8. **Tesla battery certificate feature and Model S/X Signature Edition:** Tesla is developing an in-app certificate feature for high-voltage battery repairs or replacements, intended to improve resale value and buyer confidence in the used market. Separately, official Model S/X Signature Edition badge and animation assets were revealed, suggesting a limited edition variant is in preparation — though no pricing or availability details were disclosed.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — Tesla Semi is gaining real commercial momentum with nearly 400 trucks committed in a single day, FSD is making tangible regulatory progress in Europe, and Tesla's energy and EV dominance in key markets remains intact while competitors struggle.

articles.title: Tesla's 'Battery Shortage' Mystery Solved (It wasn't the 4680)
articles.body:
This video by Jordan Giesige of The Limiting Factor investigates the "battery shortage" Tesla has intermittently referenced over the past year, revealing that the constraint is not a cell supply problem but rather battery *pack* assembly capacity. The core thesis is that Tesla is deliberately creating a temporary, self-imposed bottleneck by upgrading and insourcing battery pack production across multiple factories — a strategic move to reduce costs and improve margins in an increasingly competitive EV market.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Battery Pack Assembly — Not Cells — Is the Bottleneck:** In Q1's earnings call, Tesla CFO Vaibhav clarified that the limiting factor is battery pack capacity, not the cells themselves (i.e., not the 4680 or LFP cell production lines). This resolved widespread speculation that the 4680 ramp was causing the constraint. Lars reinforced this, noting that new capacity is actively being added across multiple facilities and that the situation is expected to improve over the coming months.

2. **Giga Berlin Shifting to In-House 4680 Cells:** At Giga Berlin, Tesla has launched a Model Y battery pack using in-house 4680 cells produced in the United States. This is described as ramping up and contributing to Berlin's output, helping meet the demand surge seen in Europe. These cells are cheaper than third-party alternatives both because they eliminate supplier margins and because Tesla receives a $35 per kilowatt-hour production tax credit on them.

3. **Giga Nevada Production Line Upgrades:** At Giga Nevada, Tesla is retooling battery pack production lines that were originally stood up in 2017–2018 — nearly a decade old. The upgrades are expected to yield higher production rates and lower production costs, and may also include improvements to the battery pack design itself.

4. **Giga Shanghai Insourcing LFP Modules from Sunwoda Cells:** At Giga Shanghai, Tesla has begun purchasing battery cells from Sunwoda (rather than CATL) and assembling the modules in-house. Previously, CATL supplied both cells and modules. The Sunwoda cells are expected to be cheaper than CATL's, and in-house module assembly should provide additional cost savings.

5. **Vehicle Backlog and Future Sales Upside:** Tesla exited Q1 with its highest vehicle backlog in over two years. Once the battery pack bottleneck is resolved, Jordan argues this should translate into higher vehicle sales in upcoming quarters and potentially new highs for total vehicle deliveries.

6. **Strategic Cost Reduction Thesis:** Jordan frames all three factory initiatives as part of a unified strategy: by reducing costs on the battery pack — the most expensive assembly in the vehicle — Tesla can either lower vehicle prices to compete more aggressively or capture the savings as higher margin.

## Energy

1. **Megapack Q1 Deployments Down Sharply:** Tesla's energy storage deployments in Q1 came in at 8.8 GWh, a 38% reduction from 14.2 GWh in Q4 2025. Tesla attributed the decline to the lumpy nature of the energy storage business, which is subject to customer project timelines and construction schedules.

2. **Megapack Gross Margins Hit All-Time High — But for the Wrong Reason:** Megapack gross margins reached an all-time high in Q1, but Jordan notes this was driven by adjustments related to tariffs paid in prior quarters rather than organic operational improvement. Tesla is guiding that Megapack gross margins should be expected to decline in future quarters due to increased competition and tariff impacts.

3. **Megapack U.S. Domestic Cell Supply and Future Cost Trajectory:** For U.S.-bound Megapacks, Tesla plans to increasingly use domestic LFP battery cells to avoid tariffs, though production costs will initially be higher domestically. Jordan notes that this cost dynamic could change in the future if Tesla brings prismatic LFP cell production in-house using lithium from its Corpus Christi refinery, LFP cathode material from Austin, and its dry electrode coating process.

4. **Megapack 3 Coming to Houston Later in 2026:** Tesla reaffirmed that Megapack 3 production will begin later this year in Houston, Texas. Jordan characterizes Megapack 3 as a more competitive product than Megapack 2.

5. **Giga Shanghai Megapack Capacity Listing Anomaly:** In Tesla's Q1 quarterly report, Giga Shanghai's Megapack production capacity was listed as 20 GWh, down from the usual 40 GWh figure. Tesla made no comment on this change during the earnings call. Jordan flags it as potentially worth raising at the next earnings call, but notes it doesn't appear significant given Tesla's reaffirmed strong demand and production outlook.

Notable quotes and data:
- **Vaibhav (Tesla CFO):** *"At the moment, I think the limiter is not the cells itself, it's the battery pack capacity. Like I said in my opening remarks, we're actively working on resolving this. There's more capacity being added as we speak."*
- **Lars (Tesla):** *"We started launching a Model Y battery pack with our in-house 4680 cells a few months ago, and that is ramping up nicely, adding to Berlin's output and helping with the demand surge that we've seen in Europe."*
- **Lars (Tesla):** *"We're adding additional capacity in our Reno facility, sort of retooling it as it's been building packs now for almost 10 years."*
- Q1 energy storage deployments: **8.8 GWh** (vs. 14.2 GWh in Q4 2025 — a **38% decline**)
- Megapack gross margins: **All-time high in Q1**, but driven by prior-quarter tariff adjustments
- 4680 in-house cell production tax credit: **$35 per kilowatt-hour**
- Tesla exited Q1 with its **highest vehicle backlog in over 2 years**
- Giga Nevada pack lines originally stood up in **2017–2018**
- Megapack 3 production to begin **later in 2026** in **Houston, Texas**
- Giga Shanghai Megapack capacity listed as **20 GWh** in Q1 report vs. the usual **40 GWh**

articles.title: Tesla's Robotaxi Just Did Something Insane!
articles.body:
This week's episode from The Tesla Space covers a range of technology and space news, with the central Tesla-related focus on the rapid expansion of Tesla's unsupervised robotaxi fleet in Texas and the milestone of FSD surpassing 10 billion supervised miles. The video also covers the Tesla Semi's new charging infrastructure program, Neuralink's automated surgical robot, and SpaceX's Mars colony compensation plan for Elon Musk. The core thesis is that Tesla's data-driven FSD strategy is now bearing fruit in real-world autonomous deployments, with exponential fleet growth beginning to materialize.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Hits 10 Billion Supervised Miles:** Tesla's supervised Full Self-Driving has now accumulated over 10 billion real-world miles. The video frames this as a critical threshold — Elon Musk's 2016 Master Plan Part Two originally estimated that approximately 6 billion miles of data would be needed to demonstrate that FSD is safer than the average human driver and unlock broader regulatory approval globally. With 10 billion miles now logged, Tesla has substantially exceeded that original benchmark.

2. **Regulatory Progress in Europe and China:** In the Netherlands, the RDW (the country's official vehicle regulator) has formally approved Full Self-Driving supervised, stating that when used properly with driver monitoring in place, the system is safer than other driver assistance systems and makes a positive contribution to road safety. In China, Tesla has secured partial approval for a supervised FSD release, with early owner feedback described as very positive and broader rollout still in progress.

3. **California Robotaxi Accountability Rules:** California has clarified how autonomous vehicles will be handled when they violate traffic laws. Starting July 1, 2026, robotaxis in California will be ticketed like any other vehicle — if they run a red light or fail to stop for pedestrians, the company managing the vehicle will be liable for the fine. California DMV Director Steve Gordon framed the new rule as enhancing public safety, transparency, and accountability for AV manufacturers.

## Robotaxi

1. **Rapid Unsupervised Fleet Expansion in Texas:** Tesla has expanded its robotaxi operations beyond Austin to include Houston and Dallas, Texas. According to community tracking data from RobotaxiTracker.com, approximately 36 fully unsupervised Model Y vehicles are now operating across these Texas cities. The video highlights a fleet growth chart showing an initial rollout in early 2026, followed by a period of stagnation, then a resumption of growth in early April 2026, culminating in a near-vertical acceleration in fleet size in the weeks prior to the video — described as "what the beginning of exponential growth looks like."

2. **Night Operations Now Active:** The unsupervised Tesla robotaxi fleet in Texas has extended its operating hours into nighttime driving. The video notes that night driving presents distinct challenges for a vision-only system — reduced visibility, headlight glare, and harder-to-detect objects — making the extension of night operations a meaningful signal of Tesla's confidence in FSD's around-the-clock performance.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Semi Efficiency and Cost Advantage:** The Tesla Semi is rated at under 1.7 kWh per mile. Real-world tests from companies including DHL and PepsiCo indicate it is approximately three times more efficient than a diesel truck. This translates to an operating cost of roughly 23 cents per mile for the Semi, compared to over 80 cents per mile for a traditional diesel rig — a major cost advantage for high-mileage commercial fleets.

2. **New Semi Charging for Business Program:** Tesla is launching a structured charging infrastructure program for Semi fleet operators. The Megacharger delivers 1.2 megawatts of power, enabling the Semi to recover approximately 60% of its range in 30 minutes — aligning with mandatory rest break requirements for truck drivers. A lower-cost base charger is arriving in early 2027, delivering 125 kilowatts of power and priced at around $40,000 for two units. The base charger is designed for overnight depot charging, and Tesla will handle maintenance, network operations, and driver support for both charger types under the program.

Notable quotes and data:
- FSD supervised: **10 billion miles** accumulated
- Elon Musk's original data threshold estimate (2016 Master Plan Part Two): **~6 billion miles**
- Unsupervised robotaxi fleet (Texas cities): **~36 Model Y vehicles** per RobotaxiTracker.com
- Tesla Semi energy consumption: **under 1.7 kWh per mile**
- Tesla Semi operating cost: **~23 cents per mile** vs. **over 80 cents per mile** for diesel
- Semi efficiency vs. diesel (real-world DHL/PepsiCo tests): **~3x more efficient**
- Megacharger output: **1.2 megawatts**, recovers ~60% range in **30 minutes**
- Base charger output: **125 kW**, cost: **~$40,000 for two units**, arriving **early 2027**
- California robotaxi ticketing rule effective: **July 1, 2026**
- SpaceX compensation targets: **$7.5 trillion valuation** and **1 million-person Mars colony**; award includes **200 million super voting restricted shares**

articles.title: Tesla Just Dropped Multiple Big Signals
articles.body:
This video from "brighterwithherbert" features host Herbert and guest Brian White (of the FutureAzA YouTube channel) breaking down five major Tesla-related developments from the week: the SpaceX Terafab chip fabrication filing, the Boring Company's Nashville residential loop agreement, a rumored FSD version rollout in China, new Roadster trademark filings, and a new tiered Model Y lease structure. The core thesis is that Tesla and its ecosystem companies are accelerating on multiple fronts simultaneously, reinforcing a long-term bull case centered on autonomous driving, infrastructure, and vehicle affordability.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Rumored FSD Version 14.3.2 Push to Employees in China:** According to a rumor circulating online, Tesla may have pushed FSD version 14.3.2 — described as "full functionality" — to its employees in China. Brian White notes that FSD rollout in China has been delayed from an expected March launch due to unresolved government regulatory hurdles. He explains that China must train on locally sourced and processed data, and that the driving style there differs significantly from the US. White recounts that Xiaomi engineers who conducted head-to-head comparisons told him that Chinese FSD (running version 13) is not on par with US FSD, which they described as "just about flawless." He suggests that if the rumor is true and employees are receiving the latest version, it signals the Chinese government may be preparing to approve a wider rollout — which would unlock a significant new recurring revenue stream for Tesla.

2. **Boring Company Nashville Loop to Use FSD:** The Boring Company has signed its first residential loop station agreement in Nashville, covering luxury towers at Prime Al Cove and Paramount Towers in downtown Nashville. Residents will take an elevator directly to an underground loop station, board a Tesla, and reach the airport in 9 minutes or Lower Broadway in 2 minutes. Herbert notes that the Boring Company has already begun testing Tesla Full Self-Driving inside its Las Vegas loop (as of October), with the car running robotaxi software on version 14. The Nashville project is described as privately funded, with first segments targeted for late 2026. Brian White emphasizes the economic model: the Boring Company asks only for permits and land at terminal endpoints, then recoups its investment through fares — a model made viable because its tunneling costs (targeting ~$50 million per mile) are a fraction of traditional subway construction ($500 million to $2 billion per mile).

3. **FSD Subscriber Growth and Version 14 Momentum:** Herbert mentions that Tesla gained another 170,000 FSD subscribers, describing this as a small but persistent and growing revenue stream. He and Brian White both express enthusiasm for FSD version 14, with White suggesting it may be time for Tesla to offer another free one-month trial given how good the software has become.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **New Five-Tier Model Y Lease Structure:** Tesla has rolled out a new flexible five-tier Model Y lease. The entry-level standard rear-wheel drive starts at $459/month, the dual motor all-wheel drive at $499/month, a premium tier at $569/month, premium all-wheel drive at $669/month, and the performance variant at $799/month — all requiring just over $4,000 at signing. Brian White highlights the competitiveness of these numbers by citing a comparison in which a Model 3 standard lease on a 48-month, 10,000-mile-per-year, zero-down basis came in at $299/month — cheaper than a comparable Toyota Camry or Honda Civic lease — while also saving nearly as much in fuel costs as the monthly payment itself.

2. **Leasing as a Robotaxi Pipeline Strategy:** Both hosts discuss the strategic logic of Tesla's lease pricing: by offering attractive terms, Tesla gets cars into consumers' hands with low upfront commitments, then reclaims those vehicles at lease-end (typically 3–4 years, ~30,000–40,000 miles on the odometer) and redeploys them into the robotaxi fleet. White notes this strategy dates to 2018 Model 3 leases, which contractually prevented buyers from keeping the cars. At that time, the robotaxi fleet wasn't ready, so Tesla sold the returned cars as near-new, effectively collecting margin twice. White frames this as a plan that works whether or not the robotaxi deployment is ready at lease-end.

3. **Canada's Affordable Model 3 and Model Y L Spotted in the US:** Brian White highlights a newly introduced Canadian-market rear-wheel drive Model 3 Premium priced at CAD $39,000 (approximately USD $29,000), calling it cheaper than anything "remotely comparable" even before factoring in fuel savings. Separately, White mentions that a camouflaged Model Y L (long version) was spotted in the United States, which he views as a positive signal that the vehicle may arrive sooner than Elon Musk's stated "end of year" timeline — White had publicly predicted a first-half 2026 arrival.

4. **Model Y Five-Star ANCAP Safety Rating:** The refreshed Model Y received a five-star safety rating from ANCAP (the Australian equivalent of Euro NCAP). Brian White notes this result was expected given the Model X's strong safety record and the Model Y's structural continuity, and describes it as confirmatory rather than surprising.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX Terafab — Largest Chip Fab Filing:** SpaceX filed documents with Grimes County, Texas proposing construction of what Elon Musk described as "the largest and most advanced chip fabrication facility in the world." The filing cites a $55 billion initial capital investment and up to $119 billion total. Musk confirmed the filing is real but noted Grimes County is one of several locations under consideration. A public hearing is scheduled for early June 2026. Brian White notes that Tesla has pledged $20 billion and SpaceX has pledged $20 billion toward the project, covering most of the initial $55 billion phase. He pushes back on the "most advanced" claim, suggesting the Fab Lab adjacent to Giga Texas would hold that title. He also speculates that Intel could be a funding partner, and that operational income from both Tesla and SpaceX could cover the remaining capital, potentially supplemented by debt.

2. **Next-Gen Roadster Trademarks and Hover Capability Tease:** Tesla filed three new trademarks for the next-generation Roadster. Sawyer Merritt noted the trademark filing describes lines depicting "speed, propulsion, heat or wind." In a clip from an interview at a moonshot event, Elon Musk confirmed that hover time using cold gas engines is "classified" but acknowledged there will be a hover capability and called the reveal "a cool demo." Musk also notably characterized the Roadster as "the best of the last human-driven cars," suggesting it may be one of the final vehicles designed primarily for driver enjoyment rather than autonomy.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX Terafab proposed investment: $55 billion (initial phases), $119 billion (total)
- Location under consideration: Grimes County, Texas — approximately 2 hours from Austin
- Public hearing on Terafab zoning: scheduled for early June 2026
- Tesla pledged $20B, SpaceX pledged $20B toward the Terafab project
- Boring Company tunneling cost target: ~$50 million per mile vs. traditional subway cost of $500M–$2B per mile

articles.title: The Tesla Competition Problem Just Got Worse
articles.body:
This video from "brighterwithherbert" features host Herbert and guest Brian White (of the FutureAzA YouTube channel) analyzing the deteriorating financial condition of Tesla's key competitors — Lucid, BYD, Waymo, and Uber. The core thesis is that rather than pulling ahead of Tesla, these companies are burning cash at alarming rates, struggling with unviable business models, and making increasingly desperate strategic pivots. The hosts argue that Tesla's advantages in scale, vertical integration, and data collection make it uniquely positioned to win the autonomous driving and EV race.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Lucid's catastrophic Q1 2026 results:** Lucid reported a Q1 loss of approximately $1 billion, with revenue coming in at $282 million — dramatically below the Wall Street expectation of $440 million. Loss per share was -$3.46 versus an expected -$2.64. The company suspended its full-year production guidance, citing elevated vehicle inventories, and announced plans to reduce production output. The hosts attribute the deeper structural problem to Lucid's failure to scale, overoptimization of performance at the expense of reliability and serviceability, and an inadequate service center network that leaves most Americans more than 100 miles from the nearest location.

2. **Lucid's path to survival — the midsize platform:** Brian White expresses cautious hope that Lucid's upcoming midsize SUV platform could save the company if it is priced competitively and reaches sufficient volume. He mentions Corey Stuben as the executive leading the midsize SUV effort. The hosts note that without volume, Lucid cannot achieve factory utilization, competitive parts pricing, or profitability — a classic chicken-and-egg problem with service infrastructure and sales.

3. **BYD's eight-month sales decline:** BYD reported approximately 314,000 new energy passenger vehicle sales in April 2026, representing a 15.7% year-over-year decline — its eighth straight month of falling passenger EV sales in China. Meanwhile, domestic Chinese competitors including Xiaomi, Leap Motor, and Zeekr posted new monthly highs. Exports were a bright spot, reaching a record, but the hosts argue that BYD's struggles at home will eventually constrain its overseas ambitions. Brian White notes BYD has sufficient overcapacity that it won't need new factory capital expenditures for potentially 8–10 quarters, offering some capital efficiency cushion.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Waymo's unsustainable unit economics:** Wall Street expects Google/Waymo to lose $5 billion in 2026, against a target of 1 million paid rides per week. That equates to a $100 loss per ride across approximately 52 million annual rides. Waymo's pricing is already higher than Uber's for comparable trips, making it structurally difficult to grow the market. Brian White argues Waymo's LiDAR-heavy, HD-mapping sensor approach creates prohibitively high hardware, compute, insurance, and service costs that the company has no clear mechanism to address at scale.

2. **Waymo's strategic pivot toward vision-only neural nets:** Brian White contends Waymo's only path to viability is to abandon its current LiDAR and HD-mapping architecture and transition to a vision-only, neural-net-based approach — similar to Tesla's and Xpeng's. He suggests all current expansion and losses are essentially building a base while preparing for a full platform overhaul, and that even that pivot would require changing "everything." He also speculates Waymo may eventually need to acquire an automaker to control vehicle costs.

3. **Uber's sensor-grid data strategy — skepticism warranted:** Uber announced a plan to turn its millions of drivers into a rolling sensor/data collection grid for AV companies, positioning itself as the data layer for the entire AV ecosystem. The hosts dismiss this as strategically incoherent, noting that Tesla already collects real-world driving data at a scale no other company can match, and that Uber's data (knowing where people take rides) is fundamentally different from and inferior to full telematics and edge-case scenario data. Brian White argues Waymo's location-specific data collection approach is itself flawed, and Uber's plan to support it is even worse.

## Robotaxi

1. **Uber's pivot to asset-heavy model via Lucid and Nuro:** Uber expanded its investment commitment to Lucid from $300 million to $500 million and increased its minimum vehicle order from 20,000 to 35,000 units — comprising at least 10,000 Lucid Gravity SUVs and 25,000 EVs built on Lucid's upcoming midsize platform. Separately, Uber made a multi-million dollar investment in Nuro, whose autonomous tech is being tested on Lucid Gravity SUVs on California public roads under a driverless testing permit. Lucid has delivered 75 engineering vehicles to Nuro and Uber for testing across several U.S. cities.

2. **Nuro partnership complexity raises red flags:** Brian White highlights that the Uber robotaxi stack involves at least five separate technology partners — Lucid for the vehicle, Nuro for autonomy software, Nvidia's Drive AGX for compute, plus additional camera and LiDAR hardware suppliers. He argues that none of these individual components are proven at scale and that combining unproven systems multiplies rather than mitigates risk. He also notes Nuro only recently received permission to test on public roads with no safety operator, having previously held a permit only for low-speed delivery vehicles.

## Market & Competition

1. **Shared theme: no profitable business model:** The hosts conclude that the common thread across Lucid, BYD, Waymo, and Uber's AV efforts is the absence of a sustainable, profitable business model. Brian White draws a contrast with Tesla, which endured years of losses but ultimately scaled successfully — arguing that the competitors' losses are structurally different in nature and not analogous to Tesla's early burn rate. He describes Uber as having only recently turned profitable in its core ride-hailing business after 10–15 years, while now re-entering a money-losing investment cycle.

2. **Nvidia's role as an indiscriminate backer:** Both hosts note that Nvidia has invested in or partnered with virtually every AV company, characterizing it as a self-reinforcing strategy: Nvidia provides capital to companies that then use it to buy Nvidia chips. Brian White dismisses this as evidence of conviction in any particular partner rather than a sign of sector validation.

Notable quotes and data:
- Lucid Q1 2026 revenue: $282M (vs. $440M expected); loss per share: -$3.46 (vs. -$2.64 expected); total quarterly loss: ~$1 billion
- Lucid stock down 41% year-to-date as of video date
- BYD April 2026 new energy passenger vehicle sales: ~314,000 units, -15.7% YoY; eighth consecutive month of YoY decline
- Waymo projected 2026 losses: $5 billion; target of 1 million paid rides/week = ~$100 loss per ride, ~52 million rides annually
- Waymo losses estimated at $4–8 billion per year range mentioned
- Uber commitment to Lucid expanded to $500 million minimum; vehicle order expanded to minimum 35,000 units (10,000 Gravity SUVs + 25,000 midsize platform EVs)
- Lucid delivered 75 engineering vehicles to Nuro/Uber for testing
- Uber has partnerships with 25 AV companies
- Google CEO Sundar Pichai offered special performance award tied to Waymo growth
- Waymo previously targeted 2027 for profitability
- Brian White (guest): "If you're going to lose $100,000 a car, you got a problem."
- Brian White on Uber's data claim: "I can think of one company that could gather more data and has and does every single day."
- Brian White on Waymo's pivot: "If you can just change everything then maybe you'll make a profit."

articles.title: Tesla’s 4680 battery cells are underperforming and frustrating buyers
articles.body:
Five years after Tesla's Battery Day promises, real-world data shows the 4680 cell consistently underperforms the supplier cells it is replacing — delivering lower energy density, less range, and slower charging. Tesla is now quietly substituting 4680 "8L" packs for LG cells in European Model Y vehicles, triggering consumer backlash over an undisclosed range downgrade.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Energy density gap:** Tesla's 4680 cells produced at Giga Austin measure 244 Wh/kg, versus 269 Wh/kg for the Panasonic 2170 cells they are meant to replace — a 13% deficit. Tesla has claimed higher density in a latest version, but no independent test results are available.

2. **European Model Y range downgrade:** The new 4680-based "8L" pack carries approximately 79 kWh gross (74 kWh usable), replacing an LG 5M pack rated at 82–84 kWh in the same Model Y Premium Long Range RWD trim. WLTP range drops from 661 km to 609 km — a 52 km (8%) reduction. Pack mass is 447 kg per European certification data.

3. **Charging performance:** First-generation 4680 Model Y (2023) charging power dropped below 100 kW at just 35% state of charge, with a 10–80% charge time exceeding 40 minutes, versus roughly 27–30 minutes for the 2170 Model Y Long Range. An Out of Spec 15-minute test from 10% SOC found the 4680 added only 27 kWh, while a cheaper 62 kWh LFP pack added 29 kWh in the same window. For the European 8L pack, Out of Spec Roaming found charging power already declining at 31% SOC from 155 kW, ranking it the worst battery option in the current European Model Y lineup. Tesla claims up to 250 kW on V4 Superchargers for the 2026 Model Y but no independent confirmation exists for the 8L pack specifically.

4. **Consumer backlash in Europe:** Tesla replaced the LG 5M pack with the 8L without clearly notifying customers who had already placed orders. EV communities in France and Norway are reporting order cancellations. Tesla does not disclose battery type on its configurator or in vehicle specifications, leaving buyers unable to determine which cell they will receive before delivery.

## Market & Competition
5. **Supply chain contraction signals 4680 struggles:** South Korean supplier L&F disclosed its $2.9 billion cathode materials contract with Tesla for 4680 production has been written down to just $7,386 — a 99.9% reduction — citing a "change in supply quantity." The Cybertruck, the primary 4680 vehicle, is selling at an estimated 20,000–25,000 units annually against a factory capacity of 250,000. Tesla's original production targets of 100 GWh by 2023 and 3,000 GWh by 2030 have not been met; as of 2026, the cells are going into one European Model Y trim, select US configurations, and the Cybertruck.

6. **Elon Musk acknowledged core technology failure:** At the 2025 shareholder meeting, Musk stated the dry battery electrode process — the manufacturing centerpiece acquired from Maxwell Technologies and central to Battery Day promises — turned out to be "way harder" than expected and was a mistake.

## Editorial Stance
Electrek's Fred Lambert argues Tesla's 4680 program has failed to deliver competitive battery cells after five years and billions of dollars, falling behind Panasonic on energy density, LG on charging, and even CATL's LFP chemistry. He contends the quiet cell swap in European Model Ys amounts to a "bait-and-switch" for customers and that the 4680 is at least partly responsible for the Cybertruck's commercial failure.

Notable quotes and data:
- 4680 energy density: 244 Wh/kg vs. 269 Wh/kg for Panasonic 2170 (−13%)
- 8L pack: ~79 kWh gross / 74 kWh usable; replaces LG 5M at 82–84 kWh
- WLTP range: 609 km (8L) vs. 661 km (LG 5M) — same trim, same vehicle
- 10–80% charge time, first-gen 4680 Model Y: >40 minutes vs. ~27–30 minutes for 2170 LR
- Out of Spec 15-min test: 4680 added 27 kWh; LFP (62 kWh pack) added 29 kWh
- L&F contract written down from $2.9 billion to $7,386 (−99.9%)
- Cybertruck run rate: ~20,000–25,000 units/year vs. 250,000 factory capacity
- Musk (2025 shareholder meeting): dry electrode process was "way harder" than expected — "a mistake"
- Weight difference between 4680 and 2170 Model Y per Munro teardown: 20 pounds

articles.title: Yea... Tesla just quietly lapped Waymo 50x over
articles.body:
This video from Farzad argues that Tesla has quietly lapped Waymo by roughly 50x in cumulative autonomous miles, and that mainstream coverage obsessing over fleet size is missing the metric that actually determines who wins the multi-trillion-dollar robotaxi market. The core thesis is that Wright's Law — the principle that cost falls by a fixed percentage every time cumulative production doubles — applies to autonomous miles, and Tesla's mile doubling rate combined with its manufacturing scale makes it structurally dominant over Waymo despite Waymo's larger current driverless fleet.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Tesla's cumulative FSD miles vs. Waymo:** Tesla has crossed roughly 10 billion cumulative Full Self-Driving miles, growing at approximately 1 billion miles per month and doubling roughly every 9 months. Waymo has accumulated somewhere north of 200 million cumulative driverless miles across its entire history going back to the Google self-driving car project era, and is also doubling roughly every 9 months. By this math, Tesla is approximately 50 times Waymo's cumulative mile count — hence the video's title. Farzad acknowledges the miles are not perfectly apples-to-apples, as most of Tesla's are supervised FSD miles while most of Waymo's are fully driverless, but argues the training data signal still flows through to Tesla's unsupervised system.

2. **Wright's Law applied to autonomous miles:** Farzad invokes Wright's Law — first observed in 1936 by aeronautical engineer Theodore Wright — which holds that every time cumulative production of a product doubles, the unit cost falls by a fixed percentage (historically 15–20%). He applies this principle to autonomous miles, arguing that each cumulative mile is a unit of training data, edge case experience, safety validation, and cost reduction. Whoever doubles their mile count fastest gets cheaper, smarter, and safer faster. Farzad is careful to note this is an analogy rather than a strict mathematical law, acknowledging skeptics who argue data quality matters more than raw volume.

3. **Tesla's cost per mile vs. Waymo's:** Morgan Stanley analysis cited in the video pegs Tesla's robotaxi cost per mile at roughly $0.81, while Waymo's cost per mile is estimated between $1.36 and $1.43 depending on the source. This means Tesla is already operating at roughly 60% of Waymo's cost per mile despite having a far smaller active fleet and being in the earliest stages of commercial deployment. ARK Invest projects fully autonomous robotaxi cost at roughly $0.25 per mile at scale, compared to approximately $2.00 per mile for Uber today.

4. **Unified neural network as a compounding advantage:** Farzad emphasizes that Tesla's fleet operates on a single unified neural network, meaning every mile driven in Austin improves the model for Dallas and Houston cars, and every customer-driven FSD mile worldwide trains the same neural net powering the unsupervised robotaxis. He contrasts this with Waymo, which historically required expensive HD mapping, sensor calibration, and city-specific tuning for each new market — though he notes Waymo is working to reduce its reliance on HD maps.

5. **AI5 hardware mentioned as a risk factor:** In the bear-case scenario, Farzad flags that "AI5" — Tesla's next hardware — could slip again, representing a software/hardware wall risk that could slow the doubling rate.

## Robotaxi

1. **Current unsupervised fleet size and city expansion:** Per the video (citing numbers consistent with RobotaxiTracker.com), Tesla's unsupervised robotaxi fleet spans Austin, Dallas, and Houston, with approximately 19 cars in Austin, 3 in Dallas, and 3 in Houston — totaling roughly 25 unsupervised vehicles as of the video date. Hundreds more supervised vehicles (with a person inside) are also operating. Tesla expanded unsupervised service from Austin to Dallas and Houston on April 18, 2026. Waymo by comparison has somewhere north of 3,000 commercial vehicles operating across Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and other cities, nearly all driverless with remote supervisors in the US and Philippines.

2. **Q1 2026 paid robotaxi miles and growth trajectory:** Tesla reported on its Q1 2026 earnings call that paid robotaxi miles hit roughly 1.7 million cumulative miles in the quarter, up from roughly 610,000 in Q4 2025 — nearly tripling in one quarter. Farzad projects that if the trajectory holds, Q2 2026 could reach north of 4 million paid miles and Q3 could approach 10 million or more. He suggests that by end of 2026, Tesla's paid robotaxi miles could start approaching Waymo's annual commercial volume.

3. **Cybercab production begins at Giga Texas:** Cybercab production began in April 2026 at Giga Texas. A key revelation confirmed by Tesla's head of engineering (named in the video as Lars Moravy, though Farzad stumbles on the name) is that the Cybercab is FMVSS compliant from day one. This means Tesla is not subject to the NHTSA 2,500-vehicle annual exemption cap that had been a concern for fully self-driving vehicles lacking standard safety equipment. There is therefore no regulatory production ceiling on Cybercab output beyond normal manufacturing ramp constraints.

4. **Manufacturing scale advantage over Waymo:** Tesla manufactures approximately 2 million cars per year today and can theoretically produce roughly half a million vehicles per quarter. Farzad estimates Tesla can produce roughly 100 times more self-driving capable cars per year than Waymo, which is dependent on Zeekr and Hyundai as vehicle suppliers — a combined production capacity estimated at no more than 20,000 vehicles per year under current contracts. Farzad projects Tesla could deploy several thousand to tens of thousands of Cybercabs from a single factory line within 12 months.

5. **Pony.AI break-even benchmark:** Pony.AI published a figure that Farzad calls his favorite data point in the autonomy debate: their robotaxi business reaches break-even at approximately 23 paid rides per vehicle per day. He uses this as a benchmark to frame the competitive question — who reaches 23 rides per car per day fastest, and at what cost per mile?

6. **Five additional city launches planned for H1 2026:** Tesla has publicly committed to launching robotaxi service in five more cities in the first half of 2026: Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, and Las Vegas. Farzad expresses skepticism that all launches will happen on schedule, anticipating some will slip to H2 2026 or later.

7. **Three-scenario analysis:** Farzad outlines three scenarios. Bull case: doubling math holds for 24 months, cumulative miles reach 40–80 billion by mid-2028, cost per mile drops to 35–50 cents, robotaxi fleet grows from 25 vehicles to 5,000–25,000 (mostly Cybercab), and annual robotaxi revenue exceeds $5 billion. Base/partial case: doubling rate slows to every 18–24 months due to regulatory, software, or safety headwinds; Tesla still leads on miles and cost but the timeline stretches 2–3 years. Bear case: FSD fails to generalize across geographies, a Cybercab injures someone triggering an indefinite NHTSA pause, and Waymo's architecture proves correct — though even then Tesla retains its EV business (1.6–2 million cars/year), Optimus development, and energy business.

8. **Waymo's 16-year development arc vs. Tesla's projected compression:** Farzad notes that Waymo spent roughly 15–16 years building from a Google research project to its current safety and commercial levels. He argues Tesla will compress an equivalent arc into roughly 18–36 months due to the aggressive compounding of its mile doubling rate.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla's existing fleet as the robotaxi pipeline:** Tesla's approximately 2 million annual production capacity means the existing Model Y and other vehicle lines are already pumping out robotaxi-capable cars that can be flipped into unsupervised service as regulatory and safety thresholds are met — independent of the dedicated Cybercab ramp. This is framed as a key asymmetry: the robotaxi fleet can scale without waiting for a new purpose-built vehicle line to ramp.

## Market & Competition

1. **Transportation cost disruption thesis:** ARK Invest projects autonomous robotaxi rides at roughly $0.25 per mile at scale. The average American drives roughly 13,000 miles per year; at $0.20–$0.25 per mile in a robotaxi, total annual transportation cost would be approximately $3,000 — or about $250/month. Farzad contrasts this with the average American's current car payment plus insurance plus gas plus maintenance, which he estimates at roughly $900/month, suggesting autonomous transportation could effectively collapse personal car ownership economics within 7–10 years.

2. **Waymo praised but structurally constrained:** Farzad repeatedly acknowledges Waymo's achievements as "unbelievably impressive" and calls it an "awesome company," but argues its structural dependence on third-party vehicle manufacturers and its city-by-city mapping approach create a ceiling on its ability to compound miles and reduce costs at the rate Tesla can.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla cumulative FSD miles: ~10 billion, growing ~1 billion/month, doubling ~every 9 months
- Waymo cumulative driverless miles: north of 200 million across entire history
- Tesla is ~50x Waymo on cumulative miles
- Morgan Stanley: Tesla robotaxi cost per mile ~$0.81; Waymo cost per mile ~$1.36–$1.43
- Tesla current robotaxi pricing in Austin: ~$1.00–$1.40 per mile
- ARK Invest projection: ~$0.25/mile at scale for fully autonomous robotaxi
- Uber today: ~$2.00/mile
- Tesla Q1 2026 paid robotaxi miles: ~1.7 million (up from ~610,000 in Q4 2025)
- Pony.AI robotaxi break-even: ~23 paid rides per vehicle per day
- Cybercab production began April 2026 at Giga Texas; confirmed FMVSS compliant from day one
- Waymo fleet: north of 3,000 commercial vehicles; dependent on Zeekr and Hyundai, combined ~20,000 vehicles/year max under current contracts
- Tesla can produce ~500,000 vehicles per quarter (~2 million/year currently)
- Tesla unsupervised fleet (per RobotaxiTracker.com): ~25 vehicles — Austin ~19, Dallas ~3, Houston ~3
- Expansion to Dallas and Houston: April 18, 2026
- 5 additional city launches planned H1 2026: Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, Las Vegas
- Bull case by mid-2028: 40–80 billion cumulative miles, cost/mile 35–50 cents, fleet 5,000–25,000 vehicles, robotaxi revenue north of $5 billion/year
- Average American: ~13,000 miles/year; at ~$0.25/mile robotaxi = ~$3,000/year (~$250/month) vs. ~$900/month for car ownership total cost

articles.title: Tesla’s Biggest Expansion Week
articles.body:
This FutureAzA video, hosted by Brian with guest Herbert from Brighter, covers three major expansion announcements from Elon Musk's companies during what they call Tesla's biggest expansion week. The hosts discuss SpaceX's proposed semiconductor fabrication facility in Grimes County, Texas; a large Megapack installation in Australia; and the Boring Company's first residential tunnel stop in Nashville — examining whether each announcement is real, significant, and strategically sound.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Unsupervised FSD enabling point-to-point Boring Company travel:** The hosts note that once Unsupervised FSD is operational, passengers could work the entire commute from Austin to Grimes County without touching the wheel. This is framed as a practical illustration of how autonomy adds value to longer inter-city trips, not just urban rides.

## Robotaxi
1. **Boring Company Nashville residential stop as robotaxi integration showcase:** The Boring Company announced its first residential tunnel stop, connecting three apartment buildings in Nashville to the downtown/airport trunk line. Residents would take an elevator to a lower parking level, board autonomous Model Ys, and be transported to the airport in approximately 9 minutes — compared to 14 minutes at off-peak hours and 35–40 minutes during rush hour by surface roads. The hosts argue this residential stop sets a precedent that could trigger a chain reaction of private-entity approvals (apartments, malls, city halls), similar to how Las Vegas casinos demanded inclusion once the system proved itself.

2. **Boring Company operations timeline and cost model:** The hosts expect the first Nashville tunnel stops to begin operation by end of 2026 or early 2027. The cost model discussed mirrors Las Vegas: the Boring Company pays for the main trunk, while spur connections are paid by the connecting entity — though for the residential buildings, the exact cost-sharing arrangement was described as uncertain. The hosts highlight that using existing underground parking garages as pickup/drop-off zones dramatically reduces station construction costs.

3. **Autonomous daisy-chaining as a subway substitute:** Herbert describes how autonomous robotaxi vehicles in tunnels could daisy-chain together like train cars, delivering riders point-to-point before rejoining the main corridor — offering the efficiency of a subway without fixed stops, at a fraction of the cost. Subway construction is noted as costing approximately $1 billion per mile, making city-wide coverage financially impossible with traditional infrastructure.

## Energy
1. **Large Megapack installation in Australia:** Tesla is delivering a 200 MW / 800 MWh battery installation called the Kulonga battery in Australia, valued at approximately $225 million worth of Megapacks. Brian notes this is not a new Gigafactory in Australia (a misreading he initially made), but a large grid-scale energy storage project. The hosts emphasize that Australia has repeatedly proven the Megapack business model works, with payback periods of roughly one to two years, and call for more announcements at this scale from other countries.

2. **Megapack 3 and Megablock production timeline:** Brian expects Megapack 3 units out of the new Gigafactory in Texas to ship no later than Q3 2026, with Elon's stated timeline of "this year" characterized as sandbagging. The ramp-up could be slower due to uncertainty around cell supply from LG's new factory in Lansing, Michigan. Herbert confirms he toured the Megapack factory and observed details under NDA.

## Market & Competition
1. **SpaceX semiconductor fab in Grimes County, Texas — scale and strategic rationale:** SpaceX filed for a proposed next-generation, vertically integrated semiconductor manufacturing and advanced computing fabrication facility in Grimes County, Texas, approximately two hours from Austin. The proposed capital investment is $55 billion upfront, with a potential ceiling of $119 billion across multiple phases, with a county hearing scheduled within one month. Elon Musk confirmed the announcement is real and noted several locations are under consideration, describing it as the largest and most advanced chip facility of its kind.

2. **Location analysis — proximity to Giga Texas as key criterion:** The hosts argue Grimes County's location between Houston and Austin is strategically sound. Elon Musk previously asked Samsung to build its fab as close as possible to Giga Texas, and the same logic applies here. Giga Texas is cited as the future home of a 10 million Optimus units per year production line and Cybercab manufacturing — making chip supply chain proximity critical. The hosts also cite talent access (proximity to Austin and Houston metro areas), reasonable Texas power rates, and county approval likelihood as key factors.

3. **Domestic chip manufacturing precedent:** The hosts push back on skepticism about building semiconductor fabs in the US, noting that Samsung and TSMC are already doing it, and that Tesla pioneered domestic lithium processing — something others said was impossible. The SpaceX fab is framed as part of a broader reshoring trend accelerated by tariff pressures.

Notable quotes and data:
- Proposed SpaceX fab investment: $55 billion upfront, up to $119 billion total
- Location: Grimes County, Texas — approximately 2 hours / ~124 miles from Austin
- County hearing scheduled within one month of the video's publication
- Kulonga battery: 200 MW / 800 MWh, ~$225 million in Megapacks, Australia
- Megapack 3 expected: no later than Q3 2026 per Brian; cell supply from LG's Lansing, Michigan factory
- Nashville Boring Company tunnel: airport trip in ~9 minutes underground vs. 14 min off-peak / 35–40 min rush hour on surface
- Nashville first stops expected to operate by end of 2026 or early 2027
- Giga Texas future planned output: 10 million Optimus units per year (referenced by Brian)
- Subway construction cost cited: approximately $1 billion per mile
- Elon Musk quote (paraphrased): confirmed the fab is real and described it as "the largest, most advanced chip" facility, with "several locations under consideration"

articles.title: Why Germany is at the BRINK of Revolution
articles.body:
This video from Jo Bhakdi's channel offers a political and social commentary on the current state of German politics, arguing that Germany is approaching a revolutionary inflection point driven by immigration backlash, energy policy failures, militarization, government censorship, and the surging popularity of the AFD (Alternative für Deutschland). The core thesis is that the ruling CDU-SPD coalition is deeply unpopular and losing legitimacy, while the AFD is on the verge of a polling breakthrough that could trigger a rapid, dramatic realignment of German politics. The video has no meaningful connection to Tesla, autonomous driving, robotaxis, Optimus, or any other topics tracked by The Tesla Thesis platform, with only a single passing reference to Tesla as a contributor to the decline of the German auto industry.

## Market & Competition
1. **Tesla cited as a factor in German auto industry decline:** In a brief passing mention, Jo Bhakdi notes that Tesla (along with Chinese automakers) is "destroying the German car industry," referencing the broader economic distress facing legacy German automakers such as Volkswagen. No further detail, data, or analysis is provided about Tesla in this context.

Notable quotes and data:
- AFD polling at 28% (up from 26%, then 27% in recent months), making it the largest political party in Germany per the Insa/Emnid trend polling cited.
- CDU/CSU at 24%, SPD at 14%.
- Chancellor Mertz has a 13% approval/satisfaction rating; 85% of Germans are dissatisfied with him, per the Forsa trend barometer cited.
- Germany ranked #3 globally for online speech arrests, with 3,500 arrests cited in the graphic discussed; the German government's own BKA (Federal Criminal Office) acknowledged 8,001 investigations opened for "propaganda crimes" in 2023, with 5,161 citizens currently under criminal investigation for propaganda offenses.
- Rheinmetall artillery shell production capacity cited as having grown from ~70,000 shells/year to 1.1 million rounds annually, with plans to expand to 20 million shells/year.
- Germany's special defense fund: €100 billion (~$100 billion), with a total of ~€500 billion cited for broader military spending plans.
- A YouTube interview with AFD politician Björn Höcke on the channel "Ben Unscripted" received 4 million views within 7 days.
- AFD receives only 2.8% of airtime on German public broadcasting despite holding 24% of parliamentary seats.
- Jo Bhakdi's "30/20 breakpoint theory": if the AFD crosses 30% and the CDU falls below 20%, the political narrative around the AFD collapses and a rapid further surge — potentially to 50% — becomes possible.
- Violent crime rate among Syrian nationals in Germany cited at 1,740 per 100,000 residents vs. 163 per 100,000 for Germans overall.

articles.title: Daily X Summary (2026-05-07)
articles.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts from @SawyerMerritt were light on hard robotaxi/FSD data but carried several noteworthy Tesla-specific signals: the sunset of one-time FSD purchases in Europe (deadline May 21, 2026), a new Tesla Roadster trademark filing, and ongoing Cybercab visual comparisons. The broader ecosystem themes — SpaceX's semiconductor ambitions and xAI/Anthropic compute deal — are tangential to Tesla investors but reflect the Musk-sphere's AI infrastructure buildout.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **FSD Europe Subscription Transition — Deadline May 21, 2026:** Tesla is ending one-time (perpetual) FSD purchases across Europe on May 21, 2026, affecting the UK, Germany, France, Italy, Belgium, Switzerland, Denmark, and other markets. After that date, FSD will only be available via subscription. This is a meaningful monetization model shift — transitioning European customers to recurring revenue — and gives prospective buyers roughly two weeks to lock in a one-time purchase. This mirrors a transition Tesla has already made or signaled in other markets, and has direct implications for Tesla's software revenue mix and long-term ARR modeling.

2. **Tesla Roadster Trademark Filing:** Merritt flagged a newly discovered Tesla trademark application for what appears to be a next-generation Roadster logo/badge. The filing describes the design lines as depicting "speed, propulsion, heat or wind." No launch date, specs, or pricing were mentioned. While the Roadster has long been vaporware in public perception, an active trademark filing suggests some level of internal activity around the brand, though this is a weak signal on its own.

3. **Cybercab Visual Comparisons:** Merritt shared side-by-side imagery comparing glossy vs. matte Cybercab finishes, noting that the glossy variant has a "nicer and richer gold color." No new production, pricing, or timeline data was included — this is a visual/aesthetic observation with minimal investment signal beyond confirming that multiple Cybercab finish variants exist in the wild.

4. **FSD Snow Performance — Anecdotal Validation:** Merritt shared a personal account of using FSD extensively during winter conditions, including low-visibility scenarios with obscured lane markings. He pushed back on the claim that FSD doesn't work in snow, calling it "simply not true" while acknowledging the need for increased vigilance. This is anecdotal but directionally positive for FSD's all-weather capability narrative.

5. **Tesla Semi Incentives Summary:** Merritt compiled available incentives for the Tesla Semi, highlighting California's HVIP program offering $120,000–$330,000 per Semi truck, with over $100M in total funding available on a first-come, first-served basis. Additional unspecified programs were referenced. This is relevant for Tesla Semi demand and fleet adoption velocity, as substantial per-unit subsidies materially reduce TCO for commercial buyers.

6. **Energy & Competition Context — IRENA Renewables Cost Data:** A new IRENA report cited in Merritt's posts shows solar and wind with battery storage now costs $54–$82/MWh, down from over $100/MWh in 2020, and is now cost-competitive with new coal in China ($70–$85/MWh) and cheaper than new gas globally (>$100/MWh). Total installed costs have declined significantly since 2010. This is a macro tailwind for Tesla's Energy segment (Megapack), as falling storage costs accelerate grid-scale battery deployments.

7. **Mercedes All-Electric C-Class Pricing:** Mercedes announced final pricing for its new all-electric C-Class at €68,000 (~$79,900 USD), with up to 350 miles of expected EPA range, a 94 kWh battery, 330kW peak charging, 800V architecture, 0–60 mph in 3.9 seconds, and 482 hp. This positions a premium European legacy OEM directly in Tesla Model S/Model 3 Performance territory at a high price point, suggesting legacy competition remains concentrated at the premium end rather than mass market.

8. **SpaceX/xAI Ecosystem Developments — Indirect Tesla Relevance:** SpaceX and xAI signed an agreement giving Anthropic access to the Colossus 1 supercomputer, with Anthropic citing "over 300 megawatts of additional capacity." Separately, xAI is reportedly being dissolved as a standalone entity into SpaceX ("SpaceXAI"). Also, SpaceX filed to build a $55B (up to $119B total) next-generation semiconductor and advanced computing fabrication facility in Grimes County, Texas. These are primarily SpaceX/xAI stories, but the semiconductor fab ambition — if it extends to Tesla's custom AI chip supply chain — could have long-term relevance to FSD and Dojo compute costs. No direct Tesla connection was stated in the posts.

---

## Signal Strength: **Mildly Bullish** — The FSD Europe subscription transition is a concrete monetization model upgrade, the IRENA data supports Energy segment tailwinds, and Tesla Semi incentive clarity aids commercial demand — but there were no major robotaxi fleet updates, FSD version releases, or Optimus milestones today.

articles.title: Big Week for Tesla, SpaceX, and AI
articles.body:
This episode of "brighterwithherbert" features host Herbert alongside panelists Jeff Lutz ("the rational bull"), Cern Basher ("the bot bull"), and Phil Biceel ("the engineerable," formerly of Apple and Rivian) discussing a busy week spanning the SpaceX–Anthropic compute deal, Tesla's unsupervised Robotaxi fleet expansion, FSD progress in China and Europe, the debate over a potential SpaceX–Tesla merger, and the state of Optimus humanoid robot development. The episode's core thesis is that Elon Musk is systematically positioning his companies — through compute infrastructure, chip fabrication (Terafab), autonomous driving software, and humanoid robots — further ahead of all competitors, but that Tesla investors should maintain humility about timing and unexpected risks. The panel is notably divided on the SpaceX–Tesla merger question and on whether Optimus is meaningfully delayed.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Rollout in China:** Rumors surfaced that a fully functional version of FSD 14.3.2 is being made available to Tesla employees in China under non-disclosure agreements. Supporting this signal, Tesla China is actively hiring Autopilot test engineers, which the panel interprets as a possible indication that Tesla expects to seek full FSD approval in China in the near term.

2. **FSD Expansion Across Europe:** The RDW (Dutch vehicle regulator) presented its findings on FSD to EU member states and is advocating for FSD approval across all 27 EU countries. Separately, Tesla updated FSD purchase terms — including deadlines for one-time purchase pricing — in multiple European countries including Belgium, Germany, and Sweden, which observers interpret as preparation for a broader FSD rollout. The panel noted that EU approval may still proceed country-by-country rather than bloc-wide, and that the process remains inherently messy.

3. **FSD 14 Series as the Readiness Threshold:** Both Jeff and Phil agreed that FSD was not genuinely ready for regulatory approval until the FSD 14 series. Phil noted that FSD 14.3 specifically rewrote the runtime, dramatically improving performance and creating headroom for model inference frequency, and also established a reinforcement learning pipeline enabling rapid fine-tuning of specific operational issues encountered in the field. The panel acknowledged ongoing "whack-a-mole" regression risks when fine-tuning but expressed confidence that the tooling to address this quickly is now in place.

4. **FSD Variant in Robotaxi Fleet:** Ashok confirmed at Tesla's earnings call that the Robotaxi fleet runs a variant of the FSD 14.3 series. The panel assessed that the Robotaxi fleet is likely running software somewhat ahead of what is deployed to consumer vehicles, and that as FSD 14.3.2 reaches wider consumer deployment (estimated at ~50% of Tesla fleet at time of recording, with full rollout expected within one to two weeks), the broader fleet will help surface remaining edge cases faster.

## Robotaxi

1. **Unsupervised Fleet Growth:** Per RobotaxiTracker.com, the unsupervised Robotaxi fleet grew from 26 to 38 vehicles in the five days preceding the episode — a 46% increase. The breakdown is 27 unsupervised vehicles in Austin, 5 in Dallas, and 6 in Houston. Dallas and Houston are noted as 100% unsupervised (no safety monitor in any vehicle). The panel emphasized that the percentage rate of change, not the absolute number, is the meaningful signal at this early stage.

2. **Brian Wang's 60-Day Projection:** Brian Wang predicted that if Tesla converts all Austin vehicles to unsupervised (potentially adding ~24 more), and Dallas and Houston each reach at least 10 unsupervised vehicles, the total could reach approximately 70 unsupervised vehicles by end of the following week, with each city potentially reaching 100 unsupervised and an overall fleet of 80+ parked Robotaxi-badged vehicles per city including Cybercabs. Wang argued that extending evening driving hours combined with a 10x vehicle increase would produce approximately 20x the Robotaxi miles.

3. **Cybercab Integration Into Robotaxi Fleet:** Joe Tegtmeyer documented 40–50 Cybercabs now spotted at and around Giga Texas (up from ~20 previously), and a Tesla Semi was filmed transporting a batch of new Cybercabs. Phil assessed that the Cybercab camera placement differs slightly from the Model Y but that Tesla has abstracted this in software, making it straightforward to integrate. He believes Cybercabs are already operating within the Robotaxi network in Austin but are not yet available for customer hailing — they are conducting autonomous test runs without passengers. The panel sees Cybercabs as ultimately replacing Model Ys in the fleet over time.

4. **Operational Constraints as the Binding Limitation:** The panel consensus was that safety is no longer the primary constraint on Robotaxi scaling — operational issues are. These include proper pickup and drop-off behavior, situations where the vehicle sits idle awaiting a remote operations decision, and the need to keep the ratio of remote operations interventions extremely low (Elon's stated goal being a service scalable without frequent human intervention). Jeff noted a concern about wireless charging not yet visibly deployed, which he flagged as a future scaling bottleneck if vehicles must be manually plugged in. Rumors suggest the wireless charging system has been significantly delayed and has not yet received regulatory approval.

5. **Mystery Covered Vehicle:** Joe Tegtmeyer captured footage of a mystery vehicle covered with a tarp and wheels masked with white vinyl at what appeared to be a Tesla facility. Size comparisons to a Cybertruck and Model Y suggest it may be a Model Y variant, though the panel acknowledged they are rarely correct when speculating on covered vehicles.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Tesla's Communication Blackout on Optimus:** Tesla made a deliberate decision to stop releasing short demo videos and public event appearances for Optimus, citing competitive intelligence concerns — Elon stated that revealing too much too soon allows competitors to copy the design frame by frame. A promised reveal that was expected in Q1 2026 did not happen; Elon stated the bot was not yet performing enough use cases at the required level. Phil expressed comfort with this communications policy, drawing a parallel to Apple's product secrecy culture.

2. **Acknowledged Delays vs. Real Capital Commitment:** The panel agreed Optimus is delayed relative to earlier promises (e.g., the original target of 5,000 units that required building an entirely new actuator supply chain). However, Herbert countered that Tesla is actively spending real capital converting the Fremont factory to an Optimus production facility and building out infrastructure at Giga Texas. He argued that if Tesla were truly shelving Optimus, Elon would delay capital spending as he did with Giga Mexico — the continued spending signals near-term intent to ramp. Herbert described the current Fremont conversion as a "10 million per year line."

3. **AI5 Chip as a Prerequisite:** Phil stated his view that Optimus will not enter meaningful production until Tesla's AI5 chip is available to power it, framing this as a hard dependency.

4. **Competitive Landscape — Figure, 1X, Boston Dynamics:** Figure and 1X both publicly revealed factory footage and claimed pre-production volumes. Jeff was skeptical, noting that pre-production unit counts reveal nothing about spec compliance, yield rates, or supply chain readiness. He drew on his smartphone industry experience — it took five years to scale from a few million units per year to one billion in smartphones — and warned that the humanoid bot supply chain, particularly for constrained components, is not ready for mass ramp. He identified China as potentially moving 10x faster in bot deployment but questioned whether functionality and usefulness would match. Jeff also noted Boston Dynamics' 20+ year history with no mass-market product, and that its original CEO acknowledged the platform was never designed to be a commercial product. The panel saw Hyundai's ownership of Boston Dynamics as a potential improvement but not a near-term threat.

5. **Tesla's Manufacturing Credibility:** Despite the delays, the panel's consistent view was that Tesla has the most credible path from prototype to scaled production of any company in the humanoid bot space, given its existing manufacturing culture and supply chain expertise. Phil's key evaluative framework: the only milestones that truly matter are when the first 100,000 units and first million units are available for consumers to purchase — all demos, start-of-production events, and interim milestones are "squishy."

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX–Anthropic Compute Deal:** SpaceX agreed to lease its Colossus 1 data center (~300 megawatts of capacity) to Anthropic, which had been severely compute-constrained and throttling its Claude LLM. Elon stated that XAI had already migrated training workloads to Colossus 2, making Colossus 1 available. The deal allows Anthropic to double its rate limits, remove peak-hour restrictions, and substantially raise API limits (Tier 1 input tokens per minute jumping from 30,000 to 500,000, and context limits from 2 million to 10 million tokens). Revenue estimates for SpaceX from this deal ranged from $5 billion to $16 billion per year in the discussion, with Brian Wang's AWS-comparable estimate cited as closer to $20–28 billion per year. The panel interpreted this as strategically weakening OpenAI by strengthening its top competitor while SpaceX monetizes excess compute.

2. **SpaceX–Tesla Merger Debate:** A significant portion of the episode addressed the heated community debate over a potential SpaceX–Tesla merger. Polymarket odds were cited at approximately 70% probability that a merger occurs. Cern Basher laid out the bull case for merger (Tesla would otherwise pay SpaceX for Starlink connectivity, Grok/XAI AI services, Terafab chips, and orbital data centers anyway — so "economic leakage" to SpaceX happens regardless of merger structure) and the bear case (dilution of Tesla's robotaxi upside to SpaceX shareholders; uncertainty about regulatory timelines; risk of chip constraints if Terafab is not built). SpaceX's valuation was noted as having surged from $400 billion last summer to a potential $2 trillion IPO valuation. Cern noted he holds 20x more Tesla exposure than SpaceX. The panel consensus was that the debate is currently "low data" — no merger has been proposed and Elon has not publicly stated he wants one.

3. **Terafab as a Strategic Necessity:** Multiple panelists flagged Terafab as critical infrastructure. A new SpaceX filing was cited showing Terafab numbers of $55 billion upfront and up to $119 billion total, potentially sited in Grimes County, Texas (~2 hours from Austin). The panel argued that without domestic chip fabrication at this scale, both Robotaxi and Optimus face a chip supply constraint within approximately five years that could cap Tesla's growth and compress its valuation multiples regardless of software progress.

4. **European and China EV Sales Data:** Jeff noted that April 2026 European sales data was very positive, with Germany posting its best-ever April sales. China April data was also described as one of the strongest Aprils on record. A deal reportedly in the works for over $100 million in Tesla Semi purchases was also cited as a positive signal. Tesla Semi was described as entering production.

5. **Tesla Stock Technical Analysis:** Jeff referenced analysis from a technical analyst on X (handle: "retro tech") noting that Tesla's stock had broken out of a downward channel for the third time, and that the prior two such breakouts preceded runs to all-time highs. The stock was noted to have closed above its 200-day moving average (in the low $400s, around $402–$404), and is currently trading between Fibonacci sequence levels.

Notable quotes and data:
- Elon Musk on the Anthropic deal: *"I spent a lot of time last week with senior members of the Anthropic team to understand what they do to ensure Claude is good for humanity and was impressed. Everyone I met was highly competent and cared a great deal about doing the right thing. No one set off my evil detector."*
- Elon on Grok: *"We have many Grok models training simultaneously in Colossus 2. I'm confident they will bear fruit and work on the Grok built harness is progressing well."*
- SpaceX–Anthropic deal revenue estimates: $5B–$16B/year (various analysts); Brian Wang estimate ~$20–28B/year (AWS-comparable pricing)
- Terafab filing: $55 billion upfront, up to $119 billion total; potentially in Grimes County, Texas
- Unsupervised Robotaxi fleet per RobotaxiTracker.com: 38 total (Austin 27, Dallas 5, Houston 6) — up from 26 five days prior
- Total active Robotaxi fleet per RobotaxiTracker.com: ~550+ in Bay Area, 104 Austin, with Cybercab counts at Giga Texas now 40–50 units
- FSD 14.3.2 estimated at ~50% of Tesla fleet at time of recording; full fleet rollout expected within 1–2 weeks
- SpaceX valuation: $400B last summer → potential $2T IPO valuation
- Polymarket odds of SpaceX–Tesla merger: ~70%
- Cern Basher: holds 20x more Tesla exposure than SpaceX
- Fremont Optimus conversion: described as a "10 million per year line"
- Anthropic Tier 1 API: input tokens/minute increased from 30,000 → 500,000; context from 2M → 10M tokens
- Tesla stock 200-day moving average: approximately $402–$404
- Boston Dynamics: ~20 years of operation with no mass-market product shipped

articles.title: Tesla Model Y first to pass NHTSA’s new ADAS tests — but they test the basics
articles.body:
The 2026 Tesla Model Y became the first vehicle to pass NHTSA's updated NCAP ADAS benchmark tests, clearing all eight pass/fail evaluations. The article reports this as a legitimate but heavily caveated milestone, with significant editorial skepticism about the announcement's framing and context.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **What the Model Y passed:** NHTSA's updated NCAP added four new pass/fail ADAS evaluations — pedestrian automatic emergency braking, lane keeping assistance, blind spot warning, and blind spot intervention — plus four original criteria: forward collision warning, crash imminent braking, dynamic brake support, and lane departure warning. The tested Model Y must have been manufactured on or after November 12, 2025.

2. **Why Tesla is "first" — and why that's misleading:** NHTSA finalized the NCAP updates in late 2024 for model year 2026 vehicles, but the Trump administration delayed full implementation by one year to model year 2027 in September 2025, following a request from the Alliance for Automotive Innovation. Most automakers have not yet submitted vehicles for testing because of that delay — not because they lack the capabilities. These features are standard or widely available across vehicles from Toyota, Hyundai, Honda, BMW, and others.

3. **Concurrent FSD investigation:** NHTSA is simultaneously conducting an Engineering Analysis investigation into Tesla's "Full Self-Driving" system covering approximately 3.2 million vehicles — the stage that typically precedes a recall. That investigation found FSD's camera-based system fails to detect common visibility-impairing conditions such as sun glare and fog, and doesn't adequately warn drivers before crashes. NHTSA has also noted Tesla may be under-reporting related crashes.

4. **Political framing:** The press release was titled "Trump's Transportation Department Announces Tesla Model Y Is the First Vehicle to Pass NHTSA's New 'Advanced Driver Assistance System' Tests" — an unusual practice for a government safety announcement. The article notes Tesla's CEO has a well-documented relationship with the current administration.

5. **Cybercab context:** Tesla has begun Cybercab production without approval for unsupervised autonomous driving, adding further complexity to the regulatory picture.

## Editorial Stance
The author credits the Model Y's ADAS test results as a genuine consumer safety achievement but argues the announcement is packaged as a PR win rather than a meaningful safety milestone, citing political branding, delayed NCAP implementation, and the irony of simultaneous FSD safety investigations. The author also expresses doubt that the FSD investigation will result in a recall.

Notable quotes and data:
- NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison: the Model Y "demonstrates the lifesaving potential of driver assistance technologies and sets a high bar for the industry."
- ~2 million Model Ys sold per year (per article's characterization of buyer volume)
- FSD Engineering Analysis covers approximately 3.2 million vehicles
- NCAP full implementation delayed from model year 2026 to model year 2027
- ADAS test results are pass/fail checkmarks and do not affect a vehicle's five-star crashworthiness safety rating

articles.title: Tesla Semi battery sizes confirmed: 822 kWh and 548 kWh officially revealed
articles.body:
California's Air Resources Board has officially confirmed Tesla Semi battery capacities via regulatory filing (Executive Order A-374-0095, signed April 15), revealing the Long Range variant carries an 822 kWh usable pack and the Standard Range 548 kWh — both using NCMA lithium-ion chemistry with 4680 cells.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Battery specs smaller than Musk's 2022 estimate, same range achieved:** Elon Musk estimated ~900 kWh for the 500-mile Long Range Semi in December 2022. The certified 822 kWh pack is roughly 80 kWh smaller, yet Tesla still rates the truck at 500 miles at full 82,000-lb GCW. The efficiency gain is partly explained by the production version weighing nearly 1,000 lbs less than the prototype, as revealed in Tesla's March refreshed design.

2. **Shared powertrain specs across both trims:** Both variants use an 800 kW (1,072 hp) tri-motor drivetrain with 525 kW sustained output and support 1.2 MW Megacharger speeds via an MCS 3.2 connector. At 1.2 MW, the Long Range can recover roughly 60% charge in 30 minutes.

3. **Standard Range as strategic product:** The 548 kWh Standard Range is estimated at $260,000 — $30,000 less than the $290,000 Long Range — and covers 325 miles, sufficient for the majority of Class 8 regional haul routes under 300 miles. The article notes the modular battery architecture appears to remove one of three parallel modules, yielding almost exactly a one-third reduction from 822 kWh to 548 kWh.

## Market & Competition

4. **Tesla Semi leads competitors on range and efficiency:** The Freightliner eCascadia tops out at 550 kWh for 230 miles; the Volvo VNR Electric at 564 kWh for 275 miles; the Nikola Tre BEV claims 330 miles. At 1.7 kWh per mile (~0.6 miles/kWh), the Semi is materially more efficient than competitors at roughly 0.4–0.5 miles/kWh.

## Financials

5. **Cost of ownership and delivery projections:** The article cites a TCO analysis showing Semi energy costs of approximately $0.20/mile at $0.12/kWh versus $0.67/mile for diesel at $5.35/gallon, with estimated 10-year savings exceeding $400,000. Analyst projections for 2026 deliveries range from 5,000 to 15,000 units, with the author noting even 1,000 deliveries would be a positive signal for the Nevada production ramp. Tesla's Megacharger network currently spans 66 locations across 15 states, with pricing starting at $188,000 for a two-post setup.

## Editorial Stance
The author argues the 822 kWh Long Range pack achieving 500 miles is more impressive than a 900 kWh pack doing the same — reflecting genuine efficiency gains — but contends the Standard Range at $260,000 will be the more impactful product for fleet adoption, as most Class 8 operations run regional routes where the cheaper, lighter truck wins on economics.

**Notable quotes and data:**
- 822 kWh (Long Range) and 548 kWh (Standard Range), NCMA/4680 chemistry — CARB Executive Order A-374-0095, April 15
- Long Range: 500-mile rating at 82,000 lb GCW; Standard Range: 325 miles
- 1.7 kWh/mile efficiency; ~0.6 miles/kWh vs. competitors' 0.4–0.5 miles/kWh
- Both trims: 800 kW tri-motor, 1.2 MW Megacharger support
- Production Semi ~1,000 lbs lighter than prototype
- Standard Range estimated $260,000; Long Range $290,000
- Energy cost: ~$0.20/mile (electric) vs. ~$0.67/mile (diesel); ~$400,000 10-year savings
- Megacharger network: 66 locations, 15 states; starting at $188,000 (two-post)
- 2026 delivery analyst range: 5,000–15,000 units

articles.title: Tesla Semi Demand Just Hit Another Level
articles.body:
This episode of FutureAzA features host Brian and guest Mark from The Tesla Life discussing a wave of new Tesla Semi orders announced at the ACT Expo in Las Vegas, the official pricing release for the Semi, and the confirmation that Semi production has begun at Giga Nevada. The hosts also walk through recent aerial footage from Zanegler showing construction and equipment activity at the Giga Nevada Semi facility, and close with a community Q&A and "Wrong Answers Only" humor segment.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **New Tesla Semi Orders Announced at ACT Expo:** Several fleet operators announced Tesla Semi orders at the ACT Expo trucking conference in Las Vegas. Watt EV's CEO ordered 370 Tesla Semis, with the first 50 deliveries beginning in 2026 and the full fleet expected by the end of 2027. Additionally, Big F Transport ordered 40 Semis after recently demoing a unit, and NA Container Freight Lines announced a purchase of 20 Semis. The hosts note that the ACT Expo is a natural venue for these announcements, as the trucks either make financial sense for a given operator or they don't.

2. **Official Tesla Semi Pricing Released:** Official pricing for the Tesla Semi has been confirmed: $290,000 for the long-range version and $260,000 for the standard range. Mark notes he had previously estimated $300,000 as the "sweet spot" threshold — below which the economics make sense for fleet operators — and had suggested $240,000–$260,000 would be leaving money on the table. Brian suggests Tesla's strategy may be to maximize volume at $290,000 first and work backward from there.

3. **Semi Production Has Officially Begun:** The first Tesla Semi has come off the production line at the Giga Nevada Semi facility (referred to as "Giga Iowa West" or "Giga Eye West" in context of the new dedicated building). Brian expects the production ramp to be, in his words, "painfully slow" initially, consistent with Tesla's typical ramp trajectory on new products.

4. **MCS 3.2 Charging Standard Adopted:** Tesla has transitioned the Semi to the MCS (Megawatt Charging System) 3.2 standard, moving away from its previous proprietary square connector. The new connector is more triangular in shape. This was confirmed via video footage shown during the Semi pricing announcement. The hosts note this is a positive industry alignment move, not an attempt to impose a proprietary standard.

5. **Semi Delivery Logistics via Reno Airport:** A viewer pointed out that Tesla is opening a Semi delivery station near the Reno airport, including a charging location so drivers can charge up before their first trip out. Fleet operators will fly their drivers into Reno to pick up vehicles. The hosts note most initial deliveries are expected to go to California and Southern California.
