6. **Production Capacity and Market Share Context:** A viewer comment suggested 50,000 units per year as a likely production bottleneck at the facility, which the hosts contextualize as less than 25% of the U.S. Class 8 truck market. Mark notes that not all fleet operators will convert immediately, and early adopters will set the pace. Brian adds that based on the facility's square footage, 50,000 units may assume only two or three shifts, leaving room for higher volume. Tesla also has known plans to manufacture Semis in Europe, with Asia as a possible future market.

7. **Watt EV's Prior Pilot and White Papers:** The Watt EV order is not a cold purchase — the company had previously conducted a pilot program with a Tesla Semi, wrapped it in their branding colors, and published white papers detailing their positive findings on efficiency and performance during those test runs.

## Market & Competition

1. **Legacy Trucking OEMs Caught Off Guard:** The hosts note that until now, no U.S. manufacturer was offering Class 8 trucks for under $400,000–$500,000, meaning incumbents like Freightliner were effectively only competing with other similarly priced legacy competitors. Tesla's sub-$300,000 pricing represents a structural disruption to that dynamic. The hosts suggest legacy players have not yet taken the competitive threat seriously enough.

## Giga Nevada Site Activity (Aerial Footage)

1. **Equipment and Packing Materials Indicate Active Factory Buildout:** Recent aerial footage from Zanegler shows large quantities of opened wooden crates and packing materials strewn outside the Giga Nevada Semi facility, indicating significant equipment has recently been moved inside. Bridge crane components are also visible, consistent with the type of overhead infrastructure needed for vehicle assembly.

2. **Stamping Press Likely Installed:** A Griffin crane near the building appears to be in the process of being disassembled rather than assembled, leading Zanegler and the hosts to theorize that something large — most likely a stamping press — was recently moved into the stamping building while they weren't watching. A heavy-duty truck with additional steel ballast weighting it down was spotted nearby, consistent with heavy equipment transport.

3. **Paint Shop Confirmed Operational:** Silver paint vents are visible on the factory roof in the footage, confirming that the paint shop is operational and giving observers a rough sense of where in the factory floor layout the paint stage sits within the assembly line.

4. **Traffic Circle Under Construction:** A new traffic circle is being installed behind the factory toward the road connecting to the main Giga Nevada building, suggesting increased vehicle traffic is anticipated as production ramps.

5. **Battery Pack Assembly Location Unclear:** The hosts and viewers debated where Semi battery pack assembly will occur. Because the Semi's battery packs are configured in a cube format (unlike the flat packs in passenger cars), Mark speculates pack assembly may happen at the Semi facility itself. Brian raises the possibility that it could be done at Giga Texas (where cells are made) or at the Giga Nevada Semi building. No confirmed answer is given.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla Semi long-range price: **$290,000**; standard range: **$260,000**
- Watt EV order: **370 Semis** — first 50 deliveries in 2026, full fleet by end of 2027
- Big F Transport order: **40 Semis** (post-demo)
- NA Container Freight Lines order: **20 Semis**
- Estimated production capacity ceiling discussed: **50,000 units/year** (viewer estimate; hosts note this may assume 2–3 shifts, not maximum capacity)
- 50,000 units/year cited as representing less than **25% of the U.S. Class 8 truck market**
- Semi facility requires approximately **40 GWh of cells**, comparable to the entirety of the adjacent Giga Nevada battery facility
- Tesla Semi uses **center-driver seating**, making it compatible with both left- and right-hand-drive countries without modification
- Tesla has adopted the **MCS 3.2 standard** for Semi charging (triangular connector replacing the proprietary square one)
- Mark: *"290 for the long range, 260 for the standard. I've been saying 300 is the sweet spot. If you're under that, it makes sense."*
- Brian: *"I expect the ramp to be, as Elon would say, painfully slow."*

articles.title: Semi, Neuralink, FSD, & SO MUCH MORE to cover before the weekend - Live with Joe, John, and Matthew
articles.body:
Episode 145 of "The Tesla Beat," hosted by John, Joe, Brian, and Matthew, covers a broad range of Tesla and tech news heading into the weekend, including Tesla Semi updates, FSD milestones, new vehicle launches, Model S/X end-of-life, and market dynamics. The panel is broadly bullish on Tesla's product pipeline and the company's competitive positioning across EVs, autonomous driving, and energy.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Semi at ACT Expo:** Tesla's Dan Priestley presented the Tesla Semi at the ACT Expo in Las Vegas in a roughly 43-minute on-stage appearance. The panel praised his transparency and engineering philosophy. Key highlights included the Semi's one-speed direct drive transmission — contrasted with competitors (Cascadia, Kenworth) who use two- to four-speed transmissions, adding 500 lb to over 2,000 lb of weight. The front end was redesigned from a single replaceable piece into three sections to reduce repair costs and improve total cost of ownership. Competitor electric semis were described as electrified versions of existing diesel platforms, while Tesla's is a purpose-built vehicle priced approximately 25% below competing trucks (which are in the $400,000–$500,000 range). NA Container Freight Line ordered 20 units, with the first truck slated to operate next year. Watt EV was noted as having placed an order of approximately 370 units. In California, the cost per mile for the Semi is reportedly 50% cheaper than diesel; outside California, approximately 20% cheaper.

2. **Model Y L Incoming:** A covered Model Y L was spotted this week, consistent with earlier reports. Matthew shared that Giga Texas is reportedly preparing for two large SUV variants — one likely being the Model Y L and potentially a Cyber SUV built on the Cybertruck platform. Elon had previously responded (approximately six weeks prior to the episode) to a comment about needing larger family vehicles. The Model Y L is expected to be built on the same production line as the Model Y in Austin and potentially Fremont, requiring no new line build-out. The panel estimated the Model Y L could arrive at approximately $55,000–$60,000 at launch, with an unveil possible within 60 days and deliveries potentially beginning around October. The panel dismissed Osborne Effect concerns, noting that Model Y L availability in other markets has not hindered standard Model Y sales.

3. **Model S and Model X End of Production:** The last Model S and Model X units rolled off the production line, with Tesla employees holding a signing event for the final vehicles. The panel acknowledged the Model S as historically significant for kicking off EV mass production. The Model Y L and potential Cyber SUV were cited as likely volume successors, particularly given the Model X's relatively low production volumes.

4. **Model 3 Now Available in Canada from Giga Shanghai:** Tesla began selling the Giga Shanghai-manufactured Model 3 in Canada at approximately $30,000 USD — described as the cheapest Tesla has ever been offered anywhere in the world and roughly 35% below the average new vehicle price in Canada. The panel noted the import cap is 49,000 units for this year (rising through 2030), and that Tesla is positioned to take the lion's share of that quota. Model Y is not expected to be imported from China to Canada as it already arrives from Giga Berlin under a preferred trade agreement.

5. **Model Y: Top-Selling Vehicle Globally and in Norway:** The Model Y was confirmed as the bestselling EV in the world in March. In Norway, BEVs represent nearly 98% of the total market, with the Model Y selling approximately 5,400 units and Model 3 approximately 2,000 units. BYD was noted to have posted its 10th consecutive month of sales decline, and Tesla passed BYD in Q1 2026 — though the panel noted the media will prominently report if BYD reclaims the lead.

6. **New Colors for Model 3 and Model Y:** Tesla released two new colors — Frost Blue and Marine Blue — for the Model 3 and Model Y in the US. Frost Blue was confirmed available on the Model 3 Performance trim. The panel noted this is one of the first recent color launches to debut in the US rather than Giga Berlin or Giga Shanghai.

7. **Tesla Brand Loyalty:** Tesla was cited as leading all automotive brands in owner return-to-purchase loyalty, ahead of Subaru and Toyota. The panel attributed this to software updates, FSD capability, safety ratings, low maintenance costs, and the seamless ownership experience.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Hits 10 Billion Miles:** Tesla's Full Self-Driving cumulative miles reached 10 billion, a milestone the panel noted as significant for unsupervised autonomy validation. As of the recording, the counter had already moved to 10.133 billion miles on Tesla's live website tracker, illustrating the pace of accumulation. The panel noted 42% (described loosely as "4% of vehicles FSD-based") are now running Tesla self-driving — though the phrasing in the transcript was ambiguous. FSD versions 13 and 14 were discussed qualitatively, with version 14 described as so capable that users don't go back after experiencing it.

2. **FSD Ethics and Pricing Debate:** The panel debated whether Tesla has an ethical responsibility to make FSD more widely accessible given its demonstrated safety benefits. Brian argued that paywalling supervised FSD at $100/month is arguably too restrictive given lives that could be saved, and proposed splitting supervised (potentially free or cheaper) from unsupervised (premium, akin to a chauffeur service). Matthew noted Tesla does zero advertising for FSD, calling it a missed opportunity. The panel also discussed frustration that FSD subscriptions do not follow the person across vehicles (e.g., on Turo rentals), with Matthew recounting paying a Turo owner separately for a one-month FSD subscription in Hawaii.

## Robotaxi

1. **Robotaxi Loyalty and Consumer Experience:** The panel discussed the expectation that once consumers use a Tesla robotaxi, they will not return to traditional ride-share platforms. The key value drivers cited were: faster arrival than Uber, lower cost, no tipping, and consistent vehicle/experience quality regardless of which unit arrives. No specific fleet counts or fare data were mentioned.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus 3 in the Pipeline:** Optimus 3 was briefly mentioned by John as part of a broader observation about the unprecedented number of simultaneous product releases Tesla is managing — alongside the Model Y L, Roadster, Semi, and potential Cyber SUV. No technical details about Optimus 3 were provided.

## Energy

1. **Solar and Battery Storage Cost Decline:** The panel discussed an IRENA report (cited via Sawyer Merritt) showing the cost of solar and wind with battery storage has fallen from $100/MWh in 2020 to $54–$82/MWh today. New coal capacity in China was cited at $70–$85/MWh, making renewable-plus-storage cost-competitive with new coal. The panel connected this to Tesla's Megapack business and broader energy transition momentum.

2. **EV Charging Lounges:** Tesla is building a 28-charger station designed as an experiential lounge, competing with convenience-store-style charging stations from other networks. The panel noted constraints on upgrading existing supercharger sites (insufficient grid capacity, leased parking lots) but praised the lounge concept where feasible.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla Stock Up 11% on the Week:** Tesla's stock rose approximately 11% over the past week, attributed partly to broader market optimism around trade war resolution and potentially to positive momentum from the OpenAI trial (where Elon Musk's odds of winning on Prediction Market platform Poly Market also improved). The panel warned against selling covered calls on Tesla given the potential for 10%+ weekly moves.

2. **XAI / SpaceX Restructuring:** XAI, previously a subsidiary of SpaceX, is being dissolved as a separate entity and folded into SpaceX as a division. The panel viewed this as a defensive antitrust posture — Elon's practice of opening up patents, offering FSD licensing to other OEMs, adopting the North American charging standard, and partnering with Anthropic (via the assistant integration) was cited as evidence of intentional competitive friendliness to reduce breakup risk. Historical analogies to Standard Oil and AT&T breakups were discussed, with Brian noting breakups often increase total enterprise value.

3. **Neuralink Surgical Robot:** Neuralink announced a new surgical robot capable of reaching any region of the brain, described as enabling a generalized neural interface to address any neurological condition originating in the brain. No financial or timeline details were provided.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla Semi cost per mile: **50% cheaper** than diesel in California; **~20% cheaper** outside California
- Competitor electric semis priced at **$400,000–$500,000**; Tesla Semi at minimum **25% cheaper**
- FSD cumulative miles: **10.133 billion** (live counter as of recording)
- Model 3 Canada price: **~$30,000 USD** (Giga Shanghai-built)
- Canada Chinese-vehicle import cap: **49,000 units** in 2026, rising through 2030
- Norway BEV market share: **~98%**; Model Y ~5,400 units, Model 3 ~2,000 units in Norway
- Solar + battery storage cost: **$54–$82/MWh** today vs. **$100/MWh** in 2020
- New coal in China: **$70–$85/MWh**
- Model Y L expected launch price: **~$55,000–$60,000**; deliveries potentially starting **~October 2026**
- Canada import cap retail threshold: **$39,000 CAD** (retail price of base Model 3), import value cap **$35,000 CAD**
- Watt EV Semi order: **~370 units**
- NA Container Freight Line Semi order: **20 units**, first truck operating **next year (2027)**
- Brian (re: FSD): *"FSD is so safe. The fact that Tesla is not really promoting FSD at all, making no effort to get it into the mainstream, doing essentially zero advertising… it starts to become an ethical decision."*
- Matthew (re: robotaxi loyalty): *"Once somebody uses a robotaxi, they're never going to go back to traditional ride share."*

articles.title: Is The SpaceX Merge UNFAIR For Tesla Shareholders? My Rebellionaire Takedown!
articles.body:
Jo Bhakdi responds directly to a viral X post by Rebellionaire (211,000 views) arguing that Tesla shareholders are being treated unfairly in a potential SpaceX merger, having endured years of drawdowns and missed FSD timelines without yet receiving the financial payoff from robotaxi scaling. Bhakdi pushes back on both the "merger is unfair" camp and the uncritical "support Elon, we're going to the moon" camp, arguing instead that rational investors must understand how markets price stocks — and that Tesla, given the level of public attention and information transparency, is unlikely to be as dramatically mispriced as Rebellionaire implies. His core thesis is that any merger price, assuming adequate premium, is by definition a reasonable reflection of known risks and probabilities, and that the assumption Tesla is obviously worth far more is structurally unsound.

## Market & Competition

1. **The Rebellionaire Argument — Tesla Shareholders Deserve More:** Rebellionaire's viral video argues that Tesla shareholders endured years of missed FSD timelines, ridicule, and drawdowns while believing in the robotaxi vision, and that merging Tesla into SpaceX before robotaxi revenue scales to hundreds of thousands or millions of vehicles would cheat them out of the payoff. Bhakdi acknowledges this is emotionally compelling and represents a real concern within the Tesla shareholder community, but ultimately rejects its logical foundation.

2. **Bhakdi's Core Rebuttal — Markets Are Not Dramatically Mispriced:** Bhakdi argues that with this level of YouTuber, analyst (Dan Ives, Adam Jonas/Morgan Stanley), and public attention on Tesla's robotaxi and Optimus verticals, there is no credible case for a lack of information transparency. He contends that over 50% of Tesla's current stock price already reflects anticipated future value from robotaxi and Optimus, discounted for risk. Therefore, the claim that Tesla is obviously and dramatically undervalued — and that a merger would be categorically unfair — is what he calls "structurally unsound."

3. **SpaceX Can Make the Same Argument in Reverse:** Bhakdi notes that SpaceX shareholders could equally argue they are being undervalued in a merger, pointing to SpaceX's theoretically infinite total addressable market (Starlink, Starship, space colonization) versus Tesla's more bounded TAM. He expects SpaceX may be somewhat overhyped at IPO and Tesla slightly undervalued, but says the gap is not "worlds apart." He does not believe Tesla shareholders require a significant merger premium beyond a roughly equal exchange, though he acknowledges the merger price is not yet known.

4. **Alexandra Merz and the Uncritical Bull Camp:** Bhakdi also pushes back on commentators like Alexandra Merz who dismiss shareholder valuation concerns entirely in favor of enthusiasm about SpaceX and Elon Musk's broader mission. He frames this as equally flawed — rational investors must assess intrinsic value, not defer to mission-driven sentiment.

## Financials

1. **Bhakdi's DCF Model — Fair Value of ~$600 for 2026:** Bhakdi shares his discounted cash flow model, which he describes as the most conservative valuation approach available. After pushing his original timelines back by 12–18 months to account for delays, his model produces a 2026 fair value (intrinsic value) of approximately $600 per share — contingent on Tesla deploying 10,000 robotaxis by end of 2026 and scaling from there. He emphasizes this is intrinsic value, not a price target, and that the actual market price could significantly exceed or fall below this figure in any given year.

2. **Risk-Discounting Methodology:** Bhakdi applies a probability discount on top of his raw DCF output. As an example, if robotaxi generates a raw model value of $300–$400 per share but carries a 20% risk of failure, that value is further discounted by 20%. This layered risk discount is how he arrives at the ~$600 intrinsic value figure for 2026, making it explicitly conditional on deployment milestones being met.

3. **Timeline Shift Lowers Near-Term Price Targets:** Bhakdi notes he pushed his original model timelines back by 12 to 18 months, which reduces his 2030 price target relative to earlier estimates. He does not give a specific revised 2030 number in the transcript but characterizes it as "still pretty good" though "a little lower" than before.

## Robotaxi

1. **Conservative 2026 Deployment Assumption of 10,000 Robotaxis:** Bhakdi's base model assumes 10,000 robotaxis deployed by end of 2026, which he describes as conservative — noting that other analysts (he references "Herbert") believe the number will be higher, and that he himself thinks it will likely be more. His $600 intrinsic value is directly contingent on hitting this 10,000 figure.

2. **Scaling Trajectory — 100K in 2027, Millions by Mid-2030s:** From the 2026 base of 10,000, Bhakdi projects 100,000 robotaxis in 2027 (an inflection point), 200,000 by 2028, and then aggressive growth toward millions — reaching approximately 10 million by 2034–2035. He frames 2028 as the year when the technical problem should be "thoroughly solved" and regulatory readiness across jurisdictions should enable true mass scaling.

3. **Stock Price Could Significantly Exceed Intrinsic Value:** Bhakdi believes that if Tesla does deploy 10,000+ robotaxis in 2026, the actual market price will likely run well above the $600 intrinsic value — potentially dramatically so — but warns investors to be prepared for a subsequent correction, since intrinsic value remains the true long-run anchor.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus Deployment Assumptions Through 2030:** Bhakdi's base model projects 10,000 Optimus units delivered in 2026, scaling to 50,000 in 2027, 200,000 in 2028, and 1.5 million deployed by 2030 with a production rate of approximately 900,000 units in 2030. He characterizes these as reasonable but speculative estimates that could come in higher or lower.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Credibility Gap Was Real, But Now Priced In:** Bhakdi acknowledges that Tesla shareholders endured years of "FSD is impossible" criticism and missed timelines, validating Rebellionaire's characterization of the suffering. However, he argues that this history is now factored into the market price through risk discounts — the market has not ignored the past delays but has probabilistically weighted them into current valuation.

---

Notable quotes and data:
- Rebellionaire's X video received 211,000 views, described as "not easy to achieve."
- Bhakdi's 2026 intrinsic value (DCF): ~$600/share, contingent on 10,000 robotaxis deployed by year-end.
- Robotaxi deployment projections: 10,000 (2026) → 100,000 (2027) → 200,000 (2028) → ~10 million (~2034–2035).
- Optimus projections: 10,000 (2026) → 50,000 (2027) → 200,000 (2028) → 1.5 million deployed / ~900,000 produced (2030).
- "Over 50% of the stock price is already anticipating the future discounted with the risks and unknown factors."
- "The argument that anything in a public market with this level of attention, this level of coverage is totally mispriced and the deal is unfair, I think is structurally unsound."
- Bhakdi pushed his model timelines back 12–18 months from earlier projections.
- He believes Tesla will have a "generational run" in 2026 or 2027 — possibly 100%, 200%, or 300% — but cautions this does not change his intrinsic value framework.
- Potential merger price range referenced (not confirmed): ~$450–$600/share mentioned illustratively.

articles.title: Inside Rivian’s Future with CEO RJ Scaringe | R2 Updates, Fleet Strategy & ACT Expo
articles.body:
This video is an interview conducted at the ACT Expo 2026 between a Munro Live representative and Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe. The conversation covers Rivian's fleet strategy across commercial and consumer vehicles, its software-defined vehicle architecture, and key partnership deals. The core thesis is that Rivian is positioning itself as a horizontally integrated technology platform company — not just a vehicle manufacturer — with its software, connectivity, and autonomy stacks deployable across very different vehicle types and brands.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **EDV fleet scaling with Amazon:** Rivian's Electric Delivery Van (EDV), developed in deep partnership with Amazon specifically for last-mile delivery, now has well in excess of 30,000 units on the road. Scaringe noted that output is expected to ramp significantly over the coming year, driven by Amazon's recognition of a meaningful total cost of ownership (TCO) and operational cost advantage. Beyond electrification, the value proposition includes vehicle connectivity, built-in prognostics, predictive service interval capabilities, and deep integration into Amazon's software architecture.

2. **R2 as Rivian's first mass-market vehicle:** Scaringe described the R2 as Rivian's first high-volume, mass-market vehicle, targeting the mid-size SUV segment — which he characterized as the largest segment in the market. He contrasted it with the R1, which was successful but limited to the premium/flagship space. Scaringe also teased that R2 represents a significant engineering improvement over R1 and expressed excitement about having it torn down by Munro Live.

3. **Software-defined architecture enabling lower price points:** Scaringe attributed Rivian's ability to offer vehicles at lower price points to its software-defined, zonal ECU architecture, which consolidates compute into a small number of zonal computers, dramatically simplifies the wiring harness, and brings software development fully in-house. He noted this platform is scalable across different price points, content levels, form factors, and brands.

4. **Volkswagen partnership and the ~$20,000 ID1:** Rivian completed a $5.8 billion software licensing deal with Volkswagen approximately a year and a half ago. The first vehicle to emerge from this partnership is the VW ID1, priced at around $20,000 — an EV not intended for the U.S. market — which Scaringe said dramatically demonstrates the simplification of the electronic stack and wiring harness made possible by Rivian's technology.

## Market & Competition
1. **Robotaxi deal with Uber on the R2 platform:** Rivian recently signed a large deal with Uber to build a robotaxi on its R2 platform. Scaringe positioned this as a distinct type of fleet business focused on moving people, with self-driving technology as a central element. He framed this alongside the Amazon delivery van as part of a broader fleet strategy encompassing both goods movement and people movement.

2. **"Also" micromobility company and DoorDash deal:** Rivian created a micromobility subsidiary called "Also," which recently announced a deal with DoorDash to operate a fleet of small delivery bots for food delivery. Scaringe described this as another expression of the same fleet-oriented, autonomy-forward, AI-defined platform strategy.

3. **Horizontal technology platforms as the organizing principle:** Scaringe described Rivian's strategic organization around horizontal technology platforms — including its autonomous driving platform, connected vehicle platform, and diagnostics/prognostics platform — that are shared across very different vehicle types (vans, R1, R2, R3, micromobility, VW products). He said the company is shifting its language from "software-defined vehicles" to "AI-defined vehicles," reflecting a focus on leveraging data collection across vehicles for better decisioning.

Notable quotes and data:
- "Well in excess of 30,000" EDVs on the road as of the interview, with significant ramp expected over the coming year.
- $5.8 billion software licensing deal with Volkswagen, signed approximately a year and a half before the interview (i.e., roughly late 2024).
- VW ID1 priced at approximately $20,000 — an EV enabled by Rivian's architecture, not sold in the U.S.
- Rivian robotaxi deal with Uber to be built on the R2 platform.
- Rivian micromobility subsidiary "Also" signed a deal with DoorDash for small food delivery bots.
- Scaringe: "We used to always say software-defined vehicles. We're increasingly thinking about these vehicles as being AI-defined."
- Scaringe on R2: "It's a giant improvement" over R1.
- R3 referenced as an upcoming vehicle after R2 in Rivian's consumer roadmap.

articles.title: Daily X Summary (2026-05-08)
articles.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts were headlined by two significant regulatory and milestone developments: NHTSA officially certifying the 2026 Tesla Model Y as the first vehicle to pass its new advanced driver assistance system tests, and Tesla announcing that FSD (Supervised) has surpassed 10 billion miles of real-world driving. Supporting these was strong global EV sales data showing record-breaking April performance across multiple markets, reinforcing demand recovery narratives heading into Q2 2026.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **NHTSA Certifies 2026 Model Y as First Vehicle to Pass New ADAS Tests:** In a high-engagement post (3.5K likes, 541 reposts), Sawyer Merritt reported that NHTSA officially announced the 2026 Tesla Model Y is the first vehicle model to pass the agency's newly established advanced driver assistance system tests. Vehicles manufactured on or after November 12, 2025 successfully met the new criteria across four test categories. NHTSA itself stated: *"By successfully passing these new tests, the 2026 Tesla Model Y demonstrates the lifesaving potential of driver assistance technologies and sets a high bar for the industry. We hope to see many more manufacturers develop vehicles that can meet these requirements."* This is a meaningful regulatory endorsement that reinforces Tesla's ADAS leadership, potentially influencing future policy frameworks, fleet purchasing decisions, and the regulatory pathway for more advanced autonomy deployments.

2. **FSD (Supervised) Crosses 10 Billion Miles:** Tesla sent an official email to customers announcing that FSD (Supervised) has now surpassed 10 billion miles of real-world driving. The email noted that Tesla's Self-Driving computer has "navigated nearly every driving scenario possible and continues to learn, adapt and improve on each additional drive." This milestone is significant for the autonomous driving thesis: the cumulative real-world data corpus underpinning Tesla's neural network training is a core competitive moat argument, and 10 billion supervised miles represents a scale that is extremely difficult for competitors to replicate.

3. **Tesla Semi Battery Specs Revealed via Regulatory Filing:** A regulatory filing disclosed the official production battery specifications for both Tesla Semi trims. The Long Range variant features an 822 kWh usable battery capacity using NMCA chemistry (4680 cells), a 500-mile range at 82,000 lbs gross combination weight, and a peak charging speed that was partially truncated in the post. While not directly tied to the robotaxi or Optimus thesis, this confirms large-scale 4680 cell deployment in a commercial vehicle context, relevant to Tesla's manufacturing scale and energy cost dynamics.

4. **Global EV Sales Show Strong April Recovery:** Multiple posts highlighted record-breaking April 2026 sales across key markets. Tesla China-made EV deliveries jumped 36% year-over-year to 79,478 units — the best April ever for the China operation. In South Korea, Tesla sold a record 13,190 vehicles in April, its highest monthly total ever in the country, exceeding the prior record (set in March 2026) by approximately 2,000 units, and outselling BMW and Mercedes combined. Tesla sales in Germany also posted the best April ever, with Merritt characterizing Europe broadly as seeing a "BIG comeback." Collectively, these data points suggest meaningful demand recovery following the challenging early-2026 period, which is relevant to near-term revenue and margin trajectory.

5. **OTA "Recall" Media Coverage Criticized:** Merritt pushed back on media framing of a Tesla software recall, noting that Tesla issued a free over-the-air update to resolve the issue, and that 30 articles covering the story buried this context — misleading readers into implying a physical recall. While not a new data point, this is relevant for investors monitoring headline risk around Tesla's regulatory relationship with NHTSA.

6. **Tesla Semi Hauling Cybercabs (Visual):** A video post showed a Tesla Semi transporting Cybercabs, generating notable engagement (2.5K likes, 199 reposts). While primarily visual, it signals active Cybercab logistics and distribution activity, consistent with scaling fleet operations.

7. **Lexus TZ All-Electric SUV Unveiled (Competition Context):** Lexus unveiled the TZ, an all-electric three-row SUV for the US market, with up to 300 miles of range, 77 kWh or 96 kWh battery options, 150 kW peak charging, a 35-minute 10–80% charge time, and NACS port compatibility. Merritt noted — somewhat dismissively — that the vehicle includes fake gear shifts and simulated gas engine sounds, a design choice he described negatively. The 150 kW peak charging rate and 300-mile range ceiling position the TZ below Tesla's performance benchmarks in comparable segments.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — The dual headlines of NHTSA's first-ever ADAS certification going to Tesla and FSD crossing 10 billion miles provide strong regulatory and data-scale validation for the autonomous driving thesis, while simultaneously, record April sales across China, South Korea, and Germany indicate that the demand recovery is real and broad-based.

articles.title: Elon Just Changed The AI War Again
articles.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel covers the announcement of a major compute partnership between SpaceX and Anthropic, in which Anthropic has signed an agreement to use all of the capacity at SpaceX's Colossus 1 supercomputer facility. Host Herbert is joined by serial entrepreneur and venture capital investor Larry Goldberg (website: lumacenti.com) to discuss the strategic implications of this deal for SpaceX, XAI, Grok, Anthropic, and the broader AI competitive landscape. The core thesis is that this deal validates Elon Musk's "compute as infrastructure" strategy and fundamentally transforms SpaceX into a recurring-revenue cloud business.

## Market & Competition

1. **Anthropic-SpaceX Colossus 1 Deal:** Anthropic (maker of Claude) has signed a partnership with SpaceX to use all of the compute capacity at the Colossus 1 data center — 220,000 Nvidia GPUs with over 300 megawatts of power. Anthropic stated the capacity would be online within the month, and that Claude inference on Colossus 1 would begin ramping up within days. Anthropic's Tom Brown credited SpaceX's ability to "move atoms" quickly, hinting at potential future collaboration extending beyond terrestrial data centers. Nvidia publicly congratulated the partnership, calling Colossus 1 "two Frontier Labs, one accelerated computing platform."

2. **XAI Dissolved as Separate Entity; SpaceX AI Born:** Elon Musk announced that XAI will be dissolved as a separate company and folded into SpaceX as a product group called "SpaceX AI." Elon confirmed a new logo is planned and possibly a new name for the AI division. Larry Goldberg framed this as SpaceX becoming, overnight, a massive recurring-revenue company earning from both its Starlink satellite network and its Colossus compute infrastructure — directly countering critics who argued XAI's losses would erode SpaceX's profitability.

3. **Musk's Strategic Rationale — Coherence and Compute Allocation:** Elon explained that XAI's Grok models have already moved training to Colossus 2, making Colossus 1 available to lease. Goldberg explained this is due to the technical concept of "coherence" — all training processes must run simultaneously on a single, unified compute cluster and cannot be mixed across architecturally distinct systems. Because Grok's inference demand has not yet matched Claude's scale, Colossus 1 was underutilized for SpaceX AI's own needs, creating the opportunity to lease it.

4. **SpaceX as AI Infrastructure Landlord:** Elon stated that just as SpaceX launches satellites for competitors on fair terms, SpaceX will lease compute to AI companies that are "taking the right steps to ensure it is good for humanity," with the explicit right to reclaim compute if an AI engages in actions that harm humanity. Herbert cited Brian Wang's calculation that this rental arrangement could generate approximately $16.8 billion per year in revenue for SpaceX. Goldberg suggested the combined SpaceX entity could show roughly $20 billion in profit in its first year from these combined revenue streams.

5. **Anthropic's Compute Crisis and Near-IPO Risk:** Both Herbert and Goldberg described Anthropic as having been in a serious compute bottleneck prior to this deal, with Claude being throttled — slower response times, reduced token limits, peak-hour restrictions, and pricing increases — to the point that users (including Herbert himself) were migrating to alternatives like OpenAI's Codex. Despite existing agreements with Amazon (5 gigawatts), Google (5 gigawatts), and strategic partnerships with Microsoft and Nvidia, Anthropic still lacked sufficient live inference capacity. Goldberg noted that Anthropic was planning an IPO — with speculation around a valuation of over $1 trillion — and that the compute shortage threatened both that IPO and the company's competitive standing. The SpaceX deal, Herbert argued, effectively saved Anthropic.

6. **Competitive Squeeze on OpenAI:** Herbert framed the deal as OpenAI being squeezed from both sides: Elon is in an active lawsuit against Sam Altman, and Anthropic — led by former OpenAI employee Dario Amodei — is now empowered with SpaceX compute. Goldberg was less focused on the adversarial framing, noting Elon has historically welcomed competition and would likely be willing to lease compute to OpenAI and Google as well, subject to the same ethical guardrails.

7. **Musk's Foresight on Compute Scarcity and Energy Bottlenecks:** Goldberg credited Musk with having recognized compute as the critical bottleneck before it became widely understood, and having built Colossus 1 before the market caught on. Herbert noted that Musk had also predicted energy would be the next bottleneck, which appears to be materializing — with 50% of data center projects reportedly stalled due to inability to secure energy or permitting. Musk's off-planet data center strategy (space-based compute via Starlink infrastructure) was cited as the long-term play that validates this vision.

8. **Musk's Cybertruck 48V Open-Sourcing as Precedent for Competition Philosophy:** Goldberg cited as evidence of Musk's pro-competition worldview the fact that when Tesla developed and implemented the 48-volt electrical architecture on the Cybertruck, Musk produced a detailed book explaining the system and vendor relationships and sent it to every major automotive CEO — none of whom, Goldberg noted, acted on it.

9. **SpaceX-Tesla Merger Speculation:** Herbert briefly raised the possibility of a SpaceX-Tesla merger, noting that if it occurred, Tesla investors could own a piece of the company now sitting at the center of global AI infrastructure. Goldberg did not dismiss the idea but noted that whether or not a merger occurs, SpaceX and Tesla already have a natural fluidity in assigning compute work and financial flows between them, making the merger question "not material" to the underlying thesis.

10. **Grok as Tesla/FSD AI vs. Claude as General/Coding AI:** Goldberg expressed his view that the partnership with Anthropic is strictly a client-vendor compute relationship and that Grok — not Claude — is the intended AI for Tesla's cars, Full Self-Driving, and Optimus. He noted that Grok's integration into Tesla vehicles is already progressing at a "pretty rapid clip," while Claude's strength is in generalized and coding applications. He does not foresee the Anthropic-SpaceX relationship deepening beyond compute leasing.

Notable quotes and data:
- Colossus 1: 220,000 Nvidia GPUs, over 300 megawatts of power
- Anthropic's Claude API rate limits reportedly increased from ranges like 30,000 to 500,000 and 450,000 to 2 million and 2 million to 10 million tokens (exact tier definitions not fully specified in transcript)
- Brian Wang's estimated SpaceX compute rental revenue: ~$16.8 billion per year
- Goldberg's estimate: combined SpaceX entity could show ~$20 billion in profit in its first year
- Elon (quoted): "Nobody set off my evil detector" — on meeting Anthropic's senior team
- Elon (quoted): "Just as SpaceX launches hundreds of satellites for competitors with fair terms and pricing, we will provide compute to AI companies that are taking the right steps to ensure it is good for humanity."
- Elon (quoted): GB300 is "the best AI computer"
- Herbert: "50% of all data center projects are not moving forward — they can't get the energy"
- Goldberg: "He's going to be the only large-scale AI company in the world making profits next year" — referring to Musk's combined SpaceX/XAI entity
- Anthropic's existing agreements cited: 5-gigawatt deal with Amazon, 5-gigawatt deal with Google, strategic partnership with Microsoft and Nvidia, $50 billion investment in American AI infrastructure with Fluid Stack

articles.title: Tesla Beats Every Other Mag 7! Here's Why
articles.body:
This video from "brighterwithherbert" argues that the traditional investing playbook — finding companies with moats, solid fundamentals, and growing TAMs — is no longer sufficient in the age of rapidly accelerating AI. The host presents a framework called the "10 Titans," co-developed with Chamath Palihapitiya, which holds that by the end of this decade, roughly 10 companies will own the future by controlling the compute, chips, data centers, and robots needed to build artificial superintelligence (ASI). The core thesis is that Tesla (and SpaceX) are uniquely positioned among the Mag 7 and beyond because they own the "physical world layer" of AI — something Microsoft, Google, and Meta cannot replicate.

## Market & Competition

1. **The Old Investing Playbook Is Broken:** The host argues that traditional moats — brand (Coca-Cola), switching costs (Microsoft), network effects (Visa) — are becoming obsolete as AI can perform the work of entire departments for pennies. AI agents buying products autonomously undermines brand moats; stablecoins undermine payment network moats; AI-generated documents undermine productivity software moats. The speed of AI development has compressed from major model updates every 6–12 months in 2024 to updates every few weeks or days in 2026, making the old "find a slow compounder" strategy increasingly ineffective.

2. **The 10 Titans Framework:** The host and Chamath Palihapitiya argue that by end of decade, perhaps 10 or fewer companies will dominate by owning the infrastructure for ASI — chips, data centers, power, and robotics. Candidates include the Mag 7 (Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, Apple, Nvidia, Tesla), potentially one or two Chinese national champions, OpenAI if it goes public, and SpaceX. The key insight is that the barrier to entry for ASI is no longer the algorithm (increasingly open or commoditized) but the balance sheet — the ability to write $200 billion annual checks for compute infrastructure.

3. **Hyperscaler AI CapEx Scale:** The four major hyperscalers are collectively on track to spend close to $700 billion on AI CapEx in 2026, up approximately 70% year-over-year. Microsoft and Google are each at $190 billion, Amazon at $200 billion, and Meta at $145 billion. Total global AI data center CapEx for 2026 is estimated at $400–$450 billion, with projections reaching $1 trillion per year by 2028. The host argues this scale of spending creates an unbridgeable gap between Titans and everyone else.

4. **Three Scenarios for ASI Timeline:** The host outlines three investor scenarios. In the slow scenario, ASI arrives by 2035 or later — indexing still works but underperforms concentrated Titan bets. In the middle scenario, ASI lands by 2030 — concentrated Titan positions massively outperform. In the fast scenario — which the host notes Elon Musk has actually been suggesting — recursive self-improvement breaks containment and ASI arrives by 2028, compressing the Titan list from 10 to perhaps 5 and creating the largest wealth transfer in human history.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Tesla's Real-World AI Advantage:** The host cites Elon Musk's framing that Tesla has three ingredients no other Mag 7 company possesses simultaneously: real-world AI (cameras, sensors, cars on roads, robots in factories, trillions of miles of data), electromechanical engineering developed over 20 years, and manufacturing at scale. Waymo is cited as Google's attempt at real-world AI, but is described as still small — approximately 3,000 cars confined to a few cities — by comparison to Tesla's scale.

2. **AI Chip Roadmap for FSD and Beyond:** The host outlines Tesla's stated AI hardware progression: AI 4 is described as getting self-driving safety far beyond human levels; AI 5 makes cars "almost perfect" and greatly enhances Optimus; AI 6 is targeted at Optimus and data centers; and AI 7 (also called Dojo 3) is described as space-based AI compute. The AI 5 chip is cited as delivering 2,500 TOPS, 144 gigabytes of memory, and up to a 40x system-level improvement over Hardware 4.

## Robotaxi

1. **Robotaxi Fleet as a Leading Indicator:** The host identifies robotaxi fleet count and Cybercab unit count as key leading indicators to watch for Tesla's physical-world AI thesis. No specific fleet counts or fare economics are discussed in the video beyond this framing. The host's overall argument is that the market is still pricing Tesla as a car company with optionality rather than as the owner of the physical world layer of ASI, and that this gap represents the investment asymmetry.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus as the "Infinite Money Glitch":** The host quotes Elon Musk calling Optimus the "infinite money glitch," describing it as three exponential forces multiplied recursively: production capacity, capability, and cost reduction — all compounding simultaneously. Elon's long-term stated target is cited as one billion humanoid robots per year. At $30,000 per unit, the host calculates that as $30 trillion in annual revenue, noting that even 1% of that figure — $300 billion — would exceed Tesla's entire current revenue base. The host is careful to note this is not a 2030 prediction.

2. **Optimus Factory Conversion and Production Path:** Tesla has reportedly discontinued the Model S and Model X and is converting that factory space into an Optimus production line, which the host characterizes as a strategic rather than incremental move. Elon did not offer specific guidance on Optimus units for 2026 or 2027, but a path to eventually one million units per year per production line is mentioned. The host notes Elon has said "next year" for Optimus production across multiple consecutive years — flagging timeline risk — but argues even a 1–2 year delay doesn't break the thesis.

3. **Optimus as a Von Neumann Probe:** The host cites Elon hinting at an endgame in which Optimus can manufacture Optimus — a self-replicating "Von Neumann probe" — making the production curve recursive rather than linear, mirroring the recursive self-improvement dynamic in AI software.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **2026 Tesla Product Pipeline:** The host lists several products expected from Tesla in 2026: Optimus Gen 3, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Megapack 3, and potentially a new solar product. This is framed as evidence of Tesla's manufacturing breadth across physical-world AI categories, not just automotive.

## Financials

1. **Terafab — Tesla's Vertically Integrated Chip Fab:** On March 21st, Tesla announced Terafab, described as a vertically integrated chip fabrication facility covering logic, memory, and advanced packaging, with a capital expenditure of approximately $25 billion. The first chip planned to roll off is the AI 5. Elon stated on X that Tesla plans to build more AI chips than every other company combined — more than Nvidia, Google's TPUs, AMD, and every hyperscaler's custom silicon combined — which the host describes as potentially the largest captive chip supply in the world.

2. **Optimus Revenue Math:** At Elon's stated long-term target of one billion humanoid robots per year at $30,000 per unit, the implied annual revenue would be $30 trillion. The host uses 1% of that ($300 billion) as a near-term benchmark, noting it alone would exceed Tesla's current total revenue base.

## Notable Quotes and Data

- Elon Musk (paraphrased): "Humans are gradually getting less and less in a loop on the recursive self-improvement."
- Elon Musk (paraphrased): "Solving real-world AI for Optimus will be 100 times harder than cars."
- Elon Musk (paraphrased): Called Optimus the "infinite money glitch" and described it as three exponential forces — production capacity, capability, and cost reduction — multiplying recursively.
- Elon Musk (paraphrased): Said Tesla plans to build more AI chips than every other company combined.
- Elon Musk (to Cathie Wood/Ark Invest, paraphrased): "Satellites with localized AI compute will be the lowest cost way to generate AI bit streams in under 3 years. The fastest way to scale within four."
- Elon Musk (paraphrased): "It is a hard path to 100 gigawatts per year of AI in space, but we know what to do."
- SpaceX filed plans in late January for a one-million satellite orbital data center constellation.
- Waymo fleet cited at ~3,000 cars confined to a few cities.
- AI 5 specs: 2,500 TOPS, 144 GB memory, up to 40x system-level improvement over Hardware 4.
- Terafab CapEx: ~$25 billion.
- Global AI data center CapEx 2026: $400–$450 billion; projected to reach $1 trillion/year by 2028.
- Combined hyperscaler AI CapEx 2026: ~$700 billion (Microsoft $190B, Google $190B, Amazon $200B, Meta $145B), up ~70% YoY.
- Optimus long-term target: 1 billion units/year at $30,000/unit = $30 trillion annual revenue.
- SpaceX orbital AI target: 100 gigawatts, described as ~20% of all US electricity consumption today.

articles.title: Why Elon May Have To Merge Tesla And SpaceX
articles.body:
This episode of the Cern Basher channel features host Cern alongside regular guest Phil and new guest Kenyon Wells — a longtime Tesla investor and enterprise IT professional with decades of experience — discussing the potential merger of Tesla and SpaceX, the looming compute supply crisis driven by AI demand, Tesla's Etherloop/Ethernet wiring architecture in the Cybercab, and the political and societal risks of AI deployment ahead of the 2028 U.S. election. The central thesis is that the demand for AI inference compute is growing so fast (approximately 3.4x per year) that terrestrial chip production cannot keep up, pointing toward orbital data centers and eventually lunar manufacturing as the only viable long-term solution — and that a Tesla-SpaceX merger is the logical outcome of Elon Musk's vertically integrated vision. The conversation also explores how Tesla's robotaxi rollout, Optimus, and the broader "Musconomy" ecosystem represent the clearest near-term path to demonstrating tangible AI benefits to ordinary consumers and voters.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX–Anthropic Partnership and the Compute Supply Crisis:** Phil opens by discussing the newly announced deal between SpaceX (operating as "SpaceX AI" following the dissolution of xAI as a separate brand) and Anthropic, in which Anthropic — whose primary cloud host is Amazon AWS, with additional presence on Azure and Google Cloud — will gain access to Colossus 1, while Colossus 2 remains dedicated to xAI's work. Colossus 1 is described as housing 220,000 Nvidia GPUs including H100s, H200s, and GB200s. Phil frames this as a symptom of a broader supply wall: AI inference demand is growing at approximately 3.4x per year, far outpacing semiconductor production capacity, and Anthropic had little practical alternative but to partner with SpaceX for orbital compute capacity.

2. **The Compute Demand Curve and Terafab:** Phil presents a detailed analysis showing that global AI compute capacity today stands at approximately 30 gigawatts (he notes Elon's own chart uses ~20 GW, but calls the difference immaterial). Growing at the historical CPU-era rate of 1.58x per year, it would take 7.7 years to reach 1 terawatt and 17 years (approximately 2043) to reach 100 terawatts. But at the current AI growth rate of 3.4x per year, 1 terawatt is reachable in just 3 years, and 100 terawatts in 7 years. Adjusting for hardware efficiency gains, Phil revises these estimates to 4.3 years for 1 terawatt and 10 years for 100 terawatts. He argues that Terafab — described as producing 1 terawatt of compute capacity annually and requiring at minimum a 100-million-square-foot facility (five Pentagons or two Central Parks) — is necessary but insufficient on its own; one Terafab eventually cannot keep pace with accelerating demand.

3. **Orbital and Lunar Computing as the Long-Term Answer:** Phil argues that within 5–10 years, terrestrial chip production will dominate, but beyond that, the industrialization of chip fabrication on the Moon becomes inevitable. He estimates that 90% or more of all AI inference will ultimately be delivered to Earth via space, while terrestrial data centers will be mostly dedicated to AI training (which requires coherent supercomputer-scale clusters). He describes a starting concept of 100-kilowatt satellites each hosting roughly 250 GPU-equivalent chips (at approximately 400 watts per chip), scalable to a million satellites. Elon has stated approximately 80% of Terafab chips will go to space; Phil believes the true long-term figure will be even higher.

4. **Tesla–SpaceX Merger Debate:** The hosts debate the merits of combining Tesla and SpaceX. Phil's core argument is not primarily economic but operational: managing two separate companies with deeply intertwined intellectual property (Tesla's AI chip design team building chips for both Tesla and SpaceX; Terafab; Optimus for off-planet manufacturing; Starlink benefiting Tesla's connectivity) is "dilutive" to Elon's focus and energy. Cern notes a critical economic nuance for Tesla shareholders: if Tesla doubles in value but SpaceX triples before a merger, Tesla shareholders have not improved their relative ownership stake in a combined entity — making the pre-merger stock price largely beside the point. Both hosts agree that a SpaceX IPO (described as being in a quiet period) is imminent and that pre-IPO hype is currently drawing narrative attention away from Tesla. Phil speculates that if a merger were perceived as likely, Tesla's stock price would begin to track a "pretend merger value," allowing Tesla shareholders to benefit from SpaceX's momentum.

5. **Legacy Auto's Inability to Catch Up:** Phil, drawing on his experience at Rivian (including attempted deals with General Motors — rejected by Rivian — and an executed partnership with Ford involving a skunk works team to reimagine vehicle architecture), argues there is no viable path for legacy automakers to catch up with Tesla's software-defined vehicle architecture. The core problem is that legacy OEMs are assemblers of supplier-built components, making it structurally impossible to rearchitect the vehicle from scratch without rejecting their entire supply chain model. He describes a BMW engineer spending a career extracting 1% more efficiency from a combustion engine per product cycle as emblematic of the cultural barrier.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD and Robotaxi Safety Posture:** Kenyon raises the question of whether Tesla is being too cautious in its robotaxi rollout given the 2028 election timeline. He concludes that the incidents observed so far have been minor, and he does not believe safety is the primary remaining obstacle. He suggests Tesla is working through "the long tail of operational related things" rather than fundamental safety barriers. He adds that he will not be seriously concerned unless, by the end of 2026, Tesla is still not fully rolling out robotaxi at scale.

2. **Etherloop Architecture in the Cybercab:** Phil provides a detailed technical breakdown of Tesla's Etherloop technology — a zonal Ethernet-based architecture that replaces traditional wiring harnesses, eliminating approximately 80–100 pounds of wiring per vehicle. In the Cybercab's "unbox" manufacturing process, major vehicle assemblies snap together, with wiring and power connections reduced to essentially two small connectors at each junction. The Cybercab uses a zonal architecture with compute surfaces embedded in each major assembly, connected by Ethernet and power rather than complex harnesses. Phil notes that a key Tesla innovation within Etherloop is time-division multiplexing, where every controller has a fixed address and a synchronized time slot on the wire, enhancing system reliability and safety. He traces the lineage: Cybertruck was the technology demonstration platform (including the move to 48V), and the Cybercab is the elegant realization of everything Cybertruck proved. Kenyon notes that other automakers — with the exception of Chinese manufacturers — have not meaningfully adopted these advances despite Tesla demonstrating them at scale.

## Robotaxi

1. **Robotaxi Deployment Strategy and Geography:** Kenyon suggests Tesla will likely roll out robotaxi more geographically broadly than the current city-by-city handful of vehicles implies. He specifically highlights the triangle of the three major Texas cities (Austin, Dallas, Houston) as a near-ideal initial expansion zone, covering both urban and suburban environments and representing a large share of the second-largest U.S. state economy. He also raises the broader potential for robotaxi infrastructure in home delivery and last-mile logistics, particularly when combined with Optimus for the final 50 feet of delivery.

2. **Fleet Management as the Software Monetization Layer:** Cern and Phil discuss how the operational software stack built for robotaxi — managing fleets and subfleets of robotic entities — is directly transferable to Tesla Semi logistics and Optimus warehouse deployment. Phil describes a future in which a Tesla Semi communicates its manifest to a cloud orchestration layer, and Optimus units at a loading dock know exactly what to unload and where to place it before the truck even arrives. Kenyon adds that this orchestration layer — which he compares favorably to Grok or a similar solution — represents a high-value, recurring subscription service that Tesla will first develop for internal use, then sell as a platform. Cern references "Tesla One" software as a potential unified platform tying all of these systems together.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus as the Enabler of Off-Planet Industrialization:** Phil argues that Optimus is the critical piece that makes lunar and Martian industrialization viable, providing generalized robotic labor in environments hostile to humans. He reiterates a point from a prior episode that Optimus units will outnumber humans on Mars or the Moon by orders of magnitude. He draws a direct line from Tesla's decade of manufacturing innovation — culminating in the Cybercab's unbox process — to the manufacturability and scalability of Optimus.

2. **Etherloop Principles Applied to Optimus:** Phil and Kenyon discuss how the internal wiring and network architecture developed for Cybercab will be applied to Optimus, with Ethernet connecting controlling extremities (e.g., a forearm controller articulating hand movements) using the same time-division synchronization approach. Phil clarifies that inter-bot communication will not use peer-to-peer Etherloop but rather a cloud-based fleet orchestration system, likely using in-building Wi-Fi and 5G/Starlink mobile for connectivity.

3. **Optimus Supply Chain Is Entirely New:** Phil notes a fundamental difference between Optimus and the automotive supply chain: virtually every Optimus component is new, meaning suppliers cannot simply pull a part from existing inventory. This makes scaling harder initially but also means Tesla carries no legacy architecture debt — a structural advantage over any competitor attempting to build humanoid robots using existing industrial supply chains.

## Market & Competition (AI Policy)

1. **The 2028 Election and the Risk of AI Backlash:** Kenyon's primary contribution centers on his concern that AI and data center construction are becoming a partisan political issue ahead of the 2028 U.S. election. He warns that fear-mongering narratives — including proposed bans on data center construction, restrictions on AI, and increased AI liability — could gain enough votes to become policy. He draws an analogy to "Dutch disease," where the AI industry is crowding out investment capital, talent, and attention from the broader economy in a way that, while not yet manifesting in labor displacement, is already distorting where money flows. He argues the industry must shift its messaging from cost-cutting and job displacement to demonstrable consumer benefits — reduced grocery costs, cheaper energy, lower cell bills via Starlink — to make AI politically safe before the election.

2. **Jensen Huang and the "Leadership Lacks Imagination" Thesis:** Cern recounts an interview in which CNBC's Jim Cramer asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang why companies were using AI to cut workers rather than to grow revenue. Huang's answer: "Leadership lacks imagination." Kenyon elaborates, arguing that companies announcing 10% workforce cuts due to AI represent either a business failure or a leadership failure — the correct approach is to use AI to grow the top line by more than 10% rather than shrink the bottom line by 10%.

Notable quotes and data:
- Phil: "I estimate that 90% or greater of all inference will basically be delivered to Earth via space. Period. End of story."
- Phil: "One Terafab is not good enough."
- Jensen Huang (via Cern): "Leadership lacks imagination. They don't know how to grow their businesses with this beautiful productivity tool."
- Kenyon: "If Tesla doubles and SpaceX triples, then Tesla shareholders haven't gained anything vis-à-vis their share in a combined company."
- Phil on the Cybercab unbox process: "CyberCab has developed with the unbox process... when they snap together at the wiring and power, it's literally like two little connects that connect together at this point."
- Kenyon on legacy auto: "They should have bought a Cybertruck, torn it down themselves, looked at how much the tech has changed, and after they changed their underwear, they can get to — all right, we're going to change a lot of things about our business."
- Kenyon on AI adoption: "AI's adoption is nowhere near as strong as many members of the industry would like to think."
- Colossus 1: 220,000 Nvidia GPUs (H100s, H200s, GB200s)
- AI compute demand growth rate: ~3.4x per year
- Current global AI compute capacity: ~30 gigawatts (Phil's estimate; Elon's chart uses ~20 GW)
- Time to 1 terawatt at 3.4x/yr with efficiency gains: ~4.3 years
- Time to 100 terawatts at 3.4x/yr with efficiency gains: ~10 years
- Terafab minimum facility size: ~100 million square feet (five Pentagons or two Central Parks)
- Elon's stated target: ~80% of Terafab chips destined for space
- Satellite compute concept: 100-kilowatt satellites, ~250 GPU-equivalent chips each, ~400 watts per chip
- Etherloop wiring reduction: approximately 80–100 pounds of wiring eliminated per vehicle

articles.title: Tesla Cybertruck PCS2 Board Failure Breakdown
articles.body:
This video is a collaborative discussion between Brian (FutureAzA) and Craig (Red Review) breaking down a hardware failure affecting Cybertruck owners — specifically the PCS2 board, which manages AC-to-DC power conversion for home charging, Supercharging, and PowerShare (vehicle-to-home). The hosts explain the nature of the failure, how to detect it, warranty coverage, and Tesla's response to affected owners.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **What the PCS2 Board Does:** The PCS2 (Power Conversion System 2) board is described as the nerve center for electricity flow in the Cybertruck. It handles home AC charging (converting AC to DC for the high-voltage battery), DC Supercharging, and PowerShare/vehicle-to-home back-feeding functionality. Craig first discovered the issue when attempting to film a PowerShare demonstration and the truck failed to back-feed the home, followed shortly by the charging rate dropping to 24 amps.

2. **Nature of the Failure — Redundancy Masks the Problem:** The PCS2 board has two AC-side components for redundancy. When one fails, the charge rate drops from the normal 48 amps (or 40 amps depending on the home electrical system) down to 24 amps — but no driver-facing error notification is generated because partial functionality remains. The vehicle only throws a front-facing alert when the second AC component also fails and AC charging is lost entirely. This design means many owners are unaware they have a fault.

3. **How to Detect the Failure:** Owners can check the Tesla app to see if their Cybertruck is capped at 24 amps during home charging. A more definitive check is to enter service mode on the vehicle, where error codes PCS_049 or PCS_048 will appear if the board has failed. Craig notes he has tutorial videos on how to access service mode on his Red Review channel. He also cautions that owners who primarily use Supercharging and rarely plug into AC at home may have a failed board without knowing it, since the triggering event (AC charging) may not have occurred.

4. **Warranty Coverage — A Split Situation:** The PCS2 failure is covered under the basic vehicle warranty, which Craig states is 4 years / 50,000 miles. However, many high-mileage Cybertruck owners have already exceeded 50,000 miles. The 2026 Cybertruck is covered under a new warranty Tesla is offering called the "high-priced propulsion related parts ZEV limited warranty" — a 7-year / 70,000-mile warranty — but this is not retroactive and does not apply to 2024 or 2025 trucks.

5. **Out-of-Warranty Costs and Tesla's Goodwill Response:** For owners out of warranty, replacement costs initially ranged from $4,000 to $7,000 depending on labor time, as Tesla gave no clear guidance to service centers. More recently, as a goodwill gesture, Tesla has been charging approximately $1,000 — roughly the cost of parts — for out-of-warranty repairs, though Craig describes this as "hit or miss." Tesla has a broader reputation for goodwill repairs; Craig cites an example of a Model S owner whose battery was replaced when they were only a few hundred miles beyond warranty.

6. **Parts Shortage and Free Supercharging Workaround:** Tesla service centers across the country have run out of replacement PCS2 boards, leading to wait times of 4 to 6 weeks, and in some cases up to 8 weeks or roughly 2.5 months. Owners have reported being as far back as 13th in line for the repair. In response, when an owner files a service ticket through the app for a verified PCS issue, Tesla in some cases sends an over-the-air update via cellular — without requiring Wi-Fi — that enables free Supercharging for the affected truck until the repair date. This is not free lifetime Supercharging but is intended to allow owners to continue charging their vehicles while waiting for parts.

7. **Distinction from Inverter Recall and Wiring Harness Service Bulletin:** Craig clarifies that this issue is entirely separate from a prior drive inverter recall that affected many Cybertrucks. The PCS2 is a power conversion system, not a drive inverter. There is also a separate service bulletin for a wiring harness that connects the PCS board to the rest of the system; Tesla replaces both the harness and the board together when performing the PCS repair. The wiring harness was initially thought to be the root cause, but the board itself is the primary issue.

8. **Scope of Affected Vehicles and Call for a Recall:** Craig has been tracking VIN numbers of affected trucks and reports failures going back to the earliest VIN numbers. The highest VIN number he has observed with the issue is approximately 77,000, with the majority of failures concentrated in the VIN 25,000–35,000 range. He has observed at least three different versions of the PCS2 board, with at least two of them consistently failing. He argues that a formal recall is warranted given the scale of affected vehicles, and notes Tesla has been tight-lipped about the issue — apparently reluctant to invite further negative press after the Cybertruck's already turbulent public reception. Whether 2026 Cybertrucks are at risk remains uncertain, as the root cause of the board flaw has not been publicly identified.

9. **Community Awareness vs. Sudden Surge:** Craig pushes back against social media speculation that a recent software update caused a sudden wave of failures. He argues the failures have been a dormant, ongoing issue — the apparent spike in reports is driven by growing community awareness following his earlier video, which prompted many owners to check their apps and service mode for the first time. Munro Live previously conducted a teardown that included the PCS2 board.

Notable quotes and data:
- Normal home charge rate: 48 amps (or 40 amps depending on home electrical system); failure causes a drop to 24 amps
- Error codes to look for in service mode: PCS_049 or PCS_048
- Basic warranty: 4 years / 50,000 miles (2024–2025 Cybertrucks)
- New ZEV limited warranty: 7 years / 70,000 miles (2026 Cybertruck and beyond, non-retroactive)
- Out-of-warranty repair cost: initially $4,000–$7,000; now approximately $1,000 as a goodwill gesture
- Parts wait time: 4–8 weeks, up to approximately 2.5 months
- Highest affected VIN observed: approximately 77,000; majority of failures between VIN 25,000–35,000
- At least 3 versions of the PCS2 board identified; at least 2 have consistently failed
- Craig: "I think we can all agree at this point there's so many vehicles affected that there needs to be a recall on this part."

articles.title: How Anthropic and OpenAI PLAN To Destroy MILLIONS OF JOBS By Xmas
articles.body:
Jo Bhakdi argues that two newly announced joint ventures — one by Anthropic and one by OpenAI, each partnering with major private equity and asset management firms — represent a structural turning point in the deployment of AI as a mass labor replacement technology. His core thesis is that the primary barrier to widespread job displacement is no longer capability (which he claims is already sufficient to replace the majority of white-collar workers) but distribution, and that these deals solve the distribution problem by routing AI deployment through private equity firms that collectively own or control vast numbers of mid-sized companies. He predicts a tsunami of job destruction arriving by 2027, with early signals potentially appearing by January of that year.

## Market & Competition

1. **Anthropic's joint venture with private equity:** On Monday (relative to the video's publish date), Anthropic announced a joint venture focused on deploying enterprise AI services. Founding partners include Blackstone, Helman and Friedman, and Goldman Sachs. Additional backers include Apollo Global Management, General Atlantic, GIC, Leonard Green, and Sequoia Capital. The Wall Street Journal reported the venture is valued at $1.5 billion, with $300 million committed each from Anthropic, Blackstone, and Helman and Friedman.

2. **OpenAI's parallel "Development Company" venture:** Hours after the Anthropic announcement, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI is raising funds for a new venture called "the Development Company," targeting $4 billion from 19 investors against a $10 billion valuation. Named investors include TPG, Brookfield Asset Management, and Bain Capital. Bhakdi notes there is no apparent overlap between OpenAI's and Anthropic's respective investor groups, suggesting the two ventures together cover a broad swath of the private equity market.

3. **The distribution logic: private equity as the deployment channel:** Bhakdi's central structural argument is that the critical missing link between AI capability and mass enterprise deployment is mid-sized companies, which represent the majority of the economy in his view. Large enterprises (Fortune 500) are already being served directly by AI labs and consulting firms like Accenture, McKinsey, and BCG. Small businesses are too fragmented to matter at scale. Mid-sized companies, however, are heavily owned or controlled by private equity — making private equity the ideal distribution partner. These ventures give Anthropic and OpenAI preferred sales access to the portfolio companies of their PE partners, while the PE firms gain early access to AI tools they can use to cut labor costs and drive margins.

4. **"Forward deployed engineers" as the implementation model:** Bhakdi notes that Anthropic's announcement explicitly references the "forward deployed engineer" model popularized by Palantir, in which AI consultants embed with a company's existing teams (clinicians, IT staff, etc.) to build tools that fit into existing workflows. He interprets this as a sanitized description of a process that ultimately results in large-scale workforce reduction.

5. **AI funding at scale:** Bhakdi cites OpenAI announcing $122 billion in new funding at the end of March 2026 against a valuation of $852 billion. He also cites a TechCrunch report that Anthropic is in the final stages of a funding round seeking $50 billion in new funding against a $900 billion valuation. He additionally references Anthropic doing compute deals with SpaceX (Colossus One), Google (TPU access), and Amazon.

6. **Bhakdi's labor displacement thesis:** Bhakdi claims that as of the video's publish date, AI agents are already capable of replacing over 50% of white-collar and administrative jobs, and that within 8–12 weeks this figure will rise to approximately 80%. He defines the affected category broadly: any job involving sitting at a screen, typing, and emailing — spanning healthcare administration, law firms, accounting firms, insurance companies, hospital management, and government administration. He frames the technology barrier as fully solved and the remaining challenge as purely one of deployment and distribution.

7. **2027 job destruction prediction:** Bhakdi states he made this prediction roughly 16 months prior to the video and reaffirms it: 2027 will be the year a "tsunami" of job destruction becomes visible to the public, with the inflection potentially arriving as early as January 2027 or as late as July–August 2027. He explicitly discounts official U.S. unemployment statistics as structurally incapable of capturing this displacement, arguing that the survey methodology (which counts any paid work, including informal gigs) means measured unemployment cannot rise meaningfully even in a scenario of mass job loss.

8. **Economic decoupling thesis:** Bhakdi predicts that mass job destruction will not trigger a traditional recession. Instead, he argues the economy will increasingly decouple — with companies and shareholders capturing enormous value from AI productivity while a large share of the population loses income. He frames this as a theoretical possibility within AGI-era economics where aggregate output growth does not require broad consumer purchasing power.

Notable quotes and data:
- Anthropic reportedly growing at 80x (8,000%) versus an expected 10x (1,000%)
- Anthropic joint venture valued at $1.5 billion; $300 million committed each from Anthropic, Blackstone, and Helman and Friedman
- OpenAI's "Development Company" raising $4 billion from 19 investors at a $10 billion valuation
- OpenAI: $122 billion in new funding (end of March 2026), valuation $852 billion
- Anthropic: seeking $50 billion in new funding, valuation $900 billion (per TechCrunch)
- Bhakdi: "We have already reached mostly across the board AGI economic AGI meaning AGI that can replace people on mass"
- Bhakdi: "I think we are right there now that we can replace over 50% of white collar jobs probably as of today and in 8 or 12 weeks it will be 80%"
- Bhakdi: "2027 will be the year where the storm arrives and panic will break out in the economy"
- Bhakdi: "The biggest gaslighting operation in history literally is that these people tell the rest of the world AI is going to create more jobs than it destroys"
- The global labor market the video targets is described as a "$25 trillion labor market"

articles.title: Daily X Summary (2026-05-09)
articles.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts were dominated by Tesla product news — new exterior color launches for Model Y and Model 3, the Model S/X Signature delivery event announcement, and a website redesign spotlighting FSD mileage — alongside a regulatory clarification from Denmark pushing back on a Reuters FSD criticism story. The overall signal is mildly bullish: no major robotaxi or Optimus updates, but FSD brand-building and product momentum are intact.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **New Blue Paint Colors Launched for Model 3 and Model Y:** Tesla introduced two new exterior blue paint options in the U.S., replacing Deep Blue Metallic (which has been discontinued). Marine Blue is now available on the Model Y Premium and Model 3 Premium for $1,000. Frost Blue is available on the Model Y Performance and Model 3 Performance. This was among the highest-engagement content of the day, with the main announcement post drawing 4.3K likes and 307 reposts, suggesting meaningful consumer interest. A Model 3 Performance in Frost Blue was also spotted in the wild shortly after launch.

2. **Model S/X Signature Production Underway — Delivery Event Next Tuesday:** Tesla confirmed that production of the Model S/X Signature edition is now well underway, with the delivery event scheduled for Tuesday, May 12, 2026. This is a notable near-term catalyst for Tesla's flagship sedan and SUV lineup.

3. **Tesla Website Redesign Spotlights FSD Mile Counter:** Tesla redesigned its homepage to prominently feature the live FSD (Supervised) cumulative mile counter alongside owner-recorded FSD videos. With 4.3K likes on the post, this was the day's most-engaged item. The move signals Tesla's intent to use real-world FSD data as a marketing and credibility tool, reinforcing the autonomous driving narrative directly to consumers and prospective buyers.

4. **Danish Regulator Pushes Back on Reuters FSD Criticism Report:** The Danish Road Traffic Authority (DRTA) issued an official statement clarifying that it has "at no time expressed either positive or negative opinions about the approval of Tesla's FSD" — directly contradicting a recent Reuters report suggesting the DRTA had criticized FSD. This is a meaningful regulatory clarification that removes what could have been a bearish FSD narrative in Europe, at least as it pertains to Denmark.

5. **Honda Delays Five Next-Gen Models Due to EV Losses of $15.7B:** Honda is reportedly delaying five vehicle redesigns — including the Odyssey, Accord, and HR-V — by multiple years (several pushed to 2030), citing losses of $15.7 billion on its EV program. This underscores the competitive struggles of legacy automakers in the EV transition and reinforces Tesla's structural advantages in the space.

6. **SpaceX/Tesla Merger Speculation — Merritt Urges Caution:** Merritt addressed circulating speculation about a potential SpaceX/Tesla merger, emphasizing it is "purely speculation" with no confirmed timeline, and noting that even if proposed, it would require more than 50% of all outstanding Tesla shares to vote yes. No new facts were presented; this is primarily a signal-dampening post for investors tracking the merger narrative.

7. **Jay Leno Praises Tesla Semi; Grok Launches on Apple CarPlay:** Jay Leno described the Tesla Semi as impressive in a new interview, noting its acceleration, range of 500 miles, and 60% recharge in 30 minutes. Separately, Grok officially launched on Apple CarPlay — a distribution milestone for xAI, with potential downstream relevance for Tesla's AI ecosystem positioning, though no Tesla-specific integration details were provided.

---

## Signal Strength: **Mildly Bullish** — FSD brand-building via the homepage redesign, the Model S/X Signature delivery event on the horizon, and the Danish regulatory clarification removing a potential FSD headwind are all modest positive signals, though the day lacked major robotaxi, Optimus, or financial catalysts.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Breaking Down Tesla’s Robotaxi Ramp Scenarios
articles.body:
This video features host Herbert alongside retail analysts Cern Basher and Brian Wang (Next Big Future) breaking down near-term Tesla robotaxi ramp scenarios for 2026.
