This runs in parallel with the 2026 Model Y becoming the first vehicle to pass all eight NHTSA NCAP ADAS evaluations, including four new criteria added for MY2026.

- **Consumer unsupervised FSD targeted Q4 2026 or Q1 2027.** Elon on the Q1 earnings call suggested FSD version 15 — described as featuring a model ~10x larger than the current small model — may be needed before truly scaled unsupervised consumer deployment.

## Robotaxi

- **Cybercab confirmed FMVSS-compliant from day one** per Tesla's head of engineering. This eliminates the NHTSA 2,500-vehicle annual exemption cap as a ceiling risk for the purpose-built driverless vehicle — production ramp at Giga Texas is now constrained by manufacturing, not regulation. Production began in April 2026 at approximately 20 units/day, with ~40–50 units documented near the factory.

- **Unsupervised expansion: Dallas and Houston are 100% driverless.** Both cities launched directly into unsupervised service with no prior ride-hail supervised phase. Austin's remaining supervised vehicles are expected to convert within approximately 10 days. Per Brian Wang, the Texas triangle could reach 300+ unsupervised vehicles by end of June. The operational binding constraint is now software orchestration (pickup/drop-off behavior, remote ops frequency) rather than safety performance.

- **Paid robotaxi miles tripled quarter-over-quarter**: ~1.7 million miles in Q1 2026, up from ~610,000 in Q4 2025. Farzad projects Q2 could exceed 4 million and Q3 could approach 10 million paid miles.

- **Five additional city launches committed for H1 2026:** Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, and Las Vegas. Field response specialist hiring is active in Las Vegas and Doral, Florida — the same pre-launch role Tesla staffed ahead of Dallas and Houston. California unsupervised service is unlikely before 2027; Tesla has not applied for a CPUC AV permit and faces a 6–9 month processing window once it does.

- **California AV traffic law takes effect July 1, 2026.** Law enforcement may issue citations directly to AV manufacturers; accumulated violations can restrict or suspend driverless operating licenses. A separate 50,000-mile pre-commercial safety test is required.

## Optimus

- **Model S/X production discontinued; Fremont line converting to Optimus manufacturing.** The factory conversion is a deliberate reallocation of production capacity — a formal signal Tesla has transitioned its strategic identity from car company to physical AI company. Fremont targets 1M units/year; Giga Texas targets 10M units/year. V3 production is set to begin summer 2026; 2027–2028 targets are 100,000–300,000 units across both facilities at a cost target of $20,000–$25,000/unit.

- **Optimus reveal expected within 90 days per Bhakdi**, who describes it as a major soft catalyst. Tesla has maintained a communications blackout on Optimus citing competitive intelligence concerns — Elon cited frame-by-frame copying by rivals. A "paused production line to retool for faster assembly" news item was read as active development signal, not a setback.

- **Optimus supply chain does not yet exist.** Elon on the Q3 earnings call: "With humanoid robots, there is no supply chain." Tesla is building actuators, sensors, hands, and forearms internally; Elon described the hand and forearm as "more difficult than the entire rest of the robot." The Etherloop (Ethernet-based time-division multiplexing developed for Cybercab) will apply directly to Optimus limb control architecture.

- **AI5 chip is a hard prerequisite for meaningful Optimus production**, per Phil Biceel. AI5 delivers 2,500 TOPS and 144 GB memory — up to 40x system-level improvement over HW4. Elon's roadmap: AI4 achieves safety far beyond human levels; AI5 makes cars "almost perfect"; AI6 targets Optimus and data centers.

## Tesla Semi

- **High-volume production line is live at Giga Nevada.** The first unit came off the dedicated facility on April 29; the 1.7 million sq ft Sparks plant is designed for 50,000 trucks/year. Analyst 2026 delivery estimates range from 5,000 to 15,000 units. CARB regulatory filings confirmed specs: 822 kWh (Long Range) and 548 kWh (Standard Range), both NCMA/4680 chemistry; LR achieves 500 miles at 82,000 lb GCW.

- **430+ units ordered at ACT Expo.** Watt EV: 370 units (~$100M), first 50 in 2026. Big F Transport: 40 units after a single demo. NA Container Freight Lines: 20 units, first operating 2027. Semi pricing is 25–35% below competing electric Class 8 trucks ($400K–$500K range); official pricing confirmed at $290,000 LR / $260,000 SR.

- **New charging suite removes depot infrastructure barrier.** Mega Charger: 1.2 MW, 60% in 30 minutes, ~$188,000 per two-post setup, 66 planned locations across 15 states. Base Charger: 125 kW, 60% overnight, ~$40,000 installed for two units, daisy-chainable on a single breaker. Jordan (The Limiting Factor): "I'm no longer concerned that the charging network will be the rate-limiting factor for semi production."

- **Incentives make economics compelling.** Washington State WEZI program: up to $175,000 rebate, reducing the LR Semi to ~$115,000. California HVIP: $120,000–$330,000 per truck with $100M+ available. Tesla Semi captured 965 of 1,067 California clean truck voucher applications between January 2025 and February 2026.

## Energy

- **Tesla loses ~$400M/year 45X tax credit in 2026.** IRS Notice 2026-15 introduced Prohibited Foreign Entity rules; Tesla's use of imported CATL cells at the Lathrop Megapack factory immediately exceeds the PFE allowance, eliminating the $10/kWh module assembly credit. Nevada LFP factory expected to restore eligibility — but ~99% of LFP cathode supply is China-based, creating a substantial compliance hurdle even after the domestic line opens.

- **Q1 2026 energy gross margin of ~39% included non-recurring tariff benefits.** Management flagged the record margin reflected "tariff recognitions"; Benchmark's Iola Hughes describes the most likely explanation as an overpayment during tariff turbulence — not a recurring benefit.

- **Giga-scale project pipeline accelerating sharply.** Q1 2026 saw 11 projects over 1 GWh come online; the full-year 2026 pipeline stands at 122 projects, versus 50 in all of 2025 and 17 in 2024. Australia became the second-largest global market with over 8 GWh installed in Q1 alone. Ex-China markets grew ~112% year-over-year in Q1.

- **Chinese competition intensifying.** BYD took top global energy storage shipment rank in 2025. Chinese competitors deploy systems in China at under $100/kWh versus Tesla's ~$190–$200/kWh — a structural gap in unprotected markets. Hughes: "Tesla's potentially lagging some of what we see from the Chinese players." Powin, previously the third-largest US integrator, declared bankruptcy.

## Electric Vehicles

- **Record April China deliveries: 79,478 units, +36% YoY** — best April ever for China operations. South Korea posted a record 13,190 units, outselling BMW and Mercedes combined. Germany posted its best April ever. Model Y confirmed as the world's best-selling EV in March 2026; Tesla passed BYD in Q1 2026 overall.

- **Canada Model 3 RWD (Giga Shanghai) priced at ~CAD $39,990 (~USD $29,000)** — enabled by Canada's quota mechanism allowing ~49,000 Chinese-built vehicles at 6% import tariff in 2026. Delivery estimates slipped from June to October on strong order intake; Chinese EV brands have no Canadian sales infrastructure to compete for the quota this year.

- **New five-tier Model Y lease starting at $459/month.** Tesla reclaims vehicles at lease-end (~30,000–40,000 miles) and redeploys them into the robotaxi fleet — a model generating margin twice regardless of robotaxi readiness at return. Model Y L mule spotted in the US with an unveil possible within 60 days; deliveries projected ~October 2026 at ~$55,000–$60,000.

- **Cybertruck Frost Blue and Model 3 Marine Blue launched.** Model S/X Signature Edition delivery event — originally scheduled May 12 — postponed with no new date announced.

## Financials

- **Tesla guided to negative free cash flow for the remainder of 2026.** Capital commitments include Terafab ($55B upfront, $119B total), xAI's Colossus 2 supercomputer ($18B in chips), and the Optimus supply chain buildout. Terafab is jointly owned by Tesla, xAI, SpaceX, and Intel; a Grimes County public hearing is scheduled for early June 2026.

- **FSD Europe perpetual purchase ends May 21, 2026** across UK, Germany, France, Italy, Belgium, Switzerland, Denmark, and other markets — shifting to subscription-only and converting one-time revenue to recurring ARR.

- **Bhakdi DCF: ~$600/share intrinsic value for 2026**, explicitly conditioned on 10,000 robotaxis deployed by year-end. He pushed original model timelines back 12–18 months from earlier projections. Stock up ~11% on the week, closing above its 200-day moving average (~$402–$404).

## Market & Competition

- **xAI dissolved; folded into SpaceX as "SpaceX AI."** Colossus 1 (~220,000 Nvidia GPUs, ~300 MW) leased to Anthropic for inference; Colossus 2 remains dedicated to Grok training. Larry Goldberg estimates the combined SpaceX entity could show ~$20B in profit in its first year. SpaceX–Tesla merger speculation is at ~70% on Polymarket; Sawyer Merritt characterized it as "purely speculation" with no confirmed timeline.

- **Goldman Sachs: autonomous trucking is a $560B market by 2035**, larger than the $415B robotaxi market. Autonomous truck cost per mile projected to fall from $8.56 today to ~$2.30 by 2035, with crossover versus human-driven trucks around 2028.

- **Waymo projected to lose ~$5B in 2026 — roughly $100 per ride** across ~52 million annual rides. Morgan Stanley pegs Tesla's robotaxi cost per mile at ~$0.81 versus Waymo's ~$1.36–$1.43. Multiple analysts argue Waymo must abandon its LiDAR/HD-mapping architecture entirely to reach viable unit economics.

- **BYD April 2026 passenger EV sales: ~314,000 units, -15.7% YoY** — eighth consecutive month of domestic China decline. Domestic rivals Xiaomi, Leap Motor, and Zeekr posted new monthly highs.

## Bear Case of the Week

- **FSD 14.3.2 navigation confirmed regressing.** A real-world review found the vehicle looping a bank parking lot entrance three times — behavior a passenger confirmed "didn't used to" happen. The reviewer's verdict: "The navigation has absolutely gotten worse." This is a concrete regression, not a framing complaint, in a build that has reached ~50–60% of the HW4 consumer fleet.

- **NHTSA Engineering Analysis covers ~3.2 million Tesla vehicles**, the stage typically preceding a recall, specifically focused on FSD's camera system failing in sun glare and fog and potential underreporting of related crashes. Running concurrently with the positive NCAP result — the duality is a material regulatory risk.

- **4680 "8L" pack quietly substituted in European Model Y without disclosure.** The swap cuts WLTP range 52 km (−8%) versus the LG 5M pack it replaced in the same Premium Long Range RWD trim, with slower charging (155 kW curve already declining at 31% SOC, ranked worst in the current EU lineup). Consumer backlash triggered cancellations in France and Norway. South Korean cathode supplier L&F confirmed the scale of 4680 commercial disappointment: a $2.9B Tesla contract written down to $7,386 (−99.9%), citing "change in supply quantity."

- **Cybertruck PCS2 board failures widespread.** Failures documented across a wide VIN range with concentration between VINs 25,000–35,000; the board manages AC charging, Supercharging, and PowerShare. Charge rate drops silently from 48A to 24A with no driver alert. Out-of-warranty repair cost was $4,000–$7,000 before Tesla offered a goodwill rate of ~$1,000; parts are backordered 4–8 weeks. Per Craig (Red Review): "There needs to be a recall on this part." 2024–2025 trucks are covered only by the standard 4-year/50,000-mile warranty, which many high-mileage owners have already exceeded.

- **45X credit loss of ~$400M/year is effective immediately in 2026** due to PFE rules triggered by CATL cell imports at Lathrop. The Nevada LFP line that could restore eligibility faces a further obstacle: ~99% of LFP cathode supply is currently China-based, and cathode accounts for ~40% of cell cost — meaning domestic manufacturing alone does not resolve the compliance gap.

- **Tesla guided to negative free cash flow for the remainder of 2026** while simultaneously absorbing Terafab ($55B upfront), Colossus 2 ($18B in chips), and the Optimus supply chain — with Q1's record energy gross margin

articles.title: Analysts Think Tesla Optimus Is Basically Free! Here's Why
articles.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel covers a broad update on Tesla's investment thesis, anchored by a new Piper Sandler analyst note arguing that at $400/share, investors are getting Optimus "for free." Host Herbert is joined by Jeff Lutz, a multi-decade supply chain executive and CEO of a high-tech manufacturing consulting firm, to discuss analyst forecasts, technical momentum in the stock, Optimus supply chain signals, Cortex 2 progress, and Cathie Wood's robotaxi and Starlink commentary.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Piper Sandler: Optimus Valued at Zero in Current Stock Price:** Piper Sandler analyst Alexander Potter published a note arguing that at $400 per share, Tesla investors are receiving Optimus for free — meaning the market has not yet assigned any value to the humanoid robot business. Potter's 17-business-line model forecasting $1.8 trillion in annual revenue by 2045 does not include Optimus at all, which the hosts note is a deliberate omission because including it would produce numbers too large for most investors to accept. Jeff Lutz draws a parallel to how Tesla's energy business and FSD were similarly excluded from analyst models until they became undeniable, suggesting Optimus will follow the same pattern and trigger another valuation re-rating when analysts are eventually forced to add it.

2. **China Supply Chain Reports: First Bulk Purchase Orders Placed:** According to chatter from China's humanoid robot supply chain, Tesla has officially placed its first bulk purchase order with humanoid robot component suppliers. The reports characterize this as a move beyond sample testing and validation into small-scale mass production and delivery, involving actual payments, and laying the groundwork for mass production in July and August 2026. Jeff Lutz contextualized this by noting that if Tesla is targeting a July–August production start as stated on its earnings call, mechanical and electromechanical suppliers would have had to begin production in April, and silicon and other externally sourced components would require purchase orders even earlier. He described the convergence of Tesla's public guidance and supplier intelligence as corroborating evidence that the timeline is credible.

3. **Optimus Factory and Cortex 2 Investment Signals:** Joe Tegtmeyer's video footage of Giga Texas shows Cortex 2 making significant progress, with roughly 50% of the facility already operational. Installed Megapacks, chiller system assembly, and superstructure work are all visible. The hosts note that just north of the Cortex 2 facility is the future site of Tesla's planned Optimus factory, described as targeting a production capacity of 10 million units per year. Elon Musk also toured Intel's Oregon fab, interpreted as a sign that Terafab development is moving quickly. The hosts argue that the scale of capital being deployed across Cortex 2, Terafab, and Optimus supply chain orders is itself evidence of Tesla's commitment to mass-scale humanoid robot production.

4. **AND-Gate Framework for Bot Success:** Jeff Lutz articulated a framework for evaluating which humanoid robot companies will succeed: product, AI/engineering capability, and manufacturing must all be present — if any one is absent, the result is zero. He argued Tesla is at "one" on all three dimensions, making it one of very few companies with a realistic path to mass production. He noted that of the roughly ten humanoid robots Jensen Huang displayed on stage at Nvidia, perhaps only one will ship in volume. He also flagged that a wave of Chinese bots is coming, but questioned whether any will achieve Tesla's combination of proven AI, manufacturing scale, and commercial viability.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **FSD Licensing and Hardware Sales Included in Piper Sandler Model:** Piper Sandler's 17-business model includes FSD software licensing and FSD hardware sales to other automakers, with both projected to begin around 2032. Jeff Lutz suggested the licensing opportunity could be accelerated by two factors: first, competitive pressure as automakers see FSD becoming a purchase decision driver and risk losing sales without it; second, potential regulatory mandates, given that FSD is claimed to be approximately eight to nine times safer than human driving, which could motivate Congress or the executive branch to push for broad adoption to reduce the approximately 43,000 annual US traffic deaths.

2. **Coast-to-Coast FSD Drive as Competitive Benchmark:** The hosts referenced Tesla's recent coast-to-coast drive from Los Angeles to New York City completed without intervention as a demonstration of FSD's lead. Jeff Lutz framed the competitive question simply: no other vehicle available at any US dealership can be given an address and autonomously navigate there. He noted no competitor — domestic or foreign — has a credible near-term timeline to replicate this, citing it as the second recent example (after profitable global EV manufacturing) of Tesla building a lead that no one has closed.

## Robotaxi
1. **Unsupervised Robotaxi Fleet Growth Cited as Market Signal:** Jeff Lutz noted that Tesla has grown from approximately two cars operating autonomously to nearly 40 in the past month or two, characterizing this as a meaningful inflection — sufficient to offer real public service and signal that the robotaxi program is past the "will it work?" binary question. Per RobotaxiTracker.com, the unsupervised (driverless) fleet stands at 39 vehicles as of 2026-05-09, with the broader active robotaxi fleet at 668 vehicles across Bay Area, Austin, Dallas, and Houston. The hosts described Cybercab production startup and Q2 2026 milestones as significant near-term catalysts.

2. **Cathie Wood: Robotaxi Cost Structure at 25 Cents Per Mile vs. Waymo at 50% Higher:** Cathie Wood of ARK Invest was featured in two interview clips arguing that Tesla's vertical integration will produce the lowest robotaxi cost structure by far. She stated Tesla's costs will drop to $0.25 per mile as robotaxis scale, compared to Waymo's cost structure which ARK estimates will remain approximately 50% higher than Tesla's in 2030 due to Waymo's dependence on third-party automakers and supply chain partners. She framed the current pricing umbrella as $3+ per mile using Uber as a reference. Jeff Lutz argued 50% may actually be conservative in Tesla's favor, drawing an analogy to a car manufacturer who can produce at $20,000 what competitors cannot build below $30,000 — effectively locking them out of an entire market segment.

3. **Piper Sandler Robotaxi Revenue Projections — Conservative and Delayed:** Piper Sandler's model does not show robotaxi becoming a meaningful business until 2028, with significant revenue ramp occurring from 2031 onward and accelerating sharply through 2033. The hosts characterized these projections as very conservative relative to Tesla's own pace of deployment, consistent with how Morgan Stanley has also modeled a delayed ramp. They argued analysts are constrained by the information available and will revise upward as Tesla executes faster than modeled.

## Financials
1. **Piper Sandler 17-Business Model: $1.8 Trillion Revenue by 2045:** Alexander Potter of Piper Sandler projects Tesla approaching $1.8 trillion in annual revenue by 2045 across 17 discrete business lines, implying a market capitalization on the order of $17 trillion if a 10x revenue multiple is applied. The model includes FSD licensing, FSD hardware sales to automakers, robotaxi, supercharging, insurance, subscriptions, and vehicle sales, among others. Vehicle sales are projected to be essentially flat or declining as a share of revenue over time, at approximately $48–$50 billion by 2045, illustrating the degree to which software and services dominate the long-term model. Optimus is entirely excluded.

2. **Tesla Energy Miss in Q1 and Potential Q2 Recovery:** Jeff Lutz flagged that Tesla missed consensus estimates for its energy business in Q1 2026 by approximately 38–39%, a miss that would have caused severe market reactions for other energy storage companies. He suggested this sets up a potentially large Q2 rebound in energy, alongside what appears to be recovering auto sales based on April momentum.

3. **Cathie Wood: Starlink Revenue Potential of $160 Billion:** Cathie Wood's ARK Invest research estimates that Starlink alone could generate $160 billion in revenue for SpaceX. ARK's SpaceX position represents a mid-teens percentage of its private fund; Wood indicated ARK would likely reduce this position as SpaceX moves toward a public listing, since a public vehicle would offer a less expensive access point. The hosts noted this figure is not included in any Tesla valuation but is mentioned in the context of Elon Musk's broader infrastructure buildout.

## Market & Competition
1. **Tesla's Competitive Moat: Two Proven Examples, Robotaxi as the Third:** Jeff Lutz structured the competitive argument around two recent precedents where Tesla built a durable lead that no competitor has closed: profitable global EV manufacturing, and Full Self-Driving capability. He argued Chinese EV manufacturers cannot demonstrate profitability even in their domestic market and cannot establish profitable global operations. He predicted robotaxi will become the third such example — other systems will exist and operate but will be limited in scale, unable to reach Tesla's deployment volume. He named Xpeng as a potential second-place competitor in China, possibly one to two years behind Tesla, with Xiaomi also flagged as a credible EV contender following a highly automated design and production model.

2. **Colossus 1 Leased to Anthropic — Framed as Strategic, Not a Concern:** The hosts addressed criticism on X regarding Tesla/xAI leasing Colossus 1 to Anthropic. Jeff Lutz argued this reflects the reality of building compute capacity at speed — timing will not be perfect, and excess capacity will exist at certain points. He framed it as a revenue opportunity for xAI in the near term, with Tesla able to reclaim the capacity when needed for Cybercab fleet inference and Optimus training at scale. He noted Elon Musk is simultaneously building Colossus 1, Colossus 2, Cortex 1, Cortex 2, Macrohard, and Dojo, and suggested the possibility of an "Elon Web Services" offering — terrestrial and space-based compute available to third parties — which he said is not in any current valuation model.

Notable quotes and data:
- Piper Sandler price target: $500/share; Optimus described as "free" at $400/share
- Piper Sandler 2045 revenue forecast: ~$1.8 trillion across 17 business lines; implied valuation ~$17 trillion at 10x revenue
- FSD licensing and hardware sales to automakers projected to begin ~2032 per Piper Sandler
- Robotaxi meaningful revenue in Piper Sandler model: begins ~2028, accelerates sharply 2031–2033
- Vehicle sales in Piper Sandler 2045 model: ~$48–50 billion (flat/declining share)
- ARK Invest robotaxi cost estimate: $0.25/mile for Tesla at scale; Waymo estimated 50% higher cost than Tesla in 2030
- Current robotaxi pricing reference: ~$3+/mile (Uber umbrella per ARK)
- Active robotaxi fleet: 668 per RobotaxiTracker.com; unsupervised fleet: ~39 per RobotaxiTracker.com
- Tesla Q1 2026 energy business miss vs. consensus: ~38–39%
- Cortex 2: approximately 50% operational as of video date
- Planned Optimus factory capacity: 10 million units per year
- Optimus mass production start: July–August 2026 per Tesla earnings guidance
- ARK Starlink revenue estimate: $160 billion
- FSD safety claim: ~8–9x safer than human driving (stated in transcript, unverified)
- US annual traffic deaths reference: ~43,000 (used to frame regulatory licensing argument)
- Jeff Lutz: "Tesla has built something. I think 50%'s a huge advantage. I think actually think it may be more."
- Jeff Lutz: "Tesla is definitely setting up for scale."
- On Colossus 1/Anthropic: "This is small potatoes" in context of multi-year infrastructure buildout

articles.title: Tesla Just Got Several Massive Catalysts
articles.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel features host Herbert and guest Jo Bhakdi, an economist, investor, and tech entrepreneur, discussing several major catalysts driving Tesla's stock higher over the previous five days. The conversation covers Tesla's stock trajectory, Elon Musk's invitation to join President Trump on a China trip, robotaxi fleet expansion, Waymo's recall and competitive weaknesses, and Giga Berlin's production expansion. The core thesis is that Tesla's stock recovery toward all-time highs is justified by fundamentals alone — with robotaxi and Optimus representing additional upside catalysts layered on top.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla stock up $42 (11%) in five days:** Tesla's stock rose over $45 in the five days preceding the video, with Jo Bhakdi arguing the move is not driven by any specific catalyst but rather a logical mean-reversion after an unjustified post-earnings selloff. Bhakdi contends that Tesla's fundamentals are at least as strong as they were when the stock hit its all-time high of $490 on December 16, 2025, and with the broader market also near all-time highs, there is a natural "magnet" pulling Tesla back toward that level.

2. **All-time high of $490 as base target, larger repricing contingent on robotaxi scale:** Bhakdi separates his analysis into layers: a baseline return to ~$490 independent of any robotaxi or Optimus catalyst, and a potential "great repricing" to somewhere between $600 and $1,000 once the market becomes convinced that robotaxi is scaling to multiple millions of vehicles. He argues the market will cross that threshold well before the fleet reaches 10,000 units, at which point a dramatic repricing could occur at any moment.

3. **Elon Musk invited to join Trump's China trip alongside major U.S. executives:** President Trump invited Elon Musk, Tim Cook (Apple), and representatives from Boeing, Goldman Sachs, Blackstone, BlackRock, Citigroup, Meta, General Electric, Cargill, Micron, Qualcomm, Visa, Alumina, and Coherent Corp on his trip to China. Bhakdi interprets the inclusion of top corporate leaders as a strong signal that the U.S.-China trade war is de-escalating behind the scenes and that deal announcements are imminent. Notably, Jensen Huang (Nvidia) was not invited, which Bhakdi reads as evidence that semiconductor export restrictions remain a sticking point.

4. **FSD approval in China signaled by owner's manual update:** The Chinese owner's manual has been updated, with the FSD supervised version now renamed "Tesla Assisted Driving." Tesla has also been hiring Autopilot engineers in China. Herbert suggests this points toward an imminent, expanded FSD launch in China, potentially accelerated by Elon Musk's presence on the China trip.

5. **Optimus supply chain dependency on China:** Bhakdi notes that major key components for Optimus come from China, making a de-escalation of trade tensions particularly important for Tesla shareholders. He frames the warming U.S.-China relationship as directly beneficial to Optimus manufacturing economics.

6. **Waymo loses $5–$6 billion per year, approximately $100 per ride:** Herbert states that Waymo is losing $5 to $6 billion annually, which translates to roughly $100 in losses per ride. He predicts Waymo will eventually announce plans to acquire a car factory and move to a vision-only system, abandoning lidar. Bhakdi argues Waymo's lidar dependency represents a fundamental architectural dead end — transitioning to vision-only would take roughly a year of rework — and that the earliest Waymo could solve its core technology problems is around 2028.

7. **Waymo recalls 3,800 robotaxis over flooded road software issue:** Waymo issued a recall of nearly 3,800 robotaxis (fifth and sixth generation automated driving systems) after a software issue caused vehicles to drive onto flooded roads. The recall reveals the true scale of the Waymo fleet. Waymo's response includes a software fix and narrowing its operating scope to exclude areas prone to flash flooding during intense rain. A separate NHTSA investigation involves a Waymo vehicle striking a child near an elementary school, resulting in minor injuries.

8. **AV Ride (Uber partner) under NHTSA investigation for 16 crashes:** AV Ride, which partners with Uber, is under NHTSA investigation for 16 self-driving crashes involving failures to properly change lanes, respond to vehicles in the same lane, and respond to stationary objects. Herbert notes these incidents occurred even with a safety monitor present in the driver's seat.

9. **Competitors structurally far behind Tesla on data, compute, and time:** Bhakdi argues that autonomous driving is not magic — it requires data, compute, time, and talent. When comparing companies on these metrics, he asserts that competitors outside of Waymo are at roughly 1% or less of Tesla's infrastructure stack, and that even Waymo does not have access to Google's full compute resources. He concludes there is effectively no meaningful competition for Tesla in the near term.

10. **Global auto market consolidation favors Tesla:** Bhakdi predicts that by 2027, the broader auto industry will see widespread bankruptcies among legacy OEMs (German, Japanese, American), with Tesla as the last major profitable player. He notes that in China, over 40% of all cars sold are now battery EVs, and if PHEVs are included, the figure exceeds 50%. He describes a clear EV inflection point in Europe, particularly among Scandinavian countries, benefiting Tesla as the market leader.

## Robotaxi

1. **39 unsupervised Tesla robotaxi vehicles across Austin, Houston, and Dallas:** Per RobotaxiTracker.com, there are 39 unsupervised (driverless) Tesla robotaxi vehicles deployed across Austin, Houston, and Dallas. Herbert notes Tesla appears to be converting supervised vehicles to unsupervised and expects approximately 20 more conversions to fill out the next tier. He also notes the overall active fleet across all modes stands at 668 per RobotaxiTracker.com.

2. **64% of Austin robotaxi rides unsupervised in the last 7 days:** Over the seven days prior to the video, 64% of all Tesla robotaxi rides in Austin were unsupervised, signaling a meaningful operational transition. Herbert cautions that the total number of rides and vehicles remains small, characterizing the current phase as a test pilot.

3. **Cybercab production estimate: 300–600 units per month currently, targeting 1,800 as inflection point:** Jo Tegtmeyer spotted 37 new Cybercabs, and Herbert references a prior sighting of 40. Bhakdi estimates that if the ~30–40 Cybercabs visible in the parking lot cycle out even twice a week, minimum production is approximately 10 per day, implying 300 to 600 Cybercabs per month. Bhakdi states his personal inflection point for the thesis is 1,800 total produced Cybercabs, which he believes will be reached within roughly one month at current trajectory.

4. **Cybercab fleet projected to reach ~10,000 by end of 2026:** Bhakdi projects that at the current ramp rate, Tesla will be producing over 1,000 Cybercabs per month within three months, putting the cumulative fleet at approximately 10,000 by end of 2026. He frames this as nearly impossible for bears to dispute, arguing the only bear case is that Tesla builds the vehicles but never deploys them — a bet he considers very unlikely.

5. **Fleet deployment structure: ~1,000 Cybercabs plus ~100 Model Y's per city:** Herbert describes the expected deployment structure as approximately 1,000 Cybercabs per city supplemented by roughly 100 Model Y's per city to handle trips requiring more than two passengers (estimated at ~10% of rides). This is described as the current observable rollout pattern.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Giga Berlin hits 750,000 cars produced, planning 20% production increase:** Tesla's Giga Berlin plant announced it has produced 750,000 vehicles, with plant manager André stating the goal is to reach the first million cars as quickly as possible. Tesla is planning to scale production at Giga Berlin by 20%, which will require new hiring.

2. **$250 million investment to expand 4680 battery cell production at Giga Berlin:** Tesla announced a $250 million investment to expand 4680 battery cell production at Giga Berlin. The expansion will more than double existing capacity, with an annual production capacity target of 18 GWh — more than twice the previously stated 8 GWh target for the site. The expansion is expected to create over 1,500 new jobs.

3. **Affordable Cybertruck variant spotted at Giga Texas:** Joe Tegtmeyer observed what appears to be early production of a new $59,000 Cybertruck variant at Giga Texas, though he notes it is difficult to visually distinguish from the premium all-wheel drive version.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla stock up ~$42 (11%) over the prior five days as of midday recording
- Tesla all-time high: $490, reached December 16, 2025
- Bhakdi's stock price targets: $490 baseline (no catalyst), $600–$1,000 with confirmed robotaxi scale
- Optimus launch referenced as approximately 70 days away from recording date
- 39 unsupervised Tesla robotaxi vehicles per RobotaxiTracker.com (Austin 28, Dallas 5, Houston 6)
- 668 total active Tesla robotaxi vehicles (all modes) per RobotaxiTracker.com
- 64% of Austin robotaxi rides unsupervised in last 7 days
- 37 Cybercabs spotted by Joe Tegtmeyer; prior sighting of 40
- Bhakdi's Cybercab production estimate: 300–600 units/month currently
- Bhakdi's inflection point: 1,800 total Cybercabs produced
- Bhakdi's year-end 2026 Cybercab fleet projection: ~10,000
- Waymo fleet size confirmed at 3,800 vehicles via NHTSA recall
- Waymo losses: $5–$6 billion per year, ~$100 per ride
- Giga Berlin: 750,000 cars built; 20% production increase planned
- Giga Berlin 4680 investment: $250 million; capacity target raised from 8 GWh to 18 GWh; 1,500+ new jobs
- China EV market share: 40%+ battery EVs; 50%+ including PHEVs
- FSD supervised version renamed "Tesla Assisted Driving" in updated China owner's manual
- Bhakdi on Waymo: "The earliest where Waymo could solve the technology thing... is maybe 2028"
- Bhakdi on competitors: "They're at 1% or less of Tesla" on data, compute, and infrastructure

articles.title: Tesla Robotaxi’s ‘convenience issues’ are hiding the real safety bottleneck
articles.body:
A Reuters investigation documents severe availability and routing problems across Tesla's three-city Robotaxi service. The article argues these are not mere convenience issues but direct symptoms of a safety system that cannot scale — a framing supported by Elon Musk's own comments at the Q1 2026 earnings call.

## Robotaxi

1. **Service reliability is severely limited across all three cities:** Reuters reporters tested the service in Austin, Dallas, and Houston over the past month. In Dallas, a reporter spent nearly two hours on what should have been a 20-minute, 5-mile trip — including a 36-minute wait before a car appeared, followed by a 35-minute surface-street detour that avoided North Central Expressway and dropped them at a parking lot 15 minutes from the destination. In Houston, one ride was completed before the app canceled a second booking and showed no vehicles for 30 minutes. In Austin, where the service has run for nearly a year, a Reuters reporter tracking availability eight times daily for three weeks in April found wait times exceeded 15 minutes roughly half the time, exceeded 25 minutes more than a quarter of the time, and in 27% of checks, no cars were available at all.

2. **Fleet size is extremely small relative to stated ambitions:** Tesla operates approximately 50 vehicles in Austin, according to city officials, versus more than 250 Waymo vehicles in the same city. Across Dallas and Houston combined, roughly 25 unsupervised vehicles are operating. The article attributes the tiny fleet directly to crash-rate math: Tesla has reported 15 crashes in Austin to NHTSA since August, working out to approximately one crash every 57,000 miles — about 4x worse than the average human driver rate of one per 229,000 miles, based on Tesla's own vehicle safety data. Tesla has asked regulators to redact all crash details.

3. **Musk cited safety validation — not software or manufacturing — as the scaling bottleneck:** On the Q1 2026 earnings call on April 22, Musk said the limiting factor for expansion is "rigorous validation, making sure things are completely safe," adding that Tesla does not want "a single accidental injury" and described the approach as "very cautious." He also walked back his expansion timeline: last July he predicted robotaxis would serve half the U.S. population by end of 2025; on the Q1 2026 call he downgraded that to "a dozen or so states" by end of 2026. Tesla has also delayed its five-city expansion that was originally planned for the first half of 2026.

## Market & Competition

4. **Waymo's scale contrasts sharply with Tesla's:** Waymo is delivering over 500,000 paid robotaxi rides per week across 10 U.S. cities — fully driverless, no chase cars or safety monitors, operating 24 hours a day. The article notes that Waymo's HD-mapping and extensive pre-launch testing approach is the same methodology Musk has repeatedly mocked.

## Editorial Stance
Lambert argues the "convenience issues" framing is generous to Tesla — the real problem is that the underlying crash rate makes scaling mathematically dangerous, and Tesla's vision-only system without supervision is not confident enough for highway driving. He states that "the idea that Tesla would somehow quickly outscale Waymo because of its vision-only approach is officially dead."

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla Austin crash rate: ~1 per 57,000 miles vs. human average of ~1 per 229,000 miles (per Tesla's own vehicle safety data) — approximately 4x worse
- Tesla Austin fleet: ~50 vehicles (per city officials); Waymo Austin fleet: 250+
- Unsupervised Tesla vehicles across Dallas and Houston combined: ~25
- Austin availability: no cars available in 27% of checks; wait >15 min ~50% of the time; wait >25 min in >25% of checks (Reuters, three weeks in April 2026)
- Waymo: 500,000+ paid rides/week across 10 U.S. cities, fully driverless
- Musk Q1 2026 call (April 22): safety validation is the limiting factor; expansion target downgraded to "a dozen or so states" by end of 2026
- Tesla has requested NHTSA redact all crash information
- Dallas trip: 5-mile ride took nearly 2 hours; car failed to make a left turn four times at one intersection; remote attendant intervened

articles.title: Tesla invests $250M more in Giga Berlin battery cells, boosting capacity to 18 GWh
articles.body:
Tesla announced a ~$250 million additional investment in battery cell production at its Grünheide (Giga Berlin) factory, more than doubling the planned capacity target from 8 GWh to 18 GWh annually and adding over 1,500 battery-related jobs.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Giga Berlin recovery underway:** The factory was reportedly running at just 40% capacity earlier this year following a 28% collapse in European sales in 2025 (German registrations down 48%) and the shedding of ~1,700 jobs. Rising demand for the refreshed Model Y has reversed the trajectory — in April Tesla announced plans to hire 1,000 new workers, boost production by 20%, and convert ~500 temporary workers to permanent contracts.

## Energy
1. **Battery capacity expansion:** Tesla raised its Grünheide cell production target from 8 GWh (announced December 2025) to 18 GWh. Total cumulative investment in the site's cell production unit now approaches €1 billion (~$1.2 billion). At 18 GWh, the facility would produce enough cells for an estimated 250,000–350,000 vehicles per year, depending on pack size. Cell production is expected to start in the first half of 2027.

2. **Vertical integration goal:** Tesla's stated ambition is to produce everything from battery cells to finished EVs at a single European location by 2027 — a scale of vertical integration it claims no other European automaker has achieved. Tesla has already begun recruiting for the 1,500+ battery production roles.

## Market & Competition
1. **Union vote controversy:** Two months before this announcement, CEO Elon Musk sent workers a video warning that expansion would not proceed if IG Metall gained a works council majority. IG Metall's vote share fell from 39.4% (2024) to 31.1% in the March 2026 election; Tesla's management-aligned list, Giga United, won 24 of 37 seats. IG Metall has filed a legal challenge alleging unlawful interference. The investment announcement followed immediately after the union's defeat.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert notes healthy skepticism is warranted given Tesla's repeated history of announcing and re-announcing Grünheide battery plans since 2021 without delivery, while acknowledging the 18 GWh target, €1 billion cumulative investment, and active recruiting make this more concrete than past promises. He characterizes the union-investment sequence as a "troubling precedent for labor relations in European manufacturing," regardless of one's view of the underlying tactic.

**Notable quotes and data:**
- New investment: ~$250 million; cumulative cell production investment: ~€1 billion (~$1.2 billion)
- Capacity target: 8 GWh → 18 GWh (more than doubled)
- Jobs created: 1,500+ battery production roles; hiring already begun
- Cell production start: first half of 2027
- Estimated vehicle output at 18 GWh: 250,000–350,000 vehicles/year
- Giga Berlin capacity utilization earlier in 2026: reported at ~40%
- European Tesla sales 2025: down 28%; German registrations down 48%
- IG Metall vote share: 39.4% (2024) → 31.1% (March 2026); Giga United won 24/37 seats
- Tesla quote: "From battery cells to electric vehicles, everything is expected to be produced at a single location starting in 2027."

articles.title: Tesla finally launches Supercharger virtual queue pilot after fights broke out
articles.body:
Tesla has launched a virtual waitlist pilot at five Supercharger locations, allowing drivers to join a queue via the Tesla app rather than physically waiting — arriving over a year behind the originally announced Q2 2025 timeline.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Virtual queue pilot details:** Drivers at capacity Supercharger stations can join a virtual queue through the Tesla app, which displays their position and wait time via a Live Activity notification. Tesla uses both vehicle and phone location to determine eligibility. The system does not technically enforce queue order — it displays a prompt asking drivers if they want to skip the queue, relying on the honor system.

2. **Five pilot locations:** Los Gatos CA, Mountain View CA, San Francisco CA (Lombard St.), San Jose CA, and Bronx NY. Four of the five are in the Bay Area, Tesla's highest-density market. The Bronx location is notable given past congestion from ride-hailing drivers at NYC Superchargers.

3. **Background and timeline:** Tesla first promised the feature following a viral fight video at a crowded Supercharger, then announced a Q2 2025 pilot launch in February 2025. The pilot is launching in Q2 2026 — one year late. A separate congestion measure, a $1/minute fee for charging past 90% at busy stations, was introduced in 2023 to address dwell time rather than wait-queue management.

## Market & Competition
1. **Non-Tesla EV access:** The virtual queue feature supports non-Tesla EVs through the Tesla app. Approximately 70% of Tesla's 80,000+ Supercharging stalls are now open to other automakers, contributing to higher station utilization and making congestion management increasingly relevant.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert welcomes the launch but criticizes the year-long delay for what is a software-only feature, notes that 1% congestion across 53 million Q1 2026 charging sessions implies hundreds of thousands of affected visits annually, and flags that the honor-system enforcement model may prove insufficient as network utilization grows.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla announced the pilot on X, inviting driver feedback through the Tesla app
- Original timeline: Q2 2025 pilot announced February 2025; actual launch: Q2 2026
- Tesla acknowledged wait times occur ~1% of the time across the Supercharger network
- 53 million charging sessions in Q1 2026 (cited in editorial section)
- 80,000+ Supercharging stalls total; ~70% open to non-Tesla EVs
- Congestion fee of $1/minute for charging past 90% at busy stations, launched 2023

articles.title: Tesla moves Basic Autopilot features to paid FSD where available
articles.body:
Tesla has quietly removed Basic Autopilot from its Dutch configurator, making the Netherlands the first European market where buyers must pay for FSD (Supervised) to access any active driver-assistance features beyond GSR2-mandated emergency lane-keeping.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Netherlands becomes FSD-subscription-only market:** Tesla's Dutch configurator now offers only FSD (Supervised) — at €99/month, a €7,500 one-time purchase, or "Add later" — with no Basic Autopilot option at any price. The change mirrors Tesla's January 2026 move in North America, where Autosteer was paywalled behind the FSD subscription, leaving new vehicles with only Traffic-Aware Cruise Control as standard. The Netherlands was the first European country to grant FSD Supervised type approval, via Dutch RDW under UN R-171, in approximately mid-April 2026, enabling this rollout.

2. **Broader European rollout likely imminent:** Other EU markets (Germany, France) still include Basic Autopilot as standard ("Inklusive" on Tesla's German configurator, with Enhanced Autopilot available for €3,800). However, Tesla has set a May 21, 2026 deadline for one-time FSD purchases across other European markets, signaling an imminent shift to subscription-only. Flanders is described as already moving toward FSD recognition.

## Market & Competition
3. **Competitive disadvantage on standard features:** EU GSR2 regulations (in force since July 2024) require emergency lane-keeping on all new cars, but competitors including Toyota, Hyundai, and Volkswagen include active lane-centering as standard on vehicles priced below a Model 3. A base Model 3 in the Netherlands starts at €36,990 and now ships with only the GSR2 safety nudge — no Autosteer — unless buyers pay €99/month. Comparable vehicles like the VW ID.4 and Hyundai Ioniq 5 include those features standard at similar price points.

## Editorial Stance
Electrek views this as Tesla deliberately padding FSD's perceived value by moving standard features behind a paywall rather than delivering genuine self-driving capability. The author is skeptical the strategy will succeed in Europe, where alternatives with standard driver assistance are widely available and the backlash is expected to be stronger than in North America.

Notable quotes and data:
- FSD (Supervised) pricing in Netherlands: €99/month or €7,500 one-time purchase
- One-time FSD purchase deadline in Netherlands: May 15, 2026
- One-time FSD purchase deadline across other European markets: May 21, 2026
- Base Model 3 Netherlands price: €36,990
- Enhanced Autopilot price on German configurator: €3,800
- Dutch RDW granted FSD Supervised type approval under UN R-171; rollout to Dutch owners began mid-April 2026
- Netherlands is described as "a small market" used as a contained test for the subscription-first strategy

articles.title: When Tesla Will Deploy Cybercab to the Robotaxi Network ⚡️
articles.body:
This video from Dillon Loomis of the "Electrified" channel centers on the question of when Tesla will deploy the Cybercab onto its paid robotaxi network. Loomis argues that despite production of Cybercabs already underway at Giga Texas, a September 2026 deployment timeline is more realistic than the 1–2 month window many observers are expecting. The video also covers a notable Piper Sandler analyst note projecting Tesla's revenue across 17 business lines through 2045, along with updates on Optimus, FSD regulatory validation, Uber's AV lobbying push, and several Tesla business items.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab Production Underway but Deployment Not Imminent:** Joe Tegtmeyer reported that Cybercab production is proceeding slowly — as Tesla said it would — but that dozens of Cybercabs are now visible in the outbound lot at Giga Texas. Loomis interprets this as validating activity rather than pre-deployment staging, arguing that Tesla needs real-world and simulation miles to validate the new vehicle platform before any paid rides begin.

2. **Predicted Cybercab Robotaxi Launch: ~September 15, 2026:** Loomis's central prediction is that Tesla will deploy the first Cybercab onto the paid robotaxi network around September 15, 2026 — approximately six months from the start of Cybercab production. He bases this on the Cybertruck FSD precedent, where it took roughly a year-plus to fully retrain and validate Tesla's neural network for that new vehicle platform, and notes that the Cybercab presents even more novel engineering challenges.

3. **Why Cybercab Integration Is More Complex Than Cybertruck:** Loomis argues that for the Cybertruck, the primary challenge was not perception but the control stack — specifically, remapping Tesla's mechanically linked steering rack model to the Cybertruck's variable-ratio steer-by-wire and four-wheel steering system. The Cybercab introduces additional novel challenges: it is Tesla's first front-wheel-drive-only vehicle, it has no steering wheel or pedals (requiring the FSD stack to output entirely new control commands), different camera angles, different suspension, and different B-pillars. Unlike the Cybertruck, Cybercab will likely launch unsupervised for paid rides, raising the stakes for validation.

4. **Model Y Continues to Anchor the Robotaxi Fleet:** Loomis notes that Tesla does not need the Cybercab to keep expanding its robotaxi network — Model Y deployments can continue scaling without issue. This removes urgency and allows Tesla to take whatever time is needed to get the Cybercab right before fleet introduction.

5. **FSD V15 as a Potential Gating Factor:** Loomis raises — without asserting — that Elon Musk has indicated in a roundabout way that they are waiting for FSD V15 to really scale, and flags that Tesla might also wait for V15 before deploying the Cybercab. He does not argue this is likely, but includes it as a consideration.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Model Y Passes All NHTSA Advanced Driver Assistance Tests:** Tesla's Model Y became the first — and as of the video, only — vehicle to pass NHTSA's new advanced driver assistance system tests. NHTSA confirmed that Model Y vehicles made on or after November 12, 2025 successfully met criteria for four newly integrated safety tests: pedestrian automatic emergency braking, lane-keeping assistance, blind spot warning, and blind spot intervention. NHTSA's administrator said the 2026 Model Y "sets a high bar for the industry." Loomis emphasizes this is a significant federal-level validation of Tesla's vision-only system at a moment when congressional debates about LiDAR vs. vision-only are ongoing.

2. **Tesla Hiring Autopilot Test Engineers Across Chinese Cities:** Tesla is hiring for Autopilot test engineer roles in China, with Shanghai listed as the preferred location and additional cities including Shenzhen, Chongqing, and Wuhan also listed. Loomis notes this is the first time Tesla has specified cities and provinces for this role, suggesting active expansion of FSD testing and validation in China.

3. **Elon Musk's China Trip and FSD Approval Prospects:** The White House invited Elon Musk to join President Trump's trip to China. Loomis draws a parallel to Elon's April 2024 surprise Beijing visit, after which Tesla passed a key data privacy assessment and secured a mapping deal with BYD — both steps that enabled Tesla's current limited FSD approval in China. Loomis suggests this trip could advance the broader FSD approval in China.

4. **Uber Launches AV Policy Push:** Uber's director of autonomy announced a new public policy paper advocating for autonomous vehicle deployment across the US, including in challenging markets like Chicago, Boston, and New York City. Uber argues for a hybrid network where AVs and human drivers coexist long-term, while calling out infrastructure (charging/cleaning), mapping/validation, and density as the three main barriers. AV legislation has stalled in at least eight states. Loomis frames Uber's lobbying as a net positive for the broader AV industry and for Tesla.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus V3 Entering Small-Scale Trial Production in May 2026:** Chinese supply chain account Ming — who Loomis says has a credible track record — reported that Optimus V3 has successfully cleared its engineering verification and is entering small-scale trial production in May 2026. Core suppliers are expected to receive their first mass production orders in mid-July, paving the way for a large-scale production ramp in August. Seven key Chinese partners have already passed Tesla's PPA (production part approval) certification.

2. **Piper Sandler: Optimus Still Too Unknown to Model Formally:** Piper Sandler analyst Alex Potter acknowledged that the humanoid robot and "inference as a service" businesses "arguably will be worth more than Tesla's other businesses combined," but has not yet formally attempted to forecast them. Loomis notes that Optimus remains too uncertain even for firms like ARK Invest to model seriously. Potter's current base case assigns zero value to Optimus, while arguing that at ~$400/share, investors are effectively getting the Optimus business for free.

## Financials

1. **Piper Sandler 17-Business-Line Tesla Model:** Analyst Alex Potter published a new Tesla model covering 17 product lines, yielding a price target of approximately $400 per share without assigning any value to Optimus. The model includes previously overlooked business lines such as in-house insurance, Supercharging, and a standalone robotaxi evaluation separate from the FSD software business. Potter's near-term estimates for 2026 and 2027 are below consensus, reflecting declining deliveries from discontinued products and lower regulatory credit contributions, but he argues traditional metrics are becoming less relevant as FSD subscriber counts and robotaxi metrics take center stage.

2. **Piper Sandler Long-Range Revenue Projections (Selected Figures):**
   - FSD subscriptions: ~$600 million in 2026, growing to $10.6 billion by 2030
   - FSD licensing: $0 through 2031, then ramping to $400 billion by 2045
   - Robotaxi rides: $400 million in 2027, $2.2 billion in 2028, $18.6 billion by 2030
   - Energy revenue: $13.1 billion in 2026, growing to ~$20.9 billion by 2030 (Loomis believes this is too conservative given Tesla's solar and Megapack plans)
   - Total Tesla revenue: ~$96 billion in 2026, $155 billion in 2030, $1.7 trillion by 2045
   - First trillion-dollar revenue year projected: 2039
   - Regulatory credits projected to go to zero by 2029
   - Vehicle sales revenue projected to begin a steady decline after 2031 as Tesla transitions to transportation-as-a-service

## Electric Vehicles

1. **$59,000 Cybertruck May Have Started Production:** Joe Tegtmeyer reported that the $59,000 Cybertruck variant may have begun production in Austin, though this was presented as preliminary observation rather than confirmed news.

2. **Model S/X Signature Edition Delivery Event Rescheduled:** Tesla officially changed the Model S/X Signature Edition delivery event to May 20, 2026, to be held in Fremont, California.

3. **Tesla Supercharger Waitlist Feature Testing:** Tesla is testing a waitlist feature at five Supercharger locations — four in California and one in the Bronx, New York. Non-Tesla vehicles can join the waitlist through the Tesla app. The feature shows estimated wait time (under 5 minutes in the demo) and number of cars ahead in queue, with an option to leave the waitlist.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla Stock Performance — Relative Context:** Tesla stock closed at $445, up 3.89% on the day, with volume 18% above average, while the Nasdaq 100 was up 2.9%. Tesla is up 32% over the prior 35 days. However, Loomis cautions against attributing this to a Tesla-specific catalyst: the S&P 500 is up 16% over the prior six weeks, which is the 11th-largest six-week gain for that index since 1950 — and the only instance in the top 20 that did not occur during or just after a bear market.

2. **Ford Enters Battery Energy Storage Market:** Ford announced a new subsidiary, Ford Energy, planning to deploy at least 20 gigawatt-hours of battery storage annually, with first customer deliveries planned for late 2027. Their flagship product is the Ford Energy DC Block — a standardized 20-foot containerized battery energy storage system using 512 amp-hour LFP prismatic cells. Ford is repurposing existing US battery manufacturing capacity in Glendale, Kentucky. Loomis frames this as validation of the attractive margins in the BESS market, consistent with a prior interview discussion about EV battery factories being repurposed for energy storage.

3. **Redwood Materials: Tesla's Former CFO Joins:** Tesla's former CFO Deepak Ahuja joined Redwood Materials as CFO, citing his longstanding relationship with JB Straubel. Redwood recently cut approximately 10% of its headcount (135 people) to refocus resources on its energy division.

Notable quotes and data:
- Joe Tegtmeyer: "CyberCab production is proceeding slowly as Tesla said it would, but there are dozens of Cybercabs in the outbound lot."
- Alex Potter (Piper Sandler): "At $400 a share, we think investors can buy Optimus for free."
- Alex Potter: "The humanoid robot and inference as a service businesses arguably will be worth more than Tesla's other businesses combined."
- NHTSA administrator on Model Y: "By successfully passing these new tests, the 2026 Model Y demonstrates the life-saving potential of driver assistance tech and sets a high bar for the industry."
- Uber: There are 8,000 cities in the US alone that Uber serves, which "likely won't be workable for AVs in the foreseeable future."
- Piper Sandler robotaxi revenue: $400M (2027) → $2.2B (2028) → $18.6B (2030)
- Piper Sandler FSD licensing revenue: $0 through 2031 → $400B by 2045
- Piper Sandler total Tesla revenue: ~$96B (2026) → $155B (2030) → $1.7T (2045)
- Tesla stock: $445/share, +32% over prior 35 days, +3.89% on the day
- Optimus V3 supply chain report: engineering verification cleared, small-scale trial production May 2026, mass production orders to suppliers mid-July, large-scale ramp in August 2026

articles.title: Tesla Stock Surges As Major Product Changes Hit
articles.body:
This episode of FutureAzA features host Brian and correspondent Randy Kirk discussing a cluster of Tesla news items from the week, including the end of the Model S and Model X era, a postponed delivery event, battery technology developments, brand loyalty data, and Tesla/SpaceX's partnership with Intel on a semiconductor fabrication facility. The hosts offer context on whether each headline materially matters to Tesla's stock and long-term thesis, generally concluding that strong sales volume and the robotaxi ramp are the dominant drivers of the current stock rally.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **End of the Model S and Model X Era:** The final Model S has been produced, marking the end of the SNX lineup. The hosts note that the last car was reportedly graffitied before delivery to its buyer, Steve Jurvetson, who they speculate will apply clear PPF wrap to preserve it. Randy argues the retirement is a natural business decision: as Tesla scales, products that once represented a major revenue line become "a rounding error," and maintaining the factory space and cost structure for low-volume models is increasingly hard to justify. The hosts suggest Tesla still has halo-car appeal through the Cybertruck, Cybercab, and the forthcoming Roadster.

2. **Delivery Event Postponed with 72 Hours Notice:** A scheduled celebration and handover event for the final Model S/X vehicles, planned for May 12, 2026, was postponed with only 72 hours notice and no new date provided. The hosts speculate the likely reason is Elon Musk's expected participation in a presidential trade trip to China alongside other tech executives including Tim Cook. They acknowledge this is inconvenient for loyal customers who booked non-refundable travel, but conclude it will have zero impact on the stock price.

3. **Giga Shanghai Posts Strongest April Ever:** Tesla's Giga Shanghai recorded its strongest April on record, delivering approximately 80,000 vehicles in the month. The hosts note this puts the factory on an annualized run rate of close to one million units. They highlight that while China domestic sales have been somewhat soft, Tesla is increasingly exporting from Shanghai to markets including Canada, Europe, and South Korea, describing a broad surge in global demand.

4. **Tesla Brand Loyalty Still Above 60%:** A brand loyalty study found Tesla owners return to buy another Tesla at a rate above 60%, still ranking first among automakers, though slightly lower than historical highs. The hosts attribute the modest decline primarily to political backlash (including incidents of vandalism at Tesla locations) earlier in the year, which they say has since largely faded. They view the retention figure as consistent with Tesla's positioning as a premium product with demonstrable advantages in safety and ADAS.

## Market & Competition

1. **4680 Battery Underperforms vs. LFP and 2170:** Reports surfaced that the 4680 cell has fallen short of expectations on both energy density (watt-hours per kilogram) and charging speed, failing to surpass the older 2170 cell on either metric. Meanwhile, LFP chemistry has advanced significantly — offering higher charge/discharge rates, more cycles, cheaper materials, and now competitive fast-charging speeds. The hosts discuss a battery deep-dive interview on Dillon Loomis's show with a guest named Iona covering Tesla batteries and Megapack technology. Randy notes Tesla remains the leader in high-nickel (NMC/NCA) chemistries, but acknowledges LFP is closing the performance gap, particularly relevant in China where apartment dwellers depend on public fast charging. Tesla has reportedly adopted a very fast-charging LFP battery (described as 5C or 3C) for the Chinese market.

2. **China Battery Competition Intensifying:** Chinese manufacturers including CATL and BYD are aggressively scaling battery production, overbuilding factory capacity and driving down prices. The hosts frame this as a familiar pattern of Chinese industrial overinvestment creating intense price competition, while noting Tesla retains a differentiated position on the high-nickel chemistry side.

## Financials

1. **Stock Up ~4% on the Day of Recording:** Tesla's stock was up approximately 4%, or $16.73 per share, on the day of recording (Monday, May 12, 2026). The hosts note the stock is now within approximately 10% of its all-time high of $495, meaning nearly all current shareholders are in a profit position. They attribute roughly 50% of the recent rally to strong car sales numbers, with the robotaxi ramp cited as the other major catalyst expected to drive an all-time high later in 2026.

## Autonomous Driving / Market & Competition

1. **Tesla and SpaceX Partner with Intel on Terafab Semiconductor Fab:** Elon Musk toured Intel's semiconductor fabrication plant in Hillsborough, Oregon, ahead of a formal Tesla and SpaceX partnership with Intel to build a chip fabrication facility called the "Terafab." The hosts recount that Tesla first approached Samsung (who allowed a factory tour but apparently didn't satisfy Musk's ambitions) and then TSMC (who declined to partner), before landing on Intel, which agreed to share its new chip architecture and manufacturing methodology. The first phase of the Terafab is planned to cost $55 billion, split between Tesla and SpaceX, making the financial burden more manageable for both. The hosts argue the deal is arguably even more significant for SpaceX than Tesla, as it de-risks a key question ahead of SpaceX's anticipated IPO. They also note that Samsung subsequently announced it would dedicate more chip capacity — suggesting the Intel deal sparked competitive pressure.

Notable quotes and data:
- Giga Shanghai: "strongest April ever" — approximately 80,000 vehicles, implying an annualized run rate of close to 1 million units
- Tesla stock up ~4% (~$16.73/share) on May 12, 2026; all-time high was $495, currently ~10% below that
- Tesla brand loyalty: still #1 at over 60% retention rate
- Terafab Phase 1 estimated cost: $55 billion, shared between Tesla and SpaceX
- Randy: "I think [the Shanghai sales number] is about 50% of the reason why we're up right now"
- Randy on SNX retirement: "a product that used to be a major thing all of a sudden turns into a rounding error"
- On Intel partnership: "partnering with Intel, one of the very few companies in the world that knows how to do this, especially when Intel is in a position of modest duress"

articles.title: Jeep Wagoneer S Review From A Tesla Owner’s Perspective
articles.body:
This video features FutureAzA's host visiting Platt Auto, a used car dealership with a significant Tesla inventory, to test drive and review a 2025 Jeep Wagoneer S from the perspective of Tesla owners and EV enthusiasts. The core thesis is that the Wagoneer S, available used at roughly half its new price (~$40,000), offers a compelling premium EV option for buyers who prioritize interior quality, ride comfort, ground clearance, and light off-road capability — though it has notable calibration and software shortcomings compared to Tesla. The video is casual and conversational, with dealership rep Jack providing hands-on context.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Jeep Wagoneer S specs and pricing:** The 2025 Jeep Wagoneer S on the lot is priced at approximately $40,000 used — described as "almost half off" its new price. It features a ~100 kWh battery pack, stated range of just over 300 miles, all-wheel drive, and NMC (not LFP) battery chemistry. Both the vehicle and batteries are described as made in the US. The car has approximately 4,000 miles on it, making it a very low-mileage used example.

2. **Performance and handling characteristics:** The Wagoneer S is described as "rocket ship fast" in a straight line, with the front end lifting noticeably under hard acceleration — a "boat-like" feel the hosts find acceptable given the vehicle's weight (just under 6,000 lbs curb weight). Sport mode automatically disables traction control, which both hosts criticize as a poor design decision, as the front wheels visibly spin out.

3. **Regenerative braking calibration issues:** The host's primary complaint is the throttle/regen pedal calibration in high-regen mode, describing the transition from acceleration to regeneration as an abrupt on/off switch with no granularity or smoothness. He notes that Nissan has handled one-pedal driving more gracefully for over a decade, and that he resorts to the lower regen mode to achieve acceptable drivability.

4. **Interior quality and features:** Both hosts praise the interior, highlighting plush, well-bolstered ventilated seats, high-quality leather feel, thoughtful dash patterns, a square-ish steering wheel that improves dashboard visibility, and high-definition surround-view cameras. The interior is described as more premium-feeling than comparable Teslas, which is cited as the primary reason cross-shoppers are seriously considering it.

5. **Practicality and off-road capability:** The Wagoneer S has approximately 8-point-something inches of ground clearance, compared to the Model Y's ~6.5 inches. The hosts consider it well-suited for light off-roading such as forest service roads and trail heads, with the 300-mile range sufficient for regional trips (e.g., Portland to Mount Hood at 80 miles). It seats five with a flat rear floor, generous legroom, and a large trunk — but is deemed too small for a practical third row.

6. **Exterior pedestrian sound alert:** At low speeds (switching on around 26 mph), the Wagoneer S emits a loud exterior pedestrian alert sound, similar to Chevy/Blazer EV behavior, which the host finds so intrusive it creates an urge to accelerate past the threshold just to silence it.

## Market & Competition
1. **Cross-shopping dynamics at the dealership:** Customers showing interest in the Wagoneer S are primarily cross-shopping against top-trim Model Y's and Chevy Blazer EVs — vehicles of similar size in the large two-row SUV segment. The Wagoneer S attracts buyers seeking a more premium interior experience than either of those alternatives.

2. **Competitive comparison to other EVs:** The hosts compare the Wagoneer S to the Hyundai Ioniq 5 (similar range, slightly better charging, but much lower ground clearance making it less capable on rough terrain) and loosely to Mercedes GLE/GLS EVs and BMW X5/X7 in terms of pricing tier and positioning. The Wagoneer S is described as sitting at the top of the two-row SUV size class, just below vehicles large enough to offer a meaningful third row.

3. **Tesla Autopilot removal noted:** The hosts briefly discuss that Tesla has removed Autopilot from new vehicles entirely (not just the base trim), attributing the decision to Tesla not wanting to maintain a separate software stack alongside FSD. This leaves new Tesla buyers with either basic cruise control or full FSD — no intermediate Autopilot tier.

4. **Platt Auto's Tesla inventory:** The dealership carries a broad Tesla lineup including a 2020 Model S, a 2018 Model X, Highland and older Model 3s, and multiple Model Y's — described as "the whole sexy arrangement," missing only a Roadster and Cybertruck.

Notable quotes and data:
- Wagoneer S used price: ~$40,000 ("almost half off" new)
- Battery: ~100 kWh, NMC chemistry, US-made
- Stated range: just over 300 miles
- Curb weight: just under 6,000 lbs
- Ground clearance: ~8-point-something inches (vs. Model Y's ~6.5 inches)
- Mileage on this example: ~4,000 miles
- "Sport mode automatically turns off traction control, which I think is ridiculous."
- "Nissan has been doing a decent job of [one-pedal calibration] for over a decade."
- "People that have been showing interest in this have been cross-shopping to top-end Model Y's."
- Tesla Autopilot described as fully removed from new vehicles, leaving buyers with "nothing or FSD."

articles.title: Why The SpaceX Timeline Just ACCELERATED
articles.body:
This video from Jo Bhakdi covers the emerging thesis around orbital AI data centers, centered on SpaceX's growing partnerships with major tech companies (Google and Anthropic) to deploy compute satellites in space. Bhakdi argues that a severe terrestrial energy crisis — driven by surging AI electricity demand — makes space-based compute not just viable but inevitable, and that SpaceX's Starship is the critical bottleneck and monopoly asset enabling this transition. The video also touches on implications for Tesla shareholders in the context of a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger.

## Market & Competition

1. **Google and Anthropic Partner with SpaceX for Orbital AI Compute:** Bhakdi highlights two major breaking developments: Anthropic announced a deal to access SpaceX's Colossus One terrestrial AI data center (described as a massive compute facility originally built by xAI and then acquired by SpaceX), and as part of that agreement, expressed interest in partnering with SpaceX to develop "multiple gigawatts" of orbital AI compute capacity. Shortly after, Google announced it is in talks with SpaceX to place an orbital data center in outer space. Bhakdi claims he was among the first to model the economics of orbital AI compute, doing so in November of the prior year.

2. **Terrestrial Energy Crisis as the Core Driver:** Bhakdi presents data showing AI and cloud compute consumed 4% of total U.S. electricity in 2023, rising to 7% in 2026, projected to reach 20% by 2030 and 50% by 2035 — a trajectory he describes as completely unsustainable. He notes that gas turbines are the only near-term tactical solution, but that the three companies that manufacture them globally (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, and Mitsubishi Power) have order books stretched to 2029–2030, and turbine prices have nearly tripled since 2019, reaching approximately $600 per kilowatt by end of 2027. He concludes that the energy buildout cannot keep pace with AI demand on Earth.

3. **Space Compute as the Energy Solution:** Bhakdi argues that orbital data centers solve the energy crisis because space provides approximately five times more solar energy per square foot per day compared to Earth, with 24/7 sunlight, 40% higher solar flux, and no need for batteries. He adds that space requires no land lease, no water cooling, and no grid infrastructure. The only meaningful cost becomes orbital lift, which he frames as entirely dependent on Starship's cost-per-kilogram trajectory.

4. **Starship Lift Cost as the Unlock:** Bhakdi states that current heavy-lift costs run approximately $25,000 per kilogram, and that Starship is projected to bring this down to $200 per kilogram — which he describes as a 10x cut he expects to be achievable by 2027. He further references a theoretical endpoint of $10 per kilogram but says he'll believe it when he sees it. He argues that the $200/kg figure alone is sufficient to economically justify shifting all AI compute buildout to space, and predicts this transition will begin in earnest in 2027, not 2029 or 2030.

5. **SpaceX's Satellite Launch Dominance:** Bhakdi cites a chart from analyst Christian Kyle showing that SpaceX is now only approximately 200 satellites away from having launched as many satellites as the rest of the world combined in all of history — with the rest of the world at 15,662 total historical launches. He uses this to characterize SpaceX as holding a monopoly on orbital access, comparing it to having a monopoly on ships during the age of exploration.

6. **Hyperscaler Race to Space:** Bhakdi predicts that rather than purchasing Elon's satellites, major hyperscalers will each book Starship capacity to launch their own proprietary space compute. He forecasts that Amazon will be the next announced partner, followed by Microsoft and Oracle, with a final landscape of approximately five or six "space clouds" — SpaceX, Google, Anthropic, Amazon, Microsoft, and possibly Oracle — each owning orbital AI infrastructure. He argues Elon is strategically correct not to monopolize all space compute, as diversity prevents political and reputational backlash.

7. **Ron Baron on SpaceX IPO Mechanics:** Bhakdi closes with a clip of investor Ron Baron discussing the SpaceX IPO. Baron notes that approximately $70 billion of the offering would be available to public investors, and describes an accelerated index inclusion timeline in which SpaceX would be added to one index five days post-IPO, a second index at ten days, and a third at fifteen days. Baron confirms SpaceX has chosen to list on NASDAQ rather than the NYSE. Baron also explains the "not in my backyard" political dynamic — citing governors in New Jersey and Virginia running on platforms opposing data center construction due to rising electricity bills and water usage — as a further political tailwind for moving compute to space.

## Financials

1. **Tesla-SpaceX Merger Thesis and Robotaxi Cash Flow:** Bhakdi argues that Tesla's robotaxi cash flows — which he projects to reach "hundreds of billions of dollars" in 2027 and 2028 — will need to be channeled into SpaceX to fund Starship production at the scale required for the orbital AI buildout. He frames the Tesla-SpaceX merger as a necessary capital formation mechanism for building what he calls "infinity starships." He expresses personal comfort with the merger timing, dismissing debates about whether Tesla should delay the merger to let its stock price run higher first.

Notable quotes and data:
- "By 2030, that's three years from now, it's going to be 20% of the entire US energy is going to be sucked into AI data centers. By 2035, projected 50%."
- "Turbine prices have nearly tripled since 2019, being $600 per kilowatt by end of 2027."
- "You cannot buy a new gas turbine until 2030. Order books at GE, Siemens Energy stretch to 2029."
- "SpaceX is only 200 satellites away from having launched as many satellites as the rest of the world combined." (Rest of world total: 15,662 historical launches, per Christian Kyle chart)
- Starship lift cost trajectory: ~$25,000/kg today → $200/kg projected by ~2027 → theoretical $10/kg long-term
- Space solar energy advantage: 5x more energy per square foot per day vs. Earth; 40% higher solar flux; 24/7 sunlight
- Anthropic deal includes expressed interest in "multiple gigawatts of orbital AI compute capacity"
- Ron Baron: ~$70 billion of SpaceX IPO available to public; index inclusions at 5, 10, and 15 days post-IPO; NASDAQ listing confirmed
- "We will need to get the robo taxi cash flow in 2027 and 8, which will be hundreds of billions of dollars, into SpaceX so they can build infinity starships."
- SpaceX valuation referenced: $2.2 trillion (attributed to institutional investor framing around the IPO)

articles.title: Tesla Semi Walkaround & Discussion at ACT Expo w/ Dan Priestley
articles.body:
This video features a walkthrough and technical discussion of the Tesla Semi at the ACT Expo, conducted by Munro Live with Dan Priestley, Tesla's Director of Engineering for the Semi truck. The conversation covers the engineering philosophy behind the Semi's design — particularly aerodynamics, drivetrain architecture, battery integration, and total cost of ownership — and how Tesla's experience from its passenger car lineup informed the Semi's development. The overarching thesis is that Tesla's integrated, efficiency-first approach gives the Semi a meaningful structural and economic advantage over both traditional diesel trucks and competing electric heavy-duty vehicles.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Aerodynamics as the primary efficiency lever:** Dan Priestley explains that aerodynamic drag accounts for approximately 50% of the energy required to move the truck down the road. Tesla's approach to minimizing drag compounds into significant savings: less drag means less battery needed, which means less mass, which in turn requires even less structural support — a cascading efficiency benefit. This philosophy drove decisions from the ground up, borrowing lessons from Tesla's passenger car side, including smooth underbody treatment, careful study of airflow around wheels and tires, and extensive wind tunnel testing.
