2. **Hard-mounted cab eliminates gap-related drag:** Unlike traditional trucks where the cab is independently suspended and creates large gaps relative to the chassis — gaps that are aerodynamically costly — the Tesla Semi uses a hard-mounted cab integrated directly with the frame structure. Priestley explains this was made possible in part because the electric drivetrain eliminates the longitudinal driveshaft found in diesel trucks, which causes the whole chassis to twist under torque. By treating the battery structure and chassis as a unified system — analogous to a unibody — Tesla was able to lock down the integrated "skateboard" (chassis, drivetrain, battery, front subframe) and eliminate the need for cab compliance, enabling a cleaner aerodynamic envelope.

3. **Two variants targeting different operational needs:** The long-range variant offers 500 miles on a single charge and can haul a 45,000 lb payload with a typical drive van, achieving both time parity and payload parity with diesel operations. Charging is designed to occur during mandatory driver rest periods (per hours-of-service regulations), meaning no dedicated charge downtime. The standard-range variant is positioned for operators who are more mass-sensitive or don't require the extended range, offering a lighter and potentially more cost-effective option.

4. **Dual e-axle drivetrain architecture:** Rather than a longitudinal driveshaft, the Semi uses directly mounted motors on the drive axles. The mid (fourth) axle is the "torque axle," equipped with two independently driven motors — one per wheel — optimized for high-power events like takeoffs and steep-grade overtaking. The rear axle is the "efficiency axle." The two axles are geared differently but share many common components including oil pumps, rotor/stator assemblies, and inverters. At highway cruise speeds, the torque axle disconnects entirely — wheels continue to spin freely with no internal windage losses — delivering the traction benefits of a 6x4 configuration with the efficiency of a 6x2.

5. **Cross-platform component sharing from Tesla's broader lineup:** Priestley highlights significant parts commonality across Tesla's vehicle family as a key enabler of reliability and cost control. The drive inverter and stator are shared with the Cybertruck. The HVAC compressor is shared with the Cybercab. Light modules are shared from other Tesla vehicles. Screens are also carried over. This commonization reduces bespoke component costs and leverages proven reliability from high-volume production.

6. **Total cost of ownership as the central design ethos:** Priestley frames TCO as the unifying objective that benefits all three key stakeholders: the driver, the fleet owner, and the shipper. For drivers, Tesla has developed an in-house seat architecture and focused on comfort. For fleet managers, the emphasis is on day-in, day-out reliability. For shippers, the benefit is reduced freight costs through lower energy throughput. Priestley stresses that the product must work for all three simultaneously to be commercially viable.

7. **Charging infrastructure buildout underway:** Tesla currently has approximately 50 charging sites in various stages of development for the Semi, with some expected to open within the next month or two (from the time of filming). Priestley states that Tesla's philosophy is that every truck delivered must have a charging solution already identified and available on day one — charging deployment must match truck delivery. Tesla is also now selling charging hardware directly online: a V4 fast charger with 1.2 megawatt capability and a base charger rated at 125 kilowatts, available for fleet operators or third parties building out charging infrastructure. The broader Tesla Supercharger team has deployed more than 80,000 DC fast charging posts worldwide, providing institutional expertise in utility coordination and rapid deployment.

Notable quotes and data:
- "Aerodynamics are key because it's about 50% of the energy that you use just to move the truck down the road." — Dan Priestley
- Long-range variant: 500 miles on a single charge, 45,000 lb payload capacity with a typical drive van
- ~50 Semi charging sites currently in some stage of development
- V4 Semi charger: 1.2 megawatt capability; base charger: 125 kilowatts
- Tesla Supercharger network: more than 80,000 DC fast charging posts deployed worldwide
- Drive inverter and stator shared with Cybertruck; HVAC compressor shared with Cybercab
- "The twin axle setup here really gives an operator all the benefits of a 6x4 in terms of maximum traction, torque, and power to do the job while also then all of the efficiency of a 6x2." — Dan Priestley
- Future plans: Priestley confirmed ongoing improvements are in development and expressed enthusiasm about getting the Semi into high volume production

articles.title: Daily X Summary (2026-05-12)
articles.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts paint a broadly bullish picture for Tesla investors, led by a strong stock performance note (TSLA +33% over the past month, approaching all-time highs), a notable analyst call from Piper Sandler arguing Optimus is essentially "free" at current valuations, and meaningful operational milestones at Giga Berlin. Secondary themes include new vehicle color/model launches, Tesla Semi's European website appearance, FSD deployment in a factory context, and a Supercharger infrastructure update. No major negative catalysts were flagged.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **TSLA Stock Performance — Near All-Time High After Historic Month:** Sawyer flagged that $TSLA is up 33% over the past month — described as one of its best months ever — and now sits just 11.5% away from a new all-time high. With 4,300 likes and 294 retweets, this was the highest-engagement post of the day and reflects significant retail and investor attention. No specific price target or dollar figure was stated, but the momentum framing is a relevant sentiment signal for Tesla thesis tracking.

2. **Piper Sandler: Optimus "Free" at $400/Share; FSD Metrics Gaining Primacy:** Piper Sandler analyst Alex Potter made a notable bull case, writing that at $400/share investors are effectively getting Optimus for free. Potter also noted that traditionally relevant financial metrics are becoming less important as FSD subscriber counts grow — a direct signal that the sell-side is beginning to weight the autonomous/robotics thesis more heavily in valuation frameworks. No specific Optimus revenue estimate or DCF input was provided, but the framing reinforces the long-term optionality argument central to the Tesla Thesis.

3. **Giga Berlin Milestones — 750K Model Ys Built, 20% Production Scale-Up Underway, 93K FSD Miles on Factory Floor:** Tesla announced it has produced over 750,000 Model Ys at Giga Berlin since the factory opened in 2022 and is currently scaling production by 20%. Separately, Tesla disclosed that Model Ys rolling off the Berlin production line have now autonomously driven a combined 93,000 miles on FSD from the end of the production line to the outbound lot — a real-world FSD deployment milestone that also serves as a safety and reliability data point in a controlled but operationally meaningful environment.

4. **Tesla Semi Appears on European Websites — 2027 Launch Window, Key Specs Listed:** The Tesla Semi is now appearing on Tesla's European websites including the UK. Only the Standard Range trim is listed. Specs disclosed: ~550 km range, 1.0 kWh per kilometer energy consumption. European launch is expected in 2027 at the earliest. The kWh/km figure is a directly usable efficiency datapoint (equivalent to approximately 1.61 kWh per mile).

5. **New Marine Blue Color Launches on Model 3 and Model Y Premium; Model S/X Signature Event Rescheduled:** Tesla introduced a new "Marine Blue" exterior color on the Model 3 Premium and Model Y Premium in the U.S. last week. The color is described as darker than Tesla's existing Glacier Blue and Frost Blue options. Deep Blue Metallic was simultaneously discontinued after a decade in Tesla's lineup. Separately, the Model S and Model X Signature Edition delivery event has been rescheduled to May 20, 2026.

6. **Supercharger Infrastructure Updates — Virtual Queue Live at 5 Locations, Site Maps Now in Canada:** Tesla's new virtual queue feature for Superchargers is now live at 5 locations. Additionally, the Supercharger Site Maps feature — which provides a detailed visual layout of charging stations on the vehicle touchscreen — has officially launched in Canada. Both are incremental infrastructure quality-of-life improvements relevant to network utilization and customer experience.

7. **Ford Energy Launch — Competitive Context for Tesla Energy:** Ford officially introduced "Ford Energy," offering U.S.-assembled LFP prismatic battery energy storage systems in 2-hour and 4-hour configurations, with availability planned for late 2027. While this signals growing competition in the stationary storage space, Tesla's Megapack business has a substantial head start in scale, deployment, and manufacturing maturity.

8. **Former Tesla CFO Deepak Ahuja Joins Redwood Materials:** Deepak Ahuja, Tesla's CFO during two stints (2008–2015 and 2017–early 2019), has joined EV battery recycler Redwood Materials as its new CFO. Redwood was founded by JB Straubel, a current Tesla board member and former CTO. Tangential to Tesla but relevant for battery supply chain dynamics.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — Strong stock momentum, a high-profile analyst arguing Optimus carries zero cost at current prices, and tangible FSD + production milestones at Giga Berlin collectively reinforce the core Tesla Thesis without any meaningful negative datapoints today.

articles.title: SpaceX Could Become The World’s Biggest Company
articles.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel features host Herbert and guest Jo Bhakdi, an economist, investor, and tech entrepreneur, discussing Ron Baron's long-term bets on Elon Musk, the impending SpaceX IPO, the emerging space-based AI compute thesis, and the debate among Tesla shareholders over a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger. The core argument is that SpaceX's ability to deploy orbital AI data centers represents a virtually limitless economic opportunity, and that the SpaceX IPO — expected in June 2026 — will be a defining moment for both SpaceX and Tesla investors.

## Market & Competition

1. **Ron Baron's Elon Musk investment thesis:** Legendary investor Ron Baron of Baron Funds is highlighted as having made approximately $20 billion in profits for clients through investments tied to Elon Musk. Baron's firm holds roughly $15 billion in SpaceX and $5 billion in Tesla. Baron began investing in Tesla between 2014 and 2016, putting in approximately $400 million and generating about $8 billion in profit so far. He started investing in SpaceX in 2017, putting in approximately $1.7 billion, which is now worth approximately $15 billion at current market prices — nearly a 10x return.

2. **SpaceX valuation and IPO expectations:** Ron Baron believes SpaceX will be worth $10 trillion, $20 trillion, or even $30 trillion over the next 10 to 15 years, stating he could be "very low" on those projections. The SpaceX IPO is described as coming in late June 2026 on NASDAQ. Betting markets are projecting the SpaceX IPO will close above $2.2 trillion on its first day, with the IPO itself expected to price around $1.7 trillion. Baron also notes that after the IPO, SpaceX will be added to multiple indexes within 5, 10, and 15 days respectively, forcing large institutional investors and pension funds to buy the stock.

3. **Space-based AI compute as the core SpaceX thesis:** Jo Bhakdi argues that space-based AI data centers represent the single most transformative economic opportunity in human history, comparing it to the colonial-era race to capture global resources. The thesis is that there is unlimited demand for AI compute, the only bottleneck is energy, and deploying AI satellites in orbit circumvents terrestrial energy and regulatory constraints. Jo Bhakdi identifies four dominant players as likely owners of this orbital compute layer: SpaceX, Google, Amazon, and Microsoft.

4. **Anthropic and Google partnerships signaling orbital compute buildout:** The video highlights two key recent deals: SpaceX's deal with Anthropic, reportedly generating $5–6 billion per year from leasing the Colossus One terrestrial data center in Memphis, with a planned space-based component as well; and ongoing negotiations between SpaceX and Google to explore orbital data centers under Google's "Project Suncatcher," with Google planning to launch prototype satellites in early 2027. Google is noted to hold approximately a 5–6% stake in SpaceX from a 2015 investment. Jo Bhakdi expects Amazon to announce a similar deal soon.

5. **Jo Bhakdi's tactical caution on the SpaceX IPO:** Despite being "infinitely bullish" on SpaceX's long-term value — calling $30 trillion achievable "sooner than later" — Jo Bhakdi says he will not buy the IPO. His reasoning is that there is significant forward pull into the IPO price, the broader market has run up strongly, and he believes there is a high probability of getting SpaceX at a lower price during a market correction in the following 12–24 months. He estimates the real "forcing function" for SpaceX's exponential trajectory begins around 2028 or 2029.

## Robotaxi

1. **Tesla-SpaceX merger debate among Tesla shareholders:** Betting markets are currently giving a 50% probability that Tesla and SpaceX merge within the next year. A significant debate exists in the Tesla investor community, with one camp arguing a merger would be unfair to Tesla shareholders who have waited years for the robotaxi revenue ramp to materialize, and another camp viewing SpaceX as a merger of equals that brings enormous value. Jo Bhakdi argues that the premise of the anti-merger argument — that Tesla is massively underpriced right now but will be fairly priced in a few months — is flawed because markets have become much more efficient and informed about the Tesla robotaxi thesis.

2. **Merger ratio and "magnet effect" thesis:** Jo Bhakdi develops a qualitative thesis that if a Tesla-SpaceX merger is widely anticipated, the two companies' market caps will converge toward a one-to-one ratio. His reasoning: it would be unusual for Tesla to be valued higher than SpaceX in a merger, and a ratio significantly below one-to-one would likely be rejected by Tesla shareholders. This creates what he calls a "magnet effect," where Tesla's market cap is pulled toward SpaceX's market cap. Tesla's market cap at time of discussion is cited as approximately $1.33 trillion, while SpaceX's IPO valuation is expected around $2.2 trillion, implying meaningful upside for Tesla if the thesis holds.

3. **SpaceX IPO as a potential catalyst for Tesla stock:** Host Herbert relays a view from commentator "Larry" that the SpaceX IPO alone — even without any merger announcement — could push Tesla's stock up 10–15%. Jo Bhakdi is skeptical of this specific claim, arguing the IPO is not new information to markets, though he acknowledges the magnet effect thesis could provide some mechanism for Tesla appreciation if merger speculation remains active.

Notable quotes and data:
- Ron Baron: "I've invested about a billion 7 since 2017 and that's now worth about 15 billion at current market prices."
- Ron Baron on SpaceX future value: "I think that the company over the next 10 or 15 years is going to be worth 10 trillion, 20 trillion, 30 trillion. And I could be very low."
- Jo Bhakdi: "I think it's going to be 2028 or 29 when this infinity trajectory starts. Then there's no hold back."
- Jo Bhakdi on SpaceX IPO tactics: "The odds that you get this cheaper are just insanely high. So I'm definitely waiting."
- Betting markets: 50% probability of Tesla-SpaceX merger within the next year.
- Betting markets: SpaceX IPO projected to close above $2.2 trillion.
- SpaceX IPO expected on NASDAQ in late June 2026.
- SpaceX to be added to three separate indexes within 5, 10, and 15 days post-IPO.
- Baron Funds total profits tied to Elon Musk investments: approximately $20 billion.
- Baron's Tesla investment: approximately $400 million invested 2014–2016, approximately $8 billion profit to date.
- Anthropic deal cited as potentially generating $5–6 billion per year for SpaceX from Colossus One.
- Google holds approximately 5–6% of SpaceX from a 2015 investment.
- Google "Project Suncatcher" prototype satellites planned for early 2027.
- Tesla market cap referenced at approximately $1.33 trillion at time of discussion.

articles.title: Two Theories on How Cybercab Actually Rolls Out
articles.body:
This video from "brighterwithherbert" presents two contrarian theories about how Tesla's Cybercab will actually roll out into commercial robotaxi service. The host argues that despite Cybercabs actively rolling off the line at Giga Texas, the vehicle will stay out of live passenger service for at least two to three months while accumulating form-factor-specific training miles — and that when it does launch, it will do so at scale across multiple cities simultaneously rather than as a slow trickle.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab production is ramping but not yet in passenger service:** Based on drone footage from Joe Tegtmeyer, Cybercabs are currently being produced at an estimated 20–40 units per day at Giga Texas. By early March, 25 units were spotted in a single day across three locations; by late April, groupings of 50–60+ were visible in the staging lot. Despite this production ramp, not a single Cybercab has entered the live robotaxi fleet — all 39 unsupervised vehicles currently in service (per RobotaxiTracker.com) are Model Ys, split across Austin (28), Dallas (5), and Houston (6).

2. **Theory One — Cybercab stays out of live service for two to three months:** The host argues Tesla needs to accumulate roughly 50–100 million miles of Cybercab-specific real-world driving data before trusting the new form factor with unsupervised passenger service. The Cybercab has a different ride height, camera placement, weight distribution, sensor configuration, and autonomous-only steering and braking system compared to the Model Y fleet that generated Tesla's 10 billion FSD supervised miles. The host estimates a fleet of roughly 1,000 Cybercabs driving constantly for two to three months — with Tesla employees behind the wheel and engineers in the passenger seat — would be sufficient to validate the platform's unique characteristics.

3. **Brand protection as a second rationale for slow-rolling Cybercab:** The host cites the Cruise implosion in 2023 — where a single pedestrian-dragging incident shut down the entire program — as a cautionary tale. He argues Tesla cannot afford an early high-profile Cybercab incident, since the vehicle is the visible face of the company's entire autonomous thesis. Any symbolic one-off Cybercab passenger ride before the full launch (e.g., at a Q2 earnings event or via an Elon Musk tweet) should be treated as a PR moment, not a real transition.

4. **Theory Two — Fleet composition of 100 Model Ys plus 900 Cybercabs per city:** The host proposes a target fleet structure based on Uber and Lyft ride-share data showing roughly 90% of rides involve two passengers or fewer. Since Cybercab seats exactly two and Model Y seats five, the host argues the natural fleet ratio is 90% Cybercab and 10% Model Y. At 1,000 vehicles per city, that means 900 Cybercabs handling the bulk volume and 100 Model Ys covering the 10% of rides requiring more than two seats. This is described not as a fleet composition but as a deliberate service design.

5. **Phased rollout timeline — summer Model Y density, Q3/Q4 Cybercab launch:** The host projects that by August or September 2026, the Model Y unsupervised fleet will have grown to 100 vehicles each in Austin, Dallas, and Houston, and Tesla will have launched Model Y robotaxi service in expansion cities including Phoenix, Miami, Las Vegas, Orlando, Tampa, and possibly San Antonio. After Cybercab accumulates ~70–80 million internal miles, the host expects Tesla to deploy roughly 1,000 Cybercabs simultaneously in each of the three Texas cities — choosing a large simultaneous launch over a trickle to create a demonstration moment.

6. **33-city signal from Tesla job postings:** The host highlights that a researcher reviewing Tesla's open autonomy operations job postings on X identified 33 US cities where Tesla is actively hiring for robotaxi-related roles. The host treats this as a more reliable forward signal than any public Elon Musk statement, noting that quiet staffing decisions reflect real operational intent. At even 100 vehicles per city across all 33, that yields 3,300 vehicles from expansion markets alone, before factoring in Texas density.

7. **End-of-year fleet size range — 3,300 to 15,000 robotaxis:** The host lays out a production math check: at 30 Cybercabs per day average over roughly 150 days from May to October, Tesla could produce approximately 4,500 units, with the ramp expected to accelerate to potentially 5,000–10,000 by year-end. Three Texas cities at ~1,100 vehicles each (~3,300) plus 5–7 expansion cities at 500–1,500 vehicles each yields a combined range of roughly 6,000–12,000, putting total fleet near 15,000 in the optimistic scenario. The conservative floor of 3,300 assumes only Texas density and 33-city breadth at minimal vehicle counts.

8. **Three investor scenarios for H2 2026:** Scenario one: Tesla executes the full plan — Model Y density grows through summer, Cybercab data period runs in parallel, Q3/Q4 brings a simultaneous multi-city Cybercab launch, year ends at ~15,000+ robotaxis, and the stock gets re-rated as a transport platform. Scenario two: Tesla executes a careful version — Cybercab pushes to early 2027, year ends at 3,000–5,000 robotaxis, stock holds current multiples without a re-rating. Scenario three: A regulatory snag, tech issue, or high-profile incident leaves the fleet under 1,000 unsupervised vehicles at year-end, with a negative stock impact. The host suggests the market is currently pricing in somewhere between scenarios two and three, implying real upside if scenario one materializes.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Version 15 as a gating event for full-scale launch:** The host notes Tesla has stated it is waiting for FSD version 15 before launching at "super scale." He flags the FSD version release cadence as a key monitoring signal — a version bump to 15 would be a meaningful indicator that the large-scale Cybercab rollout is imminent.

2. **10 billion supervised FSD miles — but almost all on Model Y and Model 3:** Tesla recently hit the 10 billion FSD supervised mile milestone, which Elon Musk previously cited as the threshold needed for safe unsupervised driving. However, the host emphasizes that nearly all of those miles were accumulated on Model Y and Model 3 platforms, meaning the Cybercab restarts a form-factor-specific learning curve — not from zero, but not from 10 billion miles either.

## Market & Competition

1. **Waymo as the baseline for fleet scale context:** The host notes that even with 100 unsupervised Model Ys per Texas city (300 total), Tesla's fleet would still be well below what Waymo operates in Phoenix and San Francisco, framing this as a meaningful growth step but not yet competitive parity in those markets.

2. **Cruise as the cautionary tale for premature deployment:** The host explicitly references Cruise's 2023 collapse — a single pedestrian-dragging incident led to the entire program being shut down and the company effectively folding — as the primary case study driving Tesla's expected caution. This is presented as the institutional memory shaping Tesla's brand-protection rationale for delaying Cybercab's live passenger debut.

---

**Notable quotes and data:**

- Current unsupervised robotaxi fleet per RobotaxiTracker.com: 39 vehicles — Austin 28, Dallas 5, Houston 6 — all Model Ys, zero Cybercabs
- Cybercab production rate: estimated 20–40 units/day currently at Giga Texas, based on Joe Tegtmeyer drone footage
- Elon Musk's long-term Cybercab production target: one every 10 seconds, eventually one every 5 seconds
- Tesla hit 10 billion FSD supervised miles; Elon Musk cited this as the threshold for safe unsupervised driving
- Tesla is actively hiring for robotaxi-related roles in 33 US cities per job posting analysis on X
- Tesla reportedly delayed 5 of 7 planned city launches and softened language from "first half of 2026" to "a dozen states by end of year"
- Q2 2026 earnings call (late July) flagged as the first opportunity to get official Cybercab production numbers from Tesla
- Proposed fleet target: 900 Cybercabs + 100 Model Ys per city, based on ride-share data showing ~90% of rides involve two or fewer passengers
- Production math: 30/day × 150 days = ~4,500 Cybercabs producible May–October; modest ramp could yield 5,000–10,000 by year-end
- Proposed Cybercab data accumulation target before passenger service: 50–100 million miles over ~2–3 months on ~1,000 units
- "You don't get a second chance to launch a brand."
- Switch-flip timing estimate: "somewhere between September and November"

articles.title: BYD surpasses Tesla as world’s top energy storage deployer
articles.body:
BYD overtook Tesla in 2025 to become the world's largest battery energy storage system (BESS) integrator, capturing 13% of the global market versus Tesla's 10%, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence data.

## Energy
1. **BYD ships 60+ GWh vs. Tesla's 46.7 GWh in 2025:** BYD shipped over 60 GWh of energy storage systems globally in 2025, ranking first among all BESS integrators. Tesla deployed 46.7 GWh — a 49% year-over-year increase — but still lost its top position it had held in 2023 and 2024. Sungrow ranked third at 9% market share, followed by CRRC Zhuzhou, CATL, and Hyper Strong (6% each), Huawei and Envision (5% each), and Fluence and Sunwoda (4% each). Eight of the top 10 integrators are Chinese companies.

2. **Global BESS market nearly doubled:** Global BESS installations jumped 51% in 2025 to approximately 315 GWh, while cell shipments for stationary storage nearly doubled to over 600 GWh. China installed 65 GWh of large-scale battery storage in December 2025 alone — more than the entire U.S. deployed over the full year.

3. **BYD's HaoHan vs. Tesla's Megapack 3:** BYD unveiled its HaoHan storage system in September 2025 with a 14.5 MWh standard configuration (nearly three times Tesla's Megapack capacity), plus a 20-foot container variant at 10 MWh. A HaoHan deployment of 12.5 GWh is underway in Saudi Arabia with the Saudi Electricity Company. Tesla responded in the same month with Megapack 3 and Megablock, featuring 5 MWh per unit (up from 3.9 MWh in Megapack 2). Tesla is building its Houston Megafactory toward 50 GWh annual capacity by late 2026 and signed a $4.3 billion LFP battery deal with LG Energy Solution for cells starting August 2027.

4. **Structural cost dynamics — integrators vs. vertically integrated players:** Benchmark data shows vertically integrated cell-BESS companies have been losing market share since 2023 as falling battery prices expanded options for pure integrators. Pure integrators grew their combined share from 20% in 2023 to 30% in H1 2025. BYD is the exception — its battery division produced over 113 GWh in the first three quarters of 2025 alone. Tesla, by contrast, sources Megapack cells from CATL, BYD, and soon LG.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert argues BYD's ascent was inevitable given HaoHan's capacity advantage and BYD's vertically integrated structure, and warns that Tesla's reliance on competitors (CATL and BYD) for cells is a structural vulnerability the Houston Megafactory and LG deal must urgently address, as Chinese dominance of the market is already overwhelming.

Notable quotes and data:
- BYD: 13% global BESS market share in 2025; Tesla: 10%
- BYD shipped >60 GWh; Tesla deployed 46.7 GWh (+49% YoY)
- Global BESS installations: ~315 GWh in 2025 (+51% YoY); cell shipments >600 GWh
- China installed 65 GWh in December 2025 alone
- BYD HaoHan: 14.5 MWh standard config; 10 MWh container variant
- BYD's 12.5 GWh project in Saudi Arabia — among world's largest grid-scale BESS deployments
- Tesla Megapack 3: ~5 MWh per unit (up from 3.9 MWh)
- Tesla Houston Megafactory target: 50 GWh annual capacity by late 2026
- Tesla–LG Energy Solution deal: $4.3 billion, LFP cells for Megapack 3 starting August 2027
- BYD battery division: 113 GWh produced in first three quarters of 2025
- 8 of top 10 BESS integrators are Chinese; only Fluence (Siemens/AES JV) joins Tesla as non-Chinese

articles.title: I Was Wrong About Tesla's Cybercab (Important Update) ⚡️
articles.body:
In this video, host Dillon Loomis of the "electrified" channel walks back his earlier prediction that the Cybercab would hit the robotaxi network by September 15th, replacing it with a revised July 2026 timeline. He explains why he was wrong — specifically that the challenges Tesla faced getting FSD to work on the Cybertruck (rear-wheel steering, variable steering ratio, camera placement) do not apply to the Cybercab — and argues that Tesla is actually very well-positioned to port FSD to the Cybercab relatively easily. He also introduces a new self-built robotaxi tracking dashboard called "Tesla Autonomy" and covers broader Tesla news including Dallas and Austin robotaxi experience reports, Giga Shanghai production records, a Giga Berlin cell factory investment, and Waymo's expansion plans.

## Robotaxi

1. **Revised Cybercab deployment timeline — now July 2026:** Loomis formally revises his Cybercab robotaxi deployment prediction from September 15th to July 2026. He reasons that Tesla needs roughly three full months from the start of production to validate the unboxed manufacturing method, confirm safety tolerances, and ensure the Etherloop is working reliably across all production units. He acknowledges the timeline could be even sooner, but notes Tesla has no reason to rush since the Model Y is functioning adequately at the current small scale.

2. **Dallas robotaxi service struggling with navigation and availability:** A report from Spencer described the worst robotaxi move he had seen in recent months — a car attempting to turn onto a street, getting stuck, and blocking the road for nearly a minute. Reuters also tested the Dallas service and found it plagued by long wait times and sometimes no availability at all, with drop-off spots sometimes far from the rider's destination. One reporter tried for 30 minutes to book a ride, was repeatedly met with "high demand" or "service unavailable," and after 36 minutes finally got a ride with a 19-minute wait. On another ride, what should have been a 20-minute drive to city hall took nearly 2 hours, and Tesla support confirmed the area around city hall was not yet in the service zone.

3. **Austin robotaxi wait time data — half of rides over 15 minutes:** Reuters cited a recent slideshow from Austin officials indicating Tesla is operating approximately 50 vehicles in Austin, compared to more than 250 Waymo vehicles in Austin. A reporter who spent 3 weeks in April 2026 tracking wait times found that wait times exceeded 15 minutes about half the time, were at least 25 minutes more than 25% of the time, and 27% of the time no cars were available at all. Loomis acknowledges the Reuters framing tends to be negative on Tesla but believes in this case it is a realistic representation of the experience for non-Tesla fans.

4. **Cybercab FSD porting should be easier than Cybertruck:** Loomis corrects his prior video's implicit assumption that FSD porting to the Cybercab would be as difficult as it was on the Cybertruck. He clarifies that the Cybertruck's challenges — rear-wheel (four-wheel) steering, variable steering ratio, and non-standard camera placements — do not apply to the Cybercab. The Cybercab has no rear-wheel steering, no physical steering wheel (so no traditional variable steering ratio), is front-wheel drive, uses steer-by-wire with AI-controlled actuators, and has camera placements much closer to the Model 3. He concludes that porting FSD to the Cybercab should be far more straightforward than it was for the Cybertruck.

5. **Cybercab production observed at Giga Texas:** Joe Tegtmeyer reported over 70 Cybercabs in the Giga Texas outbound lot across three major areas, with vehicles driving around — described as the largest single gathering of Cybercabs observed to date. Loomis estimates the daily production rate is still likely in the neighborhood of 5 to 15 units per day and expects hundreds to be shipped across the country for testing and validation.

6. **Pony AI break-even benchmark — 23 rides per vehicle per day:** Loomis highlights that Pony AI announced reaching unit economics break-even in two Tier 1 Chinese cities, with the key metric being an average of 23 orders (rides) per vehicle per day. Loomis flags this as a useful benchmark to store in memory for when Tesla eventually begins reporting its own ride-level data.

7. **Tesla Autonomy dashboard introduced:** Loomis introduces a new self-built robotaxi tracking dashboard called "Tesla Autonomy," vibe-coded using Perplexity Computer (the video's sponsor). Features include an interactive map of active robotaxi cities, a countdown showing days remaining for Tesla to launch in its officially announced cities, a hiring watch list that populates new cities on the map, a head-to-head Tesla vs. Waymo comparison with clickable data points, NHTSA incident data broken down by pre-crash movement, injury severity, and geography (noting 5 of Tesla's 15 incidents involved a stopped Tesla vehicle), and real-time Tesla and NASDAQ prices. The dashboard is available at electrified.plx.app.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Cortex 2 now online and ramping training workloads:** Loomis notes that Cortex 2 has come online and begun running training workloads, as disclosed in Tesla's Q1 earnings deck. Cortex 1 was over 100,000 H100 equivalents; Cortex 2 will be over 130,000 H100 equivalents, though it is still in an early ramp phase. Loomis flags that Tesla likely has materially more compute available now than when it was working on getting FSD running on the Cybertruck, though the exact frontier model status of Cortex 2's workloads is unknown.

2. **Etherloop architecture enables unboxed manufacturing and FSD redundancy:** Loomis explains Tesla's Etherloop system — a high-speed gigabit Ethernet ring running around the car in both directions — as the key enabler of the unboxed manufacturing process. It replaces traditional copper wiring, reducing wiring from approximately 490 wires on the Model 3 to around 155 on the Cybertruck (roughly a 70% reduction), while increasing connection points. Because it is a closed loop running in two directions, it provides built-in redundancy, meaning a severed wire won't interrupt signal delivery. Running on 48 volts, it can carry both power and data, enabling features like active road noise cancellation, integrated audio, and UI controls over the same network. The system runs approximately 200 times faster than older CAN bus wiring with millisecond-level latency, providing headroom for future capabilities including FSD command and camera feed transmission.

3. **Cybercab to use 100% Tesla-designed controllers:** Tesla's own chart shows that controller in-house design has grown from 20% on the Model S to 85% on the Cybertruck, with the Cybercab targeted at 100% Tesla-designed controllers. Loomis contrasts this with Ford, where CEO Jim Farley noted they work with 150 different controller suppliers, each with its own software and language. Waymo also does not develop its own controllers. Loomis argues this vertical integration is part of why Tesla can offer the Cybercab for under $30,000.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Giga Shanghai sets production record through April 2026:** Roland reported that Giga Shanghai produced more cars than ever during the first four months of 2026, with the through-April cumulative production at its highest level ever — ahead of both 2024 and significantly ahead of early 2025 (which was impacted by the Model Y and Model 3 changeover). Loomis notes this is before broader FSD approval in China or the EU.

2. **Giga Berlin $250 million cell factory investment:** André Turinge announced a $250 million investment in a Giga Berlin cell factory that will enable 18 GWh of annual 4680 cell production and create more than 1,500 new jobs. At that production level, Loomis estimates the output would be sufficient for approximately 240,000 vehicles annually, potentially allowing Giga Berlin to supply nearly 100% of its vehicles with in-house 4680 cells once fully ramped. He views this as a signal of Tesla's confidence in its 4680 technology, noting the export of that manufacturing process likely includes dry battery electrode (DBE) technology for both the anode and cathode.

3. **Tesla Semi 500-mile variant demo with Covenant Logistics:** Matt Mullen posted on LinkedIn that Covenant Logistics is running a 3-week demo of the Tesla Semi using the 500-mile variant on a 200-mile round trip, with more details forthcoming.

## Market & Competition

1. **Waymo expanding to Miami, targeting 1,400+ square miles across 11 cities:** Waymo announced expansion into Miami, with Austin, Atlanta, Houston, and the Bay Area listed as next in the pipeline. The company projects coverage of 1,400+ square miles across 11 cities. Loomis plans to incorporate total square miles covered as a comparative metric in his Tesla Autonomy dashboard.

Notable quotes and data:
- Reuters: Tesla operating ~50 vehicles in Austin vs. more than 250 Waymo vehicles in Austin (per Austin officials slideshow)
- Austin wait time study (3 weeks in April 2026): >15 min wait ~50% of the time; ≥25 min wait >25% of the time; no cars available 27% of the time
- Pony AI break-even benchmark: 23 rides per vehicle per day in two Tier 1 Chinese cities
- Cybertruck wiring reduction: ~490 wires (Model 3) → ~155 wires (Cybertruck), ~70% fewer wires
- Etherloop speed: ~200x faster than older CAN bus wiring, millisecond-level latency
- Cortex 1: >100,000 H100 equivalents; Cortex 2: >130,000 H100 equivalents (early ramp)
- Tesla controller in-house design: Model S 20% → Cybertruck 85% → Cybercab 100% (target)
- Cybercab price target referenced: under $30,000
- Joe Tegtmeyer: 70+ Cybercabs observed in Giga Texas outbound lot; estimated production rate 5–15/day
- Giga Berlin: $250M investment, 18 GWh annual 4680 capacity, ~1,500 new jobs, ~240,000 vehicles' worth of cells annually
- Tesla stock close: $445.27, up 2.73%; NASDAQ up 1.04%; volume 4% above average
- Revised Cybercab robotaxi deployment timeline: July 2026 (updated from September 15th prior prediction)

articles.title: Tesla Semi Economics Are Shocking Fleets
articles.body:
This episode of FutureAzA, hosted by Brian with co-host Mark from the Tesla Life, covers recent Tesla Semi news including confirmed battery pack sizes, European market expansion, available government incentives, and a tour of Fremont factory drone footage. The video also addresses viewer questions about Tesla Semi capabilities, payload, charging infrastructure, and competition, along with a recurring "Wrong Answers Only" comedy segment. There is no substantive discussion of autonomous driving, robotaxi, Optimus, or financial results.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Semi Battery Capacity Officially Confirmed:** The official battery capacity for the Tesla Semi has been published: the standard range trim is 548 kWh and the long range trim is 822 kWh. The hosts note these figures confirm the Semi's strong efficiency, as the numbers align closely with what could previously be estimated from known range and efficiency data. The standard range pack is described as roughly one-third smaller than the long range pack, which the hosts note has implications for 4680 cell supply and European manufacturing strategy.

2. **Tesla Semi Arriving on European Websites, Launch Expected 2027 at Earliest:** Tesla Semi has begun appearing on Tesla's websites in Europe, including the UK. Only the standard range trim is listed. The hosts speculate that the shorter distances typical of European trucking make the standard range variant a practical starting point. A European semi factory is speculated to be most likely located at or near Giga Berlin, given existing land, permits, and infrastructure.

3. **Government Incentives Make Tesla Semi Cost-Competitive with Diesel:** California's HVIP program offers between $120,000 and $330,000 in funding per truck. The hosts note the Tesla Semi does not cost $330,000, and that even at the $120,000 incentive level, the net cost drops to approximately $170,000 — described as roughly price parity with a comparable diesel truck. Oregon and Washington state also have incentive programs in place, with more expected. The hosts emphasize that the Semi already makes economic sense for many buyers in incentive-eligible states, particularly on the West Coast.

4. **Tesla Semi Payload Advantage Over Diesel Competitors:** The Tesla Semi is legally permitted to operate at a gross vehicle weight of 82,000 lbs versus the standard 80,000 lb limit for conventional trucks, due to an EV weight exemption. The hosts note that despite the heavier battery pack, Tesla's engineering choices result in only approximately a 2,000 lb weight penalty compared to a comparable diesel truck, meaning Tesla Semi operators can still haul approximately 45,000 lbs of cargo — on par with diesel.

5. **Weight Savings Through Transmission-Free Design:** Unlike other EV semi manufacturers in the US and Europe, Tesla is described as the only company that builds its semi with no traditional transmission. Competitors use two-speed or four-speed transmissions that can weigh up to roughly 1,000–1,500 lbs. Tesla instead uses a clutch system that disengages the second axle during normal loads and engages all motors under heavy load for efficiency. Additional weight savings come from a less reinforced frame (because in-wheel motors eliminate drivetrain torque stress on the chassis) and potentially lighter brakes due to regenerative braking, though the hosts are uncertain on the brakes point. These savings are attributed in part to a video discussion with Dan Priestley and Jordan from Munro Live.

6. **Bobtail Range Estimated at 600–800+ Miles:** A viewer asked about the Tesla Semi's range when running bobtail (no trailer). The hosts note there is no official figure, and that trucking operators generally don't track this metric since an unloaded truck isn't generating revenue. Driver consensus estimates range from approximately 600 to 800 miles, with some suggesting it could reach 900 miles. The hosts clarify this is unconfirmed speculation from driver community feedback.

7. **Nicola Semi Production Context:** The hosts note that Nikola appears to have produced only approximately 2,200 semis in total before ceasing operations, and speculate that Tesla may have already surpassed that cumulative production figure, though they acknowledge uncertainty and ask viewers to research the comparison. One customer, identified in context as Watt EV, placed an order for 370 Tesla Semis — described as a single customer purchase following a trial of the vehicle.

8. **Fremont Factory Observations from Drone Footage:** Drone footage of the Fremont factory from a creator running a new dedicated technical channel (a second channel from an existing creator) shows a congested, space-constrained facility compared to newer Tesla gigafactories. Notable observations include: a patchwork of solar panels on rooftops not originally designed for solar, Starlink gateway terminals on the test track, large quantities of castings staged outdoors near two mostly open-air casting buildings, and surplus empty racks. The hosts note the factory site is smaller than when it was the NUMI plant, as Toyota sold off the northern logistics lot — now converted to condominiums.

9. **Charging Infrastructure and Semi Megacharger Economics:** The hosts address a claim that charging a Tesla Semi requires as much electricity as 3,000 homes — describing this as incorrect. They state that even at its peak draw of one megawatt, the Semi charges at a rate equivalent to roughly 200 homes. They also discuss Tesla's charging network economics, noting that Tesla historically has not profited significantly from charging, instead reinvesting revenues to expand the network. For Semi megachargers, the hosts suggest Tesla would charge a markup but keep margins lean to encourage fleet adoption, consistent with the strategy used for passenger car Superchargers in the early days.

## Market & Competition

1. **Electric Trucks Gaining Traction in China:** The hosts reference a recent admission by commentator Electric Viking, who acknowledged he had previously doubted the viability of electric trucks but noted that electric trucks now hold approximately 25% market share in China. The hosts commend him for publicly acknowledging his prior skepticism was wrong.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla Semi standard range battery: **548 kWh**
- Tesla Semi long range battery: **822 kWh**
- California HVIP incentive range: **$120,000–$330,000 per truck**
- Net cost after minimum HVIP incentive: approximately **$170,000** — described as roughly price parity with diesel
- Tesla Semi gross vehicle weight allowance: **82,000 lbs** vs. standard **80,000 lbs**
- Estimated cargo payload: approximately **45,000 lbs** — on par with diesel
- Competitor transmission weight: estimated **700 lbs to ~1,500 lbs**
- Bobtail range community estimate: **600–900 miles** (unofficial)
- Peak Semi charging draw: **1 megawatt**, equivalent to approximately **200 homes**
- Nikola Semi total production: approximately **2,200 units** (cited by hosts, unverified)
- Single Watt EV Semi order: **370 trucks**
- Electric trucks market share in China: approximately **25%** (per Electric Viking)
- Tesla Semi European launch: **2027 at earliest**, standard range only

articles.title: This Cadillac EV Feels Too Premium
articles.body:
This video is a hands-on test drive review of a used Cadillac Lyriq EV, filmed at Platt Auto in Milwaukie, Oregon with dealer Jack. The hosts evaluate the Lyriq's interior quality, driving dynamics, driver assistance features, and charging specs, ultimately concluding it's a luxury-feel purchase driven by aesthetics and comfort rather than best-in-class EV specs.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cadillac Lyriq Overview and Platform:** The Cadillac Lyriq is built on GM's Ultium platform and is described as the best vehicle GM produces on that platform. It features a 102 kWh battery pack, a stated range of just over 300 miles, and is manufactured in Spring Hill, Tennessee — as is the battery. The battery uses NMCA chemistry. The specific unit on the lot is listed for $45,900 used, with new well-optioned examples having originally sold into the $70,000s.

2. **Driving Dynamics and Performance:** The Lyriq is noted to be front-wheel drive in base configuration, rated at 365 horsepower. The hosts observe that torque delivery is intentionally suppressed at low speeds to avoid wheel spin, with power ramping in more noticeably at higher speeds (around 30–40 mph). The ride is described as composed and well-balanced given the vehicle's weight, with very low road and wind noise inside the cabin.

3. **Interior Quality and Features:** The Lyriq is praised for its premium feel — supple seats, metal door handles, wood trim accents, and a generally upscale tactile experience that surpasses other Ultium-platform vehicles like the Blazer EV. It includes heated and ventilated seats, massaging seats (via a lumbar air bladder that inflates and deflates), an AKG sound system (which the host finds underwhelming for the space), haptic seat vibration alerts for proximity warnings and lane departure, and headrest-integrated speakers. Physical buttons are present in large quantity but criticized for being uniform in size and shape, making them hard to distinguish by feel alone.

4. **Charging Speed Criticism:** The Lyriq charges at a maximum of 190 kW DC, which is the standard rate across all Ultium-platform vehicles (including the Equinox EV, Blazer EV, and others). The hosts note the quoted 10–80% charge time of 30–40 minutes is a best-case figure. They compare this unfavorably to Tesla and the Hyundai/Kia 800-volt architecture vehicles, noting the Lyriq's charge time is roughly double. The large ~102 kWh battery makes the relatively modest charge rate more impactful in real-world use.

5. **Driver Assistance — Super Cruise:** The Lyriq includes GM's Super Cruise system, which operates hands-free on over 400,000 miles of pre-mapped divided highways and supports automatic lane changes (including blinker-initiated lane changes). It does not work on city streets or undivided highways. Super Cruise is a paid subscription service, which the host criticizes, contrasting it with Nissan's ProPilot Assist 2.0 — a comparable pre-mapped hands-free lane-change system that is not subscription-based.

6. **Used Market Availability and Comparable Inventory:** The dealer Platt Auto has been receiving multiple Lyriq units regularly. The lot also has Ford Lightning pickups priced at approximately $36,000 and $42,000 used (Flash and a higher trim), and recently sold six Silverado EVs (large battery variants) to a fleet customer. The hosts note used EV truck inventory has grown as prices have come down to accessible levels.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla FSD vs. Subscription ADAS:** A brief comparison is made between Tesla's Full Self-Driving and GM's Super Cruise subscription model. One host notes they have FSD on one of their two Tesla vehicles because they drive it enough to justify it, while their coworker uses FSD heavily on a 2021 or 2022 Model 3 for a long highway commute in rush-hour traffic. The host expresses a general objection to charging subscriptions for driver assistance features already embedded in the vehicle.

2. **Cadillac's EV Lineup Context:** The hosts briefly survey Cadillac's broader EV lineup, including the Escalade IQ (larger), the Vistiq (mid-size, position relative to Lyriq uncertain), and the Celestiq — described as a hand-built, extremely expensive halo vehicle of which they expect very few to be sold. The Lyriq is positioned as Cadillac's smallest EV.

3. **Charging Rate Competitive Landscape:** The hosts note that while 190 kW is disappointing relative to Tesla and 800-volt Hyundai/Kia products, it is not the worst in the segment — the 2025 Subaru Solterra is still at 100 kW, some Volkswagen ID.4s were at 130 kW for a period, Ford Mustang Mach-E was around 150 kW, and Ford Lightning is 150 kW.

Notable quotes and data:
- Cadillac Lyriq battery: ~102 kWh; stated range: just over 300 miles
- Used asking price at Platt Auto: $45,900; original new price (well-optioned): up to ~$70,000s
- Max DC charging rate: 190 kW (consistent across all Ultium-platform vehicles)
- Quoted 10–80% charge time: 30–40 minutes (best case)
- Horsepower (base trim): 365 hp
- Super Cruise covers 400,000+ miles of pre-mapped divided highways; subscription-based
- Ford Lightning used prices on lot: ~$36,000 and ~$42,000
- Platt Auto recently sold six Silverado EVs (large battery) to a fleet customer
- Jack has been selling EVs for seven and a half years
- Location: Milwaukie, Oregon (just south of Portland)
- *"Tesla dominates"* — host's summary on EV specs comparison
- *"I wouldn't pay the new price for this. The used price is more interesting."*

articles.title: Rating Brokerage Platforms #investing #tsla #trading #stocks #optionstrading
articles.body:
This short video from the "investingagainstthegrain" channel offers a tier-ranking of popular brokerage and trading platforms, evaluating them on criteria such as live data, user interface, ease of trade execution, and available features like implied volatility rank and paper trading. The video is not Tesla-specific and contains no content related to the Tesla Thesis (autonomous driving, robotaxi, Optimus, energy, or EV sales). The core argument is that tastytrade is the best platform for active traders, while most mainstream brokerages fall short.

## Market & Competition
1. **Brokerage Platform Tier Rankings:** The host ranks six platforms across a tier system (S through F). tastytrade receives S tier as the top pick, praised for its clean UI, fewest clicks to execute trades, and its origins among market makers from the CBOE and Wall Street. Interactive Brokers receives A tier, highlighted for broad international accessibility and the availability of Implied Volatility Rank (IVR), a metric the host considers rare and valuable. Thinkorswim receives B tier for its paper trading feature despite a "wonky" user interface. Robinhood is debated between B and C tier, ultimately landing at B tier due to its live 24/7 market data and watchlist feature, though it is characterized as "amateur hour" in terms of full feature depth. Fidelity receives C tier, criticized for lacking live data without manual page refreshes and for its Active Trader Pro platform being considered not genuinely professional. E*TRADE and all remaining unspecified brokerages receive F tier, faulted for poor live data, weak user interfaces, and not being designed for active trading or investing.

Notable quotes and data:
- "They are the ones who created Thinkorswim." — Host on tastytrade's origins
- "It was built by market makers from the CBOE, from Wall Street." — On tastytrade
- "IVR, implied volatility rank… you don't see it on most others." — On Interactive Brokers' standout feature
- "The Active Trader Pro, honestly, there's nothing pro about it." — On Fidelity
- "Use the best tools, my take." — Host's closing philosophy on platform selection

articles.title: Tesla Stock, Trump, Elon And China - The Great WINNING Has Started
articles.body:
Jo Bhakdi delivers a live commentary session covering the macro significance of President Trump's state visit to China — with Elon Musk prominently featured in the delegation — and what it means for Tesla, particularly for Optimus supply chains and trade relations. The video weaves together geopolitical analysis, Tesla stock commentary, and community Q&A, with Bhakdi arguing that easing US-China tensions represent a major bullish catalyst for Tesla and for the broader market. His central thesis is that "the great winning has started" — geopolitical friction is receding, animal spirits are returning, and Tesla is on a trajectory back to $490.

## Market & Competition

1. **Trump's China State Visit as Macro Bullish Signal:** Bhakdi frames Trump's state visit to China — featuring Elon Musk walking off Air Force One immediately behind Trump, ahead of the Secretary of State, Secretary of Defense, US Trade Representative, and Jensen Huang — as a carefully choreographed signal that major deals are already prepared. He argues that such a high-profile delegation would not be assembled unless outcomes were largely pre-agreed, and that the market is responding accordingly, with the NASDAQ up 1.26% and Tesla up approximately 3% on the day.

2. **US-China Trade Relations and Tesla's Strategic Position:** Bhakdi emphasizes that a constructive US-China relationship is critical for Tesla specifically because of Optimus supply chain dependencies on China. He notes that high tariffs or a continued trade war would be damaging for Tesla's humanoid robot program, and expresses hope that any trade deal would include carve-outs or favorable terms for Tesla's operations — both selling into China and exporting out of China into the United States.

3. **SpaceX and Starship as a Geopolitical Wild Card:** Bhakdi raises the question of whether Chinese hyperscalers could be permitted to use Starship for orbital AI infrastructure buildout, noting that Elon has already opened Starship access to Google, Anthropic, and expects Amazon, Oracle, Microsoft, and Meta to follow. He finds the China question unresolved — strategically interesting but fraught with national security implications — and offers no firm prediction, framing it as one of the most consequential open questions from the visit.

4. **Iran Conflict Wind-Down and Return of Animal Spirits:** Bhakdi briefly notes that the Iran conflict has effectively ended because neither side could afford to continue it, and that Trump is now refocused on his core agenda of global trade deals and economic growth. He argues this shift restores investor confidence and is broadly bullish for equities.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus Mass Production Entering This Year:** Bhakdi references a December leak from "Tesla Ming" — described as a well-sourced Chinese industry source — indicating that Chinese suppliers for Optimus were preparing supply chain readiness for 70,000 units in 2026. He clarifies this does not guarantee 70,000 units will be delivered, but interprets it as confirmation that Optimus is entering mass production this year. He equates the credibility of this signal to that of the Cybercab ramp, noting these are capital expenditure commitments that suppliers must make in advance.

2. **AI4 Sufficient for Unsupervised Operation; AI5 Not Required:** In response to a viewer question about whether AI4 hardware is sufficient for unsupervised Cybercab operation, Bhakdi states that Elon was "crystal clear" on the earnings call that AI5 is not required for fully unsupervised operation. He acknowledges AI5 will be a significant boost but emphasizes Elon was explicit that AI4 is sufficient.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab Ramp Continuing — 70 Spotted:** Bhakdi references sightings reported by Joe Tegtmeyer of 70 Cybercabs spotted on a single day, characterizing this as evidence of an ongoing and accelerating production ramp. He treats this as a meaningful data point and pushes back on skeptics who might dismiss the sighting volume as insignificant.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Stock Trajectory — Target of $490:** Bhakdi reiterates his price target of $490 for Tesla stock, noting the stock is up approximately 3% on the day after a brief pullback. He describes the movement as "creeping up" — expecting a pattern of gains interspersed with small retracements rather than a straight-line rise — and expresses a preference for slow, steady appreciation to maximize alpha from his short put options strategy.

## Financials

1. **Pioneer Alpha Portfolio Performance:** Bhakdi reports his Pioneer Alpha portfolio is up 36% year-to-date and is outperforming Tesla by 43 percentage points, while also beating all other benchmarks he tracks. He notes he made a minor risk reduction move (taking roughly 20% off the table) during the previous day's dip before re-entering. He states his preferred scenario for maximum alpha is a slow, sideways-to-up grind in Tesla stock, as steep upward moves are harder for his short put strategy to capitalize on, and sharp drops would be harmful.

2. **SpaceX-Tesla Merger Speculation:** Bhakdi discusses the possibility of a SpaceX-Tesla merger, sharing his view that a one-to-one share exchange is the most likely outcome due to a "magnetic pull" toward symmetry. He notes that Tesla is currently valued around $1.3–1.4 trillion, and that SpaceX is anticipated to be valued around $2.2 trillion at IPO (expected around June 2026). He argues this creates a valuation convergence dynamic for Tesla stock independent of fundamentals, and states he is not concerned about Tesla shareholders being disadvantaged, expressing trust in Elon's stewardship. He credits Alexandra Merz with producing detailed written analysis on the merger mechanics.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla stock up approximately 3% on the day of recording; NASDAQ up 1.26%
- Pioneer Alpha portfolio: +36% year-to-date, +43 percentage points alpha over Tesla
- Tesla price target: $490 (Bhakdi's stated prediction, unchanged)
- Preferred weekly close range: $440–$450 (Bhakdi calls this a win for his options strategy)
- Cybercab sightings: 70 units spotted in a single day, per Joe Tegtmeyer
- Optimus Chinese supplier readiness: 70,000 units supply chain commitment for 2026, per Tesla Ming (leaked December 2025)
- SpaceX anticipated IPO valuation: ~$2.2 trillion (Bhakdi's expectation, around June 2026)
- Tesla current market cap: ~$1.3–1.4 trillion
- AI4 confirmed sufficient for unsupervised Cybercab operation per Elon on earnings call; AI5 not required
- Elon Musk walked off Air Force One second in line behind Trump, ahead of Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense, US Trade Representative, and Jensen Huang
- Blue Origin and Chinese government rockets estimated "at absolute minimum 5 years behind" Starship

articles.title: Daily X Summary (2026-05-13)
articles.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts were dominated by Ron Baron's bullish commentary on Tesla and SpaceX, Belgium's imminent approval of FSD supervised testing on public roads, and Tesla's ~$250M investment to more than double 4680 battery capacity at Giga Berlin. SpaceX-related content (Starship V3, FCC spectrum acquisition) was prominent but carries limited direct Tesla investor signal. The overall tone is cautiously bullish, driven by regulatory progress in Europe for FSD and a major capex commitment signaling confidence in the EV production roadmap.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Ron Baron's Mega-Bullish Tesla and SpaceX Outlook:** In a new interview, legendary investor Ron Baron made several high-profile statements. On Tesla ($TSLA), he projected the stock reaching **$2,000–$2,500 over the next 10 years**, which at $2,500 would imply a market cap of roughly **$8.3 trillion** — approximately 5.7x today's value. On SpaceX, Baron revealed his firm's **$1.7 billion invested** is now worth **over $15 billion**, and that roughly **one-third of Baron Capital's lifetime profits (~$60 billion total)** have come from investing in Elon Musk companies. He plans to purchase an additional **$1 billion of SpaceX stock at IPO**, though he acknowledged fill uncertainty. He called SpaceX potentially worth **$10–$30 trillion over 10–15 years**. On a potential SpaceX/Tesla merger, Baron was agnostic, saying whatever Elon decides "it's very unlikely it's not a good idea." These comments reflect the thesis that Musk's broader ecosystem — including Tesla — remains a generational investment opportunity.

2. **Belgium Moving Toward FSD (Supervised) Testing Approval:** Flemish mobility minister Annick De Ridder stated that Tesla FSD (Supervised) testing on public roads in Flanders, Belgium, could begin **"within days"** as regulators review Tesla's documentation. This marks meaningful regulatory progress for FSD in Europe, a market where autonomous driving approvals have historically lagged the U.S. The minister noted the vehicle will remain under supervision during testing. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis also commented positively on Tesla FSD, though the specific content of his quote was not captured in the post text.

3. **Tesla Invests ~$250 Million to Expand 4680 Production at Giga Berlin:** Tesla announced it is investing **almost $250 million** to expand 4680 battery cell production at its Giga Berlin factory. The investment more than **doubles the site's annual production capacity target to 18 GWh**. This is a significant capex commitment underscoring Tesla's confidence in the 4680 cell platform and European manufacturing scale. Higher 4680 output supports both cost reduction efforts and supply for future vehicle and energy storage programs.

4. **SpaceX Starship V3 and FCC Spectrum — Indirect Tesla Signal:** SpaceX officially scheduled **Starship V3's first test flight for May 19th** (launch window opens at **6:30 PM ET**), with a wide range of engineering changes including a redesigned Super Heavy with 3 (down from 4) grid fins that are 50% larger. Starship V3 features **50 cameras** and **480 Mbps Starlink connectivity**. Separately, SpaceX received **FCC approval to acquire ~65 MHz of nationwide spectrum from EchoStar** for its next-gen direct-to-device Starlink Mobile service. While these are SpaceX-specific developments, they are relevant to Tesla investors insofar as SpaceX's valuation trajectory and Musk's capital allocation decisions (e.g., potential merger speculation) affect the Tesla narrative.

5. **FSD Subscription Pricing Ideas and Competitor Commentary:** Sawyer Merritt shared his personal wishlist for Tesla FSD monetization options, including an **annual FSD subscription starting at $999/year** (with prices rising as FSD improves) and a **short-term pass (~$99/month or less)** targeted at rental fleets and Turo operators. These are speculative/opinion-based ideas, not official Tesla announcements. In a separate post, he highlighted Audi's new **Q9 three-row SUV** for the U.S. market, dismissing its interior design as looking "8 years old" — a qualitative competitive jab rather than a data-driven comparison.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — FSD regulatory momentum in Europe, a substantial 4680 capex expansion, and Ron Baron's high-conviction long-term Tesla price targets collectively reinforce the core autonomous driving and EV manufacturing thesis, though no near-term catalysts were announced.

articles.title: Tesla’s BIGGEST Transition Is Happening Now
articles.body:
The video, hosted by "brighterwithherbert" with guest Brian White (FutureAzA), covers a broad sweep of Tesla milestones happening simultaneously: the end of Model S production and the factory's conversion to Optimus assembly, accelerating FSD regulatory approvals across Europe, Cybercab sightings proliferating across U.S. cities, and expanding hiring signals for both autonomous driving data collection and Optimus training. The core thesis is that Tesla is undergoing its most significant product transition in company history — from a car manufacturer into an autonomous and robotics platform — and that multiple converging signals suggest this transition is happening now, not in some distant future.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **End of the Model S Era:** The very last Tesla Model S rolled off the production line at the Fremont factory. The final unit will be displayed at the factory and was signed by employees. Steve Jurvetson, who bought the very first Model S off the line, is reported to be buying the last one as well. The hosts reflect on the Model S's legacy as the first ground-up EV that demonstrated electric vehicles could be aspirational, high-performance products — not compliance cars — and note that the car underwent roughly 97% of changes over its lifetime.

2. **Factory Conversion to Optimus Production:** With Model S and Model X production ending, Tesla is now pulling out the manufacturing equipment at Fremont and installing the Optimus assembly line. The hosts draw a parallel to how Tesla built Giga Shanghai, Giga Berlin, and Giga Texas — in each case, production began as soon as (or before) the factory was complete, suggesting the product is ready when the factory is being built.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus Hiring Surge Signals Imminent Training Deployment:** Tesla is actively hiring for "data collection operator – Optimus" roles across multiple locations including Austin, Fremont, Palo Alto, San Diego, Marina del Rey, Henderson (Nevada), and Lyra. The hiring spans Tesla's engineering offices and factories, consistent with Elon Musk's stated plan to deploy the first 5,000 Optimus units internally for training purposes. Commentator Phil Trouy noted this is a positive signal that Optimus production this summer remains on track.

2. **Training Scale and Facility Uncertainty:** The hosts discuss that Tesla's total number of facilities is not fully publicly known — people occasionally discover large Tesla-operated buildings that weren't previously publicized. The first 5,000 Optimus units are expected to be distributed across these locations, with the primary goal of generating training data and accumulating experience interacting with humans for safety development.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Belgium Moving Toward FSD Supervised Approval:** The Director of Transportation for Flanders (Belgium) announced that Belgium will test Tesla's FSD Supervised system on Flemish roads over 5,000 kilometers (approximately 3,000 miles) to evaluate any differences between Dutch and Belgian road infrastructure. The goal is a provisional European type approval valid across the entire Belgian territory. Officials indicated Tesla could begin testing "tomorrow" with administrative monitoring, and stated they are removing all obstacles to be first.

2. **Sweden Issues Supportive Statement:** The Swedish Transport Agency issued a public statement affirming support for FSD and the ongoing EU approval process. Sweden has already permitted a trial of FSD on Swedish roads. The agency noted that a broader consumer launch could become possible at the earliest during the summer or autumn of 2026, aligning with the expected EU member state vote timeline.

3. **Ireland in Active Talks with Tesla:** Ireland was asked directly about the approval timeline and confirmed it is in active talks with Tesla. The hosts interpret this as Tesla conducting an education and lobbying campaign — getting EU member states informed and prepared to vote in the affirmative when the EU-wide approval vote occurs, rather than conducting binding independent test regimens.

4. **Tesla Hiring Self-Driving Data Collection Supervisors in 33 Cities:** Tesla is actively hiring self-driving data collection supervisors across 33 cities, including Bellevue, Washington. The hosts note this list will only grow over time and frame it as further evidence that unsupervised robotaxi deployment is imminent, with the Model Y already a proven data-rich platform and the Cybercab validation ongoing.

## Robotaxi
1. **Cybercab Spotted Across Multiple U.S. Cities:** Cybercabs have been spotted on public roads in Miami, San Francisco, and Houston. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis commented on the Miami sighting, expressing curiosity about public reaction. The hosts note that production Cybercabs are visually distinguishable from validation units — production models are shiny, while validation units are matte gold.

2. **Cybercab Production Rate and Timeline to Service:** Guest Brian White reports that Cybercabs are currently being produced at approximately 20–40 units per day, with output expected to slowly increase. Approximately 70+ Cybercabs were spotted in the outbound lot at the factory (per Joe Tegtmeyer's reporting). The hosts debate timeline to actual robotaxi service: the host suggests it may take one to three months before Cybercabs enter true commercial robotaxi service in Austin, as the new form factor needs additional real-world validation miles even though the FSD software stack is well-tested. Brian White agrees the validation need is more about the physical vehicle than the FSD software.

3. **Cybercab Interior and Charging Design:** Close-up photos of the Cybercab interior show a makeshift steering wheel and pedal setup — consistent with the vehicle being designed without them originally, with controls added for testing/validation purposes. The steering interface uses a Cybertruck-style yoke with an airbag. The charge port is located at the bottom rear of the vehicle, described as a provisional solution until wireless charging is available. The hosts note that wideband FCC approval needed for precise vehicle-over-charger positioning was only granted in approximately February–May 2026, making mass wireless charging hardware deployment in that timeframe physically impossible.

4. **Robotaxi Adoption and Competitive Dynamics:** The hosts debate what will drive initial consumer adoption of Cybercab robotaxi service. The host argues price will be the primary driver — citing Uber's disruption of taxis via lower prices — while Brian White counters that convenience and the elimination of tipping, music/temperature negotiation, and social friction will matter equally or more, even at price parity with Uber. Both agree Waymo's demonstrated willingness to pay a premium for driverless rides confirms driverlessness is valued as a feature. Brian White asserts Uber will be "crushed" before any price war erupts, simply because consumers will prefer the driverless experience.

## Market & Competition
1. **Florida's Governor Signals Openness Despite EV Skepticism:** Governor Ron DeSantis stated he has "always opposed EV mandates" and prefers traditional engines, but acknowledged Tesla products are "absolutely top-notch" with a "dedicated following." He also noted he has friends who "never touch the wheel anymore because of FSD," a notably strong public endorsement of Full Self-Driving from a prominent non-EV-aligned political figure. The hosts view this as significant precisely because Florida does not have incumbent auto manufacturers whose interests DeSantis would need to protect.

2. **Blackberry vs. iPhone Analogy for Cybercab:** A photo of a Cybercab alongside a Waymo vehicle in San Francisco was described by community members as "the world's Blackberry vs. iPhone moment," framing the Cybercab as the paradigm-shifting successor displacing an incumbent autonomous vehicle player.

Notable quotes and data:
- Last Model S to be displayed at Fremont factory; Steve Jurvetson purchasing the final unit.
- Optimus hiring in at least 7+ locations: Austin, Fremont, Palo Alto, San Diego, Marina del Rey, Henderson (NV), Lyra.
- Belgium to test FSD over 5,000 km (3,000 miles) before issuing provisional EU type approval.
- EU member state vote on FSD approval expected summer or autumn 2026.
- Tesla hiring self-driving data collection supervisors in 33 cities.
- ~70+ Cybercabs spotted in outbound lot at factory (per Joe Tegtmeyer).
- Cybercab production estimated at 20–40 units/day, increasing over time.
- FSD has accumulated 8 billion supervised miles across the Model 3/Y fleet.
- Wideband FCC approval for wireless charging positioning granted approximately February–May 2026.
- Governor DeSantis: "I have friends who never touch the wheel anymore because of [FSD]."
- Brian White (FutureAzA): "Uber will be crushed way before a price war could ever erupt."
- Herbert: "As soon as you've gone unsupervised, there's very little reason to not stop using the Model Y. Get the Cybercab out there."

articles.title: Legacy Automakers Are Running Out Of Time! Here’s Why
articles.body:
This video features host Herbert and guest Brian White (of the FutureAzA YouTube channel) discussing the deteriorating competitive position of legacy automakers globally as the automotive industry transitions toward electric and self-driving vehicles. The core thesis is that legacy automakers — particularly Japanese and European brands — are in a slow, painful decline, retreating to their home markets and doubling down on hybrids while Tesla continues to extend its lead in EVs and approaches full autonomy as a genuine demand driver.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla's Dominant U.S. EV Sales in Q1:** A chart sourced from KBB (Kelly Blue Book) / EV Wire shows Tesla sold approximately 78,000 Model Y units and 31,000 Model 3 units in Q1 in the U.S., totaling roughly 110,000 EVs. The Cybertruck came in at only 3,519 units — described as "very tiny." The Model S and Model X were also on the list but near the bottom of the rankings. Brian White noted that the rounding error in Herbert's "100,000" estimate was itself larger than some competitors' total sales, illustrating Tesla's commanding lead.

2. **Legacy EV Sales Are Alarmingly Small:** Of the 69 EV models tracked in the U.S. Q1 data, only 21 sold more than 1,000 units. The Toyota BZ sold around 10,000 units — cited as one of the stronger non-Tesla results, attributed largely to brand loyalty. The Kia EV9 sold 2,700, the Ioniq 5 sold around 10,000, and Rivian sold approximately 5,000 — noted as essentially its global number since Rivian barely sells outside the U.S. The Mercedes EQE/EQS sold only about 200 units. The Jeep Wagoneer S (priced around $80,000) and Cadillac Vistiq were called out as poor products, with one already appearing at a dealership at half price with minimal miles.

3. **Cybertruck Struggles, Lower-Priced Variant Anticipated:** The Cybertruck's Q1 sales of ~3,519 were described as a failure relative to the vehicle's potential. A new lower-cost variant (referenced at a $59,000 price point) is expected to begin deliveries in June 2026, but as of the video, steel wheels — the visual indicator of the budget variant — had not yet been spotted in drone footage from Joe Tegtmeyer's coverage. Brian White expressed hope the new price point would boost volumes, noting the production line is running well below capacity.

4. **Scale Threshold for EV Viability:** Herbert argued that an automaker needs to be selling at least 200,000 EVs per year globally to achieve meaningful scale benefits in pricing, suppliers, and manufacturing efficiency. By that measure, virtually every non-Tesla EV brand in the U.S. market is failing to reach viability.

## Market & Competition

1. **Japanese Automakers in Serious Trouble:** Honda, Nissan, and Mazda were all cited as likely non-survivors. Honda's CEO tore up his company's strategic plan following the company's first-ever full-year loss, described as an "historic loss from a bad bet on EVs." Nissan is deep in financial distress. A proposed Honda-Nissan merger fell apart, and the view expressed is that individually none of them are "too big to fail" — the Japanese government may allow them to collapse. Toyota, by contrast, was considered too big to fail due to scale and current profitability.

2. **Mazda Delays EVs, Doubles Down on Hybrids:** Mazda announced it is delaying its first dedicated EV platform until at least 2029 and cutting its EV investment through 2030 roughly in half — from approximately 1.5 trillion yen down to about 830 billion yen — redirecting resources toward hybrids and internal combustion development. The CEO framed this as a wise early decision. Brian White strongly disagreed, calling it a post-hoc rationalization of "laziness and complacency," and noted that Toyota introduced the Prius hybrid over 30 years ago, meaning Mazda had ample time to follow and chose not to.

3. **Porsche Cutting Jobs and Exiting Business Lines:** Porsche announced it will cut more than 500 jobs and exit three non-car-making business lines to refocus on core luxury vehicles. Despite these struggles, both hosts agreed Porsche as a brand will likely survive, partly because it sits within the Volkswagen Group (considered too big to fail) and partly due to enduring brand desirability. However, the broader concern raised was that EVs are eroding the performance mystique of gas-powered sports cars as consumers experience instant EV torque firsthand.

4. **Global EV Adoption Varies by Region:** China has already surpassed 40% battery EV penetration of new car sales (with combined BEV+hybrid well over 50% since the prior year), essentially completing its transition and squeezing out German and American legacy brands that once held ~15% market share there. Europe is also rebounding toward EVs. The U.S. lags significantly, with only around 9% EV share and projected to reach perhaps 10% in 2026 — giving U.S.-focused legacy automakers a longer runway but at the cost of shrinking global relevance.
