10. **Voltera and Revel Merge to Build AV-Focused Charging Infrastructure:** Voltera and Revel announced a definitive agreement to combine businesses, creating a charging infrastructure platform purpose-built for autonomous vehicles, electric fleets, and ride-hail deployment in dense urban markets. The combined company will operate more than 1,000 charging stalls across 11 major US metro markets and will not be open to public charging. Loomis noted this would primarily serve non-Tesla AV companies, as Tesla robotaxis would likely use Superchargers.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Tesla Granted Patent for Autonomous Camera Lens Cleaning System:** Tesla received a new patent for a camera lens cleaning system that uses a controller to detect debris via image quality degradation, then automatically triggers a fluid dispenser and wiper to clean the lens — without requiring human intervention. The camera lens is spherical, requiring a contoured wiper blade. Loomis noted this is critical for unsupervised autonomy in snowy and dirty climates and that Optimus is not named in the patent but could also benefit from the technology. He speculated this could potentially be tied to a future FSD version Elon mentioned as possibly coming next year.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab Sightings in Houston with Starlink Equipment:** The Cybercab Spotter account reported multiple tandem Cybercab sightings, all appearing to be equipped with Starlink — confirming this is not a one-off. SC Robinson shared new footage from Houston showing 14 Cybercabs on site.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Figure Announces Commercial Deployment with Catalyst Brands:** Figure signed a commercial agreement with Catalyst Brands — which operates JC Penney, Aeropostale, and Brooks Brothers — to deploy humanoid robots at scale, starting in Reno, Nevada, within Catalyst's distribution and logistics network. The initial focus will be on the facility's Joey Pouch sorting system. No pricing, timeline specifics, or deployment scale details were disclosed.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cybertruck Dual Motor AWD VINs Now Being Assigned:** Sawyer confirmed Tesla has officially started assigning VINs to customers who ordered the $59,000 Cybertruck dual motor all-wheel drive, with first deliveries expected in the coming weeks.

2. **Tesla Roadster to Be Built at Giga Texas:** Lars confirmed on the Ride the Lightning podcast that the Roadster will be built at Giga Texas, with "a lot of things unfolding in the next months." The unveil event will not take place in May 2026.

3. **Volvo Expands Tesla Supercharger Access in Europe:** Starting Q4 2026, Volvo owners will be able to use the Volvo app to charge at more than 20,000 Tesla Supercharger stations across 29 European countries. Volvo is also planning to transition selected models to NACS in Japan and South Korea by 2029.

4. **Tesla Opens Supercharger Prepaid Passes to Non-Tesla EVs in China via WeChat:** Tesla expanded Supercharger network access in China to non-Tesla EV owners through prepaid charging passes purchasable via WeChat, usable at V3 and V4 Supercharger stations. The trial pass is approximately $12 for 50 kWh (~$0.23/kWh) and the enjoy pass is $88 for 400 kWh (~$0.22/kWh). Loomis noted this improves asset utilization during off-peak periods and generates upfront cash flow.

5. **First Tesla Supercharger Goes Live in Colombia:** Tesla Charging announced the first Supercharger is now live in Bogotá, Colombia.

6. **Elon Corrects Overstated Battery Patent Claim:** Elon Musk corrected a viral post claiming Tesla's new patent would cut battery production costs by nearly half, clarifying it will "significantly reduce the cost of battery cathode production" — not halve total battery costs. The patent relates to Tesla's full dry battery electrode (DBE) process for the cathode, which also accelerates 4680 cell cathode production.

## Financials

1. **Tesla Stock Performance:** Tesla stock closed at $433.59, up 1.78% on the day, roughly in line with the NDX (up 1.76%). Volume was 25% below the average.

Notable quotes and data:

articles.title: SpaceX IPO Could Create The Biggest Wealth Explosion Ever
articles.body:
This video from FutureAzA features host Brian in conversation with guest Randy Kirk, discussing the anticipated SpaceX IPO, its unique structural characteristics, potential valuation, and the competitive landscape for SpaceX's launch business. The core thesis is that the SpaceX IPO could be the most consequential and unusual public offering in history, with enormous wealth creation potential — but also significant short-term volatility risk.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX's 10,000 Annual Launches Ambition:** SpaceX has stated a goal of 10,000 annual launches within five years — roughly one launch every two minutes. FAA Administrator Brian Bedford, following a meeting with SpaceX President Gwen Shotwell, acknowledged the goal as ambitious but stated that significantly greater reliability would need to be demonstrated first. The hosts noted that SpaceX's Falcon 9 Block 5 has logged approximately 550–580 launches with only one unsuccessful mission, attributed to a second-stage relight failure, and that landing reliability is nearly perfect, with only minor mishaps causing no damage or injuries.

2. **Need for New Launch Sites:** The hosts discussed that achieving 10,000 annual launches would require far more than the two existing heavy-lift sites at Vandenberg and Cape Canaveral, potentially requiring 10 to 20 launch sites globally. At least three new launch towers are reportedly under construction at Cape Canaveral. Candidate locations discussed included the U.S. Southwest (Nevada, Arizona, New Mexico — citing the remote Virgin Galactic site as a precedent), as well as international island locations for orbital trajectories. Proximity to the equator was noted as a key geographic advantage. Noise and community impact (referencing Joe Tegtmeyer's footage showing glass flexing miles from a Starship launch) were identified as major constraints for any new site.

3. **SpaceX IPO — Structure and Uniqueness:** Randy Kirk described the SpaceX IPO as potentially the most unique in history across roughly a dozen dimensions. Key features include: a minimum raise of $75 billion, with some estimates suggesting $100 billion or more; an IPO valuation starting around $3 trillion; only approximately 4% float at launch; an expedited NASDAQ listing almost immediately and S&P 500 inclusion within six months — both described as unprecedented. The phased lockup expiration structure is also highly unusual, with some insiders coming out of lockup as early as the first day of trading, others tied to earnings calls, creating a deliberately staggered mechanism the managing banks designed to reduce volatility — though the hosts expressed doubt it would succeed in doing so.

4. **Tesla Shareholder Access to the IPO:** Elon Musk had indicated Tesla shareholders should be rewarded in connection with the SpaceX IPO. The hosts explained that brokers such as E*TRADE and Robinhood are offering access with no stated minimum balance requirement (Robinhood allows partial shares), while some brokers require minimum account balances of $100,000–$500,000. There does not appear to be a clear prior ownership date requirement for Tesla shares to qualify. Investors apply for a target number of shares at a maximum price they are willing to pay, with the final IPO price set within approximately 24 hours before the offering. The IPO date was stated as the 12th (month unspecified).

5. **Valuation Potential and Long-Term Upside:** Randy Kirk stated that a 10x return within 10 years — from roughly $3 trillion to $30 trillion market cap — is "easy." He noted that the Moonshots podcast community believes the company could reach $100 trillion market cap. Elon Musk has cited a total addressable market (TAM) of $27 trillion in annual revenue; the hosts speculated that even capturing 20% of that TAM would imply $6 trillion in annual revenue, with an indeterminate but very large implied P/E multiple. Starlink was cited as a major driver, with former SpaceX engineers telling the host that one billion Starlink subscribers is mathematically feasible given global coverage.

6. **Volatility and Risk Warning:** Both hosts cautioned that the IPO will be highly volatile in the short term, potentially swinging dramatically in either direction in the first days of trading. They drew comparisons to Facebook's IPO, where lockup expiration selling caused a prolonged decline below the IPO price. Randy Kirk stated his personal plan is to allocate a "very very small percentage" of his portfolio to SpaceX at IPO, and advised against it for investors with low risk tolerance.

7. **European Rocket Competition — Skepticism:** A headline from Daily Galaxy claimed Europe has revealed a rocket that could outperform SpaceX's Starship in efficiency, claiming a 70-ton lift capacity. The hosts were dismissive, noting the "rocket" is purely conceptual — an artist's rendering with no real design, no funding, and no timeline. They framed it as consistent with a broader pattern of vaporware "next-generation" technology announcements that rarely materialize. Randy Kirk speculated that the most likely future advancement in rocketry would be a nuclear-chemical hybrid, with nuclear propulsion activating above a certain altitude, though the host expressed skepticism about nuclear propulsion near Earth due to atmospheric and satellite risks.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX target: 10,000 annual launches within 5 years (~1 launch every 2 minutes)
- Falcon 9 Block 5: ~550–580 launches; 1 failure (second-stage relight); near-perfect landing record
- SpaceX IPO minimum raise: $75 billion; some estimates suggest $100 billion+
- IPO valuation: implied ~$3 trillion at listing
- Float at IPO: approximately 4%
- NASDAQ listing: near-immediate; S&P 500 inclusion: within 6 months (both described as unprecedented)
- IPO date: the 12th (month not specified)
- Elon Musk's cited TAM for SpaceX: $27 trillion in annual revenue
- 20% TAM capture scenario: ~$6 trillion annual revenue
- Moonshots podcast community projection: $100 trillion market cap
- Former SpaceX engineers confirmed 1 billion Starlink subscribers is mathematically feasible
- Randy Kirk: "Oh, yeah. Oh, easy" on 10x in 10 years (from ~$3T to ~$30T)
- European competitor rocket: artist's rendering only — no funding, no design, no timeline
- At least 3 new launch towers reportedly under construction at Cape Canaveral

articles.title: Tesla Is About To Hit All Time Highs.. But Is There A Bubble?
articles.body:
This video from "investingagainstthegrain" is a Memorial Day market update in which the host argues that Tesla is technically set up to break out to all-time highs, walking through multi-timeframe chart analysis to support the thesis. He also addresses macro concerns — including geopolitical tensions involving Iran, Russia/Ukraine, and Israel/Lebanon — as well as pushback against popular "bubble" narratives circulating in financial media. The video blends Tesla-specific technical analysis with broader market commentary and options trading education.

## Market & Competition
1. **Bubble Narrative Rebuttal — Short Interest as Bullish Signal:** The host addresses a circulating narrative that S&P 500 short interest hitting 3% — its highest level in more than a decade — is a bearish signal. He argues the opposite: historically, elevated short interest tends to precede market rallies rather than crashes, citing the GameStop short squeeze as an example. He notes that short interest was at its lowest around COVID, which was actually a poor contrarian signal for bears.

2. **IPO Liquidity Risk — SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic:** The host acknowledges a thesis circulating on social media that the simultaneous IPOs of SpaceX (framed as a ~$2 trillion company), OpenAI (~$1 trillion), and Anthropic (~$1 trillion) could force markets to absorb roughly $200 billion in new supply, pressuring existing winners like Nvidia, SK Hynix, and Micron as funds rotate. He partially agrees — money has to come from somewhere — but counters that over $8 trillion is sitting in U.S. money market funds, providing a significant reservoir of sidelined capital. He also cautions against rushing into the IPOs themselves, noting that Facebook traded below its IPO price after its listing and suggesting waiting for the first 5–10% flush before entering.

3. **Sector Rotation Opportunity — Software and "Hated" Names:** Citing analyst Amit, the host highlights that many software stocks have been compounding earnings but receiving no market love due to sector rotation toward semis and AI hardware. He singles out Meta as a particularly underappreciated AI beneficiary, arguing its advertising flywheel — where AI improves ad targeting and ROI — creates a self-reinforcing revenue engine. He also mentions Microsoft as potentially entering a "lost decade" similar to the early 2000s, preferring Google, Amazon, or neo-cloud plays for cloud exposure. AppLovin is flagged as another advertising-adjacent trade where he has sold puts.

4. **Tesla as the Third Underperforming Mag-7 Name:** The host notes that of the "Magnificent 7" stocks, only three are unprofitable year-to-date: Meta, Microsoft, and Tesla — framing Tesla as the most glaring omission from lists of beaten-down but fundamentally strong opportunities.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Tesla at Historically High Seasonal Price:** The host emphasizes that Tesla at approximately $426 per share in late May 2026 represents a historically unprecedented price for this time of year. He contrasts this with the same period in prior years when Tesla was trading in the $200s, arguing this elevated base makes the technical setup even more significant.

## Autonomous Driving & Robotaxi
1. **Cybercab and Robotaxi Expansion as Upcoming Catalysts:** The host cites the first Cybercab entering the robotaxi fleet and Tesla surpassing Waymo's vehicle count as two milestone catalysts on the near-term horizon. He argues that once Tesla's fleet exceeds Waymo's, the competitive race is effectively over — no other player could catch up. He notes Waymo is currently dealing with its own recall issues related to driving through flooded streets.

2. **Unsupervised Fleet Trajectory — Incremental but Accelerating:** Referencing a current count of roughly 30-something unsupervised robotaxi vehicles (consistent with RobotaxiTracker.com's figure of 39 as of 2026-05-09), the host argues Tesla is not stuck but rather "gearing up" for a significant sprint. He speculates Tesla could plausibly move from ~30 unsupervised vehicles to 100–200, which he describes as "market-making news" that would command broad investor attention. He frames the FSD rollout cadence as the analogy — incremental versions, not a single magic launch moment.

3. **Tesla's Quality-First Deployment Philosophy:** The host argues Tesla is deliberately taking longer than Waymo to expand its robotaxi service because it wants to deliver a polished, "feature-complete" product rather than a beta experience. He frames Waymo's approach as typical software-industry practice — ship GA, let early adopters find bugs — while Tesla is trying to skip that phase.

## Technical Analysis (Tesla)
1. **Monthly BX Trender — Historical Pattern Repeating:** The host walks through a multi-instance pattern on Tesla's monthly BX Trender indicator. He identifies three prior instances where the indicator moved from a dark red bar to a lighter red bar on a monthly timeframe, each preceding a major rally: (1) September 2022 to September 2023 — stock moved from $107 to $281; (2) May 2024 to January 2025 — stock moved from $156 to $440; (3) July 2025 to February 2026 — stock moved from $289 to $499 (the all-time high). He notes the monthly bar for May 2026 is currently printing a lighter red, signaling a potential fourth instance of this pattern — this time starting from $426.

2. **Weekly and Daily Confirmation:** The host notes the weekly BX Trender has already turned bullish, showing four consecutive green weekly bars, and the daily indicator is also transitioning from dark red to lighter red as of the Friday close preceding this video. He describes this alignment — daily leading, weekly confirming, monthly about to confirm — as a high-conviction setup for a move to new all-time highs.

3. **Covered Call Strategy Implications:** The host states he exited covered calls on Tesla approximately one week prior (around the Monday before Memorial Day weekend) and explicitly says he would not sell covered calls on Tesla at this stage, citing the bullish technical setup. He frames this as a practical application of the options strategies taught in his courses.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla currently trading at approximately **$426/share** as of video recording (late May 2026)
- Tesla all-time high: **$499**, reached during the July 2025–February 2026 rally per the host's chart analysis
- Prior Tesla BX Trender rally instances: **$107→$281**, **$156→$440**, **$289→$499**
- S&P 500 short interest at **3%**, described as the highest in more than a decade
- U.S. money market assets: **over $8 trillion**
- SpaceX framed as ~**$2 trillion** company; OpenAI and Anthropic each ~**$1 trillion**; combined new IPO supply potentially ~**$200 billion**
- WTI oil pre-market: ~**$90.30/barrel**, down ~**6–6.5%** on Iran deal hopes
- Bitcoin: approximately **+1%** in pre-market
- NASDAQ pre-market: **+1.26%**; Dow and S&P 500 pre-market each up ~**1%**
- RobotaxiTracker.com unsupervised fleet (as of 2026-05-09): **39 vehicles** (Austin 28, Dallas 5, Houston 6)
- Host's speculative robotaxi fleet sprint target: **100–200 unsupervised vehicles**
- *"Once Tesla surpasses the amount of vehicles Waymo has, it's over. It's game set match."*
- *"Tesla has never been at this point this time of year, ever."*

articles.title: Why Tesla Stock Could Start A 60 Day Bull Run
articles.body:
In this update, Jo Bhakdi reviews the recent performance of his Pioneer Reserve trading strategy following a difficult stretch of six trading days, then pivots to a bullish outlook on Tesla over the next 60–90 days. His core thesis is that Tesla is approaching a convergence of hard catalysts — Cybercab production ramping, Optimus v3 unveiling, and unsupervised robotaxi scaling — that could drive the stock back to its prior all-time high of ~$490 (reached December 16, 2025) and potentially beyond. He also discusses macro conditions, particularly the Iran conflict and bond yield volatility, as near-term risks to monitor.

## Robotaxi
1. **Cybercab Production Ramp as the Key Indicator:** Jo Bhakdi argues that the Cybercab production ramp — not the robotaxi tracker fleet deployment numbers — is the most reliable indicator of Tesla's autonomous vehicle progress. He states that Cybercabs are now being deployed across the United States and that hiring activity is visible in multiple cities. He emphasizes that since these vehicles effectively have no functional steering wheel, they can only be used as robotaxis, making commercial deployment this year essentially inevitable.

2. **Thousands of Cybercabs Per Month Projected Soon:** Bhakdi predicts that Cybercab production will reach thousands of units per month, estimating this could happen as soon as next month (June 2026) or within two months (July 2026). He frames this acceleration as a hard forcing function that has been absent until recently, noting that mass manufacturing of the Cybercab only began "last month" (approximately April–May 2026).

3. **Unsupervised Robotaxi Scale by August:** Bhakdi expects that by August 2026, Tesla could have multiple hundreds of unsupervised robotaxis operating, which he identifies as a significant near-term catalyst. He acknowledges uncertainty about whether robotaxi scaling will reach that level by August but says it is "more likely than not."

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus v3 Unveiling Expected in July–August 2026:** Referencing Elon Musk's statement on the April 22, 2026 earnings call that Optimus version 3 would be unveiled in approximately 90 days, Bhakdi calculates that the reveal is now roughly 60 days away — pointing to July, with August as a conservative estimate. He describes this as an above-$500 catalyst for Tesla stock if the unveiling impresses.

2. **Optimus Consumer Sales Potential Underestimated:** Bhakdi argues that Optimus's consumer sales potential is being underestimated on timeline. He contends that even a barely functional Optimus could sell millions of units to both enterprise/industrial customers and end consumers at a price point of $30,000–$40,000 per unit, simply due to novelty and coolness. He frames selling millions of Optimus units at ~$40,000 each as equivalent in revenue impact to doubling Model Y sales. He expects critical functionality to be present "latest next year" (2027), though he notes it doesn't need to be economically optimal to generate mass demand.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Commercial Deployment This Year Based on Vehicle Design:** Bhakdi reiterates his long-standing view that the Cybercab's design — lacking a conventional steering wheel — makes it a one-purpose vehicle that must become commercial in 2026. He sees this as the clearest signal yet that Tesla's autonomous driving ambitions are transitioning from promise to execution.

## Market & Competition
1. **Tesla Target of $490 Without New Catalysts:** Bhakdi argues that Tesla's fundamentals are at least as strong now as they were when the stock hit its all-time high of approximately $490 on December 16, 2025, and that the broader market is at or above those levels. He therefore believes Tesla should return to $490 even without new catalysts, and could go above $490 if the Cybercab ramp and Optimus v3 catalysts materialize within the 60–90 day window.

2. **Macro Risk: Iran Conflict and Bond Yields:** Bhakdi identifies two near-term macro risks — the Iran conflict and U.S. bond yield volatility. He notes that bond yields spiked to approximately 4.6–4.8% but have since pulled back to 4.48%. He believes the Iran situation will be resolved within one to two weeks due to enormous economic and geopolitical pressure to reopen trade, and that the market broadly shares this view, as evidenced by oil prices remaining subdued even after recent bombing activity.

## Financials
1. **Pioneer Reserve Strategy Performance:** Bhakdi reports that his Pioneer Reserve portfolio is down 4.61% for the prior week — its worst weekly performance of 2026 — driven by heavily leveraged short put positions on Tesla that were hurt by a rapid two-day drop from $443 to approximately $390. Despite this, the portfolio is up approximately 20% month-to-date for May 2026, with a 7.8% alpha over Tesla, and up approximately 27% year-to-date with a 32% alpha over Tesla.

2. **Options Strategy Adjustment:** Following the losses, Bhakdi is resetting to a more cautious synthetic leverage posture. He plans to re-enter short put positions on Tesla at strike prices in the $425–$430 range but intends to avoid heavy leverage. He identifies the $445–$450 zone as a key resistance area to watch before committing more aggressively.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla all-time high: ~$490, reached December 16, 2025
- Tesla stock at $426 pre-market at time of recording (May 26, 2026)
- Pioneer Reserve: down 4.61% last week; up ~20% month-to-date (May 2026); up ~27% year-to-date; alpha over Tesla of ~32% YTD
- Bond yields peaked at approximately 4.6–4.8%, now at 4.48%
- Optimus v3 reveal: ~60 days from publish date (July–August 2026), per Elon Musk's April 22, 2026 earnings call statement of "90 days"
- Optimus potential price: $30,000–$40,000 per unit for consumer/enterprise sales
- Cybercab production ramp: described as reaching "thousands per month" within one to two months
- Unsupervised robotaxi fleet: "multiple hundreds" expected by August 2026
- "Only since last month have we seen mass manufacturing of the vehicle that can only be used as a robotaxi."
- "If you sell millions of Optimus for $40,000 bucks each, that's like doubling Model Y sales."
- "$490 is my target without catalysts; with catalysts, we go above."

articles.body:

---

This is a modest but meaningful signal that Tesla is broadening the pre-deployment testing footprint of the Cybercab ahead of anticipated commercial rollout.

While Ferrari is not a direct Tesla competitor at volume, the contrast reinforces Tesla's design credibility in the EV space.

4. **SpaceX IPO Preparation Guide (Tangential):** A detailed post on how retail investors can position to access SpaceX's IPO through specific brokerages (including Fidelity, with a noted $500,000 minimum account balance requirement) garnered strong engagement (4.1K likes, 478 reposts). This is not directly Tesla-relevant but may be of interest to Tesla investors who are also SpaceX watchers, given Elon Musk's cross-portfolio significance.

---

## Signal Strength: **Mildly Bullish** — Cybercab testing expanding to Arizona signals continued pre-commercial momentum, and Cybertruck's extended delivery window suggests healthy demand, while legacy EV design stumbles reinforce Tesla's competitive differentiation.

articles.title: Elon Musk Doubled Down On This Massive Bet
articles.body:
This video features a conversation between host Herbert and guest Jo Bhakdi, an economist, investor, and tech entrepreneur, focused on Elon Musk's AI strategy through xAI and SpaceX. The central thesis is that Elon's acquisition of Cursor — the leading AI "scaffolding" company — combined with Grok's large language models and SpaceX's massive compute infrastructure, positions xAI to leapfrog Anthropic and OpenAI within months rather than years. The discussion also covers Starship's economics, orbital AI data centers, and xAI's compute-rental business model (dubbed "Elon Web Services").

## Market & Competition

1. **xAI's Strategic Position — Hyperscaler Over Best Model:** Peter Diamandis argued that Elon does not need to run the best AI model — only to control the best hardware, comparing the strategy to Nvidia's dominance despite not having the most popular model. Elon responded by agreeing with Diamandis's framing but doubling down, saying "our AI will be great" and vowing never to give up. He noted xAI is only three years old — half the age of Anthropic and a quarter the age of OpenAI — and said, "Let's see where things stand 3 years from now," implying a competitive horizon around 2029.

2. **SpaceX's Historical Precedent for Long Games:** Elon drew a parallel between xAI's current position and SpaceX's early years, noting that SpaceX had "achieved nothing of note after three years" and was "written off as dead after six years with three consecutive launch failures." The implication is that xAI is following a similar long-game trajectory and should not be counted out.

3. **Cursor Acquisition — The Scaffolding Thesis:** Jo Bhakdi argued that the real competitive advantage in AI is no longer the core LLM but the "scaffolding" — the prompting infrastructure, pipelines, and agent orchestration wrapped around it. He identified Cursor as the world's best scaffolding company, better than Anthropic itself, evidenced by the fact that Cursor using Kimmy (described as a second-tier Chinese model) achieved near-parity with ChatGPT and the latest Claude model in coding benchmarks — proving Cursor's scaffolding alone is more powerful than Anthropic's. Elon reportedly offered a $10 billion call option to acquire Cursor for $60 billion (exercisable 60 days after Cursor's IPO, with an execution deadline of approximately August 11, 2026). OpenAI had previously tried to buy Cursor for $3 billion and was turned down.

4. **Grok Model Lineup — Multiple Models in Parallel:** The transcript describes two Grok models currently in development: a 1.5 trillion parameter model (training complete, evaluations positive, Cursor data incorporated in supplementary training, fine-tuning underway, reinforcement learning beginning imminently, with public release in two to three weeks from the publish date) and a 0.5 trillion parameter model (currently serving all Grok production traffic, especially for difficult coding tasks, with an open release planned toward the end of 2026). Jo Bhakdi argued the multi-model approach — running several frontier models simultaneously — is a structural advantage enabled by xAI's outsized compute capacity.

5. **Compute Rental Revenue — "Elon Web Services":** A financial analyst identified as Phil Duan calculated that Colossus 1, with approximately 220,000 GPUs (broken down into H100s, H200s, and GB200s at typical market pricing), generates approximately $5 billion in annual compute revenue paid by Anthropic to xAI. Because Anthropic applies that compute to inference (charging customers), that $5 billion of compute cost translates to approximately $15 billion in annual revenue for Anthropic at a 60–70% gross margin. Herbert noted that the $15 billion figure implies Anthropic is renting only about 150,000–200,000 GB200s from Colossus 2 — roughly one-third of Colossus 2's 550,000 GB200 capacity — meaning xAI retains two-thirds of Colossus 2 for its own use or further rental. Jo Bhakdi and Herbert compared this flywheel to Amazon AWS: overbuild for internal needs, rent out excess, use that revenue to fund even more buildout.

6. **Cursor's Enterprise Moat:** A key strategic insight raised by Jo Bhakdi is that Cursor is already deeply embedded in every Fortune 500 company through developer adoption. This gives xAI an enterprise sales channel that would otherwise require a partnership with Salesforce, Oracle, or a private equity rollup. Herbert had predicted Elon would need such an enterprise partner; Bhakdi corrected this, saying Cursor already provides that penetration without any additional sales effort.

7. **Orbital AI Data Centers — Timeline and Economics:** The discussion covered Elon's plans for AI satellite data centers in orbit, with a stated deployment target of 2028 (referenced from xAI's S-1 filing). Jo Bhakdi predicted orbital prototype satellites in 2027. A technical question from a user named Pierre Farerugi raised a power budget concern (three to four hundred kilowatts of solar panels for one hundred kilowatts of compute, factoring in panel decay). Elon responded that he will present a more detailed AI satellite design "in a few weeks." Bhakdi rated the engineering complexity of AI satellites as "medium to high" — well within Elon's execution sweet spot — and expressed 100% confidence in success.

8. **Starship Economics and Launch 12 Success:** Jo Bhakdi broke down the risk hierarchy for Starship launches: (1) avoiding an explosion at launch with cargo aboard is the highest priority because it affects insurance/cost reserves for the next ~20 flights; (2) successful cargo deployment is next; (3) booster catch and reuse matters for economics but is less catastrophic if failed; (4) Starship vehicle reuse is the least economically critical because even without reuse, Starship's cost per launch (~$40 million for 150 tons of payload) compares favorably to current alternatives (~$70 million for 15 tons). He concluded that orbital AI data centers are economically feasible even without Starship reuse. Launch 12 was described as a near-complete success — one engine failure out of 33 engines but cargo deployed successfully; booster relanding failed but was deemed economically minor.

Notable quotes and data:
- Elon: "Our AI will be great. Whether it is the best remains to be seen, but I will never give up. Never."
- Elon: "SpaceX had achieved nothing of note after three years and was written off as dead after six years with three consecutive launch failures. You may have noticed things are different now."
- Elon (on AI satellites): "I will present a more detailed AI satellite design in a few weeks."
- xAI's option to acquire Cursor: $10 billion call option, full acquisition price $60 billion, exercisable 60 days after Cursor's IPO (~August 11, 2026 deadline)
- OpenAI reportedly offered $3 billion for Cursor and was rejected
- Colossus 1: ~220,000 GPUs; estimated $5 billion/year in compute revenue from Anthropic
- Anthropic reportedly generating ~$15 billion/year in revenue from that inference capacity (60–70% gross margin)
- Colossus 2: ~550,000 GB200s; Anthropic using ~150,000–200,000 (~one-third), leaving two-thirds available
- Grok 1.5T model: training complete, public release ~2–3 weeks from publish date (estimated ~mid-June 2026)
- Grok 0.5T model: currently serving all production traffic; open release planned late 2026
- xAI is described as three years old; Anthropic ~six years old; OpenAI ~twelve years old
- AI satellite deployment: 2028 target (commercial); 2027 predicted for prototypes (Jo Bhakdi)
- Starship booster cost: ~$80 million; per-use cost at 10 reuses ~$8 million; Starship vehicle cost ~$40 million
- Jo Bhakdi's estimate: xAI will reach Anthropic's current capability level within ~3 months; will be competitive with OpenAI and Anthropic by end of 2026

articles.title: Elon Musk Just Dropped Massive New Clues
articles.body:
This video from "brighterwithherbert" analyzes 20+ posts Elon Musk made on X over a three-day period (approximately May 24–27, 2026), arguing that these posts collectively function as forward guidance for Tesla investors — more informative, in the host's view, than the next earnings call. The core thesis is that developments across xAI (Grok V9), Starlink, and SpaceX's Pentagon relationship are directly relevant to Tesla's valuation because they share the same operator, talent pool, and compounding S-curve logic that applies to Tesla's robotaxi, Optimus, and AI compute buildout.

## Market & Competition

1. **Grok V9 Medium Training Complete — Implications for Tesla's xAI Stake:** Elon posted that Grok foundation model V9 medium, at 1.5 trillion parameters, has finished pre-training. This is triple the size of the current 0.5 trillion parameter V8 small model that handles all Grok production traffic. Cursor coding data was bolted onto supplementary training, reinforcement learning is starting imminently, and public release is targeted for mid-to-late June 2026 (a 2–3 week window from the post). The host flags this as the biggest news of the three days because Tesla holds a direct equity position in xAI — approved by the board — meaning when xAI is marked higher in private rounds, the Tesla balance sheet line moves with it. The host also notes that xAI's Colossus compute cluster in Memphis and Tesla's own AI training infrastructure draw from the same engineering labor market.

2. **xAI Open-Source Strategy and Agentic Coding Product:** In follow-up posts on the same thread, Elon stated the current 0.5 trillion V8 model will be open-sourced by end of 2025 (resolved to end of 2026 given publish date context), framed as a developer mindshare play against OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta. He also noted that Grok Build — xAI's agentic coding product — is still in beta for another month or so but is "already quite useful for production tasks." The host frames this as a full-stack play: flagship model shipping in weeks, prior model open-sourced, agentic coding product in beta — and Tesla owns a piece of it.

3. **xAI Private Valuation and Tesla Read-Through:** The host notes xAI is currently being marked around the $200 billion zone in private rounds. Tesla holds a fractional stake, so the read-through is real but bounded. The host explicitly cautions that anyone claiming a V9 release adds $50 to Tesla's stock price is "reaching," but the directional exposure is genuine.

4. **Starlink Land Grab — Airlines, Countries, and the 100,000 Satellite Vision:** Elon posted that Starlink will ultimately carry more than 100,000 V3/V4/V5 satellites for broadband and direct-to-cell connectivity, and that if growth continues, Starlink will one day carry the majority of internet traffic. The host notes the operational fleet sits around 10,000 satellites today, making this a 10x buildout. American Airlines — described as the largest airline in the world by fleet size — announced Starlink will be on its flights in 2027. Starlink also went live in the Kyrgyz Republic, putting the country count past 130. The host draws a direct parallel to Tesla's robotaxi and Optimus ramp: the same operator, the same compounding S-curve.

5. **Space Solar Power Scaling as Compounding Precedent:** Elon cited a 10x-per-generation scaling trend in solar power capacity on Starlink satellites: 10 megawatts on Gen 1, 100 megawatts on Gen 2, and a planned 1,000 megawatts on Gen 3. Elon added that this trend will continue for many years. The host uses this as an analog for the compounding curves Tesla is attempting to run on robotaxi miles, Optimus units, and battery storage.

6. **SpaceX/Pentagon Reuters Story — Star Shield vs. Starlink Distinction:** A Reuters story circulated Tuesday claiming a problem between SpaceX and the Pentagon. Elon responded by drawing a firm line: Starlink is the civilian system; Star Shield is the separate US government constellation. A defense contractor making suicide drones incorrectly used the civilian Starlink system instead of Star Shield, violating terms of service. The Department of War (the Pentagon's current name per the transcript) publicly backed SpaceX in writing via Sean Parnell's account, stating SpaceX "remains a strong and valued partner." The host notes that SpaceX is the largest single launch provider for US national security payloads and Star Shield contracts run multi-billion dollars — any crack in that relationship would reprice the SpaceX private mark, which investors use as a comp for Tesla's AI and robotics businesses.

## Robotaxi

1. **Tesla's AI and Robotics Buildout in the "Year 3 to Year 6" Window:** Three of Elon's posts this week were framed as vision statements about timelines. He noted xAI is only 3 years old — half the age of Anthropic and a quarter the age of OpenAI — and explicitly reminded followers that SpaceX "had achieved nothing of note after 3 years and was written off as dead after 6 years with three consecutive launch failures." The host maps this directly onto Tesla's robotaxi and Optimus ramp, arguing Tesla's AI and robotics buildout is sitting in the same year-3-to-year-6 window where SpaceX looked dead before it didn't. The host draws on personal experience holding the stock since 2012, recalling a similar "impatient story" in 2018.

2. **Robotaxi and Optimus as Catalyst Triggers to Watch:** The host frames the current 20+ posts as "leading indicators," not catalysts. The actual catalyst events to watch are: Grok V9 shipping cleanly in mid-June, American Airlines lighting up Starlink in-cabin, an AI satellite design unveiling (Elon said "a few weeks," pointing to mid-to-late June), and Optimus and robotaxi miles compounding. No specific fleet size, fare, or deployment numbers are mentioned in the transcript.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus Hiring Filter — Same Engineering Screen Across the Empire:** Elon posted his hiring philosophy: evidence of exceptional ability assessed by drilling down to the "brass tacks" level of how hard problems were actually solved. The host notes this is the same filter used for xAI, Tesla AI, and Optimus engineering hires — described as "the same screen on every engineering hire across the empire right now." No Optimus production or deployment numbers are cited.

2. **Bandwidth Risk — Multiple Mandates Mid-Ramp:** The host flags a genuine bear case concern: Elon keeps adding new mandates (Boring Company, Star Shield, xAI, Optimus, robotaxi) while existing ones are still mid-ramp. This is described as the "bandwidth question" and a fair risk to size for.

## Financials

1. **Tesla's xAI Equity Position and Balance Sheet Exposure:** The board-approved Tesla investment in xAI gives Tesla a direct equity position. With xAI marked around $200 billion in private rounds, any upward remarking of xAI reprices that balance sheet line. The host is explicit that the impact is real but bounded — not a $50/share event from a single model release.

2. **Bear, Base, and Bull Case Framework:** The host lays out three scenarios. Bull case: Grok V9 lands clean in mid-June, xAI remarked higher, Tesla stake reprices with it, Starlink maintains monopoly path in aviation, Star Shield revenue compounds, Tesla AI narrative hardens and the multiple holds or expands. Base case: V9 ships late (early July), Starlink keeps growing, defense headline risk flares occasionally, Tesla's xAI stake quietly appreciates — slow ground compounding. Bear case: Reinforcement learning takes longer than expected, a real Starlink misuse incident hits the press in a way the Pentagon doesn't bail out, FCC pushes back on the 100,000 constellation, xAI mark stays flat, Tesla decouples from the AI narrative and trades on auto fundamentals only.

Notable quotes and data:
- Grok V9 medium: 1.5 trillion parameters, vs. 0.5 trillion for current V8 small (3x increase)
- Public release target: mid-to-late June 2026 (2–3 weeks from ~May 25, 2026)
- xAI private market valuation: approximately $200 billion
- Starlink long-term target: more than 100,000 satellites (V3/V4/V5); current fleet ~10,000 (implied 10x buildout)
- Starlink in-flight: American Airlines announced Starlink on flights in 2027; country count now past 130
- Space solar scaling: 10 MW (Gen 1) → 100 MW (Gen 2) → 1,000 MW planned (Gen 3) — 10x per generation
- SpaceX launch cadence 2026: ~200–250 launches; Elon's long-term target is ~10,000 per year
- xAI age: 3 years old; Anthropic: ~6 years; OpenAI: ~12 years (implied from "half" and "quarter" framing)
- Tesla has held xAI equity since a board-approved investment made in 2025 (resolved from "last year" against publish date of 2026-05-27)
- Host has held Tesla stock since 2012
- "Tesla is the public market expression of that same operator."
- "The work compounds. It compounds even when the calendar slips."
- "Anyone underwriting the impatient frame today is going to regret it."

articles.title: Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX merger would be Musk’s 4th billion-dollar self-deal
articles.body:
Electrek reports that Elon Musk is reportedly considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, framing it as the fourth in a pattern of billion-dollar self-dealing transactions between companies Musk controls. The article argues this would be the largest such deal yet, raising serious fiduciary concerns for Tesla shareholders.

## Market & Competition
1. **SpaceX IPO context and merger odds:** SpaceX filed its S-1 on May 20 and is expected to begin trading on Nasdaq under ticker SPCX on June 12, targeting a valuation of up to $1.75 trillion and raising approximately $75 billion — described as the largest IPO in history. Tesla's market cap currently sits around $1.6 trillion. Wedbush analyst Dan Ives puts merger odds at "80 to 90 percent" by early 2027; Kalshi prediction markets assign only 33% odds before May 2027. A combined entity could exceed $3 trillion in market cap. SpaceX reported revenue of $18.7 billion and a net loss of $4.9 billion ahead of the IPO.

2. **Pattern of self-dealing transactions:** The article catalogs three prior billion-dollar transactions: (1) Tesla's 2016 acquisition of SolarCity for $2.6 billion in stock, where Musk chaired both boards; other Tesla directors settled related litigation for $60 million. (2) Musk's $44 billion Twitter acquisition in 2022, which Fidelity later marked down ~65%; by October 2024 the platform was valued at roughly $9–10 billion. In March 2025, xAI acquired X for $33 billion ($45 billion including $12 billion in debt). (3) Tesla disclosed a $2 billion investment in Musk's xAI in January 2026; shortly after, SpaceX acquired xAI in a deal valued at approximately $250 billion. Musk subsequently admitted xAI was "not built right."

3. **Structural conflict of interest:** Musk holds approximately 20% of Tesla's equity but controls 85.1% of SpaceX's voting power through a super-voting share class. The article argues this asymmetry means Musk effectively negotiates merger terms with himself, with Tesla shareholders absorbing disproportionate risk. Tesla shareholders are already suing Musk for breach of fiduciary duty over the xAI investment.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert argues this potential merger represents the "logical culmination" of Musk using Tesla as a "piggy bank" for private ventures, contending that Musk's playbook — shuffling assets between entities he controls to stamp higher valuations on combinations — benefits his private holdings at Tesla shareholders' expense. Lambert is skeptical of Dan Ives' pro-merger thesis and notes Ives "has been extremely wrong in predicting Tesla's progress in robotics."

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX IPO target valuation: up to $1.75 trillion; raise: ~$75 billion; expected trading date: June 12 under ticker SPCX
- SpaceX financials: $18.7 billion revenue, $4.9 billion net loss
- Tesla market cap: ~$1.6 trillion; combined entity projected at $3+ trillion
- Musk's Tesla equity: ~20%; SpaceX voting control: 85.1%
- Dan Ives merger probability: "80 to 90 percent" by early 2027
- Kalshi merger odds: 33% before May 2027
- SolarCity deal: $2.6 billion (2016); director settlement: $60 million
- Twitter acquisition: $44 billion (2022); platform value by Oct. 2024: ~$9–10 billion
- xAI/X deal: $33 billion ($45 billion including debt), March 2025
- Tesla's xAI investment: $2 billion (disclosed January 2026)
- SpaceX acquisition of xAI: ~$250 billion
- Dan Ives claim: autonomous robotics could add "$1 to $2 trillion" to combined market cap

articles.title: The Electric Car Explosion Nobody Saw Coming
articles.body:
This video is a lighthearted, comedic review by Brian (FutureAzA) and Mark (The Tesla Life) of Top Gear's list of 44 most exciting upcoming electric vehicles. The hosts work through the list car by car, offering quick reactions, design critiques, and skepticism about whether many of the featured vehicles will ever reach production in their rendered form. The core thesis, stated at the outset, is that the EV market has matured dramatically — where 10–15 years ago affordable options barely existed, today there is a wide and growing global selection, even if many are not yet available in North America.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **EV market maturity framing:** The hosts open by noting that while a decade or more ago it was genuinely true that affordable EVs were scarce, today there is a broad and expanding global selection. The caveat is that many of the most interesting options are not yet available in preferred markets, colors, or brands — but the variety is real and growing.

2. **Peugeot E208 GTI (No. 1 on Top Gear's list):** Shown only as a rendering, the car is noted as having 276 horsepower. The hosts are skeptical of render-only reveals and note that many vehicles on the list claim up to 300 miles of range on the European test cycle, which they address more fully later.

3. **European vs. EPA range cycles explained:** When discussing the Mercedes C-Class electric's claimed 473-mile range (on the CLTC Chinese cycle), the hosts clarify that non-EPA range figures are not inherently dishonest — CLTC is calibrated for slower, more congested Chinese urban driving, and WLTP is calibrated for typical European driving conditions. They argue these figures reflect real-world expectations for their respective markets.

4. **Hyundai Ioniq 3:** Noted as claiming 305 miles of range on the European cycle. The hosts caution that charging from 10–80% would reduce usable range by roughly a third, and that real-world figures would be lower still. They suggest it could be competitive if priced well, given the popularity of small SUVs.

5. **Hyundai Staria Electric:** Highlighted as significant because it fills a gap — an electric minivan segment largely absent in North America. Mark notes Hyundai also has a smaller van (the PV4 or PV5) coming to Canada later in the year (i.e., later in 2026). The hosts confirm the Staria is not made in China, with production across Korea and two final assembly plants elsewhere.

6. **BYD Denza 79 GT:** The hosts are genuinely enthusiastic about this vehicle, citing 952 brake horsepower, crab-walk capability, and instant charging. Already on sale in China and heading to Europe. They discuss its fastback/shooting brake design and note its camera-based side mirrors, confirming that Europe has permitted camera mirrors for years.

7. **Rivian R2 (No. 16):** The hosts express surprise it ranks so low given that manufacturing has already begun and the vehicle has been seen publicly. They drove it previously and found the slightly smaller size appealing, noting it could be a strong fit for both European and North American markets. They flag that it lacks even a cramped third row. Rivian will be present at the Michigan summer meetup offering test drives (of other models, not the R2).

8. **Volkswagen ID Polo / ID2 / ID Golf:** The hosts call it an early winner on nostalgia alone, noting it closely resembles a Golf. No pricing or specs confirmed yet, but they believe the heritage branding will drive strong sales.

9. **Polestar 2 Gen 2 and Polestar 4 Estate:** The Polestar 4 estate variant appears to add a rear window absent from the standard model. On Polestar generally, the hosts note that US pricing has been too high relative to perceived brand value — "it's hard to charge Mercedes pricing without the Mercedes logo."

10. **Jaguar concept:** The hosts are harshly critical of Jaguar's strategy, noting the brand has had nothing to sell for over a year and a half to two years while running brand-image advertising. They question what Jaguar dealerships have been doing during this period. Despite this, Top Gear apparently gave the prototype a drive and called it "a proper Jag of the highest order."

11. **Render quality and concept skepticism:** A running theme throughout is that a significant portion of the 44 vehicles are either pure CGI renders, early-stage concepts, or designs the hosts believe will look substantially different in production. Several entries (BMW hydrogen, Bentley Urban SUV, Ford Universal EV, Alpine A3, and others) receive particular mockery for appearing to be low-quality renders or outright placeholder images.

## Market & Competition

1. **China-origin vehicles expanding to Europe:** Multiple vehicles on the list — including the BYD Denza 79 GT and MG Cyber Stir Coupe — are already on sale in China and are now moving into European markets. The hosts note that Chinese manufacturing enables lower price points and that MG's heritage as a non-premium brand means the Cyber Stir coupe does not need to be expensive.

2. **Stellantis/Jeep credibility gap:** The hosts express skepticism about the Jeep Recon, citing Stellantis's track record of announced products that underdeliver. They predict the Jeep Recon will likely be "an overpriced, oversized pavement princess" given its apparent weight and cost trajectory.

3. **Toyota/Subaru partnership noted:** The Subaru E Outback is identified as still being a Toyota platform cousin, with the hosts noting that the latest generation of Toyota EVs has meaningfully improved in horsepower, efficiency, and range for the 2027 model year.

Notable quotes and data:
- Mercedes C-Class electric: up to 473 miles of range (CLTC Chinese cycle)
- Hyundai Ioniq 3: 305 miles claimed range (European cycle); hosts estimate ~200 miles usable at 10–80% charge
- BYD Denza 79 GT: 952 brake horsepower, crab-walk, instant charging, already on sale in China
- Honda Super N: under £20,000, 95 brake horsepower
- GV60 Magma (Genesis/Hyundai): described as having "600-something" horsepower
- Jaguar has had no production car to sell for "over a year and a half, maybe two" years (as of mid-2026)
- Polestar 4 Estate and Polestar 2 Gen 2 both appearing on the list
- Rivian R2: manufacturing confirmed underway; no third row; to be represented at Michigan summer meetup
- Hyundai PV4/PV5 van: coming to Canada later in 2026
- Brian mentions recently driving a Jeep Wagon S with 1,000 horsepower and roughly three metric tons curb weight
- "If you've got a car that small, you want to go for the cute aesthetic rather than the angry aesthetic. If you made it angry, people would call it a Chihuahua."
- European camera mirrors: confirmed legal in Germany and presumed across broader Europe

articles.title: Why Elon Just Unlocked MASSIVE New Cash Flow for SpaceX AI
articles.body:
This video from Jo Bhakdi's "Pioneer Lands" channel (cross-posted to jobhakdi) argues that Elon Musk has made a strategically brilliant move by pursuing a partnership and acquisition option with Cursor — the AI coding assistant — combining it with Grok's LLM capabilities and SpaceX's Colossus compute infrastructure to potentially leapfrog Anthropic in the AGI/enterprise AI race. Bhakdi's core thesis is that the key differentiator in AI is not raw model intelligence ("IQ") but the "scaffolding" — the organizational framework, prompt architecture, and agent management layer around the LLM — and that Cursor possesses the world's best scaffolding, making the combination with Grok and SpaceX compute a potential "holy trinity." The video is primarily a strategic analysis of the AGI landscape and SpaceX's positioning, with implications for Tesla investors given the overlap of Elon Musk's entities.

## Market & Competition

1. **AGI capability threshold imminent:** Bhakdi argues that economic AGI — defined as the ability to replace approximately 95–99% of mid-level and higher-level white collar jobs (lawyers, accountants, doctors' intellectual work, etc.) — is now within 3–6 months of being reached as of the video's publish date (May 2026). He states he originally predicted this would be completed by 2027 when he made that call in January 2025, but believes he overestimated the timeline.

2. **Anthropic's explosive growth as benchmark:** Bhakdi highlights Anthropic as currently running at a $45 billion annualized revenue run rate and doubling that run rate every six weeks. He uses Sweden's GDP as a reference point, arguing Anthropic will exceed Swedish GDP in revenue terms by end of 2026 if this trajectory holds. He positions Anthropic and OpenAI as the clear leaders in the AGI space, with Grok materially behind both.

3. **The scaffolding thesis — why Anthropic beats OpenAI and Grok:** Bhakdi's central analytical insight is that raw LLM intelligence ("IQ") is less important than the scaffolding — the hidden prompt systems, agent organization architecture, and cultural/operational structure wrapped around the model. He argues Anthropic likely does not have the best raw LLM (suggesting OpenAI or Grok may have stronger base models) but wins because its scaffolding is superior. He uses Claude Design vs. Claude Code as an internal example: same underlying model, dramatically different performance, entirely due to different scaffolding.

4. **Cursor's unique position — best scaffolding, no LLM:** Bhakdi describes Cursor as having the paradoxically weakest raw AI position (no proprietary LLM, relying on third-party models) but demonstrating through benchmark results that Composer 2.5 — now using Grok — approximates or matches OpenAI's and Anthropic's best models (including Opus and high-tier ChatGPT). He interprets this as proof that Cursor's scaffolding framework is the most advanced in the world, since it achieves near-parity results with a lower-IQ model (Kimi) than competitors use.

5. **The Elon/SpaceX-Cursor deal structure:** Bhakdi describes the deal as SpaceX paying $10 billion as a call option on Cursor, with a requirement to exercise the option within 60 days of Cursor's IPO — which Bhakdi estimates will be by approximately August 2026 — at an acquisition price of $60 billion. He characterizes $60 billion as "peanuts" relative to SpaceX's projected ~$2 trillion valuation.

6. **Anthropic's existing SpaceX compute deal and its vulnerability:** Bhakdi notes that Anthropic is currently paying $1.5 billion per month to SpaceX for compute access on Colossus. He states this deal has a short notice/cancellation period (approximately 60 days) and suggests SpaceX could terminate it if the Grok + Cursor combination proves able to displace Anthropic's product offering — creating a strategic optionality where SpaceX both profits from Anthropic today and is positioned to replace it.

7. **Cursor's enterprise deployment moat:** A key component of Bhakdi's thesis is that Cursor already has deep penetration across Fortune 500 companies — he states he believes Cursor is present in all or nearly all Fortune 500 companies — with existing account managers and a standing deployment infrastructure. He argues this gives SpaceX AI not just a sales channel but an already-installed enterprise footprint for deploying "digital human" (white collar AI replacement) products at scale.

8. **Grok's weakness acknowledged:** Bhakdi is direct in criticizing Grok/xAI's product capabilities, stating they have "no product team," are "bad at product," and have a poor scaffolding/harness layer. He frames Elon's Cursor move as a self-aware acknowledgment of this weakness and a smart solution — acquiring rather than trying to build the scaffolding capability internally.

## Financials

1. **SpaceX revenue trajectory from AI:** Bhakdi projects that the Anthropic compute deal alone — at $1.5 billion per month — has effectively doubled SpaceX's near-term revenue outlook and is now comparable in size to Starlink revenue. He then argues the larger opportunity is SpaceX AI's own "digital human" enterprise product (positioned as a direct Anthropic competitor), projecting tens of billions in revenue in 2027 and hundreds of billions in 2028, which he describes as "completely unrecognized" by the market.

2. **SpaceX valuation context:** Bhakdi references SpaceX's current or near-term valuation range as approximately $1.5–2 trillion, with his prediction being that it reaches roughly $2 trillion before experiencing a pullback, then continuing higher.

3. **Orbital AI compute as long-term infrastructure:** Bhakdi references his November 2025 video as the first coverage of SpaceX's orbital AI satellite business, arguing that orbital AI compute will replace terrestrial AI buildout at scale before 2030. He notes Elon has promised to present the AI satellite concept soon. He frames this as the third leg of the "holy trinity" alongside Cursor's scaffolding and Grok's LLM.

Notable quotes and data:
- "Anthropic is now at a $45 billion revenue run rate and they are doubling [every six weeks]."
- "Anthropic alone will be larger than the Swedish GDP by end of this year."
- "[SpaceX has] a call option that he needs to use within 60 days after IPO, which is probably by August. By August he has to pull the trigger and buy Cursor for $60 billion."
- "Anthropic is paying $1.5 billion per month to SpaceX for compute for Colossus."
- Composer 2.5 (using Grok) is described as "beating OPUS and ChatGPT" and "approximating max and extra high ChatGPT and Opus 4.7."
- "Tens of billions next year [2027] and hundreds of billions in 2028" — projected SpaceX AI revenue.
- "The bare compute lease out... within a week doubled SpaceX's outlook because it's now as big as Starlink, just the Anthropic deal."
- Bhakdi's January 2025 prediction: economic AGI completed by 2027; revised May 2026 estimate: within 6 months (by end of 2026).
- White collar labor replacement TAM cited as "$30 to $40 trillion."

articles.title: 600kW ChargePoint Express Solo - Powered by Eaton
articles.body:
This video features Armen Pashnovski from Munro Live interviewing representatives from Eaton (Sai Murhari, Global EVCI Product Manager) and ChargePoint (Erdog, Product Marketing) at ACT Expo 2026 in Las Vegas. The segment focuses on a newly announced joint product — the ChargePoint Express Solo — a 600 kW standalone DC fast charger, and the broader partnership between Eaton's power distribution expertise and ChargePoint's EV charging platform to address EV infrastructure bottlenecks.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **ChargePoint Express Solo — Fastest Standalone Charger on the Market:** The ChargePoint Express Solo is described as the fastest charging standalone solution currently available, capable of delivering up to 600 kW of output at the system level. It can charge two vehicles simultaneously at up to 300 kW per port, and can also function as a cabinet to distribute power to a side dispenser, supporting up to four ports charging simultaneously (averaging 150 kW each). The product was announced just prior to the show and is a brand-new market entry.

2. **Current EV Charging Speed Benchmarks:** The fastest-charging EV currently for sale in North America is cited as the Lucid Gravity, which was observed charging at 400 kW during testing at ChargePoint's facilities. In a theoretical scenario sustaining that power level, it could charge from 20% to 80% in approximately 15 minutes. No production EV currently on the North American market is capable of utilizing the full 600 kW output of the Express Solo.

3. **Cable Theft Prevention — Dual-Layer Security System:** ChargePoint and Eaton have developed a two-level cable theft deterrent system. The first layer consists of cut-resistant cables with embedded high-tensile metal invisible to the user. The second layer is an alarm system called "ChargePoint Protect," which triggers simultaneous alarms and flashing alerts across all chargers at a site when any single cable is cut, and notifies authorities — deterring further theft attempts.

## Energy
1. **Grid Infrastructure Bottleneck:** Eaton's representative emphasized that the existing grid infrastructure is not ready to support high-power charging installations like the 600 kW Express Solo. In approximately 99% of cases, installing such a charger would require a service upgrade, potentially including a new transformer and switchboard. This is a core problem the Eaton–ChargePoint partnership aims to address end-to-end for site owners.

2. **Direct DC Bus Integration with Battery Storage:** A technically distinctive feature of the Express Solo is its internal DC bus architecture, which allows battery storage to be integrated directly into the charger without a separate AC inverter. This reduces capital expenditure, lowers total cost of ownership, and optimizes physical footprint compared to conventional setups where battery storage requires its own inverter stack.

3. **Energy Arbitrage and Battery Storage Trends:** The representatives discussed using co-located battery storage as a practical solution for sites that cannot support 600 kW from the grid alone — charging batteries overnight at low utility rates and discharging during peak demand hours. They noted that in 2025, the U.S. added approximately 19 GW of battery storage capacity, representing roughly 30% growth over the prior year, signaling an accelerating trend toward on-site energy resilience.

4. **Prefabricated Skid Solution for Simplified Deployment:** Eaton is developing a prefabricated, pre-wired skid product that bundles a four-port charging hub, the Express Solo charger, a PowerLink dispenser, and a switchboard into a single deliverable unit. This is designed to eliminate the complexity of piecemeal procurement and installation for site operators. Eaton's Power Distribution Experience Center in Pittsburgh (described as "Disney World for engineers") will serve as a live demo site.

5. **Deployment Timeline:** ChargePoint expects the Express Solo to be available in the field by the end of 2026. One unit is already installed at ChargePoint's headquarters for ongoing testing, and an installation at Eaton's headquarters is planned.

Notable quotes and data:
- 600 kW total output — ChargePoint Express Solo (system level)
- Up to 300 kW per port (two-port simultaneous charging)
- Up to four ports supported when used as a cabinet/dispenser hub (averaging 150 kW each)
- Lucid Gravity observed at 400 kW charging rate during ChargePoint testing
- Theoretical 20–80% charge in ~15 minutes for the Lucid Gravity at sustained 400 kW
- ~99% of existing sites would require infrastructure upgrades (new transformer/switchboard) to support 600 kW
- U.S. added ~19 GW of battery storage capacity in 2025, ~30% more than the prior year
- "Engineers joke that it's Disney World for engineers" — describing Eaton's Pittsburgh Power Distribution Experience Center
- Expected field deployment: by end of 2026

articles.title: Daily X Summary (2026-05-27)
articles.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts from @SawyerMerritt were dominated by SpaceX/Starlink news with minimal direct Tesla content. The Tesla-relevant signal is thin but positive, with a new Supercharger expansion into Colombia, a Volvo NACS/Supercharger network partnership in Europe starting Q4 2026, and a new $60M Megapack installation in New Zealand going live. No autonomous driving, robotaxi, or Optimus content appeared today.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Tesla Supercharger Network Expansion — Colombia & Volvo Partnership:** Two separate posts highlight continued Supercharger network growth. The first Tesla Supercharger in Colombia is now open, extending Tesla's charging footprint into a new market. More significantly for near-term revenue, Volvo announced that starting Q4 2026, EV drivers will be able to access over 20,000 Tesla Supercharger stations across 29 European countries directly through the Volvo Cars app. This adds another OEM to Tesla's growing list of NACS/Supercharger partners in Europe, strengthening the network's role as a profit center and competitive moat. Engagement on the Volvo post was moderate (836 likes), suggesting it didn't break through to a wider audience but is substantively meaningful for the Energy/EV infrastructure thesis.

2. **Tesla Megapack Online in New Zealand:** A new $60 million Tesla Megapack battery energy storage system has come online in New Zealand. The system is capable of powering the equivalent of approximately 44,000 homes for up to two hours, storing largely renewable energy during low-demand periods and dispatching it during peak demand. This is a modest but concrete data point confirming continued Megapack deployment internationally and the real-world grid services use case.

3. **SpaceX & Starlink — Context for Tesla Investors:** The bulk of today's posts covered SpaceX milestones: American Airlines adopting Starlink (installations begin Q1 2027, 500+ narrowbody aircraft), bringing Starlink's commercial airline partners to 38 airlines and 6,300+ aircraft under contract or installed; a $2.29 billion U.S. Space Force contract for a Starshield satellite communications backbone; and NASA's Moon Base initiative featuring Starship. These are not directly Tesla-relevant but matter to Tesla investors who hold Elon Musk's broader portfolio as context for his attention and resource allocation. No direct Tesla implications were stated in the posts.

---

## Signal Strength: **Mildly Bullish** — The Supercharger network continues its geographic and OEM-partnership expansion (Colombia debut, Volvo Europe Q4 2026), and Megapack deployments remain active internationally, but the absence of any autonomous driving, robotaxi, or Optimus content makes this a low-signal day for the core TTT thesis.

articles.title: Tesla Reveals Major New Roadster Update
articles.body:
This episode of The Tesla Space covers three main stories: the long-awaited Tesla Roadster's production plans finally crystallizing around Giga Texas, the Boring Company's shift toward centralized remote tunneling operations, and Tesla's accelerating Full Self-Driving rollout across Europe. The episode's core thesis is that Tesla's most ambitious and delayed projects — the Roadster, FSD in Europe — are moving from speculation into concrete execution, while the Boring Company is quietly transforming itself from a construction contractor into an automation company.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Roadster confirmed for Giga Texas production:** Tesla VP of Vehicle Engineering Lars Morvi and chief designer Franz von Holleshausen confirmed on the Ride the Lightning podcast that the next-generation Roadster will be built at Tesla headquarters in Giga Texas. Morvi stated: "We can say it's going to be built in Texas. We've made first plans on that and you start to see a lot of things start to unfold in the next months." The video frames this as a meaningful milestone — allocating production space implies tooling, engineering validation, and factory planning are converging around a real vehicle program, not just a concept.

2. **Roadster's production location history and Tesla's strategic shift to Texas:** When the Roadster was first unveiled, Tesla planned to build it in Fremont. During the Q2 2020 earnings call, Elon Musk said the Roadster would make sense as a California-built product. That has since changed, with Tesla increasingly concentrating its newest and most ambitious programs — Cybercab, Optimus, Terafab, and now the Roadster — around Giga Texas. The video notes the symbolic fit: SpaceX's Starship is built in Texas, and the Roadster is described as a Tesla/SpaceX collaboration confirmed by Elon Musk in 2024.

3. **Original Roadster specs and the delay problem:** The Roadster was first unveiled in November 2017 at Tesla's semi-event, with specs that seemed near-impossible at the time: 0–60 mph in 1.9 seconds, 0–100 in 4.2 seconds, a quarter-mile in 8.8 seconds, over 620 miles of range, and a top speed exceeding 250 mph. Originally targeting 2020 deliveries, the car never launched. The video argues that the industry has since caught up — Tesla's own Model S Plaid (launched 2021) matched the 1.9-second 0–60 claim, and competitors like Lucid, Porsche, Rimac, and Xiaomi's SU7 Ultra (claimed 1.98 seconds at a fraction of the Roadster's expected price) have reached similar or better figures. Simply matching the original specs would no longer be revolutionary in 2026.

4. **Roadster's evolved identity — the last great driver's car:** Elon Musk has repeatedly hinted at a far more extreme version of the Roadster than originally planned. In 2018 he mentioned an optional SpaceX package using small cold gas thrusters (similar to those used on the Falcon 9 for stabilization during re-entry) to enhance acceleration, braking, and cornering. He has also claimed the car could hit 0–60 in under 1 second, and stated: "There will never be another car like this, if you could even call it a car." Most significantly, during Tesla's Q1 2026 earnings call, Musk said: "Over time, it's going to make sense for our whole lineup to be autonomous vehicles of different sizes. Long-term, the only manually driven car will be the new Tesla Roadster." This reframes the Roadster as not just the fastest car in the world, but potentially the last great manually driven car before full autonomy arrives.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Supervised approved in Lithuania — second EU country:** Tesla received regulatory approval to deploy FSD Supervised in Lithuania, making it the second European country to activate the system after the Netherlands. Lithuania used the EU's mutual recognition framework to leverage the Dutch approval rather than starting from scratch, completing its own process in under 40 days. By contrast, the Dutch Vehicle Authority had spent more than 18 months evaluating the system using 1.12 million miles of European driving data. Tesla had been quietly preparing behind the scenes — opening FSD ride-along experiences at its Vilnius showroom in late April and hiring FSD vehicle operators in Lithuania and eight other European countries around the same time.

2. **Greece poised to be the third EU country:** The Greek Secretary General of Transport has publicly stated that Greece intends to adopt FSD Supervised using the same Dutch mutual recognition framework as part of an upcoming transportation bill. Greece had hoped to be the second European country to approve it but was narrowly beaten by Lithuania. The video identifies a clear pattern: Tesla is building country-by-country momentum using mutual recognition rules already embedded in the European regulatory system, rather than waiting for a slow continent-wide process.

3. **European FSD mileage milestones and safety data:** Tesla Europe announced that drivers in the Netherlands and Lithuania have collectively logged more than 12.5 million miles (20 million kilometers) with FSD Supervised active. That milestone was reached less than three days after the same markets crossed 9.3 million miles (15 million kilometers) — meaning roughly 3 million miles were added in under 72 hours. Dutch Tesla owners alone surpassed 6.2 million miles in under a month after launch. Tesla also reported that when FSD Supervised is active, the probability of a collision per kilometer driven is up to seven times lower compared to manual driving.

Notable quotes and data:
- Lars Morvi: "We can say it's going to be built in Texas. We've made first plans on that and you start to see a lot of things start to unfold in the next months."
- Elon Musk (Q1 2026 earnings call): "Over time, it's going to make sense for our whole lineup to be autonomous vehicles of different sizes. Long-term, the only manually driven car will be the new Tesla Roadster."
- Elon Musk on the Roadster: "There will never be another car like this, if you could even call it a car."
- Roadster original specs (2017 reveal): 0–60 mph in 1.9 sec, 0–100 in 4.2 sec, quarter-mile in 8.8 sec, 620+ miles range, 250+ mph top speed.
- FSD Supervised collision probability: up to 7x lower per km vs. manual driving.
- Netherlands FSD evaluation: 18+ months using 1.12 million miles of European driving data.
- Lithuania approval timeline: under 40 days via mutual recognition framework.
- Combined Netherlands + Lithuania FSD miles: 12.5 million miles (20 million km).
- Dutch owners alone: 6.2 million miles in under one month post-launch.
- Vegas Loop full vision: ~68 miles of tunnels, 100+ stations.
- Boring Company tunnel permit timeline: up to 6 months per permit currently.
- Clark County Commissioner Jib Gibson: "The project is now ready to explode."

articles.title: Tesla Just Dropped Huge Cybercab And Roadster Updates
articles.body:
This video from brighterwithherbert features host Herbert and guest Brian White (of the FutureAzA YouTube channel) discussing a range of Tesla news updates, including new technology spotted on Cybercab test vehicles, Roadster development progress, China market developments, and Supercharger expansion. The core thesis is that multiple converging signals — Cybercab hardware refinements, FSD rebranding in China, and infrastructure buildout — reinforce Tesla's long-term autonomous and energy business thesis.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercabs Spotted with Starlink Mini Units in Austin:** Multiple Cybercab units were spotted driving in tandem around Austin with Starlink Mini satellite dishes bolted to the rear hatch. Brian White explains that while Cybercabs are known to use 5G as their primary connectivity, Starlink Mini would serve as a redundant backup communication system — critical for scenarios involving cellular dead zones, tower outages, or large-scale fleet coordination. He also raises the possibility that for a fleet eventually reaching one million vehicles, Tesla would want independence from any single carrier like AT&T, and that Starlink could be used to offload heavy data tasks (such as overnight software updates) invisibly and cost-effectively.

2. **Cybercab Confirmed at 165 Wh/Mile Efficiency:** Lars Morvy (Tesla's VP of Vehicle Engineering) confirmed in an interview on the Ride the Lightning podcast that the Cybercab has a certified efficiency of 165 Wh per mile, making it the most efficient vehicle Tesla has ever produced. Brian White noted that when he spoke with Tesla engineers, they indicated 5.5 miles per kilowatt hour is what they are "allowed to say," implying real-world performance is even better. He attributed this to a virtuous cycle of weight reduction, aerodynamic optimization (no mirrors, sleek profile), and right-sized motors — potentially using new rare-earth-free motor designs. He contrasted this with competitors, noting that Cybercab's efficiency means less time needed for charging compared to rivals like Waymo.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Next-Gen Roadster Confirmed for Giga Texas, Alpha Prototypes Testing:** Tesla executives confirmed the next-generation Roadster will be manufactured at Giga Texas. Alpha prototypes are already in testing. Lars Morvy described it as the first time Tesla has designed a motor with a "pure performance mentality." Joe Tegtmeyer also confirmed the Roadster's Texas home and highlighted that Giga Texas is becoming ground zero for Tesla's most important products — including the Model Y, Cybertruck, Cybercab, Optimus, Cortex data centers, and a SpaceX chip fab. Brian White expressed a "hope against hope" that the now-sold-out X Takeover event on October 10th could serve as the Roadster's reveal, given the new test track being built at Giga Texas and the proximity of the delivery center.

2. **New Test Track Under Construction at Giga Texas:** A new video shows Tesla building a large test track at Giga Texas. While the general purpose is vehicle testing, speculation points to the Roadster as a likely use case. Brian noted that having an on-site test track is standard for major automakers and suggested it could also be used for owner events near the delivery center.

## Market & Competition

1. **China Issues 154,000 NEV License Plate Quotas Targeting BEV Buyers:** The Chinese government introduced 154,000 new NEV license plate quotas exclusively for battery electric vehicles (not hybrids or range-extended EVs), with 119,000 reserved for families and 35,000 for individuals. The family eligibility cutoff score hit a historic low of 36 points, meaning younger, tech-savvy, middle-class urban families are now qualifying for plates. Brian White provided context on China's urban congestion-management system, explaining that license plates in major cities like Beijing are lottery-based and can cost thousands of dollars — but EV plates were historically easier to obtain as an incentive. One analyst cited in the video estimates Tesla could gain approximately 23,000 new sales if it captures roughly 15% of this quota allocation, given that Model Y and Model 3 buyers represent the exact target demographic.

2. **Tesla Rebranding FSD in China to "Tesla Assisted Driving":** Tesla China has renamed its supervised FSD offering to "Tesla Assisted Driving" in the Chinese owner's manual. Three tiers are visible: Tesla Assisted Driving, Enhanced Assisted Driving, and Basic Assisted Driving. Brian White and Herbert interpreted this as semantics rather than a capability downgrade — a signal that Tesla is preparing for a broader FSD rollout in China. Herbert noted that Tesla previously launched FSD in China in a very limited form (with restricted data usage) to satisfy the requirement for a locally sequestered data center, and that the hiring activity around that data center suggests a nationwide expansion is now possible.

3. **Optimus in China: ~80% Probability Discussed:** Herbert and Brian discussed the possibility of Tesla building an Optimus factory in China and selling Optimus robots there. Brian explained that China may require the same data-sequestration model used for FSD — local training data centers, no data in or out — before permitting a bipedal robot with indoor mobility.
