Herbert put the probability of China allowing Tesla to sell Optimus and build a factory there at approximately 80%, citing the FSD data center precedent as the blueprint.

4. **Ferrari's New Electric Flagship Criticized for Inefficiency:** As a contrast to Cybercab's efficiency, the hosts briefly discussed Ferrari's new electric flagship (referred to colloquially as "Lucy Goosey"), noting it carries a battery larger than a Cybertruck but delivers less range than a Cybertruck — requiring 800V architecture and 365 kW charging just to compensate for its inefficiency.

## Energy

1. **Tesla Supercharger Card Now Available to Non-Tesla Owners in China via WeChat:** Tesla China announced that non-Tesla EV owners can now use Tesla Superchargers by paying via WeChat prepaid cards — eliminating the need to download the Tesla app. Brian White characterized this as a frictionless payment expansion. The video cited a projection that adding just two non-Tesla charging sessions per stall daily across 1,000 open stations (averaging 10 stalls each) would generate approximately 600,000 kWh of additional daily energy sales, translating to roughly $45 million USD in annual revenue.

2. **Tesla Oasis Sets Record at 164 Stalls, Solar + Megapack Powered:** Tesla Oasis in Lost Hills, California — the world's largest charging station with 164 stalls — peaked at 112 simultaneous cars charging on Memorial Day weekend. The station is powered entirely by solar and Megapacks, with only a minimal grid connection retained as an emergency backup. Brian White explained this architecture avoided the prohibitively expensive cost of upgrading transmission lines and transformers back to a substation. He noted the station was intentionally overbuilt so it would not reach capacity even on peak holiday weekends for years to come. He discussed the economics of replicating this model: ground-mount solar (as used at Lost Hills) is the cheapest option; canopies are most expensive but justified in high-electricity-cost states like California or at premium retail locations.

3. **Tesla Superchargers Expanding Globally:** Tesla charging announced its first Supercharger stations in Colombia, continuing Latin American expansion. Additionally, Volvo announced that starting in Q4 2026, Volvo EV drivers will be able to access more than 20,000 Supercharger stations across 29 European countries directly through the Volvo cars app.

4. **Tesla Asia Megapack Factory — Two-Year Buildout Milestone:** Photos shared from Tesla Asia showed a Megapack factory that went from groundbreaking to operational in exactly two years (as of May 23rd). Discussion followed about whether a future Optimus factory in China could follow a similar rapid buildout trajectory.

Notable quotes and data:
- Cybercab efficiency: **165 Wh per mile** — confirmed by Lars Morvy; Brian White says engineers told him "5.5 miles per kWh is what we're allowed to say," implying real-world performance is better
- China NEV quota: **154,000 plates** (119,000 family, 35,000 individual), exclusively for BEVs
- Estimated Tesla China sales from quota: **~23,000 vehicles** if Tesla captures ~15% of allocation
- WeChat Supercharger revenue projection: **~$45M USD annually** from 2 extra non-Tesla sessions/stall/day across 1,000 stations at 10 stalls each
- Tesla Oasis, Lost Hills CA: **164 stalls**, world's largest charging station, **peaked at 112 cars** on Memorial Day; powered by solar + Megapacks
- Volvo EV access to Tesla Superchargers: **20,000+ stations** across **29 European countries**, starting **Q4 2026**
- Brian White (FutureAzA): "If you have a Waymo versus a Cybercab, but the Cybercab doesn't have to go into supercharging maybe two or three hours a day less than the Waymo does — you've just become more car, less cars needed to be out there servicing."
- On Starlink Mini: "If for some reason the entire fleet were to be getting too high where it's going to incur additional costs, they could determine should we shift some of the load to Starlink... entirely invisible to you and I and impossible to every one of their competitors."

articles.title: Tesla’s Rivals Keep Copying The Vision-Only Strategy
articles.body:
This video from brighterwithherbert features host Herbert and guest Brian White (of the FutureAzA YouTube channel) reviewing a series of competitive moves in the autonomous driving and EV space, including updates on Stellantis, Mercedes, Xiaomi, Waymo, and Pony AI. The central thesis is that Tesla's vision-only, neural-net-first approach is increasingly being validated as competitors either pivot toward it (Xiaomi/Xpeng) or continue struggling with lidar-dependent systems. The discussion also covers Tesla's European sales recovery and the unit economics challenges facing robotaxi competitors.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Europe Sales Rebound Continues:** New car registrations for Tesla vehicles across the European Union, UK, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, and Switzerland jumped 46.5% year-over-year last month (April 2026), totaling 10,654 units. In the EU alone, sales grew over 67% from a year earlier. This marks the third consecutive month of growth, following an improvement of over 84% in March 2026 and nearly 12% in February 2026. Brian White contextualizes this as a return to pre-refresh levels rather than a new high, noting Tesla is holding steady with the same core lineup despite intensifying competition and lower-priced alternatives.

2. **FSD Europe Approval Has Not Yet Impacted Sales:** Brian White argues that FSD approval in Lithuania and the Netherlands has had essentially no measurable effect on sales yet — perhaps five units out of roughly 10,000. He reasons that awareness is low, the product is only in very limited hands, and customers won't purchase until FSD is approved in their specific country and clearly available today.

3. **Xiaomi YU7 Standard Edition Launches at $33,000:** Xiaomi released a new standard trim of the YU7 — a vehicle frequently positioned as a Model Y competitor — priced at approximately $33,000. Brian White notes Xiaomi is losing roughly $5,000 per car, which structurally limits their ability to scale since selling more vehicles only deepens losses. He explains Xiaomi did not build its first car (the SU7) in-house but contracted a state-run manufacturer, then subsequently purchased that factory. He views it as a strong first effort but one still exhibiting early-production quirks.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Xiaomi/Xpeng Vision-Only Pivot Validates Tesla's Approach:** Xpeng CEO He Xiaopeng publicly stated the company is "absolutely adamant" they no longer need lidar, even though he acknowledged it is good technology. Brian White notes this declaration was first made in July 2024, after which lidar on existing Xpeng vehicles was deprecated and is now purely ornamental. He positions Xpeng as the current leader in end-to-end neural net autonomous driving in China, ahead of competitors still relying on Huawei's lidar-based platform. He argues that Huawei functions as the "Intel Inside" of FSD in China but has not yet fully adopted neural net approaches due to AI chip export restrictions.

2. **Stellantis Announces $70 Billion EV and Autonomy Plan with Wave AI:** Stellantis announced a €60 billion strategic plan to build 29 new EVs by 2030, with nine priced under €30,000, on a dedicated EV architecture. Their partner Wave AI announced it will bring the Wave AI driver to Stellantis's auto-drive platform, promising hands-free, door-to-door supervised automated driving across urban streets and highways, launching in 2028. Brian White acknowledges the plan has real strategic necessity — EU regulations require all-electric vehicles by 2035 — but remains skeptical Wave AI is the best partner and notes the system is still lidar-based.

3. **Mercedes Plans Automated Driving Rollout in Germany by End of 2026:** Mercedes announced plans to deploy a point-to-point automated driving system (not highway-only) in selected German cities by the end of 2026, with nationwide rollout planned for 2027. The hosts speculate it may involve Nvidia's Alpamayo platform but note that platform was only recently announced and could not realistically be integrated into production vehicles in under a year. Brian White gives roughly 10% odds this timeline is met, calling it structurally implausible for a company as large as Mercedes to execute that quickly, and notes Mercedes previously abandoned its Level 3 highway system after minimal consumer adoption.

4. **Waymo Pauses Atlanta Service Over Flooded Road Incidents:** A gold-painted Waymo driverless vehicle was spotted in Los Angeles, which the hosts note visually echoes Tesla's Cybercab. More significantly, Waymo paused service in Atlanta after vehicles repeatedly drove into flooded areas — a software recall was issued. Brian White provides context: Waymo first over-corrected by stopping for any puddle, then pushed an update to drive through them, leading to the current problem. He contrasts this with Tesla's FSD, which he says uses neural net reasoning to assess whether another vehicle's behavior in similar conditions makes the path safe.

## Robotaxi

1. **Pony AI Raises Fleet Target to 3,500 Vehicles by End of 2026:** Pony AI announced it is raising its robotaxi fleet target to 3,500 vehicles by the end of 2026 — an increase of 500 — after reporting stronger-than-expected Q1 2026 revenue of $34 million against an average estimate of $21 million. The company now expects full-year robotaxi revenue to grow 3.5 times its 2025 level. However, Pony AI reported a net loss of $58 million against that $34 million revenue, meaning they are losing nearly twice what they earn. The hosts note their fares would need to be roughly 300% higher to break even, though some costs won't scale linearly.

2. **Robotaxi Unit Economics Remain Deeply Challenged Across the Industry:** The hosts highlight systemic profitability problems across robotaxi operators. Waymo is losing approximately $5 billion per year and roughly $100 per ride. Pony AI's losses suggest fares are underpriced by approximately 70% relative to break-even. Brian White argues these are structural problems requiring fundamental fixes, not incremental fare increases, and that scale will only partially help since some costs (compute, vehicles) don't fall proportionally.

## Market & Competition

1. **Lidar vs. Vision-Only Debate Continues to Favor Vision:** The hosts argue that every lidar-first company is underperforming Tesla in autonomous driving capability. Waymo's Atlanta flood incident is cited as an example of lidar's inability to substitute for genuine intelligence and neural net reasoning. Brian White contends that FSD supervised today is "vastly safer than a human driving," citing distractions like phone use as a persistent human problem, and argues the industry is moving toward vision-centric end-to-end systems pioneered by Tesla and now being adopted by Xpeng in China.

2. **China AV Market Faces Regulatory Headwinds:** The hosts reference a prior incident in China where widespread outages of BYD robotaxis caused major traffic disruptions, prompting regulators to freeze new permits for high-level self-driving vehicles. This backdrop makes Pony AI's fleet expansion ambitions more challenging even as their revenues improve.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla Europe registrations: +46.5% YoY in April 2026; 10,654 units across EU, UK, and four other markets
- EU-only Tesla sales: +67% YoY in April 2026
- Month-over-month growth trend: +84% in March 2026, +12% in February 2026
- Xiaomi YU7 Standard Edition: ~$33,000; losing ~$5,000 per unit
- Stellantis plan: €60 billion, 29 new EVs by 2030, 9 under €30,000, autonomy partnership with Wave AI launching 2028
- Pony AI Q1 2026 revenue: $34 million (vs. $21 million average estimate); net loss: $58 million
- Pony AI full-year 2026 robotaxi revenue target: 3.5x their 2025 level
- Pony AI fleet target: 3,500 vehicles by end of 2026
- Waymo losses: ~$5 billion/year; ~$100 per ride
- Brian White on Alpamayo/Mercedes timeline: "10% odds" of deployment by end of 2026
- Brian White on Xpeng lidar deprecation: "It's ornamental. It's decorative."
- On Waymo flood issue: "This is the Michael Scott navigation."

articles.title: Tesla’s own AI trainers don’t trust ‘Full Self-Driving’ or its safety stats, Reuters finds
articles.body:
A Reuters investigation, based on interviews with nine former Tesla data labelers, a former self-driving engineer, and 11 traffic-safety researchers, finds that Tesla's FSD safety statistics are methodologically flawed and that the company's own AI trainers overwhelmingly distrust the technology.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Safety statistics inflated by a factor of three:** Tesla executives — including CEO Elon Musk, CFO Vaibhav Taneja, and Board Chair Robyn Denholm — have repeatedly claimed FSD is up to 10 times safer than human drivers, with Musk displaying a chart at a November shareholder meeting claiming "85% less crashes." Reuters found that Tesla compared airbag-deployment crashes in its own fleet against federal data that includes all crashes requiring a tow truck — a far less severe threshold. University of Michigan researcher Marco Benedetti performed the correct apples-to-apples comparison (airbag crashes vs. airbag crashes) and found the result dropped from "10x safer" to roughly three times farther between crashes. That figure itself remains unreliable due to the age gap between Tesla's fleet (4.1 years average) and the overall U.S. fleet (12.8 years). Ten of 11 traffic-safety researchers who reviewed the methodology told Reuters it amounted to misleading marketing.

2. **Tesla's own data labelers don't trust FSD:** Seven of the nine former data labelers told Reuters they wouldn't trust FSD to drive them. One said he wouldn't ride in a Tesla robotaxi "if you fucking paid me." A veteran self-driving engineer who reviewed Tesla crash data for years called the company's safety claims "bullshit" and said: "Definitely, don't trust Elon on this." Labelers described routinely seeing FSD fail to yield to emergency vehicles, give motorcyclists adequate space, brake on freeway off-ramps, and avoid construction zones. A specialized "trauma team" in Palo Alto reviewed near-misses with pedestrians, including clips of FSD-piloted vehicles nearly hitting children and failing to recognize pedestrians in crosswalks. FSD was also reported regularly exceeding speed limits by 20–30 mph after Tesla introduced a "Mad Max" aggressive driving mode, with one reported instance of 60 mph in a 25-mph zone.

3. **NHTSA scrutiny and legal exposure:** NHTSA currently has four active investigations into FSD and Autopilot, including a probe into dozens of cases where FSD ran red lights or turned into oncoming traffic, and a review of whether Tesla's 2023 Autopilot recall was sufficient. Tesla was also hit with a $243 million verdict after an Autopilot crash in Florida killed a 22-year-old woman. Despite Musk's November statement that Tesla would soon allow drivers to text while using FSD, the feature has not been enabled six months later; Tesla's own FSD website continues to state the system requires active driver supervision.

## Robotaxi

1. **Extensive pre-launch mapping contradicts Musk's "no HD maps" claim:** Reuters found that Tesla conducted weeks of intensive nightly testing and mapping at the Warner Bros. studio lot before the October 2024 Cybercab unveiling, and similarly mapped Austin's limited robotaxi zone extensively before its June 2025 launch — annotating curbs, traffic lights, road signs, and road markings. The Utah data-labeling staff doubled to approximately 300 workers in the six months before the Austin launch. This directly contradicts Musk's repeated claim that Tesla's approach does not require the "laborious local mapping" used by rivals like Waymo. One former employee described the Austin zone: "You can't get creative outside of that."

2. **Unsupervised fleet remains very small:** Nearly a year after the Austin launch, Tesla still operates only about 20 unsupervised robotaxis there within a limited and carefully mapped zone. Some vehicles still carry human safety monitors in the front seat. The Reuters findings explain the scaling difficulty: the labor-intensive, zone-specific mapping and annotation process is extremely hard to replicate broadly.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert states the Reuters findings confirm what Electrek has long documented — that Tesla's safety claims don't hold up — and calls the statistical methodology choice (using a metric that inflated safety claims 3x despite access to correct data) deliberate rather than accidental. Lambert also flags a new complacency risk: as FSD improves on HW4 hardware, drivers are becoming less attentive, making the remaining edge-case failures more dangerous, and argues Tesla is not doing enough to address this.

Notable quotes and data:
- "It's like saying: 'My jet airplane is faster than your World War II bomber.' Yeah, so, what's your point?" — Carnegie Mellon professor Phil Koopman
- "Definitely, don't trust Elon on this." — former Tesla self-driving engineer
- One labeler: he wouldn't ride in a Tesla robotaxi "if you fucking paid me"
- Tesla fleet average age: 4.1 years vs. U.S. fleet average: 12.8 years
- Safety claim inflation factor: ~3x, per University of Michigan researcher Marco Benedetti's corrected comparison
- Austin unsupervised robotaxi count: ~20 vehicles, per Reuters
- Utah labeling staff pre-Austin launch: ~300 workers (doubled in six months)
- Tesla $243 million verdict in Florida Autopilot wrongful death case
- NHTSA: 4 active FSD/Autopilot investigations currently open

articles.title: Why Tesla's Robotaxi Rollout Stalled / Many Are Wrong About Elon's Voting Percentage ⚡️
articles.body:
This episode of "Electrified," hosted by Dillon Loomis, covers the current state of Tesla's robotaxi rollout and why fleet growth has stalled, along with a detailed breakdown of Elon Musk's actual real-world voting power at Tesla versus the commonly cited beneficial ownership figure. The video also touches on Megapack 3 deployments in Europe, EU EV sales data, Optimus factory construction progress, FSD updates, and several SpaceX-related developments.

## Robotaxi

1. **Fleet Growth Has Stalled Since Mid-May:** According to the third-party tracker (RobotaxiTracker.com), fleet growth effectively paused in all three Texas cities around May 9th. Of the 26 active vehicles tracked over the past 30 days, 21 are unsupervised, and just under 80% of rides over the past 7 days have been unsupervised. A photo shared by a community member shows 13 Cybercabs parked in Dallas that "appear to be asleep for now," suggesting they are on-site but not yet deployed.

2. **Houston Depot Activity Suggests Preparation:** A community observer named Aron noted that many Model Y vehicles at the Houston robotaxi depot have their hazard lights on, speculating they may be undergoing retrofits (possibly for a rear washer camera). Some of these Model Ys are launch edition vehicles not available for sale. Separately, employees were observed removing carpeting and parts from trunks. Last week, all Model 3s, Cybertrucks, and non-robotaxi vehicles were removed from the lot, leaving only Cybercabs and Model Ys. Dillon interprets this as Tesla being in "all hands on deck" mode preparing Cybercabs for imminent deployment.

3. **Cybercab Production Timeline and Deployment Thesis:** Tesla announced the first Cybercab off the production line at Giga Texas on February 17th, with a broader production announcement on April 23rd. The pause in Model Y fleet expansion appears to coincide with the arrival of Cybercabs in Austin, Dallas, and Houston. Dillon's personal expectation is approximately 30 Cybercabs in Austin and 10–15 each in Dallas and Houston over the coming weeks. He believes serious scale will wait until a future FSD version (referred to as V15), expected later in 2025.

4. **Five New Cities Must Launch Within 33 Days:** Tesla's own slide deck commits to launching robotaxi service in five new cities, and as of the video's date, that deadline is approximately 33 days away. Dillon emphasizes that commitments in Tesla's official slide deck should carry significantly more weight than off-the-cuff comments Elon makes in interviews. He believes Tesla is hyperfocused on meeting these city-launch milestones and does not want to face the backlash of missing them.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD 14.3 Mixed Performance:** Dillon reports that FSD version 14.3 demonstrated impressive supervised FSD behavior in a complex traffic scene in the Netherlands. However, it also showed a concerning parking failure where the vehicle would have driven into a shopping cart stall without human intervention. Dillon has also experienced some phantom braking on 14.3 in limited testing. He emphasizes that the most significant aspect of 14.3 is Tesla's rewrite of the compiler and runtime from the ground up, positioning it as a foundational building block for future releases rather than a polished end product.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus Factory Steel Structure Goes Up:** Joe Tegtmeyer reported that the first steel structure has been erected at the construction site for an Optimus factory with a stated capacity of 10 million units per year, and that the second phase of land reclamation is underway. A screenshot was shared showing the first steel going up at the site.

## Energy

1. **Megapack 3 Heading to Belgium:** Tesla's newest Megapack 3 will be deployed in one of Europe's most significant battery storage projects, with Belgian company Spy installing 180 units on the site of a former power plant. Installation and grid connection work is scheduled to begin in November 2025, with testing and commissioning expected to be completed by end of 2027. The project will have a storage capacity of several hundred megawatt hours and a total project value exceeding $116 million. This will be one of the first large-scale Megapack 3 deployments in Europe.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla EU Sales Up 45.8% Year-to-Date:** New ACA data through April shows Tesla sold 89,429 vehicles in the EU, EFTA, and UK year-to-date, up from 61,343 in the same period last year — a 45.8% increase. Tesla's overall market share rose from 1.4% to 1.9%. Dillon cautions that comparisons are distorted because Q1 and Q2 of last year saw Tesla transitioning to the refreshed Model Y and Model 3. He hopes a broader supervised FSD rollout later in the year will accelerate momentum further.

2. **Chinese Automakers Outpacing Tesla in Europe:** BYD sold over 101,000 vehicles in EU/EFTA/UK markets in the first four months of the year, up nearly 144% year-over-year, exceeding Tesla's volume. Chery Auto also outsold Tesla in this period with sales growth of 338% year-over-year. Dillon notes that lower price points and more available models contribute to these figures, but flags the Chinese automaker surge as a significant storyline. Hybrids continue to dominate EU consumer preference at 38.2% market share versus full BEVs at 19.7%.

## Market & Competition

1. **Elon's Real-World Voting Power Is 11%, Not 20%:** Dillon provides a detailed breakdown of the difference between Elon Musk's SEC-reported beneficial ownership and his actual real-world voting power. The 13G/A filing shows approximately 717 million shares classified as beneficial ownership (~20.3%), but this includes 303 million unexercised options from the 2018 compensation award that do not currently carry voting rights. Elon's actual real-world voting power today is based only on the ~413 million shares he fully owns in a revocable trust, divided by Tesla's actual outstanding share count of approximately 3.75 billion — yielding an 11% real-world voting percentage.

2. **Options Exercise Window Opens Path to 17.6%:** Per a new implementation agreement following the Delaware court case, Elon's window to exercise the 303 million 2018 award options runs from May 21st through August 15th of this year. If Elon doesn't exercise them himself, Tesla will exercise them on his behalf. Once exercised, those shares will be added to both the numerator and denominator: 717 million divided by approximately 4.059 billion outstanding shares would give Elon a 17.6% real-world voting stake. The tax event for those shares is expected to be pushed to 2028 when shares vest, not at the time of exercise, with a 5-year holding period extending through 2033.

3. **2025 Award and Path to 28.1%:** The newer 2025 compensation award covers approximately 423 million shares already included in Tesla's outstanding share count. These shares are currently subject to a voting proxy given to Tesla's secretary, voted proportionately to other shareholders — meaning Elon has no voting control over them now. The award has 12 tranches, each worth approximately 35 million shares. As Elon earns each tranche by hitting market cap and operational milestones (implying Tesla reaching approximately an $8.5 trillion market cap for full vesting), voting rights transfer to him. If all tranches are earned, Elon's total voting control would reach approximately 28.1% — near or above his stated goal of 25%, estimated to occur around tranches 8 or 9.

4. **SpaceX Merger Speculation:** Peter Diamandis, a friend of Elon Musk and early SpaceX investor, stated that a post-IPO merger between SpaceX and Tesla is "inevitable" and a question of timing, primarily because Elon would want to consolidate voting power across his companies. Elon currently holds 85.1% voting control at SpaceX (prior to IPO filing). The FTSE Russell indices announced fast-entry enhancements allowing qualifying IPOs to join relevant indices just 5 days after IPO, changes Dillon notes were largely put in place for SpaceX, enabling more forced institutional buying shortly after listing.

5. **Rivian R2 Launch June 9th:** Rivian announced the R2 will launch on June 9th with order invites, first customer deliveries, and demo drives beginning. Dillon characterizes the R2's success or failure as likely a make-or-break moment for Rivian.

Notable quotes and data:
- Active robotaxi fleet per RobotaxiTracker.com: 696 total (Bay Area 579, Austin 104, Dallas 6, Houston 7); unsupervised fleet: 39 (Austin 28, Dallas 5, Houston 6)
- ~80% of robotaxi rides over past 7 days have been unsupervised per third-party tracker
- 21 of 26 active vehicles tracked over past 30 days are unsupervised
- First Cybercab off production line at Giga Texas: February 17th
- "Cybercab in production now at Giga Texas" announced April 23rd
- Tesla must launch in 5 new cities within ~33 days of video publish date (by ~June 30, 2026)
- Dillon's near-term expectation: ~30 Cybercabs in Austin, ~10–15 each in Dallas and Houston
- Elon's beneficial ownership (SEC form): ~20.3% (717M shares ÷ 3.5B)
- Elon's current real-world voting power: ~11% (413M shares ÷ 3.75B outstanding)
- Elon's voting power post-options exercise: ~17.6% (717M ÷ 4.059B)
- Elon's potential maximum voting power if all 2025 award tranches earned: ~28.1% (1.14B ÷ 4.059B)
- Elon's SpaceX voting control prior to IPO filing: 85.1%
- Megapack 3 Belgium project: 180 units, total value >$116M, several hundred MWh capacity
- Tesla EU/EFTA/UK YTD sales through April: 89,429 (+45.8% YoY)
- BYD EU/EFTA/UK YTD sales: >101,000 (+144% YoY)
- Chery Auto EU sales growth YTD: +338% YoY
- EU full BEV market share YTD: 19.7% (up from 15.3% a year ago)

articles.title: The Biggest IPO in Human History is Happening
articles.body:
This video covers the SpaceX S-1 IPO filing submitted on May 20th, 2026, which the host argues represents the largest IPO in human history, targeting a valuation nearing $2.5 trillion. The core thesis is that SpaceX is no longer just a rocket company — it has quietly transformed into three distinct businesses (rockets, satellite internet, and AI) and a landmark $15 billion/year compute deal with Anthropic fundamentally reframes what looks like a money-losing enterprise into a strategic infrastructure play for the AI era. Tesla is briefly mentioned as a parallel example of a company using a cash-cow business to fund long-term moonshots.

## Market & Competition
1. **SpaceX IPO targeting record-breaking valuation:** SpaceX filed an S-1 with the US government on May 20th, 2026, setting the stage for what is described as the largest IPO in stock market history. The previous record was Saudi Aramco's ~$25 billion raise in 2019; SpaceX is reportedly targeting roughly three times that amount at a valuation nearing $2.5 trillion. Shares are set to go live on NASDAQ on June 12th.

2. **SpaceX acquires xAI, transforming into a three-segment company:** On February 2nd of 2026, SpaceX closed an all-stock deal to acquire xAI — Elon Musk's AI company — which includes the Grok chatbot, the X social media platform (formerly Twitter), and data centers called Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 housing over half a million GPUs. As a result, SpaceX now reports financials across three segments: Space (rockets), Connectivity (Starlink), and AI (xAI).

3. **Anthropic deal: $15 billion/year in compute revenue from a single customer:** In May 2026, SpaceX signed an agreement for Anthropic — a top-tier AI company behind the Claude models and a direct competitor to Grok and ChatGPT — to pay $1.255 billion per month through May 2029 for access to SpaceX's computing capacity. This amounts to approximately $15 billion per year from a single customer. Either side can cancel on 90 days' notice, but the host considers cancellation unlikely given AI compute demand. Elon Musk publicly framed this as SpaceX offering "AI compute as a service at significant scale" and noted discussions with other companies for similar arrangements.

4. **AnySphere/Cursor deal and potential acquisition:** In April 2026, SpaceX also signed a computing deal with AnySphere, the company behind the AI coding tool Cursor, and SpaceX holds an option to acquire Cursor outright at an implied value of $60 billion, which the host suggests SpaceX is likely to exercise post-IPO based on recent reporting.

5. **SpaceX as the "picks and shovels" of the AI era:** The host frames SpaceX's strategic ambition as becoming the dominant infrastructure provider for AI — owning the compute, power, and eventually the orbital data center capacity that other AI companies must pay to use. This is explicitly compared to the Gold Rush analogy: the companies selling the tools to miners, not the miners themselves, got rich. Tesla is cited as a parallel, using car sales to fund Full Self-Driving software and the Optimus robot.

## Financials
1. **Total 2025 revenue of $18 billion, dominated by Starlink:** SpaceX's 2025 total revenue was approximately $18 billion. The Connectivity (Starlink) segment contributed roughly $11 billion, representing approximately 61% of total revenue — up nearly 50% year-over-year. The Space segment contributed roughly $5 billion, and the AI segment contributed approximately $3 billion.

2. **Starlink is massively profitable at software-like margins:** The Connectivity segment generated over $4 billion in operating income. On an adjusted EBITDA basis, Starlink produced over $7 billion on $11.4 billion in revenue — approximately a 63% margin, which the host describes as comparable to software company economics. As of end of March 2026, Starlink had roughly 10 million subscribers across 164 countries, with over 10,000 satellites in low Earth orbit, and its direct satellite-to-phone service was reaching approximately 7 million devices per month.

3. **AI segment losing over $6 billion, but Anthropic deal changes the math:** The AI segment (xAI) had an operating loss of over $6 billion (specifically cited as $6.4 billion) in 2025, which is the source of the headline-grabbing ~$5 billion overall company loss. SpaceX poured $3 billion in R&D into Starship in 2025 alone, dragging the Space segment to an operating loss of approximately $657 million. However, the host argues that with the Anthropic deal pouring $15 billion/year into the AI segment, the entire company could turn profitable as early as 2026.

4. **Severe cash burn in Q1 2026:** SpaceX's cash position fell from approximately $24 billion at the end of December 2025 to approximately $15 billion at the end of March 2026 — a roughly $9 billion decline in a single quarter. The host notes this burn rate is expected to slow significantly once Anthropic deal revenues begin flowing.

5. **Governance: Elon Musk controls ~85% of voting power pre-IPO:** SpaceX uses a dual-class share structure — Class A shares (1 vote each, available to the public) and Class B shares (10 votes each, held by insiders). Prior to the IPO, Elon Musk controlled approximately 85% of total voting power. Post-IPO, this percentage will decrease slightly but Musk will remain firmly in control. SpaceX qualifies as a "controlled company" under NASDAQ rules, allowing it to bypass certain independent board requirements. The host draws a parallel to Mark Zuckerberg's voting control at Meta.

6. **Orbital AI compute satellites planned for 2028:** The S-1 filing states SpaceX expects to begin deploying orbital AI compute satellites as early as 2028. The thesis is that satellites in sun-synchronous orbit can access effectively unlimited solar power (the filing cites the sun as holding ~99.8% of all energy in the solar system), eliminating the terrestrial grid and cooling constraints that are currently limiting AI data center expansion.

Notable quotes and data:
- Anthropic payment: $1,255,000,000 per month through May 2029 (~$15 billion/year) — disclosed in the S-1 filing
- Elon Musk quote from tweet: "As a recently expanded partnership with Anthropic demonstrates, SpaceX is offering AI compute as a service at significant scale. We are in discussions with other companies to do the same. Over time, especially with orbital data centers, we expect to serve AI at extremely high scale."
- S-1 filing quote on orbital data centers: "We expect to begin deploying our orbital AI compute satellites as early as 2028."
- S-1 filing quote on key person risk: SpaceX is "highly dependent on the continued services of Mr. Musk," and losing him "could significantly disrupt the company."
- Starlink adjusted EBITDA margin: ~63% ($7B+ on $11.4B revenue)
- SpaceX total 2025 revenue: ~$18 billion; Starlink share: ~61%
- Starlink subscribers: ~10 million across 164 countries as of end of March 2026
- Starlink satellites in orbit: over 10,000
- Cursor (AnySphere) implied acquisition value: $60 billion
- Colossus 1 & 2 data centers: over 500,000 GPUs
- SpaceX cash position: ~$24B (Dec 2025) → ~$15B (Mar 2026), ~$9B burn in one quarter
- Previous IPO record: Saudi Aramco ~$25 billion raised in 2019
- SpaceX NASDAQ listing date: June 12th
- Tesla mentioned as using car revenue to fund Full Self-Driving and Optimus

articles.title: Tesla Just Flipped The Entire Europe EV Narrative Upside Down
articles.body:
This video from FutureAzA features host Brian and co-host Herbert discussing Tesla's resurgent EV sales in Europe and emerging markets like Colombia and Chile, while also exploring the broader strategic question of whether traditional vehicle sales still matter given Tesla's pivot toward robotaxi and autonomous driving. The core thesis is that Tesla's 13-month European sales losing streak has ended, the rebound is real and accelerating, and the long-term value of selling cars today lies less in unit revenue and more in building the FSD-enabled fleet and autonomous vehicle ecosystem.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Colombia EV Market Surges:** Colombia's BEV market share reached nearly 20% in April 2026, up from 7.4% a year prior, representing over 300% growth year-over-year in EV sales. The hosts attribute early growth (2022–2025) to organic adoption from pent-up demand, while the more recent spike is linked to rising gas prices. Tesla responded by expanding its Supercharger network in Colombia, signaling confidence in continued growth. Total market volume remains small — estimated around 5,000 cars — but the trend is notable.

2. **Chile: Small Market, Meaningful Share:** Roland Percher's data shows Tesla reported 242 sales in Chile in April, capturing 16% of the BEV market, while overall BEV penetration in Chile sits at 5%. The hosts highlight this as an example of Tesla entering smaller markets that legacy automakers typically bypass due to cost and complexity.

3. **Europe Sales Rebound Is Real:** Tesla ended a 13-month European sales losing streak, with 13,740 cars sold across the EU, UK, and European Free Trade Association in the most recently reported month — a 29% increase year-over-year. Weekly data for May 18–24 showed 3,600 sales across tracked European countries, up 32% week-over-week and 67% versus the same week last year. Year-to-date European sales are up approximately 28,000 units, or 45.8%, from the prior year. France and Spain are reportedly at record highs. The hosts attribute the prior-year decline primarily to factory retooling for the refreshed Model Y, not demand destruction.

4. **Third Consecutive Month of European Growth:** According to a report referenced from ACEA (described as "APAC/AA"), Tesla has now posted three consecutive months of year-over-year growth across European markets, with April up 47% compared to April of the prior year. The tracked countries include the UK, Norway, Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, Czech Republic, and Iceland — representing approximately 60% of European Tesla sales.

5. **Norway Standout:** The hosts note Tesla sold approximately 400 units in Norway in a single day, describing it as exceptional for a small country and a sign of strong enthusiasm for the brand there.

6. **Legacy Automakers Losing Ground:** Volkswagen and Stellantis are each reportedly reducing total production capacity by approximately one million cars. The hosts argue that brand loyalty, historically bulletproof for European automakers, is eroding as consumers shift toward technology-first vehicles. BYD is also expanding dealer presence in Europe with aggressive pricing and a reported 185% sales increase, yet legacy OEMs are still the ones losing the most ground.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Version 13.3 Reduces Nag Frequency:** The hosts discuss a version of FSD (described as version 13.3, with the key change in the point-three update over point-two being reduced driver attention prompts). Users are reportedly driving for extended periods — one user cited over an hour — without receiving an attention nag. Herbert emphasizes this is supervised FSD and recommends all Tesla owners enable it, while both hosts caution against distracted driving.

2. **FSD Approval in Europe as a Demand Catalyst:** FSD has reportedly been approved in the Netherlands and is in test trials across multiple European countries. The hosts speculate that EU-wide approval across all 28 member states is possible and frame it as a significant future demand driver. Herbert argues that once consumers experience what FSD can do, it becomes a compelling purchase reason — one that other EVs cannot match.

3. **FSD Revenue as the Real Value of Current Sales:** Brian argues that the primary value of selling Model 3s and Model Ys today is generating FSD subscription or purchase revenue, rather than the vehicle margin itself. The hosts discuss how Tesla's strategic decision to cancel the Model 2 and prioritize the Cybercab — as described in the Walter Isaacson book — reflects a deliberate shift away from maximizing traditional car sales volume.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab Strategy Over Model 2:** The hosts recount the internal Tesla decision, sourced from the Walter Isaacson biography, in which Elon Musk chose to build the Cybercab robotaxi-first vehicle instead of a sub-$30,000 Model 2. Executives reportedly convinced him to design the Cybercab so it could function as a conventional car if FSD was not ready in time. This is framed as a clear signal that Tesla's corporate focus has fundamentally shifted away from traditional volume car sales.

2. **Customer-Owned Vehicles in the Robotaxi Network — Uncertain Future:** Brian raises Elon Musk's repeated promises that Model 3 and Model Y owners would be able to add their vehicles to Tesla's robotaxi network. He notes this model makes business sense for handling peak demand (analogous to Uber surge), but expresses concern that Tesla may be moving away from this plan. Herbert shares the concern, noting that Austin-deployed robotaxis appear to have hardware additions — such as camera washers and Starlink Mini — that existing consumer vehicles lack, which could disqualify them from network participation.

3. **Cybercab Revenue Superiority Over Consumer Vehicle Sales:** The hosts estimate that Tesla earns approximately $4,000–$5,000 profit selling a Model Y, versus potentially $25,000 per year in revenue by keeping one Cybercab in a robotaxi fleet. Brian initially suggests one Cybercab equals five consumer cars in revenue terms; Herbert revises this to three to four, accounting for the concentration of driving hours when roads are actually used. Both agree the Cybercab economics are dramatically superior to consumer vehicle sales.

## Market & Competition

1. **BYD Growing in Europe But Not Dominating:** Despite a 185% sales increase in Europe, BYD is described as not yet selling as much as it wants to in the region. The hosts note that Chinese EV brands broadly have made inroads but have not captured the market share they targeted, leaving room for Tesla's rebound.

2. **Media Coverage Criticized:** The hosts mock an Automotive News story framing the Dacia Sandero reclaiming Europe's monthly sales lead in April as Tesla "tumbling," calling it a failure to understand delivery wave dynamics at the start of a quarter. They also critique an Investor's Business Daily article suggesting investors should wait for Tesla stock to reach a buy point before purchasing, calling it a misunderstanding of how to evaluate a long-term thesis stock.

Notable quotes and data:
- Colombia BEV market share: ~20% in April 2026, up from 7.4% a year prior; over 300% year-over-year sales growth
- Chile: 242 Tesla sales in April, 16% BEV market share, overall BEV penetration at 5%
- Europe weekly sales (May 18–24): ~3,600 units, +32% week-over-week, +67% year-over-year
- Europe monthly sales: 13,740 units, +29% year-over-year; third consecutive month of growth
- Europe year-to-date: +28,000 units / +45.8% vs. prior year; France and Spain at record highs
- Tracked countries represent ~60% of European Tesla sales
- Norway: ~400 Tesla sales in a single day
- Volkswagen and Stellantis each reportedly cutting ~1 million units of production capacity
- BYD: +185% sales growth in Europe
- FSD version referenced: 13.3 (reduced nag frequency vs. prior point-two version)
- One user reported driving over an hour without an FSD attention prompt
- Cybercab revenue estimate: ~$25,000/year per vehicle vs. ~$4,000–$5,000 profit on a Model Y sale
- Cybercab-to-consumer-car revenue equivalence: ~3–5x per year (debated between hosts)
- Source: Roland Percher (data charts for Chile and European weekly sales)

articles.title: Legacy Auto Still Does Not Understand What Tesla Is Building
articles.body:
This video from FutureAzA features host Brian and recurring guest Randy Kirk discussing why legacy automakers — particularly GM, Ford, and Stellantis — fundamentally misunderstand what Tesla is building and why their current investment strategies signal long-term decline. The core thesis is that legacy auto is doubling down on internal combustion technology (transmissions, V8 engines) while retreating from EVs, effectively forfeiting global markets and leaving themselves wholly unprepared for the autonomous vehicle disruption ahead.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **GM's EV retreat masked as domestic investment:** GM is investing heavily in transmission production — $300 million to increase capacity near Detroit, another $300 million the prior year (2025), $40 million for transmission production in Ohio, and over half a billion for propulsion plants in Ontario building sixth-generation V8 engines for the Corvette and full-size pickup trucks. GM noted total investments of more than $6 billion since 2025, largely geared toward the redesigned Silverado. Brian and Randy frame this as analogous to investing in steam engines — profitable in the short term but strategically backwards.

2. **GM and Samsung pause $3.5 billion battery plant:** GM and Samsung have confirmed a full pause on construction of their jointly planned $3.5 billion battery plant dubbed "Synergy Cells," with county officials citing economic factors and the end of EV incentives. The companies still nominally aim to meet a "substantial completion" deadline by end of 2027, but Brian clarifies this only means finishing the building shell — no equipment will be installed. He interprets this as a complete retreat from serious EV ambitions and a forfeiture of international markets where GM has competed for over 70 years.

3. **Ford's "all in" on EVs rings hollow:** Ford has written down $6 billion in EV-related charges and is effectively retreating to its ICE roots. Jim Farley's pivot back to gas was framed not as a cost-saving move but as a profitability move. Randy notes Ford leads all automakers in recalls by a wide margin with no apparent fix in sight. Brian jokes that claiming to be "all in" on EVs while still maintaining multiple combustion commitments and writing down billions doesn't reflect the meaning of the phrase.

4. **Stellantis ranked worst-positioned of the Big Three:** Both hosts agree Stellantis is in the worst strategic position — described as "rudderless," with weak EV offerings in the US market despite having better EV products in Europe that never make it stateside. Stellantis is reportedly spending $7 billion on retrofits and new vehicles but without a coherent direction.

## Market & Competition
1. **Legacy auto's failure to partner with Tesla:** Randy argues that any of the Big Three could have simply called Elon Musk, offered a royalty arrangement, and licensed Tesla's drivetrain or skateboard platform rather than spending billions developing flawed proprietary systems like GM's Ultium. Brian extends the analogy — a single proven skateboard platform on which to build multiple vehicles would have been far more efficient than what GM attempted with Ultium, which he describes as "one size fits all, except it's all size fits none."

2. **Autonomous vehicles as the deeper existential threat:** Randy argues the real long-term threat to legacy automakers isn't just electrification — it's autonomy. He predicts robotaxis could offer rides at 30 cents to $1 per mile (citing Elon Musk's public predictions at the low end), eliminating the need for personal car ownership for many consumers. Randy notes his own household has already reduced to one Tesla, relying on Uber for some trips despite the higher per-mile cost. He expects robotaxis to become massive within the next one to two years (i.e., by 2027–2028) and to begin cutting into all car sales broadly.

3. **Blockbuster/Nokia/Xerox analogies for legacy auto:** Randy repeatedly draws parallels between GM's trajectory and famous corporate failures — Blockbuster (still profitable as Netflix disrupted it), Nokia (dominant until Apple's iPhone arrived), and Xerox (invented the personal computer mouse but failed to develop it). The point in each case: being profitable today does not protect against rapid disruption, and legacy automakers may not see the future clearly enough to adapt.

4. **Global market forfeiture:** Brian argues that legacy automakers are retreating to their domestic strengths — high-margin trucks in the US — while surrendering international markets. Developed markets abroad demand competitive EVs that GM and Ford cannot provide, and developing markets want cheaper cars than legacy OEMs can profitably build. The pivot back to ICE is framed as an irreversible forfeiture of global automotive market share.

Notable quotes and data:
- Randy Kirk: "The future is going to be autonomy... robotaxis are here. It's happening. And it's going to be massive by next year or the next following year."
- Randy Kirk on robotaxi pricing: "30 cents a mile as Elon predicts" at the low end, up to "a buck a mile or half a buck a mile"
- Randy Kirk: "We are a one-car family... you just don't need it anymore even with Uber at three bucks a mile for most of my trips."
- Brian on GM's Ultium: "One size fits all, except it's not one size, it's all size fits none."
- GM investments cited: $300M (transmission near Detroit) + $300M (prior year) + $40M (Ohio transmissions) + $500M+ (Ontario V8 propulsion) = $640M+ directly mentioned, plus $6B+ total since 2025
- GM/Samsung "Synergy Cells" battery plant: $3.5 billion, fully paused, targeting "substantial completion" by end of 2027
- Stellantis reportedly spending $7 billion on retrofits and new vehicles

articles.title: Why June Could Be BIG For Tesla Stock
articles.body:
Jo Bhakdi presents a tactical investment thesis arguing that June 2026 will be a significant catalyst month for Tesla stock, driven primarily by the expected expansion of Cybercab robotaxi deployments to new cities. He connects Tesla's official Q4 2024 earnings commitments, recent drone footage of Cybercab production activity, and nationwide AI safety operator hiring as converging signals that Tesla is preparing a major robotaxi rollout before June 30th. Layered on top of this, he cites the SpaceX IPO (anticipated around June 12th) and potential Optimus news as additional bullish macro tailwinds, leading him to execute an aggressive short-put options strategy on Tesla.

## Robotaxi

1. **Tesla's Official June 30th Robotaxi Expansion Commitment:** In the Q4 2024 earnings report (published in January 2026), Tesla officially stated plans for robotaxi coverage in Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Miami, and Phoenix — cities where it does not currently operate — by June 30th, 2026. Bhakdi emphasizes this was not an Elon Musk tweet but a formal, legally and compliance-reviewed investor relations document, making it significantly more credible and harder to miss without reputational consequence. He views this 31–32 day deadline as a powerful forcing function for near-term deployment.

2. **Cybercab Production Activity at Giga Texas:** Citing drone footage from Joe Tegtmeyer dated May 27th, 2026, Bhakdi notes that Cybercabs are being consistently churned out at Giga Texas, rolling in and out of the parking lot on what appears to be a daily or every-other-day cadence. He estimates that over 200 serially produced Cybercabs are already "in the wild" and deployed to their destinations, though he acknowledges the exact count is uncertain. He also notes Cybercabs being observed lining up in Dallas, Texas — separate from Austin — suggesting multi-city staging.

3. **Nationwide AI Safety Operator Hiring as Deployment Signal:** Bhakdi highlights a post from "Tesla Yoda" (dated approximately May 27th, 2026) showing Tesla actively recruiting AI safety operators across a large number of U.S. states including Washington, Nevada, Utah, Tennessee, Pennsylvania, New York, New Jersey, Kansas, Georgia, Texas, District of Columbia, Louisiana, Maryland, Missouri, and North Carolina. He interprets this broad, simultaneous hiring push as a strong operational indicator that a significant nationwide robotaxi expansion is imminent.

4. **June as the One-Year Anniversary of Robotaxi Launch:** Bhakdi notes that June also happens to be the one-year anniversary of Tesla's original robotaxi launch, adding symbolic alignment to his thesis that a major expansion announcement or deployment wave in June is likely.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO as a Secondary Tesla Catalyst:** Bhakdi expresses high confidence — characterizing it as somewhere between "very likely" and "guaranteed" — that SpaceX will go public around June 12th, 2026. He argues this IPO was engineered to be a buy and that the stock will rise, with secondary positive effects on Tesla stock through association, merger speculation (a SpaceX-Tesla merger has resurfaced in discussion), and forced buying by index funds upon index inclusion. He expects this to be an additional bullish layer for Tesla in June, though he considers it slightly more uncertain than the robotaxi catalyst.

2. **Optimus as a Third Catalyst:** Bhakdi briefly flags Optimus as a third potential catalyst, noting that a presentation or reveal is theoretically expected in July or August 2026. He expresses some personal skepticism about the timing but acknowledges it represents another bullish narrative layer for Tesla stock in the near term.

3. **Tesla Stock Technical Setup — Resistance at $445:** Bhakdi describes Tesla stock as repeatedly bumping against a $445 resistance level, which previously rejected the price harshly twice (including on May 11th, 2026, which he calls his worst trading day of 2026). He argues this time is different given the convergence of catalysts, and that the stock is set to break through toward a target of approximately $490, potentially within June. He also references an uptrend line from the April 8th, 2026 lows as technically supportive.

4. **Options Strategy — Short Puts at $450 Strike:** Rather than buying calls (which he finds too expensive) or more stock on margin, Bhakdi describes executing a short-put strategy with a $450 strike price and approximately one-month duration. He notes the premiums are nearly $30 (approximately $28–$30), with about $8 of intrinsic value, which he views as favorable for a seller. He frames the trade as: winning if Tesla stays above $430, fully winning above $450, and generating 10–20 percentage points of alpha over Tesla if his thesis plays out. He acknowledges the risk of a move to $420–$430 but says he has enough conviction to double down in that scenario.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla's Q4 2024 earnings (published January 2026) committed to robotaxi coverage in Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Miami, Phoenix, Houston, Dallas, Austin, and the San Francisco Bay Area by **June 30th, 2026**.
- June 30th deadline is approximately **31–32 days** from the video's publish date of May 28th, 2026.
- Bhakdi estimates **over 200 serially produced Cybercabs** are currently deployed "in the wild."
- Joe Tegtmeyer drone footage from **May 27th, 2026** shows Cybercabs rolling in and out of Giga Texas.
- Cybercabs also observed staging in **Dallas, Texas**.
- AI safety operator hiring spotted across approximately **15+ U.S. states** simultaneously.
- SpaceX IPO anticipated around **June 12th, 2026**.
- Tesla short-put strike: **$450**, ~1-month duration, premium of approximately **$28–$30**.
- Price target discussed: **$490**; minimum threshold for trade success: **above $430**.
- Bhakdi's estimated stock move from a significant robotaxi deployment: **5–10%**, potentially more.
- Optimus presentation expected in **July or August 2026** (Bhakdi expresses some skepticism on timing).
- April 8th, 2026 cited as the recent price low from which the current uptrend line originates.

articles.title: Inspire Robots RH56DFQ: Dexterous Hand Demo
articles.body:
This video from Munro Live features Mike Kasein, a senior electrical engineer at Munro and Associates, demonstrating and explaining the Inspire Robotics RH56DFQ dexterous robotic hand. The video serves as an introductory explainer on how robotic hands work — covering degrees of movement, actuation mechanisms, and sensor design — while previewing a forthcoming full teardown of the unit. The core argument is that robotic hands are among the most mechanically complex components of humanoid robots, and the video positions this as the first in a series exploring how these components are built.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Inspire Robotics RH56DFQ Overview:** The hand being demonstrated is the Inspire Robotics RH56DFQ, a six-degrees-of-freedom robotic hand. Six degrees of movement means the hand can move in six distinct ways — covering the five individual fingers plus a thumb that can articulate back and forth laterally. The hand is described as a commercially available, modular unit that can be purchased independently and integrated onto compatible robots, with Python programmability supported.

2. **Degrees of Freedom Explained:** Kasein uses a cheap 3D-printed hand as a visual aid to explain the concept of degrees of movement. A single degree means a finger can only move one way (curl/extend). Additional degrees add lateral finger movement, thumb abduction, and other articulations. He notes that a human hand has significantly more degrees of movement than this unit — for example, the ability to splay fingers sideways is a degree of movement the RH56DFQ does not possess.

3. **Actuation Mechanism — Micro Linear Actuators:** The RH56DFQ uses micro linear actuators (pistons that extend and retract) to drive each finger. A spring at the top of the finger assembly provides passive return force when the actuator retracts. This is a simpler and lower-cost approach compared to alternatives such as gear-driven or individual-motor-per-joint designs used in more expensive hands.

4. **Sensor Design — Pressure at Actuator Base, Not Fingertip:** A notable design detail is that the hand does not have sensors embedded in the fingertips. Instead, pressure sensors are located at the base of each actuator. This means tactile feedback is detected through mechanical resistance transmitted down to the actuator, not via direct fingertip contact sensing. Kasein demonstrates this by showing that separating the finger from the actuator eliminates any sensor response.

5. **Pricing and Market Positioning:** The RH56DFQ is priced at approximately $10,000 per hand and is described as one of the cheaper commercially available robotic hands on the market. At the high end of the spectrum, Kasein references a hand called the "Sharper Wave" (name as stated in transcript), which costs approximately $100,000, features approximately 26 degrees of movement, has sensors in every finger, and includes cameras embedded in the fingers as well.

6. **Force Specifications:** This lower-end model is capable of approximately 4 newtons of gripping force on the fingers and 6 newtons on the thumb. Higher-spec models from the same or competing manufacturers can reach approximately 6 newtons on fingers and 12 newtons on the thumb. Kasein notes that the current unit can grip objects but would likely not maintain grip under impact or resistance.

7. **Software Demo and Control:** The hand ships with test software that includes preloaded gesture commands. Kasein demonstrates several gestures including an "okay" sign, a pointing/flicking gesture, and a closed fist. Individual finger control is also demonstrated through the software interface, with each finger adjustable independently via sliders or similar controls.

8. **Upcoming Teardown Series:** Kasein announces that a full teardown of the RH56DFQ is planned as a follow-up video, and that Munro Live also has plans to tear down a full humanoid robot. This video is framed as the first installment in a broader series examining humanoid robot components.

Notable quotes and data:
- RH56DFQ hand price: ~$10,000 (described as lower end of the market)
- "Sharper Wave" hand price: ~$100,000 with ~26 degrees of movement, fingertip sensors, and cameras in fingers
- Finger gripping force (RH56DFQ): ~4 newtons; thumb: ~6 newtons
- Higher-spec model force: ~6 newtons (fingers), ~12 newtons (thumb)
- Six degrees of movement: five individual fingers + lateral thumb abduction
- Sensor location: pressure sensor at actuator base, not in fingertips
- Actuation type: micro linear actuators with spring return
- *"If you look at your hand, it's probably one of the most complex part of the robot."*
- *"A lot of people think there is actually a sensor in the fingertips. It really is down at the bottom of the actuator."*

articles.title: Daily X Summary (2026-05-28)
articles.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts from @SawyerMerritt were relatively light on high-signal Tesla investment content, with no autonomous driving, robotaxi, or Optimus updates. The most notable data points were strong European EV sales figures showing a 46.5% YoY jump, and a new Megapack facility breaking ground in Belgium. Overall, the day's content skewed toward general Tesla/tech news rather than thesis-driving developments.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **European Tesla Sales Surge 46.5% YoY in April:** Tesla new-car registrations across the EU, UK, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, and Switzerland jumped 46.5% year-over-year last month to 10,654 units, according to ACEA data. Within the EU alone, growth was even stronger — over 67% from a year earlier — reaching 9,000+ units (the post appears truncated). This is a meaningful demand signal for Tesla in Europe, particularly relevant given the brand headwinds and competitive EV landscape the company has faced in the region over the past year.

2. **New Tesla Megapack Facility Breaks Ground in Belgium:** A $116 million Megapack battery energy storage facility has begun construction in Belgium. The project will deploy 180 Megapack units for a total capacity of 700 MWh. Testing and commissioning are expected to be completed by end of 2027. This adds to Tesla's growing Energy division order book and represents continued international demand for grid-scale storage infrastructure.

3. **Tesla Spring Software Update Rolling Out:** Sawyer noted that Tesla's Spring software update appears to be rolling out more broadly, soliciting community feedback. No specific version number or feature details were mentioned in the post. Low engagement (75 likes) suggests this is early/informal, but worth monitoring for FSD-related feature announcements.

4. **Ferrari Enters EV Market with "Luce":** The Pope was photographed with the new Ferrari Luce EV, and Ferrari's CEO responded to design criticism by stating, "Real innovation is not democratic. Breakthrough ideas rarely emerge from immediate consensus." While this is primarily a competitor/market color item, it signals continued luxury EV market expansion — a segment where Tesla's Model S competes. Low direct relevance to Tesla's core thesis.

5. **Signature Edition Model S and Model X on Display at Fremont:** Tesla has placed both Signature Edition vehicles — limited to 250 Model S and 100 Model X units — on public display at the Fremont factory showroom. Primarily a brand/collector interest note; minimal investment signal.

6. **SpaceX/NASA and Starlink Spectrum (Tangential):** NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman praised SpaceX as the greatest commercial space company, and the European Commission opened mobile satellite spectrum bidding to non-European operators including SpaceX. These are SpaceX-specific developments with no direct Tesla financial impact, though Starlink's spectrum access in Europe could have indirect relevance to Tesla's connectivity services long-term.

---

## Signal Strength: **Mildly Bullish** — The strong European sales rebound (+46.5% YoY) and new Megapack deployment in Belgium provide incremental positive data points for Tesla's EV demand recovery and Energy division growth, but there were no major autonomous driving, robotaxi, or Optimus developments to advance the core long-term thesis.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Wall Street Star Alex Potter Says You're Getting Optimus Free
articles.body:
This video features an extended interview with Alex Potter, Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst at Piper Sandler, discussing his firm's newly released report titled "The Definitive Guide to Investing in Tesla" — a 77-page second edition that models 17 separate Tesla revenue streams out to 2045 using a detailed DCF framework. The core thesis is that Tesla's modeled businesses (excluding Optimus and distributed inference) already justify approximately $400 per share, meaning the market is effectively giving Optimus away for free at current prices around the $450s. Joining the conversation are hosts Herbert, Alexandra Merz, and Jeff Lutz, who probe Potter on robotaxi economics, FSD licensing, the competitive landscape, a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger, and China's role in the EV and robotics ecosystem.

## Robotaxi

1. **Bottom-up city-level ridership model:** Potter describes a rigorous methodology starting with all global cities of 500,000 people or more — approximately 900 cities. For each city, the model estimates population, per-capita one-way trips, the share made by car, the share eventually captured by robotaxi, and Tesla's share of that robotaxi market. Many cities (e.g., Pyongyang) were zeroed out entirely. This demand-side approach was used to back-calculate the number of vehicles Tesla would need to produce rather than starting from a vehicle production capacity figure.

2. **Tesla assumed at 50% robotaxi market share in a duopoly:** Potter explicitly assumes a duopolistic outcome in the global robotaxi market, with Tesla capturing approximately 50% market share. He does not name the second dominant player but implies a large Chinese platform as the likely counterpart, given China's ability to replicate successful business models with a domestic cost structure.

3. **Cybercab production peaks around 2 million per year in the mid-2030s:** Potter's model backs into a peak annual Cybercab production of approximately 2 million units per year, which he notes is close to the capacity figures Elon Musk has discussed. This peak production level is not reached until the mid-2030s in his forecast.

4. **Global active robotaxi fleet reaches 14–15 million by 2045:** By the end of the 20-year forecast period, Potter's model projects approximately 14 to 15 million active Tesla robotaxis globally. He notes this reflects a ride-hailing framing rather than full transportation-as-a-service, with the latter partially captured through personal vehicle FSD subscriptions.

5. **Vehicle useful life assumed at six years with straight-line depreciation:** Potter states that in his model, Cybercabs are assumed to stay in service for six years, with depreciation spread over that period. He identifies this depreciation assumption as a significant driver of cost per mile calculations.

6. **Cost per mile modeled at 25 cents:** Working from first principles — charging station output and build cost, connectors per station, sessions per day, wholesale electricity cost, cleaning costs, depreciation per mile, and other inputs — Potter's model arrived at approximately 25 cents per mile as the cost to deliver a robotaxi ride. He notes this aligns with Tesla's own stated targets and validates the directional accuracy of those one-liner figures.

7. **Robotaxi becomes ~45% of revenue and nearly half of gross profit by 2045:** The report projects that by 2045, robotaxi rides will represent approximately 45% of Tesla's total revenue and close to half of all gross profit. By contrast, new car sales become "basically a rounding error" by that point.

8. **Model previously assumed asset-light software subscription approach:** Potter acknowledges that in an earlier version of his model, he assumed Tesla would not own or manage a robotaxi fleet but would instead sell Cybercabs to third parties and monetize through self-driving software subscriptions. He has since revised this view, now modeling Tesla as directly owning and operating the fleet and selling rides.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD subscription priced at $99/month — Potter calls it "quasi-free":** Potter uses FSD himself daily and argues that $99 per month — approximately $1,200 per year — dramatically underprices the productivity value being delivered. He draws a parallel to Steve Ballmer's dismissal of the iPhone, suggesting most people today similarly underestimate FSD's transformative value. He expects the monthly price to rise substantially as capability becomes undeniable.

2. **FSD licensing to other OEMs modeled to grow to ~$400 billion by 2045:** The report models FSD licensing to third-party automakers as a revenue stream that eventually scales to approximately $400 billion — described as roughly "four Teslas" in revenue terms. However, the inflection point for this licensing business is pushed out to roughly the mid-2030s due to the multi-year process OEMs would face: first acknowledging the need (perhaps around 2029), then redesigning vehicles around Tesla's electrical architecture, cameras, and compute.

3. **One in three vehicles on Earth modeled on Tesla's platform by 2045:** By the end of the forecast horizon, Potter's model assumes approximately one out of every three vehicles globally is built around Tesla's electrical architecture, sensors, and compute. He notes this is an assumption subject to geopolitical uncertainty and acknowledges the number could be 20% or 40% rather than ~33%.

4. **Western OEMs expected to eventually capitulate and license FSD:** Potter argues that Western OEMs are using a "Franken-monster" approach to self-driving — relying on consortia and tier-one suppliers — and will ultimately fail to match Tesla's cost-effectiveness and integration. He draws an analogy to the Supercharger network adoption, where Ford and others eventually switched to NACS after resisting, and predicts the same domino effect will occur with FSD licensing. He suggests the first OEM to announce FSD licensing could see a significant stock re-rating.

5. **S-curve timing shifts have outsized DCF impact:** Potter explicitly notes that shifting his robotaxi and FSD licensing S-curves forward or backward by one to three years has a significant effect on the DCF valuation due to time value of money, even if the long-run endpoints remain the same.

6. **Current FSD version meaningfully reduces driver nag:** Co-host Jeff Lutz mentions he is on FSD version 14.3.3 and describes a meaningful reduction in the nag prompt in the most recent release, saying he is now able to read emails and messages during drives — corroborating Potter's description of FSD nearing a genuine productivity unlock.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus excluded from the $400/share valuation — Potter calls it too hard to model:** Potter explicitly excludes Optimus from his DCF, not out of skepticism but because he cannot conceptualize a credible bottom-up model. He says he genuinely believes Elon Musk's characterization of Optimus as an "infinite money glitch" that will make GDP metrics and labor market concepts unrecognizable, but that the scope of disruption makes it nearly impossible to put into a spreadsheet. His threshold was: if the 17 modeled businesses already justified a valuation above current stock price, he did not need to force an Optimus number.

2. **Optimus deployment in China raises US national security questions:** The panel raises the question of whether the US government will permit Tesla to manufacture Optimus robots in China given their strategic importance as humanoid AI systems. Potter and the co-hosts agree that China will likely want Tesla to build Optimus there, but flag US regulatory restrictions as the key open question — a dynamic distinct from EVs and software.

3. **Very few companies will survive the humanoid filter:** Jeff Lutz argues that while hundreds of companies may attempt to build humanoid robots, the number that can credibly combine a capable AI brain, manufacturable hardware, and cost-effective production will fit on "one or two hands." Potter agrees.

## Market & Competition

1. **China's EV success traced directly to Tesla's factory entry:** Potter gives a detailed account from his time covering China pre- and post-Tesla. Before Tesla's 100%-owned Giga Shanghai opened (he references the 2017–2018 period), Chinese EV companies were copying 20th-century Western OEM supply chains, relying on tier-one suppliers, and producing vehicles that nobody voluntarily bought. Government subsidies were being gamed. Tesla's arrival gave Chinese companies a modern, vertically integrated template to copy — and within a few years, companies like BYD, NIO, Li Auto, Leap Motor, and Xpeng had built compelling EVs with domestic cost structures.

2. **Chinese upstream battery and mineral supply chain was already being built pre-Tesla:** Potter acknowledges a significant blind spot in his earlier China analysis: while the EV vehicles were poor quality and subsidy-driven, Chinese investment in actual lithium and graphite refineries upstream was real and long-term. Today, critical battery materials can essentially only be refined in China, giving it a structural supply chain advantage that predates Tesla's involvement.

3. **Rivian identified as the closest Western analog to Tesla's vertical integration approach:** Potter credits Rivian with taking a page from Tesla's playbook — vertically integrated, direct consumer relationship, in-house electronics and electrical architecture. He is skeptical of their continued reliance on lidar (calling it an unnecessary "crutch") but distinguishes them favorably from OEMs that outsource their core technology stack. He notes Rivian lacks Tesla's massive, purpose-built data-harvesting fleet.

4. **Volkswagen's investment in Rivian cited as "anything but Tesla" strategy:** Alexandra Merz references Volkswagen's investment in Rivian as emblematic of OEMs doing "anything but Tesla" despite the mathematical reality that Tesla's approach is superior. Potter does not dispute this characterization.

5. **Chinese cars increasingly visible in European markets:** Alexandra Merz reports observing numerous BYD SUVs and Omoda vehicles in Italy during a recent visit, parked alongside BMWs and Mercedes at roughly half the price — evidence of China's export juggernaut reaching even brand-loyal European markets.

6. **Tesla's supply chain ranked #14 globally by Gartner in 2023, #1 among automakers:** Jeff Lutz cites a 2023 Gartner supply chain ranking placing Tesla at number 14 globally and first among all automakers — ahead of Toyota — as evidence of Tesla's underappreciated hardware and manufacturing capability. He argues Tesla's internal AI and robotics adoption (referencing Terafab and acquired robotics/hardware companies) will further widen this lead.

## Financials

1. **DCF covers 17 revenue streams over a 20-year horizon to 2045:** The Piper Sandler model is built bottom-up with 17 distinct revenue and gross profit streams, each modeled with specific assumptions about ramp timing, pricing, cost structure, and market penetration. Potter describes it as extremely detailed — the model takes roughly 30 seconds just to open due to file size.

2. **Sum-of-parts value approximately $400/share excluding Optimus and distributed inference:** After modeling all 17 businesses, Potter's DCF yields approximately $400 per share. Since Tesla was trading around the $450s at the time of the report, the delta implies the market is assigning a positive value to Optimus and other excluded items (like distributed inference) — or equivalently, getting them "for free."

3. **Conservative assumptions driven by regulatory uncertainty, not technical skepticism:** Potter stresses that his conservatism in modeling robotaxi and FSD licensing timelines reflects uncertainty about regulatory and societal responses — particularly outside the US — rather than any doubt about Tesla's technical capability. He explicitly says the technical lead is real and the cost structure is superior.

## Market & Competition (SpaceX-Tesla Merger)

1. **Potter personally expects a merger to ultimately happen:** Potter says that if asked years ago whether all of Elon Musk's companies would eventually be one entity, his assumption was always yes. He views the companies as pursuing the same existential mission, with extensive engineering cross-pollination already in place. He does not see Elon mentally delineating between them.

2. **Alexandra Merz projects merger announcement in three months, completion in Q2–Q3 2027:** Merz shares her specific scenario: an announcement approximately three months from the video's publish date (i.e., around August–September 2026), with the actual merger completing in Q2 or Q3 of 2027 — a process she estimates would take approximately 12–14 months.

3. **Merger governance risks flagged — SpaceX structure described as a "bunker":** Alexandra Merz raises concerns that the SpaceX corporate structure, unlike Tesla's 2010 IPO structure, is designed to protect Elon Musk's control on "all sides" with over 50% voting rights. She describes this as unprecedented and potentially problematic for institutional investors, regulators, and geopolitical counterparties (especially China). Potter acknowledges monopolistic power concentration as the biggest long-term risk.

4. **Merger seen as potentially complicating FSD licensing and China operations:** Alexandra Merz raises the possibility that a merged SpaceX-Tesla entity could make OEM licensing deals more politically fraught due to national security associations with SpaceX. Potter acknowledges the logic and says he left room in his model for some vehicles to use alternative (non-Tesla) self-driving solutions for geopolitical reasons.

5. **Post-merger SpaceX IPO could cause short-term Tesla capital reallocation:** Potter flags that a SpaceX IPO accompanying a merger could cause money currently in Tesla to rotate into SpaceX, potentially creating near-term pressure on Tesla's valuation — a risk more relevant to benchmark-constrained institutional investors than to long-term holders.

Notable quotes and data:
- Alex Potter: "If I was allowed to own stocks in my own portfolio that I cover, Tesla would be the biggest holding and I would just hold it until the day I retire."
- Potter on Optimus: "I actually think that it's really true. I don't think it's hyperbolic. When he says these things, I really do think the world is going to look fundamentally unrecognizable."
- Potter on FSD at $99/month: "$99 a month is quasi-free... it's like Steve Balmer saying 'why would you pay $1,000 for a phone.'"
- Potter on Tesla's competitive moat: "You can't see second place with a telescope."
- Potter on OEM FSD adoption: "It's not something that they are falling over themselves to do... but in the end, Tesla's approach is just fundamentally different and better and more cost effective."
- Piper Sandler DCF sum-of-parts value: ~$400/share (excluding Optimus and distributed inference)
- Tesla stock price at time of report: ~$450s
- Robotaxi cost per mile (modeled from first principles): $0.25
- FSD subscription price: $99/month ($1,200/year)
- Cybercab vehicle useful life assumption: 6 years
- Peak annual Cybercab production in model: ~2 million units/year (mid-2030s)
- Global active robotaxi fleet by 2045: ~14–15 million
- Robotaxi share of revenue by 2045: ~45%
- FSD licensing revenue by 2045: ~$400 billion
- Share of global vehicles on Tesla's platform by 2045: ~1 in 3
- FSD licensing inflection point: approximately mid-2030s
- Piper Sandler report length: ~77 pages, second edition, firm has covered Tesla for 10 years
- Gartner 2023 supply chain ranking: Tesla #14 globally, #1 among automakers (ahead of Toyota)

articles.title: Tesla Already Solved The Hard Part Of Robotaxi
articles.body:
