This video from "brighterwithherbert" features host Herbert and guest Brian White (of the FutureAzA YouTube channel) discussing a convergence of positive signals for Tesla's autonomous driving and robotaxi thesis, including FSD regulatory approvals spreading across Europe, an analyst declaring Tesla has solved self-driving, Cybercab fleet buildups in Texas, and strong real-world vehicle efficiency and durability data. The core argument is that third parties — regulators, analysts, and consumer testing organizations — are increasingly validating what Tesla bulls have long believed: that FSD is genuinely safer than human driving and that Tesla vehicles are exceptionally durable and efficient. The hosts suggest Tesla's robotaxi rollout may be nearing an inflection point, evidenced by growing Cybercab registrations and parking lot accumulations in Texas cities.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Supervised approved in Belgium and Denmark, now five European countries total:** Belgium's Ministry of Transport of Flanders signed approval for FSD Supervised covering the entire Belgian territory (both Flemish and Belgian roads), coming just days after Elon Musk and Tesla Europe announced approval in Denmark. This brings the total number of European countries with FSD Supervised approval to five: Belgium, Netherlands, Denmark, Lithuania, and Estonia — representing approximately 11% of all European countries. Brian White speculates Spain may be next, given its apparent eagerness, followed potentially by Ireland.

2. **Piper Sandler analyst declares Tesla has achieved Level 4 autonomy in most conditions:** In a note released on Wednesday (approximately June 11, 2026), Alex Potter of Piper Sandler wrote that "Tesla has solved the self-driving puzzle" and that FSD is "ready for dissemination beyond early adopters." Potter cited his personal experience having FSD drive him from Missoula, Montana to Minneapolis, Minnesota in April as evidence, stating "there is no substitute for personal experience." Herbert notes he interviewed Potter at a Cyberbulls event a couple of weeks prior.

3. **FSD Supervised surpasses 11 billion cumulative miles globally:** Tesla's global fleet just crossed 11 billion miles driven on FSD Supervised, up from 10 billion just one month prior — meaning Tesla owners are collectively driving approximately 1 billion FSD miles every 37 days. The hosts note that as more European countries gain approval and Tesla's fleet continues to grow, the average daily FSD miles figure is accelerating. Brian White mentions personally using FSD 98% of the time over roughly 8,000–9,000 miles driven.

4. **FSD data from Denmark shows 3.5x safety improvement over human drivers:** Herbert references data presented a few days prior showing that in Denmark — after four months of FSD Supervised use on European roads — FSD Supervised is approximately 3.5 times safer than human drivers across key metrics including less hard braking and fewer hard turns. The hosts argue this real-world European safety data should compel regulators to accelerate approvals, since every day of delay effectively costs lives.

5. **Hardware 3 vs. Hardware 4 capability gap widening; FSD version 14 "light" expected:** Brian White drove a Hardware 3 Model 3 with 158,000 miles and found it still impressive, but noted the capability gap between Hardware 3 and Hardware 4 continues to widen as Hardware 4 keeps improving. Herbert notes that a "FSD version 14 light" port for Hardware 3 vehicles had been discussed as potentially arriving by end of June 2026, though nothing has been heard. Brian references statements by Ashok Elluswamy as the source of that timeline but cautions he does not follow Elon Musk's timelines closely.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab fleet accumulating rapidly in Texas, ~10 new vehicles registered per day:** As of the filming date (Wednesday, approximately June 11, 2026), approximately 69 Cybercab vehicles are registered with the Texas DMV, up by roughly 10 vehicles in a short period, with registrations increasing at a rate of at least 10 per day. Photos from community members show large clusters of parked Cybercabs in both North Houston and Dallas parking lots. Brian White frames this as a deliberate strategic buildup: "When you see troops amassing at your border... they're doing this because they have a plan."

2. **Munro Live interview flags safety readiness for robotaxi deployment:** Brian White references a recent interview between Munro Live and Will from Tesla Jigsaw, in which Munro Live was characteristically direct in arguing that FSD is already safer and questioning why regulators — particularly in Europe — are holding it back. Munro Live's position is that while zero deaths cannot be guaranteed due to unpredictable variables, the system is already demonstrably safer than human drivers.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **European Tesla sales up ~95,000 units year-over-year in first five months of 2026:** Data from analyst Roland Percher (tracked at "Poli") shows that across the European countries he monitors, Tesla sold approximately 95,000 more vehicles in the first five months of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025 — close to 100,000 units of surplus. Year-over-year monthly comparisons for May 2026 vs. May 2025 show a difference of approximately 24,000 vehicles in his tracked subset. The hosts note this comparison is somewhat skewed by factory retooling shutdowns in early 2025, and prefer comparison to 2024 data. Brand sentiment negativity has also diminished, aiding sales.

2. **BYD records eighth straight month of sales decline in China, down ~30% year-to-date:** Data highlighted by Michael Dunn (former CEO of GM Indonesia) shows BYD Auto has experienced eight consecutive months of declining sales in China, with approximately a 30% drop since the start of 2026. Geely, Changan, and SAIC are cited as applying competitive pressure. The April top three in China were Geely, Xiaomi SU7, and Model Y — though Model Y was number one in the prior month.

3. **Xiaomi losing approximately $5,000 per vehicle sold:** Brian White notes that Xiaomi is losing roughly $5,000 on every car it sells, which he argues makes a long-term path to profitability difficult even given the brand's broader tech conglomerate revenue streams. He draws a parallel to Tesla's own "production hell" era with the Model 3, suggesting Xiaomi will need to replicate that cost-reduction journey.

4. **2026 Tesla Model 3 RWD named most efficient EV in Edmunds real-world testing:** Edmunds tested the 2026 Model 3 rear-wheel drive and found it traveled 393 miles on a full charge — 30 miles (8.3%) beyond its EPA-rated 363-mile figure. More significantly, it consumed only 21.7 kWh per 100 miles in real-world testing, 13% better than the EPA rating of 25 kWh per 100 miles, making it the most efficient EV currently in production that Edmunds has tested. The review also noted improved cabin finish quality.

5. **Tesla ranks sixth in long-term vehicle durability study, beating Mazda, Subaru, and Porsche:** A study by iSeeCars analyzing 174 million vehicles found Tesla twice as likely to reach 250,000 miles as Subaru. Toyota, Lexus, Honda, and Acura led the rankings, with Tesla ranking higher than Mazda, Subaru, and Porsche. The hosts attribute Tesla's ranking — which they consider understated — to the car's relative newness limiting sample size, and predict Tesla will ultimately rank number one as more vehicles accumulate high mileage. Brian White cites battery degradation of approximately 1% per year as a key data point, meaning roughly 15% capacity loss over 15 years.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX going public cited as potential catalyst for Tesla robotaxi acceleration:** Herbert opens by suggesting that with SpaceX now a public company, Tesla's robotaxi ramp may be beginning — initially slow but soon gaining speed. The implication is that Elon Musk's bandwidth and/or strategic prioritization may now shift more toward Tesla's robotaxi deployment.

Notable quotes and data:
- Alex Potter, Piper Sandler: *"Tesla has solved the self-driving puzzle and FSD is ready for dissemination beyond early adopters."*
- Brian White on Cybercab buildups: *"When you see troops amassing at your border, if you think nothing's going on, I would ask you to study any amount of history."*
- Belgium Ministry of Transport letter: *"Regarding the approval for FSD technology on both our Flemish and Belgian roads... I just signed the approval."*
- FSD Supervised cumulative miles: **11 billion miles**, up from 10 billion one month prior (~1 billion miles every 37 days)
- Denmark FSD Supervised data: **3.5x safer than human drivers**
- Texas Cybercab DMV registrations: **~69 vehicles**, growing at ~10/day
- European Tesla sales surplus Jan–May 2026 vs. Jan–May 2025: **~95,000 units**
- BYD China sales decline: **~30% drop** year-to-date, eighth consecutive month of declines
- 2026 Model 3 RWD real-world range: **393 miles** (EPA: 363 miles); real-world efficiency: **21.7 kWh/100 miles** (EPA: 25 kWh/100 miles)
- iSeeCars study sample size: **174 million vehicles**
- Xiaomi estimated loss per vehicle: **~$5,000**
- Brian White's personal FSD usage rate: **98%** of miles driven
- FSD countries in Europe approved: **5** (Belgium, Netherlands, Denmark, Lithuania, Estonia) = **~11% of all European countries**

articles.title: SpaceX Is Now a $2 Trillion Company
articles.body:
This video covers the SpaceX IPO on Friday, June 12, 2026, which the host and guest Larry Goldberg describe as the largest public offering in the history of capital markets. The core thesis is that SpaceX is vastly underappreciated as an AI and cloud computing company — not merely a rocket company — and that Starlink's total addressable market and terrestrial data center ambitions make it a generational investment. Elon Musk is noted to have rung the NASDAQ bell for the second time, the first being for Tesla's IPO in June 2010.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO size and debut performance:** SpaceX priced its IPO at $135 per share and closed its first trading day up 20% at $161, giving it a market capitalization of approximately $2.1 trillion. The offering raised approximately $86 billion (including a green shoe overallotment), which is described as roughly three times the size of Saudi Aramco's record-breaking IPO debut in 2019. By number of shares traded on debut day, SpaceX ranked second to Facebook (580 million shares vs. SpaceX's approximately 518 million), but in dollar value of a single stock traded in a single day, SpaceX set an all-time record.

2. **SpaceX's position among the world's largest companies:** Following the IPO, SpaceX is ranked the seventh-largest company in the world at $2.1 trillion. Tesla is cited as the tenth-largest company at $1.46 trillion. Elon Musk now owns two of the top ten largest companies on Earth, with both having gone public at NASDAQ — Tesla in June 2010 and SpaceX on June 12, 2026, exactly 16 years later.

3. **SpaceX as an AI and cloud computing company:** Guest Larry Goldberg and early SpaceX investor Gavin Baker of Atradus both argue that SpaceX is fundamentally misunderstood as a rocket company. Baker notes that a month prior to the IPO, SpaceX had no cloud computing business, but by IPO day it had become the fourth-largest cloud provider by some measures, surpassing Oracle — an achievement accomplished in one month. Baker points to SpaceX's ability to bring gigawatts of terrestrial compute online, reuse Starship to deploy Starlink V3 satellites, enable direct-to-cell service, and eventually develop orbital compute as a series of investor-trackable milestones.

4. **Colossus data centers and chip strategy:** The discussion references Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 data centers. Colossus 1 was originally intended for Tesla's use, but latency issues led to a shift toward Colossus 2, which is associated with Vera Rubin chips in a deal with Google. Colossus 1 was then made available to Anthropic. Larry Goldberg argues that SpaceX/xAI will always prioritize its own compute needs first and rent out capacity secondarily — a strategy he says will make them the leading AI entity in time. He also suggests Grok and Cursor will merge into a single product.

5. **Starlink total addressable market revision:** Cathie Wood of ARK Invest bought approximately 3.3 million SpaceX shares — worth close to $500 million — on the open market on the day of the IPO across four funds. She explains that ARK originally sized the Starlink opportunity at $34 billion, interpreting it as a rural/maritime connectivity play. SpaceX itself now sizes the total addressable market at $1.6 trillion, encompassing all of telecommunications and the internet, enabled by SpaceX's decision to manufacture its own phased array antennas and drive hardware costs down dramatically. A phased array antenna previously cost approximately $27,000; SpaceX's in-house manufacturing has collapsed that cost curve.

6. **Starlink terminal manufacturing scale:** Larry Goldberg describes visiting the Starlink terminal factory in Bastrop, Texas (near Austin), where fully automated manufacturing produces phased array antennas with no human workers on the floor. He notes that this already enormous factory was doubled in size after his first visit, and that SpaceX plans to build four factories at Bastrop, some up to three times the size of the current facility, to manufacture data satellites at scale.

7. **Analyst coverage and investor demand:** Oppenheimer initiated coverage on SpaceX with an Outperform rating and a $190 price target, which would imply a valuation of approximately $2.5 trillion. The firm's thesis is that SpaceX will leverage its terrestrial compute expertise as a bridge to becoming the largest communications, cloud, and AI company in the world, citing a very large total addressable market with high barriers to entry. Black Rock reportedly put in an order for $5 billion of SpaceX shares. Options trading on SpaceX is set to begin Tuesday, June 17, 2026, and both the host and Goldberg warn of extreme volatility and danger for retail options traders.

8. **Competitive moat and SpaceX's lead over rivals:** Goldberg argues SpaceX's competitive moat is essentially insurmountable in the near term. He notes that China has not yet successfully returned a single booster to Earth, and Blue Origin — the only other company to have done so — is approximately nine to ten years behind SpaceX. SpaceX's Starship is described as ten times larger than competitors' rockets and designed for 100% reusability. Goldberg attributes SpaceX's technological lead to its willingness to push the frontier aggressively rather than waiting years between tests.

9. **SpaceX employee wealth creation:** Approximately 4,000 SpaceX employees, including blue-collar workers such as welders, reportedly became millionaires or multi-millionaires as a result of the IPO, due to SpaceX's practice of granting stock options to all employees.

10. **OpenAI and Anthropic IPO expectations:** The host notes that both OpenAI and Anthropic are expected to go public soon and that rumors suggest each could raise approximately $100 billion, which would surpass SpaceX's $86 billion raise and make SpaceX's record temporary.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX IPO priced at $135, closed at $161 (+20%) on June 12, 2026
- SpaceX market cap post-IPO: ~$2.1 trillion (ranked #7 globally)
- Tesla market cap at time of video: ~$1.46 trillion (ranked #10 globally)
- IPO raised ~$86 billion including green shoe, vs. Saudi Aramco's previous record
- Cathie Wood purchased ~3.3 million SpaceX shares (~$500 million) on IPO day
- Black Rock reportedly submitted a $5 billion order
- ARK's original Starlink TAM estimate: $34 billion; SpaceX's own TAM estimate: $1.6 trillion
- Phased array antenna previously cost ~$27,000 before SpaceX's in-house manufacturing
- Oppenheimer price target: $190 (implying ~$2.5 trillion market cap), rated Outperform
- SpaceX options trading begins Tuesday, June 17, 2026
- ~4,000 SpaceX employees became millionaires or multi-millionaires via the IPO
- Gavin Baker: "A month ago SpaceX did not have a cloud computing business. Now by some measures it is the fourth largest cloud ahead of Oracle and they did that in one month."
- Cathie Wood: "[SpaceX] thinks that this TAM is $1.6 trillion. And it's because it's not just [rural/maritime]. It is really all of telecommunications and all of the internet."
- OpenAI and Anthropic each rumored to raise ~$100 billion in upcoming IPOs

articles.title: Elon Musk's Biggest Tesla Bet Is Finally Taking Shape
articles.body:
This FutureAzA episode, hosted by Brian and Herbert, covers a broad range of Tesla news centered on the slow but steady robotaxi rollout, Cybertruck FSD feature updates, Tesla's strong China sales in May 2026, and a tangential discussion of SpaceX's orbital AI data center announcement. The core thesis is that Tesla's cautious, data-driven approach to scaling its robotaxi and Cybercab programs is deliberate and justified by safety data — and that near-term acceleration is likely once sufficient supervised miles are accumulated.

## Robotaxi

1. **Texas DMV registration count vs. RobotaxiTracker:** Only 69 Cybercabs are registered with the Texas DMV as of the time of recording — up from 42 previously. The hosts acknowledge this is the verified official figure, while noting that RobotaxiTracker.com has been a useful but imperfect community tool for monitoring the broader fleet. Both hosts agree that this number is far below what most observers expected a year after launch.

2. **NHTSA safety data since June 2025 launch:** The hosts walk through NHTSA-reported incident data covering the period from December through the recording date. There have been 17 reported incidents since the Austin robotaxi launch in June 2025. Only one involved a speed of 17 mph; the rest were described as fender benders. Of those, only seven were attributed to Tesla's fault, and two of those seven involved human remote operators — not the autonomous system itself. The hosts argue that the NHTSA "crash" classification is overly broad, as it includes events like a tire touching a curb with no damage.

3. **Cybercab lots spotted in Dallas and Houston:** The hosts note recent reports of lots containing 20–30 Cybercabs sitting idle in Dallas and Houston. Their interpretation is that these vehicles are ready to deploy but are awaiting the green light, likely pending additional supervised FSD miles and regulatory confidence specifically for the Cybercab form factor.

4. **Theory: SpaceX IPO timing influenced rollout pacing:** One host speculates that Tesla/Elon Musk deliberately avoided a large-scale Cybercab rollout to prevent any high-profile crash from dominating news cycles and potentially undermining the SpaceX IPO. Now that the IPO has occurred, the host expects more robotaxi news to emerge, though he believes true mass-scale deployment won't happen until a potential Tesla-SpaceX acquisition announcement, which he speculates could come in late July or August 2026.

5. **Cybercab form factor requires its own data set:** The hosts argue — using the Cybertruck Smart Summon delay as a direct analogy — that each new Tesla vehicle form factor requires its own dataset before FSD can be confidently deployed at scale. The Cybercab's unique design means Tesla needs to accumulate sufficient supervised miles specific to that vehicle before mass unsupervised deployment, regardless of how well FSD performs on existing Model 3/Y platforms.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Cybertruck Smart Summon launching soon:** Tesla's official Cybertruck account announced that Smart Summon is coming soon to the Cybertruck — described as overdue after years of silence on this FSD feature for the vehicle. Engineers reportedly cited the Cybertruck's rear-wheel steering and variable front steering as the technical challenges that extended development time.

2. **Ashok Elluswamy presentation on camera perception:** One host references a recent presentation by Ashok Elluswamy (Tesla VP AI/Autopilot) in which he demonstrated that Tesla's cameras can perceive scenes even under blinding sunlight conditions — seeing individual photons and cleaning up the image in ways the human eye cannot. The host uses this to raise the question of whether matrix headlights provide meaningful benefit to FSD's perception systems at night.

3. **Tesla patents smaller, cheaper matrix headlights:** Tesla has filed a patent for a more compact and less expensive method of producing matrix headlights. The significance noted is that Cybertruck's existing small front headlights are too compact to house a traditional projector — this new approach could enable matrix headlights on the Cybertruck. One host describes matrix headlights as a meaningful improvement for nighttime driving, citing over a thousand miles of personal nighttime FSD experience.

4. **Waymo criticized for traffic-blocking incidents:** The hosts argue that NHTSA's crash-reporting framework fails to capture dangerous-but-non-collision events, using Waymo as the primary example. They contend that Waymo vehicles frequently block traffic — creating hazardous conditions for other drivers — without these events appearing in crash statistics, making the safety comparison between Tesla and Waymo misleading.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla China May 2026 sales surge:** Tesla's China sales for May 2026 reached 85,982 vehicles (Model 3 and Model Y combined), up 39% year-over-year and up 8% from April 2026. Herbert notes that April is typically a weak month in China because it is the first month of the quarter and production is directed toward export deliveries; May reflects domestic sales more accurately. Annualized, this pace approaches roughly one million units per year from Giga Shanghai. Tesla has also rolled out purchase incentives and charging benefits in China.

2. **Tesla holding premium position despite macro headwinds:** Both hosts express surprise that Tesla continues to sell well at a premium price point in China despite macroeconomic weakness in that market. Herbert also notes that Chinese local governments have reintroduced EV subsidies following a period of intense price wars that left many Chinese EV makers losing money — a dynamic that indirectly supports Tesla's sales environment.

3. **Chinese EV import threat assessed skeptically:** The hosts push back on the narrative that Chinese automakers would easily displace Tesla in the US market even if tariffs were reduced. Herbert argues that Chinese automakers' cost advantages are deeply tied to local supply chains, low-cost domestic labor, and high sales volume — none of which would transfer easily to US manufacturing. Additionally, current tariffs would raise Chinese EV prices significantly in the US market. The hosts also point out that Tesla already competes successfully against Chinese brands in China itself, suggesting the competitive threat is overstated.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX orbital AI data center — context for Tesla investors:** The hosts briefly cover SpaceX's unveiling of its first-generation orbital data center satellites, dubbed "AI1," with a peak compute capacity of 150 kilowatts and an average of 120 kilowatts, at an efficiency of 70 kilowatts per ton. Elon Musk has stated a target of one gigawatt of compute capacity in space by 2027. The manufacturing facility (referred to as "Gigasat") will expand an existing facility already used for V3 Starlink satellites. The hosts frame this as relevant context for Tesla investors given the interconnected Musk ecosystem, though they note the primary gating factor is whether sufficient Starship launches can be achieved by 2027.

Notable quotes and data:
- 69 Cybercabs registered with Texas DMV as of recording (up from 42)
- 17 NHTSA-reported incidents since June 2025 robotaxi launch; only one at 17 mph, rest fender benders; only 7 attributed to Tesla fault; 2 of those 7 involved human remote operators
- 85,982 Model 3 and Y units sold in China in May 2026 — up 39% YoY, up 8% from April 2026
- SpaceX AI1 orbital data center: 150 kW peak / 120 kW average compute, 70 kW/ton efficiency
- Elon Musk target: 1 gigawatt of compute in orbit by 2027
- Lots of 20–30 Cybercabs reportedly sitting idle in Dallas and Houston, ready to deploy
- Host Herbert: "It's actually very surprising that Tesla specifically at the high premium category [is] still selling so well despite what's happening with the macro economy in China."
- On NHTSA reporting: "A crash instead of incident, and curb rashes are included in that. So the data is looking great. There are months where zero impact."

articles.title: SpaceX’s Secret Weapon Is NOT Elon
articles.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel features host Herbert and guest Larry Goldberg (serial entrepreneur and venture capital investor) analyzing multiple interviews of SpaceX President and COO Gwyn Shotwell, focusing primarily on her response to questions about a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger, as well as her comments on SpaceX's AI satellite plans, chip manufacturing ambitions, and Starship progress. The core thesis is that Shotwell's non-denial of a Tesla-SpaceX merger — combined with other signals — indicates a merger/acquisition is likely, and that Shotwell would be an ideal COO for a combined entity.

## Market & Competition

1. **Gwyn Shotwell's Non-Denial of a SpaceX-Tesla Merger:** In a CNBC interview conducted by Morgan Brennan, Shotwell was asked to respond to analyst Dan Ives of Wedbush's assertion that SpaceX and Tesla will eventually merge, with Ives putting the probability at over 80% and targeting 2027, and claiming the groundwork is already in place. Shotwell responded that a merger "might make Elon's life a little easier," acknowledged "there's no question that there are synergies between Tesla and SpaceX," and said there is "definitely a convergence of what we're all trying to accomplish in the future," before adding she was not currently focused on "that part of the future, at least." Herbert and Larry Goldberg interpret this as a tacit confirmation rather than a denial, with Goldberg noting he predicted this outcome in a white paper published in February 2026.

2. **Timing of a Potential Merger/Acquisition:** Larry Goldberg argues that an acquisition offer will not materialize immediately but rather sometime in early next year (i.e., early 2027), citing several reasons: Tesla's robotaxi rollout needs more time to establish clarity and drive Tesla's share price higher; SpaceX shareholders face lockup periods on their newly issued public stock and would not want a massive merger before those expire; and SpaceX has a large operational workload to manage in the near term. He contrasts his view with another commentator ("Alexandra") who reportedly believes an acquisition could happen sooner.

3. **SpaceX S-1 Amendment and Acquisition Capacity:** Herbert references language in SpaceX's S-1 amendment stating that SpaceX may be increasing its available shares in order to potentially conduct large acquisitions, which he cites as a structural signal supporting the merger thesis.

4. **Key SpaceX Executives Cited as Merger Assets:** Larry Goldberg highlights SpaceX CFO Brett Johnson as a key figure who has managed SpaceX's public market process and steered the company through multiple financing rounds. Goldberg suggests that a combined Tesla-SpaceX quarterly earnings call featuring both Shotwell and Johnson would represent a dramatic upgrade in executive communication quality. Shotwell herself is described as an engineer with over 20 years at SpaceX, employee number 11 at founding in 2002, and estimated by Herbert to have accumulated approximately $2 billion in SpaceX stock.

5. **SpaceX's AI Satellite and Chip Plans:** In her CNBC interview, Shotwell stated that AI satellites are "simpler" to develop than Starlink satellites, though she cautioned it is "not a slam dunk." She cited supply chain challenges, specifically the need to get solar cells right and the need to build a lot of chips — not because SpaceX wants to be a chip manufacturer, but because she believes chip manufacturers are not "thinking about scaling in the same ways" SpaceX is, or do not believe SpaceX's scale ambitions. Herbert frames this in the context of Elon Musk's previously stated goal of getting 1 gigawatt of compute into space by 2027, a timeline Musk reportedly pulled forward by one year. Goldberg revised his own forecast, saying he had not modeled orbital data centers until 2028 but now believes SpaceX could reach perhaps half a gigawatt of operational orbital compute by the end of next year (end of 2027).

6. **Starship Flight Progress and Orbital Timeline:** During a factory tour with Morgan Brennan of CNBC, Shotwell indicated that Starship flight 13 was approximately one month away from the time of filming (placing it around early-to-mid July 2026 based on her "beginning of June" reference), that flight 14 would attempt at least an orbital injection, and that she expects Starship to be in orbit "by the end of this year" (2026). She also stated SpaceX aims to fly "every month." Goldberg expressed skepticism about reaching a cadence of one launch every two days by the end of next year (2027), suggesting one every five days with successful booster recovery would represent a strong outcome.

7. **SpaceX IPO Day and XAI Acquisition:** At the SpaceX IPO, Shotwell gave a speech highlighting the company's history of achieving things critics said were impossible — including getting the first liquid-fueled private rocket to orbit in 2008, achieving 165 Falcon 9 launches in the prior year, and developing Starship. She also announced that through the merger/acquisition of xAI, SpaceX as a group now owns "the largest coherent gigawatt-class compute on the planet." She noted that more than half of SpaceX's approximately 22,000 employees purchased additional stock at the IPO opening, totaling almost $1 billion.

8. **SpaceX Natural Gas Infrastructure Plans:** Goldberg and Herbert note that Shotwell mentioned in her CNBC interview that SpaceX plans to build its own natural gas pipelines and is possibly looking at extracting natural gas itself — though Herbert corrected himself to note she said "possibly extracting," not definitively. This is framed as consistent with SpaceX's pattern of vertical integration.

9. **Potential AI Company Acquisitions by SpaceX:** Shotwell mentioned in her interview that AI companies are among the types of companies SpaceX could potentially acquire using its newly public stock. Goldberg speculates that "Cursor" (a coding AI product) could be one such target, citing its potential fit with Grok and its position at the forefront of technology, while noting cultural fit would be a requirement.

Notable quotes and data:
- Gwyn Shotwell on Tesla-SpaceX merger: *"That might make Elon's life a little easier, actually... there's no question that there are synergies between Tesla and SpaceX and our futures. Definitely there's a convergence of kind of what we're all trying to accomplish in the future... I'm not focused on that part of the future, at least."*
- Dan Ives of Wedbush (cited in interview question): 80%+ probability of SpaceX-Tesla merger, targeting 2027, with groundwork already in place.
- Shotwell on AI satellites: *"AI satellites are simpler [than Starlink satellites]... we have some supply chain challenges in front of us. We've got to get solar cells right, and we have to build a lot of chips."*
- Shotwell on Starship: Flight 13 approximately one month away (from early June 2026 reference point); orbital injection attempt targeted for flight 14; orbit expected "by the end of this year."
- SpaceX IPO: More than half of ~22,000 employees purchased additional stock totaling "almost a billion dollars."
- SpaceX Falcon 9: 165 launches in the prior year (referenced in Shotwell's IPO speech).
- Shotwell on xAI merger: SpaceX group now owns "the largest coherent gigawatt-class compute on the planet."
- Gwyn Shotwell: Employee #11 at SpaceX founding in 2002; estimated ~$2 billion in SpaceX stock per Herbert.
- Larry Goldberg's white paper predicting merger: Published February 2026.

articles.title: Elon Is Building 7 Megafactories At Once
articles.body:
This video from brighterwithherbert argues that Elon Musk is simultaneously constructing seven megafactories across Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI that collectively represent a vertically integrated industrial stack — one that redefines chips, transportation, orbital communications, AI compute, labor, and energy as delivered services. The host's core thesis is that each factory is not just a manufacturing site but a "category reset," and that the interdependence of all seven sites creates a competitive moat no single rival — domestic or Chinese — can replicate. The video walks through each facility in detail, then closes with five specific milestones to monitor through the rest of 2026.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus Factory at Giga Texas North Campus — Steel Already Up:** A new dedicated Optimus factory at Giga Texas North Campus covers 5.2 million square feet per permit filings. First steel went up May 27, 2026. The footprint stretches nearly the full length of the main Giga Texas building. Tesla's framing suggests low-volume production could begin as early as summer 2026, with the real production ramp running through 2027.

2. **10 Million Robots Per Year Long-Term Target:** The stated long-term output target for the North Campus Optimus factory is 10 million units per year — a figure the host explicitly labels as a target, not existing capacity. For context, the host compares this to Hyundai's Asan complex (roughly 1.5 million vehicles per year) and Apple's iPhone output (~230 million per year spread across multiple Foxconn campuses). The host frames 10 million complex humanoid robots from a single site as "smartphone-scale output with no precedent for that ratio of output to footprint."

3. **Cortex 2 Training Optimus Neural Nets:** Cortex 2 at Giga Texas is described as the compute backbone for Optimus training alongside FSD training. The first 250-megawatt phase came online in April 2026; the full 500-megawatt activation is targeted for mid-2026. By secondary reporting figures cited loosely, Cortex 2 runs more than 130,000 H100-equivalent GPUs; combined with Cortex 1 next door, the campus has passed 230,000 H100 equivalents. The host notes the cluster dwarfs the largest national lab supercomputers (El Capitan, Frontier) at roughly 40,000 GPUs each.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Terafab Chips Feed FSD Directly:** The Terafab semiconductor megafacility is described as the upstream supply chain for FSD compute. The first chip off the line is the Tesla AI5, with a pilot small batch targeted for 2026 and volume production targeted for 2027. The host frames Terafab as ending Tesla's dependency on Nvidia-tier margins for every FSD and Optimus compute upgrade.

2. **Cortex 2 Removes Training Bottleneck for Robotaxi:** The host argues that the key bear-case question on robotaxi deployment — whether Tesla can train FSD fast enough — is structurally answered by Cortex 2's scale. With the campus running at multiples of the largest national lab supercomputers, compute is explicitly removed as the bottleneck for FSD improvement and robotaxi scaling.

## Robotaxi
1. **Robotaxi Scale Still Concentrated in Austin and Phoenix:** The host acknowledges the honest pushback that robotaxi scale is "still mostly just Austin and Phoenix" as of mid-2026, framing this as a legitimate criticism alongside timeline slippage across all seven projects.

## Energy
1. **Houston Megapack Factory — $200M Investment, 50 GWh Per Year:** Tesla's new Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas carries a $200 million initial investment and targets 50 gigawatt-hours per year of grid-scale storage once online. Construction is underway; production is targeted for late 2026, though the host flags this date as likely to slip. The new flagship product is "Mega Block" — each unit packs 20 megawatt-hours of AC capacity (four Megapack 3 units, a medium-voltage transformer, and switchgear in a plug-and-play format). Tesla claims 23% faster installation and up to 40% lower construction cost versus traditional builds.

2. **Combined Tesla Grid Storage Capacity to Exceed 130 GWh/Year:** Adding Houston to Lathrop and Giga Shanghai, Tesla's combined Megapack manufacturing capacity climbs past 130 gigawatt-hours per year. Total global battery storage deployed in 2024 came in around 200 gigawatt-hours; Tesla's factory capacity alone would cover roughly two-thirds of that figure once Houston is online.

3. **Cortex 2 On-Site Battery Integration:** The host notes a specific loop: Cortex 2 leans on roughly 150 megawatts of on-site battery storage plus new turbines for primary power — Tesla-made batteries powering the AI training that trains the cars and robots Tesla sells.

## Financials
1. **Terafab Financing — $55B Phase 1, $119B Full Buildout:** Per the SpaceX S-1 IPO filing, Terafab carries $55 billion for phase 1 scaling to $119 billion for full buildout. The S-1 explicitly calls this a "framework," and the host cautions treating the larger number as a road map rather than a binding budget. The host notes this single private project is more than twice the $52 billion in direct chip subsidies set aside by the CHIPS Act.

2. **Colossus 2 Silicon Cost — ~$18B for GPUs Alone:** The Colossus 2 cluster in Memphis has 555,000 Nvidia GPUs purchased at roughly $18 billion just for the silicon. The host acknowledges skeptics — satellite imagery analysts who argue operating capacity runs well below headline claims.

3. **Tesla's $2B xAI Investment Converted to SpaceX Stake:** After SpaceX absorbed xAI in February 2026, Tesla's $2 billion xAI investment converted into a small SpaceX stake. The host explicitly states Tesla holds no direct xAI equity anymore, though Tesla products (FSD, in-vehicle Grok assistant) run on Colossus's output.

## Market & Competition
1. **No Comparable Industrial Stack Globally:** The host's central competitive claim is that no single operator — among the Mag-7 or in China — is simultaneously building chip fabs, launch capacity, energy storage, and labor production. The Mag-7 are spending more raw dollars on AI data centers, but none cover all layers. China has no single operator running all layers either.

2. **Colossus 2 vs. Hyperscaler AI Clusters:** At roughly 1 gigawatt operating and building toward 2 gigawatts, Colossus 2 is described as the largest single-site AI cluster on Earth right now with the clearest path to two. For comparison: Meta Hyperion in Louisiana targets 5 gigawatts eventually but is pre-operational; Microsoft's biggest single Azure AI campus runs under 1 gigawatt; OpenAI's Stargate flagship in Abilene is online at partial power heading for ~1.2 gigawatts this year, with the full 5-gigawatt vision stretching toward 2029.

3. **SpaceX Launch Capacity vs. Global Industry:** Global orbital launches in 2025 came in around 324 — an all-time record. SpaceX flew about 170 of those. Gigabay is designed to support up to 1,000 reusable Starships per year by end of decade — roughly three times the entire world's 2025 launch cadence. The host explicitly labels this an end-of-decade design goal. SpaceX already produces about 70 Starlink satellites per week; the rest of the US industry combined builds on the order of a few hundred per year.

4. **Gigasat — 11 Million Square Feet of Satellite Manufacturing:** Unveiled June 9, 2026, Gigasat in Bastrop, Texas covers 11 million square feet of planned building capacity on over 1,000 acres. For comparison, Tesla Fremont is 5.3 million square feet; Boeing Everett is 4.3 million. A 10-gigawatt-per-year solar cell sub-facility broke ground in late March 2026. Output target: 1 gigawatt of orbital AI compute by end of 2027, scaling roughly 10x per year after that. Grok Edge AI is reported to ride into orbit on Starlink V3 this year; AI1 satellites prototyping early 2027.

5. **Grimes County Tax Abatement Already Approved:** Grimes County commissioners approved a 100% 10-year tax abatement for Terafab on June 3, 2026, by a 4-to-1 vote. Intel joined the Terafab venture on April 7, 2026, contributing the 18A process node.

Notable quotes and data:
- Elon Musk stated Terafab is "around 100 million square feet" — 10 times Giga Texas's ~10 million square feet
- Terafab stated output target: 1 terawatt of AI compute per year
- Cortex 2: 130,000+ H100-equivalent GPUs per secondary reporting; campus total past 230,000 H100 equivalents combined with Cortex 1
- Colossus 2: 555,000 Nvidia GPUs, ~$18B in silicon, ~1 gigawatt operating, building toward 2 gigawatts
- Gigabay (Starbase): 380 ft tall, 46.5 million cubic feet interior, 11× the square footage of the existing Mega Bay, 2× crane capacity, 19 additional work cells; construction started July 2025, full operations targeted December 2026
- Houston Megapack factory: $200M initial investment, 50 GWh/year target, Mega Block = 20 MWh AC capacity per unit
- Combined Tesla grid storage manufacturing capacity: 130+ GWh/year (Lathrop + Giga Shanghai + Houston)
- Global battery storage deployed in 2024: ~200 GWh
- Optimus factory: 5.2 million sq ft, first steel May 27, 2026; 10 million units/year long-term target
- Elon on AI1 satellites: "much simpler than a Starlink satellite — mostly solar cells and laser links"
- Joe Tegtmeyer credited for weekly drone construction documentation

articles.title: I Wanted to Recommend the Rivian R2 Until I Saw This
articles.body:
FutureAzA host Brian delivers a critical assessment of the Rivian R2, arguing that while it is a promising concept, it is not ready for mainstream buyers at launch. His core thesis is that Rivian faces compounding problems — pricing pressure, manufacturing limitations, cash burn, reliability concerns, and the loss of key government incentives — that make the R2 a risky purchase today. Brian also expresses deep skepticism about Rivian's autonomous driving ambitions relative to established players.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Pricing has ballooned from the original announcement:** When the R2 was announced in 2024, it was positioned as a $45,000 vehicle. As of the video, the base launch edition sits at approximately $58,000 on the configurator, with a landed cost closer to $59,500 after delivery charges. Color upgrades push the price over $60,000. Brian notes the originally promised $44,900 price point is not expected until spring 2027 at the earliest — roughly a year away — and expresses doubt it will actually be achieved.

2. **Manufacturing constraints limit cost savings:** The R2 was originally intended to be built in a new, state-of-the-art factory in Georgia, which would have delivered efficiency and cost savings at scale. That factory has been delayed due to Rivian's cash crunch, so the R2 is being built in existing facilities. Brian argues this eliminates the anticipated cost savings and raises the concern that Rivian may be losing money on every unit sold at high volume.

3. **Reliability is a serious concern:** Brian cites a Consumer Reports ranking that placed Rivian dead last in reliability — behind Jaguar and every other brand surveyed. He also references a reported 19,000 recalls due to botched service, and notes a software incident during an R2 demo drive in Pasadena where a battery failure message appeared. He acknowledges he could not independently validate every claim but flags the pattern as concerning for prospective buyers.

4. **Content creators and early reservers are being locked out:** Brian notes that none of the content creators or reviewers he is aware of — including people who reserved in the first five minutes and own multiple R1 vehicles — have received invitations to configure an R2 for purchase. He also describes being repeatedly denied access to R2 demo events, including being told the night before a California event to simply livestream it rather than attend in person. He interprets this as a sign Rivian may be managing a product that isn't ready for close scrutiny.

5. **Charging speed is underwhelming:** The R2's charging speed is approximately 29 minutes from 10% to 80%, covering 70% of a stated 330-mile range. Brian calculates this yields roughly 230–240 miles of practically usable range per charge, translating to about 30 minutes of charging for every 3 hours of driving — a ratio he finds unappealing.

## Market & Competition

1. **Loss of EV incentives is a major headwind:** Brian outlines several layers of lost government support that hit Rivian particularly hard. The $7,500 federal consumer EV tax credit is gone. The commercial clean vehicle credit (which allowed leasing to qualify) is also gone. ZEV credits — which Brian estimates Rivian earned approximately $590 million from — have been eliminated in the U.S. Charging infrastructure grant funding, which Rivian had tapped to build out its adventure network, has also been cut. Brian frames this as an enormous stack of headwinds with no comparable offsets.

2. **Existential financial pressure and insider signals:** Brian cites cumulative cash burn of $24.4 billion (as of February 2026) across pure-play EV automakers tracked by analyst AJ, with Rivian included. He flags declining deliveries, insider share sales, and leadership changes as warning signs. His core concern is that if Rivian does not survive, buyers will be left without warranty support.

3. **Volkswagen's software pivot undermines Rivian's software value:** Rivian's software stack was seen as a key asset, with Volkswagen as a notable partner. Brian points out that Volkswagen Group has entered a new agreement with Xpeng for fast joint development of two smart EVs using Xpeng's software for certain markets — suggesting that Rivian's software partnership with VW may be less comprehensive or durable than previously assumed.

4. **Autonomous driving ambitions are deeply skeptical:** Brian argues that Rivian's autonomy plans are not credible in the near term. He states Rivian lacks the real-world training miles (contrasting with Tesla's 11 billion miles), lacks visible compute infrastructure of the scale operated by Tesla, Waymo, Huawei, BYD, or Xpeng, and relies heavily on simulation that cannot substitute for real-world data. He also flags a problematic unit economics issue: Rivian reportedly plans to install approximately $2,500 worth of sensors and sell the autonomy package for $2,500, meaning any take rate below 100% results in a loss on every unit.

5. **Competition from gas and other EVs remains stiff:** Brian acknowledges Rivian has wisely carved out a niche in the adventure/overlanding market where it has genuine advantages over mainstream EVs like the Model Y. However, he argues that traditional off-road vehicles like Jeeps remain compelling alternatives, especially given Rivian's U.S.-centric focus and the difficulty of expanding internationally.

Notable quotes and data:
- R2 launch edition price: ~$58,000 on configurator; ~$59,500 landed; over $60,000 with color options
- Originally announced price (2024): $45,000; $44,900 price not expected until spring 2027
- Cumulative EV cash burn tracked by AJ (as of February 2026): $24.4 billion across pure-play EVs including Rivian
- Rivian estimated ZEV credit earnings: ~$590 million
- Consumer Reports reliability ranking: Rivian placed last, behind Jaguar and all other brands
- Recall example cited: 19,000 vehicles recalled due to botched service
- Charging: 29 minutes from 10% to 80% on a stated 330-mile range (~230–240 miles usable)
- Autonomy sensor cost concern: ~$2,500 in sensors sold for ~$2,500, making sub-100% take rates loss-generating
- "If there's no company left, there's no warranty left."
- "Don't buy one. Maybe when they come down to $45,000, maybe when they've sold 30–40,000 of them and the reliability is more predictable."

articles.title: Tesla and SpaceX Stock ACCELERATION: The Week Ahead
articles.body:
Jo Bhakdi hosts a Sunday livestream reviewing the week ahead for Tesla and SpaceX investors, with a primary focus on Cybercab deployment signals, the latest FSD release, and his tactical trading posture on Tesla stock. A secondary thread covers his bearish short-term / bullish long-term view on the newly public SpaceX, including index inclusion catalysts. The core thesis is that Cybercab production is the most reliable forcing function for estimating robotaxi launch timing, and that multiple early signals point toward an imminent supervised or unsupervised Cybercab deployment event that could push Tesla back to all-time highs.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab production trajectory and fleet size estimate:** Jo Bhakdi presents his own conservative production estimates based on drone footage (attributed to Joe Tegtmeyer) and sightings across multiple cities. He estimates a minimum of 10 Cybercabs per day produced in April (≈220 units), 20 per day in May across 22 production days (≈440 units), and 30 per day so far in June (≈360 units), putting the total produced above 1,000 Cybercabs as of mid-June 2026. He projects roughly another 1,000 units added by the first week of July, reaching approximately 2,000 by July and 3,000–4,000 by August, arguing that no manufacturing operation of this scale proceeds without a high-conviction deployment plan.

2. **Cybercab sightings in Houston, Las Vegas, and beyond:** Bhakdi shows images dated June 13, 2026 of Cybercabs staged in a parking lot in Houston and a separate batch in Las Vegas, both fitted with decorative wheel caps. He interprets the wheel caps — which were absent during earlier testing — as a cosmetic preparation signal suggesting public deployment is near. He also references sightings in California (Palo Alto), Nevada, Texas (Austin), Chicago, Boston, and Florida.

3. **Near-term deployment prediction and stock impact:** Bhakdi states he remains convinced that "multiple dozens" of Cybercabs will be deployed (likely unsupervised) in June 2026. He estimates that a release of 40–50 unsupervised Cybercabs would be a 10–20% short-term catalyst for the stock, sufficient to push Tesla back to its prior all-time high area of approximately $490. He notes that 1,800 unsupervised robotaxis would represent a more fundamental repricing of the stock — sufficient to add roughly 5% to free cash flow — and could push Tesla to $600–$800 or higher with exuberance.

4. **Elon's earnings call statement on FSD version gating:** Bhakdi references Elon Musk's comments from the most recent Tesla earnings call, in which Elon stated clearly that robotaxi rollout does not require waiting for FSD version 15. Bhakdi summarizes: the rollout will happen at "huge scale" on version 14, and version 15 is scheduled for approximately end of 2026.

5. **Tesla comment on new robotaxi cities:** A viewer (Marty) comments that four to five new robotaxi cities should be going online in the next two weeks, referencing something Tesla said. Bhakdi acknowledges this but expresses uncertainty about whether Tesla's stated timeline can be relied upon.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD 14.3.4 released and receiving exceptional reviews:** FSD version 14.3.4 was released on Friday, June 13, 2026. Bhakdi shares detailed feedback from a prominent Tesla community member ("Doge Army General") who reports driving 250 miles on the build. Key highlights from the review: it is described as "by far the best overall FSD build by a wide margin," more refined than 14.3.3 (which was in some respects a regression from 14.3.2), the car no longer brakes hard for animals but eases off the accelerator more naturally, parking destination selection is improved, and the reviewer describes it as "one step closer to robotaxi." The reviewer notes that major upgrades are arriving roughly every two to three weeks and that the pace is accelerating.

2. **Architectural significance of the 14.3.x rebuild:** Bhakdi explains that the FSD 14.3 release (the major one in the series) represented a fundamental rebuild of the underlying system that removed legacy components, enabling faster iteration cadence going forward. He emphasizes that a change in the slope of progress — not just a new release — is the meaningful signal, and that 14.3.x represents exactly such an inflection.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla demand signals looking positive heading into Q2 2026:** Bhakdi briefly notes that Model Y wait times in China are elevated, European Tesla sales are rebounding "like crazy," and competing automakers including Chinese brands are facing significant problems. He characterizes Tesla as being in a strong position even setting aside the robotaxi thesis, and expects the upcoming earnings report to look very good.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO and short-term index inclusion catalysts:** SpaceX went public the prior week in what Bhakdi describes as the largest IPO in the history of capitalism, with the stock rising approximately 20% to around $165 (vs. an IPO price he references as $135). He lays out a calendar of forced buying pressure from index inclusion events: Russell US Indexes fast-entry inclusion on June 26, 2026; NASDAQ fast-entry rebalance on approximately July 6, 2026; and a Russell semiannual reconstitution in December 2026. He notes the S&P 500 rejected a rules change that would have allowed SpaceX inclusion, so the earliest possible S&P 500 entry is approximately one year away.

2. **Bhakdi's bearish short-term / bullish long-term SpaceX stance:** Bhakdi states he is not a SpaceX shareholder and does not intend to buy near current prices, believing the stock is running on hype and that fundamentals (current cash flow) do not support the valuation. He predicts a classic IPO cycle pattern: hype peak, a crash or prolonged weakness ("valley of tears"), followed by a steep re-acceleration driven by actual cash flow. He estimates the "valley of tears" period will be one to two years, but possibly shorter and steeper than typical due to SpaceX's fundamentals. He says he cannot determine a floor (could be $160, $135 IPO price, or lower) but is willing to wait, expecting to buy meaningfully in roughly nine months to a year.

3. **Tesla stock tactical positioning:** Bhakdi describes Tesla as currently trading around $406, which he views as a clear strong buy. He sees upside to the $490 all-time high area if Cybercab deployment materializes, but warns of resistance/mean reversion at that level unless robotaxi scaling continues. He acknowledges getting over-leveraged at end of May 2026 and suffering losses before partially recovering. He warns viewers against excessive leverage, noting Tesla can always pull back to around $380 with no apparent reason.

Notable quotes and data:
- Doge Army General: *"I have driven 250 miles on 14.3.4. It is by far the best overall FSD build by a wide margin... The pace of improvements is mind-boggling. Essentially every two to three weeks, we are getting upgrades. This will only go faster as the AI learns more."*
- Bhakdi on Cybercab: *"There are probably over 1,000 Cybercabs out in the wild and another thousand being added by probably the first week of July."*
- Bhakdi on robotaxi repricing: *"At the moment we hit 1,800 unsupervised robotaxis and see the growth accelerating... yes, we can absolutely reprice the entire stock"* — suggesting $600–$800 or higher.
- Bhakdi on deployment catalyst: *"If we get 48–50 of these Cybercabs actually unsupervised deployed... I would estimate we are up to all-time highs in June in the next two weeks."*
- Bhakdi on Elon's earnings call comments: *"We do not have to wait for version 15 for robotaxi rollout... We will roll it out before version 15, which is scheduled for probably end of the year."*
- Cybercab production estimates (Bhakdi's own): April ≈ 220 units (10/day), May ≈ 440 units (20/day), June to date ≈ 360 units (30/day) — total >1,000 as of mid-June 2026.
- SpaceX IPO: ~20% gain on first week of trading, stock at approximately $165; IPO price referenced as $135.
- SpaceX NASDAQ inclusion: approximately July 6, 2026.
- Tesla current price referenced: ~$406; prior all-time high referenced: ~$490.

articles.title: Daily X Summary (2026-06-14)
articles.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts from @SawyerMerritt center on Tesla's expanding robotaxi footprint (Cybercabs spotted in Houston), FSD V14.3.4 UI updates that signal robotaxi readiness, and broader ecosystem context including updated valuations of Elon Musk's companies. Rivian's CEO signaling a supervised FSD-equivalent product for late 2026 is a notable competitive data point. Overall signal is modestly bullish, with robotaxi expansion and FSD polish as the headline themes.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Cybercab fleet expanding into Houston:** A post with significant engagement (4.1K likes, 308 reposts) shared video of "tons of Tesla Cybercabs in Houston, Texas." This is consistent with the canonical RobotaxiTracker.com data showing 10 active robotaxis in Houston as of 2026-06-13, suggesting the fleet may be growing beyond that reported figure or the footage predates the latest tracker update. This geographic expansion beyond Austin and the Bay Area is a meaningful signal for investors tracking robotaxi rollout velocity.

2. **FSD V14.3.4 introduces robotaxi-style UI messaging:** Merritt highlighted new on-screen messages in FSD V14.3.4, describing them as "the kind of stuff a robotaxi would show." Specific new messages include: "Vehicle will pull over near destination," "Approaching destination. Will pull over near destination," and "Driving to Market Basket." These UI additions suggest Tesla is actively preparing the FSD software stack for a passenger-facing, driverless experience — a meaningful qualitative step toward unsupervised robotaxi deployment.

3. **Rivian CEO signals supervised FSD-equivalent coming late 2026, unsupervised in 2027:** In a new interview, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe stated the company will launch "full supervised point-to-point" autonomy (explicitly compared to Tesla FSD) across all Gen 2 vehicles and R2 later in 2026, with unsupervised capability targeted for 2027. While Rivian remains far behind Tesla in autonomous driving maturity, this is a notable competitive benchmark — it suggests the broader EV industry is coalescing around FSD-like supervised autonomy as the near-term standard, with unsupervised as the next frontier.

4. **Updated Elon Musk company valuations — Tesla at $1.5 trillion:** A widely circulated post (5K likes, 568 reposts) listed publicly available valuations: SpaceX at $2.1 trillion, Tesla at $1.5 trillion, Neuralink at $9 billion, and The Boring Company at $7 billion, totaling $3.62 trillion combined. No source methodology was specified. These figures provide a market-context snapshot but are based on informal/publicly circulated estimates rather than official filings.

5. **Tesla Solar Tile Roof — largest U.S. residential installation:** A Maui home listed for $26.5 million features a $1.4 million Tesla Solar Tile Roof, claimed to be the largest residential installation in the U.S. No kilowatt capacity was disclosed. While a niche data point, it illustrates the high-end residential energy market opportunity and serves as a brand showcase for Tesla Energy.

6. **SpaceX-adjacent news (limited Tesla relevance):** Posts covered the U.S. State Department signing a two-year MOU with SpaceX/Starlink for humanitarian disaster response, Jim Cramer's commentary on a potential SpaceX IPO, and ARK Invest reportedly purchasing ~$500 million in SpaceX stock. These are primarily SpaceX stories with no direct Tesla investment thesis implications, though ARK's continued SpaceX conviction indirectly reflects broader confidence in Elon Musk's portfolio companies.

---

## Signal Strength: **Mildly Bullish** — Cybercab geographic expansion into Houston and FSD V14.3.4's robotaxi-oriented UI polish are incremental positive signals for the autonomous driving and robotaxi thesis, though no major milestones or data breakthroughs were reported today.

articles.title: SpaceX Is Public. Tesla's Turn Starts Now
articles.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel argues that the SpaceX IPO — described as the biggest IPO in stock market history — has set the stage for Tesla's own stock repricing, driven by a dense calendar of over 20 milestones between now and December 31, 2026. The host Herbert (alongside collaborator Cern Basher) walks through a milestone tracking table covering robotaxi expansion, FSD international rollouts, Optimus development, energy products, financials, and the dominant wild card: a possible SpaceX-Tesla merger as early as late July 2026. The core thesis is that even without a merger, Tesla's second-half 2026 milestone slate is the strongest the company has ever had, and the merger represents an asymmetric option layered on top.

## Robotaxi
1. **Current unsupervised fleet status:** Unsupervised robotaxi service (no safety driver, paying customers) is live in three cities — Austin, Dallas, and Houston. The existing paying-ride fleet is still composed of Model Y vehicles; no Cybercab has yet carried a paying passenger. Five additional cities are pending — Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, and Las Vegas — though Tesla's language softened from "first half" to "preparations underway" as of April, suggesting some may slip into Q3 2026.

2. **City-by-city strategic significance:** Each new city launch serves as proof that the FSD system generalizes without city-specific mapping or depot infrastructure. Phoenix is highlighted as a direct competitive signal, as it is Waymo's home turf. Las Vegas offers friendly regulators, year-round weather, and the Boring Company tunnel infrastructure. Miami, Orlando, and Tampa are tourist markets where first-time riders (non-Tesla owners) become word-of-mouth ambassadors.

3. **Scale ramp as the key inflection:** Herbert identifies the Q3 unsupervised ramp — going from dozens of cars per city to hundreds and then thousands — as the milestone that transforms robotaxi from a headline into a modelable revenue line. FSD miles have crossed 11 billion cumulative, with a projection past 17 billion by year-end 2026; the most recent 1 billion miles took just 37 days, with over 4 billion total logged on city streets.

4. **Federal autonomous driving framework:** A national regulatory standard replacing the current state-by-state patchwork is tracked as a Q4 2026 milestone. If it lands, the city-by-city rollout map effectively becomes a national rollout map, though Herbert acknowledges Tesla controls nothing in Washington.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **FSD Europe rollout accelerating:** The Netherlands granted the first European approval for FSD (supervised) on April 10, 2026, through the Dutch authority RDW, with rollout to Dutch owners beginning the next day. Denmark followed, and Belgium approved on June 10, 2026 — with Tesla publishing roughly two months of Dutch safety and usage stats alongside the Belgium approval. The count now stands at 13 countries globally with FSD supervised, five of them in Europe. Tesla is targeting broader European rollout through summer 2026, country by country, with the possibility of an EU-wide approval.

2. **FSD China launch and scale potential:** Tesla made FSD supervised officially available in China on May 21, 2026, priced as a one-time purchase of approximately 64,01 RMB (~$9,400 USD). Tesla built a dedicated data center in Shanghai, partnered with BYD for mapping, and is hiring test drivers across nine major cities. Full fleet-wide regulatory approval (over-the-air to all eligible cars) is targeted for Q3 2026. With over 2 million Teslas on Chinese roads, Herbert notes that every 10% of the fleet purchasing FSD at $9,400 represents roughly $2 billion of high-margin software revenue (flagged as rough math with hedged attach rates).

3. **Self-reinforcing regulatory flywheel:** Each country that goes live generates local safety data that serves as evidence for the next country in the queue. Herbert argues this is why five European approvals in two months could look slow compared to the next six months, and why the approval pace is accelerating in pairs.

4. **FSD on customer-owned vehicles (unsupervised) — Q4 target:** Elon Musk stated on the Q1 2026 earnings call that unsupervised FSD reaching customer-owned vehicles (i.e., your own car driving with no one watching) should happen in Q4 2026. Herbert expresses skepticism about on-time delivery of this milestone.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Cybercab production underway:** Cybercab production began at Giga Texas on April 24, 2026, targeting hundreds of units per week with a ramp in progress. The table tracks two remaining Cybercab milestones for 2026: the first paid Cybercab ride (likely with an event) and Cybercab opening for customer orders in Q4 2026, the latter of which Herbert is skeptical will hit on schedule.

2. **Tesla Semi in production:** Tesla Semi started production in 2026 (already checked off the milestone table), retiring what Herbert describes as the "science project" bear-case narrative.

3. **10 million cumulative deliveries milestone:** Somewhere in Q3 2026, Tesla is expected to cross 10 million cumulative vehicles delivered — a brand milestone Herbert expects to land while the robotaxi narrative is peaking, amplifying headline impact.

4. **Next-gen Roadster demo:** Originally targeted for April 1, 2026, then pushed to late spring, and now pointed at August 2026. The car is reportedly ready; the SpaceX thruster package is described as the long pole. Herbert notes that Franz von Holzhausen stated in an interview just days before the video that the Roadster is "coming very soon" and will "blow people away" — which Herbert treats as more credible than prior schedule promises.

5. **Model S and Model X sunset:** The table tracks the winding down of the Model S and Model X lines, partly to free up tooling capacity for Optimus manufacturing.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus factory construction underway:** Construction started in Q2 2026 on a dedicated Optimus factory in Austin. Tesla's stated plan for the first-generation line is capacity for 1 million robots per year. Optimus units are currently being tested inside Tesla factories, though Tesla has not provided an officially confirmed unit count and has not given a 2026 production target. Wall Street models citing ~50,000 units for 2026 are characterized as analyst math, not company guidance.

2. **Optimus Gen 3 reveal and pilot production — Q3 target:** Gen 3 is penciled for a Q3 2026 reveal, possibly at the annual shareholder meeting. Leaked information on Gen 3 hand design points to approximately 50 actuators of dexterity. Herbert argues that if the reveal demonstrates hands capable of real factory tasks, the million-robot factory transitions from a prototype bet to a manufacturing bet — the thing Tesla has proven it can do. Gen 3 pilot production is also tracked for Q3.

3. **Digital Optimus / Macrohard — Q4 wild card:** A Q4 2026 row on the table tracks what Herbert calls the "digital Optimus reveal" — the Macrohard project — described as a software-only version of the robot brain doing knowledge work.

4. **Compute buildout supporting Optimus:** Cortex 2.0, the AI training cluster in Austin, is hitting 50% capacity in Q2 2026 and full capacity in Q3. Construction on an advanced technology chip fab (the follow-through on the Terafab chip project launched in Q1 2026) is also beginning, with Herbert describing Tesla making its own AI chips at scale as a 5-to-10-year statement.

## Energy
1. **Megapack 3 and Megablock production launch:** Megapack 3 and a new product called Megablock are set to begin production at a new Houston Megapack factory late in 2026. Each unit delivers 5 MWh — 28% more than Megapack 2 in the same footprint — out of a factory built for 50 GWh per year of capacity. Herbert describes energy as Tesla's best-margin hardware business and frames this as its "next gear."

## Financials
1. **Q2 2026 production and delivery report:** Q2 production and delivery numbers are expected to land in the first week of July 2026, providing the first data point on Cybercab ramp and robotaxi fleet growth.

2. **Q2 2026 earnings call — late July:** The Q2 2026 earnings call in late July is flagged as the event where robotaxi unit economics, city-by-city color, Cybercab ramp numbers, and FSD take rates following the Europe and China launches will be disclosed. Herbert frames this as the call where the story moves from narrative to arithmetic.

## Market & Competition
1. **SpaceX IPO as the catalyst:** SpaceX's IPO — described as the biggest in stock market history — put a live public market price on "Elon execution," and Herbert argues the capital that watched SpaceX get repriced will now look directly at Tesla. The two companies entered the IPO week at nearly the same market capitalization.

2. **SpaceX-Tesla merger: the dominant wild card:** A possible merger between SpaceX and Tesla emerged from podcast speculation into mainstream financial discourse after CNBC reported in May 2026, citing a Tesla employee and others familiar with the talks, that the two companies are weighing a combination. Wolf Research says the idea has moved into the Wall Street mainstream. Dan Ives puts the odds at 80%; the prediction market Kalshi (referred to as "Calry" in the transcript) has it around 52% within the next year.

3. **Merger financial math and strategic logic:** Analysts running merger math are publishing a combined company valuation of around $3.4 trillion. Herbert describes a stock-for-stock "merger of equals" scenario where the exchange ratio is the critical variable — a near-par ratio would pull Tesla's price toward SpaceX's trading price at announcement, while a ratio favoring SpaceX holders would shrink Tesla's upside. SpaceX's own S1 filing language — stating the company "may issue a significant amount of equity in connection with future transactions" — is noted as potentially meaningful. Fortune's Sean Tully interpreted this as a forward signal of a large stock-funded acquisition, with Tesla being the only target that fits "significant" at SpaceX's scale.

4. **Why the IPO itself raised merger odds:** Herbert argues that a private SpaceX could not practically acquire Tesla with stock because there was no market price, no liquidity, and no way for a Tesla board to present shareholders with a fairness opinion. The IPO created a ticker, a tape, and a price the lawyers can use — meaning the structural tool to do the deal now exists for the first time.

5. **Bear case on the merger:** A national security review is flagged as a serious obstacle — SpaceX is a major defense contractor while Tesla runs major operations in China. SpaceX is also described as still posting losses (revenue up, profits negative), meaning no positive cash flow on day one of a combined company. Board committees, shareholder votes, and fairness reviews on both sides add further delay risk.

6. **Waymo competitive framing:** Herbert notes that Tesla's ability to light up new robotaxi cities in weeks rather than years — without city-specific maps or depot infrastructure — directly undermines Waymo's cost structure argument, which Herbert describes as "most of the long-term valuation debate."

Notable quotes and data:
- FSD cumulative miles: crossed 11 billion; the last 1 billion miles took 37 days; over 4 billion miles on city streets; projected to exceed 17 billion by year-end 2026
- Cybercab production began April 24, 2026 at Giga Texas
- FSD China price: approximately 64,01 RMB (~$9,400 USD), one-time purchase
- Over 2 million Teslas on Chinese roads; every 10% FSD attach rate ≈ ~$2 billion high-margin software revenue
- 13 countries globally with FSD supervised as of the video date; 5 in Europe
- Belgium FSD approval: June 10, 2026
- Netherlands FSD approval: April 10, 2026 (RDW)
- Megapack 3: 5 MWh per unit, 28% more than Megapack 2; Houston factory rated at 50 GWh/year
- Dan Ives merger odds: 80%; Kalshi prediction market: ~52% within one year
- Analysts' combined SpaceX + Tesla valuation: ~$3.4 trillion
- Optimus Gen 3 leaked hand design: ~50 actuators
- Cortex 2.0 training cluster: 50% capacity in Q2 2026, full capacity in Q3 2026
- Franz von Holzhausen, days before the video: Roadster is "coming very soon" and will "blow people away"
- SpaceX S1 language: "may issue a significant amount of equity in connection with future transactions"
- CNBC reported in May 2026 (citing a Tesla employee and others familiar with talks) that the two companies are weighing a merger
- Terafab chip project: launched Q1 2026; advanced technology fab construction beginning
- Active robotaxi fleet operating in Austin, Dallas, and Houston with no safety driver and paying customers

articles.title: Everyone Is Suddenly Chasing Tesla
articles.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel reviews several Tesla-related developments over the weekend of June 13–15, 2026, all centering on the robotaxi rollout and FSD progress. Host Herbert is joined by guest Jeff Lutz, a former supply chain executive from Motorola, Google, and Lenovo who now runs his own consulting firm serving mega-tech companies. The core thesis is that Tesla is approaching a meaningful tipping point in Cybercab production, FSD software quality, and regulatory momentum — while competitors are still years behind.

## Robotaxi

1. **Record Cybercab count at Giga Texas outbound lot:** A drone flyover by Airwave/General Westside captured a record 102 Cybercabs in the outbound lot at Giga Texas — the highest single-lot count observed to date. Jeff Lutz interprets this as evidence of a production ramp transitioning from dozens to hundreds to thousands of units, noting that Tesla only began Cybercab production near the end of April (the first month of Q2 2026), meaning fewer than two full months of production have elapsed. He emphasizes that Tesla's decision to move vehicles out to remote city locations — rather than keeping them near the factory — signals growing confidence in both hardware and FSD software readiness.

2. **Cybercab fleet buildup at Houston and Dallas robotaxi hubs:** As of June 13, 2026, 31 Cybercabs were spotted at a Houston robotaxi hub (up from approximately 20 just a few weeks prior), and 50 Cybercabs were spotted in Dallas — with 19 of the Dallas units described as fully badged and ready. Lutz notes that production-worthy signals include wheel caps, front license plates, and decals being attached — details that would not be applied to pure test vehicles. He argues steering wheels are likely field-retrofitable and not a permanent indicator of test-only status.

3. **Cybercabs spotted in new cities:** Cybercabs were reported spotted in Seattle (described as a first sighting since the prior week), Mesa, Arizona, and Las Vegas — with Las Vegas reportedly preparing dedicated robotaxi support infrastructure. The broad geographic distribution is cited by both host and guest as another indicator of growing operational deployment rather than purely localized testing.

4. **Tesla robotaxi safety data — one new NHTSA-reported crash, not Tesla's fault:** The monthly NHTSA update (covering April 15 to May 15, 2026) showed one new crash for Tesla's robotaxi program, bringing the cumulative total to 18. Of those 18, only 7 are described as Tesla at fault, and those involved minor incidents such as remote-driving errors and curb scrapes. The new incident involved a robotaxi stopped at a solid red left-turn arrow that was rear-ended by a pickup truck — fully the other driver's fault. The host notes that Tesla's robotaxi latest 3-month rolling crash rate remains better than the average human driver baseline.

5. **One-year anniversary of Austin robotaxi launch — progress slower than expected:** The host acknowledges that June 22, 2025 was the original robotaxi launch date in Austin, and that by June 15, 2026 — a full year later — the network remains limited to Austin, a handful of Cybercabs in Dallas and Houston, and has not yet achieved widespread deployment. He expresses measured disappointment but points to the safety data and accumulating Cybercab inventory as grounds for optimism that broader deployment will arrive later in 2026 or in 2027.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD version 14.3.4 described as a meaningful step:** Jeff Lutz shares that he received FSD version 14.3.4 over the weekend on both of his vehicles and describes it as a bigger improvement than a typical dot release. He highlights smoother lane-keeping, more informed lane changes, reduced nag, and notably improved end-of-ride behavior — including new destination approach options and a UI that presents the car as acting like a chauffeur or robotaxi. Parking performance is also cited as materially improved, with the system more consistently completing parking in a single attempt.

2. **FSD evasive action video goes viral:** A video showing FSD reacting to an oncoming out-of-control truck — initiating evasive action before the human driver perceived the threat and before the car immediately ahead reacted — was highlighted as an example of FSD's real-time safety capability. A Tesla AI team member commented that FSD responded at the frame level even before the vehicle ahead. Jeff Lutz and the host connect this to a claimed FSD reaction time of 0.13 seconds, though this figure was attributed to separate experiments by "AI Driver and David Moss."

3. **Forbes article declares FSD a "de facto robotaxi":** A Forbes article by Brook Kthers, testing a 2026 Model 3 Premium AWD in Los Angeles, concluded that FSD version 14.3 "feels more like a level four or driverless ADS than past versions" and that Tesla is "a headway ahead" of all other car manufacturers pursuing advanced driver assistance. The article also notes that the author tested a 2026 Toyota BZ and found it to be basic lane-centering technology. General Motors' Super Cruise and Ford's Blue Cruise were described as more advanced than Toyota but still far short of FSD.

4. **FSD China approval rumors and naming change:** Tesla has accelerated recruitment across nine Chinese cities for data labeling and FSD validation. Rumors circulating online suggest FSD approval in China could come as early as June 19, 2026 (before the Dragon Boat Festival), though the host characterizes these as unverified and personally expects approval no earlier than Q3 2026. Tesla has rebranded FSD in China, moving through several names — from "FS Intelligent Assisted Driving" to "Intelligent Assisted Driving" to the current "Tesla Assisted Driving" — for regulatory and marketing reasons.

5. **AV ride (Uber partner) accident goes viral:** A video of a passenger who hailed an Uber and was picked up by an AV ride autonomous vehicle — which then was involved in an accident during what appeared to be a supervised test run — circulated widely. Sawyer Merritt noted that the vehicle was equipped with five lidars, 13 cameras, and four radars, and commented it "needs better intelligence." The host and Lutz contrast this with Tesla FSD's performance, arguing that sensor count alone does not guarantee safety.

## Market & Competition

1. **Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe claims supervised FSD equivalent coming later in 2026:** In a new interview, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe stated that Rivian will offer full supervised point-to-point driving — described as "very similar to Tesla's FSD" — rolling out to all Gen 2 vehicles and R2 later in 2026.
