2. **FSD Subscription Revenue as a Rising Revenue Wave:** The hosts briefly discuss the revenue implications of the global FSD subscription rollout. With the one-time purchase option being phased out (most recently in New Zealand/Taiwan markets by July 1st), all new FSD users will be on recurring subscriptions. Brian White references Elon Musk's next compensation plan target of 10 million FSD subscribers as the scale milestone, estimating the revenue potential at roughly $100/month per subscriber across that base.

Notable quotes and data:
- "When the facts are on your side, you bang on the facts. When the truth is on your side, you bang on the truth. And when nothing's on your side, you just bang on the table." — Brian White
- "It's pretty ironic that the only crashes involving Tesla's robotaxi fleet in recent months have been humans in other vehicles rear-ending them." — Sawyer Merritt (affirmed by Elon Musk)
- Dutch RDW independent review: 18-month review, 1.6 million km of road tests, 4,500 track tests, 13,000 customer ride-alongs
- Post-approval Dutch data: zero highway collisions across 23.6 million km of FSD driving in Netherlands; Dutch transportation officials cited 24 million miles
- 578 people killed in New Jersey traffic accidents in 2025; 94%+ of serious crashes attributed to human error
- FSD one-time purchase option discontinued in Taiwan (and previously New Zealand), moving to subscription-only starting July 1st
- Elon Musk's next compensation plan target referenced as 10 million FSD subscribers
- "People who are delaying the autonomous vehicle being rolled out have blood on their hands." — Brian White
- "The people I follow who go to Austin specifically to take the rides are still getting rides." — Brian White, rebutting claims the robotaxi fleet is inactive

articles.title: New SECRETS About The Cybercab Discovered
articles.body:
This video from "brighterwithherbert" features host Herbert and guest Brian White (of the YouTube channel FutureAzA) discussing newly revealed technical specifications for the Tesla Cybercab, sourced from recent EPA filings, alongside analysis of accelerating production and deployment signals. The core thesis is that the Cybercab is farther along in regulatory, manufacturing, and distribution readiness than most investors appreciate, and that a commercial robotaxi launch is weeks to a couple of months away rather than years.

## Robotaxi

1. **EPA Certificate of Conformity — a critical regulatory unlock:** The Cybercab has officially received its EPA Certificate of Conformity, which is required before any vehicle can be legally introduced into US commerce. Brian White argues this was the primary reason no paid Cybercab rides had occurred yet — not software or hardware issues — and that this regulatory milestone clears the path to commercial deployment. He also notes the EPA, not NHTSA, enforces the 8-year/100,000-mile minimum battery warranty requirement.

2. **Cybercab production numbers suggest imminent deployment:** Over 100 Cybercabs were spotted in the outbound lot at Giga Texas, 55 were spotted in Dallas, and additional units have appeared at robo taxi hubs across Texas and beyond — including one sighted at an event in Austria. Brian White estimates the total number produced is in the "high hundreds" and says he "would be very surprised if it's under a thousand." He draws a direct analogy to tanks massing at a border: mass production at this scale signals imminent rollout, not extended testing.

3. **Infrastructure buildout underway in multiple cities:** A ~51,000 square foot facility is being built in Grand Prairie, Texas (in the Dallas metro area) that will serve as a combined service, repair, and charging/cleaning hub dedicated to the Cybercab. A similar permitted facility was identified in Las Vegas. Brian White notes these service hubs only need to exist in each deployment market — a logistical advantage of Tesla's vertically integrated, fleet-owned model versus consumer-owned vehicles.

4. **Software remains the final gating factor:** Brian White states there are no remaining physical or regulatory hurdles to deployment — the only remaining question is when Tesla decides the software is ready. He is skeptical that the end-of-June deadline for a specific FSD milestone will be met ("low" probability), but says the only FSD timelines he trusts are those posted by Ashok Elluswamy with a specific date attached.

5. **Autonomous Cybercabs spotted driving without steering wheels:** Joe Tegtmeyer captured footage of a Cybercab operating autonomously — without a steering wheel — making a graceful arrival and backing smoothly into a parking space at Giga Texas. Other units on the lot retain steering wheels, which Brian White notes can be removed. The absence of wheel covers on many units is explained as standard Tesla shipping procedure, not a production anomaly.

6. **Owner-vehicle robotaxi network remains uncertain and unlikely near-term:** The hosts discuss skepticism about Tesla's previously promised ability for owners to add their personal vehicles to the robotaxi fleet. Brian White identifies camera washers and potentially Starlink terminals as hardware retrofits that would be difficult or impossible to add aftermarket. He suggests owner vehicles are unlikely to be included in the first or even second round of fleet deployment. Herbert notes this could create legal exposure given how consistently Tesla executives promised the feature — comparing it to the hardware 3 / unsupervised FSD coast-to-coast promise.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD on Hardware 3 vehicles — revenue motivation for Tesla to deliver:** Brian White states that FSD is currently unavailable outside the US for Hardware 3 vehicles, and that unlocking Hardware 3 for international markets represents "millions, tens, maybe hundreds of millions of dollars a month" in potential revenue. He argues Tesla is therefore more motivated than owners to make Hardware 3 unsupervised FSD work, and considers it "100% a priority," though the timeline remains unknown.

2. **Ashok Elluswamy's milestone track record cited as credibility benchmark:** Brian White references a post from "last summer" (summer 2025) in which Ashok Elluswamy published eight to ten FSD milestones with specific dates, and the worst performer missed by only one day. He uses this as his personal standard for trusting FSD timelines — only believing dates when Elluswamy posts them publicly.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cybercab technical specifications revealed via EPA filing:** The EPA documents disclose that the Cybercab uses approximately a 48 kWh battery pack, weighs approximately 3,000–3,100 lbs (the lightest vehicle in Tesla's lineup, lighter than a Model 3), produces approximately 219 horsepower, uses a front-wheel drive configuration, and achieves an equivalent range of approximately 418 miles. Brian White previously broke the front-wheel drive detail. He notes the vehicle uses a non-standard voltage architecture — neither 400V nor 800V, but something around 326V or 362V — suggesting it was specifically tuned for its commercial use case.

2. **Front-wheel drive justified by commercial use case:** Brian White explains that torque steer (normally a concern with front-wheel drive EVs) is a non-issue for the Cybercab because hard acceleration will essentially never occur in robotaxi service. The weight distribution with the battery pack makes front vs. rear wheel drive largely inconsequential for this application.

3. **48 kWh battery sized for durability, not just range:** Brian White explains that a larger-than-minimum battery pack is necessary to allow full regenerative braking capacity and to enable Tesla to operate the vehicle in a narrow state-of-charge window (e.g., 20–70%) in daily fleet operations, which dramatically extends battery longevity — potentially to 800,000 miles instead of 300,000 miles. The 418-mile rated range gives Tesla significant headroom to manage battery degradation over the vehicle's commercial life.

4. **165 Wh/mile efficiency rated best in North America:** The Cybercab's energy consumption figure of 165 Wh per mile is described as the best efficiency rating of any vehicle in North America. Brian White attributes this to the vehicle's light weight and the fact that its use profile will almost never include hard acceleration. He notes the 5.5 miles/kWh figure previously cited by Tesla engineers was described to him as what they were "allowed to say," and the EPA data now confirms the real-world efficiency is better.

5. **3,100 lb curb weight designed for durability and repairability, not lightness:** Brian White clarifies the Cybercab is not designed to be lightweight — it is designed to be rugged and easily repairable. Body panels are plastic and can be swapped quickly and cheaply, in contrast to a vehicle like the Jaguar I-Pace where a fender repair involves bodywork, paint matching, and significant downtime. This design philosophy adds some weight but reduces total cost of ownership for a fleet operator dramatically.

6. **Cybercab range vs. Waymo fleet efficiency comparison:** Brian White estimates that for every one Cybercab, a fleet operator would need approximately three Waymo vehicles to provide equivalent coverage, due to the Waymo's higher energy consumption (attributed partly to the power demands of its sensor compute stack) and shorter effective range. He notes the Cybercab has "a little bit more than half" the battery of a Waymo but substantially more range.

Notable quotes and data:
- EPA-reported Cybercab specs: ~48 kWh battery, ~3,000–3,100 lbs, ~219 hp, front-wheel drive, ~418 miles equivalent range
- Energy efficiency: 165 Wh/mile — described as best in North America
- Voltage architecture: neither 400V nor 800V; approximately 326V or 362V (Brian White flagging this as unusual and seeking clarification from electrical engineer contacts)
- 100+ Cybercabs spotted in outbound lot at Giga Texas; 55 spotted in Dallas
- Brian White's estimate: total Cybercabs produced is in the "high hundreds," likely over 1,000
- ~51,000 sq ft Cybercab service/charging/cleaning facility under construction in Grand Prairie, Texas
- Brian White on deployment timing: "weeks, perhaps a couple months" — not years
- Brian White on owner-vehicle robotaxi inclusion: "I'm deeply skeptical that owner vehicles would be in the first round of deployment. And I'm also a bit skeptical we'd be in the second round."
- On the EPA certificate: "You have to have this certificate before you can engage in commerce… that obstacle has been passed."
- Ashok Elluswamy's last summer milestone post: 8–10 milestones with dates, worst miss was by one day
- Brian White on end-of-June FSD deadline probability: "Low."

articles.title: What Happens The Day Tesla Turns On Robotaxi
articles.body:
This wide-ranging episode of the Cern Basher podcast features hosts Cern Basher and Phil Beisel alongside special guest Robert Scoble — a longtime tech journalist, author, and early Tesla rider — covering the SpaceX IPO, the Cursor acquisition, and Tesla's robotaxi rollout strategy. The core thesis is that Elon Musk and his companies are building a fundamentally new technological and economic order, and that Tesla's robotaxi deployment represents a coming inflection point that most of the world has not yet grasped. The conversation weaves together AI infrastructure, autonomous vehicles, humanoid robots, and big-tech competitive dynamics into a unified "who wins the AI future" framework.

## Robotaxi

1. **"Storm the parking lot" deployment thesis:** Robert Scoble argues that Tesla is deliberately accumulating Cybercabs in parking lots rather than deploying them piecemeal, with the goal of launching a large fleet simultaneously. His view: Tesla should wait until it has roughly 2,000 Cybercabs staged, then turn on the robotaxi service all at once so that the sheer visible scale creates its own news cycle and demonstrates capability to the public immediately. He frames this as both a PR and a software-readiness strategy — the FSD software may need one or two more updates before the lawyers sign off, and Tesla does not want 2,000 new vehicles causing traffic jams on day one.

2. **Cybercab production ramp comparison to Model 3:** Scoble draws a direct analogy to his own experience buying the 749th Model 3 off the Fremont line roughly six months after the line started. He notes the current Cybercab ramp is slower at the front end, but argues the manufacturing process — modular, built in place rather than on a long line — means it will scale faster once it reaches full speed. He predicts that by end of 2025 (resolved from "end of this year" against publish date 2026-06-18, suggesting late 2025 context in the anecdote, though the speaker appears to mean end of the current ramp year) there could be 10,000–20,000 Cybercabs on the road, and that the Cybercab production curve should eventually surpass the Model 3 ramp rate.

3. **Outbound lot at Giga Texas identified as staging area:** The hosts confirm, crediting Joe Tegtmeyer's reporting, that the parking lot where Cybercabs are being staged is the outbound lot at Giga Texas — the same lot used to stage finished vehicles before they are loaded onto transport trucks. Sawyer Merritt is also cited as having published photos of the lot.

4. **Robotaxi adoption still in its infancy globally:** Scoble notes that if you aggregate all customers of Tesla, Waymo, Zoox, Nuro, BYD, and Chinese autonomous vehicle operators, fewer than 10 million people out of 8 billion have ever ridden in an autonomous vehicle. He frames this as evidence that the world is at the very beginning of autonomous vehicle adoption, not near saturation.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD's data flywheel acknowledged across the robotics industry:** Scoble states that "everybody in the robotics industry talks about the Tesla data flywheel" — the advantage Tesla built by putting cameras and an AI computer in every vehicle it sold, regardless of whether the buyer purchased FSD, and then charging an additional fee (he references the $6,000 FSD price) to activate the software. He credits this fleet — described as roughly 10 million vehicles — as the foundation for Tesla's world-model training advantage.

2. **Legacy automakers' failure traced to executive resistance:** Scoble gives a detailed account of Mercedes having autonomous driving technology in its labs more than a decade ago but killing the project because executives did not want to add $6,000 per car to the retail price. He also notes that Volkswagen sponsored the Stanford University autonomous car project that became Waymo, but could not get budget approval to deploy the technology in production vehicles. Phil Beisel reinforces the theme, arguing that all these failures trace back to leadership: Elon Musk simply directed Tesla to do it, bypassing the institutional resistance that paralyzed legacy OEMs.

3. **Robert Scoble's consumer research timeline:** Scoble describes conducting consumer research roughly 15 years ago (implying around 2011) going around America asking people about autonomous cars, and finding unanimous resistance — he recounts one respondent in Kansas describing himself as "a narcissistic control freak" who would never let a computer drive him. He contrasts that with current Waymo riders in San Francisco and Phoenix who are now enthusiastic converts, illustrating how attitudes shift once people experience the technology.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus timeline estimates from industry insiders:** Scoble reports that when he asks people collecting training data for humanoid robots — including those building sensor gloves, egocentric camera rigs, and force-sensing devices — when a generalized humanoid will be capable of doing 20% of jobs in a factory like Tesla's, most answer "two to seven years." He notes that people who work at Tesla tend to give the more optimistic end of that range, around 18 months, while others are more cautious. His own view is that it will be "a couple of years" before Optimus can safely walk around, interact with people, listen to instructions, and perform a variety of factory tasks.

2. **Giga Texas SNX line closure linked to Optimus co-location:** Scoble argues that Elon closed the Model S/X (SNX) line at Fremont in order to place the Optimus development team physically adjacent to an active car production line. The logic: rapid iteration requires Optimus to be deployed on the factory floor, fail, be brought back to the lab in the afternoon for software and hardware adjustments, and redeployed — the same tight iteration loop that China's manufacturing ecosystem enables for consumer electronics. He frames this as Tesla deliberately engineering the feedback cycle that will accelerate Optimus to commercial readiness.

3. **Egocentric data and sensor gloves as key training inputs:** Scoble describes the hardware infrastructure being built to train humanoid robots — hats with two to six cameras capturing egocentric (first-person) data of human hand manipulation, and gloves with hundreds of sensors per finger measuring grip force (using a Diet Coke can as a tactile example). He notes that Apple Vision Pro is being used in parts of the robotics industry specifically to capture this egocentric training data.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cybercab's large screen validated by the conversation:** The hosts reference the Cybercab's large interior screen as a concrete example of why big screens make sense in a self-driving vehicle — when the car drives itself, the screen becomes purely an entertainment and information interface. Scoble explicitly says riders will be "watching movies and doing video calls" in their Cybercabs, and that the screen real estate will be fully utilized in ways that were hard to articulate in advance, just as large screens in earlier EVs seemed hard to justify until the use cases emerged.

2. **Model 3's software-defined architecture cited as paradigm shift:** Scoble recounts buying his Model 3 and experiencing continuous over-the-air improvements to acceleration, audio, headlights, braking, and FSD over the ownership period, calling this the definitive advantage of a software-defined vehicle. He frames this as something Mercedes engineers he spoke with roughly 12 years ago understood intellectually but could not execute because their executives feared hacking and did not want to enable persistent cloud connectivity.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO and Cursor acquisition framed as linked maneuvers:** The hosts open by discussing the SpaceX IPO, noting SpaceX's market cap of approximately $2.6 trillion at the time of recording, with the stock having briefly traded around $222 per share after hours. They then analyze SpaceX's June 16 announcement that it will exercise its option to acquire Cursor — the AI coding tool used by 64% of Fortune 500 companies and 75% of Salesforce developers — in an all-stock transaction at approximately 10 times Cursor's projected annual revenue. Because SpaceX trades at roughly 40 times revenue, the hosts calculate that SpaceX is effectively acquiring Cursor at about 0.25 times SpaceX's revenue multiple, making it a highly favorable deal for SpaceX. They describe this as a "Trojan horse" entry into the enterprise market, which they note represents $26.5 trillion of SpaceX's stated $28 trillion total addressable market.

2. **Space-based compute framed as the inevitable AI infrastructure endgame:** A central thesis of the episode is that AI compute demand will outstrip Earth-based data center capacity, and that the only scalable path is orbital data centers powered by free solar energy, with no corrosion, no land-use conflicts, no community resistance, and no vulnerability to physical infrastructure attacks. Scoble describes companies already building satellites carrying Nvidia Vera Rubin chips and solar arrays that unfurl in orbit, launched and connected via SpaceX and Starlink respectively — meaning SpaceX profits from the trend regardless of whether it owns the data centers. Elon Musk is quoted (from a post described as made "a couple of days ago") saying that harnessing 1 millionth of the sun's power for AI would represent more than a million times the intelligence of all humanity, and that doing so would ultimately require manufacturing solar panels and radiators on the moon and launching them into deep space with a mass driver.

3. **Chinese competition identified as the primary long-term threat:** Scoble argues that the real competitive threat to Apple, Tesla, and other American tech leaders is not from European or Japanese incumbents but from a new generation of Chinese entrepreneurs — citing DJI, Insta360, Xiaomi, Huawei, Xpeng, and Unitree — who are building original brands rather than copying American ones. He notes that Xpeng's founder explicitly wants to be Elon Musk and that Xpeng's investor presentation cited Tesla as the only American competitor worth naming. He argues China's manufacturing iteration speed — where designers can walk across the street to the factory and prototype overnight — gives Chinese companies a structural advantage that Elon Musk has consciously tried to replicate by co-locating engineering with production at Tesla.

4. **Big Tech competitive rankings:** The hosts walk through a global market cap list placing Tesla at approximately $1.5 trillion and SpaceX at approximately $2.6 trillion, with SpaceX briefly surpassing Microsoft. They frame having two Elon Musk companies in the global top 10 as historically remarkable. Meta is characterized by Scoble as a "cigarettes company" — effective at creating addiction but generating no positive emotional association — and as internally chaotic, with its spatial computing ambitions hampered by leadership that grew up in a 2D world. Google is described as a data-rich utility that consumers trust but do not feel warmly toward, and as lacking a fashion brand suitable for wearable computing. Apple is assessed as well-positioned to enter the wearables market late but effectively, with incoming CEO Terri (the name used in the transcript) credited as an engineer with Vision Pro experience who avoids internal politics.

Notable quotes and data:
- Elon Musk (quoted from a recent post): "It's humbling to consider that if we harness just 1 millionth of the sun's power for AI, that'll be much more than a million times the intelligence of all humanity." He added that doing so would require manufacturing solar panels and radiators on the moon and launching them into deep space with a mass driver, and that "conventional money will no longer be relevant — mass and energy will take the place of dollars."
- Elon Musk (quoted from a May presentation): "In 2027 you won't even bother doing coding. XAI would just create the binary directly… There's an intermediate step there that probably won't even be needed by the end of 2026."
- Robert Scoble on Elon's mental time horizon: "I think about 15 years."
- Scoble on Cybercab deployment strategy: "If I was Elon, I'd wait until I had 2,000 in parking lots. And then I would turn on robotaxi, and all of a sudden one day you don't see any gold cars rolling around Austin, Texas, and the next day you see a f***load of them roll."
- Scoble on Meta: "Meta is perceived as a cigarettes company… you might be addicted to nicotine or social media, but you're not feeling good about it."
- Cursor used by 64% of Fortune 500 companies and ~70% of Fortune 1000; 75% of Salesforce developers use it.
- SpaceX Cursor acquisition: all-stock deal at ~10x Cursor's projected 2026 revenue; SpaceX trades at ~40x revenue, implying an effective acquisition cost of ~0.25x SpaceX revenue.
- SpaceX market cap at time of recording: approximately $2.6 trillion; Tesla approximately $1.5 trillion.
- Global autonomous vehicle ridership estimate (Scoble): fewer than 10 million people out of 8 billion have ever ridden in an autonomous vehicle.
- Humanoid robot capability timeline (Scoble's industry contacts): 2–7 years to achieve 20% of Tesla factory tasks; Tesla employees say ~18 months.
- Jensen Huang quote on Cursor: "My favorite enterprise AI service is Cursor. Every one of our engineers, some 40,000, are now assisted by AI, and our productivity has gone up incredibly."

articles.title: Tesla Just Checked Another Critical Box
articles.body:
This FutureAzA video hosted by Brian, joined by guest Herbert, does a deep dive into the newly published EPA Certificate of Conformity for the Tesla Cybercab, analyzing every key engineering specification line by line. The core thesis is that the Cybercab's specifications — particularly its weight, efficiency, and custom-tuned architecture — represent a decisive structural advantage over competitors like Waymo, and that the EPA filing itself is a critical regulatory milestone that clears the path for commercial deployment. The hosts also discuss the current state of FSD version 14 and offer a realistic timeline for Cybercab fleet scaling.

## Robotaxi

1. **EPA Certificate of Conformity is the critical regulatory unlock:** The hosts emphasize that the EPA Certificate of Conformity is not merely a data document — it is a required regulatory filing that must be approved before Cybercabs can be placed into commercial revenue-generating service. Herbert flags this as the buried lead: now that this certificate is filed and approved, the clock on commercial Cybercab deployment can truly begin. Brian estimates commercial-scale rollout is still roughly one to two months away, not imminent, as Tesla continues accumulating FSD training data on a brand-new vehicle platform.

2. **Cybercab curb weight of 3,113 lbs makes it the lightest EV in the US market:** The EPA filing confirms a curb weight of 3,113 lbs, which the hosts note is approximately 700 lbs lighter than the lightest Model 3 currently on the market. For context, the Model 3 weighs approximately 3,700 lbs and the Model Y approximately 4,000 lbs. The hosts argue this weight reduction is a foundational competitive advantage, enabling superior efficiency, lower operating costs, and longer operational range.

3. **EPA-estimated range of ~400 miles — far exceeding earlier expectations:** The EPA filing shows an estimated range in the vicinity of 400 miles (Herbert cites approximately 411 miles), well above the ~300-mile figure that had been discussed when the Cybercab was first revealed. Combined with the 165 watt-hours per mile efficiency rating, the hosts argue Tesla only needs roughly one-third as many Cybercabs as Waymo vehicles to deliver equivalent service miles — Herbert frames this as "Tesla needs only 1,000 vehicles to match Waymo's 3,500."

4. **Front-wheel drive layout explained as a deliberate manufacturing and engineering choice:** Brian explains that the Cybercab's front-wheel drive configuration is not a cost-cutting compromise but a consequence of consolidating all major components — motor, cooling, HVAC — under the front service-access panel. This approach simplifies manufacturing by concentrating all complex sub-assemblies in one area. Additionally, the rear wheels have a larger diameter than the front wheels for aerodynamic advantage, a detail confirmed by Ian Pavevelo from Fast Wheels in a prior segment.

5. **Custom 326V electrical architecture reflects Tesla's vertical integration philosophy:** Unlike the industry-standard 400V or 800V architectures, the Cybercab runs on a custom 326V system. Brian argues this is an expression of Tesla's broader strategy of fine-tuning every component specifically for the vehicle rather than adopting off-the-shelf standards — drawing an analogy to Tesla's custom actuator development for Optimus. The hosts acknowledge this introduces early compatibility risk, but note that since Tesla retains ownership of the entire fleet, any issues can be resolved without public recalls.

6. **219 horsepower motor is a byproduct of engineering for durability, not performance:** The 219 horsepower output from the single front-mounted permanent magnet motor is described as intentionally oversized relative to the vehicle's operational needs. Running the motor below its maximum capacity extends its operational lifespan — an important consideration for a commercial fleet vehicle expected to run continuously.

7. **Gross vehicle weight rating accommodates up to ~700 lbs of cargo:** At a curb weight of 3,113 lbs, the gross vehicle weight rating leaves room for substantial payload. The hosts note this makes the Cybercab suitable not just for passenger transport but potentially for delivery use cases, reinforcing the multi-purpose nature of the platform.

8. **Fleet scaling projection: Herbert estimates 10,000–15,000 active robotaxis by end of 2026:** Herbert's forward model envisions each city receiving approximately 1,000 robotaxis, with a roughly 90/10 split between Cybercabs and Model Y vehicles — reflecting his estimate that ~90% of trips involve two passengers or fewer. He believes approximately 1,000 Cybercabs have already been produced as of the video date, with production running at perhaps 50–100 units per day, though he acknowledges the exact rate is difficult to verify from external observation.

9. **Four months of NHTSA reporting showing zero Tesla robotaxi at-fault incidents:** Herbert notes that Tesla has now accumulated four consecutive months of NHTSA reports showing no at-fault robotaxi incidents, and argues this safety data record is itself an asset — providing a statistical baseline that will contextualize any future incident when fleet scaling begins.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD version 14.3.4 described as a meaningful step-change improvement over prior 14.x releases:** Both Brian and Herbert have recently downloaded FSD v14.3.4 and describe it as a larger jump than a typical point release. Herbert notes that v14.3 exhibited minor brake-stabbing behavior in certain situations (e.g., exiting a driveway), which v14.3.4 reportedly resolves. Brian's first two drives on v14.3.4 showed the system correctly detecting and slowing for a small animal that crossed the road — behavior he describes as appropriate and human-like.

2. **FSD version 14 broadly considered "good enough to show friends and family":** The hosts agree that any version in the v14.x range represents a qualitative threshold where the system is impressive enough to demonstrate to skeptical passengers. Herbert recounts a v14.3 drive where the car appropriately yielded to a vehicle cutting into an intersection — behavior he found correct even though his passenger found the slight jerk unsettling.

3. **Navigation remains an unresolved weakness in FSD:** Brian notes the car missed the turn for his street on a v14.3.4 drive, and references an article describing Tesla's navigation as a stitched system drawing from four different sources including its own. Both hosts agree this is a genuine and persistent problem that has not yet been solved.

4. **Timeline delays attributed to FSD version 13/14/15 parameter scaling falling behind schedule:** Herbert explains that Elon Musk's earlier promise of covering half the US population with robotaxis by end-2025 was contingent on FSD scaling faster than it did. The "10x parameter" milestone was associated with version 15, which has not yet arrived. Version 14 has deployed but is described as months behind the original roadmap. The hosts treat this as an honest engineering delay rather than a strategic decision.

## Market & Competition

1. **Waymo's efficiency disadvantage quantified at approximately 3x energy per mile:** Herbert estimates the Waymo fleet consumes roughly three times more energy per mile than the Cybercab's 165 watt-hours per mile. Combined with Tesla's ownership of the Supercharger network — eliminating middlemen in charging cost — the hosts argue Tesla's per-mile operating cost will be structurally lower than Waymo's, even if Waymo currently has approximately 3,500 vehicles deployed versus Tesla's much smaller current fleet.

2. **Waymo's vehicle strategy criticized as reactive rather than purpose-built:** The hosts contrast Tesla's vertically integrated approach — designing the Cybercab from the ground up for autonomous commercial operation — with Waymo's history of selecting existing vehicles (including the Jaguar I-Pace built by Magna) and upfitting them for autonomy. The analogy drawn is to Waymo's situation being similar to a robotics company still relying on off-the-shelf actuators a decade into development.

Notable quotes and data:
- Cybercab curb weight: **3,113 lbs** (lightest EV currently on US roads per EPA filing)
- Cybercab estimated range: approximately **400 miles** (Herbert cites ~411 miles); earlier public estimates had been ~300 miles
- Cybercab efficiency: **165 watt-hours per mile** (EPA certified)
- Cybercab motor: **219 horsepower**, single front-mounted permanent magnet, front-wheel drive
- Cybercab electrical architecture: **326 volts** (custom, not industry-standard 400V or 800V)
- Gross vehicle weight allows approximately **700 lbs of payload**
- Waymo fleet cited at approximately **3,500 vehicles**; Herbert's estimate that **~1,000 Cybercabs** already produced
- Herbert's end-of-2026 forecast: **10,000–15,000 active robotaxis**, ~900 Cybercabs + ~100 Model Y per city
- FSD navigation issue: described as stitching **four different navigation sources**
- *"Tesla needs only a thousand [Cybercabs] to match [Waymo's 3,500]"* — Herbert
- *"Heaping quarter cup"* of salt on Elon timelines — Brian and Herbert, in agreement
- *"We are now there"* — Herbert, on FSD version 14 readiness for scale deployment

articles.title: Daily X Summary (2026-06-18)
articles.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts centered on three high-signal themes for Tesla investors: a record Cybercab sighting at Giga Texas reinforcing production ramp momentum, Dutch regulatory validation of FSD (Supervised) in Europe signaling international regulatory progress, and Elon Musk's exercise of 304 million stock options from his 2018 compensation package with important clarifications on lock-up structure. FSD real-world intervention data and a Texas DOT executive's enthusiastic first-hand Cybercab reaction added further bullish texture to the autonomous driving and robotaxi thesis.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Record Cybercab sighting at Giga Texas signals production ramp acceleration:** A record 120 Cybercabs were spotted at Giga Texas on June 17, the highest single-day count reported to date. This is a meaningful production signal, suggesting the factory is materially scaling Cybercab output ahead of broader fleet deployment. Separately, the Texas Department of Transportation Executive Director rode in the production version of the Cybercab and issued a notably enthusiastic statement: *"The complete absence of traditional driver controls underscores a significant shift in mobility and vehicle design. No steering wheel, no accelerator, no brake."* The combination of a senior state transportation official publicly validating the vehicle design and a record unit count on the factory floor is a strong near-term signal for robotaxi launch readiness.

2. **Dutch vehicle authority (RDW) defends FSD (Supervised) approval in Europe:** The Dutch RDW released a formal public statement defending its decision to approve Tesla's FSD (Supervised) after receiving public criticism. The authority stated it *"carefully assessed and tested this driver assistance system before approval was granted,"* including analysis and evaluation prior to sign-off. This is a meaningful regulatory milestone — it confirms FSD (Supervised) has cleared a formal European regulatory review and that the approving body is willing to publicly stand behind its process. This post received significant engagement (2.9K likes, 343 reposts), reflecting investor awareness of its importance for Tesla's international FSD expansion.

3. **FSD intervention data: destination parking is the dominant friction point, critical safety events rare:** Results from what appears to be an in-app or community FSD feedback survey indicate that destination parking is by far the most common reason users intervene with FSD, while critical safety interventions are described as "extremely rare." This qualitative data point is consistent with Tesla's broader narrative that FSD has matured beyond safety-critical failures and is now primarily limited by edge-case convenience scenarios. While not an official Tesla dataset, it reinforces the thesis that the remaining barriers to unsupervised deployment are operational rather than safety-fundamental.

4. **Elon Musk exercises 304 million Tesla stock options; no shares sold, long lock-up ahead:** Elon Musk exercised 304 million Tesla stock options from his 2018 compensation package, per an SEC filing. Tesla withheld 17.53 million shares at an average price of $404.66/share as part of net share settlement — no open-market Tesla stock sale occurred. Critically, the received shares are restricted and do not vest until January 19, 2028, after which a 5-year lockup period begins, meaning Musk cannot sell the shares until 2033. This clarification is important for investors concerned about near-term supply overhang: there is effectively no sell pressure from this transaction for at least seven years.

5. **Market & Competition — 2027 Porsche Taycan reveals simulated gear shifting ("E-Shift"):** Porsche revealed the 2027 Taycan lineup featuring a system called "E-Shift," which simulates an eight-speed gearbox via paddle shifters, including a virtual rev limiter and gear-specific drag torque. Sawyer Merritt covered this without explicit editorial commentary, but the implicit framing — that Porsche is adding mechanical simulation to mask the EV experience — positions Tesla's software-forward, minimalist approach as a contrasting design philosophy. This is mildly relevant context for Tesla's competitive positioning in the premium EV segment.

6. **Energy macro context — renewables vs. fossil fuel capacity additions in 2025:** A post noted that in 2025, the world installed 814 GW of new solar and wind capacity versus 158 GW of gross fossil fuel capacity, with renewables overtaking coal globally. While not Tesla-specific, this macro backdrop supports long-term demand for Tesla Energy products (Megapack, solar) as grid electrification accelerates.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — The record Cybercab production sighting, formal European regulatory defense of FSD, real-world FSD safety data showing rare critical interventions, and a Texas DOT executive's firsthand validation of the Cybercab collectively reinforce the near-term robotaxi and autonomous driving deployment thesis, while the Musk option exercise carries no near-term dilution or sell-pressure risk.

articles.title: Why Elon Increased His Tesla Voting Power
articles.body:
This panel discussion on "brighterwithherbert" features host Herbert alongside guests Jeff Lutz ("the rational bull"), Cern Basher ("the bot bull"), and Larry Goldberg ("the golden bull") analyzing Elon Musk's decision to exercise 304 million Tesla stock options, the implications for a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger, and a series of fresh FSD and Grok-in-car announcements. The video's core thesis is that Elon's consolidation of voting power signals increasing probability of a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla, while simultaneously FSD and Cybercab deployment breadcrumbs suggest the robotaxi rollout is approaching a meaningful inflection point.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Elon's FSD parking memory announcement:** Elon Musk posted that upcoming FSD releases will remember users' parking preferences, allowing the car to navigate autonomously to the correct spot at home, office, or school drop-off. The panel agreed this is significant — host Herbert and guests noted that destination parking is now the primary reason FSD users intervene, with critical safety interventions described by Elon as "extremely rare." One guest (Larry Goldberg) noted he had experienced a regression in garage parking capability since a recent FSD version, and flagged that memory storage on existing hardware may be a limiting factor going forward.

2. **Grok voice control of FSD coming in ~3 months:** Elon replied to a user requesting conversational Grok control of the car — the ability to say things like "turn right here," "drop us off here," or "park far away while we go in" — saying this functionality will arrive in approximately 3 months. The panel emphasized this is qualitatively different from Grok answering questions: it represents direct vehicle control via AI. Jeff Lutz noted the current cloud-based Grok latency would be unacceptable for real-time vehicle control, and that Elon's 3-month timeline implies the existing HW4 (AI4) processor can handle this — contrary to earlier expectations that it would require AI5. Larry Goldberg speculated that memory (not processing power) is the binding constraint on AI4, and that future AI5 and AI6 chips will have dramatically more memory.

3. **FSD safety record and global expansion:** Herbert noted that FSD has gone approximately four months since February without any at-fault incidents (per the host, unconfirmed). The panel discussed FSD approvals expanding globally and expressed frustration at Tesla's perceived lack of marketing around the technology. Jeff Lutz argued Tesla has an "awareness problem" — the engineering moat is growing faster than the marketing and awareness moat — and called on Tesla to measure and publicly report FSD adoption rates regionally, especially for recently approved European markets.

4. **Memory and personalization as FSD's next frontier:** Cern Basher and Larry Goldberg explored the broader implications of persistent memory in FSD beyond parking — including remembering preferred routes, mapping unique navigation challenges in specific parking garages, and building personalized driving profiles per driver. Larry noted that memory accumulated on the car's storage stick would be relatively slow to access, and that existing vehicles were not designed to store very large amounts of persistent data. He suggested a memory stick upgrade (e.g., 5–10 GB) would be an inexpensive future option.

## Robotaxi

1. **102 Cybercabs spotted at Giga Texas Albon lot:** Herbert reported that 102 Cybercabs were spotted at the Albon lot near Giga Texas — described as a record accumulation, up from earlier sightings of 20, then 30, then 50 units. Jeff Lutz interpreted the staging of vehicles away from the factory as a bullish signal, explaining that in manufacturing, you only add value (decals, hubcaps, external branding) when you are close to deployment, because rework costs increase with each value-added step. He said he expected Cybercab production to scale from dozens of units in April to hundreds in May, targeting thousands per week by end of June, though he acknowledged uncertainty about whether software or hardware is the pacing constraint.

2. **Cybercabs spotted in New Zealand:** The panel noted that several Cybercabs were spotted in New Zealand, which Cern Basher interpreted as likely testing for right-hand-traffic road conditions (driving on the opposite side of the road) and possibly cold-weather testing. The host noted Tesla has used New Zealand as a testing ground for vehicles in the past.

3. **Cybercabs now exiting Giga Texas autonomously:** Joe Tegtmeyer, upon returning from a trip to Europe, reportedly spotted a Cybercab driving autonomously out of the Giga Texas factory and parking itself — described by the host as a first. The panel viewed this as another indicator of imminent commercial deployment readiness.

4. **Cybercabs coming out of factory with branding installed:** Cern Basher noted that Cybercabs are now coming out of the factory with "cyber cables on the sides and the back" (branding/service markings), indicating preparation for vehicles that will actually be put into service rather than held for testing.

5. **Robotaxi Q2 city expansion still possible:** Cern Basher noted that Tesla had stated they would roll out robotaxi service in additional cities before the end of Q2 (i.e., before end of June 2026). He said Miami and other cities could potentially see an announcement imminently, possibly over the coming weekend (around June 22, 2026 — the one-year anniversary of the first robotaxi). Jeff Lutz was skeptical that Tesla would time an announcement to a calendar milestone, believing they will deploy when operational readiness criteria are met. The EPA certificate of conformity was flagged as a potential gate for commercial charging of rides — without it, per the discussion, Tesla may be unable to charge customers for Cybercab rides.

6. **Delivery estimates for Q2:** Goldman Sachs and Wolf Research are projecting approximately 420,000 vehicle deliveries for Q2 2026; Barclays at 418,000; consensus (per Grok) between 397,000–401,000 depending on the data source. Notably, bear analyst Gordon Johnson's GLJ Research has the highest estimate at 426,000 — which the panel found ironic given his historically negative Tesla ratings. Q2 delivery volume is expected to be released around July 2nd or 3rd.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus mentioned as beneficiary of Grok memory integration:** Jeff Lutz briefly connected the Grok-in-car voice control development to Optimus, noting that memory and conversational AI control will be essential for humanoid robot operation as well. Larry Goldberg mentioned getting "the first robots out of the factory or into the factory" by June 30, 2027 as a key valuation milestone that should precede any merger announcement, to allow proper price discovery.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Q2 2026 vehicle delivery outlook positive:** Jeff Lutz noted that Tesla started Q2 from a strong inventory position (similar to Q2 2025 pattern), and that the absence of meaningful incentives and inventory discounts — which typically appear at quarter-end — suggests strong underlying demand. He cited improving monthly numbers across Europe, China, and rest of world. Goldman Sachs revised its Q2 delivery estimate upward to 420,000, above the prior 400,000–405,000 range.

2. **Tesla stock underperforming despite broader market strength:** Herbert noted Tesla stock is trading around $400 — sometimes below — while the S&P 500 is near 7,500 and the NASDAQ is above 26,000, both near all-time highs. Jeff Lutz attributed Tesla's relative weakness to its long-duration earnings profile (more sensitive to interest rate/hawkish Fed signals), a new Fed chairman perceived as slightly more hawkish, and potential liquidity rotation toward SpaceX following its IPO.

## Financials

1. **Q2 gross margins and COGS trajectory:** Jeff Lutz said Tesla has been outperforming on cost of goods sold (COGS), and that filling factories drives fixed cost absorption and continued improvement down the COGS curve. He expects gross margins to potentially surprise to the upside again in Q2. He noted Tesla will likely show elevated capex, which will pressure free cash flow but not operating margin. He also flagged that Tesla will need to recognize an increase in the value of its SpaceX stock holdings on the balance sheet.

2. **Energy business: lumpy but potentially strong in Q2:** Larry Goldberg noted a large amount of work-in-progress in Tesla's energy business (Megapack) that was carried into Q2. If that work-in-progress converts to revenue in Q2, it could be a "big number." Jeff Lutz noted that Q1 energy expectations were approximately 14.5 gigawatt-hours and Tesla meaningfully underperformed by approximately 40%, attributing the miss to interconnection queue timing and the inherently lumpy nature of the energy business. He recommended evaluating energy on a trailing 12-month basis.

3. **Cybercab as a future production and delivery line item:** The panel discussed when Tesla might break out Cybercab production volumes separately in its production and delivery reports. Jeff Lutz suggested it will likely appear in an "other" category initially, with a separate line item when volumes become significant (5–10% of total, per the general discussion). The panel expressed hope Tesla will also begin reporting robotaxi ride miles and FSD adoption rates.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX-Tesla merger: breadcrumbs analyzed, deal mechanics debated:** The central segment of the video analyzed Elon Musk's exercise of 304 million Tesla stock options (from his 2018 performance award), at an average strike price of $44/share, bringing his Tesla ownership to approximately 19.9%. The shares are subject to a 5-year lockup and cannot be sold until 2033; Elon did not sell any stock. The panel's consensus read is that consolidating voting power positions Elon for a potential SpaceX acquisition or merger-of-equals vote, though all guests emphasized they are analyzing likelihood — not advocating for the deal. Per Grok (flagged as unverified), Elon was required to exercise these options before August 15, 2026, which contradicts Gemini's answer (per Larry Goldberg) that there was no deadline this year — the panel acknowledged disagreement between the two AIs.

2. **Larry Goldberg's merger timeline argument:** Larry Goldberg argued that a merger announcement with deal terms cannot realistically happen until after June 30, 2027, because (a) a large number of "OG" (early) Tesla shareholders are locked up until June 30, 2027, and those shareholders should be able to vote their own shares; (b) a true merger of equals requires months-long due diligence, independent board negotiations, and pricing work — a process Larry said takes close to a year based on his experience with two such mergers; and (c) price discovery for both companies will be materially better after key milestones (robotaxi scaling, Optimus factory deployment) are achieved. He allowed that an announcement of intent could come earlier, with a closing date set for after the lockup period.

3. **Jeff Lutz's counter: Elon moves fast, synergies are undeniable:** Jeff Lutz agreed with Larry's procedural points but argued Elon historically does not move slowly, and that the synergies between the two companies are so numerous — shared AI (Grok + FSD), shared GPU clusters, Terafab, solar, and more — that the pressure to combine sooner is real. He noted that the absence of an Elon denial, despite rampant public speculation, is itself a signal. He also flagged that Tesla and SpaceX each buying GPUs separately, with potentially underutilized compute between training runs, is a major driver for combining resources.

4. **Cern Basher's Blockbuster analogy clarified:** Cern Basher clarified a widely misread post he made on X: his point was not that Tesla will become "the next Blockbuster" if it doesn't merge with SpaceX. Rather, the analogy was about the necessity of always looking forward to the next platform — from cars to autonomy to Terafab — to avoid being disrupted. He noted that Elon himself embodies this forward-looking mindset, which is why critics simultaneously complain he never finishes one thing before moving to the next.

5. **Elon sentiment and political environment:** The panel briefly addressed the political backlash against Elon following SpaceX's IPO making him a trillionaire. Larry Goldberg argued the current political climate around wealth and socialism — particularly among younger demographics and academia — is more intense than past periods of political unrest he has witnessed. Jeff Lutz was more optimistic, arguing that the arguments against Elon collapse under scrutiny given his contributions to clean energy, US manufacturing, and technology, and that technology and FSD/robotaxi improvements will ultimately win the narrative.

Notable quotes and data:
- Elon Musk (via X post): "Upcoming releases of FSD will remember your parking preferences so that the car goes to the right location at your home, office, school drop off. Destination parking is by far the biggest reason people now intervene with FSD."
- Elon Musk (via X post): Critical safety interventions are now "extremely rare."
- Elon Musk (via X reply): Grok voice control of the car "will be there in about 3 months or so."
- 304 million Tesla stock options exercised by Elon Musk at an average strike price of $44/share; shares locked up until 2033.
- Elon's Tesla ownership after exercise: ~19.9% (referred to as "20%").
- 102 Cybercabs spotted at the Albon lot near Giga Texas — described as a record.
- Q2 2026 vehicle delivery estimates: Goldman Sachs & Wolf Research at ~420,000; Barclays at 418,000; consensus (per Grok) 397,000–401,000; GLJ Research (Gordon Johnson) at 426,000.
- Q1 2026 energy expectations: ~14.5 GWh; actual performance came in approximately 40% below that figure (per Jeff Lutz).
- Tesla stock price at time of filming: ~$400 (sometimes below); S&P 500 ~7,500; NASDAQ ~26,000.
- FSD described as having gone ~4 months since February without an at-fault incident (per host Herbert, unconfirmed).
- Q2 2026 production and delivery report expected around July 2–3, 2026; earnings call expected around July 20, 2026 (implied).
- Lockup period for "OG shareholders" cited by Larry Goldberg: through June 30, 2027.

articles.title: Investors May Be Missing SpaceX’s Biggest Opportunity
articles.body:
This video features host "brighterwithherbert" interviewing Brian Wang, futurist and blogger at nextbigfuture.com, who argues that investors are dramatically underestimating SpaceX's valuation potential. Wang's core thesis is that SpaceX is transitioning from a launch/satellite company into a major AI infrastructure and data center rental business — driven by its Colossus supercomputer, Cursor acquisition, Grok AI, and upcoming Rubin chip deployments — and that this transformation could drive revenue and stock appreciation far faster than the widely-cited Micron analogy suggests. The discussion is entirely focused on SpaceX and XAI, with Tesla mentioned only briefly in passing comparisons.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX as AI Infrastructure Giant — The Core Thesis:** Wang argues that most investors still view SpaceX primarily as a launch and Starlink company, but the company is rapidly becoming an AI infrastructure and data center rental business. He draws a direct analogy to Micron, which grew from roughly $6 billion per quarter in revenue to nearly $25 billion per quarter over two years as AI demand exploded, with its stock going from around $100 to over $1,000. Wang believes SpaceX could be growing even faster than Micron did.

2. **Revenue Growth Trajectory — Q1 2026 to Q4 2026:** Wang presents a quarter-by-quarter analysis. He states SpaceX was at approximately $4.6 billion per quarter in Q1 2026, and estimates it will reach roughly $15 billion per quarter by Q4 2026 — driven by AI rental revenue (from deals with Anthropic and Google), the Cursor acquisition contributing approximately $1 billion per quarter now and heading toward approximately $0.7 billion per month, plus approximately $6–7 billion from ongoing Starlink and launch revenue. He says this is roughly twice as fast as Micron's comparable growth window.

3. **Full-Year and Annual Run Rate Projections:** Wang states SpaceX had approximately $18.7 billion in revenue in 2025 and projects the company will reach approximately $46 billion in revenue by end of 2026. He agrees with others who project a $60 billion run rate by Q4 2026, and says SpaceX could reach $120–150 billion in revenue and approximately $100 billion in earnings as Rubin chips come online, potentially reaching $200 billion in revenue if Rubin deployments scale.

4. **Colossus Compute — Existing and Planned Capacity:** Wang outlines the current Colossus supercomputer infrastructure. He states Colossus 1 has approximately 230,000 chips (context suggests H100/H200 class). The S1 filing disclosed plans for an additional 220,000 GB300 chips with 400 megawatts of power for Colossus 2, potentially bringing the total to approximately 550,000–700,000 chips. Wang notes that approximately 345,000 chips remain available for rental beyond what is already committed, and that every 100,000–110,000 chips rented at Blackwell rates generates approximately $10–11 billion in rental revenue per year (per Wang's estimate). He notes that Anthropic received approximately 230,000 chips under its deal.

5. **Rubin Chip Allocation and Revenue Multiplier:** Wang cites Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker on the Altimeter BG2 podcast as saying XAI/SpaceX has approximately 20% market share of Nvidia Rubin chip allocations reserved. He states Rubin chips offer approximately 10x the inference compute of Blackwell chips, and that a fully monetized Rubin deployment could generate $100 billion or more per year in rental revenue — potentially $1.5–2 trillion at full scale per figures Wang attributes to comments by "Chamath" on the All-In podcast. Wang believes Rubin rack production is already underway from Dell and others, with meaningful scale likely by September–October 2026, and 100,000 Rubin chips per quarter potentially achievable by Q4 2026 or Q1 2027.

6. **Cursor Acquisition and AI Monetization Upside:** Wang states SpaceX acquired Cursor, which he says is currently at a $4 billion run rate heading toward a $10 billion run rate. He cites the host's figure that Cursor is used by approximately 70% of Fortune 1000 companies. Wang argues that if Grok with SpaceX inference becomes competitive with Anthropic Claude, SpaceX could replace Anthropic as the AI provider within Cursor — effectively internalizing what Anthropic currently earns (which Wang estimates at approximately $50 billion in revenue run rate). He notes Anthropic grew from a $9 billion run rate to a $50 billion run rate in approximately five to six months after releasing Claude Code.

7. **Third Data Center Location — "Macrohard" in Mississippi:** Wang describes a third XAI/SpaceX data center facility, which he refers to as "Macrohard," located in Mississippi. He states it is approximately 810,000 square feet (48 acres), was a former logistics warehouse acquired around December 2025–February 2026, and has been under internal buildout preparation for approximately four to five months. He says it is ready for power and chip installation but notes no recent public updates on it. He suggests it could eventually support 0.5–2 gigawatts of power capacity.

8. **Energy Infrastructure — Gas Turbines and Power Sourcing:** Wang details SpaceX/XAI's power strategy. He states Korean gas turbine maker Doosan makes 388-megawatt gas turbines, and XAI/SpaceX has an order for 12 of them — with 2 expected by end of 2026, approximately 5 more in 2027, and another 7 starting in 2029, totaling approximately 4.66 gigawatts when fully delivered. He also describes a joint venture in which XAI/SpaceX owns 49.9% of Solar Turbines (a Caterpillar subsidiary), securing approximately 67% of their turbine capacity — locking up approximately 1.4 gigawatts of mobile natural gas generation. Wang also mentions the Tennessee Valley Authority providing approximately 150 megawatts of grid power per new data center location. He estimates total current on-the-ground power for Colossus 1 and 2 combined at just under 2 gigawatts.

9. **Space-Based AI — Starship Launch Path to 1 Gigawatt:** Wang explains SpaceX's plan for space-based AI compute. He states current Starship Version 3 can launch approximately 100 tons, with AI satellite systems consuming approximately 70 kilowatts per ton, yielding approximately 7 megawatts of AI compute per launch. At current regulatory approval of approximately 120 launches, that caps space-based AI at approximately 700 megawatts — just under 1 gigawatt. Reaching 1 gigawatt would require approximately 130 dedicated AI launches plus FAA approval to increase launches to 160–200. Wang says SpaceX is building five Starship launch towers (two at Boca Chica, two at Kennedy Space Center LC-39A, and two integrated towers at Cape Canaveral SLC-37). He estimates Starship Version 4, planned by end of 2027, will double per-launch payload to approximately 14 megawatts. Wang values each 7-megawatt launch at approximately $700 million per year in rental revenue at current Blackwell rates, rising to approximately $2.1 billion per launch per year if full Anthropic-level monetization is achieved, and potentially $5–10 billion per launch with Rubin-class chips.

10. **Valuation Floor and Comparable Analysis:** Wang argues that SpaceX's terrestrial data center business alone — excluding Starlink, launch, and space AI — justifies a valuation floor of approximately $2 trillion today, rising to approximately $5 trillion or more by end of 2027. He compares SpaceX's projected Q4 2026 revenue profile to Broadcom (approximately $88 billion annual run rate, approximately 65% margins, valued at approximately $1.9 trillion) and to Nvidia in 2025 (approximately $88 billion revenue run rate at the time of its $4–4.5 trillion valuation). He argues SpaceX at $60 billion revenue with faster growth and 70–80% margins would not trade below those comparable valuations.

11. **IPO Structure and Stock Inclusion Schedule:** Wang describes SpaceX's IPO as having raised approximately $85 billion (including the greenshoe option, up from an initial $75 billion), at approximately 5% liquidity. He states the stock has fluctuated between $2.5–3 trillion market cap since IPO. He outlines a schedule of index inclusion events: Russell inclusion on approximately June 26, 2026 (estimated $12 billion of passive buying); NASDAQ inclusion on approximately July 6, 2026 (estimated additional $12–15 billion); NASDAQ rebalancing September 18, 2026; and Russell/NASDAQ rebalances in December 2026. He notes large shareholder unlocks in August and December 2026, but argues each unlock is followed within three to five weeks by a major index rebalancing buying event. He also mentions a potential S&P 500 inclusion in June 2027 if not accelerated earlier.

Notable quotes and data:
- Wang: "In nine months, beginning of the year, April to December or to October, you go from 4.6 to 15 billion per quarter run rate. So twice as fast as Micron."
- Wang on Rubin: "Every 100,000–110,000 chips you're tossing on these massive amounts of revenue... adding $22 billion of revenue per quarter [annualized]."
- Wang on Rubin economics: "The Rubin stuff monetizes at $100 billion per year on rental — at least."
- Wang on Cursor: "Cursor is already being used by 70% of Fortune 1000 companies."
- Wang on SpaceX valuation: "The 2027 $5 trillion plus will be fully justified by about Q1, Q2 of next year."
- SpaceX 2025 reported revenue: approximately $18.7 billion
- SpaceX projected 2026 full-year revenue: approximately $46 billion (per Wang)
- SpaceX IPO size: approximately $85 billion (including greenshoe)
- Colossus current/planned chip count: ~550,000–700,000 GB300-class chips across Colossus 1 and 2
- Doosan turbine order: 12 units × 388 MW = ~4.66 GW total future power
- Solar Turbines JV: 49.9% XAI/SpaceX ownership, 67% capacity allocation, ~1.4 GW
- Current on-ground power estimate: just under 2 GW
- Space AI per-launch compute: ~7 MW (Version 3), ~14 MW (Version 4 planned)
- Rubin chip share: ~20% of Nvidia Rubin allocation, per Altimeter/BG2 podcast (Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker)

articles.title: Which Investing Strategy Actually Performs Better
articles.body:
This video from FutureAzA features host Brian and guest Randy Kirk discussing general personal investing strategies — specifically dollar cost averaging, tactical/value investing, and buy-and-hold — with no Tesla-specific content. The central thesis, drawn from a Morningstar-cited Fidelity internal study, is that the best-performing investors tend to be those who trade least, illustrated humorously by the finding that deceased Fidelity account holders outperformed active traders. The video is a general financial education discussion and does not cover Tesla, EVs, autonomous driving, or any other TTT thesis topics in any substantive way.

## Market & Competition

1. **Dollar Cost Averaging as a baseline strategy:** Randy Kirk describes dollar cost averaging (DCA) as a method where an investor allocates a fixed amount on a regular schedule — for example, $100 per month rather than a lump sum of $1,200 per year — rather than attempting to time the market. He references Steve Mark Ryan as a prominent advocate of this approach, noting that Ryan has argued in detail that DCA tends to perform comparably to attempts at picking bottoms and tops, which most investors execute poorly. Randy acknowledges he personally does not use DCA and instead attempts to pick entry points on individual stocks.

2. **Tactical allocation / market timing underperforms:** Brian presents data (sourced from what appears to be a third-party investment research clip) showing that only 24% of fund managers who attempt tactical allocation — waiting for dips below trailing 12-month levels before deploying capital — generate positive alpha after controlling for risk factors via regression analysis. The remaining three-quarters of managers attempting market timing delivered negative alpha. Randy characterizes this approach as generally worse than DCA for the average individual investor, noting that managing a portfolio of 20 to 100 companies makes it impractical to monitor every ticker daily.

3. **The Fidelity "dead investors" study — buy-and-hold as the winning strategy:** Brian cites a Morningstar reference to an internal Fidelity study examining which self-directed investors performed best. The counterintuitive finding, per the study's reported conclusions, was that deceased account holders outperformed active investors — because they did not trade, did not incur fees, and made no emotional decisions. Women investors were also noted to outperform men on average, attributed to lower risk-taking behavior and a tendency toward more passive strategies such as index investing or DCA. Randy and Brian frame this as validation for a simple buy-and-hold approach with minimal trading activity.

4. **Options income strategy as a complement to buy-and-hold:** Randy briefly notes that many investment advisors appearing on his channel recommend selling options (such as covered calls or cash-secured puts) against a long-term buy-and-hold portfolio as a way to generate income. He stresses he does not personally understand the mechanics in detail and explicitly frames this as not investment advice.

Notable quotes and data:
- Only 24% of tactical allocation managers generated positive alpha, per the data clip shown; three-quarters delivered negative alpha.
- Randy Kirk claims a single year of aggressive intraday out-of-the-money options trading returned 33x his money, but described it as exhausting and potentially health-affecting.
- Brian notes that the Fidelity dead-investor study is an internal study and that the actual primary source is difficult to locate — the "general notion" rather than a verified published finding.
- Upcoming event mentioned: Fourth of July EV festival (July 2nd–4th, 2026) at Lakes Actia Park in Long View, Washington, where David Moss will be present to answer FSD questions on July 2nd and 3rd.
- SpaceX (SPCX) mentioned in passing by Randy as an example of entry-point picking, with reference to price levels of $150 and $170 as discussed entry targets, and a current price noted as approximately $191 at time of recording.

articles.title: Tesla Getting Love by US AND EU Gov'ts?!? Tesla Beat Podcast w/ special guest Randy Kirk
articles.body:
This episode of the Tesla Beat Podcast (episode 148) from FutureAzA features host John alongside regulars Brian and Joe, plus first-time guest Randy Kirk. The discussion covers a wide range of Tesla and SpaceX topics including the Grok AI integration in Tesla vehicles, Cybertruck Smart Summon, Cybercab regulatory progress and deployment readiness, FSD expansion into new international markets, and Q2 2026 delivery and energy expectations. The broader framing is bullish on both Tesla and SpaceX, with considerable time spent on the SpaceX IPO and its terrestrial data center business as a near-term profit driver.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cybertruck Smart Summon (V14 Update):** The panel celebrates the rollout of actual Smart Summon for Cybertruck via the V14 update, which they describe as one of the biggest Cybertruck updates since FSD itself was rolled out. Joe, who owns Cybertruck unit #1387, describes using it as a "chariot" at events, noting the visual impact of such a large vehicle navigating a parking lot autonomously. The host mentions a $60,000 Cybertruck variant is rolling out and expresses excitement for more owners to experience the feature.

2. **FSD in Australia:** Joe references a video released showing FSD operating in Australia — driving on the left side of the road — and describes it as performing impressively. The panel jokes that it's doing well "upside down and backwards."

3. **Grok AI Integration Roadmap:** Randy Kirk and Brian discuss the current and near-future state of Grok integration in Tesla vehicles. Brian describes wanting Grok to proactively manage parking preferences, curate playlists intelligently, and become more conversational and context-aware. He notes Tesla is rolling Grok out cautiously, citing an incident in China (in a non-Tesla vehicle) where an AI assistant turned off headlights on a highway when asked to "turn off the lights." The panel expects deeper vehicle-wide Grok integration — including controlling rear entertainment screens — as a significant upcoming catalyst.

4. **EV Tax Credit Removal — Competitive Advantage:** The host argues that the removal of EV tax credits, widely predicted to hurt Tesla, has instead created a "perfect storm" for the company. Competitors relying on those credits now face higher effective prices, while Tesla, having already optimized its cost structure, continues to move vehicles. He cites a friend who started using FSD on shorter trips and found he no longer enjoys manual driving.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Approval Rumor — Spain:** Randy Kirk shares a rumor from what he describes as a very reliable source in Spain that FSD could receive regulatory approval there by the end of the current month (June 2026). He notes the source is excellent but advises taking it with "a grain of salt." He was unable to independently confirm it fully.

2. **Sweden Blocking FSD Over Speed Limit Compliance:** Randy Kirk reports that Sweden has stated it will not approve FSD unless Tesla removes the ability for the vehicle to exceed the speed limit. The panel finds this absurd, noting that human drivers also speed and that locking FSD to the speed limit would make it effectively unusable in most real-world driving conditions, particularly in the US where 10 mph over is described as the norm. Brian notes the EU framework would make approval easier but not mandatory, and individual countries can maintain more restrictive local laws.

3. **EU Regulatory Framework:** Brian explains that EU-level FSD approval would create an easy permitting pathway but would not override local country laws. Countries could still impose additional restrictions. He draws a parallel to the US federal framework discussion, where federal approval would simplify but not automatically legalize deployment across all states.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab EPA Certificate of Conformity:** Joe reports that the Tesla Cybercab has received an EPA Certificate of Conformity, confirming it meets all applicable federal emissions requirements and can legally be introduced into US commerce. Randy clarifies that while it sounds counterintuitive for an electric vehicle with no tailpipe, the certificate is a required regulatory step before commercial deployment or fare collection — and notes that this box is now checked.

2. **Texas Deployment Readiness:** Randy states that Texas already has the permitting in place and is not subject to the federal 2,500-vehicle cap. He argues Tesla could deploy Cybercab commercially in Texas today and believes the remaining holdup is likely a software tweak. He characterizes the situation as "getting real close."

3. **Austin Cybercab Observations:** The host describes visiting Austin the prior Friday and seeing approximately 10 Cybercab units on the road within 2–3 hours, plus roughly 30 more staged behind a black fence at Tesla's robotaxi hub. He notes all current Model Y rides in Austin are unsupervised. He also mentions recent reports of accidents caused by other drivers hitting the autonomous vehicles.

4. **Active Robotaxi Fleet and City Expansion:** The host describes seeing Cybercab units appearing in Las Vegas, Florida, the Boston area, and even reportedly New Zealand, suggesting Tesla is pre-positioning vehicles across multiple cities. Per RobotaxiTracker.com, the active robotaxi fleet (all modes) stands at 732 as of 2026-06-20, with 605 in the Bay Area and 104 in Austin.

5. **"Four Weeks Away" Estimate:** Randy relays (per "Jeff Le," unconfirmed) that each city's robotaxi operation is like a small factory requiring setup — charging infrastructure, repair capability, fast responders, remote support staff — and that Jeff Le believes these city-level factories are "just about there," putting full commercial launch approximately four weeks away at most.

6. **Cybercab Track Testing at Giga Texas:** The host references footage from Joe Tegtmeyer showing a dedicated test track at Giga Texas that is nearly complete. The track is designed not only for high-speed testing but also includes suspension and braking challenges — bumps, slaloms — mirroring the setup at the Fremont factory.

7. **Waymo Comparison:** The host mentions seeing Waymo vehicles operating unsupervised throughout the Bay Area and expresses hope that Tesla can light up robotaxi service in California cities like Palo Alto. He also references a Waymo recall currently underway (unspecified details).

## Financials

1. **Q2 2026 Delivery Expectations:** Randy Kirk discusses upcoming Q2 2026 delivery numbers expected around July 2, 2026. He consulted Grok, which estimated a maximum of 575,000 vehicles if everything executes perfectly, with a more likely range of 475,000–525,000. Randy expresses personal belief there is a good chance Tesla gets close to or over 500,000 units, which he expects would be a positive surprise for the stock and could generate pre-announcement FOMO.

2. **Energy Deployment Expectations — Q2 2026:** Randy notes Tesla is manufacturing approximately 17 gigawatt-hours of Megapack per quarter. Last quarter came in at 8.8 GWh, implying significant "lumpiness" with roughly 8 GWh of undeployed capacity. He suggests Q2 2026 could see anywhere from 14 to 25 GWh deployed depending on timing, which he believes would be a major positive shock to the market. The range of 17 GWh (normal quarter) to ~25 GWh (with carryover) is cited as the realistic band.

3. **SpaceX Stock Mark-to-Market Impact on Tesla:** Randy raises that Tesla holds SpaceX stock and, now that SpaceX is public, that position must be marked to market each quarter. He estimates this could contribute approximately $2 billion in profit — roughly $0.75 per share — to Tesla's Q2 2026 earnings. He notes he believes he read this figure in a major financial publication (he thinks Fortune) the prior day, though he is not certain of the outlet.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO and Valuation:** The panel discusses the SpaceX IPO extensively. The stock IPO'd at $135, and at the time of recording had reached approximately $185, with an intraday high the panel estimates around $200–$210 — representing roughly a 60% gain from IPO price. Tesla's stock is noted at approximately $400 at time of recording. Randy cites analysis from Brian Wong projecting SpaceX at approximately $40 billion in revenue in the current year (2026), growing to approximately $80 billion in 2027, with roughly $35 billion in profit driven largely by data center rental income (including a reported ~$1 billion/month from Anthropic). He argues this shifts SpaceX's valuation multiple from ~95x sales to ~40x sales with real earnings.

2. **SpaceX Terrestrial Data Centers as Near-Term Driver:** Randy argues that SpaceX's ability to build and light up data centers faster than any competitor — in roughly one year versus the three-to-four years typical for others — is the key near-term value driver. He cites a rumor (attributed to Brian Wong and Cern Basher, per Randy) that the Macrohard building may be converted into a fourth data center, with Cern Basher reportedly identifying the energy supply source. Randy estimates SpaceX could add two new data centers in 2027 and two to three more in 2028.

3. **Space-Based Data Centers — Longer Timeline:** Randy tempers enthusiasm for orbital data centers, personally estimating significant revenue from that segment is unlikely before 2031, even as Elon Musk has suggested 2029. He cites outstanding uncertainties including the lack of an orbital Starship trip and no successful ship landing to date.

4. **Nvidia Chip Allocation Claim:** Randy relays a claim attributed to "Peter the Amandas" via the Moonshots podcast (unconfirmed) that Elon Musk/xAI has placed an order representing 22% of Nvidia's total output capacity. The panel treats this as credible but unverified, noting it aligns with xAI's aggressive GPU cluster buildout strategy and the Terafab chip manufacturing ambitions.

5. **US Government Visit to Tesla Fremont:** Joe reports that US Trade Representative Ambassador Greer toured Tesla's Fremont manufacturing facility, viewing the production line and Optimus. The Texas Department of Transportation's executive director also visited to observe the Cybercab. The panel frames these visits as meaningful government recognition of Tesla as an American manufacturing leader — a shift from the prior administration's posture.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla stock at ~$400; SpaceX stock at ~$185 at time of recording, with IPO at $135 and estimated intraday high of ~$200–$210

articles.title: How Tesla and SpaceX Investors Create Cash Flow Without Selling
articles.body:
This video features host Herbert interviewing Cern Basher, a chartered financial analyst and founder of Brilliant Advice, a wealth management firm. The conversation addresses a core challenge facing successful Tesla, SpaceX, and other concentrated-position investors: how to generate cash flow from highly appreciated stock holdings without selling shares, triggering capital gains taxes, or sacrificing long-term upside. Eight potential strategies are presented and evaluated, with particular depth on options strategies and a margin-plus-income-securities approach using preferred stocks.

## Financials

1. **The Concentrated Position Problem:** The central dilemma is that investors with large, appreciated stock positions — the video uses Tesla and SpaceX as primary examples — see their net worth rise but not their cash flow. Selling triggers capital gains taxes, while simply holding provides no income. The video frames the challenge as having three dimensions: generating cash flow while keeping upside, generating cash flow while reducing downside risk, and generating cash flow without triggering capital gains events.

2. **Income Needs vs. Portfolio Size:** Cern Basher presents a framework matching annual income needs to portfolio size. On a $5 million portfolio, $100,000/year represents 2% (described as doable), $200,000 is 4% (potentially achievable), and pushing into the 6–8% range starts to carry meaningful risk.
