5. **Scenario analysis — deal without a ratchet:** Bhakdi presents a model assuming a 50% premium acquisition offer at $600/share for Tesla (implying a $1.88 trillion Tesla market cap), based on a then-current Tesla share price of approximately $400. He models the outcome for Tesla shareholders depending on where SpaceX trades at the vote date: if SpaceX is flat at $183 (market cap $2.43T), Tesla shareholders own 44% of the new entity; if SpaceX rises 20% to $220 (market cap ~$2.9T), Tesla shareholders own only 39%; if SpaceX falls 20% to $146 (market cap ~$1.94T), Tesla shareholders own nearly 50%; if SpaceX falls 50% to $92 (market cap ~$1.22T), Tesla shareholders own 61%. He argues this variability creates perverse incentives — Tesla shareholders would want SpaceX to fall, SpaceX shareholders would want to push the price up to minimize dilution — opening the door to manipulation, resentment, and vote failure.

6. **The ratchet proposal:** Bhakdi proposes a one-line addendum to the deal: Tesla shareholders will receive the greater of either $1.88 trillion (the 50%-premium fixed offer) or the full SpaceX market cap at the moment of the vote (a one-to-one merger of equals). Under this structure, if SpaceX stays flat ($2.43T market cap), Tesla is acquired for $2.43T at ~$778/share and owns 50% of the combined entity. If SpaceX rises 20% to $2.9T, Tesla is acquired for $2.9T at ~$933/share and still owns 50%. If SpaceX falls 20% to $1.94T, Tesla is acquired for $1.94T at ~$622/share and still owns 50%. Only if SpaceX falls below the $1.88T floor does the fixed minimum kick in — e.g., if SpaceX falls 50% to $1.22T, Tesla is still acquired at $1.88T ($600/share) and owns 61% of the new entity. He argues this ratchet eliminates manipulation risk, stabilizes the vote, and ensures Tesla shareholders are never worse off if SpaceX rises in value.

7. **Fiduciary and legal risk of a bad deal:** Bhakdi argues that if institutional Tesla shareholders (including those like Ron Baron who also hold SpaceX) vote to approve a deal that disadvantages Tesla shareholders in order to benefit their SpaceX holdings, this creates a fiduciary breach and exposes the Tesla board to significant legal liability. He contends the deal must be genuinely attractive to Tesla shareholders or the vote will fail, and believes all parties — including Elon Musk — have strong incentives to structure it cleanly.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla share price assumed in model: ~$400; SpaceX share price at time of video: ~$183
- SpaceX IPO price: $161; post-IPO high: ~$218; current price cited: ~$185
- SpaceX authorized shares: 36 billion; SpaceX outstanding shares: 13 billion (~300% ratio)
- SpaceX float at IPO: ~5% of total shares; expected to expand to ~20%
- 50% premium Tesla offer = $600/share = $1.88 trillion market cap
- 30% premium Tesla offer = $520/share = $1.63 trillion market cap
- Ratchet scenario: Tesla acquired for greater of $1.88T or SpaceX market cap at vote date
- Cursor acquisition cited as precedent: $60 billion firm-dollar offer ≈ ~3% of SpaceX
- "No ratchet, no deal." — Jo Bhakdi
- Jo Bhakdi on SpaceX: "in my opinion the most important company that ever existed, in my opinion currently totally undervalued. I'm still not buying a single share right now because I'm very sure I get it much cheaper very soon."
- SpaceX selling pressure expected to intensify around August 2026 as float expands
- Merger vote expected no earlier than September 2026 if offer comes in July; more likely November 2026 shareholder meeting

articles.title: GM's future of home energy and V2G technology.
articles.body:
This short video from Munro Live features a walkthrough of GM's home energy and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology, showcasing how a GM vehicle's battery can power a home — and even external loads like a coffee bar — during a blackout or to support the grid. The demonstration highlights a home energy storage system that integrates seamlessly with the vehicle battery through an app. The core thesis is that GM is entering the bidirectional energy space, enabling vehicles to serve as mobile power sources for both residential backup and grid services.

## Energy
1. **Home Energy Storage System with NMC Chemistry:** The system on display features a 17.7 kWh battery unit using NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) based lithium-ion chemistry. These units can be paralleled together to double capacity, reaching 35.4 kWh on a single system, offering meaningful scalability for home energy storage applications.

2. **Vehicle-to-Home and Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) Capability:** The demonstration shows the vehicle's battery integrated into the home energy system, enabling bidirectional power flow. Power from the vehicle is used not only for home backup during a blackout but also to supply external loads — in this case, a coffee bar on-site — and to support the broader grid. The system is managed through a dedicated app that displays charging and discharging status and estimates remaining backup duration.

3. **Seamless App-Based Integration:** The home energy stack — comprising the battery unit and a power converter — connects wirelessly to the vehicle and is monitored and controlled through a smartphone app, allowing users to track energy flow and backup capacity in real time.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **GM Vehicle as Bidirectional Energy Node:** The GM vehicle featured in the demonstration is central to the V2G system, with its onboard battery serving as an active participant in home and grid energy management — not merely as a passive transport device. This positions GM's EVs as dual-purpose assets in the broader energy ecosystem.

Notable quotes and data:
- "We are providing power not just to the home but to this coffee bar off to the side and it's all done from the vehicle."
- Battery chemistry: 17.7 kWh NMC-based lithium-ion
- Two units in parallel: 35.4 kWh total capacity
- System components: battery stack + converter + vehicle, all connected via app
- Use cases demonstrated: home backup power during blackout, external load support (coffee bar), and grid support via V2G

articles.title: Daily X Summary (2026-06-22)
articles.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts from @SawyerMerritt are relatively low in signal, centered on two main themes: a personal FSD long-distance milestone demonstrating supervised autonomy capability, and Tesla's pushback on media framing of a Texas crash incident involving a Tesla vehicle. A peripheral note on Hyundai's consolidation of Boston Dynamics is the only competition-adjacent item. No major product, financial, or fleet deployment news was posted.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **FSD Long-Distance Milestone — 500-Mile Supervised Streak:** Merritt reported completing a ~500-mile round trip between New Hampshire and New York City using Tesla FSD in supervised mode on his Model Y, with him present in the driver's seat but not actively driving. He framed this as a demonstration of FSD's real-world capability, noting that Tesla FSD is currently the only system enabling this kind of long-distance supervised autonomy. The post drew strong engagement (3.4K likes, 195 reposts), suggesting meaningful resonance with Tesla's retail and enthusiast audience.

2. **Texas Tesla Crash — Autopilot/FSD Not Likely Involved:** Merritt addressed a viral story about a Tesla crashing into a house in Texas, sharing real-time video of the incident and noting the vehicle was traveling at an extremely high speed. He made two key points: (a) Autopilot is not "self-driving mode" — a distinction he stressed is frequently misrepresented in media coverage — and (b) Tesla's vehicle logs will determine whether any driver-assist system was active, but he expressed strong confidence it was not, citing that neither Autopilot nor FSD operates at those speeds in residential areas. He also noted that historically, nearly all similar incidents turn out to be the result of human driver error. Post [4] ("Well well well 👀") appears to be a teaser or reaction tied to this story or its follow-up, but no substantive content was included in the digest. Combined, these posts received ~5.2K likes across three related entries, indicating high visibility on a reputationally sensitive topic.

3. **Hyundai Acquires Remaining Boston Dynamics Stake:** Hyundai is acquiring the remaining 9.65% stake in U.S. robotics firm Boston Dynamics from SoftBank for $325 million, giving Hyundai full ownership. Merritt posted this without editorial commentary. This is relevant context for Tesla investors tracking the humanoid robotics competitive landscape, as Boston Dynamics represents a well-capitalized, now fully consolidated competitor in the broader robotics space — though Boston Dynamics' focus differs from Tesla Optimus's manufacturing-oriented humanoid use case.

---

## Signal Strength: **Neutral** — The FSD milestone is a positive anecdotal data point for supervised autonomy capability, but the day's posts are dominated by defensive media commentary on the Texas crash story and a competitor news item, with no new product, fleet, financial, or regulatory developments disclosed.

articles.title: Weekly Tesla Brief (Jun 15 – Jun 21, 2026)
articles.body:
## Brief

- Katy, TX fatal crash: Autopilot cited by driver; NHTSA engineering analysis covers 2.9M vehicles.
- Texas DOT Executive Director rode a Cybercab, says it will "dramatically scale" operations.
- Cybercab EPA Certificate of Conformity cleared; no remaining federal regulatory gate to commerce.
- FSD now in 12 countries; Spain testing data (275K km, zero serious incidents) published by regulator.
- Elon exercises 304M options; shares locked until 2033 — zero near-term sell pressure.
- Tesla files "Megapod" trademark for distributed compute at Supercharger sites.
- SpaceX–Tesla merger thesis intensifies; ITAR flagged as the structural blocker.

---

## Robotaxi

- **Texas DOT Executive Director Mark Williams rode a production Cybercab and publicly endorsed the program**, stating the vehicle's "complete absence of traditional driver controls underscores a significant shift in mobility and vehicle design" and that the Cybercab will "dramatically scale these operations over the coming months." A senior state transportation official issuing an on-record endorsement — after almost certainly receiving a prior briefing from Tesla — is the clearest near-term institutional signal of launch readiness to date.

- **Cybercab EPA Certificate of Conformity cleared**, removing the last federal regulatory gate to commercial fare collection in the US. Both brighterwithherbert and FutureAzA identify this as the primary compliance hurdle that had been blocking paid rides; with it cleared, the remaining hold-up is software readiness. Brian White estimates commercial-scale rollout is roughly one to two months out.

- **Tesla received SFO ride-hailing permits**, extending the Bay Area robotaxi footprint into a major high-revenue transit hub. Cybercabs have also been spotted in New Zealand, Las Vegas, Florida, and the Boston area — consistent with multi-city pre-positioning ahead of launches. A second Dallas-area depot (Grand Prairie, TX: ~51,000 sq ft) is under construction, and a Las Vegas facility on Mohawk Street is already under renovation.

- **June 30 IR commitment is broken.** Tesla's Q4 2025 earnings deck committed to paid service in Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Miami, and Phoenix by June 30; as of June 21, only Austin, Dallas, and Houston are operational. Bhakdi still sees June as a "local probabilistic maximum" for a launch but acknowledges his June thesis has so far been wrong; he names August as the next window.

- **Cybercab inventory is building, not yet deploying.** Drone footage across the week showed the lot at Giga Texas reaching a new record of 120 units by June 17. Per RobotaxiTracker.com, the active fleet (all modes) stands at 737 as of June 21. Bhakdi states explicitly that Wall Street will not reward Tesla for undeployed inventory, and that even ~50 deployed units would be a meaningful catalyst.

---

## Autonomous Driving

- **Spain's DGT published independent FSD safety data:** 275,471 km (171,170 miles) of supervised FSD testing by Tesla's 30-vehicle Spanish fleet since November 2025, with zero serious incidents — government-sourced, not Tesla-produced. This is the second major European regulator-published FSD dataset this month, following the Netherlands' 23.6 million km figure (3.5x safer than manual driving; zero highway collisions) released last week.

- **FSD now approved or available in 12 countries**, with Australia and New Zealand receiving V14 for the first time this week. Taiwan formally submitted its regulatory application; a technical committee is expected within two to four weeks. An unconfirmed but described-as-reliable source cited Spain approval by end of June. Sweden is blocking approval pending Tesla's agreement to remove the ability to exceed speed limits, which the panelists characterized as unworkable.

- **Elon clarified the FSD intervention breakdown publicly:** destination parking is "by far the biggest reason people now intervene with FSD" and "critical safety interventions are extremely rare." A forthcoming FSD release will add parking-preference memory, which Elon identified as a direct fix for the dominant intervention trigger. Separately, the first owner crossed 10,000 continuous hands-free miles on Tesla's streak counter — a qualitative maturity signal.

- **New Jersey proposed legislation would effectively prohibit driverless AV deployment** in the state. Tesla emailed NJ owners directly urging opposition, citing 578 traffic fatalities in 2025 with 94%+ attributed to human error. Brian White flagged the bill appears designed to target Tesla's FSD specifically while leaving other ADAS systems unaffected.

---

## Optimus

- **Optimus V3 reveal targeted for approximately late July 2026**, per Bhakdi citing Tesla guidance. Bhakdi flags that if a merger vote is simultaneously in motion, the reveal could be pushed into 2027. Cortex 2 at Giga Texas — partially operational since April, full capacity targeted mid-2026 — has been designated the primary Optimus training cluster, running alongside Cortex 1's FSD workloads.

- **Hand dexterity remains the central unsolved problem.** Dr. Knowit All (FutureAzA guest) identifies the robot hand as the primary bottleneck for the industry and Tesla specifically; Elon reportedly acknowledged in ~May 2026 that the most recently patented hand design "didn't work," implying Tesla is already on its fourth or fifth hand iteration.

- **AI 5 chip is being built primarily for Optimus, not vehicles.** Dr. Knowit All noted AI 4 is already sufficient for autonomous driving; AI 5 is targeted at the humanoid form factor. The broader humanoid industry has standardized on Nvidia's Jetson and Thor platforms; Tesla is developing a proprietary chip for Optimus — a differentiation bet that concentrates execution risk.

---

## Tesla Semi

- **New-design Semis with a full-width headlight bar spotted at the Giga Nevada production facility**, including two long-cab and four short-cab variants. ABF Freight added two Semis to its fleet as of June 15, continuing the commercial validation cadence that includes ArcBest, PepsiCo, Covenant, DHL, and CEVA. Most 2026 output is reportedly allocated; Goldman Sachs' Q2 delivery revision includes Semi production ramp contributions.

---

## Energy

- **Tesla filed a "Megapod" trademark** for distributed micro-scale AI GPU compute units deployed at existing Supercharger sites, leveraging existing electrical permits to bypass multi-year data center permitting delays. Bhakdi argues this could bring gigawatts of compute online faster than centralized competitors; he estimates a few gigawatts of deployed Megapod capacity could double or triple Tesla's ~$3.5–4B annual free cash flow. The filing was made under Tesla rather than SpaceX.

- **Lathrop Megapack inventory at highest observed levels**, with Sawyer Merritt estimating approximately $500M worth of units on site — a strong indicator for Q2 Energy revenue. Q2 Megapack deployment is tracking toward 14–25 GWh, versus Q1's 8.8 GWh and an ~14.5 GWh Q1 consensus estimate that was missed by ~40%. Houston Megapack factory (50 GWh/year capacity) is targeting production start in late 2026.

---

## Electric Vehicles

- **Goldman Sachs raised its Q2 2026 delivery forecast to 420,000 units** (from 405,000), stating deliveries are "likely tracking ahead of consensus." Full-year estimate is 1.72–1.73 million. Bhakdi's bull case for Q2 is 475,000–525,000. Delivery report is due approximately July 2–3.

- **Elon confirmed Tesla sales rose after the $7,500 federal EV tax credit was removed**, as buyers shifted from other EV makers to Tesla. Herbert Ong frames this as disproving a central 2025 bear case, with one quarter of data as a signal rather than proof.

- **Q2 gross margins may surprise to the upside** per brighterwithherbert, driven by high factory utilization and COGS outperformance. SpaceX mark-to-market on Tesla's equity stake is estimated at ~$2B / ~$0.75/share in Q2 earnings contribution (unconfirmed source cited as Fortune).

---

## Market & Competition

- **SpaceX–Tesla merger thesis intensified.** Bhakdi and Herbert Ong both published detailed analyses converging on a late-July to mid-August 2026 announcement window, timed around Q2 earnings (~August 11). Bhakdi's proposed structure: SpaceX acquires Tesla at ~$600/share with a ratchet mechanism; combined entity ~$4T valuation. Herbert Ong identifies ITAR — merging a top US defense contractor with a company producing ~one-third of its cars in Shanghai — as the single biggest structural risk to close timing, likely pushing completion into 2027 even if an announcement comes this summer.

- **SpaceX acquired Cursor for $60B**, giving the post-xAI-merger entity all three layers of the enterprise AI stack simultaneously: harness (Cursor, used by 64% of Fortune 500), frontier LLM (Grok), and compute (Colossus). Herbert Ong argues SpaceX's public market presence now provides analysts an undeniable comp when pricing Tesla's AI, robotaxi, and Optimus businesses.

- **Terafab chip fab confirmed with Intel partnership** targeting a non-EUV sub-5nm process node. The FutureAzA guest characterized the technical target as a "Hail Mary" that, if successful, would be transformative; expressed significant skepticism about it being operational within a year. Samsung and TSMC will continue building Tesla chips while Terafab is constructed. Production remains at minimum three-plus years out.

---

## Bear Case of the Week

- **Fatal crash in Katy, TX with Autopilot cited.** Around 8 p.m. on June 20, a Tesla failed to make a right turn, drove through the front wall of a home, and killed a 76-year-old woman inside. The 44-year-old driver told Harris County deputies the car was on Autopilot; Harris County Sheriff's Office confirmed Autopilot is "a line of investigation." No charges filed and the claim remains unverified — but the incident arrives while NHTSA's engineering analysis covering 2.9 million Tesla vehicles for FSD running red lights and wrong-way driving is already at the final pre-recall stage (upgraded March 2026). A separate NHTSA probe into alleged crash underreporting also remains open. Fred Lambert's self-disclosure that FSD v14 is "making me dangerously complacent" adds an anecdotal but pointed behavioral risk signal.

- **Electrek documents a contracting unsupervised fleet.** Fred Lambert, citing Texas DMV data, reports Tesla holds only 42 driverless operation authorizations in Texas versus Waymo's 577 and Avride's 317. The unsupervised fleet peaked at 25 in late April 2026 and has declined to 14 per Lambert's read of the data — well short of Musk's original Austin target of 500 by end of 2025 and the subsequently revised ~60. Musk is now citing FSD v15 as the prerequisite for aggressive scaling, implicitly pushing any real ramp to late 2026 or 2027. (Note: this figure contradicts the RobotaxiTracker.com snapshot, which has been static since May 9; Lambert's 14-vehicle figure attributes to his independent reading of the Texas DMV database and is flagged as a data discrepancy investors should monitor.)

- **June 30 IR commitment will not be met.** Tesla's binding investor relations commitment — paid service in Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Miami, and Phoenix by June 30 — has nine days remaining with zero of those five cities operational. This is the second consecutive weekly brief in which this deadline appears; unlike last week, there is now no credible scenario in which it is met. Bhakdi has shifted his primary deployment window to August.

- **Reuters documented misleading FSD safety data presented to European regulators.** Ten of eleven independent traffic-safety researchers called Tesla's methodology "misleading marketing"; Norway's roads administration stated Tesla's figures "are self-produced," making it "difficult to find correlation with the authorities' accident statistics." The Dutch RDW formally defended its independent 18-month review in response — but the Reuters investigation adds concentrated litigation and regulatory credibility risk exactly as Tesla pursues EU-wide approval. Belgium's FSD promo video containing five documented traffic violations (from last week's brief) remains unaddressed by Tesla.

- **Optimus hand design confirmed failing on the fourth or fifth iteration.** Elon reportedly acknowledged in ~May 2026 that the most recently patented design "didn't work." Combined with ~18 months of public silence since the last substantive demo, the October 2024 vintage of public Optimus capability data may be materially stale. The V3 reveal — targeted late July — is the next opportunity to update the public record; if delayed by a merger process, as Bhakdi flagged, the information vacuum extends further.

articles.title: SpaceX Just Added Another Billion-Dollar Customer
articles.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel focuses primarily on SpaceX's emerging AI compute business, its recent IPO and financial milestones, and the broader debate over whether SpaceX is a near-term revenue story or a long-term moonshot. Host Herbert is joined by Jeff Watts, a multi-decade supply chain executive and chief quality officer who now runs a high-tech manufacturing consulting firm. The pair argue that SpaceX's terrestrial data center business — anchored by deals with Anthropic, Google, and now Reflection AI — represents a significant and underappreciated near-term revenue stream, while also touching on Tesla-adjacent topics such as Optimus and FSD as competitive moats.

## Market & Competition

1. **Reflection AI signs $6.3B compute deal with SpaceX:** SpaceX has reportedly signed a new AI compute agreement with Reflection AI worth up to $6.3 billion through 2029, with Reflection paying approximately $150 million per month for access to SpaceX's Colossus 2 infrastructure and NVIDIA GB300 chips, starting July 1, 2026. The host notes this is less than what Anthropic and Google are paying — described as $975 million and $1.25 billion per month respectively (figures presented without clear attribution) — but still highly significant. Jeff Watts characterizes this as confirmation that SpaceX has built a genuine commercial AI compute business, not a one-off arrangement.

2. **SpaceX as a growing AI compute platform:** Watts argues that SpaceX is systematically filling excess compute capacity between its own major training runs for Grok by signing commercial customers. He contends this creates a flywheel: SpaceX can stand up data centers faster and more cost-efficiently than hyperscalers, acquire Nvidia hardware at scale, and now monetize utilization that would otherwise be idle. He frames the Anthropic deal (signed earlier) not as a rescue of a struggling Grok but as the beginning of a deliberate hosting business that will eventually extend to space-based data centers, giving early terrestrial customers an additional incentive to stay.

3. **Cursor acquisition as potential Grok accelerant:** The host and Watts discuss SpaceX's acquisition of Cursor (an AI coding tool), whose compute product is referred to as "Composer." Watts notes that Cursor's core problem was lack of compute, which SpaceX now solves. He cites Jensen Huang as being on record saying Cursor may have a better coding product than alternatives. Both speakers suggest that combining Cursor's product quality with SpaceX's compute scale and cost efficiency — potentially subsidized by paying customers like Anthropic — could push Grok back into the top tier of frontier models. Watts emphasizes that the moat in AI chatbot models is narrow and that the landscape can shift quickly, pointing to Anthropic's own rise from obscurity as an example.

4. **"Macrohard" as a potential near-term wildcard:** The host references a product or service called "Macrohard" (also described as "digital optimist"), which he says is expected to launch soon. He frames it as a potential near-term revenue generator comparable to Anthropic's business, though both speakers acknowledge deep uncertainty — it could be a flop or a breakout. The host suggests that if Macrohard proves competitive, it could start generating revenue immediately, similar to terrestrial data center contracts, without waiting on any longer-horizon infrastructure.

5. **AI polling below Congress — social acceptance risk:** Watts raises the concern that public polling on AI has fallen below approval ratings for Congress, and that this sentiment is translating into protests against data centers and potential regulatory headwinds. He attributes part of this to AI companies leading with narratives about job loss and displacement rather than abundance and medical breakthroughs, and warns this could slow AI development in the U.S. relative to other countries, particularly China.

## Financials

1. **SpaceX IPO and investment-grade ratings:** Following its IPO, SpaceX reportedly raised $87.5 billion (described as oversubscribed) and now holds approximately $100–101 billion in cash and cash equivalents. SpaceX also launched its first bond offering and received investment-grade credit ratings from all three major agencies: Fitch (BBB+), Moody's, and S&P. The host notes the bond proceeds are reportedly intended to repay outstanding borrowings under a bridge loan facility, though the size, maturity, and pricing of the bond were not disclosed. Watts calls the financial engineering of the IPO comparable in quality to SpaceX's rocket engineering.

2. **$101 billion may not be enough for SpaceX's ambitions:** Watts cautions that while $101 billion in cash sounds large, SpaceX's capital needs for AI infrastructure buildout and Starship development are enormous, and the current cash position is "nowhere near enough" to fund the full master plan. He anticipates SpaceX will need to raise much larger sums going forward, but points to Starlink and Tesla's robotaxi business (mentioned in passing) as future cash-flow engines that could fund longer-horizon investments.

3. **Revenue growth targets vs. analyst models:** The host references Elon Musk's stated goal of $1 trillion in revenue by approximately 2030–2031, while noting that even the most optimistic sell-side analysts model only $300–400 billion in revenue by that timeframe. Watts acknowledges the gap and suggests that SpaceX's current portfolio of businesses may not be the same entity four or five years from now — implying new revenue lines will need to emerge to close the difference.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus cited as a durable competitive moat:** While discussing AI moats broadly, Watts contrasts the relatively narrow moat in AI chatbot/LLM models with the much wider and more durable leads he expects Tesla to hold in physical AI — specifically calling out FSD and Optimus. He says leads in those domains will be "measured in half and full decades," implying he views Tesla's robotics and autonomous driving advantages as structurally harder to close than software model gaps.

2. **Elon's "Amazing Abundance" framing and Optimus scale claims:** The host references a post (dated June 21, 2026) in which someone named David states that 5 million humanoid robots working 24/7 could build Manhattan in 6 months, and imagines 10 billion humanoid robots by 2045. Elon Musk reportedly trademarked the phrase "Amazing Abundance" and has been publicly posting about this vision. Both speakers are skeptical the framing is landing well with general audiences, who the host says are more focused on near-term concerns.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD cited as one of Tesla's widest moats:** In the context of comparing Tesla's competitive position to SpaceX's AI compute business, Watts specifically names FSD (alongside Optimus) as one of the areas where Tesla's lead is most durable and hardest to replicate, distinguishing it sharply from the more contestable LLM/chatbot space. No specific FSD version numbers or performance data are discussed.

Notable quotes and data:
- Reflection AI deal: up to $6.3 billion through 2029; ~$150 million/month starting July 1, 2026
- Anthropic reportedly paying ~$975 million/month (per host, unconfirmed); also described as $1.25 billion/month in a separate reference — figures are inconsistent in the transcript
- SpaceX IPO raised $87.5 billion (oversubscribed); ~$101 billion cash post-IPO
- Fitch rating: BBB+ (investment grade); Moody's and S&P also rated SpaceX investment grade
- Elon's stated revenue target: ~$1 trillion by 2030–2031 (per host); most bullish analyst models reportedly in the $300–400 billion range
- "5 million humanoid robots working 24/7 can build Manhattan in 6 months" — attributed to "David" in an Elon Musk post, June 21, 2026
- Jeff Watts: "The leads [in FSD and Optimus] are going to be measured in half and full decades"
- Watts on AI moats: "The moat here is not big. It's not like FSD, physical AI and FSD, vehicle FSD, and of course what's going to happen with Optimus"
- Host: "AI is polling lower than Congress in terms of approval ratings"
- Elon reportedly trademarked the phrase "Amazing Abundance"
- 4,500 SpaceX employees described as having become millionaires via the IPO

articles.title: Tesla's Biggest Problem Isn't Competition
articles.body:
This video from brighterwithherbert features host Herbert and guest Jo Bhakdi (economist, investor, and tech entrepreneur at pioneerlands.org) discussing what they argue is Tesla's biggest challenge: not competition, but hostile media narratives and misinformation. The episode covers a viral Autopilot crash story that they contend was falsely framed, Cybercab fleet testing progress, FSD expansion into new countries, Optimus factory construction, and a broader market sentiment discussion around why Tesla stock is underperforming despite what they see as meaningful operational progress.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Texas crash misattributed to Autopilot:** Multiple major media outlets — including Business Insider — reported that a Tesla on Autopilot crashed into a Texas home, killing a woman. According to Ashok Elluswamy (identified in the transcript as Tesla's AI VP), the driver had manually overridden the self-driving system by pressing the accelerator pedal to 100%, reached 73 mph in a residential area, and had the accelerator pressed even after the crash. Elon Musk also responded publicly, stating that FSD drives slowly through neighborhood streets and that a high-speed crash was inconsistent with how FSD operates. Sawyer Merritt noted that Tesla's vehicle logs would clarify whether any system was active, and Chuck Cook called the reporting "blatantly irresponsible." The hosts argue this is part of a pattern — they claim there has not been a single confirmed case where a legal investigation proved FSD caused a crash.

2. **FSD expansion into Europe:** FSD version 14.2.2.6 reportedly shows two new countries — Spain and the UK — appearing in the software, suggesting those markets may be in active testing or approaching regulatory approval. Tesla is hiring Autopilot data collection supervisors in London, Paris, and Barcelona, which the host interprets as a standard pre-launch signal. A source cited in the transcript — described as employees the host spoke with when testing FSD in Spain — reportedly expected approval in Spain to come around June 30, 2026. A fleet of vehicles in Spain reportedly grew from 19 to approximately 30 cars and has driven around 80,000 kilometers since November 2025. The Netherlands and Estonia are also mentioned as recently having come online for FSD.

## Robotaxi

1. **Largest Cybercab pack spotted at Giga Texas:** Joe Tegtmeyer captured video of approximately 10 Cybercabs testing together in formation at Giga Texas on what the host notes was the one-year anniversary of the robotaxi service going live. The test track where this occurred appears to have been newly built, possibly specifically for Cybercab testing. Joe Tegtmeyer described it as the largest group of Cybercabs he had seen on the track at any one time and expressed hope that they would soon be taking paying passengers.

2. **Cybercab deployment to multiple cities accelerating:** Jo Bhakdi notes that Cybercab counts in parking lots in Houston and Dallas have been climbing — he references a figure of approximately 45 units growing to around 55 in one city (per a ground reporter on X, attributed by the host to Houston or Dallas, unconfirmed). The hosts draw a contrast with how Model Y robotaxi testing operated, arguing that deploying dozens of vehicles in multiple new cities is consistent with launch preparation rather than mere testing. Cities mentioned as targets include Austin, Dallas, Houston, Los Angeles, Silicon Valley, Las Vegas, Miami, and Phoenix — though the hosts acknowledge the full seven-city rollout promised in Q1 2026 has not yet materialized as of June 23, 2026.

3. **Four months of no at-fault incidents:** The host states that Tesla's robotaxi safety data shows four months without any at-fault issues, which they argue provides a strong basis for expanded deployment.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus factory construction at Giga Texas progressing:** Joe Tegtmeyer documented the construction of Tesla's dedicated Optimus factory at Giga Texas with time-lapse footage from March through April and into subsequent weeks. As of the time of recording, the steel structure assembly is visible, the structure appears to have four floors, and footings have been completed. The host states the factory is planned for a target capacity of 10 million units per year once fully ramped and that the structure is currently on track for a late 2027 completion.

2. **Optimus supply chain expanding with new supplier deals:** Per a report in Taiwan Economic Daily cited by the host, Tesla has signed deals with Merl Automation and Asia Optical to accelerate mass production of Optimus 3. Merl Automation will supply harmonic reducers and joint modules, and has established a joint venture in Thailand to manufacture harmonic reducers, robot actuators, and other precision parts, taking advantage of existing factory space. Asia Optical will supply spherical and aspherical lens components to serve as the robot's "eyes." These parts are slated to enter mass production in the second half of 2026 and into 2027. The host notes that the scale of Tesla's orders is large enough that suppliers are creating entirely new joint ventures and factories.

3. **Strategic framing of Optimus scale bet:** Jo Bhakdi argues that Elon Musk's key strategic insight with Optimus is the same playbook used with compute (xAI's Colossus): rather than guaranteeing the best underlying technology, Tesla is making a decisive bet on massive manufacturing scale. The logic, per Bhakdi, is that if Tesla builds the world's largest humanoid robot factory, any competitor with superior technology will ultimately need to partner with or be acquired by Tesla. He draws a parallel to how Google and Anthropic reportedly became customers of xAI's Colossus compute infrastructure despite potentially having superior AI models.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla stock down ~5% on day of recording; inverse relationship with SpaceX suspected:** As of recording on June 23, 2026, Tesla was down approximately 5.18% while SpaceX was up approximately 5.16% — nearly mirror images. Jo Bhakdi notes that the prior day showed the reverse: SpaceX down approximately 16% while Tesla was up approximately 1.5% against the broader market. He speculates this reflects a mechanical cash-flow relationship between the two stocks, possibly related to a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger thesis (with a dedicated episode on merger pricing teased for the following day). He explicitly attributes less than half a percent of the day's Tesla decline to the Autopilot crash headlines.

2. **Investor rotation into "shiny object" AI and semiconductor stocks:** Jo Bhakdi argues Tesla is experiencing selling pressure from investors rotating into high-momentum names like Micron Technologies (noted as up sharply in recent months and down approximately 11% on the day of recording) and SpaceX. He warns that chasing high-momentum stocks is a common beginner mistake and that Tesla's upside could be hyperbolic once robotaxi or Optimus scaling becomes tangible — speculating that meaningful robotaxi progress could push the stock not to $600–$700 but potentially to $1,000 and beyond in the current market sentiment environment, given how quickly SpaceX moved in a short period. He compares SpaceX's recent run to a $3 trillion valuation as an example of how quickly sentiment can shift.

Notable quotes and data:
- Ashok Elluswamy (per transcript): "The driver manually overrode self-driving by pressing the accelerator all the way to 100% of the accelerator pedal in this residential area. They reached a speed of 73 mph during this crash and had the accelerator press even after the crash."
- Jo Bhakdi: "120 people die per day in the United States because of motor vehicle crashes. Yesterday when that happened, 120 people died in car accidents. But guess what? 119 of them were not covered."
- Jo Bhakdi on robotaxi scale: "I think if we have scaling of robotaxi we go to 600–700 — I think we go straight to a thousand and beyond."
- Host on Optimus factory: planned for 10 million units per year once fully ramped; steel structure with approximately four floors visible; on track for late 2027 structural completion.
- FSD version 14.2.2.6 reportedly includes Spain and UK.
- Spain FSD testing fleet: grew from 19 to approximately 30 vehicles; approximately 80,000 km driven since November 2025; approval reportedly expected around June 30, 2026 (per employees cited by host, unconfirmed).
- Active Cybercab lot in one city (host believes Houston): approximately 45 units growing to approximately 55 (per ground reporter on X, unconfirmed).
- SpaceX on day of recording: +5.16%; Tesla: -5.18%.
- Prior day: SpaceX -16%, Tesla +1.5%.

articles.title: Tesla, NatPower strike $5B deal for 25 GWh of Megapack storage
articles.body:
Tesla and UK-based independent energy firm NatPower have struck a deal to deploy 25 GWh of Megapack battery storage across Italy and Britain, the first phase of a program worth up to $5 billion.

## Energy
1. **Deal structure and scope:** The multiyear agreement covers five initial projects totaling 25 GWh across Italy and the UK, with a construction cost of $4–$5 billion. Beyond hardware, Tesla is also supplying its energy trading software to manage charging and discharging cycles for grid arbitrage — embedding its software stack into NatPower's operations. NatPower CEO Fabrizio Zago framed the arrangement as "an ecosystem that enables alignment between capital and execution" that can be replicated across markets.

2. **Long-term program ceiling:** NatPower says the broader program aims to exceed 100 GWh of total storage capacity, with revenue potentially topping $15 billion over 20 years. The article notes the 25 GWh phase-one figure alone exceeds half of Tesla's entire global energy storage deployment in 2025.

3. **Context — Tesla's energy growth:** Tesla deployed a record 46.7 GWh of energy storage in 2025, up roughly 48% year-over-year. Analysts pegged Q1 2026 deployments at a record ~14.4 GWh. In September 2025, Tesla unveiled the Megablock and Megapack 3, pre-integrated systems designed to reduce installation time. The article notes Tesla secured a separate multi-billion-dollar Megapack contract in 2024.

## Financials
1. **Market reaction:** TSLA was down approximately 3.3% in pre-market trading Tuesday, attributed to separate reports of a ransomware group leaking confidential documents tied to Tesla and Apple — not to the NatPower deal itself.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert calls this "a meaningful win" in Tesla's strongest business segment, highlighting the software component as an underrated, stickier, higher-margin moat. He cautions that "up to $5 billion" and "$15 billion over 20 years" are headline figures dependent on execution, permitting, and grid interconnection — noting Europe's interconnection queues are "notoriously slow."

Notable quotes and data:
- 25 GWh phase-one across Italy and UK; construction cost $4B–$5B
- Broader program target: >100 GWh; >$15B revenue over 20 years
- Tesla 2025 energy deployments: 46.7 GWh (+~48% YoY)
- Analysts' Q1 2026 deployment estimate: ~14.4 GWh (record)
- TSLA pre-market: –3.3% Tuesday
- NatPower CEO Fabrizio Zago: "What we have built with Tesla is an ecosystem that enables alignment between capital and execution, and that can be replicated across multiple markets."

articles.title: Tesla admits FSD was on in fatal Texas crash, blames driver for ‘overriding’ it
articles.body:
Tesla has confirmed that its Full Self-Driving system was engaged when a Model 3 driven by 44-year-old Michael Butler left a residential road in Katy, Texas, and killed 76-year-old Martha Avila Mantilla inside her home. Tesla attributes the crash to the driver "manually overriding" FSD by pressing the accelerator to 100%, reaching 73 mph in a residential area — but the article argues this framing sidesteps the deeper question of why the override happened.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Tesla's account of the crash:** Tesla's Head of AI Ashok Elluswamy stated that vehicle data shows Butler pressed the accelerator to 100% while FSD was active, overriding the system. The car reached 73 mph, and the pedal remained floored after the vehicle struck the house. Driver Butler had told Harris County deputies the vehicle was on Autopilot at the time. Elon Musk had earlier posted that "FSD drives slowly through neighborhood streets and this was a high speed crash!" — a framing now contradicted by Tesla's own account placing FSD in the loop at the moment of impact.

2. **The complacency argument:** The article contends that Tesla's "driver overrode it" defense does not constitute exoneration. The most plausible scenario, per the author, is that FSD did something unexpected, prompting an emergency intervention in which the driver — whose feet were not already over the pedals because the system was doing the driving — hit the accelerator instead of the brake. The article argues this "out-of-the-loop" failure mode is structurally created by Level 2 systems that condition drivers to disengage, making emergency takeovers harder to execute.

3. **Florida precedent:** In August 2025, a Miami federal jury found Tesla 33% responsible for a 2019 Key Largo crash in which driver George McGee, on Autopilot, struck and killed Naibel Benavides Leon. The jury placed 67% of fault on McGee but still assigned Tesla partial liability, resulting in a $243 million judgment upheld by a federal judge in February 2026. The jury concluded Tesla's marketing and weak steering-torque-based driver monitoring fostered complacency — the same dynamic the author sees in the Katy crash.

4. **Data credibility concerns:** Tesla is already under an NHTSA Engineering Analysis covering roughly 3.2 million vehicles and a separate probe into whether it properly reported Autopilot/FSD crashes. The article notes that in the Florida litigation, Tesla told plaintiffs crash data didn't exist until an independent researcher recovered a "collision snapshot" showing the system had detected the pedestrian. The article treats Tesla's public interpretation of its own logs with skepticism, and notes NHTSA has opened a Special Crash Investigation to independently pull the event data recorder and onboard logs.

## Editorial Stance
The author argues that Tesla's confirmation of FSD engagement is a bigger admission than the company's framing acknowledges, and that pinning the crash entirely on a "100% accelerator" input is "technically convenient and substantively hollow." The article calls for Tesla to take the complacency problem — its marketing, system naming, and easily-gamed driver monitoring — seriously, and withholds full judgment pending NHTSA's independent data readout.

Notable quotes and data:
- Ashok Elluswamy: driver "manually overrode self-driving by pressing the accelerator all the way to 100% of the accel pedal in this residential area"
- Vehicle reached 73 mph with accelerator floored; pedal still pressed after striking the home
- Elon Musk posted: "FSD drives slowly through neighborhood streets and this was a high speed crash!"
- Florida verdict: $243 million judgment, Tesla held 33% liable, upheld by federal judge February 2026
- NHTSA Engineering Analysis covers ~3.2 million vehicles; separate crash-reporting probe also ongoing
- NHTSA has opened a Special Crash Investigation into the Katy crash

articles.title: Elon Musk Signs Another Huge Deal (Musk Industry Daily)
articles.body:
This episode of "Musk Industry Daily" — a new daily members-only series launching on the farzad-fm channel — covers the top stories across the broader Elon Musk industry ecosystem for June 23rd, 2026. The video spans SpaceX AI infrastructure deals, a Texas court ruling on Starbase access, Starlink aviation expansion, SpaceX's balance sheet disclosure, and a Tesla crash incident in Katy, Texas involving a Model 3. The host frames these stories through an investor lens, emphasizing second-order effects on capital allocation, narrative risk, and long-term infrastructure positioning.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Katy, Texas Model 3 Crash — Driver Override Narrative:** Tesla VP of AI Software Ashok Elluswamy publicly stated that the driver of a Model 3 that crashed into a home in Katy, Texas manually overrode the vehicle's self-driving system by pressing the accelerator pedal to 100%. Elluswamy said the vehicle reached 73 mph during the crash and that the accelerator pedal remained pressed afterward. The crash killed a 76-year-old woman inside the home. The incident had drawn scrutiny because early reports linked the vehicle to an automated driving assistance system; Elluswamy's statement, as reported by Sawyer Merritt, reframed the incident as caused by driver input rather than autonomy software. One X user cited in the discussion cautioned that Tesla's account should be treated cautiously until investigators release their findings. The host notes this illustrates Tesla's recurring "speed gap" problem — the narrative forms before the technical facts become public.

2. **Tesla Vision Airbag Deployment Video:** Tesla published a video explaining how its camera-based Tesla Vision system can help identify unavoidable collisions and support airbag deployment decisions up to 70 milliseconds earlier, while impact sensors still make the final airbag deployment decision. The host frames this as Tesla positioning vehicle perception as a broader safety layer beyond driver assistance.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus Factory Construction Progress at Giga Texas:** New drone imagery from Joe Tegtmeyer showed continued steel assembly at Tesla's planned Optimus factory at Giga Texas, including a section that appears to have at least four floors. Sawyer Merritt noted the factory is going up quickly. Joe Tegtmeyer said the structure remains on track for substantive completion in late 2027. The host flags whether physical construction progress will begin matching Tesla's longer-term robot production ambitions.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Tesla Model 3 Crash Scrutiny and Liability Framing:** Beyond the autonomy angle, the Katy, Texas crash involving a Model 3 is flagged as a liability and public perception risk for Tesla. The host notes that if the driver override data holds up in official investigations, it materially changes the story for Tesla's legal exposure. Investigators could still clarify system status via an official crash report.

## Market & Competition
1. **SpaceX Signs AI Compute Lease with Reflection AI:** SpaceX has signed an AI compute lease with Reflection AI, an open-source AI startup, per reporting from CNBC and posts from Sawyer Merritt, Herbert Ang, and Musconomy. The agreement gives Reflection access to SpaceX AI infrastructure and Nvidia GB300 chips, with payments of approximately $150 million per month starting July 1st, 2026. If the agreement runs through 2029, total payments would reach roughly $6.3 billion. Either side can terminate with 90 days' notice after the first three months, meaning the headline contract value is not equivalent to guaranteed revenue. CNBC also reported that SpaceX has had compute-related deals with Anthropic, Google, and Cursor. Musconomy noted that SpaceX built Colossus to train Grok and is now renting that compute to outside firms. The host argues this positions SpaceX's build capacity as an AI balance sheet asset, making the company harder to categorize within a single industry.

2. **SpaceX Cash Balance Disclosure:** Sawyer Merritt reported that SpaceX held $100.88 billion in cash as of June 19th, 2026, citing an SEC filing connected to a proposed offering of senior unsecured notes. The filing noted that the cash balance could be materially different as of June 30th, and that proceeds from the notes offering are intended to repay outstanding borrowings under a bridge loan facility, pay related fees and expenses, and support general corporate purposes. Commentary was split: Sawyer Merritt framed it positively, while Craig Moffett pushed back saying cash on hand is less relevant than burn rate, and The Gild Standard noted much of the cash is already earmarked for Starship and other projects.

3. **Texas Supreme Court Rules for SpaceX on Boca Chica Beach Access:** The Texas Supreme Court unanimously ruled in favor of SpaceX and state officials in a year-long dispute over temporary Boca Chica Beach closures during Starship launch activity. The Texas Tribune reported the court dismissed the lawsuit with prejudice, holding that a 2009 constitutional amendment preserves public beach access but does not give private groups the right to sue to enforce it. The case was brought by environmental groups including Save RGV under a 2013 state law, with the Texas Attorney General's office intervening on behalf of the state. The host notes this reduces legal friction for Starship's launch cadence, though different plaintiffs or separate regulatory disputes remain possible.

4. **United Airlines Flies First Transatlantic Starlink-Equipped Widebody Flight:** United Airlines flew its first widebody transatlantic customer flight with Starlink, using a Boeing 777-200 from Newark to London Heathrow. United said this aircraft is the first of nearly 60 widebody jets it plans to equip with Starlink in 2026, with the entire widebody fleet expected to have Starlink by summer 2027. Musconomy reported that United already has Starlink installed on more than 400 aircraft and expects to approach 1,000 aircraft by the end of 2026. United CEO Scott Kirby wrote on LinkedIn that international routes are the ones he is most excited about for Starlink. The host views widebody long-haul as the real aviation proving ground for Starlink transitioning from an amenity to default airline infrastructure.

5. **Air Force One Fitted with Starlink:** President Trump stated that the new interim Air Force One — a Boeing 747-8 — is fitted with Starlink, per Musconomy and Tesla reporting. The host flags this as a high-profile government aviation installation in a mission-critical connectivity market.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX–Reflection AI lease: ~$150M/month starting July 1, 2026; ~$6.3B total if held through 2029; terminable with 90 days' notice after first 3 months
- SpaceX cash balance: $100.88 billion as of June 19th, 2026 (per SEC filing cited by Sawyer Merritt)
- Katy, TX crash: driver pressed accelerator to 100%; vehicle reached 73 mph; crash killed a 76-year-old woman inside the home (per Ashok Elluswamy)
- Tesla Vision: camera system can support airbag deployment decisions up to 70 milliseconds earlier
- United Airlines: 400+ aircraft already equipped with Starlink; targeting ~1,000 by end of 2026; ~60 widebody installs planned in 2026; full widebody fleet by summer 2027
- Optimus factory at Giga Texas: steel assembly ongoing, appears to have at least four floors; substantive completion targeted for late 2027 (per Joe Tegtmeyer)
- Ashok Elluswamy (re: Katy crash): driver "manually overrode the vehicle's self-driving system by pressing the accelerator pedal to 100%"
- Host: "Tesla's problem is not just safety data. It is the speed gap between an incident, media framing, and the technical record."

articles.title: Tesla FSD UK Approval Explained
articles.body:
This video is a conversation between Brian (FutureAzA) and Will from Tesla Jigsaw discussing the current state of FSD approval in the UK, the regulatory hurdles involved, and what UK Tesla owners can expect and when. The core argument is that the UK remains significantly behind other markets in approving supervised FSD due to a combination of post-Brexit regulatory complexity, strict type approval requirements, and Tesla's apparent prioritization of EU momentum first. The hosts are cautiously optimistic that, whenever FSD does arrive in the UK, it will be a far more refined product than early adopters in other markets had to endure.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **UK FSD subscription currently delivers only Enhanced Autopilot features:** Will tested the FSD subscription in the UK and found it provides only summon, navigate on autopilot, and lane changes — functionally equivalent to Enhanced Autopilot. Critically, these features are hobbled by UK-specific regulation, including "system-initiated maneuvers" that require the driver to touch the steering wheel within 3 seconds during a lane change or the system aborts the maneuver. Will found this dangerous and frustrating, and canceled his subscription. He emphasized this is not Tesla's fault but the result of regulatory constraints.

2. **Tesla has not yet formally submitted a type approval application to the VCA:** Will explained that there is no public confirmation that Tesla has formally submitted an FSD type approval application to the UK's Vehicle Certification Agency (VCA). He believes Tesla is likely prioritizing EU momentum first, using the Dutch RDW approval as the foundation, before tackling the separate post-Brexit GB type approval process. UK-specific requirements include testing on British roads, roundabouts, and narrow lanes.

3. **Tesla has been collecting UK road data for a long time:** Will noted that Tesla has been gathering shadow mode data from UK drivers using Autopilot, and Tesla employees have been testing the system on UK roads for over a year. He referenced a video of Tesla's system navigating Swindon's Magic Roundabout well over a year ago, and a Tesla-released video of a vehicle driving autonomously around London. He argued Tesla has substantial data; the remaining challenge is formal regulatory compliance demonstration.

4. **Supervised FSD timeline for the UK is late 2026 or early 2027 at best:** Will assessed the most optimistic realistic timeline for supervised FSD reaching UK customer vehicles as late 2026 or early 2027. He described the UK as likely being "the last domino to fall" among markets receiving FSD, which he found deeply frustrating given that FSD is already rolling out across multiple EU countries (Belgium, Denmark, Lithuania, Estonia) and beyond.

5. **UK automated vehicles safety principles consultation began June 17, 2026:** Will shared that the UK Department for Transport launched a consultation on draft safety principles for automated vehicles on June 17, 2026, with a closing date of September 9, 2026. He described this as a small but genuine positive signal, as these principles will feed into permanent UK rules covering supervised FSD, unsupervised FSD, and eventually robotaxi operations. Brian framed the meetings and consultations as necessary hurdles on the path to approval.

6. **Australia and New Zealand received FSD version 14 on June 19, 2026:** Brian noted that Australia and New Zealand — both right-hand drive markets — received FSD version 14 on June 19, 2026. He speculated that data gathered from right-hand drive operation in those markets may be transferable and beneficial for the UK approval process. Will agreed that by the time FSD reaches the UK, it could be version 14 or potentially much later versions, meaning UK users will receive a dramatically more mature product.

7. **FSD versions 13 and above described as transformatively better:** Both hosts agreed that FSD version 13 and above represents a qualitative leap that most UK users don't appreciate. Will described it as "silky smooth" and "utterly boring because it does the job so well." Brian shared his own experience struggling to make FSD videos because the system handles challenges without incident, and noted that on version 14 he no longer feels urgency to test new updates because the system simply works. Will's personal FSD experience was on a Cybertruck running version 12.5.5 (outside the UK).

## Market & Competition

1. **Waymo is testing in London under the Autonomous Vehicles Act 2024:** Will explained that Waymo is able to test on London roads because the UK's Autonomous Vehicles Act of 2024 permits commercial robotaxi and autonomous vehicle testing. He noted that Waymo's stated goal (as of Will's last knowledge) was to offer actual public robotaxi rides in London by September 2026. He clarified this has no direct bearing on FSD approval, since Waymo operates at Level 4+ autonomy whereas FSD is a Level 2 supervised system subject to different regulatory rules.

2. **Tesla could theoretically deploy Cybercabs in London under existing AV law:** Will observed that because the Autonomous Vehicles Act of 2024 covers Level 4 and above autonomy, Tesla could in theory place Cybercabs in London for testing under the same framework Waymo is using. The regulatory bottleneck specific to UK customers is the Level 2 supervised FSD product in customer-owned vehicles, which requires separate type approval.

3. **UK-based AV company Wave also testing vision-only system:** Will mentioned a UK company called Wave that operates a vision-only, AI-based autonomous system using a bolt-on unit fitted to existing cars. Wave's longer-term goal is to have their technology integrated directly into manufacturers' vehicles. Will described them as an interesting company to watch alongside Waymo in the UK AV landscape.

4. **Competing automakers' autonomy claims met with skepticism:** Brian expressed strong skepticism toward other automakers claiming they will catch up to Tesla in autonomy "next year," arguing that those manufacturers underestimate the challenge, have far less real-world training data, and cannot substitute simulation for real-world miles. He said the idea that best-in-class AI engineers alone will close the gap misunderstands the scope of the problem.

Notable quotes and data:
- Will: "It's absolutely insane and dangerous, and it's not Tesla's fault, it's regulation interfering with a system that would otherwise work beautifully."
- Will on the UK FSD timeline: "Late 2026 or early 2027 for supervised FSD at best."
- Will: "It very much looks to me like we will be the last domino to fall at this rate with FSD."
- Brian on FSD v13+: "I didn't encounter a challenge that it didn't accomplish."
- Brian: "I don't even get excited for [a new update]. It's like, oh, I got 14.3.4. I mean, I guess download it, but I'm not going to rush out and check it — I don't even know what you're working on. It's working."
- Will on FSD v13+: "It's silky smooth and it's utterly boring because it does the job so well."
- UK Department for Transport automated vehicles safety principles consultation: opened June 17, 2026; closes September 9, 2026.
- Australia and New Zealand received FSD version 14 on June 19, 2026 (right-hand drive markets).
- Waymo's reported target for public robotaxi rides in London: September 2026 (per Will's last known information, flagged as possibly changed).
- Supercharged UK (Tesla Owners Club annual event) at Millbrook Proving Ground: June 27, 2026.

articles.title: Elon Isn't Sandbagging and Here's the Proof
articles.body:
This video from FutureAzA features host Brian and guest Randy Kirk pushing back against a circulating theory that Elon Musk is deliberately sandbagging Tesla's progress — on Cybercab, robotaxi deployment, FSD, and Optimus — in order to suppress Tesla's stock price ahead of a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger. The hosts argue the premise is logically, legally, and structurally flawed, and walk through multiple reasons why coordinated sandbagging at Tesla's scale would be impossible and self-defeating.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Unsupervised FSD as a near-term catalyst:** Randy argues that unsupervised FSD — if it rolls out this year (2026) — would meaningfully increase both the number of customers subscribing to FSD and the number of people motivated to buy a Tesla vehicle. He treats this as one of three major near-term catalysts that could dramatically lift Tesla's stock price before any hypothetical merger close, undermining the sandbagging thesis.

## Robotaxi
1. **Cybercab and robotaxi deployment pace criticized — then rebutted:** Commenters in the video claim that Cybercab is "not rolling out at all" and that the robotaxi is "slower than molasses." Brian and Randy counter that this pace is not evidence of sandbagging, and that even if Cybercab were fully ready today, it could not be deployed overnight. Randy suggests that scaling to 5,000–15,000 robotaxis on the road before a merger close is an in-play possibility for Q3 or Q4 2026, and that doing so would be a massive stock catalyst — the opposite of what sandbagging would produce.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus reveal and pricing as a stock catalyst:** Randy argues that if Tesla delivers a compelling Optimus demonstration — showing the robot performing useful factory functions — and announces a rental price of approximately $100,000 per year (which he and co-host "Cern" believe is appropriate based on market value, per Randy's characterization), it could push Tesla's stock toward $600–$800. He frames this as one of three near-term catalysts that would make it irrational for Elon to be suppressing Tesla's valuation ahead of a merger.

## Market & Competition
1. **The sandbagging thesis deconstructed — merger valuation process:** Randy explains that a SpaceX-Tesla merger valuation would not simply be based on market cap on the day of closing. Instead, it would involve three independent committees: one for Tesla, one for SpaceX, and a joint committee. Each company's committee would conduct a full forward-looking DCF-style valuation (projecting 5, 10, and 15 years out, discounting at a rate such as 12–14%), and the joint committee would reconcile the two to determine the merger ratio. Randy states this is not speculative — he describes it as 100% certain to be the process used. Boards could override committee recommendations but would be required to show shareholders the full methodology, enabling an informed shareholder vote.

2. **Whistleblower incentive makes coordinated sandbagging implausible:** Brian argues that Tesla employs thousands of millionaires — product leads, department engineers, distribution managers — who would all need to stay silent while personally losing millions from a suppressed stock price. Federal whistleblower laws would entitle any such person to 10–30% of hundreds of billions of dollars in recovery. Randy adds that beyond financial incentive, Tesla's internal culture is strongly ethics-driven, making it even more likely that someone would come forward if genuine wrongdoing were occurring. Both hosts note that no whistle has been blown, and that the sandbagging comments largely come from accounts that have never previously engaged with Brian's channel.

3. **Elon's ownership stake makes suppressing Tesla stock irrational:** Brian points out that Elon Musk would not need to suppress Tesla's price to maintain voting control after a merger — control can be maintained at around 25% ownership rather than 50%. Given the stock awards still pending from Tesla's second compensation plan and any future SpaceX compensation restructuring, suppressing Tesla's stock price would cost Elon far more than it would benefit him in a merger ratio, making the theory economically self-defeating.

4. **Tesla-SpaceX merger premium debate:** Brian notes that there has been substantial public discussion about Tesla deserving a premium above its market cap in any merger with SpaceX, on the grounds that Tesla is further along in its various ventures than the stock price reflects. Even within the merger-ratio debate, no consensus has formed on the size of that premium — further undermining the idea that Elon could reliably engineer a favorable outcome by sandbagging.

Notable quotes and data:
- Randy: "If all three things happen between now and the end of the year... the price of Tesla stock would in my opinion be going to closer to $600, maybe even $650, maybe even $800 if the Optimus is really really good."
- Randy on three near-term catalysts: robotaxi scaling to 5,000–15,000 units, a compelling Optimus reveal at ~$100,000/year rental, and unsupervised FSD rollout — all described as possible in Q3 or Q4 2026.
- Randy on merger valuation: "This is not like maybe this is how it's going to be done. I can assure you 100% this is how it's going to be done" — referring to the three-committee DCF process.
- Brian on whistleblowers: people would be "eligible for up to 10 to 30% of money collected on what would be hundreds of billions of dollars."
- Brian: "You don't need 50% to maintain control. You can do that with like 25%."
- Discount rate mentioned for DCF committees: "14 or 12 or whatever percent" (Randy's illustrative range, not a firm Tesla figure).
- Optimus rental price cited: ~$100,000/year (Randy's and "Cern's" view of appropriate market value — not a Tesla announcement).

articles.title: Why Is Tesla Stock DROPPING Today?
articles.body:
Jo Bhakdi hosts a live session explaining a sharp Tesla stock decline of approximately 5.79% on 2026-06-23, arguing it was driven almost entirely by misleading media coverage of a crash incident rather than any fundamental deterioration in Tesla's business. He also addresses the broader NASDAQ selloff, contextualizing it as a knock-on effect from the South Korean stock market dropping 10% in a single session. His core thesis is that the drop represents a buying opportunity created by fake news, and that Tesla's underlying trajectory — particularly Cybercab deployment and FSD progress — remains intact.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Harris County crash misrepresented as FSD/Autopilot failure:** A crash in Harris County, Texas, in which a driver allegedly drove a Tesla into a home at 73 mph and killed an elderly woman, was widely reported with headlines suggesting Autopilot or FSD was responsible. Jo Bhakdi argues these headlines are outright lies. He cites Ashok Elluswamy's statement (posted approximately 22 hours before the session, i.e., around 2026-06-22) that the driver manually overrode self-driving by pressing the accelerator to 100%, reached 73 mph in a residential area, and had the accelerator pressed even after the crash. Bhakdi contends that Autopilot and FSD disengage when the driver fully depresses the accelerator, making the headlines — including one from the New York Times reading "Tesla driver using Autopilot crashes into home" — factually false and potentially actionable. He calls for Elon Musk to sue the New York Times and Texas Monthly over these headlines, analogizing the situation to other defamation cases.

2. **FSD version 14.3.4 noted by a viewer as a significant improvement:** A viewer in the live chat mentioned FSD version 14.3.4 as a notable leap in capability. Bhakdi did not independently verify this claim but acknowledged the comment, asking the viewer whether they had that version. He also relayed a viewer's personal account of using FSD for two hours that day with no issues, describing it as getting "better and better."

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab deployment accelerating across multiple cities:** Bhakdi states that Cybercabs are being deployed in increasing numbers to parking lots across multiple cities beyond Austin, including Houston and other unspecified locations. He estimates Tesla is already at a production run rate of approximately 1,000 Cybercabs per month (his own estimate, unverified), and argues the act of parking dozens of Cybercabs in distributed city parking lots is unambiguous evidence of impending commercial deployment. He asks rhetorically why Tesla would distribute 50–60 units to parking lots in various cities if not to operationally deploy them, and suggests each lot may eventually hold up to ~200 units before they are put into service.

2. **Cybercabs will not be sold to consumers:** Bhakdi states he heard from "a good source" (unspecified, unconfirmed) that Tesla will not sell Cybercabs to individual buyers. He says this aligns with his own financial modeling, which shows it makes no economic sense to sell the vehicle when the robotaxi revenue model is far more lucrative. He adds he believes a robotaxi commercial announcement could come by June 30, 2026, citing a viewer's comment — though he does not personally confirm this timeline.

3. **Commercial robotaxi launch timeline optimism:** Bhakdi reiterates he believed a meaningful robotaxi milestone would occur in June 2026. He acknowledges it may slip, but says this does not materially change his conviction that commercial deployment is imminent. He frames the Cybercab parking lot deployments across the nation as the clearest signal available.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **European sales up sharply in May 2026:** Bhakdi highlights Tesla's European registration data for May 2026, which showed a 107.9% year-over-year increase to 28,610 units, marking four consecutive months of gains. He expresses frustration that at least one news outlet ran a headline suggesting a "hit to Europe sales" while the article itself reported these strong numbers — calling it a factual inversion that likely contributed to retail investor confusion and selling pressure.

2. **UBS delivery forecast raised:** Bhakdi briefly references a UBS estimate (attributed to a news article he was reading) that bumped Tesla's delivery forecast to approximately 405,000 vehicles, representing a 5% rise from the prior year and 13% higher than two years prior. He presents this as further evidence that the stock's decline is disconnected from fundamentals.

## Market & Competition

1. **South Korean KOSPI crash dragged down NASDAQ:** The primary macro driver of the NASDAQ's ~2% decline on 2026-06-23, per Bhakdi, was the South Korean KOSPI (referred to colloquially as the "Cosby" in the transcript) falling approximately 10% in a single session. He notes this is alarming in isolation but contextualizes it: the KOSPI was up approximately 90% year-to-date in 2026 as of that session, driven by SK Hynix and Samsung dominating the global DRAM and semiconductor market. He argues this is a breather within an intact uptrend rather than a bubble pop, pointing to a similar ~10% intraday dip on June 4, 2026 that recovered to higher highs.

2. **Micron and semiconductor stocks hit hardest:** Bhakdi identifies Micron Technologies as the most notable American casualty, down approximately 13–14% on the day, which he attributes directly to Korea semiconductor exposure. He notes Micron is up approximately 267% year-to-date in 2026, with a market cap of roughly $1.1 trillion, describing it as the only major American DRAM maker. He contrasts this with the Mac-7 stocks: Amazon was up, Meta was flat, Microsoft was up, and Google was approximately flat — suggesting Tesla's drop was not part of a broad tech selloff but rather a Tesla-specific reaction to the fake news headlines.

3. **SpaceX IPO dynamics creating Tesla selling pressure:** Bhakdi argues that SpaceX's IPO has been a persistent headwind for Tesla, as investors sell Tesla shares to fund SpaceX purchases. He says SpaceX's current revenue multiple would imply a stock price of approximately $35 if valued on the same 13x revenue multiple Tesla trades at. He warns of massive selling pressure beginning August 11, 2026, when SpaceX lockup periods begin expiring, with approximately 400% of current float coming to market through November 2026. He states he will not take a SpaceX position until November at the earliest, when he believes price discovery will be more complete.

4. **Tesla/SpaceX merger theory discussed but skeptically assessed:** Bhakdi engages with the Tesla-SpaceX merger thesis (associated in the chat with "Alexandra Merz" — though he refers to her as both "Alexander Mertz" and "Alexandra") and a prior discussion with someone named "Herbert." He argues a merger of equals is structurally problematic right now: SpaceX's float is immature at ~5% with 400% more shares coming, SpaceX's valuation is unstable, the IPO just occurred placing both companies under heavy SEC scrutiny, and standard merger-of-equals agreements include price deviation clauses (~20%) that would invalidate a deal if either stock moved dramatically between announcement and shareholder vote. He concludes the earliest a safe merger could occur is well after November 2026.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla closed down approximately **5.79%** on 2026-06-23.
- NASDAQ down approximately **2.1%**; S&P 500 down approximately **1.38%**; Dow Jones approximately flat.
- Tesla European registrations in May 2026: **28,610 units, up 107.9% year-over-year** — four consecutive months of gains.
- UBS delivery forecast cited in article: approximately **405,000 vehicles**, up ~5% year-over-year and ~13% vs. two years prior.
- South Korean KOSPI down approximately **10%** on the session; up approximately **90% year-to-date** in 2026.
- Micron Technologies down approximately **13–14%** on the day; up approximately **267% year-to-date** in 2026; market cap cited as approximately **$1.1 trillion**.
- SpaceX: if valued at Tesla's revenue multiple of **13x**, would imply a stock price of approximately **$35**.
- SpaceX lockup expirations: beginning **August 11, 2026**, running through **November 2026**; approximately **400% of current float** coming to market.
- Bhakdi estimates Tesla Cybercab production run rate: approximately **1,000 units per month** (his own unverified estimate).
- Bhakdi's Tesla allocation in long-term portfolio: approximately **60%** (excluding derivatives).
- Ashok Elluswamy on the Harris County crash (posted ~2026-06-22): *"In this case, the driver manually overrode self-driving by pressing the accelerator all the way to 100% of the acceleration pedal in this residential area. They reached a speed of 73 miles per hour during the crash and had the accelerator pressed even after the crash."*
- Bhakdi: *"I come to the terrible conclusion that this piece of fake news is indeed the main driver."*
- On Cybercab deployment: *"Why would you put them into parking lots across the nation and have like 40, 50, 60 of these things in parking lots neatly parked next to each other in all of these different cities? The only reason for that is to actually use them."*

articles.title: Daily X Summary (2026-06-23)
articles.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts center on three Tesla-relevant themes: a significant FSD safety vindication (driver manually overrode autopilot in the Texas crash), a one-year anniversary milestone for Tesla's robotaxi service with Austin now running unsupervised, and first-hand FSD V14.3.4 performance praise. The overall signal is mildly bullish — the safety clarification removes a reputational overhang, robotaxi momentum continues, and Optimus factory construction is visibly accelerating.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **FSD Safety Vindication — Texas Crash Driver Manually Overrode System:** Tesla officially confirmed that the driver of the Model 3 that crashed into a Texas home at 73 mph manually overrode the vehicle's self-driving system by pressing the accelerator pedal. Merritt called out multiple mainstream media outlets — explicitly naming the *New York Times* — for framing headlines to imply Autopilot was engaged despite zero evidence at the time. The NYT post drew 7.6K likes and 433 retweets, indicating significant viral reach on a claim with direct reputational implications for Tesla. Tesla's official confirmation, shared subsequently, received 5.3K likes and 683 retweets. This removes a meaningful near-term liability narrative and reframes the incident as driver error rather than an FSD/Autopilot failure.

2. **Robotaxi One-Year Anniversary — Austin Fleet Now Fully Unsupervised:** Merritt marked the one-year anniversary of Tesla's first robotaxi rides and noted that Tesla's Austin fleet has transitioned to unsupervised operation. This is a qualitative milestone but a meaningful one: it signals Tesla's internal confidence in the Austin deployment has reached the threshold for full driverless operation. Per RobotaxiTracker.com (as of 2026-06-21), the active robotaxi fleet stands at 737 vehicles across the Bay Area (609), Austin (104), Dallas (13), and Houston (11). The unsupervised subset was last tracked at 39 vehicles as of 2026-05-09, but Merritt's characterization of the Austin fleet as now fully unsupervised suggests that figure may be materially higher.

3. **FSD V14.3.4 First-Hand Performance — Zero Disengagements in NYC:** Merritt reported driving throughout New York City on FSD V14.3.4 with zero disengagements, describing the system as handling all situations "flawlessly." Specific behaviors noted included stopping for a child on a scooter entering the street, navigating tight urban spaces, and a self-driven trip from New Haven to New York City. NYC is one of the most challenging urban driving environments, making a zero-disengagement report on this version noteworthy for FSD capability tracking.

4. **Optimus Factory Construction Accelerating:** Merritt shared imagery of Tesla's new Optimus factory going up quickly, with no additional specifics on timeline or capacity. The visual signal of rapid construction pace is consistent with Tesla's stated ramp ambitions for Optimus and is relevant to the humanoid robotics thesis.

5. **Competitive Landscape — Lucid Cutting 18% of U.S. Workforce; Xiaomi Robotic Charging Arm:** Lucid announced it is cutting 18% of its U.S. workforce and that COO Marc Winterhoff is departing immediately, citing the need to align production with demand and reduce inventory — a sign of continued stress among EV challengers.
