12. **New Delhi EV scrapping incentive:** New Delhi announced a program offering residents approximately $1,000 to scrap old EV vehicles to curb air pollution, paired with lower registration fees and road tax exemptions up to 3 million rupees (approximately 4–10% of vehicle price).

13. **Volkswagen ID Buzz coming to US:** VW's ID Buzz camper van is returning to the US market, with US-bound equipment packages priced under $3,000.

## Market & Competition

1. **Legacy automaker strategic incoherence:** The host's overarching critique of GM, VW, and Lucid is that they continue to hedge between ICE and EV rather than committing, which produces neither competitive EVs nor cost savings. VW's plan to reduce lineup complexity while simultaneously maintaining both powertrain types is singled out as self-defeating. By contrast, Model Y's global bestselling status with a tight, focused lineup is held up as proof that focus beats breadth.

2. **China's AI chip restrictions tightening:** In response to a viewer question about how Chinese AV companies solve compute challenges, the host notes that Huawei manufactures AI chips domestically for inference workloads. He adds that China has now banned the import of advanced AI chips from companies like Nvidia (reversing the prior situation where the US banned export to China but China had not restricted import). He observes that Chinese AV companies are notably reluctant to discuss their chip sourcing publicly.

Notable quotes and data:
- FSD V14 Lite is distilled from hardware 4 to hardware 3; early access rollout underway as of June 29, 2026.
- Lucid cutting ~18% of workforce; savings of $158 million/year; COO role eliminated.
- VW job cuts potentially doubling to 100,000; four factories (Zwickau, Emden, Hanover, Neckarsulm) targeted for closure.

articles.title: Is Tesla SandBagging RoboTaxi? Is the Market Crashing?
articles.body:
The video from "investingagainstthegrain" (hosted by Nick) pushes back against the prevailing bearish narrative surrounding markets, AI, and Tesla, arguing that June's weakness is historically normal and that July typically rebounds strongly. The host's core thesis is that Tesla is not sandbagging its robotaxi rollout, that the Cybercab launch is imminent and on track, and that the real AI opportunity lies in autonomy and humanoids — not LLMs, which he argues are already commoditized.

## Market & Competition
1. **June weakness is seasonal, not structural:** The host presents historical S&P 500 data going back to 1950 showing June averages only a 0.22% return, with the back half of June being among the worst periods of the year. He attributes this to institutional rebalancing at the half-year mark, reduced market volume due to vacations, and the amplifying effect that lower volume has on any selling pressure. July, by contrast, is historically one of the strongest months.

2. **MAG 7 underperformance creates opportunity:** A chart shared in the video shows year-to-date performance as of late June 2026, with Meta down 16%, Tesla down 16%, Amazon up only 2%, Nvidia up 5%, Apple up 6%, and Google up 8%. The host contrasts this with outsized gains in names like Marll (up ~230%), Micron (up ~260%), and SanDisk (up ~781%), which he attributes to investors treating memory and storage infrastructure as an inflationary hedge and a defensive play on guaranteed AI capex from the hyperscalers. He views the MAG 7 dislocation as a buying opportunity.

3. **Bitcoin and MicroStrategy as risk-capital barometers:** Bitcoin is cited as down 52.5% from all-time highs and MicroStrategy down 82.6% from all-time highs as of the video date. The host argues risk capital has rotated out of these assets into AI infrastructure plays (Micron, SanDisk, Marll, Bloom Energy) and prediction/sports betting markets. He notes the Fed holding rates — with markets pricing in potential rate hikes — is an additional headwind for Bitcoin since rate cuts would be needed to fuel another Bitcoin rally.

4. **LLM commoditization thesis:** The host reiterates a prediction he says he made over two years ago: that LLMs would be commoditized and the real AI ROI would come from autonomy and humanoids. He points to China's GLM 5.2 — described as the most powerful downloadable open-source model, comparable to frontier models like GPT and Claude Opus — as evidence of commoditization via distillation. He references Gavin Baker on the All-In podcast discussing how China used massive distillation of frontier model outputs to train competitive models at far lower capex cost.

5. **Micron earnings as AI demand proof:** Micron's most recent earnings are cited as showing 346% year-over-year revenue growth and 86% margins, with management stating on the conference call that they have "no line of sight" for when supply will catch up to demand — not by 2027, 2028, or 2029. The host views this as definitive evidence against an AI bubble narrative and argues Micron could approach a $5 trillion market cap. He notes Apple's subsequent announcement of $200 price hikes on Macs and iPads — which Apple attributed to memory costs — as further corroboration, and suggests Apple deliberately timed that announcement to follow Micron's earnings call.

## Robotaxi
1. **Cybercab sandbagging narrative rejected:** The host forcefully dismisses the theory that Tesla and Elon Musk are deliberately delaying the Cybercab rollout — whether for merger negotiating leverage, valuation reasons, or shareholder vote strategy. He argues the logic is self-defeating: depressing the stock ahead of a shareholder vote would only alienate the voters Tesla needs. He frames the "sandbagging" narrative as a projection of bad faith onto a management team he views as consistently shareholder-aligned.

2. **Cybercab first-responder documentation released:** The host highlights that Tesla released official first-responder information for the Cybercab over the weekend prior to the video, calling it a significant and concrete milestone. He pairs this with NHTSA's recent approval of rules allowing autonomous vehicles to operate without steering wheels or pedals, framing both as regulatory prerequisites that Tesla was likely waiting for before scaling deployment.

3. **Fleet staging underway across multiple cities:** The host references a report of 78 Cybercabs counted in a Houston fleet lot at Tesla Cypress, noted as being observed the day before the video. He also references Model Y robotaxis (described as red and black units) being staged alongside Cybercabs, arguing visible fleet preparation across cities is evidence of an imminent launch rather than a delay. Per RobotaxiTracker.com, the active robotaxi fleet stood at 748 as of 2026-06-25, with Houston at 11 units in supervised operation.

4. **Cybercab-vs.-Model Y functionality debate:** The host references a community debate about whether standard Model Y, Model 3, and Cybertruck vehicles can replicate Cybercab functionality. He quotes Larry Goldberg arguing there is no hardware in the Cybercab that cannot be replicated by existing fleet vehicles, and software capabilities should transfer easily. The host sides with this view and recalls Elon's statements on the earnings call that Tesla would set up stations to upgrade Hardware 3 and Hardware 4 vehicles for the robotaxi network, arguing it is in Tesla's financial interest to maximize fleet size.

5. **July flagged as a potentially significant month:** Without citing a specific event, the host strongly hints that July 2026 could bring major Tesla robotaxi news, suggesting that if a launch or significant announcement comes around July 4th or during July, the roughly three-month delay from earlier expectations will seem minor in retrospect.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Terafab as a vertically integrated memory and chip play:** The host discusses the Terafab facility — described as a joint project originally between Tesla, xAI, and SpaceX, now primarily SpaceX and Tesla — and reveals it is intended to manufacture not just GPUs and CPUs but also high-bandwidth memory, positioning it as a vertically integrated semiconductor and compute facility. He draws a parallel to Tesla's history of being told it couldn't build cars, design chips, run data centers, or manufacture batteries — and then doing all of those things — to argue skeptics of Terafab's memory ambitions will similarly be proven wrong.

Notable quotes and data:
- S&P 500 average June return since 1950: 0.22%, with the back half of June historically among the worst periods of the year.
- Year-to-date performance as of late June 2026: Meta −16%, Tesla −16%, Amazon +2%, Nvidia +5%, Apple +6%, Google +8%, Marll +~230%, Micron +~260%, SanDisk +~781%.
- Bitcoin down 52.5% from all-time highs; MicroStrategy down 82.6% from all-time highs.
- Micron most recent earnings: 346% year-over-year revenue growth, 86% margins; management said no supply/demand equilibrium in sight through at least 2029.
- 78 Cybercabs counted at Tesla's Houston Cypress fleet lot the day before the video.
- Active robotaxi fleet: 748 per RobotaxiTracker.com (as of 2026-06-25), with Houston at 11.
- Tesla released Cybercab first-responder documentation the weekend before the video.
- NHTSA approved rules permitting autonomous vehicles to operate without steering wheels or pedals (timing described as recent).
- China's GLM 5.2 described as an open-source model comparable in capability to frontier GPT and Claude Opus models, achieved via distillation.
- Host states his options-based strategy has his portfolio up for the year despite Tesla stock being down ~15–16% year-to-date.

articles.title: Why Tesla Stock RALLIES Today
articles.body:
Jo Bhakdi hosts a live session reacting to Tesla's roughly 8–9% single-day stock rally on June 29, 2026, which he attributes primarily to Morgan Stanley raising its Q2 2026 delivery estimate rather than to Cybercab news. He argues the rally simply returns the stock to where it was the previous Monday after what he describes as an unjustified drop, and uses the session to walk through Cybercab scaling signals, his options positioning, and his continued conviction that Tesla is approaching a major re-pricing event tied to robotaxi deployment.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Morgan Stanley delivery upgrade as the primary rally driver:** Jo Bhakdi is confident the day's outsized move was driven by Morgan Stanley raising its Q2 2026 Tesla delivery forecast from approximately 373,000 vehicles to approximately 413,000 vehicles, citing stronger-than-expected sales trends in Europe and China. He notes Europe was up 100% year-over-year and China was also tracking positively. He stresses that Morgan Stanley's distribution reach — covering a large share of institutional fund clients — translates a research note directly into buy orders from investors who may not follow Tesla granularly.

2. **Deliveries now priced in:** Bhakdi cautions viewers not to expect the delivery beat to continue driving the stock after the numbers are officially released, warning of a potential "sell the news" dynamic. He believes the Morgan Stanley upgrade has already front-run the actual delivery print.

## Robotaxi
1. **Texas first-responder interaction plans filed and integrated:** Bhakdi reports that Texas has now officially integrated connected autonomous vehicle first-responder interaction plans into the Texas Department of Public Safety page, mirroring similar documentation already filed for Arizona. He describes these regulatory filings as a necessary precondition for Cybercab commercial launch and notes the effort required to produce and integrate them is a meaningful scaling signal, even if it does not guarantee an imminent launch.

2. **Lars Moravy teases a July 8 announcement tied to Giga Texas scaling:** Bhakdi plays a clip of Lars Moravy stating that approximately one week from the recording — identified by Bhakdi as Tuesday, July 7, 2026 (after the July 4th weekend) — there will be "cool news" about things happening on the Giga Texas campus related to the scaling effort, though Moravy declines to elaborate. Bhakdi acknowledges he does not know what the announcement is and says it could be something relatively modest such as a factory expansion update rather than a Cybercab commercial launch.

3. **Cybercab inventory building in Dallas and Houston:** Bhakdi cites Sawyer Merritt reporting over 70 Cybercabs now visible in a parking lot in Dallas, and notes similar accumulation has been observed in Houston. He also shows footage from Joe Tegtmeyer of Cybercabs rolling off the Giga Texas production line daily. Bhakdi interprets the growing inventory stockpiles as evidence that a deployment event is being prepared, arguing the accumulation is not sustainable indefinitely without an operational purpose.

4. **Cybercab commercial launch timeline — high conviction on July, missed May and June:** Bhakdi acknowledges he predicted a Cybercab launch in May and then in June, both of which did not materialize. He explicitly states he missed his June target (which included a $490 price target). He argues, however, that each missed month raises the probability of the next month, and he now has his highest conviction yet that something significant happens in July. He does not give a specific date. He believes today's rally had nothing to do with Cybercab and that Cybercab news therefore remains unpriced, giving further upside potential.

5. **Re-pricing thresholds and price targets:** Bhakdi outlines his view that any significant Cybercab deployment above roughly 20 units operating commercially could push Tesla to all-time highs. He believes a fleet in the range of a few thousand — with a clear trajectory toward tens of thousands — would trigger a major re-pricing toward $700 and potentially overshoot to $1,000 or beyond. He speculates that 10,000 Cybercabs could be reached within three months but acknowledges it might not occur until December. For a longer horizon, he estimates Tesla could reach $1,800–$2,000 by end of 2027.

## Market & Competition
1. **NASDAQ recovery and Iran de-escalation as macro tailwinds:** Bhakdi notes the NASDAQ was up approximately 2–2.8% on the day, which he attributes to continued de-escalation of the Iran conflict. He frames Tesla's ~8–9% move as roughly double the NASDAQ's beta-adjusted expected return, with the excess driven by the Morgan Stanley delivery upgrade.

2. **Short-term consolidation risk flagged:** Despite his bullishness, Bhakdi switches from long calls (which he says returned roughly 100% on August-expiration $380 strikes bought at approximately $25 during the prior week's dip) back to short puts at strikes of $400, $405, $407.50, $410, and $412. He argues consolidation or a modest pullback is possible in the near term as the delivery news gets priced in and the NASDAQ potentially digests recent gains.

3. **California AB 1777 remote-operator requirement — not a major concern:** In response to a viewer question, Bhakdi dismisses California's AB 1777 legislation requiring remote operators for autonomous vehicles as a minor operational issue. He argues a single remote operator could be on call for a very large fleet and would simply be contacted if a robotaxi is pulled over by police, which he does not view as a meaningful business obstacle.

Notable quotes and data:
- Morgan Stanley raised its Q2 2026 Tesla delivery estimate from ~373,000 to ~413,000 vehicles.
- Europe deliveries reportedly up ~100% year-over-year per Bhakdi.
- Tesla stock up approximately 8–9% on June 29, 2026, reaching around $412–$413.
- Lars Moravy clip: "In a week from Tuesday there'll be some cool news about things happening on the campus at Texas… as part of the scaling effort."
- Sawyer Merritt reported over 70 Cybercabs observed in a Dallas parking lot.
- Bhakdi's August-expiration $380 call position purchased at ~$25, sold for ~100% gain.
- Short put strikes: $400, $405, $407.50, $410, $412.
- Tesla trading volume on the day: ~48 million shares vs. a stated average of ~46 million.
- Bhakdi's long-term price targets: $490 near-term; $700+ on initial robotaxi re-pricing; $1,000+ on scale conviction; $1,800–$2,000 by end of 2027.

articles.title: Slate Auto's Structural Continuity
articles.body:
This video from Munro Live features a brief technical walkthrough of Slate Auto's vehicle structure, focusing on how the SUV conversion kit integrates with the base truck platform. The core discussion centers on structural engineering decisions — specifically how the roll cage and body structure were designed to achieve torsional rigidity while maintaining the vehicle's flatpack, customer-assembled concept. The segment is short and appears to be a clip from a larger teardown or design review.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **SUV Conversion Roll Cage Integration:** The Slate Auto engineer explains that rather than tucking the roll cage structure into the catwalk area, the team designed it to plug into the truck bed interior, hugging the wheel well. This approach allows the truck and SUV structures to work together without adding unnecessary structure to the base truck platform that would only be needed for the SUV configuration.

2. **Flatpack Design Philosophy:** A key engineering requirement was that the SUV conversion be shippable in a flatpacked form to the customer's driveway and assembled over time. Achieving the required torsional rigidity for the SUV body while keeping the design flatpackable was a central constraint that shaped the structural engineering decisions.

3. **Load Path and Structural Continuity:** The Munro Live host traces the structural load path from the rear suspension up through the body and into the B-pillar (referred to as the SE-pillar in the transcript), confirming structural continuity throughout. The Slate Auto engineer acknowledges this and notes the approach reflects lessons learned from working with Munro Live approximately 15 years prior.

4. **Requirements-Driven Engineering:** The engineer emphasizes that having well-defined functional requirements — driven by the multiple constraints of dual-use (truck and SUV), flatpack delivery, and structural performance — was what enabled the engineering team to execute the design effectively.

Notable quotes and data:
- "We didn't want to add structure to the truck that didn't have to be there for the SUV."
- "It hugs the wheel well and allows the structures to work together."
- "That's stuff that we learned from you guys back way back in the day, 15 years ago or so."
- The SUV roll cage plugs into the truck bed interior and is designed to be customer-installed after delivery.

articles.title: Slate Auto's Frunk
articles.body:
This short video clip from the Munro Live channel features a representative from Slate Auto discussing the design and functionality of the frunk (front trunk) on their upcoming two-door pickup truck. The segment focuses on the engineering decisions made to optimize the frunk's usability, highlighting benchmarking work done in collaboration with Munro Live. The clip is brief and appears to be an excerpt from a longer vehicle teardown or design review.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Frunk design optimized for low lift-over height:** The Slate Auto spokesperson explains that the entire front end and cooling module was repositioned — tipped back — to minimize the lift-over height required to load items into the frunk, making it easier to hoist luggage and other cargo into the space.

2. **Large, lockable, sealable storage as a design priority:** The team intentionally preserved maximum frunk volume and ensured the space is lockable and sealable, citing this as a critical feature for a two-door truck format where bed access may be limited. The frunk also includes a drain plug, adding utility for wet or messy cargo.

3. **Munro Live benchmarking collaboration:** The Slate Auto representative credits Munro Live with benchmarking assistance that informed the frunk engineering decisions, suggesting an ongoing teardown or evaluation partnership between the two organizations.

Notable quotes and data:
- "We knew that lockable, sealable storage was a big deal for a two-door truck like this."
- "We dropped it, and we tipped it back to be able to have the lift-over be as low as possible."
- The frunk includes cup holders — described lightheartedly as a feature no frunk would be "complete without."

articles.title: Daily X Summary (2026-06-29)
articles.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's digest is a small three-post set with two substantive Tesla data points: a notable expansion of the Cybercab test fleet in Houston and a new market entry announcement for Uruguay. The primary investment signal comes from the Houston robotaxi test fleet growth, which suggests Tesla is scaling its Cybercab testing operations significantly beyond what current operational tracker data reflects.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Cybercab Houston test fleet grows to ~80:** Merritt reports approximately 80 Cybercabs are now present in Houston as a test fleet, describing it as "growing and growing." This figure is materially higher than the 11 active/operational Robotaxis currently logged for Houston on RobotaxiTracker.com (as of 2026-06-25), suggesting the bulk of these vehicles are in a pre-revenue testing phase rather than live commercial service. The distinction matters: a large test fleet staging in Houston could be a leading indicator of an imminent commercial launch in that market, consistent with Tesla's pattern of fleet staging before activation. The post included media (likely photos or video) supporting the count.

2. **Tesla announces entry into Uruguay:** Tesla has officially announced it will launch vehicle sales in Uruguay, which Merritt notes would make it the third South American country where Tesla vehicles are available. No launch date, model lineup, or pricing details were specified. This is an incremental geographic expansion story — relevant for long-term EV demand growth but not a near-term financial mover.

---

## Signal Strength: **Mildly Bullish** — The Houston Cybercab test fleet reaching ~80 units suggests meaningful behind-the-scenes scaling of the robotaxi program, even if commercial activation in that market hasn't yet followed.

articles.title: Weekly Tesla Brief (Jun 22 – Jun 28, 2026)
articles.body:
## Brief

- Official Cybercab first-responder PDFs published June 28, including Arizona appendix — legal pre-deployment requirement.
- NHTSA removes manual brake pedal mandate for fully autonomous vehicles.
- Tesla–NatPower $5B / 25 GWh Megapack deal — largest energy storage contract in Tesla history.
- June 30 IR commitment officially broken; Bhakdi shifts window to "two to eight weeks."
- Fatal Katy, TX crash: FSD was active; driver pressed accelerator to 100%.
- Optimus V3 supply chain activating; Taiwan component suppliers entering mass production H2 2026.
- Q2 delivery consensus 406K; Giga Berlin targeting 7,500 units/week by October.

---

## Robotaxi

- **Official Cybercab first-responder documentation published June 28** — ~30-page PDFs covering vehicle ID, camera placement, battery caution zones, and emergency QR codes, with an Arizona-specific appendix. Per Bhakdi, these filings are legally required before commercial AV operations begin in a state; Sawyer Merritt characterized the release as signaling "first public Cybercab rides are going to start very soon." Production spec confirmed in the filings: no steering wheel, no accelerator, no brake pedal. Vehicles observed with a wheel are explicitly classified as SAE Level 2 test units, not production configuration.

- **Cybercab staging inventory at record levels across multiple cities.** More than 150 units were counted at Giga Texas by June 26, up from prior milestones of 30, 50, and 100. Houston staging reached approximately 84 units per Bhakdi. Separately, a content creator documented Cybercabs arriving in the Washington D.C. area, the first confirmed sighting on the East Coast. Jeff Lutz noted that shipping units away from the factory — where rework is cheapest — is an implicit hardware-readiness signal.

- **June 30 IR commitment is definitively broken.** Tesla's Q4 2025 earnings deck committed to paid robotaxi service in Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Miami, and Phoenix by June 30; zero of those five cities are operational as the deadline expires. The Q1 2026 earnings deck quietly downgraded remaining target cities from date-specific language to "preparations underway." Bhakdi, who had held June as his primary window, now targets a two-to-eight-week horizon and stated explicitly: "As long as [Cybercab scale] doesn't happen, we have a problem… this stock will remain under pressure and trend down."

- **Demand is deliberately throttled; pricing at $3 drop + $1.40–$1.50/mile.** Per FutureAzA guest John, Tesla is intentionally holding prices high — up from launch-era $0.42/mile — to keep wait times under ~10 minutes given fleet constraints. John estimates Tesla could profitably price as low as $0.15/mile but is avoiding demand it cannot yet service. Waymo, for comparison, is running approximately 500,000 paid driverless rides per week across ~10 metros.

- **Cybercab engineered for 500,000-mile fleet duty life** versus approximately 150,000 miles for a consumer vehicle, and contains roughly 4,000 total parts — approximately half the Model 3's count. Waymo's sensor suite alone reportedly consists of ~4,000 parts, illustrating the structural cost gap between purpose-built and sensor-bolted-on approaches. Conversion from steering-wheel-equipped to pedal-free configuration can be performed in the field in hours.

---

## Autonomous Driving

- **NHTSA removed the manual brake pedal requirement for vehicles designed exclusively for automated operation**, opening a 30-day public comment period before a final DOT ruling. The agency framed the move as an effort to "safely unleash American innovation." For Tesla, it reduces the risk of NHTSA challenging the Cybercab's existing self-certification under FMVSS. Separately, the UNECE adopted the first-ever global AV framework — hardware-agnostic, no LiDAR mandate — backed by the US, EU, China, Japan, Canada, and the UK; binding only after domestic incorporation.

- **FSD 14.3.4 demonstrated zero disengagements across New York City**, including a full unsupervised trip from New Haven to NYC per Sawyer Merritt. A sideswipe-avoidance maneuver — briefly crossing a double yellow line to avoid a drifting vehicle — circulated widely and was cited by multiple commentators as evidence of reactive capability beyond conventional coded responses. FSD cumulative miles crossed 11.3 billion; the fleet now uploads approximately 30 million fresh miles daily.

- **Spain approval expected around June 30** per employees cited by the FutureAzA host; the Spanish testing fleet has grown from 19 to ~30 vehicles and covered ~275,000 km since November 2025 with zero serious incidents. Finland's Traficom stated FSD "is considered to have significant potential to reduce accidents" and may approve independently ahead of the EU-wide vote, now pushed to October 2026 at the earliest. China FSD full-fleet approval targeted Q3 2026; 200-vehicle test fleet is active, uploading ~1.7 TB/day.

---

## Optimus

- **Optimus V3 supply chain activating in Taiwan and Southeast Asia.** Tesla signed agreements with Merl Automation (harmonic reducers and joint modules, with a new Thailand joint venture) and Asia Optical (spherical and aspherical lens components for the vision system). Parts are slated for mass production H2 2026 into 2027 — supplier-level ramp preceding Tesla's own production line.

- **V3 reveal targeted late July to early August; Fremont line conversion on track for late summer.** V3's headline upgrade is 22 degrees of freedom per hand, doubled from 11, with actuators relocated to the forearm to reduce hand weight and increase speed. The former Model S/X line at Fremont is being converted for Optimus production, expected to complete around late summer 2026. First ~5,000 units are expected to be deployed across five to eight Tesla-owned facilities in California and Las Vegas.

- **Giga Texas Optimus factory steel now four stories tall**, projected at ~4,000+ feet in length at full build, targeting ~10 million units per year at full ramp. Realistic production-ready estimate from on-site observers remains end-2027 to 2028. Approximately 208 Optimus job listings are open across North America and Greece, led by 65 manufacturing/industrialization roles.

- **Digital Optimus emerging as a distinct near-term software product.** Ashok Elluswamy showed Digital Optimus on a slide during the week. Six of 17 AI/ML Optimus job listings explicitly name "Digital Optimus" — an agent running on the AI4 chip that operates computers via screen vision rather than APIs. Brian Wang (Next Big Future) expects a Macrohard/Digital Optimus demo by ~September 2026 and frames it as a potential near-term revenue catalyst. Caveat from brighterwithherbert: Anthropic shipped computer-use agents in 2024 and holds ~40% of enterprise API spend; Digital Optimus has no public benchmark.

---

## Tesla Semi

- **A second Tesla Semi was spotted in Palo Alto with autonomy validation hardware mounted on the roof**, drawing the highest single-post engagement of the day on June 28 (4.6K likes per Sawyer Merritt). Tesla's own materials describe the Semi as "autonomy ready" with 10 cameras with washers. Loomis does not expect unsupervised Semi FSD in serious consideration until 2028, but active validation testing is confirmed.

- **California incentives now stack to up to $240,000 off per Semi**: $120,000 via HVIP (up to 20 trucks) plus $120,000 via Clean Fuel Rewards with no truck cap. Real-world efficiency data from an Oklahoma fleet pilot: 1.55 kWh/mile — approximately 25% better than competing electric semis EPA-rated at 2.1+ kWh/mile.

---

## Energy

- **Tesla–NatPower deal is the largest energy storage contract in Tesla history**: 25+ GWh phase one across Italy and the UK, approximately $5 billion in construction value, with the full program targeting 100+ GWh and over $15 billion in revenues over 20 years. The prior largest single-source battery storage installation was approximately 12.3 GWh, making phase one alone more than twice that scale. The deal also embeds Tesla's Autobidder AI energy trading software — the stickier, higher-margin component.

- **Tesla–Giga Storage LOI for 2.8 GWh Megablock project in Limburg, Belgium** — the first Megablock deal at GWh scale, estimated value ~$700 million per Sawyer Merritt. Final contracts expected summer 2026. Combined with the NatPower deal and a $1 GWh Scotland project, Sawyer Merritt cited more than $6 billion in new Megapack announcements over recent weeks.

- **Tesla–Sunrun–Renew Home VPP aggregates 16.8 GW of flexible capacity** across hundreds of thousands of residential Powerwalls, EVs, and 8 million+ smart thermostats. Over 300 MW is immediately deployable in Virginia's Data Center Alley. Q2 2026 analyst consensus for energy storage is 13.8 GWh; Q1 came in at 8.8 GWh with record 39.5% gross margin, though management flagged some margin compression ahead from tariffs on Chinese cells.

- **Megapod trademark filed June 18**: modular AI inference data centers co-located at Supercharger stations, which already carry approximately 7 GW of permitted grid connections. Elon Musk confirmed the name and described eventual scale as millions of units. The AI4 chip ($650) serves as shared silicon across FSD vehicles, Optimus, and Megapod — a single inference platform across three form factors.

---

## Electric Vehicles

- **Giga Berlin targeting 7,500 Model Y/week by October 2026**, a second consecutive ~20% production increase adding ~1,000 workers. At full rate, ~375,000 units/year from Berlin alone. Electrified estimates the incremental step adds ~$6.2 billion in annual revenue and over $1.2 billion in gross profit at a 20% margin.

- **Q2 2026 delivery consensus is 406,000 units** (Tesla-compiled street estimate per Sawyer Merritt); Goldman Sachs is at 420,000, saying deliveries are "tracking ahead of consensus." Q1 2026 was 358,000. Report due approximately July 2–3. Europe is carrying the quarter (+108% YoY in May registrations); China is tracking ~-11% YoY and the US is down mid-teens percent YoY.

- **Model YL US production targeting August–September 2026 at Giga Texas**, priced at approximately $54,000 — roughly $4,000 above the current AWD Model Y. Adds ~6 inches of wheelbase and a 2-2-2 seating configuration with heated/ventilated captain's chairs in row 2. Source is Not a Tesla App; unconfirmed by Tesla.

- **Cybertruck earned IIHS Top Safety Pick+ for 2026** — the only pickup of any powertrain to clear all four pedestrian front crash prevention scenarios. Tesla Vision airbag deployment now up to 70 milliseconds faster via OTA, using exterior cameras to identify contact timing before impact sensors alone would trigger.

---

## Financials

- **Over $500 million in Q-period Tesla revenue sourced from other Musk entities**: Megapack deployments to xAI, $78 million in additional xAI revenue, and $143 million in Cybertruck purchases by SpaceX and xAI. Analysts also flagged $480 million in non-recurring tariff and warranty margin adjustments in the same period. Hosts expect Megapack revenue from xAI to recur; Cybertruck fleet purchases are viewed as unlikely to repeat at the same scale.

- **Q2 2026 earnings setup**: brighterwithherbert cites European sales recovery (+108% YoY in May), Megapack demand momentum, and Cybercab manufacturing ramp as the three pillars. SpaceX mark-to-market on Tesla's equity stake estimated at ~$2B / ~$0.75/share Q2 contribution (unconfirmed). Q2 earnings expected third to fourth week of July.

---

## Market & Competition

- **SpaceX joins the Nasdaq-100 effective July 7, 2026.** Index fund purchases begin after market close July 6. Further MSCI and potential S&P 500 inclusion expected, though S&P has historically been less accommodating to Musk-affiliated entities. Bhakdi warns of significant Tesla selling pressure through November 2026 when SpaceX lockup expirations bring approximately 400% of current float to market.

- **VW reportedly weighing up to 100,000 job cuts and closure of four German factories** — potentially the largest restructuring in automotive history, driven by weak sales. VW stock is down ~60% over three years. BMW discontinued its Personal Pilot L3 system entirely; Mercedes paused Drive Pilot from upcoming facelifts. FSD Supervised is now the most capable driver-assistance system widely available in Europe.

- **Musk compensation restructured from stock options to restricted stock with a five-year lock-up** around June 17, 2026, per Alexandra Merz — giving him voting rights but binding him to Tesla as a key person for five years. Framed as a strong long-term commitment signal, though the structural conflict between Musk's personal financial timeline (options expiring August 15) and operational milestone requirements remains.

---

## Bear Case of the Week

- **Katy, TX fatal crash: FSD was confirmed active.** Ashok Elluswamy confirmed via public statement that FSD was engaged when driver Michael Butler manually overrode the system by pressing the accelerator to 100% pedal travel, reaching 73–75 mph in a residential 25 mph zone and striking a home, killing 76-year-old Martha Avila Mantilla. NHTSA opened a Special Crash Investigation and maintains a separate Engineering Analysis covering ~3.2 million vehicles. Elon initially posted "FSD drives slowly through neighborhood streets" — a claim his own company's telemetry then contradicted. Electrek argues the "driver overrode it" defense does not constitute exoneration: the most plausible behavioral scenario is an out-of-the-loop emergency response where the driver hit the accelerator instead of the brake — identical to the grounds on which a Florida jury found Tesla 33% liable in a $243 million judgment upheld February 2026.

- **June 30 IR commitment missed with no credible successor date.** Tesla's binding Q4 2025 earnings deck commitment to paid robotaxi service in Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Miami, and Phoenix by June 30 expires this week with zero of five cities operational. The Q1 2026 earnings deck quietly replaced date-specific language with "preparations underway." Bhakdi — who had defended June as his primary window across multiple prior briefs — has now shifted to a two-to-eight-week horizon. The miss is the third consecutive weekly brief in which this deadline has appeared; it is now factually closed.

- **Paid robotaxi miles remain negligible.** The Q1 2026 earnings deck disclosed paid robotaxi miles "nearly doubled sequentially" in Q1 — from approximately one million to approximately 1.7 million cumulative miles. That figure represents roughly three to four days of Waymo's current weekly output of 500,000 paid driverless rides. Musk's original Austin target of 500 unsupervised vehicles by end of 2025 and Bhakdi's prior projection of 1,800 unsupervised units by April–May 2026 have both been missed by a wide margin. The unsupervised fleet count tracked by RobotaxiTracker.com has not updated since May 9, 2026 — now 51 days stale.

- **Two FSD 14.3.4 edge-case failures documented this week.** In one incident, FSD drove over a gas can that had fallen from a trailer without detecting it; Tesla's Yun Tasai acknowledged the clip. In a second, FSD prepared to proceed through a lowered railroad crossing arm. Loomis noted the inconsistency with FSD's demonstrated ability to brake hard for small animals — the same object-detection pipeline. Both clips circulated publicly during the same week Tesla is seeking EU-wide regulatory approval.

- **Optimus missed 2025 production targets; V3 hand design previously failed.** Brighterwithherbert explicitly states Tesla missed its 2025 Optimus unit numbers and that most current Optimus robots work inside Tesla's own factories. Elon reportedly acknowledged in ~May 2026 that the most recently patented hand design "didn't work," implying the program is on its fourth or fifth hand iteration. China's Unitree shipped thousands of cheaper humanoids in 2025; Figure has a live factory pilot with BMW. The 2026 targets of 50,000–100,000 units are described by the FutureAzA host as definitively unachievable: "it's going to be much less."

articles.title: Tesla’s Biggest Competitors Are Falling Behind
articles.body:
This video features host Herbert and guest Jeff Lutz — a former C-suite supply chain executive at Google, Lenovo, and Motorola, now running his own consulting firm — discussing how Tesla's biggest predicted competitors in autonomous driving and EVs have largely failed to execute, while Tesla continues to expand. The core thesis is that a famous analyst chart from years ago ranked Tesla near the bottom of the autonomous driving race and legacy OEMs at the top, but real-world outcomes have inverted that prediction almost entirely. The conversation covers the collapse or retreat of competitors like GM Cruise, Volkswagen/Bosch, Polestar, and Waymo's strained Uber partnership, alongside Tesla's Giga Berlin expansion and the imminent US launch of the Model Y L.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **The "leaders" chart has aged poorly:** Herbert and Jeff reference a widely circulated analyst chart from several years ago that ranked GM Cruise, Waymo, Volkswagen, Daimler, Ford, and others as autonomous driving leaders, with Tesla near the bottom as a "challenger." Jeff notes the chart was never signed by its author and has since been weaponized by Tesla bears. In practice, nearly every company ranked above Tesla has either shut down its program, scaled it back dramatically, or failed to achieve commercial viability, while Tesla's FSD has continued advancing toward mass-market deployment.

2. **SAE level framing was the wrong metric:** Jeff argues that analysts and legacy OEMs obsessed over SAE autonomy levels — a certification-style taxonomy — rather than focusing on consumer-relevant outcomes: miles driven under automation, cost per mile, and scalability. He compares it to marketing a phone by its IP water-resistance rating (e.g., IP67 vs. IP68) instead of explaining what that means practically. Tesla, he says, was always focused on getting the most miles done under automation at the right price point, which is the only metric that ultimately matters commercially.

3. **Volkswagen ends Bosch autonomous driving partnership:** Volkswagen ended its self-driving partnership with Bosch after determining the technology was not competitive with other systems, specifically citing Tesla's FSD as the benchmark. This came alongside Volkswagen cutting up to 100,000 jobs and planning to close four factories in Germany. Herbert notes that just a year prior (approximately June 2025), Volkswagen had publicly stated its goal to overtake Tesla in the robotaxi race by launching an autonomous ID. Buzz in 2026. Elon Musk's response to that claim, per the discussion, was simply: "Guess not."

4. **Mercedes/Daimler's Level 3 quietly dropped:** Herbert points out that Mercedes (with Bosch) claimed to be the first to offer Level 3 autonomy, but with severe restrictions — only on certain highway segments, under 40 mph, only with a lead vehicle, only during certain hours. The feature was eventually discontinued because adoption was negligible and practical utility was near zero, undermining the credibility of their claimed leadership position.

5. **Tesla's lead measured in years, not months:** Jeff pushes back hard on the analyst view that autonomous driving is standard software that competitors can replicate within six months of Tesla solving it. He argues the lead is measurable in multiple years — possibly half a decade — because it requires simultaneously mastering AI capability, manufacturing scale, and unit economics under one roof, a combination no competitor currently has. He references Lars Moravy's articulation of Tesla's integrated manufacturing and AI capability as evidence of a qualitatively different league.

## Robotaxi

1. **Waymo–Uber relationship shows signs of strain:** Uber no longer offers Waymo rides in Phoenix, a development Herbert frames as a second signal of friction between the two companies, following reports of Uber's CTO publicly criticizing Waymo around a month prior. Jeff's interpretation is that this reflects a margin conflict: Waymo may have concluded that offering rides through its own app directly captures more economics than routing through Uber's platform. Jeff warns this is precisely the risk of Uber's platform model — it depends on third-party AV operators who have their own incentive to disintermediate it.

2. **Uber's platform thesis increasingly challenged:** Jeff corrects Herbert's characterization that Uber's stock has been performing well, noting it is down approximately 18% on a 12-month basis and down roughly 8–10% year-to-date. He observes that on days with strong Tesla news, Uber tends to dip, suggesting the market is beginning to price in robotaxi displacement risk. Jeff is skeptical of Uber's stated strategy of aggregating 20-plus AV vendors as a commodity platform, arguing the company's value proposition erodes if Tesla offers rides at a materially lower price point through a vertically integrated stack.

3. **Tesla's vertically integrated unit economics as structural advantage:** Jeff emphasizes that Tesla's strategic choice to own the entire unit economic stack — vehicle hardware, FSD software, fleet management, and ride delivery — is the correct one for long-term margin capture. Outsourcing any layer, as Uber's model requires, creates the exact friction now visible in the Waymo situation. He believes Tesla's robotaxi pricing will be substantially lower than incumbents due to this integration, which will drive adoption beyond the current ride-hailing addressable market into second-car and third-car replacement decisions.

4. **Robotaxi supply remains a binding constraint today:** Jeff recounts personal experience attempting to hail both a Waymo and a Tesla robotaxi in the Bay Area and being unable to get either due to insufficient fleet size. He describes the space as still "very nascent" and flags that the total addressable market analysis for robotaxi is being systematically undercounted by analysts who simply apply current ride-hailing rates rather than modeling the incremental demand created once price and availability reach mass-market thresholds.

5. **Cybercab production ramp and risk assessment:** Herbert references a community analyst (identified as "Xander") who used VIN numbers to estimate approximately 850 Cybercabs may already have been produced, up from earlier estimates of 100–200. Jeff argues Tesla's robotaxi risk is lower than it appears because: (a) Tesla has a profitable base auto business generating 1.7–2 million units per year; (b) the Cybercab platform uses Tesla's Unboxed manufacturing process and meets Tesla's safety standards; and (c) the fundamental question is no longer "will FSD work" but rather "when does it get calibrated to the Cybercab form factor," given it already works in Model Y today.

6. **Robotaxi as a re-rating, not a base business event:** Jeff frames robotaxi deployment as a "re-rating event" for Tesla — not essential to the core auto business case, but potentially transformative if it succeeds. He draws a parallel to the smartphone emergence, noting that at the time of the iPhone's launch no one anticipated scaling from hundreds of thousands to hundreds of millions of units annually. He suggests a similar non-linear outcome is possible if robotaxi displaces second-car ownership decisions at scale.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Giga Berlin double production expansion:** Tesla executive André Thierig announced that Giga Berlin is expanding production in two stages: first from 5,000 to 6,200 vehicles per week starting in July (with 1,000 new hires), and then a further increase to 7,500 vehicles per week beginning a ramp from October, adding another 1,000 employees — totaling approximately 3,500 additional hires for the year. This is occurring while Volkswagen is simultaneously closing four German factories and cutting up to 100,000 jobs, a stark contrast Herbert emphasizes.

2. **Herbert's theory: FSD Europe approval driving Berlin expansion:** Herbert offers his own hypothesis that the Berlin production expansion is driven by two catalysts: introduction of the refreshed Model Y at Giga Berlin, and early signals that FSD regulatory approval is expanding across Europe. He notes FSD has already received approval in approximately five to six European countries, and speculates Germany, Italy, and Spain — larger markets — may be next, which would justify front-loading hiring and capacity.

3. **Model Y L spotted in California, US launch described as imminent:** A camouflaged Tesla Model Y L (the extended, six-seat version) was spotted in Palo Alto, California on 19- or 20-inch wheels, with a community observer describing the US launch as "imminent." Jeff and Herbert both believe the Model Y L will outperform the standard Model Y in North America specifically because American consumers have a demonstrated preference for larger vehicles. Jeff suggests it could enter production as soon as the current quarter and become a major volume driver through the remainder of 2026. Herbert notes the Model Y L has already launched in other global markets, with North America being the last region to receive it.

4. **Polestar exits the US market:** Herbert and Jeff discuss Polestar's withdrawal from the United States, noting the brand had previously run advertising explicitly mocking Tesla. Jeff explains the exit was driven by a US trade ruling that ended the credit arrangement under which Polestar (owned by Geely) was importing China-built vehicles offset by Volvo US plant exports. Jeff's view is that the trade ruling was a final blow to a brand that was already failing on its own merits — no meaningful sales traction, products priced too high, and no self-driving capability.

## Market & Competition

1. **GM Cruise: collapsed and only partially revived:** Herbert recounts that GM Cruise, ranked as an autonomous driving leader on the famous analyst chart, was shut down following a serious accident and has since been revived only in a much smaller, limited form with no meaningful commercial-scale activity currently. Uber had announced a partnership with GM Cruise within approximately 90 days of Cruise's shutdown, which Jeff cites as evidence that Uber's partnership announcements lack due diligence rigor.

2. **Chinese EV manufacturers overhyped as European threat:** Jeff dismisses the narrative that Chinese EV manufacturers would rapidly take over Western European auto factories as "absurd." He argues that no rational Chinese OEM would want to acquire aging legacy factory infrastructure incompatible with their manufacturing methods. He notes that Chinese imports into Europe remain a slow-moving glut rather than a manufacturing takeover, and that Tesla's established brand, Supercharger network, service infrastructure, and FSD approvals in Europe give it a durable competitive position against Chinese entrants who still need to build all of that from scratch.

3. **Legacy OEM failure pattern: make vs. buy misjudgment:** Jeff identifies a structural cause for legacy OEM autonomous driving failures: C-suite executives made "build it ourselves" decisions without the engineering capability to execute, then failed to maintain accountability through to launch. He contrasts this with companies that were essentially using autonomous driving announcements as fundraising vehicles — deploying prototypes on curated routes to impress investors rather than solving the underlying engineering problem. Tesla, he argues, actually hired the engineers, built the compute (referencing Dojo implicitly), and did the work.

Notable quotes and data:
- Uber stock: down approximately 18% on a 12-month basis, down approximately 8–10% year-to-date (per Jeff Lutz)
- Giga Berlin production targets: 5,000/week (prior) → 6,200/week from July → 7,500/week ramping from October
- Giga Berlin new hires: 1,000 (first announcement) + 1,000 more (second announcement) = approximately 3,500 total additional employees in 2026
- Waymo active fleet cited by Herbert: approximately 3,800 cars across 10 metro areas (Herbert's figure; materially higher than RobotaxiTracker.com's canonical 748 active Tesla robotaxi fleet, which covers a different operator)
- Estimated Cybercab units produced (community VIN analysis, per "Xander"): approximately 850
- Tesla conventional vehicle annual run rate cited by Jeff: 1.7–2 million units per year
- Jeff on Tesla's competitive lead: "It's measured in many years… maybe talking half decade, full decade kind of thing"
- Jeff on robotaxi TAM: "People are going to start replacing rides where they would have gone and rented a vehicle or purchased a second or third vehicle… it's going to be much bigger"
- Elon Musk's response to Volkswagen's 2025 claim it would overtake Tesla in 2026: "Guess not"
- An interview between Herbert, Jeff Lutz, and Tesla VP Lars Moravy was recorded and set to publish on the same day as this video, around 11:30 AM

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Tesla VP Announces Big Event Coming | Lars Moravy
articles.body:
This video features an in-depth interview with Lars Moravy, Tesla's VP of Vehicle Engineering, conducted by the "brighterwithherbert" channel alongside guest Jeff Lutz, a former Fortune 100 supply chain executive. Moravy covers the Cybercab production ramp, Optimus manufacturing buildout at Fremont, Tesla's expanding use of AI across factories and operations, and the competitive moat Tesla has built through vertical integration and manufacturing excellence. A headline moment is Moravy's teaser of a major announcement coming Tuesday, July 7, 2026, related to scaling activity on the Giga Texas campus.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab production ramp status — on track, burn-in underway:** Moravy confirms that Cybercab production lines are installed and running at Giga Texas. He characterizes the ramp as being roughly where the team expected. When pressed on the reported figure of approximately 150 units built, he says "I'll stick with that number." He notes that the majority of vehicles produced so far have gone into the Autopilot training fleet rather than commercial deployment, and that Tesla has just started the burn-in process on the dedicated burn-in track built on the edge of the Giga Texas campus.

2. **Automation ahead of schedule, lines over 90% automated:** Moravy states that the factory automation for Cybercab is actually ahead of schedule, and that he was impressed by the speeds already being achieved. He confirms the Cybercab production lines are over 90% automated end-to-end — a figure he describes as significant — and attributes the smoother ramp compared to prior vehicles to hard-won lessons from previous "production hell" experiences, more virtual commissioning before physical installation, and greater rigor in pre-shipment machine testing.

3. **Major announcement teased for July 7, 2026:** Moravy twice references an imminent announcement, stating: "In a week from Tuesday, there'll be some cool news about things happening on the campus of Texas, and I can't talk about it right now, but that's part of the scaling effort." The channel's intro identifies this date as Tuesday, July 7, 2026.

4. **Cybercab built as a standalone platform for unprecedented scale:** Moravy explains that Cybercab was designed on a clean sheet because Tesla believes it will build more of these than any vehicle it has ever made. He draws an analogy to the transition from hard disk to solid-state storage — where the new technology was better on nearly every dimension — to argue that autonomous transportation will similarly displace conventional car ownership over perhaps 10–15 years. He notes that whether additional vehicle models are built on the Cybercab platform will depend on the adoption rate of autonomous vehicles.

5. **Waymo's approach contrasted with Tesla's:** Moravy argues that analysts and investors are dramatically underestimating Cybercab's efficiency advantage, stating that Waymo's model of taking an existing car and adding compute on top is "probably not efficient enough." He says Tesla's vertically integrated approach — controlling raw materials, compute, software, charging, and service — creates a cost-per-mile advantage that business analysts haven't fully modeled. He credits Elon Musk with pushing this integrated vision since 2014.

6. **Consumer Cybercab sale bet referenced:** The hosts raise the reported bet between Elon Musk and MKBHD over whether a Cybercab would be sold to a consumer by end of 2025 (per the show's framing). Moravy declines to comment on the bet specifically, saying his job is to make a safe product and get it into lots, and that "the deployment will happen."

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus production line installation underway at Fremont:** Moravy confirms that the first Optimus production line has been delivered and installation has begun at the Fremont factory, where Model S and X production has ended. The automation equipment was built by Tesla's own automation groups located in the Midwest and in Germany, and units are going through final field acceptance testing (FAT) before being commissioned. He says the line is modular by design, and because Optimus is smaller than a car, a line can theoretically be taken down, shipped, and brought back online in two to three days, with full commissioning in about a week.

2. **Approximately 40 more lines to go:** When describing the scale of the Optimus manufacturing buildout, Moravy says "we got 40 more to go," referencing the total number of production lines to be installed. He notes the high line count is driven by the many subcomponent lines needed — actuators, limbs, torso, battery, and other subassemblies — in a tributary-to-final-assembly layout that he describes as resembling the unboxed manufacturing philosophy.

3. **Tesla's three advantages in humanoid robotics:** Moravy enumerates what he sees as Tesla's three structural advantages over other humanoid robot companies: (1) scale manufacturing expertise, (2) proprietary design of high-power-density electric motors and actuators that no competitor has, and (3) real-world AI implementation. He pushes back on the investor argument that humanoid robots are more analogous to consumer electronics than automobiles, stating that functional safety requirements, multi-axis mechanical complexity, and supply chain demands make them far more like vehicles.

4. **Limbic resonance as the design priority for first-generation Optimus:** Moravy says that Elon Musk has been emphatic that the first generation of Optimus must achieve "limbic resonance" — meaning it must feel natural and non-threatening in human spaces — before expanding to other form factors. He acknowledges the R2-D2-style (non-humanoid) form factor will likely come eventually but says the C3PO humanoid form must succeed first to drive social acceptance.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD awareness and public perception:** Following a reference by the hosts to a recent FSD-related incident ("what happened on Monday," not further specified), Moravy reaffirms that safety is Tesla's top priority. He argues that public acceptance of autonomous driving will come from direct experience rather than advertising or media coverage, and that Tesla's approach is to "keep calm and carry on" rather than aggressively rebutting negative press. He believes the Cybercab ride-hailing service will ultimately drive adoption by giving people firsthand experience.

2. **"Full Self-Hearing" — autonomous quality inspection on the production line:** Moravy shares that Tesla vehicles now drive themselves from end-of-line to the logistics yard, and also independently traverse the bump, squeak, and rattle track, using onboard microphones to listen for noise issues and automatically document findings for the production team. He calls this capability "full self-hearing" — a play on Full Self-Driving — and describes it as an example of Tesla using its own AI-enabled vehicles to improve manufacturing quality feedback loops.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Model Y global changeover described as historically fast:** Moravy references what he describes as Tesla's simultaneous Model Y refresh across four factories, completed in approximately three to four weeks. He characterizes this as the largest automated product changeover at that scale since Ford's transition between the Model T and Model A, which he notes took Ford six months under very different conditions.

2. **Cybercab vehicle efficiency — 10–15% further improvement targeted:** Moravy acknowledges that Tesla deliberately left some efficiency on the table with the current Cybercab design and believes a further 10–15% improvement in vehicle efficiency is achievable. He describes mass and energy efficiency as a personal passion, noting the downstream unit economics impact of even small per-unit gains.

## Financials

1. **Cybercab cost structure positioned to surprise analysts:** Moravy contends that published business outlooks from firms he mentions — including Ark and Wells Fargo — do not actually understand Cybercab's operational cost efficiency. He predicts that when real-world cost-per-mile figures emerge, they will "blow their minds." He ties this to Tesla's ability to control everything from raw materials to software to charging infrastructure, eliminating layers of margin and waste that competitors cannot.

## Market & Competition

1. **JD Power IQS ranking — Tesla now number three:** Moravy states that JD Power released its Initial Quality Study results approximately two days before the interview, and Tesla ranked number three. He attributes this partly to AI-driven quality anomaly detection on the production line — systems that now connect manufacturing data streams so that upstream processes can be adjusted in near-real-time based on downstream quality signals.

2. **Tariff flexibility through localization:** On tariffs, Moravy notes that Tesla's localized manufacturing largely insulates it from tariff exposure, though he mentions that the Canada situation was more challenging and that Tesla switched which factory was supplying Canada approximately three times in 2026.

3. **Zoox acknowledged as a legitimate competitor:** When discussing clean-sheet autonomous vehicle design, Moravy says that Zoox "gets it" because it also started from a blank sheet of paper, contrasting it favorably with Waymo's approach of adapting existing vehicles.

4. **Starlink integration for Cybercab in rural areas:** Moravy confirms Tesla is exploring Starlink as a connectivity option for Cybercab, particularly for rural coverage, and says it is likely to appear in future versions. He also references a joint project between Tesla and SpaceX called Terafab, describing it as a "joint project for real" that the two companies are working on together, in the context of Starlink's high-volume manufacturing scale-up.

Notable quotes and data:
- "In a week from Tuesday, there'll be some cool news about things happening on the campus of Texas... that's part of the scaling effort." — Lars Moravy (teasing July 7, 2026 announcement)
- "Lines [are] over 90% automated all in." — Lars Moravy on Cybercab factory automation
- "We maybe made 150. I'll stick with that number if that's what you think we built." — Lars Moravy confirming ~150 Cybercabs produced in burst build
- "I think the automation is ahead of schedule actually." — Lars Moravy on Cybercab factory ramp
- "We've left some vehicle efficiency on the table... maybe 10–15% is a good goal to cut out." — Lars Moravy on future Cybercab efficiency improvements
- "We got 40 more [lines] to go." — Lars Moravy on Optimus production line buildout at Fremont
- "The first line has landed... we've already started to install that." — Lars Moravy confirming Optimus line 1 installation begun
- "JD Power came out with this like two days ago. We're like number three in IQS now." — Lars Moravy
- "I think the amount of real world AI that's going to be around you because of us is going to be mind-blowing." — Lars Moravy on the 5-year outlook
- Elon Musk has been pushing autonomous and integrated vehicle strategy since 2014, per Moravy
- Tesla has approximately 140,000 employees, per Moravy
- Cybercab final assembly line is approximately 20–25 cells, versus ~200 cells for a typical general assembly line
- Starship uses Tesla drive units, per Moravy

articles.title: Big Short’s Michael Burry discloses new Tesla (TSLA) position
articles.body:
Michael Burry has disclosed a new short position against Tesla (TSLA), entered at $416.22 on June 30, 2026 — shorting into a roughly 10% intraday rally from Tesla's prior close of $379.71. The position is one leg of a broader basket of shorts Burry opened the same day against what he characterizes as an AI and semiconductor bubble.

## Market & Competition
1. **Burry's Tesla short is part of a multi-name basket:** The disclosure appeared in Burry's paid "Cassandra Unchained" Substack post ("Trading Post June 30, 2026"). Alongside Tesla, he also shorted Caterpillar (CAT) at $1,060.98, Nvidia (NVDA) at $198.09, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) at $642.80, and Applied Materials (AMAT) at $729.40. The bulk of the note focuses on semiconductors: Burry argues the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index is trading more than 65% above its 200-day moving average — a level he says has only been seen once before, in 2000 — and cites a price-to-sales ratio above 16x for the index. He rolled his SOXX puts from January 2027 to March 2027 at low-to-mid $400s strikes while holding QQQ January puts.

2. **No size disclosed; history of misreporting:** Burry did not reveal the dollar figure, share count, or options structure for the TSLA short. The article warns against repeating the 2021 error, when press reported his put options tied to 800,100 Tesla shares as a "$534 million" bet — a figure representing notional value (shares × closing price), not actual capital at risk. Burry covered that position by November 2021.

3. **Continued bearish stance on Tesla valuation:** Burry has remained publicly negative on Tesla, previously calling its valuation "ridiculously overvalued" in December and criticizing the ~$1 trillion pay package shareholders approved. He shut down his hedge fund in late 2025 and launched the Substack to discuss the AI bubble freely.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert agrees Tesla is "grossly overvalued" — trading around 295 times earnings on declining profits with ~3.6% annual dilution — but calls shorting it "super risky," arguing the stock is driven by hype and that a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger narrative gives Musk another catalyst to sustain investor enthusiasm. Lambert views Optimus as "vaporware."

Notable quotes and data:
- Burry: "And finally I shorted Tesla (TSLA) at 416.22. Happy it jumped back to this level."
- Burry: "It is only a matter of time now" (on a semiconductor drawdown)
- Tesla prior session close before the short: $379.71; Burry entered on ~10% intraday rally
- Burry previously called Tesla's dilution "ridiculous" and valuation "ridiculously overvalued" (December)
- Lambert's figures: Tesla ~295x earnings, ~3.6% annual dilution, ~$1 trillion pay package

articles.title: Tesla Stock Soars on Cybercab & FSD Developments ⚡️
articles.body:
This episode of Electrified, hosted by Dillon Loomis, covers a wave of Cybercab deployment signals including the publication of first responder guides, ongoing fleet stockpiling across multiple cities, and a major FSD software milestone with V14 Lite rolling out to Hardware 3 vehicles. The core thesis is that Tesla is nearing meaningful Cybercab deployment in Austin and potentially Houston, while the FSD V14 Lite release for Hardware 3 opens a large incremental monetization opportunity. The video also touches on Waymo's Uber partnership ending in Phoenix and VW's autonomous driving struggles.

## Robotaxi
1. **Cybercab First Responder Guide Now Live — Last Major Pre-Deployment Hurdle Cleared:** The Cybercab first responder guide is now officially published on the Texas Department of Public Safety website, which Dillon Loomis characterizes as the last major hurdle before Tesla can deploy the Cybercab in Austin. He notes that when Tesla uploaded the Model Y first responder guide, deployment followed within a few weeks, but that timeline could be shorter now that the service has been operating for over a year. He cautions that even after deployment, the initial fleet size will likely be under 10 vehicles for at least the first week or two.

2. **Major Announcement Teased for July 7th:** Lars Moravy stated that a "big announcement" related to scaling efforts on the Giga Texas campus is coming on Tuesday, July 7th, though he did not specify what it is. Dillon Loomis interprets this as most likely relating to the Cybercab, but acknowledges it could be any number of things.

3. **Cybercab Houston Launch Rumor — Mid-to-Late July:** Per the host (unconfirmed), a rumor attributed to Kobe Pierce — citing a "very reputable source" — suggests a Cybercab launch in Houston is expected in mid-to-late July. The source also indicated a service area expansion in Houston is coming, potentially encompassing two distinct areas including NRG Stadium and George Bush Intercontinental Airport, with the service area reportedly expected to be roughly 50% larger than Waymo's current Houston service area. The host flags this as speculative.

4. **Cybercab Stockpiling Across Multiple Cities Without Deployment Decals:** Large numbers of Cybercabs are being reported in staging lots across Houston (78 vehicles per SE Robinson), Dallas (dozens visible in a Reddit-shared image), and Phoenix. Critically, none of the vehicles in Houston, Dallas, or Phoenix have the Cybercab word mark decals — which, per the first responder guide, are present on vehicles actually in robotaxi service. This is presented as evidence these vehicles are not yet deployment-ready or cleared for service.

5. **Cybercab Testing at Giga Texas — Fully Autonomous, No Steering Wheel:** Per Joe Tegtmeyer, Cybercabs continue testing on the Giga Texas track, with recent sightings showing vehicles with Cybercab logos being driven fully autonomously. Separately, a Cybercab was spotted at the test track with no steering wheel and a safety monitor on the passenger side.

6. **Austin Robotaxi Fleet at 84 Registered Vehicles:** Per the host's robotaxi dashboard (sourced from RobotaxiTracker.com), Tesla now has 84 vehicles officially registered for the robotaxi service in Austin, with 15 vehicles added on June 27th (Saturday).

7. **Five New Cities Deadline Missed — Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, Las Vegas:** Tesla's Q4 2025 slide deck had targeted the first half of 2026 for launching robotaxi service in five new cities (Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, Las Vegas), but the Q1 2026 slide deck (uploaded in April 2026) downgraded this to "preparations underway." With June 30th being the last day of H1 2026, the host confirms Tesla has missed this self-imposed deadline. He attributes the slowdown to Tesla internally seeing promising results with V15 and deciding to wait for that model before expanding.

8. **Cybercab First Responder Guide — Key Technical Details:** The guide reveals several notable Cybercab specifications: it features a 400V high voltage battery system (not 800V) with the battery enclosure serving as the cabin floor with only a thin high-strength steel layer separating the two; it does run the new 48V low voltage architecture (Etherloop-capable); 10 airbags in the production version (five per side); an active hood pedestrian protection system that activates between approximately 15–32 mph using pyrotechnic actuators; two-way speakers and exterior microphones on the B-pillars; infrared webbing on seat belts for night passenger visibility; and no wireless charging hardware noted anywhere in the documentation. The vehicle can operate on all public and private roadways at all hours and under light-to-moderate precipitation. It is designed to stop and park if a seatbelt becomes unbuckled or a door remains open.

9. **Cybercab Test Vehicles Being Converted to Production Configuration in the Field:** Per Bradford at Rebellionaire (as cited by the host), Tesla has been observed removing the steering wheel and associated hardware from test vehicles to convert them to the production (no-steering-wheel) configuration out in the field.

10. **FSD Responding to Police Hand Signals — Impressive Real-World Demo:** A video shared by DJ showed a Tesla running FSD stopping at a green light because a police officer was directing traffic in the intersection, then proceeding only after the officer waved the vehicle through — with the host noting the car appeared to anticipate the officer's signal slightly before it was given.

11. **Dallas and Houston Unsupervised Service Remains Very Limited:** Dillon Loomis reiterates that since Tesla's April 2026 launch in Dallas and Houston (each with one vehicle), service in those cities has been very limited and sometimes unavailable entirely, suggesting the launches were timed to provide a talking point for Q1 earnings.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **FSD V14 Lite Rolls Out to Hardware 3 Early Access Customers:** A show (unspecified) confirmed FSD V14 Lite is now rolling out to Hardware 3 early access customers, with broader rollout expected over the following few weeks. The build distills the driving behavior from Hardware 4's V14 series into the camera and compute configuration of Hardware 3. It includes destination options and speed profiles on city roads and, most importantly per the notes, significantly improved safety. Elon Musk congratulated the AI team on X, noting that Hardware 3 has only approximately 15% of the effective memory bandwidth of Hardware 4, making this a technically difficult achievement.

2. **V14 Lite Limitations and Missing Features:** V14 Lite for Hardware 3 will not include the MadMax speed profile, the FSD stats app in the car UI, FSD streak counters or celebrations, or the unified smart summon model. Automatic pulling over for emergency vehicles is listed as TBD. Early reviews are described as very positive, and the host notes that Hardware 3 vehicles never received version 13, making this a significant generational leap.

3. **Hardware 3 Fleet Monetization Opportunity:** The host estimates there are somewhere between 3 and 4 million vehicles equipped with Hardware 3. As of recording, fewer than 1% of these vehicles have V14 Lite. He frames this as a meaningful future FSD subscription revenue opportunity, as FSD subscriptions are highly margin-accretive. He suggests Tesla may run another free 30-day FSD trial once the rollout broadens to drive subscription conversions.

## Market & Competition
1. **Waymo Ends Uber Partnership in Phoenix:** Waymo robotaxis are no longer available on Uber's ride-hail app in Phoenix, ending a three-year partnership. Waymo said the vehicles from the Uber pilot have been integrated into its own Phoenix fleet available through the Waymo app. Waymo's vehicles remain available on Uber in Austin and Atlanta, and the two companies are set to compete against each other in London later in 2026.

2. **Uber Teasing a New Autonomous Partner in Phoenix — Speculation Swirls:** Uber announced it is preparing to launch a new autonomous vehicle partnership in Phoenix but did not name the partner. Given the Tesla stock move on the same day, some are speculating Tesla is the unnamed partner. The host says he thinks the most likely candidate is Lucid and Mobileye (Nuro), noting Lucid builds vehicles in Arizona, has said its robotaxi will start operations later this year, and that Uber has already committed to adding approximately 20,000 Lucid vehicles to its fleet over the next few years. The host is skeptical Lucid and its partner will be meaningfully operational this year. He reiterates his long-standing view that Tesla does not need Uber — Uber needs Tesla.

3. **VW Reportedly Ending Autonomous Driving Partnership with Bosch:** Days after VW announced potential layoffs of 100,000 employees and closure of four plants, German reporting citing internal sources indicates VW plans to end its automated driving partnership with Bosch, ending a collaboration launched in 2022 through VW's software unit Cariad. Internal assessments reportedly found the technology was not yet competitive after approximately $1.7 billion invested. VW is said to be seeking a new hardware and software partner. Bosch and Cariad issued a statement saying they do not comment on market rumors. The host suggests the right answer would be Tesla, but speculates it will likely be Nvidia.

4. **Tesla Expands to Uruguay:** Tesla announced it will begin selling vehicles in Uruguay. The host notes light vehicle sales in Uruguay run approximately 6,000 units per month (~75,000/year), with BEVs having reached approximately 20% market share in 2025 (~13,500 BEVs annually). National policies and incentives are favorable toward EVs, though lower-priced Chinese EVs are already present in the market.

5. **NHTSA Closes Power Steering Loss Probe into Tesla:** NHTSA announced it has closed its engineering analysis into Tesla vehicles over power steering loss. The investigation, which began in 2023 and was upgraded to an engineering analysis, was closed following an over-the-air software recall Tesla issued in early 2025. Tesla stated the recall was not in response to NHTSA's investigation.

6. **Munro Live Involvement in Slate Auto:** Munro Live released a video over the weekend revealing it was "seemingly very involved" in the development of Slate Auto's vehicle platform. The host views this as a positive signal for Slate's ability to keep costs low and make sound engineering decisions early on.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla stock closed at $411.84, up 8.46% on the day, vs. the NASDAQ up 2.25%.
- SpaceX closed at $164.19, up 7.15%.
- Austin registered robotaxi fleet: 84 vehicles (per RobotaxiTracker.com), with 15 added on June 27th, 2026.
- Cybercabs spotted in Houston staging: 78 vehicles (per SE Robinson), none with Cybercab decals.
- Hardware 3 estimated vehicle count: between 3 and 4 million (host estimate).
- Hardware 3 has approximately 15% of the effective memory bandwidth of Hardware 4 (per Elon Musk on X).
- Cybercab battery: 400V high voltage system; 48V low voltage system.
- Cybercab production version: 10 airbags (5 per side).
- Active hood pedestrian protection system activates between ~15–32 mph.
- No wireless charging hardware found anywhere in the Cybercab first responder documentation.
- VW/Bosch autonomous driving partnership investment: approximately $1.7 billion.
- Uruguay BEV market share in 2025: approximately 20% (~13,500 BEVs/year).
- SpaceX 2025 revenue: just over $18.6 billion; Elon said he would be "disappointed" if SpaceX didn't significantly exceed projections of ~$37B (2026), ~$68B (2027), ~$97B (2028).
- Lars Moravy: "In a week from Tuesday, there'll be some cool news about things happening on the campus of Texas… it's part of the scaling efforts."
- Host on Cybercab initial fleet size: "I just think based on what we've seen to date, when the Cyber Cab is deployed, it will be at a number under 10 for at least a week, if not a few weeks."

articles.title: The Real Reason Tesla Stock Is Soaring
articles.body:
FutureAzA hosts Brian and Randy analyze the reasons behind Tesla's stock surge of approximately $32/share (roughly 8.5%) on the Monday prior to the video's Tuesday, June 30, 2026 publication. The video systematically works through popular theories — SpaceX collaboration, merger speculation, macro recovery, strong Q2 delivery expectations, and a couple of comedically implausible ones — to separate credible drivers from noise. The hosts ultimately land on anticipated Q2 delivery numbers and macro catch-up buying as the most defensible explanations.

## Market & Competition

1. **Sorting through stock-surge theories:** The hosts review several theories circulating in financial media for the roughly 8.5% single-day stock gain. They dismiss the Barron's-reported SpaceX–Tesla collaboration angle (shared use of Grok 4.5 AI, exploring AI applications on idle Tesla computing power) as too speculative and far-out to move the stock meaningfully in one session. They similarly dismiss a NHTSA closure of a power steering probe affecting roughly 376,000 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles from the 2023 model year — noting the fix had already been delivered via an over-the-air update long before this headline — and a favorable comparison of the Mazda 6E against the Model 3, which they treat as essentially irrelevant to investor decision-making.

2. **SpaceX IPO overhang as a possible factor:** Brian notes that investors who had set aside capital to buy SpaceX shares at the $135 pre-IPO price were largely shut out (receiving far fewer shares than ordered) and declined to chase the stock when it opened above $150. He says some of those investors messaged him to say they rotated back into Tesla. Randy adds that a more meaningful unlock-period effect may arrive in early August, after SpaceX's earnings report, when early SpaceX shareholders could trim positions and naturally redeploy into another Elon Musk company — i.e., Tesla.
