2026-04-30.title: The Tesla Debate Just Got Heated
2026-04-30.body:
This video is a conversational debate between host Brian (Futurazza) and Herbert (from Brighter), addressing widespread investor frustration with Tesla across multiple fronts — FSD/Hardware 3 upgrades, robotaxi delays, the Tesla Semi and Roadster, and AI focus. The core argument is that while delays are real and Elon Musk has repeatedly missed self-imposed milestones, most of these frustrations were already priced into reasonable expectations well before the Q1 2026 earnings call, and the long-term thesis centered on autonomy and robotaxi economics remains intact.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Hardware 3 upgrade path announced:** Herbert, himself a Hardware 3 owner, describes the Q1 2026 earnings call announcement as positive news for the roughly 200,000 remaining Hardware 3 owners in the US (out of an estimated 400,000 original one-time FSD purchasers, with at least half already having upgraded to Hardware 4 cars). Tesla announced two paths: a discount to trade in and purchase a new car, or a direct hardware upgrade of the existing car — new cameras and a new computer — at what Herbert assumes will be Tesla's expense, given that owners paid $8,000–$15,000 for FSD. Tesla said it would need to create "mini factories" in major cities to perform these upgrades, requiring owners to drop off their vehicles for approximately a week.

2. **V14 Light for Hardware 3:** Herbert states that a software update called "V14 light" is expected to drop in June 2026 or sometime later in Q2 2026. He describes it as covering most driving scenarios from parking to highway, and expresses enthusiasm that it will make the car feel like it's "driving itself." He notes his personal experience using the current FSD version in Los Angeles for a week and finding it "flawless."

3. **Unsupervised FSD — region-by-region rollout:** The hosts clarify that Hardware 3 vehicles will not achieve unsupervised FSD capability under the current hardware. However, Herbert notes that if a Hardware 3 car is upgraded to the new hardware and is located in a geography where unsupervised FSD has been approved, it could qualify — since the unsupervised rollout is expected to be region-by-region.

4. **Tesla's AI and compute investment:** Herbert describes Tesla's AI infrastructure as centered on Cortex (described as the second-largest supercomputer in the world after XAI's Colossus) and the under-construction Cortex 2, which he says will be among the largest supercomputers in the world. He frames Tesla's vision-based AI as the "holy grail" — physics-aware, context-aware, and camera-only — and argues no competitor has replicated it at scale. He also mentions Terafab (a joint Tesla/SpaceX chip project) as a major development, allowing Tesla to produce its own GPUs rather than relying entirely on Nvidia, and notes Elon Musk has spent "every single weekend" for the past seven to eight months focused on the AI5 chip before it was "taped out."

5. **Elon's missed predictions — misled but not lied:** Both hosts agree that Elon Musk has repeatedly set FSD and robotaxi milestones that did not materialize — Herbert calls him "the boy who cried FSD" — but both resist calling it dishonest lying, arguing instead that Musk genuinely believed the timelines and always included verbal caveats. They draw comparisons to Toyota, GM, and Waymo executives who made similarly overconfident predictions between 2012 and 2016 about autonomous driving timelines.

## Robotaxi

1. **Earnings call guidance shift — not material in 2026:** Herbert recounts that on the Q1 2026 earnings call, Elon Musk walked back prior guidance suggesting robotaxi would be "meaningfully impacting the bottom line" in the second half of 2026, instead saying it would not be "super material" by end of 2026 but would be material in 2027. Herbert argues this was not surprising — he had already adjusted his expectations in December 2025 after Tesla missed its stated goal of 50% US market access to robotaxi by end of 2025, and after the doubling-every-month cadence Elon cited in January 2026 did not materialize.

2. **Herbert's personal Cybercab fleet estimate for 2026:** Herbert states his own estimate for Cybercab production/deployment by end of 2026 is approximately 15,000 units — a figure he says he has been communicating for months. He contrasts this with more bullish community estimates of 50,000, and uses it to define what "not super material" means in practical terms.

3. **Robotaxi unit economics framing:** Herbert sketches a high-level contrast between Tesla's current car business — generating approximately $5,000–$7,000 in one-time profit per vehicle sale — versus a robotaxi generating approximately $30,000 per year in revenue, recurring for at least three to five years. He frames this transition as the central investment thesis.

4. **Tesla Semi delayed for autonomy integration:** Both hosts converge on the view that the Tesla Semi has been deliberately delayed not due to incompetence but because Tesla is waiting to redesign it for autonomous (robo-trucking) capability. Herbert argues that FSD for commercial trucking will be priced at a substantially higher commercial rate than consumer FSD — analogous to commercial vs. personal Starlink pricing — making the wait worthwhile. He also notes that battery supply constraints in 2020 would have made a full Semi launch impossible regardless.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **20 million unit target abandoned:** The hosts briefly acknowledge that Tesla's previously stated goal of 20 million vehicles per year is no longer in play, citing it among the list of investor grievances without extensive discussion.

2. **Tesla Semi and Roadster as non-priorities:** Herbert frames both the Semi and the Roadster as products that have been de-prioritized in favor of solving autonomy first. He is explicit that the Roadster "shouldn't be the priority" and that the Semi makes far more strategic sense once robo-trucking is ready.

## Market & Competition

1. **Compute constraints hitting AI competitors:** Herbert notes that Anthropic's Claude (referencing "Opus 4.7") has been "nerfed" and "dumbed down" due to compute constraints, while Tesla and XAI are building Cortex 2, Colossus 2, and Colossus 3 — and eventually plan space-based compute infrastructure through a Tesla/SpaceX collaboration. He argues this trajectory will put Tesla/XAI beyond what any Earth-bound competitor can match in AI compute.

2. **Elon distraction narrative dismissed:** Both hosts push back on media narratives that Elon Musk is distracted by SpaceX, Neurolink, or the Boring Company. Herbert argues his role at Neurolink and the Boring Company is likely advisory (an hour or two per week), that Gwen Shotwell runs SpaceX day-to-day effectively, and that Musk's recent intensive focus has been specifically on Tesla's AI5 chip. Brian jokes that even if "distracted," Musk is still working more hours on Tesla than most CEOs work total.

## Financials

1. **Investor frustration is time-horizon dependent:** Herbert segments the Tesla investor base into distinct groups — recent buyers (weeks to months), options traders who expected a post-earnings pop, and long-term holders — and argues that frustration is rational for those who bought in the past two to three years and are sitting on flat or negative returns, but less so for long-term holders. He frames Tesla as a "startup-like" investment where the valuation is predominantly built on promises of future capability, not current earnings.

Notable quotes and data:
- Herbert: "By the end of 2025, 50% of the US market will have access to robo taxi." — Elon's stated target, confirmed missed.
- Herbert: "He said [in January earnings] we should be doubling how many robo taxis are in service in Austin and California every single month." — Confirmed not achieved.
- Herbert on the earnings call shift: "He said 'I don't see it to be super material by the end of this year. It'll be material next year.'"
- Herbert's Cybercab end-of-2026 estimate: ~15,000 units.
- Herbert on robotaxi economics: "$5,000 or $7,000 one-time [car profit] vs. $30,000 per year at the minimum, every year for at least three to five years" for robotaxi.
- Estimated ~400,000 original one-time FSD purchasers in the US; ~200,000 remain on Hardware 3.
- FSD upgrade cost paid by owners: $8,000, $12,000, or $15,000 depending on when purchased.
- V14 light expected: June 2026 or later in Q2 2026.
- Hardware 3 upgrade drop-off time: approximately one week.
- Cortex described as the second-largest supercomputer in the world (after XAI's Colossus).
- Terafab described as a joint Tesla/SpaceX chip manufacturing initiative.
- Brian Wang estimate cited: in a space-based data center, ~80% of costs would be Tesla (chips).

2026-04-30.title: The Used EV Strategy Nobody Talks About
2026-04-30.body:
This video is a recorded talk by a retired biologist and sustainability volunteer in Portland, Oregon, who advocates for buying used electric vehicles as a low-risk, affordable entry point into EV ownership. Her core thesis is that most people overestimate how much range and vehicle capability they actually need for daily driving, and that a used EV — matched carefully to real driving habits — offers exceptional value. The talk is personal and anecdotal rather than data-driven, drawing on her own decade-plus experience owning two minimalist EVs.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Personal EV ownership history — 2007 Zap Zebra:** The speaker's first EV was a 2007 Zap Zebra three-wheeler, a Chinese-made vehicle with a 40 mph top speed, four doors, four seat belts, no airbags, and a 20-mile range using lead-acid batteries. She drove it for eight years, primarily for a 3.5-mile commute and school runs, finding that her typical daily driving was 10 miles and a busy Saturday rarely exceeded 15–20 miles. The vehicle eventually became impossible to maintain due to parts unavailability — each of the three production years used different parts — and she gave it to a hobbyist.

2. **Second EV — 2012 Mitsubishi i-MiEV purchased used:** After eight years with the Zap Zebra, she transitioned to a 2012 Mitsubishi i-MiEV purchased in 2016 from a CarMax in Clackamas for $9,000. The car had only 13,000 miles on it, was 10 miles from her home (drivable without shipping), had a 62-mile EPA range, freeway speeds, and airbags. She has now owned it for approximately 10 years and reports virtually no battery degradation until recently — the car was even reading slightly above its rated range (around 67 miles) until a tire issue arose. The current problem involves a flat tire; Dunlop no longer makes the original tire size, and the heavier Continental replacements have reduced her range to approximately 55 miles.

3. **Core used EV argument — match vehicle to real driving patterns:** The speaker's central recommendation is that buyers should carefully audit their actual daily driving needs before purchasing any EV. She argues that most urban dwellers drive far fewer miles per day than they assume, and that a modest used EV with a shorter range is sufficient for the vast majority of trips. For longer, occasional trips — such as a road trip to national parks — she suggests simply using a gas car or renting, rather than buying a large, expensive EV to cover every possible use case.

4. **Battery longevity and chemistry improvements:** The speaker notes that lithium-ion batteries are dramatically more durable than the lead-acid batteries in her first EV. She observes that battery chemistry has continued to improve over time — becoming less toxic and less reliant on materials from conflict regions — and that her 2012 i-MiEV battery held its charge with minimal degradation for roughly a decade.

5. **Used Nissan Leaf caution — pre-2016 battery cooling issues:** The speaker references a handout from a Washington DC EV group that warns buyers about used Nissan Leafs, noting the handout contained a typo ("pre-2026" instead of "pre-2016"). She explains that Nissan Leafs manufactured before approximately 2016 had inadequate battery cooling systems, making battery pack longevity a concern — especially for cars that originated in hot climates like Arizona. She credits Nissan for being the first automaker to commit fully to selling an electric car to the public without hedging (no fleet-only or lease-only restrictions), but expresses disappointment that Nissan rested on its laurels with range improvements for too long.

6. **Chevy Bolt as high-value option:** The speaker highlights the Chevy Bolt as offering exceptional dollar-per-mile-of-range value, noting the base model is currently around $30,000 new and has approximately 250 miles of range. She notes that consumers complained loudly enough when GM tried to discontinue the Bolt that the company brought it back, which she views as a strong endorsement. She mentions watching for a used Bolt in five to six years at roughly half the new price as her own potential next vehicle.

7. **Automotive industry trend toward luxury over minimalism:** The speaker observes that automakers find it difficult to generate profit margins on minimalist, affordable vehicles and have increasingly shifted toward luxury and feature-heavy models. She uses the example of the Chevy Spark EV — a compliance car sold only in a handful of states with limited cargo space — as a case where GM failed to commit to an affordable EV segment, ultimately discontinuing it in favor of the higher-priced Bolt. She expresses concern that lower-income workers who need basic, affordable transportation to commute are being left behind by this trend.

8. **Local used EV dealership — Platt Auto Group:** The speaker recommends a local Portland-area dealer called Platt Auto Group, located on 99E between Milwaukie and Oregon City, as a starting point for used EV shoppers. She describes them as brand-neutral, no-haggle, knowledgeable about EVs, and thorough in servicing vehicles (e.g., taking a used Bolt to a Chevy dealer to ensure all recalls have been addressed). She states she has personally referred seven buyers to them. She also mentions other channels including Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, and national online platforms (with the caveat of added shipping costs).

9. **Autonomous driving and aging-in-place consideration:** An audience member raised the topic of Tesla's driver-assistance technology as a potential benefit for aging drivers — the idea that advanced safety features could help older individuals remain independent longer. The speaker acknowledged some merit in this argument, noting that safety expectations have progressively increased (from seat belts to airbags and beyond), while also referencing a personal experience riding in a Waymo in Austin that "got us where we needed to go and seemed to be doing it safely." She did not advocate for or against Tesla specifically, noting her own discomfort with the brand without elaborating further.

Notable quotes and data:
- 2007 Zap Zebra: 40 mph top speed, 20-mile range, lead-acid batteries, purchased for approximately $10,000 new
- 2012 Mitsubishi i-MiEV: 62-mile EPA range, purchased used in 2016 for $9,000 with 13,000 miles
- Speaker's typical daily driving: ~10 miles; busy Saturday: 15–20 miles
- i-MiEV battery reading: ~67 miles (above EPA) until recent tire-related range drop to ~55 miles
- Chevy Bolt base model: ~$30,000 new, ~250-mile range
- Nissan Leaf pre-2016: flagged for battery cooling issues, especially cars from hot climates
- Platt Auto Group: speaker has referred 7 buyers; described as brand-neutral, no-haggle, used EV focused
- On Waymo: "It got us where we needed to go and it seemed to be doing it safely"
- Speaker's used EV strategy for next vehicle: "We're looking so that five years from now, we're going to buy one of these cars used for half price"

2026-04-30.title: LIVE: Tesla Robotaxi BREAKS New Record And Market Updates
2026-04-30.body:
In this live session, Jo Bhakdi delivers a bullish update on Tesla's robotaxi rollout, arguing that the deployment of Cybercabs and the growth of the unsupervised robotaxi fleet represent a historic inflection in transportation that the market is undervaluing. He frames the current moment as a rare investment opportunity obscured by retail investor pessimism and short-term earnings noise. The session blends Tesla fundamental analysis with Bhakdi's personal options trading methodology and market commentary.

## Robotaxi

1. **Unsupervised Fleet Hitting New Record — 25 Vehicles Across Three Cities:** Per RobotaxiTracker.com, the unsupervised robotaxi fleet has reached 25 vehicles: 19 in Austin, 3 in Dallas, and 3 in Houston. Bhakdi highlights this as the most important chart to watch, describing it as a decisive and exciting milestone even if still small in absolute terms.

2. **1,800 Unsupervised Robotaxis as the "Forcing Function":** Bhakdi reiterates his thesis that 1,800 deployed robotaxis — primarily unsupervised — represents a "forcing function," not merely an inflection point. At that scale, he calculates the annualized free cash flow contribution would equal approximately 5% of Tesla's entire 2024 free cash flow, making it impossible for even skeptical analysts to ignore. He now estimates this target may be reached by September–November 2026, acknowledging a potential 6-month delay from his earlier projection, but maintains the thesis is intact.

3. **Cybercab Production Ramping at Giga Texas:** Bhakdi references Joe Tegtmeyer's tracking work, noting that Cybercabs are rolling off the production line at Giga Texas at a rate of roughly 10–20 units per day. He predicts production could reach thousands of Cybercabs per month by June 2026. Vehicles have been spotted in Illinois, Massachusetts, Florida, the Bay Area, Texas, Phoenix, and potentially Georgia, suggesting broad geographic pre-deployment distribution. He notes that some Cybercabs are being manufactured and shipped without a steering wheel, which he treats as meaningful signal about their intended autonomous-only use case.

4. **Regulatory Environment Seen as Non-Issue for Scale:** Responding to a viewer arguing that regulation will block Cybercab scaling, Bhakdi disagrees strongly. He contends that in states like Georgia, Arizona, Florida, and Texas, the environment is largely self-regulated with no major hurdles. He frames Cybercab deployment as purely a function of FSD technology quality, not regulatory barriers — with California and New York being the notable exceptions, which he says Tesla does not need in the near term.

5. **Total Addressable Market Requires Replacing Car Ownership:** Bhakdi argues that for Cybercab to justify a multi-trillion-dollar TAM, it must go beyond replacing Uber, Lyft, and taxis — it must eat deeply into personal car ownership and replace public transport. He treats this as the core economic assumption underpinning the long-term Tesla bull case.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD End-to-End Neural Net as the Competitive Moat:** Bhakdi dismisses Waymo and Chinese autonomous competitors by arguing they cannot scale due to technology limitations — relying on what he characterizes as "bandaging and taping" their way to pseudo-success. He contrasts this with Tesla's vision-only, end-to-end FSD neural net system, which he believes is the only architecture capable of true massive scale.

2. **Tesla Semi Autonomy Predicted for 2027:** Bhakdi flags the Tesla Semi as an underappreciated asset, noting that the first production units are now rolling off the line. He argues that highway autonomy for trucking is technically simpler than urban driving (though higher risk) and predicts Tesla will deploy autonomous Semi trucks by 2027. He describes the trucking and rail market as an enormous, largely uncontested TAM with zero autonomous competition currently, and characterizes the Semi as highly profitable.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Semi Now in Production:** Bhakdi highlights that the Tesla Semi has moved beyond prototype phase and into actual production, with a first and second production unit visible. He believes several thousand units will deploy in 2026 and emphasizes the vehicle's 500-mile range as a major competitive advantage in the trucking market.

## Market & Competition

1. **Institutional Investors Holding the Line Post-Earnings:** Bhakdi notes that after Tesla's most recent earnings — which he describes as a beat — institutional investors largely maintained or raised their price targets (citing targets in the range of $500–$600), while retail investors reacted negatively. He finds this role reversal notable and uses it to support his thesis that the market is mispricing Tesla's near-term robotaxi catalyst.

2. **Share Price Probabilistic Scenarios:** Bhakdi outlines his current probabilistic view on Tesla's stock: (1) most likely scenario — stock moves toward $400; (2) second most likely — flat or slight upside; (3) third most likely — runs to $420+ on a catalyst; (4) least likely — drops below $370 and stays there. He describes himself as positioned with short puts at strikes of $372.50, $375, $380, and $385 expiring May 1 and May 4, 2026.

3. **Long-Term Price Target Being Refined Downward for Conservatism:** Bhakdi mentions he is working on a revised long-term Tesla price target that will come in below $6,000 (previously cited by others) but with an additive "plus X" factor for SpaceX exposure. He frames this as a deliberate effort to be conservative on timelines and upgrade later rather than overpromise.

## Financials

1. **Options Strategy — Short Puts as Alpha Engine:** Bhakdi spends significant time explaining his short put options strategy as a tool to engineer returns when he has conviction on a stock's near-term range. He argues short options systematically put the statistical odds in the seller's favor, unlike long options which require precise directional accuracy. He describes collecting approximately $10 in weekly premium on at-the-money short puts at the $380 strike, breaking even down to approximately $370.

Notable quotes and data:
- Active robotaxi fleet: 650 total (Bay Area 543, Austin 101, Dallas 3, Houston 3) per RobotaxiTracker.com
- Unsupervised robotaxi fleet: 25 total (Austin 19, Dallas 3, Houston 3) per RobotaxiTracker.com
- Cybercab production rate cited: "10, 12, 15, 20 Cybercabs per day" rolling off Giga Texas
- Predicted Cybercab monthly production by June 2026: "thousands per month"
- 1,800 unsupervised robotaxis = estimated 5% addition to Tesla's 2024 free cash flow on an annualized basis
- Estimated timeline to reach 1,800 unsupervised robotaxis: September–November 2026
- Institutional price targets cited post-earnings: $500, $580, $600
- Bhakdi's short put strikes: $372.50, $375, $380, $385 (expiring May 1 and May 4, 2026)
- Tesla Semi autonomy prediction: 2027
- Optimus Gen 3 release: described as "90 days" away (implying approximately late July 2026)
- "At 1,800 truly deployed robo taxis unsupervised in full operation, that is an easy $600, $700, $800 share price."
- "It's purely a technology function" (on Cybercab regulatory risk)
- "Zero autonomous competition" in trucking

2026-04-30.title: First Drive: Nissan e-POWER Hybrid System
2026-04-30.body:
This video from Munro Live features host Paul Turnbull test-driving the Nissan e-POWER hybrid system in Farmington Hills, Michigan at Nissan's North American headquarters. The segment covers the technical architecture of Nissan's third-generation series hybrid system and previews its upcoming introduction in the US-market Nissan Rogue later in 2026. The video has no direct connection to Tesla, autonomous driving, or the core TTT investment thesis.

## Market & Competition

1. **Nissan e-POWER Series Hybrid Architecture:** Nissan's e-POWER system is a series hybrid, meaning the wheels are driven purely by an electric motor with no mechanical connection between the gasoline engine and the drivetrain. The engine functions solely as a generator to charge the battery, which then powers the electric motor. This delivers an EV-like driving feel without requiring plug-in charging, while retaining the convenience of gasoline refueling. The system debuted in Japan in 2016 on the Nissan Note.

2. **Third-Generation 5-in-1 Modular Unit:** The third-generation e-POWER system features a 5-in-1 modular unit that integrates components to reduce mass, improve modularity, and increase efficiency. This was described as essential for the US market, which demands higher driving speeds, higher payloads, and longer road-trip capability that earlier-generation systems could not support. Paul Turnbull noted that the integrated design aligns with Munro's philosophy of eliminating excess cables, brackets, and connectors to improve quality and reduce failure points.

3. **US Rogue Launch with All-Wheel Drive:** The European version of the Rogue tested in the video is front-wheel-drive only, with the front motor integrated into the 5-in-1 unit. The US-market Nissan Rogue e-POWER will be offered with all-wheel drive, adding a second electric motor at the rear axle for additional power. Launch is expected later in 2026, described as "later this summer or fall."

4. **NVH Tuning and Engine Behavior:** A known challenge with series hybrids is acoustic disconnection — the engine can run at full power while the vehicle is stationary, which feels unnatural to drivers. Nissan engineers targeted this specifically, tuning the system so the engine shuts off at idle, runs quietly at low speeds, and ramps up in proportion to vehicle power demand. Turnbull noted the engine startup produced virtually no torque bump and minimal noise, calling the transition "seamless."

5. **Powertrain Specs and Competitive Positioning:** The system uses a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine as the generator and an electric motor shared with the Nissan Leaf, producing 210 horsepower. Turnbull argued that because the vehicle does not carry a large battery pack, it avoids excessive weight, allowing the 210 hp to feel adequate. He suggested the 1.5L turbo offers strong thermodynamic efficiency at highway speeds, enabling competitive fuel economy. Turnbull concluded that Toyota and Honda will have difficulty matching the smoothness of this system and that the average buyer could save hundreds of dollars annually on fuel versus a comparable ICE vehicle.

Notable quotes and data:
- "The wheels are purely motor driven. There is no mechanical connection between the gas engine on board and the wheels." — Kurt (Nissan engineer)
- "That'll be later this year, 2026." — Kurt, on the US Rogue e-POWER launch
- "Toyota and Honda should be paying attention to what this car is able to do." — Paul Turnbull
- 210 horsepower output stated for the e-POWER system
- 1.5-liter turbocharged engine used as the onboard generator
- e-POWER system first debuted in Japan in 2016 on the Nissan Note
- Third-generation system features a 5-in-1 modular unit
- US-market Rogue will add a rear electric motor for AWD capability

2026-04-30.title: Daily X Summary (2026-04-30)
2026-04-30.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts were dominated by two major signals: Tesla's unsupervised robotaxi fleet continuing its steady multi-city expansion (now at 24 total vehicles across Austin, Dallas, and Houston), and the official start of Tesla Semi mass production. A FSD V14 Lite update for HW3 owners and an Italian senator formally pushing for FSD approval in Italy added further autonomous driving momentum. The overall tone is bullish across multiple thesis pillars.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Unsupervised Robotaxi Fleet Expansion Accelerating Across Texas:** Tesla's unsupervised Model Y robotaxi fleet grew meaningfully throughout the day, with multiple fleet additions tracked across three Texas cities. By end of day, the total stood at 24 unsupervised vehicles: Austin (19), Dallas (3), and Houston (2), up from an earlier intraday count of 20 (Austin: 16, Dallas: 2, Houston: 2). The continued daily additions — including the first spotted unsupervised unit in Dallas — signal an active, ongoing ramp rather than a static deployment. This is the clearest real-time evidence of Tesla scaling its unsupervised robotaxi operations ahead of any formal commercial launch announcement.

2. **Tesla Semi Mass Production Officially Begins:** A high-engagement post (2.7K likes, 307 retweets) confirmed that Tesla Semi mass production has officially started. The Long Range version specs include: ~500-mile range, 4680 cells, fully electric steering assist (replacing prior hydraulic system), Cybertruck-derived actuators (beefed up), 48-volt architecture, and 3 independent motors on the rear axles. This is a significant milestone for Tesla's commercial vehicle ambitions and validates the Semi program after years of delays, directly rebutting earlier skepticism (e.g., Bill Gates's 2020 claim that electric semis would never be practical).

3. **FSD V14 Lite Rolls Out to HW3 Owners:** Tesla pushed an FSD V14 Lite update specifically for HW3 hardware owners. While no specific capability details were included in the post, this represents an active software release event and signals continued investment in serving the legacy HW3 install base with the latest FSD generation.

4. **Italian Senator Formally Pushes for FSD Approval:** Italian Senator Carlo Calenda filed a formal parliamentary question to Italy's Minister of Infrastructure and Transport, asking whether the government intends to prioritize approval of Tesla's FSD (Supervised) in Italy and urging the minister to evaluate direct action. This is a notable regulatory catalyst development — government-level political advocacy for FSD approval in a major European market.

5. **Tesla Opens Autonomy Pop-Up in Miami Featuring Optimus:** Tesla launched an "Autonomy Pop-Up" event in Miami running April 29–30 (2–6 PM) and May 1–3, 2026 (12–6 PM), with Optimus on display alongside autonomy demonstrations. This is a consumer-facing public engagement effort ahead of what is likely a broader robotaxi or autonomy commercial push, and represents Optimus's continued public visibility role.

6. **Tesla Files to Enter Bulgarian Market:** Tesla officially filed to launch vehicle sales and service in Bulgaria, covering import, operation, distribution, sales, servicing, maintenance, and repair. Minor but incremental market expansion signal.

7. **Competitive Landscape — Ford EV Losses, VW and BMW New Models:** Ford's EV division posted an $800M loss in Q1 2026 (flat year-over-year) on $1.2B in revenue, with a deeply negative EBIT margin of -63%. VW unveiled an all-electric ID. Polo for Europe starting at €24,995, and BMW revealed its new iX3 with up to 434 miles of EPA-expected range starting at $60,000. These updates underscore that traditional OEM EV economics remain severely challenged, while Tesla's cost and software advantages continue to widen.

8. **Figure Humanoid Robot Manufacturing Rate — Competitive Context:** Competing humanoid robot company Figure disclosed it is now manufacturing 55 humanoid robots per week, or roughly one per hour. While this is a competitor metric (not Tesla/Optimus), it establishes a production rate benchmark relevant to evaluating Tesla Optimus's manufacturing ramp by comparison.

9. **China Suspends New Autonomous Vehicle Licenses After Baidu Incident:** China suspended issuing new robotaxi licenses after dozens of Baidu Apollo Go vehicles simultaneously stopped in Wuhan last month, stranding passengers. The suspension prevents self-driving companies from adding new vehicles to Chinese fleets. This is a meaningful competitive/regulatory development — it constrains China-based AV rivals and may create indirect advantages for Tesla's U.S.-focused robotaxi ramp.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — Multiple concurrent thesis catalysts fired today: unsupervised robotaxi fleet actively expanding across Texas cities, Tesla Semi mass production confirmed, FSD V14 Lite released to HW3 owners, and a European regulator formally advocating for FSD approval, while key competitors continue to post heavy losses or face regulatory setbacks.

2026-05-01.title: Tesla’s Timeline Just Shifted
2026-05-01.body:
This episode of "brighterwithherbert" is a roundtable discussion with panelists Jeff Lutz, Alexandra Merz, and Cern Basher reviewing what was accomplished and missed in April 2026, the current state of Tesla's unsupervised robotaxi fleet, upcoming milestones, and broader topics including the Elon Musk vs. Sam Altman/OpenAI trial and Tesla's corporate governance developments. The panel generally maintains a bullish but measured outlook, acknowledging Tesla missed several high-profile April targets while arguing the foundational work for a major autonomous driving and robotics ramp is being laid. A recurring theme is managing investor expectations relative to Tesla's longer-term, potentially double-exponential growth trajectory.

## Robotaxi

1. **Unsupervised Fleet at 26 Vehicles Per RobotaxiTracker.com:** The unsupervised robotaxi fleet now stands at 26 vehicles per RobotaxiTracker.com, up from 17 just a few days prior. The panel acknowledges the tracker may have delays or miscounting, but treats it as the best available public data. Dallas and Houston each have 3 unsupervised vehicles, representing early-stage presence in those cities with teams reportedly hired on the ground. The panel views the recent acceleration in deployment as meaningful, even if absolute numbers remain low.

2. **Android App Launch — Necessary but Limited Impact:** The Tesla robotaxi app is now available on Android, which Alexandra Merz called "the basic minimum" given the iOS app launched approximately nine to ten months earlier. She framed the Android app as part of a third category of requirements for robotaxi success — alongside hardware and software — covering regulatory permits, charging infrastructure, washing, and operational logistics. She noted it sparked some first rides among newly enabled Android users in Austin but expected the excitement to settle quickly given very few vehicles and long wait times.

3. **Cybercab on the Robotaxi Network — Imminent but Uncertain Timing:** The panel discussed when the first Cybercab (VIN zero having already been produced) will be available to hail on the robotaxi network. Jeff Lutz called it "imminent," noting Cybercab validation vehicles are being spotted in multiple cities and states, laying regulatory and operational groundwork. Cern Basher agreed it could be weeks away in Austin. Herbert, however, expressed more caution — suggesting three months or longer — citing the Cybercab as a brand-new form factor with less FSD testing history than the Model Y, and stressing that the first public incidents involving the iconic vehicle would be permanently damaging to brand perception. The panel noted Tesla would likely distribute many of the first hundreds or possibly up to a thousand units internally or to a small trusted user group before broader launch.

4. **Fleet Expansion Strategy — Slow Start, Then Scale:** Jeff Lutz described Tesla's production line for the Cybercab as being engineered to run at several times the speed of the Model Y line (which is capacitized for approximately 1.5 million units per year), with the Cybercab ultimately targeted to be Tesla's highest-volume vehicle. He argued Tesla is building toward a "double exponential" ramp — very slow at the start, then near-vertical — and cautioned against interpreting the current low fleet count as a systemic failure. He predicted Tesla could surpass Waymo's robotaxi count within months in 2026, possibly by 2x or more, if the recent acceleration in deployment continues.

5. **Next Cities on Deck — Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, Las Vegas:** The panel identified Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, and Las Vegas as the next five cities likely to receive robotaxi service, potentially at any moment. Herbert noted Miami's F1 race weekend would have been a high-profile opportunity. He speculated the Florida cities (Miami, Orlando, Tampa) may launch roughly simultaneously. Las Vegas was tied to a later F1 event in the year as a potential target window. The panel debated whether launching with only two or three cars in a city constitutes a true "launch," with Cern suggesting Tesla may need a new internal vocabulary to distinguish first-production-unit milestones from a meaningful public launch.

6. **FSD Supervised Approval in China — Rumored Trump Visit Timing:** Alexandra Merz shared a rumor (explicitly flagged as unconfirmed) that FSD supervised approval in China could be announced around a presidential visit by President Trump approximately two weeks from the recording date, with Elon Musk potentially part of the delegation. She said this would be a logical moment to formalize the launch but emphasized it is speculation. Israel was also mentioned as another market where FSD supervised approval is on deck.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Version 14.3 Rolled Out in April:** FSD version 14.3 did roll out in April 2026 as anticipated. Elon Musk noted on the earnings call that the remaining issues being addressed are not primarily safety concerns but rather convenience and operational quality issues — such as ensuring correct pickup and drop-off locations and eliminating awkward edge-case behaviors. The panel framed this as a positive signal that safety, while always improvable, is no longer the critical gating factor.

2. **10 Billion FSD Miles Milestone Approaching:** Per the FSD miles counter, Tesla is on track to clock 10 billion cumulative FSD miles around May 3, 2026. Cern noted that extrapolating the current counter pace without accounting for growth, Tesla would reach approximately 16.5 billion total miles and about 6.5 billion city miles by year-end 2026. The panel contextualized Elon's prior statement that ~10 billion miles is the threshold at which safety is sufficiently validated for scale deployment — though they stressed safety improvements are continuous (e.g., 5x, then 10x, then 20x safer than a human driver).

3. **Cortex 2 Coming Online:** Part of Cortex 2 (Tesla's AI training supercomputer) came online in April as expected, with fans reportedly already spinning. The panel indicated it may be approaching approximately 50% capacity, though the exact figure is unclear. Full ramp of Cortex 2 remains ongoing.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus Gen 3 Reveal Delayed — Production Timeline Pushed:** The planned Optimus Gen 3 demo/reveal did not occur in April as anticipated. The panel treated this as a delay rather than a cancellation. Cern noted that based on Elon's earnings call comments, the Model S/X (SNX) production line sunsetting — necessary to free up factory space — is expected in May, with the Optimus production line build-out then beginning. Jeff Lutz expressed surprise at a July–August start-of-production timeline for Optimus, suggesting "end of summer" is more realistic. The first Optimus units rolling off the line may not come until late Q3 or Q4 2026. Elon described the transition as a "herculean effort."

2. **Competitive Pressure from China on Humanoid Robots:** Jeff Lutz noted that 2026 is shaping up as a convergence year for humanoid robots, with both Chinese and U.S. competitors targeting several thousand units built this year. The panel agreed Tesla must stay on track with Optimus version 3 and meaningful production volume. Alexandra Merz argued Tesla's strategy of showing less publicly is likely intentional given rampant copycat risk, particularly from China — noting that visual similarities can be manufactured even if functional parity does not exist.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Semi Start of Production — Confirmed or Near-Confirmed:** The Tesla Semi's first unit off the high-volume line was announced, with the panel treating this as effectively equivalent to start of production. A post from Dan Priestley (a Tesla-affiliated account) was cited as using the phrase "start of production," though the panel acknowledged some ambiguity about the precise wording. The panel drew a parallel to the Cybercab's February first-unit-off-line milestone, which was followed by official start of production approximately two months later.

2. **Q1 2026 Backlog and Gross Margins Better Than Expected:** Cern noted that Tesla described its Q1 2026 order backlog as one of the stronger Q1 backlogs in a couple of years. Gross margins were characterized as good across both the automotive and energy segments, with some one-time items — including a warranty true-down — described as constructive rather than concerning. These positives were contrasted with the disappointment around robotaxi fleet growth guidance from the prior earnings call (doubling every 90 days) not being met.

3. **Model S/X Line Sunsetting in May:** Tesla is expected to sunset the Model S and Model X production lines sometime in May 2026 to make way for the Optimus manufacturing line. This was described as a planned transition with significant logistical complexity.

## Market & Competition

1. **Legacy Auto and EV Competitors Struggling:** Jeff Lutz noted that across the broader auto industry, Q1 reporting has been poor for nearly all manufacturers. EV-specific results from competitors were described as "atrocious," with some Western European legacy automakers posting single-digit gross margins — an unusual deterioration. Rivian was noted as a small-volume niche player. Chinese EV names were also described as struggling. Tesla, by contrast, was seen as gaining EV market share. Legacy automakers were criticized for pivoting to hybrids, which Lutz characterized as an inefficient "sugar high" given the cost of dual powertrains.

2. **Vanguard SEC Filing — No Share Sale, Just Restructuring:** Alexandra Merz clarified a Vanguard 13G filing that caused confusion in financial media. Vanguard restructured its operations into two distinct companies; the reporting entity went from 250 million to 210 million Tesla shares, but the second unit (holding the ~40 million shares) did not yet file separately. Total Vanguard holdings are unchanged. The total outstanding share count used by Vanguard in the filing was 3.75 billion, which includes the 2018 restricted shares, the new compensation package, and 2025 restricted shares.

3. **Elon's 2018 Compensation Package — Converted to Restricted Stock:** Alexandra Merz explained that following Tesla's departure from Delaware jurisdiction, the board converted Elon's 2018 stock options (covering 303 million shares, for which all milestones were completed between 2018 and 2022) into restricted stock. These shares are fully accounted for in Tesla's books (no new dilution). Elon now holds full voting rights on these shares. They vest in January 2028, at which point Tesla intends to facilitate a structured repurchase to cover his tax obligation without open-market selling. Elon is required to hold 55% of the remaining shares until 2033. Merz characterized media headlines suggesting Elon was about to sell shares as deliberately misleading.

## Financials

1. **Energy Segment Weak in Q1 — Expected Q2 Recovery:** Cern flagged the energy segment as a miss in Q1 2026, noting management characterized the weakness as "lumpy" rather than systemic. He expressed hope for a strong Q2 energy recovery as a result, while noting it is too early to conclude there is a structural issue. He observed broader demand shifting toward long-duration energy storage.

2. **SpaceX CEO Performance Award — Aggressive Milestones Including Mars Colony:** The board of SpaceX approved a CEO performance award for Elon Musk in January 2026, details of which emerged as SpaceX conducts a roadshow. The ultimate market cap milestone is $7.5 trillion for SpaceX (compared to $8.5 trillion for Tesla — a combined $16 trillion goal). Operational milestones include building a 1-million-person Mars colony and achieving 100 terawatts of compute in space (described as equivalent to 100,000 one-gigawatt nuclear reactors), with 60 million restricted shares tied to the compute milestone. Elon holds 10-to-1 super voting shares in SpaceX. Alexandra Merz speculated that in a Tesla-SpaceX merger scenario, the operational milestones in both packages could potentially disappear while the super-voting rights and market cap milestones would be restructured proportionally — though she noted this is speculation pending review of SpaceX's bylaws.

Notable quotes and data:
- Active unsupervised robotaxi fleet: **26 vehicles** per RobotaxiTracker.com (up from 17 days earlier) — Bay Area, Austin, Dallas (3), Houston (3)
- Cybercab production line designed to run at **several times the speed of the Model Y line** (Model Y capacitized at ~1.5 million units/year); Cybercab targeted as Tesla's **highest-volume vehicle**
- FSD miles: ~**10 billion** expected to clock on approximately **May 3, 2026**; projected to reach ~**16.5 billion total** and ~**6.5 billion city miles** by end of 2026
- SpaceX market cap goal: **$7.5 trillion**; Tesla market cap goal: **$8.5 trillion**; combined: **~$16 trillion**
- SpaceX milestone: **1 million person Mars colony**; **100 terawatts of compute in space** (= ~100,000 one-gigawatt nuclear reactors)
- Elon's 2018 Tesla comp: **303 million shares**, vesting **January 2028**, 55% must be held until **2033**; Elon receives **zero cash** until 2028
- Elon's SpaceX base salary reportedly: **$54,000/year**
- X Money: Missing money transmitter licenses in **8 states** — Florida, Hawaii, Massachusetts, Montana, New Jersey, New York, Washington State, Wisconsin; New York previously withdrew application in 2024 and has not resubmitted
- X Money savings rate reportedly **6%**, deposit limit reportedly **$150,000**; **3% cash back** on card
- Vanguard 13G filing used total Tesla share count of **3.75 billion** (includes all restricted share packages)
- Next robotaxi cities identified: **Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, Las Vegas**
- Optimus production line start: estimated **July–August 2026** per earnings call; Jeff Lutz suggested more likely **end of summer**; first units off line possibly **late Q3 or Q4 2026**
- Jeff Lutz: "If [deployment pace] continues at this pace, it's going to pass the number one provider of robotaxis in months this year. And I still predict that it may surpass it maybe by 2x or more."
- Cern Basher on FSD miles: "We'll be at 16.5 billion by the end of the year... in the city, we'll be at about 6.5 billion."

2026-05-01.title: Uber Just Made Waymo's Trap Worse
2026-05-01.body:
This video features a conversation between Cern Basher and a co-host (Roberto) analyzing Uber's strategic partnership with Waymo and arguing that Uber is fundamentally miscalculating the long-term competitive dynamics of the autonomous vehicle market. The core thesis is that Uber's "hybrid network" model — combining human drivers with autonomous vehicles — is optimized for a transitional phase rather than the end state, and that Tesla's Cybercab will ultimately destroy Waymo's economics while rendering Uber's strategy obsolete. The hosts conclude with the ironic observation that Tesla is effectively becoming "the new Uber" by aggregating demand from a fragmented supply of personal vehicle owners.

## Robotaxi

1. **Waymo's unit economics are structurally broken at scale:** The hosts explain, citing New Street Research, that Waymo commands higher fares per mile than Uber because many customers prefer a driverless ride — but this premium is a finite, skimmable market. As Waymo adds more vehicles to a given city, it exhausts the high-fare opportunity and must accept lower fares per mile while its cost structure remains high. The result is expensive vehicles sitting idle, earning less money — a compounding economic problem. This is why Waymo's rational strategy is to keep expanding to new cities rather than scaling deeply in any single market: it can skim the cream from each new market without facing the idle-fleet penalty.

2. **Uber's "hybrid network" argument applies only to Waymo, not Tesla:** Uber argues that a hybrid model — AVs handling stable base load demand, human drivers filling peak demand spikes — is more efficient than a pure AV fleet, because an AV-only competitor would need to hold significant underutilized supply to match Uber's reliability. The hosts acknowledge this logic is valid for Waymo, which reportedly has roughly 300 vehicles in Austin and cannot economically add more without facing prolonged idle periods during low-demand windows (e.g., Monday through Wednesday). However, they argue Uber is "wishful thinking" by failing to account for Tesla's dramatically lower cost structure.

3. **Cybercab will undercut Waymo and reshape the market entirely:** The hosts argue Tesla's Cybercab, with its extremely low cost to manufacture and operate, will directly compete with Waymo at the premium end of the market — giving consumers who prefer driverless rides a choice between Waymo and Cybercab. Tesla can undercut Waymo's fares easily, destroying Waymo's economic niche. Furthermore, if Tesla can bring fares down to approximately $1.00–$1.50 per mile (compared to Uber's roughly $4–$5 per mile and Waymo's roughly $5 per mile), ride-hailing is no longer an occasional service — it becomes a substitute for personal vehicle ownership for many people, unlocking demand that is not linear but exponential with each incremental price reduction. Uber itself has reportedly said that reducing prices to a certain threshold would 10x their addressable market.

4. **Demand expansion makes the idle-fleet problem disappear for Tesla:** The hosts argue that at sufficiently low price points, the demand curve shifts so dramatically that a city could support not 300 or 500 vehicles but 1,000 or 10,000 vehicles operating at stable, full utilization — eliminating the idle-fleet penalty that constrains Waymo. This is the end state Tesla is optimizing for, whereas Uber is optimizing for the transition phase.

5. **Tesla as the new Uber — aggregating fragmented personal vehicle supply:** The hosts note the irony that Tesla is effectively replicating Uber's original model, but in reverse: rather than recruiting human drivers, Tesla is reaching out to personal vehicle owners and offering to pay them (described hypothetically as something like $5 per hour or per minute) for access to their cars during periods of peak demand. This allows Tesla to aggregate a fragmented supply of vehicles on demand, functioning as a platform operator in the same way Uber aggregated human drivers.

6. **Robotaxi as a multi-use platform beyond ride-hailing:** The hosts argue Tesla's robotaxi is not merely a ride-hailing tool but a platform for a wide range of services not yet fully identified — drawing a parallel to how every major new technology platform has spawned unanticipated use cases. One specifically highlighted emerging use case is deploying these vehicles as **mobile compute nodes**, which the hosts describe as an increasingly significant and promising advantage for Tesla, though the economics of this use case are not yet known.

7. **Uber is optimizing for the transition, Tesla for the end state:** The hosts argue Uber's miscalculation is assuming time is on its side — that regulations will be slow, edge cases will persist, and the transition to full autonomy will take a decade or more. Tesla, by contrast, is building toward the end state where AVs dominate entirely, and while the transition phase may be frustrating for Tesla shareholders, the end-state rewards are where the real value lies.

## Market & Competition

1. **Waymo's selective Uber partnership reveals strategic inconsistency:** Waymo has partnered with Uber in Austin (and possibly one other city), allowing Uber app users to be matched with a Waymo vehicle when available. However, Waymo has also launched in multiple new cities without Uber partnerships, which the hosts argue undermines Uber's core claim that the hybrid model is essential for AV operators. If the hybrid model were truly critical, Waymo would use it everywhere.

2. **Price per mile comparison across competitors:** The hosts reference approximate fare benchmarks: Uber is characterized at roughly $4 per mile (human driver cost basis), Waymo at roughly $5 per mile (premium driverless niche), and Tesla's potential target range at $1.00–$1.50 per mile — with Ark Invest cited as projecting approximately $0.70 per mile. The cost of personal vehicle ownership is discussed as ranging from roughly $0.50 per mile (paid-off vehicle, easy use) to $1.50 per mile (subprime auto borrower), making Tesla's potential price point competitive with or cheaper than car ownership for many consumers.

Notable quotes and data:
- Waymo fare: approximately $5 per mile (premium over Uber's ~$4 per mile)
- Tesla Cybercab target fare range: ~$1.00–$1.50 per mile (hosts' estimate); Ark Invest projects ~$0.70/mile
- Personal vehicle cost of ownership: ~$0.50–$1.50 per mile depending on individual circumstances
- Uber has reportedly stated that reducing fares to a certain price point would 10x their addressable market
- Waymo Austin fleet estimated at approximately 300 vehicles (hosts' rough estimate, used illustratively)
- New Street Research cited as the source for analysis of Waymo's deteriorating unit economics at scale
- "Tesla is the new Uber" — Roberto and Cern Basher, on Tesla aggregating personal vehicle owner supply
- "Uber's optimizing for the transition phase. They're not optimizing for the end state. Tesla is optimizing for the end state."
- Mobile compute nodes described as "increasingly appearing to be a significant advantage for Tesla"

2026-05-01.title: Tesla (TSLA) reveals $573M web of transactions between Elon Musk’s companies
2026-05-01.body:
Tesla's amended 10-K/A filing (submitted to the SEC on April 30, 2026) reveals $573.4 million in revenue from Elon Musk's other companies in fiscal year 2025, alongside tens of millions in expenses paid to entities Musk controls, plus a $2 billion equity investment that converted from xAI stock into SpaceX stock.

## Financials
1. **Related-party revenue totals $573.4 million:** Tesla recognized $430.1 million in revenue from xAI — primarily Megapack sales to power xAI's data centers — and $143.3 million from SpaceX, primarily vehicle sales. Megapack sales to xAI continued into 2026, with $78.1 million in additional revenue recognized through February alone. Tesla's total 2025 revenue was approximately $97.7 billion, making the xAI Megapack sales alone roughly 3.4% of Tesla's entire energy segment revenue.

2. **Expenses paid to Musk-affiliated entities:** Tesla paid $11.4 million to SpaceX under commercial, licensing, and support agreements; $400,000 for use of a SpaceX aircraft; $4 million to xAI for consulting and support; $3.3 million to X (formerly Twitter) for advertising; $900,000 to The Boring Company under commercial agreements; and $4.8 million to a Musk-owned security company for services provided to Musk, including in connection with his Tesla duties. Total expenses to Musk-affiliated entities: $24.8 million.

3. **$2 billion investment converts from xAI to SpaceX equity:** On January 16, 2026, Tesla agreed to invest $2 billion in xAI Holdings' Series E round. After SpaceX subsequently acquired xAI Holdings, Tesla's xAI preferred stock converted into SpaceX Class A common stock. Tesla completed the investment on March 12, 2026. The filing does not disclose Tesla's resulting stake, though reporting indicates it is less than 1% of SpaceX.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **SpaceX Cybertruck purchases inflate sales figures:** SpaceX purchased 1,279 Cybertrucks in Q4 2025 alone — representing 18% of all U.S. Cybertruck registrations that quarter — at a time when the Cybertruck was facing weak consumer demand. These purchases account for the bulk of the $143.3 million in revenue Tesla recognized from SpaceX.

## Energy
1. **Megapack sales to xAI are material to energy segment:** The $430.1 million in Megapack revenue from xAI in 2025, plus $78.1 million already recognized in early 2026, represents a significant and ongoing related-party revenue stream. The filing states transactions were conducted at rates generally available to unaffiliated third parties and were reviewed by Tesla's Audit Committee.

## Editorial Stance
Electrek views the cumulative scale of related-party entanglement as a genuine governance concern — not because any individual transaction is unreasonable on its face, but because Tesla's CEO controls counterparties on both sides of hundreds of millions of dollars in transactions, and a shareholder-approved $2 billion AI investment ultimately converted into stock in yet another Musk-controlled company, raising questions about whether Audit Committee review constitutes sufficient oversight.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla revenue from Musk entities (2025): $573.4M ($430.1M xAI + $143.3M SpaceX)
- Tesla expenses to Musk entities (2025): $24.8M total
- xAI Megapack revenue as % of Tesla energy segment: ~3.4%
- SpaceX Cybertruck purchases: 1,279 units in Q4 2025 = 18% of U.S. Cybertruck registrations that quarter
- $2 billion xAI investment completed March 12, 2026; converted to SpaceX Class A common stock; stake reportedly <1% of SpaceX
- Tesla also disclosed $3.3M paid to Redwood Materials (JB Straubel's battery recycling firm) and $12.9M in cost-of-revenue reductions from selling scrap to Redwood
- Filing states all transactions were at "rates generally available to unaffiliated third parties" and reviewed by Audit Committee

2026-05-01.title: Tesla launches Basecharger for Semi, reveals $188,000 Megacharger
2026-05-01.body:
Tesla has launched a "Semi Charging for Business" program enabling fleet operators to purchase and install two distinct Semi charging products: the existing Megacharger and a new lower-power Basecharger. The program includes transparent pricing via an online configurator and a per-kWh fee structure for revenue-generating sites.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Two-product Semi charging lineup:** Tesla is offering the Megacharger (up to 1.2 MW, adds ~60% range in 30 minutes) for en-route fast charging and the new Basecharger (125 kW, adds ~60% range in four hours) for depot and overnight use. Both use the open MCS 3.2 standard and support ISO 15118-2 and OCPI protocols — not locked to Tesla's ecosystem. Payment terminals are optional on both units.

## Energy
2. **Megacharger pricing and specs:** The minimum purchase is two Megacharger posts, starting at $188,000 excluding taxes and installation. The cabinet delivers 1,200 kW shared across two posts, weighs 1,100 kg, and operates at greater than 96% efficiency with cable runs up to 100 meters. The Megacharger is already being deployed, with 66 planned locations and the first public station open in Ontario, California.

3. **Basecharger pricing and availability:** The Basecharger starts at $40,000 — a compact 100 kg unit (340 × 1200 × 2000 mm) with a 6-meter cable, suited for depot layouts. Deliveries are estimated to begin in early 2027. For revenue-generating sites, Tesla charges $0.08/kWh all-inclusive — lower than the $0.10/kWh fee on the Supercharger for Business program.

## Market & Competition
4. **Competitive landscape and Tesla's positioning:** Kempower has deployed MCS-capable infrastructure in California (up to 1.2 MW at EV Realty's hub in San Bernardino); ABB and ChargePoint have announced MCS support but have not deployed at scale in the US. Tesla's vertical integration — building trucks, chargers, and operating a network — is its stated differentiator. MCS 3.2 compliance means Daimler, Volvo, and Scania MCS-compatible trucks could theoretically use Tesla's hardware.

## Editorial Stance
Electrek views the Basecharger as the more strategically significant product, arguing depot charging has been the bigger bottleneck for fleet electrification. The author notes the $0.08/kWh network fee is higher than Tesla's original 2017 claim of $0.07/kWh total electricity cost for Semi customers, which Electrek had previously flagged as unrealistic.

Notable quotes and data:
- Megacharger starting price: **$188,000** for two posts (excl. taxes and installation)
- Basecharger starting price: **$40,000**
- Revenue-site fee: **$0.08/kWh** (vs. $0.10/kWh for Supercharger for Business — 20% cheaper)
- Megacharger: **1.2 MW**, 60% range in **30 minutes**; Basecharger: **125 kW**, 60% range in **4 hours**
- Basecharger delivery estimated: **early 2027**
- Tesla Megacharger network: **66 planned locations**; first public station in **Ontario, California**
- Original 2017 Tesla Semi electricity cost claim: **$0.07/kWh** (now superseded)

2026-05-01.title: Tesla Is Becoming The Ultimate Machine
2026-05-01.body:
This video is a tour of Unplugged Performance, an aftermarket Tesla modification shop located near SpaceX's Hawthorne facility in Los Angeles. The host, Brian of Futurazza, speaks with company representatives Ben and Danny about the most popular Tesla modifications, their Pikes Peak race car, and their growing police/law enforcement vehicle program. The video's core thesis is that Teslas are highly customizable platforms that can be upgraded for performance, comfort, off-road use, and law enforcement applications.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Unplugged Performance Background and Tesla Focus:** Unplugged Performance started 26 years ago focused on Japanese sports cars, but pivoted toward Tesla modifications after becoming neighbors with Tesla's design studio in 2013. The company now offers close to 1,000 products for Tesla vehicles, covering suspension, wheels, brakes, wraps, police upfits, and motorsports builds. Ben emphasizes that Tesla's continuous over-the-air firmware upgrades are considered "untouchable" — Unplugged Performance does not attempt to modify powertrain software.

2. **Luxury Suspension for Model Y — Most Popular Consumer Modification:** The most popular consumer product is the luxury suspension kit for the pre-refresh Model Y, which softens the ride without invasive chassis changes. Ben notes it can be installed and removed the same day, and describes it as making older Model Y models feel comparable to the refreshed version. He attributes the original stiffness to spring rates and damping rigidity, and says the kit hits the right balance of valving and spring rate without requiring bushing replacement.

3. **Road Warrior Wheels — Lifetime Guarantee, Aerodynamic, and Indestructible:** Unplugged Performance's Road Warrior forged aluminum wheels come with a lifetime guarantee against damage, a claim they back up by noting zero replacement wheels have been needed by law enforcement clients who intentionally drive over curbs. The wheels also feature an integrated aerodynamic design (described as an "aero disk") that users report saves meaningful range. A curb guard accessory pops on and off for additional protection.

4. **Lowering for Range Gains:** Ben states that lowering a Model Y by one inch can yield approximately 7–10% range improvement by reducing the coefficient of drag. He references published data comparing one-inch, one-and-a-half-inch, and two-inch drops. He notes that Tesla's air-suspension vehicles (Model S, Model X, Cybertruck) automatically lower at highway speeds for the same reason.

5. **Pikes Peak Race Car "Dark Helmet" — Factory Firmware, Unlimited Class Winner:** The company built a heavily modified Tesla Model S Plaid called "Dark Helmet" that won Pikes Peak competing in the unlimited class against LMP4 race cars, open-wheel cars, and gasoline-powered cars with over 1,000 horsepower. The car runs factory Tesla firmware and technically retains FSD capability, though Ben jokes it is not a practical FSD use case. It generates 4,000 lbs (two tons) of downforce, runs 19x13-inch wide wheels with 350-wide tires front and rear, and features Öhlins TTX four-way adjustable coilovers. The main weakness is battery and drivetrain heat management, as the factory firmware still enforces thermal limits. During qualifying at Pikes Peak (approximately 70 cars total), Dark Helmet consistently placed in the top 15 of all categories and came within approximately one second of a multi-million dollar Porsche 935 motorsports car.

6. **Law Enforcement Cybertruck and Model Y Police Upfits — Rapidly Growing Segment:** Unplugged Performance is currently building hundreds of Cybertruck patrol vehicles alongside Model Y police units. Ben says demand is surging partly due to rising gas prices. Police departments benefit from lower fuel costs, no idling losses, low center of gravity, and instant torque that ends pursuits faster because suspects cannot pull away. The company hosts EVOC (Emergency Vehicle Operations Course) training events to let officers experience the vehicles firsthand. Most departments are currently ordering all-wheel-drive Model Y configurations; a newer standard all-wheel-drive trim (launched less than two months prior to filming) is expected to become the majority choice due to its lower price — approximately $7,000 less than the premium all-wheel-drive trim — while still being suitable for law enforcement use. Zero wheel damage has been recorded across all law enforcement deployments despite intentional curb strikes.

7. **Other Popular Modifications and Products:** Beyond suspension and wheels, Unplugged Performance does a high volume of camber arm adjustments (for Model S, X, 3, and Y) to correct tire wear, sway bar upgrades for sharper handling response, steel bullbars, side-step rockers, and steel bumpers for Cybertruck, and full vehicle wraps. All modifications are designed to be installable by any standard mechanic shop without specialized tools. Products ship worldwide.

8. **Commentary on the Robotaxi Future and Car Ownership:** Ben briefly reflects that people are currently in a window where they can buy, modify, and enjoy personal vehicles, but that the coming robotaxi era will reduce personal car ownership over time. He frames this as a reason to enjoy car modification while it lasts.

Notable quotes and data:
- "We're building hundreds of Cybertruck patrol vehicles right now, as well as a whole bunch of Model Y that we're getting out there." — Ben
- "A 1-inch drop is actually a really good thing... somewhere in the neighborhood of 7 to 10% range [improvement]."
- "4,000 lbs of downforce" on Dark Helmet; "factory firmware, technically has FSD."
- "Within a second of the Porsche 935, which is a couple million dollar Porsche motorsports car."
- "70 cars in total" at Pikes Peak; Dark Helmet "in the top 15 of every category for qualifying."
- "Zero replacement wheels" supplied to law enforcement despite intentional curb abuse.
- Standard all-wheel-drive Model Y trim is approximately $7,000 less than premium all-wheel-drive trim.
- Close to 1,000 products in Unplugged Performance's catalog.
- Road Warrior wheels have been shipping for approximately 6 months or more as of filming.
- "Someday people aren't going to be buying cars... we're getting into this robotaxi world where there's going to be less and less of that." — Ben

2026-05-01.title: Merger Rumors Reach Peak Fever, but I'm not feeling it - Tesla Beat Friday News
2026-05-01.body:
This weekly Tesla news roundup from the "futureaza" channel covers a broad range of topics including the OpenAI trial involving Elon Musk, Cybercab production updates, FSD V14 rollout plans, the Samsung chip factory ceremony in Taylor, Texas, Giga Berlin milestones, Tesla Semi production ramp, and Optimus building permits at Tesla's north campus. The hosts — joined by co-hosts Brian and Matthew — maintain a broadly bullish thesis on Tesla's autonomous driving and robotaxi future while expressing skepticism toward competitors like Waymo and GM's self-driving timeline claims.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD V14 Light Coming to Hardware 3 and International Markets:** Tesla posted on X announcing that following the future rollout of FSD V14 Light for Hardware 3 vehicles in the US, the company plans to expand V14 to additional international markets. This update is intended to ensure Hardware 3 vehicles continue receiving ongoing software updates. The hosts confirmed that as of the recording, V14 Light had not yet rolled out to Hardware 3 in the US. The international rollout is subject to regulatory approval, and Tesla stated it cannot provide definitive dates at this time.

2. **GM's 2028 Full Self-Driving Claim Met with Heavy Skepticism:** GM announced that its cars will drive themselves by 2028. The hosts were dismissive, noting that virtually every automaker and software company made similar claims targeting 2020 back in 2012–2016 — including Nissan — and none delivered. The panel argued GM has no credible path to achieve this and that the AI landscape is evolving so rapidly that whatever GM is building now will likely be obsolete by 2028.

3. **Tickets for Autonomous Vehicle Violations:** The panel discussed emerging policy around issuing traffic violations to autonomous vehicles. A recent incident involving a Waymo being part of a multi-car collision — and appearing to drive away — was cited as a key example. The hosts argued it is reasonable and necessary to hold autonomous vehicles accountable for traffic law violations, just as human drivers are held accountable.

4. **FSD on Cybertruck Through San Francisco:** The host shared a personal experience using FSD on his Cybertruck on a challenging route through downtown San Francisco, including Lombard Street, noting the system performed smoothly on steep inclines that limit the driver's own line of sight. The anecdote was used to illustrate FSD's sensory advantages over human drivers.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab Is in Production:** The hosts confirmed that Cybercab production has begun, with an estimated roughly a dozen Cybercabs being produced per day currently. One host argued this already exceeds the daily rate at which Waymo is adding vehicles to its fleet. The expectation expressed is that production will scale to 100 vehicles per day and eventually 1,000 vehicles per day. Many units are reportedly rolling off the production line without a steering wheel or pedals, which the hosts interpreted as a signal that Elon Musk is confident in FSD's readiness for unsupervised public road deployment.

2. **Cybercab Individual Ownership Debate:** The panel debated whether Cybercabs should be sold to individual customers. One host argued they are too valuable to sell privately and should be kept in the fleet. Another saw a limited case for selling to individuals in remote or rural markets where Tesla has no interest in operating its own fleet — such as small hotels or rural areas — or to customers who simply want personal ownership. A third host noted that Elon Musk has publicly commented that the Cybercab would be available for sale by end of next year, with the panel suggesting that realistically means 2028 at the earliest, with a handful of private sales potentially starting in 2028–2029.

3. **Waymo's Fleet Scaling Limitations Highlighted:** The hosts argued that Waymo, despite having a larger current fleet, faces a fundamental manufacturing bottleneck: its vehicle platform (the Jaguar I-Pace) is out of production, has no finalized next design, and Waymo has no scalable pipeline to add new vehicles. By contrast, Tesla's Cybercab is purpose-built for mass production at scale.

4. **Unsupervised Robotaxi Expansion Underway:** The hosts noted that Tesla is actively launching unsupervised robotaxi operations in new cities, referencing three cities in Texas where unsupervised FSD is currently active using Model Y vehicles with Hardware 4. They acknowledged that regulatory hurdles remain significant but expressed confidence the expansion is progressing.

5. **Cruz/Uber Failures as Cautionary Backdrop:** The hosts referenced Cruise's shutdown following its incident where a vehicle dragged a pedestrian, noting the real failure was the cover-up rather than the accident itself. Uber's earlier exit from autonomous driving after a single serious incident was also cited. These were framed as cautionary examples of how fragile public trust is in this space.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus Building Permits Filed at Tesla North Campus:** Joe Tegtmeyer reported that building permits have been filed in Travis County related to groundbreaking activity at Tesla's northwest campus, specifically for Optimus production facilities. The hosts expressed surprise at the speed of land preparation, noting the site appeared to have been cleared and prepped very rapidly.

2. **Neuralink Patients Control Robotic Arm:** The hosts highlighted a recent demonstration in which Neuralink patients were able to control a robotic arm, performing tasks such as putting on hats. This was framed as a significant milestone in human-machine integration, building on the freedom Neuralink has already provided to paralyzed patients.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Giga Berlin Reaches 1 Million Drive Units Built:** Giga Berlin announced it has produced 1 million drive units — a milestone the hosts celebrated as evidence of Tesla's continued global manufacturing scale, even if Giga Berlin's volumes remain well below Giga Shanghai's.

2. **Tesla Semi Production Has Officially Begun:** Tesla Semi production has commenced, with footage from Zanegler confirming the facility has moved from a dirt lot to an active manufacturing floor. The hosts noted that at a landed cost of around $300,000, electric semis make financial sense for fleet operators, while legacy competitors like Freightliner are pricing their electric semis in the $400,000–$500,000 range. Freightliner's eCascadia production reportedly dropped from approximately 1,000 units in the prior year to a target of around 100 units this year.

3. **Model X Is the Fastest-Selling Used Vehicle in the US:** Used Model X vehicles are reportedly selling faster than any other used vehicle in the United States, including gas-powered cars. The hosts attributed this partly to tax refund season and the growing consumer appeal of a vehicle that can drive itself, especially as older used Tesla models become more affordable.

4. **Model Y Long (Model Y L) Coming to US and Expanding Globally:** Strong signals suggest the Model Y L — first launched in China — is coming to the US, based on a Tesla webpage listing and recent visits by prominent Tesla YouTubers (Kyle Connor and others) to Chinese showrooms. The hosts also noted the Model Y L is now available in India. They speculated Tesla is deliberately not announcing the US launch yet to avoid cannibalizing current Model Y sales ("Osborning" the product).

5. **Supercharger Virtual Queue Feature Launched:** Tesla has built out a virtual queue feature for Superchargers, allowing owners to join a digital queue when a Supercharger is at capacity rather than waiting in a physical line. The system will manage charge order based on when vehicles joined the queue. The hosts noted this has been a long-requested feature and will require user adoption and in-vehicle prompting to work effectively.

## Market & Competition

1. **Samsung Equipment Move-In Ceremony for AI4 Chips:** Samsung held an equipment move-in ceremony at its Taylor, Texas chip plant, formally installing chip-making machines that will begin producing Tesla's AI4 self-driving chips and products for other customers later in 2026. The facility represents a nearly $37 billion investment and was approximately two years delayed after breaking ground in late 2022. Elon Musk had reportedly toured the factory with Samsung executives prior to the ceremony.

2. **SpaceX Solar Cell Factory Revealed in Bastrop, Texas:** SpaceX is constructing what is described as one of the world's most advanced solar cell factories in Bastrop, Texas. A job posting for a SpaceX Director of Solar Production was cited as evidence of active recruiting. The hosts found this surprising and noted it adds credibility to ongoing Tesla-SpaceX merger speculation, as solar is a natural fit for Tesla Energy's product ecosystem.

3. **Tesla-SpaceX Merger Speculation Remains Elevated:** Merger rumors between Tesla and SpaceX have intensified following the Terafab announcement (combining xAI and SpaceX data infrastructure) and now the SpaceX solar factory news. One host noted that new SpaceX compensation guidelines for Elon — including goals around a data center constellation and putting a million people on Mars — make the merger puzzle harder to solve, since you don't need to merge companies to do business together. Elon reportedly liked a post on X by a user making a detailed case for why a merger is feasible.

4. **Boring Company to Take Over Montreal Infrastructure in Las Vegas:** The Boring Company has announced it will take control of the existing Las Vegas Monorail infrastructure when it reaches end-of-life in a few years. Plans include removing the existing rail tracks, laying precast road on top, and integrating it into the Vegas Loop network. The hosts noted this will dramatically increase the visibility of Tesla vehicles operating in the Vegas Loop, serving as a major advertisement for Tesla given the volume of international visitors.

5. **Union and Legislative Pushback on Autonomous Vehicles:** A union for Uber drivers in Seattle has formed and is protesting autonomous vehicles. Montana legislation was also referenced that would require semi-trucks to maintain a human driver behind the wheel. The hosts acknowledged this as a near-term political reality while arguing such restrictions should not become permanent policy.

Notable quotes and data:
- Cybercab current production: approximately a dozen units per day, per host estimate
- Samsung Taylor, Texas chip plant investment: ~$37 billion; broke ground late 2022; ~2-year delay
- Elon reportedly invested $38 million in OpenAI (figure cited in court proceedings); seeking $150 billion in damages and restoration to nonprofit status
- Freightliner eCascadia production: ~1,000 units last year → targeting ~100 units this year
- Electric semi break-even cost threshold cited: ~$300,000 landed cost; legacy competitors pricing at $400,000–$500,000
- Elon has publicly stated Cybercab will be available for sale "by end of next year" (implying end of 2026/2027 per Elon's framing)
- Three Texas cities confirmed with unsupervised FSD active (Austin, Dallas, Houston implied)
- Giga Berlin: 1 million drive units produced milestone reached
- "I don't think we should sell a single one to private customers. These things are too valuable." — host on Cybercab fleet strategy
- "Waymo can't add thousands. There's no mechanism to do that. The I-Pace is out of production." — host on Waymo's scaling limitations

2026-05-01.title: How THIS Investment Method BEAT Tesla And The Stock Market Since 2023
2026-05-01.body:
This video, published by Jo Bhakdi on his "jobhakdi" / Pioneer Lands channel, presents his proprietary investment methodology — which he calls the "Pioneer Alpha / Pioneer Lens" method — explaining how it has outperformed both Tesla and the S&P 500 since inception in early 2024.
