The fleet is currently averaging 1,000 miles every 3 seconds, equating to approximately 28.8 million FSD miles per day. A follow-up post provided important context on the pace of accumulation: it took 5.5 years for the fleet to reach the first 10 billion miles, but the fleet is now adding another 10 billion miles every 11.5 months — a dramatic compression in the time required to generate each successive data tranche. This exponentially growing real-world data pipeline is a core input to Tesla's FSD improvement flywheel and a key competitive moat.

2. **Unsupervised Robotaxi Fleet Continues Daily Expansion:** Two separate posts documented incremental growth in Tesla's unsupervised (driverless) Model Y robotaxi fleet. As of approximately 15:00–15:19 UTC on May 3, RobotaxiTracker.com reported the unsupervised fleet had grown to 29 vehicles, up from 26, with the breakdown: Austin 20, Houston 5, Dallas 4. Two newly confirmed additions were one vehicle in Dallas and one in Houston, with a potential third in Houston pending confirmation. By end of day (per RobotaxiTracker.com canonical data as of 2026-05-03), the unsupervised fleet had reached 32 vehicles across Austin (21), Dallas (5), and Houston (6) — reflecting continued intraday additions. The broader active robotaxi fleet (all modes, including supervised) stands at 663 per RobotaxiTracker.com, with Bay Area (550), Austin (102), Dallas (5), and Houston (6).

3. **FSD V14.3.2 Rollout — Two Waves:** Merritt flagged two separate rollout waves of FSD V14.3.2 on the same day. An early wave (03:52 UTC) went to Tesla owners with AI4 hardware and included a redesigned FSD popup interface. A second broader wave went out later (20:38 UTC). The back-to-back waves within a single day suggest an active staged rollout. No specific capability changes beyond the redesigned popup were detailed in the posts.

4. **Tesla Semi Spotted at ACT Expo (Las Vegas):** A Tesla Semi was spotted at the Las Vegas Convention Center ahead of the ACT Expo — described as the largest North American trade show for advanced commercial vehicles. Notably, the Semi features three cameras on each side mirror and an additional front bumper camera. No pricing, production timeline, or delivery updates were included, but the trade show presence signals Tesla's continued push into the commercial trucking segment.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — The 10-billion FSD mile milestone with a sharply accelerating data run-rate, combined with daily driverless robotaxi fleet additions across three cities, reinforces the core autonomous driving thesis ahead of what is expected to be a critical commercial ramp period.

2026-05-05.title: Elon Musk Is Thinking Bigger Than You Realize
2026-05-05.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel features host Herbert and guest Jeff Lutz — a multi-decade supply chain executive, former chief quality officer, and current CEO of a high-tech manufacturing consulting firm — discussing Elon Musk's long-term ambitions across Tesla, SpaceX, and his broader portfolio of companies. The central thesis is that Musk's seemingly outsized goals (including a "10 trillion or bust" net worth declaration) are better understood as milestone-driven resource allocation rather than personal wealth accumulation, and that his pattern of scaling the "impossible" — from Starlink to Full Self-Driving to Optimus — is a deliberate and rational strategy. The conversation spans humanoid robotics competitive dynamics, SpaceX's anticipated IPO, the economics of cost-per-kilogram to orbit, and why FSD at scale could have an impact comparable to solving a major disease.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **FSD as a decade-long marathon now bearing fruit:** Jeff Lutz notes that Full Self-Driving was widely criticized as a repeated failure for approximately ten years, but frames the current moment as vindication — the technology is now "starting to happen." He argues that once FSD and robotaxi services reach mass scale, the societal impact could rival major medical breakthroughs, given that car accidents are one of the leading causes of emergency room visits. He emphasizes that Tesla's AI team should receive significant credit for addressing a problem that has been "killing and maiming people for decades."

2. **Autonomy cash flow as the financial backstop for Optimus risk:** Lutz argues that by the time Optimus is genuinely scaling, Tesla's autonomy business will be "throwing off so much cash" that the capital risk of the humanoid program becomes relatively small. This framing positions FSD/robotaxi revenue as the financial foundation that de-risks Tesla's most capital-intensive moonshots.

## Robotaxi
1. **Robotaxi scale as the tipping point for public and regulatory perception:** The hosts discuss the predictable arc of public reaction to Tesla's autonomous ambitions — first "impossible," then "only a couple cars, who cares," and eventually "it's unfair he controls everything." Lutz advises investors to plan for this cycle rather than be surprised by it. The conversation frames unsupervised FSD and robotaxi deployment as the catalyst that will most visibly demonstrate Tesla's AI leadership.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus production scale targets referenced:** Herbert describes Tesla as currently "building massive factories" for Optimus, referencing targets of 1 million units per year at Fremont and 10 million units per year at a larger facility. Lutz cautions that Tesla would "stair step" capacity investment over time in line with market acceptance, rather than committing full capex upfront — reducing enterprise-level risk.

2. **Lutz's competitive filter — only one or two humanoid companies will succeed at scale:** Lutz draws a direct parallel to the Chinese EV market, where roughly 80–100 companies started and only one or two are genuinely viable businesses. He argues the same dynamic will play out in humanoid robotics. To succeed at scale, a company needs: proven mass manufacturing capability, vertical integration, strong engineering assets, proprietary AI/autonomy capability, and ideally its own chip (to avoid paying what he characterizes as ~70% gross margin to Nvidia/Jensen Huang). He estimates 80–90% of companies currently showcasing humanoid robots will either never reach market or never become a real business.

3. **Labor arbitrage paradox — humanoids more economically compelling in the West than in China:** Lutz identifies a counterintuitive dynamic: the business case for humanoid robots is actually stronger in the US and Western Europe, where displacing $55/hour union labor yields an immediate, large ROI. In China, where labor costs are roughly $3.50–$5.00/hour, the economics require a much longer curve before humanoids become profitable. He notes that China also faces political disincentives to displace large numbers of workers. Lutz acknowledges China's supply base advantage in components like linear actuators and planetary rollers, but argues the US needs to develop its own supply chain in these areas.

4. **$44 trillion labor replacement TAM cited:** Herbert references the humanoid robotics total addressable market as $44 trillion in labor replacement value, arguing this creates more room for multiple profitable competitors than the EV market does — though Lutz ultimately disagrees and maintains the winner pool will be small.

5. **Tesla's structural advantages vs. all other humanoid entrants:** Lutz argues that Tesla uniquely possesses under one roof (or one CEO): proven scaling ability, manufacturing capacity, vertical integration, engineering talent, autonomy software, AI capability, and proprietary chip design. He states no other humanoid competitor currently combines all of these, and acquiring them independently would be extraordinarily difficult.

## Market & Competition
1. **China's AI model gap smaller than assumed, but physical AI lead is more considerable:** Lutz states that on the language model side of AI, China is approximately 3–6 months behind leading US models — a much smaller gap than commonly assumed. However, he argues the US lead on "physical AI" (robotics, embodied intelligence) is more substantial, which is a key factor in the humanoid competition.

2. **Chinese EV market as a cautionary parallel for humanoid hype:** Lutz pushes back on media narratives that portray 10 Chinese EV companies as global threats, noting most are unprofitable and lack a viable business model. He uses this as a template for how humanoid robot coverage will likely inflate the apparent competitive field before reality narrows it to a handful of true contenders.

## Financials (SpaceX / Broader Elon Portfolio)
1. **SpaceX IPO targeting $1.75 trillion valuation, $75 billion raise:** Herbert cites Arc Fund data and road show activity pointing to a $1.75 trillion market cap target for the SpaceX IPO and a planned $75 billion capital raise. Starlink currently has 10 million subscribers. SpaceX is executing approximately 165 launches per year (nearly one every two days), with that cadence expected to at least double. SpaceX accounts for approximately 85% of all spacecraft deployed globally.

2. **S&P 500 fast-track rule changes could force massive index buying within 6 months of IPO:** S&P Dow Jones Indices has officially proposed rule changes for mega-cap companies that would allow SpaceX to be added to the S&P 500 as soon as 6 months after its IPO (down from the previous 12-month minimum), with waivers on public float requirements and profitability requirements. Lutz notes that index inclusion would trigger forced buying from pension funds, university endowments, and other institutional index-tracking vehicles — potentially representing hundreds of billions of dollars in demand.

3. **Elon's "10 trillion or bust" framing contextualized:** Herbert references Peter Diamandis's observation that Elon Musk's net worth recently crossed $800 billion, approximately 2.7% of US GDP — matching John D. Rockefeller's proportional wealth in 1913. Lutz emphasizes that Musk's stated "10 trillion or bust" is milestone-based, not cash accumulation — and that his Tesla compensation structure includes lock-up provisions preventing him from selling shares for 5 years after exercising options.

4. **Starship cost-per-kilogram targets — 500x reduction from shuttle era:** Herbert cites data showing Falcon 9 reduced cost-per-kilogram to orbit from ~$54,500 (Space Shuttle era) to ~$1,500. Starship targets ~$100 per kilogram — a roughly 500x total reduction over 25 years from the shuttle era. Lutz frames this as Elon's signature approach: only enter a category if you can deliver an order-of-magnitude improvement.

5. **Arc Fund's SpaceX weighting and $160 billion Starlink TAM:** Arc Fund has allocated SpaceX as 17% of its venture fund. The estimated TAM for Starlink at scale is cited as $160 billion.

Notable quotes and data:
- Elon Musk: "It is impossible to become a multiplanetary civilization without reusable rockets, just as it would have been impossible to colonize America without reusable boats."
- Elon Musk (on net worth): "10 trillion or bust."
- Jeff Lutz: "There's no other company that actually has the assets under one roof or one CEO that Elon has."
- Jeff Lutz on Optimus risk: "If this were 2020, I think the Optimus project could sink Tesla, to be honest with you."
- Jeff Lutz on humanoid winners: "I think 80 or 90% of those things either never get to market or they're never a business success at all."
- Yan Tatasai (Tesla AI executive): "It is widely misunderstood that Elon's crazy for running so many companies. In fact, he's rolling out as many trajectories as possible in a given unit of time and performing group policy optimizations."
- Sundar Pichai (Google CEO): "Data centers in space will be the new normal within a decade."
- SpaceX: ~10 million Starlink subscribers; ~165 launches/year in 2025; ~85% of global spacecraft deployed
- Falcon 9 cost to orbit: ~$1,500/kg vs. Space Shuttle era ~$54,500/kg; Starship target: ~$100/kg
- SpaceX IPO target valuation: $1.75 trillion; planned raise: $75 billion
- Starlink TAM at scale: $160 billion (Arc Fund estimate)
- Arc Fund SpaceX position: 17% of fund weighting
- US union labor displaced by humanoids: ~$55/hour; China labor: ~$3.50–$5.00/hour
- Humanoid robot labor replacement TAM cited: $44 trillion
- S&P 500 fast-track: 6 months post-IPO eligibility (proposed rule change for mega-caps)
- Google ownership of SpaceX: ~7–8% stake mentioned

2026-05-05.title: This July Law Makes FSD Essential
2026-05-05.body:
This video from brighterwithherbert features host Herbert and guest Jo Bhakdi discussing a cluster of Tesla-related developments: new robotaxi hiring signals pointing to Las Vegas and Doral, Florida as next expansion cities; a major EU regulatory meeting on FSD approval; an upcoming EU law mandating driver monitoring systems in every new car by July 2026; and Cybercab production and deployment progress at Giga Texas. The core thesis is that converging signals — FSD readiness, hiring patterns, Cybercab production ramp, and regulatory tailwinds — suggest Tesla's robotaxi network is on the verge of a significant expansion.

## Robotaxi

1. **Hiring signals point to Las Vegas and Doral, Florida as next unsupervised robotaxi cities:** Tesla is actively hiring robotaxi field response specialists in Doral, Florida and Las Vegas, Nevada — the same roles it staffed in Dallas and Houston ahead of those cities' launches. Herbert and Jo Bhakdi interpret this as a strong signal that unsupervised robotaxi service in these two cities is imminent. Bhakdi notes that field operators are only needed once actual deployment begins, reinforcing the view that something is already in motion.

2. **Current unsupervised robotaxi fleet is small but scaling across three cities:** Bhakdi references the current unsupervised robotaxi footprint in Austin, Houston, and Dallas, noting figures of roughly 25 in Austin, and five and six vehicles respectively in Houston and Dallas (consistent with RobotaxiTracker.com data). He characterizes this as "mini scaling" that is happening fast and serves as proof of concept for broader rollout.

3. **Cybercab integration into the robotaxi fleet debated — timeline likely months, not weeks:** Herbert argues that Cybercab cannot enter the robotaxi fleet immediately because, as a brand-new vehicle with no existing fleet data, Tesla will need hundreds or potentially thousands of Cybercabs accumulating real-world miles before a public robotaxi launch. A first-week accident would be catastrophic for brand perception. Bhakdi partially agrees but counters that the camera layout, Hardware 4 chip, and control systems are nearly identical to Model Y, meaning the FSD fine-tuning required is minimal rather than a year-long effort.

4. **Fleet size projections for Cybercab robotaxi by end of 2026:** Bhakdi and Herbert converge on an estimate of 10,000–15,000 Cybercabs deployed as robotaxis by end of 2026. Bhakdi notes that even using the painful Cybertruck ramp as a worst-case analog — which reached roughly 30,000 units in its first nine months — a Cybercab ramp (described as easier to produce) cut in half still yields 15,000 units. Herbert reiterates his consistent estimate of 10,000–15,000 Cybercab robotaxis deployed by year-end.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **EU regulatory vote on FSD approval set for late June or early October 2026:** The European Commission's TCMV (Technical Committee for Motor Vehicles) held a meeting in Brussels where the Dutch RDW presented 18 months and 1 million miles of FSD testing results to EU member states. A vote to approve FSD across the entire EU — without requiring individual country retesting — is expected at either the late June or early October meeting. Approval requires at least 15 of 27 countries representing at least 65% of the EU population.

2. **Belgium's Flanders region moves immediately to fast-track FSD approval:** Immediately following the Brussels meeting, the Minister of Mobility for Flanders, Belgium posted that she had asked Tesla to transfer its FSD test dossier to her administration, with instructions to provide clarity on a rapid homologation process by end of the week. Herbert and Bhakdi note she is responsible for Flanders specifically, not all of Belgium, but characterize the move as a meaningful early signal of regional appetite for approval.

3. **Bhakdi assigns 30–50% probability to EU-wide FSD approval, calls it an upside surprise:** Bhakdi's base case is that the EU rejects the proposal, given institutional inertia, though he puts the odds of approval at somewhere between 30% and just under 50%. He frames EU-wide approval as a significant upside surprise. If the EU rejects it, he expects multiple individual countries — including the Netherlands, Czech Republic, Sweden, and potentially Bavaria — to approve FSD independently in 2026, driven by competitive pressure among regions to attract innovation.

4. **FSD performance in European urban environments highlighted via video:** The segment includes footage of Keith using FSD in Amsterdam, navigating extremely tight streets, cyclists, narrow bridges, and dense urban conditions. Both Herbert and Bhakdi express genuine amazement at FSD's ability to handle environments as varied as Amsterdam's canals, San Francisco, rural South Dakota, and China — characterizing it as evidence of a deeply generalized AI rather than a route-memorization system.

5. **FSD v13/14.3 cited as an important breakthrough enabling faster iteration:** Bhakdi references FSD version 14.3 as a significant milestone, describing it as a revamp that enabled high iteration speed and noting that the system is now proven to work at the level needed for unsupervised deployment.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cybercab production at Giga Texas observed at 25–30 units on-site, with vehicles being transported away:** Joe Tegtmeyer's drone footage identified between 25 and 30 Cybercabs around Giga Texas, including at the factory exit point and outbound lot, with many being transported away over the prior week. Vehicles have been spotted on roads, supercharging, and in surrounding areas. Herbert and Bhakdi estimate current production at roughly 10–25 units per day, implying 300–500+ per month, and project this will scale rapidly. Bhakdi believes the cumulative number of Cybercabs already outside the factory is likely well over 200.

2. **Cybercab easier to produce than Cybertruck due to unboxed manufacturing method:** Bhakdi emphasizes that Cybercabs are being produced using Tesla's unboxed manufacturing method and are structurally simpler than Cybertruck, making them easier and faster to ramp. He uses Cybertruck's first-year production of roughly 30,000 units over nine months as a conservative floor for what Cybercab production could achieve, noting Cybercab should be significantly easier.

## Market & Competition

1. **EU mandatory driver monitoring law takes effect July 7, 2026 — applies to all new car registrations:** A regulation stemming from EU law (referenced as EU 2019/2014) requires that every new car registered in the EU from July 7, 2026 onward must include a mandatory driver monitoring system — interior cameras tracking eye movement, head position, and attention levels, with mandatory alerts for distraction or drowsiness. This applies to all manufacturers, not just Tesla. Herbert frames this as creating a bifurcation: either a car drives itself (FSD), or drivers face constant monitoring nags, making FSD a more attractive proposition.

2. **Ford filing driver monitoring patents in the US, including emotion and biometric sensing:** Ford has filed multiple patents related to in-cabin driver monitoring, including a distracted driving detection patent (2020), driver fatigue prevention patent (2022), and a lip-reading, facial expression, and emotion sensing patent filed in April 2026, as well as an in-cabin biometric system patent. A video clip from another creator warns that Ford's patents envision preventing the vehicle from shifting out of park if onboard sensors detect the driver is emotionally unfit to drive.

3. **Broader privacy and civil liberties concerns raised around vehicle AI and government access:** Bhakdi raises substantive concerns about the trajectory of in-car AI surveillance, arguing that driver monitoring systems — while starting benign — create infrastructure that governments could compel automakers to use for tracking, locking vehicles, or routing them. He specifically flags risks in the EU and China, noting that Tesla (and Optimus) operating at scale will face government pressure to cooperate with law enforcement or censorship mandates. Herbert partially pushes back, noting that smartphones and smart TVs already enable similar surveillance, though Bhakdi distinguishes physical vehicle control as a qualitatively new risk.

Notable quotes and data:
- Bhakdi: "I think 14.3 was kind of an important breakthrough because now we have high iteration speed."
- Bhakdi on EU FSD approval odds: "30 to 50%... it's under 50% because the EU, they're masters in [bureaucracy]."
- Herbert on Cybercab robotaxi timeline: "My number — I'm at 10,000–15,000 Cybercabs, therefore 10–15,000 robotaxis by the end of the year."
- Bhakdi: "Even the slowest possible scale — Cybertruck would get you to 30,000 Cybercabs in year one with nine months. Cut that in half, then it's more than 15,000."
- Flanders Minister of Mobility (via Keith's post): "I have asked Tesla to transfer their file to us... I have instructed [my administration] to provide clarity by end of the week on a possible rapid homologation."
- RobotaxiTracker.com canonical data: Active robotaxi fleet 664 (Bay Area 551, Austin 102, Dallas 5, Houston 6); Unsupervised fleet 36 (Austin 25, Dallas 5, Houston 6) as of 2026-05-05.
- EU driver monitoring regulation: mandatory for all new car registrations from July 7, 2026.
- Cybercab units spotted at Giga Texas: 25–30, with many being transported away.
- Bhakdi estimate of Cybercabs already outside factory: "probably over 200."
- Current estimated Cybercab production rate: 10–25 units/day (implying 300–500+/month).

2026-05-05.title: Tesla Semi lands 60-truck order from port drayage fleets in California
2026-05-05.body:
Two California port trucking operators — Big F Transport (40 units) and NICA Container Freight Line (20 units) — have placed a combined 60-truck Tesla Semi order through Forum Mobility, marking one of the largest drayage-sector fleet commitments for the Semi to date. Both fleets will operate out of Forum Mobility's FM Santa Fe depot in Rancho Dominguez, California, expected to begin operations in early 2027.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **60-truck combined order from port drayage operators:** Big F Transport committed to 40 units and NICA Container Freight Line ordered 20, both to be deployed from Forum Mobility's charging depot in Rancho Dominguez. Big F Transport notably already operates nine Daimler eCascadia trucks and conducted real-world Tesla Semi testing before switching — a direct competitive comparison that Tesla apparently won. NICA Container, a family-owned company founded in 2014, operates out of the Ports of Long Beach, Los Angeles, and Houston.

2. **Nevada Gigafactory production ramp underway:** Tesla confirmed last week that the first Semi rolled off its new high-volume production line at Gigafactory Nevada — a 1.7-million-square-foot facility designed for annual capacity of 50,000 trucks. The Long Range model is priced at $290,000 (500-mile range); the Standard Range is approximately $260,000 (325-mile range), per quotes obtained by Electrek.

3. **Dominant demand signal in California voucher program:** In California's Clean Truck & Bus Voucher program between January 2025 and February 2026, the Tesla Semi accounted for 965 of 1,067 applications. Daimler, PACCAR, and Volvo combined received fewer than 100. Port drayage is emerging as the Tesla Semi's primary early market, with additional pilots and deliveries from MDB Transportation and Hight Logistics at the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach.

## Market & Competition

4. **Charging infrastructure ecosystem expanding:** Tesla has revealed 64 Megacharger locations across 15 states and launched its Semi Charging for Business program, with Megacharger units starting at $188,000 for two posts. Forum Mobility — backed by Amazon's Climate Pledge Fund, Edison International, and Obvious Ventures, with $15 million in Series A funding and a $400 million joint venture with CBRE Investment Management — operates as a third-party charging depot provider targeting smaller drayage carriers. The FM Santa Fe depot will feature 14 megawatt-class chargers supporting over 200 zero-emission trucks. Forum Mobility plans to commission four additional shared depots in 2026 and into 2027.

## Editorial Stance
Electrek's Fred Lambert argues port drayage is the ideal beachhead market for the Tesla Semi given short, predictable routes and favorable TCO math in California. He flags production execution — not demand — as the key risk: Tesla's Nevada factory just began ramping and must prove it can deliver at scale.

**Notable quotes and data:**
- 60 total trucks ordered: Big F Transport (40), NICA Container (20)
- Operations expected to begin: early 2027, FM Santa Fe depot, Rancho Dominguez, CA
- Gigafactory Nevada annual capacity: 50,000 trucks
- Long Range Semi price: $290,000 / 500 miles; Standard Range: ~$260,000 / 325 miles
- California voucher program: Tesla Semi — 965 of 1,067 applications (Jan 2025–Feb 2026)
- Daimler, PACCAR, Volvo combined: fewer than 100 voucher applications in same period
- Forum Mobility funding: $15M Series A; $400M JV with CBRE Investment Management
- Megacharger units: starting at $188,000 for two posts; 64 locations across 15 states

2026-05-05.title: I Spoke to Regulators: Tesla's Unsupervised Timeline ⚡️
2026-05-05.body:
This episode of Electrified, hosted by Dillon Loomis, covers a wide range of Tesla-related developments with a particular focus on the regulatory landscape for Tesla's unsupervised robotaxi operations — both in California and Texas. The central thesis is that California's evolving AV rulemaking process means Tesla's true unsupervised paid robotaxi service there is unlikely before 2027, while Texas operations are gradually expanding. Additional topics include FSD software rollout, Cybercab production observations, the Model Y L sighting in the US, Figure's humanoid robot progress, Tesla Semi charging infrastructure, and new California AV regulations that will affect all AV operators.

## Robotaxi

1. **California Regulatory Status — No AV Permit Applied For:** Dillon Loomis contacted the CPUC (referred to as the "CPU") in California and received an official response confirming Tesla has not applied for any autonomous vehicle permits. Tesla currently operates under a TCP (Transportation Charter Party permit), which classifies the service as a chauffeur/limousine-type operation rather than a true autonomous vehicle service in California's eyes. Loomis believes the reason Tesla has not yet applied is that new rulemaking is underway at the CPUC specifically covering autonomous vehicle passenger transportation services, and Tesla has been confirmed to be making public commentary on those proposed rules — suggesting Tesla is trying to shape the regulatory framework before formally entering it.

2. **California Unsupervised Timeline Pushed to 2027:** Based on the regulatory situation, Loomis estimates it will be at least 6 to 9 months — and possibly longer — before Tesla sees an actual unsupervised paid customer ride service in California. He notes that other companies like Waymo have historically taken 6 to 9 months to obtain a true AV permit. He does allow for the possibility that Tesla could hit the 50,000 miles of AV testing California currently requires sometime later in 2026, but concludes that a commercial unsupervised paid service in California is unlikely until sometime in 2027.

3. **Austin Expands to Evening Unsupervised Hours:** Tesla's robotaxis in Austin began operating unsupervised in the evenings for the first time as of the prior Sunday, a meaningful operational expansion. Previously, unsupervised operation in Austin ended in the mid-afternoon. Loomis notes that a majority of Tesla's incidents reported to NHTSA under the SGO standing order did occur at night, making evening expansion a notable safety and operational milestone to watch.

4. **Fleet Count and New City Ramp — Houston and Dallas:** Per RobotaxiTracker.com, the unsupervised robotaxi fleet stands at 35 total: 24 in Austin, 6 in Houston, and 5 in Dallas. Tesla's official robotaxi website lists service hours of 6:00 a.m. to 2:00 a.m. Central time, but Loomis notes anecdotal reports suggest Houston robotaxis are not starting until 9:00 a.m., and that the new cities are likely shutting down well before 2:00 a.m. He expects Tesla to reach 10 to 15 unsupervised vehicles in both Houston and Dallas within the next two to three weeks, describing growth as slow but in line with expectations.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Tesla Crosses 10 Billion Supervised FSD Miles:** Tesla officially crossed the 10 billion miles driven mark on supervised Full Self-Driving. Loomis contextualizes this as equivalent to driving coast to coast in the US roughly 3.5 million times. However, he cautions this milestone does not appear to be a "light switch" moment for scaling unsupervised operations, walking back an earlier period of optimism on that front.

2. **FSD 14.3.2 Rolling Out, Not Yet Wide Release:** FSD version 14.3.2 is being rolled out to additional AI4 customers in North America, with the fleet estimated at roughly 55–60% having received the update. Early user feedback is mixed — most early recipients report no major issues, but some users report degraded performance compared to the 14.2 branch, including jittery behavior, start-stop issues, and at least one instance of the system requesting an immediate takeover. The intervene popup was also modified again. Loomis concludes the software is approaching but has not yet reached a true wide release.

3. **FSD Subscription Expands in Netherlands; Outright Purchase Ending:** After launching FSD subscriptions in the Netherlands last month, Tesla announced it will end the one-time FSD outright purchase option as of May 15th, 2026, leaving the monthly subscription as the only option. Tesla also reported that Netherlands owners drove 10 million km on supervised Full Self-Driving in under one month — approximately 6.2 million miles, or just over 200,000 miles per day.

4. **New California AV Regulations Effective July 1, 2026:** The California DMV announced that law enforcement will be allowed to issue tickets directly to autonomous vehicle manufacturers for traffic violations starting July 1st. New rules include: a required 50,000-mile safety test before a commercial permit is issued; remote operations personnel must meet state licensing and training requirements; vehicles must have an onboard communication system enabling first responders to reach a company representative within 30 seconds; and local officials can enact temporary electronic geofencing zones to exclude AVs during emergencies. Loomis notes these rules would have put Waymo in trouble had they been in place for the past two years, referencing past incidents of Waymo vehicles stalling in San Francisco streets and blocking first responders, and the revelation that some Waymo safety operators were based in the Philippines.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Figure 3 Robot — Capabilities and Production Rate:** Figure released extensive factory access and promotional content for its Figure 3 humanoid robot. Key specs: approximately 130 lbs, 5'6" tall, with a foam/clothing outer layer, fifth-generation hands with palm-mounted cameras and improved grip, able to lift 40 lb boxes, 4–5 hours battery life per charge, and about 1 hour to recharge via wireless inductive charging through foot pads at 2 kW total. All movement is controlled by their Helix 2.0 neural network. The current production facility has a stated capacity of 40,000–50,000 units per year at full capacity, with a long-term goal of one million units per year. Brett Adcock stated they produced 55 humanoid robots in one week, suggesting a rate of roughly 1 to 200 robots per week, up from one per day just 120 days prior. New customer announcements are expected within the next 90 days.

2. **Tesla Model X Line Shutting Down for Optimus Production:** Tesla shared a photo of the last Model X ever produced, consistent with Elon Musk's statement on the earnings call that the S/X production lines would be shut down in May to prepare for Optimus production. This signals a concrete step in factory conversion for Optimus manufacturing.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cybercab Production Rate — Early Stage:** Joe Tegtmeyer reported approximately 25 to 30 Cybercabs located around the Giga Texas site early Monday, implying a current production rate of roughly 5 to 15 units per day at this early stage.

2. **Model Y L Spotted in the United States:** Multiple reports have emerged of Tesla testing the Model Y L in the US, specifically in Palo Alto. Loomis notes that months ago a source told him the Model Y L was indeed coming to the US despite Elon Musk's skeptical comments. He views these sightings as a strong indication of an imminent US launch and notes the timing would be well-suited to fill the gap left by the shutting down of the Model X line.

3. **Model 3 Pricing in Canada Drops Significantly:** Following Canada signing a deal with China reducing import tariffs on Chinese EVs from 100% down to 6%, the Model 3 from Giga Shanghai is now available in Canada at approximately CAD equivalent of $29,000 USD for the premium rear-wheel drive variant — described as the lowest pricing seen in some time in North America. The performance variant also dropped over 15%. The 6% tariff rate is capped at approximately 49,000 vehicles per year on a first-come, first-served basis, growing to about 70,000 by 2030. The Model 3 from China does not qualify for Canada's $5,000 EV incentive.

4. **Tesla Semi — Major Washington State Rebate and Charging Infrastructure:** Washington State announced a $175,000 rebate (via the WEZI program) for Class 8 electric trucks including the long-range Tesla Semi. If the long-range Tesla Semi costs approximately $290,000, this rebate would bring the effective price down to roughly $115,000 — below the average cost of a new diesel Class 8 truck (~$175,000). Additionally, Tesla's semi-charging suite now includes the 1.2 MW Megacharger for quick stops and a new 125 kW base charger for longer dwell/overnight charging. The base charger has no separate cabinet, uses V4 post and electronics components, features a 6-meter cable (vs. 3 meters on the Megacharger), and up to three units can be daisy-chained on a single breaker. One base charger costs approximately $20,000; one Megacharger approximately $94,000. The base charger can add up to 60% range in 4 hours. Deliveries of the base charger are estimated to begin early 2027. For revenue-generating charging sites, Tesla charges an all-inclusive fee of 8 cents per kWh (not the retail price end customers pay). Big F Transport ordered 40 Tesla Semi units through Forum Mobility, to operate out of a depot in Rancho Dominguez expected to go online in Q1 2027.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla European Registrations Rebounding:** Tesla's European registrations reportedly jumped 111% in Sweden, 102% in Denmark, 112% in France, and 23% in the Netherlands in April. Loomis cautions this is single-month data and more noise than signal, preferring to wait for Q2 year-to-date figures. He notes Europe's overall BEV share of new car registrations reached 20.5% in Q1 2026, up from 13.2% in Q1 2025, trending toward 25%.

Notable quotes and data:
- CPUC official response: *"We have not received any applications from Tesla for any CPU autonomous vehicle permits."*
- Unsupervised fleet per RobotaxiTracker.com: 35 total — 24 Austin, 6 Houston, 5 Dallas (as of ~May 4, 2026)
- Tesla FSD supervised miles milestone: 10 billion miles driven
- FSD 14.3.2 rollout: ~55–60% of AI4 fleet
- Netherlands FSD: 10 million km driven in under one month (~200,000 miles/day)
- Figure 3: 40–50K unit/year factory capacity; 55 robots produced in one week
- Washington State Tesla Semi rebate: $175,000, reducing effective price from ~$290,000 to ~$115,000
- Cybercab observed units at Giga Texas: ~25–30, implying ~5–15/day production rate
- Tesla stock closed at $392.51, up 4.3%, on volume 30% below average
- Canada Model 3 (from Giga Shanghai): ~$29,000 USD equivalent after tariff reduction to 6%
- Base charger: ~$20,000 each; Megacharger: ~$94,000 each; Tesla charges site owners 8¢/kWh all-inclusive fee

2026-05-05.title: Elon's Battle With The $130 Billion Charity Scam
2026-05-05.body:
This video from the farzad-fm channel covers the landmark federal trial — Elon Musk versus Sam Altman and OpenAI — which officially began on April 27th, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The core thesis is that this case is far more consequential than a billionaire feud or an "AI trial": it is a foundational legal challenge to whether a 501(c)(3) public charity can convert itself into a for-profit entity while insiders pocket equity, a question whose answer will shape nonprofit law in America for the next century. The host frames this as one of the most important legal precedents in modern history, touching every hospital system, university endowment, religious institution, and charitable foundation in the country.

## Market & Competition

1. **The Trial's Origins and Core Legal Question:** The trial began April 27th, 2026, with jury selection underway before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, who will make the final binding call on liability and remedies — the nine-juror advisory verdict is non-binding in equity cases. The central question is whether a 501(c)(3) charity, after accepting tax-deductible donations under an explicit public benefit promise, can convert into a for-profit entity in which insiders, employees, and outside investors hold equity worth tens of billions of dollars. Elon Musk is seeking damages reportedly in the range of $134 to $150 billion, which — if awarded — would flow to OpenAI's charitable arm, not to Musk personally.

2. **OpenAI's Founding and Elon Musk's Donations:** In December 2015, OpenAI was founded as a 501(c)(3) public charity by a group including Elon Musk, Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, Ilya Sutskever, Reid Hoffman, Peter Thiel, and Y Combinator Research. The founding charter explicitly promised to freely collaborate with other institutions, oppose corporate concentration of power, publish research openly, and operate for the benefit of humanity. Elon Musk donated between approximately $38 million (per OpenAI's court disclosures) and $45 million (per Musk's own filings and public statements) between 2015 and 2017, taking the associated IRS charitable deduction.

3. **The Structural Evolution of OpenAI — From Nonprofit to For-Profit:** In 2019, OpenAI created a capped-profit subsidiary (OpenAI LP), bringing in Microsoft with a $1 billion anchor investment while the nonprofit OpenAI Inc. remained the controlling entity. In 2024–2025, the full restructure converted the for-profit arm into a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC) under Delaware law called OpenAI Group PBC. The nonprofit was renamed the OpenAI Foundation and retained approximately 26% equity in the for-profit entity, valued at roughly $130 billion at the time of conversion. Microsoft holds approximately 27%, with employees and outside investors holding the remainder. The conversion was board-approved, reviewed by outside counsel, and disclosed to the IRS, the California Attorney General, and the Delaware Attorney General.

4. **Claims That Survived to Trial:** Several of Musk's original claims were dropped before trial. The Lanham Act false advertising counts were dismissed in pre-trial motions. On the Friday before trial, Musk himself moved to dismiss his fraud and constructive fraud claims to streamline the case, which the judge approved. What proceeds to the jury are the breach of charitable trust claim and the unjust enrichment claim — both equity claims, which is why the jury's verdict is advisory rather than binding.

5. **Elon Musk's Strongest Arguments:** Musk's case rests on five pillars. First, he donated under explicit 501(c)(3) terms, which carry a century-old legal rule that assets held in public trust cannot be distributed to private individuals. Second, the 2025 PBC conversion functionally shifted governance away from the nonprofit even if the foundation retained nominal control on paper, because a foundation coexisting alongside a 27% Microsoft stake and a majority cap table held by investors and employees is in a materially different position than a nonprofit directing its own subsidiary. Third, the precedent argument: if this conversion is deemed lawful, every nonprofit founder in America gains a blueprint to take tax-deductible donations, build value, convert to for-profit, and have insiders pocket the equity. Fourth, the founding charter language — anti-monopoly, anti-corporate concentration, open collaboration, open research — is in direct contradiction with OpenAI's 2026 reality of closed-source models, aggressive commercial deployment, and a partnership with the largest software company on earth. Fifth, the procedural argument: the 1990s nonprofit hospital conversion rule book required state AG review with findings, fair market value paid for assets, proceeds to a successor charity, and no insider equity in the for-profit successor — and Musk argues OpenAI checked boxes on paper without satisfying the spirit of those requirements.

6. **OpenAI and Sam Altman's Strongest Defense:** OpenAI's defense rests on six pillars. First, all conversions were board-approved, reviewed by top-tier outside counsel, and disclosed to three regulators — the IRS, the California AG, and the Delaware AG — none of whom brought enforcement actions, which OpenAI argues is a meaningful legal signal. Second, the PBC structure retains an explicit fiduciary duty to balance shareholder returns against the stated public benefit purpose, and the foundation's ~26% stake — reported at approximately $130 billion — is, by a wide margin, the largest charitable endowment created in modern philanthropic history, larger than the Ford Foundation (~$16 billion) and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (~$67 billion) combined. Third, training frontier AI models requires tens of billions of dollars in data center investment, a scale no 501(c)(3) can raise through charitable donations, meaning the conversion preserved the mission rather than abandoning it by giving OpenAI the capital structure needed to compete at the frontier. Fourth, ChatGPT serves more than 900 million weekly users globally, with a free tier, published safety research, and alignment research contributions — a broad public benefit output that few traditional charities can match. Fifth, OpenAI publicly stated in October 2025 that Sam Altman does not receive direct equity in the for-profit successor entity, and Musk has not produced public documentation contradicting that denial. Sixth, Musk left the OpenAI board voluntarily in 2018 after his own proposal to take over leadership was rejected, and subsequently founded XAI, a competing for-profit AI lab — OpenAI will argue the lawsuit is at least partially competitive in motivation.

7. **The Historical Analogues and Why This Case Is Bigger:** The closest historical analogues are the nonprofit hospital and Blue Cross AG oversight battles of the 1990s. Blue Cross of California's conversion produced two successor charitable foundations — the California Endowment and the California Health Care Foundation — and triggered legislation locking in AG review for future nonprofit hospital sales. The key structural difference from the OpenAI case: in the 1990s conversions, insiders did not generally end up holding direct equity in the for-profit successor; value flowed to a successor charity. The case also invokes Waltz v. Tax Commission (1970), which established the basic legal architecture for nonprofit status, and Bob Jones University v. United States (1983), which established that 501(c)(3) status is conditional rather than permanent.

8. **The Scale of What Is At Stake — The U.S. Charitable Sector:** The host lays out the full surface area of entities governed by the same nonprofit law being argued in court: nonprofit hospitals operating within a $5 trillion U.S. healthcare system; research foundations including the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (~$25 billion endowment), the Rockefeller Foundation, the Carnegie Corporation, the Ford Foundation, and the Mayo Clinic; university endowments including Harvard (over $50 billion), Yale (over $40 billion), Stanford (over $35 billion), and others whose combined endowments run into the hundreds of billions; religious institutions of all denominations; conservation organizations; arts and culture institutions; and tens of thousands of family foundations and donor-advised funds. The U.S. charitable sector moves over $1 trillion per year — more than 3% of annual U.S. GDP.

9. **Three Scenarios and Their Cascading Implications:** The host outlines three possible outcomes. In Scenario 1 (OpenAI wins outright), the conversion stands, likely triggering a wave of nonprofit-to-for-profit conversions over 5–10 years in tech, biotech, and academic spinout sectors; donors demand more aggressive contractual language at the moment of giving; the IRS likely issues new regulation within 2–3 years; and the Anthropic-as-PBC-from-day-one model becomes the default for mission-aligned founders. In Scenario 2 (Musk wins outright), the conversion is unwound or significantly constrained, insider equity claims are contested or clawed back, Microsoft's stake position is revisited, nonprofit-to-for-profit conversions with insider equity become generally impermissible, and capital flows into PBC and B-Corp structures from day one. In Scenario 3 (mixed verdict), the conversion is partially upheld but with constraints — future conversions require explicit donor notifications, mandatory state AG reviews with findings, fair market value paid by insiders for any equity received, and increased disclosure obligations; the case becomes the foundational precedent lawyers cite for the next half century, and nonprofit law evolves rather than locks or breaks. The host notes that juries rarely deliver clean total wins in cases this complex and that appellate review is near certain regardless of outcome.

Notable quotes and data:
- Trial start date: April 27th, 2026, U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California; Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers
- Nine jurors seated, no alternates; jury verdict is advisory (non-binding)
- Charitable assets at issue: approximately $130 billion
- Musk's donations to OpenAI: ~$38 million (OpenAI's court disclosures) to ~$45 million (Musk's own filings), donated 2015–2017
- Damages sought by Musk: reportedly $134 to $150 billion (would flow to OpenAI's charitable arm, not Musk personally)
- OpenAI Foundation equity stake: approximately 26% of the for-profit entity, valued at ~$130 billion at time of conversion
- Microsoft equity stake: approximately 27%
- OpenAI Foundation endowment on paper: ~$130 billion — larger than Ford Foundation (~$16B) and Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (~$67B) combined
- ChatGPT weekly users: more than 900 million globally
- OpenAI stated in October 2025 that Sam Altman does not receive direct equity in the for-profit successor
- U.S. charitable sector: moves over $1 trillion per year, more than 3% of U.S. GDP
- Harvard endowment: over $50 billion; Yale: over $40 billion; Stanford: over $35 billion
- Howard Hughes Medical Institute endowment: ~$25 billion
- Musk on X during jury selection: "Scam Altman and Greg Stockman stole a charity. Do you want to set legal precedent in the United States that it is okay to loot a charity? If so, you undermine all charitable giving in the United States forever."
- Anthropic, founded as a PBC from day one, is cited throughout as the structurally cleaner alternative model
- Microsoft's 2019 anchor investment in OpenAI LP: $1 billion

2026-05-05.title: Tesla May Be Building The Most Valuable Platform
2026-05-05.body:
This video from Futuraza features host Brian and co-host Randy in a wide-ranging discussion comparing Tesla's long-term platform strategy against Ford's near-term truck-and-software approach. The central thesis is that Tesla is building a recurring-revenue platform — spanning FSD subscriptions, robotaxi fleets, and Optimus rentals — that fundamentally outclasses one-time vehicle sales, and that traditional automakers like Ford are optimizing for a world that is rapidly becoming obsolete. The hosts use analogies to Sears Roebuck and Craftsman tools to illustrate how incumbents can appear stable while their underlying relevance erodes.

## Market & Competition

1. **Ford's short-term strategy vs. Tesla's long-term platform:** The hosts argue that Ford's plan — generating margins on Super Duty trucks, F-150s, Transits, and Ford Pro software subscriptions — may work well over the next several years, but is fundamentally misaligned with where value is heading. Ford Pro software subscription revenue is characterized as not remotely comparable in scale or nature to FSD recurring revenue, Cybercab fleet revenue, or Optimus rental income. The hosts acknowledge Ford can likely extract another decade of profitability from its truck lineup, but question whether that matters in a world trending toward autonomous vehicles.

2. **The Sears Roebuck / Craftsman analogy:** Randy draws an extended parallel between Ford and Sears Roebuck, arguing that Sears could have survived by shedding underperforming divisions and focusing on its strongest assets (appliances, Craftsman tools), but even that survival would only have delayed an inevitable decline. The Craftsman brand is cited as a case study in brand dilution — once the gold standard with a no-receipt lifetime replacement guarantee, it eroded through quality cuts until the name meant nothing. The hosts use this to argue Ford's brand faces similar structural risks.

3. **Global EV sales data — Model Y and Model 3 dominance:** The hosts briefly review a worldwide EV sales chart showing the Tesla Model Y at number one and Model 3 at number two globally. They note the Xiaomi SU7 — heavily marketed as a "Model 3 killer" — does not appear in the top 20, with only the Xiaomi U7 present. A BYD model (the Seal) appears on the list but only because its BEV and plug-in hybrid numbers are combined.

4. **Peak vehicle sales and the ICE endgame:** Randy estimates that a peak in new vehicle sales is coming — he had originally projected 2028 but now considers that too aggressive, suggesting 2030 or 2031 as a more realistic inflection point. His argument is that once autonomous vehicles reach sufficient scale, the economics of manufacturing non-autonomous ICE or even non-autonomous electric vehicles will collapse. Brian adds nuance, suggesting people who prefer ownership ("gatherers") will still want to own vehicles, but that human-operated controls in new cars may eventually be regulated away, much as cars without seatbelts or headrests were phased out.

## Financials

1. **Tesla Q1 earnings beat and FSD subscription growth:** The hosts reference Tesla's most recent quarterly results as posting strong margins and beating GAAP EPS estimates by a meaningful margin. FSD paid subscriptions grew by 170,000 new users in the quarter, which the hosts describe as a trajectory that is unlikely to stop, though growth may be lumpy. Megapack revenue is also called out as continuing to grow and expected to expand significantly over coming years.

2. **Concordia Genuity price target raise:** An article is cited noting that Canaccord Genuity raised its Tesla price target to $450 from $420 on April 23rd, maintaining a buy rating. The hosts treat this as a data point but spend more time mocking the surrounding media commentary than analyzing the target itself.

3. **Tesla vs. Ford profitability contrast:** Ford is noted to have taken a loss in the same period due to one-time impairments. The hosts contrast Ford's 5–10% margins on trucks (translating to roughly $5,000–$8,000 per unit) against Tesla's higher-margin but lower-volume model, arguing the one-time sale model is structurally inferior to recurring revenue streams.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Unsupervised FSD as the pivotal milestone:** The hosts discuss unsupervised Full Self-Driving as the hinge event for Tesla's stock and valuation. Brian argues that virtually every Tesla all-time high has been preceded by excitement about imminent autonomous capability, and every major selloff has followed disappointment that it hadn't arrived yet. He characterizes the current moment as similar — the stock is down year-to-date as investors wait for execution proof. He expresses confidence that unsupervised driving will eventually arrive, noting even skeptics are not saying "never," only debating timing.

2. **Robotaxi fleet count referenced:** Brian mentions approximately 33 vehicles operating unsupervised in Austin at the time of recording, framing this as the beginning of a ramp — adding 5, then 10, then 20–30 at a time — that he believes will push the stock back toward all-time highs later in 2026.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab pricing as a disruptive threshold:** Randy poses the question of what it would mean if a consumer could summon a Cybercab in under five minutes and travel for a dollar per mile. He describes this as "extraordinarily disruptive" and suggests that once this is demonstrably real and scalable, modeling the market opportunity becomes more tractable — investors will be able to observe how much market share the service is capturing in real time.

2. **Recurring revenue vs. one-time sale framing:** The hosts argue that Cybercab revenue — daily recurring fleet income — is categorically different from and superior to Ford's one-time truck sale model. They extend this to Optimus, noting Tesla can sell robots outright or rent them, and that the sale price of a robot will naturally correlate with its rental value, giving Tesla pricing power in both modes.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus rental and sale pricing framed as commercially rational:** Randy argues that figures like $300,000 to purchase an Optimus or $100,000 per year to rent one are not extreme when viewed through a commercial and industrial lens rather than a consumer lens. He attributes these numbers to "Cern and many others" and notes they were discussed on the channel roughly three and a half years ago. The hosts argue that businesses already willingly spend $50,000 on a simple autonomous floor-cleaning robot that requires manual route programming and is prone to failure — demonstrating that commercial buyers will pay substantial sums for labor automation even when the product is mediocre.

2. **Current robot competition is primitive:** Brian recounts observing a $50,000 autonomous floor-cleaning robot at a grocery store get jammed on a drainage mat in front of the produce section, despite having cameras. He notes the robot has no real intelligence — it must be manually driven and taught its route before operating autonomously, and even then is unreliable. He contrasts this with Optimus, arguing that Optimus would not make that mistake, and certainly not twice, illustrating how far ahead Tesla's robotics ambitions are relative to current commercial alternatives.

3. **Optimus capability as the key valuation unlock:** Randy frames Optimus's value as directly tied to the breadth of tasks it can perform — not just simple pick-and-place operations, but removing bottles from blow-molding machines, pulling garments off silk-screen printing lines, turning screws, or welding. He argues that once Optimus demonstrably handles a wide range of industrial tasks, pricing it based on labor displacement becomes straightforward and the investment case becomes clear.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla FSD paid subscriptions added **170,000 new users** last quarter
- Canaccord Genuity raised Tesla price target to **$450 from $420** on April 23rd, maintaining buy
- Ford margins on trucks cited as **5–10%**, or roughly **$5,000–$8,000 per unit**
- Unsupervised Tesla robotaxi fleet in Austin referenced as approximately **33 vehicles** at time of recording (per RobotaxiTracker.com canonical data, unsupervised Austin fleet = 25 as of 2026-05-05; host's figure of ~33 is materially different, suggesting either a slightly different date or definition)
- Grocery store autonomous floor cleaner costs **$50,000**, requires manual route teaching, and is prone to failure
- Optimus purchase price cited as **$300,000**; rental cited as **$100,000/year** (attributed to "Cern and many others")
- Cybercab fare target mentioned: **$1 per mile**, with a goal of availability in **under 5 minutes**
- Randy's estimate for peak ICE/non-autonomous vehicle sales: **2030–2031**
- Tesla stock: **+33% over the past year**, **-13.8% year-to-date** at time of article referenced
- Model Y ranked **#1** and Model 3 ranked **#2** in global EV sales chart shown; Xiaomi SU7 not in top 20

2026-05-05.title: Why Tesla Stock Is Setting Up to RUN

In this video, Jo Bhakdi delivers a market and Tesla update on May 5, 2026, arguing that Tesla stock is set up for a near-term run back toward its all-time high of $490, driven by continued robotaxi progress and the broader AI bull market. He outlines his current portfolio positioning and options strategy, while providing his assessment of macro risks and Tesla's competitive standing relative to other Mag 7 stocks.

## Market & Competition
1. **Macro Risk Assessment — Iran/US Stalemate:** Bhakdi argues that the Iran-US conflict is effectively over as an escalation risk, because neither side can afford to escalate — an escalation would be catastrophic for both parties. He notes that markets appear to agree, having trended upward throughout April and with futures up at the time of recording. He believes this geopolitical backdrop supports a continued bull run in equities.

2. **Tesla as the "Laggard" Mag 7 — But With Unique Upside:** Bhakdi positions Tesla as structurally different from the other Magnificent 7 stocks. While Nvidia, Google, Meta, and Microsoft are seeing direct earnings boosts from AI spending, Tesla is not currently scaling profits and EBITDA at the same rate. However, he argues Tesla is the only Mag 7 company with major new revenue and margin streams — specifically robotaxi and Optimus — that could "eclipse everything else" once they materialize.

3. **Waymo Comparison — Scale vs. Technology Quality:** Bhakdi acknowledges that Waymo currently operates approximately 3,000 robotaxis — roughly 90x Tesla's unsupervised fleet. He dismisses the direct comparison, arguing that Waymo relies on lidar and manual adjustments, while Tesla's robotaxis have "real autonomy and real visual sight that actually understands the world." His thesis is that Tesla's approach is more scalable once proven, potentially reaching millions or tens of millions of vehicles including semi-trucks.

1. **Current Unsupervised Fleet — 36 Vehicles Per RobotaxiTracker.com:** Per RobotaxiTracker.com, the unsupervised (driverless) robotaxi fleet stands at 36 as of the video date, with growth concentrated in Texas cities — Austin, Houston, and Dallas. Bhakdi notes Houston and Dallas are "growing rapidly on a low basis" and that the Austin unsupervised fleet is expanding as well.

2. **Year-End Fleet Target — Above 10,000:** Bhakdi states his personal estimate is that Tesla will exceed 10,000 robotaxis by end of 2026. He acknowledges this cannot be extrapolated linearly from current growth rates but believes the trajectory supports it. He explicitly states that at the current growth rate, a figure of 100,000 is theoretically possible but not what he is forecasting.

3. **Stock Price Catalyst — Robotaxi Scale Drives $1,000+ Target:** Bhakdi argues that if Tesla reaches multiple thousands of robotaxis with a high monthly growth rate by end of 2026, the stock could reprice above $1,000, though he frames this as a momentum-driven overshoot that may not be sustained. He notes Cybercab mass production has started and the Tesla Semi is out, making Tesla a stronger company than it was at its December 16th all-time high.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Unsupervised FSD Now Live in Texas Cities:** Bhakdi highlights that unsupervised robotaxis are now operating openly in Austin, Houston, and Dallas — all Texas locations — representing real-world autonomous deployment without remote driver intervention, per his characterization.

2. **Tesla Stronger Than at December All-Time High:** Bhakdi argues that Tesla is fundamentally a stronger company now than when it hit its all-time high of $490 on December 16th, citing unsupervised FSD deployment, open robotaxi operations, Cybercab mass production having started, and the Tesla Semi being in production.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Cybercab Mass Production Has Started:** Bhakdi states as a matter of fact that Cybercab has started mass production, citing this as one of the reasons Tesla is a stronger company today than at its December 2025 all-time high. No production volume or ramp figures are provided.

1. **Post-Earnings Drop Called a Buying Opportunity:** Bhakdi recounts that after Tesla's most recent earnings call, the stock dropped to the high $360s — which he characterized at the time as unjustified given what he described as strong underlying earnings. He attributes the drop to Elon Musk's perceived lack of energy on the earnings call rather than fundamental weakness. His portfolio subsequently rose 9.41% (as of May 1st), with Tesla up 3.86% during that move from the $360s back toward $390.

He frames this as a return to the prior all-time high level set on December 16th, and notes that if the stock reaches $490 without meaningful robotaxi scale (i.e., still under 100 unsupervised vehicles), he would become cautious about a pullback.
