2026-05-14.title: Elon Just Became the Landlord of AI
2026-05-14.body:
This video analyzes the partnership deal between SpaceX and Anthropic, in which SpaceX is providing Anthropic with 300 megawatts of compute capacity and access to over 220,000 Nvidia GPUs at the Colossus 1 data center in Memphis, Tennessee. The host's core thesis is that SpaceX has quietly assembled the only fully vertically integrated AI infrastructure stack on Earth — spanning rockets, chip fabrication, power, satellites, developer surfaces, and now frontier model tenants — repositioning itself not as a rocket company or even an AI lab, but as the "landlord" of the entire AI economy. The video argues this structural shift mirrors Tesla's vertical integration playbook in EVs and has profound consequences for the competitive dynamics among OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and Amazon.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX–Anthropic compute deal:** Anthropic announced a partnership with SpaceX granting access to all compute capacity at Colossus 1, the Memphis, Tennessee data center originally built to train Grok. This provides over 300 megawatts of additional capacity and more than 220,000 Nvidia GPUs — primarily H100s, H200s, and GB200 chips — expected to come online within a month of the announcement. The immediate effect is that rate limits for Claude Pro, Max, Code, Team, and Enterprise products will effectively double, peak-hour throttling on Pro and Max accounts is removed, and API limits on Opus models are raised.

2. **Background: Anthropic's demand-strangled growth:** Throughout the first half of 2026, Anthropic was severely compute-constrained despite having what many consider the best AI models available. Claude Code users were hitting rate limits in hours rather than days. The host cites Anthropic's annual revenue run rate climbing from roughly $9 billion at the end of 2025, to approximately $19 billion by March 2026, to approximately $30 billion by the first week of April 2026 — described as the fastest revenue ramp of any company in history. Anthropic's valuation at the time of recording is cited at approximately $1.2 trillion.

3. **SpaceX's transformation into an AI hyperscaler:** The host argues SpaceX is no longer meaningfully a rocket company. Following its absorption of XAI in an all-stock transaction on February 2nd, 2026 — described by Reuters as the largest corporate merger ever recorded, valuing the combined entity at roughly $1.25 trillion at announcement and closer to $2 trillion at current estimated valuations — SpaceX gained ownership of XAI, Grok, and the Colossus data center complex. SpaceX now owns Colossus 1 (220,000+ GPUs), Colossus 2 (a gigawatt-scale facility with 335,000+ GPUs), and a third site coming online in South Haven, Mississippi, with a roadmap to 1 million GPUs by late 2026 and approximately $18 billion invested in the Memphis complex alone.

4. **Terafab chip fabrication venture:** SpaceX, along with Tesla, is building Terafab, a 2nm chip fabrication facility in Austin, Texas. Originally announced as a $20–$22 billion project, it is now described as on pace to be closer to $200 billion. A report published three hours before the Anthropic announcement cited SpaceX proposing $55 billion in capital expenditure for Phase 1 of Terafab, potentially rising to $119 billion across all phases. Intel joined the project in April as a manufacturing partner. The roadmap targets 100,000 wafer starts per month ramping to 1 million per month, which the host notes would be roughly 70% of TSMC's entire global output.

5. **SpaceX's vertically integrated AI stack:** The host enumerates six layers of the AI infrastructure stack that SpaceX now owns: (1) launches via Falcon 9 and Starship, with Starship targeting $10–$100 per kilogram to orbit when flying at cadence, representing a 30x–300x reduction from current Falcon 9 prices and over 1,000x from industry prices a decade ago; (2) chips via Terafab; (3) power and compute via the Colossus data centers; (4) network via Starlink, with over 10,000 satellites in orbit; (5) models via Grok/XAI; and (6) a developer surface via a $60 billion option to acquire Cursor by end of 2026 with a $10 billion breakup fee. The host argues no competitor owns more than four of these layers.

6. **Winners and losers from the deal:** Anthropic wins by breaking its compute bottleneck and gaining the runway to deploy its next model, called Mythos, which reportedly features a 1 million token context window and was previewed to limited partners in April; the host describes benchmark reports as indicating it is highly capable. SpaceX wins by proving its thesis as an AI infrastructure company and gaining a recurring revenue stream that supports its targeted IPO valuation of $1.5–$2 trillion or more, per Bank of America projections, with the IPO targeted for sometime in mid-2026. The relative loser is Grok/XAI: Colossus 1, originally built for Grok's training, has been entirely rented to Anthropic, and the host notes that essentially every original XAI co-founder besides Elon Musk has left in 2026.

7. **OpenAI's structural squeeze:** The host argues OpenAI is under serious pressure. Its CFO recently capped the Microsoft revenue share. OpenAI pulled back from a Stargate Norway data center project, which Microsoft then picked up directly through a company called Nscale, contracting 30,000 Rubin GPUs itself. OpenAI has committed $250 billion to Microsoft Azure over six years. Microsoft's 2026 capex of $190 billion and a doubling of AI infrastructure in two years signals Microsoft has the upper hand. The host frames the SpaceX–Anthropic deal as Elon Musk and Dario Amodei — both former OpenAI colleagues who departed over safety and leadership concerns — effectively uniting against Sam Altman and OpenAI.

8. **The "landlord of AI" thesis:** The host's central argument is that the AI competitive landscape has fundamentally shifted. The moat used to be the model; now it is everything beneath the model. Models are commoditizing rapidly due to open-source releases from China, Mistral, and Meta compressing the gap from best-in-class to adequate from years to months. SpaceX's strategy, the host argues, is not to win the model race but to be the infrastructure landlord that all frontier labs — including competitors — must pay rent to. This is compared directly to Tesla's vertical integration of the EV supply chain, which left legacy automakers unable to compete because they did not own the underlying industrial layers.

Notable quotes and data:
- Anthropic annual revenue run rate: ~$9B (end of 2025) → ~$19B (March 2026) → ~$30B (first week of April 2026)
- Anthropic valuation at time of recording: ~$1.2 trillion
- SpaceX/XAI merger valuation: ~$1.25 trillion at announcement (February 2, 2026), ~$2 trillion at current estimated valuations
- Colossus 1: 220,000+ GPUs (H100s, H200s, GB200s), 300+ megawatts — now fully rented to Anthropic
- Colossus 2: 335,000+ GPUs, gigawatt-scale
- South Haven, Mississippi site: roadmap to 1 million GPUs by late 2026
- Total Memphis complex investment: ~$18 billion
- Terafab Phase 1 proposed capex: $55 billion; total across all phases: up to $119 billion
- Terafab target: 100,000 wafer starts/month ramping to 1 million/month (~70% of TSMC's global output)
- Starship target cost to orbit: $10–$100/kg (30x–300x reduction vs. Falcon 9; 1,000x+ vs. industry a decade ago)
- SpaceX Cursor acquisition option: $60 billion by end of 2026 with $10 billion breakup fee
- SpaceX IPO target: mid-2026; Bank of America projection: $1.5–$2 trillion+
- OpenAI's commitment to Microsoft Azure: $250 billion over 6 years
- Microsoft 2026 capex: $190 billion
- Starlink constellation: over 10,000 satellites in orbit
- Anthropic's next model "Mythos": previewed in April to limited partners, 1 million token context window

2026-05-14.title: Tesla Bears Missed This Massive Rebound
2026-05-14.body:
This video features FutureAzA host Brian in conversation with Herbert from Brighter, discussing Tesla's Q1 2026 delivery numbers, sales performance across global markets, and the trajectory of Full Self-Driving as a future demand driver. The core thesis is that pessimistic narratives around Tesla's China and Europe sales miss critical context — particularly the delivery wave mechanics and the Model Y refresh disruption from the prior year — and that Tesla's fundamentals are stronger than headlines suggest.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla's delivery wave explained:** The hosts walk through Tesla's well-known "delivery wave" pattern, where cars destined for distant markets (exports via ship to Europe, the US, etc.) are produced early in the quarter to allow for transit time, while domestic deliveries are fulfilled later. This explains why Tesla's April China domestic sales appear weak — Giga Shanghai prioritizes exports at the start of the quarter. The hosts note this pattern is not new and that media outlets covering it as a negative story are being deliberately misleading or ignoring known context.

2. **China April data — exports vs. domestic sales:** Tesla's April numbers out of Giga Shanghai showed strong export figures, with the hosts characterizing it as record exports from China since 2022. Brian references a post from Tesla Owner Silicon Valley showing approximately 79,478 Model 3 and Y units produced. A Yahoo Finance/Benzinga article cited a 36% jump in China sales in April, which included exports. The framing of Tesla "falling out of the top 10" in China's NEV domestic market was criticized as misleading because it excluded the export component.

3. **US sales dominance in Q1 2026:** The hosts highlight that the Model Y and Model 3 ranked first and second in US EV sales in Q1 2026, with the Model Y selling over 70,000 units and the Model 3 over 30,000 units, totaling approximately 110,000 combined. The next closest competitor — identified as a Toyota BZ model — sold around 10,000 units in the quarter, meaning the Model Y outsold the next competitor by roughly seven times.

4. **Europe sales rebound and Giga Berlin expansion:** Tesla broke a 13-month sales losing streak in Europe, selling 13,740 cars across the EU, UK, and EFTA countries in the reported period, up 29% year-over-year. The hosts contextualize the prior year's weakness as a result of the Model Y refresh requiring factory downtime. Germany is highlighted as a key benchmark market that has shown signs of recovery. Giga Berlin announced it has produced 750,000 cumulative vehicles and plans to increase production by 20%, which the hosts interpret as a strong forward-looking demand signal.

5. **South Korea and other markets:** Tesla is noted as the top imported car brand in South Korea, a market where Hyundai and Kia together hold approximately 90% domestic market share — making Tesla's import performance there particularly notable.

6. **EV adoption trends in Europe:** The hosts reference recent data showing gas car sales in Europe fell 17% and diesel fell 13.5%, describing these as accelerating structural trends. They suggest rising gas prices will further push consumers toward EVs, with early signs of this appearing in Australia and New Zealand export demand from China.

7. **Oregon's weight-mile tax proposal:** The video briefly covers a proposed Oregon measure that would replace the gas tax with a biannual weight-mile fee requiring vehicle owners to bring cars to testing stations twice a year to measure weight and miles driven. Both hosts criticize this as impractical and unfair to EV owners. Brian notes Washington State charges an EV premium of roughly $250–$300 on annual vehicle tabs to offset lost gas tax revenue.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD as a future demand driver in Europe:** Herbert argues that the rollout of Full Self-Driving in Europe will become a significant demand driver for Tesla, potentially converting consumers who were previously indifferent to EVs. He notes that the Netherlands has already approved FSD, Ireland is in talks, Sweden and Belgium are also progressing (Belgium conducting a 5,000 km Tesla FSD trial), and that consumer awareness of self-driving capability is already changing purchasing intent anecdotally.

2. **FSD version 14.3.2 user experience:** Brian shares a first-person account of driving with FSD version 14.3.2, describing an impressive real-world scenario where the car detected a stopped vehicle with hazards on ahead, began reversing and signaling to go around, then cancelled the maneuver when the car ahead resumed driving — all without driver input. He contrasts the impressive driving capability with frustration over navigation routing, which he jokes is overtrained on circuitous routing patterns.

3. **FSD market size estimate:** Brian estimates that if Full Self-Driving appeals to even 10% of US car buyers, that translates to roughly 1–2 million additional vehicle sales per year in the US alone, framing it as a "ginormous" incremental demand opportunity.

## Market & Competition

1. **Legacy automaker struggles vs. Tesla:** The hosts contrast Tesla's production expansion at Giga Berlin with GM laying off hundreds to thousands of IT and salaried workers. They acknowledge that many EV startups and legacy players are still losing money overall but note that per-unit profitability is improving across the industry, citing a Honda engineer working in China as a source. The broader narrative is that electrification is not reversing — the competitive threat to Tesla is rising but so is the overall market.

2. **Europe's 2035 ICE ban:** The hosts debate whether the 2035 European ban on new internal combustion engine vehicles will hold. Herbert predicts the deadline will be repeatedly pushed back under lobbying pressure, while Brian argues that feasibility objections are harder to sustain now that Tesla, Chinese automakers, and Volkswagen (ID.4, ID.3, ID Buzz) have demonstrated mass-market EV production is viable.

Notable quotes and data:
- ~79,478 Model 3 and Y units produced at Giga Shanghai in April (per Tesla Owner Silicon Valley post)
- China sales up 36% in April including exports — described as record exports from China since 2022
- Model Y + Model 3 combined US Q1 sales: ~110,000 units (Model Y ~70,000+, Model 3 ~30,000+)
- Next closest US EV competitor (Toyota BZ): ~10,000 units in Q1 — roughly 7x fewer than Model Y
- Europe sales: 13,740 cars across EU/UK/EFTA, up 29% year-over-year
- Giga Berlin cumulative production milestone: 750,000 vehicles; production increase of 20% announced
- Hyundai + Kia combined South Korea domestic market share: ~90%
- European gas car sales down 17%; diesel down 13.5% (as of the prior month)
- FSD approved in Netherlands; Ireland in talks; Sweden and Belgium progressing (Belgium: 5,000 km trial)
- FSD version referenced by Brian: 14.3.2
- Brian's estimate: FSD demand could drive 1–2 million additional US car sales per year if it resonates with 10% of buyers
- Washington State EV tab premium: approximately $250–$300/year

2026-05-14.title: Will Tesla Stockholders GET SCREWED In The SpaceX Merger? - FULL ANALYSIS
2026-05-14.body:
In this video, Jo Bhakdi presents a quantitative model analyzing whether a Tesla-SpaceX merger would benefit or harm Tesla shareholders. His core thesis is that on an 18-month horizon the merger is mildly negative for Tesla shareholders, but beyond that window — particularly by 2028–2029 — the combined entity outperforms Tesla standalone, driven by SpaceX's orbital AI data center opportunity. The video is framed as a direct response to criticism from a commentator named Rich Chu, who argued the merger is a clear downside risk for Tesla shareholders.

## Market & Competition

1. **Rich Chu's bearish merger case:** Rich Chu published a critical assessment arguing the 1:1 merger is a significant downside risk for Tesla shareholders. His key points: SpaceX's IPO valuation will be artificially inflated by supply-demand imbalance and retail/index fund demand; once lockup periods expire and insider shares flood the market, SpaceX will act as an anchor dragging Tesla down rather than a magnet pulling it up. He also argued the two companies have diverging duration profiles — Tesla is entering a cash flow harvest season via robotaxi, while SpaceX is burning capital on early-stage orbital infrastructure that is years from maturity.

2. **Jo Bhakdi's partial agreement with Rich Chu:** Bhakdi agrees with virtually all of Rich's short-term analysis. He concurs that SpaceX's IPO will be overhyped, that a post-IPO deflation is likely (he estimates roughly 30% down from IPO price as "very likely, very possible"), and that for approximately the next 18 months, Tesla shareholders are better off without the merger. He explicitly states he would bet that the merger is worse for Tesla shareholders through the end of 2027.

3. **Merger-of-equals framing and conspiracy concerns:** Bhakdi notes that initial narratives involved SpaceX acquiring Tesla at only a 20–30% premium, which faced retail investor pushback, leading to a pivot toward a "merger of equals" framing. Rich Chu characterizes this as a coordinated manipulation against Tesla shareholders' interests, though Bhakdi distances himself from the conspiracy framing while acknowledging it as a legitimate concern worth noting.

4. **Elon Musk control as a practical constraint:** Bhakdi raises the pragmatic point that regardless of shareholder sentiment, Elon Musk is in control, and voting against the merger is unlikely to produce an alternative plan — it would simply derail Elon's plan without substituting a better one. He treats this as a strong factual constraint on shareholder agency, even if it is an uncomfortable moral argument.

5. **SpaceX orbital AI data center thesis:** Bhakdi's long-term bullish case for SpaceX rests on the concept of orbital data centers — launching AI compute infrastructure into space, powered by solar flux, creating what he describes as an infinitely scalable business model. He argues that the global energy bottleneck for AI compute makes space-based infrastructure inevitable, and that everything hinges on Starship becoming commercially ready and scalable. He believes Starship's commercial operations timeline is not subject to indefinite delay.

6. **Starship as the key risk factor:** Bhakdi identifies Starship's commercial readiness as the singular critical risk for SpaceX's valuation trajectory. He believes commercial Starship operations could begin as early as this year (2026), with scaling in 2027, and that if this timeline holds, SpaceX's growth rate will ultimately exceed Tesla's because the addressable market for space-based AI compute is theoretically infinite.

## Financials

1. **Tesla standalone market cap projections:** Bhakdi's discounted cash flow model (described as conservative, based on robotaxi and Optimus scaling) projects Tesla's market cap as follows: approximately $1.5 trillion at present (mid-2026); $2 trillion by end of 2026; $3 trillion by end of 2027; $5 trillion by end of 2028; $8 trillion by end of 2029. He frames these as his most reasonable base-case estimates, acknowledging scenarios could be higher or lower.

2. **SpaceX IPO and near-term valuation trajectory:** Bhakdi projects SpaceX will IPO at approximately $2.2 trillion, which he sees as realistic but acknowledges uncertainty. He then expects a roughly 30% post-IPO deflation, with SpaceX likely remaining below its IPO valuation through end of 2027 due to lagging cash flows. He projects SpaceX reaches approximately $2 trillion by end of 2027, after which it enters a hyper-growth trajectory he believes will ultimately exceed Tesla's long-term growth rate.

3. **Merger impact on Tesla shareholder returns — 18-month horizon:** Using a simplified merger-of-equals model (summing the two market caps), Bhakdi computes that over the next 18–20 months a merged entity underperforms Tesla standalone. Specifically: in 2027, the merged entity delivers approximately 38% growth versus Tesla standalone's projected 50%. On a $1 million investment post-merger, he estimates shareholders would earn approximately $380,000 versus $500,000 without the merger — a meaningful but not catastrophic shortfall.

4. **Merger impact on Tesla shareholder returns — long-term horizon:** By 2028, Bhakdi's model shows the merged entity outperforming Tesla standalone (approximately $800,000 return vs. $666,000 on a $1 million investment). By 2029, the outperformance widens further ($880,000 for the merged entity vs. $600,000 for Tesla alone). He concludes that by December 2029, SpaceX alone would be larger than Tesla, and the merger will have been net positive for Tesla shareholders on a cumulative basis.

5. **SpaceX long-term growth rate vs. Tesla:** Bhakdi argues SpaceX's long-term sustainable growth rate will exceed Tesla's because the addressable market for space-based AI compute is unlimited, whereas Tesla's robotaxi and Optimus markets, while enormous, are finite. He projects Tesla growing at roughly 40–50% annually in the near term, with SpaceX ultimately growing faster once orbital infrastructure reaches maturity.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla market cap projections (standalone, no merger): $1.5T (mid-2026) → $2T (end-2026) → $3T (end-2027) → $5T (end-2028) → $8T (end-2029)
- SpaceX IPO projected valuation: ~$2.2 trillion
- SpaceX post-IPO deflation estimate: ~30% decline "very likely, very possible"
- SpaceX projected market cap end-2027: ~$2 trillion
- Merger verdict on 18-month horizon: "SpaceX Tesla merger is bad for Tesla shareholders but not really bad"
- Merger verdict on 3-year horizon: "By December 2029, SpaceX alone would be bigger than Tesla"
- On Starship: "Everything hinges on Starship being ready"
- On Rich Chu's critique: "I 100% agree... I wholeheartedly agree this is exactly what's going to happen" (re: post-IPO SpaceX deflation)
- "For the next 18 months the odds that a SpaceX merger is bad for Tesla shareholders is high"
- "Already in 2028, the merged entity will outperform Tesla"
- Fidelity's head of private investments described as publicly endorsing the orbital AI data center thesis

Today's posts from @SawyerMerritt were largely low-signal for Tesla's core investment thesis, with no meaningful updates on FSD, Robotaxi, or Optimus. The most relevant themes for Tesla investors were the Tesla Semi beginning a commercial demo with a logistics company, a small municipal Model Y fleet adoption, and high-level U.S.-China diplomatic activity involving Elon Musk that could have downstream tariff and market access implications.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Tesla Semi enters commercial demo with Covenant Logistics:** Covenant Logistics kicked off a 3-week Tesla Semi demo on May 13, with an executive accompanying a professional driver on the first delivery run in California — a full freight load using the 500-mile range variant, starting with a 200-mile round trip. This is a notable commercial validation moment for the Semi, as a major logistics operator is actively evaluating the vehicle under real operating conditions. The demo's outcome could influence fleet purchase decisions across the trucking industry.

2. **Model Y municipal fleet adoption in Covington, KY:** The city of Covington, Kentucky announced it is adding seven Tesla Model Y vehicles to its police fleet, directly replacing seven internal combustion vehicles. Research sponsored by the city estimates the switch will save approximately $23,000 annually in fuel and maintenance costs. While a small deployment, municipal fleet adoptions provide steady, visible demand and serve as credibility signals for broader EV fleet procurement decisions.

3. **Trump-Elon-Jensen Huang meet China VP in Beijing:** President Trump, Elon Musk, and Nvidia's Jensen Huang met with Chinese Vice President Han Zheng in Beijing on May 13, as part of a larger delegation of U.S. business leaders. No specific announcements were reported in the posts, but the meeting is notable for Tesla investors given Tesla's significant manufacturing and sales exposure in China. Any outcomes related to tariff relief, market access, or trade normalization could be materially relevant to Tesla's near-term financials and China demand trajectory.

4. **Model Y new "Frost Blue" color:** Tesla appears to have introduced a new "Frost Blue" color option for the Model Y, which Merritt noted approvingly with an image. Minor product news, but new color variants can modestly refresh demand and average selling price mix.

5. **Competition — Mercedes AMG GT EV with simulated engine sounds:** The upcoming all-electric Mercedes AMG GT 4-Door EV features artificial V8 engine noises and simulated gear shifts. This is a market color data point illustrating how legacy automakers are navigating EV adoption by preserving internal combustion sensory cues — a strategy Tesla has not pursued. Noteworthy as a differentiation and brand philosophy contrast.

6. **Starlink displacement of legacy satellite broadband (tangential):** Hughesnet has lost 57% of its broadband subscribers (~880,000) since Starlink launched in December 2020 and has issued a going-concern warning citing insufficient cash to service its debt. While primarily a SpaceX/Starlink story, it reinforces the competitive moat and cash-generating potential of the broader Elon Musk enterprise ecosystem, which some Tesla bull cases incorporate through conglomerate or Elon-premium valuation frameworks.

---

## Signal Strength: **Mildly Bullish** — The Tesla Semi commercial demo with a major logistics operator and continued Model Y fleet adoption provide incremental demand validation, while the high-level U.S.-China diplomatic engagement involving Musk introduces optionality on tariff/market access improvements, though no concrete Tesla-specific catalysts were confirmed today.

2026-05-14.title: How Tesla's AI Will Save Your Life!
2026-05-14.body:
This episode of The Tesla Space covers several major Tesla and adjacent tech developments, with the central focus on Tesla Vision's new predictive safety feature and its growing validation from federal regulators. The video also touches on the end of Model S and Model X production, Optimus manufacturing plans, SpaceX/xAI orbital compute developments, and The Boring Company's Nashville expansion.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Predictive Pre-Crash Safety via Tesla Vision:** Tesla has revealed a new safety feature that uses Tesla Vision — its camera-based AI system — to predict a crash before physical impact occurs. Rather than waiting for traditional impact sensors to detect a collision as it begins, the AI analyzes camera data to recognize an imminent crash and pre-deploys airbags and seat belt tensioners up to 70 milliseconds earlier than conventional systems. Tesla notes that body position at the moment of airbag deployment significantly affects injury outcomes, and those additional milliseconds can reduce injuries in certain crash types. The feature will come standard on all new Tesla vehicles and will be delivered via a free over-the-air software update to existing vehicles running the camera-based vision system.

2. **Photon Count Reconstruction for Extreme Glare:** Elon Musk posted on X a demonstration of Tesla's AI capability to reconstruct a driving scene obscured by direct sunlight glare. He shared two images of the same scene: the first showed a washed-out road indistinguishable to the human eye, while the second — processed using what Musk described as "photon count reconstruction" — clearly showed the road, nearby cars, lane markings, and trees. The AI analyzes raw light data underneath the standard visual capture, rebuilding a clearer environmental picture even when the camera sensor is overwhelmed by brightness, directly supporting the case for a cameras-only perception approach.

3. **NHTSA Validation: 2026 Model Y Passes Advanced Driver Assistance Benchmarks:** The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration announced that the 2026 Tesla Model Y became the first vehicle in the United States to pass NHTSA's new advanced driver assistance system benchmark tests. The Model Y passed evaluations for pedestrian automatic emergency braking, lane-keeping assistance, blind spot warning, and blind spot intervention, as well as earlier benchmarks including forward collision warning and crash imminent braking. NHTSA administrator Jonathan Morrison called the results "a significant step forward" and said the Model Y "demonstrated the life-saving potential of driver assistance technologies and sets a high bar for the industry."

## Electric Vehicles

1. **End of Model S and Model X Production:** Tesla has officially ended production of both the Model S and Model X at the Fremont factory. The company shared photos of the final vehicles rolling off the line and confirmed a farewell delivery event for the final Signature Edition versions of both models is scheduled for May 20th. Videos showed the Tesla team personally signing the last Model S ever produced. The Model S launched in 2012 and the Model X in 2015, and together the two models delivered approximately 750,000 vehicles combined worldwide over their production lifetimes.

2. **Giga Berlin Milestone Mirrors Combined S/X Legacy:** Giga Berlin, which began production in 2022, announced it has now built 750,000 vehicles of its own — all of a single mass-market model. The video highlights this as a striking contrast: what took two flagship models more than a decade to achieve, a single modern factory producing one car matched in just a few years.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Fremont Production Line Repurposed for Optimus:** With Model S and Model X production ending, Tesla plans to repurpose the freed production line at the Fremont factory for Optimus, its humanoid robot. Long-term plans call for eventually producing up to 1 million Optimus units per year at the facility. The video frames this as a thematic passing of the torch — the same factory floor that once hosted Tesla's biggest early gamble is now being handed to what the host describes as an even larger and riskier one.

## Market & Competition

1. **xAI Leases Colossus 1 to Anthropic, Eyes Orbital Compute:** xAI announced a compute partnership with Anthropic, giving Anthropic access to Colossus 1, xAI's supercomputer built using more than 220,000 high-end Nvidia GPUs. According to Elon Musk, xAI has already moved its own AI training to Colossus 2, making Colossus 1 available for lease. Notably, the announcement included Anthropic expressing interest in partnering to develop multiple gigawatts of orbital AI compute capacity — meaning AI supercomputers in space. The video connects this to Terafab, described as a joint project between Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI aimed at producing 1 terawatt-hour of chips annually, with the majority intended for orbital data centers powered by unlimited solar energy.

2. **SpaceX Starship Flight 12 Rehearsal Completed:** SpaceX completed a full launch rehearsal for Starship Flight 12, loading more than 5,000 metric tons of supercooled rocket fuel into the fully assembled Version 3 Starship and its Superheavy booster for the first time. Starship V3 is described as the largest and most powerful rocket SpaceX has ever built. Elon Musk indicated Flight 12 could happen around mid-May if final testing continues to go well. The video frames Starship's progress as critical infrastructure for the orbital data center thesis, as well as for eventual transport of humans and Optimus robots to the moon and Mars.

3. **The Boring Company Enters Residential Infrastructure in Nashville:** The Boring Company announced its first residential station agreement for the Music City Loop in Nashville, covering three downtown residential towers: Prime, Alcove, and Paramount. Residents will be able to take an elevator directly to an underground loop station inside their building, board a Tesla, and travel to Nashville International Airport in approximately 9 minutes or to lower Broadway in roughly 2 minutes. The video characterizes this as a significant shift from connecting large destination infrastructure to integrating the loop system into everyday residential life.

Notable quotes and data:
- NHTSA frontal airbags have saved more than 50,000 lives in the United States over the last three decades, per the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.
- Tesla Vision can pre-deploy airbags and seat belts up to **70 milliseconds** earlier than traditional physical-sensor systems.
- The 2026 Model Y is the **first vehicle in the US** to pass NHTSA's new advanced driver assistance system benchmark tests.
- NHTSA administrator Jonathan Morrison: the Model Y "demonstrated the life-saving potential of driver assistance technologies and sets a high bar for the industry."
- Model S launched in 2012; Model X launched in 2015; combined lifetime deliveries approximately **750,000 vehicles**.
- Giga Berlin, started in 2022, has also built **750,000 vehicles**.
- Tesla plans Optimus production at Fremont with a long-term target of up to **1 million units per year**.
- Colossus 1 built with more than **220,000 high-end Nvidia GPUs**.
- Terafab described as targeting **1 terawatt-hour of chips annually**, majority for orbital data centers.
- Starship Flight 12 rehearsal loaded more than **5,000 metric tons** of supercooled rocket fuel.
- Nashville Music City Loop: airport in ~**9 minutes**, lower Broadway in ~**2 minutes** from residential towers.
- Farewell delivery event for final Signature Edition Model S and Model X: **May 20th**.

2026-05-15.title: Something Big May Be Coming For Tesla
2026-05-15.body:
This live panel discussion hosted by "brighterwithherbert" features James from Invest Answers, Cern Basher, and Jeff Lutz covering a wide range of Tesla news and thesis items, including stock technicals, Elon Musk's China visit, Cybercab production sightings, a Las Vegas robotaxi maintenance facility permit, Tesla's evolving profit mix across business lines, the SpaceX IPO implications, a Piper Sandler analyst report, and the state of Optimus and humanoid robot competition. The core argument is that Tesla is transitioning from a car company into a multi-line technology business, and that analysts and investors are only beginning to price in the non-automotive revenue streams. The panel is broadly bullish and believes multiple catalysts — FSD approval in China, robotaxi expansion, Cybercab production ramp, and eventual Optimus deployment — are converging in the near term.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Stock Surge and Technical Setup:** James described Tesla climbing $105 in 30 days, reaching near the $450 resistance level before pulling back. The 200-day moving average sits around $410 and the stock is cleanly above it. The long-term support/resistance line around $330 provided a clean bounce. James predicted a new all-time high within 3 to 6 months, while Jeff and Cern Basher suggested it could happen more quickly depending on news catalysts, particularly out of China.

2. **FSD and Word-of-Mouth Driving Car Sales:** Jeff argued that FSD is increasingly driving car sales through word of mouth in the US, and that rising oil prices (with California at $7 per gallon cited) are pushing consumers toward EVs. He also noted that Panasonic has signaled a capacity increase specifically naming Tesla as the demand source — a meaningful signal given that Tesla has been stagnant or slightly down on total units for the past couple of years, meaning any net demand increase is significant.

3. **Cybercab Sightings at Giga Texas:** Approximately 70 Cybercabs were spotted in the outbound lot at Giga Texas, up from previous sightings of 30–40 units. Joe Tegtmeyer confirmed that most appear to be the same units observed the prior day, meaning they sit for multiple days before being moved — so the 70 figure does not necessarily represent a single day's output. The panel interpreted this as evidence of a ramping production line. Large numbers of Model Ys and Cybertrucks were also visible in the same lot.

4. **Cybercab Production Pacing and Deployment Strategy:** Jeff explained his view that Tesla is calibrating Cybercab production relative to robotaxi deployment readiness rather than rushing to peak production. He suggested Tesla may be building and staging Cybercabs across its 39 tested cities to conduct vehicle-level testing on a new form factor, and that the fleet may need substantial supervised FSD miles before unsupervised deployment scales. The panel noted that there is no point ramping Cybercab production sharply if the software isn't ready to deploy them commercially at scale.

## Financials

1. **Q1 2026 Profit Breakdown — Tesla as a Multi-Line Business:** James presented a profit attribution chart showing Tesla generated approximately $63 million in profit per day in Q1 2026. Of that, roughly 62.8% came from automotive (car sales), 17.5% from energy storage, approximately 6.9% from FSD subscriptions (coincidentally equal to regulatory credit revenue), and a small but growing slice from robotaxi/internet/services/charging. The panel emphasized this is a profit chart, not revenue, explaining why high-margin lines like FSD subscriptions and regulatory credits punch above their weight.

2. **FSD Subscriptions as a Recurring High-Margin Revenue Stream:** The panel highlighted that FSD subscriptions representing close to 7% of Q1 profit was higher than expected. Cern Basher noted that some one-time FSD sales and deferred FSD revenue recognition may have contributed, but argued the more important story is the expanding base of recurring FSD subscriptions. The flywheel effect was discussed: FSD drives car sales, which drives charging revenue, which feeds the broader ecosystem.

3. **Revenue Timeline for New Business Lines:** James presented a slide estimating when each new Tesla business line becomes "significant" (defined as roughly 3–5% of revenue, or approximately $3–5 billion). His sandbagged timeline: Tesla Semi sales already ramping with close to 1,000 orders at approximately $300,000 per unit (with some states offering up to $150,000 in tax credits); FSD significant by early 2027; robotaxi significant toward end of 2028; humanoid robots significant by late 2028; software and services/Digital Optimus by late 2029; in-car inference around 2030. Cern Basher pushed back, suggesting robotaxi could move sooner given Cybercab production ramp, and that Digital Optimus (described as a combination of Tesla FSD and Grok) could be massive by 2027 since it has no manufacturing constraints.

4. **Piper Sandler / Alex Potter Report:** Alex Potter of Piper Sandler released a detailed note arguing that at $400/share (the price at time of writing), Tesla shareholders are effectively getting Optimus for free — it is not priced in at all. His price target is $500. His model includes FSD licensing, automaker hardware purchases, and robotaxi revenue, but with dates pushed to 2030 and beyond. Jeff flagged several specifics from the report: FSD subscription revenue modeled at $900 million in 2027, growing to $1.8 billion in 2028, $4.1 billion shortly after, and more than doubling repeatedly through 2031. Megapack revenue was modeled at $9.7 billion this year, not exceeding $12 billion until 2030, which the panel found inconsistent with company guidance. Tesla insurance was modeled growing to $26 billion by 2035 and nearly $300 billion by 2045. Optimus was excluded entirely from the model. The panel noted that Potter will be joining the show within approximately two weeks.

## Robotaxi

1. **Current Fleet Size and Unsupervised Expansion:** The panel referenced a fleet of approximately 39 unsupervised (driverless) robotaxis currently operating, describing this as a figure they're watching closely. Jeff argued the current fleet has likely hit a performance ceiling under the existing FSD release and is effectively waiting for the next software update before expanding. He noted a coincidence that Tesla is testing in approximately 39 cities and has approximately 39 supervised unsupervised cars. James mentioned that Elon stated on a prior earnings call that there were over 500 robotaxis operating in the Bay Area, and that he personally observes them operating even outside mapped areas.

2. **Las Vegas Cybercab Car Wash / Maintenance Facility:** Tesla filed a permit with Clark County in Las Vegas for what is described as a "Tesla Center Cybercab Phase 2 car wash" — a 36,000 square foot facility involving interior and exterior improvements to an existing structure, including a car wash enclosure, relocation of tire service equipment, and installation of power raceways. The panel interpreted this as a full-service autonomous fleet maintenance hub. AI was cited as estimating the space could hold approximately 60 cars at once, though panelists were uncertain of that figure. Jeff highlighted that this is the kind of ancillary infrastructure required to run an autonomous fleet at scale, and that competitors like Waymo are still largely in manual mode for such operations. The panel speculated that cleaning cadence may coincide with charging cadence to maximize efficiency.

3. **City and State Expansion Strategy:** The panel noted a predominance of politically red states (Texas, Florida, Nevada, Arizona) among Tesla's approximately 39 tested cities, attributing this to more favorable autonomous vehicle legislation already on the books. Cern Basher noted Tesla can follow Waymo's regulatory footprint in many cases. Federal AV legislation was mentioned as a future tailwind. The panel agreed that Florida, Texas, Arizona, and Nevada alone provide massive fleet scaling capacity. James noted Sparks, Nevada and Las Vegas are both on the list.

4. **FSD Approval in China and Robotaxi Launch Path:** Tesla's job postings in China have had the word "urgent" added recently, which the panel interpreted as a strong signal that FSD approval in China is imminent. Separately, a robotaxi-specific job role was posted in China — the first time the word "robotaxi" (rather than just FSD) appeared in a Chinese job posting. The panel's view is that the logical sequence is: FSD approval in China → robotaxi launch in China → Cybercab production in China (with Giga Shanghai or a new facility, since importing from the US is impractical). Cern Basher noted Elon already announced Cybercab and 4680 production at Giga Berlin, suggesting a similar announcement for China is plausible. Jeff also noted that Cybercab production in China would open export markets in South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, and Japan.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Elon Musk's China Visit and FSD Approval Expectations:** Elon Musk traveled to China with President Trump and approximately 16 other CEOs, with Musk and Jensen Huang (Nvidia) reported to have flown together on Air Force One. The panel's consensus view is that deals are largely pre-negotiated before such high-level visits, and that the trip is partly ceremonial. The expectation is that FSD approval in China is very close and that the urgency language in Tesla's China job postings supports this. Jeff explained that China wants to learn from Tesla's vision-only approach as the economically viable path to broad global expansion, and that getting Tesla fully operational in China will catalyze a broader autonomy boom there — similar to what Tesla's 2019 Giga Shanghai entry did for EVs.

2. **FSD Software Release Gating Unsupervised Fleet Growth:** Jeff theorized that Tesla operates robotaxi expansion against a mathematical performance model, and that the unsupervised fleet size is held at a ceiling until a new FSD release is validated to meet performance thresholds. He suggested this is why the approximately 39-vehicle unsupervised fleet has plateaued, and that the next meaningful expansion will coincide with the next validated FSD release. He also raised a concern about wireless charging infrastructure — arguing that Tesla needs to demonstrate autonomous wireless charging at scale (e.g., in outbound lots) before the fleet can grow without manual charging intervention.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus Factory and Hiring Activity:** The panel noted that Tesla has stopped production on the Model S/X line and is replacing it with an Optimus production line at Giga Texas, targeting capacity for one million robots. Ground has been broken and the foundation is being laid for the Optimus factory at Giga Texas. Tesla has also been hiring data collection operators for Optimus across approximately 12 Tesla offices and factories, consistent with Elon's stated goal of having approximately 5,000 Optimus units training in Tesla facilities. Reports indicate these robots are being stress-tested carrying 30 pounds continuously — a load the panel noted is beyond what a human can sustain for a full workday.

2. **Wall Street Reluctance to Model Optimus:** Despite concrete manufacturing steps, no major Wall Street analysts — including Alex Potter's Piper Sandler report — have yet included Optimus revenue in their models. The panel debated what inflection point would cause analysts to add even a small Optimus estimate. Cern Basher suggested ARK Invest confirmed they are working on Optimus research papers and will add it to their model eventually, possibly waiting for a robotaxi inflection point first. The panel argued analysts should take Tesla's manufacturing announcements more seriously than those of any other company given Tesla's execution track record.

3. **Figure Robotics 50+ Hour Live Stress Test:** Figure ran a live-streamed autonomous robot test that was originally planned for 8 hours but extended past 50 hours, with a team of four robots sorting over 63,000 packages. Brett Adcock stated the test will run until a point of failure. The panel gave Figure credit for the transparency and endurance of the demo, but noted technical limitations — Figure's robots still use a claw-style hand without forearm actuators, limiting them to domestic/sorting use cases rather than the heavy industrial use case Optimus is targeting. Cern Basher cited Figure's progress in making approximately 50 robots per day (Jeff was uncertain of the exact number), and argued this makes Tesla's automated manufacturing capability even more impressive by comparison.

4. **Scale as the Decisive Factor in Humanoid Robots:** The panel repeatedly emphasized that the decisive factors in humanoid robotics are: (1) the right AI brain, (2) the right physical product, and (3) manufacturing capability and supply chain at scale — and that very few companies will check all three. Herbert drew an analogy to EV announcements: many companies announced EV ambitions and are now quietly canceling them, and the same pattern is expected in humanoid robots. The panel agreed that fleet scale creates a compounding training advantage — more robots doing more diverse tasks accelerates AI capability across the entire fleet simultaneously — and that this favors whoever can scale manufacturing fastest.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO and Tesla Halo Effect:** The SpaceX IPO prospectus is expected as soon as the following week, with a road show slated for approximately June 8 and the IPO expected around mid-June, which would make it the largest IPO of all time. Ron Baron reportedly stated that SpaceX will be added to three index funds within 15 days of the IPO (one every 5 days), which is unprecedented and would create sustained institutional buying pressure. James argued that the IPO proceeds will fund Terafab, from which Tesla (via Optimus and xAI) would be a long-term beneficiary. The panel's consensus was that Tesla shareholders are unlikely to sell Tesla stock to rotate into SpaceX in any significant way — due to tax consequences, the differing time horizons (Tesla's robotaxi story is closer-term), and the fact that many SpaceX holders are already in via Echelon/SBVS and may actually trim on the IPO pop. If anything, the panel agreed with Larry Goldberg's view that the SpaceX IPO would create a halo effect lifting Tesla stock by approximately 10–15%.

2. **Waymo vs. Uber and Competitive Dynamics:** James briefly noted that Waymo and Uber leadership have begun publicly attacking each other, which he characterized as a sign of weakness ("zombies fighting"). He contrasted this with the collaborative and mutually respectful relationship between Elon Musk and Jensen Huang, calling it a masterclass in CEO partnerships built on shared AI vision and cooperation.

3. **Nvidia and Terafab Partnership Speculation:** Cern Basher raised the question of whether Nvidia might become a partner in the Terafab venture. Jeff responded that Nvidia is not a fabricator — they have no process capability — so any partnership would only make sense if Tesla anticipated demand- or funding-gap issues. Jeff noted Nvidia partners broadly across the industry ("they sleep around with anything that moves"), so a partnership is conceivable but not necessarily meaningful. The panel noted there were rumors of H200 chips becoming more accessible in China, which could have implications for Tesla's FSD and Optimus programs there.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla Q1 2026 profit: approximately $63 million per day
- Profit breakdown: ~62.8% automotive, ~17.5% energy, ~6.9% FSD subscriptions, ~6.9% regulatory credits, small slice from robotaxi/services/charging
- FSD subscriptions = ~6.9% of Q1 2026 profit (described as "nearly 6%" to "6.9%" in different moments)
- Approximately 70 Cybercabs spotted in Giga Texas outbound lot (most likely same units from prior day per Joe Tegtmeyer)
- Las Vegas Cybercab car wash permit: 36,000 square feet, described as "Tesla Center Cybercab Phase 2 car wash," filed with Clark County
- Active unsupervised robotaxi fleet referenced at approximately 39 vehicles (per RobotaxiTracker.com as of 2026-05-09: 39 unsupervised, breakdown Austin 28, Dallas 5, Houston 6)
- Elon previously stated 500+ robotaxis operating in the Bay Area on a prior earnings call
- Tesla Semi: close to 1,000 orders cited, priced at approximately $300,000 per unit, with some states offering up to $150,000 in tax credits
- Piper Sandler (Alex Potter) price target: $500/share; thesis: Optimus unpriced at $400/share
- Alex Potter FSD subscription revenue projections: $900M (2027) → $1.8B (2028) → $4.1B (shortly after) → doubles again in 2030 and 2031
- Alex Potter Megapack revenue: $9.7B in 2026, not exceeding $12B until 2030
- Alex Potter Tesla insurance: $1.6B in 2026, $26B by 2035, ~$300B by 2045
- SpaceX IPO road show reportedly slated for June 8; expected to enter three index funds within 15 days of listing
- SpaceX pre-IPO implied valuation cited at approximately $1.75–$2.2 trillion
- $8 trillion reportedly sitting in money market accounts
- Figure robots sorted over 63,000 packages across 50+ hours of live streaming with a team of four robots
- Tesla reportedly hiring data collection operators for Optimus across approximately 12 offices/factories
- Optimus stress test: reportedly carrying 30 pounds continuously
- Tesla reportedly replacing Model S/X production line with Optimus production line, targeting 1 million robot capacity
- James's "significant revenue" definition: 3–5% of revenue, approximately $3–5 billion
- Jeff: "I think Tesla's manufacturing plans [should be taken] more serious than any other [manufacturer]"
- Cern Basher on Digital Optimus: "you could roll that out and have that be a massive impact in 2027"

2026-05-15.title: Tesla finally reveals what happened in 17 ‘Robotaxi’ crashes
2026-05-15.body:
Tesla has quietly unredacted all 17 of its autonomous driving crash narratives filed with NHTSA — covering July 2025 through March 2026 — revealing for the first time what happened in each incident during its Austin "Robotaxi" testing program. The data shows most crashes were caused by other drivers, but several incidents reveal genuine limitations of Tesla's ADS and its teleoperator backup.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Tesla was uniquely opaque in NHTSA crash reporting:** Tesla had been the only ADS operator to fully redact its crash narratives under NHTSA's Standing General Order 2021-01, citing potential "financial harm" from competitors assessing its autonomous progress. Waymo, Zoox, Avride, May Mobility, and all other operators provided detailed crash narratives throughout this period. Tesla has now filed updated reports removing the confidential designation.

2. **Crash summary across 17 incidents:** All 17 incidents involve a 2026 Model Y with the ADS engaged and a safety monitor present, all in Austin, TX. Injury breakdown: 13 property damage only, 2 no injuries, 1 minor injury without hospitalization, 1 minor injury requiring hospitalization (the most serious). A significant portion were not Tesla's fault — multiple incidents involved the ADS being rear-ended while stopped at red lights, stop signs, or in traffic; a pedicab clipped its mirror; a city bus sideswiped it; and an SUV struck it from behind at a yield lane.

3. **Teleoperator failures are a distinct concern:** Two crashes occurred when a remote teleoperator took over from the ADS. In July 2025, a teleoperator responding to an ADS that wouldn't proceed forward drove the vehicle up a curb and into a metal fence at 8 mph, causing a minor injury. In January 2026, a teleoperator took over a stopped vehicle and drove it into a construction barricade at 9 mph. Both incidents raise questions about the reliability of human backup intervention.

4. **ADS spatial awareness failures:** Several crashes reflect the system's difficulty detecting small or unusual obstacles, particularly while reversing — including hitting a metal chain entering a parking lot, clipping a dump trailer's gooseneck hitch protruding into the street, backing into a wooden electrical pole at 1 mph, and hitting a curb while reversing into a parking space.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert argues Tesla's year-long redaction was a "self-inflicted wound" — had the data been public earlier, the safety narrative would have looked more favorable, since many crashes mirror the rear-ending patterns seen in Waymo's data. However, Lambert flags the teleoperator crashes and spatial awareness failures as genuine concerns, especially as Tesla moves toward removing safety monitors, and suggests ultrasonics and radar may have helped prevent some incidents.

Notable quotes and data:
- All 17 incidents: 2026 Model Y, ADS engaged, safety monitor present, Austin TX, July 2025–March 2026
- Injury severity: 13 property damage only, 2 no injuries, 1 minor non-hospitalization, 1 minor with hospitalization
- Teleoperator crash speeds: 8 mph (fence, July 2025), 9 mph (construction barricade, January 2026)
- ADS spatial incidents: metal chain (6 mph), trailer hitch (18 mph), electrical pole (1 mph), curb while reversing (2 mph)
- Most serious injury: ADS creeping at 2 mph in slip lane, rear-ended by SUV; safety monitor later sought medical evaluation
- Tesla argued disclosure would cause "financial harm" because competitors could assess its autonomous progress
- Dog strike at 27 mph: ADS reduced speed and steered left; dog ran toward vehicle and pushed it into path of a van; dog seen running away afterward

2026-05-15.title: Tesla Just Unredacted Its Robotaxi Reports: Scaling Questions Answered ⚡️
2026-05-15.body:
This episode of Electrified, hosted by Dillon Loomis, covers Tesla's newly unredacted NHTSA Standing General Order (SGO) robotaxi incident reports, fleet scaling constraints, the Uber-Waymo rift, competitive developments in humanoid robotics (Figure AI), and a range of Tesla-adjacent news items. The core thesis is cautionary: while Tesla's robotaxi safety profile and driving performance are encouraging, infrastructure problems — TA operator errors, connectivity issues, limited geofences, and product bugs — make near-term scaling to thousands of vehicles unrealistic. Dillon also argues that Uber's public criticism of Waymo is strategically motivated by self-preservation as autonomous vehicle operators increasingly go direct-to-consumer.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Tesla Unredacts NHTSA SGO Incident Data:** Tesla had previously been the only automaker to redact certain incident details under Confidential Business Information (CBI) rules, but has now chosen to disclose specific information about its robotaxi incidents. The updated data shows a total of 17 incidents since the Austin robotaxi launch in June 2025. Seven of those occurred when the Tesla vehicle was traveling at 0 mph, indicating Tesla was not at fault. The two new April incidents were both at 0 mph, making it another clean month from a fault perspective. Dillon notes he has updated his Teslaomy dashboard (electrified.plx.app) with this data.

2. **Specific Incident Details Reveal ADS Limitations:** The unredacted reports expose several categories of edge-case failures. In one incident, the ADS reversed into a wooden electrical pole after encountering a blocked alley. In another, the side mirror struck a heavy-duty tow truck in a narrow street. A third involved the ADS making contact with a metal chain while entering a parking lot after an unprotected left turn — an issue Dillon links to known FSD limitations with metal chains, citing Chuck Cook's testing even with a newer FSD version. Another incident involved a goose-neck trailer hitch sticking into the street from a driveway, with the ADS side mirror making contact. Dillon characterizes these as evidence that the camera system still struggles to consistently detect smaller, thinner objects at certain height levels.

3. **TA (Remote) Operator Errors Documented Twice:** Two separate incidents involve the TEA (Tesla remote operator) taking control of a vehicle and causing an accident. In the first, the operator gradually increased speed and turned the vehicle left, driving it up a curb and into a metal fence. In the second, the operator took control of a stopped vehicle and drove it into a temporary construction barricade at approximately 9 mph, scraping the front left fender and tire. No passengers were present in either incident. Dillon connects these TA operator issues to previously reported connectivity problems and flags them as a systemic concern for scaling.

4. **Approaching 2 Million Autonomous Miles; Safety Profile Remains Strong:** Despite the specific incidents detailed, Dillon notes Tesla's robotaxi service is approaching approximately 2 million autonomous miles driven, with no new injuries in April. He frames the overall safety record as encouraging, while stressing that back-end infrastructure, TA operations reliability, and object recognition limitations are the real challenges that must be resolved before meaningful scaling can occur.

5. **FSD Data Labeling Job Listing in China:** Tesla posted a new job listing in China for a data labeler who will label images and videos from the fleet and from Optimus data collectors, feeding Tesla's deep learning network. Dillon interprets this as a positive signal that Tesla is now collecting China-specific fleet data to train a localized FSD model — which he identifies as the primary limiting factor for supervised FSD performance in China to date.

## Robotaxi

1. **Scaling Constraints: Geofence Size and Operational Gaps:** Dillon pushes back on expectations of rapid fleet expansion, noting that Tesla's geofences in Houston and Dallas remain very small, with Houston's zone excluding downtown in favor of a more rural area. He argues there is no realistic scenario where Tesla floods those cities with 500 robotaxis in the near term. He explicitly states he is "very confident" anyone expecting 1,000 robotaxis across Austin, Dallas, and Houston will be disappointed absent significant geofence expansion.

2. **Austin Operational Hours Gap After 5 PM:** Rider Ethan McConno reported that while unsupervised robotaxi rides in Austin officially stop around 5:00 PM on weekdays, supervised cars are also sparse after that time — effectively only one or two unmarked driver-monitor cars operating. This creates high service demand and 20–30 minute waits in the post-5 PM window during weekdays. Dillon notes this is a product and operational limitation that contradicts Tesla's official stated operating hours.

3. **Product Bugs Beyond Driving Performance:** Ethan McConno, after stress-testing the Austin robotaxi service over several days, praised the driving performance as impressive in complex, high-traffic scenarios, but catalogued a "long list of important product issues": bad PUDOs (pickup and drop-off locations), broken audio, connectivity issues, and UI/UX problems. Dillon uses this to argue that raw driving quality — while solid — is only one component of what is needed to scale a commercial robotaxi service.

4. **Cybercab Spotted with Starlink Unit; Patent Clarification:** A photo shared by Cybercab Spotter appears to show a Cybercab with a Starlink unit mounted on the back. Dillon treats this as a testing observation only, not confirmation of production integration. He clarifies that the equipment visible on the back of Model Y robotaxis is telecommunications and GPS hardware for remote operations — not built-in Starlink. He also addresses a misunderstood patent involving a new polymer roof material designed to make vehicles radio-frequency transparent, allowing removal of traditional shark fins, but notes that Starlink was not mentioned in that patent.

5. **Las Vegas Robotaxi Launch Anticipated Within ~45 Days:** Dillon references Tesla's permit filings for a dedicated facility in Las Vegas branded "Tesla Center Mohawk Cybercab Phase 2 Car Wash" — approximately 36,000 square feet with roughly 55 parking spots. The facility is described as a full-service maintenance hub for the autonomous fleet, including a car wash enclosure, tire service equipment relocation, and power raceway installation. The location is noted to be approximately a 7-hour drive from Giga Nevada. Dillon states Tesla is planning a Las Vegas robotaxi launch "hopefully sometime in the next 45 days."

6. **Waymo vs. Uber Rift: Competitive Dynamics and Tesla Implications:** Uber executives have taken public shots at Waymo, criticizing its deployment strategy, warning AV operators against going direct-to-consumer, and sharing a video titled "scary Waymo moment." Uber's CEO Dara Khosrowshahi stated that AVs are "still far from capable of meeting the level of reliability and ubiquity that customers and cities expect." Uber also attempted to portray Waymo as withholding service from cities like Oakland and Santa Monica where it allegedly has permits — but Dillon fact-checks this, noting that Waymo's CPUC permit expansion to Oakland is currently suspended through June 27, 2026, pending further staff review, meaning Waymo cannot legally charge for rides there. Dillon concludes Uber's criticism is strategically motivated: Uber's business model is threatened by Tesla and Waymo operating independently, and Uber has every incentive to slow them down through public narrative.

7. **Waymo Recall and San Antonio Suspension:** Waymo issued a recall for 3,800 vehicles due to software issues that could allow its robotaxis to drive onto flooded roadways. An interim software update has been shipped; a permanent fix is still in progress. Waymo's San Antonio service remains temporarily suspended after a vehicle drove into a flooded road and was swept into a creek (no passengers on board). Austin Waymo vehicles were also filmed driving onto a flooded street and stalling.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Figure AI's Live Transparency and F.04 Development:** Figure AI is on day three of a public live-stream marathon showing its robot sorting packages. CEO Brett Adcock clarified that arm-lift motions near the conveyor belt are part of programmed safety policy, not teleoperation. Phil Trouay conducted an interview with Brett, revealing that Figure's next robot (F.04) has completed design lock and is expected to debut in fall 2026, described as the biggest performance leap between versions to date. Figure is also nearly fully localized in its supply chain away from China, expected to be complete by Q3 2026.

2. **Cross-Training Boosts Reliability; Actuator Design Diverges from Tesla:** Brett Adcock is a strong proponent of cross-training robots across many unrelated tasks, citing an example where fridge-loading reliability jumped from 60% to 90% after adding kitchen shelving training to the same model. Figure spends nearly all development time on pre-training its unified Helix model to capture these cross-training benefits. On hardware, Figure's Gen 4 hands have all actuators embedded in the hand itself — the opposite of Tesla's initially patented tendon-driven forearm approach. Dillon notes that Elon Musk recently indicated Tesla has changed course on the hand design described in that patent, making Optimus hand architecture a key area to watch.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla China Denies Model Y Price Increase:** Tesla China officially denied reports of a domestic Model Y price increase. Dillon notes that rising global memory chip (DRAM) prices since September 2025 — driven by surging demand and constrained capacity — have pushed up the cost of advanced driver assistance systems. BYD recently raised the price of its optional lidar-assisted driving package, and NIO's CEO estimated rising memory chip prices could add 3,000–5,000 yuan (roughly up to ~$750) to the cost of high-end new energy vehicles. Tesla and BYD are reportedly among the two largest global consumers of memory DRAM. Dillon assesses the margin impact on Tesla as likely minor and notes Tesla is working to bring memory production in-house as a long-term mitigation.

2. **Panasonic Forecasts 19% Growth in US Battery Sales, Driven by Tesla Recovery:** Panasonic told investors it expects US EV battery sales to grow 19% to 46 GWh in its current fiscal year (ending March 2027), citing Tesla's ongoing market share recovery despite significant lineup revisions. Panasonic projects broader US EV market sales will remain roughly flat year-over-year, while Tesla-specific demand is expected to increase — implying Panasonic expects Tesla to outperform the broader EV market. Dillon notes Panasonic has strong visibility into Tesla's business given their partnership at Giga Nevada.

3. **Tesla Semi Pilot at Covenant Receives Positive Early Results:** Matt Mullen, VP of Sustainability at Covenant, reported the Tesla Semi pilot went off without issues. He praised Tesla's trip planner for accounting for distance, traffic, wind direction, air temperature, weather, grade, and driver inputs to manage range. The driver reported a positive first-day experience despite the center-drive seating position requiring adjustment. Mullen noted more information on the economics of the pilot will be shared soon.

4. **Honda Posts First Annual Loss in ~70 Years:** Honda reported its worst financial results since listing on the stock exchange in 1957, booking more than $9 billion in costs to restructure its EV business. Honda is scrapping its target of EVs comprising 20% of new car sales by 2030 and abandoning its goal of a full EV/fuel cell transition by 2040. It is also indefinitely suspending an $11 billion EV and battery manufacturing investment in Canada. Dillon cites Honda's results as evidence of how risky the EV pivot is for legacy automakers facing weaker-than-expected demand.

## Market & Competition

1. **Uber's Data Collection Play Won't Match Tesla's Fleet Advantage:** Uber announced ambitions to outfit its human-driven cars with sensors to collect real-world data for AV companies and AI training. Uber argued that outfitting even a fraction of its millions of global drivers would create a data platform dwarfing any individual AV company's own data collection. Dillon directly challenges this claim, noting Tesla already has millions of vehicles globally functioning as data collection platforms — and with far more consistency and integration than third-party sensor kits bolted onto Uber driver vehicles. He is skeptical Uber can execute this at scale.

2. **SpaceX IPO Timeline Disclosed:** SpaceX is reportedly planning to disclose its IPO prospectus filing as soon as the following week, with an IPO date of June 12, 2026, under the ticker SPCX, targeting a valuation of approximately $2 trillion.

Notable quotes and data:
- Total Tesla robotaxi incidents since June 2025 launch: **17** (as of April data)
- Incidents at 0 mph (Tesla not at fault): **7 of 17**
- April 2026: **2 new incidents**, both at 0 mph, **0 new injuries**
- TA operator-caused accidents: **2 documented instances**
- Remote operator collision speed (barricade incident): **~9 mph**
- Tesla robotaxi approaching **~2 million autonomous miles**
- Austin post-5 PM wait times: **20–30 minutes**; effectively 1–2 unmarked cars operating
- Las Vegas Cybercab maintenance facility: **~36,000 sq ft**, **~55 parking spots**, ~7-hour drive from Giga Nevada
- Las Vegas robotaxi launch target: **within ~45 days**
- Waymo recall: **3,800 vehicles** for software allowing flooded road entry; San Antonio service **suspended**
- Waymo Oakland CPUC permit expansion: **suspended through June 27, 2026**
- Figure F.04: **design lock complete**, debut expected **fall 2026**
- Figure fridge-loading accuracy: **60% → 90%** after cross-training with kitchen shelving tasks
- Panasonic US battery sales forecast: **+19% to 46 GWh** (fiscal year ending March 2027)
- Memory chip cost impact on EVs: **3,000–5,000 yuan (~up to ~$750)** per vehicle (NIO CEO estimate)
- Honda restructuring costs: **>$9 billion**; suspended **$11 billion** Canada EV/battery project
