2026-05-15.title: Tesla Stock Ready For Another Breakout
2026-05-15.body:
FutureAzA hosts Brian and Randy Kirk discuss the state of Tesla's stock following its rally to its highest level since January, arguing the move reflects the "sum of the parts" thesis coming together across multiple business lines. The video covers Piper Sandler's note that Optimus is not yet priced into Wall Street models, the Anthropic/xAI compute deal, and the ongoing robotaxi ramp as the key catalyst Randy watches daily. The core argument is that missed expectations over the prior months have finally bottomed, and the stock is now beginning a recovery as those expectations are met.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Piper Sandler Says Optimus Is "Free" at Current Valuations:** Piper Sandler released a note stating that Tesla investors are getting Optimus for free at current valuations because the firm had not been modeling it. Brian and Randy are dismissive of this as a "you problem," noting that some analysts — including Cathie Wood and commentators like Cern Basher — have already been assigning value to Optimus. Randy's view is that Optimus either becomes a transformative product or it doesn't, and he sees little middle ground.

2. **Optimus V3 Reportedly Signed Off:** Randy references an unverified but trusted source on X who has stated that Optimus V3 has been signed off on — meaning the design is finalized. Randy interprets this as a strong signal that the robot is capable enough to satisfy Elon Musk's standards, even if this is not an official factory announcement. He frames this as one of four key milestones to watch: production start, factory ramp at Fremont, pricing/billing model announcement, and a demonstration of real-world capabilities.

3. **World-Changing Timeline Debate:** The hosts discuss whether humanoid robots will "change the world" in 2027 or whether a slip to early 2028 would matter much. Randy pushes back on near-term hyperbole, noting that widespread industrial adoption will take years — using his own plastic molding business as an example of a small company that would be far back in the queue to receive an Optimus unit.

4. **TAM Framing:** Randy argues that the total addressable market for Optimus is the largest TAM humans have ever contemplated — larger even than Megapack — because the products (humanoid robots) are more expensive. He references figures of $100,000 per year in revenue or $400,000 in cash value per unit as the types of numbers being discussed, though he does not claim precision on these.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **FSD Momentum Across Geographies:** Randy cites a range of FSD-related progress as part of the "sum of the parts" thesis: China testing FSD, Europe passing FSD tests, and NHTSA reportedly naming Tesla's ADAS the best in the world. He sees these as compounding catalysts rather than any single breakout event.

2. **China FSD Revenue — Modest Near-Term Impact:** Brian is skeptical that the "Thank China AI" framing used in a Barron's/MSN article fully explains the stock's 4% move, noting that FSD revenue from China would be a relatively small portion of Tesla's overall valuation drivers.

## Robotaxi
1. **Robotaxi Fleet Tracking as Primary Daily Indicator:** Randy says the first thing he checks every morning is how many Tesla robotaxis are on the road, how many miles they are driving, and what is happening in Austin, Dallas, and Houston — and whether any new cities are opening. He frames this as what serious investors are watching to decide whether to add to their positions.

## Market & Competition
1. **Anthropic/xAI Compute Deal:** The hosts discuss a deal in which Anthropic (maker of Claude) is purchasing inference compute from xAI because it could not source enough capacity elsewhere — including from Amazon Web Services. Randy frames this as xAI monetizing spare compute capacity from what he describes as one of the largest computers in the world, ahead of an even larger facility being built next door. Reported deal estimates discussed range from $4 billion on the low end to $16 billion on the high end, with a cluster of estimates around $5–6 billion annually. Brian and Randy treat this as significant revenue for xAI and as evidence that xAI may be the only viable option at scale for inference compute at this time.

## Financials
1. **Stock Rally Context and Randy's Prediction:** Tesla stock hit its highest level since January, trading as low as $416 before rallying to $445 on a day the S&P 500 rose only 0.2%. Randy claims he predicted five to six months ago that missed expectations would drag the stock down, and that once the bottom was hit and expectations began being met, the stock would recover. He declares a "victory lap," arguing that recovery is now underway.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla stock rallied from $416 to $445 on the day discussed; the stock had not closed above $445 since late January
- S&P 500 rose only 0.2% on the same day
- Piper Sandler: Optimus not included in their Tesla valuation model — investors are "getting it for free"
- Optimus V3 reportedly signed off, per an unverified but trusted source on X
- Anthropic/xAI compute deal: estimates range from $4B to $16B, with $5–6B cited most commonly
- Randy: "You either believe that Optimus is going to be a thing and it's going to be valuable, or you don't — it's kind of hard to have middle ground"
- Randy on robotaxi: "That's the first thing I check every morning — how many cars we got on the road now, how many miles are they driving, what do we know about those cars in Austin, Dallas, and Houston?"
- Active robotaxi fleet tracking in cities mentioned: Austin, Dallas, Houston (per RobotaxiTracker.com: Austin 104, Dallas 5, Houston 6 as of 2026-05-15)
- FutureAzA Summer Meetup: June 5–6 in Muskegon, Michigan (teslamichigan.org)

2026-05-15.title: Clean Cabs, Superhuman Vision, FSD Cannonball Record, & a whole lot more at 8am Pacific
2026-05-15.body:
This episode of the Tesla Beat podcast (episode 146) covers a wide range of Tesla news including FSD safety improvements, the Cannonball Run cross-country FSD record, Model S/X end of production, Giga Berlin milestones, Cybercab robotaxi infrastructure developments, and Tesla Semi updates. The hosts — Joe, Brian, and the main presenter — also promote their upcoming "X Takeover" community event at Giga Texas on October 10th, featuring Maye Musk as keynote speaker.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Tesla Vision Superhuman Capability Highlighted:** Elon Musk posted a comparison between a human-perceived RGB image and Tesla AI's photon count reconstruction image, illustrating why FSD can see well at night and through extreme glare. The hosts noted that FSD V14 represents a major improvement over V12 and V13 in handling glare and adverse weather conditions, with one host recounting a rainy night drive where the car autonomously reduced its maximum available speed in response to road conditions without driver input.

2. **FSD Cannonball Run Record Set:** A team including David, Zach (Zack Black Model 3), and Dan completed a coast-to-coast Cannonball Run from California to New York using FSD version 143.2, covering 2,833 miles in 49 hours and 55 minutes with zero disengagements or human interventions. This beat the previous FSD Cannonball record by 8.5 hours. The hosts emphasized this as a demonstration that a Tesla can now effectively drive cross-country autonomously, needing only human assistance for charging.

3. **Early Airbag Deployment via Camera Detection:** Tesla Vision enables airbags to be deployed up to 70 milliseconds earlier than traditional sensor-triggered systems by detecting an unavoidable collision via cameras before physical impact occurs. The hosts noted that a prior episode reported FSD now reacts approximately 20% faster than a previous version, and that FSD is statistically six to seven times safer per mile than human drivers.

4. **FSD Expansion into EU Underway:** Ireland is in active talks with Tesla regarding FSD approval, with plans to adopt EU-level regulations permitting FSD rather than create independent rules. The hosts noted that Tesla is proactively engaging individual EU member states — telling each country "tell us what you need to see" — to ensure affirmative votes when EU-wide FSD policy comes up. The Netherlands has already approved FSD, and Belgium was cited as likely next.

## Robotaxi
1. **Cybercab Car Wash Facility Planned for Las Vegas:** Tesla reportedly filed a permit with Clark County on May 12th describing a "Cybercab Phase 2 car wash" at an existing facility in Las Vegas. The project involves interior and exterior improvements, construction of a car wash enclosure, and relocation of tire service equipment. The hosts noted this signals Tesla is planning robotaxi infrastructure in Las Vegas even before public robotaxi service has been announced there, and contrasted Tesla's likely automated approach with Waymo's heavily manual cleaning operation.

2. **Cybercab Spotted with Starlink Mini:** A Cybercab was observed with a Starlink Mini mounted on the back. The hosts speculated that Starlink connectivity will eventually be integrated directly into Tesla vehicles, making the robotaxi network more resilient — referencing the San Francisco power outage that caused Waymo vehicles to fail while Tesla's vision-based system was unaffected. The hosts also noted that the Fremont factory already has numerous large Starlink installations visible on the test track, suggesting deep existing integration between Tesla and SpaceX connectivity infrastructure.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Model S and Model X Production Ends at Fremont:** The last Model S and Model X vehicles have been produced at the Fremont factory, ending 14 years of Model S production and 11 years of Model X production. The hosts reflected on the Model S's legacy as the first genuinely desirable mass-market EV and noted that the final Model S is expected to go to Steve Jurvetson, who received the first one. The hosts framed the end of production as a deliberate pivot toward Optimus and autonomous vehicles.

2. **Giga Berlin Reaches 750,000 Model Y Milestone:** Giga Berlin has produced 750,000 Model Y vehicles, and separately announced a million drive units produced. The hosts noted that 4680 cells are being or will soon be manufactured on the Giga Berlin campus, which should drive down vehicle costs. Tesla is also routing Model Y production from Berlin to Canada to optimize around tariff structures, and shipping Model 3s to Canada from Giga Shanghai.

3. **$250 Million Investment in Giga Berlin Cell Factory:** Tesla announced a $250 million investment in its Giga Berlin 4680 cell factory, targeting 18 gigawatt-hours of annual cell production capacity and creating 1,500 new jobs. Brian noted the factory footprint is far smaller than Giga Nevada (which has 35 GWh capacity), demonstrating dramatically improved energy density per square foot of manufacturing space.

4. **Model Y L Expanding to Singapore and Southeast Asia:** Kyle Connor (6'1") tested the Model Y L at the Beijing Auto Show and confirmed adequate knee clearance in the third row at that height. The vehicle is being delivered in Singapore and spreading across Oceania and Southeast Asia. Test models have been spotted in both Texas and Germany. The hosts expressed confidence it will arrive in the US before the end of 2026, citing a brief appearance on Tesla's website (quickly removed) and Bay Area sightings as signals.

## Energy
1. **Tesla Semi E-PTO Powers Refrigerated Trailers:** Tesla Semi's Electric Power Take-Off (E-PTO) now delivers up to 25 kW to power trailer refrigeration units, eliminating the need for diesel auxiliary motors. The hosts noted this is a significant efficiency gain for truckers — particularly those running refrigerated loads — and referenced a 50% cost-per-mile savings in California versus diesel. They also discussed how semi drivers may increasingly use the power capability for in-cab living amenities.

## Market & Competition
1. **Waymo's LiDAR Limitations Contrasted with Tesla Vision:** The hosts compared Tesla's camera-only FSD approach favorably to Waymo's LiDAR-dependent system, noting that Waymo vehicles are regularly observed getting stuck in challenging conditions (fog, glare, unusual scenarios) while Tesla's photon-count reconstruction vision system handles those scenarios by seeing through noise that would confuse both LiDAR and human eyes.

2. **Chinese EV Competition in Europe:** Despite strong Chinese EV presence in Europe and Germany's competitive domestic auto market (BMW, Mercedes, Porsche, Volkswagen), Tesla's Model Y continues to outsell most Chinese competitors. Brian attributed part of this to Tesla's superior ride quality and suspension tuning, areas where even premium Chinese brands like Xiaomi and BYD still lag. The hosts also noted that the Model Y is the best-selling car in the world.

Notable quotes and data:
- FSD version 143.2 completed 2,833 miles coast-to-coast in 49 hours 55 minutes, zero disengagements, beating the previous record by 8.5 hours
- Tesla Vision enables airbag deployment up to 70 milliseconds earlier than conventional sensor-triggered systems
- FSD is stated as 6–7× safer per mile than human drivers
- $250 million invested in Giga Berlin 4680 cell factory; target: 18 GWh annual production; 1,500 new jobs created
- Giga Nevada capacity cited at 35 GWh for comparison
- Giga Berlin: 750,000 Model Y produced; 1 million drive units produced
- Tesla Semi E-PTO output: up to 25 kW; ~50% cheaper per mile than diesel in California
- Kyle Connor (6'1") had knee clearance in Model Y L third row
- Ron Baron suggested a combined Tesla/SpaceX entity could be worth $10–$30 trillion, calling that a conservative estimate
- X Takeover event: Giga Texas, October 10th; 570+ tickets sold in first 24 hours; capacity 1,500
- Tesla stock: ~$427 at time of recording; -2.3% year-to-date; has been hovering around $440
- Las Vegas Cybercab car wash permit filed with Clark County on May 12th
- SpaceX filed trademark for "SpaceX AI" word mark, now accepted

2026-05-15.title: Tesla Stock CRASHES - What Happens NEXT?
2026-05-15.body:
In this live session, Jo Bhakdi reacts to a sharp Tesla stock decline on what he describes as a low-volume, post-"sell-the-news" day following the Trump-Xi Beijing summit, arguing the drop is a normal market retracement rather than a thesis-breaking event. His core argument is that Tesla's bull run toward a $490 price target remains intact, supported by Cybercab ramp-up, global EV sales strength, Terafab developments, and a potential SpaceX merger catalyst. The session blends tactical options commentary with broader macro context and audience Q&A.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla underperforms NASDAQ on low volume:** Tesla fell approximately 4.3% on the day versus NASDAQ's decline of roughly 1.23–1.26%, which Bhakdi notes far exceeds what Tesla's beta would imply (approximately 2.5% down). He attributes much of this to a "sell the news" dynamic following the Trump-Xi Beijing summit, where markets had priced in enthusiasm and then retreated. He emphasizes the drop occurred on notably low volume — approximately 40 million shares versus an average of approximately 65 million — which he interprets as a weak bearish signal, suggesting the move lacks conviction.

2. **Weekly and monthly context remains bullish:** Despite the daily decline, Bhakdi notes Tesla is still positive for the week after a significant run-up. Over one month, he notes Tesla is up nearly 8%. He frames the day's drop as a normal breather after an approximately 20% run-up since April 9th, pointing to NASDAQ's roughly 9.44% gain over the prior month as evidence the broader bull run is intact.

3. **Trump-Xi summit framed as a macro positive, not a Tesla catalyst:** Bhakdi dismisses expectations that the Beijing summit would produce specific Tesla announcements (such as FSD approval in China), noting that Xi Jinping's agenda encompassed far larger geopolitical issues including Taiwan, Iran, and nuclear weapons. He views the most meaningful outcome as Trump inviting Xi to the White House in September and the generally cooperative tone, which he sees as positive for supply chain preparation for Optimus and potentially lower tariffs over time.

4. **Oil shock viewed as transient and positive for EVs:** Bhakdi argues that rising oil prices represent a supply shock rather than sustained monetary inflation, and that prices will revert rather than continue compounding year over year. He views elevated oil prices as a net positive for Tesla EV and Semi sales while they persist, and expects the Strait of Hormuz situation to resolve because both the US and Iran face too much geopolitical pressure from their respective allies to sustain the disruption.

5. **AGI crossing a threshold in real time:** Bhakdi expresses a strong view that economic AGI — defined as AI replacing workers at scale — is being crossed "as we speak," with capability parity for most jobs potentially achieved within three months, leaving deployment as the primary remaining constraint.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab ramp characterized as ongoing and on track:** Bhakdi dismisses a viewer comment that the robotaxi rollout is stalling, saying "they're printing all these Cybercabs and they're doing pretty well." He frames the deployment as deliberate and step-by-step rather than stalled. He does not cite specific fleet numbers but references the Cybercab launch as a thesis-supporting milestone that did not exist at the December 2025 all-time high.

2. **Viewer robotaxi experience in Bay Area:** A viewer reported taking their first robotaxi ride in the Bay Area, describing wait times as poor but the ride experience as "amazing" and notably cheaper than Uber, with no tip required. Bhakdi responds that cautious, step-by-step rollout will address wait times and that he believes meaningful scale is approaching.

3. **RobotaxiTracker.com referenced indirectly:** A viewer asks why the robotaxi page isn't updating, which Bhakdi acknowledges without explanation.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus supply chain from China cited as a key quiet benefit of the summit:** Bhakdi notes that while no formal announcements were made, the Beijing visit was likely preparing better supply chain arrangements for Optimus production, pointing to this as a more realistic near-term benefit than headline deals.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Global EV sales rebound cited as thesis support:** Bhakdi references a "pretty significant" sales rebound, stating Tesla is "killing it and getting very strong globally on the EV side," using this alongside Cybercab launch and Terafab as reasons the $490 price target thesis is stronger now than when Tesla hit that level in December 2025.

## Financials

1. **Long-term price target revised to $4,000 base case by 2030:** Bhakdi discloses that he has shifted his 2030 base case price target from $6,000 to $4,000, citing increased caution around the timing of robotaxi and Optimus scaling. He describes the underlying DCF model as conservative on revenue expectations and margins but base case (not conservative) on cash flow assumptions. He adds that a 10x outcome (implying roughly $4,500+ from current levels) is possible if millions of robotaxis and approximately one million humanoid robots are deployed by 2030.

2. **Pioneer Alpha fund performance disclosed:** Bhakdi reports Pioneer Alpha is up approximately 36% year-to-date, achieving approximately 41% alpha over Tesla stock, which is itself down approximately 4.75% year-to-date. Over two years and five months, he states the fund is up approximately 166%. He attributes outperformance to correctly predicting Q1 weakness, shifting to cautious positioning, then turning aggressively bullish near the $360 low.

3. **Options positioning disclosed:** Bhakdi describes holding a large number of short puts, including 420 and 430 strike puts sold for approximately $10 in premium the prior week (characterized as still profitable). For the current week, he describes positions requiring Tesla to return to approximately $430–$435 to break even, with losses mounting if the stock falls to $410. He also describes selling large quantities of 430-strike calls expiring the same day as a tactical hedge, which he estimates saved approximately 2% of portfolio value on the down day.

4. **SpaceX IPO mentioned as a near-term catalyst:** Bhakdi references a reported SpaceX IPO date of June 12th (described as unconfirmed but probable), framing it as at least a short-term tactical positive catalyst for Tesla stock, tied to the broader SpaceX-Tesla merger thesis he has covered in prior videos.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla down ~4.3% vs. NASDAQ down ~1.23–1.26% on the day
- Tesla volume: ~40 million shares vs. ~65 million average (low volume day)
- NASDAQ up ~9.44% over the prior month
- Tesla up ~8% over the prior month despite the day's decline
- Tesla up ~20% since April 9th
- Pioneer Alpha: +166% over 2 years and 5 months; +36% YTD; +41% alpha over Tesla YTD
- Tesla stock YTD: approximately -4.75%
- 2030 base case price target revised from $6,000 to $4,000
- 10x by 2030 possible "if you see millions of robotaxis and a million humanoids in 2030"
- SpaceX IPO rumored for June 12th (unconfirmed)
- Viewer robotaxi ride in Bay Area: "amazing" experience, "way cheaper than Uber," but poor wait times
- $490 cited as Tesla's December 2025 effective all-time high and near-term bull case target
- Tactical support/resistance levels cited: $420 (channel floor), $445–$450 (resistance), $490 (bull target)

2026-05-15.title: Rivian R2 First Look at ACT Expo | Improvements From the R1
2026-05-15.body:
This video features a walkthrough of the Rivian R2 at ACT Expo 2026, conducted by Munro Live with Sam Anderson, Rivian's Fleet Sales Customer Success Manager. The discussion covers the R2's key specifications, exterior design philosophy, interior features, and the deliberate engineering and cost-reduction decisions that differentiate it from Rivian's R1 platform.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Launch Edition Specs:** The R2 launch edition features approximately 330 miles of range from an 87–89 kWh usable battery pack, 0–60 mph in 3.5 seconds, and just over 650 horsepower. It uses a dual-motor all-wheel drive configuration with motors that are entirely new and bespoke to the R2 — described as smaller, more powerful, and more efficient than those found in the R1 lineup.

2. **Design Identity and Proportions:** The R2's exterior deliberately carries over Rivian's brand DNA — including the halo headlights and classic SUV silhouette — but features several distinguishing design elements including a clamshell hood, more exaggerated wheelbase proportions, squared-off mirror arms, and a rear charge port positioned on the driver's rear side. The overall effect was described as a scaled-down R1S, maintaining short front and rear overhangs for interior headroom and occupant space.

3. **Aerodynamic Rear Spoiler and Rear Wiper:** The R2 features a rear spoiler to maintain aerodynamic efficiency and silhouette continuity. Unlike some competitors (noted comparisons include Hyundai Ioniq and Jaguar/JLR models) that sacrifice a rear wiper for aerodynamic gains, Rivian retained a rear wiper on the R2, housed in a recessed "garage." Extensive testing was conducted on drainage, ice, and debris accumulation in this recessed area.

4. **Frunk Cost Reduction and Simplification:** The R2's frunk reflects a deliberate cost-reduction effort compared to the R1. Changes include relocating the frunk release button to a touch-capacitive button centered near the logo (moved from the bottom of the fascia), switching from a powered opening mechanism to gas strut operation, eliminating the two-stage load floor with reversible rubberized/carpeted mat from the R1, and reducing overall part count and fasteners. The hood liner is now a compression-molded PET piece serving primarily an NVH/acoustic function, contrasted with the finished injected-molded piece used in the R1.

5. **Interior Value Retention Despite Cost Focus:** Despite targeting a lower price point, the R2's interior retains numerous premium elements including fabric-wrapped IP components with live stitching (not faux stitch), vinyl wrap components with live stitching, vinyl seats with stitching patterns and perforation, ventilation and heating, backlit ambient LED lighting, and magnetic wireless charging in the center console. Simplifications include a single-hinge, manually lifted center console door replacing the two-hinge electronically released design from the R1.

6. **Halo Haptic Steering Wheel Controls:** The R2 features electromechanical steering wheel scroll wheels called "Halo haptic wheels." These wheels scroll up and down, toggle left and right, and can be pressed from both the front and rear. Critically, the detents are not mechanical — they are electromechanically generated, allowing the force, throw, and detent count to be adjusted contextually in software depending on what is being controlled. For example, fan speed uses seven distinct detents with resistance at the end of travel, while temperature control uses a finer, more granular resolution. This allows over-the-air software updates to modify the tactile feel. The Munro Live host noted these appear to be among the only examples of this electromechanical (non-mechanical) application in this form factor in the automotive industry.

## Market & Competition

1. **Segment Positioning and Competitive Context:** The R2 is explicitly positioned to be cost-competitive in a segment below the R1S, with cost reduction described as "the name of the game." Aerodynamic comparisons were drawn to Hyundai Ioniq and Jaguar/JLR vehicles. Rivian claims the R2 has one of the largest — if not the largest — frunks in its segment.

Notable quotes and data:
- ~330 miles of range (launch edition)
- 87–89 kWh usable battery pack
- 0–60 mph: 3.5 seconds
- Just over 650 horsepower
- Dual-motor all-wheel drive
- New motors bespoke to R2, not shared with R1 platform
- Frunk button: relocated and changed to touch-capacitive
- Frunk hood liner: compression-molded PET (NVH/acoustic function)
- Halo haptic wheels: electromechanically controlled, software-defined detents, OTA updatable
- Fan speed: 7 detents with end-of-travel resistance; temperature: finer/more granular detent resolution
- Sam Anderson title: Fleet Sales Customer Success Manager, Rivian

2026-05-15.body:

Today's posts centered on Robotaxi infrastructure expansion signals (a Las Vegas dedicated Cybercab carwash permit and a Starlink Mini spotted on a Cybercab), alongside broader Tesla demand recovery evidence from Panasonic's raised battery outlook and continued geographic expansion into India. The overall picture is one of steady operational buildout rather than a single major catalyst, with incremental but consistent bullish signals across the autonomy and EV thesis.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Robotaxi Infrastructure Expanding to Las Vegas — Carwash Permit Filed:** Tesla reportedly submitted plans to Clark County, Nevada for a dedicated Robotaxi carwash facility, with a permit filed on May 12. The project is described as "Tesla Center Cybercab Phase 2 Car Wash" and involves interior and exterior improvements. The "Phase 2" designation implies prior or concurrent Phase 1 work at the same site, suggesting Tesla is actively standing up operational support infrastructure in Las Vegas — a city not yet listed among active Robotaxi markets in canonical tracker data. This is a meaningful signal that Las Vegas is a near-term target for Robotaxi deployment expansion. The post drew 2,500 likes and 260 reposts, indicating high community interest.

2. **Cybercab Spotted with Starlink Mini Integration:** A Cybercab was photographed with a Starlink Mini unit mounted on the back — reported as the first known public sighting of this configuration. This is notable for the Tesla investment thesis on multiple levels: it suggests Tesla may be evaluating satellite connectivity as a redundant or primary data link for its autonomous fleet, potentially relevant for coverage in areas with weaker terrestrial LTE/5G infrastructure. No official confirmation or context was provided beyond the image.

3. **FSD (Supervised) Pilot for Community Transit in Germany:** A pilot program in Germany's Eifel region is actively using Tesla vehicles running FSD (Supervised) to transport students and senior citizens in rural communities with limited public transit. A passenger was quoted: "I think the ride is great. It's so relaxing. I feel safer than if I were driving." While this is supervised (not driverless) and in a non-U.S. regulatory context, it represents a real-world FSD deployment in a structured mobility service role — directly adjacent to the supervised-to-unsupervised commercialization pathway and a positive anecdotal safety data point.

4. **Panasonic Raises EV Battery Outlook on Tesla Demand Recovery:** Panasonic raised its EV battery outlook, explicitly citing increased Tesla sales. The company stated: "Demand is expected to exceed full-year 2026 levels, supported by strategic customer's recent recovery in market share, despite significant revisions to their model lineups." This is a third-party corroboration of Tesla's volume recovery trajectory in 2026 and a positive leading indicator for Tesla's Q2 2026 deliveries. The reference to "significant revisions to their model lineups" appears to acknowledge the Model Y refresh and related product transitions.

5. **Elon Musk Visits China with Tom Zhu:** Elon Musk was photographed in China today alongside his son and Tom Zhu, Tesla's SVP of Asia-Pacific and Global Vehicle Manufacturing. The visit drew 5,100 likes — the highest-engagement post of the day. No specific agenda or announcement was disclosed, but a direct visit by Musk to China alongside the executive overseeing both APAC operations and global manufacturing is a notable signal for investors monitoring Tesla's China market recovery, FSD regulatory progress in China, or potential new product/manufacturing announcements.

6. **Tesla Expands India Retail Footprint — Fourth Showroom Opens in Bengaluru:** Tesla opened its fourth showroom in India, located in Bengaluru (Karnataka). This continues the rollout of Tesla's India market entry and represents geographic diversification into a major growth market. No delivery volumes or pricing details were mentioned.

7. **Uber vs. Waymo Tension — Competitive Robotaxi Dynamics:** A post flagged that Uber and its executives have been taking "direct and indirect shots" at Waymo, cautioning against autonomous vehicle operators attempting to scale independently and criticizing Waymo's deployment strategy and technology. While this primarily concerns the Uber-Waymo relationship, it is relevant context for Tesla's robotaxi strategy: Tesla has consistently signaled intent to operate its own fleet (not partner with ride-hailing platforms), and any fragmentation or tension in the Waymo-Uber partnership could affect the competitive landscape Tesla enters.

8. **Honda Abandons 2040 Full-EV Target:** Honda's CEO stated the company has officially withdrawn its goal to go fully electric by 2040, saying "It's not realistic. We have judged that it'll be difficult to achieve." This is a continued retreat by legacy OEMs from aggressive EV commitments, which may reduce near-term competitive pressure on Tesla in the pure-EV segment while also signaling ongoing challenges in the broader EV transition.

9. **New 64-Stall Supercharger Opens in Jean, Nevada (325kW, $0.46/kWh):** A large new Supercharger station opened in Jean, Nevada with 64 stalls, trailer-friendly configurations, peak charging speed of 325kW, and a base rate of $0.46/kWh for Tesla owners. While routine infrastructure, the $0.46/kWh rate is a concrete data point for Tesla's charging economics.

---

## Signal Strength: **Mildly Bullish** — Robotaxi infrastructure expansion (Las Vegas carwash permit), Starlink Mini integration on Cybercab, third-party demand validation from Panasonic, and continued geographic expansion collectively reinforce the Tesla thesis without a single transformative catalyst.

2026-05-16.title: Tesla Delays Usually Mean Something Bigger
2026-05-16.body:
This video features host Herbert (brighterwithherbert) in conversation with Cern Basher, a chartered financial analyst and founder of Brilliant Advice wealth management, exploring the thesis that Tesla's repeated delays are not a unique flaw but a pattern consistent with virtually every major technological breakthrough in history. The core argument is that inventing something is easy — making it affordable, reliable, manufacturable, scalable, and infrastructure-supported is the hard part — and that Tesla's delays are often strategic, waiting until all conditions align for dominance at scale rather than launching prematurely for headlines. The Tesla Semi serves as the primary case study, used to illustrate how multiple converging constraints (batteries, charging, manufacturing, autonomy readiness) forced a roughly nine-year delay from announcement to production, which may have ultimately positioned the product better for market adoption.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Historical pattern of EV delays — a 100-year gap:** Cern Basher traces the EV concept back to the early 1900s, noting that electric vehicles were once serious competitors to gasoline cars — they were quieter, cleaner, and easier to operate — but lost out because batteries were weak, gasoline became cheap, and the internal combustion supply chain scaled faster. The modern EV revival, driven primarily by Tesla, only became viable once lithium-ion batteries, better motors, electronics, and software converged to make the economics viable. The hosts frame this as a century-long delay in a technology whose fundamental concept was always sound.

2. **Tesla Semi: nine years from announcement to production:** Introduced at an event on December 7, 2017, with Elon Musk promising deliveries by 2019, the Tesla Semi did not make its first deliveries — to PepsiCo — until December 2022, and those were described as pilot units only. The first vehicle came off a completed production line in Nevada in April 2026, roughly nine years after the announcement. The hosts acknowledge this is an unambiguously large delay but argue the intervening period produced a substantially better product, with Dan Priestley noted as having mentioned approximately 1,000 pounds of weight reduction achieved over the development period, and the truck described as "autonomy ready."

3. **Battery constraints as the primary bottleneck for the Semi:** The discussion identifies battery cell supply as the dominant reason for the Semi's delay. The battery pack in the Semi is described as significantly larger than that of a Model 3 — Herbert estimates it may be seven to ten times the battery content — meaning that during periods of constrained cell supply, Tesla had to prioritize between Megapacks, Model 3s, Model Ys, Cybertrucks, and the Semi. The 4680 battery cell development, including challenges with the dry cathode process and achieving adequate manufacturing yield, is cited as a critical underlying technology that the Semi's economics depended on.

4. **Semi economics: ~35 cents per mile in savings, $60,000–$80,000 annual fuel savings per truck:** Cern cites a figure of approximately 35 cents per mile in cost savings versus diesel, and an estimated annual fuel saving of $60,000 to $80,000 per truck when using a Tesla Semi Megacharger. The hosts note this implies a payback period of roughly three to five years, and that a product with this economic profile "will sell itself" provided reliability is established. Early orders are described as coming in strongly, with one example of a 340-unit order mentioned.

5. **Hub-and-spoke deployment strategy as the commercial go-to-market:** The hosts discuss Tesla's strategy of initially targeting fleet operators with depot-based charging rather than building out a public Megacharger network immediately. In this model, trucks leave a central hub in the morning and return in the evening to charge on-site, with the customer responsible for installing charging infrastructure. This approach lets Tesla sell trucks without bearing the capital cost of a national charging network, while building reliability data at scale before pursuing the long-haul trucking segment. The hosts describe this as "really smart."

6. **Aerodynamics of the Semi surpassing a Bugatti:** From the 2017 presentation, Cern notes that the Tesla Semi has a drag coefficient of 0.36 compared to 0.38 for a Bugatti sports car, making it more aerodynamic than a high-performance sports car and dramatically better than a conventional diesel truck.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD readiness vs. robotaxi rollout timing:** The hosts discuss the apparent gap between FSD software being functionally capable of enabling robotaxi service and Tesla's deliberate pace of rollout. Cern suggests that Tesla may be choosing to delay broader robotaxi deployment not because the software cannot function, but because it is continuing to improve rapidly — pickup/drop-off optimization, rider comfort features — and Tesla is waiting for a higher-quality product rather than deploying something that will be meaningfully better in three to four months. This is framed as the opposite dynamic from Duke Nukem Forever, where a product chased a moving finish line; here, the finish line is improving ahead of Tesla rather than receding from it.

2. **Tesla Semi described as "autonomy ready":** Dan Priestley is cited as having stated that the Tesla Semi is designed to be ready for autonomous trucking operation. The hosts speculate that some of the design changes made during the nine-year development period may have been specifically oriented toward future FSD integration on the truck, though they note the exterior design has not changed dramatically. The prospect of daisy-chaining autonomous semi trucks behind a single supervised lead driver is raised as a near-term intermediate step.

## Robotaxi

1. **Waymo characterized as a "demo" losing ~$100 per ride:** Herbert argues that Waymo's current operation — described as operating in approximately 10 cities — still constitutes a demonstration rather than a scalable business. He estimates Waymo is losing approximately $100 per ride, derived from a claimed five to six billion dollar annual loss divided by the number of rides. Issues cited include approximately 1,000 incidents per month, vehicles stopping unexpectedly, inability to navigate flooding, and frequent remote operator interventions. The hosts acknowledge Tesla's own robotaxi operation is currently an even more limited demo.

2. **36,000 sq ft Cybercab car wash facility permitted in Las Vegas:** Herbert cites a recently permitted 36,000 square foot car wash facility in Las Vegas specifically for Cybercabs, described as a robotic/automated operation requiring minimal human staff. This is presented as evidence that Tesla is building out the physical infrastructure for scaled robotaxi operations before the vehicles themselves are deployed at volume, with Herbert suggesting every major city will eventually have a similar facility. The scale of the facility implies planning for thousands of Cybercabs per city.

3. **Delay attributed to infrastructure setup rather than software unreadiness:** The overarching explanation offered for why Tesla's robotaxi service is not yet at scale is not software capability but rather physical infrastructure — car wash facilities, charging depots, and operational support systems. The hosts frame this as consistent with Tesla's broader pattern of waiting until the full system is ready before scaling, analogous to Apple building data center infrastructure years before the app store explosion.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus framed as the right technology arriving at the right time:** Herbert argues that earlier humanoid robot prototypes — specifically citing Honda's ASIMO, which could walk up stairs and shake hands — were demonstrations without a path to scale. The key enabling technologies that make Optimus different, according to the hosts, are FSD-derived motion intelligence, AI maturity, and Tesla's existing manufacturing expertise. Elon Musk is credited with recognizing when the AI and robotics technology stack had converged sufficiently and launching Optimus at that moment, which in turn catalyzed broader industry formation around humanoid robotics.

2. **Supply chain complexity compared to Boeing Dreamliner challenges:** The Boeing 787 Dreamliner's delays — caused by outsourcing components globally and discovering that parts didn't fit or meet quality standards when assembled — are cited as a direct analogy for challenges Tesla may face building a new global supply chain for Optimus. The hosts note that planning a supply chain on paper and executing it reliably are entirely different problems, and that this kind of challenge is inherent to any genuinely new product with new materials, new production methods, and new supply relationships.

## Market & Competition

1. **Thesis that breakthrough technologies are universally late:** Cern's research covers more than a dozen historical examples of delayed technologies to establish a pattern: AT&T's Picturephone (demoed 1964, never successfully commercialized as a dedicated device), the first commercial cell phone (first call 1973, first commercial handset 1983), the James Webb Space Telescope (expected ~2007, launched Christmas Day 2021), Duke Nukem Forever (14 years in development, released 2011), Windows Vista, the Boeing 787 Dreamliner, Dyson's bagless vacuum, Bluetooth, the Channel Tunnel (idea dating to early 1800s, opened 1994), HDTV, the tablet computer (concept from late 1960s, commercialized decades later), Netflix streaming (began 2007), the Kindle, 3D printing, virtual reality, and Webvan. The consistent finding is that delays arise from multiple dependencies — batteries, infrastructure, standards, regulation, manufacturing, consumer readiness — that must converge simultaneously.

2. **Incumbents and regulation as structural sources of delay:** The Dyson bagless vacuum example is highlighted as analogous to EV adoption resistance: the existing vacuum bag industry had no incentive to adopt the new technology (a razor-and-blades revenue model), so Dyson had to route around the industry by launching in Japan first. The hosts draw a parallel to the resistance Tesla faced from incumbent automakers and regulators, noting that consumer inertia and regulatory friction compound purely technical delays.

3. **Inflation and driver shortages improving Semi market receptivity:** Cern argues that the nine-year delay for the Tesla Semi may have inadvertently improved its commercial prospects. Since 2017, inflation has raised the cost of transporting goods, and the truck driver shortage has worsened — both factors increasing the pain point that the Semi addresses. The market in 2026 is described as "truly primed" for the product in a way it may not have been in 2019 had the Semi launched on schedule.

Notable quotes and data:
- "Prototypes are easy, production is hard." — Elon Musk, quoted by Cern
- "The future arrives when the system is ready." — Cern Basher
- Tesla Semi announced: December 7, 2017; promised delivery: 2019; first deliveries (PepsiCo pilots): December 2022; first production-line vehicle: April 2026
- Tesla Semi drag coefficient: 0.36 vs. Bugatti at 0.38
- Estimated Tesla Semi annual fuel savings: $60,000–$80,000 per truck using a Megacharger
- Estimated cost savings: ~35 cents per mile vs. diesel
- Payback period estimate: 3–5 years
- Waymo estimated loss: ~$100 per ride; ~$5–6 billion per year across ~10 cities; ~1,000 incidents per month cited
- Las Vegas Cybercab car wash facility: 36,000 square feet, permitted, robotic/automated
- Netflix began streaming: 2007
- James Webb Telescope: expected ~2007, launched Christmas Day 2021
- First commercial cell phone: 1983 (first call made 1973); cost ~$4,000, weighed ~2.5 lbs, 30 minutes talk time
- Duke Nukem Forever: ~14 years in development, released 2011
- Dyson: ~5,000 prototypes built before commercializing the cyclonic vacuum design
- Cern Basher's firm: Brilliant Advice (brilliantadvice.net)

2026-05-16.title: Why Elon Musk Is Now Too Valuable to Ignore
2026-05-16.body:
The video argues that Elon Musk and his companies — Tesla and SpaceX — have become indispensable strategic infrastructure across six critical domains: energy, communications, missile defense, AI computing, humanoid robotics, and space access. The core thesis is that the market is currently pricing Tesla somewhere between a car company and a car-plus-energy company, while the "strategic infrastructure" valuation — which the host believes is increasingly justified — is being given away for free. The video uses a series of recent signed deals and government contracts to ground this argument in current reality rather than future promises.

## Energy

1. **Megapack as national grid infrastructure:** The host emphasizes that Tesla's Megapack is not a consumer product but a grid-scale storage solution that addresses the fundamental instability problem of solar and wind energy — intermittency. As countries pursue energy independence and move away from imported fuels, Tesla has emerged as one of the few companies capable of delivering at the required scale and speed, making Elon a recurring presence in energy security conversations at the head-of-state level.

2. **Major Megapack contracts already signed:** The video cites several large, recently executed deals as evidence of Tesla Energy's strategic scale: a $2.7 billion deal with Georgia Power for more than 3 gigawatts of storage; a 1 gigawatt-hour project in Scotland; a 240 megawatt site in France described as one of the largest in that country; a $556 million grid battery project in China; and a new Megablock product ramping later in 2026 (i.e., later this year relative to the publish date of 2026-05-16). The host frames these as signed purchase orders, not projections.

3. **Tesla Energy as an underappreciated bull case:** The host specifically calls out Tesla's energy backlog as something investors should monitor closely in upcoming earnings calls, arguing that national-scale grid contracts represent a "quiet part of the bull case nobody talks about enough."

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Giga Shanghai as proof of concept for impossible deals:** The host recounts the July 2018 deal in which Elon flew to Shanghai and signed for Giga Shanghai — the first time China ever allowed a foreign automaker to own 100% of a local factory with no joint venture requirement. The factory was built in approximately 10 months, at around 65% lower cost per unit than the U.S. production line, and reached peak exports of around 35,000 vehicles per month. Tesla Shanghai sold almost 293,000 cars in just the first four months of 2026, demonstrating sustained, large-scale output.

2. **FSD approval in China as the near-term catalyst to watch:** During the May 13, 2026 Beijing trip — in which Elon accompanied President Trump along with Tim Cook, Jensen Huang, and executives from Boeing, Goldman Sachs, Blackstone, BlackRock, Citi, and Meta — Elon's stated priority was reportedly FSD approval in China. The host flags this as the highest near-term deal with the biggest potential impact for Tesla shareholders.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD China approval as the pivotal near-term event:** Beyond the EV sales angle, the host identifies Chinese regulatory approval for Full Self-Driving as the single most important near-term catalyst to watch coming out of the Beijing diplomatic trip. A successful approval would open a massive market for Tesla's software stack, which currently cannot operate in China.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus as consensus strategic asset, not a hot take:** The host notes that the market has broadly converged on the view that if any company will mass-produce humanoid robots, it is Tesla — given its existing capability to mass-produce millions of complex machines annually. Optimus is currently being tested inside Tesla's factories but is not yet doing autonomous production work, and Tesla has not issued an official 2026 production number.

2. **Analyst projections and Elon's long-term vision:** Without citing a specific source, the host mentions that analysts are modeling approximately 50,000 Optimus units in 2027 and 500,000 units in 2028. Elon's stated long-term vision is 1 million units per year per production line. The host is careful to note these are analyst models and Elon's aspirational targets, not official Tesla guidance.

3. **Robots as strategic leverage analogous to energy and satellites:** The host frames scaled humanoid robot manufacturing as a strategic asset that countries and corporations will seek to access — drawing a direct parallel to how nations depend on Tesla for grid storage and SpaceX for communications. Control of the supply creates leverage, and Tesla is currently the consensus front-runner for that supply.

## Market & Competition

1. **Three valuation frameworks for Tesla:** The host lays out three distinct ways investors can think about Tesla's value: (1) purely as a car company with auto margins and a normal multiple — where he says much of the market is still stuck; (2) as a car company plus a major energy business signing multi-billion-dollar national grid contracts; and (3) as strategic infrastructure spanning energy, defense, communications, AI, robotics, and space — a framing where the valuation conversation is fundamentally different. He argues all three are partially true today, but the market is pricing somewhere between the first and second, meaning the third is currently "free."

2. **Elon's unique negotiating position is structural, not personal:** The host explicitly distinguishes between Elon being a skilled negotiator and Elon being structurally irreplaceable. His companies provide things — grid-scale storage, unjammable satellite communications, rocket launch capacity, AI compute at scale, humanoid robots — that no other single entity can supply. This is why China, Google, and Anthropic all approached him within the same two-week window (around early-to-mid May 2026), and why Trump brought him to Beijing.

3. **Anthropic and Google as AI compute clients:** On May 6, 2026, Anthropic signed a deal to use the full computing power of SpaceX's Colossus 1 facility in Memphis — described as over 220,000 Nvidia GPUs and 300 megawatts of capacity added within one month. This came despite Elon having publicly called Anthropic "evil" approximately three months prior. The Wall Street Journal reported on May 12, 2026 that Google is in talks with SpaceX to launch Google data centers into orbit, citing power, land, and cooling constraints on Earth. The host notes that the xAI and SpaceX merger — which closed in February (2026) — created a combined entity valued at $1.25 trillion, potentially rising to $1.75 trillion at IPO, making it the largest merger ever by the host's characterization.

4. **Key catalysts and risks to monitor:** Identified risks include Elon's history of missing timelines (FSD, robotaxi, Optimus), key-man risk given how much value is concentrated in a single individual, and political risk from proximity to Trump. Catalysts to watch include FSD approval in China, Tesla Energy Megapack backlog figures at the next earnings call, Golden Dome milestone awards to SpaceX, a signed Google orbital data center contract, and the SpaceX IPO filing — which the host says the company is targeting at a valuation between $1.75 and $2 trillion, with a date of June 12th mentioned.

Notable quotes and data:

- Scotland project: 1 gigawatt-hour
- France project: 240 megawatts, described as one of the largest in the country
- China grid battery project: $556 million

- Star Shield: Pentagon placed 3,000 Ukrainian terminals on the military network
- Golden Dome contract pool: up to $3.2 billion across 12 companies; SpaceX won a $57 million data-link contract and a $178 million satellite launch contract; total Golden Dome program estimated at ~$185 billion
- Colossus 1 (Memphis): over 220,000 Nvidia GPUs, 300 megawatts of new capacity
- Anthropic growth: described as growing 80x in a single quarter
- xAI + SpaceX combined value: $1.25 trillion, potentially $1.75 trillion at IPO; described as the largest merger ever
- SpaceX IPO target valuation: $1.75–$2 trillion; targeting June 12th
- Giga Shanghai: built in ~10 months, ~65% cheaper per unit than U.S. line, peak exports ~35,000/month, ~293,000 cars sold in first four months of 2026
- Optimus analyst models: ~50,000 units in 2027, ~500,000 units in 2028; Elon's vision: 1 million units/year per production line
- "Tesla still trades like a car company with a little software upside. That's the gap and that's the trade."
- "He's not in that room because people like him. He's in that room because his companies are the leverage."

2026-05-16.title: Elon Called Out The Real Robotaxi Bottleneck
2026-05-16.body:
This video from the Cern Basher channel features a multi-person discussion analyzing comments made by Elon Musk and Tesla executives (including Ashok and Vibob) during what appears to be a recent earnings call or investor event. The core thesis is that the primary bottleneck for Tesla's robotaxi expansion is not safety — Tesla has had zero incidents to date — but rather operational "convenience" issues such as cars getting stuck in infinite routing loops or becoming overly cautious in ambiguous situations. The hosts argue that these issues are solvable within the FSD 14.3 series of updates, without needing to wait for the full version 15 architectural overhaul.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD 14.3 as the key unlocking version:** Elon Musk characterized FSD version 14.3 as a "major architectural update" for Full Self-Driving and robotaxi. The hosts interpret his comments to mean that the 14.3 series — not the forthcoming version 15 — is sufficient to enable unsupervised Full Self-Driving deployment. One host notes that version 14.3.1 introduced reasoning capabilities, but initially only applied them to end-destination parking, implying that reasoning will be extended to more edge cases (e.g., railroad crossings, prolonged stops at red lights) in subsequent point releases within the 14.3 series.

2. **Version 15 as a longer-term architectural overhaul:** Elon said version 15 will be a "complete overhaul of the software architecture" and will run on AI 4 hardware — clarifying that AI 5 is not a prerequisite. He described it as arriving "hopefully later this year" but "certainly by early next year" (i.e., by early 2027). Version 15 is framed not as the enabler of unsupervised FSD, but as a further leap in safety magnitude beyond what 14.3 already provides.

3. **Safety level claims:** Elon stated that even with version 14, Tesla FSD is "significantly safer than human" driving. He suggested version 15 will take safety to "another level," though Tesla has not publicly quantified a specific safety multiple (e.g., 2x or 5x safer than humans). The hosts note Tesla does not officially state it is a specific multiple above human safety level — just "above."

4. **Unsupervised FSD global rollout ambition:** Elon stated Tesla has "a whole pipeline of major improvements to Full Self-Driving" that they believe will lead to unsupervised Full Self-Driving being available "anywhere in the world that it is legal to do so." He also indicated unsupervised Full Self-Driving should be available in certain regions by end of 2026.

## Robotaxi

1. **Real bottleneck is operational, not safety:** Elon identified the primary limiter on wider robotaxi deployment as not safety failures but "convenience issues" — situations where the car "gets paranoid and gets stuck." Specific examples cited include infinite routing loops (where the car repeatedly routes back to the same blocked road) and excessive caution in ambiguous environments like road construction. Elon stated explicitly: "Those are by far the issues that we have had to resolve as opposed to direct safety issues." One host confirmed experiencing an infinite loop personally in his own Cybertruck.

2. **Zero incidents to date:** Both Elon and Ashok emphasized that Tesla's robotaxi program has had zero accidental injuries across its entire deployment history. The hosts characterize Tesla as being "more cautious than Waymo," noting that Waymo has historically been more willing to accept risk in its expansion approach.

3. **Expansion to Dallas and Houston:** Tesla has expanded its robotaxi service to Dallas and Houston using the same software stack as the Bay Area deployment. The hosts note that the Dallas and Houston vehicles are operating unsupervised (without safety drivers), which they view as a positive signal that the core safety bar has been met. Current fleet figures referenced are consistent with RobotaxiTracker.com data: approximately 5 vehicles in Dallas and 6 in Houston operating unsupervised.

4. **QA fleet vs. customer fleet dynamic:** Ashok explained that Tesla is increasing its QA (quality assurance) fleet to conduct rigorous validation across many U.S. cities — including rural areas — while also wanting to grow the customer-facing fleet to generate "useful metrics" for safe scaling. The hosts observe that Cybercab engineering prototype vehicles have been spotted in many cities and rural areas around the country, suggesting broad geographic validation activity.

5. **Cybercab production has begun — fleet deployment implications:** The hosts assert that Cybercab production has started at Giga Texas (referencing Joe Tegtmeyer's drone video coverage), and that the newly produced Cybercabs are being moved off the lot rather than accumulating in parking. Approximately 14 new production Cybercabs were reportedly spotted recently. The hosts argue it would make no logical sense to begin production without intent to deploy those vehicles into the robotaxi fleet, and they expect these vehicles to begin appearing in Austin, Dallas, and Houston in the near term. They note that Cybercabs without steering wheels would logically go directly into robotaxi expansion rather than QA fleet service.

6. **Scale and revenue ambiguity:** Elon said unsupervised FSD and robotaxi revenue would "not be super material this year" but would be "material, probably in a significant way, next year" (i.e., 2027). The hosts express frustration that neither "super material" nor "material in a significant way" are quantified. Similarly, Vibob stated Tesla "grew the robotaxi fleet quarter over quarter" and expects to keep ramping — without specifying absolute numbers. One host speculatively floated 10,000 robotaxis by end of 2026, but immediately acknowledged this is unconfirmed and may not align with Tesla's actual plans.

7. **Expansion pace uncertainty:** The hosts note that the language Tesla used — "ramping the fleet," "wider deployment," "expanding geographies" — is entirely unquantified, making it impossible to set reliable expectations for fleet size milestones. They caution viewers that any specific numerical expectation risks being wrong because Tesla is not providing target numbers.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cybertruck FSD behavior anecdote:** One host mentioned experiencing an infinite routing loop personally in his own Cybertruck (not in a robotaxi context), corroborating Elon's description of the operational issues limiting robotaxi deployment. This illustrates that the edge-case loop problem is not unique to the robotaxi program but exists in the broader FSD consumer experience.

---

**Notable quotes and data:**

- Elon: "A lot of what limits wider deployment of robotaxi are actually not safety issues, but convenience issues where the car basically gets paranoid and gets stuck."
- Elon: "Those are by far the issues that we have had to resolve as opposed to direct safety issues."
- Elon: "I think probably unsupervised FSD or robotaxi revenue would not be super material this year."
- Elon: "I do think it'll be material. It'll be material probably in a significant way next year." (implying 2027)
- Elon on version 15: "Hopefully later this year, but certainly by early next year" — described as a "complete overhaul of the software architecture" running on AI 4.
- Elon: "Even with version 14 we are significantly safer than human."
- Ashok: "We are increasing the amount of our QA fleet, but we also want to increase the customer fleet to give us the useful metrics back so that we can scale it safely."
- Vibob: "We grew the robotaxi fleet quarter over quarter and we expect to keep on ramping the fleet as we accelerate and get into other geographies."
- Active robotaxi fleet per RobotaxiTracker.com (as of 2026-05-15): 670 total — Bay Area 555, Austin 104, Dallas 5, Houston 6.
- Unsupervised robotaxi fleet per RobotaxiTracker.com (as of 2026-05-09): 39 total — Austin 28, Dallas 5, Houston 6.
- ~14 newly produced Cybercabs reportedly spotted recently (production units, not engineering prototypes).
- Host speculative estimate: possibly 10,000 robotaxis by end of 2026 (explicitly flagged as uncertain and unconfirmed).

2026-05-16.title: Tesla (TSLA) raises Model Y prices by up to $1,000 — first increase in two years
2026-05-16.body:
Tesla has raised Model Y prices in the US by up to $1,000 on its Premium and Performance trims — the first price increase on the model in two years, ending a prolonged period of aggressive discounting.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **New Model Y pricing:** The increases apply to the Premium RWD ($45,990, +$1,000), Premium AWD ($49,990, +$1,000), and Performance AWD ($57,990, +$500). The base RWD ($39,990) and base AWD ($41,990) remain unchanged. Increases are under 3% on affected trims.

2. **Prior pricing history:** Tesla had slashed Model Y prices by up to $2,000 in April 2024, reaching the model's then-lowest price. A broader series of cuts beginning in early 2023 had removed as much as $13,000 from the sticker price.

## Financials
1. **Margin trajectory:** Automotive gross margins dropped from above 25% in early 2023 to below 18% by mid-2025 amid sustained price cuts. Tesla's Q1 2026 deliveries showed a 50,000-vehicle inventory build and missed expectations. Full-year 2025 deliveries totaled 1.636 million, down from 2023's peak.

## Market & Competition
1. **Competitive positioning:** The price increase comes as BYD, Hyundai's Ioniq 5, and the Ford Mustang Mach-E compete aggressively in the mid-size EV SUV segment. The Model Y Premium AWD at $49,990 now sits above the Ioniq 5 AWD (starting ~$45,000) and the Mach-E Select AWD ($42,995).

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert views the increase as a selective confidence signal — Tesla is capturing more margin on higher-trim, higher-profitability configurations while protecting the entry-level price point, suggesting strength in a specific segment rather than a broad demand recovery. He notes lower US gas prices are likely contributing to improved demand.

Notable quotes and data:
- Model Y Premium AWD: $49,990 (+$1,000)
- Model Y Performance AWD: $57,990 (+$500)
- Base trims: unchanged
- Automotive gross margins: fell from 25%+ (early 2023) to below 18% (mid-2025)
- Full-year 2025 deliveries: 1.636 million (down from 2023 peak)
- Q1 2026: ~50,000-vehicle inventory build, missed delivery expectations

2026-05-16.title: Tesla Could Dominate Canada Very Fast
2026-05-16.body:
This video from FutureAzA features host Brian and Canadian correspondent Mark discussing Tesla's strategic advantage in Canada's newly established low-tariff import quota for Chinese-made electric vehicles. The core thesis is that Tesla is uniquely positioned to dominate Canada's Chinese EV import quota due to its already-established dealer, service, and brand infrastructure in the country, while Chinese competitors like BYD, Geely, and Xpeng are still setting up operations. The discussion also covers which Chinese EV brands could realistically compete in Canada and at what price points.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Canada's Low-Tariff Chinese EV Import Quota:** Canada has established a quota of 49,000 vehicles for the first year for Chinese-made EVs at a reduced tariff rate, divided into roughly 25,000 vehicles per half-year. The program runs through 2030. The import price threshold to qualify is CAD $35,000, though retail pricing can be higher. The Canadian government is now debating whether to allocate specific shares to individual manufacturers, reportedly concerned that Tesla will consume the majority of the quota.

2. **Tesla's Structural Advantage in Canada:** Tesla has been shipping Model 3s from Giga Shanghai to Canada and is expected to claim a disproportionately large share of the quota. Mark argues this is because Tesla already has showrooms, service centers, parts infrastructure, an established website, and strong brand recognition in Canada — none of which competing Chinese brands currently have. He notes this is not Tesla's first time exporting Shanghai-built cars to Canada, so there is no additional logistical friction.

3. **Pent-Up Demand for Canadian Model 3:** The Model 3 had been absent from the Canadian lineup for over a year prior to the resumption of Chinese-made imports. The Chinese-market Model 3 being imported is reportedly priced lower than the American-built Model 3, which Mark expects to generate significant pent-up demand and strong order volumes.

4. **Model 3 Battery Specs Clarification:** There was brief speculation online that the China-exported Model 3 destined for Canada might feature the newer, faster-charging Sunwoda (SVOLT/Sunwoda) LFP cells capable of 5C charging. However, after Tesla updated its Canadian website, the specs reverted to the standard LFP chemistry already familiar in the market. Brian notes this correction had been known roughly a week before the article speculating about the Sunwoda battery was published. Brian identifies Tesla's battery partners as Panasonic, LG, BYD, CATL, and Sunwoda as the potential fifth.

5. **Model Y Top-Selling Vehicle in British Columbia:** The Tesla Model Y was the top-selling vehicle — not just top EV or top SUV, but top vehicle overall — in British Columbia, Canada for two consecutive months (March and April 2026), with over 4,000 units sold through the first four months of the year. Brian and Mark note that two consecutive months suggests a trend rather than a one-time anomaly.

## Market & Competition

1. **Chinese EV Brands Preparing for Canada:** BYD reportedly plans to open 20 Canadian sites in 2026 and is considered well-positioned to enter quickly, with the BYD Dolphin and Seal cited as likely initial models. Other brands mentioned include Chery (and its sub-brand Jaecoo), Geely (with its Zeekr-related products), and Xpeng. BYD also has a longer-term manufacturing partnership option being discussed by the Canadian government, whereby a Chinese automaker could set up a joint-venture plant in Canada using Canadian labor and parts, which would eliminate import restrictions.

2. **Skepticism About Competitor Pricing Estimates:** An article speculating on Canadian retail pricing for Chinese EVs is criticized by both hosts as likely inaccurate, possibly AI-generated. Mark argues that many of the listed prices appear too high — in some cases equal to or higher than the Tesla Model 3 — which would undermine the competitive appeal of unproven Chinese brands. As an example, Brian suggests the Xpeng P7 Plus would likely retail around CAD $38,000 rather than the CAD $50,000–$60,000 cited in the article, based on its Chinese pricing of approximately USD $25,000.

Notable quotes and data:
- Canada's Chinese EV low-tariff import quota: **49,000 vehicles/year**, split ~25,000 per half-year, through **2030**
- Import price threshold to qualify: **CAD $35,000** (retail can be higher)
- Tesla Model 3 Canadian retail price cited: **CAD $39,990**
- Model Y top-selling vehicle in British Columbia for **March and April 2026**, with **over 4,000 units** sold in the first four months of 2026
- BYD plans **20 Canadian sites** during 2026
- Xpeng P7 Plus Chinese pricing: ~**USD $25,000**; estimated Canadian retail: ~**CAD $38,000** (vs. article's CAD $50,000–$60,000 claim)
- Tesla's battery partners listed: Panasonic, LG, BYD, CATL, and Sunwoda (potential fifth)
- *"Tesla is going to take as much as they can, especially out of the gate because they have a huge advantage having showrooms, service, parts all set up and running in Canada."* — Mark

2026-05-16.title: Daily X Summary (2026-05-16)
2026-05-16.body:
