2026-05-21.title: SpaceX Just Dropped IPO S1. Here's EVERYTHING To Know.
2026-05-21.body:
This video covers the SpaceX S1 IPO filing dropped on May 20, 2026, with Alexandra Merz (also known as "Tesla Boomer Mama") walking host Herbert and guest Jeff through her deep-dive analysis of the 308-page prospectus and linked documents. Her core thesis is that multiple structural elements embedded in the filing — from voting rights architecture to board composition to lockup schedules — appear deliberately designed to facilitate a future merger of equals between SpaceX and Tesla, with Elon Musk retaining majority voting control of the combined entity.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX Texas Reincorporation as the Legal Foundation:** SpaceX originally incorporated in Delaware in 2002 but reincorporated in Texas on February 14, 2024, effectively resetting its legal foundation. Alexandra Merz notes that Tesla similarly reincorporated in Texas in the summer of 2024, shortly after its shareholder meeting. She argues the Texas certificate of formation and its subsequent amendments — not the original Delaware documents — are the critical documents for understanding SpaceX's current governance structure.

2. **Dual-Class Share Structure and Elon's 85% Voting Control:** SpaceX has Class A shares (one vote per share, available to public investors) and Class B shares (10 votes per share, held by Elon Musk and a small group). This gives Elon approximately 85.1% of total voting rights. This structure has existed since at least February 2024 and likely throughout SpaceX's Delaware history, predating the IPO. Alexandra notes that early investors who were surprised by this figure should have known, as it was embedded in founding documents accessible to accredited investors.

3. **Merger Veto Clause — A Key Structural Breadcrumb:** The certificate of formation includes a dual-condition requirement for any merger to pass: first, a combined vote of all share classes must approve it; second, the Class B shares alone must independently approve it as a separate condition. Alexandra argues this is a deliberate protection ensuring Elon retains a decisive "thumb on the scale" even if future dilution brings his combined-entity voting share below 50%. She calculates that a merger of equals between SpaceX (Elon at 85% voting) and Tesla (Elon at approximately 20.3% voting) would yield roughly 52.5% combined voting control for Elon — still a majority but much closer to the threshold where dilution becomes a risk.

4. **Controlled Company Status — When the Language First Appeared:** SpaceX qualifies as a "controlled company" under NASDAQ rules because a single person (Elon Musk) holds more than 50% of voting power. This status exempts SpaceX from requirements such as a majority of independent directors or a fully independent nominating/governance committee. Crucially, Alexandra notes this "controlled company" language did not appear in any 2024 or early 2026 filings, suggesting the IPO decision crystallized in January or February 2026. She compares this to Meta (Zuckerberg at 57–60%), Alphabet (Page and Brin at 51–53%), and Snap (Spiegel and Murphy at ~60%), all of which established dual-class structures at their IPOs — something Tesla did not do at its 2010 IPO, which Alexandra characterizes as a missed opportunity.

5. **Board Composition and the Ira Ehrenpreis Signal:** SpaceX had six board members as of February 2024 and has since expanded to eight, with a ninth position to be filled within one year. The only board member overlapping between Tesla and SpaceX (other than Elon) is Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs SpaceX's Compensation and Nominating Committee — the same role he played in structuring Tesla's performance awards for Elon. Alexandra interprets his presence on both boards as a meaningful breadcrumb suggesting he may be positioned to draft a compensation plan for a combined entity. Gwen Shotwell is also on the SpaceX board. Antonio Garcia (of Valor Partners) is the only non-employee, non-Elon board member classified as non-independent, due to his firm's significant SpaceX shareholding.

6. **Share Class Amendment History as an IPO Timeline Indicator:** Alexandra traced all amendments to SpaceX's Texas certificate of formation from February 2024 through May 2026. Key milestones: (1) Initial Texas filing, February 14, 2024 — legal move only; (2) First amendment — authorized Class B shares increased from 1 billion to 1.2 billion; (3) A new Class D common stock was introduced, likely for employees; (4) On May 4, 2026 (morning) — preferred shareholders given the option to convert to common stock ahead of IPO; (5) On May 4, 2026 (evening) — a 5-for-1 stock split of Classes A, B, and C, with Class C subsequently closed. SpaceX also filed a DBA under the name "Adustra." Elon is known to have purchased secondary shares from employees and early investors over this period, which Alexandra argues makes sense only if he anticipated dilution from a future merger.

7. **Shareholder Litigation Rights Severely Restricted in New Bylaws:** The IPO bylaws (linked within the S1 and considered filed) include three provisions that Alexandra says make suing the company extremely difficult: (1) all disputes must first go to private arbitration in Houston; (2) all shareholders irrevocably waive jury trials; and (3) class actions and collective lawsuits are explicitly banned. Combined with a Texas law requiring 3% of outstanding shares to bring a derivative suit — and only 4.3% of shares being floated — Alexandra notes that organizing any meaningful legal challenge would be nearly impossible. She acknowledges that a lawyer contact (Warren) believes some of these provisions may not survive legal challenge.

8. **Amended and Restated Investor Rights Agreement (IRA) — No Preferential Exits:** The S1 links to an amended and restated investor rights agreement covering early investors (series up through Series N, last updated August 2020). Alexandra reviewed it and concluded that no early investor class has preferential or accelerated lockup rights. All large investors are subject to the same lockup schedule. Elon himself, when approached by investors wanting to exit early, has historically purchased those secondary shares himself rather than letting them hit the open market.

## Financials

1. **IPO Valuation, Float Size, and Offering Amount:** The IPO is rumored to be priced at a total market cap of approximately $1.75 trillion (with some rumors suggesting $2.25 trillion). The offering raises approximately $75 billion, representing only 4.3% of the total market cap — an extremely small public float. Alexandra notes $75 billion would be more than double the size of previous record IPOs. If the market cap is actually $2.25 trillion, the float percentage would be even smaller than 4.3%.

2. **Lockup Period Structure — Staggered Selling Windows:** Directors and executive officers face a 180-day lockup. Elon Musk faces a stricter 366-day lockup from the date of the prospectus, meaning he cannot sell until approximately June or July 2027. For all other major shareholders (e.g., ARK Invest, Valor Partners), a staggered selling schedule applies: after Q2 earnings (approximately July 20–25, 2026), they may sell up to 20% of holdings (or 30% if the stock is 30% above IPO price); on approximately August 21 (day 70), another 7%; approximately September 10, another 7%; approximately September 25, another 7%; after Q3 earnings, another 28%; in October, another 7%; with all remaining shares unlockable by December 9, 2026. Cathie Wood of ARK Invest has publicly stated ARK intends to sell a portion of its SpaceX holdings given the scale of expected profits. Goldman Sachs is the lead manager overseeing lockup compliance.

3. **Index Inclusion Timeline and Buying Pressure:** Within the first 15 trading days after the June 12, 2026 IPO (approximately by July 6–7, 2026), SpaceX is expected to qualify for inclusion in the NASDAQ 100, FTSE Russell, and CRSP indices under their respective rules. All three are float-adjusted, meaning their initial purchases will be limited by the 4.3% float — Alexandra estimates these three indices will each need to purchase approximately $10 billion worth of shares (roughly $30 billion combined), but the constrained float means they may not be able to acquire their full target allocation immediately, creating upward price pressure. These indices will conduct quarterly rebalancing in September 2026, at which point the expanded float (from staggered seller windows in July–September) will allow larger purchases. The S&P 500 currently requires 12 months post-IPO for inclusion, but the S&P is conducting a consultation on new rules that would reduce the waiting period to 6 months, eliminate the 10% minimum float requirement, and remove the profitability requirement. If approved (a decision expected on June 8, 2026 — four days before the IPO), SpaceX could be eligible for S&P 500 inclusion as early as December 2026. Alexandra's S&P inclusion purchase estimates by float size: at 5% float, ~$19 billion; at 10% float, ~$39 billion; at 20% float, ~$77 billion; at 40–50% float, proportionally higher. She describes a potential S&P inclusion as "the tightest S&P inclusion ever."

4. **Merger of Equals Scenario — Potential Impact on Tesla:** Alexandra's working hypothesis is a "merger of equals" in which SpaceX and Tesla combine at equivalent market caps. Under this scenario, Tesla shareholders would see the Tesla ticker eventually replaced by SpaceX's ticker, and the S&P 500 would replace Tesla's weighting with SpaceX rather than executing a new inclusion. Alexandra estimates Tesla is currently trading around $420 and suggests a merger announcement could push it to approximately $650 in a matter of days. She models the Tesla shareholder vote as requiring approval from 50% of approximately 3.75 billion outstanding shares, which she characterizes as "an uphill battle." On timing, she speculates the merger announcement could come before SpaceX's Q2 2026 earnings call (around July 2026), with the actual merger closing most likely in Q2 2027 (with Q1 2027 being ambitious and end of 2026 being unlikely).

5. **IPO Access for Retail Investors:** Five lead underwriters are named: Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, Citigroup, and JP Morgan. Retail access is being provided through Charles Schwab, Fidelity, Robinhood, SoFi, and E*Trade (by Morgan Stanley). Some platforms require minimum account balances (e.g., $100,000 or $500,000 depending on the institution). The IPO is reported to be multiple times oversubscribed. Alexandra notes a critical window in early June: money must be deposited by approximately June 4, and final allocation requests must be submitted by approximately June 10.

Notable quotes and data:
- Elon Musk holds approximately 85.1% of SpaceX voting rights via Class B shares (10 votes per share).
- A merger of equals would give Elon approximately 52.5% voting rights of the combined entity (85% + 20.3% ÷ 2).
- SpaceX IPO date: June 12, 2026 (rumored); total offering ~$75 billion; rumored market cap $1.75–$2.25 trillion; public float ~4.3%.
- Elon's lockup: 366 days from IPO (until approximately June–July 2027). All other directors/officers: 180 days.
- First major selling window for large early investors: after Q2 earnings ~July 20–25, 2026 (up to 20–30% of holdings).
- Final selling window: December 9, 2026.
- S&P 500 potential inclusion: December 2026 if new rules (6-month post-IPO eligibility) are approved June 8, 2026.
- Estimated S&P 500 index buying at 20% float: ~$77 billion.
- Tesla current price referenced: ~$420; merger announcement price target speculated at ~$650.
- SpaceX completed a 5-for-1 stock split on May 4, 2026.
- SpaceX DBA (doing business as) name filed with Texas Secretary of State: "Adustra."
- Ira Ehrenpreis is the only board member (besides Elon) sitting on both the Tesla and SpaceX boards.
- Alexandra Merz's birthday is May 22, 2026 (the day after the video was published).
- Alexandra Merz, Herbert, and Jeff Watts all stated they own Tesla stock and do not own SpaceX shares.
- Alexandra: "I will actually not purchase SpaceX. I will continue sitting on my Tesla and sit it all out."
- On Grok's analysis of lockup schedules: "I know quite a lot and I realized how wrong he was."

2026-05-21.title: The Math Behind Elon's Trillion-Dollar Bet
2026-05-21.body:
This video is a wide-ranging conversation between Cern Basher and Phil Beisel covering Elon Musk's interlocking empire of SpaceX, Terafab, and Tesla, framed around the thesis that Musk is positioning himself to control the entire compute supply chain for AI — from chip fabrication (Terafab) to launch infrastructure (Starship) to orbital data centers. The discussion spans the physics and economics of orbital computing, AI memory demand, the SpaceX IPO timing, and how Tesla's robotaxi and Optimus ambitions fit into this larger picture. The hosts argue that terrestrial AI compute supply cannot possibly meet demand, making Musk's space-based compute vision not just plausible but necessary.

## Market & Competition

1. **AI Compute Demand vs. Supply Gap:** Phil Beisel presents a logarithmic chart showing AI compute demand growing at approximately 3.4x per year, compared to CPU industry growth of roughly 1.5–1.6x. He argues the chip supply industry, led primarily by Taiwan Semiconductor, is growing along a trajectory that will never close the gap with demand — and that the chart is logarithmic, meaning the gap is even larger than it visually appears. Current global AI compute supply is described as approximately 30 gigawatts. The analysis does not include physical AI (robotics, autonomous vehicles) in the demand curve, meaning demand is likely understated.

2. **Terafab as the Only Solution:** Phil argues that Elon Musk's Terafab — described as a minimum 100 billion square-foot facility, roughly 10x the size of Giga Texas — is the only plausible path to closing the compute gap. He states the goal is to produce one terawatt of compute annually, which would make Taiwan Semi's current production capacity "a rounding error." He notes that all U.S. electricity consumption currently runs at roughly half a terawatt, and that within approximately 4.4 years, AI demand alone will hit one terawatt — making terrestrial deployment physically impossible at that scale. Terafab is described as vertically integrated, covering processors, memory (including high-bandwidth memory), and packaging — explicitly avoiding the geopolitical vulnerability of TSMC's Taiwan-based packaging operations. Intel's 14A node (14 angstrom, or approximately 1.4 nanometer class) is mentioned as the manufacturing process Terafab is targeting.

3. **Orbital Data Centers and SpaceX's "Railroad to Space":** The hosts discuss a social media post — reportedly liked by Elon Musk — estimating that a 1-million-satellite orbital data center constellation would require roughly 5,000 to 10,000 Starship launches. Phil frames SpaceX as the only operational "railroad to space," noting no competitor is at meaningful scale. He estimates that at three launches per day at full scale, you would need three to five launch sites with two to five towers each. The first orbital compute satellites are described as being designed around 100-kilowatt compute capacity, equivalent to roughly 250 chips at 400 watts each. Elon's stated near-term goal is described as reaching one terawatt of compute in space, which would require far more than one million satellites at that per-satellite capacity. Starlink satellites are noted to have a roughly four-to-five-year lifespan, which may align with useful chip life.

4. **SpaceX as the AI Infrastructure Gatekeeper:** Phil argues that if Terafab and orbital data centers succeed at scale, SpaceX/xAI effectively becomes the "entire bottleneck" or gatekeeper for all AI inference compute globally — analogous to owning the spice in the Dune science fiction framework. He maps out three layers of control: chip supply (Terafab), transportation (Starship), and the communications layer (Starlink). He notes SpaceX is essentially becoming the equivalent of Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure, but in orbit. He references the Anthropic deal to take over "Colossus One" as evidence that compute scarcity is already pinching frontier model providers.

5. **Nvidia and Google as Potential Terafab Partners:** The hosts speculate about whether Nvidia could become an investor in Terafab. Phil suggests Jensen Huang and Elon Musk recently spent time together on an airplane. He frames the likely deal structure as Nvidia providing capital investment without receiving chip manufacturing commitments, and SpaceX using its launch business to serve Nvidia's own orbital compute ambitions. For Google, the hosts note Google already owns approximately 7% of SpaceX (figure to be confirmed in the S-1), and that Google has reportedly expressed interest in using Starship to launch its own orbital data centers. Phil argues Google's logical move is to become a launch customer and potentially fund additional launch infrastructure, as SpaceX is the only viable option at scale.

6. **SpaceX IPO Timing and Scale:** The hosts discuss the SpaceX IPO as imminent, noting Elon is planning to launch a new Starship (the V3 stack, with 33 Raptor V3 engines in the booster) before the IPO. They estimate SpaceX could raise approximately $75–100 billion in the IPO, though they note even that sum is likely a "rounding error" relative to Terafab's capital requirements (previously discussed numbers in the $50–100 billion range for SpaceX investments in Terafab). The last Starship launch is noted as having occurred on October 13th of the prior year (implying October 13, 2025).

7. **Taiwan Semiconductor Geopolitical Risk:** Phil flags that current U.S. chip supply is heavily dependent on TSMC in Taiwan, and that even TSMC's Arizona fab currently ships chips back to Taiwan for packaging — leaving the geopolitical vulnerability intact. He suggests Terafab, by handling fabrication, memory, and packaging domestically, would fundamentally de-risk the supply chain. He also raises the speculative possibility that Elon could eventually build a Terafab in China, given Tesla's existing fully-owned Giga Shanghai operation.

8. **AI Memory Demand Hockey Stick:** The hosts walk through an analysis of AI memory demand, citing a Google Gemini estimate that a 400-billion-weight AI model requires approximately 800 gigabytes of memory (equivalent to roughly 200 HD movies). Per-conversation inference memory is estimated at 50–200 gigabytes per session. Nvidia's own roadmap shows a 10x increase in DRAM allocation per GPU from 2022 through 2028, a trend the hosts expect to continue beyond that period. They discuss high-bandwidth memory (HBM) architecture — stacking memory physically closer to the compute core — as the key innovation addressing memory latency, and note Terafab's vertical integration explicitly includes memory production.

## Robotaxi

1. **Scale vs. Waymo's Operational Model:** Cern Basher argues Tesla's robotaxi program is being engineered specifically for massive scale, which creates a fundamentally different engineering problem than Waymo's approach. He uses the example of call center staffing: if 1,000 cars require 100 call center staff, scaling linearly to 1 million cars would be destructive to unit economics. Tesla's goal, he argues, is to scale from 1,000 to 1 million vehicles while only growing the support operation from 100 to approximately 300 staff — requiring dramatically fewer operational incidents per vehicle. He draws a parallel to Starship's reusability challenge as the same type of "build for scale" engineering discipline.

2. **Robotaxi Safety and Patience:** The hosts frame the deliberate pace of robotaxi rollout as analogous to Starship launch cadence — getting it right before scaling is the first-order priority. Cern notes that Tesla's approach appears to treat safety as largely sufficient but operational polish (customer experience, edge cases, remote support) as the remaining work before aggressive expansion.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus as Primary Driver of Terafab Chip Demand:** Phil notes that the March announcement framing for Terafab positioned its chips primarily as serving Optimus and FSD requirements, with some training-side demand. He describes Elon having conversations with Samsung (at its Taylor, Texas fab) and TSMC about chip supply for Optimus, and finding that Samsung's Taylor facility — while having ample land — would only satisfy roughly half a year of the first three years of Optimus production plans. This inability to secure sufficient external supply is described as a key catalyst for Elon deciding to build Terafab himself. Phil also notes that the SNX (Model S/X) production line was wound down to free up manufacturing space for Optimus.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla's Shift Away from Traditional Car Models:** Cern argues that Elon's long-term vision has effectively moved Tesla beyond being primarily a car company. He suggests that within two years, Tesla may not be building Model Y or Model 3 at meaningful scale, and that deploying one million Cybercabs makes producing 100,000 Model Ys largely irrelevant from a capital allocation standpoint. He frames the SNX discontinuation as evidence of this prioritization shift, noting manufacturing space is desperately needed for Optimus production.

Notable quotes and data:
- "There is no place to go but space for this problem. There's not enough energy on Earth." — Phil Beisel
- "If Elon's Terafab came online, the rest of the manufacturing of GPU silicon is a rounding error." — Phil Beisel
- "He is owning the spice. He owns the transportation network. He owns the comm layer." — Phil Beisel on Elon Musk's strategic position
- "What is Elon doing here? He becomes the entire bottleneck for compute in all of AI." — Phil Beisel
- "AI is a memory hungry hippo." — Phil Beisel
- "If you could put a million Cybercabs into business, what do you need to do 100,000 Model Ys for?" — Cern Basher
- 1 million satellite orbital data center constellation = ~5,000–10,000 Starship launches (post liked by Elon Musk)
- Current global AI compute supply: ~30 gigawatts
- Total U.S. electricity consumption: ~0.5 terawatt
- AI demand hits 1 terawatt in approximately 4.4 years from present
- AI compute demand growth rate: ~3.4x per year
- GPU DRAM allocation: 10x increase from 2022 to 2028 per Nvidia roadmap
- 400-billion-weight AI model memory requirement: ~800 GB (per Google Gemini estimate)
- Per-conversation inference memory: 50–200 GB
- Terafab target node: Intel 14A (14 angstrom / ~1.4 nanometer class)
- First orbital compute satellites: ~100 kilowatt compute capacity (~250 × 400W chips)
- Elon's near-term space compute goal: 1 terawatt
- Terafab minimum size: ~100 billion square feet (~10x Giga Texas)
- SpaceX IPO estimated raise: ~$75–100 billion
- Terafab capital requirements: previously discussed in $50–100 billion range
- Google's reported SpaceX ownership stake: ~7%
- Starlink revenue: ~$15 billion (referenced by Phil)
- Last Starship launch prior to this recording: October 13, 2025
- Starlink satellite lifespan: ~4–5 years

2026-05-21.title: SpaceX S-1 reveals Tesla’s Terafab deal is far from done
2026-05-21.body:
SpaceX's S-1 filing with the SEC, ahead of what could be the largest IPO in history, reveals that Tesla's two hyped joint ventures with SpaceX — Terafab and Macrohard — are in "very early stages" with no binding financial terms, no IP rights allocated, and no committed timelines.

## Financials
1. **$650M in Tesla-SpaceX/xAI related-party transactions in 2025:** SpaceX purchased $144 million in goods and services from Tesla in 2025 (up from $4 million in 2024). xAI — absorbed by SpaceX in February 2026 — purchased $506 million from Tesla in 2025 and another $34 million in the first two months of 2026, primarily Megapack battery systems for xAI data centers. Combined, Tesla received roughly $650 million from SpaceX/xAI entities in 2025. Tesla also holds 18,990,195 shares of SpaceX Class A common stock (less than 1% ownership), converted from its $2 billion xAI investment. Tesla additionally spent $4 million on X advertising in 2025.

## Humanoid Bots / Market & Competition
2. **Terafab: $25B chip fab announcement vs. legal reality:** Musk announced Terafab in March 2026 as a $25 billion semiconductor facility targeting "one terawatt of compute hardware per year," with chips for both Optimus robots/Tesla vehicles and SpaceX's orbital compute infrastructure. Intel was added as a partner in April 2026. However, SpaceX's S-1 describes only "a general framework for the future development of Terafab," with all specific projects, timelines, milestones, and capex subject to separate future negotiations. The filing explicitly warns that "neither Tesla nor Intel are obligated to remain a part of the project" and that definitive agreements "have not yet been determined."

3. **Macrohard: AI platform with no disclosed terms:** Macrohard is described in the S-1 as an "agentic AI platform" designed to fully emulate digital workflows and "create a fully AI-operated software company," being developed jointly with Tesla. As with Terafab, no financial terms, IP ownership structure, or revenue-sharing arrangement has been disclosed, and the same "very early stages" language applies.

4. **Musk's divided attention disclosed:** The S-1 candidly states Musk "does not devote his full time and attention" to SpaceX, citing his roles at Tesla, Neuralink, The Boring Company, and his prior role as Senior Advisor to the President. SpaceX carries no key-person life insurance on Musk, and its charter explicitly renounces certain corporate opportunities that come to Musk — meaning he has no legal duty to bring opportunities to SpaceX first. The same applies to his relationship with Tesla.

## Editorial Stance
Lambert argues that Musk rushed to announce Terafab and Macrohard before the SpaceX IPO without concrete agreements in place, framing the announcements as narrative-building for capital-raising — consistent with a pattern he sees across prior Tesla announcements — while SpaceX's own risk factors warn investors not to count on these projects materializing.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX S-1: "Any specific projects undertaken pursuant to this framework will be subject to separate negotiations and agreements... and have not yet been determined."
- SpaceX S-1: "Neither Tesla nor Intel are obligated to remain a part of the project, and we may not enter into any such definitive agreements."
- SpaceX S-1: "Certain of these projects, including Macrohard and Terafab, are in the very early stages, as a result of which we and Tesla have not finalized a variety of details relating to our collaboration, including, but not limited to, financial terms, intellectual property rights, and the ultimate term of our collaboration."
- Tesla received ~$650M from SpaceX/xAI entities in 2025
- SpaceX's Tesla purchases jumped 36x in one year: $4M (2024) → $144M (2025)
- Tesla holds 18,990,195 SpaceX Class A shares, less than 1% ownership

2026-05-21.title: Why AI Data Centers Are Running Into Massive Bottlenecks
2026-05-21.body:
This episode of FutureAzA features host Brian and Herbert from Brighter discussing three news stories: Tesla's lithium refinery discharge controversy in Corpus Christi, the Siemens transformer shortage driven by AI data center demand, and the collapse of Donut Labs' battery claims. The video's core thesis is that both extreme hype and extreme fear-mongering distort public understanding of genuinely important infrastructure and technology stories, and that critical thinking and multi-source verification are essential.

## Energy

1. **Tesla Lithium Refinery Discharge in Corpus Christi:** A Texas drainage district discovered an unrecognized pipe discharging approximately 231,000 gallons of black wastewater per day from Tesla's approximately $1 billion lithium refinery near Corpus Christi, which launched in late 2024 or early 2025. An official investigation concluded in February found no heavy metals and no violations, with all samples in compliance on chloride, sulfates, oil and grease. An independent test commissioned by the drainage district found only trace amounts of hexavalent chromium (just above detection limits) and arsenic below drinking water standards. The hosts note Tesla is currently in full compliance with its permits, though the permit did not require monitoring for lithium itself. The proposed long-term solution is installation of a filtration plant to bring discharge water to drinking-water quality — similar to the water reuse approach used at Giga Berlin — though the hosts acknowledge this is expensive. The drainage district is pursuing further investigation but has not yet filed suit.

2. **AI Data Center Demand Creating Transformer Shortage:** A post attributed to a Siemens employee describes an extreme surge in demand for power transformers and electrical equipment driven by AI data center buildout. Orders have reportedly scaled from 20–30 megawatt orders to 200–500 megawatt orders. Margins for this equipment have jumped from 4–6% to 20–23%, and in some cases as high as 40%, and clients are accepting these prices without resistance. Backlog for some equipment has reached 5–6 years, with average large power transformer lead times rising from approximately 2.5 years to 3–5 years. The hosts note that roughly 50% of planned 2026 US data centers are facing delays and cancellations due to energy and transformer bottlenecks. The supply crunch is described as largely a Western-world problem, as India and China were still ramping their electrical infrastructure when demand surged and could scale more incrementally. The hosts caution that some orders may be double-counted as buyers rush to secure queue positions, which could cause apparent demand to overshoot real demand. A former Tesla employee named Drew Baglo is noted to have left Tesla to start a transformer company focused on a solid-state solution. Herbert notes that Elon Musk had previously predicted this sequence: first chips, then transformers, then energy would become the binding constraints on AI infrastructure.

## Market & Competition

1. **Donut Labs Battery Claims Collapse:** Donut Labs, a spinoff from Verge motorcycles, generated significant buzz at CES by claiming a breakthrough battery with a 5-minute full charge, 100,000 charge cycles (described as roughly 20 times more than standard lithium-ion), approximately 400 watt-hours per kilogram energy density, and pricing cheaper than existing lithium batteries — with the website stating the product was "available today." The hosts, particularly Brian, were skeptical from the outset, citing the gap between lab results and mass production readiness. As of the time of recording, the company has shipped only one unit — to itself — missing its stated Q1 shipping target. The company's own technology partner has become a whistleblower and is suing, alleging the claims are not real. It has since been acknowledged that the batteries being delivered do not meet the stated specifications, and that the technology is semi-solid rather than solid-state. The hosts draw a parallel to Elon Musk's longstanding caution that lab breakthroughs face an enormous leap before viable mass-scale production. Brian also notes that the same founder previously claimed to have solved AGI and made unmet performance claims for the hubless Verge motorcycle.

Notable quotes and data:
- ~231,000 gallons of black wastewater per day discharged from Tesla's Corpus Christi lithium refinery
- Tesla lithium refinery cost: approximately $1 billion; launched late 2024 or early 2025
- Independent testing found trace hexavalent chromium (just above detection) and arsenic below drinking water standards; February investigation found no violations
- Siemens transformer order sizes have grown from 20–30 MW to 200–500 MW
- Equipment margins up from 4–6% to 20–23%, in some cases 40%
- Large power transformer lead times: formerly ~2.5 years, now 3–5 years; some equipment backlog at 5–6 years
- ~50% of planned 2026 US data centers reportedly facing delays and cancellations
- Donut Labs shipped one unit (to itself) as of Q1 2026; technology partner is now suing as a whistleblower
- Donut Labs claimed: 5-minute full charge, 100,000 cycles, ~400 Wh/kg, cheaper than lithium — none independently verified
- "If Nvidia wasn't themselves able to create more, if they were able to create more, they'd sell two, three trillion dollars worth." (Herbert, paraphrasing analyst sentiment on Nvidia demand)
- "First it was chips, then it's going to be transformers, then it's going to be energy." (Herbert, attributing the prediction to Elon Musk)

2026-05-21.title: Battery Storage Solutions For AI Data Centers And Power Grids
2026-05-21.body:
This video features FutureAzA host Brian interviewing Quincy from Electric Era Charging, a Washington State company founded by former SpaceX engineers, about their newly announced "CoPower Platform" — a power capacity-as-a-service product targeting edge AI data centers. The core thesis is that battery-based energy storage, managed by sophisticated software, can dramatically reduce electricity costs for edge data centers while simultaneously alleviating strain on the power grid through load shifting. The video explores the technical, economic, and national security dimensions of battery storage as a foundational technology for the AI-driven energy future.

## Energy

1. **CoPower Platform Announcement:** Electric Era is publicly announcing its CoPower Platform, described as a "power capacity as a service" offering for edge AI data centers. The product has been in stealth development for approximately six to seven months. It integrates multiple third-party hardware vendors — battery systems, power conversion systems, medium voltage switchgear, and transformers — all managed by Electric Era's proprietary software platform originally developed for their EV fast charging business.

2. **Physical System Configuration:** A representative deployment shown during the video features approximately six energy storage systems, each with roughly 5 megawatt hours of capacity and approximately 2 megawatts of discharge power. This yields a total of approximately 30 megawatt hours and roughly 12 megawatts of deliverable power to a data center at any given time.

3. **Load Shifting as the Core Value Proposition:** The platform's primary economic mechanism is load shifting — charging batteries during low-demand, low-cost periods (typically mornings) and discharging during peak demand periods (typically 4–9 p.m.). This reduces both the energy cost (cost per electron) and the infrastructure/demand charge component of the data center's electricity bill, which Quincy describes as saving "a shocking amount of money."

4. **Autonomous Software-Driven Grid Optimization:** The software platform autonomously monitors a variety of grid price signals throughout the day and programmatically decides how to charge and discharge the storage systems to optimize costs. This is described as an extension of the same software Electric Era already deploys across the country for EV fast charging, simply applied to a larger load with bigger hardware.

5. **Edge Data Centers as the Target Market:** Electric Era is explicitly not targeting large hyperscale AI superfactories, which run at full load continuously and require on-site generation (solar, natural gas, or nuclear) rather than load shifting. Instead, the focus is on smaller edge data centers running real-time, low-latency workloads — such as AI call centers, ordering kiosks, or autonomous vehicle inference systems — which have a diurnal demand shape aligned with human activity patterns, making time-of-use arbitrage viable.

6. **Voltage Flicker Mitigation as a Secondary Use Case:** Beyond load shifting, Quincy explains that battery systems also act as power quality filters. AI data centers training large models can cause "voltage flicker" on the local grid — rapid voltage swings caused by large numbers of GPUs switching on and off synchronously. Battery storage can absorb and smooth these fluctuations before they propagate to the broader electrical service territory, benefiting all ratepayers.

7. **Grid Scale Context and Long-Term Industry Outlook:** The U.S. currently has approximately 1 terawatt of grid capacity but averages only about 500 gigawatts of consumption. Quincy argues that battery storage allows more of that existing capacity to be utilized by raising the average load closer to the peak. He projects that the industry will need to deploy terawatt-hours of energy storage over the next dozen or so years, calling it a "major major shift" in how the grid operates.

8. **Battery Price Trends:** Battery pack prices have declined dramatically over recent years. When Quincy first began building battery-backed power infrastructure, pack prices were approximately $200 or more per kilowatt hour. Today, cell-level prices are approximately $70 per kilowatt hour, with pack-level prices running roughly 20–30% higher. A lithium price spike occurred around November 2022, followed by a sharp decline, and prices are now described as stabilizing and beginning to rise again in a more sustainable fashion.

9. **LG Energy as Selected Vendor; Domestic Manufacturing Emphasis:** Electric Era has selected LG Energy as its battery vendor for the CoPower Platform, noting that LG Energy produces batteries in America. Quincy frames domestic manufacturing as important both for job creation and supply chain resilience, citing lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic and the Ukraine war as examples of how apparently secure global supply chains can rapidly fail under pressure. Brian echoes this, framing energy independence as a matter of national security.

10. **Shared Technology Stack Across EV Charging and Data Centers:** Quincy emphasizes that the software "secret sauce" powering the CoPower Platform is the same platform developed for Electric Era's EV fast charging network, already deployed across the country. The company views these two product lines as increasingly intertwined and hints at future announcements as the two applications converge further technically.

Notable quotes and data:
- Approximate deployment size: ~6 storage units × ~5 MWh each = ~30 MWh total; ~12 MW deliverable power
- Battery pack prices: from ~$200+/kWh historically → ~$70/kWh at cell level today; pack level adds ~20–30% on top
- Lithium price spike: approximately November 2022, followed by a sharp decline
- U.S. grid capacity: ~1 terawatt total; average consumption ~500 gigawatts
- Industry projection: terawatt-hours of storage deployment needed over the next ~12 years
- Peak electricity pricing window cited: 4–9 p.m.
- Selected battery vendor: LG Energy (U.S. manufacturing)
- Electric Era founders: former SpaceX engineers
- CoPower Platform stealth development period: ~6–7 months
- Brian: "I'm of the opinion that energy independence is national security."
- Quincy: "Batteries are just absolutely paramount for us to solve the future of the grid."

2026-05-21.title: Starship Flight 12 - The Casual Watch Channel - SCRUBBED! COME BACK TOMORROW
2026-05-21.body:
This video is a casual live-stream watch party hosted by Brian of FutureAzA, gathered to observe the SpaceX Starship Version 3 Flight 12 test launch. The stream covers the pre-launch buildup, technical details about the new Starship V3 hardware, and ultimately ends with a scrub — the launch was stood down due to unresolved issues with the quick disconnect arm on the tower during the T-minus 40 second hold. The content has essentially no relevance to Tesla's autonomous driving, robotaxi, Optimus, or financial investment thesis.

## Market & Competition
1. **SpaceX Starship V3 Flight 12 Scrubbed:** The launch of Starship Version 3 (Flight 12) was scrubbed after multiple holds at T-minus 40 seconds during the countdown. The flight control team encountered repeated issues with the quick disconnect arm on the tower and pressures in the ship's quick disconnect system. After exhausting available hold time, the team stood down, describing it effectively as a "wet dress rehearsal." A new flight attempt was expected the following day, with SpaceX directing viewers to social media and spacex.com for updates.

2. **Starship V3 Hardware Overhaul:** The SpaceX live stream embedded in the broadcast described Starship V3 as the most significant hardware redesign since the program began. Key changes include: 33 Raptor V3 engines on the Super Heavy booster generating 18 million pounds of thrust (over twice the thrust of the Saturn V), a new integrated hot stage adapter replacing the previously disposable ring, three grid fins (down from four) made 50% bigger and higher strength, a redesigned fuel transfer tube described as approximately the size of a Falcon 9 first stage, a clean-sheet propulsion redesign on the ship, increased propellant tank volume, new docking ports for future ship-to-ship propellant transfer, and an enhanced Starlink PEZ dispenser capable of deploying up to 60 Starlink V3 satellites. The new Pad 2 features a bidirectional flame diverter trench, shorter electromechanical chopstick arms, and loads propellant approximately 20% faster than Pad 1.

3. **Raptor V3 Engine Improvements:** Raptor V3 thrust was increased from 230 to 250 tons for sea-level engines and from 258 to 275 tons for vacuum-optimized engines. The redesign eliminated bulky heat shields and engine shrouds, internally integrated propulsion avionics, and dramatically reduced engine weight — enabling simultaneous ignition of all 33 engines at once rather than staged startup. The engines are manufactured in Hawthorne, California and tested in McGregor, Texas.

4. **Payload and Mission Profile:** Today's flight carried the heaviest payload ever flown on Starship: 20 Starlink simulator satellites plus two modified "Dodger Dog" Starlink satellites (stretched V2 mini satellites serving as technology demonstrators between V2 and V3 Starlink hardware). The planned flight profile included a booster soft splashdown in the Gulf, and the Starship upper stage targeting a flip, landing burn, and soft splashdown in the Indian Ocean. No catch of the booster or ship was planned for this flight.

5. **SpaceX Future Launch Infrastructure:** SpaceX described ongoing construction of a second launch tower at Launch Complex 39A in Florida (which has flown 126 Falcon missions since reactivation in 2017), a new Starship launchpad at Slick 37, and "Gigabay" — a giant assembly and maintenance facility designed to hold 24 work cells across over 800,000 square feet. SpaceX also announced plans for a Starlink constellation around the moon capable of gigabit connectivity on the lunar surface using laser relay technology.

6. **Terafab AI Infrastructure Event Referenced:** The SpaceX Starlink segment referenced the Terafab event in Austin "a few months ago" (relative to the publish date of 2026-05-21, placing this in early 2026) at which Elon Musk outlined a path to 100 gigawatts to 1 terawatt of AI computing power annually, leveraging Starship to launch AI satellites.

7. **Community Events — Tesla Michigan and Giga Texas:** The host promoted two upcoming community events. The Tesla Michigan summer meetup is scheduled for June 5–6, 2026, at Heritage Landing Park in Muskegon, Michigan, featuring speakers, a light show by Simon, test drives by both Rivian (potentially including an R2) and Tesla (Model Y, Model 3, possibly Cybertruck), and panelists discussing robotaxis. The X Takeover event is scheduled for October 10, 2026, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. at Giga Texas in Austin, with approximately 130 tickets remaining and May Musk confirmed as a speaker.

8. **Legacy Auto and EV Competition Commentary:** Brian offered commentary on the struggles of legacy automakers, particularly Stellantis (citing the electric Charger and Wagoneer as poorly conceived products) and the challenges of competing with Chinese EV makers. He noted that Buick-branded vehicles in China are effectively Chinese-designed cars with Buick badges, sharing no common components with GM's American lineup. He also discussed Lucid and Rivian's precarious financial positions, characterizing both as significant money-burning operations, and expressed hope that Rivian's R2 and Lucid's Cosmos could improve their trajectories.

9. **BYD Seal Mentioned as Competitive Concern:** The host mentioned driving a BYD Seal in Mexico, describing it as "a very good car" that was approximately one-third cheaper than a comparable Tesla, calling the price gap "concerning" from a competitive standpoint.

10. **SpaceX IPO Commentary:** Brian briefly commented on the SpaceX IPO, noting it had been confirmed that Tesla shareholders would not receive special treatment or preferential pricing, which he described as expected given fiduciary obligations to SpaceX shareholders.

Notable quotes and data:
- Starship V3: 407+ feet tall fully stacked, slightly taller than V2
- 33 Raptor V3 engines generating 18 million pounds of thrust — "over twice the thrust of the Saturn V"
- Raptor V3 sea-level thrust: 230 → 250 tons; vacuum-optimized: 258 → 275 tons
- Pad 2 propellant loading is approximately 20% faster than Pad 1
- Ship can carry up to 100 metric tons to Earth orbit, the moon, and Mars
- Gigabay: 24 work cells, 800,000+ square feet
- LC-39A: 126 Falcon missions since SpaceX reactivation in 2017
- Starlink satellites perform approximately 1,000 collision avoidance maneuvers daily
- SpaceX currently tracking approximately 50% of objects with perigees below 600 km via the Stargaze program
- SpaceX flew 165 missions to space last year (2025, per publish date context)
- Terafab event (early 2026): Elon described path to 100 GW–1 TW of AI computing power annually
- Tesla Michigan meetup: June 5–6, 2026, Muskegon, Michigan
- Giga Texas X Takeover: October 10, 2026, ~130 tickets remaining, May Musk confirmed speaker
- Host's theatrical performance: "Three Bandits and a Baby," July 10–26, 2026
- Host's EV outreach: Go Forth Festival, Longview, Washington, July 2–4, 2026
- Dan Hwitt (SpaceX): "New rocket, new pad. We're learning about a lot of these systems as we execute them for the first time."
- Chun Wang confirmed as crew for first Starship Mars flyby mission, also planned lunar flyby

2026-05-21.title: Will Tesla Robotaxi Scale OVER 10,000 THIS YEAR? w/ CERN BASHER
2026-05-21.body:
Jo Bhakdi hosts Cern Basher for a deep-dive discussion on the pace and timing of Tesla's robotaxi scaling, centered on the question of whether the unsupervised Cybercab fleet will reach 10,000 vehicles by end of 2026. The core thesis is that Cybercab production volume is the most reliable leading indicator of imminent deployment, and that Tesla is likely engineering a "switch flip" moment — moving from a few hundred validation vehicles to thousands of deployed robotaxis nearly overnight — rather than a smooth, linear ramp. Both guests converge on a year-end 2026 target of 10,000+ robotaxis, with Q3 2026 seen as a potential inflection point.

## Robotaxi

1. **"Switch Flip" vs. Linear Ramp Theory:** Cern Basher argues that what many observers interpret as repeated robotaxi delays is actually Tesla deliberately accumulating readiness — in software, production, and regulatory positioning — for a large-scale simultaneous deployment. Rather than a month-by-month stair-step increase, Cern expects a sudden jump from a few hundred vehicles to potentially tens of thousands. He points to Cybercabs being tested in states without favorable robotaxi legislation (including Alaska and rural areas) as evidence Tesla is preparing for a broad national deployment, not just incremental city-by-city rollout.

2. **Cybercab Production as the Primary Leading Indicator:** Both hosts agree that Cybercab manufacturing volume is the most trackable and reliable signal of deployment timing. Cern estimates that hundreds of Cybercabs have already been manufactured within the first month of production, and projects output could reach thousands per month within the next three months. He reasons that Tesla would not ramp production to 1,000+ units per month and then park them indefinitely — the capital cost of doing so would be prohibitive and contrary to Tesla's operational discipline. Therefore, a sustained production ramp with no corresponding deployment would itself be a warning sign.

3. **Steering Wheel Removal as a Deployment Signal:** Cern identifies the transition away from steering-wheel-equipped validation Cybercabs to production units without steering wheels as a critical near-term signal. Validation vehicles (described as having messy, truck-style steering wheels) are currently being used for testing across the country. Once Tesla stops manufacturing Cybercabs with steering wheels entirely, Cern views that as a near-certain indicator that commercial driverless deployment is imminent.

4. **Current Unsupervised Fleet and City Expansion:** The discussion references the existing small unsupervised robotaxi fleet operating in Austin, Dallas, and Houston (with Austin as the primary market), noting the count is currently around 39 unsupervised vehicles per RobotaxiTracker.com. Cern expects additional cities — including Miami, Tampa, Orlando, Las Vegas, and Phoenix — to see some form of robotaxi rollout before year-end 2026, though initial deployments in new cities may start with only five or six vehicles, potentially still supervised.

5. **Timeline Predictions — Q3 vs. Q4 for Scale:** Jo Bhakdi expresses conviction that Q3 2026 (July–September) is a more likely inflection point than Q4 for reaching a meaningful unsupervised fleet, while Cern assigns higher probability to Q4 for hitting ~1,000 unsupervised vehicles, citing unknown FSD issue resolution timelines. However, both agree that if 1,000 unsupervised units are reached in Q3, then by Q4 Tesla could already have close to 10,000 Cybercabs manufactured and ready. Cern's stated prediction is 10,000+ robotaxis in service by end of 2026, a figure Jo and a third commentator referenced as "Herbert" also share.

6. **From 1,000 to 10,000 — Speed of the Next Phase:** Cern argues that once 1,000 unsupervised robotaxis are operational, the jump to 10,000 could happen very rapidly — primarily constrained by Cybercab production rates rather than software or regulatory factors. He anticipates the fleet will shift toward predominantly Cybercabs over time, with Model Y representation in the fleet declining, assuming the Cybercab passes ongoing validation without major hardware issues.

7. **Infrastructure as a Potential Gating Factor:** The hosts raise the question of whether city-specific infrastructure — such as the car wash facility being built in Las Vegas for vehicle cleaning — must be operational before Tesla is comfortable scaling in a given market. Cern notes this is an open question: if Tesla requires dedicated cleaning and servicing infrastructure before each city launch, that introduces an additional milestone that could pace geographic expansion.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Software Progress and the Convenience Gap:** Cern references Elon Musk's comments from a recent earnings call stating that safety for robotaxi operation has been solved and the remaining work is about "convenience" — refining behaviors like pickup and drop-off, handling parking lot slow-speed scenarios, and managing passenger comfort edge cases (e.g., finding covered parking in rain). A newer FSD version, described as version 14.3.3, is noted as a meaningful improvement over the prior 14.3.2 release. Cern believes the software will reach sufficient convenience quality within one to two months, without needing to wait for a version 15 release.

2. **Robotaxi Software Leads Consumer FSD:** Cern notes that the software running on robotaxi vehicles is presumed to be one development build ahead of what consumer FSD owners receive. He points to firsthand experience with consumer FSD improvements as evidence that progress is real and accelerating, arguing it would be a different situation entirely if FSD had not improved materially over the past year.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla's Valuation Depends Heavily on Robotaxi and Optimus:** Jo Bhakdi frames the current Tesla stock price (referenced as being around $410–$490) as unsustainable without robotaxi and Optimus delivering on their thesis. He argues that stripping out those two catalysts leaves Tesla's valuation difficult to justify, making the timing of robotaxi deployment critically important not just for bulls but for anyone managing short-to-medium-term capital risk.

2. **Institutional Investor Behavior and Stock Reaction Thresholds:** Both hosts discuss how institutional investors cannot afford to hold Tesla through multi-month delays while other assets (e.g., Nvidia) outperform. Cern and Jo theorize that the unsupervised robotaxi count reaching triple digits (100+) will start generating stock reactions to fleet size milestones, with four-digit counts (1,000+) making it irrational for large capital to remain underweight Tesla. Cern floats the possibility that the stock could surge 10–20% in a single day before the public sees evidence on the roads, driven by informed institutional positioning ahead of a deployment announcement.

3. **Macro Risk Acknowledged:** Jo raises geopolitical and macro risks — specifically referencing potential oil price volatility tied to Iran — as factors that could pressure Tesla's stock in the near term regardless of robotaxi progress, creating buying opportunities for investors who track Cybercab production closely enough to have conviction during drawdowns.

Notable quotes and data:
- Cern Basher: "By the end of this year, I think we're looking in the 10,000 plus range of robo taxis."
- Jo Bhakdi: "I think in the next 2 months or something we are getting to a thousand per month manufacturing [of Cybercabs]."
- Cern Basher: "The longer this period of it doesn't happen, the bigger, the more sudden it happens."
- Cern Basher, on the steering wheel signal: "When we start seeing production vehicles, they're not making any more with steering wheels — that to me is a very strong signal that deployment is near."
- Jo Bhakdi: "If you would remove robo taxi and Optimus, [Tesla's valuation is] a huge problem."
- Unsupervised robotaxi fleet as of discussion: ~39 vehicles per RobotaxiTracker.com (Austin 28, Dallas 5, Houston 6)
- Active robotaxi fleet (all modes): 690 per RobotaxiTracker.com (Bay Area 573, Austin 104, Dallas 6, Houston 7)
- FSD version 14.3.3 described as meaningfully better than 14.3.2
- Cities expected to see robotaxi rollout before end of 2026: Miami, Tampa, Orlando, Las Vegas, Phoenix (in addition to existing Texas markets)
- Jo Bhakdi's threshold for stock significance: 1,000 unsupervised robotaxis as the point of "high conviction" that large-scale deployment is underway

With SpaceX planning to list on Nasdaq under ticker SPCX and the filing revealing significant business scale (Connectivity segment including Starlink generated $11.38B in revenue and $3.25B in Q1 2026 alone), Tesla's equity stake represents meaningful balance-sheet optionality that was previously unquantifiable in public filings.
