2026-05-28.title: The Biggest IPO in Human History is Happening
2026-05-28.body:
This video covers the SpaceX S-1 IPO filing submitted on May 20th, 2026, which the host argues represents the largest IPO in human history, targeting a valuation nearing $2.5 trillion. The core thesis is that SpaceX is no longer just a rocket company — it has quietly transformed into three distinct businesses (rockets, satellite internet, and AI) and a landmark $15 billion/year compute deal with Anthropic fundamentally reframes what looks like a money-losing enterprise into a strategic infrastructure play for the AI era. Tesla is briefly mentioned as a parallel example of a company using a cash-cow business to fund long-term moonshots.

## Market & Competition
1. **SpaceX IPO targeting record-breaking valuation:** SpaceX filed an S-1 with the US government on May 20th, 2026, setting the stage for what is described as the largest IPO in stock market history. The previous record was Saudi Aramco's ~$25 billion raise in 2019; SpaceX is reportedly targeting roughly three times that amount at a valuation nearing $2.5 trillion. Shares are set to go live on NASDAQ on June 12th.

2. **SpaceX acquires xAI, transforming into a three-segment company:** On February 2nd of 2026, SpaceX closed an all-stock deal to acquire xAI — Elon Musk's AI company — which includes the Grok chatbot, the X social media platform (formerly Twitter), and data centers called Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 housing over half a million GPUs. As a result, SpaceX now reports financials across three segments: Space (rockets), Connectivity (Starlink), and AI (xAI).

3. **Anthropic deal: $15 billion/year in compute revenue from a single customer:** In May 2026, SpaceX signed an agreement for Anthropic — a top-tier AI company behind the Claude models and a direct competitor to Grok and ChatGPT — to pay $1.255 billion per month through May 2029 for access to SpaceX's computing capacity. This amounts to approximately $15 billion per year from a single customer. Either side can cancel on 90 days' notice, but the host considers cancellation unlikely given AI compute demand. Elon Musk publicly framed this as SpaceX offering "AI compute as a service at significant scale" and noted discussions with other companies for similar arrangements.

4. **AnySphere/Cursor deal and potential acquisition:** In April 2026, SpaceX also signed a computing deal with AnySphere, the company behind the AI coding tool Cursor, and SpaceX holds an option to acquire Cursor outright at an implied value of $60 billion, which the host suggests SpaceX is likely to exercise post-IPO based on recent reporting.

5. **SpaceX as the "picks and shovels" of the AI era:** The host frames SpaceX's strategic ambition as becoming the dominant infrastructure provider for AI — owning the compute, power, and eventually the orbital data center capacity that other AI companies must pay to use. This is explicitly compared to the Gold Rush analogy: the companies selling the tools to miners, not the miners themselves, got rich. Tesla is cited as a parallel, using car sales to fund Full Self-Driving software and the Optimus robot.

## Financials
1. **Total 2025 revenue of $18 billion, dominated by Starlink:** SpaceX's 2025 total revenue was approximately $18 billion. The Connectivity (Starlink) segment contributed roughly $11 billion, representing approximately 61% of total revenue — up nearly 50% year-over-year. The Space segment contributed roughly $5 billion, and the AI segment contributed approximately $3 billion.

2. **Starlink is massively profitable at software-like margins:** The Connectivity segment generated over $4 billion in operating income. On an adjusted EBITDA basis, Starlink produced over $7 billion on $11.4 billion in revenue — approximately a 63% margin, which the host describes as comparable to software company economics. As of end of March 2026, Starlink had roughly 10 million subscribers across 164 countries, with over 10,000 satellites in low Earth orbit, and its direct satellite-to-phone service was reaching approximately 7 million devices per month.

3. **AI segment losing over $6 billion, but Anthropic deal changes the math:** The AI segment (xAI) had an operating loss of over $6 billion (specifically cited as $6.4 billion) in 2025, which is the source of the headline-grabbing ~$5 billion overall company loss. SpaceX poured $3 billion in R&D into Starship in 2025 alone, dragging the Space segment to an operating loss of approximately $657 million. However, the host argues that with the Anthropic deal pouring $15 billion/year into the AI segment, the entire company could turn profitable as early as 2026.

4. **Severe cash burn in Q1 2026:** SpaceX's cash position fell from approximately $24 billion at the end of December 2025 to approximately $15 billion at the end of March 2026 — a roughly $9 billion decline in a single quarter. The host notes this burn rate is expected to slow significantly once Anthropic deal revenues begin flowing.

5. **Governance: Elon Musk controls ~85% of voting power pre-IPO:** SpaceX uses a dual-class share structure — Class A shares (1 vote each, available to the public) and Class B shares (10 votes each, held by insiders). Prior to the IPO, Elon Musk controlled approximately 85% of total voting power. Post-IPO, this percentage will decrease slightly but Musk will remain firmly in control. SpaceX qualifies as a "controlled company" under NASDAQ rules, allowing it to bypass certain independent board requirements. The host draws a parallel to Mark Zuckerberg's voting control at Meta.

6. **Orbital AI compute satellites planned for 2028:** The S-1 filing states SpaceX expects to begin deploying orbital AI compute satellites as early as 2028. The thesis is that satellites in sun-synchronous orbit can access effectively unlimited solar power (the filing cites the sun as holding ~99.8% of all energy in the solar system), eliminating the terrestrial grid and cooling constraints that are currently limiting AI data center expansion.

Notable quotes and data:
- Anthropic payment: $1,255,000,000 per month through May 2029 (~$15 billion/year) — disclosed in the S-1 filing
- Elon Musk quote from tweet: "As a recently expanded partnership with Anthropic demonstrates, SpaceX is offering AI compute as a service at significant scale. We are in discussions with other companies to do the same. Over time, especially with orbital data centers, we expect to serve AI at extremely high scale."
- S-1 filing quote on orbital data centers: "We expect to begin deploying our orbital AI compute satellites as early as 2028."
- S-1 filing quote on key person risk: SpaceX is "highly dependent on the continued services of Mr. Musk," and losing him "could significantly disrupt the company."
- Starlink adjusted EBITDA margin: ~63% ($7B+ on $11.4B revenue)
- SpaceX total 2025 revenue: ~$18 billion; Starlink share: ~61%
- Starlink subscribers: ~10 million across 164 countries as of end of March 2026
- Starlink satellites in orbit: over 10,000
- Cursor (AnySphere) implied acquisition value: $60 billion
- Colossus 1 & 2 data centers: over 500,000 GPUs
- SpaceX cash position: ~$24B (Dec 2025) → ~$15B (Mar 2026), ~$9B burn in one quarter
- Previous IPO record: Saudi Aramco ~$25 billion raised in 2019
- SpaceX NASDAQ listing date: June 12th
- Tesla mentioned as using car revenue to fund Full Self-Driving and Optimus

2026-05-28.title: Tesla Just Flipped The Entire Europe EV Narrative Upside Down
2026-05-28.body:
This video from FutureAzA features host Brian and co-host Herbert discussing Tesla's resurgent EV sales in Europe and emerging markets like Colombia and Chile, while also exploring the broader strategic question of whether traditional vehicle sales still matter given Tesla's pivot toward robotaxi and autonomous driving. The core thesis is that Tesla's 13-month European sales losing streak has ended, the rebound is real and accelerating, and the long-term value of selling cars today lies less in unit revenue and more in building the FSD-enabled fleet and autonomous vehicle ecosystem.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Colombia EV Market Surges:** Colombia's BEV market share reached nearly 20% in April 2026, up from 7.4% a year prior, representing over 300% growth year-over-year in EV sales. The hosts attribute early growth (2022–2025) to organic adoption from pent-up demand, while the more recent spike is linked to rising gas prices. Tesla responded by expanding its Supercharger network in Colombia, signaling confidence in continued growth. Total market volume remains small — estimated around 5,000 cars — but the trend is notable.

2. **Chile: Small Market, Meaningful Share:** Roland Percher's data shows Tesla reported 242 sales in Chile in April, capturing 16% of the BEV market, while overall BEV penetration in Chile sits at 5%. The hosts highlight this as an example of Tesla entering smaller markets that legacy automakers typically bypass due to cost and complexity.

3. **Europe Sales Rebound Is Real:** Tesla ended a 13-month European sales losing streak, with 13,740 cars sold across the EU, UK, and European Free Trade Association in the most recently reported month — a 29% increase year-over-year. Weekly data for May 18–24 showed 3,600 sales across tracked European countries, up 32% week-over-week and 67% versus the same week last year. Year-to-date European sales are up approximately 28,000 units, or 45.8%, from the prior year. France and Spain are reportedly at record highs. The hosts attribute the prior-year decline primarily to factory retooling for the refreshed Model Y, not demand destruction.

4. **Third Consecutive Month of European Growth:** According to a report referenced from ACEA (described as "APAC/AA"), Tesla has now posted three consecutive months of year-over-year growth across European markets, with April up 47% compared to April of the prior year. The tracked countries include the UK, Norway, Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, Czech Republic, and Iceland — representing approximately 60% of European Tesla sales.

5. **Norway Standout:** The hosts note Tesla sold approximately 400 units in Norway in a single day, describing it as exceptional for a small country and a sign of strong enthusiasm for the brand there.

6. **Legacy Automakers Losing Ground:** Volkswagen and Stellantis are each reportedly reducing total production capacity by approximately one million cars. The hosts argue that brand loyalty, historically bulletproof for European automakers, is eroding as consumers shift toward technology-first vehicles. BYD is also expanding dealer presence in Europe with aggressive pricing and a reported 185% sales increase, yet legacy OEMs are still the ones losing the most ground.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Version 13.3 Reduces Nag Frequency:** The hosts discuss a version of FSD (described as version 13.3, with the key change in the point-three update over point-two being reduced driver attention prompts). Users are reportedly driving for extended periods — one user cited over an hour — without receiving an attention nag. Herbert emphasizes this is supervised FSD and recommends all Tesla owners enable it, while both hosts caution against distracted driving.

2. **FSD Approval in Europe as a Demand Catalyst:** FSD has reportedly been approved in the Netherlands and is in test trials across multiple European countries. The hosts speculate that EU-wide approval across all 28 member states is possible and frame it as a significant future demand driver. Herbert argues that once consumers experience what FSD can do, it becomes a compelling purchase reason — one that other EVs cannot match.

3. **FSD Revenue as the Real Value of Current Sales:** Brian argues that the primary value of selling Model 3s and Model Ys today is generating FSD subscription or purchase revenue, rather than the vehicle margin itself. The hosts discuss how Tesla's strategic decision to cancel the Model 2 and prioritize the Cybercab — as described in the Walter Isaacson book — reflects a deliberate shift away from maximizing traditional car sales volume.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab Strategy Over Model 2:** The hosts recount the internal Tesla decision, sourced from the Walter Isaacson biography, in which Elon Musk chose to build the Cybercab robotaxi-first vehicle instead of a sub-$30,000 Model 2. Executives reportedly convinced him to design the Cybercab so it could function as a conventional car if FSD was not ready in time. This is framed as a clear signal that Tesla's corporate focus has fundamentally shifted away from traditional volume car sales.

2. **Customer-Owned Vehicles in the Robotaxi Network — Uncertain Future:** Brian raises Elon Musk's repeated promises that Model 3 and Model Y owners would be able to add their vehicles to Tesla's robotaxi network. He notes this model makes business sense for handling peak demand (analogous to Uber surge), but expresses concern that Tesla may be moving away from this plan. Herbert shares the concern, noting that Austin-deployed robotaxis appear to have hardware additions — such as camera washers and Starlink Mini — that existing consumer vehicles lack, which could disqualify them from network participation.

3. **Cybercab Revenue Superiority Over Consumer Vehicle Sales:** The hosts estimate that Tesla earns approximately $4,000–$5,000 profit selling a Model Y, versus potentially $25,000 per year in revenue by keeping one Cybercab in a robotaxi fleet. Brian initially suggests one Cybercab equals five consumer cars in revenue terms; Herbert revises this to three to four, accounting for the concentration of driving hours when roads are actually used. Both agree the Cybercab economics are dramatically superior to consumer vehicle sales.

## Market & Competition

1. **BYD Growing in Europe But Not Dominating:** Despite a 185% sales increase in Europe, BYD is described as not yet selling as much as it wants to in the region. The hosts note that Chinese EV brands broadly have made inroads but have not captured the market share they targeted, leaving room for Tesla's rebound.

2. **Media Coverage Criticized:** The hosts mock an Automotive News story framing the Dacia Sandero reclaiming Europe's monthly sales lead in April as Tesla "tumbling," calling it a failure to understand delivery wave dynamics at the start of a quarter. They also critique an Investor's Business Daily article suggesting investors should wait for Tesla stock to reach a buy point before purchasing, calling it a misunderstanding of how to evaluate a long-term thesis stock.

Notable quotes and data:
- Colombia BEV market share: ~20% in April 2026, up from 7.4% a year prior; over 300% year-over-year sales growth
- Chile: 242 Tesla sales in April, 16% BEV market share, overall BEV penetration at 5%
- Europe weekly sales (May 18–24): ~3,600 units, +32% week-over-week, +67% year-over-year
- Europe monthly sales: 13,740 units, +29% year-over-year; third consecutive month of growth
- Europe year-to-date: +28,000 units / +45.8% vs. prior year; France and Spain at record highs
- Tracked countries represent ~60% of European Tesla sales
- Norway: ~400 Tesla sales in a single day
- Volkswagen and Stellantis each reportedly cutting ~1 million units of production capacity
- BYD: +185% sales growth in Europe
- FSD version referenced: 13.3 (reduced nag frequency vs. prior point-two version)
- One user reported driving over an hour without an FSD attention prompt
- Cybercab revenue estimate: ~$25,000/year per vehicle vs. ~$4,000–$5,000 profit on a Model Y sale
- Cybercab-to-consumer-car revenue equivalence: ~3–5x per year (debated between hosts)
- Source: Roland Percher (data charts for Chile and European weekly sales)

2026-05-28.title: Legacy Auto Still Does Not Understand What Tesla Is Building
2026-05-28.body:
This video from FutureAzA features host Brian and recurring guest Randy Kirk discussing why legacy automakers — particularly GM, Ford, and Stellantis — fundamentally misunderstand what Tesla is building and why their current investment strategies signal long-term decline. The core thesis is that legacy auto is doubling down on internal combustion technology (transmissions, V8 engines) while retreating from EVs, effectively forfeiting global markets and leaving themselves wholly unprepared for the autonomous vehicle disruption ahead.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **GM's EV retreat masked as domestic investment:** GM is investing heavily in transmission production — $300 million to increase capacity near Detroit, another $300 million the prior year (2025), $40 million for transmission production in Ohio, and over half a billion for propulsion plants in Ontario building sixth-generation V8 engines for the Corvette and full-size pickup trucks. GM noted total investments of more than $6 billion since 2025, largely geared toward the redesigned Silverado. Brian and Randy frame this as analogous to investing in steam engines — profitable in the short term but strategically backwards.

2. **GM and Samsung pause $3.5 billion battery plant:** GM and Samsung have confirmed a full pause on construction of their jointly planned $3.5 billion battery plant dubbed "Synergy Cells," with county officials citing economic factors and the end of EV incentives. The companies still nominally aim to meet a "substantial completion" deadline by end of 2027, but Brian clarifies this only means finishing the building shell — no equipment will be installed. He interprets this as a complete retreat from serious EV ambitions and a forfeiture of international markets where GM has competed for over 70 years.

3. **Ford's "all in" on EVs rings hollow:** Ford has written down $6 billion in EV-related charges and is effectively retreating to its ICE roots. Jim Farley's pivot back to gas was framed not as a cost-saving move but as a profitability move. Randy notes Ford leads all automakers in recalls by a wide margin with no apparent fix in sight. Brian jokes that claiming to be "all in" on EVs while still maintaining multiple combustion commitments and writing down billions doesn't reflect the meaning of the phrase.

4. **Stellantis ranked worst-positioned of the Big Three:** Both hosts agree Stellantis is in the worst strategic position — described as "rudderless," with weak EV offerings in the US market despite having better EV products in Europe that never make it stateside. Stellantis is reportedly spending $7 billion on retrofits and new vehicles but without a coherent direction.

## Market & Competition
1. **Legacy auto's failure to partner with Tesla:** Randy argues that any of the Big Three could have simply called Elon Musk, offered a royalty arrangement, and licensed Tesla's drivetrain or skateboard platform rather than spending billions developing flawed proprietary systems like GM's Ultium. Brian extends the analogy — a single proven skateboard platform on which to build multiple vehicles would have been far more efficient than what GM attempted with Ultium, which he describes as "one size fits all, except it's all size fits none."

2. **Autonomous vehicles as the deeper existential threat:** Randy argues the real long-term threat to legacy automakers isn't just electrification — it's autonomy. He predicts robotaxis could offer rides at 30 cents to $1 per mile (citing Elon Musk's public predictions at the low end), eliminating the need for personal car ownership for many consumers. Randy notes his own household has already reduced to one Tesla, relying on Uber for some trips despite the higher per-mile cost. He expects robotaxis to become massive within the next one to two years (i.e., by 2027–2028) and to begin cutting into all car sales broadly.

3. **Blockbuster/Nokia/Xerox analogies for legacy auto:** Randy repeatedly draws parallels between GM's trajectory and famous corporate failures — Blockbuster (still profitable as Netflix disrupted it), Nokia (dominant until Apple's iPhone arrived), and Xerox (invented the personal computer mouse but failed to develop it). The point in each case: being profitable today does not protect against rapid disruption, and legacy automakers may not see the future clearly enough to adapt.

4. **Global market forfeiture:** Brian argues that legacy automakers are retreating to their domestic strengths — high-margin trucks in the US — while surrendering international markets. Developed markets abroad demand competitive EVs that GM and Ford cannot provide, and developing markets want cheaper cars than legacy OEMs can profitably build. The pivot back to ICE is framed as an irreversible forfeiture of global automotive market share.

Notable quotes and data:
- Randy Kirk: "The future is going to be autonomy... robotaxis are here. It's happening. And it's going to be massive by next year or the next following year."
- Randy Kirk on robotaxi pricing: "30 cents a mile as Elon predicts" at the low end, up to "a buck a mile or half a buck a mile"
- Randy Kirk: "We are a one-car family... you just don't need it anymore even with Uber at three bucks a mile for most of my trips."
- Brian on GM's Ultium: "One size fits all, except it's not one size, it's all size fits none."
- GM investments cited: $300M (transmission near Detroit) + $300M (prior year) + $40M (Ohio transmissions) + $500M+ (Ontario V8 propulsion) = $640M+ directly mentioned, plus $6B+ total since 2025
- GM/Samsung "Synergy Cells" battery plant: $3.5 billion, fully paused, targeting "substantial completion" by end of 2027
- Stellantis reportedly spending $7 billion on retrofits and new vehicles

2026-05-28.title: Why June Could Be BIG For Tesla Stock
2026-05-28.body:
Jo Bhakdi presents a tactical investment thesis arguing that June 2026 will be a significant catalyst month for Tesla stock, driven primarily by the expected expansion of Cybercab robotaxi deployments to new cities. He connects Tesla's official Q4 2024 earnings commitments, recent drone footage of Cybercab production activity, and nationwide AI safety operator hiring as converging signals that Tesla is preparing a major robotaxi rollout before June 30th. Layered on top of this, he cites the SpaceX IPO (anticipated around June 12th) and potential Optimus news as additional bullish macro tailwinds, leading him to execute an aggressive short-put options strategy on Tesla.

## Robotaxi

1. **Tesla's Official June 30th Robotaxi Expansion Commitment:** In the Q4 2024 earnings report (published in January 2026), Tesla officially stated plans for robotaxi coverage in Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Miami, and Phoenix — cities where it does not currently operate — by June 30th, 2026. Bhakdi emphasizes this was not an Elon Musk tweet but a formal, legally and compliance-reviewed investor relations document, making it significantly more credible and harder to miss without reputational consequence. He views this 31–32 day deadline as a powerful forcing function for near-term deployment.

2. **Cybercab Production Activity at Giga Texas:** Citing drone footage from Joe Tegtmeyer dated May 27th, 2026, Bhakdi notes that Cybercabs are being consistently churned out at Giga Texas, rolling in and out of the parking lot on what appears to be a daily or every-other-day cadence. He estimates that over 200 serially produced Cybercabs are already "in the wild" and deployed to their destinations, though he acknowledges the exact count is uncertain. He also notes Cybercabs being observed lining up in Dallas, Texas — separate from Austin — suggesting multi-city staging.

3. **Nationwide AI Safety Operator Hiring as Deployment Signal:** Bhakdi highlights a post from "Tesla Yoda" (dated approximately May 27th, 2026) showing Tesla actively recruiting AI safety operators across a large number of U.S. states including Washington, Nevada, Utah, Tennessee, Pennsylvania, New York, New Jersey, Kansas, Georgia, Texas, District of Columbia, Louisiana, Maryland, Missouri, and North Carolina. He interprets this broad, simultaneous hiring push as a strong operational indicator that a significant nationwide robotaxi expansion is imminent.

4. **June as the One-Year Anniversary of Robotaxi Launch:** Bhakdi notes that June also happens to be the one-year anniversary of Tesla's original robotaxi launch, adding symbolic alignment to his thesis that a major expansion announcement or deployment wave in June is likely.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO as a Secondary Tesla Catalyst:** Bhakdi expresses high confidence — characterizing it as somewhere between "very likely" and "guaranteed" — that SpaceX will go public around June 12th, 2026. He argues this IPO was engineered to be a buy and that the stock will rise, with secondary positive effects on Tesla stock through association, merger speculation (a SpaceX-Tesla merger has resurfaced in discussion), and forced buying by index funds upon index inclusion. He expects this to be an additional bullish layer for Tesla in June, though he considers it slightly more uncertain than the robotaxi catalyst.

2. **Optimus as a Third Catalyst:** Bhakdi briefly flags Optimus as a third potential catalyst, noting that a presentation or reveal is theoretically expected in July or August 2026. He expresses some personal skepticism about the timing but acknowledges it represents another bullish narrative layer for Tesla stock in the near term.

3. **Tesla Stock Technical Setup — Resistance at $445:** Bhakdi describes Tesla stock as repeatedly bumping against a $445 resistance level, which previously rejected the price harshly twice (including on May 11th, 2026, which he calls his worst trading day of 2026). He argues this time is different given the convergence of catalysts, and that the stock is set to break through toward a target of approximately $490, potentially within June. He also references an uptrend line from the April 8th, 2026 lows as technically supportive.

4. **Options Strategy — Short Puts at $450 Strike:** Rather than buying calls (which he finds too expensive) or more stock on margin, Bhakdi describes executing a short-put strategy with a $450 strike price and approximately one-month duration. He notes the premiums are nearly $30 (approximately $28–$30), with about $8 of intrinsic value, which he views as favorable for a seller. He frames the trade as: winning if Tesla stays above $430, fully winning above $450, and generating 10–20 percentage points of alpha over Tesla if his thesis plays out. He acknowledges the risk of a move to $420–$430 but says he has enough conviction to double down in that scenario.

2026-05-28.title: Inspire Robots RH56DFQ: Dexterous Hand Demo
2026-05-28.body:
This video from Munro Live features Mike Kasein, a senior electrical engineer at Munro and Associates, demonstrating and explaining the Inspire Robotics RH56DFQ dexterous robotic hand. The video serves as an introductory explainer on how robotic hands work — covering degrees of movement, actuation mechanisms, and sensor design — while previewing a forthcoming full teardown of the unit. The core argument is that robotic hands are among the most mechanically complex components of humanoid robots, and the video positions this as the first in a series exploring how these components are built.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Inspire Robotics RH56DFQ Overview:** The hand being demonstrated is the Inspire Robotics RH56DFQ, a six-degrees-of-freedom robotic hand. Six degrees of movement means the hand can move in six distinct ways — covering the five individual fingers plus a thumb that can articulate back and forth laterally. The hand is described as a commercially available, modular unit that can be purchased independently and integrated onto compatible robots, with Python programmability supported.

2. **Degrees of Freedom Explained:** Kasein uses a cheap 3D-printed hand as a visual aid to explain the concept of degrees of movement. A single degree means a finger can only move one way (curl/extend). Additional degrees add lateral finger movement, thumb abduction, and other articulations. He notes that a human hand has significantly more degrees of movement than this unit — for example, the ability to splay fingers sideways is a degree of movement the RH56DFQ does not possess.

3. **Actuation Mechanism — Micro Linear Actuators:** The RH56DFQ uses micro linear actuators (pistons that extend and retract) to drive each finger. A spring at the top of the finger assembly provides passive return force when the actuator retracts. This is a simpler and lower-cost approach compared to alternatives such as gear-driven or individual-motor-per-joint designs used in more expensive hands.

4. **Sensor Design — Pressure at Actuator Base, Not Fingertip:** A notable design detail is that the hand does not have sensors embedded in the fingertips. Instead, pressure sensors are located at the base of each actuator. This means tactile feedback is detected through mechanical resistance transmitted down to the actuator, not via direct fingertip contact sensing. Kasein demonstrates this by showing that separating the finger from the actuator eliminates any sensor response.

5. **Pricing and Market Positioning:** The RH56DFQ is priced at approximately $10,000 per hand and is described as one of the cheaper commercially available robotic hands on the market. At the high end of the spectrum, Kasein references a hand called the "Sharper Wave" (name as stated in transcript), which costs approximately $100,000, features approximately 26 degrees of movement, has sensors in every finger, and includes cameras embedded in the fingers as well.

6. **Force Specifications:** This lower-end model is capable of approximately 4 newtons of gripping force on the fingers and 6 newtons on the thumb. Higher-spec models from the same or competing manufacturers can reach approximately 6 newtons on fingers and 12 newtons on the thumb. Kasein notes that the current unit can grip objects but would likely not maintain grip under impact or resistance.

7. **Software Demo and Control:** The hand ships with test software that includes preloaded gesture commands. Kasein demonstrates several gestures including an "okay" sign, a pointing/flicking gesture, and a closed fist. Individual finger control is also demonstrated through the software interface, with each finger adjustable independently via sliders or similar controls.

8. **Upcoming Teardown Series:** Kasein announces that a full teardown of the RH56DFQ is planned as a follow-up video, and that Munro Live also has plans to tear down a full humanoid robot. This video is framed as the first installment in a broader series examining humanoid robot components.

Notable quotes and data:
- RH56DFQ hand price: ~$10,000 (described as lower end of the market)
- "Sharper Wave" hand price: ~$100,000 with ~26 degrees of movement, fingertip sensors, and cameras in fingers
- Finger gripping force (RH56DFQ): ~4 newtons; thumb: ~6 newtons
- Higher-spec model force: ~6 newtons (fingers), ~12 newtons (thumb)
- Six degrees of movement: five individual fingers + lateral thumb abduction
- Sensor location: pressure sensor at actuator base, not in fingertips
- Actuation type: micro linear actuators with spring return
- *"If you look at your hand, it's probably one of the most complex part of the robot."*
- *"A lot of people think there is actually a sensor in the fingertips. It really is down at the bottom of the actuator."*
