2026-06-01.title: Weekly Tesla Brief (May 25 – May 31, 2026)
2026-06-01.body:
## Unsupervised Robotaxi Fleet

| City | Now | 7D | 30D |
|:-----|----:|---:|----:|
| Austin | 28 | 0 | +8 |
| Houston | 6 | 0 | +3 |
| Dallas | 5 | 0 | +2 |
| **Total** | **39** | 0 | +13 |

Source: [RobotaxiTracker.com](https://robotaxitracker.com/)

---

## Brief

- Texas Level 4 self-certification live; Ashok signals Cybercab "reporting for duty" in Austin imminently.
- FSD daily miles hit 26.7M/day — up 44% in one month per Morgan Stanley.
- Reuters: Tesla's "10x safer" FSD claim inflates true ratio ~3x; NHTSA has 4 open investigations.
- June 30 IR commitment: five new robotaxi cities must launch within days.
- Optimus factory steel erection begun at Giga Texas; Fremont pilot line visible.
- China FSD fraud trial opens; 1M+ HW3 vehicles face triple-damage exposure.
- Musk pay "change in control" clause waives all operational milestones upon a merger.

---

## Robotaxi

- **Texas Level 4 authorization is the week's structural unlock.** New Texas law took effect May 28–30, allowing manufacturer self-certification for driverless commercial operation. Tesla certified Cybercab as Level 4 on day one — the regulatory gate bears had called years away is now cleared. Tesla simultaneously pre-staged Cybercabs at hubs in all three Texas cities the same week.

- **Ashok Elluswamy's "reporting for duty" post is the clearest internal signal yet.** Tesla's head of AI quote-tweeted Musk's factory self-drive video (15M views) and stated Cybercab would soon "drive itself into Austin city, reporting for duty." The brighterwithherbert analysis: because Ashok controls FSD version, safety data, and route validation, "soon" implies real-world weeks, not months. The ~20-mile public-road drive from Giga Texas to Austin would let the fleet grow itself without human transport drivers.

- **June 30 city-launch deadline is a hard IR commitment, not a Musk tweet.** Tesla's Q4 2024 investor relations document committed to robotaxi coverage in Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Miami, and Phoenix by June 30, 2026. Nationwide AI safety operator hiring across 15+ states simultaneously (per Tesla Yoda, May 27) reads as an operational pre-launch signal with roughly 30 days left on the clock.

- **Cybercab production running ~30–36 units/day per Bhakdi**, citing Tegtmeyer drone footage — implying roughly 1,000 units/month. Starlink Mini units confirmed on Cybercabs in Austin and Houston, providing redundant connectivity for dead zones and fleet-scale OTA updates. All three Giga Texas production lines (Model Y, Cybertruck, Cybercab) confirmed running simultaneously for the first time in six to eight months.

- **Staged ≠ deployed; real gaps remain.** Staged Cybercabs still have steering wheels attached. RobotaxiTracker.com shows no growth in the unsupervised count for the full week. Bhakdi estimates ~1,000 Cybercabs produced to date but acknowledges his prior April–May target of 1,800 unsupervised units was missed by roughly a year. The repricing threshold he cites begins above 1,000 deployed unsupervised units — not staged.

---

## Autonomous Driving

- **FSD daily miles hit 26.7M/day, up 44% month-over-month**, per Morgan Stanley's May note — from 18.5M/day in April. The metric is Morgan Stanley's explicit proxy for subscriber growth and engagement, and drew the highest investor engagement of the week.

- **European mutual recognition is now a copy-paste process.** Lithuania approved supervised FSD in under 40 days by leveraging the Netherlands' 18-month, 1.12M-mile evaluation; Greece is next via the same mechanism. FSD Supervised is now confirmed in three European countries, with Czech Republic, Slovenia, and Austria preparing for unsupervised approval. Combined Netherlands + Lithuania FSD mileage hit 12.5M miles, with ~3M added in under 72 hours.

- **FSD 14.5 and 14.6 confirmed in internal testing.** FSD V14 Light — delivering all V14 features to HW3 vehicles — is targeted for late June 2026 per Ashok's Q1 earnings commentary. A reasoning model is already running in FSD V14.x on production vehicles, per Ashok's October 2025 ICCV paper. A transcontinental zero-intervention Canada drive completed at 3,760 miles — the first on record.

- **Grok Build actively accelerating FSD and Cybercab development.** Tesla AI VP Yantasai confirmed Grok Build is in active use for both programs; Tesla AI engineers have effectively unlimited token access within the Musk ecosystem's compute stack. Separately, thin-barrier detection (tape or chains across a parking lot entrance) remains an open edge case, flagged via repeated employee testing in Austin.

---

## Optimus

- **Giga Texas Optimus factory has entered steel erection phase.** Beams and columns are being staged at the North Campus site, which targets at least 10M units/year across two phases — Phase 2 reclaiming an adjacent mining site to nearly double the footprint. A realistic production-ready estimate from on-site observers is end of 2027 or 2028, not 2026.

- **Fremont pilot production line is further along than public disclosures suggested.** Footage from the Model S/X Signature Edition event showed manufacturing cells, some enclosed in glass (indicating automated steps), with workers present. Lars Moravy confirmed the Model S/X discontinuation and Optimus line conversion were explicitly linked decisions. Bhakdi expects a V3 reveal in approximately 4–6 weeks (late June–early August); Elon's April 22 earnings call placed it ~90 days out.

- **Macrohard (Digital Optimus) disclosed in the SpaceX S-1**, described as a joint Tesla-SpaceX agentic AI replicating computer-based human work via vision rather than APIs. Elon targets a product launch by end of 2026. Ashok is confirmed lead engineer; his ICCV paper states the same video generation models powering FSD "also work for Optimus robots navigating the Tesla Gigafactory" — shared AI stack confirmed in writing.

- **Cortex 2 partially operational since April; full capacity targeted end of summer/fall 2026.** Roughly half capacity is live, training both FSD and Optimus. Approximately 130 Megapacks installed at Cortex 2 today; ~400 planned across all Giga Texas sites.

---

## Energy

- **SpaceX purchased ~$500M in Megapacks from Tesla in 2025**, up from ~$200M in 2024 — driven by AI data center power stabilization. Meta is confirmed as an additional Megapack customer for Wyoming AI data centers ($200M order). Tesla's Megapack is cementing a position as critical AI infrastructure.

- **Megapack 3 Belgium deployment: 180 units, 700 MWh, >$116M**, on the site of a former power plant; grid connection scheduled November 2026, commissioning by end of 2027 — one of the first large-scale Megapack 3 deployments in Europe.

- **Limondale BESS in Australia coming online: 144 Megapacks, $145M**, configured for 100 MW charge / 50 MW discharge. Tesla Energy vertical integration expanding simultaneously: Corpus Christi lithium refinery Line 1 running 24/7, Line 2 equipment arriving; cathode plant at Giga Texas receiving new equipment; 4680 area has active permit filings and new equipment installation underway.

---

## Electric Vehicles

- **Lower-cost Cybertruck ($59,990 Dual-Motor AWD) VINs assigned; deliveries mid-to-late June 2026.** Joe Tegtmeyer describes demand as "pretty big." Q1 2026 Cybertruck sales were 4,186 units, down from ~7,000 in Q1 2025 — the original $39K price promise vs. ~$95K launch price cited as the primary demand suppressor.

- **Tesla Europe April 2026: +46.5% YoY, 10,654 units** (EU-only growth exceeded 67%) — third consecutive month of YoY growth following +84% in March. YTD EU/EFTA/UK: 89,429 units, +45.8%. France and Spain reportedly at record highs.

- **Tesla Roadster confirmed for Giga Texas production** per Lars Moravy on the Ride the Lightning podcast; alpha prototypes in testing. Elon's framing from Q1 earnings: "Long-term, the only manually driven car will be the new Tesla Roadster" — positioning it as the last great driver's car, not a performance halo.

- **Model S/X final production completed** with a Giga Texas sendoff event. Lifetime sales: 755,000 units (400K Model S, 355K Model X).

---

## Financials

- **Piper Sandler 17-business DCF yields ~$400/share, excluding Optimus and distributed inference.** At ~$450s, the market is effectively pricing Optimus at zero. Robotaxi becomes ~45% of Tesla revenue and roughly half of gross profit by 2045 in the model; FSD licensing modeled at ~$400B revenue by 2045. Potter's conservatism is explicitly regulatory, not technical: "You can't see second place with a telescope."

- **Musk pay "change in control" clause waives all operational milestones upon merger.** Electrek analysis flags that the 2025 performance stock agreement language states "the Operational Milestones shall be disregarded" upon a buyout — meaning targets including 1 million commercial robotaxis and 1 million Optimus bots could be bypassed for some or all of 12 tranches of stock. The article is opinion-editorial, but the clause language is sourced from the agreement.

- **Tesla capex-to-revenue ratio cited at ~9–10x** vs. 3–5x for Microsoft, Google, and Amazon, per Cern Basher's analysis using Q1 2016-onward data. The robotaxi and Optimus periods ahead are framed as the direct test of whether that ratio holds under a >$25B annual capex regime.

---

## Market & Competition

- **SpaceX IPO targeting ~$1.75–$2T valuation, expected June 12 (ticker: SPCX).** Merger odds: Wedbush's Ives at "80–90%" by early 2027; Kalshi at 33% before May 2027. NASDAQ rule change reportedly compresses index inclusion to 10 days post-IPO, forcing passive funds to buy at peak — with dilution risk for Tesla shareholders if an all-stock merger follows.

- **BYD EU/EFTA/UK YTD: 101,000+ units, +144% YoY.** Chery Auto grew 338% YoY in the same markets. EU full BEV share reached 19.7% YTD vs. 15.3% a year ago. GM/Samsung fully paused their $3.5B Synergy Cells battery plant; GM simultaneously directed $6B+ toward ICE investments including sixth-generation V8 engines.

- **Grok fell from second to fifth most-popular AI chatbot globally** by April 2026, per Electrek; monthly active users dropped 12.5% to 12.2M versus Claude's 23M (+44%). In enterprise, only 7% of companies reported using Grok vs. 48% for Claude. xAI's 62 unpermitted gas turbines in Memphis and Southaven face NAACP/Earthjustice emergency court action.

---

## Bear Case of the Week

- **Reuters investigation: Tesla's "10x safer" FSD claim overstates the true ratio by ~3x.** University of Michigan researcher Marco Benedetti corrected Tesla's methodology — which compared airbag-deployment crashes in Tesla's newer-than-average fleet against federal data including all tow-truck crashes — and found the corrected ratio is ~3x farther between crashes, not 10x. Ten of 11 traffic-safety researchers who reviewed the methodology told Reuters it amounted to misleading marketing. NHTSA has 4 active FSD/Autopilot investigations open, including a probe into dozens of cases where FSD ran red lights or turned into oncoming traffic. Tesla was also hit with a $243M verdict after an Autopilot crash in Florida killed a 22-year-old woman.

- **Reuters documented weeks of intensive pre-launch mapping in Austin**, directly contradicting Musk's repeated claim that Tesla's approach requires no "laborious local mapping." Utah labeling staff doubled to ~300 in the six months before the Austin launch. One former employee: "You can't get creative outside of that." The operational reality — a carefully mapped geofence — is structurally different from the vision-only generalization narrative used with investors.

- **Seven of nine former Tesla data labelers told Reuters they wouldn't trust FSD to drive them.** Labelers described FSD routinely failing to yield to emergency vehicles, give motorcyclists adequate space, brake on freeway off-ramps, and avoid construction zones. FSD was also reported regularly exceeding speed limits by 20–30 mph in "Mad Max" mode, with one instance of 60 mph in a 25-mph zone. One labeler: he wouldn't ride in a Tesla robotaxi "if you fucking paid me."

- **China FSD fraud trial opened May 30; triple-damage exposure on 1M+ HW3 vehicles.** Ten owners seeking $583K allege they paid ~$7,800 each for FSD between 2019 and 2021 and were excluded when Tesla's Chinese rollout supported only HW4. Under China's Consumer Rights Protection Law, triple damages are available. Tesla renamed the system "Tesla Assisted Driving" nine days before the hearing — a move Electrek characterizes as a tacit admission the original "Full Self-Driving" branding was misleading. Total global FSD/Autopilot-related litigation: $14.5B.

- **Unsupervised fleet count has not grown in over three weeks.** RobotaxiTracker.com shows no change from the May 9 snapshot across all three Texas cities. Cybercab production is running at ~30–36 units/day, vehicles are staged, Texas Level 4 authorization is live — yet the count of vehicles operating commercially without a human remains static. Bhakdi's own prior target of 1,800 unsupervised units by April–May 2026 missed by approximately a year, and his current projection of 1,000+ by end of June faces the same structural tension between production cadence and actual deployment pace.

- **Musk pay package "change in control" clause waives all operational milestones upon a Tesla–SpaceX merger.** If a merger occurs, Tesla need not deliver 1 million commercial robotaxis, 1 million Optimus bots, 20 million vehicle deliveries, or 10 million FSD subscriptions for Musk to collect some or all of 12 compensation tranches. Merger probability is actively debated at 33–90% depending on the source; the clause creates a direct structural conflict between Musk's financial incentive and Tesla shareholder interest in hitting the milestones that justify the current valuation.

2026-06-01.title: Can Elon Musk Still Win The AI Race?
2026-06-01.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel features host Herbert and guest Larry Goldberg, a serial entrepreneur and venture capital investor, discussing whether Elon Musk and xAI can still win the AI race against Anthropic and OpenAI. The central thesis is that despite xAI being only three years old — half the age of Anthropic and a quarter the age of OpenAI — Elon Musk's first-principles engineering approach, ownership of the world's largest supercomputers, and SpaceX's full-stack positioning across every layer of the AI infrastructure give him a credible path to overtake current leaders within the next three years. The conversation also covers the Anthropic compute-leasing arrangement, SpaceX's Starship V3 launch milestone, and the long-term vision of orbital AI data centers unlocking a $28.5 trillion total addressable market.

## Market & Competition

1. **Peter Diamandis's "duopoly" claim dismissed as premature:** The video opens with a recent post by Peter Diamandis suggesting the AI frontier is consolidating into a duopoly of Anthropic and OpenAI, with Meta out of the running and xAI dissolved into SpaceX. Larry Goldberg dismisses this as "very silly," arguing the race is so early that it resembles the opening of a 10,000-meter race where the early leaders rarely win. He explicitly states that neither Google nor Elon Musk should be counted out at this stage.

2. **xAI's age relative to rivals as a key argument:** Elon Musk himself posted that xAI is only three years old — half the age of Anthropic and a quarter the age of OpenAI. He drew a parallel to SpaceX, which "achieved nothing of note after three years and was written off as dead after six years" despite three consecutive launch failures, yet ultimately succeeded. Musk's stated timeline: "Let's see where things stand three years from now," signaling confidence in catching and surpassing current leaders by then.

3. **Colossus 2 running seven models simultaneously:** Musk posted that SpaceX AI's Colossus 2 supercomputer now has seven models in training simultaneously: two variants of one trillion parameters, two variants of 1.5 trillion parameters, a six trillion parameter model, and a ten trillion parameter model. Larry Goldberg emphasizes that Musk uniquely understands the "scaling laws" — the principle that without massive compute, you simply cannot do AI — and has built the infrastructure foundation first before building the application layer.

4. **Proprietary AI training software potentially 10x faster than Google's Jax:** A major new development highlighted in the video is that SpaceX has almost finished writing version one of an in-house AI training stack written in the C programming language, designed to run on a cluster of 220,000 Nvidia GB300s with heavy use of pipeline parallelism to get close to bare metal performance. The claimed result is that for large AI training runs, this software could be over an order of magnitude — approximately 10 times — faster than Google's Jax framework. Larry describes this as "classic Elon mode" — going back to first principles and stripping away overhead. This software is confirmed to be used for Grok version 5.

5. **Cursor partnership as the missing "harness" layer:** The video discusses xAI's partnership with Cursor, a leading AI coding tool, as a critical piece xAI had been missing. With access to the Colossus 2 supercomputer, Cursor's Composer 2.5 is described as "Pareto dominant" in coding per the Cursor benchmark after only a few weeks of supplemental training and reinforcement learning. The 1.5 trillion parameter version of Grok is described as likely becoming a much better base model than Kimi (a competing model) once Cursor transitions to using Grok.

6. **SpaceX's full-stack AI positioning as the structural advantage:** Larry Goldberg argues that SpaceX's key differentiator is that it operates at every single layer of the AI stack — from launch, to Starlink connectivity, to compute infrastructure, to real-world AI applications — whereas competitors like Anthropic and OpenAI are focused primarily on the chatbot, agentic, and coding layers. He argues that providing AI at scale end-to-end is what will unlock the $28.5 trillion TAM, and that Anthropic's own compute throttling (which the host experienced personally, paying close to $2,000/month before having usage restricted) illustrates the ceiling competitors face without infrastructure ownership.

7. **Anthropic compute lease: short-term, reversible arrangement:** Elon Musk clarified in a recent post that SpaceX has not committed to leasing Colossus to Anthropic forever. The arrangement is described as a 180-day lease with 90-day notice for mutual cancellation thereafter, and Musk noted the short-term structure was SpaceX's own request. He stated: "If compute gets super tight, we might need it back at some point." The video frames this as consistent with an "Elon Web Services" (EWS) strategy — building compute capacity for internal use but renting out excess capacity to generate revenue, analogous to how Amazon built AWS.

8. **SpaceX TAM breakdown: AI is 93% of the $28.5 trillion opportunity:** Per ARK Invest's analysis cited in the video, Starship's key contribution is reducing the cost of reaching orbit by an order of magnitude, unlocking a $28.5 trillion total addressable market for SpaceX. Of that, 93% — approximately $26.5 trillion — is attributed to AI compute and platform. Within that AI TAM, enterprise AI consumption (applications, robots, cars, coding, enterprise intelligence) is described by Larry as the largest single segment, potentially $22 trillion or more. The video notes that SpaceX's share of any individual segment will be smaller the further up the stack one goes, but that even 10–20% of a multi-trillion TAM implies a company worth more than $10 trillion.

9. **Orbital data centers as the long-term winning layer:** Both the host and Larry agree that space-based AI data centers — expected around 2028 — represent the layer where SpaceX will be completely unrivaled, since no other company has the launch capability to place them in orbit. Larry clarifies that orbital data centers are not a prerequisite for solving many AI science problems, but are necessary for providing AI at scale globally, which is the true unlock for the enterprise TAM.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Real-world AI cited as area where Tesla/SpaceX ecosystem is already ahead:** Larry Goldberg specifically calls out "real world AI" — a category that encompasses Tesla's autonomous driving and Optimus robotics — as an area where Musk is already ahead of pure-play AI labs. While not discussed in depth, this framing positions Tesla's FSD and robotaxi programs as integral to the broader xAI/SpaceX AI thesis rather than separate ventures.

## Market & Competition (SpaceX Launch)

1. **Starship V3 launch deemed a "great success" on most critical metric:** The video covers the recent 12th Starship launch (described as occurring on a Friday shortly before the video was published). Larry calls it a "great success" rather than merely a success. The single most important milestone achieved was the heat shield on the ship surviving atmospheric reentry intact for the first time, enabling recovery and reuse. The ship was successfully brought down from near-Earth orbit and splashed into its targeted water landing zone. The booster was lost due to a separation anomaly on descent, which Larry characterizes as a solvable problem given SpaceX's track record.

2. **Starship V3 payload capability dramatically increased:** Larry states that Starship V3 can carry more than four times the payload to orbit compared to the previous Starship version, driven not just by added engines but by each engine being individually more powerful and lighter than before. He describes V3 as a near-complete redesign with little design commonality with its predecessor despite outward visual similarity.

3. **Orbit achievement timeline:** Larry predicts SpaceX will achieve full orbital flight within the current year (2026) or very early in 2027, calling it a potential "game over" moment for the launch industry. He estimates it will take two more launches to reach orbit, while noting some community members predict orbit on the very next launch.

Notable quotes and data:
- Elon Musk: "I just left SpaceX AI office at 2:45 in the morning. People were still going. I think we might be getting close to a significant breakthrough in training."
- Elon Musk: "XAI is only 3 years old. That's half the age of Anthropic and a quarter the age of OpenAI. Let's see where things stand three years from now."
- Elon Musk on Anthropic lease: "No, SpaceX has not committed to leasing Colossus for years… This is just a 180-day lease with 90-day notice to mutual cancellation thereafter. This short-term was our request… if compute gets super tight, we might need it back at some point."
- Larry Goldberg: "Only Elon understands the scaling laws and the scaling laws are like the bitter lesson. If you don't have that compute, you can't do AI. It's as simple as that."
- Larry Goldberg: "SpaceX is at every single layer of the stack… They are far broader in scope in the software and they're far broader in scope in the hardware… it's a done deal. In my head, it's a done deal. They're going to win this race."
- Peter Neanderis (cited in video): "Elon doesn't need to run the best AI model. He needs to control the best hardware. Nvidia is the most valuable company on earth and their models aren't the most popular, but the hyperscaler play works."
- $28.5 trillion: SpaceX total addressable market per ARK Invest analysis; 93% attributed to AI compute and platform (~$26.5 trillion)
- Colossus 2: 7 models in simultaneous training (1T×2, 1.5T×2, 6T×1, 10T×1 parameters)
- Proprietary training stack: ~220,000 Nvidia GB300s, claimed ~10x faster than Google's Jax for large training runs
- Anthropic lease: 180-day term, 90-day mutual cancellation notice; John Tisman estimate: xAI spent $3–4B on Colossus 1, leasing to Anthropic for $45B over three years; Colossus 2 being built for ~$17B at one gigawatt capacity
- Starship V3: >4x payload to orbit vs. prior version; heat shield reentry success achieved for first time

2026-06-01.title: SpaceX's S-1 Just Hinted at Tesla Acquisition
2026-06-01.body:
This episode of "brighterwithherbert" features host Bert and guest Jeff Lutz — a multi-decade supply chain executive and CEO of a high-tech manufacturing consulting firm — covering a busy weekend of Tesla-related developments. The central themes are SpaceX's IPO amendment hinting at a potential Tesla acquisition, the rapid expansion of FSD approvals across Europe, Texas regulatory authorization of Tesla's driverless commercial operations, and mounting infrastructure signals pointing toward imminent robotaxi scaling.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX S-1 Amendment Hints at Strategic Acquisitions:** SpaceX filed an amendment to its Form S-1 ahead of a planned IPO on June 12th, adding new language stating it "may issue a significant amount of equity in connection with future transactions" — notably using the plural "transactions." Bert and Jeff Lutz highlight this as a meaningful hint at a potential Tesla acquisition or merger, since the Cursor deal was already known when the original S-1 dropped, suggesting the new language covers additional undisclosed deals. Jeff emphasizes the current administration's first half as a favorable window for strategic tie-ups across tech. Elon Musk has agreed to a 366-day lockup on all his SpaceX shares following the IPO, while 5% of IPO shares have been reserved for employees, friends, and family of executive officers with no lockup period.

2. **Tesla's Competitive Moat vs. AI Hardware Cycle:** Jeff Lutz argues that Tesla and SpaceX occupy uniquely durable competitive positions compared to AI hardware plays like memory chip manufacturers, which face cyclical risk and multiple competitors. He contends no company has a consumer-facing autonomy solution comparable to FSD, no one has a robotaxi network with Tesla's cost structure and volume, and no one has anything matching Starship or Starlink — making Tesla's high valuation multiple defensible. He draws a parallel to how Nvidia's AI infrastructure thesis confounded bears like Michael Burry, who predicted an imminent crash in November/December but was proven wrong as Nvidia, Broadcom, and Micron all reached all-time highs. Jeff suggests physical real-world AI at scale may be one of the biggest market events in history, and that markets may not yet be ready for millions of autonomous cars and reasoning robots.

3. **Near-Term Milestone Slippage vs. Long-Term Thesis Intact:** Jeff candidly acknowledges Tesla has missed several near-term milestones — including robotaxi deployment targets, the Optimus reveal (originally suggested for March), and the Roadster — noting a pattern of delays. However, he argues the key question is whether short-term slippage is delaying the long-term vision (1 million Optimus per year, 10 million per year eventually, large-scale robotaxi deployment), and that current hiring and infrastructure investment signals suggest the long-term trajectory remains intact. He cautions against expecting Tesla's physical AI products to be "printing revenue" in Terafab-scale numbers before 2027–2028.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Supervised Approved in Estonia — Third European Country:** The Estonian Transport Authority approved FSD supervised driving effective May 29th, following the Netherlands and Lithuania. Belgium's Minister of Transport, Anek Ditter, publicly stated that "if all goes well, approval will follow in the coming weeks," noting Belgium has already completed the required 5,000 kilometers of testing. Tesla executive for AI, Yantasai, responded "Welcome to the autonomy future." Tesla is also hiring vehicle operators in Slovenia and Austria, which Yoda (a commentator cited in the episode) interprets as a signal those countries may be next. Jeff Lutz predicts clusters of European approvals throughout the summer, describing the regulatory process as largely a "paperwork loop" now that the Netherlands approval provides a template other EU member states can leverage.

2. **World's First Fully Autonomous Coast-to-Coast Drive Across Canada:** David Moss, Devin Olsen, and Scott completed what is described as the world's first fully autonomous coast-to-coast drive across Canada using Tesla FSD, starting at Horseshoe Bay in West Vancouver and ending in Nova Scotia. The trip covered 3,700 miles over 4 days and 21 hours, accomplished using FSD version 14.3 with zero disengagements — including in parking situations. The hosts note this is now the fourth coast-to-coast autonomous drive in the past 5 months (Los Angeles to Myrtle Beach, New York to Los Angeles, New York to Los Angeles again, and Vancouver to Halifax), totaling 12,427 miles across all four trips, all performed in regular production vehicles with no special modifications. Bert and Jeff compare the significance of this achievement to AlphaGo or GPT, with David Moss himself quoted as saying it is "a bigger step change than AlphaGo or GPT as there's no special machine behind it."

3. **FSD Daily Miles Surging Per Morgan Stanley:** In a new research note, Morgan Stanley estimates Tesla owners are now driving 26.7 million miles per day with FSD, up from 18.5 million miles per day in April — a significant jump in just a couple of months. Morgan Stanley states this metric has bearing on FSD adoption and, given FSD's approximately 90% gross margins, can meaningfully uplift Tesla's profitability. The note also cites normalized NHTSA data implying improvement in robotaxi miles per accident, and Morgan Stanley's AlphaWise data shows increased hiring in northern metro areas for AI safety operators — which they interpret as a sign Tesla is gearing up to expand robotaxi operations.

4. **FSD Reasoning Capabilities Highlighted:** Jeff Lutz shares a personal FSD reasoning anecdote: while attempting an unprotected left turn, his Tesla detected a cyclist on the sidewalk approximately 50 feet away, shifted itself into reverse to clear the crosswalk, waited for the cyclist to pass, then completed the turn — all without input. Ashok Elluswami separately shared a video of a Tesla navigating extremely tight corners in China, including backing up to reposition, demonstrating FSD operating without pre-mapped routes in a challenging real-world environment.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab Drives Itself Out of Giga Texas:** Elon Musk posted a video of the first Cybercab driving itself out of Giga Texas unassisted — exiting the factory with no steering wheel and parking itself in the lot. Ashok Elluswami added that "soon it will drive itself into Austin and report for duty," which Bert interprets as a direct statement of intent for Cybercab robotaxi deployment in Austin. Joe Tegtmeyer documented Cybercabs making autonomous two-mile trips to the west end of the Giga Texas lot, and multiple videos show dozens of Cybercabs lined up at the factory with hatch covers open and wheel covers staged for shipping.

2. **Texas Authorizes Tesla for Driverless Commercial Operations at Level 4:** Effective May 28th, under Texas's new driverless vehicle law, Tesla received authorization from the State of Texas to operate driverless vehicles commercially, self-certifying as Level 4. James Stephenson is credited with finding this regulatory filing. Jeff Lutz dismisses prior bear arguments that Tesla would fail to qualify under the new law, calling such concerns predictable and noting Tesla had clearly been working toward this qualification.

3. **Robotaxi Fleet and Infrastructure Build Signals:** The hosts reference the active robotaxi fleet count — citing approximately 700 total active robotaxis (per RobotaxiTracker.com) versus Waymo's approximately 3,700 — while noting Waymo started its first driverless rides about six years ago. Jeff argues Tesla's rollout is the fastest in history in context, and that the relevant signal is not the current fleet count but the silent infrastructure build: service centers, charging stalls, wash facilities, and now fleet supervisor hiring across multiple cities. New job postings show Tesla hiring robotaxi fleet supervisors (in addition to AI safety operators) across multiple cities. Jeff envisions a future where Cybercabs drive autonomously from the factory to city depots, self-charge wirelessly, and are distributed at a scale that fundamentally shifts the personal car ownership vs. ride-share ratio.

4. **Driverless (Unsupervised) Fleet Context:** The hosts note that not all ~700 active robotaxis are fully driverless/unsupervised, and suggest the current relative plateau in driverless vehicle numbers is tied to an anticipated upcoming software release that will address remaining edge cases — after which they expect the unsupervised fleet count to move up significantly.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **European Tesla Sales Skyrocket in May:** Tesla registrations surged dramatically across Europe in May, with France up 655%, Denmark up 136%, Spain, Sweden, and Norway all showing increases. Jeff attributes the growth to multiple converging factors: the new Model Y now being in inventory (vs. supply constraints in the comparable period of 2025), falling brand-damage headwinds, high European gasoline prices (compounded by energy import dependency), Tesla's strong net promoter score driving word-of-mouth, and FSD approval adding incremental stickiness. He also notes that electrified vehicle registrations broadly (including BEV, plug-in hybrid, and hybrid) rose approximately 21% in Europe in April and made up more than two-thirds of total regional registrations.

2. **Camouflaged Model Y L Spotted Testing at Fremont:** A camouflaged vehicle believed to be the longer-wheelbase Model Y (Model Y L) was observed testing at the Fremont factory. Jeff Lutz, drawing on his supply chain background, explains that even though the car is already built in other countries, US production requires requalification of locally sourced suppliers and localization work on component databases. He describes US launch as "imminent" and expected in the second half of 2026. Bert notes this would give consumers more choice and extend the already dominant Model Y lineup.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX S-1 amendment language: "may issue a significant amount of equity in connection with future transactions" (plural — newly added)
- Elon Musk locked up for 366 days on SpaceX shares post-IPO
- 5% of SpaceX IPO shares reserved for employees, friends, and family of executive officers, not subject to lockup
- FSD supervised approved in Estonia effective May 29th (third EU country after Netherlands and Lithuania)
- Belgium's Minister of Transport: "If all goes well, approval will follow in the coming weeks"
- Tesla hiring vehicle operators in Slovenia and Austria (next-country signal)
- France Tesla sales: +655% YoY in May; Denmark: +136%
- Cybercab self-drives out of Giga Texas; Texas authorizes Tesla driverless commercial operations under Level 4 self-certification (effective May 28th)
- Morgan Stanley: FSD miles driven = 26.7 million per day (up from 18.5 million in April); FSD gross margin cited at ~90%
- Canada coast-to-coast: 3,700 miles, 4 days 21 hours, FSD v14.3, zero disengagements
- Four coast-to-coast autonomous drives in 5 months totaling 12,427 miles
- Active robotaxi fleet: ~700 total per RobotaxiTracker.com; Waymo ~3,700 (with ~6-year head start)
- Jeff Lutz: "Tesla's physical real-world AI products will be printing significant revenue in '27 and '28"
- David Moss: "It's wild that we let customers experience FSD coast to coast themselves… this is a bigger step change than AlphaGo or GPT"

2026-06-01.title: The Tesla Semi Delay Makes Sense Now
2026-06-01.body:
This video features a conversation between Cern Basher and a co-host analyzing why the Tesla Semi has been delayed for nearly a decade since its 2017 announcement, and arguing that the delay was ultimately strategic and beneficial rather than purely a failure. The core thesis is that multiple compounding technical, infrastructure, and economic challenges — particularly battery supply constraints — forced Tesla to delay, but that waiting allowed the product, economics, charging infrastructure, and autonomy readiness to mature simultaneously, setting up a much stronger launch. The hosts use the Semi's journey as a broader lesson for Tesla investors about managing expectations around timelines for genuinely novel technology.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Semi: A Nine-Year Journey from Announcement to Production:** The Tesla Semi was introduced in December 2017, with Elon Musk promising deliveries would begin in 2019. The first actual deliveries — described as pilot units only — went to PepsiCo in December 2022, representing a five-year delay from the original promise. The factory in Nevada has since been completed and the first vehicle came off the production line in April 2026, approximately nine years after the initial announcement. The hosts note that the truck's overall shape has remained largely unchanged, though significant internal improvements have been made over the years.

2. **Battery Supply as the Primary Delay Driver:** The hosts identify cell and battery supply constraints as the single biggest reason for the Semi's delay. They argue that Tesla faced a prioritization problem — limited battery supply had to be allocated between Megapacks, Model 3s, Model Ys, and eventually Cybertrucks — and the Semi simply lost out until battery production capacity and pack design improved sufficiently. The discussion frames this not as a failure but as a rational triage of constrained resources.

3. **Weight Reduction and Ongoing Engineering Improvements:** Dan Priestley is cited as having stated that Tesla removed approximately 1,000 lbs from the weight of the truck over the development period. The hosts debate whether weight and payload constraints were truly a rate-limiting factor or simply areas of ongoing improvement, ultimately concluding that the delay gave Tesla the opportunity to make the truck more economical and efficient regardless of the original cause.

4. **Charging Strategy: Hub-and-Spoke Model Reduces Infrastructure Burden:** Rather than building out a nationwide Megacharger network in advance, Tesla's current go-to-market approach focuses on fleet operators with hub-and-spoke distribution networks, where trucks return to a central depot each night and can charge on-site. Under this model, the customer bears the cost of installing charging at their facility, reducing Tesla's capital requirements. The hosts note this is a smart near-term strategy that allows significant truck sales before Tesla needs to invest heavily in a public long-haul charging network.

5. **Economics: ~35 Cents Per Mile in Savings:** According to a source cited in the discussion, the Tesla Semi offers approximately 35 cents per mile in cost savings compared to conventional diesel trucking. The hosts emphasize that for fleet operators running millions of miles per year, this figure is highly compelling and that the product should essentially sell itself — provided reliability is proven. They suggest that reliability concerns from early PepsiCo pilot units may have been another behind-the-scenes reason for the extended delay before mass production.

6. **Early Orders Signal Strong Commercial Demand:** Now that production has begun, the hosts report that orders are coming in rapidly, with one example cited of a company ordering 340 Semi trucks. They describe the order momentum as "going bonkers" and suggest the combination of mature economics, improved reliability, and infrastructure readiness is driving strong initial commercial interest.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Semi Designed to Be Autonomy-Ready:** Dan Priestley is quoted as describing the Tesla Semi as "robo trucking ready" or effectively autonomous-ready. The hosts speculate that some of the design changes made over the nine-year development period may have been driven by autonomy considerations, though they acknowledge the exterior has not changed dramatically. They note that FSD integration into the Semi will still require further development and validation before an autonomous trucking network can be reliably operated.

2. **Autonomy as a Possible Strategic Delay Factor:** One host raises the possibility that Tesla deliberately delayed the Semi's mass launch in part to wait for autonomy technology to mature, so the vehicle could be launched already positioned for autonomous operation rather than requiring a redesign later. The other host acknowledges this is plausible but notes it is difficult to isolate as a single cause given the many other concurrent challenges over the nine-year period.

3. **Supervised Platooning as a Near-Term Autonomy Bridge:** The hosts briefly discuss a concept raised by a commenter: using a human-supervised lead driver at the front of a convoy with several Semi trucks "daisy-chained" behind it, reducing the number of drivers needed without requiring full autonomy. The hosts are uncertain about the technical feasibility of this approach versus traditional trucking platoons but acknowledge it as an interesting interim solution in an industry facing a chronic driver shortage.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla Investor Mindset: Grace for Novel Technology Timelines:** The broader framing of the conversation is a lesson for Tesla investors about tolerating delays on genuinely unprecedented projects. The hosts draw parallels to Apple with the iPhone and Netflix, arguing that transformative products often take longer than initially promised but that getting the execution right ultimately matters more than hitting early deadlines. They caution investors not to expect rapid quarterly ramp-ups on products like Cybercab simply because production has begun.

Notable quotes and data:
- "The first deliveries were made to Pepsico in December of 2022. So 5 years late." — co-host
- "The first time I came off [production line] in April 2026, nine years later."
- Dan Priestley (cited): Tesla removed approximately 1,000 lbs from the weight of the Semi over development.
- Dan Priestley (cited): The Semi is "robo trucking ready" / autonomous-ready.
- Cost savings cited: approximately **35 cents per mile** versus conventional diesel trucking.
- One company reportedly ordered **340 Semi trucks** after production began.
- Battery allocation competition cited: Megapacks, Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck all competing with Semi for cell supply.
- "Waiting until everything's perfectly set up and then you go scale, you'll go [fast] because everything's better — economics, weight, superchargers faster, quicker, autonomy's ready."
- "This product will sell itself... if you have a product that's super reliable, it will sell itself."

2026-06-01.title: BYD will pay for crashes on its FSD competitor, something Tesla never has
2026-06-01.body:
BYD has announced it will assume full, uncapped financial liability for at-fault crashes occurring while its "God's Eye" urban driving system is active in China — a commitment Tesla has never made for FSD, inverting the industry's standard Level 2 liability model.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **BYD's liability guarantee terms:** Announced May 28 at BYD's vehicle intelligence strategy event, the policy covers all direct economic losses — repairs, third-party property damage, and personal injury — when a driver is using BYD's urban navigate-on-autopilot function in compliance with regulations. There is no payout cap, no requirement to purchase separate intelligent driving insurance, and claims will not raise commercial insurance premiums. Coverage applies to God's Eye A and B systems for one year from delivery; existing owners receive it upon updating to God's Eye 5.0 OTA and it is not restricted to the first or registered owner.

2. **Precedent from parking feature:** BYD applied a similar liability guarantee to L4 smart parking in July 2025, which it says drove feature usage from 21% to 93%. The new policy extends that model to city driving, which BYD calls a "double guarantee."

3. **Tesla's contrasting position:** Tesla's FSD (Supervised) is a Level 2 system and its owner's manual explicitly states drivers bear full responsibility at all times. A Miami federal jury awarded a $243 million judgment against Tesla over a fatal Autopilot crash, assigning Tesla one-third of the blame — a liability Tesla contested rather than absorbed voluntarily.

## Market & Competition

1. **Price gap underscores the contrast:** BYD's LiDAR-equipped God's Eye B system is a one-time 12,000-yuan (~$1,770) option available across BYD's full lineup. Tesla's equivalent in China ("Tesla Assisted Driving") costs 64,000 yuan (~$9,400) as a one-off purchase with no subscription option — roughly five times more expensive, while placing all crash liability on the driver.

2. **BYD's fleet scale:** BYD states it now has 3.15 million vehicles on the road with assisted driving, generating up to 200 million kilometers of driving data per day.

## Editorial Stance
Lambert argues BYD has answered the liability question the industry has spent a decade avoiding, framing the guarantee as both a credible safety statement and a data-harvesting strategy. He contends Tesla, despite 10 billion FSD miles logged, hides behind Level 2 disclaimers and arbitration clauses, and challenges why Tesla won't make a similar commitment. He also cautions readers that God's Eye, like Tesla FSD, remains a Level 2 system requiring driver attention.

Notable quotes and data:
- BYD chairman Wang Chuanfu: "Taking on Level 3 and Level 4 liability early during the Level 2 stage demonstrates the company's absolute confidence in its own technology."
- God's Eye B one-time cost: 12,000 yuan (~$1,770) vs. Tesla Assisted Driving in China: 64,000 yuan (~$9,400)
- BYD fleet: 3.15 million assisted-driving vehicles; up to 200 million km of driving data per day
- Smart parking liability guarantee (July 2025) lifted usage from 21% to 93%
- Tesla Autopilot Miami jury verdict: $243 million, with Tesla assigned one-third of fault

2026-06-01.title: Tesla FSD v14 is so good it’s making me dangerously complacent
2026-06-01.body:
Electrek editor Fred Lambert — who has tested every version of Tesla Autopilot and FSD since before the original launch — argues that FSD v14 is the most capable version yet, and that its near-perfect performance is creating a dangerous complacency problem that Tesla's marketing is actively worsening.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD v14 performance and the complacency trap:** Lambert reports that after daily driving FSD v14 for several weeks, he now routinely travels hundreds of miles without needing to intervene. Emerging data suggests FSD v14 can travel roughly 2,000 miles between critical interventions — equating to approximately 30–40 hours of driving. He invokes the "ironies of automation" concept (documented since the 1980s) and the "vigilance decrement" effect, noting research shows drivers need 5–8 seconds to mentally reengage after an automated system requests a takeover. Lambert warns that even a 3x safety improvement over prior versions doesn't eliminate the risk of a single moment of inattention.

2. **Real-world incident and third-party warnings:** Lambert cites the crash of Raffi Krikorian — former head of Uber's self-driving division — who totaled his Tesla Model X after FSD's near-perfect performance lulled him into a false sense of security before the system failed in a turn. He also references IIHS warnings about Level 2 system design, NHTSA's expanded crash reporting requirements for Level 2 ADAS, and a Reuters report in which seven of nine former Tesla AI data labelers said they would not trust FSD to drive them.

3. **Tesla's marketing amplifying the risk:** Lambert details a pattern of Tesla's official X account and Elon Musk framing FSD as a substitute for an attentive driver. Specific examples cited: Tesla called FSD "your personal chauffeur" and said it "gives back your freedom" and "takes the stress out of driving." Tesla amplified testimonials from a 71-year-old with failing eyesight, a 93-year-old driving to church, and a man born without arms — all framing FSD as providing independent mobility for people who cannot otherwise drive. Musk replied "yes" when asked if FSD allows texting depending on traffic context, despite texting while driving being illegal in nearly all 50 states and Tesla's own terms requiring full driver supervision. Musk also posted that "by V14.3, your car will feel like it is sentient" — which Lambert characterizes as a psychological prompt to over-trust the system, not a technical claim.

## Editorial Stance
Lambert argues Tesla is actively choosing to worsen the complacency problem through its marketing rather than address it, and calls on the company to strengthen driver monitoring, stop promoting FSD as a driver substitute, and be honest about the system's real limitations. He warns that when a complacent FSD driver misses a critical intervention, third parties on public roads bear the consequences without having consented to Tesla's beta test.

Notable quotes and data:
- "FSD v14 can travel a couple thousand miles between critical interventions" — ~30–40 hours of driving without needed input
- Drivers need "5 to 8 seconds to mentally reengage after an automated system hands control back" (cited psychological research)
- Tesla's official account: "FSD Supervised can give you back your freedom" and "takes the stress out of driving so you can enjoy going places"
- Musk on texting while using FSD: "Depending on context of surrounding traffic, yes"
- Musk: "by V14.3, your car will feel like it is sentient"
- Seven of nine former Tesla AI data labelers (per Reuters) said they would not trust FSD to drive them
- Lambert: "I wrote back in October 2024 that FSD was getting more dangerous as it got better. Now, a year and a half later, the system is dramatically more capable — and the complacency problem is dramatically worse."

2026-06-01.title: Why Elon Just Bought A LOT of Land & Robotaxi Fleet Developments ⚡️
2026-06-01.body:
This episode of Electrified, hosted by Dillon Loomis, covers a wide range of Tesla and broader tech developments including the stalled robotaxi expansion in Houston and Dallas, FSD 14.3 performance impressions, Tesla's European sales surge, the Terafab land acquisition in Texas, and competitive moves from BYD and OpenAI in autonomy and robotics. The core thesis is that while Tesla's supervised FSD is showing strong real-world performance globally, the unsupervised robotaxi rollout appears to be lagging expectations, creating a confounding near-term picture for the autonomy thesis.

## Robotaxi

1. **Texas Self-Certification and Official Registry:** Tesla officially self-certified its robotaxis as Level 4 under a new Texas law that went into effect last week, allowing continued robotaxi operations in the state. This is described as largely a formality and procedural change — no new capability was added. The Texas Motor Carrier website now lists Tesla's robotaxi service with 42 VINs registered across 42 rows. For comparison, Waymo has 619 VINs listed in Texas, and AVID has 317 VINs registered.

2. **Houston and Dallas Fleet Contraction:** On-the-ground reporters indicate the Houston robotaxi fleet has dropped from six operational vehicles down to two, a situation that has persisted for several weeks. In Dallas, Spencer reported being unable to get a robotaxi two days in a row, with the app showing "no rides available nearby" — indicating no vehicles operating in the fleet rather than high demand. Dillon Loomis noted he warned on April 18th (four days before the earnings call) that if the Houston and Dallas launches didn't scale beyond a few vehicles within weeks, they may have been timed for positive earnings momentum rather than genuine readiness.

3. **Cybercab World Cup Speculation and Caution:** Many are speculating Tesla will debut the Cybercab on the robotaxi network in Houston and/or Dallas around June 14th when World Cup games begin. However, Dillon Loomis cautions that Tesla has been historically cautious and is unlikely to rush a Cybercab debut for marketing exposure. Ashoke stated that "soon the Cybercab will be driving itself into Austin City reporting for duty," though Dillon notes "soon at Tesla has many different interpretations."

4. **Supervisor Hiring for New Robotaxi Cities:** Tesla currently has six job listings for a robotaxi fleet support supervisor in Palo Alto, Tampa, San Antonio, Orlando, San Francisco, and Miami. Three of those cities — Miami, Orlando, and Tampa — match three of the five cities Tesla is reportedly targeting for robotaxi service launch by the end of June 2026. The role involves ensuring vehicles are in excellent condition for 24/7 operations, including vehicle prep, inspections, and lot management.

5. **Dallas Facility Repurposed for Autonomous Vehicles:** A court document reveals Tesla is building a 51,000 sq ft EV sales, service, and delivery center in Grand Prairie, Texas (between Dallas and Fort Worth, near Interstate 20). A revised operational plan in the document states the facility will be used for charging, cleaning, repair, and general maintenance of Tesla-owned autonomous vehicles. This signals that Tesla's existing service center and gallery infrastructure is insufficient for planned robotaxi scale. The facility is currently under construction and will not be open in time for the World Cup.

6. **RobotaxiTracker Hiring Watch List Update:** The RobotaxiTracker.com hiring watch list now shows 41 entries, including 33 active listings of cities where Tesla is currently hiring for an AI safety operator role. Historical cities where Tesla previously hired for this role are still visible, suggesting those positions have been filled.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD 14.3 Real-World Performance — Positive Signals:** Multiple noteworthy FSD demonstrations have surfaced. Joe Anderson drove through all 48 contiguous US states plus DC on FSD version 14.3.2 — over 7,200 miles across 9 days — with FSD driving every mile. Tesla's official account congratulated him. Separately, a team drove coast-to-coast across Canada — over 3,700 miles on version 14.3 — with zero disengagements of any kind. The head of research at Silicon Data was quoted saying "self-driving has been quietly completely solved with steady daily improvements." A tester in Germany drove for almost an hour through villages, country roads, and highways with no issues. FSD has also gone viral in China with testers pushing extreme scenarios. Tesla's FSD is now approved in the Netherlands, Lithuania, and Estonia across the EU.

2. **FSD 14.3 Personal Experience — Mixed:** Dillon Loomis shares his own experience with 14.3, describing it as "very far from a banger" despite Elon's public praise. He reports persistent jittery behavior, micro-braking events that would make passengers uncomfortable, poor navigation in his area, and notably poor parking behavior — the car has parked in entirely different parking lots from the intended destination on multiple occasions. He attributes some of this to Tesla rewriting the compiler and runtime from the ground up, acknowledging a few steps back may be expected. He also notes that Elon's credibility for touting upcoming FSD improvements is "as low as it's ever been" in his view.

3. **Hardware 3 Version 14 Light Expected in June:** Dillon notes that hardware 3 owners should be expecting a "version 14 light" sometime in June 2026 if Tesla delivers on its timeline.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **European Sales Surge:** Tesla sales in Europe have surged significantly in May 2026, partly reflecting low year-ago comparables from the Model Y and Model 3 changeovers. Country-level data for May: Portugal up ~350% year-over-year (January–May up 58%, outpacing a 33% rise in all EV sales); Sweden up 71%; Denmark up 136% (Model Y was Denmark's best-selling vehicle in May); Spain up 113%; Norway up 29%; France up 655%. Giga Berlin is expanding output capacity, and a broader supervised FSD rollout across the EU later in 2026 is expected to further accelerate sales.

2. **Canada Chinese-Built EV Quota:** Tesla has already used approximately 12% of Canada's available quota for Chinese-built EVs in the first allocation window. Nearly all of the roughly 2,900 Chinese-built EVs imported so far are Model 3s from Giga Shanghai. The current quota window allows up to 24,500 Chinese-built EVs to be imported between program launch and August 31st, 2026.

3. **Tesla Semi Grapevine Test:** Covenant conducted a two-week real-world test of the Tesla Semi with a major California customer on the Grapevine route — described as one of the most demanding real-world routes for any truck due to steep grades, heavy load management, and heat. The driver reported being "amazed" at the Tesla Semi's performance and felt a level of confidence hard to match in a diesel truck. A summary from Covenant is described as coming soon.

4. **Graphite Supply Chain Update:** Australia's Syrah Resources announced Tesla has withdrawn a notice of intent to end their graphite supply deal, accepting that Syrah is now producing conforming samples. Tesla had originally issued a default notice in July 2025 citing conformity issues with active anode material samples from the Vidalia facility. Dillon flags the importance of securing anode material suppliers outside of China.

## Market & Competition

1. **BYD Autonomous Driving Liability Policy:** BYD announced a new policy offering comprehensive coverage for damages incurred while its "God's Eye" autonomous driving system is engaged. BYD will cover all losses with no cap for vehicle repairs, third-party property damage, and personal injury liabilities, and the policy will not raise the owner's regular commercial insurance for the following year. The policy is valid for one year. God's Eye is technically a Level 2 system. Dillon notes a precedent: when BYD introduced a similar guarantee for automatic parking in July 2025, usage jumped from ~21% to over 90%. He flags this as a signal that automakers will increasingly need to take liability for their autonomous systems.

2. **OpenAI Robotics Entering Humanoid Space:** Sam Altman announced OpenAI Robotics is now hiring to program and manufacture robots. OpenAI's stated near-term focus is on robots to support skilled workers building infrastructure; long-term vision is a personal robot for everyone. Dillon recaps the history: OpenAI invested in Figure in 2024 and partnered to develop AI models for Figure robots, but Figure ended that partnership roughly a year later after claiming a major in-house AI breakthrough. OpenAI has since been doing data collection and teleoperation work with hands but has not yet revealed a full humanoid prototype. In January 2026, OpenAI issued an RFP seeking humanoid manufacturing partners in the US for components like gearboxes, actuators, and motors. Dillon expects partnerships given OpenAI's lack of manufacturing experience and views this as a very long game over decades.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Terafab Land Acquisition Near Austin:** SE Robinson reported that Witt LLC — a purchasing entity sharing the physical address of XAI in Palo Alto — is buying over 3,100 acres in Grimes County, Texas (at the Gibbons Creek Reservoir), just over a two-hour drive from Giga Texas. A public hearing is scheduled for June 3rd, 2026, with SpaceX listed as the property owner for the tax abatement session. The project is described as a "multi-phase next-gen vertically integrated semiconductor manufacturing and advanced computing fab facility." Estimated capital investment for initial phases is $55 billion, with a total potential investment of $119 billion if additional phases are built. XAI's general counsel James Burnham has signed on behalf of Witt LLC. Dillon identifies this as the land for the Terafab, noting Elon uses tech entities tied to his companies to acquire land ahead of formal approvals, which are still pending.

2. **Macrohard and Digital Optimus Context:** Dillon briefly references Macrohard and "something like a digital Optimus" as potential internal uses for SpaceX's compute capacity (Colossus), noting that SpaceX retaining optionality to reallocate GPUs for internal Optimus-related projects represents asymmetric long-term upside.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla: 42 VINs registered for robotaxi service in Texas; Waymo: 619 VINs; AVID: 317 VINs
- Houston robotaxi fleet: down from 6 vehicles to 2, has been that way for "a few weeks"
- Dallas: "no rides available nearby" — two consecutive days with no operational vehicles
- FSD 14.3.2: 7,200+ miles across all 48 contiguous US states + DC, zero driver interventions
- FSD 14.3 Canada coast-to-coast: 3,700+ miles, zero disengagements
- Tesla sales May 2026: Portugal +350% YoY; France +655%; Denmark +136%; Spain +113%; Sweden +71%; Norway +29%
- Model Y: Denmark's best-selling vehicle in May 2026
- Canada Chinese EV quota: Tesla used ~12% (~2,900 vehicles, nearly all Model 3 from Giga Shanghai) of 24,500-vehicle allocation window ending August 31, 2026
- BYD God's Eye: automatic parking guarantee in July 2025 drove usage from ~21% to over 90%
- Terafab: 3,100+ acres in Grimes County, TX; $55B initial phase capex, up to $119B total
- SpaceX IPO context: only Facebook and Alibaba have been valued at $100B+ after their first day on US exchanges
