2026-06-01.title: The iPhone Moment for Robots Just Happened
2026-06-01.body:
This video argues that humanoid robotics has reached its "iPhone moment" — a genuine technological inflection point where three converging S-curves (AI brain/VLA models, data flywheels, and rapidly cheapening actuator hardware) have finally made deployable, economically viable humanoid robots a reality. The host uses Figure AI's live-streamed warehouse robots (Bob, Frank, and Gary) as the defining demonstration of this shift, comparing it to the launch of the original iPhone on June 29th, 2007. The core thesis is that the $40 trillion annual global physical labor market is about to be disrupted, with near-term deployment filling genuine demographic labor vacancies, but a more disruptive and politically volatile middle wave arriving around 2030.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Figure AI's live warehouse demo as the inflection point:** Figure AI's three humanoid robots — Bob, Frank, and Gary (Figure 3 units) — have been running a publicly live-streamed, continuous warehouse mission at a facility in California since May 14th, sorting packages at human-parity speed, autonomously swapping out for battery charges, and operating end-to-end from camera pixels via neural network without teleoperation (except when errors occurred). The runtime counter had surpassed 60 hours at the time of recording. The host characterizes this as the most significant demo in technology history, comparable in significance to the original iPhone launch.

2. **Three converging S-curves making humanoids viable:** The host identifies three simultaneous technological breakthroughs. First, the "brain": Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models — a single neural network taking raw camera pixels plus natural language instructions plus body state and outputting continuous motor commands hundreds of times per second, with no hand-coded scripts. Jim Fan at NVIDIA leads a related project called Groot. Second, the "data flywheel": Tesla has been collecting real-world manipulation data inside factories with Optimus for 2 years and with its 9 million FSD vehicle fleet for longer; NVIDIA released a synthetic data generator called Cosmos running world simulations on gaming GPUs to produce robot training trajectories. Third, the "body": actuator costs have collapsed dramatically (detailed below).

3. **Actuator cost collapse enabling economics:** In 2020, a high-torque actuator (hip or knee joint) cost $2,000–$5,000 each at low volume, making the full actuator subsystem on a single robot $50,000–$100,000. By 2026, the same actuator runs $500–$2,000 at low volume. Morgan Stanley projects that at Tesla's target scale of 1 million units per year, actuator costs could fall to $100–$300 each — an order of magnitude reduction in 6 years. The Chinese EV supply chain (precision motor and gear manufacturers supplying BYD and others) is the key enabler of this commoditization.

4. **Humanoid pricing trajectory and competitive landscape:** Unitree (Chinese company) is currently selling a full humanoid for $13,500 — roughly the price of a used Honda Civic. Bank of America projects average humanoid material cost drops from approximately $35,000 today to $13,000–$17,000 by 2035. IDTechEx projects average selling price falls from $115,000 to $37,000 over the next four years. Tesla is targeting a $20,000 price point for Optimus at 1 million units, which it hopes to reach by around 2030.

5. **Current real-world humanoid deployments:** Multiple humanoid robots are already deployed in commercial settings. Figure 3 robots are working BMW's Spartanburg, South Carolina factory in the body shop, sheet metal placement, and weld inspection areas. Apollo robots (by a company called Electronics Robot/Apptronik per context) are deployed at Mercedes plants, Jabil electronics factories, and GXO logistics warehouses. Agility Robotics' Digit humanoid has crossed 100,000 totes moved at a GXO facility in Flowery Branch, Georgia. Tesla Optimus is in internal pilots at Fremont and Giga Texas, with mass production starting in summer 2026.

6. **Figure AI's production scaling and TAM:** Figure AI CEO Brett Adcock stated on X on April 23rd and in a Forbes interview that Figure's Bot Q manufacturing plant went from producing one robot per day to one robot per hour in approximately 4 months — a 24x scaling in 120 days. The plan for calendar year 2026 is north of 12,000 robots, with a long-term goal of 1 million robots per year. Adcock's total addressable market estimate is roughly half of global GDP, approximately $50 trillion per year.

7. **Tesla Optimus production targets:** Tesla has stated a goal of reaching 1 million Optimus units per year (timeframe approximately 2030). The host notes Tesla recorded production in March 2026 and aimed to 3x that by May 2026.

8. **The demographic vacancy argument (Wave 1):** The host argues the initial wave of humanoid deployment is not displacing workers who want jobs — it is filling vacancies that already exist due to demographic collapse. Amazon warehouse turnover runs 100–150% per year; one in three new fulfillment hires quits within 90 days; a New Jersey study clocked Amazon warehouse turnover at 124% vs. 72% for comparable non-Amazon warehouses. The U.S. trucking industry is short 60,000–82,000 drivers, projected to reach 160,000 by 2028, with annual driver turnover at large carriers of 90–95%. Manpower Group's 2026 survey shows 84% of Japanese employers and 83% of German employers cannot find workers to hire. Japan's elder care sector has a job-to-applicant ratio of 3.9:1 and is projected to be short 570,000 care workers by 2040.

9. **The disruptive middle wave (Wave 2, ~2030):** Around 2030, the host warns humanoids will begin displacing jobs humans actually want: fast food prep, non-high-turnover warehouse roles, light manufacturing, hotel housekeeping, big box retail stocking, construction framing, and agricultural harvesting. In the U.S. alone, he estimates roughly 10 million workers in directly automatable physical labor categories (approximately 7 million material movers at $30,000 median wage, 2 million assemblers at $44,000, 2 million in related roles at $37,000). He explicitly worries about a scenario where cost curves run faster than government response, potentially producing 20 million laid-off material handlers within 3 years and violent political backlash.

10. **The systemic flywheel thesis:** The host argues humanoid robots are not a standalone industry but the physical manufacturing endpoint of a single integrated flywheel encompassing AI, batteries, EVs, data centers, and manufacturing AI itself. Tesla builds Optimus in a factory already producing 2 million cars per year using the same AI infrastructure as FSD and feeding into Grok. Figure uses actuators from the same Chinese supply chain as EVs and residential batteries. NVIDIA's Cosmos generates humanoid training data on the same GPUs training LLMs. The flywheel cannot be stopped without abandoning AI, batteries, EVs, or domestic manufacturing competitiveness — all politically untouchable.

11. **Political and regulatory disruption as the real near-term battleground:** Unlike the iPhone's indirect, invisible labor displacement over a decade, humanoid displacement is visible — robots have name tags and are on live streams. The host predicts the political response will be driven by optics before economics, resulting in deployment bans, component tariffs, union carveouts, and city/state/country-level regulatory fragmentation. He frames the countries that get the regulatory balance right as capturing a structural multi-trillion dollar productivity advantage that others cannot recover from within the century.

## Market & Competition

1. **$40 trillion physical labor market as the disruption target:** The host estimates the total annual value of global human physical labor at approximately $40 trillion — roughly one-third of the entire global economy and ten times the size of the market created by the iPhone ($4 trillion per year). This is the market humanoid robots are positioned to disrupt.

2. **China's supply chain advantage:** The Chinese EV supply chain — precision motor and gear manufacturers serving BYD and thousands of other Chinese EV makers — is directly enabling humanoid actuator commoditization. Unitree's $13,500 full humanoid is cited as a product of this supply chain maturity. The host identifies this as a geopolitical and industrial competition dimension, noting that restricting humanoid deployment means ceding ground to China across EVs, batteries, and manufacturing simultaneously.

Notable quotes and data:
- "We had record production in March and we're going to try to 3x that by May. We want to be able to get to a million units a year." — Tesla on Optimus production
- Figure AI production: 1 robot/day → 1 robot/hour in ~4 months (24x scaling in 120 days), per Brett Adcock
- Figure AI 2026 target: north of 12,000 robots
- Actuator cost: $2,000–$5,000 (2020) → $500–$2,000 (2026 low volume) → $100–$300 (Morgan Stanley estimate at Tesla's 1M unit/year scale)
- Unitree full humanoid: $13,500 currently available
- Bank of America: average humanoid material cost from ~$35,000 today → $13,000–$17,000 by 2035
- IDTechEx: average selling price from $115,000 → $37,000 over next four years
- Tesla Optimus price target: $20,000 at 1 million units (~2030)
- U.S. trucking driver shortage: 60,000–82,000 now, projected 160,000 by 2028; 90–95% annual turnover at large carriers
- Amazon warehouse turnover: 100–150% per year; 124% per New Jersey study vs. 72% for comparable non-Amazon warehouses
- Japan: 84% of employers can't find workers (Manpower Group 2026); elder care job-to-applicant ratio 3.9:1; projected 570,000 care worker shortage by 2040; 29% of population over 65, 1 in 5 over 75
- Germany: 83% of employers can't find workers; crossed demographic threshold in 2026 where retirees outnumber new labor force entrants
- Agility Robotics' Digit: 100,000+ totes moved at GXO Flowery Branch, Georgia
- Effective robot operating cost estimate: ~$2/hour
- Brett Adcock TAM estimate: ~$50 trillion/year (half of global GDP)
- Figure AI live stream launched: May 14th (2026)
- "The market it disrupts is not 4 trillion a year. It is 40 trillion a year."
- "The political response to the optics will arrive before the political response to the economics."

2026-06-01.title: CLIFF DIVING AGAIN?!? GPS madness masked as AP/FSD Failures. 16 Hot News Items to start your week
2026-06-01.body:
This June 1st livestream from FutureAzA covers approximately 20 news items spanning Tesla safety incidents, FSD/Autopilot misreporting, regulatory developments, EV adoption trends, battery durability, and competitor news. The host's core argument is that mainstream media systematically misrepresents Tesla's driver-assistance systems — conflating Autopilot with FSD, amplifying cherry-picked negative data from label workers, and ignoring the broader safety record — while Tesla vehicles continue to demonstrate exceptional structural safety and long-term reliability. The session concludes with an extended Q&A covering Model Y purchasing advice, battery health data, and general EV ownership topics.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Tesla Model 3 survives 300-ft cliff plunge in Malibu:** A Model 3 plunged roughly 300 feet off a cliff on Mulholland Highway in Malibu on a Friday morning, with occupants surviving. The host attributes this to the Model 3's NHTSA five-star overall rating in every category and subcategory, and its record as having the lowest probability of injury of any car ever evaluated by the US New Car Assessment Program. The absence of a traditional engine provides additional crumple zone, and the rigid occupant cell structure is credited for the outcome.

2. **87-year-old driver dies after Tesla enters pond — Autopilot misreported as FSD:** In Tampa, an 87-year-old man driving a Model Y veered off the road, struck an electrical box, and drove into a pond while Autopilot was engaged. The host emphasizes that Autopilot (lane-keep assistance) is categorically different from Full Self-Driving, and that the vehicle's speed — sufficient to break through an electrical pole and still reach the pond in what he describes as a 30–35 mph zone — points strongly to human error rather than a system failure. The host criticizes media coverage that uses incidents like this to discourage adoption of what he calls demonstrably the safest driving system in the world.

3. **Reuters "fake FSD" story dismissed as misinformation:** A Reuters report claimed Tesla staff admitted to selling fake self-driving with fake numbers, citing workers at a Utah office who label video footage of crashes, near-misses with children, and animal strikes. The host argues these data labelers are deliberately shown only the most traumatic edge-case footage — perhaps 10 miles of bad driving per day — while Tesla's fleet is accumulating roughly 30 million miles of good driving daily. He notes that at 10 billion supervised FSD miles driven, the catastrophic death toll that critics imply would exist has simply not materialized, and he calls the Reuters framing deliberately misleading.

4. **Tesla owner repeatedly uses Autopilot from back seat:** A news story profiled a man who has been arrested multiple times for riding in the back seat while Autopilot is engaged. The host strongly discourages this behavior. He also notes the article falsely cited two men killed in Texas while sitting in back and passenger seats of an Autopilot-engaged Tesla — which he identifies as being the unrelated story of intoxicated occupants who crashed into a tree, calling the article "pure slop."

5. **Estonia becomes third European country to clear self-driving on public roads:** Estonia has approved self-driving vehicle operation on its roads, joining the Netherlands and Lithuania. The host notes that while this is technically classified as Level 2 driver assistance under SAE levels, he argues the SAE framework is essentially meaningless — designed before the systems existed, it lumps mild lane-keep through Full Self-Driving into the same band. Drivers remain legally responsible. Other European countries are expected to follow.

6. **Supervised FSD surpasses 10 billion miles:** The host references that Tesla's supervised Full Self-Driving has surpassed the 10 billion mile mark, and that the fleet is now accumulating approximately 30 million miles per day.

## Robotaxi

1. **Waymo's new robotaxi uses Chinese-built Zeekr vehicle, now accepting riders:** Waymo's newest robotaxi — described as the Zeekr (referred to in the transcript as the "Zeer" / "Ohigh") — is Chinese-manufactured and is now operating in California and expanding to more riders and cities. The host notes the interior is intentionally sparse and easy to clean, which he considers appropriate. However, he argues the economics are unfavorable: if the base vehicle costs $35,000, the 100% import tariff effectively doubles it to $70,000. He contends that for Waymo's robotaxi to compete economically with a Tesla Cybercab — which he says requires less cleaning, less energy, and less maintenance — the Chinese van would need to cost around $12,000 after tariffs, a price he says it will never reach even before sensor integration costs.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **72% of new EV buyers traded in a gas car despite losing the $7,500 tax credit:** EV trade-ins as a share of new EV purchases rose from 67% in January 2026 to 72% by April 2026. The host interprets this as evidence that EV adoption is expanding beyond early adopters into the broader market. Analysts cited high interest rates and more expensive gasoline as contextual factors.

2. **Model 3 reaches 360,000 miles — battery replaced at 321,000 miles for $5,000:** A Model 3 owner hit 360,000 miles, replacing the battery at 321,000 miles. A reconditioned pack cost approximately $5,000, well below the $15,000–$22,000 range for a new battery replacement. The host notes this is exceptional longevity compared to traditional vehicles, and that the original motors remain functional.

3. **Model Y with 111,000 miles retains 90–92% battery capacity despite near-total DC fast charging:** A pre-refresh Model Y at 111,000 miles had received only 36 kWh of charging from AC sources — virtually all charging was DC fast charging — yet retains 90–92% of original range capacity. The host calls the persistent narrative about fast charging destroying EV batteries "ludicrous."

4. **FSD praised by mainstream automotive press:** The host cites a piece describing Tesla's supervised Full Self-Driving as technology that "felt like sci-fi 10 years ago," with a new owner who bought a Model Y after his son recommended it, calling it "the most impressively engineered consumer product since forever." Features highlighted include voice control, Grok integration (available with the spring update), self-parking, summon, collision avoidance, and home charging convenience.

5. **Ford Escape to return as all-electric vehicle in 2029:** Ford is reportedly planning to revive the Escape nameplate as a fully electric vehicle after ending production following the 2026 model year. The host notes a parallel with the Mustang Mach-E strategy of using established nameplates to introduce new technology, though he expresses skepticism about Ford's EV execution. He also notes a Ford Explorer electric exists in Europe but is built by Volkswagen.

6. **AC Cobra electric supercar — host correction:** The host initially reported on an electric AC Cobra supercar before discovering mid-segment that the vehicle may not actually have an electric version, acknowledging the error on air.

## Market & Competition

1. **BYD charges to 97% in 12 minutes even in freezing cold:** BYD's Denza Z9 GT, powered by the second-generation Blade battery, can charge from 10% to 70% in 5 minutes and 10% to 97% in under 10 minutes in ideal conditions — now demonstrated at 12 minutes in freezing temperatures. The host notes these batteries are not available in the US due to import tariffs (cited at approximately 30% for batteries) and export restrictions on equipment to manufacture cutting-edge LFP cells, meaning US LFP factories are using older designs.

2. **Toyota cancels next-generation EV development:** Toyota announced it will cancel development of the LFZ electric sedan under the Lexus brand, reallocating management resources to SUVs. The host frames this as consistent with Toyota's stated "multi-pathway" strategy — gas, hybrid, EV, and hydrogen — which he argues amounts to committing fully to nothing.

3. **Ferrari's new Purosangue-successor criticized by chairman and Italy's deputy PM:** Ferrari's new electric vehicle (referred to as the "luche") drew criticism from Ferrari's former chairman and Italy's deputy prime minister, sending the stock down 8%. The host notes it has a larger battery than a Cybertruck but shorter range than a Cybertruck, and appears designed to compete with Chinese EVs rather than as a traditional Ferrari performance product.

4. **Xiaomi losing $5,600 per car sold; Chinese EV gross margins declining:** Xiaomi (called "Shia" in the transcript), the phone-maker-turned-EV-manufacturer praised by Ford CEO Jim Farley, is losing $5,600 per vehicle. Gross margins for EVs in the broader Chinese market fell from 23.2% to 20.1%. The host pushes back on the narrative that China is simply dumping subsidized cars, noting that a subsidy of $10,000 per car across ~33 million annual sales would amount to over three years of a trillion dollars — a figure he calls implausible.

5. **Vinfast's US factory promise collapses:** Vinfast made promises about building a US factory, went through embassy vetting, but never completed the facility, instead building plants in Indonesia and India. The host expects efforts to claw back committed funds will fail.

6. **GM wins NASA contract to build battery for Moon-bound vehicle:** GM has been awarded a NASA contract to build a battery for a lunar vehicle. The host notes GM is not building the lunar buggy itself — that contract went to Astrolab and Lunar Outpost at $220 million each — and jokes about GM's track record with battery fires.

7. **DC converting streetlights into EV chargers using Dieselgate settlement funds:** Washington DC is using existing light poles — which have surplus electrical capacity after switching from high-wattage sodium lamps to low-wattage LEDs — to install EV charging equipment funded by Dieselgate penalty money. Companies like Shell Recharge and BP have equipment that fits inside or onto the poles. The host estimates these would deliver charging speeds roughly between Level 1 and Level 2, suitable for street parking in dense urban areas.

8. **Tesla stock snapshot (as of June 1, 2026):** Down approximately 3% on the day, down approximately 2.5% over five days, up approximately 7% for the month, down slightly over six months, down slightly year-to-date, significantly up on one-year and five-year timeframes.

## Energy

1. **Tesla patents self-cleaning camera lens with built-in eyelid wiper:** Tesla filed a patent for a self-cleaning camera lens featuring a built-in wiper mechanism described as functioning like an eyelid. The host notes most patents never reach production but calls it a more elegant solution than fluid-spray approaches used by others, or the high-speed spinning lens approach used by some competitors.

Notable quotes and data:
- "10 billion miles" — supervised Full Self-Driving cumulative miles surpassed
- "~30 million miles per day" — current Tesla FSD fleet daily mileage accumulation
- 300 ft — cliff drop survived by Model 3 in Malibu
- Model 3: lowest probability of injury of any car ever evaluated by NHTSA's New Car Assessment Program, five-star rating in every category and subcategory
- 67% → 72% — share of new EV buyers trading in a gas car, January to April 2026
- 360,000 miles on one Model 3; battery replaced at 321,000 miles for ~$5,000 (reconditioned pack); full replacement would cost $15,000–$22,000
- Model Y at 111,000 miles: only 36 kWh from AC charging, rest DC fast charging; retains 90–92% range capacity
- Waymo Zeekr robotaxi: ~$35,000 base vehicle cost → ~$70,000 after 100% import tariff; Cybercab would need to cost ~$12,000 to match
- BYD Denza Z9 GT: 10–97% charge in 12 minutes in freezing conditions; 10–70% in 5 minutes in ideal conditions
- Xiaomi losing $5,600 per EV sold; Chinese EV gross margins fell from 23.2% to 20.1%
- Astrolab and Lunar Outpost each received $220 million NASA contracts for lunar buggy
- Estonia is the third European country (after Netherlands and Lithuania) to clear self-driving for public road use
- Ford Escape expected to return as all-electric in 2029, following end of current production after model year 2026
- Toyota canceling LFZ Lexus electric sedan development
- Ferrari new EV: battery larger than Cybertruck, range shorter than Cybertruck, stock down 8%
- "It will be quite a niche thing in 10 years to actually be driving your own car" — attributed to Elon Musk
- Model Y battery health from viewer: 81% at 123,000 miles (host notes progression: 83% at 90k, 86% at 60k — implying decline with age as expected)

2026-06-01.title: Bears And Bulls Are Now Calling For a Stock Market Sell OFF And Tesla Is Ready To Run.
2026-06-01.body:
This video from "investingagainstthegrain" covers three main topics: a macro market analysis arguing against imminent crash predictions, a commentary on AI job displacement narratives from OpenAI and Anthropic CEOs, and a bullish Tesla thesis centered on Cybercab production ramp and Texas Level 4 authorization. The host's core argument is that popular bearish indicators are largely noise, momentum signals remain constructive, and Tesla is uniquely positioned to hit all-time highs driven by its robotaxi buildout.

## Market & Competition

1. **Dismissing Common Bear Indicators as Noise:** The host systematically argues that the Buffett Indicator (currently at 237%), the CAPE/Shiller ratio (currently at 42.7, second only to the dot-com bubble), and record margin debt ($1.3 trillion) are unreliable signals because they fail to account for globalized corporate profits (~40% from overseas), productivity and technology advances, and the natural scaling of nominal figures over time. He characterizes these as click-bait headlines rather than actionable indicators.

2. **The Inverted Yield Curve as the One Legitimate Signal:** The host identifies the 10-year/2-year Treasury yield inversion as the only macro indicator he takes seriously, noting it has predicted every recession since the 1950s. He cautions it is imperfect — during the Great Recession, the curve inverted at end-2006 but the market didn't peak until approximately 18 months later in late 2007. Currently, the 2-year yield sits at approximately 4% and the 10-year at approximately 4.45%, which he describes as healthy and non-inverted.

3. **BX Trender Monthly Momentum as Primary Decision Tool:** The host relies heavily on a proprietary momentum indicator called the "BX Trender" on monthly timeframes to guide his portfolio decisions. He walks through historical examples: it correctly signaled exits at S&P 4,778 in January 2022 (avoiding a drop to ~3,200–3,300), during COVID (from ~3,382), and in October 2007 (~1,600, avoiding a 60%+ drop during the Great Recession). As of the end of May 2026, the monthly BX Trender has closed green, following a light-red April (higher low vs. dark-red March), which he reads as a bullish continuation signal.

4. **S&P 500 Forward P/E and Contrarian Consumer Sentiment:** The host notes the S&P 500 forward P/E peaked around 23x in 2025 but has since compressed to approximately 20–21x due to strong earnings from companies like Micron, Nvidia, and others — suggesting the market is actually less overvalued now than a year ago. He also cites consumer sentiment at all-time lows as a contrarian bullish signal: historically, when sentiment is in the bottom 3%, the S&P has returned nearly 20%, versus only ~2.2% when sentiment is in the top 3%. The Fear & Greed Index is currently at 60 (greed), which he characterizes as normal rather than euphoric.

5. **Tom Lee's 20% Selloff Warning and the Host's Rebuttal:** The host references bull analyst Tom Lee as now calling for a 20% market selloff, and uses this as a framing device to explore whether current signals justify concern. His conclusion is that with no yield curve inversion, a green monthly BX Trender, a compressed S&P forward P/E, and low consumer sentiment (a contrarian positive), the market is in good shape heading into the second half of 2026.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Texas Level 4 Self-Certification — A Pivotal Regulatory Milestone:** The host highlights a development reported by James Stephenson on May 29, 2026 (Thursday relative to the recording date of May 31, 2026): Tesla has been authorized by the state of Texas to operate driverless vehicles commercially under a new law that took effect May 28, 2026. Tesla self-certified the software running on its robotaxi as Level 4. The host characterizes this as potentially the key regulatory hurdle Tesla had been waiting for before deploying Cybercabs commercially.

2. **Cybercabs Driving Themselves Off the Production Line:** The host references Elon Musk reposting a video of Cybercabs driving themselves off the production line to parking lots — a signal he interprets as the Cybercab being close to feature-complete and ready for operational deployment. He notes this is distinct from similar demonstrations previously done with Model Y vehicles. He also references a statement from Tesla's head of AI ("Shockwami" — likely a transcription of a name) saying Cybercabs will soon be rolling off the line and heading to work in Austin.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab Physical Deployment Signals Across Multiple Cities:** The host references Joe Tegtmeyer's videos documenting Cybercab production volume and deployment spread. He notes Cybercabs are appearing in Dallas, Houston, Pennsylvania, and that dealership lots in some cities are clearing space and positioning black-and-red Model Y vehicles labeled as "Cybercab Plus" or "Robotaxi Plus." He interprets this geographic spread and physical presence as Tesla preparing for an imminent large-scale rollout.

2. **Robotaxi Tracker Crowd-Sourced Data Cautioned Against Over-Indexing:** The host acknowledges that some observers are pointing to the robotaxi tracker showing declining numbers and using that as a bearish signal. He dismisses this, arguing that crowd-sourced data is inherently incomplete and that the physical production and deployment evidence is more telling than tracker counts.

3. **FSD Version Referenced as Impressive:** The host briefly mentions using "14.3" (a version of FSD), calling it "amazing," as additional evidence that the software side is progressing in parallel with the hardware rollout.

## Electric Vehicles

2026-06-02.title: Three Robotaxi Leaders Just Changed The Game
2026-06-02.body:
This video covers three major developments in the robotaxi race: Tesla's continued infrastructure buildout in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, Waymo's launch of its new Zeekr-based "Oho" van with sixth-generation sensor hardware, and BYD's unprecedented move to offer full damage coverage for users of its "God's Eye" Level 2 autonomous driving system in China. Host Bert is joined by Jeff Lus, a former C-suite supply chain executive from Motorola, Google, and Lenovo, who provides commentary on unit economics, manufacturing strategy, and competitive dynamics. The central thesis is that all three companies are making significant strategic moves that signal the robotaxi industry is accelerating, but with very different approaches to scale, cost structure, and liability.

## Robotaxi

1. **Tesla's Fourth Known Fleet Support Facility Discovered:** A 51,000-square-foot service and delivery center is under construction in Grand Prairie, Texas — located between Dallas and Fort Worth, near Interstate 20. City documents confirm the facility's approved use includes charging, cleaning, repair, and maintenance of Tesla-owned autonomous vehicles, making it a potential robotaxi fleet support hub. This is now the fourth such facility discovered across the country: three in Texas (including a previously found 36,000-square-foot facility also in the Dallas area and one in Austin) and one in Las Vegas. Jeff Lus notes the "combo" design of combining service/delivery with fleet support maximizes both asset and labor utilization, and he interprets the infrastructure buildout as Tesla telegraphing a major, high-scale Cybercab rollout rather than a modest ride-share operation.

2. **World Cup Cybercab Launch Theory:** The video discusses a theory attributed to Jo Bhakdi that Tesla will time a Cybercab rollout in Dallas to coincide with the FIFA World Cup, which is expected to have games at Cowboys Stadium in Arlington, Texas. Bert expresses skepticism, noting the facility will not be complete in time and that FSD still requires more months of real-world data before a full unsupervised commercial deployment. Jeff Lus suggests that Cybercab hardware is likely ready given that Tesla has already committed to start of production, but the key remaining question is a software release that resolves edge cases sufficient for a large-scale public launch.

3. **Waymo Launches "Oho" Van for Public Rides:** Waymo has begun offering public rides in its new vehicle called the "Oho," a van built by Chinese automaker Zeekr that is imported to the US and retrofitted with Waymo's sixth-generation hardware at its Arizona facility. The sixth-gen hardware includes 13 cameras, four lidars, and six radars — representing 42% fewer sensors than the previous generation — but with upgraded 17-megapixel cameras that Waymo says improve performance despite the reduced sensor count. The hardware also integrates heaters, wipers, and sprayers directly into sensor pods for all-weather operation. Selected riders in San Francisco, Phoenix, and Los Angeles currently have access, with planned expansion to Denver, Las Vegas, and San Diego. Waymo also plans to add Hyundai Ioniq 5 robotaxis to its fleet soon.

4. **Waymo Oho Vehicle Cost and Unit Economics Questions:** Industry analyst "Barely AI" projects the Oho van costs $75,000–$100,000 per vehicle even after tariffs, compared to approximately $200,000 per vehicle for the current Jaguar I-Pace fleet. Jeff Lus cautions that this quoted price likely reflects a best-case scenario dependent on Zeekr achieving sufficient production volumes — if minimum volume commitments are not met, the actual all-in landed cost (including import, tariffs, and retrofitting in Arizona) could be materially higher. He notes that purpose-built low-volume platforms carry significant fixed cost risk because tooling and capex must be divided across a small unit base, unlike Tesla's Cybercab which is being planned for hundreds of thousands or potentially millions of units per year.

5. **Waymo's Ongoing Operational and Financial Challenges:** Waymo recently issued a voluntary software recall covering nearly 3,800 fifth- and sixth-generation robotaxis after some vehicles drove into standing water or flooded roads — the fix was a software update. Waymo also temporarily paused freeway rides after identifying issues around construction zones; the company says it encounters approximately 10,000 construction zones daily. On the financial side, the video references recent data showing Waymo is losing $5–6 billion and estimated to be losing approximately $100 per ride. Jeff Lus expresses frustration that financial media has not more aggressively scrutinized the cost-per-mile economics of robotaxi operators after six years of service.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Progress and Path to Unsupervised Deployment:** Bert describes personal testing of what he refers to as a newer FSD version, noting that the system has removed the driver monitoring "nag" and allows increasingly long periods without driver intervention — though it is still officially labeled supervised FSD. The discussion frames Tesla's path to unsupervised FSD as closely tied to the geofenced areas already used for robotaxi operations: if Tesla is already comfortable running driverless robotaxis in Austin, Dallas, and Houston within specific geofences, extending unsupervised personal FSD to those same areas is a logical next step.

2. **Tesla Insurance as an "Infinite Money Glitch":** Jeff Lus argues that when Tesla eventually offers insurance coverage for unsupervised FSD, it will function as an "infinite money glitch" — because Tesla's data already demonstrates the system is not at fault in accidents, the insurance product will rarely if ever need to pay out. He draws an analogy to fully waterproofed smartphones where manufacturers sell water damage plans despite knowing the product won't fail. Lus notes Tesla already sells an insurance product in multiple regions and has reportedly taken out a license or entity in China to offer insurance there, giving it the actuarial data foundation to underwrite such a product confidently.

## Market & Competition

1. **BYD Offers Industry-First Full Damage Coverage for L2 System:** BYD announced it will provide one free full year of 100% damage coverage — including vehicle repairs, third-party property damage, and personal injury liabilities with no payout cap — for owners using its "God's Eye" Level 2 urban navigation system in China, as long as the system is used properly and in compliance with traffic regulations. This is described as the first time any automaker has ever provided damage reimbursement for an advanced driving system. BYD had previously offered coverage for its intelligent parking system, and is now extending it to full driving assistance.

2. **BYD's God's Eye Problems and Regulatory Crackdown in China:** The move comes amid serious user complaints about BYD's God's Eye system, including reports of unintended acceleration, erratic steering, and navigation failures, with BYD sales reportedly dropping 36%. More broadly, China has seen a wave of AV-related incidents: hundreds of BYD vehicles automatically stopped in a manner compared to Waymo's San Francisco power outage incidents; a fatal crash involving a Xiaomi SU7 using assisted driving killed three people after striking a highway structure and catching fire. Chinese regulators responded by restricting marketing terms like "autonomous driving" and "smart driving," drafting stricter Level 2 safety rules, and scrutinizing exaggerated claims across BYD, Tesla, Xiaomi, Xpeng, NIO, and others. Tesla can no longer use the "Full Self-Driving" label in China as a result.

3. **China's AV Competitive Landscape:** The video asserts that Tesla is the leader in China for autonomous driving capability, with Xpeng believed to be second. Huawei is also noted as a significant player — many robotaxis in China use Huawei technology — but Huawei itself has faced major incidents. BYD's scale (millions of vehicles sold) gives it a potential data advantage, but the video argues BYD currently lacks neural net and vision-only capability, still relying heavily on LiDAR, and is therefore behind Tesla by roughly one to two years. Xpeng is noted as having recently shifted to vision-only and eliminating LiDAR, offering its system for free to build the data volume needed to catch edge cases — described as a move that directly follows Tesla's approach.

4. **Competitive Pressure on Tesla's FSD Pricing and Insurance:** The discussion raises whether Tesla may face competitive pressure to reduce FSD subscription pricing if Xpeng is offering its system for free, and whether Tesla will need to introduce insurance coverage if BYD is offering it at no cost. Jeff Lus suggests Tesla will monitor the competitive dynamics and may need to respond, but notes that Tesla's brand strength and customer loyalty at its price tier provide a buffer against being forced into immediate price matching.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla's Grand Prairie, Texas facility: 51,000 sq ft, approved for charging, cleaning, repair, and maintenance of Tesla-owned autonomous vehicles
- Previously discovered Tesla fleet facilities: 36,000 sq ft in Dallas area, one in Austin, one in Las Vegas — now four total known
- Waymo's current fleet: approximately 3,700 vehicles (per recent filing cited in video)
- Waymo Oho projected vehicle cost: $75,000–$100,000 per vehicle after tariffs (per Barely AI estimate cited)
- Waymo Jaguar I-Pace fleet cost: approximately $200,000 per vehicle
- Waymo sixth-gen hardware: 13 cameras, 4 lidars, 6 radars — 42% fewer sensors than prior generation; upgraded to 17-megapixel cameras
- Waymo Oho van target: 100 vehicles currently operating, 1,000 on the road by end of 2025 (resolved: year-end 2026 per publish date context — though the transcript says "year end" without specifying)
- Waymo voluntary software recall: ~3,800 fifth- and sixth-gen robotaxis for flood/standing water navigation issue
- Waymo estimated losses: $5–6 billion total; approximately $100 loss per ride
- Waymo encounters ~10,000 construction zones daily
- BYD God's Eye insurance: 1 free year, 100% damage coverage, no payout cap, covers vehicle repairs, third-party property damage, and personal injury
- BYD sales reportedly dropped 36% amid God's Eye complaints
- Global annual traffic fatalities: approximately 1.19 million per year (cited in video from BYD God's Eye 5.0 presentation)
- BYD launched God's Eye 5.0 with a self-developed "Zhuanji A3" chip
- Jeff Lus: "Tesla's telegraphing. This stuff is just all out there in the public domain. You just have to be able to put two and two together."
- Jeff Lus on Cybercab hardware: "Tesla would not have gone to start of production unless reliability and convenience hardware issues have been worked out."
- Jeff Lus on Tesla insurance: "When you've engineered and solved that problem, you've created the infinite money glitch where people still will need to carry some policy... but the policy will never have to yield."

2026-06-02.title: Every AI Giant Just Moved, Tesla's in All Four
2026-06-02.body:
This video from "brighterwithherbert" features host Herbert and guest Jo Bhakdi — an economist, investor, and tech entrepreneur with a presence at pionerlands.org — reviewing a wave of major AI industry announcements that all broke within a single 24-hour period. The core thesis is that the AI race has expanded beyond chatbots into compute infrastructure, AI agents, and humanoid robots, and that Tesla is uniquely positioned at the intersection of all four battlegrounds. The conversation weaves between the SpaceX AI/Anthropic compute deal, Anthropic's IPO filing, Google's $80 billion equity raise, Nvidia's new PC chip, and OpenAI's robotics ambitions, consistently returning to what each development means for Tesla's competitive position.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX AI / Anthropic Compute Deal and Its Limits:** Arc Invest analyst Brett Winton calculated, based on a new S-1 amendment, that Anthropic is paying SpaceX AI $24 billion in revenue per gigawatt of compute capacity, while SpaceX spent $29 billion per gigawatt to build it — effectively recovering construction costs plus profit. He projected $50 billion in cumulative pre-tax cash flow over five years if the contract holds. Elon Musk quickly pushed back, clarifying the deal is intentionally short-term at SpaceX's request, because SpaceX AI may eventually need that compute for its own AI (Macrohard/Grok). The termination clause is reportedly 180 days with auto-renewal. Jo Bhakdi framed this not as a guaranteed revenue stream but as proof-of-concept that renting AI compute is a viable and enormous business model, comparing SpaceX AI's strategic position to Nvidia's.

2. **Anthropic's Near-Trillion-Dollar IPO Filing:** Anthropic officially filed a confidential draft S-1 registration statement with the SEC for a proposed IPO, with share count and price not yet set. Simultaneously, the company raised $65 billion in a Series H funding round led by Altimeter Capital, Dragoneer, Green Oaks, and Sequoia, at a reported valuation of $965 billion — making it nearly a trillion-dollar private company on the eve of going public. Herbert noted that $5 billion of the raise is reportedly flowing to SpaceX. Jo Bhakdi observed that Anthropic's annualized recurring revenue had reportedly hit approximately $47 billion, reflecting explosive adoption, but also flagged fragility — a single harness or model update (the recent Opus 4 rollout) degraded Claude's design quality dramatically, illustrating how vulnerable enterprises relying on these systems are.

3. **Google / Alphabet's $80 Billion Equity Raise:** Alphabet announced plans to raise $80 billion by selling new shares — comprising a $30 billion underwritten public offering, a $40 billion at-the-market program, and a $10 billion investment from Berkshire Hathaway — earmarked for AI compute and infrastructure buildout. Jo Bhakdi noted this is small relative to Google's scale: the company reported $110 billion in Q1 revenue (up 22% year-over-year), a $46 billion Google Cloud backlog, and a capex plan of $180–$190 billion. He used Warren Buffett's participation as a rebuttal to "AI bubble" arguments, calling it validation from the world's most prominent value investor.

4. **Nvidia's RTX Spark Superchip and PC Market Expansion:** At Computex, Jensen Huang unveiled the RTX Spark Superchip — a new CPU for PCs featuring approximately 20–24 CPU cores and roughly 60 GPU cores, built on Blackwell architecture with high-speed NVLink integration, manufactured with TSMC and MediaTek. The chip will debut in Dell and Lenovo laptops and desktops, with Microsoft as the key software partner for an agent-first Windows environment. Jo Bhakdi predicted this will roughly double average laptop prices (from ~$1,000 to ~$2,000–$2,500), effectively doubling the entire PC TAM, with most of the price differential accruing to Nvidia. He also predicted Apple will be forced to partner with Nvidia because it cannot replicate this chip internally. Nvidia shares rose approximately 6% on the announcement.

5. **OpenAI Entering Robotics:** OpenAI publicly signaled a renewed push into humanoid robotics, posting job listings for a robotics division. Herbert and Jo Bhakdi discussed the backstory of OpenAI's prior investment in Figure and the subsequent breakup — with Figure's CEO reportedly ending the relationship, likely because Figure did not want OpenAI gaining proprietary training data to build a competing robotics platform. Both hosts were skeptical of OpenAI's ability to execute given zero factory experience and no manufacturing infrastructure. Jo Bhakdi predicted that OpenAI will ultimately have to acquire an existing humanoid robotics company, just as he predicted Waymo will need to acquire a large automaker.

6. **Competitive Landscape for Humanoid Robots:** Jo Bhakdi identified Tesla's Optimus as the leader in humanoid robotics, but named Hyundai/Boston Dynamics as a credible second competitor — pointing to Hyundai's acquisition of Boston Dynamics, its large industrial deployment capability, and South Korea's broader semiconductor and manufacturing strengths (Samsung RAM, etc.). He dismissed Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI as serious near-term robotics threats due to their software-first DNA and lack of manufacturing expertise. He expressed general skepticism about "software people" successfully building physical robots at scale.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Tesla's Vertically Integrated Advantage Across Optimus, Robotaxi, and Compute:** Jo Bhakdi argued that Tesla — like Broadcom in its domain — wins not by being a general-purpose chip or AI company but through deep vertical integration across Optimus, robotaxi, and inference compute (via Terafab). He drew a distinction between Nvidia's strength in general-purpose AI factories, training, and now general-purpose laptops versus Tesla's purpose-built inference stack. He argued Tesla cannot and should not try to compete with Nvidia on Nvidia's home turf (general-purpose compute), but is essentially unbeatable within its own vertically integrated stack.

## Autonomous Driving / Robotaxi

1. **Waymo's Path May Require an OEM Acquisition:** In the context of OpenAI's robotics ambitions and the broader "software companies buying hardware assets" theme, Jo Bhakdi predicted that Waymo will likely acquire a large automaker — which he suggested will be "very cheap next year" — as the only practical path to scaling a robotaxi platform without paying manufacturer margins. Herbert agreed this announcement is coming and that the show will cover it when it happens.

---

**Notable quotes and data:**

- Brett Winton (Arc Invest): SpaceX AI receives $24B in revenue per gigawatt of compute; spent $29B/GW to build it; projected $50B in 5-year cumulative pre-tax cash flow from Anthropic deal alone.
- Anthropic Series H: $65 billion raised; valuation ~$965 billion; led by Altimeter Capital, Dragoneer, Green Oaks, Sequoia.
- Anthropic ARR: reportedly approximately $47 billion (recently reported figure, per transcript).
- Google Q1 revenue: $110 billion, +22% YoY; Google Cloud backlog: $46 billion; capex plan: $180–$190 billion.
- Google equity raise: $80 billion total ($30B underwritten, $40B ATM, $10B Berkshire Hathaway).
- Nvidia RTX Spark Superchip: ~20–24 CPU cores, ~60 GPU cores, Blackwell architecture, TSMC/MediaTek manufacturing, debuts in Dell and Lenovo.
- Nvidia share price reaction: +~6% on announcement.
- Jo Bhakdi: "You can expect… instead of average laptop price being 900 bucks or whatever it is right now, it's going to be 2,000."
- Jo Bhakdi on Optimus: "I think it's going to be extremely hard to compete with Optimus."
- Jo Bhakdi on Hyundai: "Probably the second most formidable robotics player after Tesla in my opinion."
- Jo Bhakdi on OpenAI robotics: "Building these robots is extremely non-trivial… Zero factories right now. No factory experience at all."
- SpaceX AI IPO date referenced by Herbert: June 12th (2026).

2026-06-02.title: Tesla patents camera wiper for self-driving — resulting in more doubts for FSD owners
2026-06-02.body:
Tesla has been granted a patent (US 12,636,684 B1, May 26) for a miniature "Lens Cleaning System" that integrates a fluid dispenser and curved mechanical wiper directly into the camera assembly — designed to keep cameras clear for autonomous driving without relying on a fixed cleaning schedule.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Patent addresses a persistent FSD failure mode:** The system automatically monitors image quality from the camera feed itself and activates a cleaning sequence — spray plus wipe — only when degradation is detected. Tesla removed radar and ultrasonic sensors years ago, making a blocked camera effectively a blind spot for its vision-only FSD system. Tesla acknowledged the dirty-camera problem over a year ago, and with FSD v14 introduced targeted cleaning for front cameras on the new Model Y, but side and rear cameras remain unaddressed on consumer vehicles.

## Robotaxi
2. **Austin Robotaxi fleet already has camera washers; consumer vehicles do not:** Tesla's Austin Robotaxi fleet already uses external camera washer jets on fender repeater and B-pillar cameras — the repeater cameras have been redesigned with the turn signal light removed in favor of a washer nozzle. No production Model Y sold to consumers includes this hardware, and it is not retrofittable. The article notes this contradicts Tesla's repeated claim that its Robotaxi service uses "the same Model Y vehicles it sells to consumers." The new patent describes a potentially more integrated solution and may be critical for the Cybercab, which has begun production and must operate fully without human intervention.

## Editorial Stance
Electrek's Lambert argues that if camera cleaning is critical enough to deploy exclusively on Robotaxis, it is equally critical for any vehicle running FSD — calling the hardware gap "not a good look" and pressing Tesla to bring the technology to consumer vehicles rather than keeping it fleet-only.

Notable quotes and data:
- Patent number: US 12,636,684 B1, granted May 26
- Patent title: "Lens Cleaning System"
- Cleaning fluids supported: water, alcohol-based solutions, washer fluid, or lubricants
- FSD v14 introduced targeted front-camera cleaning on the new Model Y; side and rear cameras remain unaddressed on consumer vehicles
- Austin Robotaxi fleet has camera washers on fender repeater and B-pillar cameras; no consumer Model Y has equivalent hardware
- Cybercab "has started production" per the article
- "Tesla has made a significant point of saying its 'Robotaxi' service uses the same Model Y vehicles it sells to consumers"

2026-06-02.title: Tesla Semi tackles the Grapevine with a loaded trailer, leaves fleet operator ‘amazed’
2026-06-02.body:
Covenant Logistics, one of the largest US trucking companies (2,600+ tractors, $1.16B in 2025 revenue), completed a two-week Tesla Semi evaluation in California, including a loaded run over the Grapevine pass on I-5. The company's VP of Sustainability and Innovation reported the driver "was amazed at the performance of the Tesla Semi and felt a level of confidence that was hard to match in a diesel truck."

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Grapevine evaluation:** Covenant tested the 500-mile long-range Tesla Semi with a major customer in California. The evaluation included a loaded run over Tejon Pass (4,160 ft elevation, 6% grade for 5 miles), one of the most demanding freight corridors in the US. McLelland highlighted regenerative braking as a structural advantage on the steep southbound descent — recovering energy rather than risking brake fade. A full evaluation summary is described as "coming soon."

2. **Growing pattern of fleet evaluations:** Covenant joins a list of operators conducting structured Tesla Semi trials since Tesla began volume production at its Nevada Gigafactory on April 29. ArcBest logged 4,494 miles over three weeks, averaging 1.55 kWh/mile. DHL Supply Chain completed a 3,000-mile trial averaging 1.72 kWh/mile at full load and has since taken delivery of its first Semi. CEVA Logistics reported avoiding 4.38 metric tons of CO₂ on a West Coast trial. MDB Transportation and AiLO Logistics launched three-week port drayage pilots in late April. Tesla has also landed a 60-truck order from port drayage fleets.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert argues that driver preference for the Tesla Semi on demanding routes like the Grapevine removes a key friction point in fleet adoption, and that with positive results now spanning long-haul, regional, and port drayage operators, the bottleneck may be shifting from product validation to whether Tesla can scale production fast enough.

**Notable quotes and data:**
- Driver "was amazed at the performance of the Tesla Semi and felt a level of confidence that was hard to match in a diesel truck." — Matt McLelland, Covenant VP of Sustainability and Innovation
