2026-06-02.title: Tesla’s 4680 Secret Is Finally Starting To Make Sense
2026-06-02.body:
This video is a deep-dive conversation between FutureAzA host Brian and Jordan from The Limiting Factor, focused on Tesla's 4680 battery cell — where they're made, whether production targets are achievable, energy density competitiveness, and how supply chains for cells and packs are evolving. The discussion covers the role of Kato Road, Giga Texas, Giga Berlin, and Giga Nevada in Tesla's battery strategy, and how 4680s fit into the broader product roadmap including the Cybercab, Semi, and Optimus. A secondary theme is the "visibility problem" that causes outside observers to underestimate both Tesla's battery progress and competitors like Panasonic.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **4680 Energy Density Is Globally Competitive, Not Best-in-Class:** Jordan clarifies that Tesla's current 4680 cell achieves approximately 270 watt-hours per kilogram, placing it between the last generation of Panasonic and LG Chem cells (250–270 Wh/kg) and the newest generation of those cells (280–290+ Wh/kg). At the pack level, the new Model Y in Germany equipped with 4680s delivers roughly 5% less range than vehicles using the newest competing packs, though Jordan frames this as a value-for-money trade-off since the 4680-equipped vehicle is cheaper and buyers have other options.

2. **Giga Texas 4680 Line Status:** Joe Tegtmeyer's recent observation of the Giga Texas facility suggested roughly four lines visible but only approximately one and a half actually running. Notably, battery line equipment that had previously been stored outside has since moved indoors, leading Brian and Jordan to conclude that additional lines are being installed in the northwest corner of Giga Texas. Jordan assesses that Giga Texas should have sufficient space and equipment to meet production needs for that facility and nearby buildings, including a new Optimus facility reportedly under construction on the north campus.

3. **Giga Berlin Cells Not Yet Produced Locally:** The battery facility at Giga Berlin is advancing but does not appear to be producing cells yet. Current production involves importing cells and assembling modules in Germany. Tesla is reportedly targeting cell production at Giga Berlin beginning next year (2027). Jordan notes this timeline illustrates the complexity of manufacturing 4680s at precision scale — a challenge that has also stymied other major battery manufacturers who announced 4680 programs but have not brought competing cells to market.

4. **Kato Road Remains an Advanced Engineering Testbed:** Tesla's original Kato Road pilot line has been converted into a testing and advanced engineering facility. Jordan confirms this is consistent with what Tesla has officially communicated — it serves as a proving ground for cell advancements before they are transferred to mass production lines in Austin and eventually Germany.

5. **2170 Cells Likely to Continue for Existing Models:** Jordan's working assumption is that 2170 cells will continue supplying current passenger vehicle platforms (Model Y, etc.), as re-engineering packs and supply chains for those vehicles would be costly and unnecessary. A source Jordan cited on X indicated Tesla plans to upgrade the 2170 cell within approximately 18 months to improve charging speed and achieve similar or slightly better energy density.

6. **Panasonic Opens New 2170 Facility in Kansas City:** Panasonic has brought online a new 2170 cell facility in Kansas City. Brian and Jordan interpret this as capacity primarily destined for Tesla, reinforcing the thesis that 2170s will continue serving passenger EVs while 4680s are directed toward the Semi, Cybercab, and Optimus.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab Battery Pack Prototyping at Nevada:** During a tour of Giga Nevada, a tour guide explained the facility has three types of pack assembly lines — a high-speed automated line, a mid-speed line used as backup when the fast line goes down, and a fully manual line used for prototyping. As an example of the manual line's purpose, the guide specifically cited being able to produce 23 Cybercab battery packs on demand — indicating small-batch, custom pack work for programs still in development.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus Building Under Construction at Giga Texas North Campus:** A dedicated Optimus facility is reportedly being constructed on the north campus of Giga Texas. Jordan confirmed this when discussing whether Giga Texas's 4680 production capacity would be sufficient to supply both vehicle and robot needs at and near the site.

2. **Visibility Problem Distorts Optimus Competitive Comparisons:** Brian draws a parallel between public perception of Optimus versus competing humanoid robots, and the earlier perception gap around Dojo versus established chip designers. An IBM senior chip engineer Brian interviewed at CES noted that Tesla's practice is to show things 5–7 years ahead of current competitor roadmaps, while most chip and hardware companies do not publicize future work. The same dynamic applies to Optimus: absence of recent public demos does not mean the program is stagnant.

## Energy

1. **Tesla Likely Still Importing Most Megapack Cells:** Jordan states that to his knowledge, Tesla is still importing the majority of battery cells used in Megapack. He contrasts this with the vehicle cell situation, where he believes domestic supply is adequate. He notes that many EV cell production lines from manufacturers that have abandoned EV programs are being repurposed for energy storage cells, reflecting stronger demand in that segment.

2. **Megapack Factory Uses LFP Chemistry:** Brian recounts touring the Megapack factory and confirms through direct observation that the packs use LFP (lithium iron phosphate) chemistry. He notes Tesla has only approximately 10 gigawatt-hours of LFP capacity, while one supplier (unnamed in transcript) produces 30–40 gigawatt hours per year — indicating Tesla is dependent on external LFP supply and that 10 GWh is insufficient to meet Megapack demand internally.

3. **Battery Constraint Is at Pack Level, Not Cell Level:** At recent earnings calls, Tesla has cited battery constraints. Jordan analyzed this and determined the bottleneck is not cells (of which there is adequate supply) but battery packs. Tesla confirmed this in a follow-up on a recent earnings call. Jordan attributes the pack constraint to Tesla transitioning previously outsourced pack production in-house to reduce costs, and to ongoing upgrades of older, less efficient pack assembly lines at Giga Nevada — a process analogous to the production dip seen during the Model Y to Model Y Juniper transition in 2025.

4. **LFP and High-Nickel Cathode Manufacturing Can Share Equipment But Not Lines:** Jordan explains that LFP and NMC cells differ primarily in cathode chemistry, and that Tesla's cathode manufacturing equipment in Austin is technically capable of producing either. However, he expects Tesla will run completely separate dedicated lines for each chemistry rather than swapping between them, for the same efficiency reasons that separate gigacasting machines are used for front and rear castings.

## Financials

1. **IRA Tax Credits: $35/kWh for Cell Manufacturing:** Jordan confirms that by manufacturing 4680 cells domestically, Tesla qualifies for a $35 per kilowatt-hour production tax credit. An additional $10 per kilowatt-hour credit is available for domestic battery pack manufacturing. Brian calculates that the $10 pack credit equates to approximately $700 per vehicle, suggesting that if Tesla ships cells to Germany and packages them there, they forgo that $700 per-car benefit — implying there must be at least equivalent savings in the current arrangement to justify it.

Notable quotes and data:
- 4680 cell energy density: ~270 Wh/kg; last-gen Panasonic/LG: 250–270 Wh/kg; newest Panasonic/LG: 280–290+ Wh/kg
- New Model Y (Germany, 4680): ~5% less range than vehicles with the newest competing packs
- Tesla Semi requires approximately 11 cars' worth of batteries per unit; 50,000 Semis would require the equivalent of ~600,000 cars' worth of batteries
- IRA cell manufacturing credit: $35/kWh; pack manufacturing credit: an additional $10/kWh (~$700/vehicle)
- Tesla's internal LFP capacity: ~10 GWh; one external LFP supplier produces ~30–40 GWh/year
- Giga Texas: ~4 battery lines visible, ~1.5 operational per Joe Tegtmeyer's recent observation
- Giga Berlin: modules assembled locally, cells still imported; local cell production targeting 2027
- 2170 cell upgrade reportedly expected within ~18 months
- Jordan: "In terms of vehicle batteries, I think we have plenty… in terms of energy storage, that's a different story."
- Brian (on Tesla's weight/battery trade-off philosophy): "The question is if we do this, how much less battery do we need? How much more battery can we add for the same curb weight?"

2026-06-02.title: Tesla's Biggest Businesses Still Aren't Priced In
2026-06-02.body:
FutureAzA host Brian and guest Randy Kirk evaluate three financial media narratives about Tesla's investment thesis, pushing back on legacy automaker recommendations as alternatives to Tesla and defending the long-term bull case. The video's core argument is that mainstream financial journalists are missing Tesla's biggest growth stories — particularly energy storage and Optimus — and that critics dismissing Tesla's valuation fail to account for the scale of these businesses. The hosts also touch on near-term energy deployment dynamics and speculate about Cortex compute capacity being made available for rent.

## Market & Competition
1. **Legacy Automakers Pitched as Tesla Alternatives:** A 24/7 Wall Street article recommends General Motors, Ford, and Stellantis as "value-driven automotive stalwarts" for retirees instead of Tesla, citing Tesla's trailing price-to-earnings ratio of 373x as unsustainable. Brian and Randy reject the framing, arguing that while GM and Ford are generating near-term cash flow and buybacks, their dependence on internal combustion engines makes them poor long-term bets, as most of the world is expected to restrict or ban ICE vehicles within 5 to 10 years.

2. **Ford and GM Short-Term Metrics vs. Long-Term Risk:** Ford is noted to have produced 11.4% margins and 30% year-over-year growth in software subscriptions, while GM is buying back stock and raising guidance. Randy gives GM's Mary Barra partial credit for delivering shareholder value recently but calls both companies "dead men walking" when evaluated against a forward-looking lens. Randy also highlights Ford's chronic recall problem — described as roughly 12 recalls for every 5 at Tesla — as a fundamental operational failure.

3. **Stellantis Called the Weakest of the Group:** Stellantis is described as trading at $7.35, down 32% year-to-date, with a price-to-book ratio of 0.32. Randy calls it potentially the worst major automotive company in the world right now. Brian criticizes Stellantis's EV strategy in the US — launching large vehicles like the Charger EV and Wagoneer S when neither product resonated with buyers — and notes the Charger EV has been discontinued. The hosts acknowledge Stellantis has more compelling EV offerings in Europe but says that hasn't translated to the US market.

4. **Rivian and Lucid as Cautionary Tales:** Randy briefly notes he would want to see at least two profitable quarters before considering Rivian. Brian references a video he made roughly four years ago (circa mid-2022) warning that Lucid insiders were deeply concerned about the company's survival — a prediction that he argues was vindicated, noting that an investor who bought on the day that video published would be down 97%, with the company only surviving due to an unforeseen injection of billions from the Saudi PIF.

5. **Wall Street Bets Sentiment on Tesla:** The article notes Reddit's Wall Street Bets community has posted sentiment scores as high as 88 (very bullish) on Tesla, driven by robotaxi, Optimus, and China deal chatter. Randy interprets this positively, arguing younger retail investors who are bullish on robotaxi "get it" in a way that traditional financial media does not.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus TAM Too Large for Open AI Competition to Matter:** The video addresses a claim that Tesla stock dropped over 4% on a Monday due to a partnership between Unitree and Figure, framed as new competition from Open AI. Randy calls this "the most ridiculous reason" and argues institutional investors aren't even pricing Optimus into Tesla's valuation yet. He contends the total addressable market for functional humanoid robots is so large that even if Open AI enters the space, it will be irrelevant — Tesla will be the largest producer by a significant margin and likely producing the best product.

2. **Tesla's Optimus Production Capacity Trajectory:** Brian notes Tesla is already building capacity to produce 1 million Optimus units, with a longer-term target of 10 million, and emphasizes that Tesla's ability to construct factories quickly gives it a structural advantage over any new entrant trying to scale humanoid robot manufacturing.

## Energy
1. **Megapack Deployment Timing and Revenue Recognition Complexity:** Randy explains that Megapack revenue is recognized not when units leave the factory or arrive at a site, but when they are electrified and paid in full (or substantially completed to the point where only permitting remains). He calls the Q1 2026 energy deployment figure of 8.8 GWh a "low lump" and expects Q2 2026 to see a significant rebound — with Grok projecting a minimum of 16–17 GWh and a potential range of 21–23 GWh or higher if deferred deployments from prior quarters are counted.

2. **Cortex Compute Capacity May Be Available for Rent:** Randy raises what he describes as underreported news: Tesla's Cortex facility — designed for real-world AI training rather than standard LLM workloads — likely has surplus capacity that may be offered for rent. He contrasts this with Colossus, which was mentioned in an S1 filing update on the day of recording and is more suited to typical LLM use cases. Randy suggests this could become a meaningful revenue stream for Tesla, drawing an analogy to Amazon Web Services' success in renting out cloud and AI compute.

## Financials
1. **Tesla's Historical Stock Return and Current Valuation:** The article cited notes Tesla shares have risen 22,250% over 15 years, meaning a $4,500 investment in May 2011 would be worth $1 million today. Tesla's current market cap is stated at $1.4 trillion, with a trailing P/E of 373x. Brian and Randy push back on the implied conclusion that the stock can't repeat strong performance, with Randy suggesting most Tesla bulls expect an 8–10x return over the next 10 years, meaning a $100,000 investment today could reach $1 million.

2. **Q1 2026 Automotive Revenue and Inventory:** The article notes Tesla posted a 16% year-over-year gain in automotive revenue in Q1 but that revenue was 19% below the same period in 2023. Deliveries were up 6%. Inventory rose from what Brian characterizes as "historic lows" — which he describes as unsustainable — to a higher but still industry-low level measured in days of supply. Brian frames the inventory build as strategically sensible given oil price volatility.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla trailing P/E cited at 373x as of approximately May 19th close of $404
- Tesla market cap: $1.4 trillion
- Tesla stock up 22,250% over 15 years; $4,500 in May 2011 → $1 million today
- Q1 2026 energy deployments: 8.8 GWh (described as a "low lump"); current Megapack capacity: 17 GWh
- Grok's Q2 2026 energy deployment projection: minimum 16–17 GWh, potentially 21–23 GWh or higher
- Ford margins: 11.4%; software subscription growth: 30% YoY
- Stellantis stock: $7.35, down 32% year-to-date, price-to-book of 0.32
- "The TAM is so large that whether Open AI gets in the business or not is going to be irrelevant to Tesla." — Randy Kirk
- "If you invested on the day I published that [Lucid] video, you would be down 97%." — Brian
- Tesla building capacity for 1 million Optimus units with a longer-term target of 10 million
- Cortex described as offering "real world training, which nobody has anything like it"

2026-06-02.title: RANKING TRADING STRATEGIES
2026-06-02.body:
This video is a tier-list ranking of common options trading strategies, presented in a rapid-fire format where the host rates each strategy from S-tier down to C-tier. The content is general personal finance and options trading education with no specific connection to Tesla, autonomous driving, robotaxi deployment, or any other Tesla Thesis topics. The host shares personal preferences and risk assessments for each strategy based on their own trading experience.

## Market & Competition

1. **Iron Condor Rated C-Tier:** The host places the iron condor in C-tier, acknowledging that on paper it appears to be a sound, defined-risk strategy — particularly appealing to newer traders. However, the host criticizes it for taking too long to play out, offering lower probabilities of profit, and being difficult to manage in practice.

2. **Covered Calls Rated S-Tier:** The host gives covered calls the highest rating (S-tier), describing them as essentially a "profit engine." Key reasons cited include defined risk, predictable outcomes, the ability to sell them consistently and repeatedly, and their utility as a disciplined mechanism for selling at high prices when a trader might otherwise hesitate due to FOMO. The only downside flagged is the risk of a trader voluntarily taking a loss due to FOMO.

3. **Cash Secured Puts Rated S-Tier:** Cash secured puts also receive S-tier, described by the host as a "golden way to acquire stock" and a personal "bread and butter" strategy. The host notes they are a defined-risk trade, allow for some aggressiveness depending on cash position, and effectively allow the trader to get paid while waiting to buy stock at a desired price.

4. **Naked Puts and Calls Rated A-Tier:** The host places naked puts and calls in A-tier — one step below S-tier — also describing them as a bread and butter strategy. The rationale for not reaching S-tier is the undefined risk nature of these trades, which introduces perceived risk not present in cash secured puts or covered calls, despite their high probability of profit.

Notable quotes and data:
- "Covered calls are S-tier. Unless you choose to take a loss on them because you have FOMO, they're essentially a profit engine."
- "Cash secured puts are also S-tier. They're a golden way to acquire stock... you get paid to buy the stock."
- "Naked calls and naked puts, I put those in A-tier... they do have that risk that a cash secured or covered call don't have."
- Iron condor: C-tier — "takes too long for the trade to work out," "too difficult to manage"

2026-06-02.title: Bulls vs Bears is The Market About to Correct
2026-06-02.body:
This video from the "investingagainstthegrain" channel addresses the wave of bearish market commentary expected as the stock market sits at all-time highs entering June 2026. The host argues that most widely-cited valuation indicators are noise rather than signal, and walks viewers through a momentum-based framework — the BX Trender — as a more actionable tool for timing market exposure. The core thesis is that investors should focus on monthly momentum indicators and the yield curve rather than headline-grabbing metrics like the Buffett Indicator or CAPE ratio.

## Market & Competition

1. **Buffett Indicator dismissed as noise:** The host explains that the Buffett Indicator — which compares total U.S. stock market capitalization to U.S. GDP — is currently sitting at 237%, an all-time high. However, he argues it is fundamentally flawed because it only captures domestic GDP while roughly 40% of corporate profits now come from overseas. He dismisses it as a metric that generates clicks primarily because of Warren Buffett's name, not because of genuine predictive value.

2. **CAPE Ratio also characterized as unreliable:** The Cyclically Adjusted Price-to-Earnings (CAPE, or Shiller) ratio is currently at 42.7 — second only to the dot-com bubble peak. The host acknowledges this sounds alarming but argues the metric fails to account for productivity gains driven by AI, software, and SaaS, and is distorted by COVID-era economic anomalies from 2022. Like the Buffett Indicator, it only reflects the U.S. market and ignores global context.

3. **Margin debt and credit metrics labeled cherry-picked:** Margin debt is currently at a historic $1.3 trillion, and the host notes that credit card debt and delinquency rates are also at record highs. He argues these figures are misleading in isolation because wealth, money market balances, home values, and virtually every financial aggregate are also at all-time highs — a natural consequence of a larger, inflation-affected economy. He characterizes the selective use of these figures as fearmongering.

4. **Inverted yield curve identified as the one legitimate signal:** The host singles out the inverted yield curve — where short-term yields (e.g., the 2-year) exceed long-term yields (e.g., the 10-year) — as the only macro indicator with a consistent track record, having predicted every recession since the 1950s. He notes a key caveat: during the lead-up to the Great Recession, the yield curve inverted at the end of 2006 but the market didn't peak until approximately 18 months later in 2007, meaning early action would have felt premature. As of the video's publication, the yield curve is not inverted — the 2-year sits at approximately 4% and the 10-year at approximately 4.45%, which the host describes as healthy and normal.

5. **BX Trender (monthly) presented as the primary actionable tool:** The host introduces the BX Trender, used on a monthly timeframe, as his preferred momentum indicator. He walks through three historical case studies: (1) January 2022 — the monthly turned red at S&P 4,778, and a sell signal would have avoided a drop to approximately 3,200–3,300; (2) COVID crash — the monthly turned red near a peak of approximately 3,382, and following the signal would have avoided approximately a 25% S&P decline; (3) October 2007 — the monthly turned red the following month after the Great Recession peak near 1,600, and exiting around 1,400 would have avoided a 50–60% market collapse. He also demonstrates how the transition from dark red to lighter red bars signals upward momentum reversal.

6. **Current market momentum assessed as healthy:** As of the end of May 2026, the monthly BX Trender has printed green. The prior month (April) printed light red, and March before it printed dark red — a sequence the host says correctly tracked the rough March followed by strong April and May. He states he is not currently worried about the market based on this indicator. His personal risk-management plan, as a self-described all-in Tesla investor, is to sell covered calls if the monthly BX Trender turns red, as a defensive hedge on his holdings.

7. **RSI dismissed alongside other overbought indicators:** The host warns that the Relative Strength Index (RSI) suffers from the same flaw as the CAPE and Buffett indicators — it can remain in "overbought" territory for extended periods without being actionable. He cites the example of the RSI staying above 70 from approximately mid-1996 through mid-1998 to 1999, a stretch during which exiting the market based on RSI would have been a costly mistake.

Notable quotes and data:
- Buffett Indicator: currently at **237%** (all-time high); ~40% of corporate profits come from overseas, undermining its relevance
- CAPE Ratio: currently at **42.7**, second only to the dot-com bubble
- Margin debt: currently at a historic **$1.3 trillion**
- 2-year Treasury yield: approximately **4%**; 10-year Treasury yield: approximately **4.45%** — not inverted, described as healthy
- S&P 500 level at January 2022 BX Trender red signal: **4,778**; subsequent trough: approximately **3,200–3,300**
- S&P 500 peak during COVID BX Trender signal: approximately **3,382**; avoided approximately **25% decline**
- S&P 500 level at October 2007 BX Trender signal: approximately **1,400** (exit level); market subsequently dropped **50–60%**
- Inverted yield curve preceded the Great Recession peak by approximately **18 months** (inverted end of 2006, market peaked ~mid-2007)
- RSI remained overbought (above 70) for approximately **mid-1996 through mid-1998 to 1999** without a correction
- Host describes himself as "essentially an all-in Tesla investor"

2026-06-02.title: Is There A SECRET PLOT In The SpaceX - Tesla Merger?
2026-06-02.body:
Jo Bhakdi analyzes SpaceX's newly amended S1 IPO filing — scheduled to go public on June 12, 2026 — and argues that the authorization of 36 billion shares (against only ~12 billion currently issued) is a strong signal that SpaceX is structurally preparing to acquire Tesla, not merely raise capital. The core thesis is that the share authorization is far too large to be explained by normal capital raises or conventional acquisitions, and can only make sense in the context of a Tesla merger — potentially structured as a 1-to-2 or even 1-to-3 share exchange favoring Tesla shareholders.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX S1 share structure signals a Tesla acquisition:** The amended SpaceX S1 reveals two share classes: Class A common stock (~6.91 billion shares issued and outstanding, 1 vote per share) and Class B shares (~5.95 billion, 10 votes per share, held predominantly by Elon Musk). Total shares currently defining SpaceX ownership are ~12.86 billion. However, 36 billion shares have been authorized — roughly three times the total current share count. Bhakdi argues this cannot be explained by capital raises (which would never dilute SpaceX by 300%) or normal acquisitions (which typically involve 1–10% of shares), and can only be intended for a major acquisition of a company valued two to three times SpaceX — i.e., Tesla.

2. **Legal constraints delay a merger announcement post-IPO:** Bhakdi notes that SpaceX cannot announce a Tesla acquisition immediately after going public on June 12, 2026, as failing to disclose a known acquisition intent in the S1 would constitute a violation of disclosure duties. A meaningful gap between the IPO and any merger announcement is therefore legally necessary, placing the earliest realistic merger initiation in 2027.

3. **Predicted valuation trajectory sets up a 1-to-2 merger:** Bhakdi's central scenario for early 2027 is Tesla reaching a $3 trillion market cap (~$800/share) while SpaceX deflates approximately 25% from its IPO valuation of ~$2 trillion, landing at ~$1.5 trillion. This would make a 1-to-1 merger impractical and instead suggest a 1-to-2 structure, in which SpaceX issues ~24 billion new shares to acquire Tesla — well within the 36 billion authorized. He argues SpaceX could technically even support a 1-to-3 merger if Tesla reached $4 trillion against a $1 trillion SpaceX.

4. **Elon's control and economics remain intact under a 1-to-2 merger:** In a 1-to-1 merger (both entities at equal valuation), Elon's economic ownership of the combined entity would be ~34% and his voting control ~81%. In a 1-to-2 merger (Tesla twice the size of SpaceX), his economic ownership declines modestly to ~29–30% — a difference Bhakdi characterizes as negligible — while his voting control remains ~78%, well above both the 51% and 66% control thresholds. Even in a 1-to-3 scenario, Elon would retain a total voting majority due to his dominance of the 10x Class B shares.

5. **Tesla shareholders would have strong incentive to vote yes:** In a 1-to-2 merger, Tesla shareholders would receive two-thirds of the combined entity while effectively acquiring SpaceX at half its standalone value. Bhakdi argues this eliminates any risk of a shareholder vote rejection — particularly if Tesla shares are at $800 by the time a vote is called, with robotaxi scaling already underway. This structure, he contends, solves all alignment problems simultaneously: Elon retains control, Tesla shareholders are rewarded, and SpaceX gains a path to funding its orbital AI ambitions projected for 2028.

6. **Bhakdi's investment stance: hold Tesla, skip SpaceX IPO:** Bhakdi states he is not participating in the SpaceX IPO, citing a high probability of paper losses over the subsequent 9 months post-IPO, and believes Tesla is the superior vehicle for capturing the combined upside. He remains long-term bullish on SpaceX but views the IPO entry point as unfavorable relative to Tesla.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab scaling as a forcing function for Tesla's valuation:** Bhakdi reiterates his previously stated projection of 15,000 Cybercabs operating unsupervised by end of 2026, which he acknowledges is criticized but stands behind based on observed facts on the ground. He argues this Cybercab scaling is the key catalyst that would drive Tesla to a $3 trillion valuation (~$800/share) and eliminate the era of delays, making the merger math work in Tesla shareholders' favor.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX authorized shares: 36 billion; currently issued and outstanding: ~12.86 billion (Class A: ~6.91B, Class B: ~5.95B)
- SpaceX IPO date: June 12, 2026
- Elon Musk owns ~12% of SpaceX Class A common shares and ~93% of Class B shares; total economic ownership ~50%; voting control ~85%
- Tesla common stock: ~3.7 billion shares; Elon's beneficial ownership ~20% of votes
- Elon's voting control in 1-to-1 merger scenario: ~81%; economic ownership: ~34%
- Elon's voting control in 1-to-2 merger scenario: ~78%; economic ownership: ~29.37%
- Bhakdi's Tesla price target: ~$800/share (~$3 trillion market cap), described as "more likely than not" to occur in 2026
- Bhakdi's SpaceX post-IPO prediction: ~25% decline from IPO valuation, landing ~$1.5 trillion by early 2027
- Projected Cybercab fleet (unsupervised, end of 2026): 15,000 — per Bhakdi's estimate
- SpaceX orbital AI buildout expected: 2028
- Source credit for S1 share data: Alexandra Merz

2026-06-02.title: Daily X Summary (2026-06-02)
2026-06-02.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts were dominated by SpaceX/Anthropic IPO coverage (low direct Tesla relevance), with the most actionable Tesla signal coming from a strong European sales recovery in May 2026 — particularly France's explosive +655% YoY growth. Secondary signals include Tesla Semi commercial testing feedback and a minor FSD/camera maintenance update. Overall, the Tesla-specific content is bullish on demand recovery but limited in scope.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Tesla Europe Sales Surge in May 2026:** Tesla posted dramatic YoY registration gains across multiple European markets in May 2026. France led with +655% (described as the best-selling May ever for Tesla there), followed by Denmark at +136%, Spain at +113%, Sweden at +71%, and Norway at +29%. Notably, the Model Y was Denmark's best-selling vehicle overall in May — across all powertrains — while the Model 3 placed fifth in the same market. Denmark also set a new overall BEV record, with 15,020 BEVs out of 19,092 new passenger car registrations, pushing BEV market share to a record high. Additional European country data was noted as forthcoming later in the week. The magnitude of France's growth in particular (+655%) suggests either a very low prior-year base or a meaningful demand inflection, and the breadth of gains across markets is a positive signal for Q2 2026 deliveries.

2. **Tesla Semi Commercial Testing — Strong Fleet Operator Feedback:** Covenant Logistics completed two weeks of Tesla Semi testing and reported being "amazed at the performance" of the vehicle, noting a "level of confidence that was hard to match in a diesel truck." The post was truncated, so the specific route or payload details were not fully captured, though a "final run" tackling a challenging section was referenced. This is a meaningful data point for commercial fleet adoption sentiment, as Covenant is a publicly traded logistics company whose endorsement carries credibility beyond individual owner testimonials.

3. **Camera Maintenance Update — Minor FSD/Autonomy Infrastructure Signal:** Tesla added a new front-facing camera cleaning guide in service mode, introducing a 4-step process for technicians to address haziness buildup on cameras. The steps include cleaning the forward camera per service procedure and verifying clarity afterward. While operationally minor, this is a marginal signal for the robotaxi thesis — camera reliability and maintenance standardization become material at fleet scale.

4. **SpaceX and Anthropic IPO Activity (Indirect Tesla Relevance):** The majority of today's posts covered SpaceX's amended S-1/A IPO filing and Anthropic's confidential S-1 submission to the SEC. SpaceX's filing noted they "may issue a significant amount of equity in connection with future acquisitions, divestitures, or other strategic transactions." These posts are primarily relevant to Tesla investors who hold SpaceX exposure through Elon Musk's broader portfolio, but have no direct operational or financial impact on Tesla. Sawyer also ran a poll on SpaceX IPO purchase intent. These posts are noted but carry low Tesla-specific investment signal.

2026-06-03.title: Tom Lee Extremely BULLISH
2026-06-03.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel features host Herbert and guest Jo Bhakdi, an economist, investor, and tech entrepreneur, discussing bullish macro and tech investment theses from Tom Lee of Fundstrat and Brad Gerstner of Altimeter. The core argument is that AI-driven productivity is equivalent to a massive, costless labor force expansion, and that Elon Musk — through his unique ability to build physical compute infrastructure at unprecedented speed — is uniquely positioned to be the biggest winner of this era. The conversation covers Terafab, orbital AI data centers, FSD, Optimus, and the Cursor/XAI deal as evidence of Elon's compounding advantages.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tom Lee's "Biggest Gains of Our Lifetime" Thesis:** Tom Lee of Fundstrat argues that after 2026, the next two years could produce some of the largest stock market gains in a lifetime. He cites accelerating U.S. GDP growth (potentially reaching 4%), the U.S. being a net exporter of high-value AI products, misallocated capital shifting from private alternatives into public markets, and demographic tailwinds from millennials and Gen Z entering the workforce and beginning to inherit generational wealth as the key drivers.

2. **AI as Massless Labor Immigration:** Jo Bhakdi frames the AI productivity revolution as economically equivalent to importing hundreds of millions of highly skilled workers at near-zero cost — "100 million PhDs at $20 per day." He argues this is not a sector-specific boom but rather a fundamental fuel injection into the entire economy, comparable to but more powerful than mass immigration, because these "workers" require no food, housing, or physical infrastructure. The ripple effect is described as expanding in circles: from Nvidia chips → hyperscalers → Mag 7 → Dell/Oracle/IBM → energy → chemicals → the broader economy.

3. **Brad Gerstner's "Electrons to Tokens" Thesis:** Brad Gerstner of Altimeter is quoted as saying there is "no human being on the planet better at turning electrons into tokens than Elon Musk" — meaning converting physical compute infrastructure into AI capability. Gerstner argues that Elon's ability to build the world's largest data centers, combined with the Cursor acquisition and the Anthropic deal, fundamentally changes the valuation case for a potential SpaceX IPO, going beyond the launch and Starlink businesses alone.

4. **Colossus Data Center as Proof of Execution:** Jo Bhakdi highlights that Elon built the Colossus AI compute cluster in approximately two months — something that normally takes two years — and that even Nvidia's Jensen Huang expressed disbelief at the speed. He contrasts this with the Stargate project (involving OpenAI, Oracle, and SoftBank in Texas), which reportedly struggled to execute. Jo frames the ability to actually build coherent large-scale GPU clusters — specifically breaking the then-believed ceiling of 30,000 coherent GPUs — as a decisive, non-trivial engineering achievement.

5. **Terafab: SpaceX-Linked Semiconductor Facility in Texas:** A company called Wit Tech LLC, sharing the same physical address as XAI in Palo Alto, has filed land acquisition deed records with Grimes County, Texas on May 28, 2026 for the purchase of more than 3,100 acres. This is described as preparation for a $55–$119 billion SpaceX AI multi-phase, next-generation, vertically integrated semiconductor manufacturing and advanced computing fabrication facility, part of a SpaceX reinvestment zone. A public hearing was scheduled for June 3, 2026. Jo Bhakdi estimates that with Elon's execution speed, the first chips could emerge within three to four years — compared to the typical five-to-ten-year timeline for comparable projects like TSMC's Arizona fab.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD as a Validation of Elon's Amorphous Problem-Solving:** Jo Bhakdi acknowledges that FSD was a different category of problem for Elon than rockets or factories — an "open-ended," "vast, amorphous" challenge where even the endpoint was unclear. He expresses that he was initially more skeptical of FSD than of hardware projects. However, he credits Elon's early first-principles decisions — vision-only (no LiDAR), deploying cameras in every car since approximately 2012 to collect training data, and making the early bet on neural nets and supercomputers — as the foundational moves that ultimately made FSD possible when no other automaker was positioned to do so.

2. **Cursor/XAI Deal as an AGI Strategy Signal:** Jo Bhakdi describes Elon's acquisition of Cursor as a "genius" move that gave him a major confidence boost in Elon's ability to navigate open-ended, amorphous problems like AGI. The logic: Anthropic demonstrated that the "harness" (the developer tool layer) is at least as important as the underlying model. Elon had a strong model (Grok) but no harness; Cursor had the best harness but no model or compute. Jo predicts this deal will rapidly close the gap between XAI and Anthropic/OpenAI.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus Still an Open Question, but Confidence Growing:** Jo Bhakdi places Optimus in the same "amorphous problem" category as FSD — involving hands, embodied AI, neural nets, and actuator technology that have never been fully solved before. He notes that unlike rockets (where each sub-component has prior precedent), humanoid robots require solving a "vast array of weird problems" simultaneously. He says the economic pressure is high enough that he believes they will figure it out, but considers it less certain and less time-bounded than hardware infrastructure projects.

2. **Convergence of Enabling Technologies for Humanoid Robots:** The host notes that earlier humanoid robot efforts (Boston Dynamics, Honda ASIMO) were "just demos" because the necessary enabling technologies — advanced actuators, sufficient compute, AI intelligence, and capable batteries — were not yet available. The argument is that all of these components are converging simultaneously now, creating a window for practical humanoid robots within the next one to three years.

## Financials

1. **Orbital AI Data Centers: Cost and Timeline Projections:** Jo Bhakdi claims he calculated in November 2025 that space-based AI data centers will be approximately 60% cheaper than terrestrial equivalents over a ten-year time span. He states Elon has disclosed that each AI satellite will require five times the solar power of a Starlink satellite. Jo predicts dozens to potentially hundreds of prototype AI satellites (approximately 100 kilowatt class) could be in orbit for testing within the next year (i.e., by approximately mid-2027), with the first scaled commercial deployment by 2028. He argues the only bottleneck is Starship readiness, and that even non-reusable Starship could make the economics work.

2. **U.S. Energy Demand as an AI Infrastructure Constraint:** The discussion includes a projection that AI currently represents approximately 7% of U.S. energy use, and that this figure will reach approximately 15% next year (i.e., 2027), at which point terrestrial build-out hits a hard ceiling. Jo frames this inflection point as the precise moment when Starship's capabilities become commercially critical — and notes the timing coincidence as extraordinary and largely unforeseeable.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tom Lee: "After 2026, perhaps over the next two years, some of the biggest gains of the stock market in our lifetime."
- Tom Lee: U.S. GDP growth could reach 4%, which would be "pretty astounding" for the world's largest mature economy.
- Brad Gerstner: "There's no human being on the planet that is better at turning electrons into tokens than Elon Musk."
- Jo Bhakdi: AI is "basically importing billions of people into the US, only they are disembodied — they don't need food, they don't need housing, they just work."
- Jo Bhakdi on Colossus: Built in approximately two months, something that normally takes two years; experts previously claimed coherent GPU clusters beyond 30,000 units were impossible.
- Wit Tech LLC filed land acquisition deeds in Grimes County, Texas on May 28, 2026 for 3,100+ acres; $55–$119 billion facility scope.
- Jo Bhakdi: Space-based AI data centers projected to be 60% cheaper than terrestrial over 10 years; first scaled deployment target: 2028.
- AI energy use: ~7% of U.S. total currently; projected ~15% by 2027.
- Jo Bhakdi on Terafab timeline: "Within three to four years we could actually see the first chip out."
- Elon Musk reportedly stated orbital AI data centers are "a lot easier than people think."

2026-06-03.title: Tesla Rolls Out Unsupervised Robotaxis
2026-06-03.body:
This video from "brighterwithherbert" features host Herbert and guest Brian White (of the YouTube channel FutureAzA) discussing the latest developments in Tesla's unsupervised robotaxi rollout in Austin, the shift in Tesla's institutional vs. retail ownership, and the upcoming SpaceX IPO and its potential implications for Tesla stock. The core thesis is that Tesla's robotaxi program is quietly but steadily progressing — with the unsupervised geofence in Austin expanding to its full boundary — and that institutional investors are increasingly recognizing Tesla's long-term value even as retail investors remain in a wait-and-see mode.

## Robotaxi

1. **Unsupervised Robotaxi Geofence Expands to Full Austin Map:** Researcher Jesse Richards discovered that Tesla's unsupervised robotaxi service in Austin has expanded from a small sub-area to cover the entire Austin geofence as of the morning of the video. Richards determined this by hailing an unsupervised robotaxi on the app and repeatedly changing the drop-off destination to map out where the service would route — locations returning "route unavailable" were outside the operating zone. This expansion is interpreted by both the host and Brian White as a sign of increasing confidence in the system's capability and safety.

2. **~28 Unsupervised Robotaxis Currently Operating in Austin:** The host references approximately 28 unsupervised robotaxi vehicles currently slated for the Austin program, noting this number is small and that the rollout has been slower than many anticipated. Brian White frames this deliberate pace as intentional caution — Tesla is held to a far higher standard than competitors like Waymo, meaning any public incident would generate disproportionate media attention.

3. **Waymo Comparison and Double Standard:** Brian White argues that Tesla faces a uniquely harsh media environment compared to Waymo. He notes that when Waymo vehicles have standoffs at intersections, it does not become major news, whereas any comparable Tesla incident would dominate tech headlines. This is offered as justification for Tesla's measured rollout pace rather than evidence of failure.

4. **Cybercab Production Underway as Commitment Signal:** Both Brian White and a clip from ARK Invest's Cathie Wood (referred to as "Tasha Keiney" / Tashakini in the transcript) point to the fact that Tesla has already begun manufacturing Cybercabs and shipping them around the country as strong evidence that the robotaxi network is real and imminent. Brian White argues Cybercabs — unlike Model Y vehicles that could be redirected to consumer sales — have no alternative use case if the robotaxi network fails, making their production a credible commitment signal.

5. **Ramp Expected Before FSD Version 15:** The video addresses a concern among some investors that Tesla must wait for FSD version 15 before ramping robotaxi. ARK Invest's Cathie Wood is quoted saying that FSD 15 is compatible with the AI4 compute platform (which is in all currently sold Tesla vehicles), and that current safety data already shows Tesla FSD is safer than human drivers. Brian White reinforces this by noting FSD version 14 is already deployed and running in Austin and San Francisco today. Both guests conclude that AI4 hardware is sufficient for robotaxi operations and that waiting for version 15 or AI5 hardware is unnecessary. Brian White also speculates that version 15 may not require substantially more compute than version 14.

6. **Cross-Country Autonomous Drive Cited as Proof Point:** Brian White references a David Moss cross-continental FSD drive — including through Canada — completed without any speed profile adjustments or manual interventions, which he cites as real-world evidence that the technology already works at a high level.

## Market & Competition

1. **Institutional Ownership Surpasses Retail for First Time:** According to Alexandra Merz, institutions now hold 47.8% of Tesla stock, Elon Musk holds approximately 20%, and retail investors have fallen to just 31.9%. Brian White notes this shift was a long time coming — Tesla was previously underweight in institutional portfolios due to perceived risk, its historical absence from certain S&P inclusion criteria, and a credit rating that did not reflect the company's strong balance sheet (tens of billions in reserves, no debt). Once the credit rating improved and index fund inclusion was required, pension funds and index funds were compelled to buy. There are now approximately 4,276 institutional owners and shareholders who have filed 13F forms with the SEC.

2. **Largest Institutional Holders Identified:** The largest institutional shareholders currently include Vanguard, BlackRock, Vanguard Capital Management, State Street, Geode Capital, Jane Street, Vanguard Portfolio, and JP Morgan.

3. **Waymo Fleet Size Put in Context:** ARK Invest's Cathie Wood notes that Waymo's last reported fleet figure was approximately 3,000 cars, and that Tesla can produce more vehicles than that in a single day — underscoring Tesla's manufacturing scale advantage in any future robotaxi fleet race.

4. **SpaceX IPO Set for June 12, 2026:** Reuters reported that SpaceX plans to offer shares at a target price of $135, with approximately 555 million shares made available, raising $75 billion and implying a $1.75 trillion valuation. This would be over 50 times revenue. When asked how to justify that multiple, Elon Musk responded simply: "You shall see." Elon Musk is subject to a lockup period preventing him from selling for over one year after the IPO.

5. **Tesla Stock Impact from SpaceX IPO — Three Scenarios Discussed:** The hosts discuss three possible outcomes for Tesla stock on the SpaceX IPO date. (1) Down — some investors may rotate cash from Tesla into SpaceX. (2) Up — analyst Larry Goldberg believes a "halo effect" from SpaceX media coverage could drive Tesla up 10–15%, similar to how interest in SpaceX's first crewed mission to the space station drove money into Tesla stock when SpaceX was not publicly tradeable. (3) No change — much of the SpaceX optimism is already priced into Tesla. Brian White suggests any cash rotation out of Tesla likely already occurred during Tesla's recent run to the $420–$430 range.

6. **Potential SpaceX–Tesla Merger Theory Debated:** The hosts preview an upcoming debate between Jo Bhakdi and Alexandra Merz on the Tesla/SpaceX merger thesis. Jo Bhakdi's theory — described as unconventional — is that rather than SpaceX acquiring Tesla at a discount, Elon Musk would offer Tesla shareholders a premium, valuing Tesla at roughly double SpaceX's market cap. His reasoning: SpaceX's prospectus reportedly authorized 36 billion shares (far more than the ~12 billion needed to acquire Tesla), suggesting Tesla shareholders would receive two-thirds of the combined entity. Bhakdi argues this makes sense because Tesla provides near-term profitability while SpaceX is a longer-term story, and that without such a premium SpaceX stock might fall significantly post-IPO. Brian White notes that among the "Magnificent 7," Tesla is currently the only company without founder voting control via dual-class share structures — making a restructuring toward founder control less unusual in context.

## Financials

1. **Revenue Milestone as Potential Stock Catalyst:** Brian White suggests the Tesla stock may need to reach a new revenue level — with the price-to-earnings ratio falling out of triple digits — before the next significant institutional re-rating occurs. He offers a speculative figure of "$6 billion a year" as a revenue level from robotaxi that might trigger a broader reassessment, though he qualifies this as illustrative rather than a firm forecast. He notes that much of the robotaxi growth potential is already priced into Tesla for long-term holders.

Notable quotes and data:
- "Institutions now hold 47.8% of Tesla stock. Elon is 20% and retail is now down to just 31.9%." — Alexandra Merz, per the host
- "There are now nearly 4,300 institutional owners and shareholders" — approximately 4,276 per 13F filings
- Active robotaxi fleet in Austin (unsupervised): ~28 vehicles referenced in the video; per RobotaxiTracker.com (as of 2026-05-09), unsupervised fleet is 39 total (Austin: 28, Dallas: 5, Houston: 6)
- "Waymo, the last reported figure was they have around 3,000 cars. Tesla can produce more vehicles than that in a single day." — ARK Invest (Cathie Wood)
- SpaceX IPO: $135/share target price, ~555 million shares, $1.75 trillion valuation, $75 billion raised, IPO date June 12, 2026
- "You shall see." — Elon Musk, responding to questions about SpaceX's 50x revenue valuation
- FSD version 14 is currently deployed and running robotaxi operations in Austin and San Francisco
- Jo Bhakdi's merger theory: SpaceX prospectus reportedly authorized 36 billion shares; his thesis is Tesla would be valued at 2x SpaceX in a merger, giving Tesla shareholders two-thirds of the combined company
- Elon Musk lockup: cannot sell SpaceX shares for more than one year after IPO
- Tesla stock currently trading at over $400/share (referenced as "over 400 a share" and recent range of "$420–$430")

2026-06-03.title: Might SpaceX Buy Tesla at 2x The Price?
2026-06-03.body:
This video features a three-way discussion between host Herbert, Alexandra Merz, and Jo Bhakdi on the thesis that SpaceX will acquire Tesla following SpaceX's upcoming IPO, with speculation about the timing, structure, and valuation of such a deal. The core debate centers on whether the merger would be a one-to-one market cap deal or whether SpaceX could acquire Tesla at a significant premium — potentially two times Tesla's current valuation — and what governance and financial engineering considerations would shape the offer. The conversation draws on breadcrumbs from SpaceX's S1 amendment, share authorization numbers, Elon Musk's stock option exercise deadlines, and index fund inclusion mechanics to build a speculative but detailed case for an announcement window between end of June and August 15, 2026.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO and merger thesis overview:** SpaceX is scheduled to IPO on June 12, 2026. The hosts discuss widespread speculation that SpaceX will at some point announce an acquisition of Tesla, with the community debating whether it would be a "merger of equals" (both valued at roughly $2 trillion) or whether SpaceX might offer a significant premium. Jo Bhakdi introduces the framing that a 2-to-1 acquisition — SpaceX buying Tesla at double its own valuation, i.e., $4 trillion — is not impossible, though he stresses this is not a prediction but a scenario worth modeling.

2. **Jo Bhakdi's Elon control modeling:** Jo explains that he modeled the voting and economic implications of various merger ratios for Elon Musk. His conclusion is that whether the deal is 1-to-1 or 1-to-2 in favor of Tesla, the difference in Elon's control over the combined entity is only marginal. Specifically, he notes Elon's ownership would decline from approximately 35% to approximately 29% in a scenario where SpaceX acquires Tesla at twice its own valuation. His key takeaway is that Elon has no strong incentive to push for any particular merger ratio — he is largely indifferent between the scenarios from a control standpoint.

3. **SpaceX's 36 billion authorized shares as a breadcrumb:** SpaceX currently has approximately 12.86 billion shares outstanding, yet its S1 authorizes 36 billion shares — roughly three times the total current share count. Jo argues this is a meaningful breadcrumb suggesting SpaceX has pre-authorized enough shares to acquire Tesla at up to two or even three times SpaceX's own valuation, without needing to return to shareholders for additional authorization. Alexandra Merz counters that large authorized-vs-issued gaps are standard corporate practice, citing Tesla's own history of authorizing 2 billion shares at IPO in 2010 while issuing fewer than 100 million, a ratio that held for 12 years.

4. **Jo's directional valuation scenario — SpaceX down, Tesla up:** Jo's base case prediction for the 9–12 month horizon (i.e., by approximately mid-2027) is that SpaceX will struggle to maintain its IPO valuation over time due to missing near-term earnings catalysts, while Tesla will trend significantly upward driven by robotaxi scaling. His most likely directional scenario is SpaceX at $1.5 trillion and Tesla at $3 trillion, which would make a one-to-one merger structurally difficult from Tesla shareholders' perspective.

5. **SpaceX index inclusion mechanics — six months of forced buying:** Alexandra details that SpaceX faces three major index inclusions in its first 15 trading days (MSCI, FTSE, and NASDAQ), followed by S&P 500 inclusion potentially in mid-December 2026, which she estimates could trigger over $100 billion in passive index fund purchases — larger in impact than Tesla's own S&P inclusion in 2020. She argues lockup period expiries are staggered with these inclusion waves intentionally, and that the S&P has already softened its profitability requirements and float thresholds specifically for this IPO. This six-month engineered support structure, she argues, is designed to keep SpaceX's price elevated long enough to make a merger offer attractive to Tesla shareholders.

6. **Competitive and governance risk of waiting past midterms:** Alexandra argues that one key reason to pursue the merger quickly is political. With the Trump administration currently favorable to Elon Musk's interests, delaying past the 2026 midterms risks Democratic gains in Congress leading to hostile committee hearings, subpoenas, and targeting of Tesla. She notes that a merged Tesla-SpaceX entity would be effectively untouchable given SpaceX's critical role in U.S. defense infrastructure. Her estimated timeline for the combined entity having a single ticker is Q2 2027, after a shareholder vote (likely November 2026) and approximately four to seven months of regulatory approval.

7. **Waymo and other suitors as merger complication:** The discussion briefly notes, citing a point from a commentator named Warren, that Tesla is an attractive acquisition target for parties other than SpaceX, and that a competing offer landing on the table could put Tesla's board in an awkward position and potentially delay the process.

## Financials

1. **Elon's 2018 stock option exercise deadline — August 15, 2026:** Alexandra explains that Elon's 2018 compensation package options must be exercised before August 15, 2026, converting them into restricted stock units (RSUs) that he must hold until 2033. The exercise of these options would add approximately 300 million shares to Tesla's outstanding share count. The exercise price is $23 per share, meaning the total cost to exercise is approximately $7 billion. Alexandra notes this is not a tax event (that comes in January 2028) but purely a bureaucratic purchase. The higher Tesla's share price at the time of exercise, the less Elon needs to sell, pledge, or net-exercise to cover the $7 billion cost, giving him a direct financial incentive to have Tesla's stock price elevated before August 15.

2. **Tesla outstanding shares approaching 4 billion:** Alexandra explains that Tesla's current outstanding share count, after the 2025 compensation package added approximately 400 million shares in November 2025, will reach approximately 4 billion shares once Elon exercises his 2018 options by mid-August 2026. Tesla currently has a 6 billion share authorization. She stresses that any market cap-based merger offer must be calculated using this 4 billion share count, not a smaller number, making it a critical input for valuing the deal.

3. **Merger structure debate — ratchet vs. fixed ratio:** The panel converges on a proposed deal structure: a one-to-one market cap offer with a guaranteed minimum floor price per Tesla share (a "ratchet"), so that Tesla shareholders are protected if SpaceX's price falls between announcement and the shareholder vote. Jo argues this is necessary for game-theory reasons — without a floor, uncertainty about the vote outcome would itself destabilize both stock prices. The ratchet would allow Tesla shares to move upward with SpaceX but not downward, creating certainty that would likely make the vote self-fulfilling. Example numbers discussed include a hypothetical floor of $750 per Tesla share if Tesla is at $500 at announcement, representing a roughly 50% premium.

4. **SpaceX share math limits a strict 2-to-1 deal:** Alexandra and Jo work through the arithmetic showing that a strict 2-to-1 acquisition (SpaceX buying Tesla at twice SpaceX's market cap) is mathematically constrained by the 36 billion authorized shares. With SpaceX already at approximately 13 billion shares outstanding (including shares to be issued for Grok/xAI-related entities described as marginal at ~3%), a 2-to-1 deal would require approximately 26 billion new shares plus the existing 13 billion, totaling approximately 39 billion — exceeding the 36 billion authorization. Alexandra concludes the math works for up to approximately a 1.9-to-1 ratio but not a clean 2-to-1.

5. **SpaceX S1 amendment explicitly references Tesla acquisition:** The hosts note that SpaceX's S1 amendment contains language explicitly stating that SpaceX is reserving authorized shares to acquire Tesla, which Alexandra describes as a clear and unambiguous breadcrumb embedded in an amendment rather than the main prospectus body. She suggests this placement was intentional — visible to those reading changes but not prominently featured.

6. **Tesla shareholders need 50% plus one vote to approve merger:** Alexandra clarifies the vote threshold is 50% plus one of all outstanding shares (not 66%). She identifies the key blocs needed to pass: Elon's approximately 19.09% economic interest in Tesla, plus Vanguard (already invested in both SpaceX and Tesla), BlackRock (reportedly seeking $10 billion of the SpaceX IPO), ARK Invest, and Baron Capital, plus approximately one-third of retail shareholders. She argues this coalition is achievable but notes it requires a premium juicy enough that retail shareholders holding Tesla at elevated prices won't vote no out of fear of giving up further upside.

Notable quotes and data:
- Jo Bhakdi: "It is only a marginal difference in Elon's control over the new merged entity... Elon has no incentive of driving that merger ratio in any way."
- Alexandra Merz: "There is no cash. It will be 100% shares."
- Alexandra Merz: "My last date in my scenario is the 15th of August and my first day is probably just before the NASDAQ inclusion which is three weeks after the 12th of June."
- Alexandra Merz: "Please all keep in mind calculations of the stock price have to be based on 4 billion outstanding shares."
- Alexandra Merz on the combined entity ticker: "probably has the X ticker"
- Alexandra Merz on Q2 2027 as the single-ticker date: "a real replacement of the tickers and one entity being born — Q2 2027"
- Jo Bhakdi: "SpaceX at 1.5 trillion and Tesla at 3 trillion is in my opinion directionally the most likely scenario in 9 to 12 months."
- SpaceX current shares outstanding: ~12.86 billion; authorized: 36 billion
- Tesla outstanding shares post-August 15 exercise: ~4 billion
- Tesla's 2010 IPO: 2 billion authorized, fewer than 100 million issued
- Elon's exercise cost for 2018 options: ~$7 billion at $23/share strike price
- S&P 500 inclusion of SpaceX estimated for mid-December 2026, with passive buying potentially exceeding $100 billion
- Elon's Tesla economic ownership: ~19.09%; Tesla voting share described as equivalent to ownership
- Elon's SpaceX economic interest: ~50%; voting control: ~85% (via 10-to-1 Class B shares)
- Hypothetical merger ratchet floor discussed: ~$750/share minimum if Tesla is at $500 at announcement
- Elon's ownership dilution in a 2-to-1 scenario: from ~35% to ~29% of combined entity

2026-06-03.title: Tesla found new buyers for its Cybertruck: Kazakh emergency services
2026-06-03.body:
Kazakhstan's Ministry of Emergency Situations has confirmed plans to purchase additional Tesla Cybertrucks following successful deployment in rescue operations around Almaty, as Tesla continues searching for buyers amid collapsing domestic demand for the electric pickup.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Kazakhstan emergency services deployment:** Vice Minister Yerbolat Sadyrbayev confirmed the expansion after the first Cybertruck deployed in Almaty demonstrated effectiveness in mountainous terrain rescue operations. Officials cited high off-road mobility, vehicle-to-load power output for communications and rescue equipment, quiet operation, and extended power delivery as key advantages. The Cybertruck is positioned as a supplementary rapid-response vehicle, not a replacement for traditional fire engines, ambulances, or rescue trucks.

2. **Government and security use:** Kazakhstan's State Guard Service also deployed Cybertrucks as mobile command-and-control vehicles at the Summit of the Organization of Turkic States in Turkistan on May 15. One unit served the State Guard Service for command and coordination; a second was added to the Ministry of Emergency Situations' rapid response reserve. The State Guard cited power supply and communications deployment capabilities as the selection rationale.

## Market & Competition
3. **Cybertruck demand collapse:** Cybertruck sales fell 48% in 2025 to approximately 20,000 units — far below Tesla's original 250,000 annual production target. In Q1 2026, Tesla sold just 3,519 Cybertrucks, with registration data showing SpaceX purchased 1,279 units over the past year, artificially inflating figures. Tesla launched the Cybertruck in the Middle East in January 2026, delivering roughly 63 units in the UAE at prices starting around $110,000, and introduced a new $60,000 AWD trim in February 2026. The truck remains ineligible for export to Europe due to EU regulatory non-compliance.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert views Kazakhstan's purchase as emblematic of Tesla's desperation to find any buyer for the Cybertruck and does not expect small government contracts to reverse the demand trajectory. He identifies the $60,000 AWD trim as the vehicle's "last hope," warning that if it fails to move the needle, the Cybertruck program may follow the path of the Model S/X in terms of volume.

Notable quotes and data:
- Cybertruck sales: ~20,000 units in 2025 (–48% YoY); 3,519 units in Q1 2026
- SpaceX purchased 1,279 Cybertrucks over the past year, inflating sales figures
- UAE launch: ~63 units delivered, starting at ~$110,000
- New $60,000 AWD trim introduced February 2026
- Original Tesla production target: 250,000 Cybertrucks/year
- "The Cybertruck has shown high efficiency in responding to various emergency situations. We are talking about saving people's lives." — Vice Minister Sadyrbayev

2026-06-03.title: Tesla retroactively added ‘supervised’ to FSD contracts owners signed years ago
2026-06-03.body:
Tesla has retroactively modified "Full Self-Driving" purchase agreements to add "supervised" language absent from the originals, and in some cases has made the original contracts entirely inaccessible — an issue Electrek confirmed with multiple owners holding HW3 vehicles and FSD purchases from before 2024.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Contracts altered or inaccessible post-purchase:** Owner Oliver Abcarius discovered that his 2019 FSD purchase agreement (for a 2018 Model 3) and his wife's 2020 Model Y purchase agreement — both from the era when Tesla sold "Full Self-Driving Capability" without "supervised" language — now link to invalid pages. Every other document on both accounts opens normally; only those referencing FSD purchase details are inaccessible.

2. **Timeline of Tesla's FSD language shift:** From 2016 through early 2024, Tesla sold "Full Self-Driving Capability" for up to $15,000 with the promise of unsupervised autonomy via OTA updates. In March 2024, Tesla formally renamed the product "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)" with FSD v12.3.3. By September 2025, Tesla had abandoned the original autonomy promise, and in April 2026, Musk confirmed HW3 vehicles (produced 2016–2023) cannot achieve unsupervised FSD due to hardware limitations — with no concrete retrofit plan in place.

3. **Legal context — evidence relevance:** Tesla faces up to $14.5 billion in lawsuits covering FSD false advertising, Autopilot crash liability, and securities fraud. A certified US class action covers FSD statements made between October 2016 and August 2024. A California administrative ruling found Tesla engaged in false advertising on FSD. An arbitrator ordered Tesla to refund $10,600 to an FSD buyer for breach of contract. FSD fraud suits are also active in China and Europe. The now-inaccessible contracts are central evidence in these cases. Tesla also deleted a 2016 blog post — which promised full self-driving hardware on all vehicles — in August 2024 during the buildup of litigation; it remains accessible via the Wayback Machine.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert argues that making executed contracts inaccessible during active litigation is legally distinct from a forward-looking product rename, raising the possibility of evidence spoliation — which courts can treat with adverse inferences or sanctions — and calls the pattern "hard to ignore." He urges pre-2024 FSD owners to check and document the accessibility of their original purchase agreements.

Notable quotes and data:
- "Tesla has retroactively updated my documents from 2019 when I paid for FSD." — Oliver Abcarius
- "It's crazy because there are zero issues opening any documents on both accounts except those that would have the FSD purchase details documented. Super fishy." — Abcarius
- FSD sold for up to **$15,000** without "supervised" language, 2016–early 2024
- Tesla renamed package to "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)" in **March 2024** with FSD v12.3.3
- HW3 inability to achieve unsupervised FSD confirmed by Musk in **April 2026**
- Tesla's 2016 blog post deleted **August 2024**; still accessible via Wayback Machine
- Total litigation exposure cited: **up to $14.5 billion**
- Arbitrator-ordered FSD refund amount: **$10,600**
- Certified class action covers statements from **October 2016 to August 2024**

2026-06-03.title: Tesla expands ‘Robotaxi’ to entire Austin metro — but still has only ~20 vehicles
2026-06-03.body:
Tesla announced an expansion of its unsupervised Robotaxi geofence to cover the entire Austin metro area, but the actual fleet serving that territory has shrunk to approximately 20 active unsupervised vehicles — down from a peak of 25.

## Robotaxi
1. **Geofence expands to all of Austin metro, fleet does not:** Tesla's official Robotaxi account on X confirmed "Unsupervised Robotaxi now in the entire Austin Metro area." Previously, unsupervised vehicles were restricted to a small part of South Austin. The geofence has grown through several phases over the past year, roughly doubling each time, but the unsupervised fleet peaked at 25 cumulative vehicles in late April before declining to ~20 active. Dallas and Houston, which launched in April with tiny geofences, remain stuck at 3 and 6 vehicles respectively with zero growth since launch.

2. **Total fleet has collapsed:** The total active fleet — including supervised Bay Area vehicles — dropped from 165 to just 34 active vehicles. Per RobotaxiTracker.com, roughly 20 unsupervised vehicles now nominally cover potentially thousands of square miles of Austin metro.

3. **Scale gap vs. Waymo:** Waymo operates approximately 3,000 robotaxis across its US markets and completes over 500,000 paid trips per week, across more than 1,400 square miles in 11 cities. Waymo recently raised $16 billion to fund expansion including to London and Tokyo.

4. **FSD v15 cited as scaling prerequisite:** CEO Elon Musk has said Tesla is waiting for its FSD v15 software rewrite before aggressively scaling the fleet, pushing any meaningful ramp to late 2026 or early 2027. The article notes Musk has previously tied fleet growth to other software milestones that passed without scaling.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert argues that geofence expansions are costless and meaningless without vehicles to serve them, characterizing Tesla's pattern as moving the goalpost to the easy-to-change metric (territory) while fleet size and rides stagnate or decline. He states Tesla must demonstrate it can safely scale the fleet before any service area expansion translates into an actual business.

Notable quotes and data:
- ~20 active unsupervised vehicles in Austin as of latest RobotaxiTracker.com data
- Unsupervised fleet peaked at 25 cumulative vehicles in late April 2026
- Dallas: 3 unsupervised vehicles; Houston: 6 — zero growth since April 2026 launch
- Total active fleet (all modes) collapsed from 165 to 34
- Waymo: ~3,000 robotaxis, 500,000+ paid trips/week, 1,400+ sq miles across 11 cities, $16B raised
- Tesla Robotaxi program launched in Austin in June 2025 — now one year in
- FSD v15 rewrite cited as prerequisite for scaling; ramp expected late 2026 or early 2027

2026-06-03.title: Tesla Deploys Major Unsupervised Robotaxi Area Expansion ⚡️
2026-06-03.body:
This video from Dillon Loomis at "electrified" covers Tesla's major expansion of unsupervised robotaxi operations to the entire Austin geofence, a significant milestone in Tesla's autonomous deployment. The video also touches on Tesla Semi infrastructure buildout in Texas, strong global EV sales figures across multiple markets, and a minor FSD software update. The core thesis is that Tesla's robotaxi program may be approaching an inflection point where fleet expansion in Austin — and potentially other cities — could accelerate rapidly.

## Robotaxi

1. **Full Austin Geofence Now Covered by Unsupervised Robotaxis:** Tesla has officially made unsupervised robotaxi operations available across the entire Austin geofence, not just the primary zone where they had previously been operating. Earlier in the same morning, a partial expansion to the south was noted, and then shortly after, the full geofence was confirmed as covered. This is characterized as a clear signal of Tesla's confidence in its unsupervised operations and a meaningful positive development after a period of limited movement on the program.

2. **Safety Monitors May No Longer Be Needed in Austin:** With the full geofence now covered by unsupervised vehicles, safety monitor positions in Austin may effectively be eliminated. The host notes that the only remaining bottleneck to rapid fleet expansion would be backend infrastructure — specifically remote operations — and that if that infrastructure is in place, the "floodgates" in Austin could theoretically open at any time. Tesla may choose to hold fleet size steady for a week or two to validate operations across the expanded geofence before scaling up.

3. **Cybercabs Staging in Dallas:** A photo was shared showing 26 Cybercabs in a Dallas lot, and a second image shared the same afternoon showed over 30 Cybercabs in that lot — a strong indicator that Tesla is preparing for a near-term expansion of robotaxi operations in Dallas. Separately, a ground reporter named Saddok in Houston confirmed the addition of a Model Y as vehicle number nine in the Houston fleet, suggesting fleet additions may not be limited to Cybercabs going forward.

4. **Fleet Counts Referenced:** The video references small but growing fleet numbers across cities, consistent with community-tracked data from RobotaxiTracker.com, including nine vehicles in Houston (one of which is a Model Y).

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD 14.3 Update Mostly Bug Fixes:** A new version of FSD 14.3 is rolling out, but it is described as primarily containing bug fixes rather than major capability changes. One noted feature is improved driver monitoring sensitivity, including better eye gaze tracking, eyewear handling, and higher accuracy in variable lighting — though the official Tesla account clarified this feature had actually been released in a prior update and simply not highlighted in those release notes.

2. **Railroad Crossing Arm Incident Highlighted:** A video from a user named Platinum Patriarch OnX showed an FSD highway incident involving railroad-style gate crossing arms used to block a road. The host acknowledges this was a supervisor error but emphasizes that truly unsupervised, scalable autonomy requires these edge cases to be reliably handled. He notes that railroad-style gate arms have been a recurring challenge for multiple autonomous driving companies.

3. **FSD 14 Coming to Australia:** Tesla sent an update to Australian owners stating that FSD 14 for Hardware 4 vehicles is in its final stages of local development and testing, with no confirmed release date yet but active work underway.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Record Australia Sales in May:** Tesla posted its best-ever monthly sales figure in Australia in May, exceeding 6,400 units. The Model Y L was cited as a standout contributor by Tesla's Australia country director Tom Drew, who described the result as not isolated. Year-to-date Tesla sales in Australia are up 56% compared to last year. The Model Y was also confirmed as the bestselling vehicle of any kind in Australia for May across all fuel types — the first EV in history to lead Australia's overall sales charts.

2. **Model Y L Spotted in the U.S.:** The Model Y L, which has been driving Tesla's Australia momentum, has been spotted multiple times in the United States, including the previous day on the Fremont test track. The host speculates it could officially launch in the U.S. sometime in the summer.

3. **Strong Norway and China Sales:** In Norway, Tesla achieved over a 21% market share in May (21.5%), making it the bestselling car brand for the month. In China, Tesla's wholesale figure for May came in at 85,982 units, up 8.2% over April and up 39.4% year-over-year — the highest wholesale figure for Giga Shanghai so far in 2026. Year-to-date through May, Tesla China is up 29.4% versus the same period last year, selling over 85,900 more units than in the prior year period. The host notes this is before FSD receives broad approval in China.

4. **Japan and Germany Posting Massive Year-Over-Year Gains:** Tesla Japan saw May sales up 182% year-over-year, with year-to-date sales up 157% — over 8,100 registrations compared to 3,178 in the same period last year — despite overall foreign brand registrations in Japan being down 6%. Tesla Germany registered over 5,100 vehicles in May, up 322% year-over-year, and year-to-date registrations in Germany exceed 21,000 — up 200% versus last year and already 9% above Tesla's full-year 2025 Germany total.

5. **Used Cybertrucks Briefly Appeared on Tesla's Website:** Tesla's inventory page momentarily listed used Cybertrucks for sale, but the inventory appeared to be gone by the following day.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla Semi Dominates EV Truck Voucher Applications in California:** According to California voucher data covering January 2025 through February 2026, Tesla Semi accounted for 965 out of 1,067 total Class 8 tractor voucher applications. Daimler and Volvo combined for fewer than 100 applications. Tesla's voucher applications in this round exceeded the total of all other Class 8 tractor applications combined from 2021 through February 2026.

2. **Tesla Semi Dashboard Launched — 644 Verified Orders:** The host has built and launched an interactive Tesla Semi dashboard tracking 644 verified Semi orders across nine confirmed customers with public confirmation. In the last 18 months, 48 trucks have been delivered — 45 to Pepsi, two to WEV, and one to DHL. Tesla stated earlier in June 2026 that most of its 2026 Semi output is already accounted for, implying production is still only a handful of units per week. The dashboard also tracks 81 total known semi-charging depot sites (operational, under construction, and planned).

3. **Tesla Mega Charger Projects Filed in Texas:** According to filings with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, Tesla has new mega charger infrastructure projects tied to San Antonio (estimated cost $400,000, projected completion May 2027), Laredo (estimated cost $100,000, completion December 2026), and Houston (estimated cost $200,000, start June 22, 2026, completion June 2027). These projects are expected to support Tesla Semi charging in major Texas freight markets. The filings do not specify the number of charging stalls or which fleets will have access.

---

**Notable quotes and data:**
- "Now theoretically, the floodgates in Austin could open any time."
- "Safety monitors in Austin may no longer have jobs."
- Over 30 Cybercabs photographed in the Dallas staging lot as of June 3, 2026.
- Houston fleet: vehicle number nine confirmed, a Model Y — suggesting non-Cybercab additions are possible.
- Tesla Semi: 644 verified orders, 9 confirmed customers, 48 delivered trucks, 81 known charging depot sites.
- 48 deployed Tesla Semis already displacing nearly 600,000 gallons of diesel per year (per dashboard estimate).
- Tesla Australia May sales: 6,400+ units — record month; Model Y first EV to top all-fuel-types sales chart in Australia.
- Tesla China May wholesale: 85,982 units, +39.4% YoY, highest Giga Shanghai figure of 2026.
- Tesla Germany YTD: 21,000+ registrations, already 9% above full-year 2025 total.
- Tesla Japan YTD: 8,100+ registrations vs. 3,178 same period last year (+157%).
- California voucher data (Jan 2025–Feb 2026): Tesla Semi 965 of 1,067 applications.

2026-06-03.title: Everyone Told Elon This Was Impossible
2026-06-03.body:
