This video, hosted by Farzad, presents a sweeping macro-thesis about Elon Musk's interconnected empire of companies — Tesla, SpaceX, Neuralink, the Boring Company, and xAI — arguing they are not separate ventures but layered components of a single civilizational foundation. Using a January 2026 cross-country Full Self-Driving road trip as an entry point, the video builds toward the argument that Elon Musk is constructing the infrastructure for the next 100 years of human civilization, ultimately aimed at enabling a self-sufficient Mars colony. The core message is that Musk consistently misses deadlines but ultimately delivers paradigm-shifting results, and the convergence of near-free AI, near-free robotic labor, and near-free solar energy is rendering the existing economic system obsolete.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **13,000-Mile Unsupervised FSD Road Trip:** In January 2026, a Tesla owner named David Moss drove 13,000 miles from Tacoma, Washington coast-to-coast without touching the steering wheel or pedals once, using Full Self-Driving through varied weather and traffic conditions. The video frames this as a largely unnoticed milestone that signals a fundamental shift in transportation and civilization, not merely a novelty demo.

2. **Elon's History of Missed FSD Timelines:** The video documents a pattern of missed autonomous driving promises: in April 2019, Elon Musk predicted 1 million robotaxis on the road by 2020 (result: zero); he predicted half the US population would have robotaxi access by end of 2025 (result: a small ~10-vehicle pilot fleet in South Austin launched in June 2025); and on the Q4 2021 earnings call in January 2022, he said he would "be shocked if we do not achieve Full Self-Driving safer than a human this year" — referring to 2022 — which did not materialize in 2022, 2023, 2024, or 2025.

3. **Grok Natively Integrated into Tesla Vehicles:** Grok, the AI model from SpaceX AI (formerly xAI, which merged with SpaceX in February 2026 per the video), has been integrated natively into Tesla vehicles via a software update, connecting the car platform directly to the AI intelligence layer.

## Robotaxi
1. **Austin Robotaxi Pilot Launch:** What materialized from Elon's earlier promise of broad robotaxi access by end of 2025 was a small pilot fleet of approximately 10 vehicles operating in South Austin, launched in June 2025. The video treats this as a real but dramatically scaled-down delivery relative to the original promise.

2. **Las Vegas Loop as Commercial Robotaxi Proof Point:** The Boring Company is already deploying Tesla's Full Self-Driving technology commercially in the Las Vegas Loop, with paying customers riding in self-driving Teslas through tunnels today. The video uses this as evidence that the robotaxi use case has moved beyond pilot testing into revenue-generating deployment.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Jason Calcanis's Optimus Lab Visit:** Around CES in January 2026, investor and All-In podcast host Jason Calcanis visited Tesla's Optimus Lab on a Sunday and posted on X: "I can tell you now, nobody will remember that Tesla ever made a car. They'll only remember the Optimus robot." Elon Musk replied on X: "probably true" — the founder of a trillion-dollar-plus car company publicly agreeing that cars would not be his legacy.

2. **Fremont Factory Transition to Optimus:** Tesla is actively converting its Fremont, California factory from building the Model S and Model X to manufacturing Optimus robots, reflecting a strategic reorientation of the company's core manufacturing identity.

3. **Optimus Production Targets:** Tesla is targeting 1 million Optimus robots per year out of its Fremont facility and 10 million units per year out of Giga Texas. The video notes that once robots can build other robots fully autonomously, the cost per unit is expected to fall further.

4. **Optimus Labor Economics:** At scale, Optimus is projected to cost between $1.50 and $2.00 per hour to operate, compared to approximately $46 per hour for an American worker — a dramatic labor cost differential that underpins the thesis that physical labor is approaching free.

5. **Tesla Reframed as a Humanoid Robot Company:** The video argues Tesla is best understood as a humanoid robot company that uses cars as a training vehicle for the AI that will eventually run Optimus robots — not primarily as an automotive company.

## Energy
1. **Tesla Energy Megapacks Powering AI Infrastructure:** Tesla Energy Megapacks are being used to power SpaceX AI's data centers, which train the AI models that improve Tesla's products, which generate more sales, which fund more data center capacity — described as a self-reinforcing loop between the energy and intelligence layers.

2. **Solar Cost Collapse:** Solar panel costs have fallen from $106 per watt in 1976 to approximately $0.20 per watt today — a 99% decline — making solar the cheapest energy source on the planet and still declining. The video frames this as one of three simultaneous convergences (alongside AI cost collapse and robotic labor cost collapse) that are undermining the scarcity assumptions of the current economic system.

3. **Starlink Antennas in Tesla Roofs:** Tesla has filed a patent called "vehicle roof assembly with radio frequency transparent material," which the video describes as embedding Starlink antennas directly into every Tesla vehicle's roof, natively connecting each car to SpaceX's satellite network and ensuring uniform connectivity from rural Montana to urban Manhattan.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Model Y as the World's Best-Selling Car:** The Model Y is described as the best-selling car in the world — not just the best-selling EV — for three consecutive years as of the video's publication, costs less than the average new car price in the United States, and now drives itself via Full Self-Driving.

2. **Tesla's Near-Bankruptcy During Model 3 Ramp:** The host, a former Tesla employee, describes firsthand the 2018 Model 3 production hell: Tesla built a production line under a tent in the Fremont parking lot, was burning $6,500 per minute, Elon Musk was sleeping on the factory floor, and the company's survival balanced on a knife's edge in late Q2 2018. The video uses this as a template for understanding how Musk operates — near-catastrophic execution followed by eventual paradigm-level delivery.

## Market & Competition
1. **Anthropic Renting Compute from SpaceX AI:** In May 2026, Anthropic — widely regarded as the builder of the best AI models in the world and Elon Musk's direct AI competitor — was announced as the first major external customer for SpaceX AI's Colossus supercomputer. The video frames this as extraordinary: a frontier AI competitor forced to rent compute from a company nobody considers an AI infrastructure provider, because there is simply not enough available compute elsewhere.

2. **SpaceX AI / xAI Merger and Colossus Supercomputer:** xAI merged with SpaceX in February 2026 (per the video) and was rebranded as SpaceX AI. In 2025, SpaceX AI spent nearly $8 billion in the first 9 months and built the Colossus supercomputer — described at the time as the world's largest AI supercomputer — in 122 days, then doubled it to 200,000 GPUs in another 92 days.

3. **AI Inference Cost Collapse:** ChatGPT-4-level inference cost approximately $36 per million tokens at launch in early 2023 and fell to under $1 per million tokens by 2025 for equivalent capability — a 36x cost reduction in roughly two years. DeepSeek's R1 model was trained for approximately $6 million while American labs were spending hundreds of millions for comparable performance. The video argues AI cost curves are steeper than Moore's Law and show no signs of flattening.

4. **Keyman Risk — Elon Musk:** The video identifies Elon Musk as the single biggest risk to the entire system. Without him, Tesla remains a strong car and energy company and SpaceX retains Gwynne Shotwell for operations — but the cross-company integration strategy and the long-range vision connecting all pieces to a Mars colony in three decades would be lost. The video calls this "the biggest keyman risk of any company in the history of business."

5. **Terafab Chip Foundry:** Tesla and SpaceX are building a chip foundry called Terafab targeting production of between 100 and 200 billion custom AI chips per year — representing roughly one full terawatt of compute power annually, described as approximately the size of the entire US electrical grid. Approximately 80% of that output is earmarked for space applications.

6. **Starship Cost to Orbit:** The cost to put 1 kilogram into orbit on the Space Shuttle was between $10,000 and $54,000. Falcon 9 brought that down to approximately $2,700. Starship's target is $10 to $100 per kilogram — a 30x to 300x reduction from Falcon 9 prices and over 1,000x cheaper than where the industry was a decade ago.

7. **Starlink Scale:** Starlink has over 10,000 satellites in orbit today, with FCC filings for up to 1 million. New V3 satellites deliver 1 terabit per second of bandwidth each, with 60 fitting into a single Starship. SpaceX is targeting approximately 6,000 V3 deployments per year. Monthly subscribers exceed 10 million and annual revenue exceeds $10 billion.

Notable quotes and data:
- David Moss drove 13,000 miles coast-to-coast in January 2026 using FSD without touching the steering wheel or pedals.
- Elon on Q4 2021 earnings call: "I would be shocked if we do not achieve full self-driving safer than a human this year" (referring to 2022 — did not materialize through 2025).
- Elon on missed timelines: "I know people say I'm the boy who cried wolf, but I'm telling you, there is a damn wolf."
- Jason Calcanis after visiting Optimus Lab, January 2026: "I can tell you now, nobody will remember that Tesla ever made a car. They'll only remember the Optimus robot."
- Elon's reply to Calcanis: "probably true."
- Elon at Davos, January 2026: stated there would be "more robots than people" in the near future and that robots and AI would "saturate human needs to the point you wouldn't be able to think of something to ask for."
- Elon on X, February 2026: "That's why I say the system won't use dollars as currency in the future. Just mass and energy."
- Tesla burning $6,500 per minute during the Model 3 production ramp in 2018.
- SpaceX caught a 20-story, 275-ton booster with two metal arms ("chopsticks") on the first attempt in October 2024.
- Optimus operating cost at scale: ~$1.50–$2.00/hour vs. ~$46/hour for an American worker.
- Tesla targeting 1 million Optimus/year from Fremont, 10 million/year from Giga Texas.
- Terafab targeting 100–200 billion custom AI chips per year; ~80% earmarked for space.
- AI inference: ~$36/million tokens in early 2023 → under $1/million tokens by 2025 (36x reduction).
- DeepSeek R1 trained for ~$6 million vs. hundreds of millions for comparable US lab models.
- Solar: $106/watt in 1976 → ~$0.20/watt today (99% decline).
- Starlink: 10,000+ satellites, 10M+ monthly subscribers, $10B+ annual revenue, FCC filing for up to 1 million satellites.
- Anthropic announced as first major external compute customer of SpaceX AI's Colossus in May 2026.
- Colossus built in 122 days; doubled to 200,000 GPUs in another 92 days; ~$8B spent by SpaceX AI in first 9 months of 2025.
- Starship cost target: $10–$100/kg to orbit vs. $2,700/kg for Falcon 9.

2026-06-03.title: Tesla's Mystery Vehicle Just Appeared In Fremont
2026-06-03.body:
This episode of FutureAzA, hosted by Brian with guest Mark from Tesla Life, covers two main topics: a mysterious camouflaged vehicle spotted testing at Tesla's Fremont facility (theorized to be the Model Y Long/stretched variant, or "Model Y L"), and Tesla's early move to claim 10% of Canada's Chinese EV import quota. The video is relatively light on hard data, blending news commentary with audience Q&A and a recurring "Wrong Answers Only" comedy segment about how Ford could theoretically build a sub-$30,000 electric pickup truck.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Camouflaged vehicle at Fremont test track — likely Model Y L:** New footage captured by a creator named "Servants Life" (formerly "Met God in Wilderness") shows a camouflage-wrapped vehicle testing at Tesla's Fremont facility. Brian and Mark dismiss speculation that it is the Model Q and instead theorize it is the Model Y L — a longer, stretched version of the Model Y with three usable rows. Brian notes that Elon previously said this vehicle might be seen "at the end of '26, if at all," but argues the word "might" was the critical qualifier, not "if at all," and that he himself predicted it would appear in the first half of 2026. He describes the car as having proven very popular in every market where it has been released, making it "truly insane" not to bring it to the US market. The camo wrapping includes what appears to be a chrome-look element on the rear quarter that Mark notes doesn't correspond to any known production Tesla — consistent with disguise wrapping rather than a design feature.

2. **Model Y L interior practicality — third-row adult usability:** Mark and Brian discuss the demand case for the Model Y L, noting that the current North American Model Y's third row is unusable for adults or older teenagers due to severe legroom constraints. They reference YouTuber Kyle Connor (6'2") demonstrating that he could sit in all three rows of the Model Y L — front, second, and third — without repositioning any seats, making the case that the stretched wheelbase genuinely resolves the usability problem rather than merely adding token space.

3. **Ford sub-$30,000 electric truck skepticism:** A recurring segment examines whether Ford can realistically produce a sub-$30,000 electric pickup truck. Brian and Mark are broadly skeptical, noting that the last time Ford sold a profitable ~$30,000 truck was the F-150 work edition prior to approximately 2015 (roughly 11 years prior to the video's publish date). The Ford Lightning was sold at $39,000 briefly but at a significant loss. Brian notes that a small-battery truck (estimated 150–200 miles of range) creates real utility concerns — while 20–80% charge times remain reasonable, the total usable range is limited. He expresses cautious optimism but expects the first editions to carry a premium price targeting early adopters, consistent with standard industry ramp economics.

4. **Nissan and BYD entering the Canadian EV market:** Nissan is described as looking to enter Canada's Chinese EV import quota program with its Chinese-manufactured EVs, benefiting from its existing Canadian dealership network. BYD and other Chinese EV brands are expected to have showrooms open across Canada by the end of 2026, which would also presumably function as service centers.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla claims 10% of Canada's Chinese EV import quota:** Canada replaced a 100% punitive surtax on Chinese-made EVs with a structured quota system in January 2026. Tesla has already claimed approximately 10% of the available import allocation for the first half of 2026. Brian and Mark attribute this to Tesla's preparedness — existing shipping infrastructure, no new certification requirements, and vehicles that could be sold immediately upon arrival. Inventory from Giga Shanghai is reported to already be sitting on dedicated Tesla lots in Ottawa, Toronto, and Montreal ahead of imminent deliveries.

2. **Legacy automaker EV strategy criticized as unsustainable:** Brian and Mark argue that legacy automakers' pattern of launching a version-one EV product, achieving moderate success, and then retreating is fundamentally self-defeating. They suggest that if Tesla is moving toward an autonomous future, legacy automakers are already approximately 10 years behind — and that Nvidia's narrative of a plug-in autonomous solution is not credible without the underlying continuous development investment Tesla has made.

Notable quotes and data:
- Brian: "When Elon said last year we'll see it at the end of '26 if at all... 'might' is the critical word. It could come at any time."
- Kyle Connor (6'2") fit in all three rows of the Model Y L without adjusting seat positions.
- Canada replaced a 100% surtax on Chinese EVs with a quota system in January 2026; Tesla has claimed ~10% of the H1 2026 allocation.
- Tesla inventory from Giga Shanghai reportedly already sitting on dedicated lots in Ottawa, Toronto, and Montreal.
- BYD and other Chinese EV brands expected to have Canadian showrooms open by end of 2026.
- Last Ford truck at or near $30,000 profitably: F-150 work edition, approximately pre-2015 (~11 years ago).
- Ford Lightning briefly sold at ~$39,000 as a loss leader.
- Slate truck expected to reveal pricing "in a few weeks" from publish date (i.e., around June 2026).
- Brian predicts a Model Y L launch in the US in the first half of 2026.

2026-06-03.title: Did Nvidia Just TAKE OVER The Global PC Market?
2026-06-03.body:
This video from Jo Bhakdi covers Nvidia's announcement at a Taiwan event where CEO Jensen Huang (referred to as "Yansen Wang" in the transcript) unveiled the RTX Spark chip and a new line of AI-capable personal computers built in partnership with MediaTek and Microsoft. Bhakdi's core thesis is that this launch represents a fundamental reinvention of the PC market, dramatically expanding Nvidia's total addressable market and cementing its dominance in AI compute — now extending from data centers to edge and home computing.

## Market & Competition

1. **Nvidia RTX Spark chip announcement:** Jensen Huang unveiled the N1X chip, branded as RTX Spark, described as the product of 33 years of Nvidia development. The chip features a Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores, one petaflop of AI performance, a custom 20-core Grace CPU built in partnership with MediaTek, 128 GB of unified memory, a TSMC 3-nanometer process, and 70 billion transistors. It is designed to run the full Nvidia software stack — including CUDA applications spanning digital biology, seismic processing, astrophysics, genomics, AI, and computer graphics — as well as all Windows applications.

2. **Microsoft partnership and agentic Windows platform:** The chip was developed in close collaboration with Microsoft over approximately three years, resulting in a Windows platform optimized for AI agents. Huang indicated a joint appearance with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella was planned for the following night. Bhakdi frames this as bringing AGI and agentic intelligence directly into consumers' homes via personal computers.

3. **PC market TAM expansion thesis:** Bhakdi argues this announcement will effectively double the total addressable market for home computing — laptops and desktops. He contends average computer prices will rise from roughly $900 to $2,000 or more, with premium configurations reaching $3,000–$4,000. He estimates Nvidia will capture approximately half of that incremental revenue, representing a massive expansion of both market size and Nvidia's margins beyond its existing data center business.

4. **Edge compute and free local AI tokens:** Bhakdi highlights that running AI inference locally on these devices means tokens are effectively free for the end user, removing the per-token cost associated with cloud-based AI services. He views this as a compelling enough value proposition for consumers to justify the higher hardware prices, and notes it also represents a form of distributed compute that could alleviate some energy demands at scale.

5. **Nvidia stock and personal investment position:** Bhakdi states Nvidia is his second-largest holding after Tesla and expresses strong conviction, indicating he plans to double down. He cited Nvidia's price-to-earnings ratio as "super low" and described it as one of the most undervalued stocks given its cash generation. He predicted Nvidia stock would reach $300 during the current year (2026), noting it was already up approximately 6% on the Monday prior to recording (with the stock trading around $226 at time of recording on Tuesday, June 3, 2026).

6. **Apple competitive pressure:** Bhakdi asserts that Apple will be forced to adopt Nvidia chips in response to this announcement, arguing Apple cannot independently develop chips competitive with Nvidia at this level. He predicts Apple will eventually announce adoption of similar chips, which he expects to be bullish for Apple's stock, though he acknowledges Apple's historically slow technology adoption cycle could mean a delay of approximately one year.

Notable quotes and data:
- Jensen Huang: "We're reinventing the personal computer."
- Jensen Huang: "Every single application Nvidia has ever created and every single application that Windows has ever run."
- RTX Spark / N1X chip specs: Blackwell RTX GPU, 6,144 CUDA cores, 1 petaflop AI performance, 20-core Grace CPU (MediaTek partnership), 128 GB unified memory, TSMC 3nm process, 70 billion transistors
- Bhakdi: "If the average computer now costs maybe 900 bucks, it will cost 2,000 next year."
- Bhakdi: "Nvidia will take half of that."
- Nvidia stock up ~6% on Monday (June 2, 2026); trading around $226 at time of recording (Tuesday, June 3, 2026)
- Bhakdi's price target: $300 for Nvidia in 2026
- Bhakdi: Nvidia is his second-largest holding after Tesla
- Microsoft–Nvidia collaboration on RTX Spark spanned approximately 3 years

2026-06-03.title: Daily X Summary (2026-06-03)
2026-06-03.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts are dominated by strong global EV demand signals for Tesla, with record sales in Australia, dominant market share in Norway, and robust China wholesale volumes in May 2026. Secondary themes include Cybertruck supply/demand dynamics — used inventory selling out rapidly alongside lengthening new order lead times — and a minor software update (dashcam viewer). No Robotaxi, FSD, Optimus, or Financials news of note today; the overall signal is modestly bullish on EV demand fundamentals.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Record Tesla Sales in Australia (May 2026):** Tesla posted its highest-ever single-month sales total in Australia in May 2026, delivering 6,433 vehicles — surpassing the previous all-time record of 6,017 set in March 2024. The Model Y was the #1 best-selling EV overall, accounting for 5,605 of those deliveries, or roughly 84% of Tesla's Australian May volume. This is a meaningful demand data point heading into Q2 2026 delivery reporting.

2. **Tesla Dominates Norway in May 2026:** Tesla was the best-selling car brand in Norway in May, capturing 21.5% of all new car sales. The Model Y alone represented 1 in every 5 new vehicles sold in the country during the month. Norway's overall EV market share reached 97.8%, with only 150 gas and diesel cars sold — underscoring Tesla's continued dominance in the world's most EV-saturated market.

3. **Tesla China Wholesale Volume Surges in May 2026:** Tesla China's wholesale volume reached 85,982 vehicles in May 2026, up 39% year-over-year and the highest monthly figure recorded so far this year. The post notes Tesla's cumulative 2026 pace is outrunning both 2024 and 2025, suggesting sustained momentum in the critical China market despite ongoing competitive pressure there.

4. **Cybertruck Demand/Supply Dynamics — Used Inventory Sells Out, New Lead Times Lengthen:** Tesla began officially selling used Cybertrucks directly from its inventory, with prices starting at $66,200 for a used Foundation Series with 2,566 miles, and delivery available to any continental U.S. Tesla location for up to $2,500. The entire used inventory sold out within roughly one day of listing. Concurrently, estimated delivery dates for new Cybertruck Premium AWD orders have pushed out to September–October 2026 — extending from August–September the prior week and July–August before that, implying a 4–5 month wait. Sawyer Merritt attributes this to Tesla prioritizing production of another (unspecified) vehicle. Used Foundation Series units come with 3 free months of FSD (Supervised), 3 months of Supercharging, and 3 months of Premium Connectivity; non-Foundation Series used units receive 1-month free trials of each. The rapid sell-through of used inventory alongside elongating new lead times suggests strong net demand for the Cybertruck platform.

5. **Kazakhstan Expanding Cybertruck Emergency Fleet:** Kazakhstan's emergency response ministry announced plans to purchase additional Cybertrucks following positive results from an existing deployment. Officials cited the vehicle's "high efficiency in responding to various emergency situations." While not a large volume signal, it adds to the emerging use case of Cybertruck in government/fleet applications internationally.

6. **Tesla Software Update 2026.20 — Web-Based Dashcam Viewer:** Tesla released update 2026.20, which introduces a web-based dashcam viewer. Recordings are automatically encrypted by default using a key tied to the owner's Tesla account; owners can opt out. Encrypted recordings cannot be played back outside the account ecosystem. Low signal for investors but relevant as a product/software development data point.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — Strong May 2026 demand data across three major markets (Australia record, Norway dominance, China +39% YoY) alongside rapid Cybertruck used inventory sell-through collectively reinforce healthy EV demand heading into Q2 2026 delivery reporting.

2026-06-03.title: Do Not Buy This Model Y?  4680 '8L' Battery Pack Investigated
2026-06-03.body:
This video by Jordan Giesige of The Limiting Factor investigates claims made by several outlets that the European Model Y equipped with the new 4680 "8L" battery pack charges extremely slowly and should not be purchased. After reviewing two sets of real-world charging test data, Jordan concludes that the 8L pack's charge rate is roughly in line with Tesla's other battery packs — slightly worse than the best 2170 packs, but well within acceptable limits — and that the alarming headlines appear to stem primarily from poor testing methodology rather than a fundamental flaw in the battery.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Background and timeline of the 8L battery pack:** In January 2026, the X account Eivissa — known for sourcing battery information from European regulatory filings — reported that Tesla was introducing a European Model Y with a new battery pack coded YB8LR, which the Tesla community shortened to the "8L" battery pack. Tesla confirmed the launch of a new trim called the Standard Long Range Rear Wheel Drive Model Y within three days. At the Q4 2025 earnings call, Tesla confirmed they were beginning to use the 4680 cell in non-structural battery packs, and at the Q1 2026 earnings call they confirmed that Giga Berlin had launched a Model Y battery pack using their in-house 4680 cell. A key open question remains whether the specific 4680 cell used is the Generation 2 "Cybercell" (also used in the Cybertruck) or the newer, fully dry electrode version.

2. **Two trim versions complicate the picture:** Jordan notes that there appear to be two versions of the Model Y equipped with the 8L battery pack. The original Standard Long Range Rear Wheel Drive trim was seemingly discontinued in early spring 2026 and replaced with a Premium Long Range Rear Wheel Drive trim, with the battery pack designation remaining the same but other aspects of the trim (such as the entertainment system) being upgraded. This matters because Tesla could theoretically change the 4680 cell version within the same pack designation, potentially affecting charging results, and because different WLTP range figures (ranging from 609 to 657 km depending on wheel and tire options) were listed during this period, adding to the confusion.

3. **8L pack specifications and energy density comparison:** The 8L battery pack contains 828 cells — the same cell count as the original Gen 1 4680 pack produced in Austin and deployed in the Model Y in 2022. Usable energy capacity increased from 67.5 kWh (Gen 1) to 74 kWh, and total capacity from 71.6 kWh to 79 kWh. Pack weight decreased slightly from 452 kg to 447 kg. This yields a pack-level energy density improvement of roughly 11–12%, from 149 Wh/kg usable / 158 Wh/kg total (Gen 1) to 166 Wh/kg usable / 177 Wh/kg total (8L). For comparison, the best recently upgraded 2170 packs from Panasonic and LG Chem reach approximately 177 Wh/kg usable and 188 Wh/kg total, meaning the 8L pack is about 6% behind the best available packs on energy density and therefore range.

4. **Cell-level energy density matches the Cybertruck's Cybercell:** With 828 cells and a total pack capacity of 79 kWh, each cell in the 8L pack works out to approximately 95.4 Wh. The cells measured in the Cybertruck came in at 95.2 Wh, which Jordan notes is effectively identical given variances in cells and testing conditions. This is one of two lines of evidence he uses to argue that the 8L pack uses the same Generation 2 Cybercell as the Cybertruck.

5. **Elektro Ronny's charging tests and the methodology problem:** The most widely cited negative review came from a YouTube creator called Elektro Ronny, whose first test (posted February 24, 2026) recorded a peak charge rate of only 130 kW — roughly half the advertised 250 kW maximum. Jordan's view is that this result is best explained by the battery not being properly preconditioned before the test. A follow-up test Ronny posted about a week later used proper preconditioning but started at 31% state of charge rather than below 10%, meaning the peak charge rate window was missed. Despite this, the second test achieved 155 kW at 32% state of charge, which Jordan describes as much better than the first-generation 4680 pack, though not as strong as most Model 3 and Model Y vehicles.

6. **Fabrizio (Lampi di Tesla) provides the definitive charging dataset:** Italian automotive content creator Fabrizio, who runs the YouTube and X accounts "Lampi di Tesla" and was an FSD beta tester, was given a press vehicle by Tesla Italy. He provided Jordan with full documentation including the vehicle registration confirming the YB8LR battery pack designation, the matching licence plate number, and the complete unedited charging video. Fabrizio drove the vehicle down to 7% state of charge with active preconditioning, then charged at a Supercharger starting at 8:22 PM on March 1st, 2026, with an ambient temperature of 13°C (55°F). The charging power quickly ramped to 250 kW at 7% state of charge and tapered to 63 kW by 82% state of charge.

7. **C-rate comparison reveals the 8L pack and Cybertruck use the same cell:** Fabrizio normalized the charging curves of the 8L Model Y pack and the Cybertruck pack by c-rate (rather than absolute power) to account for the Cybertruck's much larger pack size. The two curves showed a "surprisingly similar fingerprint," which Jordan treats as strong evidence that both packs use the same 4680 cell — corroborating the energy density calculation. When plotted against other European Model Y battery packs (two LG 2170 packs and a CATL LFP pack), Fabrizio's properly preconditioned 8L result fell below the LG 2170 packs but was described by Jordan as within acceptable limits for most EV buyers.

8. **Debunking the two main criticisms of the 8L charge rate:** Jordan addresses two recurring arguments that the 4680 should be performing better. First, he pushes back on the claim that Tesla is falling dangerously behind competitors on charging speed, arguing that this reflects the preferences of a small, vocal group rather than the priorities of most EV buyers, who weight factors like value for money, safety, charging network reliability, and connectivity more heavily. He also notes that Tesla's efficiency advantage means their vehicles still rank well on miles of range added per minute. Second, he disputes the claim that Tesla promised faster charging for the 4680 due to the tabless electrode design; he states the tabless electrode was introduced to allow the cell to be made larger while maintaining the same thermal and charging characteristics, and to reduce manufacturing costs — not to improve charge speed.

Notable quotes and data:
- Gen 1 4680 pack: 828 cells, 67.5 kWh usable / 71.6 kWh total, 452 kg, 149 Wh/kg usable / 158 Wh/kg total
- 8L 4680 pack: 828 cells, 74 kWh usable / 79 kWh total, 447 kg, 166 Wh/kg usable / 177 Wh/kg total
- Energy density improvement Gen 1 → 8L: roughly 11–12%
- Best 2170 packs (Panasonic/LG Chem): ~177 Wh/kg usable / ~188 Wh/kg total; 8L is roughly 6% behind
- Cell energy density: 8L pack cells ≈ 95.4 Wh each; Cybertruck cells measured at 95.2 Wh each
- Elektro Ronny first test peak: 130 kW (likely no preconditioning)
- Elektro Ronny second test: 155 kW at 32% state of charge (preconditioned but partial charge)
- Fabrizio's test: ramped to 250 kW at 7% state of charge; 63 kW at 82%; ambient temp 13°C; March 1, 2026
- WLTP range for 8L Model Y variants: 609–657 km depending on wheel/tire options
- "It's not the fastest charging battery cell on the market, but it's a good all-around performer, and will improve because it's still only the 2nd version of Tesla's 4680 battery cell."

2026-06-03.title: The Tesla SpaceX Merger is INSANE!
2026-06-03.body:
This episode of The Tesla Space covers three major topics: the growing speculation around a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger driven by shared AI and robotics ambitions, Tesla's new lens-cleaning patent that resembles a mechanical eye (with implications for both Cybercab and Optimus), and the latest Optimus manufacturing developments at Giga Texas. The video's core thesis is that Tesla and SpaceX are not merely partners but are converging into a single strategic enterprise centered on artificial intelligence, robotics, and ultimately Mars colonization. A brief segment also discusses whether Tesla might one day build a Model 3 Plaid.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla-SpaceX Merger Speculation:** According to people familiar with the conversations, Elon Musk has seriously discussed a merger between Tesla and SpaceX with his most trusted colleagues, and the idea is reportedly discussed openly inside Tesla. The video argues the merger is less a surprise than it might seem, given how intertwined the two companies have already become over several years.

2. **Deep Financial Entanglement Between Tesla and SpaceX:** The SpaceX prospectus, filed ahead of what the video describes as potentially the largest stock market debut in history, revealed that SpaceX purchased roughly $697 million worth of Tesla Megapack battery systems in 2024 and 2025 to power AI data centers connected to XAI's Colossus facilities in Memphis, as well as $131 million in Cybertruck purchases during the same period. Tesla also invested $2 billion into XAI earlier in 2026, shortly after which XAI merged with SpaceX. In 2024, Nvidia redirected a $500 million GPU order from Tesla to XAI at Elon Musk's personal request. Suppliers have reportedly begun treating Tesla and SpaceX as a single customer.

3. **Terafab — A Joint Semiconductor Venture:** In March 2026, Elon Musk announced the Terafab, a joint semiconductor fabrication project with an initial facility being built in Texas near the Austin Gigafactory. One side of the project serves Tesla's needs — including FSD, Optimus, and future vehicle programs — while the other is aimed at SpaceX's long-term vision for computing infrastructure in space. The video frames Terafab as something neither company could have justified building independently.

4. **Shared AI Engineering Challenges as the Underlying Driver:** The video argues that Tesla and SpaceX face surprisingly similar engineering constraints — running powerful AI systems with tight limits on power consumption, cooling, reliability, and cost — Tesla inside a moving vehicle and SpaceX in orbit. This convergence of technical problems makes the same expertise in chips, power systems, and AI valuable to both organizations, providing a structural logic for deeper integration beyond financial ties.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus as a "Von Neumann Probe":** Elon Musk reportedly described Optimus as a Von Neumann probe — a concept from physicist John Von Neumann referring to a self-replicating machine that can build copies of itself from raw materials, enabling exponential growth without additional human labor. The video quotes Musk on X as saying "Optimus will be the first Von Neumann machine capable of building civilization by itself on any viable planet," positioning the robot as central to SpaceX's Mars settlement ambitions.

2. **Dedicated Optimus Factory Construction Begins at Giga Texas:** Construction officially began this week on Tesla's dedicated Optimus manufacturing facility at Giga Texas, with drone footage captured by longtime factory observer Joe Tegtmeyer showing the first steel structure now standing at the site. When completed, the building is expected to stretch nearly the full length of the main Giga Texas factory, making it one of the largest manufacturing facilities Tesla has ever built. Tesla's stated target is production of approximately 10 million Optimus units per year at the facility, equating to roughly 27,000 units per day.

3. **Mechanical Eye Patent — Implications for Optimus:** Tesla was granted a patent for a lens cleaning system that, while never using the words "eye," "blink," or "tear," features a dark circular lens resembling a pupil, a housing shaped like an eye socket, a cleaning nozzle positioned where a tear duct would be, and two curved wiper blades resembling eyelids. The system continuously monitors image quality and, upon detecting degradation, automatically sprays cleaning fluid and sweeps debris with a wiper plate — completing the full cycle in under one second. Since Tesla has confirmed that Optimus shares camera hardware with its vehicles, the video argues that robots operating in real-world environments will eventually require the same self-cleaning capability.

## Autonomous Driving / Robotaxi

1. **Lens Cleaning Patent Critical for Unsupervised Robotaxi Operation:** The video emphasizes that the lens cleaning system is especially important for robotaxi deployment because, unlike a human driver, a robotaxi cannot pull over to wipe a dirty lens. Tesla has already been spotted testing camera cleaning systems on robotaxi vehicles and Cybercab prototypes, suggesting the technology is closer to production than a newly granted patent might indicate.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Model 3 Plaid — A Dream Deferred:** Tesla VP of vehicle engineering Lars Morvi, appearing on the Ride the Lightning podcast, said when asked about a potential tri-motor Plaid version of the Model 3: "I think about it all the time. I think about carbon sleeves, all the permanent magnets. I definitely think about it." Morvi described it as a "work-forward situation," citing packaging constraints in the smaller Model 3 chassis as the primary challenge. The video notes that Tesla recently retired the Model S and Model X, effectively retiring the Plaid badge with them, and that the next-generation Roadster will not be accessible to most buyers, leaving a performance gap. The current Model 3 Performance hits 0–60 mph in approximately 2.9 seconds; a Plaid version could push that significantly further.

---

**Notable quotes and data:**
- SpaceX purchased ~$697 million in Tesla Megapack systems in 2024–2025 (per SpaceX prospectus)
- SpaceX purchased ~$131 million in Cybertrucks during the same period (per SpaceX prospectus)
- Tesla invested $2 billion into XAI earlier in 2026; XAI subsequently merged with SpaceX
- Nvidia redirected a $500 million GPU order from Tesla to XAI at Elon Musk's request (2024)
- Terafab announced March 2026, located near Austin Gigafactory
- Optimus factory target: ~10 million units/year (~27,000/day)
- Lens cleaning cycle completes in under 1 second
- Lars Morvi on Model 3 Plaid: *"I think about it all the time. I think about carbon sleeves, all the permanent magnets. I definitely think about it."*
- Elon Musk on X: *"Optimus will be the first Von Neumann machine capable of building civilization by itself on any viable planet."*
- Elon Musk posted in November 2025 that his companies are "trending towards convergence"
- Elon Musk's SpaceX compensation is tied to establishing a permanent human settlement on Mars with at least 1 million inhabitants
- Model 3 Performance: 0–60 mph in ~2.9 seconds

2026-06-04.title: Elon Musk Just Made 6 Moves That Proves He’s Brilliant
2026-06-04.body:
This video analyzes the amended SpaceX S-1A IPO filing and argues that six deliberate strategic moves embedded in the document reveal Elon Musk as an exceptionally sophisticated long-term operator. The presenter walks through each change in the filing, arguing that together they form a coherent, multi-layered strategy to protect mission continuity, reward loyalists, attract forced institutional buying, and keep maximum optionality — including a potential acquisition of Tesla. While the video is primarily about SpaceX, it carries direct implications for Tesla investors due to the acquisition language in the filing.

## Market & Competition

1. **Potential SpaceX Acquisition of Tesla via Equity Issuance:** The amended S-1A filing includes new language in the acquisitions and strategic transactions section stating SpaceX "may issue a significant amount of equity in connection with future transactions." The presenter interprets this as a deliberate signal — not boilerplate — that a large stock-funded acquisition could be forthcoming. The two most-cited targets are Tesla and Cursor (a developer coding tool). The presenter notes that Elon already folded xAI into SpaceX earlier in 2026, and that this filing language represents "the strongest hint yet" that Tesla could follow. However, the presenter explicitly cautions that the filing does not say Tesla is being acquired — only that the door is now open in writing.

2. **Anthropic Paying SpaceX ~$1.25 Billion Per Month for Compute:** The filing discloses that Anthropic — a direct competitor to xAI's Grok — is paying SpaceX approximately $1.25 billion per month for access to roughly 325,000 Nvidia GPUs, hyperscale-class CPUs, exabyte-scale storage, and high-speed networking. The total deal value is approximately $45 billion running through 2029. The presenter notes an earlier draft of the filing disclosed a lower GPU count of around 220,000, so the amendment revealed a larger footprint. Critically, either party can exit with 90 days' notice, which the presenter frames as intentional: Elon is monetizing idle compute while reserving the right to reclaim it for Grok the moment xAI needs it. The presenter characterizes this as "making the competition pay for his buildout."

3. **Index Rule Changes Creating Forced Institutional Buying:** As of May 1, 2026, Nasdaq updated its rules to allow newly listed companies ranking in the top 40 by market cap to join the Nasdaq 100 after just 15 trading days, eliminating the old minimum float requirement. For low-float stocks like SpaceX, a waiting multiplier of up to 3x effectively inflates the company's index weight beyond what its small tradable share base would normally earn. Separately, the S&P 500 opened a consultation in May 2026 proposing to cut the seasoning window from 12 months to 6 months for mega-cap IPOs and to waive the four-quarter profitability test for sufficiently large companies. FTSE Russell went further, proposing index eligibility after just five trading days for companies above the top 500 size threshold. The presenter frames this as a wall of automatic buying from index-tracking ETFs (QQQ, SPY, etc.) arriving on a predictable schedule — timed to absorb selling pressure from early holders and the no-lockup 5% directed share program.

4. **SpaceX Valuation and IPO Structure:** SpaceX is described as being valued at approximately $1.5 to $1.75 trillion, which the presenter characterizes as likely the largest IPO in history. Up to 5% of IPO shares have been reserved for selected employees and friends and family of executive officers, with no lockup period — meaning these holders can sell on day one. The presenter frames this as a deliberate loyalty mechanism, with participants selected at the discretion of executive officers (i.e., Elon and his leadership). Meanwhile, Elon himself agreed to a 366-day lockup on all of his shares with no early release provision — framed as a confidence signal to the market.

5. **Voting Control and Acquisition Power:** Elon owns approximately 42% of SpaceX's equity but controls approximately 85% of votes via a dual-class share structure — Class A shares (1 vote each, sold to the public) and Class B shares (10 votes each, held by Elon), with Elon holding roughly 93.6% of Class B stock. The filing also confirms that Elon can vote approximately 1 billion performance-based restricted shares granted in January 2026 — tied to market cap milestones across 15 tranches and to building a permanent human colony on Mars with at least 1 million people — before those shares have vested. The presenter argues that combined with the equity issuance language, this means Elon could unilaterally execute a Tesla acquisition using SpaceX stock without needing any other shareholder's approval.

6. **Float Restrictions and Worker Wealth Creation:** Over 60% of the company — approximately 7.8 billion shares — is restricted from immediate sale, with some holders locked up through the quarter ending June 2027. The presenter notes this limits selling pressure and stacks with forced index buying to support the post-IPO price. On the human side, the presenter highlights that SpaceX has historically paid lower cash salaries in exchange for richer equity — distributed not just to executives but to technicians, assembly crews, and floor workers at Starbase and Hawthorne. The IPO converts years of illiquid paper equity into real, sellable money. The presenter notes that executives like Gwen Shotwell and the CFO are crossing $1 billion each, but emphasizes that blue-collar workers who held equity for 5, 10, or 15 years are becoming millionaires. American Airlines was also added as a Starlink customer in this amended filing.

## Financials

1. **Grok/xAI Subscription Revenue Now Appearing in SpaceX Filings:** As of the end of 2025, SpaceX reported 4.1 million paid X Premium subscribers and approximately 900,000 paid Super Grok subscribers. The presenter notes this is the first time the AI subscription business has appeared in SpaceX's numbers, representing the beginning of real recurring revenue from the xAI side of the combined entity — alongside the rocket and satellite businesses.

2. **Underwriter Commission Waiver on Overallotment:** The investment banks running the IPO agreed to take no discount or commission on shares sold under the overallotment option, meaning that money stays with the company and its holders rather than going to Wall Street. The presenter flags this as an investor-friendly structural detail embedded in the filing.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX valued at approximately $1.5–$1.75 trillion (presenter's characterization of the IPO setup)
- Anthropic paying ~$1.25 billion/month; ~$45 billion total deal value through 2029
- ~325,000 Nvidia GPUs disclosed in amended filing (up from ~220,000 in earlier drafts)
- 90-day exit clause for either party in the Anthropic compute deal
- Elon controls ~85% of votes despite owning ~42% of equity
- Elon holds ~93.6% of Class B (10-vote) shares
- ~1 billion performance-based restricted shares that Elon can vote before vesting
- 366-day lockup on all of Elon's personal shares, with no early release
- Over 60% of shares (~7.8 billion) restricted from immediate sale
- Some holders locked until SpaceX reports results for the quarter ending June 2027
- 5% of IPO shares reserved for employees, friends, and family — no lockup
- 4.1 million paid X Premium subscribers (end of 2025)
- ~900,000 paid Super Grok subscribers (end of 2025)
- Nasdaq 100 fast-entry: top-40 market cap companies eligible after 15 trading days (effective May 1, 2026)
- S&P 500 consultation (May 2026): proposed cut of seasoning window from 12 months to 6 months for mega-cap IPOs
- FTSE Russell proposal: index eligibility after 5 trading days for companies above the top-500 size threshold
- Presenter on Elon's strategy: *"He's getting a rival to fund his data centers while he waits for his own AI to grow into them."*
- Presenter on Tesla acquisition risk: *"The language tells you the door is open. It does not tell you he's walking through it this year."*
- Presenter on voting control: *"The one person who decides has locked up the votes to do it without asking anyone."*

2026-06-04.title: The Biggest AI Companies Can't Escape SpaceX
2026-06-04.body:
This episode of the Cern Basher podcast features host Cern Basher and returning guest Phil Beisel covering a wide range of technology and investment topics centered on Tesla's FSD and robotaxi progress, the SpaceX IPO outlook, the explosive growth of AI compute demand, and a live demo of a networking app Phil Beisel built using AI-assisted coding tools. The core thesis is that SpaceX is the indispensable compute infrastructure company of the future — every major AI firm will eventually need SpaceX's orbital data centers and Starlink connectivity — and that Tesla's FSD and robotaxi deployment are quietly accelerating toward a tipping point that the market is not fully pricing in.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Performance and Personal Usage:** Cern Basher reports actively using FSD and building a usage streak, noting that on a recent drive the odometer read 1,433 miles. He expresses strong personal trust in the system, saying he "doesn't even bother looking at the road much at all." Phil Beisel corroborates this sentiment, stating he feels more confident in the car on the highway than in urban settings, noting the irony that Tesla historically worried about highway incidents due to higher speed consequences, yet the incident rate on divided highways with FSD appears low.

2. **FSD Driving Modes and Edge Cases:** Phil Beisel describes testing FSD in "Mad Max" mode on a mountain road near South San Jose, noting it was too aggressive for that environment and he dialed it back. He recounts FSD performing a hard brake for a bird crossing its path — an event he found slightly over-tuned — as well as braking for a snake on the road. He frames these as evidence of how well-calibrated the safety layer is, while acknowledging there are still preference and operational nuances to refine.

3. **Grok Voice Integration — Hardware Constraint on AI4:** Phil Beisel analyzes the challenge of integrating Grok voice commands natively into robotaxi vehicles. He explains that currently all Grok inference — voice recognition, speech-to-text, AI processing, and text-to-speech — is handled in the cloud, which is unreliable for a robotaxi service that may not have constant connectivity. He argues this workload cannot borrow compute cycles from FSD (running at approximately 36 frames per second) without degrading safety performance. He gives only a 20% probability that full voice integration is achievable on the current AI4 hardware platform, and states his expectation is that it will require the AI5 chip, at which point he believes hardware will be "fully capable."

## Robotaxi

1. **Unsupervised Robotaxi Expansion to Greater Austin Area:** Cern Basher cites Tesla's Ashok (referencing a public post) announcing that unsupervised robotaxi service is now available in the greater Austin area, describing it as "robotaxi the way it was intended starts in earnest today in Austin." Both hosts frame this as a pivotal moment, with Cern Basher predicting the market is "about to transition into what will be an explosion of these things" and that it will "hit everybody like a ton of bricks" given how close the program is to rounding its first year of operation.

2. **Unsupervised Robotaxis Operating on Highways:** A notable detail surfaced in the discussion is that unsupervised robotaxis are now operating on highways within the geofenced Austin area — not just surface streets. Both hosts find this significant given Tesla's historical caution around high-speed autonomous operation, and note the irony that FSD is in many ways more reliable on highway segments than in complex urban environments.

3. **Operational Nuances of Robotaxi Service:** Phil Beisel argues that the safety box for robotaxi is "largely checked" and that the remaining challenges are operational — specifically the seamless passenger experience around pickup/dropoff navigation, dynamic route adjustments, and in-vehicle communication. He uses the analogy of typical Uber driver conversations (e.g., "drop me at door nine, not door six") to illustrate how much ambient human supervision currently compensates for gaps that a driverless system must handle automatically. He frames Grok voice integration as the key unlock for making the in-vehicle robotaxi experience feel complete.

4. **Robotaxi Tracker and Data Density:** Cern Basher briefly references the robotaxi tracker website (RobotaxiTracker.com) as a public tool tracking fleet counts, and speculates about future AI-powered tools that could provide granular, real-time views of Cybercab density by intersection, cross-referenced with Waymo data and other public sources — framing this as an example of what democratized AI-powered analysis tools could deliver.

5. **Validation Coverage of Geofenced Areas:** Phil Beisel theorizes that Tesla has likely run every road segment, intersection, and decision point within its geofenced operating polygon hundreds of times through autonomous systems as part of its validation process, building a comprehensive traversal graph. He notes that situational variability (weather, pedestrians, obstructions) is the remaining challenge beyond static road topology.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus as a World-Model Data Collector:** Phil Beisel frames Optimus as ultimately one of the most important data-collection platforms for building world foundation models. He argues that current LLMs are trained on written text — an extremely condensed and filtered version of reality — whereas what AI truly needs is continuous, real-world visual observation data. He states that when Optimus is deployed at scale, it will be able to observe the world "on a constant, continuous basis" in ways that humans and current AI systems have barely scratched the surface of, enabling far richer world models than text-based training allows.

2. **Jensen Huang's Robot Capability Slide:** Cern Basher references a slide from Jensen Huang's annual presentation plotting robot capability against compute and data volume, progressing from TFLOP-level classical simulation through internet plus synthetic data, to world foundation models. Both hosts note with emphasis that "Tesla vision tech" appears in the top-right quadrant of the chart — the highest capability, highest compute position — validating Tesla's data-driven FSD approach as the leading edge of real-world robotics training data.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO Analysis — Historical IPO Comps:** Phil Beisel walks through a Market Watch table of major tech IPO performance, covering Facebook (down 45% at 3 months), Twitter (roughly flat at 12 months), Zoom (up 142% at 12 months), Uber (down 21% at 12 months), Palantir (up 153% at 12 months with a 53% drawdown), and Robinhood and Rivian (strong IPO period followed by decline). The average one-year return across the list was approximately 14%, with an average peak-to-trough drawdown of approximately 55% in the first year. Both hosts characterize the article's "scary chart" framing as purposefully negative clickbait, and suggest the more relevant question is 3–5 year performance.

2. **SpaceX as the Indispensable Compute Infrastructure Company:** Phil Beisel articulates the central thesis of the episode: every major AI company — Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, Apple — will ultimately need SpaceX to scale its compute. He argues that terrestrial chip production (including Terafab) will not be sufficient to close the compute supply-demand gap, that power availability on Earth is a binding constraint, and that orbital data centers with space-based solar arrays are not a fantasy but a necessity. He states: "Every single person in that capex chart has to come to SpaceX to get its business done."

3. **AI Capex Trajectory — Big Tech Spending:** Cern Basher presents a capex chart showing that Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, and Apple combined spent $165 billion in one recent year, rising to $268 billion the following year, then $468 billion in 2025. Projections show $785 billion for 2026 and just under $1 trillion for 2027, with the chart showing a flattening toward 2030 that both hosts dismiss as unrealistic given accelerating demand. Free cash flow for most companies on the list is projected to dip significantly during this period.

4. **Nvidia Vera Rubin — Early Adopters Signal Future Leaders:** Cern Basher highlights a Jensen Huang presentation slide showing early adopters of Nvidia's new Vera CPU (part of the Vera Rubin platform for agentic AI) as OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX. He interprets this as Jensen signaling the three fastest-growing companies of the next several years. Both hosts agree these will likely be the three largest IPOs of the next year. Phil Beisel notes the key distinction: OpenAI and Anthropic do not build data centers, while SpaceX is building both terrestrial and space-based data center infrastructure — meaning the former two must ultimately go through SpaceX for compute at scale.

5. **Anthropic–SpaceX Deal and OpenAI Competitive Risk:** Phil Beisel discusses Anthropic's deal to use SpaceX's Colossus data center, which he frames as strategically smart — effectively buying Anthropic an "e-ticket" into SpaceX's future orbital compute pipeline. He contrasts this with OpenAI, suggesting Sam Altman's company will be "starved out" of compute if it cannot secure a similar infrastructure relationship, drawing a parallel to Yahoo versus Google and Netscape versus Microsoft. He notes that Elon Musk previously referred to Anthropic as "Missanthropic" before the deal was announced, and expresses skepticism that a similar détente with OpenAI is forthcoming.

6. **Cursor AI and SpaceX Acquisition Option:** Phil Beisel mentions in passing that SpaceX holds an option to acquire Cursor AI, the coding platform he used to build his app, with a reported acquisition price of $60 billion and an option to walk away for $10 billion. He connects this to SpaceX/xAI's strategy of training Grok on coding data and techniques.

7. **Starlink as the Access Layer for Orbital Compute:** Phil Beisel argues that Starlink is not merely a consumer internet service but the access layer for future orbital compute infrastructure. He frames low-Earth-orbit satellites — currently around 10,000 and growing — as the connectivity backbone that will link users to space-based data centers, making terrestrial ISPs like Comcast progressively obsolete. He notes Starlink's round-trip ping to ground of approximately 17–18 milliseconds as evidence of the low latency that makes it viable for real-time applications.

Notable quotes and data:
- "Every single person in that capex chart has to come to SpaceX to get its business done. Every one of them."
- "We are absolutely categorically slamming into a compute demand curve supply gap."
- "Orbital data centers are absolutely required because we can't get enough compute on planet Earth."
- "Starlink is going to revolutionize the way we think about access to compute."
- "For the first time, I'm programming in a new programming language called English."
- "Unsupervised robotaxis are operating on the highways" within the Austin geofenced area.
- Phil Beisel gives 20% odds that full Grok voice integration is achievable on AI4 hardware.
- Combined Big Tech capex (Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, Apple): $468B in 2025, projected $785B in 2026, just under $1T in 2027.
- Average IPO drawdown in first year across the Market Watch comp set: ~55%; average one-year return: ~14%.
- Colossus data center: first cluster online in 121 days; Colossus 2 achieved in 91 days.
- Starlink satellites travel at approximately 17,000 miles per hour (~4.7 miles per second).
- Starlink Mini ping-to-ground measured at 17–18 milliseconds in live demo.
- SpaceX option to acquire Cursor AI: $60B acquisition price, $10B walk-away fee.
- FSD odometer reading cited by Cern Basher: 1,433 miles on current streak.
- Phil Beisel built his networking app (NetP) in approximately 3–4 weeks at ~3–4 hours/day using Cursor AI.

2026-06-04.title: Tesla hit with class action in Quebec over up to $400m in heat pump failures
2026-06-04.body:
A Quebec Tesla owner has filed a class action request against Tesla in Quebec's Superior Court, alleging the company's heat pump system constitutes a hidden defect under provincial consumer law. The suit could be worth up to $400 million and covers all Quebec owners of heat pump-equipped Tesla models.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Plaintiff's case and repair history:** Amélie Paquette purchased a 2021 Model 3 in December 2020 for $52,880. Her vehicle suffered three separate heat pump-related failures under warranty — sensor replacements, debris in the fan, and a full compressor/manifold replacement — before a smoke-accompanied failure on January 27, 2026, at 158,220 km rendered the full heat pump inoperable. Out-of-warranty, Tesla charged her $4,476.55. Tesla rejected both an in-person request for shared responsibility and a formal demand letter (refused by email March 17, 2026).

2. **Scope of the class action:** Filed by Perrier Avocats before Quebec's Superior Court, the suit targets all Quebec owners or lessees of heat pump-equipped Teslas: Model S (2021+), Model 3 (2021+), Model X (2021+), Model Y (2020+), and Cybertruck (2023+). It seeks repair cost reimbursement, purchase/lease price reductions, and punitive damages. The lawsuit argues Tesla, as a professional seller, is presumed to have known about the defect and failed to disclose it. It asserts vehicles of Tesla's price should last at least 10 years or 200,000 km without major failure.

3. **Regulatory and legal background:** NHTSA issued a recall covering certain 2021–2022 Model 3, Model Y, Model S, and Model X vehicles after confirming the heat pump problem compromised windshield defrosting, a federal safety violation. Transport Canada launched its own investigation after receiving over 170 complaints from Canadian owners, predominantly from Quebec. Tesla has previously faced authorized class actions in Quebec over paint defects and Premium Connectivity changes, and faces up to $14.5 billion in lawsuits across multiple jurisdictions. Out-of-warranty heat pump repairs in Canada typically cost $3,800–$4,700.

## Editorial Stance
The author calls the lawsuit "inevitable," citing Tesla's persistent heat pump reliability issues since 2021 and a recurring pattern of warranty-covered failures followed by expensive post-warranty bills. The author considers the suit's 10-year/200,000 km durability standard "entirely reasonable" and notes Quebec's consumer protection laws are among the strongest in North America.

Notable quotes and data:
- Repair cost paid by plaintiff: $4,476.55 CAD
- Vehicle purchase price: $52,880 CAD (2021 Model 3, purchased December 2020)
- Odometer at final failure: 158,220 km
- Warranty coverage: 4 years or 80,000 km
- Typical out-of-warranty heat pump repair cost in Canada: $3,800–$4,700
- Potential class action value: up to $400 million
- Transport Canada received over 170 complaints, majority from Quebec
- Elon Musk previously claimed a software update would fix the heat pump via valve recalibration; Tesla service centers attributed the issue to a hardware defect (ice-stuck flap/valve trapping refrigerant)

2026-06-04.title: SpaceX Makes Huge Announcement.
2026-06-04.body:
This video features Brett Johnson, SpaceX's Chief Financial Officer (and the only CFO the company has ever had), delivering a formal investor-facing presentation on SpaceX's business across three core segments: space launch, connectivity (Starlink), and AI infrastructure. The central thesis is that SpaceX's unrivaled vertical integration — from rocket manufacturing to satellite deployment to AI compute — positions it to capture a total addressable market exceeding $28 trillion across space, connectivity, and enterprise AI. The content is entirely focused on SpaceX and has no direct relevance to Tesla's autonomous driving, robotaxi, Optimus, or energy thesis.

## Market & Competition
1. **SpaceX's launch milestones and Starship roadmap:** Johnson outlines a series of industry firsts, including the first private liquid-fuel rocket to reach orbit (Falcon 1, 2008), first private docking with the International Space Station (2012), first propulsive landing of a rocket booster (2015), first reuse of an orbital-class booster (2017), and first private crewed launch to the ISS (2020). SpaceX completed 165 Falcon 9 launches in 2025. Starship version 3 is expected to carry approximately 100 metric tons to orbit, with version 4 already in design and targeting approximately 200 metric tons — a doubling of version 3's capacity.

2. **Starlink constellation scale and user growth:** SpaceX operates roughly 9,600 satellites, representing approximately 75% of all active maneuverable satellites in orbit. Starlink ended 2024 with approximately 4.4 million users, grew to approximately 8.9 million by end of 2025 (roughly 100% year-over-year growth), and reached approximately 10.3 million users by the end of Q1 2026. The network covers over 164 countries and territories, representing coverage for over 3 billion people.

3. **V3 satellite and Starship launch capacity step-change:** The current V2 Starlink satellites deliver 96 Gbits per second per satellite, with roughly 27 satellites per Falcon 9 launch. The upcoming V3 satellites represent a 20x improvement in capacity per launch relative to V2 on Falcon. On Starship, 60 V3 satellites per launch — each delivering roughly 1 terabit per second — equates to 61 terabits per second of downlink capacity per launch. Johnson states that after 20 Starship launches, SpaceX will be deploying 1.2 petabytes of capacity per year, positioning Starlink as a meaningful percentage of global internet traffic.

4. **Direct-to-device and Gen 2 expansion:** SpaceX's Gen 1 direct-to-device service was described as a proof of concept — 650 satellites deployed, service activated with 30 mobile network operators globally (largest being T-Mobile in the US), covering 1.9 billion people. Gen 2 is described as full 5G quality to existing handsets and is positioned as the transformational solution to connect the remaining ~3 billion people excluded from the digital economy.

5. **AI infrastructure — Colossus 2 and orbital compute:** SpaceX has built the Colossus 2 data center, described as the world's largest coherent supercomputer, using Nvidia GB300 chips. It is described as the first gigawatt-scale training cluster and includes the first gigawatt-scale mega battery installation. SpaceX also signed a hosting deal with Anthropic and a coding capability deal with Cursor. Johnson highlights orbital AI compute as a near-term future direction, leveraging existing Starlink hardware (ion thrusters, inter-satellite laser links, flight computers) with solar power and radiative cooling to create low-cost, clean-energy AI infrastructure in space.

6. **Total addressable market framing:** Johnson frames SpaceX's opportunity as nearly $6 trillion across its current three segments (space, connectivity, AI infrastructure), and over $28 trillion when including the broader enterprise AI market. Future growth vectors cited include point-to-point terrestrial transportation, space manufacturing, asteroid mining, and a lunar economy, with boots on the moon targeted within the next couple of years.

## Financials
1. **2025 full-year financial results:** SpaceX generated approximately $19 billion in total revenue in 2025, reflecting over 30% year-over-year growth. The connectivity segment alone grew roughly 50% year-over-year in 2025. Adjusted EBITDA for 2025 was approximately $7 billion. R&D spend in 2025 was approximately $3.6 billion. Capex in 2025 was approximately $21 billion, with the majority allocated to AI infrastructure buildout.

2. **Historical capital efficiency and prior-year EBITDA:** Johnson notes that across the life of the space and connectivity businesses, SpaceX raised only approximately $9 billion in total external capital while building to its current scale. In 2024, the company generated $7.8 billion in positive adjusted EBITDA.

3. **Q1 2026 financials:** SpaceX delivered approximately $5 billion in total revenue in Q1 2026, with the connectivity segment contributing approximately $3 billion of that.

4. **Long-term financial targets:** Management's future model targets approximately 70% gross margins and approximately 45% GAAP net income margin, with revenue growth projected to be significantly above current rates.

Notable quotes and data:
- "We're representing 75% of all active maneuverable satellites in orbit at this point."
- "After 20 launches of Starship we will be launching 1.2 petabytes of capacity per year."
- "We ended 2024 with roughly 4.4 million users… end of last year [2025], roughly doubled year-over-year to roughly 8.9 million… as of end of Q1 [2026], approximately 10.3 million users."
- "Last year alone 165 launches of our Falcon 9."
- "$19 billion in revenue [2025], over 30% growth year-over-year."
- "Roughly $21 billion of capex [2025], a large percentage of that was for AI."
- "$7.8 billion in positive adjusted EBITDA [2024]; ~$7 billion adjusted EBITDA [2025]."
- "$3.6 billion of R&D just last year [2025] alone."
- "Q1 [2026]: roughly $5 billion of topline, connectivity segment roughly $3 billion."
- Long-term model targets: ~70% gross margins, ~45% GAAP net income margin.
- Total addressable market framed as "almost $6 trillion" in near-term segments, "over 28 trillion" including enterprise AI.
- "We only raised $9 billion [total in company history across space and connectivity]."
- Gen 2 direct-to-device described as "full 5G quality to your phone."
- V3 satellites: "20x improvement related to the capacity per launch."
- Starship v4 targeting ~200 metric tons to orbit (design phase).

2026-06-04.title: CATL's Latest Battery Claims Deserve A Closer Look
2026-06-04.body:
This video features FutureAzA host Brian in conversation with Jordan from The Limiting Factor, analyzing CATL's recent battery technology presentation. The discussion focuses on three key battery developments: ultra-fast charging LFP cells, semi-solid state batteries, and sodium ion batteries. The core thesis is that while CATL and BYD are credible and generally accurate in their claims, the broader public — often driven by influencers and enthusiastic fan communities — tends to over-interpret those announcements, leading to inflated expectations about timelines and capabilities.

## Market & Competition

1. **CATL's Battery Philosophy — No Single "Best" Chemistry:** Jordan explains that CATL's own framing at their recent event was that all battery chemistries have strengths and weaknesses, and the goal is to capitalize on strengths rather than dwell on weaknesses. CATL has narrowed its automotive focus to two primary chemistries — high nickel (NMC-type) and LFP — with sodium ion as a potential future third pillar. Notably, CATL made a surprising statement at the event, suggesting that for vehicles priced over $35,000, a high-nickel battery pack is the appropriate choice and that using LFP at that price point does a disservice to customers — a remarkable comment given that LFP is CATL's flagship mass-market product. Jordan interprets this as CATL trying to push higher-margin high-nickel packs upmarket while positioning sodium ion as an expansion of the floor rather than a replacement for LFP or NMC.

2. **Ultra-Fast Charging: 10–15C Rates from CATL and BYD:** Jordan highlights that CATL and BYD have achieved charge rates of 10 to 15C, meaning a battery can be substantially or fully charged in under five to eight minutes. Brian notes this level of performance was considered implausible not long ago, when a 6C claim would have drawn skepticism. Kyle Connor reportedly tested one of these BYD fast-charging vehicles in person and confirmed the performance is real. However, Jordan cautions that the infrastructure required to deliver this level of charging is not yet widely deployed — even in China, where most media coverage focuses on cutting-edge high-power chargers, the actual network skews toward slower units. A contact in China who conducts battery teardowns reported that when testing one of these BYD batteries, the available charger lacked the necessary software updates and power capability, causing the battery to overheat — illustrating the gap between cell-level capability and real-world deployment.

3. **Cycle Life Trade-offs with Fast Charging:** Jordan and Brian discuss the practical implications of aggressive fast charging on battery longevity. Jordan's view is that while 10–15C charging will reduce cycle life compared to slower charging, the degradation is acceptable — shortening useful life from perhaps four times the expected vehicle lifespan to perhaps two times, still well beyond what most owners will ever need. This also increases the viability of second-life applications for these batteries in off-grid or stationary storage. The key trade-off is that consumers should prioritize whether they want a 5-minute charge capability or maximum long-term cycle life, and for most use cases the fast-charge option is the more practical value proposition.

4. **Sodium Ion: Promising but Volumetric Density Lags Significantly:** CATL announced in 2021 that it would build an industrial base for sodium ion batteries, but Jordan notes that mass manufacturing is only beginning to start at the end of 2025 (implied by context as late 2025/early 2026) — a roughly five-year gap that illustrates how early-sounding announcements from even credible companies can mislead audiences about timelines. Jordan estimates there is approximately a 30% gap between the gravimetric energy density (watt hours per kilogram) and volumetric energy density (watt hours per liter) of sodium ion cells. He stresses that for EVs, it is volumetric density — not weight — that limits range, because engineers run out of physical space to pack in batteries before weight becomes the binding constraint. Sodium ion's lower volumetric density means that achieving equivalent range requires a physically larger pack, which creates packaging trade-offs in vehicle design.

5. **Semi-Solid State: CATL's Claims Require Careful Interpretation:** CATL previously announced a "condensed matter" semi-solid state battery (which uses a gel electrolyte rather than a true solid electrolyte) with a claimed energy density of 500 Wh/kg. At their most recent event, CATL announced an automotive version rated at 350 Wh/kg. Jordan is skeptical: while 350 Wh/kg is respectable on a gravimetric basis, the volumetric energy density of this cell is reportedly worse than Tesla's current Panasonic battery cells. He suggests the 500 Wh/kg figure may be intended for aviation or aerospace applications where cost is less constrained. Jordan uses this as an example of CATL choosing words carefully — their claims are technically accurate, but the gap between what they say and what audiences hear is significant, often amplified by influencers and fan communities who over-extrapolate positive signals.

6. **Prologium Solid-State: A Credible Long-Term Player:** Brian briefly introduces Prologium, a solid-state battery company that has been working on the technology for 20 years and recently allowed Two Bit da Vinci to film and publish a full facility visit. Brian's read is that Prologium is making measured, credible claims — not promising revolutionary cost reductions or immediate automotive readiness — and is currently commercializing small-format solid-state cells for electronics. Jordan was not familiar with the specific details but expressed interest in reviewing Two Bit da Vinci's coverage.

7. **Credibility Framework: How to Read Battery Company Announcements:** Jordan offers a practical framework for separating signal from noise in battery industry announcements. Major manufacturers like CATL, BYD, Panasonic, LG, and SK have a track record of not making promises they cannot keep, and their official press releases and website language are chosen carefully. The problem, Jordan says, is not the companies themselves but the downstream interpretation by influencers and fan communities who amplify announcements beyond their actual meaning. As a rule of thumb, when Jordan sees an announcement like "4% efficiency improvement in two years," he accepts it as credible, methodical engineering progress — not a paradigm shift.

Notable quotes and data:
- CATL C-rate claims: 10–15C, enabling a near-full charge in under 5–7 minutes
- CATL's automotive semi-solid state battery: 350 Wh/kg (gravimetric); volumetric energy density reportedly worse than Tesla's current Panasonic cells
- CATL's previously announced condensed matter cell: 500 Wh/kg — Jordan suggests this may target aviation, not automotive
- Sodium ion volumetric energy density estimated to lag gravimetric by approximately 30%
- CATL announced sodium ion industrial base in 2021; mass manufacturing beginning approximately 5 years later
- Jordan: "You have to listen very closely to what companies like CATL and BYD say because I've never really heard them say anything that's terribly misleading, but the way they word it causes a lot of the fans to interpret it as more positive than it is."
- Brian: Fast-charge degradation shortens useful battery life "from four times longer than you will ever drive a car to two times longer — it's still going to outlive the vehicle."

2026-06-04.title: Tesla's Global Comeback Is Happening Faster Than Expected
2026-06-04.body:
This video is a conversation between Brian (FutureAzA) and Herbert from Brighter, covering Tesla's global sales rebound, Cybertruck pricing developments, and a Reuters rumor about a new smaller, cheaper Tesla SUV. The core thesis is that Tesla's global comeback is accelerating faster than many expected, driven by improved products, competitive pricing, and favorable macro conditions like higher gas prices.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla's Global Sales Rebound Across Multiple Markets:** Herbert summarizes data from analyst Roland Percher's charts showing strong year-over-year sales growth across several countries. In China, wholesale volume grew 39% in May year-over-year, described as the highest number so far in 2026 and far outpacing 2024 and 2025 performance. In Australia, the Model Y was the bestselling vehicle of any kind for the month of May — described as the first time in electric car history that an EV led overall sales in Australia. In Germany, sales rebounded and surpassed all prior years except 2023. Both hosts note this positive trend was already underway before the recent rise in gas prices, suggesting it is not purely a fuel-cost phenomenon.

2. **Tesla's EV Market Share in Australia:** Tesla achieved a record high 20% market share in Australia in May, even while carrying less inventory than competitors.
