Both hosts highlight this as a significant milestone and note that broader EV adoption in Australia continues to surge, with Tesla capturing a large share of that growth.

3. **Cybertruck Pricing and Affordability Efforts:** Tesla officially began selling used Cybertrucks directly from its inventory as of June 1, 2026, with shipping available anywhere in the country for $2,500. The starting price was listed at $66,200 for a used Foundation Series. These used units come with 1 to 3 months of FSD and 1 to 3 months of complimentary charging, but without lifetime perks, in order to keep costs down. The used inventory sold out almost immediately. A separately mentioned new lower-priced Cybertruck trim (a slightly trimmed-down new model) also sold through within roughly a week to ten days after launch. Both hosts conclude that price has been the primary barrier to Cybertruck adoption, not the product itself.

4. **Cybertruck's History of Disappointing Sales and Root Causes:** Herbert and Brian discuss how Cybertruck originally attracted 1–2 million reservations, most of which were placed at the $39,000 price point (which they adjust to approximately $53,000 in inflation-adjusted terms). The vehicle never reached that price point, launching at over $100,000, later coming down to around $80,000 and then to approximately $65,000. A prior attempt to create a cheaper variant — described as cutting $10,000 off the price by removing $30,000 worth of utility — sold only around 600–700 units. Herbert also notes that brand damage associated with Elon Musk's public profile in 2025 disproportionately affected Cybertruck compared to other Tesla models, given its more polarizing design and visual identity. Both hosts believe lower pricing will eventually overcome this lingering brand association issue.

5. **Reuters Rumor: New Smaller, Cheaper SUV:** Reuters reported, citing four anonymous sources, that Tesla is developing an entirely new model — not a variant of the Model 3 or Model Y — that would be approximately 14 feet long (notably shorter than the Model Y at 15.7 feet) and substantially cheaper than the Model 3's current starting price of $37,000. The vehicle would reportedly be manufactured in China, potentially offered with a smaller battery and a single motor. Brian and Herbert are both skeptical. Herbert argues it is highly unlikely Tesla would build a net-new platform from scratch rather than a variant of an existing line, and notes that Elon Musk himself recently stated Tesla is working on "something way cooler than a minivan, but smaller than a Model Y." Both hosts also point out logistical problems: Giga Shanghai is reportedly at capacity, and Fremont has no room. Herbert raises the possibility of a Cyber-SUV variant built on the Cybertruck line at Giga Texas, noting that Joe Tegtmeyer confirmed a very large portion of Giga Texas is dedicated to Cybertruck infrastructure — more than what is allocated to Cybercab production — and that this cannot easily be repurposed. The hosts conclude that while the rumor has some logical appeal for the Chinese market specifically, too many elements of the Reuters story don't add up.

## Market & Competition

1. **EV Cost Curve vs. ICE Pricing Trends:** Brian makes the broader market point that gas cars increase in price every year while gas prices are volatile, whereas electric vehicles have continued to move down the cost curve. He frames this as a structural advantage for Tesla and EVs generally, suggesting the growth story for EVs is far from over.

2. **Brand Damage and Its Market Impact:** Herbert argues that while Tesla's overall global sales have recovered — including in Germany — the Cybertruck remains the model most visibly affected by the brand damage Tesla experienced in 2025. He attributes this to the vehicle's bold, polarizing design, which makes it more symbolically associated with Elon Musk in the public eye than other Tesla models. He believes this effect will diminish as more units reach the road and as prices come down to attract a broader buyer base.

Notable quotes and data:
- China wholesale volume: +39% year-over-year in May 2026 — highest figure of the year so far
- Australia: Model Y was the #1 bestselling vehicle of any kind in May 2026; Tesla achieved a record 20% EV market share
- Germany: Tesla sales rebounded past all years except 2023
- Used Cybertruck Foundation Series starting at $66,200 via Tesla's direct used inventory program (launched June 1, 2026); $2,500 shipping nationwide
- Original Cybertruck reservations: 1–2 million, mostly placed at $39,000 (~$53,000 inflation-adjusted)
- Cybertruck previously launched at over $100,000; later reduced toward $80,000 then ~$65,000
- A prior "cheap" Cybertruck variant (price cut via feature removal) sold only ~600–700 units
- Rumored new SUV: ~14 ft long, cheaper than Model 3's $37,000 starting price, reportedly to be built in China
- Model Y current length: 15.7 feet
- Joe Tegtmeyer cited as confirming that a very large share of Giga Texas floor space is dedicated to Cybertruck, more than what is allocated to Cybercab
- Elon Musk quoted as recently saying Tesla is working on "something way cooler than a minivan, but smaller than a Model Y"

2026-06-04.title: Will The SpaceX Merger SCREW Tesla Shareholder? The BIG DEBATE with Alexandra Merz
2026-06-04.body:
This video features a live debate between Jo Bhakdi and Alexandra Merz, hosted by Herbert, on the topic of a potential SpaceX acquisition of Tesla following SpaceX's anticipated IPO on June 12, 2026. The central discussion revolves around whether such a merger is likely, when it might be announced, at what valuation ratio it would be structured, and whether Tesla shareholders would benefit or be harmed. Both guests broadly agree a merger is being planned but differ on the mechanics, timing, and structure of the offer.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO and valuation trajectory:** Alexandra Merz and Jo Bhakdi both accept that SpaceX is targeting an IPO around June 12, 2026, with current whisper valuations in the $2–4 trillion range. Merz believes SpaceX's price will be volatile but structurally supported upward over six months due to three major index inclusions (MSCI, FTSE, and NASDAQ) in the first 15 trading days, followed by a potentially massive S&P 500 inclusion around mid-December 2026, which she compares to Tesla's transformative S&P inclusion in 2020. She argues these index-driven inflows were deliberately engineered as part of a broader merger plan, noting that major index makers softened their rules specifically to accommodate the SpaceX IPO.

2. **The merger thesis and breadcrumbs:** Both guests argue there are strong indications that a SpaceX-Tesla merger has been in preparation for at least a year. Key "breadcrumbs" cited include: (a) language in the SpaceX S-1 amendment explicitly referencing share issuance for acquisitions; (b) SpaceX authorizing 36 billion shares while currently having only approximately 12.86 billion outstanding — roughly three times the total company — which Bhakdi argues is far more than needed for routine employee incentives or stock splits; (c) the structured setup of SpaceX's lock-up period and index inclusion timeline; and (d) Tesla's unresolved share count questions that Alexandra Merz says went unanswered when she formally inquired.

3. **Merger ratio debate — one-to-one vs. one-to-two:** Jo Bhakdi originally explored whether SpaceX might acquire Tesla at two times SpaceX's own valuation (i.e., a 1:2 ratio), arguing this would be only a marginal reduction in Elon Musk's voting control — from approximately 35% to 29% ownership — and therefore Musk has little incentive to push for any particular ratio. However, Alexandra Merz countered that there are not enough authorized SpaceX shares to support a 2:1 acquisition (13 billion SpaceX shares outstanding × 2 = 26 billion needed, plus existing issuances for Echostar and other entities, exceeds the 36 billion authorized). Both converge on the view that the offer will likely be dynamic or structured with a collar/ratchet rather than a fixed ratio.

4. **Proposed merger structure — ratchet mechanism:** After extensive back-and-forth, both guests converge on a preferred structure: a one-to-one market cap offer with a guaranteed floor (ratchet), meaning Tesla shareholders would receive at minimum a set absolute dollar amount per share regardless of SpaceX price movements between announcement and vote. Bhakdi argues this is essential for deal certainty — a pure floating one-to-one offer could fail if SpaceX declines or Tesla appreciates organically via robotaxi scaling. The ratchet would remove downside risk for Tesla shareholders, drive Tesla's price to the floor immediately upon announcement, and create a near-certain yes vote. Merz agrees a ratchet would be ideal but notes it may not be necessary if SpaceX's price is well-supported by index fund inflows.

5. **Timing of announcement — Alexandra Merz's Goldilocks scenario:** Merz argues the merger announcement could come as early as late June 2026 (just before the NASDAQ index inclusion, approximately three weeks after the June 12 IPO) and no later than August 15, 2026. Her reasoning: (a) Elon Musk must exercise his 2018 compensation package stock options by August 15, converting approximately 300 million options into restricted stock units at a strike price of $23 per share, at a cost of approximately $7 billion — a higher Tesla stock price reduces this burden; (b) politically, acting while the Trump administration is in power and regulators are favorable reduces risk; (c) an August announcement would allow Tesla's shareholder vote to be held around the November 2026 shareholder meeting, with a six-week minimum proxy publication period required for a company of Tesla's size. She estimates the full regulatory merger completion at approximately Q2 2027.

6. **Tesla share count mechanics:** Merz emphasizes that Tesla's outstanding share count is a critical variable for any market cap-based merger offer. Currently Tesla has approximately 3.7 billion shares outstanding. After Musk exercises his 2018 stock options (adding approximately 300 million shares) by mid-August 2026, Tesla's outstanding share count will reach approximately 4 billion. Separately, the 2025 compensation package already added approximately 400 million shares (inserted in November 2025). Tesla's current authorized share count is 6 billion, well above the 4 billion that will be outstanding. Merz draws a comparison to Tesla's 2010 IPO, when it authorized 2 billion shares but issued fewer than 100 million — a 20x gap that lasted 12 years — to argue that SpaceX's large authorized share count does not prove acquisition intent on its own.

7. **Governance and voting control:** Alexandra Merz focuses extensively on governance dimensions that she says few analysts are covering. SpaceX's S-1 grants Elon Musk Class B shares with 10-to-1 voting rights, giving him 85% voting control despite approximately 50% economic ownership. Tesla shareholders vote by simple majority (50% plus one of all outstanding shares). Merz identifies key institutional voters as Vanguard (already invested in both companies), BlackRock (reportedly seeking $10 billion of the SpaceX IPO), ARK Invest, and Baron Capital, and argues these plus Musk's approximately 20% Tesla stake and roughly one-third of retail could clear the 50% threshold. One governance concern she raises: unlike Meta and Google, where super-voting shares revert to ordinary shares upon the founder's death or incapacitation, SpaceX's S-1 allows Musk's Class B shares to pass to his family members — a clause she believes Tesla's board should push back on in merger negotiations.

8. **Political rationale for speed:** Merz argues the merger should happen as quickly as possible because Musk's current political leverage with the Trump administration provides a favorable regulatory environment. She warns that if Democrats win both the House and Senate in the 2026 midterms, Elon Musk becomes a political target again, committees could be weaponized, and the regulatory path becomes far harder. She also raises unresolved questions about Tesla China operations and whether they can be firewalled in a combined entity.

9. **Lock-step trading mechanics and merger arbitrage:** The guests discuss how Tesla and SpaceX stocks would trade between announcement and vote. Both agree the stocks would move in approximate lock-step driven by merger arbitrage hedge funds, but Bhakdi argues this lock-step would be asymmetric — SpaceX going up pulls Tesla up (deal remains attractive), but if Tesla organically surpasses SpaceX's implied offer price, the stocks decouple and the vote risks failure. Merz counters that a ratchet floor solves this by giving Tesla shareholders certainty on their minimum, making the Tesla price jump to the floor immediately and removing the decoupling risk. She also notes the S&P inclusion in December 2026, potentially over $100 billion in passive purchases, would provide sustained upward pressure.

## Financials

1. **Elon Musk's 2018 stock option exercise economics:** The 2018 Tesla compensation package requires Musk to exercise his options (at a $23 strike price) before August 15, 2026, in a two-step process — first exercising into shares, then converting those into restricted stock units that he must hold until 2033. The exercise adds approximately 300 million shares to Tesla's outstanding count. The cost to exercise is approximately $7 billion. The tax event from this package is not due until January 2028. Musk's options to finance the $7 billion exercise cost include selling Tesla shares (higher price = fewer shares sold), pledging shares as collateral (higher price = less pledged), or a net exercise in which Tesla effectively lends him the $7 billion in exchange for shares, resulting in slightly fewer net shares received. In all scenarios, a higher Tesla stock price at the time of exercise is financially advantageous to Musk.

2. **Elon Musk's combined voting and ownership under various merger scenarios:** Bhakdi's modeling shows that under a 1:1 market cap merger, Musk's voting rights over the combined entity remain dominant due to his 10-to-1 Class B SpaceX shares. Under a 2:1 scenario (SpaceX buys Tesla at twice SpaceX's valuation), Musk's ownership stake in the combined entity would decline from approximately 35% to approximately 29% — a reduction Bhakdi characterizes as marginal and insufficient to motivate Musk to manipulate the merger ratio in either direction. His main conclusion: Musk has no strong personal financial incentive to favor any particular merger ratio.

3. **Jo Bhakdi's directional 12-month scenario:** Bhakdi states his base case (not a firm prediction) is that over a 9–12 month horizon from mid-2026, SpaceX will face difficulty sustaining its IPO valuation due to a lag in catalysts to justify the multiple, while Tesla will appreciate significantly on robotaxi and Optimus news. His directional scenario: SpaceX at approximately $1.5 trillion and Tesla at approximately $3 trillion, making Tesla the larger company by market cap at that point. He argues this scenario does not prevent a merger but does make a simple one-to-one market cap offer more complex and potentially less favorable to SpaceX.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX authorized shares: 36 billion; SpaceX currently outstanding shares: approximately 12.86 billion
- Tesla outstanding shares post-option exercise (by mid-August 2026): approximately 4 billion
- Tesla authorized shares: 6 billion
- Elon Musk's Tesla ownership: approximately 19.09% of economic interest
- Elon Musk's SpaceX voting control: approximately 85% (via 10:1 Class B shares); economic ownership approximately 50%
- Cost to exercise Musk's 2018 Tesla options: approximately $7 billion at $23 strike price
- Tax event from 2018 package: January 2028
- 2025 compensation package shares already inserted: approximately 400 million (November 2025)
- SpaceX float at IPO: approximately 4.3% plus up to 5% friends-and-family shares
- S&P 500 inclusion wave: estimated mid-December 2026; estimated passive purchases potentially exceeding $100 billion (compared to Tesla's 2020 inclusion)
- Lock-up sellers coming after Q2 2025 results: second half of July 2026
- Three initial index inclusions (MSCI, FTSE, NASDAQ): first 15 trading days post-IPO
- Alexandra Merz's merger announcement window: end of June 2026 to August 15, 2026
- Estimated regulatory completion / single ticker trading: approximately Q2 2027
- Required Tesla shareholder vote threshold: 50% plus one of all outstanding shares
- Proxy publication minimum period for Tesla-scale companies: six weeks
- Jo Bhakdi's 12-month directional scenario: SpaceX ~$1.5 trillion, Tesla ~$3 trillion
- Alexandra Merz: "The SpaceX S-1 prospectus protects Elon like never a founder has been protected."
- Jo Bhakdi: "Elon has no incentive of driving that merger ratio in any way."
- Alexandra Merz: "Q2 2027" as her estimated date for the combined entity trading under a single ticker.

2026-06-04.title: Inside Pirelli: Ian Coke on the Future of Tire Technology
2026-06-04.body:
This Munro Live interview features Jason Hill of Munro speaking with Ian Coke, Vice President of Technical Strategy and Customer Relations in North America for Pirelli, about the engineering complexity and innovation behind modern tire technology. The conversation covers how mega-trends in the automotive industry — including EV adoption, vehicle weight increases, torque demands, noise reduction, and sustainability — are driving continuous innovation in tire design, materials science, and manufacturing. The core thesis is that tires are far more technologically sophisticated than most consumers realize, and that Pirelli's position at the premium, high-value end of the market is driven by its engineering capabilities, motorsport participation, and growing use of AI and simulation.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **EV-Specific Tire Challenges — Weight, Torque, and Rolling Resistance:** Ian Coke explains that EVs and hybrids present multiple simultaneous demands on tires: significantly greater vehicle weight (requiring higher load ratings, including "extra load" and "high load" ratings), dramatically higher torque requiring strong grip, the need for ultra-low rolling resistance to maximize battery range, and increased noise sensitivity due to the absence of a combustion engine. Coke notes these demands are often in direct conflict — a stiffer, stronger construction needed to support weight works against ride comfort, while maximizing grip can compromise rolling resistance.

2. **Early EV Tire Wear Concerns:** Coke notes that tire wear was not a high priority for early EV OEMs, which led to real-world wear rates that surprised consumers. He contrasts expected EV tire life — some early tires wearing out at 15,000–20,000 miles — against typical expectations of 40,000–50,000 miles for conventional tires. He states this has since changed, and wear is now a more deliberate design consideration, addressed through "block stability" in tread design and improved compounding that balances mileage with wet braking and rolling resistance.

3. **Noise Cancellation Technology for EVs:** With combustion engine noise eliminated, road and tire noise became newly prominent in EVs. Coke explains Pirelli had already been developing noise cancellation systems before the EV era (originally prompted by increasingly quiet luxury vehicles like Mercedes, BMW 7 Series, and Maybach), making the technology effectively plug-and-play for EV applications. The system works by breaking up the acoustic drum effect inside the tire.

## Market & Competition
1. **Pirelli's Premium Market Positioning — High-Value Technology Focus:** Coke describes Pirelli as a technology-driven premium brand, with approximately 95–96% of its production in what the company calls "high-value" tires — defined as 18-inch and above — encompassing ultra-high performance, noise cancellation systems, ultra-low rolling resistance, and mobility solutions. He contrasts this with mass-market competitors who produce hundreds of millions of tires, while Pirelli produces approximately 70 million tires annually but focuses on highly complex, small lot sizes.

2. **OEM Homologation — Bespoke Tires Per Vehicle Model:** A key differentiator Coke emphasizes is that Pirelli develops tires specifically homologated for individual vehicle models. Even if two different vehicles use the same tire size, their specifications will typically differ because the tire is tuned for that specific vehicle's lateral force, longitudinal traction, footprint, and performance targets. He uses BMW's "star mark" sidewall symbol as a consumer-visible example of this practice.

3. **Motorsport as a Technology Engine:** Pirelli has been a Formula 1 supplier for over 15 years, also participates in the World Rally Series, and produces motorcycle tires with plans to take over GP motorcycle tire supply the following year (implying 2027 per the publish date of 2026-06-04). Coke is explicit that the primary value of motorsport participation is not marketing but the engineering capability it forces — specifically the ability to design, simulate, test, and iterate rapidly under extreme conditions. He cites a dedicated tire engineer per F1 team, real-time telemetry monitoring, and the need to model dimensional rule changes before manufacturing 30,000–35,000 tires per season as examples of the pace and rigor involved.

4. **AI and Virtual Simulation — From Compound Design to Track Performance:** Pirelli invested in a dedicated AI and digital center in Bari, southern Italy, approximately five years ago (implying around 2021), staffed by approximately 50 engineers focused on AI and simulation. This center enables fully virtual tire development: compounds are designed using AI based on vehicle and tire attributes, a complete dynamic virtual tire is created, and then tested under a virtual vehicle model in various conditions (loads, pressures, temperatures). Coke estimates this process brings development approximately 90% of the way to the final physical tire before any physical prototype is built. He acknowledges that modeling snow and mud remains difficult, while other surfaces simulate more accurately.

5. **Connected and Sensorized Tires — The Next Frontier:** Coke identifies tire connectivity and sensorization as what he views as the most exciting near-future development. Beyond basic TPMS, embedded sensors can proactively track temperature and pressure in real time, measure the actual contact patch, detect aquaplaning, and feed data to vehicle systems to improve ABS reaction time and alter suspension dynamically. Pirelli has signed a cooperation agreement with Bosch (which Coke says supplies approximately 70–75% of onboard systems for major vehicle manufacturers) to enable tire sensor data to integrate with vehicle operating systems. Coke also envisions V2V (vehicle-to-vehicle) communication via 5G enabling a sensorized tire's real-time road condition data (e.g., a water patch) to be broadcast to surrounding vehicles. He notes that real-time data upload frequency remains an unresolved challenge.

6. **Sustainability Materials Innovation:** Coke states Pirelli was the first tire manufacturer — and specifically first in the US market — to use FSC (Forest Stewardship Council) certified natural rubber. Pirelli now produces an ultra-high-performance product with more than 75% biodegradable and recyclable materials, incorporating recovered carbon black from tire pyrolysis, recovered metal, and lignin as a sidewall filler reinforcement. Coke frames this as technologically and resource-driven rather than purely marketing-driven, noting that no consumer in their market has ever paid a premium specifically for sustainability.

7. **3D Printing-Inspired Manufacturing and Adaptive Tread Design:** Pirelli uses a strip-injection construction method analogous to 3D printing, building tires up in precise rubber strips to place material exactly where needed — addressing the challenge that rubber does not always conform accurately when extruded conventionally. This enables rapid design changes and small production lot sizes suited to Pirelli's bespoke, low-volume approach. On the tread design side, Coke describes "3D siping" used in winter and all-season tires, where the tread is engineered to increase the contact patch surface area as it wears, maintaining or even improving grip as the tire ages — counterintuitive to most consumers who assume worn tires always grip less.

Notable quotes and data:
- Ian Coke has been with Pirelli for "just over 40 years," always on the manufacturing, technical, and quality side.
- Pirelli produces approximately 70 million tires annually; major competitors produce in the hundreds of millions.
- Approximately 95–96% of Pirelli's production is classified as "high-value" (18-inch and above).
- Early EV tires were wearing out at 15,000–20,000 miles vs. consumer expectations of 40,000–50,000 miles.
- Summer compound glass transition point: approximately 44°F / 7°C — below this temperature, summer compounds begin to harden and lose braking capability.
- Pirelli AI/digital center in Bari, Italy: approximately 50 AI engineers, established approximately five years ago.
- Formula 1 season tire production: approximately 30,000–35,000 tires per season.
- Bosch described as supplying approximately 70–75% of onboard systems for major vehicle manufacturers.
- Pirelli ultra-high-performance product: more than 75% biodegradable and recyclable materials.
- Pirelli-Bosch cooperation agreement signed for tire sensor integration with vehicle operating systems.
- "They're not just black and round" — Coke's closing message to consumers.
- "We call ourselves a 150-year-plus startup."

2026-06-04.title: Daily X Summary (2026-06-04)
2026-06-04.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts span several bullish Tesla-relevant themes: strong EV sales momentum in Europe and Japan, an expansion of Tesla's unsupervised robotaxi operating area in Austin, a new FSD software update, and a significant insurance product validating FSD's safety record. The SpaceX IPO announcement and its $269M Megapack purchase from Tesla are notable secondary signals for Tesla's energy business and Elon Musk's broader ecosystem.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Tesla Unsupervised Robotaxi Operating Area More Than Doubles in Austin:** Sawyer Merritt noted that Tesla's unsupervised robotaxi operating area in Austin has more than doubled in size, citing apparent geofence expansion. This is a meaningful operational milestone — broader coverage translates directly to higher potential utilization and revenue per vehicle in the fleet. Per RobotaxiTracker.com (as of 2026-06-02), Tesla's active robotaxi fleet stands at 704 vehicles across all modes (Bay Area 584, Austin 104, Dallas 7, Houston 9), with 39 unsupervised/driverless vehicles (Austin 28, Dallas 5, Houston 6). A larger operating zone in Austin could accelerate the transition of more vehicles to unsupervised status.

2. **FSD V14.3.3 Rolling Out with Improved Driver Monitoring:** Tesla began rolling out FSD V14.3.3, featuring improved driver monitoring system (DMS) sensitivity — specifically better eye gaze tracking, eyewear handling, and higher accuracy in variable lighting conditions. While this is an incremental update rather than a major capability release, enhanced DMS is directly relevant to Tesla's regulatory pathway for supervised FSD and the transition toward unsupervised operation. Sawyer confirmed it was downloading on his Model Y.

3. **Lemonade Launches FSD Insurance Discount — Up to 50% Off in Indiana:** Lemonade launched an "Autonomous Car" insurance program in Indiana offering Tesla drivers up to a 50% insurance discount when using FSD (Supervised), citing FSD as "twice as safe." This is a notable commercial validation of Tesla's safety data narrative. For DCF modeling purposes, this suggests that per-mile insurance costs for FSD-equipped vehicles may be materially lower than conventional benchmarks, and the program could expand to other states. The specific framing — "twice as safe" — implies a roughly 50% reduction in actuarial risk, which Lemonade is passing through directly to consumers.

4. **Tesla EV Sales Surge in Germany and Japan:** Tesla registered 5,111 vehicles in Germany in May 2026, up 322% year-over-year per Germany's Federal Motor Transport Authority — a standout result given the difficulty of the European market. In Japan, Tesla registered 1,996 vehicles in May 2026 (+182% YoY), pushing past Audi to become the #3 luxury brand in the country for the month. Year-to-date in Japan, Tesla has registered 8,194 vehicles (+157% YoY), putting it on track for its best year ever there. Sawyer characterized Q2 European sales as "looking very strong." These data points provide meaningful positive signal ahead of Q2 2026 delivery results.

5. **SpaceX Purchases $269M in Tesla Megapacks; IPO Announced at $1.75T Valuation:** SpaceX disclosed in a new filing that it purchased $269 million worth of Tesla Megapacks in April 2026, adding to the $430 million in Megapacks purchased by SpaceX/xAI last year — bringing the cumulative known total to approximately $699 million. Separately, SpaceX officially announced its IPO targeting $74.4 billion in proceeds at $135/share (approximately 555.55 million shares), implying a $1.75 trillion valuation. With a potential overallotment option, the offering could reach ~$85.7 billion. While the IPO is not directly a Tesla event, the Megapack purchases represent a meaningful revenue relationship, and the SpaceX liquidity event has implications for Elon Musk's personal financial position and his ability to fund Tesla-adjacent ventures.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — The combination of accelerating EV sales in key international markets, Austin robotaxi geographic expansion, FSD insurance validation, and continued large-scale Megapack demand from a related-party buyer (SpaceX) presents a broadly positive picture across multiple Tesla business lines heading into Q2 2026 reporting.

2026-06-05.title: JUST RECORDED: Jamie Dimon Gets Elon’s Biggest SpaceX Answers
2026-06-05.body:
This video covers a live Q&A session between Jamie Dimon and Elon Musk hosted at JP Morgan's headquarters in New York City, broadcast simultaneously to approximately 3,500 individual investors across 100 branches. The conversation is centered almost entirely on SpaceX's public offering, its growth roadmap, and Elon Musk's broader vision for space infrastructure — with no substantive discussion of Tesla, autonomous driving, robotaxi services, or Optimus. The event appears timed to coincide with SpaceX's IPO-related investor outreach.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO Rationale — Capital for a Major Growth Phase:** Elon Musk explained that SpaceX has been cash-flow positive since approximately 2014–2015 and that prior private equity rounds were liquidity events for employees and investors rather than fundraising rounds. The reason for going public now, he said, is that SpaceX is entering a significant new capital growth phase, specifically to fund the buildout of the Starlink Version 3 satellite constellation (targeting over 100,000 satellites), space-based AI data centers, and chip fabrication infrastructure. He described revenue as now being more predictable, which added to the timing rationale.

2. **Starlink Version 3 — Generational Leap in Capability:** Musk described the V3 satellite as 10 to 20 times more capable than the current V2 satellite, delivering 100 times more bandwidth and half the latency of the existing Starlink system, due in part to a lower orbital altitude. V3 satellites are approximately 7 meters (roughly 20–23 feet) wide — too large to be launched on any rocket other than Starship — and incorporate custom chips designed by SpaceX's chip team, larger phased array antennas, more inter-satellite laser links, and W-band and E-band communications. Starship is expected to launch up to 50 V3 satellites per mission.

3. **Starship Full Reusability as the Core Breakthrough:** Musk identified full reusability as the fundamental technological breakthrough of Starship, noting that Falcon 9 achieved partial reusability but Starship will be fully reusable. Because Starship uses liquid oxygen and liquid methane — which Musk described as the cheapest propellant available — the marginal cost per launch once reusability is achieved becomes primarily the cost of propellant, which he said would be less than the cost of jet aviation fuel. Starship Version 3 is targeting 100 tons to orbit with full reusability; Version 4 is targeting over 200 tons per mission.

4. **Space-Based AI Data Centers — Simpler Than Communication Satellites:** Musk argued that space-based AI data centers are technically easier to build than Starlink communication satellites, because they essentially consist of solar power, radiators, basic satellite operations equipment, and laser links connecting to the existing Starlink constellation. He said connectivity to the ground would be weather-independent, as Starlink communicates to the ground on cloud-penetrating (and even roof-penetrating) frequencies.

5. **Terafab Chip Manufacturing — Filling a Critical Gap:** Musk stated that there is currently no high-volume computer memory fabrication facility in the United States, and that even under best-case assumptions from existing chip manufacturers, domestic supply will be insufficient to meet anticipated AI demand. He cited a Micron fab in Idaho not expected to reach volume production until approximately 2028, and other fabs in New York targeting 2029–2030, as insufficient to close the gap. He framed the Terafab initiative as essential for AI logic, memory, and packaging.

6. **Grok AI Integration into SpaceX Platform:** Musk indicated that SpaceX's AI satellites will be an open platform, allowing customers to run Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs, Amazon Trainium, or other third-party chips. SpaceX/xAI intends to also offer its own chips and AI software (including Grok) on the platform in the future, but the architecture is designed to be hardware- and software-agnostic.

7. **Moon and Mars as Long-Term Infrastructure Vision:** Musk outlined a vision in which the moon serves as an intermediary step before Mars, noting that the moon's lack of atmosphere and low gravity (approximately 1/6th of Earth's) allows for electromagnetic mass drivers (rail guns) to launch AI data center hardware into deep space without rockets. He estimated approximately 1 terawatt per year of AI space compute capacity from Earth-based launches, scaling to 1,000 terawatts or more from the moon. He described Mars as a "fixer upper of a planet" with long-term terraforming potential.

Notable quotes and data:
- Starlink V3: "10 to 20 times more capable than V2," "100 times more bandwidth," "half the latency"
- SpaceX targeting "over 100,000 satellites" in orbit for communications
- Starship V3 payload target: 100 tons to orbit with full reusability; V4: over 200 tons per mission
- Starship capable of launching up to 50 V3 satellites per mission
- V3 satellites approximately 7 meters wide — only launchable on Starship
- "There's not a single high-volume computer memory fab in America right now. Zero."
- Micron Idaho fab: volume production expected ~2028; New York fabs: ~2029–2030
- SpaceX cash-flow positive since approximately 2014–2015
- AI space compute potential: ~1 terawatt/year from Earth, ~1,000 terawatts/year from the moon
- Brent Johnson cited as SpaceX CFO with approximately 15 years of tenure
- Jamie Dimon: "Elon is the Edison of our time"
- Musk on leadership evolution: "I'm probably more chill than I used to be… it matters if they have a good heart"
- Event reached approximately 3,500 individual investors across 100 JP Morgan branches

2026-06-05.title: Tesla Executive Extremely Confident About Robotaxi
2026-06-05.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel features host Herbert in a panel discussion with three Tesla bull investors — Alexandra Merz, Jeff Lutz, and Cern Basher — covering the three topics most discussed among Tesla investors that week: robotaxi expansion, the SpaceX IPO and its implications for Tesla, and competition in autonomous driving and humanoid robotics. The panel's core thesis is that a significant convergence of Tesla catalysts is building for the second half of 2026, potentially amplified by a Tesla-SpaceX merger that Alexandra Merz believes could be announced as early as end of June through mid-August 2026.

## Robotaxi

1. **Unsupervised Robotaxi Expanded to Greater Austin Area:** Tesla VP of AI Ashok Kaliswami officially announced that unsupervised robotaxi service is now available across the entire greater Austin metro area, no longer confined to a smaller geofenced zone. Jesse Richard was credited as the first to discover the expanded boundary by testing the service limits. The panel noted the exact number of vehicles operating in this expanded zone is unknown — potentially still a small handful — and that the RobotaxiTracker app appeared to be lagging more than at launch, possibly due to increased activity.

2. **Panel Mixed on Pace — "Baby Steps" vs. "Imminent Launch":** Cern Basher characterized the Austin expansion as a "baby step," noting that nearly a year into the service, expansion to other cities has been slow and wait times remain too long for an urban ride-hail product — with one observer suggesting waits under 20 minutes are still too long. However, Jeff Lutz argued the buildup of inventory, hiring, and infrastructure feels like a product launch in progress, comparing it to supply chain readiness before a factory launch, and said he believes deployment is "imminent." He argued Tesla may have underestimated the operational complexity of running a ride-share service from scratch.

3. **Texas Permit for Unsupervised Operation — A Regulatory Milestone:** The panel noted that on May 28, 2026, Texas granted Tesla a permit to operate unsupervised robotaxi vehicles, clearing what the panel described as one of three key requirements for full robotaxi deployment: (1) regulatory approval — now done in Texas; (2) hardware/software readiness — described as largely ready or getting there; and (3) operational infrastructure — cleaning, charging, on-time logistics — still being built out.

4. **Infrastructure Buildout Signals Scale:** The panel highlighted several infrastructure developments: three large facilities (described as approximately 36,000–151,000 square feet) for car wash and charging being built or approved in the Dallas/Austin area, and a new 51,000-square-foot delivery center in Grand Prairie, Texas (between Dallas and Fort Worth). Jeff Lutz warned that if Tesla builds out this OPEX-heavy infrastructure and then doesn't deploy high volume, it would be a serious financial drag — which he takes as evidence Tesla is planning a large deployment. Cern Basher noted there are currently 36 job listings for robotaxi-related roles.

5. **Edge Cases Still Being Resolved:** The panel discussed recent testing footage showing a Model Y repeatedly practicing recognition of a chain in a parking lot, and a separate incident where FSD failed to detect a lane-closure gate on a highway and struck it. Jeff Lutz and others agreed these edge cases must be resolved before wide rollout — and that resolving them takes iterative development cycles. Jeff noted Tesla has speed-profile "dials" it can adjust post-launch to reduce risk during edge conditions.

6. **Cybercab Production Units Spotted:** A video from content creator Tech Danny was shown featuring a production Cybercab in a new color called "Gleaming Gold," with self-opening McLaren-style doors, two seats, a large center console, no rear-view mirrors, no sunroof, and no rear window. The panel discussed the Cybercab's unconventional door mechanism as a potential manufacturing risk at scale, noting the concern about misalignment or sticking at higher volumes.

7. **Six-City Expansion Timeline Under Scrutiny:** The panel acknowledged Tesla had previously suggested expanding to six cities by end of Q2 2026. As of filming (Thursday, June 5, 2026), active supervised and unsupervised robotaxi service remains in Austin, Dallas, and Houston, with California still not operating as a true robotaxi service. Cern Basher expressed belief the other three cities could still be added by end of Q2 (approximately 21–26 days away at time of filming), and the panel broadly expects a more concerted ramp through summer 2026 (July–September).

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Supervised Now Approved in 11 Countries:** Ashok Kaliswami presented a slide showing FSD supervised self-driving approved in: United States, Canada, Mexico, Netherlands, Estonia, Lithuania (and broader Europe listed), China, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, and Puerto Rico. Estonia was noted as having approved FSD supervised that same week. The panel noted some nuance — China's inclusion reflects FSD being "shipped to customers" in certain cities/regions, not a formal nationwide approval, and Ashok's language ("supervised self-driving shipped to customers in China") was parsed as technically accurate but potentially misleading.

2. **Pending Approval in 13+ Countries Covering 36% of World Population:** Kaliswami's slide showed FSD pending regulatory approval in Japan, India, Israel, Bangladesh, Thailand, Taiwan, Malaysia, Philippines, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Ethiopia, Colombia, Chile, and the rest of Europe. Nick Cruz Betain was credited for compiling the list. The panel noted 36% of the world's population lives in these pending-approval regions. Cern Basher flagged that Bangladesh and the Philippines did not appear to be highlighted on Ashok's actual map, and noted that Ethiopia was a surprise since Tesla currently only operates in Morocco within Africa. Belgium was noted as likely next in Europe, awaiting homologation data from Dutch authorities.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **202 Optimus Job Listings vs. 36 Robotaxi Listings:** The panel highlighted that Tesla currently has 202 job listings related to Optimus, compared to 36 for robotaxi roles, signaling the company's significant internal focus on humanoid robotics. An Optimus manufacturing facility is reportedly being built at Giga Texas, described as nearly as large as the main Giga Texas factory.

2. **Optimus Gen 3 Reveal Delayed, Now Tied Closely to Production Readiness:** The panel discussed that Optimus demo dates were pushed back multiple times — from December 2025, to January 2026, to March 2026 — and Elon Musk has now said the reveal will happen as close to production readiness as possible, rather than as a standalone demo event. Jeff Lutz predicted a Q3 2026 reveal; Cern Basher suggested the second half of September to first half of October; Alexandra Merz suggested it could come sooner if tied to a merger announcement. The panel interpreted the delay as Elon wanting a high-quality demo, and drew a comparison to Apple's approach of revealing products close to availability.

3. **Competition from Figure and OpenAI — Panel Unworried:** The panel addressed Figure's impressive live-streamed demo over 7+ days showing humanoid robots doing pick-and-place tasks at human-comparable speed, and OpenAI's announcement of entering robotics. Jeff Lutz argued there aren't enough companies building capable humanoid robots, and that the real filter — AI brain capability, right product specs, and mass manufacturing — will leave very few viable competitors. He cautioned that no company will produce a million useful bots in the near term, drawing a parallel to the 5-year smartphone supply chain ramp from one million to one billion units per year. The panel noted the supply chain for humanoid robots is more complex than smartphones, which benefited from a globalized assembly ecosystem.

## Market & Competition

1. **Waymo Comparison Called "Bizarre" and "Ignorant":** Jeff Lutz pushed back strongly on CNBC comparisons between Tesla's robotaxi program and Waymo's approximately 3,700-car fleet, calling the framing inaccurate and almost purposefully misleading. He argued that when Tesla is at scale, the two services will be fundamentally different, and that the broader problem is there aren't enough autonomous ride-share companies — not too many. The panel agreed competition in this space is healthy and that Tesla does not fear it, historically publishing patents openly to encourage the ecosystem.

2. **Tesla Sales Strong Internationally — Q2 Expected Solid:** Jeff Lutz cited South Korea at 11,000 car sales in a single month as an example of organic demand growth, not just easy year-over-year comps. He attributed some of the demand tailwind to oil prices and the retreat of other automakers from EVs in Western Europe and the US. Global sales data (excluding US, where rapid data was unavailable) showed net growth of approximately 27–28% over the prior year. Q2 deliveries and production numbers are expected around July 3, 2026, with a full earnings report expected in the third or fourth week of July.

3. **Cybercab Available for Public Purchase by End of 2026 — Per Elon:** Jeff Lutz noted Elon Musk has stated Cybercabs will be made available for public sale by end of 2026, and discussed how customer-owned Cybercabs could help Tesla scale the robotaxi network faster by offloading charging, cleaning, and maintenance infrastructure burdens.

## Financials

1. **SpaceX-Tesla Merger Thesis — Alexandra Merz's Detailed Scenario:** Alexandra Merz laid out her theory that SpaceX will IPO on June 12, 2026, followed by a merger announcement with Tesla between end of June and mid-August 2026. Under her scenario, a Tesla shareholder vote would occur in November 2026, with the actual merger completing in Q2 2027. At the moment of merger consummation, the merged entity would replace the Tesla ticker in the S&P 500, triggering mandatory index buying — which she estimates could exceed $60–100 billion from S&P alone, with an additional $15–20 billion each from FTSE, CRSP, and NASDAQ 100 indices. She described this S&P inclusion event as a major financial motivation to complete the merger sooner rather than later.

2. **S&P Dow Jones Declines to Change Index Inclusion Rules:** Breaking news during the filming (June 5, 2026) confirmed that S&P Dow Jones officially announced it would not change its index inclusion rules to fast-track profitable-company requirements from 12 months to 6 months. This means SpaceX on its own (without a merger) cannot be included in the S&P 500 until approximately June 2027. Jeff Lutz predicted S&P would eventually be forced by market forces to change these rules, as competing indices (NASDAQ, Russell, CRSP/Vanguard) stand to absorb capital flows from SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic, and other large companies excluded from S&P.

3. **Starlink Hits 12 Million Subscribers:** The panel noted Starlink announced 12 million subscribers, up from 10 million the prior month, as evidence of SpaceX's rapidly building profitability. Goldman Sachs (co-lead on the SpaceX IPO) projected SpaceX 2030 revenue of $322 billion; Mach 33 (Aaron Bernett and Larry Goldberg) was cited as projecting approximately $305 billion for 2030, with AI data center revenue not materializing significantly until 2031.

Notable quotes and data:
- Ashok Kaliswami: "Unsupervised robotaxi now available in the greater Austin area" (official announcement)
- 36 robotaxi-related job listings vs. 202 Optimus-related job listings at Tesla currently
- Waymo fleet cited at approximately 3,700 cars
- Texas unsupervised robotaxi permit issued May 28, 2026
- FSD supervised approved in 11 countries; pending approval in 13+ countries covering 36% of world population
- South Korea: 11,000 Tesla vehicles sold in a single month
- Global Tesla sales (ex-US) up approximately 27–28% year-over-year as of May 2026
- Starlink: 12 million subscribers (up from 10 million the prior month)
- Goldman Sachs SpaceX 2030 revenue estimate: $322 billion; Mach 33 estimate: ~$305 billion
- Alexandra Merz merger announcement window: end of June to mid-August 2026
- S&P index buying from merger event estimated at $60–100 billion+; FTSE/CRSP/NASDAQ 100 at ~$15–20 billion each

2026-06-05.title: Tesla’s Biggest Demand Driver Hasn’t Arrived Yet
2026-06-05.body:
This video from "brighterwithherbert" features host Herbert and guest Brian White (of the FutureAzA YouTube channel) arguing that Tesla's strongest demand drivers — Full Self-Driving adoption and insurance cost reduction — have not yet fully arrived, even as global Tesla sales are already surging. The core thesis is that once consumers viscerally understand that FSD is real and robotaxis are visible on public streets, a second, more powerful wave of demand will hit, compounded by insurance companies like Lemonade offering up to 50% discounts for FSD miles. The hosts review skyrocketing Tesla sales data from China, Australia, Japan, and Germany as evidence that the rebound is already underway before these catalysts fully materialize.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Lemonade Insurance Expands FSD Discount to Indiana:** Insurance provider Lemonade has expanded its Tesla autonomous driving insurance discount to Indiana, joining Oregon and Arizona. The product offers Tesla owners a 50% reduction in insurance rates for miles driven using FSD, based on Lemonade's own data showing FSD drivers have approximately 50% fewer accidents and injuries. Lemonade's CEO has reportedly suggested rates could approach near-zero over time. Lemonade has stated plans to expand to 10 states total. The hosts note a "virtue cycle" dynamic: low-risk FSD drivers concentrating in Lemonade and Tesla Insurance, potentially leaving competing insurers with a higher-risk pool and escalating premiums.

2. **FSD Version 14 Coming to Australia and New Zealand:** Tesla announced to Australian customers that FSD version 14 is in its "final stages of local development testing" and is "coming soon," though no specific date was shared. FSD supervised is currently available in approximately 11 countries, with Estonia recently added and Belgium reportedly coming soon. China has a very limited rollout of FSD. The hosts note that most countries outside the US currently have older versions (described as "13 series or something like that"), not the latest release. Brian White emphasizes that FSD version 14.3 represents a meaningful leap and that getting FSD onto Hardware 3 vehicles — the majority of cars on the road — remains a critical unlocked revenue opportunity for Tesla.

3. **FSD as a Future Demand Driver:** The hosts debate to what extent FSD is currently a demand driver versus what it will become. Brian White argues that most consumers do not yet understand the distinction between genuine end-to-end self-driving and basic driver-assistance features like those in a Chevy Blazer. He posits that even if only 5% of all new car buyers in the US demand true FSD capability, that would roughly double Tesla's US market — approximately 400,000 additional sales — since Tesla is essentially the only brand outside China offering end-to-end autonomous driving. The hosts agree that widespread robotaxi visibility will be the key catalyst that educates the public that this technology exists and is purchasable.

## Robotaxi

1. **Robotaxi Visibility as the Critical Awareness Catalyst:** Both hosts identify the robotaxi rollout as the pivotal event that will convert public awareness of autonomous driving into a consumer demand driver for Tesla vehicles. The argument is that once Cybercabs are "blanketed everywhere" and mainstream media covers robotaxis as a normalized reality — as is already beginning with Waymo coverage — consumers will ask whether they can buy that technology, and discover Tesla is the only option available outside China. One commenter's observation cited on the show: once people see a robotaxi operating, they'll realize the same software is sitting unused in their own driveway, which would drive a surge in FSD subscription adoption and meaningful margin contribution.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **China Wholesale Sales Hit Multi-Year Highs:** Tesla's Giga Shanghai wholesale volume in May 2026 (covering both domestic China sales and exports) reached 85,982 Model 3 and Model Y units, a 39.4% year-over-year increase and an 8.2% month-over-month increase. Year-to-date through May, China total wholesale volume reached 378,000 units, a 29% increase year-over-year. The hosts highlight that year-to-date sales are the highest after two months into the quarter since 2022 — meaning Q2 2026 is outpacing fully-ramped years 2023 and 2024 at this stage. This is occurring despite intense price wars in China, with BYD sales reportedly falling sharply in recent quarters.

2. **Model Y Becomes First EV to Top Australia's Overall Sales Chart:** In May 2026, the Model Y was the best-selling vehicle of any kind in Australia across all fuel types — the first time an electric car has ever led the overall Australian sales chart. Tesla ranked as the 6th best-selling brand in Australia, with Model Y being the top model and comprising 87% of Tesla's Australian sales, with Model 3 at 13%. Market share was 336 units above the three-month trailing average, representing the highest market share ever recorded and Tesla's second-best month ever in Australia. BEV adoption in Australia reached 19.9% in May 2026. The hosts attribute the surge largely to sharply rising petrol prices, which cleared out EV inventory across multiple brands rapidly.

3. **Japan Registrations Jump 182% Year-Over-Year:** Tesla registrations in Japan jumped 182% year-over-year in May 2026, reaching approximately 2,000 vehicles in the month. Year-to-date through May, Tesla registered 8,000 vehicles in Japan, up roughly 157% over the same period in 2025. The May result pushed Tesla past Audi in year-to-date figures, moving from fifth to fourth place among imported brands in Japan. Tesla's head of Asia sales, Tom Drew, commented "three more to go," interpreted as a goal to become the number one imported brand in Japan.

4. **Germany Sales Rebounding Past Most Prior Years:** In May 2026, Germany recorded approximately 5,000 Tesla sales and a 2.1% overall market share. BEV penetration in Germany stands at 25%, with Tesla holding 8.5% of the BEV segment. Year-to-date sales are up 200% over the same period in 2025 and 109% over 2025's full-year total. The hosts note results are the highest quarter after two months since Q1 (implied to be the current year's Q1), and the second-best May ever. Sales have surpassed all prior years except 2023. Brian White attributes the rebound partly to consumers' short political memories (citing the "dieselgate" precedent) and notes that FSD's arrival in Germany could be a further step-change catalyst.

5. **Production Capacity Headroom at Giga Texas and Giga Berlin:** The hosts note that while Fremont and Giga Shanghai are described as "tapped out," Giga Texas and Giga Berlin have meaningful capacity to expand production within existing footprints by adding shifts. Giga Berlin has already announced a 20% production increase, which the hosts connect directly to the expanding FSD rollout in Europe driving anticipated demand growth.

## Market & Competition

1. **China Competitive Landscape — FSD Pricing Dynamics:** In China, Tesla and Huawei are described as the only brands charging extra for their top-tier autonomous driving features. Xiaopeng (Xpeng) is offering its FSD equivalent for free to capture data and maximize fleet size. BYD's lower-tier autonomy features are also free, with only the top tier from Tesla and Huawei carrying a cost. Brian White, who recently visited China and tested Xpeng's driving system, declined to characterize whether Chinese consumers are currently aware of or choosing Tesla based on its FSD advantage, calling it an open question.

2. **Outside China, Tesla Has No Real FSD Competition:** Both hosts agree that in markets outside China, Tesla is effectively the only automaker offering end-to-end self-driving for consumer purchase. Chinese brands like Xpeng and BYD do not have regulatory approval to operate autonomously in most non-China markets. This creates a unique demand driver for Tesla in international markets once consumer awareness catches up.

Notable quotes and data:
- Lemonade offering 50% insurance discount for FSD miles; CEO quoted as expecting rates to approach "near zero"
- Lemonade currently in Oregon, Arizona, and Indiana; plans to expand to 10 states total
- FSD supervised now available in approximately 11 countries; FSD v14 confirmed coming to Australia and New Zealand
- China May 2026 wholesale: 85,982 units (+39.4% YoY, +8.2% MoM)
- China YTD through May: 378,000 units (+29% YoY)
- China YTD described as "highest after two months into the quarter since 2022"
- Australia Model Y: #1 selling vehicle of any kind in May 2026; first EV ever to top overall AU sales chart
- Australia BEV adoption: 19.9% in May 2026
- Australia: 87% of Tesla sales are Model Y, 13% Model 3
- Japan May 2026: ~2,000 registrations, +182% YoY; YTD 8,000 units, +157% vs. same period 2025
- Japan: Tesla moved from 5th to 4th among imported brands YTD
- Germany May 2026: ~5,000 sales, 2.1% overall market share, 25% BEV penetration, Tesla 8.5% of BEV segment
- Germany YTD: +200% vs. same period 2025, +109% vs. full year 2025
- Giga Berlin announced 20% production increase
- Brian White's estimate: if only 5% of US new car buyers demand true FSD, that could mean ~400,000 additional Tesla sales, roughly doubling current US market share
- FSD subscription described as "more or less free money" that will "pad some pretty nice margin in future quarters"

2026-06-05.title: Tesla pushes Roadster demo to August as SpaceX thruster work continues
2026-06-05.body:
Tesla has pushed the planned public demo of its next-generation Roadster to August or later, according to The Information, citing four sources with knowledge of the program. The delay marks at least the eighth timeline slip since the prototype was first unveiled in November 2017.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Demo delayed to August or later:** Tesla's planned Texas demo event for the Roadster has been pushed to August or later, per The Information. Previous targets included April 1, 2026 (set by Musk at the November 2025 shareholder meeting), then late May or early June, then "maybe in a month or so" during the Q1 2026 earnings call. The prototype was originally unveiled in November 2017 with a promised 2020 production start; production has since been pushed to 2027–2028.

2. **SpaceX cold gas thruster system ("A71") is the focus:** The demo is intended to showcase a cold gas thruster system developed in collaboration with SpaceX, internally codenamed "A71." Tesla and SpaceX employees demonstrated the A71 system to Musk in late April 2026 — an internal milestone that helps explain the continued public delay. The system is meant to dramatically improve acceleration, cornering, and braking, and Musk has claimed a 0–60 mph time of 1.1 seconds and the ability to briefly lift off the ground.

3. **Two Roadster variants planned:** Tesla plans to produce a limited-edition SpaceX version featuring the thruster system — which replaces the rear seats with roughly 10 cold-air rocket thrusters — alongside a "scaled down" version of the vehicle.

4. **Reservation holders still waiting:** Early reservation holders paid $50,000 (or $250,000 for the Founders Series) beginning in 2017 and have yet to receive a production vehicle. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's publicly reported attempt to cancel his reservation in October 2025 was thwarted when the reservation email address was found to be inactive. Competitors including Rimac, Lotus, and Xiaomi have shipped high-performance EVs in the interim.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert expresses exhaustion at the repeated delays and skepticism that a production vehicle is imminent, noting that real engineering work and a shipping product are "very different things." He calls the possibility that the Roadster's near-decade delay was driven by a desire for a hovering SpaceX edition "the dumbest thing I've ever heard," arguing it advances neither EVs nor Tesla's core mission.

Notable quotes and data:
- Demo target history: 2020 production → April 1, 2026 → late May/early June 2026 → "maybe in a month or so" (Q1 2026 earnings) → August 2026 or later
- Musk described the April 1 date as giving him "deniability" at the November 2025 shareholder meeting
- Founders Series reservation price: $250,000; standard reservation: $50,000
- Internal code name for thruster system: "A71"
- Claimed 0–60 mph time with thruster system: 1.1 seconds
- At least eight timeline delays since 2017
- Tesla did not respond to The Information's request for comment

2026-06-05.title: Elon Drops 3 New Bombshells (Explained) - Can We Trust Them? ⚡️
2026-06-05.body:
This video from Dillon Loomis of the "Electrified" channel covers several breaking developments across the Tesla and SpaceX ecosystems, including Elon Musk's comments on orbital AI data centers, the SpaceX IPO and its implications for Tesla shareholders, robotaxi deployment updates, and a notable Tesla stock upgrade from JP Morgan. The core thesis is that while market noise around SpaceX and macroeconomic pressures are creating short-term volatility in Tesla stock, the fundamental Tesla story — particularly around robotaxi ramp and potential SpaceX merger — remains intact and misunderstood by the market.

## Robotaxi

1. **Texas Motor Carrier VIN registrations rising:** The Texas Motor Carrier website now shows 51 registered VINs for Tesla's robotaxi service, up from 42 just a few days prior — an increase of nine vehicles. Dillon notes this represents the total number of vehicles registered and eligible for deployment, not necessarily all active at any given time.

2. **Unsupervised robotaxi activity paused in North Austin:** Community reporter "Cyber Owl" noted zero unsupervised robotaxis in North Austin since the day prior to her Thursday post. She reported her ride did include a safety monitor, the car lacked a robotaxi badge, wait times remain long, and pickup/drop-off logic still needs improvement.

3. **Cybercab steering wheel question:** Dillon highlights a key open question: what is involved in removing the steering wheel and pedals from the Cybercab before deployment? He speculates Tesla will want the Cybercab deployed as intended — without a steering wheel — for its debut experience. Since all Cybercabs currently seen in Austin, Houston, and Dallas still have steering wheels, he suggests deployment of the true driverless Cybercab form factor may be weeks away. He also raises unanswered questions about whether the removal can be done at any Tesla service location, select locations only, or via mobile service.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Belgium FSD supervised homologation test completed:** Tesla has officially completed the required 5,000-kilometer supervised FSD test in Belgium. The regulatory burden now shifts to the administration for a formal homologation advice. The Belgian mobility minister expressed support for the fastest possible homologation in Flanders and Belgium.

2. **Tesla AI team at CVPR:** Tesla's AI team presented at CVPR this week. Ashoke gave a presentation and stated the full discussion would be uploaded within a few days.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Model Y North America upgrade:** Tesla has announced that all Model Y trims sold in North America will now come standard with a black headliner and the larger 16-inch center touchscreen, replacing the previously standard gray headliner. Dillon notes the 16-inch screen is also improved in quality, not just size, and expresses hope these upgrades will eventually extend to the Model 3.

2. **Tesla Roadster delayed to August:** Per The Information, Tesla is pushing the Roadster demo to August. The Roadster will use cold gas thrusters co-developed with SpaceX — a previously known detail. Dillon is skeptical the August timeline will hold.

## Market & Competition

1. **JP Morgan Tesla price target upgrade — with caveats:** JP Morgan raised its Tesla price target from $145 to $475 after new analyst Rajat Gupta took over coverage from the long-bearish Ryan Brinkman. Dillon flags a key conflict of interest: JP Morgan is part of the underwriting syndicate for SpaceX's IPO, giving them a direct financial incentive to maintain a positive relationship with Elon Musk. Jamie Dimon's recent in-person interview with Elon is cited as further evidence of this newly aligned relationship. Dillon characterizes the upgrade as JP Morgan "moving out of Tesla Fantasy Land" rather than a purely independent analytical call.

2. **Tesla stock down ~7% on macro conditions:** At the time of recording, Tesla stock was down nearly 7%, but Dillon attributes the move largely to broad market weakness — the NASDAQ was down over 4% — and Tesla's historical beta of 1.5 to 2.3. He also notes that better-than-expected labor market data likely means the Federal Reserve will lean toward tightening rather than loosening, which is a headwind for longer-duration companies like Tesla.

3. **SpaceX IPO and S&P 500 inclusion timing:** The S&P 500 will not allow SpaceX early entry into the index, meaning if SpaceX IPOs this month, the earliest it could be added to the S&P 500 would be June 2027. Dillon notes some speculation that this delayed inclusion could accelerate a Tesla-SpaceX merger, but he views this as a secondary issue and does not expect it to materially alter SpaceX's trajectory.

4. **SpaceX Google cloud deal — $920 million/month:** A SpaceX SEC filing revealed a cloud services agreement with Google covering approximately 110,000 Nvidia GPUs and related components. Google agreed to pay SpaceX $920 million per month starting in October of this year through June 2029, with capacity ramping up through September at a reduced fee. Either party may terminate after December 31st of this year with 90 days' notice. This represents over $11 billion in annualized revenue. Combined with a previously disclosed Anthropic deal running at roughly $15 billion annually, these two deals alone exceed SpaceX's entire 2025 revenue of just over $18 billion.

5. **SpaceX IPO and Tesla shareholder allocation:** Erade has a process for IPO share allocation for SpaceX specifically for Tesla shareholders who have held Tesla in their account for at least 10 years. Dillon notes this is limited to one platform and requires a lengthy holding period, falling short of what many Tesla shareholders had hoped for.

6. **Potential Tesla-SpaceX merger confidence:** Dillon states he is confident Elon will not let Tesla shareholders "draw the short straw" in any potential merger or acquisition scenario, even if it occurs before Tesla has fully scaled its robotaxi ramp.

## Financials

1. **SpaceX revenue context for AI compute business:** SpaceX's total revenue in 2025 was just over $18 billion. The newly announced Google deal alone at $920 million per month would exceed $11 billion annually. Combined with the Anthropic deal at roughly $15 billion annually, these two contracts far surpass SpaceX's entire 2025 revenue, illustrating how transformative the compute rental business could be as a revenue driver.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla stock down ~7% at time of recording; NASDAQ down over 4%; Tesla's historical beta cited as 1.5 to 2.3

- SpaceX annualized revenue from Google deal alone: over $11 billion

2026-06-05.title: Tesla & Space X Next Trillion Dollar Opportunity Is Taking Shape
2026-06-05.body:
This video features Brian (FutureAzA) in conversation with Herbert from Brighter, discussing what they frame as the next trillion-dollar opportunity emerging from a joint Tesla/SpaceX venture to build a vertically integrated semiconductor manufacturing facility called Terafab. The hosts also explore SpaceX AI's broader valuation case, Starlink's growth trajectory, and the potential of Macrohard (an agentic AI product) as part of the SpaceX AI ecosystem.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Terafab land acquisition signals real momentum:** A purchasing entity called Terafab Wit LLC, sharing a physical address with XAI in Palo Alto, has acquired 3,000 acres in Grimes County, Texas near the Gibbons Creek Reservoir area. Herbert describes this as part of SpaceX Reinvestment Zone Number One and characterizes it as a joint Tesla/SpaceX project to manufacture chips — not just ideas on paper, but active forward movement. Herbert cautions, however, that Terafab is unlikely to be in production for at least three or more years.

2. **Chip production rationale mirrors the Giga Nevada battery logic:** The hosts draw a direct parallel between Elon Musk's decision to build Giga Nevada for battery production — when conventional wisdom said to just buy batteries — and the current Terafab chip strategy. Herbert explains that Musk calculated the number of chips needed for humanoid robots, autonomous vehicles, AI data centers, and potentially personal devices (watches, glasses, necklaces), and concluded no external supplier could meet the demand. Herbert believes chip output won't be sold like Nvidia sells chips, but rather rented as a compute service — with any excess capacity licensed out short-term, as illustrated by a referenced deal renting compute to Anthropic for $1.25 billion per month, with a 90-day exit clause Musk reportedly insisted upon.

3. **Terafab's design philosophy: optimized inference chips, not general-purpose:** Herbert argues that unlike TSMC, which must design for every conceivable use case, Terafab's chips will be narrowly optimized for end-device inference — bots, cars, and AI data centers. This focus could allow Tesla/SpaceX to skip legacy manufacturing steps that incumbents maintain due to sunk costs. Musk reportedly hinted at one such simplification on a recent podcast, suggesting he could eat a burger inside the facility — implying the sterile cleanroom environment would be limited only to the area where chips are actually moving, rather than the entire facility. Herbert also notes that a partnership with Intel brings decades of manufacturing experience, meaningfully reducing (though not eliminating) the risk of failure. Grok was cited as an early analyst of the Terafab concept, reportedly identifying legacy steps that could be eliminated.

4. **Bot form factors beyond humanoids:** Herbert emphasizes that Elon Musk frequently references not just C-3PO-style humanoids but also R2-D2-style non-humanoid robots, suggesting a wide range of bot form factors is planned. Every device — bots, cars, personal electronics — will require chips, and Herbert argues that even Terafab's projected output (described as roughly 10x current available capacity) may ultimately be insufficient to meet total demand.

## Market & Competition
1. **Morningstar's SpaceX AI bearish report challenged:** The hosts reference a Morningstar report arguing SpaceX AI is worth less than half its current valuation, which Brian and Herbert push back on. Herbert cites independent space analysts Aaron Bernett of Mach 33 and Larry Goldberg, whose modeling reportedly shows Starlink revenue is already comparable in scale to robotaxi revenue. Herbert argues Morningstar underestimates Starlink's near-term trajectory and that the AI data center and enterprise AI revenue streams are closer than a five-plus-year horizon implies.

2. **Starlink V3 represents a potential 10x capacity expansion:** Herbert describes the rollout of Starlink V3 satellites — enabled by Starship's greater launch capacity and lower per-launch cost versus Falcon 9 (whose upper stage is expendable) — as a transformational capacity upgrade. Each V3 satellite offers substantially greater bandwidth, and Starship can deploy substantially more satellites per launch. Herbert states that the current Starlink user base is approximately 10 million, and that V3 deployment could support a roughly 10x increase in capability. Starlink reportedly lost $600 million in the prior year (2025), which Brian attributes to the service still being in expansion mode rather than a structural weakness.

3. **Macrohard: agentic AI with vision-only thesis, but valuation withheld for now:** Herbert introduces Macrohard (also referred to as "Grok Build") as SpaceX AI's agentic AI product, whose competitive thesis rests on vision-only interaction — the ability to look at any screen visually and control it like a human, without requiring API integrations. Herbert argues this could give it an edge over Anthropic and OpenAI in enterprise settings. Brian, however, explicitly assigns Macrohard zero value in his current model, stating he will only assign value when revenue is demonstrably real — contrasting it with rockets and satellites, which he can see and evaluate today.

## Financials
1. **SpaceX AI TAM cited at $26.5 trillion:** Brian references a total addressable market figure of $26.5 trillion for SpaceX AI, which he uses to justify not dismissing any part of the business — though he withholds valuation credit for Macrohard until tangible revenue emerges.

2. **Compute monetization model: rent, don't sell:** Herbert argues Musk's preferred model for surplus chip and compute capacity is rental rather than outright chip sales. The referenced Anthropic arrangement — $1.25 billion per month, 90-day exit clause — is presented as the template: use what you need internally, rent out the rest on short-term terms to retain optionality.

Notable quotes and data:
- Terafab Wit LLC acquired 3,000 acres in Grimes County, Texas near Gibbons Creek Reservoir
- Estimated facility cost: $55 billion, potentially up to $119 billion, described as a multi-phase next-gen vertically integrated semiconductor manufacturing and advanced computing fabrication facility
- Herbert: Terafab production at least 3+ years away
- Terafab chip capacity described as roughly 10x what is currently available
- Starlink user base: approximately 10 million
- Starlink reportedly lost $600 million in 2025
- Compute rented to Anthropic: $1.25 billion per month, with a 90-day mutual exit clause
- SpaceX AI TAM cited: $26.5 trillion
- Herbert: "Starlink is as big as robotaxi" in revenue potential
- Brian on Macrohard: "I'm going to assign Macrohard in my valuation model zero because I don't care... when it becomes real, I'll give it a valuation"
- Musk reportedly said on a recent podcast he'd "bet he can eat a burger in the facility," implying a reduced-sterility manufacturing approach

2026-06-05.title: Unitree G1 Humanoid Robot: Overview & Upcoming Teardown
2026-06-05.body:
This video from Munro Live features Armen Fchnowski of Munro Associates introducing the Unitree G1 humanoid robot — specifically the base version — ahead of a planned full teardown series. The core argument is that humanoid robots share fundamental engineering DNA with electric vehicles (actuators, battery systems, thermal management, cost pressures), making Munro's 36 years of teardown and costing expertise directly applicable. The goal is to analyze the robot from first principles and identify opportunities for more cost-effective construction.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Unitree G1 Base Specifications:** The Unitree G1 base model stands approximately 4'4" (132 cm) tall, weighs 35 kg (75 lbs), and has 23 degrees of freedom driven by visible actuators throughout the body. It has a walking speed of approximately 2 meters per second. The presenter notes its smaller stature is actually an advantage for software developers, as it reduces risk during development if the robot falls or steps on someone.

2. **Battery and Power System:** The G1 is equipped with a 9,000 milliamp-hour battery running on approximately a 46–48 volt system, which translates to roughly half a kilowatt-hour of capacity. The battery is located in the chest of the robot. Munro notes the cells have not yet been removed for inspection and the cell chemistry/format will be revealed during the teardown.

3. **Sensor Suite and Autonomy Features:** The robot's sensor suite is located at the top of the unit and includes a LiDAR sensor and RGB cameras. While the presenter was remotely controlling the robot during the demo, the G1 does include autonomous features — the LiDAR allows it to scan a room and be set on patrol routes. The base model shown has dummy hands, though Munro Associates has separately purchased Dexterous hands (a finger from one of those hands was shown on camera) for independent evaluation.

4. **Balance and Stability Systems:** The G1 uses position encoders on all motors to track the full state of the robot at all times, combined with accelerometers and gyroscopes to calculate recovery from perturbations. The presenter demonstrated push-recovery capability live, noting the robot handles moderate pushes well but will fall if pushed too forcefully.

5. **Humanoid Robots as "Reconfigured EVs" — Munro's Thesis:** The presenter frames humanoid robots as fundamentally similar to electric vehicles in terms of core engineering: both require actuators, battery systems, thermal management for actuators, and readiness for scale manufacturing under similar cost pressures. This framing positions Munro Associates — with 36 years of teardown and costing experience on EVs — as uniquely qualified to analyze humanoid robot cost structures. The teardown series will produce a full report and explore how these systems could be built more cost-effectively.

6. **Broader Unitree G1 Capability Context:** The presenter notes that the same Unitree G1 platform (or closely related versions) is capable of backflips, acrobatics, and running, and reportedly participated in a humanoid robot marathon in Beijing. The base version being torn down is described as largely the same robot minus certain processor and hand configurations.

Notable quotes and data:
- Height: 132 cm (4'4"); Weight: 35 kg (75 lbs)
- 23 degrees of freedom
- Walking speed: ~2 meters per second
- Battery: 9,000 mAh at ~46–48V ≈ ~0.5 kWh
- "Humanoid robotics in some sense are reconfigured electric vehicles"
- Munro Associates has 36 years of teardown and costing experience
- Dexterous hands purchased separately from the G1 teardown unit
- Cell chemistry inside the battery not yet identified — to be revealed in teardown
