2026-06-07.title: EXCLUSIVE: Why SpaceX Will SURPRISE Investors
2026-06-07.body:
This video is a deep dive into SpaceX's business model and upcoming IPO, featuring Aaron Bernett of Mach 33 Financial Group and venture investor Larry Goldberg. The core thesis is that most investors are misreading SpaceX as a distant-future bet, when in fact near-term revenue drivers — particularly Starlink and terrestrial AI compute — are already materializing, with the IPO potentially pulling forward growth that many assume is years away. While this is a SpaceX-focused discussion, passing references are made to Tesla's robotaxi business and Optimus as parallel opportunities for comparison.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO framing and investor misperception:** The hosts argue that the most common mistake investors make with SpaceX is treating it as a 10-years-away story about Mars, moon cities, and orbital AI. Instead, Bernett contends the business is already generating meaningful revenue through Starlink and is approaching an inflection point. The IPO share price at the time of recording was described as $135, with speculation that it could close near $200.

2. **Starlink as the primary near-term revenue engine:** Bernett's model projects Starlink revenue of approximately $221–228 billion by 2030, driven by both broadband and direct-to-cell (Starlink Mobile) subscribers. The model shows a sharp acceleration in customer growth beginning around 2028–2029, coinciding with the deployment of V3 Starlink satellites via Starship. Bernett frames Starlink as having high IRR comparable to a telco oversubscription model, where the same infrastructure is sold to many customers simultaneously at very high margins.

3. **AI compute as a longer-term but massive opportunity:** Goldman Sachs is cited as estimating SpaceX's AI business at $322 billion by 2030 — a figure Bernett characterizes as significantly higher than his own more conservative model. Bernett's model includes both terrestrial and orbital AI data centers, with orbital compute beginning to generate meaningful revenue around 2028–2031. The model frames terrestrial AI centers as primarily for training large models, while orbital infrastructure is positioned for inference workloads. A key insight from the model: approximately 200 Starship launches would be required to put one gigawatt of AI compute into orbit — equivalent to Colossus 1 and 2 — and the model projects that cadence being reached around 2031.

4. **Capital allocation as the central modeling framework:** Rather than building a traditional top-down revenue model, Mach 33 uses an IRR-driven capital allocation framework. Each year, available capital and Starship launch capacity are allocated to the business line with the highest return on investment. Currently, that is Starlink; around 2030, the model projects that Starlink's IRR will compress (as the market saturates and broadband prices fall) and AI compute IRR will rise, triggering a capital shift toward orbital data centers and AI infrastructure.

5. **Terafab chip manufacturing as a key variable:** Bernett's team performed a bottom-up cost analysis of Terafab and estimated that at 100 wafer starts per month — described as roughly one-tenth to one-hundredth of Terafab's ultimate capacity — SpaceX could produce approximately 44 million chips (at ~70% yield). This was framed as sufficient for one chip per Optimus unit and two chips per robotaxi vehicle with chips left over. Chip availability is flagged as a key risk to the timeline for orbital compute.

6. **Valuation range and SpaceX reaching $10 trillion:** Using a traditional DCF (Gordon Growth Model), Bernett's team estimates SpaceX's end-of-2026 valuation at approximately $2.48 trillion, with an upper bound around $5.5 trillion using exit multiple methodology. The model projects SpaceX reaching $10 trillion in market capitalization somewhere between 2030 and 2035. Bernett frames this as a dollar-cost-averaging opportunity in the "core infrastructure of the future," not a trading vehicle.

7. **Launch cadence and Starship scalability:** The model projects roughly 600–700 total Starship launches by 2030, equating to approximately two launches per day across SpaceX's planned five launch towers in two locations. Larry Goldberg argues that launch revenue is being underestimated industry-wide, noting that as Starship becomes fully reusable (every component recovered intact) and costs collapse, the total addressable market for launch will expand dramatically beyond what Falcon 9 history would suggest.

8. **AI application layer as uncapped upside:** Both Goldberg and Bernett emphasize that the highest-margin opportunity is not infrastructure rental (like the Anthropic compute deal) but owning the AI application layer — what Goldberg calls "Macrohard." Bernett notes that today, roughly 80% or more of AI stack profit flows to chip manufacturers (Nvidia) and hyperscalers, but over time that margin shifts toward application owners. SpaceX's full vertical stack — chips, compute, connectivity, applications — positions it to capture margin at every layer.

9. **Tesla robotaxi parallel:** Goldberg draws an explicit parallel between Tesla's transition from EVs to robotaxi and SpaceX's transition from launch services to Starlink and AI compute. He also notes that $221 billion per year in Starlink revenue is roughly equivalent in scale to what 10 million robotaxis might generate, but argues Starlink carries far lower operational overhead than a physical robotaxi fleet.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX IPO opening price referenced: $135/share, with speculation of closing near $200
- Starlink projected revenue by 2030: ~$221–228 billion (Mach 33 model)
- Goldman Sachs AI compute estimate for SpaceX by 2030: $322 billion
- Goldman Sachs Starlink estimate by 2030: ~$140 billion
- SpaceX prospectus cited TAM for enterprise AI: $26.5 trillion
- Terafab estimated chip output at 100 wafer starts/month: ~44 million chips at ~70% yield
- Orbital AI compute: ~200 Starship launches to put 1 gigawatt into orbit (equal to Colossus 1+2)
- Model projects 210 AI compute-specific launches in 2031 = one Colossus-equivalent per year
- IRR for Starlink modeled at 172% in 2028 in one scenario
- SpaceX valuation range end-2026: $2.48 trillion (DCF low) to ~$5.5 trillion (exit multiple high)
- SpaceX projected to reach $10 trillion market cap between 2030 and 2035
- 2031 flagged as a potential "blowout year" where SpaceX could return its entire capital to investors
- Mach 33 model forecasts out to 2040; collaborates with ARK Invest on components
- "If you knew this was going to happen, you wouldn't be worried about timing one little blip up and down — you would be worried about dollar cost averaging into that over time." — Aaron Bernett
- Lock-up expirations expected in the 60–180 day window post-IPO

2026-06-07.title: The Only Public Way to Own Figure and Apptronik
2026-06-07.body:
This video from brighterwithherbert introduces Robo Strategy (ticker: BOTB on NASDAQ), a newly public closed-end fund designed to give retail investors access to private humanoid robotics companies like Figure AI and Apptronik. The host argues that the intelligent robot market represents one of the largest economic shifts in history — bigger than the PC or the internet — and that the value creation is happening almost entirely in private markets inaccessible to ordinary investors. Robo Strategy is presented as a MicroStrategy-style vehicle that bridges that gap.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **The Scale of the Robotics Opportunity:** The host frames physical AI and humanoid robots as a generational economic shift, citing a global labor market of approximately $60 trillion (derived from labor being ~52% of global GDP, with global GDP running around $118 trillion in the prior year). A projected global shortage of 85 million skilled workers by 2030 is cited as a structural tailwind. Industry forecasts place the robotics market at up to $218 billion by 2030 and past $370 billion by 2034, though the host believes these figures understate the ultimate opportunity.

2. **Figure AI's Growth as the Central Case Study:** Figure AI is highlighted as the clearest example of private market value creation being locked away from public investors. It raised at a $2.6 billion valuation in early 2024 and by its Series C in the fall of 2025 was valued at $39 billion — approximately 15x growth in under two years. The host notes that essentially none of that appreciation was accessible to a normal public investor. Figure has also signed a commercial deal with Catalyst Brands (parent of J.C. Penney, Aéropostale, and Brooks Brothers) to deploy humanoid robots at operations in Reno, Nevada, and its production line is reportedly building a robot roughly every 90 minutes.

3. **Apptronik's Momentum:** Apptronik is cited as another private company with significant momentum, having attracted investment from Google, Mercedes, and others. Its valuation is noted to have tripled to over $5 billion in the current year (2026).

4. **Robo Strategy's Portfolio:** The fund's holdings span multiple categories of robotics: Figure AI and Apptronik in humanoids, plus Dino Robotics, Standard Bots, Dexmate, Cocoa Robotics, Path Robotics, and others covering robotic arms, mobile manipulation, and compute infrastructure.

5. **Dr. Scott Walter as Due Diligence Lead:** The host emphasizes the credibility of Dr. Scott Walter — described as a 40-year veteran in humanoid robotics and a recurring guest on the channel — who recently joined Robo Strategy as Robotics Research Diligence Director (internally nicknamed "R2-D2"). The host argues that having a hands-on engineer with decades of experience vetting deals provides a meaningful edge in distinguishing real technology from hype-driven demos.

## Market & Competition

1. **The Private Market Access Problem:** The host identifies a structural problem: the most exciting robotics companies are staying private far longer than in prior technology cycles because abundant private capital means they don't need to go public. He draws parallels to OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX — companies with enormous valuations where the public largely watched from the sidelines. Andrew Kang, the fund's founder, estimates the current private robotics market at roughly $100–$150 billion, with the potential to become a tens-of-trillions industry.

2. **The MicroStrategy Playbook Applied to Robotics:** Robo Strategy explicitly models itself on MicroStrategy's approach to Bitcoin — a publicly traded company that raises capital markets money and deploys it into an asset class (in this case, equity in private robotics firms). The fund is structured as a closed-end fund listed on NASDAQ under ticker BOTB, which went public on May 11, 2026. The permanent capital structure (no fixed fund life) is highlighted as a key advantage over traditional VC funds, allowing indefinitely long holding periods suited to an early-stage industry.

3. **The NAV Premium Flywheel and Its Risks:** The host explains the mechanics in plain terms: when the stock trades at a premium to net asset value (NAV), the fund can issue new shares at inflated prices, use the proceeds to buy more private robotics assets, and incrementally increase NAV per share — a self-reinforcing flywheel. He cites MicroStrategy as precedent, noting it traded at nearly 4x its Bitcoin value at its late-2024 peak before cooling to approximately 1.2x by 2026. The key risk is premium collapse: if sentiment shifts, the fund could trade at a discount to NAV, making share issuance dilutive rather than accretive. Additional risks include the difficulty of valuing and liquidating private holdings, and the possibility that humanoid robot timelines slip relative to current hype.

4. **Capital Raise and Competitive Positioning:** Shortly after listing, Robo Strategy signed a committed equity facility of up to $2 billion with Roth Principal Investments, providing a standing mechanism to issue new shares and deploy capital into future private robotics rounds. The host notes that Andrew Kang's early $19 million investment in Figure AI (made roughly two years ago) and his early entry into Apptronik established a track record, and that Robo Strategy is now described as leading rounds and competing successfully against top-tier venture firms for allocations.

5. **Tesla and Optimus as the Public Baseline:** The host positions Tesla as his single largest holding and acknowledges Optimus as potentially the most valuable thing Tesla ever builds. However, he argues that at over $1 trillion in market cap, Tesla gives only partial, diluted exposure to robotics, making concentrated robotics vehicles like Robo Strategy a complementary rather than redundant holding.

Notable quotes and data:
- Global labor market implied at ~$60 trillion (52% of ~$118 trillion global GDP)
- Global skilled worker shortage: 85 million by 2030
- Robotics market forecast: up to $218 billion by 2030; past $370 billion by 2034
- Andrew Kang's estimate of current private robotics market: $100–$150 billion
- Figure AI valuation: $2.6 billion (early 2024) → $39 billion (Series C, fall 2025) — ~15x in under 2 years
- Apptronik valuation: described as having tripled to over $5 billion in 2026
- Robo Strategy initial investment in Figure AI: ~$19 million (approximately 2 years before recording)
- Figure AI production rate: approximately one robot every 90 minutes
- Committed equity facility: up to $2 billion with Roth Principal Investments
- BOTB listed on NASDAQ on May 11, 2026
- MicroStrategy premium at late-2024 peak: ~4x Bitcoin NAV; cooled to ~1.2x by 2026
- "Bitcoin got the micro strategy treatment. Robotics is a bigger industry than Bitcoin and far harder for a regular person to access. So robotics needs its own version." — Andrew Kang's pitch as paraphrased by the host

2026-06-07.title: Elon Musk's Next Move Is Sending Wall Street Into Panic
2026-06-07.body:
This episode of FutureAzA features host Brian and guest Randy Kirk discussing the potential SpaceX IPO and its implications for Tesla investors, Wall Street narratives, and the broader Elon Musk tech ecosystem. The central argument is that media and financial analyst fears about SpaceX harming Tesla or robbing retirement accounts are overblown, dishonest, or simply wrong — and that Tesla's fundamentals heading into the rest of 2026 are actually strengthening.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO and its real winner — Anthropic's cloud deal:** The SpaceX S1 disclosure revealed a cloud services agreement with Anthropic worth $1.25 billion per month, with capacity ramping in May and June 2026 at a reduced fee period, and a 90-day cancellation window available to either party after the first 6 months. Randy Kirk argues this deal — combined with a reported ability to train new AI models 10 times faster than a few months prior — positions SpaceX as a serious compute provider, and that the Anthropic and Cursor deals push SpaceX's projected 2026 revenue from a previously estimated $19.7 billion to approximately $40 billion, with solid profitability expected this year. Brian notes the joke thesis of the article is that Mark Zuckerberg is the "real winner" of the SpaceX IPO because he can simply copy SpaceX's cloud monetization playbook, given Meta's massive but arguably less productive AI capex spend (2026 capex guidance raised to $145 billion).

2. **Tesla-SpaceX merger speculation dominating headlines:** Brian and Randy discuss how the Tesla-SpaceX merger narrative has been the dominant headline for roughly a week at time of recording. A Fortune analysis cited a potential combined entity valued at approximately $3.4 trillion — SpaceX at an anticipated $1.75 trillion and Tesla at $1.65 trillion — which would make it nearly three times larger than the biggest merger ever completed. One analyst named Larry Goldberg is cited as predicting Tesla could reach $550 by end of June 2026, driven by investors seeking exposure to a potential SpaceX merger. Both hosts are skeptical that a merger is a "rescue mission" for Tesla, pushing back hard on that framing.

3. **SpaceX IPO impact on Tesla stock and index funds:** The hosts discuss how the SpaceX IPO could cause short-term selling pressure on Tesla, as investors raise cash to participate in the IPO — noting Tesla fell approximately 5% on the Monday of recording (around June 2, 2026), alongside drops in Amazon, Meta, and cryptocurrencies. However, they also note a potential positive offset: SpaceX insiders unlocked on IPO day may rotate some proceeds into Tesla shares. Randy estimates SpaceX could represent approximately 4% of the S&P 500 upon inclusion, requiring index funds to buy in and potentially dilute other holdings marginally. A union spokesperson and a content creator named Zack Nelson are cited as claiming the IPO will "rob" 401k accounts — claims the hosts dismiss as uninformed or dishonest. A portfolio manager named Ian McMillan (at Client First) is quoted calling the situation "100% fraud," a claim the hosts also reject as legally reckless and analytically wrong.

4. **SpaceX revenue trajectory and long-term growth:** Randy projects SpaceX revenue of $40 billion in 2026, $65 billion in 2027 (noting Brian Wong projects $80+ billion), and potentially $130 billion the year after. He argues the company could be profitable today if it stopped expanding Starlink, but that halting expansion would be strategically foolish given competition from Amazon's LEO constellation, New Glenn, and Russia's emerging low Earth orbit network. The hosts frame SpaceX as a company deliberately sacrificing near-term profits for long-term dominance — similar to early Tesla.

## Financials

1. **Tesla's trailing earnings scrutinized and defended:** A Fortune article is cited claiming Tesla's trailing GAAP earnings have collapsed from $15 billion to $3.9 billion, with core operating earnings (excluding regulatory credits and Bitcoin gains) at just $2.3 billion. Brian and Randy forcefully reject this framing, arguing the analysis cherry-picks negative line items while ignoring growing FSD subscription revenue, improving vehicle sales and margins in Q2 2026, and expanding energy (Megapack) deployment. They also note that regulatory credits represent real money paid by competitors to avoid fines, and stripping them out while not applying equivalent adjustments to competitors is intellectually dishonest.

2. **Tesla outlook for 2026 and 2027:** Randy argues Tesla is heading into very substantial profits in 2026, driven by higher Q2 vehicle unit sales (described as "up substantially"), increasing FSD subscription uptake, and approximately double the Megapack deployments in Q2 versus Q1. He projects the trajectory "goes crazy" in 2027 with the scaling of robotaxi and Optimus.

## Robotaxi

1. **Robotaxi as a key 2027 growth driver:** Randy briefly but explicitly identifies robotaxi scaling as one of the two primary catalysts (alongside Optimus) that will drive Tesla's dramatic profit acceleration in 2027. No specific fleet numbers or unit economics are provided in this episode.

## Energy

1. **Megapack deployment acceleration in Q2 2026:** Randy states Tesla is expected to deploy approximately double the number of Megapacks in Q2 2026 compared to Q1 2026, calling this a "massive increase" in both profits and revenue from the energy segment.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Vehicle sales recovering in Q2 2026:** Randy asserts that Tesla vehicle sales are "up substantially" in Q2 2026 compared to prior quarters, which he expects to translate into improved margins as Tesla will not need to discount vehicles as aggressively to move inventory.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX-Anthropic cloud deal: $1.25 billion/month, ramping May–June 2026, 90-day cancellation clause after 6 months
- SpaceX projected 2026 revenue (per Randy Kirk): ~$40 billion (up from prior estimate of $19.7 billion)
- SpaceX projected 2027 revenue: Randy at ~$65 billion; Brian Wong at $80+ billion
- SpaceX projected 2028 revenue (Randy): ~$130 billion
- Potential combined Tesla-SpaceX valuation: ~$3.4 trillion ($1.75T SpaceX + $1.65T Tesla)
- That combined entity would be nearly 3x the size of the largest merger ever completed
- SpaceX estimated to represent ~4% of S&P 500 upon inclusion
- Tesla GAAP trailing earnings cited by Fortune: collapsed from $15 billion to $3.9 billion; core operating earnings ex-credits and Bitcoin: $2.3 billion
- Meta 2026 capex guidance: $145 billion; Q1 2026 revenue growth: 33% year-over-year
- Tesla stock down ~5% on the Monday of recording (approximately June 2, 2026)
- Larry Goldberg price target: $550 Tesla by end of June 2026
- SpaceX share issuance for Tesla merger (per Fortune/Telly): new shares equal to 94% of current count, doubling share base to 8 billion
- Randy: Megapack deployments in Q2 2026 expected to be approximately double Q1 2026
- Randy: 2027 is when robotaxi and Optimus scaling begins to "go crazy" for Tesla

2026-06-07.title: Tesla's Factory Advantage Is About To Get Even Bigger
2026-06-07.body:
This video from FutureAzA features host Brian in conversation with casting expert Luca Greco, exploring the current state and future trajectory of giga casting technology in the automotive industry. The core thesis is that Tesla's in-house, vertically integrated casting process gives it a durable competitive advantage through rapid iteration, process control, and continuous improvement — advantages that suppliers and most Western OEMs cannot easily replicate.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla's casting strategy evolved away from mega-machines:** Tesla originally ordered a casting machine in the 15,000–16,000 ton range to produce a full underbody in one piece (front section, battery tray, and rear), but cancelled the order. This was widely misreported as Tesla "retreating" on giga casting. In reality, Tesla pivoted to its "unbox" manufacturing process, which uses smaller castings producible on 6,000-ton machines or smaller. The structural battery pack made a single-piece full underbody redundant, as adding a second structure through the middle of the car would have introduced complexity, new tolerances, and higher scrap rates.

2. **Front casting removal from Model Y was contextual, not a reversal:** The front underbody casting was never fully rolled out across Giga Texas, Giga Berlin, or Giga Shanghai — it remained on a separate line and was dependent on the structural 4680 battery pack. In Giga Berlin, it was tied to BYD blade pack integration, which was cancelled (possibly over battery longevity concerns). In Giga Texas, cell supply was redirected toward the Cybertruck. Additionally, thousands of robots had already been installed for a traditional front underbody, and the existing front casting design was suboptimal — reportedly weighing around 85 kg, at least 10 kg heavier than ideal per Munro Live's assessment. Importantly, both the Cybertruck and the Cybercab do use front underbody castings, confirming the technology remains valid.

3. **Vertical integration is Tesla's most underrated casting advantage:** Lars Moravi told Munro Live at the Cybertruck delivery event that Tesla's casting engineers, body-in-white engineers, and die designers all work together in the same room daily. This level of integration enables rapid iteration impossible with a supplier relationship. A key example is conformal cooling — 3D-printed inserts placed inside dies with channels that mirror the casting's shape — which dramatically improved thermal control and reduced cycle times from over 170 seconds down to 80 seconds or less. Giga Berlin recently released a video discussing this. Suppliers lack the financial capacity and incentive to pursue such innovations on behalf of OEMs.

4. **Chinese OEMs are adopting a hybrid model:** Rather than fully outsourcing casting or investing in full in-house capability, some Chinese OEMs are inviting die casting suppliers to set up operations inside their factories or industrial parks. This allows the OEM to benefit from rapid iteration and supplier expertise simultaneously. One unnamed Chinese supplier is reportedly running a machine at over 200,000 parts per year — believed to exceed Tesla's Fremont peak output. Chinese company Chery (a state-owned OEM) is also noted for using a 5,000-ton machine to produce a rear underbody casting with strong structural properties, though they also continue using traditional 9,000-ton supplier machines.

5. **Near-term casting improvements will be incremental and mostly invisible:** Over the next one to five years, visible changes to castings are unlikely. Improvements will focus on yield rates, material properties, reduced scrap, weight reduction, and lower machining cycle times. The most exciting frontier is magnesium castings, which could reduce weight by approximately 18–20 kg compared to aluminum equivalents (e.g., replacing Tesla's rear casting). Aluminum-magnesium alloys (~60% aluminum, 40% magnesium) are being studied in China to balance weight savings with corrosion resistance and flammability concerns during die casting. No consumer vehicle applications exist yet. Tesla is not expected to pursue magnesium castings in the near term.

6. **Western OEMs and newer entrants face structural limits:** Ford, Volvo, and Volkswagen are highlighted as capable of reaching good casting technology levels, partly by following Tesla's lead; Volkswagen is doing interesting work on battery trays. Rivian's R2 integrates multiple rear underbody castings sourced from suppliers — a pragmatic strategy given the investment required for in-house capability. Lucid similarly uses castings from suppliers. Lucid's plan to build a factory in Saudi Arabia is flagged as logistically difficult given the absence of a local supply chain. The broader point is that supplier-dependent OEMs cannot achieve the rapid iteration that defines Tesla's manufacturing edge.

## Market & Competition

1. **Large casting applications may have reached their practical ceiling:** Beyond battery trays (largely a China-only development) and C-pillar castings on large SUVs (seen from Huawei, NIO, and others), Luca Greco sees few new compelling large-casting applications on the horizon. The benefits of consolidation — fewer parts, fewer process steps — diminish as castings grow beyond a certain size, and integration challenges begin to outweigh savings.

2. **China leads on large and exotic casting innovation:** All current large-scale casting applications, including battery tray castings, are being developed in China. The largest casting ever made — the one-piece full underbody originally conceived by Tesla — was produced in China approximately two years before the video's publication. Multi-material innovations (plastic injection molding combined with aluminum die casting in a single shot, from a 5,000-ton machine) have been announced and built in China, though no consumer product output has been confirmed.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla cancelled an order for a casting machine reportedly in the 15,000–16,000 ton range before pivoting to the unbox process using ~6,000-ton machines.
- Conformal cooling reduced Tesla's casting cycle time from over 170 seconds to 80 seconds or less.
- One Chinese supplier is running a casting machine at over 200,000 parts per year — reportedly above Tesla's Fremont peak.
- Magnesium castings could reduce weight by approximately 18–20 kg vs. aluminum equivalents.
- Munro Live assessed Tesla's original front underbody casting design at approximately 85 kg — at least 10 kg heavier than optimal.
- Aluminum-magnesium alloys are approximately 60% aluminum and 40% magnesium.
- Chery (Chinese state-owned OEM) is producing a rear underbody casting using a 5,000-ton machine.
- "To have such a huge level of process control in-house means you can basically do whatever you want and you have no constraints from your suppliers." — Luca Greco
- "The OEM can forget rapid iteration the way Tesla did" when using an external supplier. — Luca Greco

2026-06-07.title: LIVE: Will Tesla Stock RECOVER Into The SpaceX IPO?
2026-06-07.body:
Jo Bhakdi hosts a live session reacting to a sharp Friday market selloff (NASDAQ down ~4.18%, Tesla down ~6.56%), arguing it represents a profit-taking breather in a strong bull market rather than the start of a sustained crash. He previews an in-progress SpaceX DCF model and shares his evolving view that SpaceX may be dramatically undervalued at its ~$2 trillion IPO valuation. He also flags the upcoming World Cup as a potential catalyst for a Cybercab public launch, and outlines his near-term Tesla trading posture.

## Market & Competition

1. **Friday Selloff Characterized as Profit-Taking, Not Panic:** Bhakdi describes the Friday session as the worst single day for the NASDAQ in over a year, with the NASDAQ falling 4.18% and Tesla dropping 6.56% (~$27). He argues the selling was unusually linear — not the accelerating-into-the-close pattern typical of true panic — and frames it as an inevitable breather after the NASDAQ rallied approximately 25% over the March–May period. He attributes the catalyst to widespread profit-taking in semiconductors and other high-momentum names, dismissing the strong labor data narrative as an after-the-fact rationalization.

2. **Tesla Outperformed Relative to NASDAQ Beta:** Bhakdi notes that given Tesla's historical beta versus the NASDAQ, a 4.18% NASDAQ decline would ordinarily imply a roughly 8.3–8.5% Tesla decline. Tesla's actual 6.56% decline, he argues, reflects partial support from JP Morgan's price target upgrade from $150 to $475 — which he attributes directly to JP Morgan's role as a bookrunner for the SpaceX IPO rather than a genuine analytical revision.

3. **Near-Term Tesla Price Range: $350–$490:** Bhakdi outlines a wide near-term range, noting Tesla could reach $490 within days if a Cybercab World Cup launch catalyst materializes and the broader market recovers, or could fall to $350–$380 if the market extends its selloff and/or SpaceX IPO dynamics create additional selling pressure in Tesla. He emphasizes that both scenarios are "really, really reasonable" in the next 10 days.

4. **SpaceX IPO Volatility Risk for Tesla:** Bhakdi flags the SpaceX IPO as an additional complicating variable, noting possibilities in both directions: some Tesla investors could sell Tesla to fund SpaceX purchases, while SpaceX enthusiasm could also draw new capital toward Tesla. He states the IPO is approximately $75 billion in size, which he considers manageable relative to the ~$2.5 trillion single-day market cap destruction seen on Friday. He gives a 95% probability to a Tesla–SpaceX merger occurring within two years.

5. **S&P 500 Exclusion Limits SpaceX Index Buying:** Bhakdi notes that the S&P 500 has indicated it will not include SpaceX this year, which removes what would have been the largest forced-buying driver. He expects NASDAQ 100 index inclusion to provide some upward pressure but considers it substantially less powerful. His base case remains that SpaceX shares will rise at IPO, then drop, and potentially stay depressed longer than he previously expected before recovering.

## Robotaxi

1. **World Cup as Cybercab Launch Catalyst:** Bhakdi identifies the FIFA World Cup — beginning the weekend of the video — as the most significant near-term catalyst for an unsupervised Cybercab public launch. He notes that Cybercabs are already physically present in Dallas, Houston, and Austin, and that Dallas hosts major World Cup matches, making it an ideal PR moment. He stops short of calling it a guarantee but says he "would really not be surprised if it happens" and believes a successful launch could push Tesla to $490.

2. **Current Robotaxi Fleet Status Referenced:** A viewer comment mentions approximately 30 unsupervised Cybercabs deployed entering June, which Bhakdi acknowledges without correcting or providing his own updated figure.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Acknowledged as Delayed:** In response to a viewer skeptical of Elon Musk's ability to execute, Bhakdi concedes that Full Self-Driving has been "totally delayed" and that the timeline uncertainty remains. He contrasts this with Starlink, which he says is "absolutely scaling," and uses Starlink's scaling success to argue that SpaceX's AI satellite buildout is more likely to follow a similar trajectory than FSD's delayed path.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus Radio Silence Seen as Bullish:** Bhakdi agrees with a viewer comment that the absence of recent Optimus news is a bullish signal, though he tempers this by noting Elon Musk is highly distracted by the SpaceX IPO process. He also mentions an upcoming video he plans to publish about Figure One's robot production updates, noting Figure One has released overview content on all robots produced to date.

## Financials

1. **SpaceX DCF Model: Work in Progress, Surprising Undervaluation Signal:** Bhakdi shares a preliminary SpaceX DCF model being built by his Pioneer Lens team, currently projecting a fair share price of approximately $196–$221 for 2026 — figures he explicitly flags as not yet correct due to modeling issues. The core problem he identifies is that standard DCF terminal value assumptions (dropping to ~3% growth after 2040) are unrealistic for SpaceX given his view of indefinitely high data center demand growth (30–50% annually). He is extending the model to a longer horizon to address this. His preliminary gut feeling, even unfinished, is that SpaceX is "dramatically undervalued" at a $2 trillion IPO valuation.

2. **Google's $920 Million Monthly SpaceX Compute Deal:** Bhakdi highlights a breaking news item that Google has agreed to pay SpaceX $920 million per month for access to Colossus data center compute. He notes this is on top of what he describes as $1.25–1.5 billion per month that Anthropic already pays SpaceX for compute, implying SpaceX is adding approximately $12 billion in annualized high-margin revenue from this single deal. He uses this as evidence that SpaceX has become a hyperscaler of the first order.

3. **Tesla Target: ~$750 at Merger:** Bhakdi responds to a viewer suggesting Tesla hits $1,000 per share at merger by countering with approximately $750 per share, which he estimates implies a Tesla market cap of roughly $2.2–2.5 trillion.

Notable quotes and data:
- NASDAQ decline on Friday: ~4.18%; Tesla decline: ~6.56% (~$27/share)
- NASDAQ up approximately 25% from late March through early June 2026 before the selloff
- JP Morgan price target change on Tesla: from $150 to $475
- Near-term Tesla range: $350 (downside) to $490 (upside)
- SpaceX IPO size referenced: approximately $75 billion
- Preliminary SpaceX DCF fair value (flagged as incomplete): $196–$221 per share for 2026
- Google deal: $920 million/month to SpaceX for Colossus compute
- Anthropic deal: $1.25–1.5 billion/month to SpaceX (as cited by Bhakdi)
- Probability of Tesla–SpaceX merger within two years: 95% (Bhakdi's estimate)
- Tesla at merger: "maybe $750" per share (~$2.2–2.5 trillion market cap)
- Elon Musk Freudian slip: referred to SpaceX AI satellites as "Tesla AI satellites" during a clip played in the video
- Bhakdi: "I think SpaceX is just dramatically undervalued at two trillion"
- On AI data center demand: "I think we will have 30 to 50% growth forever on data centers because there is no limit to the amount of intelligence you need"

2026-06-07.title: Daily X Summary (2026-06-07)
2026-06-07.body:
## Executive Summary
The dominant signal today is Tesla's formal permit application in Nevada to operate up to 5,000 robotaxis in Clark County (Las Vegas) — a major regulatory expansion milestone that represents the single largest fleet authorization sought to date. Secondary signals include used Cybertruck inventory being restocked at meaningfully higher prices, suggesting some pricing power recovery. Overall, today's posts skew bullish on the robotaxi deployment thesis.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Tesla files for Nevada Robotaxi permit — up to 5,000 vehicles in Year 1:** In the highest-signal post of the day (4,200 likes, 489 reposts), Tesla officially applied for an Autonomous Vehicle Network Company permit in Nevada. The application seeks approval for **up to 5,000 robotaxis during the first 12 months** after the permit is granted. The geographic scope covers **Clark County (Las Vegas), including Harry Reid International Airport** — a commercially dense, high-fare corridor. This is a significant step in Tesla's robotaxi expansion strategy beyond its current California and Texas footholds. The Las Vegas market, with its high tourism traffic, airport demand, and Strip density, is arguably one of the most attractive unit-economics environments for autonomous ride-hailing. The 5,000-unit first-year ask dwarfs the current total active fleet of ~706 vehicles per RobotaxiTracker.com (as of 2026-06-04), signaling Tesla is preparing for a step-change in fleet scale pending regulatory approval.

2. **Used Cybertruck inventory restocked at higher prices:** Tesla sold out of used Cybertruck inventory within days, then restocked with higher average pricing. The new floor is **$72,900 for a used 2024 Foundation Series Cybertruck with 32,845 miles**, up from **$66,200** for a comparable used unit just days prior — a jump of roughly $6,700. While this is secondary-market pricing rather than new-vehicle demand, the rapid sell-through followed by a price increase suggests resilient consumer appetite for Cybertruck at current levels and gives Tesla room to capture more margin on used inventory.

3. **Lucid Gravity sighted in the wild (minor competition note):** A brief post noted a first real-world sighting of a white Lucid Gravity. Low signal for Tesla investors, but serves as a reminder that the luxury EV competitive set continues to expand incrementally.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — Tesla's Nevada permit application for up to 5,000 robotaxis in Year 1 represents a concrete regulatory expansion move into one of the most economically attractive U.S. markets for autonomous ride-hailing, materially strengthening the near-term deployment thesis.

2026-06-08.title: Weekly Tesla Brief (Jun 1 – Jun 7, 2026)
2026-06-08.body:
## Unsupervised Robotaxi Fleet

| City | Now | 7D | 30D |
|:-----|----:|---:|----:|
| Austin | 28 | 0 | +1 |
| Houston | 6 | 0 | 0 |
| Dallas | 5 | 0 | 0 |
| **Total** | **39** | 0 | +1 |

Source: [RobotaxiTracker.com](https://robotaxitracker.com/)

---

## Brief

- Austin unsupervised robotaxi zone expands to entire metro; highways now included.
- Nevada permit filed: up to 5,000 robotaxis in Clark County Year 1.
- Tesla retroactively deleted FSD purchase contracts during active litigation.
- JP Morgan raises Tesla target to $475; analyst conflict flagged.
- Belgium clears 5,000 km FSD test; Estonia becomes third EU approval.
- Optimus factory steel standing at Giga Texas; 208 open job listings.
- Q2 Megapack deployments tracking ~2x Q1's 8.8 GWh.

---

## Robotaxi

- **Austin geofence now covers the entire metro**, including Pflugerville, Manor, I-35, Giga Texas, and Austin-Bergstrom International Airport — roughly doubling prior coverage and the fifth expansion since January 2026. Ashok Elluswami confirmed unsupervised service "starts in earnest today." Unsupervised vehicles are now operating highway segments within the geofence — a meaningful capability threshold Tesla had historically avoided at speed.

- **Nevada permit application targets 5,000 vehicles in Year 1.** Tesla formally applied for an Autonomous Vehicle Network Company permit in Clark County (Las Vegas), including Harry Reid International Airport. The application encompasses the full city geofence and a high-fare tourism corridor — structurally the most attractive unit-economics environment in any pending market. This is the clearest disclosed scale target Tesla has filed with any regulator to date.

- **H1 2026 six-city IR commitment is under pressure.** As of June 7, paid service remains only in Austin, Dallas, and Houston. The Q4 2025 earnings deck committed to Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Miami, and Phoenix by June 30 — 23 days away. AI safety operator hiring is active in 15+ states; infrastructure is permitted in Las Vegas and Grand Prairie, TX. Bhakdi identifies the FIFA World Cup opener in Dallas (June 14) as the most compelling near-term Cybercab launch window.

- **Operational quality gaps remain.** Community reporter Cyber Owl found zero unsupervised vehicles in North Austin on June 5; her own ride had a safety monitor. Electrek reports the active Austin fleet (all modes) collapsed from ~165 to ~34 vehicles at one point. Wait times and pickup/drop-off logic still need improvement per multiple on-the-ground observers. All Cybercabs observed in Texas still retain steering wheels.

- **Infrastructure buildout confirms scale intent.** Four confirmed Tesla fleet facilities now span Austin, Las Vegas, Grand Prairie TX (51,000 sq ft, permitted for autonomous vehicle charging/cleaning/maintenance), and a second Dallas-area site. A Senior Real Estate Manager listing covers Pennsylvania — the first East Coast expansion signal. Full-stack engineers building dynamic and surge pricing algorithms are among 36 open robotaxi roles this week.

---

## Autonomous Driving

- **Belgium clears 5,000 km supervised test; Estonia becomes third EU approval.** Flemish Minister Annick De Ridder confirmed the test file has moved to formal homologation. Estonia approved supervised FSD effective May 29 via mutual recognition of the Dutch RDW certification. Ashok confirmed at CVPR that approximately 1.3 million vehicles worldwide now have FSD access; pending markets include Germany, France, Japan, India, Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Brazil.

- **FSD 14 Light for HW3 still pending.** HW4 vehicles receive FSD the day a country approves; Tesla is targeting "later this summer 2026" for the HW3 variant, which would materially widen the installed base in newly approved markets overnight. Australia and New Zealand told customers FSD 14 is in "final stages of local development testing."

- **Lemonade launches up to 50% insurance discount for FSD miles in Indiana**, explicitly citing FSD as "twice as safe." CEO has suggested rates could approach "near-zero" over time; 10-state expansion is planned. This is the first major commercial actuarial validation of Tesla's FSD safety narrative — and introduces a compounding adverse-selection risk for competing insurers.

- **FSD daily miles: 26.7M/day**, per Morgan Stanley's May note (up from 18.5M/day in April) — the firm's explicit proxy for subscriber growth and engagement. Morgan Stanley estimates FSD gross margin at approximately 90%.

---

## Optimus

- **Optimus factory steel is standing at Giga Texas.** Drone footage from Joe Tegtmeyer shows the first steel structure erected at the North Campus dedicated facility, which when complete will stretch nearly the full length of the main factory. A realistic production-ready estimate from on-site observers is end-2027 to 2028.

- **208 open Optimus job listings across 10 cities**, versus 36 robotaxi listings — the largest internal resource concentration signal to date. The 65 manufacturing and industrialization roles (production line maintenance, precision machining, general assembly testing, power electronics, supplier quality) are the largest single category. An "Engineering Technician Optimus Hand Repair" posting confirms hands are in active field use with real-world wear. A night-shift data collection role requires 7+ hours of walking with 30 lbs of motion-capture equipment.

- **Digital Optimus emerging as a distinct software product.** 17 AI/ML listings cover Reinforcement Learning, AI Generalizability, and AI Infrastructure Engineering — roles targeting a software agent competing with Anthropic Claude and OpenAI's agentic AI. Herbert and Cern Basher identify 2026–2027 as the key market window for this product.

- **Reveal timing: Q3–early Q4 2026.** Jeff Lutz predicts Q3; Cern Basher targets second half of September to first half of October. Bhakdi characterizes the current communications blackout as bullish, attributing it partly to Musk's SpaceX IPO focus rather than any setback.

---

## Tesla Semi

- **Commercial validation accelerating.** Covenant Logistics completed a loaded run over Tejon Pass (4,160 ft, 6% grade); the driver was "amazed at the performance." ArcBest logged 4,494 miles at 1.55 kWh/mile; DHL completed 3,000 miles and took delivery of its first Semi; CEVA avoided 4.38 metric tons of CO₂. One unnamed company has ordered 340 Semis since volume production began at Giga Nevada on April 29.

- **Tesla holds 965 of 1,067 California Class 8 EV voucher applications** (January 2025–February 2026). Most 2026 Semi output is reportedly already allocated; verified orders stand at 644 across nine customers, with 48 trucks delivered.

---

## Energy

- **Q2 2026 Megapack deployments tracking ~2x Q1's 8.8 GWh**, per Randy Kirk. Current Megapack capacity is 17 GWh; Q2 projections range from 16–23 GWh depending on whether deferred prior-quarter deployments are counted. Revenue is recognized at electrification/substantial completion, not shipment.

- **SpaceX purchased $269M in Tesla Megapacks in April 2026**, bringing cumulative known related-party Megapack purchases to approximately $699M. Meta's Wyoming AI datacenter order (~$200M) and recent large contracts (Georgia Power $2.7B, Scotland 1 GWh, Belgium 180 units/700 MWh) confirm Megapack's positioning as critical AI infrastructure.

---

## Electric Vehicles

- **May 2026 global surge across seven major markets.** France +655% YoY (best May ever); Germany +322% YoY (YTD already 9% above full-year 2025); Australia record 6,433 units (Model Y first EV ever to lead overall monthly sales chart); South Korea 10,866 units (#1 overall vehicle); Japan +182% YoY; Norway 21.5% market share (97.8% EV penetration nationally); China wholesale 85,982 units (+39% YoY, highest Giga Shanghai figure of 2026).

- **Model Y L spotted testing under camouflage at Fremont** — the stretched three-row variant currently on sale in China at ~$47,000. Drone footage on the Fremont test track is the strongest North American launch signal to date; analysts estimate US production could begin around September 2026.

- **Used Cybertruck program launched June 1 at $66,200; inventory cleared in ~24 hours.** Tesla restocked at $72,900 — a $6,700 jump in days — suggesting price has been the primary adoption barrier and used-market demand is resilient. New Premium AWD lead times have extended to September–October 2026.

---

## Financials

- **JP Morgan raises Tesla target from $145 to $475.** New analyst Rajat Gupta replaced the long-bearish Ryan Brinkman. Electrified's Dillon Loomis flagged a structural conflict: JP Morgan is co-lead underwriter on the SpaceX IPO, creating financial incentive to maintain a positive relationship with Musk — raising questions about whether the upgrade reflects analytical revision or relationship management.

- **Tesla trailing GAAP earnings under pressure.** A Fortune analysis found core operating earnings — excluding regulatory credits and Bitcoin gains — at $2.3 billion, down from a $15 billion peak. Randy Kirk and FutureAzA reject the framing, citing growing FSD subscription revenue and the Q2 recovery in vehicle sales and Megapack deployments. Q2 deliveries report expected ~July 3; earnings third/fourth week of July.

- **Terafab approved 4–1 by Grimes County, Texas on June 3.** Partners: SpaceX, Tesla, xAI, Intel. $55B initial phase, $119B total; 35-year property tax exemption worth over $2 billion. Tesla's role is as customer and co-partner with a compute allocation earmarked for FSD chips and Optimus — not as project owner. Production is at minimum three-plus years out.

---

## Market & Competition

- **SpaceX IPO priced at $135/share, $1.75T valuation, targeting June 12.** $74.4B in proceeds, rising to ~$85.7B with overallotment. Musk subject to 366-day lockup. SpaceX annualized compute revenue run rate: $26B ($920M/month Google deal + $1.25–1.5B/month Anthropic deal). S&P 500 inclusion blocked until June 2027. Tesla–SpaceX merger probability: 95% within two years per Bhakdi; Alexandra Merz's proposed announcement window is end of June – August 15, 2026.

- **NASDAQ –4.18% Friday; Tesla –6.56%.** Bhakdi characterizes the move as profit-taking after a ~25% NASDAQ rally from late March, not the start of a sustained downturn. Tesla's decline was modestly below its beta-adjusted move. Bhakdi's 10-day range: $350 (downside if SpaceX IPO creates selling pressure) to $490 (upside if World Cup Cybercab launch materializes).

---

## Bear Case of the Week

- **Tesla retroactively deleted FSD purchase contracts during active litigation.** Electrek confirmed with multiple pre-2024 buyers — including Oliver Abcarius, who purchased FSD in 2019 — that original purchase agreements now link to invalid pages, while every other document on the same accounts opens normally. Tesla sold "Full Self-Driving Capability" without the word "supervised" from 2016 through March 2024. Active FSD/Autopilot litigation totals up to $14.5 billion. Electrek raises the possibility of evidence spoliation, which courts can treat with adverse inferences or sanctions.

- **Unsupervised fleet count has not grown in approximately four weeks.** RobotaxiTracker.com shows no change across all three Texas cities since the May 9 snapshot — despite Texas Level 4 self-certification being live, Cybercab production running at estimated 30–36 units/day, and vehicles staged in all three cities. All Cybercabs observed this week still retain steering wheels. The June 30 IR commitment (six cities) now has 23 days remaining with only three cities active.

- **Electrek documents conflicting active fleet data.** Fred Lambert reports the total active Austin fleet (all modes) collapsed from ~165 vehicles to ~34 at one point, and the unsupervised count shrank to approximately 20 active vehicles from a peak of 25 in late April. If accurate, these figures contradict the expansion narrative — though the discrepancy likely reflects timing differences with RobotaxiTracker.com community data, and investors should monitor for resolution.

- **FSD contract alteration allegation documented by Electrek.** Tesla reportedly retroactively added the word "supervised" to FSD contracts owners had already signed and deleted a blog post claiming all Tesla vehicles contain self-driving hardware. Tesla has not commented. Combined with the inaccessible purchase contracts, this represents a concentrated legal liability risk in the same week the company is arguing its FSD data demonstrates superior safety.

- **Tesla GAAP core operating earnings at $2.3 billion** — stripped of regulatory credits and Bitcoin gains — against a $1.4 trillion market cap and >$25B annual capex guidance. Q2 deliveries report due ~July 3 is the next hard data point. The stock is down ~6.56% on a single Friday macro session and carrying a 373x trailing P/E heading into what management guided will be a negative-free-cash-flow year.

2026-06-08.title: 4 Reasons SpaceX IPO Could Be Historic
2026-06-08.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel covers the anticipated SpaceX IPO scheduled for Friday, June 12th (2026), framing it as potentially the largest and most historic IPO ever. Host Herbert is joined by guest Larry Goldberg, a serial entrepreneur and venture capital investor, to discuss four key reasons the SpaceX IPO could be historic: its unprecedented scale, extraordinary investor demand, capital deployment into growth rather than survival, and expanding business engines including Starlink Mobile and Terafab.

## Market & Competition
1. **Largest IPO in History by Scale:** SpaceX officially launched its roadshow targeting approximately $75 billion in proceeds at a fixed price of $135 per share, implying a market capitalization of approximately $1.75 trillion. The offering consists of 555 million Class A shares. Underwriters also have the option to purchase additional shares, which would bring the total raised to $85.7 billion if exercised. For context, some earlier expectations had placed the valuation closer to $2 trillion. Prediction market Polymarket is reportedly projecting a closing valuation of $2.3 trillion on IPO day.

2. **Unprecedented Retail Investor Access:** Unlike typical large IPOs, SpaceX publicly announced that retail investors will be able to participate at the same $135 per share price as institutional investors. The ticker symbol will be SPCX. The host noted that SpaceX broke convention by setting a fixed price rather than offering a range, reflecting the company's leverage over the process. The IPO is also unusual in being scheduled for a Friday, which Larry Goldberg noted is rare — perhaps only 1 in 10 to 1 in 20 IPOs historically have launched on a Friday — due to risks around end-of-day price tapering heading into a weekend.

3. **Extraordinary Institutional Demand and Unprecedented ETF Interest:** Major banks including Goldman Sachs (lead underwriter), Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, Citigroup, JP Morgan, and Barclays are all participating. JP Morgan CEO Jamie Dimond is personally involved, hosting a live Q&A with SpaceX President Gwyn Shotwell and CFO Brett Johnson on the Thursday before the IPO. This is notable given that JP Morgan and Tesla (and by extension Elon Musk) had a long legal dispute — JP Morgan sued Tesla in 2021 over a stock options dispute, Tesla countersued, and the two sides only dropped their lawsuits in November 2024. Dimond later publicly joked that he and Musk had "hugged and made up." Additionally, an unprecedented number of ETFs have already announced SpaceX inclusion prior to the IPO.

4. **Record-Low Underwriting Fees Reflect SpaceX's Leverage:** SpaceX is reportedly negotiating to pay less than 0.75% on its approximately $75 billion IPO, far below the typical IPO underwriting fee range of 4% to 7%. Banks could still collect roughly $500 million in fees collectively, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley reportedly taking the largest shares. Goldberg noted that while unusually low, sub-1% fees are not entirely without precedent — GM achieved a similarly low rate on a $15 billion raise in 2010.

5. **Capital Deployed Into Infrastructure, Not Survival:** The filing shows IPO proceeds will be used to expand AI compute infrastructure, launch capacity, satellite constellations, and future growth initiatives — signaling that SpaceX is scaling existing businesses rather than searching for product-market fit.

6. **Starlink Mobile as a Proven Revenue Engine:** SpaceX published data showing its Starlink Mobile constellation consists of 650 satellites in low Earth orbit across six continents, accessible to more than 1.7 billion people. Australian telecom Telstra (described as a major early partner) reported over 200,000 of its customers connect to Starlink Mobile per day, with over 2.7 million customers having connected at least once in the past year. Next-generation V2 satellites are scheduled to begin launching in 2027, promising 5G speeds from space, 100 times the data density of current V1 satellites, up to 150 Mbps speeds, thousands of spatial beams, and 20 times the throughput capability compared to the first generation. Goldberg noted a notable connection: Tesla's chairperson Robyn Denholm was previously the CFO of Telstra, which he suggested explains the close relationship.

7. **Terafab: A $55 Billion Chip Manufacturing Project Linking SpaceX, xAI, and Tesla:** Grimes County, Texas commissioners voted 4-to-1 to approve major tax incentives for SpaceX's Terafab chip manufacturing project, located east of College Station. The tax abatement grants SpaceX a full exemption on property taxes tied to the project's machinery and equipment. Elon Musk noted that Terafab will increase annual tax revenue for Grimes County by 25% even with the abatement — and significantly more when employee and contractor taxes are included. The project is described as a "generational change" by county officials. Musk explained the rationale: property taxes on expensive chip-manufacturing equipment would create a serious competitive disadvantage globally. Larry Goldberg added geopolitical context, noting the US-China competition in AI and semiconductor manufacturing, and flagging TSMC's Taiwan operations as a systemic vulnerability if China were to act against Taiwan.

## Financials
1. **Employee Wealth Creation:** The host outlined projections for SpaceX employee wealth outcomes at the $1.75 trillion valuation. An estimated 4,000 employees are expected to become millionaires, and approximately 400 are expected to become "100 millionaires" (i.e., worth over $100 million). Employees who joined before SpaceX's first successful launch in 2008 and held their equity — estimated at 150 to 250 people still holding — could see returns of $100 million each. Gwyn Shotwell and CFO Brett Johnson are each reported to have cleared over $1 billion. Elon Musk also reportedly carved out 5% of the offering for friends, family, and executives, with no lock-up period. Elon Musk himself is expected to become a trillionaire as a result of the IPO, though the host and Goldberg emphasized these are stock options, not cash.

2. **Elon Musk's Economic Contribution Framed as Historic:** Goldberg stated that Musk has generated an estimated 0.4% of US GDP — a figure Goldberg described as thousands of times more than the average individual's contribution — and argued Musk has made the single biggest economic contribution of any living person in the United States. Both host and guest expressed the view that Musk's wealth is deserved given the personal sacrifices and near-bankruptcy experiences in SpaceX's early years, when the first three rocket launches failed.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX IPO price: $135 per share, fixed (no range given), ticker SPCX, listing June 12th, 2026
- Shares offered: 555 million Class A; up to 85.7 million additional shares available to underwriters
- Total proceeds targeted: approximately $75 billion; up to $85.7 billion if overallotment exercised
- Implied market cap at IPO: approximately $1.75 trillion
- Polymarket prediction: SpaceX closes IPO day at $2.3 trillion valuation
- Underwriting fee: less than 0.75% (vs. typical 4–7%); total bank fees approximately $500 million

2026-06-08.title: Big Investors Are BUYING Tesla Stock
2026-06-08.body:
The video, hosted by "brighterwithherbert" featuring guest Jeff Lutz (a former supply chain C-level executive from Motorola, Google, and Lenovo), covers a surge of bullish news for Tesla and SpaceX investors over a single weekend in early June 2026. The core thesis is that institutional "smart money" is rotating into Tesla ahead of a wave of near-term catalysts — robotaxi scaling, Optimus reveals, Cybercab, Roadster, and strong Q2 deliveries — while SpaceX's compute business is generating enormous new revenue that is drawing major financial institutions into Elon Musk's orbit. The hosts argue that Tesla's hardware-first playbook mirrors SpaceX's GPU strategy: build at scale, absorb fixed costs, then dominate on unit economics.

## Robotaxi

1. **Nevada AV Permit Filing — Up to 5,000 Robotaxis in Year One:** Tesla officially applied for an Autonomous Vehicle Network Company permit in Nevada, seeking approval for up to 5,000 robotaxis during the first 12 months after the permit is granted. The filing covers Clark County, including Harry Reid International Airport and Henderson Executive Airport, per a public notice from the Nevada Transportation Authority. Jeff Lutz emphasized that in his regulatory experience, companies do not submit inflated numbers — doing so invites scrutiny and delays — so the 5,000 figure reflects Tesla's genuine near-term deployment intention. He noted that Waymo, currently the largest robotaxi operator in the country, has approximately 3,700 vehicles nationwide, making Tesla's Nevada target alone potentially larger than the entire current Waymo fleet.

2. **Texas DMV Data — Registered Fleet at 51 Vehicles:** Texas DMV data shows that Tesla Robotaxi LLC added four more Model Y vehicles to its registered fleet, bringing the total to 51 registered robotaxi vehicles in Texas. The hosts noted this is a small but growing number and is the official mechanism by which the public can track Texas fleet size. The RobotaxiTracker.com site — which had been a community resource for real-time fleet tracking — is noted as potentially less current going forward, as Ethan (the tracker's maintainer) was hired by Tesla as a summer intern and stated publicly he cannot update the tracker for several months, at least through August.

3. **Robotaxi Demo Expected in August:** Reports indicate a robotaxi demo is expected in August 2026. Tesla's next-generation Roadster demo has also reportedly been pushed to August. The hosts connected this timing to a post-SpaceX IPO (expected in June 2026) window, when Tesla may want to showcase a cluster of catalysts simultaneously. Jeff Lutz described the current deployment phase as analogous to a product ramp-up: vehicles being staged in cities are like raw materials entering a factory, and Tesla's hundreds of open job postings for robotaxi fleet management roles signal that funding has been approved at the executive level — a sign engineering leadership has confirmed the technology is ready.

4. **Competitive Unit Economics vs. Waymo:** Jeff Lutz argued that Tesla's robotaxi economics are fundamentally different from competitors. He stated that other robotaxi vendors are "losing money per ride" at current fare levels of roughly $3–$10 per hour, which limits both their vehicle count and their ability to scale. Tesla's lower unit cost per vehicle and superior fixed-cost absorption allow it to target a much larger fleet in a concentrated area and reach profitability quickly. He drew a direct parallel to the SpaceX/xAI compute playbook: build more capacity than needed, drive utilization up, and watch cost-per-unit collapse.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **NHTSA Safety Data as Regulatory Evidence:** The hosts noted that Tesla now has approximately six months of robotaxi operational data in Texas (since the June 22, 2025 Austin launch), and that submissions to NHTSA appear to show very few — possibly zero — major accidents, with only minor incidents at most. This safety record is expected to be a central piece of evidence in Tesla's Nevada permit submission, strengthening the regulatory case for approval of the 5,000-vehicle request.

2. **FSD Word-of-Mouth Effect Driving Investment:** Jeff Lutz described a growing word-of-mouth phenomenon around Full Self-Driving, stating that people are "getting hooked" on FSD after a single ride — to the point of buying cars and making investment decisions on the spot. He recounted his own experience test-driving a Tesla 13+ years ago (before FSD existed) and investing the following Monday. He suggested that the Chinese investor Dwan Yongpin's reversal from Tesla skeptic to major shareholder was partly triggered by a recent FSD ride, and that this effect is now spreading internationally as FSD rolls out to more countries.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus Reveal as an Upcoming Catalyst:** The hosts listed an Optimus reveal as one of several major near-term milestones for Tesla. Jeff Lutz described Optimus as "a Tesla product with a SpaceX brain in it," emphasizing the cross-company technology integration. No specific date for the reveal was given beyond it being part of the broader cluster of catalysts expected over the next four to eight weeks from the video's publish date (i.e., through late July/early August 2026).

## Energy

1. **Houston Megapack Factory Exterior Completed:** Aerial footage published by an unnamed source showed that the exterior of Tesla's Houston factory for Megapack production appears to be complete. The facility is described as a 50 gigawatt-hour factory. The hosts noted that interior fit-out and capital equipment installation remain to be completed, but the pace of exterior construction suggests the factory could be operational sooner than expected, representing another significant upcoming catalyst for Tesla's energy business.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Q2 Deliveries Tracking ~28% Higher Year-Over-Year:** Jeff Lutz reported that through May 2026, Tesla's auto deliveries are tracking approximately 28% higher year-over-year on a net basis, with most countries showing meaningfully higher volumes even as some individual markets are softer. Combined with what he described as a slow energy quarter in Q1 2026, this sets up the potential for a strong Q2 report. Official Q2 results are expected in the third week of July 2026. A potential new Model Y introduction in North America was also listed as an upcoming catalyst, though no specific date or details were provided.

## Market & Competition

1. **Dwan Yongpin ("Chinese Warren Buffett") Builds ~$1.27B Tesla Position:** Chinese value investor Dwan Yongpin, widely known as the "Chinese Warren Buffett" for his concentrated, disciplined value philosophy, disclosed a position of approximately 3.4 million Tesla shares with a market value of roughly $1.27 billion as of Q1 2026, representing approximately 6.3% of his total portfolio and his fifth-largest holding. His reported average purchase price was approximately $371 per share. Notably, Dwan had historically been a vocal skeptic of Elon Musk but reversed his stance after experiencing Tesla's technology firsthand, praising it as "truly remarkable" and explicitly separating his personal views on Musk from the objective economic disruption Tesla is driving. His broader $20 billion portfolio includes Apple (36%), Berkshire Hathaway (21%), Nvidia (12%), and Pinduoduo, with Tesla showing the largest percentage portfolio increase in Q1.

2. **JP Morgan Raises Price Target from $145 to $475 — 227% Increase:** JP Morgan, described as having held a "permanent bear position" on Tesla for years with a prior price target of $145, upgraded Tesla to neutral with a new price target of $475 — a 227% increase. The hosts attributed the change primarily to JP Morgan wanting to participate in the SpaceX IPO and needing to repair its relationship with Elon Musk, noting that Jamie Dimon recently hosted Elon Musk (and his mother) for a public interview. Jeff Lutz added that the underlying cause was analytical inaccuracy from the prior analyst, who has since been replaced.

3. **Morgan Stanley Buys $1.26B of Tesla Stock in Q1 2026:** Morgan Stanley returned to Tesla as a significant buyer, purchasing approximately $1.26 billion worth of Tesla stock in Q1 2026. The hosts framed this alongside the JP Morgan upgrade and Dwan Yongpin's purchase as evidence of a major institutional rotation into Tesla, with institutions now owning over 51% of Tesla stock — up from below 50% — while retail ownership has dropped to approximately 31%.

4. **SpaceX Compute Revenue — Google Deal and Combined Run Rate:** SpaceX's amended S-1 filing revealed Google as a new compute customer, paying $920 million per month from October 2026 through June 2029, with either party able to terminate on 90 days' notice. Combined with Anthropic's existing deal, SpaceX is receiving $2.17 billion per month from these two customers alone — a revenue run rate of approximately $26 billion per year if sustained. The hosts noted the strategic irony of Google — which designs its own TPUs (manufactured by Broadcom) and operates one of the world's largest cloud infrastructures — renting 110,000 Nvidia GPUs from SpaceX. Jeff Lutz argued this is a utilization play that will dramatically lower SpaceX's cost per token, and that the 90-day termination clause means SpaceX retains effective control of the capacity faster than any competitor could acquire and deploy new hardware.

5. **Physical AI as the Next Institutional Rotation:** Jeff Lutz predicted that the next major sector rotation in institutional investing — following the shift from pure chip/Mag 7 plays to AI infrastructure (power, cooling, data center supply chain) — will be into "physical AI." He argued Tesla is uniquely positioned as the only publicly traded company with large-scale physical AI assets (autonomous vehicles, humanoid robots), and that this rotation, combined with a wave of physical AI startups going public, will drive significant re-rating of Tesla's valuation multiple.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla's Nevada AV permit application seeks up to **5,000 robotaxis** in Clark County within the first 12 months after permit approval.
- Texas DMV data: Tesla Robotaxi LLC now has **51 registered robotaxi vehicles** in Texas (up 4 from prior count).
- RobotaxiTracker.com maintainer Ethan was hired by Tesla as a summer intern and cannot update the tracker through at least August 2026.
- Waymo current nationwide fleet cited as approximately **3,700 vehicles**.
- Competing robotaxi fare rates cited as approximately **$3–$10 per hour** (per Jeff Lutz), with competitors described as losing money per ride.
- Google paying SpaceX **$920 million/month** for compute (Oct 2026–Jun 2029); combined Anthropic + Google = **$2.17 billion/month** = ~**$26 billion/year** run rate.
- SpaceX cluster running **7 models** on Colossus 2, including one model at **1.5 trillion parameters**.
- Dwan Yongpin: **3.4 million Tesla shares**, market value **~$1.27 billion**, ~**6.3% of portfolio**, reported avg price **~$371/share**.
- JP Morgan price target: **$145 → $475** (+227%).
- Morgan Stanley purchased **~$1.26 billion** of Tesla stock in Q1 2026.
- Institutions now own **>51%** of Tesla stock; retail ownership down to **~31%**.
- Houston Megapack factory: **50 GWh** capacity; exterior construction reportedly complete.
- Q2 2026 auto deliveries tracking approximately **+28% year-over-year** through May.
- Q2 2026 results expected in the **third week of July 2026**.
- Jeff Lutz: *"This is totally a utilization play... he can pull the capacity within 90 days. You can't get Nvidia chips [that fast]."*
- Herbert: *"It looks like a table's being set and dinner time is like it's close. We don't know exactly when dinner is going to be called, but you can smell it."*
