The speakers note that humanity currently uses "much less than a trillionth" of the sun's power output, making Earth effectively non-registering on the Kardashev Type 2 scale. The stated aspiration is to reach one-millionth of the sun's power output — described as "a micros[ol]" — as a meaningful near-term civilizational goal.

2. **Starship as the foundational enabler:** Starship is described as the first rocket capable of full and rapid reusability, which the speakers argue is the fundamental prerequisite for ascending the Kardashev scale. They note that SpaceX currently delivers approximately 85–90% of all mass to Earth orbit via Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy, with China accounting for most of the remainder and the rest of the world (including other U.S. operators) making up roughly 5–7%. The goal with Starship is to scale from approximately 2,500 tons per year to orbit to millions of tons per year — targeting roughly one million tons per year to orbit within approximately three years. Starship B3 is described as more than double the thrust of the Saturn V moon rocket, with Version 4 expected to reach approximately three times Saturn V's thrust. Full reusability (without refurbishment between flights) is described as not yet achieved but expected "later this year" (i.e., by end of 2026).

3. **SpaceX AI Satellite (AI1) — orbital compute design:** SpaceX has developed a draft design for an orbital AI satellite called "AI1," intended to carry roughly the compute equivalent of one Nvidia GB300 rack (72 GPUs). Key design parameters: 150 kW peak power, 120 kW sustained average power, solar arrays at 250 watts per square meter, double-sided radiators at 1,400 watts per square meter, and approximately 70-meter wingspan. The satellite is described as simpler than a Starlink satellite because it lacks complex phased-array antennas — consisting primarily of solar cells, radiators, and laser links. Connectivity is described as approximately one terabit of laser-link bandwidth. Orbital altitude is discussed as approximately 600–800 kilometers, yielding roughly 3 milliseconds of light-travel latency. Current reference chip designs include Rubin chips, GB300s, and TPUs.

4. **Terafab — ground-based chip megafactory:** To scale AI compute to terawatt levels, SpaceX/xAI is proposing a massive chip manufacturing facility called the "Terafab," described as approximately 100 million square feet — roughly 10 times the size of Giga Texas. The target output is one terawatt of chips per year, equivalent to approximately one billion full-reticle-equivalent chips each consuming one kilowatt. The current global chip industry is described as heading toward perhaps 100 gigawatts per year of AI compute, making the Terafab the mechanism to reach the next order of magnitude.

5. **Orbital compute scaling roadmap:** The speakers outline a time-phased aspiration (explicitly caveated as a best-guess, not a promise): approximately one gigawatt per year annualized rate of space-based AI compute by end of 2026 (i.e., "end of next year" from a prior reference point, though context suggests this is the near-term target); scaling by roughly one order of magnitude per year thereafter — 10 gigawatts per year by approximately 2.5 years out, 100 gigawatts per year by approximately 3.5 years out, and eventually one terawatt per year (described as twice the current total electricity consumption of the United States) with the Terafab.

6. **Moon-based mass drivers as the ultimate scaling step:** Beyond the terawatt level, the speakers discuss a further three-orders-of-magnitude scale-up using moon-based photovoltaic and radiator manufacturing, combined with electromagnetic mass drivers (linear electric motors) to launch AI satellites into deep space without rockets — exploiting the moon's lack of atmosphere and one-sixth Earth gravity. Chips could potentially be brought from Earth or eventually manufactured on the moon. This is framed as a longer-term vision enabling anyone to visit or live on the moon.

7. **Bastrop, Texas as the production hub:** The conversation takes place at SpaceX's Bastrop facility, currently manufacturing Starlink user terminals. A solar manufacturing facility is described as already under construction, with the AI satellite (ISAT) production building to follow. The speakers expect "reasonable volume" production of AI satellites and solar components at Bastrop by end of 2027 ("end of next year" relative to the video). SpaceX currently operates approximately 10,000 Starlink satellites and cites this as unique operational experience managing large constellations safely.

Notable quotes and data:
- "The sun is about 99.86% of all mass in the solar system."
- "We currently use much less than a trillionth of the power output of the sun."
- "A trillion is a million times a million" — contextualizing how far humanity is from Kardashev Type 2.
- SpaceX delivers "almost 90%" of all Earth mass to orbit via Falcon 9/Falcon Heavy.
- Target: ~1 million tons to orbit per year within ~3 years via Starship.
- Starship B3: more than 2× thrust of Saturn V; V4 expected at ~3× Saturn V.
- AI1 satellite: 150 kW peak / 120 kW sustained, ~70m wingspan, ~1 terabit laser-link connectivity.
- Terafab: ~100 million square feet, ~10× size of Giga Texas, targeting 1 terawatt/year of chip output.
- "A terowatt actually is very small" — speaker contextualizing ambition relative to the sun's output.
- Orbital compute roadmap: 1 GW/year by end of 2026 → 10 GW/year → 100 GW/year → 1 TW/year.
- "A terowatt per year... is twice the current electricity consumption of the United States."
- Starlink direct-to-cell expected to support "a few hundred million" terminals eventually.
- AI satellite latency at 600–800 km altitude: approximately 3 milliseconds (light travel).

2026-06-08.title: EXTREME MIRACLE BATTERIES vs their reality. Plus another dozen Monday News Roundup stories
2026-06-08.body:
This Monday morning news roundup from FutureAzA, recorded live from Detroit following a summer meetup, covers roughly a dozen news stories spanning EV affordability, battery technology developments, SpaceX/Starlink milestones, and miscellaneous market topics. The host's overarching theme is separating genuine technological progress from hype — particularly around next-generation battery claims — while also highlighting competitive dynamics in EVs, energy storage, and satellite internet.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Slate Auto Truck Reveal Approaching:** The host discusses Slate Auto's upcoming June 24th production-intent truck unveil, at which the actual price will also be announced. A deal with Carvana has already been announced ahead of the sales launch. The host expects the price to land under $40,000 and considers a sub-$30,000 launch price unreasonable at this stage. He also expresses concern about the truck's range and hopes Slate will switch from NMC to LFP batteries, noting that domestic sourcing incentives that originally justified NMC are no longer relevant. With LFP, buyers can charge to 100%, whereas an NMC battery charged only from 20–80% effectively cuts usable capacity by 40%, potentially leaving a range-limited truck with only ~100 usable miles.

2. **Used Cybertruck Demand Surprise:** Tesla recently uploaded a batch of used Cybertrucks to its sales site, with prices starting at $72,900 for a Foundation Series. The host notes that roughly half of the newly listed inventory sold within a day, suggesting meaningful demand at lower price points despite the vehicle's polarizing reputation.

3. **Dodge Charger Daytona Price Hike:** The Dodge Charger Daytona Scat Pack received a $12,000 price increase despite slow sales, with the base model now starting at approximately $50,000. The host is skeptical of the logic behind raising prices on an already slow-selling vehicle.

4. **Canada BYD Expansion and EV Tariff Quota:** Canada has opened an import quota allowing 49,000 EVs from China at preferred tariff rates. Tesla has already consumed roughly 10% of that allotment. BYD is moving to open Canadian showrooms to capture share, and Nissan — which manufactures some models in China — is also positioned to benefit given its existing dealership network.

## Energy

1. **CATL Sodium-Ion Commercial Rollout:** CATL, described as the world's largest lithium-ion battery maker by a significant margin, has announced a concrete roadmap for commercial sodium-ion energy storage systems, with first customer deliveries expected to begin in September 2025 (implied from context as a matter of months away from the June 2026 publish date — though the host presents this as imminent). The host notes sodium-ion is cheaper to produce but historically has had lower energy density, worse roundtrip efficiency, and shorter cycle life than lithium-ion — factors that must be factored into total cost of ownership, especially for grid storage.

2. **Lithium-Air Battery Research Paper — 12,000 Wh/kg Claim:** A research paper claiming a theoretical lithium-air battery energy density of 12,000 watt-hours per kilogram generated significant online buzz over the weekend. The host strongly cautions that this is purely theoretical — not in production, not in pilot, not even in prototype — and that the jump from ~400 Wh/kg (considered very good today) to 12,000 Wh/kg should trigger serious skepticism. He acknowledges that if it were ever real, it would be transformative across aviation, rail, and virtually every energy-intensive application.

3. **BYD Flash-Charge Battery Supply Constraints:** BYD's new fast-charge batteries — described as charging roughly four times faster than standard for a modest price premium — are experiencing supply constraints because demand has outpaced production capacity. A full-size SUV model's launch has been pushed to June as a result.

4. **Tesla Vehicle-to-Grid/Vehicle-to-Load Progress:** Tesla has rolled out vehicle-to-load functionality in Australia, at least for the Model Y Performance variant. The host notes the full vehicle-to-grid vision — where fleet-scale bidirectional charging could meaningfully support grid stability — remains limited by the fact that most Tesla vehicles lack the necessary onboard circuitry.

5. **Battery Energy Storage Bans in U.S. Towns:** Some U.S. municipalities have enacted outright bans or placed pending restrictions on large-scale battery energy storage projects (Megapacks and equivalents). The host highlights Washington State examples, including an outright ban in Black Diamond. He argues the fire concerns driving these bans are largely outdated, noting that thermal runaway incidents have become rarer even as deployments have surged, and that the industry has largely moved away from high-nickel chemistries toward lithium iron phosphate, which is significantly less prone to thermal runaway.

6. **PNNL Domestic Battery Production Line:** The Pacific Northwest National Laboratory has commissioned a 16-piece prismatic battery cell production line inside the Department of Energy's Grid Storage Launchpad, aimed at developing safer and cheaper domestic energy storage solutions. The host is mildly skeptical this represents near-term news, suggesting the research mandate changes slowly year over year.

7. **GM Battery Bet at Warren Tech Center:** GM is investing $900 million in a new battery development facility at its Warren Tech Center outside Detroit, attempting to reboot an EV battery program that was previously written down. The host is skeptical of the accounting logic but notes the investment signals continued commitment to an electric future.

## Market & Competition

1. **EU Trade Defense Against Chinese EVs:** The European Union is expanding its response to Chinese industrial overcapacity, moving beyond tariffs toward broader trade defense and industrial policy measures. The host notes that European automakers have begun producing genuinely competitive EVs (citing the VW ID.Buzz as attractive but roughly 1,000 lbs too heavy and $30,000 too expensive) but have not yet achieved the cost competitiveness needed to displace Chinese imports on price.

2. **Elon Musk / ASML Terafab Chip Plant Talks:** Elon Musk is reportedly in direct talks with ASML regarding a proposed $119 billion chip fabrication facility in Texas. The host clarifies that $119 billion refers to the total factory cost — not the ASML lithography equipment deal alone — and notes that ASML's CEO described Musk as "very serious." The ASML CEO also warned that semiconductor ambitions tied to Tesla and SpaceX could strain an already tight global chip supply, which the host finds logically confused given that building new fab capacity is precisely the solution to supply tightness.

## SpaceX / Starlink (Non-Tesla Context)

1. **Starlink Reaches 12 Million Active Subscribers:** Starlink has announced 12 million active paying customers, each with a dedicated terminal. The host frames this as the beginning of a much larger growth trajectory, citing a former SpaceX engineer (Quincy from Electric Era Tech) who believes 12 million is just the start even with the existing satellite constellation and without Starship ever flying.

2. **British Airways Starlink Pause Explained:** A headline suggested British Airways was suspending Starlink installations due to a problem with the service. The host clarifies that deep in the article, the actual reason is that the summer travel season prevents planes from being taken out of service for maintenance, and the Starlink installations will proceed alongside regular maintenance in the fall. No service issues exist.

3. **Falcon 9 Booster 35th Reuse:** A single Falcon 9 booster completed its 35th launch and landing. The host uses this as a broader point about how reusability enables higher quality rocket engineering — when boosters are expendable, there is no incentive to build them to last.

4. **Russia's Starlink Competitor Loses First Satellite:** Russia's competing constellation lost its first satellite after just 75 days in orbit. The host notes this is less alarming than it sounds for a first batch, but points to Russia's fundamental cost disadvantage from using non-reusable rockets and geopolitical barriers to market adoption.

5. **SpaceX XAI Compute Deal:** Google has signed a $920 million per month compute deal with XAI/SpaceX. The host also references a large deal with Anthropic, framing these as validation that SpaceX/XAI has meaningful, monetizable compute infrastructure.

Notable quotes and data:
- Slate Auto reveal date: June 24th; host's price expectation: under $40,000 at launch
- Used Cybertruck Foundation Series starting price: $72,900; approximately half the new listings sold within one day of posting
- Dodge Charger Daytona Scat Pack price increase: +$12,000; new base price approximately $50,000
- Canada EV import quota from China: 49,000 vehicles at preferred tariff; Tesla has used ~10% of allotment
- Lithium-air battery theoretical claim: 12,000 Wh/kg (research paper only, no prototype)
- CATL sodium-ion first deliveries: expected September (a few months out from publish date)
- GM battery facility investment: $900 million at Warren Tech Center
- Starlink active subscribers: 12 million
- Google/XAI compute deal: $920 million per month
- Falcon 9 single booster reuse record: 35 flights
- PNNL prismatic cell line: 16-piece production line at DOE Grid Storage Launchpad
- Elon Musk / ASML Terafab chip plant: $119 billion total facility cost (Texas)
- Host's personal charging note: charges at 32 amps at home (down from 42 amp capacity on electrician's advice)

2026-06-08.title: What Happen Friday With the Stock Market? Is The Bubble Popping? Is Tesla Going To Crash?
2026-06-08.body:
This video from "investingagainstthegrain" analyzes the significant market sell-off that occurred on Friday, June 6, 2026 — described as the biggest single-day sell-off in over a year — and whether it signals a broader market downturn. The host argues the sell-off was predictable and avoidable, driven by a strong jobs report that paradoxically spooked markets into pricing in rate hikes, compounded by Iran's missile attack on Israel that threatened a fragile ceasefire. The core thesis is that this is a healthy, temporary pullback within a fundamentally strong AI-driven bull market, and that Tesla remains well-positioned despite near-term technical weakness.

## Market & Competition

1. **The Friday Sell-Off Was Predictable and Avoidable:** The host argues that the June 6, 2026 sell-off — the largest since Liberation Day 2025 — was foreseeable to attentive investors. He walks through a series of posts he made on X beginning June 2nd warning subscribers about weakening momentum in the S&P 500, the misleading nature of the 70%/30% call-to-put open interest ratio (which doesn't distinguish buyers from sellers), and the risk of binary market events. He specifically identified two upcoming binary events to avoid: the SpaceX IPO (scheduled for June 11th, first trading day June 12th) and the first Fed meeting chaired by Kevin Warsh on June 17th. The trigger for Friday's sell-off was a strong jobs report that paradoxically caused markets to price in rate hikes rather than cuts.

2. **Iran-Israel Escalation Adding Weekend Uncertainty:** Iran launched four waves of approximately 10 rockets each at Israel on the weekend of June 7–8, 2026, marking the first attack since a ceasefire in April 2026. The Iron Dome intercepted all missiles with no reported damage. The host interprets this as a symbolic, face-saving retaliation by Iran rather than a genuine escalation, noting it closely resembles Iran's pre-announced symbolic strike pattern seen in 2025. He highlights reports that President Trump called Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu urging restraint, stating both sides had "done their part" and emphasizing proximity to a nuclear deal with Iran. Despite the geopolitical noise, S&P futures were only down approximately one-third of a percent overnight, which the host found encouraging.

3. **Big Tech Equity Raises Signal AI Investment Supercycle, Not a Bubble:** The host argues that the market has entered a new phase he characterizes as the "Mag Seven equity raise era," following prior phases of stock buybacks, capex announcements, and capex escalation. Google conducted an $80 billion equity raise — its first since its 2004 IPO — backed by Berkshire Hathaway. The host predicted on June 2nd that Google would not be the last, and by June 3rd, Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon confirmed at the Economic Club of New York that more companies would come to market to raise capital. Meta subsequently announced plans for a similar capital raise. The host frames these raises — alongside SpaceX's $75 billion raise — not as bubble signals but as validation that leading companies have clear line-of-sight to massive AI-driven returns, citing Amazon CEO Andy Jassy's statement that every GPU, server, and data center they stand up has demand waiting that cannot be filled.

4. **Historical Sell-Off Context and Monday Outlook:** The host references a chart compiled by Odd Stats (credited to a user named "Lord Pretty Flaco") showing historical instances of large Friday sell-offs, their intraday Monday drawdowns, and Monday closing returns. The data shows mixed outcomes — for example, on Friday April 4th (2025, Liberation Day context), the market fell 6%, saw a 4.92% intraday Monday drawdown, but ultimately closed up 0.19% on Monday. The host notes these figures are NASDAQ numbers, not S&P 500. He concludes the setup for the coming Monday looks like a possible down open but not a catastrophic continuation, and reiterates that fear-and-greed index dropping from 61 to 42 (a roughly 19-point drop from the prior week) reflects normal sentiment oscillation rather than panic.

5. **Long-Term AI Bull Market Thesis Intact:** The host draws a historical parallel between the current AI investment wave and the industrial revolution and internet era, arguing that dominant profitable companies (Tesla, Meta, Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Micron) are reinvesting profits into the AI infrastructure race — compute, energy, and data centers — that will define the next 20 years. He cites market analyst Tom Lee as agreeing this sell-off is not the start of a broader decline, though Lee does anticipate a correction that "feels like a bear market" later in the year. The host explicitly states he sees no signs of a bubble, comparing current AI to pets.com-era internet speculation and finding the current wave fundamentally different due to tangible, profitable, usable technology.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla's Technical Picture Shows Short-Term Weakness but Monthly Trend Intact:** Tesla had been declining for approximately five consecutive trading days heading into Friday, June 6, 2026. On Friday, Tesla briefly hit an intraday high of $423 before selling off to close around $391. The host notes that on daily charts, Tesla appears to be potentially bottoming out, which makes him "somewhat optimistic" on the near-term daily timeframe. On the weekly chart, Tesla had been making higher highs in prior weeks but printed a dark green (cautionary) candle this past week. On the monthly chart, the host acknowledges a lower-low signal on his BX Trender indicator but is not overly concerned, noting the longer-term monthly trend remains up and to the right and there is significant month remaining. He concludes Tesla was "set up structurally to go to all-time highs" before this pullback disrupted that setup.

2. **Tesla Positioned as a Leader in the AI and Physical-World Race:** The host briefly references Tesla and Elon Musk as "the clear leader" in the race to dominate physical-world AI, which he broadly defines as encompassing robotaxi deployment and real-world AI applications. He frames this within the broader AI infrastructure race, noting Tesla's own data center scaling as analogous to what Google and Meta are now doing — suggesting Tesla recognized the FSD breakthrough moment earlier and acted decisively. He also mentions xAI renting compute to Anthropic and Google as evidence of insatiable demand for AI infrastructure, though the specific connection to Tesla's balance sheet is not elaborated.

Notable quotes and data:
- Fear and Greed Index dropped from 61 (prior week) to 42 as of the video date — approximately a 19-point decline.
- Tesla intraday high on Friday, June 6, 2026: **$423**; sold off to approximately **$391**.
- Google equity raise: **$80 billion** — first equity raise since Google's 2004 IPO; backed by Berkshire Hathaway.
- SpaceX capital raise: **$75 billion**; IPO scheduled for June 11, 2026; first trading day June 12, 2026.
- Kevin Warsh's first Fed meeting as chair: **June 17, 2026**.
- Iran launched four waves of approximately 10 rockets each at Israel; Iron Dome intercepted all; no reported damage.
- S&P futures overnight: down approximately **0.3%** at time of recording; Bitcoin up approximately **3%** (~$2,000 gain, from ~$61,000 to ~$63,000).
- Friday April 4th (2025, Liberation Day) historical data point: market down ~6% on Friday; Monday intraday low down 4.92%; Monday close up 0.19%.
- Tom Lee view: current sell-off is a "giveback" before higher prices, but expects a correction "that feels like a bear market" later in 2026.
- Options open interest split discussed: 70% calls / 30% puts — host cautions this includes both buyers and sellers, not just bullish positioning.
- Host exited Micron (MU) position on Wednesday, June 4, 2026, after hitting 50% profit target, ahead of Thursday/Friday declines.

2026-06-08.title: Tesla Stock SURGES Back: PREPARE For The SpaceX IPO
2026-06-08.body:
Jo Bhakdi hosts a live session on his Pioneer Lands platform the Monday following a severe market selloff, analyzing Tesla's strong recovery and laying out his bullish thesis for the remainder of June 2026. The core argument is that two major catalysts — the SpaceX IPO launching Friday and an anticipated Cybercab robotaxi fleet deployment timed around the World Cup — are converging to drive Tesla toward its all-time high of $490. Bhakdi also discusses the longer-term SpaceX-Tesla merger thesis and his personal portfolio positioning.

## Market & Competition

1. **Post-selloff recovery and NASDAQ context:** The prior Friday saw the NASDAQ fall 4.18% and Tesla drop nearly $30. By Monday, the NASDAQ had recovered only about 86% of those losses, while Tesla bounced back far more strongly. Bhakdi describes Friday as a "phony selloff" and a tactical breather in an ongoing bull market, which he predicted correctly over the weekend.

2. **SpaceX IPO as the week's dominant event:** The SpaceX IPO is scheduled for Friday of the current week (approximately June 13, 2026) and is described as the largest IPO in human history. SpaceX is set to IPO at a valuation of $1.75 trillion, while Tesla is trading at approximately $1.28 trillion market cap. JP Morgan CEO Jamie Dimon personally hosted corporate and investor elites ahead of the listing. Bhakdi believes SpaceX is simultaneously the most hyped and potentially the most undervalued company ever, due to its role in transforming the economics of compute in space beginning around 2028, combined with projected compute demand growth of 20–30% per year for an extended period.

3. **Tesla-SpaceX merger thesis and magnet effect:** Bhakdi argues that a Tesla-SpaceX merger is a near-certainty and that it must be structured at a minimum as a one-to-one merger (or better for Tesla shareholders), since Tesla shareholders would vote down any deal that gave SpaceX the majority of the combined entity. He notes Alexandra Merz is also involved in this discussion. With SpaceX potentially surging past $2 trillion at IPO open, this would create a "magnet effect" pulling Tesla's valuation higher. He also dismisses the theory that investors will sell Tesla to fund SpaceX purchases, arguing that any such rotation already occurred last week.

4. **$490 price target for June 2026:** Bhakdi assigns roughly a 70% probability to Tesla reaching $490 (all-time high) within June 2026 — approximately 22 more days from the video date. He notes it historically takes only about three days for Tesla to travel from $390 to $490 given the right catalyst. He does not consider $600 a reasonable near-term target, stating the stock would either stall around $500 or reprice straight through $600 — the latter requiring sustained Cybercab scaling into the hundreds of vehicles. His DCF model projects Tesla reaching $2,000 per share in the first half of 2029.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab sightings across the U.S. as launch signal:** Cybercabs have been photographed in Seattle and observed across the country, including large parking lots of staged vehicles in Dallas, Houston, and Austin. Bhakdi cites Joe Tegtmeyer's drone footage on X as corroborating evidence of scaling preparation. He emphasizes that Cybercab only entered production approximately two months prior to this video (around early April 2026) and is actively scaling.

2. **World Cup as the robotaxi PR launch window:** Dallas is hosting World Cup matches starting Thursday and Friday of the current week and through the weekend, which Bhakdi identifies as the ideal PR canvas for a Cybercab public launch. He views the convergence of the SpaceX IPO, the World Cup, and the accumulation of Cybercabs in Texas cities as multiple probability layers stacking toward a major robotaxi announcement in June 2026.

3. **Fleet size threshold for price impact:** Bhakdi states that just two to three dozen unsupervised Cybercabs operating publicly would be sufficient to drive Tesla's stock to $490. However, he argues that sustained scaling into "multiple hundreds" of vehicles is required to push the stock through $600 and trigger a full repricing of Tesla's autonomous driving thesis.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Optimus chip mention:** A commenter references a cheap A5 chip for Optimus 2, which Bhakdi acknowledges without elaborating further.

## Financials

1. **Bhakdi's personal portfolio allocation:** Bhakdi discloses his approximate portfolio breakdown on the non-leveraged core stock side: roughly 60% Tesla, 25% Nvidia, 10% MicroStrategy, and 6% Robinhood. When factoring in leverage through short puts, the effective exposure shifts to approximately 80% Tesla and 15% Nvidia. He is currently holding short puts on Tesla with a $410 weekly strike expiring Friday, and short puts on Nvidia.

2. **Tesla valuation vs. SpaceX at IPO:** Tesla's market cap at the time of recording is approximately $1.28 trillion. SpaceX is IPOing at $1.75 trillion with Bhakdi suggesting high odds it surges to $2 trillion on day one. He describes Tesla at $1.28 trillion as "insanely cheap" — comparable to a startup valuation — and likens it to Anthropic in scale. His internal model projects Tesla reaching $2,000/share in the first half of 2029.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla market cap at time of recording: ~$1.28 trillion
- SpaceX IPO valuation: $1.75 trillion; potential day-one surge to $2 trillion
- NASDAQ Friday drop: -4.18%; NASDAQ Monday recovery: ~86% of losses
- Tesla Friday drop: nearly $30
- Tesla Monday gain: ~$17 (approximately $408–$410 level implied)
- Bhakdi's June 2026 price target: $490 (70% probability); $600 requires sustained Cybercab fleet scaling into hundreds
- Tesla $2,000/share target: first half of 2029 per Bhakdi's DCF model
- Cybercab entered production approximately two months ago (~early April 2026)
- SpaceX compute economics transformation expected around 2028
- Global compute demand growth projection: 20–30% per year
- SpaceX authorized shares: 36 billion (cited in PioneerLens AI summary)
- "It takes exactly three days for Tesla to go from $390 to $490."
- "For 600 you need sustained scaling... either it doesn't get there and drops off at 500 or it goes straight through 600 because it's repricing."

2026-06-08.title: Daily X Summary (2026-06-08)
2026-06-08.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts from @SawyerMerritt were light on hard investment data, with the dominant Tesla-relevant theme being anecdotal FSD (Supervised) user satisfaction — including elderly adopters and a viral third-party review. A follow-up post about strong truck sales demand generated notable engagement but lacks enough context to confirm the vehicle or pricing specifics. SpaceX-related posts (Ontario Teachers windfall, Starlink/Finnair) dominate the digest but are tangential to Tesla's core investment thesis.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **FSD (Supervised) User Adoption — Anecdotal Evidence of Broad, Confident Use:** Two separate user anecdotes highlight FSD Supervised adoption among older demographics. An elderly couple drove their Model Y from New Hampshire to Connecticut with zero interventions, and an 89-year-old woman reportedly uses FSD for the majority of her driving. Separately, a third-party written review (1.8K likes, 234 reposts — the highest-engagement Tesla post of the day) describes FSD Supervised as handling lane changes, passing, signaling, and parking "with almost eerie confidence" across varied environments including warehouses, banks, and fast-food locations, with no "sudden surprises" or "jerky corrections." While these are qualitative and anecdotal, the combination of zero-intervention long-distance use and strong organic review engagement suggests continued improvement in real-world FSD reliability perception. No specific software version, miles-per-intervention figures, or disengagement counts were cited.

2. **Tesla Truck Demand Signal:** A follow-up post (1.8K likes) notes that "nearly half" of an unspecified batch of Tesla trucks sold within 24 hours of availability. The referenced prior post is not included in this digest, leaving the specific truck model, total inventory size, price point, and geography unconfirmed. The strong engagement suggests this is being received as a bullish demand signal, but the lack of specifics limits its analytical utility. Likely refers to Cybertruck or Tesla Semi based on context, but this cannot be confirmed from the available post text alone.

3. **SpaceX / Starlink — Tangential but Notable for Elon Ecosystem Investors:** Two posts detail the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan's 2019 $300M SpaceX investment, which at a target IPO valuation of $1.75T would be worth approximately $11.6B — described as the pension's single most successful investment ever. A separate post covers Finnair (80-plane fleet) in talks with Starlink and Amazon for in-flight Wi-Fi, aiming to finalize a rollout strategy in 2026. These posts have no direct Tesla financial impact but may be relevant to investors tracking Elon Musk's broader asset portfolio or a potential SpaceX IPO as a valuation comparator.

---

## Signal Strength: **Mildly Bullish** — Viral FSD user reviews and anecdotal zero-intervention long-distance use reinforce the narrative of improving Supervised FSD quality and broadening adoption demographics, though no hard metrics or robotaxi/Optimus developments were reported today.

2026-06-09.title: Ron Baron Says SpaceX Could Reach $30 Trillion
2026-06-09.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel discusses the SpaceX IPO (scheduled for that Friday, around June 9, 2026) and the extraordinary valuation projections coming from Ron Baron, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley. Host Herbert is joined by guest Jeff Lutz, a former supply chain C-level executive at Motorola, Google, and Lenovo who now runs his own consulting firm serving mega-cap tech companies. The central thesis is that SpaceX's unique combination of reusable rockets, space-based AI data centers, Starlink, and XAI positions it as potentially the most valuable company ever — though both hosts acknowledge the frenzy of IPO-week hype warrants skepticism.

## Market & Competition

1. **Ron Baron's $10–$30 Trillion SpaceX Valuation:** Billionaire investor Ron Baron, speaking ahead of the SpaceX IPO, stated that SpaceX — initially expected to be valued at under $2 trillion at IPO — will ultimately be worth $10 trillion, $20 trillion, or even $30 trillion, and that it will become the largest, most profitable company on the planet. Baron added that people inside SpaceX believe he is lowballing that estimate. Elon Musk responded to Baron's remarks simply by saying "Ron is smart," and separately appeared to suggest the scale could extend beyond the planet — "largest in the sector of the galaxy." Baron also noted he personally cannot imagine ever selling his SpaceX (or Tesla) stock, and is urging friends and executives of portfolio companies to invest at IPO.

2. **Ron Baron's Existing SpaceX Position and IPO Plans:** By some estimates, Baron Capital Group and its various funds hold approximately $15 billion worth of SpaceX. Baron has publicly stated he plans to purchase an additional $1 billion worth at IPO, reflecting his conviction that this is "the greatest idea" he has ever encountered as an investor.

3. **Goldman Sachs Revenue Projections:** Goldman Sachs, one of the lead bookrunners for the SpaceX IPO, projects that SpaceX revenue will grow roughly 100 times — from approximately $3.2 billion in AI-related revenue in 2025 to $322 billion by 2030. Their broader SpaceX revenue projection reaches $474 billion by 2030, with Starlink contributing approximately $144 billion of that and rocket launch revenue contributing approximately $8.8 billion. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley both project SpaceX revenue near $160 billion by 2028. Both hosts noted the timing of these projections — released in the days immediately before the IPO by the very banks earning fees on the deal — warrants caution.

4. **Morgan Stanley Revenue Projections:** Morgan Stanley projects SpaceX revenue reaching $3.4 trillion by 2040, with profits of approximately $2.7 trillion, calling it an unprecedented revenue figure for any company. Jeff Lutz noted that while the AI buildout numbers are extraordinary, the 2040 timeframe makes them harder to dismiss outright, drawing a parallel to how AI infrastructure projections from five years ago would have seemed equally absurd.

5. **XAI Losses and the Google/Anthropic Deals:** Goldman Sachs's model notes that XAI lost $6.4 billion in 2025. However, both hosts noted that the recently announced deals with Google and Anthropic for SpaceX's space-based data center capacity appear to offset those losses, and that the XAI total addressable market is claimed at $26.5 trillion, versus $2 trillion for Starlink and space launch combined — meaning the bull case is fundamentally an XAI/data center story.

6. **SpaceX's Competitive Moat:** Jeff Lutz argued that SpaceX's core moat is its manufacturing capability for reusable rockets — a capability no competitor has yet replicated at scale. He pointed to Blue Origin/Amazon as a potential future competitor but noted the gap remains large. He also observed that many automotive companies attempted in-house autonomy programs and abandoned them, and that companies relying on Nvidia for AI infrastructure may be in a "pretty big bind." The hosts framed SpaceX's moat as: reusable rockets → exclusive pathway to space → space-based AI data centers → access to near-unlimited solar energy → largest possible AI models → compounding intelligence advantage.

7. **Elon Musk Key-Man Risk:** Ron Baron identified Elon Musk as the single biggest risk to the SpaceX investment thesis. Jeff Lutz offered a nuanced assessment: Musk's decade-long master plans, long-tenured direct reports at both SpaceX and Tesla, and well-articulated product portfolios provide meaningful continuity. However, Lutz identified specific initiatives that remain dependent on Musk's direct involvement — particularly Terafab (described as "very early") and SpaceX AI data centers (described as still being figured out) — while characterizing robotaxi as "solved" and Starship reusability as essentially a "done deal." Both hosts agreed the companies would suffer a valuation hit in a key-man scenario but would not collapse.

8. **SpaceX/Tesla Merger Speculation:** Ron Baron was asked directly about a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger. He said there have been no public announcements and that he defers entirely to Elon's judgment — if Elon says merge, Baron will support it and explain why; if Elon says don't merge, Baron will support that too. Jeff Lutz noted that whether the $10–$30 trillion figure refers to SpaceX alone or a combined SpaceX-Tesla entity is a critical and unanswered question — a combined entity including Tesla's physical AI and Optimus would make those numbers "not inconceivable at all." Both hosts also noted what appeared to be a Freudian slip by Ron Baron, who said "I can't imagine I'm ever going to sell my stock in Tesla" when apparently meaning SpaceX, before correcting himself — mirroring a similar reported slip by Elon Musk in a JP Morgan interview.

9. **China Risk and Geopolitical Dynamics:** The hosts identified China as a top-tier risk and unknown for both SpaceX and Tesla. Jeff Lutz argued that China is unlikely to lock Tesla or Optimus out of the Chinese market because doing so is more detrimental to China than to Elon's companies — "China needs Tesla more than Tesla needs China." He also argued that the U.S. government, not China, may be the more likely party to restrict export of physical AI (including Optimus) to China, drawing a parallel to ongoing U.S. government restrictions on Nvidia chips and AI model exports. Both hosts agreed SpaceX would never make any military or national-defense-related deal with China.

10. **National Defense and Government Contract Potential:** Jeff Lutz noted that while SpaceX currently derives only a small single-digit percentage of its contracts from government, the product lines have clear national defense correlaries — Star Shield being the government version of Starlink — and he speculated there could be many undisclosed or future government business units. He also raised the possibility of Tesla and/or SpaceX entering the drone manufacturing space given the U.S. shortage of reusable drone manufacturing capacity, though he noted neither company is obligated to pursue that market.

Notable quotes and data:
- Ron Baron: "We think SpaceX will be worth $10 trillion, $20 trillion, or $30 trillion... People in the company believe that I'm lowballing it."
- Elon Musk's response to Baron: "Ron is smart."
- Ron Baron on concentration: "You can't own enough of the greatest idea you've ever had. That's the way I feel about SpaceX."
- Ron Baron's Freudian slip: "I can't imagine I'm ever going to sell my stock in Tesla" — corrected to SpaceX, then "or Tesla."
- Baron Capital estimated SpaceX holdings: ~$15 billion; planned IPO purchase: $1 billion additional
- SpaceX IPO initial valuation: under $2 trillion (Baron's framing)
- Goldman Sachs SpaceX revenue projections: $322 billion by 2030 (AI segment); $474 billion total by 2030; ~$160 billion by 2028
- Goldman Sachs Starlink revenue projection: ~$144 billion by 2030
- Goldman Sachs rocket launch revenue projection: ~$8.8 billion by 2030
- XAI 2025 loss: $6.4 billion (per Goldman Sachs model)
- XAI claimed TAM: $26.5 trillion vs. $2 trillion for Starlink and space
- Morgan Stanley SpaceX revenue projection: $3.4 trillion by 2040, with ~$2.7 trillion in profit
- Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs consensus: ~$160 billion revenue by 2028
- Jeff Lutz on robotaxi: "Robotaxi is solved. He's moved on. It's now an operational thing."
- Jeff Lutz on Terafab: "Very early. Who knows if something happens to [Elon] — I would put that at risk and maybe never happening."
- Jeff Lutz on SpaceX AI data centers: "He's just now focusing on that... that is not [solved] right now."

2026-06-09.title: The SpaceX IPO Opportunity Explained
2026-06-09.body:
This video features host Herbert interviewing Alexandra Merz (known as "Tesla Boomer Mama") on the channel "brighterwithherbert," providing what they describe as the most definitive guide to the SpaceX IPO and its implications for Tesla investors. The core thesis is that the SpaceX IPO — launching Friday, June 12, 2026, at $135/share with a $1.75 trillion market cap — has been deliberately engineered with staggered index inclusions and lockup unlock periods timed to maximize SpaceX's stock price, which Alexandra believes is designed to set the stage for a SpaceX-Tesla merger announcement sometime between July 7 and late July 2026.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO Launch Details:** SpaceX is set to begin trading on Friday, June 12, 2026, under the ticker SPCX at an IPO price of $135 per share, implying a market cap of $1.75 trillion. The IPO involves issuing 555 million new Class A shares, representing approximately 4.3% of the market cap as the initial float. Underwriters have a 30-day greenshoe option that could expand the offering from approximately $75 billion to approximately $86 billion if demand warrants it. The total authorized Class A shares will rise from 6.8 billion pre-IPO to approximately 7.38 billion at minimum, or nearly 7.5 billion if the full greenshoe is exercised. Class B shares remain approximately 97% controlled by Elon Musk, and Class C shares (non-voting) remain at zero.

2. **Index Inclusion Timeline and Passive Buying:** Alexandra lays out a detailed timeline for index fund inclusions. The first wave — CRSP (Vanguard) and FTSE Russell — is expected either Thursday, June 18 or Monday, June 21, 2026, due to the Juneteenth holiday on June 19 closing markets. The second and larger wave is NASDAQ 100 inclusion on approximately July 7, 2026 (delayed from the July 4 holiday weekend). Alexandra estimates total index passive buying of between $8 billion and $18 billion, with approximately $15 billion being her central estimate, noting that purchases are float-adjusted and therefore lower than some commentators expect given only 4.3% float. Further rebalancing inclusion rounds are expected in September and December 2026 for CRSP, FTSE, and NASDAQ. The S&P 500 declined to change its 12-month profitability rule and therefore the earliest S&P 500 inclusion under current rules would be June 2027, unless a Tesla-SpaceX merger is consummated first — at which point the combined entity would be included immediately.

3. **Lockup Unlock Structure and Stock Price Projections:** Alexandra describes an unusual and deliberately engineered lockup structure where the largest early-investor unlocks are tied to SpaceX quarterly earnings calls rather than a simple 180-day period. The first major unlock — up to 30% of eligible early investor shares — occurs two business days after the Q2 earnings call, which Herbert guesses will fall on July 22, 2026. Importantly, Elon Musk personally cannot sell for 366 days from the IPO date, meaning he represents roughly 50% of the early investor pool and is excluded from near-term unlocks, so effective unlock exposure is approximately 10–15% of total shares rather than 20–30%. A Grok-generated chart (based on Alexandra's published assumptions, fed in by a community member named Aurelius) projects SpaceX stock price peaking between $275 and $300 around the July 7 NASDAQ 100 inclusion date — more than double the $135 IPO price — before declining as early investors unlock. Even in the most bearish scenario modeled (all non-Elon early investors sell 100% of holdings), Grok projects the stock does not fall below the $135 IPO price, supported by the floor of staggered index purchases.

4. **Proposed SpaceX–Tesla Merger Thesis:** Alexandra's central investment thesis is that a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla will be announced sometime between July 7 and approximately July 28, 2026 — the window between peak SpaceX stock price (at NASDAQ 100 inclusion) and the first major early investor unlock at the Q2 earnings call. Her rationale is that this window offers the highest SpaceX market cap (potentially $3–3.5 trillion), giving SpaceX maximum stock-based acquisition currency. The proposed structure is a stock-for-stock "merger of equals," meaning no cash changes hands. She speculates the new combined entity ticker would be "X," replacing both TSLA and SPCX. Alexandra holds Tesla call options expiring in August 2026, purchased at a $385 strike, as her primary expression of this thesis — she chose Tesla options over buying SpaceX IPO shares because she believes Tesla stock would double to match SpaceX's market cap if a merger of equals is announced.

5. **Tesla Shareholder Vote Math:** If a merger is announced, a Tesla shareholder vote would likely occur in approximately November 2026, with deal consummation (regulatory approvals including HSR, SEC, and Department of Defense review for SpaceX government contract firewalling) expected in Q1 2027 at best, more likely Q2 2027. To reach the required 50% plus one vote of Tesla's approximately 4 billion shares, Alexandra's math requires approximately 2 billion yes votes. Elon Musk holds approximately 17.5% post-option-exercise (~700 million shares). She estimates Vanguard and BlackRock together represent approximately 15%, and with Ron Baron and others, total friendly institutional votes reach approximately 35% — leaving approximately 15% still needed. With retail shareholders at 31% of shares, approximately half of all retail would need to vote yes. Alexandra notes that abstaining is equivalent to a no vote, making retail mobilization critical. She also theorizes that SpaceX chose Charles Schwab, Morgan Stanley, and JP Morgan as IPO underwriters/distributors specifically to obligate them to vote in favor of a Tesla acquisition, given those institutions had previously voted against Tesla shareholder proposals.

6. **Elon's August 15, 2026 Stock Option Exercise:** Alexandra flags a significant near-term financial event: Elon Musk must exercise his 2018 Tesla compensation package stock options by August 15, 2026, described as a "$7 billion event" that triggers a taxable event in January 2028. She argues this creates a strong personal financial incentive for Elon to maximize Tesla's stock price by August 15, further reinforcing her thesis that a merger announcement — which would cause Tesla stock to double — would be timed before that date.

7. **Retail Shareholder Allocation and Broker Restrictions:** Elon reportedly pushed for retail shareholders to receive priority allocation in the SpaceX IPO, requesting that every retail investor who applied receive at least one share, and specifically asked that large institutional orders not crowd out small investors. Fidelity has a firm recommendation (with consequences for future IPO access) that retail IPO buyers hold for 15 trading days — which would expire around July 7, 2026, the same date as NASDAQ 100 inclusion, which Alexandra finds notable. Schwab's minimum account threshold for SpaceX IPO participation has reportedly been reduced from $500,000 to $2,000 after pressure. Options on SPCX are not expected to be available on the first trading day; Alexandra expects them to become tradable the following Tuesday or Wednesday.

## Financials

1. **SpaceX Capital Structure Post-IPO:** Pre-IPO total Class A shares outstanding were 6.8 billion. Post-IPO at minimum issuance: approximately 7.38 billion Class A shares; at full greenshoe: approximately 7.5 billion Class A shares. Total authorized shares across all classes are capped at 36 billion, which Alexandra says is the constraint on how many shares SpaceX could issue in a stock-for-stock Tesla acquisition. She estimates SpaceX will have approximately 13 billion total shares outstanding post-IPO (across all classes), while Tesla will have approximately 4 billion shares outstanding post-option-exercise — giving an approximate 13:4 ratio relevant to merger-of-equals exchange rate calculations. Tesla's current market cap is approximately $1.5 trillion at time of recording.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX IPO price: $135/share; market cap: $1.75 trillion; float: ~4.3%
- New shares issued: 555 million Class A (greenshoe could bring total to ~86 billion in proceeds vs. ~75 billion base)
- Grok projects SpaceX stock peaks between $275–$300 around July 7, 2026 (NASDAQ 100 inclusion day)
- Even in 100% non-Elon early investor sell scenario, Grok projects stock stays above $135 IPO price
- Estimated index passive buying: $8–18 billion, central estimate ~$15 billion, float-adjusted
- First major unlock: ~2 business days after Q2 earnings call (Herbert's guess: July 22, 2026); up to 30% of eligible early investor shares, but effectively 10–15% of all shares because Elon's ~50% stake is locked for 366 days
- Elon's Tesla option exercise deadline: August 15, 2026 — a "$7 billion event" triggering a January 2028 taxable event
- Tesla retail shareholder ownership: ~31% of shares
- Votes needed for merger approval: ~2 billion of ~4 billion total Tesla shares
- Estimated friendly institutional block: Elon ~17.5% + Vanguard/BlackRock ~15% + others ~2.5% = ~35%; need ~15% more from retail
- BlackRock has publicly stated intent to buy $5–10 billion of SpaceX at IPO; Ron Baron publicly stated he will not sell and intends to buy more (~$1 billion)
- Alexandra's personal position: 100% in Tesla plus August 2026 Tesla call options purchased at $385 strike; no SpaceX stock
- Merger consummation timeline: Q1 2027 (optimistic), Q2 2027 (most probable); regulators include HSR, SEC, Department of Defense
- S&P 500 standard inclusion: June 2027 at earliest under current 12-month rule, or immediately upon merger consummation
- Alexandra's "Goldilocks" merger announcement window: July 7–28, 2026
- "I'm not participating in the SpaceX IPO because I do believe in my scenario that sometime in July or maybe early August there will be the announcement of the merger." — Alexandra Merz
- "If everybody sells everything except Elon… the stock price doesn't go below IPO price." — Alexandra Merz
- "Not voting is actually a no. Abstaining is no in this case." — Alexandra Merz / Herbert

2026-06-09.title: Tesla ‘FSD’ approved in Denmark, 4th European country in 2 months
2026-06-09.body:
Denmark's Road Traffic Authority has provisionally approved Tesla's FSD (Supervised) system, making it the fourth European country to clear the software in approximately eight weeks, following the Netherlands, Lithuania, and Estonia.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Denmark approves FSD despite prior EU-level objections:** Færdselsstyrelsen accepted the provisional type approval originally issued by the Dutch authority RDW on April 10, after conducting its own independent technical review. The approval is notable because Denmark had previously been among Nordic nations — alongside Sweden, Finland, and Norway — that raised concerns at the EU level about FSD's tendency to exceed speed limits, its performance on icy roads, and whether the "Full Self-Driving" name overstates the technology. The Danish authority emphasized that "the system does not make the car self-driving. The driver is still fully responsible for driving."

2. **EU-wide approval remains stalled, with significant downside risk:** The national-recognition route continues advancing, but EU-wide approval is not expected before October or December 2026, with full recognition potentially slipping into early 2027. A qualified majority requires at least 15 of 27 member states representing 65% of the EU population — Nordic opposition could complicate that threshold. Critically, if the EU Commission ultimately rejects the system, the Dutch provisional approval becomes invalid after six months, taking all four national approvals down with it. FSD Supervised pricing in Europe is €99/month, or €49/month for owners who previously purchased Enhanced Autopilot.

## Market & Competition

3. **Tesla gains competitive ground as German OEMs retreat from Level 3:** Both Mercedes-Benz and BMW have pulled back from Level 3 autonomous systems in Europe — Mercedes paused Drive Pilot from upcoming S-Class and EQS facelifts, and BMW discontinued its Personal Pilot L3 system. Both are pivoting to Level 2+ systems. This leaves Tesla's FSD Supervised as the most capable driver-assistance system widely available in Europe. Belgium and Greece are reportedly moving quickly toward national approvals, while Ireland, Germany, France, Italy, and Spain are still reviewing or testing.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert argues Denmark's approval — from a prior skeptic — suggests the technical documentation was more convincing than initial political objections implied, but cautions that national mutual-recognition approvals are "low-hanging fruit" and the EU Commission vote remains the real test. He notes Tesla's Level 2 approach is "winning the regulatory race in Europe by default" while Level 3 systems from German automakers proved commercially unviable, attributing much of the difference to manufacturers' willingness to take responsibility for their systems.

Notable quotes and data:
- Danish authority statement: "Færdselsstyrelsen agrees with RDW's assessment that the system will contribute positively to road safety by assisting the driver while driving."
- Swedish Transport Agency investigator wrote in April he was "quite surprised" Tesla allowed FSD to speed.
- FSD Supervised: Level 2 system requiring constant driver attention; works on any road.
- EU vote timeline: earliest realistic bloc-wide vote October or December 2026; full recognition possibly early 2027.
- FSD subscription: €99/month standard; €49/month discounted rate for prior Enhanced Autopilot purchasers.
- Four countries approved via Dutch RDW certification: Netherlands, Lithuania, Estonia, Denmark.
- RDW presented to TCMV on May 5; June 30 meeting agenda includes discussion but no vote.

2026-06-09.title: Tesla Finally Adding More Robotaxis & the SpaceX AI Satellite V1: Running the Numbers ⚡️
2026-06-09.body:
This episode of Electrified, hosted by Dillon Loomis, covers several Tesla and SpaceX developments including growth in Tesla's Texas robotaxi fleet registrations, FSD safety data from the Netherlands and new country approvals, the EU regulatory timeline for supervised FSD, and a deep numerical analysis of SpaceX's newly revealed AI1 orbital compute satellite. The video's core argument is that while Tesla's robotaxi expansion is progressing (with more VINs registered and Cybercabs spotted in multiple states), several timelines — including the Q1 slide deck city launch targets and EU-wide FSD approval — are under significant pressure. On SpaceX, Dillon runs the math to argue that Elon Musk's target of 1 gigawatt of annualized orbital AI compute by end of 2027 is highly ambitious given current Starship launch cadence.

## Robotaxi

1. **Texas fleet registrations growing rapidly:** Tesla now has 59 VINs listed on the Texas Motor Carrier website, up from just over 40 approximately two weeks ago. Dillon clarifies this does not mean all 59 vehicles are currently active in the fleet or that any are unsupervised — rather, it represents the maximum Tesla could theoretically deploy in Texas right now. All 59 are currently Model Ys.

2. **Cybercabs accumulating in Houston and Dallas lots:** A flyover of the Houston lot shared by SC Robinson showed 21 Cybercabs visible, with numerous Model Ys also appearing to be staged for deployment. A separate video of the Dallas lot showed dozens of Cybercabs lined up. Dillon cautions that until a Cybercab without a steering wheel and without pedals is spotted on-site, expectations for near-term Cybercab deployment should remain low.

3. **Cybercab testing now spanning ~20 US states:** The Cybercab has been spotted testing in approximately 20 different US states, indicating broad geographic preparation even ahead of commercial launch.

4. **Arizona first responder filing reveals broad operating domain:** A Tesla first responder interaction plan for Arizona, dated April 24th of this year, lists the robotaxi service's design domain as operating at SAE Level 4 autonomy across Chandler, Gilbert, Glendale, Maricopa County, Mesa, Paradise Valley, Phoenix, Scottsdale, and Tempe — all within Maricopa County, which has a population of approximately 4.8 million people. The robotaxi tracker lists Phoenix as the only officially called-out Arizona city, so Dillon expects the first Arizona launch there with expansion to follow.

5. **Q1 city launch timeline in serious jeopardy:** Tesla's Q1 slide deck indicated launches in five different cities within a specific window. With only 20 days remaining on that timeline as of the publish date, Dillon acknowledges that most observers would agree the target is not looking achievable.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Netherlands FSD safety data shows strong performance:** Over the last two months, Tesla reported supervised FSD has been over three times safer than manual driving on Dutch roads, with 3.5 times fewer collisions. Additional metrics include nearly 15 times fewer automatic emergency braking events, 8.8 times less harsh acceleration, 7.3 times less harsh braking, and 8 times fewer hard swerves. On highways specifically, FSD achieved 3.4 times safer performance across 16.6 million km with zero collisions. On non-highway roads, it is 1.6 times safer across 7 million km with three collisions. Combined, this implies FSD has now covered 23.6 million km in the Netherlands from April 10th to June 5th, 2026.

2. **Denmark approves supervised FSD:** Elon Musk announced that supervised FSD has been officially approved in Denmark, with rollout to begin soon. This brings the total to four countries with approval: the Netherlands, Lithuania, Estonia, and Denmark. Across these four countries, approximately 215,000 Teslas are active on the roads (a cumulative figure, with the majority in the Netherlands and Denmark), though hardware filtering for older AI4 and Hardware 3 vehicles would reduce the addressable pool.

3. **EU-wide vote unlikely before October 2026, rollout possibly delayed to early 2027:** The agenda for the June 30th Technical Committee of Motor Vehicles (TCMV) meeting shows only a continuation of discussions on the Netherlands' Act 39 authorization request — no vote is listed. Dillon assesses the probability of a surprise vote as near zero, since a formal draft act would normally be circulated to member countries at least two weeks in advance. The next window for a possible EU-wide vote would be October 2026, meaning actual software rollout across the EU could slip into early 2027.

4. **Risk of provisional approvals lapsing if EU formally rejects FSD:** Per a Danish outlet, the current approvals in the Netherlands and Denmark are provisional and only apply to EU countries that choose to recognize the Dutch approval. If the EU Commission ultimately rejects the system, the Dutch provisional approval would become invalid after six months, causing the Danish approval to lapse as well, and supervised FSD could no longer be marketed or sold in EU countries. Dillon notes that with each additional country adopting the provisional approval, a formal rejection becomes increasingly disruptive.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Model 3 RWD tops Edmunds real-world efficiency test:** Edmunds named Tesla's Model 3 rear-wheel drive the efficiency champion in their real-world range test. The tested vehicle achieved 393 miles on a full charge versus its EPA estimate of 363 miles — 30 miles further, or 8.3% beyond the official figure. On energy consumption, the car returned 21.7 kWh per 100 miles (4.61 miles per kWh), versus the EPA rating of 25 kWh per 100 miles (4 miles per kWh), making it 13.2% more efficient than the EPA estimate and the most efficient EV currently in production tested by Edmunds.

2. **Tesla durability study ranks competitively among luxury brands:** An iSeeCars study covering 174 million vehicles found Tesla ranks sixth overall and third among luxury brands for the likelihood of reaching 250,000 miles, with a 4.6% probability. This places Tesla above Cadillac, Mazda, Subaru, Volvo, Mercedes, BMW, and Porsche. Toyota led overall at 17.8%, with Lexus second at 12.8%. The luxury segment average was 3.2%, and the overall industry average was 4.8%.

3. **Tesla Semi commercial groundwork in Europe:** Tesla posted a job listing for a Business Development Manager for the Tesla Semi, based in Parsdorf near Munich, Germany — a B2B sales role focused on lining up fleet customers and expanding Semi's customer base in the region. Dillon does not expect the Tesla Semi to be deployed or sold in Europe until 2027 at the earliest.

## Market & Competition

1. **US Trade Representative visiting Tesla Fremont factory:** Jameson Greer, the US Trade Representative, is scheduled to tour Tesla's Fremont factory as part of a manufacturing tour promoting the Trump administration's reindustrialization agenda. Dillon notes that in March of last year (2025), Tesla had submitted a formal letter to Greer warning about retaliatory tariff exposure for US exporters and flagging that certain lithium battery components remain difficult or impossible to source entirely within the US despite onshoring efforts. Tesla is expected to continue making its case during the visit.

2. **SpaceX AI1 orbital satellite — numbers vs. Colossus:** Dillon runs detailed math comparing SpaceX's newly revealed AI1 satellite to ground-based compute. The AI1 satellite spans 70 meters across and 20 meters tall, with a peak power of 150 kW (0.15 MW) and sustained power of 120 kW (0.12 MW), and a power density of 70 kW per ton, implying each satellite weighs approximately 2 tons (~4,400 lbs, roughly the weight of a Model Y). SpaceX is targeting 1 gigawatt of annualized orbital AI compute by end of 2027. Using Colossus 1 at 500 MW as a benchmark, it would require between 3,333 satellites (at peak power) and 4,000 satellites (at sustained power) to match it. With Starship V3 capable of carrying ~100 tons per launch (roughly 50 satellites at 2 tons each), matching a 500 MW data center would require 67–83 Starship launches. Reaching the 1 GW annualized target would require approximately 150 Starship launches, or more than 12 per month by December 2027 — a cadence Dillon views as highly optimistic given Starship has flown only 12 times in three years and has not yet reached orbit.

Notable quotes and data:
- 59 VINs now listed on Texas Motor Carrier website for Tesla's robotaxi fleet, up from ~40 two weeks prior
- All 59 Texas-registered vehicles are currently Model Ys
- 21 Cybercabs visible in Houston lot flyover; dozens visible in Dallas lot
- Cybercab spotted testing in ~20 US states
- Arizona first responder plan covers SAE Level 4 autonomy across Maricopa County (pop. ~4.8 million)
- FSD Netherlands data (April 10 – June 5, 2026): 3.5x fewer collisions, 3.4x safer on highways (16.6M km, 0 collisions), 1.6x safer on non-highway roads (7M km, 3 collisions); total 23.6M km
- Four countries with supervised FSD approval: Netherlands, Lithuania, Estonia, Denmark; ~215,000 Teslas on road across those countries
- EU-wide vote next window: October 2026; actual rollout possibly early 2027
- Model 3 RWD: 393 miles real-world range vs. 363 EPA; 21.7 kWh/100 mi vs. 25 kWh/100 mi EPA (13.2% more efficient)
- Tesla durability: 4.6% chance of reaching 250,000 miles (6th overall, 3rd among luxury brands)
- AI1 satellite: 70m wide, 20m tall, 150 kW peak / 120 kW sustained, ~2 tons per unit
- 3,333–4,000 AI1 satellites needed to match a 500 MW data center
- 67–83 Starship launches needed to orbit enough satellites to match 500 MW; ~150 launches for 1 GW
- Starship has flown 12 times in 3 years; 5 times in all of 2025; once so far in 2026
- Tesla stock closed at $396.68, down 3%; NDX down 1.5%; volume 14% above average

2026-06-09.title: SPACE X: The Biggest Financial Event Of The Year Is Almost Here
2026-06-09.body:
This video from FutureAzA features host Brian in conversation with Randy Kirk, covering the anticipated SpaceX IPO, speculation about a potential SpaceX acquisition of Nokia, and a critical assessment of Ford's business trajectory. The core thesis is skeptical of both the Nokia acquisition rumor and Ford's long-term viability, while bullish on SpaceX's vertical integration and growth prospects.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO Pricing and Scale:** The video discusses a freshly published report indicating SpaceX's IPO is expected to be priced at $135 per share, which would raise over $1 billion — described as the largest raise of any company in history. The hosts indicate Brian plans to cover the IPO live when it goes public. Proceeds are expected to fund Nvidia chip purchases and buildout of their own Terafab infrastructure.

2. **SpaceX Nokia Acquisition Rumor:** A Yahoo Finance article speculating that SpaceX might acquire Nokia (estimated at potentially around $100 billion) rather than merge with Tesla is discussed and largely dismissed. Randy Kirk argues that SpaceX and Tesla together already possess essentially everything needed across the AI/tech stack, and that Nokia would not add sufficient value to justify the cost. Any acquisition SpaceX pursues, he argues, would more likely be done via stock rather than cash, given the massive capital requirements for building out Terafab and scaling Starship production to potentially thousands of units per year.

3. **SpaceX Starlink Subscriber Growth:** SpaceX recently announced it has surpassed 12 million active Starlink subscribers, which the hosts note makes it larger than many historically prominent ISPs. Randy Kirk adds that Starlink has been adding approximately 1 million subscribers per month, and references analyst Brian Wong's projection that with a current building expansion underway, the growth rate could reach 1.5 million per month either later in 2026 or into early 2027.

4. **XAI and Compute Revenue:** Brian notes that XAI (Elon Musk's AI company) is generating billion-dollar deals renting out compute, and is building and standing up data centers faster than competitors. The broader point is that AI infrastructure has become a legitimate revenue model, with companies spending millions monthly on tokens for staff productivity improvements.

5. **Ford's Dividend and Valuation — Skepticism:** The hosts address a Yahoo Finance article touting Ford's 4.06% dividend yield as a "no-brainer" buy in June 2026, following a 44% share price surge over the past 12 months and three out of four recent quarters beating analyst estimates. Ford's shares currently trade at a price-to-earnings multiple of 11.3x, a 56% discount to the broader S&P 500. Brian and Randy are deeply skeptical, arguing the low valuation is justified by absent long-term vision, and that a dividend cut would wipe out more than the 4% yield gain.

6. **Ford's Structural Problems:** Randy Kirk details Ford's persistent issues with warranty claims and recalls, noting Ford has led in actual factory recalls for multiple consecutive years through at least 45 days prior to the video. A former Ford engineer who helped write their warranty management software told Randy the current system is insufficiently proactive. Randy draws a parallel to Sears and Kmart, warning Ford faces a similar fate if it fails to develop a credible EV and autonomous driving strategy. Both hosts note Ford has hired former Tesla employees and is now quoting Elon Musk's manufacturing philosophy (e.g., "the best part is no part"), but question why these lessons weren't applied earlier and why Ford hasn't pursued FSD licensing.

7. **Ford's Brand and Entry-Level Strategy Failure:** Randy argues Ford made a critical error by discontinuing entry-level vehicles like the Ford Escort and Ford Focus. While those cars weren't highly profitable, they built brand loyalty.
