2026-06-17.title: Why SpaceX's $60B Cursor Deal Changes Everything
2026-06-17.body:
This video discusses SpaceX's $60 billion all-stock acquisition of Cursor, the AI coding tool company, framing it not as a simple software purchase but as the completion of a full-stack AI empire. Host Herbert and guest Jo Bhakdi argue that Cursor provides SpaceX/XAI with the critical missing piece — developer distribution and enterprise access — to compete directly with Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google in the enterprise AI market. While both are long-term bulls on SpaceX, Bhakdi warns that the current stock price is mechanically inflated by IPO lock-ups and forced index buying, and will likely correct significantly before genuine price discovery occurs.

## Market & Competition

1. **The "Holy Trinity" of AI — Harness, LLM, and Compute:** Jo Bhakdi frames the Cursor acquisition through what he calls the "holy trinity" of AI: the harness (the interface that translates user intent into LLM-readable instructions), the LLM itself, and compute. He argues Cursor is the best harness in the world — with a larger install base than Anthropic — while Grok provides the LLM and Colossus provides compute. Before the deal, SpaceX/XAI had world-class compute but lacked a strong harness and enterprise distribution. Now, Bhakdi argues, SpaceX holds all three layers simultaneously, something no other company — not Microsoft, not Google, not Anthropic — currently does. Anthropic, by comparison, has only two of the three (harness and LLM) but no proprietary compute, yet reached a trillion-dollar valuation on that basis alone.

2. **Cursor's Enterprise Penetration as the Core Value Driver:** The video emphasizes that Cursor is used by 64% of Fortune 500 companies and 70% of Fortune 1000 companies, with approximately 50,000 enterprise customers including Nvidia, Samsung, and Salesforce. Salesforce alone has 20,000 engineers using Cursor with over 90% daily adoption. Bhakdi stresses that this pre-existing enterprise footprint — which took Cursor roughly 18 months to build from launch to $1 billion in revenue (compared to Slack's seven years) — is the real strategic asset, giving SpaceX a fast-track distribution channel into the white-collar workforce that is the core of the 22.7 trillion enterprise AI TAM outlined in the SpaceX IPO deck.

3. **Cursor's Revenue Trajectory and the Deal's Valuation Context:** Cursor's ARR reportedly grew from $500 million to $3 billion in approximately 11 months, with projections of $6 billion by year-end 2026. The video notes that SpaceX paid roughly 10 times forward revenue for Cursor, contextualizing this against Microsoft paying 13 times forward revenue for its OpenAI stake. Bhakdi notes that despite these growth metrics, the $60 billion price tag represents a very high multiple even by the standards of comparably frothy companies like Palantir and Anthropic, and he argues that if SpaceX were valued on Tesla's revenue multiple it would be at $35 per share — a fraction of its current price.

4. **Colossus + Cursor Data: A Potential Leap to Frontier AI:** The video plays a clip from investor Gavin Baker, who explains that Cursor and Anthropic hold more tokens of proprietary coding training data than any other lab — more than exists on the public internet. Baker describes how Cursor's internal coding model (Composer 2) reached near-frontier performance with minimal training, and after just three weeks on the Colossus 2 cluster it became benchmark-dominant on Cursor's internal coding benchmark (CursorBench). Baker frames this as a signal that once XAI/SpaceX trains Cursor's data chinchilla-optimally with reinforcement learning, Grok has a genuine shot at becoming a leading frontier model in coding.

5. **SpaceX IPO Mechanics and Near-Term Stock Risk:** Bhakdi argues the post-IPO stock surge is largely mechanical rather than organic. He explains that most pre-IPO shareholders face lock-up periods ranging from 15–30 days (retail, broker-side) up to 180 days and 366 days for large institutional holders, meaning effectively no one is allowed to sell. Simultaneously, three indices are scheduled to include SpaceX at 5, 10, and 15 days post-IPO, creating forced buying pressure. Options trading also began at the time of the video. Bhakdi's view is that once these forced-buying mechanics fade and lock-ups expire, the stock will drop sharply into genuine price discovery — potentially to around $80 per share. He states he is waiting to buy at a lower price and is not currently purchasing.

6. **SpaceX Revenue Trajectory and Valuation Concerns:** The video states SpaceX's 2025 annual revenue was approximately $18.7 billion. Following compute-leasing deals with Anthropic, Google, and now the Cursor acquisition, its estimated annual revenue run rate has risen to approximately $55 billion. The video suggests SpaceX could exit 2026 with a run rate exceeding $60 billion. Bhakdi is more conservative, estimating SpaceX will end 2026 with $30 billion in actual (not run-rate) revenue, and could reach $120–$150 billion — possibly $200 billion — in actual revenue in 2027. However, he argues that even at $200 billion in revenue, at a Tesla-equivalent valuation multiple the stock would be worth roughly $2 trillion by end of 2027, which at current prices (~$2.8–3 trillion market cap) still implies significant downside. SpaceX raised $85.7 billion in its IPO (initially targeting $75 billion).

7. **Potential Tesla–SpaceX Merger Hinted:** Bhakdi and Herbert briefly touch on the idea that SpaceX may eventually acquire Tesla, referencing it as something Elon Musk needs SpaceX stock to be "strong enough" to execute. Bhakdi suggests the stock ratio (one-to-one, one-to-two, etc.) matters less to Elon than getting the deal done, and predicts there will be community drama around it — referencing a future debate between "Rebellionire versus Alexandra" — but that the merger will ultimately happen.

Notable quotes and data:
- Cursor ARR: grew from $500M to $3B in 11 months; projected $6B by end of 2026
- Cursor: fastest software company to reach $1B in revenue (18 months vs. Slack's 7 years)
- Cursor users: ~1 million daily users, ~1 million paying subscribers, 50,000+ enterprise customers
- Enterprise penetration: 64% of Fortune 500, 70% of Fortune 1000
- Salesforce: 20,000 engineers using Cursor with 90%+ daily adoption
- SpaceX paid ~10x forward revenue; Microsoft paid ~13x for OpenAI stake
- SpaceX IPO raised $85.7 billion (up from initial $75B target)
- SpaceX 2025 revenue: ~$18.7 billion; current estimated run rate: ~$55 billion
- SpaceX current market cap: ~$2.8–3 trillion
- Bhakdi estimate: SpaceX actual revenue ~$30B in 2026, ~$120–200B in 2027
- Colossus supercomputer described as having 1 million H100 equivalents
- AWS comparison: Amazon Web Services earns ~$110B/year from cloud infrastructure
- SpaceX IPO enterprise AI TAM: $22.7 trillion (the dominant line item in the IPO deck)
- Jo Bhakdi: "If SpaceX would trade on the revenue multiple of Tesla, it would be at $35."
- Jo Bhakdi: "I think true recursive self-improvement is at least five years away... runaway recursive self-improvement, maybe 10 years away."
- Gavin Baker (clip): "Cursor and Anthropic have more tokens of proprietary coding data than anyone else — and each has more than exists on the public internet."

2026-06-17.title: Three Signals Point To Tesla’s Next Move
2026-06-17.body:
The video covers three developments the host and guest Jo Bhakdi argue are converging to signal Tesla's next major momentum phase: strengthening robotaxi safety data, the Cybercab's EPA certification revealing better-than-expected specs, and Goldman Sachs raising its Q2 delivery forecast. The core thesis is that these signals, taken together, suggest Tesla is approaching a major robotaxi deployment inflection point that most investors are not yet connecting. Jo Bhakdi, described as an economist, investor, and tech entrepreneur with a YouTube channel covering Tesla and AGI, serves as the primary analyst throughout the discussion.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Four months of zero at-fault FSD incidents:** The latest NHTSA filing covering the period from April 15 to May 15 shows only one new incident — a stopped robotaxi that was rear-ended by a pickup truck, meaning FSD was not at fault. The two prior incidents in March also involved stationary robotaxis being rear-ended. As a result, Tesla has recorded zero incidents where FSD was at fault since the beginning of February 2026, now spanning approximately four months. Elon Musk publicly commented on a post noting the irony that all recent crashes involving Tesla's robotaxi fleet were caused by other human-driven vehicles rear-ending them. Bhakdi notes that in total, across 18 incidents since June 2022, almost none were Tesla's fault.

2. **FSD version 14.3.4 as a significant leap:** Bhakdi characterizes FSD version 14.3.4, described as having launched the prior week, as more than a minor point release — calling it a "very big leap." He frames version 14.3 as a major architectural overhaul that enabled faster iteration, and says 14.3.4 is now receiving "crazy positive reviews." On the Tesla earnings call, Elon Musk is cited as having stated that Tesla has "solved safety" and that the remaining challenge is convenience — optimizing the tradeoff between safety and ride quality along what Bhakdi describes as an "efficient frontier."

3. **Safety data accumulation as a strategic prerequisite:** The host theorizes that Tesla has been deliberately accumulating months of safety data with a small fleet before broader deployment, so they can present regulators and the public with a substantial mileage record showing, for example, five or six months of operation without a fault incident. This data cushion would allow Tesla to contextualize any future incident statistically.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab fleet buildout accelerating ahead of deployment:** Bhakdi claims Tesla has "over a thousand Cybercabs deployed right now somewhere in the country," based on his own calculations. He references reports of 100 Cybercabs on the lot at Giga Texas and 44 in Dallas, plus additional units in Houston and Austin. He argues it would be irrational for Tesla to be printing thousands of Cybercabs with no deployment plan, and frames the manufacturing ramp as a "forcing function" pointing toward imminent launch.

2. **June deployment timeline and five-city promise:** Bhakdi states his "local probabilistic maximum" for the start of commercial robotaxi deployment is June 2026, with August as the next likely window if June does not materialize. He notes that Tesla previously promised robotaxi service in five cities by the end of June 2026, and believes they will still honor that, even if it means only a few cars in a few cities initially. He and the host agree that 10,000–20,000 Cybercabs deployed by end of 2026 is their forecast, which they acknowledge most consider aggressive; Bhakdi notes the prior consensus was as high as 50,000.

3. **Cybercab EPA certification and specs:** The Cybercab received its EPA certificate of conformity, confirming it meets all federal emissions requirements and can be legally introduced into US commerce. The filing revealed: front-wheel drive, 48 kWh battery, 219 horsepower, approximately 3,000 lb curb weight (roughly 600–700 lb lighter than the Model 3 rear-wheel drive at ~3,700 lb), and a range of 418 miles — materially above the ~375 miles previously anticipated. The host also references a prior concern about a 2,800-unit cap, clarifying these vehicles are self-certified and that cap does not apply.

4. **Cybercab vs. Waymo unit economics:** Bhakdi argues that because the Cybercab's 418-mile range is roughly three times that of a Waymo vehicle, one Cybercab is operationally equivalent to three Waymos in terms of uptime. Combined with the Cybercab costing approximately one-third the price of a Waymo, he frames this as a "one to nine" structural advantage for Tesla before accounting for maintenance and other costs.

5. **SpaceX acquisition and options implications:** The host and Bhakdi discuss a speculative scenario in which a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla is announced at a price below some investors' LEAP strike prices, potentially rendering out-of-the-money options worthless. Bhakdi notes that standard Chicago-style options contracts theoretically transfer rights to the equivalent prorated SpaceX position, but expresses significant uncertainty about how this would work operationally, and says this risk makes him unwilling to put large amounts of capital into deep out-of-the-money LEAPs.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Goldman Sachs raises Q2 delivery forecast:** Goldman Sachs raised its Q2 2026 Tesla vehicle delivery forecast from 405,000 to 420,000 units, citing stronger-than-expected trends across Tesla's major markets. The bank's full-year estimate remains at 1.72–1.73 million vehicles, which is noted as slightly below 2025 levels, but the direction of revision is seen as confirming a global sales turnaround. The host cites improving China and Europe sales as consistent with this trend.

2. **Core auto business as a cash engine for platform bets:** Bhakdi frames Tesla's vehicle business not primarily as a growth story but as a validation and cash generation machine that funds and de-risks the Optimus and robotaxi platforms. He argues the Model Y's improving margins, combined with ongoing deterioration at legacy OEMs, positions Tesla to capture increasing market share. He predicts 2027 will be a "year of massive reckoning" for incumbent automakers, with potential bankruptcies, and that Tesla will emerge as one of the last major Western OEMs standing alongside a few Chinese players and possibly Toyota.

## Market & Competition

1. **Legacy automakers structurally incapable of competing on robotaxi:** Bhakdi argues that legacy OEMs like Volkswagen and Ford lack both the first-principles engineering culture and the organizational willingness to invest in a purpose-built, scalable robotaxi platform. He contends that Waymo, despite having solved autonomous driving technically, cannot scale to 200 million vehicles because it was never designed for mass manufacturing. Tesla, by contrast, engineered the entire stack — vehicle, software, and fleet infrastructure — with 200 million cars as the target endpoint.

2. **Tesla Semi as an underreported platform story:** Bhakdi briefly flags the Tesla Semi as a "massively underrated story," arguing it will become the singular platform for autonomous commercial trucking globally, mirroring what the Model Y did for passenger EVs. He notes a steady stream of fleet customer announcements but says the story gets insufficient coverage.

Notable quotes and data:
- Zero FSD-at-fault incidents since early February 2026 — approximately four months
- 18 total NHTSA incidents reported since June 2022; almost none attributed to Tesla fault
- Cybercab specs per EPA filing: 48 kWh battery, 219 hp, ~3,000 lb curb weight, 418-mile range
- Model 3 rear-wheel drive curb weight cited at ~3,700 lb for comparison
- Active Robotaxi fleet per RobotaxiTracker.com: 728 (as of 2026-06-16), including 604 Bay Area, 104 Austin, 9 Dallas, 11 Houston
- Bhakdi's independent estimate: "over a thousand Cybercabs deployed right now somewhere in the country"
- Goldman Sachs Q2 delivery forecast raised from 405,000 to 420,000; full-year at 1.72–1.73 million
- "We have 14.3.4 now out where people say it's now it's perfect. So it is just a question of time until they push the button."
- "Tesla is an incredible deal… the best Tesla deal we have had in the last 5 years in my opinion because we are very close to this inflection point."
- Bhakdi on Cybercab vs. Waymo: "One Cybercab equal to three Waymos and each Waymo three times more expensive than Cybercab. So it's a one to nine advance before you even start maintenance."

2026-06-17.title: The Latest Tesla Semi Developments
2026-06-17.body:
This episode of FutureAzA, hosted by Brian with guest Mark from The Tesla Life, focuses primarily on new drone and ground footage of the Tesla Semi Giga factory (referred to as "Giga Eye West"), captured by field reporter Zanegler. The hosts analyze visual evidence of production progress at the Tesla Semi manufacturing facility, discuss a range of viewer comments on topics ranging from solar charging to FSD legislation, and close with a "Wrong Answers Only" comedy segment.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **New Tesla Semi footage from Zanegler:** Fresh aerial and ground-level footage from the Tesla Semi production facility shows a variety of activity. The parking lot previously occupied by large equipment staging has been cleared and now serves as standard employee parking, suggesting a construction/installation phase has concluded. Employee vehicles are a mix of cars, trucks, and motorcycles — indicating a blend of contractors and regular employees — with a growing number of Teslas visible.

2. **Six new-design Tesla Semis spotted in a corral:** Six Tesla Semis were observed grouped together in a cordoned-off area near what is believed to be the end of the assembly line exit door. Two were identified as long-cab variants and four as short-cab variants. The new design is distinguished from the older "Atlas" prototype generation ("Arcus") by a headlight bar that runs all the way across the front. The hosts note that the shorter cab likely corresponds to the standard-range variant, which uses two large battery modules versus three in the long-range version.

3. **Speculation on a short-range "port version":** Brian speculates — based on no inside information, by his own admission — that Tesla could potentially produce a single-battery-module variant with roughly 100 miles of range, optimized for port operations where short-range is sufficient. He suggests this could also help margins and relieve battery supply constraints if demand outpaces battery production.

4. **Gen 1 Tesla Semi still in active use on-site:** An older-generation Tesla Semi (identifiable by the cab window design extending further back) was observed actively moving pallets and performing logistics work on the factory grounds. The hosts note this is a practical use of early prototype builds.

5. **Large custom pallets observed — likely for battery packs:** Oversized metal pallet-like racks with forklift cutouts were spotted at the facility. Brian theorizes these are purpose-built carriers for the Semi's heavy battery packs, given their size (roughly twice that of a standard pallet) and heavy-duty tubular/box steel construction.

6. **Mystery black dots on cab rooftops:** New black dots were observed on the rooflines of all the new-design cabs in the footage. The hosts are uncertain of their purpose — ruling out rear-view cameras as impractical from that position — and invite viewer speculation in the "Wrong Answers Only" format.

7. **ABF Freight adds two Tesla Semis:** A news item dated June 15, 2026 reports that ABF added two Tesla Semis to its fleet. The image accompanying the story appears to show older pilot-model Semis rather than the current production design.

8. **Costco operating older-design Tesla Semis:** The hosts confirm Costco has Tesla Semis but note these are the older design, not the current production variant.

9. **Creature comforts and future iterations:** In response to European feedback that the Tesla Semi lacks creature comforts, Mark notes Tesla iterates its vehicles quickly and issues will be addressed. Brian adds that sleeper cab variants, when introduced, will offer more amenity options; the current version is a day cab.

10. **Solar charging on vehicles — math breakdown:** Brian works through the physics of rooftop solar for EVs. At 100% panel efficiency on a 2 square meter roof, a car could capture 8–10 kWh per day — enough for roughly 24–30 miles. At realistic efficiency (approximately half), this drops to about 12 miles per day, under optimal stationary conditions (no shading, full sun, optimal tilt). Commenter Henry elaborates that automotive-grade solar integration requires curved panels, shatter-safe glass, DCDC converters (30–50V to 1000V), adds cost of $3,000+, and represents only one-third the area of a typical roof-mounted system — making rooftop home solar a far better investment. Brian and Mark conclude the technology is not yet viable for meaningful daily driving range contribution.

11. **Aptera solar EV — disappointment with production delays:** The hosts discuss Aptera, whose three-wheel, two-seat, aerodynamically optimized design is the closest real-world attempt at a solar-sufficient EV. Brian expresses disappointment that Aptera has not yet reached customer deliveries. He notes that when Aptera was pitching at ~$35,000 it was a compelling alternative to $60,000 EVs, but now that EVs can be had for under $35,000, Aptera's value proposition is harder to justify — especially with production timelines still unclear.

12. **FSD in Canada — supervised only:** Mark confirms FSD is in use across Canada but remains supervised. No legislative approvals for unsupervised FSD operation in Canadian provinces have been announced.

13. **Chinese EV tariff legislation and Tesla:** A viewer raises whether a hypothetical U.S. law blocking China-built EVs would apply to Teslas built in Giga Shanghai, given they run U.S. software rather than Chinese software. The hosts suggest Tesla may have an exemption path on that basis, though they acknowledge other Chinese automakers could simply adopt U.S. software to circumvent such a rule.

## Market & Competition

1. **Rivian commercial vans beyond Amazon:** In response to a viewer question, the hosts confirm Rivian is selling commercial vans to customers beyond Amazon, citing HelloFresh/Factor-branded vans and noting that "Also" vans recently seen at an event are a wholly owned Rivian subsidiary.

2. **Horizon Motors positioning against Tesla Semi:** The hosts reference Horizon Motors as a competitor apparently marketing itself to the small segment of buyers who dislike Tesla, rather than competing head-on. Brian interprets this as an implicit concession that they cannot match Tesla's product.

Notable quotes and data:
- "Two long caps and four small caps" — six new-design Tesla Semis visible in the factory corral area.
- Long-range Semi uses three battery modules; standard-range uses two. Brian speculates a single-module "port version" could yield ~100 miles of range.
- "At 100% efficiency on a two square meter roof, you're looking at 8 to 10 kilowatt hours per day… so if it was half that, you get four kilowatts — about 12 miles a day."
- Rooftop automotive solar estimated at $3,000+ and representing only one-third of a standard residential panel's area.
- ABF Freight added two Tesla Semis (news dated June 15, 2026).
- Studies cited linking higher EV registrations in a zip code to lower ER visits for asthma/respiratory issues — hosts flag this as relevant to the port electrification case for the Semi.
- New black dots visible on rooflines of all new-design Semi cabs — purpose unknown.

2026-06-17.title: Why Tesla + SpaceX Stocks SLIDE Today
2026-06-17.body:
Jo Bhakdi hosts a live session reviewing Tesla's and SpaceX's price action on a day dominated by the Federal Reserve's first press conference under new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh. Tesla sold off broadly in line with the NASDAQ, driven by macro concerns rather than any Tesla-specific news. The core thesis of the session is that Cybercab production is visibly ramping at Giga Texas, a senior Texas DOT official publicly endorsed the coming scale-up, yet the stock market remains unresponsive — creating both frustration and, in Bhakdi's view, a strategic buying opportunity for patient investors.

## Robotaxi

1. **Over 100 Cybercabs spotted at Giga Texas:** Drone footage reviewed on the stream — credited to Joe Tegtmeyer and a count attributed to Sawyer Merritt — showed more than 100 Cybercabs in the Giga Texas parking lot on this date. Some units were identified as production-spec Cybercabs without steering wheels, which Bhakdi and Genma JP interpret as units most likely destined for the first commercial deployments rather than supervised testing vehicles.

2. **Bhakdi's personal estimate: over 1,000 Cybercabs deployed:** Bhakdi states his own estimate that Tesla has now deployed strongly over 1,000 Cybercabs across multiple U.S. cities. He notes that Waymo has approximately 3,000 vehicles in operation and suggests Tesla could reach a comparable fleet size within roughly five weeks at the current production pace.

3. **Texas DOT Executive Director endorses dramatic scale-up:** Mark Williams, Executive Director of the Texas Department of Transportation, publicly stated at the 2026 Texas Innovation Invitational that he experienced a production version of the Tesla Cybercab firsthand. He noted that Tesla is currently operating robotaxis using Model Y vehicles around Austin, Dallas, and Houston in Full Self-Driving mode, and said "the introduction of the Cybercab will dramatically scale these operations over the coming months." Bhakdi argues that Williams, as the government official responsible for overseeing autonomous vehicle operations in Texas, almost certainly had prior briefings from Tesla before making this statement.

4. **Lack of public FSD supervision evidence for Cybercab:** Referencing a write-up by Genma JP, Bhakdi notes that despite clear evidence of production-spec Cybercabs accumulating at Giga Texas, there is still no strong public evidence of Cybercabs running FSD under supervision even for testing purposes.

5. **Model: Cybercab and robotaxi economics coming next week:** Bhakdi previews an upcoming model covering various aspects of Cybercab and robotaxi economics, expected to be published the following week. He does not believe Cybercab consumer sales will happen anytime soon, saying it makes no sense to divert vehicles from the robotaxi network at this stage.

6. **End-of-year Tesla price target conditional on deployment:** Bhakdi states that if Tesla deploys Cybercabs and scales to 15,000 units, he expects Tesla stock to reach $800–$1,000 by year-end (i.e., end of 2026). He frames this as entirely contingent on commercial deployment materializing.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Model Y operating as robotaxi in multiple Texas cities:** Per the Mark Williams quote, Tesla is currently running Model Y vehicles in Full Self-Driving robotaxi mode across Austin, Dallas, and Houston — confirming that the current operational fleet is not exclusively Cybercab.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla trades in line with NASDAQ on Fed day:** Tesla's intraday decline tracked the NASDAQ closely, bottoming near -1.6% before recovering to close down approximately 1.34%. Bhakdi attributes the entire move to macro sentiment around the Warsh press conference rather than any Tesla-specific development, and does not view it as a serious selloff.

2. **Waymo fleet comparison:** Bhakdi cites Waymo's fleet at approximately 3,000 vehicles as the competitive benchmark, arguing Tesla is closing in rapidly as it produces Cybercabs by the hundreds per week.

3. **SpaceX IPO and valuation concerns:** Bhakdi discusses his view that SpaceX is tactically overvalued despite being fundamentally undervalued. He sold naked calls at a $250 strike with one-month expiration, collecting $7 per contract, as a small bearish position. He predicts SpaceX will drop below its IPO price of $135 at some point before December 2026, driven by a large unlock event starting in mid-August when up to approximately 1.6 billion shares (roughly 20% of outstanding shares) could enter the market against a current float of only about 5% of outstanding shares. He also sold a small number of contracts expiring the next day at the $200 strike as a speculative trade.

4. **SpaceX stealing the spotlight from Tesla:** Bhakdi argues that Tesla is currently in a "valley of tears" partly because SpaceX has become the dominant Elon Musk-related investment narrative, drawing attention and capital away from Tesla. He believes investor frustration with SpaceX will eventually pivot attention back to Tesla, but cautions that the "hype era" is over for both stocks and results must now be demonstrated.

5. **Possible Tesla–SpaceX merger:** Multiple viewer questions touch on a potential merger. Bhakdi says he believes it is a real possibility, speculating that SpaceX would acquire Tesla, rename the combined entity X Corporation, and house Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI as divisions underneath it. He acknowledges complications around SpaceX's defense/national security classifications but suggests a conglomerate structure with separate divisions could resolve those issues.

## Financials

1. **Bhakdi's options strategy — back to conservative churn:** Bhakdi describes having made overly aggressive short put trades around $435 per share beginning of June 2026, which he characterizes as a mistake driven by excessive conviction that June would be an inflection point. He is shifting back to a disciplined weekly "churn strategy" — selling at-the-money or slightly out-of-the-money weekly puts. As an example, he sold $400-strike puts expiring the following Wednesday/Thursday for approximately $10 in premium, giving him a breakeven down to approximately $390.

2. **Federal Reserve: no rate change, hawkish undertone:** The Fed held rates steady at a target range of 3.5%–3.75%. Warsh did not submit a dot plot. The post-meeting statement was dramatically shortened to approximately 130 words. The 2-year Treasury yield rose approximately 14.4 basis points on the day, and the 10-year moved from approximately 4.43% to a peak near 4.50%. Bhakdi interprets the market reaction as an overreaction to Warsh's repeated emphasis on "price stability," which traders read as potentially hawkish, and does not expect a rate hike given anticipated employment pressures.

Notable quotes and data:
- Mark Williams (Texas DOT Executive Director): "The introduction of the Cybercab will dramatically scale these operations over the coming months."
- Mark Williams: "Tesla is now operating robotaxis using Model Y around Austin, Dallas, and Houston in Full Self-Driving mode."
- Bhakdi's personal Cybercab deployment estimate: "strongly over 1,000 Cybercabs deployed" across multiple cities.
- Waymo fleet cited at ~3,000 vehicles; Bhakdi estimates Tesla reaches ~3,000 Cybercabs within ~5 weeks.
- Tesla end-of-year price target: $800–$1,000, conditional on Cybercab deployment scaling to 15,000 units.
- SpaceX IPO price cited as $135; Bhakdi predicts a drop below that level before December 2026.
- SpaceX unlock: ~1.6 billion shares eligible for sale starting mid-August 2026, against a current float of ~5% of outstanding shares.
- Tesla intraday low: approximately -1.6%; closing decline: approximately -1.34%.
- Fed funds target rate: 3.5%–3.75% (held steady).
- 2-year Treasury yield move: +14.4 basis points on the day.
- 10-year Treasury yield: approximately 4.43% to ~4.50% intraday.
- SpaceX naked call sold: $250 strike, one-month expiration, $7 premium collected.

2026-06-17.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts centered on three main Tesla-relevant themes: regulatory developments around FSD/autonomous driving (New Jersey pushback, Dutch approval defense, Taiwan application), Goldman Sachs raising its Tesla delivery forecasts for Q2 and full-year 2026, and strong Megapack production activity at Lathrop. The broader backdrop includes significant SpaceX news (IPO, Cursor acquisition, index inclusion) which is largely tangential to Tesla investors but signals the health of the Musk-adjacent ecosystem.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Autonomous Driving Regulatory Battles & Milestones:** Multiple posts addressed FSD's regulatory trajectory across jurisdictions. In New Jersey, Tesla is actively fighting proposed legislation that the company says would effectively ban its autonomous vehicles from the state market; Tesla sent emails directly to NJ owners urging them to oppose the bill, calling it an "arbitrary roadblock" that delays "life-changing technology." On a more positive note, the Dutch Transport Minister publicly defended the RDW's provisional approval of FSD (Supervised), stating it was based on independent RDW testing — not Tesla-provided data — and noting that Teslas using FSD have driven 24 million miles on Dutch roads "without any noteworthy incidents." Additionally, Tesla announced it has submitted its FSD (Supervised) application documents in Taiwan to the Vehicle Safety Inspection Center, officially entering the regulatory examination process there. Together, these posts paint a picture of Tesla advancing FSD approvals internationally while facing political resistance domestically.

2. **Goldman Sachs Raises Tesla Delivery Forecasts:** Goldman Sachs raised its Tesla vehicle delivery forecast for Q2 2026 from 405,000 to 420,000 vehicles, stating it believes Tesla's Q2 deliveries are "likely tracking ahead of consensus." Goldman also raised its full-year 2026 delivery forecast from 1.72M (the post was truncated, but the upward revision is confirmed). This is a meaningful near-term demand signal heading into the Q2 delivery report.

3. **Megapack Production at Full Capacity:** Drone footage circulating online showed Tesla's Lathrop Megafactory with lots at their fullest level observed to date, with Merritt estimating approximately $500 million worth of Megapacks on site. This suggests Tesla's Energy business is running at peak output, a strong indicator for Q2 Energy revenue and deployment metrics.

4. **U.S. EV Charging Infrastructure:** Government data cited in posts indicates the U.S. now has over 250,000 public charging points, including over 73,000 DC fast chargers and 180,000 Level 2 plugs. Tesla leads in fast-charger deployments with 38,000 DC charging ports across its Supercharger network — roughly 52% of all U.S. DC fast chargers.

5. **SpaceX IPO & Financials (Tangential):** SpaceX surpassed Amazon to become the 5th most valuable company globally at a $2.79 trillion market cap, adding $263 billion in a single day. SpaceX officially announced its acquisition of Cursor for $60 billion (per an 8-K filing), with the merger expected to close in Q3 2026. SpaceX's annualized revenue run rate is estimated at ~$55B (including compute leasing deals and Cursor's reported $4B ARR), potentially reaching ~$60B by year-end. SpaceX is also being added to the CRSP and FTSE Russell indices on June 18, triggering an estimated $10–16B in combined forced buying by passive funds. While these are SpaceX stories, they are relevant to Tesla investors as context for Elon Musk's broader portfolio and any cross-ownership dynamics.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — Goldman's upward delivery revision, peak Megapack production, and international FSD regulatory progress all reinforce near-term execution momentum, even as the New Jersey legislative threat represents a real but localized headwind.

2026-06-17.title: The Fully Dry 4680 // Too little too late?
2026-06-17.body:
This video by Jordan Giesige of The Limiting Factor examines Tesla's fully dry electrode 4680 battery cell following Tesla's announcement that it can now coat electrodes using a dry process instead of a wet process. The central question is whether the 4680 is now obsolete given the rise of sodium ion and solid-state batteries, and the broader decline in lithium-ion battery prices since Battery Day. Giesige argues that the "obsolete" narrative fundamentally misunderstands both Tesla's original goals for the 4680 project and the nature of the dry electrode process itself.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla's Three Goals for the 4680 Project — In Priority Order:** Giesige frames the 4680 project around three goals ranked by importance: (1) supply chain stability — rebuilding a battery supply chain outside of China, which dominates not just cell production but also cell components and materials processing; (2) cost reduction — vertical integration offered the opportunity to cut battery costs by nearly 60% by eliminating supplier margins at each step of the supply chain; and (3) performance — producing high-performance battery cells. Performance is ranked last because Tesla always has the option to purchase best-in-class cells from third parties; supply chain disruption, by contrast, would halt production entirely.

2. **Progress Against Goals — What Tesla Has Actually Achieved:** Tesla has built an alternative supply chain for the 4680, eliminating the strategic supply chain risk. The 4680 is now described as the cheapest high-nickel battery cell available to Tesla in North America, though the cost savings are estimated at 10–20% rather than the originally projected 50–60%. Performance is described as comparable to Panasonic and LG Chem cells, but not yet best-in-class. Giesige notes it is still early days for Tesla as a cell manufacturer.

3. **Sodium Ion Batteries Cannot Replace the 4680 for Tesla Vehicles:** Sodium ion batteries do not meet the minimum range requirements for Tesla vehicles. Despite adequate gravimetric energy density, their volumetric energy density is lower, meaning EVs using sodium ion batteries can expect roughly one-third less range than those using iron-based lithium-ion batteries. This is acceptable for budget vehicles but not for an entry-level luxury vehicle like Tesla sells. Giesige notes, however, that Tesla could develop its own in-house sodium ion chemistry for grid storage applications and potentially for vehicles like the Cybercab that don't require long range.

4. **Solid-State Batteries Are Not Near-Term Displacement Threats:** Multiple companies claim they will have high-performance solid-state batteries on the market within one to two years. However, Giesige argues none of them are cheap enough or scalable enough for multi-million-unit mass-market vehicles. He does not expect solid-state batteries to significantly displace liquid electrolyte batteries like the 4680 in the next decade, especially given what BYD and CATL are achieving with LFP chemistries. He also notes that solid-state batteries typically require prismatic or pouch formats due to brittle separators that cannot be rolled — making them incompatible with the cylindrical 4680 can.

5. **Chinese Battery Competition Is Geographically Constrained:** The CATL Shenxing and BYD Blade 2.0 batteries are not "4680 killers" in the U.S. market due to import costs and legal, political, and financial barriers to direct Chinese ownership of U.S. factories. For Tesla's China-produced vehicles, Tesla already uses CATL cells and would likely adopt Shenxing batteries when ready if there are no major drawbacks. For European vehicles, Tesla can use a combination of the 4680 and whatever cells are available locally or for import.

6. **What Customers Actually Prioritize:** Giesige argues that the most important factors to customers are safety, price, and reliability, followed by charging network quality, charging speed, and range. Most customers want a top-up in under 30 minutes when fast charging and more than 300 miles of real-world range — thresholds most EV makers can now achieve. Beyond those minimums, further performance improvements yield diminishing returns for unit sales. Only a small minority of customers prioritize cutting-edge specs like solid-state batteries or maximum range.

## Energy

1. **The 4680 Is a Form Factor, Not a Chemistry — Enabling Future Flexibility:** The 4680 is a cylindrical can that can be filled with any chemistry, including LFP or sodium ion. This means Tesla's manufacturing infrastructure is not locked into high-nickel chemistry. The potential exception is solid-state batteries, which require prismatic or pouch packaging due to brittle separators that would crack if rolled.

2. **The Dry Electrode Process Is Chemistry- and Form-Factor-Agnostic:** The dry electrode coating process is compatible with every major battery chemistry and is not tied to any specific form factor. Once Tesla scales the high-nickel 4680, nothing prevents them from applying the dry electrode process to LFP, sodium ion, or solid-state batteries in whatever form factor is optimal. Giesige emphasizes this is the key point that undermines the "obsolete" narrative: the dry electrode process is not a competing chemistry — it is a fundamental manufacturing improvement that the entire battery industry will eventually adopt.

## Market & Competition

1. **The Durability of Tesla's Cost Reduction Estimates:** Giesige breaks down the original Battery Day cost reduction projections by source. He identifies which savings are still durable: 14% from better cell design (durable, as competitors haven't changed cell design significantly); 18% from dry electrode coating and other manufacturing improvements (largely durable until competitors adopt the process); 12% from in-house cathode and lithium production (durable, as it eliminates supplier margins). Items he crosses off as no longer uniquely durable: 5% from adding silicon anode (achievable by any manufacturer) and 7% from cell-to-vehicle integration (competitors have replicated this). His estimate is that up to 44% of the original 56% cost reduction target remains achievable and durable.

2. **What Actually Drove Industry-Wide Battery Price Declines:** Giesige argues that much of the lithium-ion battery cost reduction seen over the six years since Battery Day was driven by market conditions — lower materials costs, overcapacity, intense price competition, and a shift toward cheaper LFP chemistries — rather than fundamental manufacturing improvements. He estimates less than one-third of the industry-wide cost reduction came from genuine manufacturing advances, and that Tesla can benefit from some of those same component cost reductions (e.g., cheaper electrode foils, separators, and electrolyte). He concludes that approximately 44% cost savings from in-house manufacturing remains a sound estimate.

3. **Tesla as a First-Mover in Dry Electrode Manufacturing:** Giesige concludes that the entire battery industry — across all chemistries and form factors — was always heading toward dry electrode coating. Tesla, as a relatively new battery manufacturer, achieved this first, giving it a durable manufacturing advantage that extends beyond any single chemistry or form factor.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla currently purchases ~99% of batteries from third-party battery makers.
- Original Battery Day cost reduction target: ~60% (Giesige uses "almost 60%" and "56%").
- Cost reduction breakdown: 14% cell design, 18% dry electrode/manufacturing process, 5% silicon anode, 12% in-house cathode/lithium, 7% cell-to-vehicle integration.
- Giesige's estimate of still-durable cost savings: ~44% of the original ~56%.
- Current 4680 cost savings vs. third-party cells: estimated at 10–20%, not 50–60%.
- Sodium ion batteries offer roughly one-third less range than iron-based lithium-ion batteries due to lower volumetric energy density.
- "The dry electrode coating process isn't in competition with other battery chemistries because it's not a chemistry, it's a fundamental improvement to the way batteries are manufactured."
- "Tesla, as a freshman battery manufacturer, pulled a rabbit out of the hat and got there first."

2026-06-17.title: Major New Tesla Cybercab Update LEAKED!
2026-06-17.body:
This episode from The Tesla Space covers the EPA certification document leak revealing key technical specifications for the Tesla Cybercab, alongside non-Tesla stories including a Neuralink milestone, Boring Company tunneling updates, and the SpaceX IPO's impact on employee wealth. The core Tesla-focused argument is that the Cybercab's EPA filings paint a surprisingly capable and purpose-built vehicle — not a compromised pod — and that its combination of practical specs and the unboxed manufacturing process could make it historically significant for autonomous transportation.

## Robotaxi
1. **EPA Certification Reveals Cybercab Specs for the First Time:** Tesla's Cybercab cleared a mandatory EPA certification process, and the regulatory filings publicly disclosed vehicle specifications that Tesla had not previously announced. This represents the first official, third-party-verified technical portrait of the vehicle ahead of commercial launch.

2. **Powertrain and Battery Details:** The Cybercab is powered by a single front-wheel drive motor producing 219 horsepower. It is paired with a battery pack of roughly 48 kWh. For comparison, these figures are described as slightly smaller, lighter, and less powerful than the base Model 3 rear-wheel drive standard trim.

3. **Range Figures Exceed Expectations:** Despite the modest battery size, the EPA certification documents list an equivalent all-electric range of 418 miles and a highway range of 375 miles — notably higher than the base Model 3. The video notes that official EPA ratings typically come in significantly lower than pre-certification figures, but suggests Tesla is on track to meet its own stated target of 300 miles or more.

4. **Vehicle Weight and Payload Capacity:** The Cybercab weighs 3,113 lbs at curb weight, with a gross vehicle weight of 3,730 lbs, yielding just over 600 lbs of payload capacity. The video frames this practically: enough for two 200-lb adults and approximately 200 lbs of luggage — sufficient for airport travel with multiple large suitcases.

5. **Interior Design Optimized for Actual Trip Patterns:** Cybercab lead engineer Eric E, speaking at a Tesla enthusiast meetup in December 2024, explained that roughly 80% of vehicle trips involve two passengers or fewer. Tesla designed the Cybercab around that reality rather than the occasional edge-case family road trip. With no second row, interior legroom is described as exceeding many traditional sedans despite the compact exterior. Engineers also stated the vehicle can accommodate large suitcases, golf bags, bicycles, and certain foldable wheelchairs.

6. **Testing Mileage and Certified Useful Life:** The vehicle Tesla submitted for EPA testing had already accumulated more than 2,100 miles on its odometer at the time of submission. The EPA certified it for a useful life of 150,000 miles — treating it not as an experimental prototype but as a production vehicle expected to spend years transporting passengers on public roads.

7. **Unboxed Manufacturing Process as a Structural Advantage:** The Cybercab is described as the first vehicle in Tesla's lineup built using the "unboxed" process, which assembles major vehicle sections in parallel before joining them at the end. The video draws a parallel to the Ford Model T, arguing that the Cybercab's potential historical significance lies not just in the vehicle itself but in pairing a purpose-built design with a manufacturing system capable of producing it at unprecedented scale and low cost.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Cybercab Compared to Model 3 Benchmark:** Throughout the EPA spec discussion, the base Model 3 rear-wheel drive standard trim is used as the reference point. The Cybercab is lighter, has a smaller battery, and produces less horsepower than the Model 3, yet its pre-certification range figures exceed those of the Model 3 — suggesting meaningful efficiency gains from the vehicle's design optimization.

Notable quotes and data:
- Cybercab motor: single front-wheel drive, 219 horsepower
- Battery pack: ~48 kWh
- Curb weight: 3,113 lbs; Gross vehicle weight: 3,730 lbs; Payload capacity: ~600+ lbs
- EPA filing equivalent all-electric range: 418 miles; Highway range: 375 miles
- Tesla's own stated range target: 300+ miles
- Odometer at time of EPA submission: 2,100+ miles
- EPA certified useful life: 150,000 miles
- Eric E (Cybercab lead engineer), December 2024 meetup: "roughly 80% of vehicle trips involved two passengers or fewer"
- Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in October 2024
- Cybercab is the first Tesla vehicle built using the unboxed manufacturing process

2026-06-18.title: Tesla’s Biggest Challenge Isn’t Technology Anymore
2026-06-18.body:
This video, hosted by "brighterwithherbert" featuring guest Brian White of FutureAzA, argues that Tesla's primary challenge in advancing Full Self-Driving and robotaxi deployment has shifted from technology to politics and narrative warfare. The hosts present a series of positive FSD safety and regulatory developments, then contrast them with a growing wave of legislative resistance and media criticism — particularly a Reuters article challenging Tesla's safety claims in Europe and proposed restrictive legislation in New Jersey.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Supervised Submitted for Approval in Taiwan:** Tesla has officially submitted FSD Supervised for regulatory review in Taiwan through the Vehicle Safety Inspection Center. The process requires a technical committee review and road testing, with the committee expected to convene within 2–4 weeks. If deemed feasible, it then moves to the Ministry of Transport for final approval. Separately, Tesla Taiwan has discontinued the one-time FSD purchase option, moving to subscription-only starting July 1st, which the hosts interpret as a signal that FSD launch in Taiwan is imminent.

2. **FSD Now Approved or Available in 12 Countries and Regions:** The hosts enumerate the current markets where FSD is approved or available: the US, Canada, Mexico, Puerto Rico, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, Netherlands, Lithuania, Estonia, Denmark, and Belgium. Japan is also conducting road tests in metropolitan areas including Tokyo and Yokohama. Brian White notes that as approval spreads in Europe and Australia, additional Asian countries that defer to other regulators' approvals are likely to follow without conducting their own full review processes.

3. **Dutch Regulators Defend FSD Approval Against Reuters:** Reuters published an article claiming Tesla used misleading US safety statistics when presenting data to European regulators — specifically alleging that Tesla counts only serious crashes for its own vehicles and compares that to all US crashes, and that Tesla's "32,000 lives saved" figure assumes all trucks and motorcycles in America are replaced by FSD-equipped Teslas. The Dutch vehicle authority (RDW) pushed back directly, stating their approval was based on an independent 18-month review that included 1.6 million km of road tests, 4,500 track tests, and 13,000 customer ride-alongs. Post-approval, Tesla recorded zero highway collisions across 23.6 million km of FSD driving in the Netherlands (also cited as 24 million miles by Dutch transportation officials). Brian White argues Reuters wrote a technically defensible but incomplete picture, knowingly omitting context that would make Tesla's comparison methodology reasonable given that no other manufacturer provides equivalent telematics data.

4. **Reuters Senate Inquiry Criticized as Irresponsible:** Reuters publicized on X that a US Senate inquiry had been opened based on their article, which Brian White characterized as journalistically irresponsible — analogous to "standing next to a building you just burned down." He noted Reuters has shifted toward sensationalism since introducing a paywall, citing a prior false report about a Tesla factory near Mexico City airport as an example of the outlet publishing unverified claims for clicks.

5. **New Jersey Legislation Would Effectively Ban Driverless Deployment:** Tesla sent a direct email to New Jersey Tesla owners urging them to contact state legislators to oppose proposed legislation moving through Trenton that would impose restrictions severe enough to keep true driverless deployment illegal in the state. The email noted that 578 people were killed in traffic accidents in New Jersey in the prior year (2025), with more than 94% of serious crashes attributed to human error, impairment, distraction, or fatigue. Brian White and the host suspect taxi or transportation lobbying interests are behind the bill. The hosts note the proposed legislation appears to specifically target Tesla's FSD while leaving other ADAS systems such as Blue Cruise, Super Cruise, and ProPilot unaffected. Brian White argues that legislators actively blocking AV deployment now have "blood on their hands," comparing it to discovering a cancer treatment and refusing to distribute it.

6. **Real-World FSD Life-Safety Use Case:** The hosts highlight a viral story of a Model Y driver who suffered a heart attack mid-drive, called his son, and whose son remotely rerouted the vehicle to a hospital via the Tesla app. The medical team confirmed that minutes of delay could have changed the outcome. The hosts use the story to illustrate a practical life-safety dimension of FSD beyond crash statistics.

## Robotaxi

1. **Four Months Without an At-Fault Robotaxi Incident:** The latest NHTSA robotaxi data for Tesla's Austin fleet shows one new incident in the most recent reporting month: a stopped Tesla robotaxi that was rear-ended by a truck — Tesla not at fault. Combined with two prior incidents in March where the robotaxi was also stationary and rear-ended, Tesla has now gone approximately four months without a robotaxi incident where FSD was at fault. Sawyer Merritt noted the irony that all recent crashes involving Tesla's robotaxi fleet were caused by human drivers in other vehicles rear-ending the stopped Teslas. Elon Musk affirmed this observation.

2. **Robotaxi Fleet Remains Active and Taking Passengers:** In response to skeptics claiming the robotaxi fleet isn't conducting rides, Brian White cited Josh West, who visited Austin the prior week for the Cyber Rodeo event hosted by Tesla Owners of Austin and immediately took a robotaxi ride. The hosts acknowledge ride volume may be lower than peak but argue that any active mileage makes a zero at-fault accident rate meaningful.

## Market & Competition

1. **Regulatory Fragmentation as a Business and Strategic Risk:** The hosts discuss how the patchwork of regulatory environments — ranging from permissive (US, Australia) to proactive independent testing (Netherlands) to potentially hostile (New Jersey, Boston) — creates uneven FSD deployment timelines. Brian White expresses confidence that pockets of resistance like New Jersey and Boston are not a material long-term threat to Tesla's mission, as they represent a small percentage of overall drivers and the legislative prohibition strategy is unlikely to hold once the technology's safety record becomes undeniable. He predicts holdout jurisdictions will eventually flip.

2. **FSD Subscription Revenue as a Rising Revenue Wave:** The hosts briefly discuss the revenue implications of the global FSD subscription rollout. With the one-time purchase option being phased out (most recently in New Zealand/Taiwan markets by July 1st), all new FSD users will be on recurring subscriptions. Brian White references Elon Musk's next compensation plan target of 10 million FSD subscribers as the scale milestone, estimating the revenue potential at roughly $100/month per subscriber across that base.

Notable quotes and data:
- "When the facts are on your side, you bang on the facts. When the truth is on your side, you bang on the truth. And when nothing's on your side, you just bang on the table." — Brian White
- "It's pretty ironic that the only crashes involving Tesla's robotaxi fleet in recent months have been humans in other vehicles rear-ending them." — Sawyer Merritt (affirmed by Elon Musk)
- Dutch RDW independent review: 18-month review, 1.6 million km of road tests, 4,500 track tests, 13,000 customer ride-alongs
- Post-approval Dutch data: zero highway collisions across 23.6 million km of FSD driving in Netherlands; Dutch transportation officials cited 24 million miles
- 578 people killed in New Jersey traffic accidents in 2025; 94%+ of serious crashes attributed to human error
- FSD one-time purchase option discontinued in Taiwan (and previously New Zealand), moving to subscription-only starting July 1st
- Elon Musk's next compensation plan target referenced as 10 million FSD subscribers
- "People who are delaying the autonomous vehicle being rolled out have blood on their hands." — Brian White
- "The people I follow who go to Austin specifically to take the rides are still getting rides." — Brian White, rebutting claims the robotaxi fleet is inactive

2026-06-18.title: New SECRETS About The Cybercab Discovered
2026-06-18.body:
This video from "brighterwithherbert" features host Herbert and guest Brian White (of the YouTube channel FutureAzA) discussing newly revealed technical specifications for the Tesla Cybercab, sourced from recent EPA filings, alongside analysis of accelerating production and deployment signals. The core thesis is that the Cybercab is farther along in regulatory, manufacturing, and distribution readiness than most investors appreciate, and that a commercial robotaxi launch is weeks to a couple of months away rather than years.

## Robotaxi

1. **EPA Certificate of Conformity — a critical regulatory unlock:** The Cybercab has officially received its EPA Certificate of Conformity, which is required before any vehicle can be legally introduced into US commerce. Brian White argues this was the primary reason no paid Cybercab rides had occurred yet — not software or hardware issues — and that this regulatory milestone clears the path to commercial deployment. He also notes the EPA, not NHTSA, enforces the 8-year/100,000-mile minimum battery warranty requirement.

2. **Cybercab production numbers suggest imminent deployment:** Over 100 Cybercabs were spotted in the outbound lot at Giga Texas, 55 were spotted in Dallas, and additional units have appeared at robo taxi hubs across Texas and beyond — including one sighted at an event in Austria. Brian White estimates the total number produced is in the "high hundreds" and says he "would be very surprised if it's under a thousand." He draws a direct analogy to tanks massing at a border: mass production at this scale signals imminent rollout, not extended testing.

3. **Infrastructure buildout underway in multiple cities:** A ~51,000 square foot facility is being built in Grand Prairie, Texas (in the Dallas metro area) that will serve as a combined service, repair, and charging/cleaning hub dedicated to the Cybercab. A similar permitted facility was identified in Las Vegas. Brian White notes these service hubs only need to exist in each deployment market — a logistical advantage of Tesla's vertically integrated, fleet-owned model versus consumer-owned vehicles.

4. **Software remains the final gating factor:** Brian White states there are no remaining physical or regulatory hurdles to deployment — the only remaining question is when Tesla decides the software is ready. He is skeptical that the end-of-June deadline for a specific FSD milestone will be met ("low" probability), but says the only FSD timelines he trusts are those posted by Ashok Elluswamy with a specific date attached.

5. **Autonomous Cybercabs spotted driving without steering wheels:** Joe Tegtmeyer captured footage of a Cybercab operating autonomously — without a steering wheel — making a graceful arrival and backing smoothly into a parking space at Giga Texas. Other units on the lot retain steering wheels, which Brian White notes can be removed. The absence of wheel covers on many units is explained as standard Tesla shipping procedure, not a production anomaly.

6. **Owner-vehicle robotaxi network remains uncertain and unlikely near-term:** The hosts discuss skepticism about Tesla's previously promised ability for owners to add their personal vehicles to the robotaxi fleet. Brian White identifies camera washers and potentially Starlink terminals as hardware retrofits that would be difficult or impossible to add aftermarket. He suggests owner vehicles are unlikely to be included in the first or even second round of fleet deployment. Herbert notes this could create legal exposure given how consistently Tesla executives promised the feature — comparing it to the hardware 3 / unsupervised FSD coast-to-coast promise.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD on Hardware 3 vehicles — revenue motivation for Tesla to deliver:** Brian White states that FSD is currently unavailable outside the US for Hardware 3 vehicles, and that unlocking Hardware 3 for international markets represents "millions, tens, maybe hundreds of millions of dollars a month" in potential revenue. He argues Tesla is therefore more motivated than owners to make Hardware 3 unsupervised FSD work, and considers it "100% a priority," though the timeline remains unknown.

2. **Ashok Elluswamy's milestone track record cited as credibility benchmark:** Brian White references a post from "last summer" (summer 2025) in which Ashok Elluswamy published eight to ten FSD milestones with specific dates, and the worst performer missed by only one day. He uses this as his personal standard for trusting FSD timelines — only believing dates when Elluswamy posts them publicly.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cybercab technical specifications revealed via EPA filing:** The EPA documents disclose that the Cybercab uses approximately a 48 kWh battery pack, weighs approximately 3,000–3,100 lbs (the lightest vehicle in Tesla's lineup, lighter than a Model 3), produces approximately 219 horsepower, uses a front-wheel drive configuration, and achieves an equivalent range of approximately 418 miles. Brian White previously broke the front-wheel drive detail. He notes the vehicle uses a non-standard voltage architecture — neither 400V nor 800V, but something around 326V or 362V — suggesting it was specifically tuned for its commercial use case.

2. **Front-wheel drive justified by commercial use case:** Brian White explains that torque steer (normally a concern with front-wheel drive EVs) is a non-issue for the Cybercab because hard acceleration will essentially never occur in robotaxi service. The weight distribution with the battery pack makes front vs. rear wheel drive largely inconsequential for this application.

3. **48 kWh battery sized for durability, not just range:** Brian White explains that a larger-than-minimum battery pack is necessary to allow full regenerative braking capacity and to enable Tesla to operate the vehicle in a narrow state-of-charge window (e.g., 20–70%) in daily fleet operations, which dramatically extends battery longevity — potentially to 800,000 miles instead of 300,000 miles. The 418-mile rated range gives Tesla significant headroom to manage battery degradation over the vehicle's commercial life.

4. **165 Wh/mile efficiency rated best in North America:** The Cybercab's energy consumption figure of 165 Wh per mile is described as the best efficiency rating of any vehicle in North America. Brian White attributes this to the vehicle's light weight and the fact that its use profile will almost never include hard acceleration. He notes the 5.5 miles/kWh figure previously cited by Tesla engineers was described to him as what they were "allowed to say," and the EPA data now confirms the real-world efficiency is better.

5. **3,100 lb curb weight designed for durability and repairability, not lightness:** Brian White clarifies the Cybercab is not designed to be lightweight — it is designed to be rugged and easily repairable. Body panels are plastic and can be swapped quickly and cheaply, in contrast to a vehicle like the Jaguar I-Pace where a fender repair involves bodywork, paint matching, and significant downtime. This design philosophy adds some weight but reduces total cost of ownership for a fleet operator dramatically.

6. **Cybercab range vs. Waymo fleet efficiency comparison:** Brian White estimates that for every one Cybercab, a fleet operator would need approximately three Waymo vehicles to provide equivalent coverage, due to the Waymo's higher energy consumption (attributed partly to the power demands of its sensor compute stack) and shorter effective range. He notes the Cybercab has "a little bit more than half" the battery of a Waymo but substantially more range.

Notable quotes and data:
- EPA-reported Cybercab specs: ~48 kWh battery, ~3,000–3,100 lbs, ~219 hp, front-wheel drive, ~418 miles equivalent range
- Energy efficiency: 165 Wh/mile — described as best in North America
- Voltage architecture: neither 400V nor 800V; approximately 326V or 362V (Brian White flagging this as unusual and seeking clarification from electrical engineer contacts)
- 100+ Cybercabs spotted in outbound lot at Giga Texas; 55 spotted in Dallas
- Brian White's estimate: total Cybercabs produced is in the "high hundreds," likely over 1,000
- ~51,000 sq ft Cybercab service/charging/cleaning facility under construction in Grand Prairie, Texas
- Brian White on deployment timing: "weeks, perhaps a couple months" — not years
- Brian White on owner-vehicle robotaxi inclusion: "I'm deeply skeptical that owner vehicles would be in the first round of deployment. And I'm also a bit skeptical we'd be in the second round."
- On the EPA certificate: "You have to have this certificate before you can engage in commerce… that obstacle has been passed."
- Ashok Elluswamy's last summer milestone post: 8–10 milestones with dates, worst miss was by one day
- Brian White on end-of-June FSD deadline probability: "Low."

2026-06-18.title: What Happens The Day Tesla Turns On Robotaxi
2026-06-18.body:
This wide-ranging episode of the Cern Basher podcast features hosts Cern Basher and Phil Beisel alongside special guest Robert Scoble — a longtime tech journalist, author, and early Tesla rider — covering the SpaceX IPO, the Cursor acquisition, and Tesla's robotaxi rollout strategy. The core thesis is that Elon Musk and his companies are building a fundamentally new technological and economic order, and that Tesla's robotaxi deployment represents a coming inflection point that most of the world has not yet grasped. The conversation weaves together AI infrastructure, autonomous vehicles, humanoid robots, and big-tech competitive dynamics into a unified "who wins the AI future" framework.

## Robotaxi

1. **"Storm the parking lot" deployment thesis:** Robert Scoble argues that Tesla is deliberately accumulating Cybercabs in parking lots rather than deploying them piecemeal, with the goal of launching a large fleet simultaneously. His view: Tesla should wait until it has roughly 2,000 Cybercabs staged, then turn on the robotaxi service all at once so that the sheer visible scale creates its own news cycle and demonstrates capability to the public immediately. He frames this as both a PR and a software-readiness strategy — the FSD software may need one or two more updates before the lawyers sign off, and Tesla does not want 2,000 new vehicles causing traffic jams on day one.

2. **Cybercab production ramp comparison to Model 3:** Scoble draws a direct analogy to his own experience buying the 749th Model 3 off the Fremont line roughly six months after the line started. He notes the current Cybercab ramp is slower at the front end, but argues the manufacturing process — modular, built in place rather than on a long line — means it will scale faster once it reaches full speed. He predicts that by end of 2025 (resolved from "end of this year" against publish date 2026-06-18, suggesting late 2025 context in the anecdote, though the speaker appears to mean end of the current ramp year) there could be 10,000–20,000 Cybercabs on the road, and that the Cybercab production curve should eventually surpass the Model 3 ramp rate.

3. **Outbound lot at Giga Texas identified as staging area:** The hosts confirm, crediting Joe Tegtmeyer's reporting, that the parking lot where Cybercabs are being staged is the outbound lot at Giga Texas — the same lot used to stage finished vehicles before they are loaded onto transport trucks. Sawyer Merritt is also cited as having published photos of the lot.

4. **Robotaxi adoption still in its infancy globally:** Scoble notes that if you aggregate all customers of Tesla, Waymo, Zoox, Nuro, BYD, and Chinese autonomous vehicle operators, fewer than 10 million people out of 8 billion have ever ridden in an autonomous vehicle. He frames this as evidence that the world is at the very beginning of autonomous vehicle adoption, not near saturation.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD's data flywheel acknowledged across the robotics industry:** Scoble states that "everybody in the robotics industry talks about the Tesla data flywheel" — the advantage Tesla built by putting cameras and an AI computer in every vehicle it sold, regardless of whether the buyer purchased FSD, and then charging an additional fee (he references the $6,000 FSD price) to activate the software. He credits this fleet — described as roughly 10 million vehicles — as the foundation for Tesla's world-model training advantage.

2. **Legacy automakers' failure traced to executive resistance:** Scoble gives a detailed account of Mercedes having autonomous driving technology in its labs more than a decade ago but killing the project because executives did not want to add $6,000 per car to the retail price. He also notes that Volkswagen sponsored the Stanford University autonomous car project that became Waymo, but could not get budget approval to deploy the technology in production vehicles. Phil Beisel reinforces the theme, arguing that all these failures trace back to leadership: Elon Musk simply directed Tesla to do it, bypassing the institutional resistance that paralyzed legacy OEMs.

3. **Robert Scoble's consumer research timeline:** Scoble describes conducting consumer research roughly 15 years ago (implying around 2011) going around America asking people about autonomous cars, and finding unanimous resistance — he recounts one respondent in Kansas describing himself as "a narcissistic control freak" who would never let a computer drive him. He contrasts that with current Waymo riders in San Francisco and Phoenix who are now enthusiastic converts, illustrating how attitudes shift once people experience the technology.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus timeline estimates from industry insiders:** Scoble reports that when he asks people collecting training data for humanoid robots — including those building sensor gloves, egocentric camera rigs, and force-sensing devices — when a generalized humanoid will be capable of doing 20% of jobs in a factory like Tesla's, most answer "two to seven years." He notes that people who work at Tesla tend to give the more optimistic end of that range, around 18 months, while others are more cautious. His own view is that it will be "a couple of years" before Optimus can safely walk around, interact with people, listen to instructions, and perform a variety of factory tasks.

2. **Giga Texas SNX line closure linked to Optimus co-location:** Scoble argues that Elon closed the Model S/X (SNX) line at Fremont in order to place the Optimus development team physically adjacent to an active car production line. The logic: rapid iteration requires Optimus to be deployed on the factory floor, fail, be brought back to the lab in the afternoon for software and hardware adjustments, and redeployed — the same tight iteration loop that China's manufacturing ecosystem enables for consumer electronics. He frames this as Tesla deliberately engineering the feedback cycle that will accelerate Optimus to commercial readiness.

3. **Egocentric data and sensor gloves as key training inputs:** Scoble describes the hardware infrastructure being built to train humanoid robots — hats with two to six cameras capturing egocentric (first-person) data of human hand manipulation, and gloves with hundreds of sensors per finger measuring grip force (using a Diet Coke can as a tactile example). He notes that Apple Vision Pro is being used in parts of the robotics industry specifically to capture this egocentric training data.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cybercab's large screen validated by the conversation:** The hosts reference the Cybercab's large interior screen as a concrete example of why big screens make sense in a self-driving vehicle — when the car drives itself, the screen becomes purely an entertainment and information interface. Scoble explicitly says riders will be "watching movies and doing video calls" in their Cybercabs, and that the screen real estate will be fully utilized in ways that were hard to articulate in advance, just as large screens in earlier EVs seemed hard to justify until the use cases emerged.

2. **Model 3's software-defined architecture cited as paradigm shift:** Scoble recounts buying his Model 3 and experiencing continuous over-the-air improvements to acceleration, audio, headlights, braking, and FSD over the ownership period, calling this the definitive advantage of a software-defined vehicle. He frames this as something Mercedes engineers he spoke with roughly 12 years ago understood intellectually but could not execute because their executives feared hacking and did not want to enable persistent cloud connectivity.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO and Cursor acquisition framed as linked maneuvers:** The hosts open by discussing the SpaceX IPO, noting SpaceX's market cap of approximately $2.6 trillion at the time of recording, with the stock having briefly traded around $222 per share after hours. They then analyze SpaceX's June 16 announcement that it will exercise its option to acquire Cursor — the AI coding tool used by 64% of Fortune 500 companies and 75% of Salesforce developers — in an all-stock transaction at approximately 10 times Cursor's projected annual revenue. Because SpaceX trades at roughly 40 times revenue, the hosts calculate that SpaceX is effectively acquiring Cursor at about 0.25 times SpaceX's revenue multiple, making it a highly favorable deal for SpaceX. They describe this as a "Trojan horse" entry into the enterprise market, which they note represents $26.5 trillion of SpaceX's stated $28 trillion total addressable market.

2. **Space-based compute framed as the inevitable AI infrastructure endgame:** A central thesis of the episode is that AI compute demand will outstrip Earth-based data center capacity, and that the only scalable path is orbital data centers powered by free solar energy, with no corrosion, no land-use conflicts, no community resistance, and no vulnerability to physical infrastructure attacks. Scoble describes companies already building satellites carrying Nvidia Vera Rubin chips and solar arrays that unfurl in orbit, launched and connected via SpaceX and Starlink respectively — meaning SpaceX profits from the trend regardless of whether it owns the data centers. Elon Musk is quoted (from a post described as made "a couple of days ago") saying that harnessing 1 millionth of the sun's power for AI would represent more than a million times the intelligence of all humanity, and that doing so would ultimately require manufacturing solar panels and radiators on the moon and launching them into deep space with a mass driver.

3. **Chinese competition identified as the primary long-term threat:** Scoble argues that the real competitive threat to Apple, Tesla, and other American tech leaders is not from European or Japanese incumbents but from a new generation of Chinese entrepreneurs — citing DJI, Insta360, Xiaomi, Huawei, Xpeng, and Unitree — who are building original brands rather than copying American ones. He notes that Xpeng's founder explicitly wants to be Elon Musk and that Xpeng's investor presentation cited Tesla as the only American competitor worth naming. He argues China's manufacturing iteration speed — where designers can walk across the street to the factory and prototype overnight — gives Chinese companies a structural advantage that Elon Musk has consciously tried to replicate by co-locating engineering with production at Tesla.

4. **Big Tech competitive rankings:** The hosts walk through a global market cap list placing Tesla at approximately $1.5 trillion and SpaceX at approximately $2.6 trillion, with SpaceX briefly surpassing Microsoft. They frame having two Elon Musk companies in the global top 10 as historically remarkable. Meta is characterized by Scoble as a "cigarettes company" — effective at creating addiction but generating no positive emotional association — and as internally chaotic, with its spatial computing ambitions hampered by leadership that grew up in a 2D world. Google is described as a data-rich utility that consumers trust but do not feel warmly toward, and as lacking a fashion brand suitable for wearable computing. Apple is assessed as well-positioned to enter the wearables market late but effectively, with incoming CEO Terri (the name used in the transcript) credited as an engineer with Vision Pro experience who avoids internal politics.

Notable quotes and data:
- Elon Musk (quoted from a recent post): "It's humbling to consider that if we harness just 1 millionth of the sun's power for AI, that'll be much more than a million times the intelligence of all humanity." He added that doing so would require manufacturing solar panels and radiators on the moon and launching them into deep space with a mass driver, and that "conventional money will no longer be relevant — mass and energy will take the place of dollars."
- Elon Musk (quoted from a May presentation): "In 2027 you won't even bother doing coding. XAI would just create the binary directly… There's an intermediate step there that probably won't even be needed by the end of 2026."
- Robert Scoble on Elon's mental time horizon: "I think about 15 years."
- Scoble on Cybercab deployment strategy: "If I was Elon, I'd wait until I had 2,000 in parking lots. And then I would turn on robotaxi, and all of a sudden one day you don't see any gold cars rolling around Austin, Texas, and the next day you see a f***load of them roll."
- Scoble on Meta: "Meta is perceived as a cigarettes company… you might be addicted to nicotine or social media, but you're not feeling good about it."
- Cursor used by 64% of Fortune 500 companies and ~70% of Fortune 1000; 75% of Salesforce developers use it.
- SpaceX Cursor acquisition: all-stock deal at ~10x Cursor's projected 2026 revenue; SpaceX trades at ~40x revenue, implying an effective acquisition cost of ~0.25x SpaceX revenue.
- SpaceX market cap at time of recording: approximately $2.6 trillion; Tesla approximately $1.5 trillion.
- Global autonomous vehicle ridership estimate (Scoble): fewer than 10 million people out of 8 billion have ever ridden in an autonomous vehicle.
- Humanoid robot capability timeline (Scoble's industry contacts): 2–7 years to achieve 20% of Tesla factory tasks; Tesla employees say ~18 months.
- Jensen Huang quote on Cursor: "My favorite enterprise AI service is Cursor. Every one of our engineers, some 40,000, are now assisted by AI, and our productivity has gone up incredibly."

2026-06-18.title: Tesla Just Checked Another Critical Box
2026-06-18.body:
This FutureAzA video hosted by Brian, joined by guest Herbert, does a deep dive into the newly published EPA Certificate of Conformity for the Tesla Cybercab, analyzing every key engineering specification line by line. The core thesis is that the Cybercab's specifications — particularly its weight, efficiency, and custom-tuned architecture — represent a decisive structural advantage over competitors like Waymo, and that the EPA filing itself is a critical regulatory milestone that clears the path for commercial deployment. The hosts also discuss the current state of FSD version 14 and offer a realistic timeline for Cybercab fleet scaling.

## Robotaxi
