- Megapod: "intent to use" trademark — not yet deployed
- Loomis personal note: drove ~3,500 miles in first year of Model 3 ownership

2026-06-22.title: Elon Built Something Wall Street Can't Price
2026-06-22.body:
This video from the farzad-fm channel presents a macro-philosophical argument about why the SpaceX IPO represents something Wall Street cannot properly price: the potential to become the world's dominant energy-to-intelligence company. The host's central thesis is that intelligence has always been the binding constraint on economic output, and AI is converting that constraint from a human labor problem into an energy problem — making cheap, abundant energy the defining competitive variable of the coming decades. Tesla, autonomous driving, and robotaxis receive only glancing references; the video is primarily a SpaceX/AI/energy essay.

## Market & Competition
1. **SpaceX IPO and the $2 trillion milestone:** SpaceX officially became a public company on Friday, June 12th (2026), with a market valuation that reportedly reached over $2 trillion at launch, making it the sixth-largest company in the world. The host describes it as breaking "every single record related to the stock market," though he is careful to note it is widely misunderstood by markets.

2. **The brain-as-arbitrage framework:** The host builds his entire thesis around a single napkin-math figure: a human brain runs on roughly 20 watts of power, consuming approximately 175 kilowatt-hours of electricity per year at a cost of about $20 in American electricity rates. Against that, the average U.S. worker generates roughly $65,000 per year in labor value — a ratio the host describes loosely as approximately 3,000-to-1 between what intelligence produces and what it costs to run. He frames this as "easily the single biggest arbitrage in the entire world economy," while explicitly cautioning it is an order-of-magnitude frame, not a precise figure.

3. **AI converts intelligence into an energy business:** The host argues that AI closes the historical arbitrage by manufacturing cognition out of electricity rather than human labor. The competitive race — chips, data centers, model wars, corporate feuds — ultimately reduces to one question: who can produce the cheapest electricity and deploy compute on top of it most efficiently. He cites Microsoft's reported revival of Three Mile Island nuclear plant and year-long waiting lists to connect data centers to the power grid as evidence that the industry has already internalized this logic.

4. **How the surplus migrates — and the GDP trap:** The host warns that the 3,000-to-1 arbitrage erodes as competition scales. The sequence he describes: surplus first sits with existing wage earners, briefly migrates to early AI deployers (naming Anthropic as an example of a company enjoying fat early margins), then gets competed away toward the energy cost floor, ultimately manifesting as cheaper goods and services for consumers. He also flags a measurement problem: because GDP counts prices times quantity, if the price of cognitive work collapses toward zero while real output explodes, measured GDP could stagnate or shrink even as actual living standards surge. He argues purchasing power and standard of living are the correct measuring sticks, not GDP.

5. **The energy ceiling — sun vs. Earth:** The host introduces a physical upper bound for the opportunity. The sun delivers energy to Earth at approximately 170,000 trillion watts; all of human civilization currently uses roughly 20 trillion watts — meaning the sun already delivers about 10,000 times more energy to Earth than civilization consumes. He argues this makes the real ceiling on AI-driven abundance not the number of human brains (which he calls the "floor," approximated at roughly $60 trillion per year of cognitive labor globally), but available energy — ultimately solar.

6. **Orbital solar compute — SpaceX's AI1 satellite:** Alongside the IPO, SpaceX announced a project called "AI1," described by the host as essentially a data center in space: a satellite carrying a computing payload of approximately 150 kilowatts, powered by a large solar array, using the vacuum of space as a radiator for waste heat, with Starship as the delivery vehicle. The host notes 150 kilowatts of compute is roughly 1/1,000th of a single large hyperscale data center on Earth, making a single satellite a "rounding error" — the bet only works as a massive constellation of thousands of satellites, mirroring the Starlink playbook. He cites orbital compute economics as currently about four times more expensive than a warehouse in Texas, with cost parity potentially not arriving until the 2030s, and the whole thesis gated on continued Starlink launch cost reductions via Starship.

7. **Vertical integration as SpaceX's true moat:** The host's core argument for why SpaceX is differentiated despite competitors (he mentions Google's "Suncatcher" project and a company called StarCloud): SpaceX controls the rocket (launch), the satellite bus (manufacturing), solar cell production reportedly in Bastrop, Texas (described as a SpaceX-Tesla partnership), and the anchor AI customer (xAI/Grok, which the host says was folded into SpaceX before the IPO). He also states that competitors including Anthropic and Google are already renting compute from xAI/SpaceX for over $20 billion per year. No competing entity, he argues, owns all layers of this stack simultaneously.

8. **Practical takeaways — energy as the macro variable:** The host closes with three action points. First, treat cheap energy access — dollars per kilowatt-hour, grid interconnect queues, nuclear restarts, solar deployment — as the macro variable of the next decade, analogous to how investors watch interest rates. Second, treat the AI1/orbital story as a 2030s thesis, not a 2026 trade, and apply appropriate skepticism given it was disclosed in an IPO pitch. Third, recognize that long-run competition drives cognition costs toward the energy floor, effectively making everyone richer in purchasing power — not necessarily in dollar terms — by making scarce human labor no longer the binding input in the economy.

## Energy
1. **SpaceX solar cell manufacturing in Bastrop, Texas:** The host claims SpaceX is manufacturing solar cells in Bastrop, Texas, described as a partnership with Tesla, to supply the solar arrays for orbital compute satellites. No production figures or capacity numbers are provided.

2. **Nuclear and grid investment as AI infrastructure:** The host briefly references Microsoft reviving Three Mile Island — the nuclear plant associated with a famous 1979 incident — as an example of tech giants becoming de facto energy companies. He also cites year-long waiting lists to connect new data centers to the power grid as structural evidence that energy supply, not software or chips, is the binding AI constraint.

Notable quotes and data:
- Human brain power consumption: ~20 watts, ~175 kWh/year, ~$20/year in U.S. electricity costs
- Average U.S. worker labor value: ~$65,000/year
- Implied intelligence arbitrage ratio: ~3,000-to-1 (host's framing, explicitly approximate)
- Global cognitive labor floor estimate: ~$60 trillion/year from ~3.5 billion workers
- Sun's energy delivery to Earth: ~170,000 trillion watts
- Human civilization total energy use: ~20 trillion watts (sun delivers ~10,000× more than civilization uses)
- AI1 satellite compute payload: ~150 kilowatts (~1/1,000th of one large hyperscale data center)
- Orbital compute cost vs. ground: ~4× more expensive than a Texas warehouse today; parity potentially in the 2030s
- xAI/SpaceX compute rental revenue from competitors (including Anthropic and Google): stated as over $20 billion per year
- SpaceX IPO market cap: over $2 trillion (as of June 12, 2026), described as the sixth-largest company in the world
- "The ceiling is energy. Human brains are the floor. Sunlight is the ceiling."
- "A wage is the price of scarce human thinking power."
- "The measured dollar number stalls out or even shrinks while the real abundance is going through the roof."

2026-06-22.title: Tesla's Running Changes Explained
2026-06-22.body:
This video features FutureAzA host interviewing Will from the Tesla Jigsaw YouTube channel about delivery delays affecting certain Model Y variants in the UK. The core issue is that Tesla introduced mid-cycle hardware upgrades to Giga Berlin-produced all-wheel-drive and performance Model Y vehicles — specifically more energy-dense battery cells and rear motor improvements — which caused those vehicles to fall out of compliance with existing type approval certifications, blocking registration in the UK and parts of Europe. The conversation also touches on UK Tesla demand more broadly and comparisons between the Model 3 and Model Y for European driving conditions.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **UK Delivery Delays Caused by Running-Change Type Approval Gap:** Tesla introduced hardware upgrades mid-production cycle to Giga Berlin-built all-wheel-drive and performance Model Y variants. The changes included more energy-dense battery cells (to improve range) and updates to the rear motor (to improve performance). Because these changes meant the vehicles no longer matched the existing type approval specifications on file, the UK's Vehicle Certification Agency (VCA) had not yet issued updated certificates of conformity, and the DVLA system consequently blocked those vehicles from being registered and handed over to customers. The delays had reportedly been building for a couple of months, with some customers seeing their delivery dates pushed back repeatedly — in some cases to September or later.

2. **Cars Built and In-Country But Undeliverable:** Affected vehicles are physically present in the UK — stockpiled at ports, airport overflow sites, industrial estates, and other temporary locations — but cannot legally be handed over pending the updated certification. Will notes this is unusual in that the vehicles are not defective; they actually exceed the specifications on file, delivering better range and performance than the approved spec.

3. **Resolution Underway — Customers Receiving Self-Schedule Links:** As of the video's recording date (around 2026-06-22), the Tesla Owners UK community had posted that notifications were being sent to affected customers, who would receive self-scheduling links within 24–48 hours to rebook their deliveries. Tesla asked affected customers to wait for those links rather than contacting Tesla directly, to avoid overwhelming support. Will also notes that goodwill gestures — including free Supercharging and free premium connectivity — had been offered to some affected customers.

4. **Only All-Wheel-Drive and Performance Variants Affected:** Standard (rear-wheel-drive) Model Y variants, both long-range and short-range, are unaffected and delivering normally. Model 3 vehicles are also unaffected. The delay is limited to the all-wheel-drive long-range and performance Model Y variants produced at Giga Berlin.

5. **Tesla's Running-Change Manufacturing Model Creates Certification Risk:** Will observes that Tesla continuously updates its vehicles rather than waiting for annual model-year changeovers like most automakers, which should make it well-practised at managing type approval implications of mid-cycle changes. He expresses some surprise that Tesla did not proactively notify the VCA of these specific hardware changes before vehicles were produced and shipped. The VCA's normal processing time for such updates is reportedly 3 to 6 weeks (per Will). Will notes that while this situation is frustrating, mid-cycle technical issues are not unique to Tesla — other manufacturers experience similar problems.

6. **UK Demand and Sales Appear Strong Despite Controversy:** Will describes Tesla as doing "quite well" in the UK, noting (per his belief) that the Model 3 was among the best-selling cars in the market. He also observes that Teslas are increasingly visible on UK roads and that both updated Model Y and Model 3 vehicles are easily distinguishable from older versions. Giga Berlin's production capacity is said to be up 20% as of July (the host attributes this claim to Will without further sourcing). Will also mentions that the UK-market lower-cost rear-wheel-drive standard Model Y retains larger wheels compared to some other markets — reportedly due to UK insurance considerations and customer preference for residual value, particularly for leased vehicles, per a conversation Will had with Tesla UK.

7. **Model Y Practicality vs. Model 3 Dynamics in European Context:** Will, who has driven a Model Y across the UK and into Austria on the autobahn, says the car is no larger than most SUVs already on UK roads and poses no meaningful obstacle on typical routes, including tight roads in rural Wales. He and the host agree that while the Model 3 is sportier and more engaging to drive, the Model Y's higher seating position and ease of ingress/egress make it more practical for everyday family use.

Notable quotes and data:
- Will: "Cars are built and in the country, but can't be handed over to the customers."
- The VCA's standard processing time for type approval updates: reportedly 3–6 weeks (per Will).
- Vehicles stockpiled at: ports, airport overflow sites, industrial estates, and other temporary locations.
- Affected models: Giga Berlin-produced Model Y all-wheel-drive long-range and performance variants only.
- Unaffected models: Model Y rear-wheel-drive (both standard and long-range versions), Model 3.
- Resolution status (as of ~2026-06-22): Tesla Owners UK reported self-schedule delivery links being sent within 24–48 hours.
- Goodwill gestures offered: free Supercharging, free premium connectivity.
- Giga Berlin capacity reportedly up 20% as of July (attributed to Will, unverified).
- Will: "Tesla manufacture vehicles very differently to most car companies. Instead of waiting every 4 years to make a small change, Tesla are continually updating the vehicle."
- No public statement from Tesla UK to customers had been issued at the time of filming.

2026-06-22.title: MORE  TESLA YL leaks, Slate price leak, megabig batteries, & LOTS more in the Monday News Roundup
2026-06-22.body:
This is FutureAzA's Monday news roundup for June 22, 2026, hosted by Brian, covering a wide range of Tesla and EV industry stories. The episode touches on Tesla Model Y L leaks, Slate EV pricing speculation, autonomous trucking developments, robotaxi competitive dynamics, energy storage alternatives, and various EV industry moves from Ford, Honda, GM, Rivian, and others. Brian's tone is editorially opinionated throughout, mixing confirmed news with personal analysis and viewer Q&A.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Model YL Coming to the US This Summer:** Brian reports that according to information from what he describes as a credible source, the Tesla Model Y Long (YL) — a larger, third-row variant of the Model Y — will begin production in Texas in August or September 2026. Brian says his own source separately confirmed August production. Visually, the YL is identical to the standard Model Y from the waist up, but notably larger from the hips down; the key visual tell in spy shots is a significantly larger third rear window. One published article speculates a price of $539.90, but Brian believes the price will be $549.90, estimating a roughly $4,000 premium over the standard Model Y — consistent with the pricing differential seen in China.

2. **Slate EV Pricing Speculation:** A code examination of Slate's website revealed a price of $24,950 still embedded in the site's deprecated code. Brian is skeptical this reflects the actual launch price, calling it likely outdated and noting that inflation alone would have driven the price up. He argues that if Slate launches under $30,000 it could be a viable product, but expresses serious doubt about profitability at the $24,950 figure unless the company is willing to absorb losses at low volume and offset them through stock offerings.

3. **Cybertruck Pricing and Demand:** A viewer raises the possibility that a dual-motor all-wheel-drive Cybertruck at $60,000 could generate overwhelming demand. Brian agrees the truck would sell well at that price, noting that $60,000 in 2026 dollars is equivalent to roughly $48,000 in 2019 terms — "a whole lot of truck" for that inflation-adjusted price. He expresses hope Tesla can make that version profitable enough to reintroduce it.

4. **Ford's LFP Battery Push and EV Pivot Confusion:** Ford revealed plans for a new LFP battery aimed at mass-market EV pricing, with hiring underway at Blue Oval Battery Park in Michigan — over 500 employees hired so far, with plans to reach 800 by end of 2026. Brian is skeptical of Ford's direction, noting the company has repeatedly reversed its EV ambitions. He also raises the issue that China has placed export restrictions on the equipment used to manufacture the latest-generation LFP batteries, meaning any U.S. or Western factory would at best be producing the prior generation — adequate for stationary energy storage but competitively disadvantaged against Chinese EVs. Brian notes Tesla's Nevada facility faces the same constraint. He also mentions (without a sourced article) that Ford may be discontinuing the Mustang Mach-E.

5. **BYD Shark Hybrid Truck and Brazil Battery Production:** Brian covers the BYD Shark, a hybrid (not fully electric) pickup truck available in Hawaii, noting it sidesteps EV range challenges by using a hybrid drivetrain. He highlights that BYD is ramping battery production in Brazil, which he views as strategically significant — localizing production removes Chinese sourcing concerns and, given U.S.-Brazil trade relations, could eventually open a path for those batteries to enter the U.S. market.

6. **Honda + QuantumScape Solid-State Partnership:** Honda has announced a partnership with QuantumScape for solid-state EV batteries. Brian is dismissive of Honda's current EV urgency, quipping they're "in neutral and coasting," and jokes the timing may actually work out since QuantumScape hasn't reached scale production either.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Tesla Semi Spotted with Autonomous Validation Equipment:** An enthusiast spotted a Tesla Semi in Sunnyvale equipped with what Brian describes as LIDAR gear on the roof and ground-truthing equipment on the cabin exterior — indicating Tesla is actively preparing the Semi for FSD capability. Brian treats this as unsurprising and largely expected, consistent with Tesla's broader autonomy roadmap.

2. **Tesla Megapod Trademark Filing — AI Data Center Speculation:** Tesla quietly filed a trademark for "Megapod," which Brian connects to the previously discussed pre-assembled Megacharger patent for the Tesla Semi. He speculates the concept could extend to a standalone product — potentially a prefabricated AI compute node co-located with charging infrastructure. He acknowledges the idea runs into latency challenges but finds it worth watching.

3. **Tesla Pre-Assembled Megacharger Patent for Semi:** A patent has surfaced showing Tesla's plan to build pre-assembled, prefabricated Megacharger units for the Tesla Semi. Brian views this as straightforwardly positive — moving permitting and contractor complexity back to the factory improves speed and quality control.

4. **Aurora + Volvo Autonomous Trucks on I-35:** Aurora and Volvo have partnered to run driverless semi trucks on a roughly 200-mile route between Dallas and Oklahoma City, operating up to five days per week. Brian praises the development, noting Aurora has had considerable success testing driverless semis in Texas and that non-Tesla companies blazing the autonomy trail is broadly beneficial for the industry.

## Robotaxi

1. **Robotaxi Competitive Scorecard — China Leading:** A company called OTM AI has developed a generative AI benchmarking platform that evaluates all robotaxi operators every 12 hours using publicly available and Creative Commons data. As of the Friday before air date, the top-ranked robotaxi operator was Baidu's Apollo Go program, narrowly edging out Waymo in second place, followed by Pony AI and WeRide, with Tesla in fifth. The system evaluates safety records, deployment numbers, and other publicly available metrics.

2. **Texas AV Registrations — Waymo and Tesla Growth:** Per the OTM AI scorecard data cited in the transcript: as of the video date, Waymo had 620 autonomous vehicles registered in Texas — up from 577 in May, a roughly 7.5% increase. Tesla had 69 registered autonomous vehicles in Texas, up 64% from 42 in May. Zoox had 35 registered vehicles but lacks the correct permit to charge for rides.

3. **Uber Premium Robotaxi Coming to Houston in 2027:** Uber is bringing a premium robotaxi service to Houston in 2027, using a Lucid Gravity vehicle powered by Nuro's self-driving software (rather than Lucid's proprietary system). Brian questions the unit economics, noting the Lucid Gravity costs roughly three times what competing vehicles cost, and that revenue must be split among Uber, Lucid, and Nuro.

4. **Mobileye Plans U.S. Robotaxi Launch in 2027:** Mobileye (Intel subsidiary) announced plans to launch a robotaxi service in the U.S. in 2027, positioning itself as both a hardware/technology supplier and a finished-service operator. Mobileye has cited a target of 17,000 vehicles over the following five years. Brian is skeptical, comparing it to competitors still "lacing up their shoes" 10–15 years into the autonomous vehicle race.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **SoftBank Sells Boston Dynamics Stake for $325 Million:** SoftBank walked away from its investment in Boston Dynamics, selling its roughly 10% stake to Hyundai for $325 million — implying a total company valuation of just over $3 billion. Brian uses this to push back against viewers who cite Boston Dynamics as a credible Optimus competitor, arguing the company lacks the compute infrastructure, data centers, and manufacturing scale to compete — and that the valuation reflects this. A viewer separately mentions having toured the Optimus factory and calling it "mind-blowing," which Brian notes with interest.

2. **GM vs. UAW Over Factory Robots:** Brian briefly covers a GM and UAW dispute in which the union is pushing back against the use of collaborative robots (cobots) on the factory floor. Brian is openly critical of the union's position.

## Energy

1. **Gravity Battery Tower — Skepticism on Concrete Block Energy Storage:** A company is building a 40-story windowless concrete tower that stores energy by lifting 35-ton concrete blocks when power is available (e.g., from wind) and recovering energy as the blocks are lowered. Brian references Wired's math: one 55-gallon drum of concrete stores enough energy to charge roughly four to eight cell phones, and it would take more than 50 such drums to equal the storage of a single Tesla Powerwall. He concludes the economics are unlikely to pencil out at scale due to weight, wear and tear, and construction costs — but supports the attempt as a necessary proof-of-concept exercise.

2. **GM Vehicle-to-Grid Development:** GM is working on a vehicle-to-grid / vehicle-to-load system that could enable time-of-use energy shifting for consumers. Brian notes there is no specific product announcement, only that development is ongoing, and that the fragmented U.S. utility landscape (roughly 4,000 utilities) complicates widespread deployment.

## Market & Competition

1. **Rivian Class Action Lawsuit Over Gen 1 Autonomy Claims:** Rivian is reportedly facing a class action lawsuit alleging fraud, negligent misrepresentation, and unjust enrichment over claims made about the autonomous capabilities of its Gen 1 vehicles — specifically that no software update could deliver the advertised autonomy. Brian notes the lawsuit echoes similar challenges faced by Tesla over early FSD marketing. He doubts the lawsuit will go anywhere because any reasonable settlement would be existentially threatening to Rivian given its low sales volume.

2. **Global EV Adoption Trends:** EV adoption data shows China growing very rapidly (steep upward trend), Europe showing a flattened but recovering trajectory, and the U.S. hovering at a low adoption rate by comparison. Brian frames this as a signal that investors not in EV-exposed equities may be missing the longer-term growth story.

3. **SpaceX Beach Access Ruling:** The Texas Supreme Court unanimously denied an environmental group's request to require beach access during SpaceX launches at Boca Chica. Brian supports the ruling on safety grounds. (Note: this is a SpaceX story, included as general context.)

Notable quotes and data:
- Brian on Model YL price: "I think it's going to be $549.90" — $1,000 above the article's $539.90 estimate
- On Slate pricing: "If it launches under 30 you've got a potential winner on your hands. $24,950 to me deeply concerning because that price is old and inflation is real."
- Tesla had 69 registered autonomous vehicles in Texas as of the video date, up 64% from 42 in May (per OTM AI scorecard data)
- Waymo had 620 registered autonomous vehicles in Texas, up from 577 in May (~7.5% increase)
- Boston Dynamics implied valuation: just over $3 billion (SoftBank's ~10% stake sold for $325 million)
- Ford Blue Oval Battery Park: 500+ employees hired, targeting 800 by end of 2026
- One 55-gallon drum of concrete stores enough energy to charge approximately 4–8 cell phones; 50+ drums needed to equal one Tesla Powerwall
- Mobileye targets 17,000 robotaxi vehicles over five years following a planned 2027 U.S. launch
- Aurora/Volvo autonomous trucks: ~200-mile Dallas-to-Oklahoma City route, up to 5 days/week

2026-06-22.title: Tesla and SpaceX Merger: How Iran and Fed Moves Are Affecting Markets
2026-06-22.body:
This video from the "investingagainstthegrain" channel is a casual, Father's Day commentary delivered by a visibly ill host who covers a broad range of market topics including Iran-US tensions, the Federal Reserve's new direction under Kevin Warsh, Micron earnings, Tesla's Cybercab rollout, and the rumored Tesla-SpaceX merger. The host's core thesis is that Tesla's robotaxi buildout is clearly accelerating — evidenced by growing Cybercab counts in cities like Houston — and that the stock is positioned to reach all-time highs. The tone is personal and conversational, with the host emphasizing his investment approach around options trading and disciplined portfolio management.

## Market & Competition
1. **Iran-Strait of Hormuz Tension:** The host describes ongoing drama around Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, with US-Iran nuclear negotiations in Switzerland reportedly still ongoing despite rumors that Iran walked out after Trump issued threats. The host notes that vessels are still moving through the strait, which he reads as a positive sign, and observes that gasoline prices nationally fell below $4 per gallon for the first time since the conflict began. He views the geopolitical noise as something markets will largely look through, though short-term volatility is possible.

2. **Federal Reserve Under Kevin Warsh:** The host characterizes Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first press conference as a "nothing burger" in terms of immediate market disruption, but views his longer-term direction positively. He describes Warsh as pushing to modernize the Fed by moving away from archaic inflation measurement methods toward more real-time data — what the host likens to a "trueflation-type approach." He believes the market will reward this change in leadership and philosophy.

3. **Micron Earnings as AI Infrastructure Bellwether:** The host identifies Micron's upcoming Wednesday earnings as the most significant near-term market event, describing it as a key signal for the entire AI infrastructure investment thesis. He acknowledges near-universal agreement that AI chip demand is insatiable and backlogged, but flags a realistic downside risk: a supply-chain bottleneck on a single component could prevent Micron from fulfilling demand and cause a miss versus guidance. He believes Micron will likely crush earnings but warns of a roughly 16% implied move (plus or minus) and notes the results will reverberate into companies like SanDisk and the broader AI infrastructure sector.

## Robotaxi
1. **Houston Cybercab Hub Expanding Rapidly:** The host highlights a community-reported observation from June 20, 2026, showing 45 Cybercabs spotted at the Houston robotaxi hub — up from 31 the prior week. He notes none of the vehicles had Cybercab decals at the time of observation. He also references a photo of a Cybercab (and a Cybertruck) equipped with what he describes as geospacing/LAR equipment on the roof, which he says Tesla has previously deployed before launching or expanding to new geographic areas. He frames this as strong circumstantial evidence of an imminent large-scale launch.

2. **"Slow at First, Then All at Once" Thesis:** The host argues that Tesla's consistent use of the phrase "slow at first, then all at once" regarding robotaxi deployment is intentional and meaningful. He contends that the sheer volume of Cybercabs being produced and positioned across multiple cities makes the counter-thesis — that it's all vaporware or for show — irrational. He also notes that Tesla had previously indicated it would expand to new cities in the first half of 2026, which has not yet happened, suggesting a significant announcement may be imminent before Tesla's next earnings call.

3. **Tesla-SpaceX Merger Speculation:** The host expresses a growing belief that a Tesla-SpaceX merger is likely to happen within 2026, citing a third-party estimate of a 70% probability. He traces the public narrative from what he says were wink-wink comments by Chamath Palihapitiya and Jason Calacanis on stage in December 2025, through podcast discussions in January 2026, to more recent commentary — including, per the host, Andrew Ross Sorkin on a Piers Morgan appearance over the weekend and even Tom Sosnoff (founder of tastytrade and thinkorswim), whom the host describes as an Elon skeptic who nonetheless called it "a done deal." The host believes the sustained public narrative has been deliberately seeded to normalize the merger and reduce pushback. He also flags that Elon Musk recently exercised options to increase his Tesla voting rights to up to 19%, which the host finds notable given the timing — Musk could have waited until August but chose to act now.

Notable quotes and data:

2026-06-22.title: SHOCKING SpaceX Merger Price For Tesla Stock?
2026-06-22.body:
This video, from the channel "jobhakdi" (Jo Bhakdi), argues that a SpaceX-Tesla merger is inevitable and imminent, and focuses almost entirely on the mechanics of how such a deal would be structured, priced, and voted on. The core thesis is that the acquisition offer will be denominated in absolute dollars (not as a percentage of SpaceX), that SpaceX's post-IPO volatility creates dangerous uncertainty for Tesla shareholders, and that a "ratchet" mechanism must be built into the deal to protect Tesla shareholders and ensure a clean vote.

## Market & Competition

1. **Merger inevitability and timing:** Jo Bhakdi argues the SpaceX-Tesla merger is certain to happen, citing Elon Musk's need to consolidate companies into a singular entity (possibly renamed X Corp) to eliminate governance friction and maximize management focus. He references Chamath Palihapitiya as sharing this view. He believes the merger will happen sooner rather than later, citing upcoming U.S. midterm elections and current political momentum as reasons not to delay. He speculatively suggests an offer could come within one to three months of the video's publication.

2. **Structural mechanics — SpaceX acquires Tesla, not vice versa:** Bhakdi states clearly that SpaceX must be the acquiring entity (the surviving legal entity) because Elon Musk holds majority 10x supervoting shares in SpaceX. He uses the Cursor acquisition — reportedly done at a firm price of $60 billion (equivalent to roughly 3% of SpaceX at the time) — as a precedent to argue that all acquisitions are denominated in absolute dollar amounts, not percentages of the acquirer. Therefore, the Tesla deal will be announced as a specific dollar market cap offer, payable in SpaceX shares, with the exact number of SpaceX shares determined only at the moment the vote closes, based on SpaceX's market price at that time.

3. **SpaceX share structure enabling the deal:** Bhakdi notes that SpaceX has 36 billion authorized shares versus only 13 billion outstanding — meaning authorized shares are approximately 300% of outstanding shares. He argues this ratio is highly unusual (far beyond a typical employee options pool reserve of 10–20%) and signals deliberate pre-authorization for a large acquisition. He says SpaceX would not need additional board approval to issue shares for a Tesla acquisition.

4. **SpaceX post-IPO volatility as a deal risk:** Bhakdi describes SpaceX's post-IPO price action as extremely volatile — IPO'd at $161, ran to $218 (roughly +35%), then fell back to approximately $185 (about +14% from IPO, net). He argues the current float is only about 5% of total shares, which could expand to 20% soon as lockups expire, creating significant selling pressure starting around August 2026. He expects SpaceX to retreat toward or below IPO price in that window, which he says is nearly inevitable regardless of the company's long-term value. He explicitly states he is not buying SpaceX shares currently, expecting a cheaper entry point.

5. **Scenario analysis — deal without a ratchet:** Bhakdi presents a model assuming a 50% premium acquisition offer at $600/share for Tesla (implying a $1.88 trillion Tesla market cap), based on a then-current Tesla share price of approximately $400. He models the outcome for Tesla shareholders depending on where SpaceX trades at the vote date: if SpaceX is flat at $183 (market cap $2.43T), Tesla shareholders own 44% of the new entity; if SpaceX rises 20% to $220 (market cap ~$2.9T), Tesla shareholders own only 39%; if SpaceX falls 20% to $146 (market cap ~$1.94T), Tesla shareholders own nearly 50%; if SpaceX falls 50% to $92 (market cap ~$1.22T), Tesla shareholders own 61%. He argues this variability creates perverse incentives — Tesla shareholders would want SpaceX to fall, SpaceX shareholders would want to push the price up to minimize dilution — opening the door to manipulation, resentment, and vote failure.

6. **The ratchet proposal:** Bhakdi proposes a one-line addendum to the deal: Tesla shareholders will receive the greater of either $1.88 trillion (the 50%-premium fixed offer) or the full SpaceX market cap at the moment of the vote (a one-to-one merger of equals). Under this structure, if SpaceX stays flat ($2.43T market cap), Tesla is acquired for $2.43T at ~$778/share and owns 50% of the combined entity. If SpaceX rises 20% to $2.9T, Tesla is acquired for $2.9T at ~$933/share and still owns 50%. If SpaceX falls 20% to $1.94T, Tesla is acquired for $1.94T at ~$622/share and still owns 50%. Only if SpaceX falls below the $1.88T floor does the fixed minimum kick in — e.g., if SpaceX falls 50% to $1.22T, Tesla is still acquired at $1.88T ($600/share) and owns 61% of the new entity. He argues this ratchet eliminates manipulation risk, stabilizes the vote, and ensures Tesla shareholders are never worse off if SpaceX rises in value.

7. **Fiduciary and legal risk of a bad deal:** Bhakdi argues that if institutional Tesla shareholders (including those like Ron Baron who also hold SpaceX) vote to approve a deal that disadvantages Tesla shareholders in order to benefit their SpaceX holdings, this creates a fiduciary breach and exposes the Tesla board to significant legal liability. He contends the deal must be genuinely attractive to Tesla shareholders or the vote will fail, and believes all parties — including Elon Musk — have strong incentives to structure it cleanly.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla share price assumed in model: ~$400; SpaceX share price at time of video: ~$183
- SpaceX IPO price: $161; post-IPO high: ~$218; current price cited: ~$185
- SpaceX authorized shares: 36 billion; SpaceX outstanding shares: 13 billion (~300% ratio)
- SpaceX float at IPO: ~5% of total shares; expected to expand to ~20%
- 50% premium Tesla offer = $600/share = $1.88 trillion market cap
- 30% premium Tesla offer = $520/share = $1.63 trillion market cap
- Ratchet scenario: Tesla acquired for greater of $1.88T or SpaceX market cap at vote date
- Cursor acquisition cited as precedent: $60 billion firm-dollar offer ≈ ~3% of SpaceX
- "No ratchet, no deal." — Jo Bhakdi
- Jo Bhakdi on SpaceX: "in my opinion the most important company that ever existed, in my opinion currently totally undervalued. I'm still not buying a single share right now because I'm very sure I get it much cheaper very soon."
- SpaceX selling pressure expected to intensify around August 2026 as float expands
- Merger vote expected no earlier than September 2026 if offer comes in July; more likely November 2026 shareholder meeting

2026-06-22.title: GM's future of home energy and V2G technology.
2026-06-22.body:
This short video from Munro Live features a walkthrough of GM's home energy and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology, showcasing how a GM vehicle's battery can power a home — and even external loads like a coffee bar — during a blackout or to support the grid. The demonstration highlights a home energy storage system that integrates seamlessly with the vehicle battery through an app. The core thesis is that GM is entering the bidirectional energy space, enabling vehicles to serve as mobile power sources for both residential backup and grid services.

## Energy
1. **Home Energy Storage System with NMC Chemistry:** The system on display features a 17.7 kWh battery unit using NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) based lithium-ion chemistry. These units can be paralleled together to double capacity, reaching 35.4 kWh on a single system, offering meaningful scalability for home energy storage applications.

2. **Vehicle-to-Home and Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) Capability:** The demonstration shows the vehicle's battery integrated into the home energy system, enabling bidirectional power flow. Power from the vehicle is used not only for home backup during a blackout but also to supply external loads — in this case, a coffee bar on-site — and to support the broader grid. The system is managed through a dedicated app that displays charging and discharging status and estimates remaining backup duration.

3. **Seamless App-Based Integration:** The home energy stack — comprising the battery unit and a power converter — connects wirelessly to the vehicle and is monitored and controlled through a smartphone app, allowing users to track energy flow and backup capacity in real time.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **GM Vehicle as Bidirectional Energy Node:** The GM vehicle featured in the demonstration is central to the V2G system, with its onboard battery serving as an active participant in home and grid energy management — not merely as a passive transport device. This positions GM's EVs as dual-purpose assets in the broader energy ecosystem.

Notable quotes and data:
- "We are providing power not just to the home but to this coffee bar off to the side and it's all done from the vehicle."
- Battery chemistry: 17.7 kWh NMC-based lithium-ion
- Two units in parallel: 35.4 kWh total capacity
- System components: battery stack + converter + vehicle, all connected via app
- Use cases demonstrated: home backup power during blackout, external load support (coffee bar), and grid support via V2G

2026-06-22.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts from @SawyerMerritt are relatively low in signal, centered on two main themes: a personal FSD long-distance milestone demonstrating supervised autonomy capability, and Tesla's pushback on media framing of a Texas crash incident involving a Tesla vehicle. A peripheral note on Hyundai's consolidation of Boston Dynamics is the only competition-adjacent item. No major product, financial, or fleet deployment news was posted.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **FSD Long-Distance Milestone — 500-Mile Supervised Streak:** Merritt reported completing a ~500-mile round trip between New Hampshire and New York City using Tesla FSD in supervised mode on his Model Y, with him present in the driver's seat but not actively driving. He framed this as a demonstration of FSD's real-world capability, noting that Tesla FSD is currently the only system enabling this kind of long-distance supervised autonomy. The post drew strong engagement (3.4K likes, 195 reposts), suggesting meaningful resonance with Tesla's retail and enthusiast audience.

2. **Texas Tesla Crash — Autopilot/FSD Not Likely Involved:** Merritt addressed a viral story about a Tesla crashing into a house in Texas, sharing real-time video of the incident and noting the vehicle was traveling at an extremely high speed. He made two key points: (a) Autopilot is not "self-driving mode" — a distinction he stressed is frequently misrepresented in media coverage — and (b) Tesla's vehicle logs will determine whether any driver-assist system was active, but he expressed strong confidence it was not, citing that neither Autopilot nor FSD operates at those speeds in residential areas. He also noted that historically, nearly all similar incidents turn out to be the result of human driver error. Post [4] ("Well well well 👀") appears to be a teaser or reaction tied to this story or its follow-up, but no substantive content was included in the digest. Combined, these posts received ~5.2K likes across three related entries, indicating high visibility on a reputationally sensitive topic.

3. **Hyundai Acquires Remaining Boston Dynamics Stake:** Hyundai is acquiring the remaining 9.65% stake in U.S. robotics firm Boston Dynamics from SoftBank for $325 million, giving Hyundai full ownership. Merritt posted this without editorial commentary. This is relevant context for Tesla investors tracking the humanoid robotics competitive landscape, as Boston Dynamics represents a well-capitalized, now fully consolidated competitor in the broader robotics space — though Boston Dynamics' focus differs from Tesla Optimus's manufacturing-oriented humanoid use case.

---

## Signal Strength: **Neutral** — The FSD milestone is a positive anecdotal data point for supervised autonomy capability, but the day's posts are dominated by defensive media commentary on the Texas crash story and a competitor news item, with no new product, fleet, financial, or regulatory developments disclosed.

2026-06-23.title: SpaceX Just Added Another Billion-Dollar Customer
2026-06-23.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel focuses primarily on SpaceX's emerging AI compute business, its recent IPO and financial milestones, and the broader debate over whether SpaceX is a near-term revenue story or a long-term moonshot. Host Herbert is joined by Jeff Watts, a multi-decade supply chain executive and chief quality officer who now runs a high-tech manufacturing consulting firm. The pair argue that SpaceX's terrestrial data center business — anchored by deals with Anthropic, Google, and now Reflection AI — represents a significant and underappreciated near-term revenue stream, while also touching on Tesla-adjacent topics such as Optimus and FSD as competitive moats.

## Market & Competition

1. **Reflection AI signs $6.3B compute deal with SpaceX:** SpaceX has reportedly signed a new AI compute agreement with Reflection AI worth up to $6.3 billion through 2029, with Reflection paying approximately $150 million per month for access to SpaceX's Colossus 2 infrastructure and NVIDIA GB300 chips, starting July 1, 2026. The host notes this is less than what Anthropic and Google are paying — described as $975 million and $1.25 billion per month respectively (figures presented without clear attribution) — but still highly significant. Jeff Watts characterizes this as confirmation that SpaceX has built a genuine commercial AI compute business, not a one-off arrangement.

2. **SpaceX as a growing AI compute platform:** Watts argues that SpaceX is systematically filling excess compute capacity between its own major training runs for Grok by signing commercial customers. He contends this creates a flywheel: SpaceX can stand up data centers faster and more cost-efficiently than hyperscalers, acquire Nvidia hardware at scale, and now monetize utilization that would otherwise be idle. He frames the Anthropic deal (signed earlier) not as a rescue of a struggling Grok but as the beginning of a deliberate hosting business that will eventually extend to space-based data centers, giving early terrestrial customers an additional incentive to stay.

3. **Cursor acquisition as potential Grok accelerant:** The host and Watts discuss SpaceX's acquisition of Cursor (an AI coding tool), whose compute product is referred to as "Composer." Watts notes that Cursor's core problem was lack of compute, which SpaceX now solves. He cites Jensen Huang as being on record saying Cursor may have a better coding product than alternatives. Both speakers suggest that combining Cursor's product quality with SpaceX's compute scale and cost efficiency — potentially subsidized by paying customers like Anthropic — could push Grok back into the top tier of frontier models. Watts emphasizes that the moat in AI chatbot models is narrow and that the landscape can shift quickly, pointing to Anthropic's own rise from obscurity as an example.

4. **"Macrohard" as a potential near-term wildcard:** The host references a product or service called "Macrohard" (also described as "digital optimist"), which he says is expected to launch soon. He frames it as a potential near-term revenue generator comparable to Anthropic's business, though both speakers acknowledge deep uncertainty — it could be a flop or a breakout. The host suggests that if Macrohard proves competitive, it could start generating revenue immediately, similar to terrestrial data center contracts, without waiting on any longer-horizon infrastructure.

5. **AI polling below Congress — social acceptance risk:** Watts raises the concern that public polling on AI has fallen below approval ratings for Congress, and that this sentiment is translating into protests against data centers and potential regulatory headwinds. He attributes part of this to AI companies leading with narratives about job loss and displacement rather than abundance and medical breakthroughs, and warns this could slow AI development in the U.S. relative to other countries, particularly China.

## Financials

1. **SpaceX IPO and investment-grade ratings:** Following its IPO, SpaceX reportedly raised $87.5 billion (described as oversubscribed) and now holds approximately $100–101 billion in cash and cash equivalents. SpaceX also launched its first bond offering and received investment-grade credit ratings from all three major agencies: Fitch (BBB+), Moody's, and S&P. The host notes the bond proceeds are reportedly intended to repay outstanding borrowings under a bridge loan facility, though the size, maturity, and pricing of the bond were not disclosed. Watts calls the financial engineering of the IPO comparable in quality to SpaceX's rocket engineering.

2. **$101 billion may not be enough for SpaceX's ambitions:** Watts cautions that while $101 billion in cash sounds large, SpaceX's capital needs for AI infrastructure buildout and Starship development are enormous, and the current cash position is "nowhere near enough" to fund the full master plan. He anticipates SpaceX will need to raise much larger sums going forward, but points to Starlink and Tesla's robotaxi business (mentioned in passing) as future cash-flow engines that could fund longer-horizon investments.

3. **Revenue growth targets vs. analyst models:** The host references Elon Musk's stated goal of $1 trillion in revenue by approximately 2030–2031, while noting that even the most optimistic sell-side analysts model only $300–400 billion in revenue by that timeframe. Watts acknowledges the gap and suggests that SpaceX's current portfolio of businesses may not be the same entity four or five years from now — implying new revenue lines will need to emerge to close the difference.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus cited as a durable competitive moat:** While discussing AI moats broadly, Watts contrasts the relatively narrow moat in AI chatbot/LLM models with the much wider and more durable leads he expects Tesla to hold in physical AI — specifically calling out FSD and Optimus. He says leads in those domains will be "measured in half and full decades," implying he views Tesla's robotics and autonomous driving advantages as structurally harder to close than software model gaps.

2. **Elon's "Amazing Abundance" framing and Optimus scale claims:** The host references a post (dated June 21, 2026) in which someone named David states that 5 million humanoid robots working 24/7 could build Manhattan in 6 months, and imagines 10 billion humanoid robots by 2045. Elon Musk reportedly trademarked the phrase "Amazing Abundance" and has been publicly posting about this vision. Both speakers are skeptical the framing is landing well with general audiences, who the host says are more focused on near-term concerns.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD cited as one of Tesla's widest moats:** In the context of comparing Tesla's competitive position to SpaceX's AI compute business, Watts specifically names FSD (alongside Optimus) as one of the areas where Tesla's lead is most durable and hardest to replicate, distinguishing it sharply from the more contestable LLM/chatbot space. No specific FSD version numbers or performance data are discussed.

Notable quotes and data:
- Reflection AI deal: up to $6.3 billion through 2029; ~$150 million/month starting July 1, 2026
- Anthropic reportedly paying ~$975 million/month (per host, unconfirmed); also described as $1.25 billion/month in a separate reference — figures are inconsistent in the transcript
- SpaceX IPO raised $87.5 billion (oversubscribed); ~$101 billion cash post-IPO
- Fitch rating: BBB+ (investment grade); Moody's and S&P also rated SpaceX investment grade
- Elon's stated revenue target: ~$1 trillion by 2030–2031 (per host); most bullish analyst models reportedly in the $300–400 billion range
- "5 million humanoid robots working 24/7 can build Manhattan in 6 months" — attributed to "David" in an Elon Musk post, June 21, 2026
- Jeff Watts: "The leads [in FSD and Optimus] are going to be measured in half and full decades"
- Watts on AI moats: "The moat here is not big. It's not like FSD, physical AI and FSD, vehicle FSD, and of course what's going to happen with Optimus"
- Host: "AI is polling lower than Congress in terms of approval ratings"
- Elon reportedly trademarked the phrase "Amazing Abundance"
- 4,500 SpaceX employees described as having become millionaires via the IPO

2026-06-23.title: Tesla's Biggest Problem Isn't Competition
2026-06-23.body:
This video from brighterwithherbert features host Herbert and guest Jo Bhakdi (economist, investor, and tech entrepreneur at pioneerlands.org) discussing what they argue is Tesla's biggest challenge: not competition, but hostile media narratives and misinformation. The episode covers a viral Autopilot crash story that they contend was falsely framed, Cybercab fleet testing progress, FSD expansion into new countries, Optimus factory construction, and a broader market sentiment discussion around why Tesla stock is underperforming despite what they see as meaningful operational progress.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Texas crash misattributed to Autopilot:** Multiple major media outlets — including Business Insider — reported that a Tesla on Autopilot crashed into a Texas home, killing a woman. According to Ashok Elluswamy (identified in the transcript as Tesla's AI VP), the driver had manually overridden the self-driving system by pressing the accelerator pedal to 100%, reached 73 mph in a residential area, and had the accelerator pressed even after the crash. Elon Musk also responded publicly, stating that FSD drives slowly through neighborhood streets and that a high-speed crash was inconsistent with how FSD operates. Sawyer Merritt noted that Tesla's vehicle logs would clarify whether any system was active, and Chuck Cook called the reporting "blatantly irresponsible." The hosts argue this is part of a pattern — they claim there has not been a single confirmed case where a legal investigation proved FSD caused a crash.

2. **FSD expansion into Europe:** FSD version 14.2.2.6 reportedly shows two new countries — Spain and the UK — appearing in the software, suggesting those markets may be in active testing or approaching regulatory approval. Tesla is hiring Autopilot data collection supervisors in London, Paris, and Barcelona, which the host interprets as a standard pre-launch signal. A source cited in the transcript — described as employees the host spoke with when testing FSD in Spain — reportedly expected approval in Spain to come around June 30, 2026. A fleet of vehicles in Spain reportedly grew from 19 to approximately 30 cars and has driven around 80,000 kilometers since November 2025. The Netherlands and Estonia are also mentioned as recently having come online for FSD.

## Robotaxi

1. **Largest Cybercab pack spotted at Giga Texas:** Joe Tegtmeyer captured video of approximately 10 Cybercabs testing together in formation at Giga Texas on what the host notes was the one-year anniversary of the robotaxi service going live. The test track where this occurred appears to have been newly built, possibly specifically for Cybercab testing. Joe Tegtmeyer described it as the largest group of Cybercabs he had seen on the track at any one time and expressed hope that they would soon be taking paying passengers.

2. **Cybercab deployment to multiple cities accelerating:** Jo Bhakdi notes that Cybercab counts in parking lots in Houston and Dallas have been climbing — he references a figure of approximately 45 units growing to around 55 in one city (per a ground reporter on X, attributed by the host to Houston or Dallas, unconfirmed). The hosts draw a contrast with how Model Y robotaxi testing operated, arguing that deploying dozens of vehicles in multiple new cities is consistent with launch preparation rather than mere testing. Cities mentioned as targets include Austin, Dallas, Houston, Los Angeles, Silicon Valley, Las Vegas, Miami, and Phoenix — though the hosts acknowledge the full seven-city rollout promised in Q1 2026 has not yet materialized as of June 23, 2026.

3. **Four months of no at-fault incidents:** The host states that Tesla's robotaxi safety data shows four months without any at-fault issues, which they argue provides a strong basis for expanded deployment.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus factory construction at Giga Texas progressing:** Joe Tegtmeyer documented the construction of Tesla's dedicated Optimus factory at Giga Texas with time-lapse footage from March through April and into subsequent weeks. As of the time of recording, the steel structure assembly is visible, the structure appears to have four floors, and footings have been completed. The host states the factory is planned for a target capacity of 10 million units per year once fully ramped and that the structure is currently on track for a late 2027 completion.

2. **Optimus supply chain expanding with new supplier deals:** Per a report in Taiwan Economic Daily cited by the host, Tesla has signed deals with Merl Automation and Asia Optical to accelerate mass production of Optimus 3. Merl Automation will supply harmonic reducers and joint modules, and has established a joint venture in Thailand to manufacture harmonic reducers, robot actuators, and other precision parts, taking advantage of existing factory space. Asia Optical will supply spherical and aspherical lens components to serve as the robot's "eyes." These parts are slated to enter mass production in the second half of 2026 and into 2027. The host notes that the scale of Tesla's orders is large enough that suppliers are creating entirely new joint ventures and factories.

3. **Strategic framing of Optimus scale bet:** Jo Bhakdi argues that Elon Musk's key strategic insight with Optimus is the same playbook used with compute (xAI's Colossus): rather than guaranteeing the best underlying technology, Tesla is making a decisive bet on massive manufacturing scale. The logic, per Bhakdi, is that if Tesla builds the world's largest humanoid robot factory, any competitor with superior technology will ultimately need to partner with or be acquired by Tesla. He draws a parallel to how Google and Anthropic reportedly became customers of xAI's Colossus compute infrastructure despite potentially having superior AI models.

## Market & Competition

1. **Tesla stock down ~5% on day of recording; inverse relationship with SpaceX suspected:** As of recording on June 23, 2026, Tesla was down approximately 5.18% while SpaceX was up approximately 5.16% — nearly mirror images. Jo Bhakdi notes that the prior day showed the reverse: SpaceX down approximately 16% while Tesla was up approximately 1.5% against the broader market. He speculates this reflects a mechanical cash-flow relationship between the two stocks, possibly related to a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger thesis (with a dedicated episode on merger pricing teased for the following day). He explicitly attributes less than half a percent of the day's Tesla decline to the Autopilot crash headlines.

2. **Investor rotation into "shiny object" AI and semiconductor stocks:** Jo Bhakdi argues Tesla is experiencing selling pressure from investors rotating into high-momentum names like Micron Technologies (noted as up sharply in recent months and down approximately 11% on the day of recording) and SpaceX. He warns that chasing high-momentum stocks is a common beginner mistake and that Tesla's upside could be hyperbolic once robotaxi or Optimus scaling becomes tangible — speculating that meaningful robotaxi progress could push the stock not to $600–$700 but potentially to $1,000 and beyond in the current market sentiment environment, given how quickly SpaceX moved in a short period. He compares SpaceX's recent run to a $3 trillion valuation as an example of how quickly sentiment can shift.

Notable quotes and data:
- Ashok Elluswamy (per transcript): "The driver manually overrode self-driving by pressing the accelerator all the way to 100% of the accelerator pedal in this residential area. They reached a speed of 73 mph during this crash and had the accelerator press even after the crash."
- Jo Bhakdi: "120 people die per day in the United States because of motor vehicle crashes. Yesterday when that happened, 120 people died in car accidents. But guess what? 119 of them were not covered."
- Jo Bhakdi on robotaxi scale: "I think if we have scaling of robotaxi we go to 600–700 — I think we go straight to a thousand and beyond."
- Host on Optimus factory: planned for 10 million units per year once fully ramped; steel structure with approximately four floors visible; on track for late 2027 structural completion.
- FSD version 14.2.2.6 reportedly includes Spain and UK.
- Spain FSD testing fleet: grew from 19 to approximately 30 vehicles; approximately 80,000 km driven since November 2025; approval reportedly expected around June 30, 2026 (per employees cited by host, unconfirmed).
- Active Cybercab lot in one city (host believes Houston): approximately 45 units growing to approximately 55 (per ground reporter on X, unconfirmed).
- SpaceX on day of recording: +5.16%; Tesla: -5.18%.
- Prior day: SpaceX -16%, Tesla +1.5%.

2026-06-23.title: Tesla, NatPower strike $5B deal for 25 GWh of Megapack storage
2026-06-23.body:
Tesla and UK-based independent energy firm NatPower have struck a deal to deploy 25 GWh of Megapack battery storage across Italy and Britain, the first phase of a program worth up to $5 billion.

## Energy
1. **Deal structure and scope:** The multiyear agreement covers five initial projects totaling 25 GWh across Italy and the UK, with a construction cost of $4–$5 billion. Beyond hardware, Tesla is also supplying its energy trading software to manage charging and discharging cycles for grid arbitrage — embedding its software stack into NatPower's operations. NatPower CEO Fabrizio Zago framed the arrangement as "an ecosystem that enables alignment between capital and execution" that can be replicated across markets.

2. **Long-term program ceiling:** NatPower says the broader program aims to exceed 100 GWh of total storage capacity, with revenue potentially topping $15 billion over 20 years. The article notes the 25 GWh phase-one figure alone exceeds half of Tesla's entire global energy storage deployment in 2025.

3. **Context — Tesla's energy growth:** Tesla deployed a record 46.7 GWh of energy storage in 2025, up roughly 48% year-over-year. Analysts pegged Q1 2026 deployments at a record ~14.4 GWh. In September 2025, Tesla unveiled the Megablock and Megapack 3, pre-integrated systems designed to reduce installation time. The article notes Tesla secured a separate multi-billion-dollar Megapack contract in 2024.

## Financials
1. **Market reaction:** TSLA was down approximately 3.3% in pre-market trading Tuesday, attributed to separate reports of a ransomware group leaking confidential documents tied to Tesla and Apple — not to the NatPower deal itself.

## Editorial Stance
Author Fred Lambert calls this "a meaningful win" in Tesla's strongest business segment, highlighting the software component as an underrated, stickier, higher-margin moat. He cautions that "up to $5 billion" and "$15 billion over 20 years" are headline figures dependent on execution, permitting, and grid interconnection — noting Europe's interconnection queues are "notoriously slow."

Notable quotes and data:
- 25 GWh phase-one across Italy and UK; construction cost $4B–$5B
- Broader program target: >100 GWh; >$15B revenue over 20 years
- Tesla 2025 energy deployments: 46.7 GWh (+~48% YoY)
