2026-06-24.title: Tesla Launches Brilliant New Business Partnership / Slate EV Details Drop ⚡️
2026-06-24.body:
This episode of Electrified, hosted by Dillon Loomis, covers three main stories: a major new energy partnership between Tesla, Sunrun, and Renew Home to create a distributed virtual power plant; the Cybertruck earning a 2026 Top Safety Pick Plus rating; and details on the Slate EV startup's barebones electric truck. The video also touches on Zoox's robotaxi redesign and Slate's pre-order opening. The host's core thesis is that Tesla's energy business is deeply underappreciated and that the Cybercab's parts simplicity represents a structural robotaxi advantage over competitors like Waymo.

## Robotaxi
1. **Cybercab Parts Efficiency vs. Waymo:** Per FutureAzA's Brian (as cited by the host), the Model 3 contains somewhere between 8,000 and 10,000 parts. The Cybercab is expected to have roughly 50% of that — approximately 4,000 parts total. By comparison, Waymo's sensor suite alone — the hardware Waymo must add on top of third-party vehicles — reportedly consists of around 4,000 parts. The host argues this illustrates Tesla's structural manufacturing advantage in the robotaxi space, where the entire Cybercab has roughly the same part count as just Waymo's add-on sensor kit.

2. **Zoox Robotaxi Redesign and Expansion:** Zoox announced a redesign of its robotaxi (which some are calling "the Toaster"), featuring higher-quality touchscreens, more comfortable seats and headrests, and exterior tweaks to help riders distinguish front from back. Zoox has served more than 500,000 riders since opening service in Las Vegas last September. It currently offers free rides in parts of Las Vegas and San Francisco, allows select users to hail robotaxis in small areas in Miami and Austin, and is testing in six other US cities. Zoox signed a deal with Uber in March 2026 to make its robotaxis available through Uber's ride-hailing app in Las Vegas, though it is still awaiting NHTSA approval for an exemption to commercially deploy up to 2,500 vehicles on public roads. Zoox expects to introduce the redesigned model to its fleet later in 2026 and plans to eventually produce 10,000 vehicles per year at its Bay Area manufacturing site that opened last June.

## Energy
1. **Tesla–Sunrun–Renew Home Virtual Power Plant Partnership:** Tesla, Sunrun, and Renew Home have announced an agreement to deliver more than 16 gigawatts of flexible energy capacity to hyperscalers and utilities. The framework aggregates hundreds of thousands of home battery systems operated by Sunrun and Tesla, alongside flexible peak capacity from more than 8 million smart thermostats and devices managed by Renew Home — forming what would be the largest distributed power plant in the country. Critically, the deal requires no additional hardware, software, interconnection, water, or land usage for off-taking parties and is described as deployable in months, not years. The mechanism for smart thermostats involves the software raising thermostat temperatures during high-usage periods to reduce AC load, easing grid stress and redirecting power elsewhere while compensating participating homeowners.

2. **Immediate and Near-Term Capacity:** In Virginia — described as the heart of "data center alley" — the three companies already have more than 300 megawatts of capacity available for immediate deployment. By 2030, that figure is expected to grow to at least 500 megawatts, rivaling some of the largest generation facilities in the state. The companies have also committed to provide capacity to PJM's proposed reliability backstop process; if accepted, PJM would immediately unlock over a gigawatt of capacity. New analysis from the Brattle Group cited in the video found that better utilization of the existing power grid could reduce US electricity bills by between $110 billion and $170 billion over the next decade and could accelerate data center interconnection by several years.

3. **Household and Grid Benefits:** The host emphasizes that the deal is structured to benefit multiple parties simultaneously: hyperscalers get faster access to power, utilities gain grid relief without new infrastructure, and participating homeowners earn credits on their utility bills. The host frames this as a largely overlooked Tesla initiative that deserves wider public attention, particularly in the context of criticism directed at data centers and Elon Musk.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Cybertruck Earns 2026 Top Safety Pick Plus:** The Cybertruck was awarded the 2026 IIHS Top Safety Pick Plus rating, making it the safest truck tested and the only truck to receive the designation. Its two weak spots were a "marginal" rating for seat belt reminders and an "acceptable" rating for latch ease of use. The re-evaluation this year was triggered by Tesla updating the front underbody structure and driver footwell area geometry, stiffening certain parts to improve crashworthiness. For context, the Model Y retains its Top Safety Pick Plus from last year (no structural changes warranted a new evaluation), while the Model 3 received only Top Safety Pick — not the Plus — in last year's assessment, partly due to headlight performance.

2. **Slate EV Truck Details:** Slate Auto, a startup making a barebones electric pickup truck starting under $25,000, is approaching production. The CEO stated that every vehicle produced will be gross margin positive, targeting positive free cash flow and EBITDA by 2027. The company's break-even point is approximately 80,000 vehicles per year, just over half of the 150,000-unit annual production capacity planned at its assembly plant in Warsaw, Indiana. The truck offers 205 miles of estimated EV range and 181 horsepower. It is exclusively rear-wheel drive, features hand crank windows (upgradeable), no built-in modem or large infotainment screen, and no paint — instead engineered for vinyl wrap. More than 100 standard wrap colors are available for under $500. The truck can be converted into a five-passenger SUV for an additional $5,000. Slate will offer more than 175 accessories at launch, with over 80 priced under $500. The company has received more than 180,000 reservations and is officially opening pre-orders. Deliveries are expected to begin in Q4 2026. The CEO indicated a potential IPO is possible but said 2027 is likely too soon. Slate plans to sell direct-to-consumer, bypassing franchise dealers, and has not ruled out four-door models in the future. Currently, Slate is building about three vehicles per day while still completing federal vehicle validation and certification.

## Market & Competition
1. **Starlink Maritime Expansion:** Marlink and Oldendorff Carriers are expanding their partnership beyond hardware installation to a unified, flexible, shared data pool model. Oldendorff's fleet will use hybrid LEO/GEO routing, with Marlink's smart routing hardware dynamically directing critical ship-to-shore telematics through the most stable link while offloading crew internet traffic to Starlink. The host notes that over 15 major shipping providers have publicly committed to large-scale Starlink deployments, driven in part by a maritime industry trend of treating high-speed onboard Wi-Fi as a crew retention tool rather than a luxury.

Notable quotes and data:
- Cybercab total parts: ~4,000 (per FutureAzA's Brian, cited by host) vs. Model 3's ~8,000–10,000
- Waymo's sensor suite alone reportedly ~4,000 parts
- Tesla–Sunrun–Renew Home deal: >16 GW of flexible energy capacity aggregated
- Combined resource: hundreds of thousands of home batteries + 8 million+ smart thermostats/devices
- Virginia capacity: 300 MW immediately available, expected to grow to 500 MW by 2030
- PJM potential unlock: over 1 GW immediately if accepted into reliability backstop process
- Brattle Group analysis: better grid utilization could cut US electricity bills by $110B–$170B over the next decade
- Cybertruck: only truck to earn 2026 IIHS Top Safety Pick Plus
- Slate: >180,000 reservations; break-even ~80,000 units/year; 150,000 unit/year production capacity target; ~3 vehicles/day currently in build
- Slate specs: 205-mile range, 181 hp, RWD only, starting under $25,000; SUV conversion kit +$5,000
- Zoox: 500,000+ riders served since Las Vegas launch (September 2025); awaiting NHTSA exemption for up to 2,500 commercial vehicles; 10,000 vehicles/year production target at full scale
- Tesla stock closed at $375.53, down 1.59%; SpaceX closed at $154.54, down 1.01%; NDX down 0.43%
- Host quote on the energy deal: "It's literally just using the hardware that's in place. Brilliant."

2026-06-24.title: Why Tesla Semi Is Pulling Ahead of Competitors
2026-06-24.body:
This episode of FutureAzA is a weekly Tesla Semi-focused news roundup hosted by Brian, joined by Mark from The Tesla Life. The video covers a range of topics including Tesla Semi charging infrastructure, FSD preparation for the Semi, real-world efficiency results from fleet pilots, competition from Chinese and European electric truck makers, and autonomous trucking startups. The tone is conversational and humor-heavy, with a recurring "wrong answers only" community segment mixed in throughout.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Tesla Pre-Assembling Mega Chargers for Semi:** Tesla was reported (not officially announced, but discovered by the hosts) to be building pre-assembled Mega Chargers for the Tesla Semi. The hosts draw a parallel to Tesla's Supercharger deployment strategy, where pre-assembly at a factory allows for faster on-site installation, less field wiring, and smoother utility hookups. The expectation is that this approach could enable Semi charging locations to go live in 24–48 hours once a site is prepped, mirroring what Tesla has done with Superchargers.

2. **ArcBest Fleet Expansion and Efficiency Results:** ArcBest expanded its Tesla Semi fleet after a pilot program. The hosts highlight the efficiency data as the main story: the industry benchmark target is around 2 kilowatts per mile; competing electric semis like the eCascadia, Volvo, and Mercedes trucks come in around 2.1 kWh/mile; Tesla's Semi is rated at 1.8 kWh/mile. The ArcBest real-world pilot result came in at 1.55 kWh/mile — which the hosts characterize as approximately a 25% energy savings compared to competing electric trucks, attributed to Tesla designing the Semi from the ground up as an electric vehicle.

3. **Chinese OEM SAIC Expanding in European Electric Truck Market:** A Chinese OEM, SAIC, is expanding into the European electric truck market. The hosts note that European regulations limiting overall vehicle length have long driven the use of flat-front cab-over designs, which this truck follows. Of greater interest to the hosts is the truck's use of sodium-ion batteries, which reportedly maintain more than 90% of usable capacity at temperatures as low as 40 degrees below Fahrenheit, while still supporting fast charging and long cycle life. The hosts suggest this chemistry could become relevant for cold-weather markets in Europe and North America.

4. **Battery Swap Networks for Electric Semis (China's CATL):** A Chinese company, CATL, is developing a global battery swap network for electric semi trucks, pitched as an alternative to long charging stops for operators with known fixed routes. The hosts discuss the logic of swap stations for predictable routes but note that increasingly fast charging speeds are eroding the advantage of battery swapping. They also reference an Australian company that had previously converted diesel trucks to electric using large battery skids swapped by forklift at a home base.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Tesla Semi Equipped with Autonomous Validation Equipment:** A report surfaced that a Tesla Semi was spotted equipped with autonomous validation equipment, described as hardware used to confirm road position by cross-referencing camera views with ground truth data — essentially calibrating the truck's camera placement and field of view for autonomous driving purposes. The hosts note this has been expected since Tesla first introduced the Semi, when convoy mode was discussed as early as 2017 (per the host, citing a viewer comment, though the host could not locate the original Elon Musk quote). No timeline for FSD deployment on the Semi is given; the hosts characterize this as early-stage validation work.

## Market & Competition
1. **Autonomous Logging Truck Concept (T-Log):** The hosts briefly cover a concept for an autonomous electric logging truck called the "T-Log," published on trans.info. The electric truck has a range of approximately 200 kilometers, which the hosts flag as likely insufficient for most commercial logging operations in countries like Canada, where the vast majority of logging by volume takes place well beyond that range from urban centers. The hosts treat this as an interesting concept but note the range limitation is a significant practical barrier.

2. **Autonomous Freight Startup Targeting California Roads:** A startup aiming to bring driverless freight trucks to California's roads was covered briefly. The company has raised $24 million to build a demo unit. The hosts express some skepticism about whether that funding level is sufficient and note the concept resembles a shipping container on a sled. Labor unions and safety advocates are cited as opposing the effort, though the hosts do not dwell on that angle.

3. **Aptera and Nicola Viability Concerns:** In the comments segment, the hosts briefly acknowledge viewer skepticism about Aptera, with one commenter suggesting it will never reach market — a concern the hosts say they share. Nicola is mentioned in the same breath as a cautionary example of investors pulling out of an electric trucking venture.

Notable quotes and data:
- ArcBest Tesla Semi real-world efficiency: **1.55 kWh/mile** (vs. 2.1 kWh/mile for eCascadia/Volvo/Mercedes, and Tesla's rated 1.8 kWh/mile)
- Hosts characterize ArcBest result as approximately **25% energy savings** vs. competing electric semis
- Sodium-ion batteries on Chinese OEM truck: maintain **>90% usable capacity at -40°F** while supporting fast charging and long cycle life
- Autonomous logging truck range: **~200 km**
- Autonomous freight startup (California): raised **$24 million** to build a demo unit
- Host (quoting a viewer): "Elon said in 2017 that the trucks could already do convoy mode" — host notes he could not verify the original quote
- On the ArcBest results: "That's what happens when you build the truck from scratch to be electric." — Mark

2026-06-24.title: Tesla Semi Update 2026: Full Self Driving
2026-06-24.body:
This episode of The Tesla Space covers three main topics: Tesla Semi's apparent preparation for Full Self-Driving capability (evidenced by a recent sensor-rig sighting), the upcoming North American launch of the Model YL, and a triple update from The Boring Company across its tunneling projects. The video's core thesis is that Tesla has been quietly building toward autonomous trucking since the Semi's 2017 unveiling, and that recent hardware and data-collection activity suggests that long-term plan is now accelerating.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Tesla Semi spotted with ground-truthing equipment:** A Tesla Semi was recently spotted in Sunnyvale, California, carrying a tall sensor rig above the cab typically associated with ground truthing — a process that creates highly accurate environmental reference data to validate what an autonomous vehicle perceives versus what is actually present. The host frames this as evidence that Tesla is actively collecting the kind of training data needed to bring autonomous capability to the Semi, though notes that the sighting alone does not confirm a rollout timeline.

2. **Semi's 2025 redesign was built with autonomy in mind:** When Tesla rolled out the Semi's updated design in late 2025, it included a revised camera layout with 10 external cameras and an interior driver monitoring camera, plus new side-mounted camera pods above the front wheel arches to reduce blind spots. The host argues these changes, taken together, indicate Tesla was deliberately building a platform suited to a modern vision-based autonomous driving system rather than simply refreshing an existing product.

3. **Highway freight as an early autonomy use case:** The video argues that long-haul trucking is, in several respects, an easier environment for autonomous driving than urban passenger vehicles, because trucks spend most of their operating life on highways with relatively predictable routes. The economic case is amplified by utilization: a long-haul truck can exceed 100,000 miles per year versus roughly 12,000 miles for a typical passenger car, meaning efficiency and safety improvements compound dramatically across a fleet.

4. **FSD safety figures cited for the Semi opportunity:** Tesla's own safety data is cited: vehicles operating with Full Self-Driving supervised engage reportedly experience one serious collision approximately every 5.3 million miles, compared to the U.S. average of one every 660,000 miles for human drivers. The host acknowledges uncertainty about whether these numbers hold at scale but notes they illustrate why Tesla is motivated to bring its autonomy stack to the Semi, given that large trucks are involved in roughly 5,000–6,000 fatal crashes annually in the U.S., with the majority of fatalities occurring in the other vehicle.

5. **Convoy mode ambition traces back to 2017:** At the Semi's original 2017 unveiling, Tesla introduced the concept of "convoy mode," in which a lead truck driven by a human would be followed autonomously by additional Semis drafting closely to reduce wind resistance. Elon Musk claimed at the time that a three-truck convoy could bring freight costs down to approximately $0.85 per mile versus roughly $1.25 for diesel trucking, and argued the system could operate 10 times more safely than a human driver. The host positions the current ground-truthing activity as a continuation of that vision rather than a new initiative.

6. **FSD fleet milestone referenced:** Tesla's Full Self-Driving supervised fleet has now accumulated more than 11.3 billion miles of real-world experience, which the host cites as context for how far the underlying technology has matured since the Semi was first unveiled.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Model YL targeting August–September North American launch:** According to a report from Not a Tesla App, Tesla is targeting an August or September 2026 launch for the Model YL in North America — a longer-wheelbase version of the Model Y already available in China, Australia, and New Zealand. The vehicle is expected to be built at Giga Texas, where tooling changes are reportedly underway. Tesla has not officially confirmed the timeline.

2. **Physical dimensions and seating configuration:** The Model YL features a wheelbase approximately 6 inches longer and an overall length roughly 7 inches greater than the standard Model Y. This extra space enables a 2-2-2 seating configuration — two captain's chairs (heated and ventilated) in the middle row and two seats in the third row — creating a genuine six-seat family vehicle rather than the cramped third-row arrangement of the standard Model Y.

3. **Market positioning and expected pricing:** The Model YL is positioned to bridge the gap between the standard Model Y and the significantly more expensive Model X, offering real third-row usability at a more accessible price point. Based on overseas market pricing, the North American version is expected to carry roughly a $4,000 premium over the current all-wheel drive Model Y, placing it around $54,000 before incentives — above the premium all-wheel drive trim but below the Model Y Performance. North American pricing has not been officially announced.

4. **Pre-launch evidence accumulating:** Earlier in spring 2026, observers spotted a Model YL body-in-white at Giga Texas; more recently, camouflage prototypes have been seen testing on public roads in both California and Florida, suggesting the program is progressing toward production readiness.

## Market & Competition *(The Boring Company)*

1. **Vegas Loop expands to UNLV campus:** The Nevada System of Higher Education Board of Regents approved an agreement for a Vegas Loop station on the UNLV campus, with The Boring Company covering construction costs and the university owning the completed station. The plan includes a 25% student discount on fares.

2. **Emergency preparedness milestone in Las Vegas:** The Boring Company completed a large-scale tunnel rescue exercise with the Clark County Fire Department inside a Vegas Loop tunnel. More than 200 firefighters and first responders have participated in over 150 hours of tunnel-specific training, which the host frames as a critical but underappreciated step in gaining regulatory and public confidence for long-term operations.

3. **Nashville Music City Loop machinery commissioned and scaling:** The Boring Company's second Prufrock boring machine (MB2) is now fully commissioned and ready to begin tunneling for the Music City Loop in Nashville. A third machine (MB3) is already scheduled to ship in August 2026. The host interprets this as a sign the company has moved past proving faster tunneling is possible and is now focused on the harder challenge of scaling across multiple cities simultaneously.

---

**Notable quotes and data:**
- Tesla Semi spotted with ground-truthing sensor rig in Sunnyvale, California
- Semi redesign (late 2025): 10 external cameras + 1 interior driver monitoring camera; new side-mounted camera pods above front wheel arches
- FSD supervised fleet: 11.3+ billion miles accumulated
- FSD safety stat: ~1 serious collision per 5.3 million miles (FSD supervised) vs. ~1 per 660,000 miles (U.S. human driver average)
- U.S. fatal large-truck crashes per year: roughly 5,000–6,000
- Typical passenger vehicle: ~12,000 miles/year; long-haul truck: can exceed 100,000 miles/year
- 2017 convoy mode claim: ~$0.85/mile (3-truck Tesla convoy) vs. ~$1.25/mile (diesel), with a claimed 10x safety advantage
- Model YL wheelbase: ~6 inches longer; overall length: ~7 inches longer than standard Model Y
- Model YL seating: 2-2-2 configuration with heated/ventilated captain's chairs in row 2
- Expected Model YL U.S. pricing: ~$54,000 before incentives (~$4,000 premium over AWD Model Y) — per Not a Tesla App, unconfirmed by Tesla
- Model YL target launch: August–September 2026 (per Not a Tesla App; unconfirmed by Tesla)
- Vegas Loop/UNLV: 25% student fare discount; Boring Company covers construction costs
- Las Vegas emergency training: 200+ first responders, 150+ hours of tunnel-specific drills
- Nashville MB2: fully commissioned; MB3 scheduled to ship August 2026

2026-06-25.title: SpaceX And Tesla Just Added Billions!
2026-06-25.body:
This video from brighterwithherbert covers several major business developments across SpaceX and Tesla that the hosts argue are being overlooked by mainstream media and analysts. The core thesis is that while public attention remains fixed on rockets and EV sales figures, SpaceX and Tesla are quietly building AI compute and energy businesses — through orbital AI satellites, terrestrial data center deals, large-scale Megapack contracts, and distributed grid partnerships — that could generate tens of billions in new revenue. Host Herbert is joined by Brian from the YouTube channel FutureAzA, who contributes factory-floor insight and broader context on Tesla's energy business.

## Energy
1. **Tesla–Nat Power Megapack Partnership (Phase One):** Tesla signed what the hosts describe as a landmark energy storage partnership with Nat Power. Phase one covers 25 gigawatt-hours of battery storage across sites in Italy and Britain, representing roughly $5 billion in revenue. The full buildout could potentially exceed 100 gigawatt-hours and generate up to $15 billion in revenue over 20 years. The hosts note this is the first time battery energy storage has been procured, financed, and executed across multiple locations under a single integrated framework. Brian points out that the previous largest single-source installation of this type was reportedly 12.3 gigawatt-hours, making phase one alone more than twice that size.

2. **Scale Relative to Tesla's Megapack Production Capacity:** The hosts contextualize the 25 gigawatt-hour contract against Tesla's existing production footprint. Tesla's Megapack factory in Lathrop is said to have approximately 40 gigawatt-hours of annual capacity, and a new Megapack factory in Houston is reportedly planned at 50 gigawatt-hours when it comes online. Brian notes that Tesla's Megapack factory in Shanghai is still ramping and has not yet reached its final run rate, contributing to a backlog of deployments that could cause a future quarter where deployed gigawatt-hours substantially exceed production. Brian also confirms — based on personal factory tours — that Tesla's Megapack battery supplier is a major manufacturer with no supply concerns, though he declines to name them on-record.

3. **Expectation of Strong Q2 Energy Numbers:** The hosts discuss the upcoming Tesla Q2 earnings call, expected in late July 2026. They note that Q1 energy deployments came in below expectations, but attribute this to pipeline timing rather than slowing demand. Brian expresses confidence that a large catch-up deployment quarter is coming — potentially showing 25–30 gigawatt-hours deployed in a single quarter — though he does not commit to Q2 specifically. Some observers the host references expect the energy segment to "really surprise" on the upside.

4. **Tesla–Sunrun–Renew Home Distributed Virtual Power Plant:** Tesla, Sunrun, and Renew Home announced a partnership to create what is described as the largest distributed power plant in the United States, aggregating more than 16 gigawatt-hours of flexible power capacity. The system draws on hundreds of thousands of residential battery systems (including Powerwalls), EVs, and more than 8 million smart thermostats. Brian explains the mechanism: rather than pulling energy back from vehicles or homes (vehicle-to-grid), the system primarily works by deferring charging and adjusting thermostat setpoints during peak demand — a demand-response model. Participants receive compensation incentives for participating. The hosts note that the data center corridor in Virginia alone reportedly has 300 megawatts available for immediate use under this framework. The partnership is projected to potentially reduce overall U.S. electricity bills by up to $170 billion over the next decade, per the hosts' cited figures.

5. **Case for a European Megapack Factory:** Brian argues that the scale of the Nat Power deal — effectively requiring output comparable to an entire factory — makes a strong case for Tesla building a dedicated Megapack manufacturing facility in Europe to serve both this contract and broader continental demand.

## Market & Competition
1. **SpaceX AI Compute Business — Reflection AI Deal:** SpaceX signed a new AI compute agreement with Reflection AI, who will pay approximately $150 million per month — or up to $6.3 billion through 2029 — for access to SpaceX's Colossus 2 data center and Nvidia GB300 chips. This joins previously announced deals with Google and Anthropic (each reportedly paying $950 million to $1.25 billion, per the hosts' figures). A table compiled by commentator Steve Mark Ryan, as cited by the host, puts SpaceX's total AI compute annual run rate across all signed deals at approximately $27.84 billion, or roughly $2.32 billion per month. The hosts note these figures assume deals run to their stated end dates, which they consider unlikely.

2. **SpaceX "Star Mind" Orbital AI Satellite Brand:** Elon Musk confirmed (per a social media exchange cited by the host) that the name "Star Mind" — a trademark pending application filed by SpaceX — will be the official brand for SpaceX's orbital AI satellite constellation. The hosts note SpaceX has reportedly requested regulatory approval for up to 1 million AI satellites. The branding joins a growing "Star" product family (Starlink, Star Pipe, etc.). Brian and the host discuss the concept's defensibility against skeptics, noting that even if the orbital concept fails, much of the underlying technology could be repurposed for ground-based standalone closed-loop systems.

3. **SpaceX "Star Pipe" Natural Gas Pipeline:** SpaceX has notified the Texas Railroad Commission of plans to build an 8.1-mile, 16-inch natural gas pipeline at Starbase, Texas, dubbed "Star Pipe," with construction scheduled to begin July 7, 2026. Brian explains this is critical for scaling Starship launch cadence — currently, fuel must be trucked in on a single congested road, which limits rapid reuse capability. A 16-inch diameter pipeline is described as substantial for natural gas flow, and an 8-mile stretch is relatively low cost compared to typical pipeline projects.

4. **Tesla "Megapods" — Distributed AI Data Centers:** The hosts briefly reference Tesla's trademarked "Megapods" concept — portable, packaged AI data center units designed to be deployed at or near Supercharger locations. The idea combines existing electrical infrastructure with Megapack storage and compute chips (H100s, B100s, B300s are mentioned). Brian frames this as consistent with Tesla's product philosophy of pre-packaging complexity inside the unit, similar to Megapack 2. He notes potential use cases including data-security-sensitive customers who need on-premises compute, and arbitrage opportunities in municipalities with very low overnight electricity rates.

5. **Contrast with GM and Ford:** Brian expresses skepticism toward legacy automakers, noting that announcements of electrification pullbacks are often followed almost immediately by new electrification commitment announcements, making it difficult to take their strategic direction seriously compared to Tesla's demonstrated scaling in both EVs and energy.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX annual AI compute run rate across all signed deals: ~$27.84 billion (per Steve Mark Ryan's table, as cited by host)
- SpaceX monthly AI compute run rate: ~$2.32 billion/month
- Reflection AI deal: ~$150 million/month, up to $6.3 billion through 2029, for Colossus 2 / Nvidia GB300 access
- Tesla–Nat Power deal: Phase 1 = 25 gigawatt-hours / ~$5 billion; full buildout potentially >100 gigawatt-hours / up to $15 billion over 20 years
- Previous largest single-source battery storage installation: reportedly 12.3 gigawatt-hours (per Brian)
- First South Australia Megapack installation: reportedly ~100 megawatts (per Brian)
- Tesla Megapack factory in Lathrop: ~40 gigawatt-hours annual capacity; planned Houston factory: ~50 gigawatt-hours
- Tesla–Sunrun–Renew Home distributed power plant: >16 gigawatt-hours flexible capacity, >8 million smart thermostats, enough to power ~12 million average homes
- Virginia data center corridor: reportedly 300 megawatts available for immediate use under the distributed power plant framework
- Projected U.S. electricity bill savings from the distributed power plant: up to $170 billion over the next decade
- Star Pipe: 8.1-mile, 16-inch natural gas pipeline at Starbase, TX; construction start date July 7, 2026
- SpaceX requested approval for up to 1 million AI satellites (per host, citing reports)
- Brian (FutureAzA): confirms Megapack battery supplier is a "significant battery manufacturer" with no supply concerns; declines to name them
- Brian: "If Tesla stopped selling any kind of car, forget autonomy, forget cars, they've still got all that FSD revenue pouring in... And you've got Mega, which is not stopping. It's still accelerating."

2026-06-25.title: Tesla’s Biggest Achievement Isn’t What You Think
2026-06-25.body:
This video from the "brighterwithherbert" channel, featuring guest Brian White of FutureAzA, argues that Tesla's most underappreciated achievements are not its headline autonomous driving or robotaxi ambitions, but rather its core contributions to vehicle safety, American manufacturing, and accelerating the global energy transition. The hosts walk through a series of recent data points — FSD safety footage, Cybertruck IIHS results, Tesla Vision airbag technology, and American-made vehicle rankings — to counter what they describe as unfair media narratives against Tesla. The discussion also touches on Goldman Sachs's projection for EV-driven oil demand reduction and the Model Y L's anticipated US launch.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Version 14.3.4 Sideswipe Avoidance Footage:** A recently circulated real-world clip showed an owner's Tesla running FSD version 14.3.4 executing a lateral maneuver to avoid a vehicle that had drifted into its lane. The owner described it as avoiding a potentially dangerous sideswipe situation and stated they believed no human could have reacted as effectively, calling it "superhuman driving skill." The hosts discuss how the system briefly crossed the double yellow line to avoid the collision — noting there was no oncoming traffic — and contrast this with a handcoded system that might only apply the brakes.

2. **Media Misattribution of a Recent Crash to FSD:** The hosts reference a news story from roughly 48 hours prior (approximately June 23, 2026) in which global media outlets attributed a crash — in which a vehicle traveling at 70 mph in a residential area struck a home and killed a woman inside — to Tesla's FSD or Autopilot. The hosts state that Tesla responded with vehicle data showing the accelerator was pressed fully to the floor, indicating human control at the time of the crash. They argue that flooring the accelerator is not a known failure mode of FSD, drawing an analogy to a blender unexpectedly exploding.

3. **FSD Version 14 Rolling Out to New Markets and Models:** FSD version 14 is described as now rolling out in Australia and New Zealand. Notably, the hosts highlight that the Model Y L received its first-ever FSD activation update, marking the first time that variant could access Full Self-Driving anywhere in the world.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cybertruck Earns IIHS Top Safety Pick for 2026:** The Cybertruck became the only pickup truck to earn the IIHS Top Safety Pick Plus — the organization's highest award — for 2026. In the pedestrian front crash prevention test, it avoided every single collision across all scenarios tested: daytime, nighttime, crossing child, and parallel adult. The hosts contrast this with the Ford F-150 and Ram 1500, which rated "very poor" in the moderate overlap front test. The Toyota Tundra also performed well, but the Cybertruck was the only EV in the category.

2. **Tesla Vision Enables Earlier Airbag Deployment:** Tesla released footage explaining a new safety feature in which the vehicle's camera system supplements existing accelerometers to make airbag deployment decisions up to 70 milliseconds earlier. The system works by using exterior cameras to identify when contact will be made and how severe a crash will be, passing that information to the airbag controller before impact sensors alone would trigger deployment. Tesla states this was developed over several years with thousands of simulations and physical sled tests, and that it rolls out as an over-the-air software update to existing vehicles — described as "outside the bounds of the five-star safety ratings."

3. **Cybertruck Real-World Crash Survivability:** An owner reported striking a utility pole head-on at speed while attempting to avoid a child running a red light on a bike. The owner reported the impact was absorbed with no serious injury to occupants and that even the utility pole was undamaged, crediting the vehicle's crumple zone design. Brian White contextualizes this by noting that the Cybertruck's aluminum front rail is scalloped and widens toward the rear, designed to deform progressively rather than buckle uniformly.

4. **Model Y L US Launch Described as Imminent:** The hosts discuss strong rumors that the Model Y L (a slightly longer, taller variant with a larger battery and more interior space) is coming to the United States imminently. Per the host, a source indicated it will be built at Giga Texas, and a Verge article published the prior week reportedly cited multiple sources confirming a Texas build location with potential deliveries as early as August 2026. The hosts frame it as a logical complement to the Cybercab in a future robotaxi network — the Cybercab satisfies most demand, but a larger vehicle is needed for versatility.

5. **Tesla Ranked Most American-Made Vehicle for Sixth Consecutive Year:** According to cars.com rankings for 2026, the Model Y and Model 3 hold the number one and number two spots respectively for most American-made vehicles — across all vehicle types, including gas cars. The hosts note this is the sixth consecutive year Tesla has claimed the top spot and contrast it with popular perception that traditional American brands like Ford have more US-made content.

## Market & Competition

1. **Goldman Sachs EV Oil Demand Projection:** A Goldman Sachs note projects that the global EV surge could reduce oil demand by up to 320,000 barrels per day by late 2027. The hosts note that Goldman itself acknowledged this understates the full picture, as the analysis only accounts for passenger car fleet additions and excludes two- and three-wheeler EVs, which account for 92% of total EV sales in India and 80% in Vietnam. The hosts credit Tesla's entry into China — particularly the Model 3 and Giga Shanghai — as a catalyst for China's EV transition, noting China is now at over 50% battery electric plus hybrid vehicle sales.

2. **LiDAR vs. Vision Debate:** Brian White briefly addresses the ongoing LiDAR vs. camera-only debate, asserting that Tesla without LiDAR performs substantially better than Waymo and other LiDAR-equipped competitors. He argues LiDAR is "not a silver bullet" and that Waymo and others have demonstrated as much in practice.

Notable quotes and data:
- FSD version 14.3.4 described by owner as "superhuman driving skill" in avoiding a sideswipe.
- Tesla Vision airbag system: up to **70 milliseconds** earlier airbag deployment decisions.
- Cybertruck: only pickup truck to earn **IIHS Top Safety Pick Plus for 2026**; avoided **every** pedestrian collision scenario tested.
- Goldman Sachs: EV surge may cut global oil demand by up to **320,000 barrels per day by late 2027**.
- Model Y and Model 3 ranked **#1 and #2 most American-made vehicles** per cars.com — **sixth consecutive year** for Tesla.
- Model Y L US deliveries potentially as early as **August 2026**, reportedly built at Giga Texas (per host's source and a Verge report).
- China EV + hybrid penetration: host states "well over 50% of all cars are battery electric vehicles plus hybrids."
- Transportation's share of carbon emissions: host believes it is approximately 15–30% (stated with uncertainty).
- Brian White: "Best crash is no crash."
- On Tesla's manufacturing legacy: "A company had not reached mass production of a vehicle in the US since Jeep, what, 60–70 years prior."

2026-06-25.title: Tesla to hire 1,000 more Giga Berlin workers as Europe demand returns
2026-06-25.body:
Tesla confirmed plans to hire 1,000 additional workers at Giga Berlin, targeting 7,500 vehicles per week by October, as European sales stage a meaningful recovery after two years of declines.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Second hiring wave at Giga Berlin:** The new 1,000 hires follow a separate 1,000-worker expansion announced in April, intended to lift output to ~6,000 vehicles per week by end of June. The October target of 7,500 units/week would represent a further ~25% increase, equating to roughly 390,000 vehicles per year — the factory's highest-ever sustained output, though still below the 500,000-unit annual capacity Tesla targeted at launch. Giga Berlin produces only the Model Y for the European market.

2. **Battery staffing also expanding:** In May, Tesla announced plans to recruit more than 1,500 employees for battery cell production in Germany, revisiting Elon Musk's 2020 pledge to make Grünheide the world's largest battery factory.

## Market & Competition
3. **European demand rebound:** After roughly a 27% sales drop last year, Tesla's EU registrations have grown for several consecutive months — up 67% year-over-year in April, with European registrations reportedly more than doubling in June. A key external driver is rising fuel prices across Europe since late February, which have broadly boosted EV adoption; battery-electric cars reached 19.7% of new EU registrations through April, up from 15.3% a year earlier. Renewed national incentive programs and a recovering overall auto market have added to the tailwind, with France, Sweden, Denmark, and Ireland all posting triple-digit percentage increases in April.

## Editorial Stance
Lambert views the hiring push as a clear signal Tesla's European slump is over for now, but cautions that the recovery is driven largely by external tailwinds — rising fuel prices and a low prior-year comparison — rather than product strength. He flags Chinese competition (BYD in particular) and any fading of the fuel-price tailwind as the real tests of whether Tesla can sustain these gains.

Notable quotes and data:
- October target: 7,500 vehicles/week at Giga Berlin (~390,000/year)
- April hiring wave: +1,000 workers, targeting ~6,000 units/week by end of June
- May battery hiring: 1,500+ employees for cell production
- EU BEV share through April 2026: 19.7% vs. 15.3% a year earlier
- Tesla EU registrations: +67% YoY in April; "more than doubling" in June
- Last year's European sales decline: ~27%
- Giga Berlin original capacity target: 500,000 units/year

2026-06-25.title: Big Robotaxi Rule Changes / Tesla Finally Growing Again / Tesla Semi Production ⚡️
2026-06-25.body:
This episode of Electrified, hosted by Dillon Loomis, covers a wide range of Tesla and broader tech news including a significant NHTSA regulatory update removing the manual brake pedal requirement for autonomous vehicles, Giga Berlin's production expansion announcements, FSD developments in China, Tesla Semi production scale hints, and several adjacent stories involving SpaceX, OpenAI, and Polestar. The core thesis is that regulatory tailwinds for autonomous vehicles are gradually building, Tesla's manufacturing base is finally approaching full utilization, and the longer-term robotaxi and Optimus narratives remain the dominant drivers of Tesla's valuation.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **NHTSA drops manual brake pedal mandate for AV-only vehicles:** NHTSA announced it is updating federal safety standards to remove the requirement for hand or foot-operated brake controls in vehicles designed exclusively for automated operation. The NHTSA administrator framed this as necessary for America to lead the "greatest technological revolution in vehicle tech since the Model T." Braking performance requirements will be preserved, but the method of achieving them is now open. The public has 30 days to comment before the Department of Transportation decides whether to approve the changes, so this is not yet finalized. For Tesla, this matters because Tesla has already self-certified the Cybercab as meeting all FMVSS regulations without needing an exemption through Part 555; removing the brake requirement reduces the chances NHTSA challenges that self-certification later. For companies like Zoox still going through the Part 555 exemption process (which carries a 2,500-unit annual cap), this also simplifies their path.

2. **UN adopts first global autonomous vehicle framework (not yet binding law):** The UNECE adopted what it describes as the first-ever global rules allowing fully autonomous vehicles, backed by the US, China, the EU, Japan, Canada, and the UK. The framework mandates safety management systems, credible testing, safety case validation, and continuous in-service monitoring. Importantly for Tesla, the framework is hardware-agnostic — there is no requirement for lidar, radar, or any specific hardware, only a requirement to demonstrate safety. However, one notable clause states the requirements are written with the expectation that ADS software does not include online in-vehicle learning that self-modifies system behavior. Dillon Loomis notes Tesla's current over-the-air update model (training done offboard, static software pushed to vehicles) should be compliant today, but flags this could become a point of contention in the 2030s as on-the-fly AI learning matures. The framework is entered into the UN registry and is "in force" internationally, but is not binding on any manufacturer until individual countries write it into national law — the US has supported and helped draft the framework but has not yet taken adoption steps. The most likely path is that parts of the framework are eventually incorporated into FMVSS standards.

3. **FSD in China: test fleet at 200 vehicles, targeting 600:** A Chinese source reported that Tesla's FSD test fleet in China has reached 200 vehicles with a target of 600. Each vehicle averages over 280 km (~173 miles) per day, and the 200-car fleet uploads approximately 1.7 terabytes of data daily. Underlying compute and storage is estimated at 6 petabytes or more, housed in Tesla's Phase 2 factory in Shanghai to keep data within China. OTA approval timelines in China have stretched from 2 weeks to 60 days, constraining Tesla's normal update cadence. Tesla has partnered with BYD for mapping in China due to data security requirements. FSD 14 will only be available on AI4 hardware. The host notes that the technology is reportedly ready, but the bottlenecks are policy approvals and localization, with a broader approval hoped for in Q3 2026.

4. **FSD 14.3.4 safety incidents flagged:** Two FSD incidents were highlighted by the community. In one, FSD 14.3.4 failed to detect a gas can that had fallen off a trailer and drove over it; Tesla's Yun Tasai acknowledged the clip and said it was forwarded to the team. In another, FSD was prepared to drive through a lowered railroad crossing arm despite red warning squares affixed to it. The host notes the inconsistency — FSD has been observed braking hard for small animals but failed to react to these more prominent obstacles.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab conversion capability confirmed:** Per Bradford Ferguson, Cybercabs can be converted from having a steering wheel and pedals to a pedal/wheel-free configuration anywhere — including on-site at a lot — and reportedly in a matter of hours. A conversion was observed performed in a small tent. This suggests Tesla could rapidly convert existing staged inventory should deployment decisions warrant it.

2. **Cybercabs accumulating at lots; Tesla hiring robotaxi logistics senior analyst:** Cybercabs continue to accumulate at staging lots, including one in Dallas. Tesla posted a job listing for a Senior Analyst for Robotaxi Logistics in Austin, whose responsibilities include owning final-mile logistics for robotaxi deployments across North America, optimizing routes, selecting carriers, managing rail partners, and improving logistics hub and distribution workflows. The host interprets this as Tesla actively preparing for broad North American robotaxi distribution.

3. **4680 cell expansion tied to Cybercab and Semi demand:** Joe Tegtmeyer noted (the host characterizes it as somewhat tongue-in-cheek) the expansion of 4680 production at Giga Texas, hinting at significantly higher production volumes ahead. The 4680 cell is used in the Cybercab, Tesla Semi, and Cybertruck. The host also notes Tesla may still be shipping some 4680s from Austin to Giga Berlin for use in Model Y there, at least until Giga Berlin's own 4680 production scales up.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Micron says Optimus could become a bigger memory customer than Tesla's cars:** During Micron's recent earnings call, the CEO outlined a long-term vision in which humanoid robots become a significant new memory market, stating that humanoid robots carry 10 times the memory of an average Level 2+ vehicle. The CEO said Micron expects "a sustained, substantial multi-decade memory demand cycle to begin in the latter part of this decade," driven by advances in simulation, foundation models, and integrated hardware/software for physical AI. The host also notes Tesla's Terafab is expected to address memory needs as well.

## Energy

1. **Tesla signs LOI for Green Turtle battery storage project in Belgium:** Tesla and Giga Storage signed a letter of intent for the Green Turtle project in the Belgian province of Limburg (rendered as "Lindberg" in captions). The project will have a storage capacity of 2,800 MWh (2.8 GWh), making it one of the largest battery storage projects in Europe. Tesla will be responsible for full EPC (engineering, procurement, and construction), battery supply, commissioning, and long-term maintenance. Tesla will deploy its latest-generation Megablock technology. Final contracts are expected to be signed in summer 2026, after which project financing will be finalized. The host notes this is the first Megablock announcement at gigawatt-hour scale; a prior Megablock deal with Neoen was under 1 GWh.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Giga Berlin production ramping to 7,500 units/week — approaching full capacity:** Giga Berlin plant manager André Tütig previously announced a production increase from 5,000 to 6,200 units per week starting in July, adding 1,000 new jobs, plus substantial new investment in the cell factory to enable 18 GWh of 4680 manufacturing capacity starting in 2027, adding 1,500 further jobs. A new announcement followed: production will be further increased to 7,500 units per week, beginning to ramp in October 2026, with another 1,000 employees hired. At 7,500 units/week × 50 weeks, that equals 375,000 units per year — matching the Model Y annual capacity figure shown in Tesla's most recent slide deck, meaning Tesla is finally planning to utilize nearly full capacity at Giga Berlin roughly five years after opening. Across recent weeks, these announcements total 3,500 new jobs at Giga Berlin, representing over a 30% headcount increase from a base of ~11,000 employees. The host calculates the incremental 125,000 annual units would add roughly $6.2 billion in revenue; applying a 20% gross margin yields over $1.2 billion in incremental gross profit.

2. **Polestar banned from US market:** The US Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security refused Polestar the clearance needed to continue selling new cars in the US, citing the connected vehicle rule that bars vehicles with Chinese or Russian software and hardware in connectivity systems on national security grounds. Polestar's majority owner is Geely, a Chinese company. Existing Polestar 3 and 4 inventory will remain on sale until stock runs out; 2027 model year vehicles will not be authorized. Volvo, also Geely-owned, received a waiver in May 2026. The software restrictions take effect for 2027 model year vehicles; hardware restrictions follow in 2030. In Q1 2026, 94% of Polestar's retail sales were outside the US, so the US was not central to its strategy, though the fate of its US manufacturing facility is now in question.

## Financials

1. **Tesla Semi production: high confidence in doubling total North American Class 7/8 EV registrations in year one:** In a recently aired interview, Dan Priestley stated there are currently 2,829 Class 7 and 8 electric trucks registered in aggregate in the US and Canada. When asked if Tesla could double that number in its first year of Semi production, he said he had "very high confidence" in that outcome — implying Tesla could manufacture somewhere in the neighborhood of over 3,000 Tesla Semis in that timeframe. The Tesla careers page currently lists dozens of Semi-related positions across the country, including service adviser roles nationally.

## Market & Competition

1. **OpenAI builds first in-house AI chip "Jalapeño":** OpenAI announced its first custom AI chip, Jalapeño, designed from the ground up by OpenAI and brought to production with Broadcom. It is purpose-built for LLM inference workloads (not training), powering GPT, the API, and future agentic products. Per analyst Patrick Collison (the host's attribution), the chip is likely the first virtually entirely developed by Codex and GPT. It is expected to be manufactured by TSMC and is the first in a planned series of chips between OpenAI and Broadcom. The host's framing: custom ASICs are now "table stakes" for any frontier AI company.

Notable quotes and data:
- NHTSA administrator: *"We're at the cusp of the greatest technological revolution in vehicle tech since the innovation of the Model T. If we want America to lead the way, we have to reimagine our regulatory framework."*
- Micron CEO: *"Humanoid robots carry 10 times the amount of memory as an average Level 2+ vehicle. We expect a sustained, substantial multi-decade memory demand cycle to begin in the latter part of this decade."*
- Dan Priestley on Tesla Semi: asked if Tesla could double the ~2,829 Class 7/8 EVs currently registered in North America in year one of production, he replied: *"I have very high confidence in that."*
- Giga Berlin capacity at 7,500 units/week × 50 weeks = **375,000 units/year** — matching Tesla's stated annual capacity
- Incremental 125,000 units/year from Giga Berlin ≈ **$6.2 billion additional revenue** at ~20% gross margin = **$1.2 billion+ incremental gross profit** (host's estimate)
- FSD China test fleet: **200 vehicles** active, target **600**; averaging **280 km/day** (~173 miles); uploading **~1.7 TB/day**; estimated compute/storage **6+ petabytes**
- Green Turtle Megablock project: **2,800 MWh (2.8 GWh)** — first Megablock deal at GWh scale
- Tesla stock closed at **$375.12, down 0.11%**; SpaceX at **$153, down 1%**; NASDAQ up **0.75%**
- Giga Berlin new jobs announced in recent weeks: **3,500** (>30% headcount increase from ~11,000 base)
- UNECE AV framework: hardware-agnostic, no lidar/radar mandate; does not permit online in-vehicle learning that self-modifies system behavior

2026-06-25.title: What Really Happened in the Texas Tesla Crash
2026-06-25.body:
This video is a joint discussion between the host of FutureAzA and Herbert from Brighter, reacting to widespread media coverage blaming Tesla's Full Self-Driving system for a fatal crash in Texas. Their core argument is that the crash was caused by a driver pressing the accelerator pedal — not by FSD — and that journalists are irresponsibly amplifying unverified claims while ignoring Tesla's same-day rebuttal from Elon Musk and Ashok Elluswamy. The hosts situate this incident within a long pattern of FSD-related media misrepresentation that they argue actively harms public safety by discouraging adoption of technology they believe saves lives.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **The Texas crash was driver-caused, not FSD-caused:** The hosts describe footage of a Tesla traveling at approximately 70 mph in a 25 mph zone — roughly double to triple the speed limit — and going airborne before crashing through a house. They argue the accelerator pedal was pressed the entire time, including after the car hit a wall, which they say definitively rules out FSD as the cause. The host states that pressing the gas pedal too long or moving the steering wheel causes FSD to disengage, reverting control to the human driver.

2. **Elon Musk and Ashok Elluswamy responded with data the same day:** The hosts note that both Elon Musk and Ashok Elluswamy publicly rebutted the FSD narrative within the same day using telemetry data showing the pedal was depressed throughout the incident. Despite this, subsequent media articles — published hours after the rebuttal — continued to frame the story as an FSD failure without using the word "allegedly."

3. **FSD's known failure mode is caution, not acceleration:** The host argues that when FSD fails, it fails by stopping, hesitating, or slowing down — not by accelerating uncontrollably to 70 mph through a residential area. He frames the Texas incident as inconsistent with any documented FSD failure mode, comparing it to a computer blue-screening in an unrecognized way.

4. **Tesla FSD is claimed to be seven times safer than human drivers (supervised):** The hosts assert that Tesla's supervised FSD has been shown to be seven times safer than human drivers, and reference reporting — attributed generally to doctors writing in the New York Times and other outlets — suggesting that Waymo's autonomous driving data is so compelling that, were it a clinical trial, it would be unethical to continue a control group. The hosts use this to argue the media narrative actively delays life-saving technology.

5. **A pattern of debunked FSD crash claims:** The hosts cite more than ten prior cases where articles claimed Tesla's FSD caused crashes or deaths, all of which were subsequently found not to be caused by FSD. Examples mentioned include: a 2022 fatal crash where the driver was reportedly three times the legal limit; a San Francisco incident (from 2025 per the headline shown); and a Chinese case where a woman made brake-failure claims, lost a lawsuit, was fined, and was required to publicly apologize after protests at Tesla showrooms and car shows.

6. **January 2026 NHTSA robotaxi incident report misrepresented:** The hosts describe a NHTSA report from January 2026 citing five robotaxi incidents in one month, which media outlets used to claim Tesla's robotaxi was four times worse than human drivers. The hosts say not a single article disclosed what those five incidents actually were. Upon investigation, the hosts say all five turned out to be low-speed contacts — described as under 4 mph, occurring in parking lots, essentially just touching another vehicle while parking — and that none constituted meaningful crashes.

7. **Tesla's full robotaxi incident disclosure:** The hosts reference a disclosure by Tesla — described as occurring approximately one to two months before the video, so roughly April–May 2026 — in which Tesla released unredacted details of all 17 robotaxi incidents since June of the prior year (i.e., June 2025). The hosts say a review of all 17 showed Tesla's automated system was not at fault: incidents included cars hitting a parked Tesla (which Tesla is still required to report), a tire touching a curb, and the worst incidents being caused by human remote operators — which the hosts argue proves autonomous operation is safer than human remote control.

## Market & Competition

1. **Media bias in crash reporting by brand:** The hosts argue that when non-Tesla vehicles crash into homes or cause fatalities, articles do not mention the manufacturer. One host describes a user on X who posted multiple examples of cars crashing into houses where no brand was named. Another example given: a Reddit post blaming Tesla's Dog Mode for a child's death was actually, per the host's research, a Hyundai Sonata where a child was left in a running gas car that ran out of fuel.

2. **Anti-Elon sentiment driving coverage:** The hosts acknowledge that dislike of Elon Musk as a political figure is understandable, but argue that weaponizing crash narratives to harm him personally results in delaying life-saving technology — which they frame as a net harm to humanity regardless of the motivation.

Notable quotes and data:
- "Tesla FSD is seven times safer supervised than human drivers." (hosts' claim, sourced generally to Tesla data)
- "44,000 people dying [annually on US roads]" — hosts argue FSD deployment could prevent these deaths; they also note global road deaths are much larger.
- "It's equivalent to a passenger jet falling out of the sky every day." (host's framing of US road fatality scale)
- "Someone said it's equivalent to solving cancer" — host flags this as unconfirmed: "I haven't confirmed this."
- The Texas crash: approximately 70 mph in a 25 mph zone; car was airborne; accelerator pedal remained depressed after the vehicle crashed through a house.
- 17 total robotaxi incidents reported since June 2025; Tesla released unredacted details approximately one to two months before this video (per hosts).
- January 2026 NHTSA report: 5 robotaxi incidents in one month, all described by hosts as under-4-mph parking lot contacts.
- A user named David Moss is cited by the host as having driven 30,000 miles on FSD in the past year, used as an example of an experienced FSD user who could have been consulted for fact-checking.
- The Chinese brake-failure woman: lost her lawsuit, paid a fine described as "substantial for an individual, inconsequential to Tesla," and was required to publicly apologize.

2026-06-25.title: Will Tesla Stock RECOVER?
2026-06-25.body:
Jo Bhakdi hosts a live stream addressing Tesla's steep five-day stock decline, arguing the selloff is driven by inorganic market distortions — likely linked to SpaceX liquidity flows and broader sector rotation — rather than any fundamental deterioration at Tesla. His core thesis is that the accelerating Cybercab manufacturing ramp makes an inflection point in commercial robotaxi deployment inevitable and imminent, and that the stock's weakness is temporary and increasingly irrational given the company's improving fundamentals. He draws on a technical analysis shared by "Lord Pretty Flaco" and fields extensive viewer questions about trading strategy, FSD readiness, a potential Tesla–SpaceX merger, and the broader market.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab production already exceeding 1,000 units:** Jo Bhakdi estimates Tesla has already produced over 1,000 Cybercabs, based on visual sightings across multiple locations. He reports seeing over 100 units in the Giga Texas parking lot in Austin, over 50 in Houston, over 50 in Dallas, an unspecified number in Los Angeles and Phoenix, and a large contingent in the Bay Area. He projects that Cybercab production will exceed 1,000 units in July alone, putting the cumulative total at roughly 2,000 by end of July.

2. **Manufacturing scale as the core bull argument:** Bhakdi's central thesis is that Tesla's operational, finance, and manufacturing departments — which he describes as best-in-class — would not greenlight mass-scale Cybercab production without a clear line of sight to commercial deployment. He argues it is economically irrational to accumulate thousands of Cybercabs (which cannot be sold and serve only one purpose — paid robotaxi operation) unless deployment is imminent. He dismisses the idea that Tesla needs thousands of units purely for testing purposes as "ridiculous."

3. **Geofenced rollout as bridge to full autonomy:** Bhakdi argues Tesla does not need perfect, ungated FSD to begin monetizing Cybercabs. He believes a transition period has already begun in which geofenced areas, remote operators, remote monitoring, and default safety systems can enable meaningful fleet deployment — potentially absorbing multiple thousands of Cybercabs — even before FSD achieves complete autonomy. He estimates full, un-geofenced autonomy may still be 12+ months away (possibly end of 2026 or into Q1 2027), but this does not preclude an early commercial rollout.

4. **Tesla vs. Waymo competitive framing:** Bhakdi contends Tesla only needs to be "more effective" than Waymo in geofenced areas to begin winning the robotaxi market, not perfect in absolute terms. He believes this competitive threshold has already been crossed or is very close, supporting the case for near-term deployment.

5. **Path to $1,000+ per share tied to Cybercab scale:** Bhakdi states that once Cybercab deployment reaches 1,000–2,000 units on a steep month-over-month scaling curve, he believes Tesla's stock can run to $1,000 per share extremely quickly. He says reaching $1,000 in 2026 is possible (not certain) if a commercial rollout occurs. He views $1,500 as a stretch in the near term.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD still not ready for full unsupervised deployment — but close:** Bhakdi is more measured on FSD than some commentators he references. He acknowledges ongoing user complaints about edge cases and says he takes them seriously. He believes FSD will not achieve complete autonomy until probably end of 2026 or Q1 2027, possibly even another year out. His bullishness on Tesla is not predicated on FSD being perfect today, but on Tesla's organizational competence and the inference drawn from the Cybercab manufacturing ramp.

2. **FSD version 14.3.4 referenced:** A viewer comment references FSD version 14.3.4 as the current build, and Bhakdi acknowledges some users may not yet be on it. He does not offer independent confirmation of the version number.

3. **FSD version 15 as potential geofence unlock:** Bhakdi references a view — which he attributes to some community members — that version 15 (expected around October–December 2026) may be the version enabling truly un-geofenced commercial operation. He does not endorse a specific timeline but uses this framing to argue that geofenced deployments can begin well before that milestone.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla Semi autonomous driving teased by community observers:** Bhakdi briefly references a community figure (Herbert) who claimed the Tesla Semi will "soon be driving autonomously," though Bhakdi characterizes Herbert as sometimes overly optimistic and does not confirm this himself.

2. **European sales turnaround cited as fundamental positive:** Bhakdi mentions 100% year-over-year growth in European Tesla sales as one of several fundamental improvements that make the stock's weakness appear irrational. He does not provide a specific volume figure.

## Market & Competition

1. **Inorganic stock movements linked to SpaceX liquidity:** Bhakdi's primary explanation for the erratic Tesla price action — a strong rally on Monday with no news, followed by a severe drop on Tuesday with no meaningful news — is that SpaceX-related liquidity flows are distorting Tesla trading. He explicitly distinguishes this from market manipulation, calling it a distortion caused by cash being pushed in and out non-organically. SpaceX shares reportedly fell ~16% on one day of the week discussed.

2. **Broader market sector rotation observed:** Bhakdi notes unusual cross-market behavior: Micron Technologies surged ~15% on strong earnings (validating the AI memory cycle), yet Nvidia, Amazon, and Apple all declined on the same day for no obvious reason. He also observes biotech and diagnostic stocks (Tempus, Personalis, Garden Health cited by name) rising ~10% with no catalyst, suggesting a rotation out of AI and into other sectors that he finds fundamentally unexplained.

3. **Uber and Lyft viewed as uninvestable:** Bhakdi states he cannot understand why anyone would buy Uber or Lyft stock, characterizing them as effectively dead once Tesla's robotaxi deployment materializes as widely expected. He uses the phrase "Russian roulette with seven bullets."

4. **SpaceX stock expected to fall significantly:** Bhakdi expresses a strongly bearish view on SpaceX's publicly traded shares. He does not see how SpaceX avoids falling below $135 and likely below $100, citing increasing selling pressure expected through November 2026. He views $75 as a reasonable entry point for accumulation but says he will wait for momentum and chart confirmation rather than a specific price level. He cites a viewer's $75 price target and calls it "reasonable." He notes SpaceX trades at a multiple far above comparable companies including Palantir, Tesla, Anthropic, and OpenAI.

5. **Tesla–SpaceX merger discussed but seen as unlikely in 2026:** Bhakdi addresses persistent community speculation about a Tesla–SpaceX merger. He believes a merger will ultimately happen and would add a significant premium to Tesla shares (he says he would vote yes at $750 per share and would be skeptical at $500). However, he argues the deal is far more legally and operationally complex than most commentators acknowledge. Key concern: Tesla conducting a merger of this scale just months after SpaceX's IPO would invite SEC scrutiny over whether merger plans were known at IPO and not disclosed. He thinks 2027 is a more realistic and de-risked timeline. He also dismisses the "merger of equals" structure as impractical given the extreme volatility of both stocks (a standard 20% deal-break clause would be triggered almost daily).

## Financials

1. **Q2 2026 earnings expected to be positive:** Bhakdi expresses confidence that Tesla's second-quarter 2026 earnings will be strong, citing the European sales recovery, energy business growth, and Cybercab ramp as tailwinds. He does not provide specific guidance figures.

2. **Trading position disclosed:** Bhakdi discloses he is holding short puts at strike prices of $375, $380, and $390 (weekly expiration) and has begun adding near-the-money call options (August expiration, $380 strike) at approximately $25–$26 each. He frames the calls as a probabilistic bet that Tesla will be at or above $405 by end of August, which he considers far more likely than remaining below $400. He describes his June trading as having been hurt by over-optimism following Monday's rally. He emphasizes not using margin to a degree that risks being forced out of positions.

3. **Personal price target of $490 by end of June reiterated but acknowledged as unlikely:** Bhakdi reiterates his end-of-June target of $490 but acknowledges the stock is more than $100 below that level with one week remaining. He describes reaching it as "possible" but "unlikely," and frames it humorously as "being down 10 goals with two minutes left."

Notable quotes and data:
- "This is 1 million percent a giant screaming buy, but not on margin."
- "A stock cannot endlessly crash when there is only good news all over the place."
- "You do not need thousands of Cybercabs for testing. That is so ridiculous."
- Jo Bhakdi estimates over 1,000 Cybercabs already produced; projects ~2,000 cumulative by end of July 2026.
- Cybercab visual sightings: 100+ at Giga Texas (Austin), 50+ in Houston, 50+ in Dallas, unknown quantities in LA, Phoenix, and the Bay Area.
- Tesla stock approximately $110 below Bhakdi's end-of-June $490 target at time of recording (~$370–$380 range implied).
- NASDAQ down ~3.38% on the day of the stream.
- Micron Technologies up ~15% on earnings day; market cap cited as just over $150 billion.
- SpaceX reportedly down ~16% earlier in the week.
- Oil price cited at ~$70/barrel.
- FSD version 14.3.4 referenced by a viewer as the current build.
- $380 August call options priced at approximately $25–$26 at time of recording.
- Bhakdi's merger vote threshold: yes at $750/share offered, skeptical at $500/share.
- SpaceX price targets discussed: $75 as a reasonable entry (viewer's estimate endorsed by Bhakdi); Bhakdi sees sub-$100 as likely eventually.
- "Once Cybercab starts scaling in earnest — 10,000 plus — Tesla can run up extremely fast to $1,000 per share."
- European Tesla sales cited as up 100% year-over-year (no absolute volume given).

2026-06-25.title: Daily X Summary (2026-06-25)
2026-06-25.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts from @SawyerMerritt were dominated by energy partnership news (a major Tesla-Sunrun-Renew Home distributed power deal), EV competitive dynamics (Slate Auto pricing, Zoox robotaxi update), and Cybertruck safety accolades from the IIHS. There were no major FSD/autonomy or Optimus updates, but the energy story and Cybertruck safety ratings carry meaningful signal for Tesla investors.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Tesla-Sunrun-Renew Home Virtual Power Plant Partnership:** Tesla, Sunrun, and Renew Home announced a partnership to create what they describe as the largest distributed power plant in the U.S., aggregating more than 16 GW of flexible power capacity from hundreds of thousands of distributed energy assets (home batteries, solar, EVs) to serve utilities and hyperscale data centers. This is a significant energy story — 16 GW is a substantial figure that signals Tesla's ambition to monetize its installed base of Powerwall and energy assets as a grid services platform, with hyperscale data centers as a key demand driver.

2. **Tesla Megapack Belgium Deal (~$700M):** Tesla has partnered with GIGA Storage to install a ~$700 million (estimated) Megapack battery energy storage facility in Belgium, designed to power approximately 385,000 homes. The project will utilize Tesla's next-generation Megablock technology with Megapack version 3, which is described as beginning production in late [the post appears truncated]. This represents a large international Megapack deployment using next-gen hardware, reinforcing the Energy segment's growth trajectory.

3. **Cybertruck Earns Top IIHS Safety Rating — Only Pickup to Avoid All Pedestrian Collisions:** The IIHS updated its Cybertruck crash test ratings, awarding it Top Safety Pick+ — the highest possible rating — making it the top-ranked large pickup truck for safety among both EVs and gas vehicles. Notably, the Cybertruck avoided every single pedestrian collision in testing, including a crossing child (day), crossing adult (night), and parallel adult (night). This is a meaningful demand and brand signal for Cybertruck, which has faced public perception challenges; IIHS Top Safety Pick+ is a credible third-party endorsement.

4. **Slate Auto Announces Budget EV Truck Pricing — Competitive Context for Tesla:** Slate Auto unveiled pricing for its small EV truck starting at $24,950 (pickup) and $29,950 (SUV version), with first deliveries targeted for Q4 2026. Specs include 205-mile range, a 63 kWh battery, 0–60 mph in 8.0 seconds, 90 mph top speed, and curb weights of 4,048 lbs (pickup) / 4,335 lbs (SUV). This is notable competitive context — a sub-$25K EV truck entering the market in late 2026 could pressure Tesla's entry-level positioning, though Tesla does not currently have a directly competing product in that price range.

5. **Zoox (Amazon) Unveils Updated Mass-Production Robotaxi Design:** Zoox revealed an updated robotaxi design it says will be the version going into mass production, with a claimed production capacity of up to 100 units per week. Updates include improved seating, new interior colors, and other refinements. This is a competitive data point for Tesla's robotaxi ambitions — Zoox's 100/week production rate claim is modest compared to Tesla's stated manufacturing scale aspirations, but it signals the competitive robotaxi market is progressing toward production-stage hardware.

6. **Starlink Expansion (SpaceX — Tangential):** Starlink announced installations on 80+ Oldendorff bulk shipping vessels and completed its first flight on an Iberia Airlines plane (Iberia plans to equip 35% of its long-haul fleet with Starlink in 2026). These are SpaceX/Starlink stories with no direct Tesla relevance; included for completeness given Elon Musk's role but low signal for Tesla investors specifically.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — The 16 GW distributed power plant partnership and the ~$700M Belgian Megapack deal reinforce Tesla's Energy segment as a serious, scaling business, while the Cybertruck's IIHS Top Safety Pick+ (the only pickup to avoid all pedestrian collisions) provides a credible demand catalyst for an otherwise challenged product line.

2026-06-26.title: Tesla's Robotaxi Pieces Are Falling Into Place
2026-06-26.body:
The video is a roundtable discussion hosted by "brighterwithherbert" featuring Tesla community commentators Alexandra Merz and Jeff Lutz, covering the accelerating regulatory tailwinds for autonomous vehicles, the visible buildup of Cybercabs at Giga Texas, and the broader strategic picture around Tesla's robotaxi rollout. The panel's core thesis is that multiple signals — NHTSA regulatory changes, a record Cybercab sighting at the Giga Texas lot, and Tesla's logistics hiring — are converging to suggest a coordinated, large-scale robotaxi launch is being carefully staged rather than indefinitely delayed. The hosts also address a viral media controversy over a Texas crash falsely attributed to Tesla's Autopilot, and discuss Elon Musk's naming of new AI infrastructure products (Starmind, Megapod).

## Autonomous Driving

1. **NHTSA drops manual brake pedal requirement for fully autonomous vehicles:** NHTSA announced it is removing the requirement for autonomous vehicles to carry manual brake pedals, provided the vehicle is designed exclusively for automated driving system operation. The panel views this as a significant regulatory unlock, with Jeff Lutz framing it as removing a major "fourth bucket" of readiness — regulatory — that had been constraining the robotaxi launch timeline alongside hardware, software, and field readiness. The announcement was also noted to have coincided with two high-profile autonomous vehicle accident news cycles, which the panel felt made the timing especially meaningful as a signal of government confidence in the technology.

2. **NHTSA joins global autonomous vehicle technical regulation framework:** NHTSA announced it voted in support of the world's first global technical regulation for autonomous driving systems at the UN World Forum. Alexandra Merz emphasized this as the highest-level regulatory approval yet, arguing it would make it significantly harder for individual nations — she specifically named Germany and the EU — to continue lobbying to slow autonomous vehicle deployment. The host expressed some skepticism about whether international bureaucratic frameworks translate quickly into practical change.

3. **Texas crash falsely attributed to Autopilot — media backlash:** A fatal crash in Texas went viral with widespread media headlines attributing it to Tesla's Autopilot or FSD. Ashok Elluswamy publicly clarified that the driver had manually overridden Full Self-Driving by pressing the accelerator pedal to 100% in a residential area, reaching 73–75 mph at the time of the crash, with the accelerator still pressed after impact. Elon Musk replied to a post calling the reporting "blatantly irresponsible," citing over 10 billion miles of data showing FSD is far safer than manual driving. The panel discussed whether FSD fully disengages steering when the accelerator is held to the floor, noting the investigation is ongoing. Alexandra Merz noted that Tesla shareholders — approximately 1,700 of them — had sent a letter to the Tesla board in January 2025 requesting Tesla sue media outlets for false reporting, with no follow-up. The panel expressed frustration that NTSB and NHTSA have both opened probes but that factual corrections never receive the same media amplification as the initial misleading headlines.

4. **FSD safety statistics not being communicated effectively:** Jeff Lutz argued that Tesla's safety data — showing FSD as many times safer than human driving — is not being effectively communicated to the public, and that media incidents risk repeating the dynamic that has kept US EV adoption at roughly 6–9%, where persistent negative coverage brainwashed a significant portion of the population with inaccurate information about EVs. He proposed Tesla work with media outlets to pair incident reporting with avoidance statistics, and Alexandra Merz advocated for Tesla to both sue the most egregious offenders and build a structured PR operation that ensures reporters can always reach someone at Tesla for a factual response.

## Robotaxi
