His thesis, maintained for five weeks, is that Trump cannot afford to let oil prices spike, making full escalation irrational and effectively off the table. He expects the situation to remain contained.

## Robotaxi
1. **Houston Cybercab fleet building rapidly:** Bhakdi highlights that Houston now has approximately 84 Cybercabs, with visible parking lots full of units. He frames this alongside hundreds reportedly staged in Austin as evidence of a deliberate, large-scale pre-deployment buildup across multiple cities, arguing Tesla would not be accumulating this inventory without an imminent rollout plan.

2. **First responder documentation signals commercial deployment prep:** Tesla published detailed first responder interaction plan PDFs for the Cybercab on June 28, 2026 — including an Arizona-specific appendix. Bhakdi describes the documents as comprehensive (~30 pages), covering vehicle identification, camera placement, VIN information, interior access, chainsaw-safe battery caution zones, and QR codes for emergency personnel. He emphasizes these filings are legally required by states before commercial autonomous vehicle operations can begin, and their publication strongly implies Tesla is preparing for imminent real-world deployment.

3. **Cybercab rollout timeline — weeks, not months:** Bhakdi had predicted June 2026 as the Cybercab commercial launch month and acknowledges he was wrong on that specific timing call. However, he argues the accumulating signals — fleet staging, first responder filings, regulatory documentation across states — make it "madness" to bet against a rollout within the next two to eight weeks. He stops short of committing to a specific date but says "something has to happen very soon."

4. **Stock price thesis tied directly to Cybercab action:** At the time of the stream, Tesla is trading at approximately $379, which Bhakdi describes as "completely ridiculous" given the operational progress. He believes Q3 2026 is the likely window for meaningful stock appreciation, contingent on Cybercab deployment. He holds August 21st at-the-money call options (strike ~$380) as his primary tactical position. He believes Tesla could double from current levels and potentially overshoot significantly if multiple thousands of robotaxis are rolling out with real momentum — he floats a range of $1,000 to potentially $10,000–$20,000 per share in a bull case, though he acknowledges $1,000 would already be an overshoot relative to near-term fundamentals.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Q2 2026 delivery consensus and Europe rebound:** Analyst consensus for Tesla Q2 2026 deliveries is approximately 46,000 (average) to 48,000 (median) per Bhakdi's reading of analyst estimates. He notes Giga Berlin is reportedly expanding Model Y production from 5,000 to 7,500 units per week in response to strong European demand, and that China also appears to be performing well in the quarter. He argues these delivery dynamics make the current stock price suppression even more anomalous.

Notable quotes and data:
- Fear & Greed Index: 25 (extreme fear) as of late June 2026
- Put/call ratio: approaching 0.9
- Tesla stock price at time of stream: ~$379
- Houston Cybercab count: ~84 units staged (per Bhakdi's observation)
- Analyst Q2 2026 Tesla delivery consensus: ~46,000 (average) / ~48,000 (median)
- Giga Berlin Model Y production: reportedly expanding from 5,000 → 7,500 units/week
- Tesla first responder Cybercab PDFs published: June 28, 2026
- Bhakdi's current options position: August 21 calls at ~$380 strike (at the money)
- Bull case stock target (robotaxi deployment scenario): $1,000 near-term overshoot; $10,000–$20,000 cited as possible in a "multiple thousands of robotaxis" scenario
- "When they cry, we buy" — Bhakdi's recurring mantra on sentiment extremes
- "Betting on Cybercab not rolling out very, very soon… would be madness"

2026-06-28.title: Daily X Summary (2026-06-28)
2026-06-28.body:
## Executive Summary
Today's posts were dominated by new official Cybercab documentation surfaced by Sawyer Merritt, confirming production-intent specs (no steering wheel, no pedals) and hinting that first public rides are imminent. A Tesla Semi autonomy testing sighting and a negative Waymo experience in Nashville rounded out the day's content, with a minor regulatory win on a closed NHTSA probe adding to the EV picture.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Cybercab official documentation reveals production specs and imminent public launch:** Multiple posts drew from newly released official Tesla Cybercab documentation, collectively painting the clearest picture yet of how the vehicle is designed. The standard production Cybercab has **two seats and is not equipped with a steering wheel, acceleration pedal, or brake pedal** — a hardware-level commitment to full autonomy. Vehicles spotted with a steering wheel are explicitly classified as engineering or test vehicles operating at **SAE Level 2**, not the production autonomous configuration. The documents also confirmed several notable hardware details: an **Active Hood** system that raises during certain pedestrian impacts to reduce injuries; **pressurized air canisters and camera washers** for sensor maintenance; and emergency protocols for situations where a Cybercab is stranded in the roadway or in a dangerous position. Sawyer's framing — "feels like the first public Cybercab rides are going to start very soon" — signals he reads the documentation release as a pre-launch signal. This is a meaningful milestone: official safety and operational documentation is typically finalized just ahead of public deployment. (Posts [1]–[5]; post [5] had 2.4K likes and 152 RTs, the highest single-post engagement of the day on a Tesla topic.)

2. **Tesla Semi spotted testing with autonomy validation gear:** A Tesla Semi was filmed in Palo Alto with **ground truth validation equipment** mounted on its roof — hardware used to benchmark and verify autonomous driving perception systems. The vehicle features **10 cameras and camera washers**, and Tesla's own materials describe it as **"autonomy ready."** This is a concrete data point that Tesla is actively developing autonomous capability for the Semi platform, beyond passenger vehicles. For investors tracking the long-term autonomous freight opportunity, this confirms active field testing is underway. (Post [8]; 4.6K likes and 319 RTs — the highest-engagement Tesla post of the day.)

3. **Waymo Nashville failure anecdote — competitive context:** Sawyer shared a firsthand negative Waymo experience in Nashville: the vehicle became confused and stuck within 4 minutes, required ~10 minutes of remote intervention from rider support, was unable to continue after that, and required escalation to a second specialist before ultimately completing the trip late. He noted the experience was "not great" (implied by the anecdote's structure). While one data point isn't statistically meaningful, this kind of visceral competitor stumble — shared by a high-profile Tesla bull to a large audience — reinforces the narrative that Waymo's operational reliability has room to improve, which contextually benefits Tesla's robotaxi positioning as it prepares to launch. (Post [6]; 2K likes, 129 RTs.)

4. **NHTSA closes power steering probe on 376,000 Tesla vehicles:** The NHTSA formally closed its preliminary evaluation (opened July 2023) into loss of steering control reports affecting **Model 3 and Model Y** vehicles. Tesla resolved the issue via an **over-the-air software update** (recall) issued last year, which satisfied the regulator. This is a clean regulatory closure with no hardware action required — a minor but positive signal for Tesla's regulatory standing and its OTA-update-as-recall model. (Post [7].)

5. **SpaceX joins Nasdaq-100 (tangential):** Nasdaq officially announced SpaceX will join the Nasdaq-100 effective **July 7, 2026**, with index funds beginning share purchases after market close on **July 6**. While SpaceX is a separate entity from Tesla, Elon Musk's involvement in both companies means SpaceX's rising institutional profile is a peripheral consideration for Tesla investors monitoring Musk's attention and capital allocation. This is low-signal for Tesla specifically but noted for completeness. (Post [10].)

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — The release of official Cybercab production documentation (confirming no steering wheel/pedals and detailing safety systems) combined with Sawyer's "very soon" public launch comment represents a concrete step toward robotaxi commercialization, while the autonomous Semi sighting extends the addressable market narrative.

2026-06-29.title: Weekly Tesla Brief (Jun 22 – Jun 28, 2026)
2026-06-29.body:
## Brief

- Official Cybercab first-responder PDFs published June 28, including Arizona appendix — legal pre-deployment requirement.
- NHTSA removes manual brake pedal mandate for fully autonomous vehicles.
- Tesla–NatPower $5B / 25 GWh Megapack deal — largest energy storage contract in Tesla history.
- June 30 IR commitment officially broken; Bhakdi shifts window to "two to eight weeks."
- Fatal Katy, TX crash: FSD was active; driver pressed accelerator to 100%.
- Optimus V3 supply chain activating; Taiwan component suppliers entering mass production H2 2026.
- Q2 delivery consensus 406K; Giga Berlin targeting 7,500 units/week by October.

---

## Robotaxi

- **Official Cybercab first-responder documentation published June 28** — ~30-page PDFs covering vehicle ID, camera placement, battery caution zones, and emergency QR codes, with an Arizona-specific appendix. Per Bhakdi, these filings are legally required before commercial AV operations begin in a state; Sawyer Merritt characterized the release as signaling "first public Cybercab rides are going to start very soon." Production spec confirmed in the filings: no steering wheel, no accelerator, no brake pedal. Vehicles observed with a wheel are explicitly classified as SAE Level 2 test units, not production configuration.

- **Cybercab staging inventory at record levels across multiple cities.** More than 150 units were counted at Giga Texas by June 26, up from prior milestones of 30, 50, and 100. Houston staging reached approximately 84 units per Bhakdi. Separately, a content creator documented Cybercabs arriving in the Washington D.C. area, the first confirmed sighting on the East Coast. Jeff Lutz noted that shipping units away from the factory — where rework is cheapest — is an implicit hardware-readiness signal.

- **June 30 IR commitment is definitively broken.** Tesla's Q4 2025 earnings deck committed to paid robotaxi service in Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Miami, and Phoenix by June 30; zero of those five cities are operational as the deadline expires. The Q1 2026 earnings deck quietly downgraded remaining target cities from date-specific language to "preparations underway." Bhakdi, who had held June as his primary window, now targets a two-to-eight-week horizon and stated explicitly: "As long as [Cybercab scale] doesn't happen, we have a problem… this stock will remain under pressure and trend down."

- **Demand is deliberately throttled; pricing at $3 drop + $1.40–$1.50/mile.** Per FutureAzA guest John, Tesla is intentionally holding prices high — up from launch-era $0.42/mile — to keep wait times under ~10 minutes given fleet constraints. John estimates Tesla could profitably price as low as $0.15/mile but is avoiding demand it cannot yet service. Waymo, for comparison, is running approximately 500,000 paid driverless rides per week across ~10 metros.

- **Cybercab engineered for 500,000-mile fleet duty life** versus approximately 150,000 miles for a consumer vehicle, and contains roughly 4,000 total parts — approximately half the Model 3's count. Waymo's sensor suite alone reportedly consists of ~4,000 parts, illustrating the structural cost gap between purpose-built and sensor-bolted-on approaches. Conversion from steering-wheel-equipped to pedal-free configuration can be performed in the field in hours.

---

## Autonomous Driving

- **NHTSA removed the manual brake pedal requirement for vehicles designed exclusively for automated operation**, opening a 30-day public comment period before a final DOT ruling. The agency framed the move as an effort to "safely unleash American innovation." For Tesla, it reduces the risk of NHTSA challenging the Cybercab's existing self-certification under FMVSS. Separately, the UNECE adopted the first-ever global AV framework — hardware-agnostic, no LiDAR mandate — backed by the US, EU, China, Japan, Canada, and the UK; binding only after domestic incorporation.

- **FSD 14.3.4 demonstrated zero disengagements across New York City**, including a full unsupervised trip from New Haven to NYC per Sawyer Merritt. A sideswipe-avoidance maneuver — briefly crossing a double yellow line to avoid a drifting vehicle — circulated widely and was cited by multiple commentators as evidence of reactive capability beyond conventional coded responses. FSD cumulative miles crossed 11.3 billion; the fleet now uploads approximately 30 million fresh miles daily.

- **Spain approval expected around June 30** per employees cited by the FutureAzA host; the Spanish testing fleet has grown from 19 to ~30 vehicles and covered ~275,000 km since November 2025 with zero serious incidents. Finland's Traficom stated FSD "is considered to have significant potential to reduce accidents" and may approve independently ahead of the EU-wide vote, now pushed to October 2026 at the earliest. China FSD full-fleet approval targeted Q3 2026; 200-vehicle test fleet is active, uploading ~1.7 TB/day.

---

## Optimus

- **Optimus V3 supply chain activating in Taiwan and Southeast Asia.** Tesla signed agreements with Merl Automation (harmonic reducers and joint modules, with a new Thailand joint venture) and Asia Optical (spherical and aspherical lens components for the vision system). Parts are slated for mass production H2 2026 into 2027 — supplier-level ramp preceding Tesla's own production line.

- **V3 reveal targeted late July to early August; Fremont line conversion on track for late summer.** V3's headline upgrade is 22 degrees of freedom per hand, doubled from 11, with actuators relocated to the forearm to reduce hand weight and increase speed. The former Model S/X line at Fremont is being converted for Optimus production, expected to complete around late summer 2026. First ~5,000 units are expected to be deployed across five to eight Tesla-owned facilities in California and Las Vegas.

- **Giga Texas Optimus factory steel now four stories tall**, projected at ~4,000+ feet in length at full build, targeting ~10 million units per year at full ramp. Realistic production-ready estimate from on-site observers remains end-2027 to 2028. Approximately 208 Optimus job listings are open across North America and Greece, led by 65 manufacturing/industrialization roles.

- **Digital Optimus emerging as a distinct near-term software product.** Ashok Elluswamy showed Digital Optimus on a slide during the week. Six of 17 AI/ML Optimus job listings explicitly name "Digital Optimus" — an agent running on the AI4 chip that operates computers via screen vision rather than APIs. Brian Wang (Next Big Future) expects a Macrohard/Digital Optimus demo by ~September 2026 and frames it as a potential near-term revenue catalyst. Caveat from brighterwithherbert: Anthropic shipped computer-use agents in 2024 and holds ~40% of enterprise API spend; Digital Optimus has no public benchmark.

---

## Tesla Semi

- **A second Tesla Semi was spotted in Palo Alto with autonomy validation hardware mounted on the roof**, drawing the highest single-post engagement of the day on June 28 (4.6K likes per Sawyer Merritt). Tesla's own materials describe the Semi as "autonomy ready" with 10 cameras with washers. Loomis does not expect unsupervised Semi FSD in serious consideration until 2028, but active validation testing is confirmed.

- **California incentives now stack to up to $240,000 off per Semi**: $120,000 via HVIP (up to 20 trucks) plus $120,000 via Clean Fuel Rewards with no truck cap. Real-world efficiency data from an Oklahoma fleet pilot: 1.55 kWh/mile — approximately 25% better than competing electric semis EPA-rated at 2.1+ kWh/mile.

---

## Energy

- **Tesla–NatPower deal is the largest energy storage contract in Tesla history**: 25+ GWh phase one across Italy and the UK, approximately $5 billion in construction value, with the full program targeting 100+ GWh and over $15 billion in revenues over 20 years. The prior largest single-source battery storage installation was approximately 12.3 GWh, making phase one alone more than twice that scale. The deal also embeds Tesla's Autobidder AI energy trading software — the stickier, higher-margin component.

- **Tesla–Giga Storage LOI for 2.8 GWh Megablock project in Limburg, Belgium** — the first Megablock deal at GWh scale, estimated value ~$700 million per Sawyer Merritt. Final contracts expected summer 2026. Combined with the NatPower deal and a $1 GWh Scotland project, Sawyer Merritt cited more than $6 billion in new Megapack announcements over recent weeks.

- **Tesla–Sunrun–Renew Home VPP aggregates 16.8 GW of flexible capacity** across hundreds of thousands of residential Powerwalls, EVs, and 8 million+ smart thermostats. Over 300 MW is immediately deployable in Virginia's Data Center Alley. Q2 2026 analyst consensus for energy storage is 13.8 GWh; Q1 came in at 8.8 GWh with record 39.5% gross margin, though management flagged some margin compression ahead from tariffs on Chinese cells.

- **Megapod trademark filed June 18**: modular AI inference data centers co-located at Supercharger stations, which already carry approximately 7 GW of permitted grid connections. Elon Musk confirmed the name and described eventual scale as millions of units. The AI4 chip ($650) serves as shared silicon across FSD vehicles, Optimus, and Megapod — a single inference platform across three form factors.

---

## Electric Vehicles

- **Giga Berlin targeting 7,500 Model Y/week by October 2026**, a second consecutive ~20% production increase adding ~1,000 workers. At full rate, ~375,000 units/year from Berlin alone. Electrified estimates the incremental step adds ~$6.2 billion in annual revenue and over $1.2 billion in gross profit at a 20% margin.

- **Q2 2026 delivery consensus is 406,000 units** (Tesla-compiled street estimate per Sawyer Merritt); Goldman Sachs is at 420,000, saying deliveries are "tracking ahead of consensus." Q1 2026 was 358,000. Report due approximately July 2–3. Europe is carrying the quarter (+108% YoY in May registrations); China is tracking ~-11% YoY and the US is down mid-teens percent YoY.

- **Model YL US production targeting August–September 2026 at Giga Texas**, priced at approximately $54,000 — roughly $4,000 above the current AWD Model Y. Adds ~6 inches of wheelbase and a 2-2-2 seating configuration with heated/ventilated captain's chairs in row 2. Source is Not a Tesla App; unconfirmed by Tesla.

- **Cybertruck earned IIHS Top Safety Pick+ for 2026** — the only pickup of any powertrain to clear all four pedestrian front crash prevention scenarios. Tesla Vision airbag deployment now up to 70 milliseconds faster via OTA, using exterior cameras to identify contact timing before impact sensors alone would trigger.

---

## Financials

- **Over $500 million in Q-period Tesla revenue sourced from other Musk entities**: Megapack deployments to xAI, $78 million in additional xAI revenue, and $143 million in Cybertruck purchases by SpaceX and xAI. Analysts also flagged $480 million in non-recurring tariff and warranty margin adjustments in the same period. Hosts expect Megapack revenue from xAI to recur; Cybertruck fleet purchases are viewed as unlikely to repeat at the same scale.

- **Q2 2026 earnings setup**: brighterwithherbert cites European sales recovery (+108% YoY in May), Megapack demand momentum, and Cybercab manufacturing ramp as the three pillars. SpaceX mark-to-market on Tesla's equity stake estimated at ~$2B / ~$0.75/share Q2 contribution (unconfirmed). Q2 earnings expected third to fourth week of July.

---

## Market & Competition

- **SpaceX joins the Nasdaq-100 effective July 7, 2026.** Index fund purchases begin after market close July 6. Further MSCI and potential S&P 500 inclusion expected, though S&P has historically been less accommodating to Musk-affiliated entities. Bhakdi warns of significant Tesla selling pressure through November 2026 when SpaceX lockup expirations bring approximately 400% of current float to market.

- **VW reportedly weighing up to 100,000 job cuts and closure of four German factories** — potentially the largest restructuring in automotive history, driven by weak sales. VW stock is down ~60% over three years. BMW discontinued its Personal Pilot L3 system entirely; Mercedes paused Drive Pilot from upcoming facelifts. FSD Supervised is now the most capable driver-assistance system widely available in Europe.

- **Musk compensation restructured from stock options to restricted stock with a five-year lock-up** around June 17, 2026, per Alexandra Merz — giving him voting rights but binding him to Tesla as a key person for five years. Framed as a strong long-term commitment signal, though the structural conflict between Musk's personal financial timeline (options expiring August 15) and operational milestone requirements remains.

---

## Bear Case of the Week

- **Katy, TX fatal crash: FSD was confirmed active.** Ashok Elluswamy confirmed via public statement that FSD was engaged when driver Michael Butler manually overrode the system by pressing the accelerator to 100% pedal travel, reaching 73–75 mph in a residential 25 mph zone and striking a home, killing 76-year-old Martha Avila Mantilla. NHTSA opened a Special Crash Investigation and maintains a separate Engineering Analysis covering ~3.2 million vehicles. Elon initially posted "FSD drives slowly through neighborhood streets" — a claim his own company's telemetry then contradicted. Electrek argues the "driver overrode it" defense does not constitute exoneration: the most plausible behavioral scenario is an out-of-the-loop emergency response where the driver hit the accelerator instead of the brake — identical to the grounds on which a Florida jury found Tesla 33% liable in a $243 million judgment upheld February 2026.

- **June 30 IR commitment missed with no credible successor date.** Tesla's binding Q4 2025 earnings deck commitment to paid robotaxi service in Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Miami, and Phoenix by June 30 expires this week with zero of five cities operational. The Q1 2026 earnings deck quietly replaced date-specific language with "preparations underway." Bhakdi — who had defended June as his primary window across multiple prior briefs — has now shifted to a two-to-eight-week horizon. The miss is the third consecutive weekly brief in which this deadline has appeared; it is now factually closed.

- **Paid robotaxi miles remain negligible.** The Q1 2026 earnings deck disclosed paid robotaxi miles "nearly doubled sequentially" in Q1 — from approximately one million to approximately 1.7 million cumulative miles. That figure represents roughly three to four days of Waymo's current weekly output of 500,000 paid driverless rides. Musk's original Austin target of 500 unsupervised vehicles by end of 2025 and Bhakdi's prior projection of 1,800 unsupervised units by April–May 2026 have both been missed by a wide margin. The unsupervised fleet count tracked by RobotaxiTracker.com has not updated since May 9, 2026 — now 51 days stale.

- **Two FSD 14.3.4 edge-case failures documented this week.** In one incident, FSD drove over a gas can that had fallen from a trailer without detecting it; Tesla's Yun Tasai acknowledged the clip. In a second, FSD prepared to proceed through a lowered railroad crossing arm. Loomis noted the inconsistency with FSD's demonstrated ability to brake hard for small animals — the same object-detection pipeline. Both clips circulated publicly during the same week Tesla is seeking EU-wide regulatory approval.

- **Optimus missed 2025 production targets; V3 hand design previously failed.** Brighterwithherbert explicitly states Tesla missed its 2025 Optimus unit numbers and that most current Optimus robots work inside Tesla's own factories. Elon reportedly acknowledged in ~May 2026 that the most recently patented hand design "didn't work," implying the program is on its fourth or fifth hand iteration. China's Unitree shipped thousands of cheaper humanoids in 2025; Figure has a live factory pilot with BMW. The 2026 targets of 50,000–100,000 units are described by the FutureAzA host as definitively unachievable: "it's going to be much less."

2026-06-29.title: The Rules Just Changed For Robotaxis
2026-06-29.body:
This video from brighterwithherbert features host Herbert and guest Larry Goldberg, a serial entrepreneur and venture capital investor, discussing a wave of regulatory milestones for autonomous vehicles alongside the scrutiny Tesla continues to face over FSD-related incidents. The central argument is that the regulatory environment is meaningfully improving for the entire AV industry — including Tesla's Cybercab — but that Tesla is held to a far higher public and media standard than competitors like Waymo, making a cautious, deliberate rollout strategically necessary.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **NHTSA eliminates manual brake pedal requirement for fully autonomous vehicles:** NHTSA announced it will remove the mandate for hand- or foot-operated brake controls on vehicles designed never to be operated by a human. Existing rules continue to apply to AVs that retain manual controls, and all vehicles must still meet the same stopping distance performance criteria via alternative testing procedures. The host notes this builds on a 2022 loosening of rules that had already removed steering wheel and pedal requirements in principle — the new announcement solidifies and extends that framework specifically for brake controls.

2. **United Nations adopts first-ever global regulatory framework for autonomous driving:** The UN Economic Commission for Europe (UN ECE) adopted the world's first global technical regulation for automated driving systems, with a positive vote expected in June 2026. The framework incorporates elements of the U.S. DOT's AV framework and is intended to help streamline AV approvals across Europe and other participating countries. Larry Goldberg cautions that Europe has a history of layering additional regulatory complexity onto global frameworks, and notes that Tesla's association with Elon Musk makes it a political football in Europe, creating further uncertainty about whether full autonomy will materialize there on any near-term timeline.

3. **NTSB opens investigation into Texas crash; Tesla disputes FSD involvement:** The NTSB has joined NHTSA in investigating a recent Texas crash in which a woman in a house was killed when a vehicle struck it. Tesla and Ashok Elluswamy stated that telemetry data shows the driver had the accelerator floored the entire time, reaching 73 mph, and that the car was not operating under FSD in the manner portrayed. The family of the victim has filed a lawsuit against both the driver (identified as Michael Butler) and Tesla, alleging negligence. The host and guest emphasize this will not be the last such incident and that media coverage consistently attributes crashes to FSD regardless of actual fault.

4. **FSD safety vs. public perception disconnect:** Larry Goldberg argues that supervised FSD is already demonstrably safer than human driving and cites a personal anecdote from the same day — FSD automatically stopped his vehicle when a car ran a red light and turned directly in front of him at speed. He contends that even a genuine FSD-caused fatality in the future will be covered crash-by-crash rather than in the context of the dramatic overall reduction in road deaths that autonomy could deliver. The host notes the U.S. sees roughly 44,000 motor vehicle deaths per year, with approximately 30% attributed to texting, and argues that autonomous driving could reduce that figure dramatically even if it cannot reach zero.

5. **Waymo accumulates serious operational incidents while receiving minimal media scrutiny:** Dillon Loomis is cited as having compiled a list of recent Waymo incidents that the host argues have received far less public attention than any Tesla incident would. These include: hitting a child; illegally passing school buses with active red lights; fully blocking a street and obstructing ambulance and first responders during a mass shooting; six vehicles failing to recognize ramp closure signs and driving into active freeway construction zones in Texas; seven vehicles driving between cones and entering freeway construction lanes in California — prompting Waymo to voluntarily restrict its entire fleet from all freeway and highway operations. NHTSA also recalled approximately 3,800 Waymo vehicles after they drove into flooded roads, and Waymo suspended service in Atlanta, Dallas, Houston, San Antonio, and Nashville. The host argues Tesla could likely already scale beyond its current deployment but will not receive the same lenient treatment from media and regulators that Waymo appears to get.

## Robotaxi

1. **Regulatory clarity may be a factor in Tesla's Cybercab rollout pace:** The host speculates that Tesla may have been waiting for regulatory paperwork — specifically, formal confirmation that vehicles without steering wheels or brake pedals are permissible — before scaling Cybercab deployment on its robotaxi service. He notes that Tesla was able to self-certify the Cybercab without steering wheels or pedals under the existing framework, unlike Zoox, which sought self-certification and was denied by NHTSA due to insufficient crash test data. The guest suggests the delay reflects Tesla designing deliberately for true scale rather than a forced slowdown.

2. **Zoox unveils refined robotaxi vehicle, targets 100 units per week:** Zoox revealed a refined version of its robotaxi, featuring elevator-style sliding doors, face-to-face bench seating with no steering wheel or pedals, improved seat padding and ergonomics, an updated touchscreen, redesigned wireless charging, larger cup holders, and a two-way audio system. The vehicle is intended for Zoox's mass-production fleet, to be built at its Hayward manufacturing facility, with a stated target of up to 100 units per week. Larry Goldberg dismisses 100 units per week as nowhere near true mass production, arguing that scale requires something closer to 100 units per day at minimum, and that Zoox's volume cap (noted by the host as approximately 2,500–2,600 vehicles under current self-certification limits) makes it fatally constrained as a business. He contrasts this with Tesla's stated ambition of producing one Cybercab roughly every two minutes — approximately 30 per hour.

3. **Tesla's scale advantage remains decisive despite delays:** Both the host and guest agree that Tesla is uniquely positioned to reach the scale required to replace human drivers in meaningful numbers, pointing to its existing production infrastructure, its fleet of millions of consumer vehicles gathering real-world FSD data, and its purpose-built Cybercab. Larry Goldberg frames Waymo and Zoox as "playing at the edges" — producing on the order of 5,000 vehicles per year each — and argues that robotaxi economics only work at a scale of hundreds of millions of vehicles. He also notes the Cybercab will almost certainly be less expensive to produce than the Zoox vehicle. The host acknowledges the rollout has taken longer than anticipated but argues Tesla's higher self-imposed safety standard is the correct strategic choice given the asymmetric media and regulatory risk it faces.

## Market & Competition

1. **New York City blocking autonomous vehicle entry; pattern mirrors Uber resistance:** The host notes that New York City has effectively said no to Waymo operating there, drawing a parallel to the city's earlier resistance to Uber. He argues NYC has a pattern of using regulatory tools to block innovation rather than promote it, citing also the city's rejection of Amazon and Citadel headquarters. Larry Goldberg describes the broader dynamic as cities becoming resistant to change, though neither speaker expects this to ultimately stop the national or global trajectory toward autonomy.

2. **Rivian and Lucid called out as noise, not competitors:** The host briefly dismisses Rivian and Lucid as companies whose autonomous or robotaxi ambitions will remain "talk and promises for years to come" with no real scale or volume, contrasting them with Tesla's actual deployment progress.

---

**Notable quotes and data:**

- ~44,000 motor vehicle deaths per year in the U.S. (host's figure); ~30% attributed to distracted driving/texting.
- Host's hypothetical: reducing 44,000 annual deaths to ~5,000 through autonomous driving — still generating public backlash focused on individual incidents.
- Zoox production target: up to 100 units per week at Hayward facility.
- Tesla's stated Cybercab production ambition: approximately one every two minutes (~30/hour), per Larry Goldberg.
- Waymo NHTSA recall: approximately 3,800 vehicles for driving into flooded roads.
- Waymo voluntarily restricted its entire fleet from freeway and highway operations following repeated construction-zone failures.
- Larry Goldberg: "We've reached a point where the car is fully capable of autonomy. Fully capable of autonomy. That's where we're at."
- Larry Goldberg on Zoox/Waymo volumes: "When you're making 5,000 cars a year or 15,000 cars a year, that's not a business."
- Texas crash: Tesla telemetry data shows driver had accelerator floored, vehicle travelling at 73 mph; Ashok Elluswamy cited as having confirmed this publicly.

2026-06-29.title: Ashok Delivered Early, Fleet Growing, Amsterdam Hiring—It's Happening
2026-06-29.body:
The video covers three major Tesla developments: Ashok Elluswamy's rollout of FSD version 14 Light to Hardware 3 vehicles, continued growth of Tesla's robotaxi fleet across Texas and Fremont, and the quiet release of Tesla's first official Cybercab first responder guide. The host Herbert and guest Jeff Lutz also preview an exclusive interview they conducted with Tesla VP of Vehicle Engineering Lars Moravy at the Fremont factory, teasing significant announcements about Cybercab production volume, Optimus manufacturing progress, and a Giga Texas announcement expected July 7, 2026.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Version 14 Light rolls out to Hardware 3 on schedule:** Ashok Elluswamy announced that FSD version 14 Light is now rolling out to Hardware 3 (AI3) vehicles, hitting his self-imposed end-of-June deadline. The build distills the driving behavior from Hardware 4's version 14 series into the camera and compute configuration of Hardware 3. It includes destination options and speed profiles on city roads, along with significantly improved safety. Improvements cited in the release notes include better navigation handling, merges and forks, pedestrian interactions, traffic light and vehicle-cutting scenarios, smoother steering, more consistent lane centering, parking/unparking/reverse, and added speed profiles. Elon Musk publicly acknowledged the rollout with "Nice work."

2. **Engineering challenge of AI3's hardware constraints:** Jeff Lutz highlights that Hardware 3 has only approximately 15% of the effective memory bandwidth of Hardware 4, making this a significant engineering achievement. He notes there are an estimated 3–4 million Hardware 3 vehicles in the fleet, making this a commercially important update that could unlock FSD subscription revenue and fulfill obligations to customers who purchased FSD outright. He flags that whether Hardware 3 vehicles will ever reach unsupervised capability remains an open question, though he believes Tesla is committed to pursuing it.

3. **Early user feedback strongly positive:** Early access testers, including one named Kristen, tested the build across highway, residential, and back-road conditions and found it comparable in feel to version 14 on a Hardware 4 vehicle. Another early tester (Zach) described it as a "big leap in capability and feature set from version 12.6." The host notes the build is tuned for safety as a priority.

4. **Hardware upgrade path for AI3 owners remains complex:** Jeff Lutz cautions that upgrading Hardware 3 vehicles to Hardware 4 is not a simple swap — harnesses and cameras differ, making it a significant field rework effort. He suggests Tesla may need differentiated strategies: field upgrades for lower-volume Model S/X owners and purchase incentives (potentially tied to FSD subscriptions) for the higher-volume Model 3/Y base.

## Robotaxi

1. **Texas robotaxi fleet reaches 84 registered Model Ys:** Texas DMV records show 15 new 2026 Model Y vehicles were added to Tesla's robotaxi fleet, bringing the total registered in Texas to 84. The host argues the continued addition of Model Ys alongside Cybercab production is evidence the robotaxi program is operationally ready, not stalled.

2. **78 Cybercabs spotted actively testing in Houston lot:** Independent observer SE Robinson counted 78 Cybercabs in a Houston fleet lot, with the host noting additional units were out on active test runs at the time of the count. Jeff Lutz contextualizes this as typical of an early production ramp, where vehicles serve multiple purposes — engineering testing, marketing, and pre-launch staging — before production-ready units begin to dominate.

3. **Hundreds of Cybercabs spotted staged at Fremont factory:** John from Tesla Own Silicon Valley flew a drone over the Fremont factory and discovered a newly identified lot containing hundreds of robotaxi vehicles — Cybercabs and Model Ys — apparently staged for launch. The host describes this as a previously unknown lot that had not been publicly observed before.

4. **Lars Moravy confirms Cybercab production on schedule and teases July 7 announcement:** In the preview of the exclusive interview, Lars Moravy confirms Cybercab production is on schedule and says the factory automation ramp — which he had anticipated would be the hardest part — went more smoothly than expected, crediting accumulated experience from prior vehicle launches. He teased that on Tuesday, July 7, 2026, there will be "cool news about things happening on the campus of Giga Texas" related to the scaling effort, volunteering this information unprompted after a detailed discussion of Cybercab. Moravy also reportedly emphasized that "people have no idea what the volume of this thing is going to be," which Jeff Lutz calls one of the most compelling statements of the entire interview.

5. **Cybercab described as a fundamentally different manufacturing paradigm:** Jeff Lutz emphasizes that Cybercab is not just a different form factor from Model Y or Model 3 — it represents a different method of manufacturing entirely, years in development. He describes the current period (approximately 9–10 weeks into production) as the first quarter of ramp, characterized by yield improvement and station optimization before production run rates are increased.

6. **First official Cybercab first responder guide released:** Tesla quietly released its first official Cybercab first responder guide, distributed to police, fire departments, and city officials. The guide confirms the production Cybercab operates as a SAE Level 4 robotaxi with no steering wheel or pedals. Key confirmed details include: 10 airbags; an active hood that raises pre-impact to reduce pedestrian injuries; pressurized air canisters and camera washers; exterior microphones and speakers for two-way communication; two first responder emergency loops (one under the hood, one behind the passenger-side pillar); a 400V and 48V dual-voltage battery system; an orange-colored battery pack coolant; a charge port centered below the trunk with a hidden manual emergency charge cable release behind the rear wheel liner; and the ability for first responders to manually move the vehicle using onboard controls. The guide also confirms autonomous operation capability on all public roadways (freeways, highways, city streets, rural roads) and private roadways (parking lots, charging stations, car washes, parking garages), at all times of day and night, and under light to moderate precipitation including rain, fog, and snow. In extreme weather, the vehicle is designed to pull over and notify Tesla's robotaxi operations team.

7. **Cybercab branding confirmed; steering wheel units are test/engineering vehicles:** The first responder guide confirms that in-service Cybercabs will carry the "Cybercab" wordmark on the sides and trunk lid. Cybercabs equipped with steering wheels, brake pedals, and acceleration pedals are designated engineering or test vehicles operating at Level 2 autonomy. The host notes Tesla may use "Cybercab" rather than "robotaxi" in some jurisdictions where use of the word "taxi" or "cab" is legally restricted, though the decal can easily be changed.

8. **Tesla hiring for robotaxi service operations in Amsterdam:** Tesla posted a vehicle software engineer internship role in Amsterdam focused on robotaxi and service operations, signaling that the robotaxi network is being developed for international expansion into Europe. Jeff Lutz suggests this likely involves localization work for European markets.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Lars Moravy gives detailed update on Optimus production line status:** In the Lars Moravy interview preview, Moravy provided a detailed answer about where Optimus manufacturing currently stands, including the level of automation in place and whether the production approach follows a serial modular "unbox-type" manufacturing model. Jeff Lutz states that based on Moravy's answer — particularly the specific stage of automation he described — it signals they are "getting very close" on the Optimus production line. Lutz notes the answer was technically detailed and that the implications are more optimistic than a casual listener might initially interpret.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cybercab as a new sales channel for Model Y inventory:** Jeff Lutz notes that Tesla's ability to channel Model Y production directly into the robotaxi fleet represents a new and efficient sales channel, complementing what he describes as already best-in-class inventory management. He frames this as a structural advantage: Tesla can produce Model Ys just-in-time for fleet deployment without accumulating unsold inventory.

Notable quotes and data:
- Lars Moravy (per host preview): "People have no idea what the volume of this thing is going to be" — referring to Cybercab production volumes.
- Lars Moravy (per clip): "From Tuesday, there'll be some cool news about things happening on the campus of [Giga] Texas… as part of the scaling effort." — announcement expected July 7, 2026.
- Ashok Elluswamy on FSD version 14 Light: "This build distills the driving behavior from AI4's version 14 series into both the camera and compute config of AI3… significantly improved safety."
- Elon Musk on FSD version 14 Light: "Nice work."
- Early tester Kristen: "Feels as good as version 14 to me on an AI4 vehicle."
- Hardware 3 has approximately 15% of the effective memory bandwidth of Hardware 4.
- Estimated 3–4 million Hardware 3 vehicles in the Tesla fleet.
- 84 Model Ys now registered as Tesla robotaxi vehicles in Texas (up 15 from prior count).
- 78 Cybercabs counted by independent observer in Houston fleet lot.
- Cybercab first responder guide confirms: SAE Level 4, no steering wheel/pedals in production version, 10 airbags, operates in rain/fog/snow, all road types including private roadways.
- Cybercab production entered approximately 9–10 weeks ago per Jeff Lutz's estimate.
- Tesla hiring for robotaxi service operations internship in Amsterdam.
- Full interview with Lars Moravy to be published the day after this video (i.e., June 30, 2026).

2026-06-29.title: Where Tesla's Robotaxi Rollout Actually Stands
2026-06-29.body:
This video from the Cern Basher channel covers the current state of Tesla's robotaxi rollout, with particular focus on new FSD capability announcements from Elon Musk, Cybercab production and staging activity at Giga Texas, and what various field observations suggest about the pace of autonomous deployment. The hosts analyze a cluster of signals — fleet movements, decal applications, overseas testing — to argue that Tesla is methodically preparing for a broader robotaxi launch rather than experiencing delays. The core thesis is that while there is no single dramatic announcement, the accumulating evidence points toward an imminent expansion of robotaxi service to new cities.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD Four-Month Safety Milestone and Parking as the Last Friction Point:** The hosts note that FSD has now gone approximately four months since February without any at-fault incidents, and that global regulatory approvals continue to expand. Elon Musk responded to a user post celebrating a 13-day, 96% autonomous driving streak by stating that upcoming FSD releases will remember individual parking preferences — home, office, school drop-off — calling destination parking "by far the biggest reason people now intervene with FSD." The hosts interpret this as Elon confirming that critical safety is no longer the primary challenge; the remaining friction is convenience and personalization.

2. **Grok Voice Control of FSD Coming in ~3 Months:** In a separate exchange on X, Elon replied to a user requesting the ability to give conversational commands to the car — such as directing drop-off location or instructing the vehicle to park itself remotely — saying this functionality would arrive "in about 3 months or so." The hosts characterize this as robotaxi-level capability: not just a question-and-answer interface like ChatGPT, but direct natural-language control of vehicle behavior while FSD is active.

3. **Persistent Memory as a Platform Shift for FSD:** The hosts discuss at length what it means for FSD to gain persistent memory. Currently, they note, FSD reacts purely to real-time conditions, which is why it can behave differently in identical-looking situations. With memory, the system could learn preferred routes, preferred parking lots at specific locations (not just at home), and even user-specific behavioral patterns. One host raises the possibility that memory could extend to things like known speed enforcement zones. Another host flags a hardware constraint: existing vehicles were not designed to store large amounts of persistent data, though upgrading the onboard storage stick to 5 GB or 10 GB is described as technically trivial and inexpensive. The hosts also note that the upcoming AI5 and AI6 chips will carry significantly larger memory capacity, though they clarify that chip memory is volatile rather than persistent storage.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab Staging at Giga Texas Reaching Record Levels:** The hosts report that 102 Cybercabs were spotted in the open lot at Giga Texas — described as a record — up from earlier observations of 20, then 30, then 50 units. One host, drawing on manufacturing experience, interprets the outward movement of vehicles from the factory as a positive signal: companies typically keep brand-new products close to the factory during early reliability validation, and the decision to stage cars at distributed sites suggests Tesla has passed a meaningful maturity threshold. He also notes that available parking near the factory is not the constraint, meaning Tesla is actively choosing to move the vehicles — suggesting something is "forcing their hand" toward deployment.

2. **Cybercabs Now Appearing with Service Decals:** The hosts observe that Cybercabs coming out of the factory are now being fitted with Tesla robotaxi decals on the sides and back, which one host interprets as preparation for vehicles that will actually be put into revenue service rather than held for internal testing. He notes the timeline remains uncertain — Tesla could stage cars in multiple cities before any formal unveil — but this cosmetic preparation is a meaningful signal of forward progress.

3. **Cybercabs Spotted in New Zealand for Testing:** Several Cybercabs were reportedly spotted in New Zealand, which the hosts attribute to a combination of cold-weather testing and left-hand-traffic testing for FSD. One host notes Tesla has used New Zealand as a testing ground for vehicles before, calling it unsurprising. The hosts also note the reaction of local observers who had no idea what the vehicle was.

4. **Q2 Robotaxi City Expansion Deadline Approaching:** The hosts reference a prior Tesla statement that robotaxi service would roll out to additional cities before the end of Q2 2026. Given the video's publish date of June 29, 2026, they note the deadline is essentially upon them and that if Tesla is still on track, an announcement should be imminent. The combination of decal application, large-scale staging, and distributed vehicle movement is presented as circumstantial evidence that Tesla remains on that timeline.

5. **Cybercab Ramp-Up Cadence:** One host shares his expectation that Cybercab production would ramp from dozens of units in April to hundreds in May, reaching thousands of units per week by the end of June. He frames this as his personal projection rather than confirmed data, and notes that without continuous drone coverage it is difficult to track actual output. He also raises the open question of whether Tesla is intentionally pacing Cybercab scale relative to the autonomous network rollout rather than pushing maximum production volume.

Notable quotes and data:
- Elon Musk on FSD: *"Upcoming releases of FSD will remember your parking preferences so that the car goes to the right location at your home, office, school drop-off. Destination parking is by far the biggest reason people now intervene with FSD."*
- Elon Musk on Grok integration: *"This functionality will be there in about 3 months or so"* (in response to a request for natural-language vehicle control via Grok).
- 102 Cybercabs spotted in the open lot at Giga Texas — described as a record, up from prior counts of ~20, ~30, and ~50.
- FSD has gone approximately four months since February 2026 without an at-fault incident.
- One host's personal production ramp estimate: dozens of Cybercabs in April, hundreds in May, thousands per week by end of June 2026 (unconfirmed).
- Joe Tegtmeyer referenced by name as the drone videographer covering Giga Texas, noted as having been in Europe for ~2 weeks.

2026-06-29.title: We've Been Asking the Wrong Question About Nvidia
2026-06-29.body:
This video from farzad-fm argues that the conventional framing of the AI chip war — "who will beat Nvidia?" — is the wrong question entirely. The host contends that most serious chip competitors are not attacking Nvidia's training stronghold but are instead staking out differentiated positions in the rapidly expanding inference market. The core thesis is that as inference (running AI models) displaces training (building them) as the dominant compute workload, the real prize is collecting the toll on every AI interaction — and that Nvidia, AMD, Groq, Cerebras, and Tesla are each pursuing fundamentally different strategies to claim a piece of that.

## Market & Competition

1. **Nvidia's dominant position and the CUDA moat:** Nvidia's data center business generated approximately $75 billion in revenue in the quarter ending April 2026, up roughly 92% year-over-year, with gross margins near 75%. The host attributes this dominance not primarily to chip hardware but to CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture), a software layer Nvidia has been building since 2006. With roughly 18 years of accumulated ecosystem — university curricula, engineering workflows, tooling — CUDA functions as an effectively insurmountable switching cost for anyone trying to compete on identical terms. Nvidia's current-generation chip (Blackwell) is shipping in volume, and the next generation (Rubin) is expected to ramp in the second half of 2026.

2. **The training-to-inference shift as the structural thesis:** The host argues that the center of gravity in AI compute has decisively shifted. As of 2026, inference already accounts for roughly two-thirds of all AI computing globally and is still growing toward 70–80%. Training was the original gold rush; inference is described as "the forever money" — because a model is trained once but queried potentially billions of times daily. This shift is framed as the single most important variable for evaluating every chip company's long-term position.

3. **AMD's strategy — direct competition with a software handicap:** AMD is characterized as the only credible general-purpose number-two in AI chips. Its bet is straightforward: build a faster, cheaper version of Nvidia's own product. In one major independent benchmark cited from 2026, AMD's top chip came within a few percentage points of Nvidia's best on inference workloads. AMD's next-generation chip reportedly includes more high-speed memory than Nvidia's current flagship. The persistent obstacle is ROCm, AMD's answer to CUDA, which the host says has improved significantly but remains the wall AMD keeps "slamming into." The host's outlook: AMD is unlikely to dethrone Nvidia soon but has a solid path to staying a strong distant number two, particularly as large cloud customers seek a second supplier to avoid full pricing dependence on Nvidia.

4. **Groq's inference-speed play and Nvidia's acquisition maneuver:** Groq, founded in 2016 by Jonathan Ross (who previously built Google's first TPU as an internal side project), built its LPU (Language Processing Unit) specifically for inference speed. The chip delivers a time-to-first-token of approximately 18 milliseconds versus 200–400 milliseconds on typical GPU cloud setups — roughly 10–20 times faster — by storing model weights in on-chip SRAM rather than external memory. The tradeoff is that each chip holds only about 230 megabytes versus an Nvidia H100's 80 gigabytes, requiring hundreds of chips wired together to run large models. On Christmas Eve 2025, Nvidia struck a deal the host values at approximately $20 billion: a perpetual, non-exclusive license to Groq's entire patent portfolio and software stack, combined with the hiring of Jonathan Ross, president Sunny Madra, and approximately 80% of Groq's staff. The host underscores that Nvidia deliberately avoided a full acquisition — licensing technology and hiring people rather than buying the company outright — to sidestep antitrust scrutiny.

5. **Cerebras — wafer-scale chips and customer concentration risk:** Cerebras took an extreme architectural bet: instead of slicing a silicon wafer into hundreds of standard chips, it kept the entire wafer as a single chip — approximately 57 times the size of a standard Nvidia GPU, with 4 trillion transistors and 900,000 cores. The advantage is eliminating the "memory wall," the latency penalty incurred when data is shuffled between thousands of separate chips. Cerebras recently went public and reportedly signed an inference deal with OpenAI with a backlog described as worth tens of billions of dollars. The host flags severe customer concentration risk: for years the bulk of revenue traced to a single UAE-based customer (G42), and now the future is heavily dependent on OpenAI. The host treats this concentration as the primary risk — strong technology with one or two customers is described as fragile.

6. **Tesla's private-mountain chip strategy:** Tesla builds its own AI chips — the Dojo project and the current AI 4 generation, with AI 5 and subsequent generations in development — exclusively for internal use: FSD, Optimus, and, per the host, upcoming SpaceX orbital satellites. The host explicitly draws the Apple/Intel analogy. AI 5 completed tape-out in April 2026 and is expected to ramp to meaningful volume in 2027. The host notes Tesla's historical pattern of missing self-imposed deadlines (including building and then disbanding and reconstituting the Dojo team) as a key risk. For Tesla investors, the chip program is framed as an enabler of the FSD, Optimus, and inference satellite thesis rather than a standalone investment case — but success would give Tesla meaningful margin leverage by controlling its own cost structure.

## Autonomous Driving / Humanoid Bots

1. **Tesla's chips as infrastructure for FSD and Optimus:** The host briefly situates Tesla's chip ambitions within the broader autonomous driving and robotics thesis. AI 4, AI 5, and subsequent in-house chips are described as the computational backbone for Full Self-Driving, Optimus, and SpaceX satellite inference. The host is clear that the chip program's investment value is derivative — it matters insofar as it makes FSD and Optimus economically stronger by removing Nvidia from Tesla's cost structure — not as a chip business in its own right.

## Financials

1. **Nvidia margin sustainability as a long-term concern:** The host argues that Nvidia's ~75% gross margins are unlikely to be sustainable as inference becomes the dominant workload. Large cloud providers (Google with TPU, Amazon with Trainium, Microsoft with Maya) are building proprietary inference chips specifically to avoid paying what the host calls "Nvidia's tax." The host declines to predict exactly when margin compression will arrive, noting the current AI boom obscures timing, but treats it as a structural inevitability.

Notable quotes and data:
- Nvidia data center revenue: ~$75 billion in the quarter ending April 2026, up ~92% year-over-year
- Nvidia gross margin: ~75%
- Nvidia market cap: surpassed $5 trillion in 2026 (described as the highest in world history)
- Inference share of all AI compute as of 2026: ~two-thirds, trending toward 70–80%
- CUDA has been in development since 2006 (~18 years)
- Groq LPU time-to-first-token: ~18 ms vs. 200–400 ms on typical GPU cloud setups (~10–20× faster)
- Groq on-chip SRAM per chip: ~230 MB vs. Nvidia H100's 80 GB
- Nvidia–Groq deal value: ~$20 billion for perpetual non-exclusive license to Groq's patents and software stack, announced Christmas Eve 2025; included hiring of Jonathan Ross, Sunny Madra, and ~80% of Groq's staff
- Cerebras chip: ~57× the size of a standard Nvidia GPU; 4 trillion transistors; 900,000 cores
- Cerebras–OpenAI inference deal backlog: reportedly "tens of billions of dollars" (host characterization, not confirmed)
- Tesla AI 5 tape-out: April 2026; volume ramp expected 2027
- "The recipe is a one-time cost, the cooking never, ever stops."
- "Who owns inference" is framed as the correct question replacing "who beats Nvidia"

2026-06-29.title: This Country Just Killed Gas Cars
2026-06-29.body:
This video from FutureAzA examines Ethiopia's emergence as an unlikely leader in EV adoption, driven primarily by economic pressures rather than environmental idealism. The host argues that Ethiopia's ban on importing internal combustion engine vehicles (enacted in 2024), combined with dramatically cheap hydroelectric power, has rapidly transformed the country's vehicle fleet. The video also serves as a fundraising appeal for the host to travel to Ethiopia in late 2025 to report on the story firsthand.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Ethiopia's ICE import ban:** In 2024, Ethiopia became the first country in the world to ban imports of petrol and diesel vehicles entirely. The policy was driven primarily by fiscal pressure — Ethiopia was spending roughly $4.5 billion per year on imported petrol, money that left the country and did not return to the local economy. By contrast, domestically generated electricity keeps spending within the local economy.

2. **Rapid EV adoption from a near-zero base:** EV adoption in Ethiopia has grown from less than 1% to nearly 5–6% of all vehicles (not just new car sales), placing it above the global average of approximately 4% of all vehicles. Within Africa, Ethiopia is the clear outlier — its roughly 15,000 EV passenger cars represent more than four times the EV stock in South Africa. The government's target is 500,000 EVs on the road by 2030, up from approximately 115,000 currently (though the host notes the article citing that figure is about nine months old).

3. **Policy levers — carrots and sticks:** Beyond the import ban, Ethiopia has zeroed out VAT and import taxes on EVs, introduced 100 new electric buses in the capital Addis Ababa (population 4.2 million), and announced plans to build 17 EV assembly plants using imported parts, primarily from China. Middle-class consumers are finding it easier to obtain credit for new EVs than for secondhand petrol cars, lowering the financial barrier despite relatively high sticker prices for a low-income country (a BYD Seagull hatchback is cited at approximately $23,000).

4. **Ultra-low electricity costs as a structural advantage:** The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam — which took 14 years to build and came online roughly a year and a half before the video's publication — is the foundation of the country's EV economics. A chart cited in the video places Ethiopia's electricity rate at approximately 0.6 cents per kilowatt hour, which the host calculates would cost under $1 to fully charge a large EV. Even at a higher government-cited figure of 10 cents per kilowatt hour — roughly half the rate of neighboring countries — a full charge would cost approximately $8, still dramatically cheaper than petrol given chronic fuel shortages and long queues.

5. **Domestic manufacturing ambitions:** Ethiopia launched what it describes as its largest EV factory, a $52 million facility targeting production of 1,000 cars per year. The host acknowledges that figure is modest but expects capacity to grow. Plans for 17 assembly plants using Chinese knockdown or semi-knockdown kits are underway, partly because Ethiopian labor costs are among the lowest in the world — a key incentive for Chinese manufacturers like BYD to agree to final assembly in-country. An earlier assembly partnership with Hyundai in 2020 collapsed due to foreign currency shortages.

## Market & Competition

1. **BYD's dominance in emerging EV markets:** BYD is described as the most prevalent EV brand on Ethiopian roads and is noted as having overtaken Tesla as the world's largest EV maker. The host emphasizes that BYD is not hesitant about entering emerging markets, which Western brands have historically avoided.

2. **U.S. policy contrast:** The host briefly notes that under Republican leadership, the U.S. has cut EV subsidies, forcing automakers to scale back production and absorb significant financial losses as demand-side incentives were removed — a contrast to Ethiopia's aggressive pro-EV stance.

Notable quotes and data:
- Ethiopia spends roughly **$4.5 billion/year** on imported petrol.
- EV share of **all vehicles** in Ethiopia: ~**4.7–6%** (depending on data source cited), vs. ~2.7% for the USA and ~32% for Norway.
- Ethiopia's electricity rate: approximately **0.6 cents per kilowatt hour** (per cited chart); government figures suggest **10 cents/kWh**, about half the rate of neighboring countries.
- Full EV charge cost at 0.6 cents/kWh: estimated at **under $1** for a large vehicle.
- **115,000 EVs** currently on Ethiopian roads out of 1.5 million total vehicles (data ~9 months old per host).
- Government target: **500,000 EVs by 2030**.
- Ethiopia's EV stock is **more than 4× that of South Africa**.
- Largest domestic EV factory: **$52 million**, capacity **1,000 cars/year**.
- Plans for **17 EV assembly plants** using imported Chinese parts.
- **100 electric buses** introduced in Addis Ababa.
- Global average EV share of all vehicles: approximately **4%**.
- Host is planning a reporting trip to Ethiopia, approximately **November 30 – December 22, 2025**, and is soliciting donated airline miles (Portland to Addis Ababa) and PayPal donations.

2026-06-29.title: v14 LITE!!! US EVs are Lost, EU Close Behind, & Some INSANE Battery Stuff - Monday News Roundup
2026-06-29.body:
This Monday news roundup from FutureAzA (June 29, 2026) covers a wide range of Tesla and EV-industry headlines, with the host moving briskly through roughly two dozen stories. The central themes are FSD V14 Lite's arrival for hardware 3 vehicles, the ongoing struggles of legacy automakers (Volkswagen, GM, Lucid) to compete in the EV and autonomy space, and the rising threat from Chinese manufacturers — particularly BYD's new flagship SUV and Xpeng's XNGP 2.0 going global. The host's core argument is that Tesla's software and manufacturing advantages continue to compound while competitors either retreat from electrification or fail to grasp the difficulty of autonomous driving.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD V14 Lite distilled to hardware 3:** The biggest news of the day, per the host, is the arrival of FSD V14 Lite for hardware 3 vehicles. Ashok Elluswamy — whom the host credits as reliable ("does not play games") — announced that version 14 has been distilled from hardware 4 down to hardware 3, allowing hardware 3 to directly learn how to handle scenarios using V14 as a guide. The update unlocks implementations previously exclusive to hardware 4, including reinforcement learning, improved proactive and reactive responses, fewer false slowdowns, smoother steering, new parking/unparking/reversing capabilities (distinct from Summon), arrival options for selecting where FSD should park, and speed profiles. The host notes it is currently rolling out to the early access group and treats that as a near-certain signal of broader release, citing the precedent that early-access releases are almost always followed by full rollout.

2. **Pricing incentive argument for hardware 3:** The host floats the idea that Tesla should reduce the monthly FSD subscription price for hardware 3 subscribers — suggesting something like $79.99/month rather than $99/month — to reflect the lesser feature set and to drive uptake. He frames this as a good A/B pricing test opportunity.

3. **Volkswagen's autonomous ID Buzz ambitions dismissed:** VW announced plans to launch an autonomous ID Buzz in 2026 with a new self-driving partnership with Bosch (replacing, or supplementing, a prior Bosch arrangement — the host finds the details contradictory). VW has stated it hopes to "overtake Tesla in the driverless taxi race." The host is deeply skeptical, noting the core lesson of the autonomy space is that the challenge is far harder than anyone anticipates, especially because roads are filled with human drivers creating endless edge cases.

4. **Xpeng XNGP 2.0 going global:** Xpeng's CEO announced that XNGP 2.0 is going global, including to Europe. The host pushes back on criticism that this is irrelevant because it won't reach the US, arguing the US is only one market. He discloses he was (per his own claim) the first Western media to drive XNGP 2.0 and holds a Chinese driver's license. His assessment: XNGP 2.0 was at least equivalent to a late version of FSD version 12 at the time of his test, and has likely improved since. He notes Xpeng has less direct government entanglement than BYD or Huawei, making its international expansion more credible.

5. **Robotaxi difficulty and competitor stumbles:** The host recounts a report of a Motional robotaxi ride where the safety supervisor had to disengage twice in a single trip, with a safety driver still present. He argues that any company claiming a robotaxi product will arrive "next year or the year after" while still at that stage fundamentally doesn't understand the scope of the problem. He also references a reported Waymo incident where the vehicle spent approximately 10 minutes unable to navigate the final 60–70 feet of a journey due to a railroad crossing — drawing a parallel to similar Tesla FSD behavior in Austin.

## Robotaxi

1. **Trump administration proposes removing brake pedal and steering wheel requirements for AVs:** The Trump administration has proposed new federal vehicle regulation changes that would allow companies to omit brake pedals and steering wheels from vehicles not designed to have them. The host views this as a meaningful regulatory boost for Tesla's Cybercab and other robotaxi operators, calling it sensible policy — though he jokes that governments doing sensible things is "not their brand."

2. **Cybercab vs. Waymo vehicle cost comparison:** In response to a viewer comment about Waymo potentially using Chinese-made vans, the host does a back-of-envelope unit economics argument: a ~$35,000 Chinese van with a 100% import tariff becomes $70,000 before upfit, putting the total vehicle cost at roughly three times the price of a Cybercab. He adds that those vans are designed for ~150,000 miles while the Cybercab is designed for 300,000–500,000 miles minimum, making Waymo's potential approach "untenable."

3. **Tesla setting up robotaxi operations in Amsterdam (host skeptical, then surprised):** A viewer or report mentioned Tesla standing up robotaxi service operations in Amsterdam. The host's initial reaction is strong skepticism ("this is never going to happen, not in my lifetime, definitely not in the next 10 years"), followed immediately by self-correction questioning whether he might be wrong.

4. **Uber–Waymo relationship in Phoenix:** A viewer noted that Uber has pulled back from Waymo in Phoenix. The host quips that when you work with everyone, you work with no one, framing Uber's retreat as predictable.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Tesla delivery consensus and Q2 outlook:** The host previews a follow-up video for the next day covering his delivery estimates. He states the analyst consensus for Q2 2026 total deliveries is approximately 406,000 — roughly 50,000 higher than Q1 2026. He offers several bullish supporting factors: Q1 ended with ~50,000 units added to inventory that may have since been drawn down; gasoline prices have skyrocketed, boosting EV demand; Q2 has no major holidays and one or two more production days than Q1; and Model Y Long Range sales have been strong. He is cautious about his own precision but leans positive.

2. **Tesla stock up ~$22 on delivery volume expectations:** Tesla's share price was up approximately $22 on the day of filming, which the host attributes to market anticipation of strong Q2 production and delivery numbers representing a reversal of a prior downward trend.

3. **Tesla leads Cars.com American-Made Index:** Tesla again topped the Cars.com American-Made Index, with Model 3 and Model Y taking the first and second spots. The host attributes this to Tesla's consistent practice of localizing production wherever it operates.

4. **Lucid layoffs and COO departure:** Lucid announced layoffs of roughly 18% of its workforce, expected to save $158 million per year. The COO role has been eliminated. The departing COO spoke about robotaxi ambitions, acknowledging Lucid cannot build an autonomous vehicle stack in-house (which would require billions) and has made partnerships — including a deal the host characterizes as Uber offering ~$500 million in exchange for 35,000 vehicles including 10,000 Gravity SUVs, which he frames as a purchase order with strings attached rather than a research grant.

5. **GM retreating from LFP, pivoting to lithium manganese-rich batteries:** GM is reportedly considering dropping LFP batteries from its future EV portfolio, citing China's export restrictions on equipment to manufacture the latest-generation LFP cells. The alternative being considered is lithium manganese-rich (LMR) batteries, which the host notes offer NMC-like performance at lower cost — but do not yet exist at commercial scale. GM simultaneously announced a $275 million investment in its Spring Hill, Tennessee plant, of which $150 million is earmarked for a future internal combustion Cadillac product. GM is also developing a third-generation EV platform (following Ultium and its successor).

6. **BYD Great Tang flagship SUV:** BYD launched the Great Tang, a full-size flagship crossover priced at approximately $35,000 in China, securing over 150,000 pre-orders. Key specs cited: up to 130–135 kWh battery, approximately 590 miles of CLTC range (host estimates ~450 miles on an EPA cycle), 10C battery capable of charging 10–70% in five minutes and 0–97% in approximately nine minutes, 1,000-volt architecture, and megawatt charging capability. BYD already has 6,600 megawatt chargers installed in China and is expanding internationally. The host estimates the car could reach other global markets under $55,000, calling it "one heck of a value proposition."

7. **Polestar forced out of US market:** The Trump administration forced Polestar out of the US market over concerns about Chinese-connected software. The host criticizes the move as inconsistent — Volvo, also owned by Geely and with similar Chinese software ties, has not been similarly targeted. He also raises geopolitical concerns, noting that antagonizing China puts Tesla's Giga Shanghai (Tesla's most productive factory) and its largest car market at risk.

8. **Volkswagen's deepening crisis:** VW faces potential cuts of up to 100,000 jobs (doubling earlier reports of 50,000), and plans to close at least four factories — Zwickau, Emden, Hanover, and Neckarsulm — as current model runs end. The affected models include the ID.3, ID.4, ID.5, and several SEAT/Cupra models. The host interprets this as a de facto retreat from EVs, noting VW's strategy of simultaneously pursuing ICE and EV development is the opposite of focus.

9. **Xiaomi electric sports car leak:** A leaked two-door Xiaomi electric sports car featuring a carbon fiber track wing was shown. The host notes the camouflage wrap conceals little of the car's design.

10. **Ferrari Luce GU launch in China:** Ferrari launched the Luce GU in China at approximately 586,000 (currency not specified in transcript), with all 88 units sold out immediately.

11. **Nio solid-state battery progress:** Nio is reportedly using 588 amp-hour liquid solid-state cells to address supply chain bottlenecks. The host briefly flags Nio's track record of battery development innovation for a company of its size.

12. **New Delhi EV scrapping incentive:** New Delhi announced a program offering residents approximately $1,000 to scrap old EV vehicles to curb air pollution, paired with lower registration fees and road tax exemptions up to 3 million rupees (approximately 4–10% of vehicle price).

13. **Volkswagen ID Buzz coming to US:** VW's ID Buzz camper van is returning to the US market, with US-bound equipment packages priced under $3,000.

## Market & Competition

1. **Legacy automaker strategic incoherence:** The host's overarching critique of GM, VW, and Lucid is that they continue to hedge between ICE and EV rather than committing, which produces neither competitive EVs nor cost savings. VW's plan to reduce lineup complexity while simultaneously maintaining both powertrain types is singled out as self-defeating. By contrast, Model Y's global bestselling status with a tight, focused lineup is held up as proof that focus beats breadth.

2. **China's AI chip restrictions tightening:** In response to a viewer question about how Chinese AV companies solve compute challenges, the host notes that Huawei manufactures AI chips domestically for inference workloads. He adds that China has now banned the import of advanced AI chips from companies like Nvidia (reversing the prior situation where the US banned export to China but China had not restricted import). He observes that Chinese AV companies are notably reluctant to discuss their chip sourcing publicly.

Notable quotes and data:
- FSD V14 Lite is distilled from hardware 4 to hardware 3; early access rollout underway as of June 29, 2026.
- Lucid cutting ~18% of workforce; savings of $158 million/year; COO role eliminated.
- VW job cuts potentially doubling to 100,000; four factories (Zwickau, Emden, Hanover, Neckarsulm) targeted for closure.
- GM earmarking $150 million of a $275 million Spring Hill investment for a future ICE Cadillac.
- BYD Great Tang: ~$35,000, 130–135 kWh, ~590 miles CLTC, 10–70% charge in 5 minutes, 10C battery, 6,600 megawatt chargers already in China.
- Q2 2026 delivery consensus: ~406,000 vehicles.
- Cybercab designed for 300,000–500,000 miles; host estimates competing Chinese vans would cost ~3× as much after tariffs and upfit.
- Host's XNGP 2.0 assessment: "Easily late version 12 [FSD] at worst" at the time of his test, likely better now.
- Motional robotaxi: safety driver still present, two disengagements in one ride reported.
- Tesla stock up ~$22 on June 29, 2026, attributed to delivery volume expectations.

2026-06-29.title: Is Tesla SandBagging RoboTaxi? Is the Market Crashing?
2026-06-29.body:
The video from "investingagainstthegrain" (hosted by Nick) pushes back against the prevailing bearish narrative surrounding markets, AI, and Tesla, arguing that June's weakness is historically normal and that July typically rebounds strongly. The host's core thesis is that Tesla is not sandbagging its robotaxi rollout, that the Cybercab launch is imminent and on track, and that the real AI opportunity lies in autonomy and humanoids — not LLMs, which he argues are already commoditized.

## Market & Competition
1. **June weakness is seasonal, not structural:** The host presents historical S&P 500 data going back to 1950 showing June averages only a 0.22% return, with the back half of June being among the worst periods of the year. He attributes this to institutional rebalancing at the half-year mark, reduced market volume due to vacations, and the amplifying effect that lower volume has on any selling pressure. July, by contrast, is historically one of the strongest months.

2. **MAG 7 underperformance creates opportunity:** A chart shared in the video shows year-to-date performance as of late June 2026, with Meta down 16%, Tesla down 16%, Amazon up only 2%, Nvidia up 5%, Apple up 6%, and Google up 8%. The host contrasts this with outsized gains in names like Marll (up ~230%), Micron (up ~260%), and SanDisk (up ~781%), which he attributes to investors treating memory and storage infrastructure as an inflationary hedge and a defensive play on guaranteed AI capex from the hyperscalers. He views the MAG 7 dislocation as a buying opportunity.

3. **Bitcoin and MicroStrategy as risk-capital barometers:** Bitcoin is cited as down 52.5% from all-time highs and MicroStrategy down 82.6% from all-time highs as of the video date. The host argues risk capital has rotated out of these assets into AI infrastructure plays (Micron, SanDisk, Marll, Bloom Energy) and prediction/sports betting markets. He notes the Fed holding rates — with markets pricing in potential rate hikes — is an additional headwind for Bitcoin since rate cuts would be needed to fuel another Bitcoin rally.

4. **LLM commoditization thesis:** The host reiterates a prediction he says he made over two years ago: that LLMs would be commoditized and the real AI ROI would come from autonomy and humanoids. He points to China's GLM 5.2 — described as the most powerful downloadable open-source model, comparable to frontier models like GPT and Claude Opus — as evidence of commoditization via distillation. He references Gavin Baker on the All-In podcast discussing how China used massive distillation of frontier model outputs to train competitive models at far lower capex cost.
