2026-07-01.title: Daily X Summary (2026-07-01)
2026-07-01.body:
## Executive Summary
The dominant signal from today's posts is Tesla's major milestone: production Cybercabs with no steering wheel or pedals are now testing on public roads in Austin, representing a concrete step toward commercial robotaxi deployment. Secondary signals include Tesla's first significant Terafab chip-fab hire, a large Megapack project reaching commercial operation in Australia, and Tesla expanding EV sales into Uruguay. Overall sentiment is bullish, with hardware and infrastructure moves advancing the autonomous driving thesis simultaneously.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **Production Cybercab testing on public roads — a key robotaxi milestone:** Tesla officially announced it has begun testing production Cybercabs — with no steering wheel or pedals — on public roads in Austin. This was confirmed both by Tesla's own announcement (post [8], 8.8K likes / 795 retweets, the day's highest-engagement post) and by a follow-up sighting of the vehicle testing in Austin (post [1]). A separate post (post [7]) shared an image of the Cybercab's interior screen. The significance here is the transition from prototype/development vehicles to production-spec hardware operating on open public roads without traditional manual controls — a regulatory and engineering threshold that directly precedes commercial robotaxi deployment. This is distinct from the supervised robotaxi fleet already operating in Austin; these are production-configuration vehicles being validated on public roads.

2. **Tesla's Terafab chip-fab project lands first major hire:** Tesla has made its first prominent hire for its in-house semiconductor fabrication project, dubbed "Terafab," based in Austin. Gary Jiang — a semiconductor manufacturing veteran with nearly 18 years at Intel — has joined as Director of Tera Fab (post [2], 3.3K likes / 292 retweets). This is notable for the Tesla investment thesis because vertical integration into chip manufacturing would reduce dependency on third-party suppliers (e.g., Nvidia) for AI training and inference hardware powering FSD and Optimus. The hire of an Intel-pedigreed manufacturing executive signals this project is moving from planning into execution.

3. **Tesla Megapack: 415 MW / 1.66 GWh Australia facility reaches commercial operation:** A new Tesla Megapack battery energy storage facility — the Orana BESS — has reached commercial operation in New South Wales, Australia (post [10]). The project has a capacity of 415 MW and can deliver up to four hours of storage, totaling 1.66 GWh. The facility is valued at $415 million. This represents a meaningful revenue and deployment data point for Tesla's Energy division, which has become an increasingly important contributor to Tesla's financials.

4. **Market & Competition — BMW iX5 unveiled; Ford CEO on Chinese EV dominance:** BMW officially unveiled the all-electric iX5, priced at $81,250 with a 435-mile EPA range, 144 kWh battery, 460 kW peak charging, 800V architecture, bidirectional charging, and a 0–60 time of 4.4 seconds (post [5]). This represents a well-spec'd premium competitor to Tesla's lineup in the high-end segment. Separately, Ford CEO Jim Farley made pointed comments in a new interview, stating that Chinese automakers are "completely dominating the EV landscape globally" and that "there's no real competition from Tesla, GM or Ford" with what's coming from China (post [11]). Sawyer Merritt noted pointedly that the Tesla Model Y is one of the best-selling cars in China — implying Farley's framing may be overstated or inaccurate with respect to Tesla specifically. Farley also discussed Ford's upcoming $30K all-electric pickup truck in the same interview (post [12]).

5. **Tesla expands EV sales to Uruguay:** Tesla officially announced that Model 3 and Model Y sales will begin soon in Uruguay (post [13]), representing incremental international market expansion in Latin America.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — The confirmation of production-spec, steeringwheel-free Cybercabs testing on public Austin roads is a concrete, verifiable step in the robotaxi commercialization timeline, while the Terafab hire and Megapack milestone further support Tesla's vertical integration and energy revenue narratives.

2026-07-01.title: SpaceX - Tesla Merger?  //  My thoughts
2026-07-01.body:
This video from Jordan Giesige (The Limiting Factor) offers his personal perspective as a Tesla shareholder on the increasingly discussed prospect of a Tesla–SpaceX merger, following SpaceX's completion of its IPO. The core argument is that while a merger makes strategic sense in principle, the timing is poor for Tesla shareholders because Tesla's near-term robotaxi-driven revaluation is likely 1–2 years away, whereas SpaceX's comparable revaluation may be 2–4 years out — meaning a merger of equals now would dilute Tesla holders and delay their expected gains.

## Market & Competition

1. **SpaceX IPO as the merger catalyst:** SpaceX recently completed its IPO, pricing shares at $135 per share, implying a market cap of approximately $1.77 trillion. The S-1 filed with the SEC showed the company is not currently profitable enough to justify a ~$2 trillion valuation on current earnings, but investors are pricing in rapid growth and an extra-planetary total addressable market (TAM) spanning space-based compute, lunar operations, and Mars colonization. Elon Musk's close associates are now describing a merger as imminent, and prediction markets have bets placed that it will occur before spring 2027.

2. **The "Schrödinger's Valuation" framing:** Jordan introduces the concept that stock valuations are inherently observer-dependent — a stock can be simultaneously over- and undervalued depending on the investing framework, risk tolerance, and time horizon applied. He uses this to frame the merger debate: each shareholder must independently decide whether a merger offer is fair and vote accordingly, because there is no single objective answer.

3. **Differing TAMs and timelines:** Jordan argues that SpaceX has a larger TAM due to its extra-planetary ambitions, but that tapping into it meaningfully depends on a fully and rapidly reusable Starship, which he estimates is roughly 1–2 years away if development goes well. After that, ramping launch cadence and converting that into meaningful profit will take additional time, all while SpaceX continues to consume capital for factories and launch infrastructure. He estimates SpaceX's stock could trade sideways for several years. Tesla, by contrast, has an earthbound but nearer-term TAM, with robotaxi revenues appearing on the horizon and a potential stock revaluation he expects within 1–2 years; he considers humanoid robots (Optimus) a longer-dated story, 2–4 years from generating significant revenue.

4. **Merger dilution risk for Tesla shareholders:** If a merger happened now, Jordan argues it would dilute Tesla shareholders by blending Tesla's near-term revaluation potential with SpaceX's longer-dated one, delaying potential gains by 2–3 years or more. He frames the time-value cost at roughly 15–20% annual opportunity cost — what the capital could earn elsewhere if not tied up in a sideways-trading merged entity. A merged company could also be net cash-flow negative if SpaceX's capital expenditure requirements exceed the combined FSD and Starlink revenue streams, potentially meaning the stock "flounders" for multiple years.

5. **Jordan's preferred merger terms:** If a merger does occur, Jordan states he would want either (a) at least $800 per share for Tesla stock, or (b) Tesla to represent at least 60% of the combined company's value. Under scenario (a) combined with the 60% framing, this would imply a ~$3 trillion valuation for Tesla and ~$2 trillion for SpaceX (approximately $150/share for SpaceX). He acknowledges that $800/share would mean forgoing the 2-year standalone gains he anticipates, but views it as a fair premium for accepting merger synergies. He notes the most likely deal is probably a merger of equals, which would imply Tesla shareholders receive roughly a 30–50% premium over the current share price — approximately $500–$600 per share.

6. **Post-merger portfolio strategy:** Jordan says he would hold through the merger period to capture whatever premium is offered, then reassess. His expectation is that he would sell a significant portion of the merged company's stock, redeploying capital into other positions he considers undervalued (he names Upstart and Lemonade as current holdings). He explicitly frames this as a rational, unemotional response — "there's no crying in the casino."

7. **Strategic rationale for a merger:** Jordan lists three reasons he supports a merger in principle: (1) it would reduce bureaucratic and regulatory overhead on Elon Musk; (2) it would eliminate duplicated resources between the two companies; and (3) a combined entity would have greater capacity to attract and retain talent. The overarching goal he attributes to Elon Musk is concentrating more cognitive capacity on execution and problem-solving while cutting costs. He also acknowledges Elon's perspective — that the combined companies could create such abundance that money itself becomes irrelevant — while noting that this vision will take decades regardless, making a 1–2 year delay to let Tesla realize its next revaluation event immaterial to the long-term mission.

Notable quotes and data:
- SpaceX IPO price: $135/share; implied market cap: ~$1.77 trillion
- Both Tesla and SpaceX estimated at ~$2 trillion each based on discounted future cash flows (per online analysis and AI chatbot conversations, as noted by Jordan — not his own independent DCF)
- Jordan's minimum acceptable Tesla merger price: **$800/share** (implying ~$3 trillion Tesla valuation)
- Jordan's minimum acceptable Tesla share of combined company: **60%**
- Implied SpaceX valuation under those terms: ~$2 trillion (~$150/share)
- Most likely deal scenario (Jordan's estimate): merger of equals, ~30–50% premium, or roughly **$500–$600/share** for Tesla
- Starship full reusability timeline (Jordan's estimate): approximately **1–2 years** if development proceeds well
- SpaceX stock may trade sideways for **"several years"** due to capital expenditure outflows
- Tesla robotaxi revaluation expected within **1–2 years**; significant Optimus revenues **2–4 years** out
- Merger dilution could delay Tesla shareholder gains by **2–3 years or more**
- Opportunity cost of delay estimated at **15–20% annual growth**
- Prediction markets: bets placed that a merger will occur **before spring 2027**
- *"As much as I'm fond of Tesla and SpaceX, they aren't the only opportunities in the stock market."*
- *"If it doesn't turn out my way, as they say, there's no crying in the casino."*

2026-07-01.title: SpaceX Is About to Take Over The Internet
2026-07-01.body:
This week's episode from The Tesla Space covers three major stories: SpaceX's emerging ambition to become a global mobile communications provider via Starlink (including a potential T-Mobile acquisition), Tesla's newly published Cybercab first responder guide that offers the clearest public look yet at how the driverless robotaxi is designed to operate, and a California incentive stack that can bring the price of a Tesla Semi down to roughly Model Y levels. The video's core thesis is that transformative technologies — whether satellite internet or autonomous vehicles — win by becoming invisible infrastructure that people rely on without thinking about it.

## Market & Competition

1. **Starlink's evolution from rural internet to global communications platform:** Starlink has grown well beyond its original niche as connectivity for remote areas. Commercial aircraft, cruise ships, and emergency responders now rely on it, and major airlines — including United, Southwest, Alaska Airlines, American Airlines, Emirates, and the Lufthansa Group — have either deployed Starlink or committed to it. In 2025, Starlink generated $11.4 billion of SpaceX's $18.7 billion in total revenue, meaning more than half of SpaceX's business now comes from selling connectivity rather than launching rockets.

2. **SpaceX's IPO filing positions Starlink as a direct telecom competitor:** In its IPO filing, SpaceX openly described Starlink Mobile as a direct competitor to Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile, and projected an addressable market of roughly $740 billion. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell told investors the company is planning to launch a Starlink-branded retail product and is possibly building its own ground-based network to support it. SpaceX has already spent $17 billion acquiring wireless spectrum from Echostar — a purchase the FCC approved in May — signaling serious preparation for a full mobile offering.

3. **Analyst speculation about a T-Mobile acquisition:** Analysts at TD Cowen suggested that if SpaceX wants Starlink to become a global communications platform quickly, acquiring T-Mobile — its longest-running partner for direct-to-device satellite connectivity — would be one of the fastest paths. The logic: major U.S. carriers have publicly refused to lease network access to SpaceX, so buying a carrier outright becomes the simplest alternative. Reuters also reportedly covered SpaceX exploring a dedicated Starlink phone earlier this year, though Elon Musk publicly denied that report.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab first responder guide reveals fleet-wide coordination capabilities:** Tesla published a Cybercab first responder guide — a safety manual for firefighters, police, and emergency personnel — that provides one of the clearest public looks yet at how the driverless robotaxi is designed to behave. A standout capability: if responders need to close an area, they can call Tesla's robotaxi support team to request a temporary geofence, blocking Cybercab traffic within roughly 1,000 feet of a location and rerouting the entire fleet before any vehicle arrives. This connected, fleet-wide logic is described as something no individual human-driven car could replicate.

2. **Cybercab's emergency vehicle response and post-crash behavior:** The Cybercab uses cameras and a dedicated sound detection system to recognize flashing lights and sirens, yield, and pull over to the nearest safe spot if an emergency vehicle remains behind it. Once stopped, it disengages autonomous driving, unlocks the doors, and opens a two-way audio line to Tesla support so responders can coordinate before touching the vehicle. The guide also notes the Cybercab is designed to respond to a first responder's hand signals and follow a path marked by cones. After a crash — if airbags deploy or a safety-critical event is detected — the car parks itself, rapidly flashes its hazards, unlocks the doors, rolls down the windows to vent the cabin, and automatically connects to Tesla support, who can then contact 911.

3. **Confirmed Cybercab interior and structural details:** The guide confirms several features Tesla had not previously detailed publicly: electrically adjustable seats controlled via touchscreen, power windows, exterior microphones on the B-pillars enabling responders to talk to Tesla support from outside the vehicle, and a minimalist two-seat cabin built around a single landscape touchscreen with no glove box, no steering wheel, and no pedals. A Tesla-released video of a production Cybercab driving on public roads in Austin during engineering validation also revealed notably thick A-pillars — key structural components in crash integrity — suggesting the Cybercab was engineered with the same safety-first philosophy behind Tesla's top-rated crash test performance on other models.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **California incentive stack brings Tesla Semi to ~$50,000 for qualifying buyers:** Qualifying businesses in California can now purchase a Tesla Semi for roughly the price of a well-equipped Model Y by stacking two state incentive programs. The first is California's HVIP clean truck voucher program, covering up to $120,000 per truck; the second is the California Clean Fuel Reward, which can add another $120,000. Combined, eligible small fleets can deduct as much as $240,000 from a single truck's price, bringing an estimated sticker of around $290,000 down to roughly $50,000. The Semi is a Class 8 truck capable of a gross combined weight of 82,000 pounds, approximately 500 miles of range on a single charge, and is described as eventually gaining more autonomous driving capability.

2. **Tesla Semi's economic case to fleet operators:** The video frames the incentive story not just as a price discount but as a removal of the single biggest adoption barrier — upfront purchase cost. Tesla's argument is that the Semi's significantly lower energy costs per mile, fewer moving parts requiring maintenance, and advanced safety systems deliver total cost-of-ownership savings worth hundreds of thousands of dollars over the vehicle's life, even before incentives. The host argues that at ~$50,000 with lower operating costs, fleet managers' purchasing calculus changes entirely.

Notable quotes and data:
- Starlink 2025 revenue: **$11.4 billion** out of SpaceX's total **$18.7 billion**
- Starlink projected addressable market (per SpaceX IPO filing): **~$740 billion**
- SpaceX spectrum acquisition from Echostar: **$17 billion** (FCC-approved in May)
- Starlink active subscribers: **more than 10 million** across **over 160 countries**
- SpaceX valuation reference: **$2+ trillion**
- Cybercab geofence radius for emergency road closures: **~1,000 feet**
- Tesla fleet real-world driving data cited: **more than 11 billion miles**
- Tesla Semi gross combined weight capacity: **82,000 lbs**
- Tesla Semi range: **~500 miles** on a single charge
- Tesla Semi estimated base price: **~$290,000**; after California incentive stack: **~$50,000**
- HVIP voucher: up to **$120,000**; California Clean Fuel Reward: up to **$120,000**; combined max: **$240,000**

2026-07-02.title: Tesla Q2 2026 Production, Deliveries & Deployments
2026-07-02.body:
Tesla released its official Q2 2026 production, deliveries and deployments figures pre-market on July 2: 451,758 vehicles produced, 480,126 vehicles delivered, and 13.5 GWh of energy storage deployed. Deliveries beat the company-published Wall Street consensus of 406,024 by roughly 74,000 units (+18%) and set a new Q2 record, surpassing Q2 2023's 466,140.

| Q2 2026 | Production | Deliveries | Energy Storage |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Model 3/Y | 442,936 | 467,762 | — |
| Other Models | 8,822 | 12,364 | — |
| **Total** | **451,758** | **480,126** | **13.5 GWh** |
| QoQ change | +10.6% | +34.1% | +53.4% |
| YoY change | +10.1% | +25.0% | +40.6% |

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Official Q2 2026 figures:** Model 3/Y production 442,936 and deliveries 467,762; Other Models production 8,822 and deliveries 12,364; totals of **451,758 produced** and **480,126 delivered**. 2% of deliveries were subject to operating lease accounting (both segments).

2. **Deliveries outpaced production by 28,368 units**, drawing down the inventory built in prior quarters (Q1 2026 alone added ~50,000 units to inventory on production of 408,386 vs. deliveries of 358,023). Quarter over quarter, deliveries grew ~34% from Q1's 358,023.

3. **Best Q2 in company history.** The 480,126 total exceeds the prior Q2 record of 466,140 (Q2 2023) and comes against a depressed Q2 2025 comparison base, when volumes were held back by factory retooling.

## Energy

1. **13.5 GWh of energy storage deployed** — up ~53% from Q1 2026's 8.8 GWh, slightly below the 13.8 GWh Wall Street consensus.

## Financials

1. **Forecast scoreboard:** The result landed far above the Tesla-published analyst consensus of 406,024 and above nearly every community estimate tracked ahead of the report — Gary Black 420K, FutureAzA 431K, Troy Teslike 466K, Khi 468K. The 482K calls (James Stephenson, "PY") were closest; FutureAzA's Randy had flagged 490K+ as possible on inventory drawdown.

2. **Q2 earnings scheduled for Wednesday, July 22, 2026**, after market close, with the Q2 update and management Q&A webcast at 4:30 p.m. Central Time. Net income and cash flow results will be reported then.

Notable quotes and data:
- Total production: **451,758** (Model 3/Y 442,936; Other Models 8,822)
- Total deliveries: **480,126** (Model 3/Y 467,762; Other Models 12,364)
- Energy storage deployed: **13.5 GWh** (vs. 8.8 GWh in Q1 2026; consensus 13.8 GWh)
- Deliveries subject to operating lease accounting: 2%
- Consensus beat: +74,102 vs. Tesla-published 406,024 (~+18%)
- Prior Q2 record: 466,140 (Q2 2023) — surpassed
- QoQ baseline (Q1 2026): production 408,386, deliveries 358,023, energy storage 8.8 GWh → +10.6% / +34.1% / +53.4%
- YoY baseline (Q2 2025): production 410,244, deliveries 384,122, energy storage 9.6 GWh → +10.1% / +25.0% / +40.6%
- Deliveries minus production: +28,368 (inventory drawdown)
- Q2 2026 earnings: Wednesday, July 22, 2026, after market close

2026-07-02.title: Tesla Just Hit Its Biggest Robotaxi Milestone
2026-07-02.body:
The video covers a cluster of Tesla milestones centered on the Cybercab robotaxi program: the first confirmed production Cybercab (no steering wheel, no pedals) driving autonomously on public roads in Austin, two new regulatory steps in Texas and Florida signaling imminent commercial deployment, and Tesla's first major Terafab leadership hire. Host Herbert (brighterwithherbert) is joined by Brian White of the FutureAzA YouTube channel to analyze what these developments collectively mean for Tesla's near-term robotaxi launch timeline.

## Robotaxi

1. **Production Cybercab confirmed driving autonomously in Austin:** Elon Musk publicly confirmed that a production Cybercab — with no steering wheel and no pedals — is driving on public roads in Austin in what Tesla calls an "engineering test." A safety monitor is present in the vehicle but is not operating it. Ashok Elluswamy separately confirmed the vehicle is driving by itself. The hosts note that multiple Cybercab storage lots and depots have been discovered around the country by community spotters, and that over a thousand units are believed to be out and ready, which the hosts argue is inconsistent with a timeline that is still a year or more from deployment.

2. **Vast majority of produced Cybercabs still in supervised FSD data-collection phase:** Per Brian White, citing his interview with Lars Moravy, the vast majority of Cybercabs currently produced are still in a supervised testing phase accumulating FSD autonomy miles in the new form factor. White estimates this phase will require a few more months before broader commercial deployment, noting the Cybercab's different form factor requires its own dataset before Tesla can confidently scale unsupervised operation.

3. **Texas DPS adds Cybercab to connected autonomous vehicles registry:** The Texas Department of Public Safety officially added the Tesla Cybercab robotaxi to its connected autonomous vehicles first-responder interaction plans page. The hosts describe this as a strict regulatory prerequisite for Level 4 operations at scale, meaning police, fire, and EMS in Texas now have a standardized protocol for interacting with a driverless Cybercab — a concrete operational step ahead of a wider Texas launch.

4. **Miami-area first responders complete Cybercab safety training:** In Coral Gables, Florida, fire personnel participated in a specialized training session with Tesla covering vehicle safety features, battery systems, emergency access points, and best practices for autonomous vehicle incidents. The hosts note Tesla has no active robotaxi service in Miami yet, framing this training as a strong signal of planned near-term deployment in the region at meaningful scale.

5. **Tesla missed its end-of-June five-city robotaxi expansion target:** Tesla had committed on earnings calls and in investor materials to launching robotaxi service in five additional cities by the end of June 2026. That deadline passed without the launches. Brian White characterizes autonomy timeline misses as expected, but the host emphasizes this was a formal investor-deck commitment reiterated as recently as months before the deadline — not a casual Elon prediction — and therefore a meaningful miss. The hosts speculate that a July 7 event teased by Lars Moravy around Giga Texas may be the occasion for announcing those city launches, with the holiday weekend cited as the likely reason for the brief delay.

6. **Lars Moravy teases July 7 announcement related to Giga Texas and Cybercab scaling:** In a recently published interview (discussed in detail in a companion video on the FutureAzA channel), Lars Moravy indicated he has "cool news" about something happening around Giga Texas related to Cybercab scaling. Brian White interprets this as likely a deployment or scaling announcement rather than a manufacturing update, reasoning there is no point in continuing to ramp Cybercab production without a corresponding deployment plan. Moravy also stated that Tesla is not building five or ten Cybercabs — they expect it to outsell the Model Y.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD version 14 "light" rollout to Hardware 3 vehicles began by June 30:** Ashok Elluswamy had committed to delivering FSD v14 light to Hardware 3 vehicles by June 30, 2026. The hosts confirm a small number of Hardware 3 cars received it by that date, including some in Canada. Brian White notes the rollout appears broader than just influencers, since regular owners who receive it typically do not post publicly. The host's own Hardware 3 vehicle had not yet received it as of filming.

2. **Gap between Hardware 3 and Hardware 4 FSD performance may be narrowing with v14 light:** Brian White, who drove a Hardware 3 vehicle for several days last December and noted it was "very good but not Hardware 4," observed in June 2026 that the gap between the two was widening. Based on videos from trusted channels, he now believes v14 light has narrowed that gap again. He is uncertain whether Hardware 3 can reach unsupervised capability and suggests Tesla may offer a discounted FSD subscription tier (around $65–70 vs. the current $99) for Hardware 3 owners who do not need unsupervised driving, alongside a paid Hardware 4 chip upgrade path for those who do.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Q2 2026 delivery numbers expected to show improvement:** Filming took place on a Wednesday (July 2, 2026), with delivery results due out the following morning (Thursday, July 3). Brian White expresses confidence the numbers will show growth, noting Tesla is growing while competitors are shrinking, and pushing back on the narrative that Tesla is "just a car company."

## Market & Competition

1. **Terafab hires first major semiconductor executive — Gary Jang from Intel:** Tesla (in a joint venture with SpaceX) hired Gary Jang, a semiconductor manufacturing veteran with nearly 18 years at Intel, as Director of Terafab — the planned chip fabrication facility in Austin. The hosts frame this as Tesla building custom chips optimized for its specific AI and autonomy workloads rather than general-purpose silicon, drawing a parallel to a Swiss Army knife trimmed of unnecessary tools. They note the Intel partnership context makes the hire a natural fit rather than a simple talent raid, and argue it applies competitive pressure on existing chip suppliers — pointing to Samsung announcing a production increase and Intel reactivating mothballed fabs as early signs.

Notable quotes and data:
- Lars Moravy (per Brian White): "We are not building five or ten of these — we expect [the Cybercab] to outsell the Model Y."
- Lars Moravy (per Brian White): "The vast majority of the Cybercabs that are produced right now are still in test phase for Full Self-Driving autonomy."
- Coral Gables Fire Department statement: "The class covered vehicle safety features, battery systems, emergency access points, best practices for managing incidents involving autonomous vehicles."
- Brian White on the Terafab hire: Gary Jang, ~18 years at Intel, named Director of Terafab chip fabrication project in Austin.
- Brian White on Hardware 3 FSD pricing suggestion: "Maybe do it for $65–70 instead of $99" for a supervised-only tier.
- Host on the five-city miss: "That is written on an earnings call, on the investment deck, multiple earnings — it's right there. You cannot give that a grain of salt. That is a miss, big time."
- Over 1,000 Cybercabs described by the host as "out there ready to go" — an informal estimate, not sourced to a tracker.

2026-07-02.title: Tesla Exec Reveals Tesla’s Scaling Plan
2026-07-02.body:
This video from brighterwithherbert features host Herbert and guest Brian White (of FutureAzA) analyzing key revelations from Herbert's exclusive interview with Lars Moravy, Tesla's VP of Vehicle Engineering, covering Optimus production line installation, Cybercab manufacturing readiness, and FSD training requirements. The core thesis is that Tesla is closer to high-volume Cybercab and Optimus production than most investors appreciate, with manufacturing automation and automotive experience giving Tesla structural advantages over competitors. The discussion also incorporates unverified supply chain rumors from China suggesting an Optimus Gen 3 launch window of July–August 2026.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus production line installation underway in Fremont:** Lars Moravy confirmed that space has been cleared in Fremont (the former Model S/X area) and the first Optimus production subline has arrived from automation partners in the Midwest and Germany. Installation is underway, with machines going through final stages of field acceptance testing (FAT). Lars indicated a single subline takes two to three days to install and about a week to get operational.

2. **40 additional sublines planned after first is proven:** The first subline is described as modular, making it relatively quick to bring up. Once proven, Tesla plans to replicate the process across roughly 40 more sublines covering different Optimus components — actuators, torso, battery, and limbs. The host clarifies this is not a sequential 40-week process but a staged rollout.

3. **Elon Musk visits Optimus production line:** Elon Musk posted a photo of himself walking the Optimus production line in Fremont, which Herbert and Brian treat as a meaningful milestone signal — consistent with the factory being in active installation and validation, not just planning.

4. **Automotive manufacturing expertise directly transfers to Optimus:** Lars Moravy stated that Tesla's experience scaling vehicle production — supply chain management, multi-sourcing, crisis management, production line software, and functional safety — directly applies to Optimus. He noted Optimus is more analogous to a car than a consumer electronics device due to functional safety requirements and multi-axis mechanical complexity. Lars also indicated that over time, an Optimus robot could cost less to build than one of Tesla's cars.

5. **Tesla ran crash-test simulations on Optimus from the start:** Brian White highlights that at Tesla's first Optimus demo, they showed crash-test simulation results run on the robot — something rival humanoid robot companies reportedly had not thought to do, owing to Tesla's deep automotive safety background.

6. **Unverified China supply chain rumors on Optimus volumes:** Herbert cites what he attributes to a Nomura research report (described as China-sourced rumors — take with caution) claiming: Tesla has raised its annualized Optimus Gen 3 production capacity target at Fremont from 50,000 to 70,000 units; Tesla plans to add approximately 70,000 units of capacity in Austin in 2028; long-term capacity is targeted at 1.5 million units per year; 2026 Optimus shipments are estimated at 25,000 units (with a margin of error of ±10,000); and a weekly production target of 1,000 units per week is expected by September 2026. Brian White notes these figures could be directionally accurate if a supplier has visibility into one component, but cautions that stated targets are frequently not met.

7. **UBS reportedly pegs Optimus Gen 3 official launch window as July–August 2026:** Herbert cites what he describes as a UBS research report placing the Gen 3 official launch window in July–August 2026. Neither he nor Brian White express high conviction in this specific timing.

8. **Humanoid robot form factor chosen deliberately:** Lars told Herbert that Tesla is starting with a humanoid form factor because society is not yet comfortable with non-humanoid robots. He cited coffee-pouring robots as an example of how even small robotic movements still unsettle people. Tesla plans to expand to other robot form factors after establishing humanoid robots as normalized.

## Robotaxi

1. **Cybercab manufacturing line is 90% automated:** Lars Moravy confirmed that the Cybercab production line is already approximately 90% automated, factoring in everything. Brian White notes this is more automated than most finished lines, not just early-production lines, and expects the figure to improve over time.

2. **Lars expects Cybercab to be Tesla's highest-volume vehicle ever:** Lars Moravy stated he expects Tesla to build more Cybercabs than any other vehicle in the company's history. The host describes this as reiterating a massive volume target, using the tongue-in-cheek term "a cajillion" to characterize its scale.

3. **Cybercab FSD requires its own dedicated training — not a copy-paste from Model Y:** Lars explicitly confirmed that FSD for Cybercab is not a copy-paste from Model Y. It has different model weights, requires retraining, and cannot be done solely with simulation — it needs real-world data. Lars stated the majority of the current Cybercab test fleet has been deployed for FSD/Autopilot training, not commercial robotaxi service. Herbert frames this as the explanation for why Cybercab robotaxi launch has been slower than many expected.

4. **Cybercab currently in infant mortality and validation testing:** Lars confirmed that because Cybercab has many new components and new manufacturing processes, the team is currently conducting infant mortality testing and validation — a standard but necessary phase before scaling production.

5. **Cybercab is not expected to be sold to consumers with a steering wheel:** When Herbert asked Lars about the MKBHD bet (whether Tesla would sell a Cybercab to a consumer under $30,000 by end of 2026), Lars reportedly laughed and declined to answer directly. Both Herbert and Brian interpret his non-answer and demeanor as signaling that Cybercab is being built exclusively as a robotaxi, not a consumer vehicle. Brian argues the economics strongly favor robotaxi deployment (~$5,000/month per car) over a one-time consumer sale.

6. **Cybercab described as a platform unto itself:** In response to a question from Jeff during the interview, Lars said Cybercab is a platform, but Tesla expects to build so many of them that it functions as a platform in its own right. Whether additional vehicles will be built off this platform will depend on autonomous vehicle adoption rates. Brian notes the underlying structure is minimal — essentially a front, rear, and structural battery pack.

7. **Waymo's approach contrasted unfavorably with Cybercab:** Brian White characterizes Waymo's method — buying a production car and adding sensor hardware — as fundamentally inferior to Tesla's purpose-built, deeply integrated approach, and argues Waymo could not replicate Cybercab's design at any price.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **Tesla using AI extensively in manufacturing quality control:** Lars described Tesla deploying AI vision systems on the production line to detect defects — going beyond simple defect identification to intelligently understanding upstream causes and feeding corrections back into the manufacturing process. Cybercabs leaving Giga Texas are driven over speed bumps and monitored for rattles, with AI used to interpret acoustic data and trigger factory corrections.

2. **End-of-line AI-assisted burn-in track reduces testing cost dramatically:** Brian White explains Tesla's AI-assisted burn-in track allows comprehensive NVH (noise, vibration, harshness) and quality testing at a cost he estimates at approximately $0.30 per car in electricity — a capability competitors cannot replicate, giving Tesla a lasting quality-assurance advantage.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cybercab unboxed manufacturing represents a step-change in assembly complexity:** Brian White notes that whereas a traditional vehicle might require 200 manufacturing cells, the Cybercab's unboxed process uses roughly 20–25, representing a fundamentally different manufacturing paradigm that reduces complexity and enables higher automation rates.

---

**Notable quotes and data:**

- Lars Moravy (per Herbert's interview): *"The majority of our CyberCab test fleet has gone into training for Autopilot. You know, our models are great, but they still need to train. You've seen the training vehicles with the steering wheels and pedals."*
- Lars on Cybercab FSD: confirmed it is not a copy-paste from Model Y, has different weights, requires retraining, and needs real-world data — not just simulation.
- Lars on Optimus subline installation: first line takes two to three days to install and about a week to get going; 40 more sublines to follow after the first is proven.
- Lars on Optimus cost: suggested that over time, an Optimus robot could cost less to build than one of Tesla's cars.
- Cybercab production line: ~90% automated (per Lars Moravy).
- Lars's production volume target for Cybercab: more than any other vehicle Tesla has ever built.
- Unverified Nomura/China supply chain figures (treat as rumor): 70,000 Optimus units/year capacity at Fremont (raised from 50,000); 70,000 units/year planned for Austin in 2028; 1.5 million units/year long-term target; ~25,000 units shipped in 2026 (±10,000); 1,000 units/week target by September 2026.
- UBS (per Herbert, unconfirmed): Optimus Gen 3 official launch window July–August 2026.
- Brian White on Cybercab economics: *"I don't see why you would want to make $5,000 off a car when you can make $5,000 a month off a car."*

2026-07-02.title: Elon Is Building the Entire Stack
2026-07-02.body:
Recorded on July 1, 2026 (Canada Day), this episode of the Cern Basher podcast features host Cern Basher and guest Phil Beisel reviewing the past two weeks of Tesla, SpaceX, and broader AI/tech developments. The central thesis is that Elon Musk is systematically building a vertically integrated "full stack" — spanning FSD software, robotaxi operations, Optimus manufacturing, chip fabrication (Terafab), orbital compute (Star Mine), and wireless spectrum (Starlink/Echostar) — and that this positions him to win the AI race not just at the model level but at the infrastructure and inference-at-scale level. The hosts argue that the coming wave of embodied AI and autonomous deployment will be far larger and more disruptive than most observers appreciate, and that a Tesla–SpaceX merger is increasingly logical given the deepening operational and financial entanglement between the two companies.

## Humanoid Bots

1. **Optimus production line opens at Fremont:** Elon shared an image walking the Optimus production line at the Fremont factory, confirming that the Model S/X line has been cleared from that space to make room. Lars Moravy mentioned in a separate interview with Herbert and Jeff Lutz that one line has been assembled at Fremont for Optimus. A Tesla post cited by the hosts (attributed to Tesla Zoa) indicates that Optimus is being built and validated in Germany with approximately 40 sublines to be constructed. A Tesla video released roughly one to two months prior depicted 40 lines with multiple stations for producing various robot sub-components; that same video stated 12,000 human jobs will be created in the process.

2. **Manufacturing philosophy — more like a car than a phone:** Lars Moravy pushed back on the criticism that Tesla lacks consumer-product manufacturing expertise, arguing that building Optimus is far more analogous to building a car than a cell phone, given the three-dimensional nature of assembly and the safety requirements. The hosts agreed, noting that Optimus — like a car — has a large number of moving parts and dense electronics, whereas a phone is largely static. Phil Beisel expects Optimus manufacturing to begin human-in-the-loop, with automation introduced progressively as processes are understood.

3. **Scale trajectory — Fremont as prototype, Texas as mass production:** The hosts characterize Fremont as effectively a prototype factory regardless of unit count, with initial thousands of units likely absorbed internally by Tesla and SpaceX before reaching external customers. The hosts believe a 10-million-unit annualized production factory in Texas is the eventual destination. Early Optimus units are expected to be deployed first in manufacturing, then in service industries (retail, restaurants), and eventually in the home — though the hosts note that home deployment faces unique consumer-acceptance and safety hurdles.

4. **Societal integration — novelty to normalcy:** The hosts discuss a two-stage transition: first, the novelty phase where Optimus in public will be a head-turning spectacle (analogous to early Waymo reactions in San Francisco), and second, a normalization phase where robots are simply background fixtures of daily life. They also flag an anticipated period of public misbehavior toward Optimus units, noting that the robots are expected to be trained not to fight back or self-protect, drawing parallels to people harassing Waymo vehicles in San Francisco.

## Robotaxi

1. **Austin unsupervised expansion imminent:** Phil Beisel states with conviction that Austin unsupervised robotaxi operation is close, acknowledging he had previously (and incorrectly) predicted a May–June 2026 launch. He cites the growing number of Cybercabs observed running in Austin, testing on public roads without a driver, steering wheel, or pedals, and what he interprets as a manufacturing build-up — including images of Cybercabs accumulating in parking lots — as evidence of an imminent fleet release. He estimates that within two weeks to two months, Tesla will announce a fleet of approximately 150 cars operating as a commercial service in Austin.

2. **Lars Moravy: Cybercab production ahead of expectations:** The hosts reference Lars Moravy's interview with Herbert and Jeff Lutz in which Lars indicated that Cybercab production is going better than he expected, while also emphasizing that high volumes must be produced simply to learn how to produce at high volumes — a point the hosts interpret as Tesla making many more Cybercabs than the publicly known service numbers suggest.

3. **Operational complexity is the hidden bottleneck:** Phil Beisel argues that the broader investment community and media are overly focused on FSD/AI as the gating factor for robotaxi scale, when in fact a large set of non-AI operational challenges — customer service systems, fleet maintenance (tire changes, cleaning), navigation edge cases, and incident response automation — are equally or more constraining. He draws an analogy: if Waymo handles N incidents per day at its fleet size, Tesla cannot simply hire a proportionally larger call center when running 10x the fleet; the entire operational loop must itself be autonomous. He believes this is what is occupying significant Tesla engineering bandwidth beyond the FSD team.

4. **Cybercab spotted near Silicon Valley suburbs:** The host (Cern Basher) recounts personally seeing a Cybercab driving on Yerba Buena Road in a remote southeast corner of San Jose — approximately one mile from his home and roughly 20 minutes outside of Palo Alto — describing it as a striking surprise even for someone deeply familiar with the vehicle. Testing on public roads without driver controls is confirmed by both hosts.

5. **Fleet size context:** The hosts reference Lars Moravy having commented in the Herbert/Jeff Lutz interview that roughly 150 Cybercabs may be in existence (Herbert's estimate), with the hosts speculating the true production number could be substantially higher (e.g., 450+), reflecting manufacturing learning rather than service deployment intent alone.

6. **Mixed fleet model — Cybercab plus Model Y:** The hosts note that a functioning robotaxi network will still require a significant proportion of Model Y vehicles (perhaps ~20% of fleet) to accommodate rides with more than two passengers, and that a larger Model Y rollout alongside Cybercabs has not yet been publicly visible.

## Autonomous Driving

1. **FSD V14 "light" for Hardware 3 — an impressive feat with caveats:** Phil Beisel characterizes the delivery of a supervised FSD experience on Hardware 3 as a remarkable engineering achievement, given that Hardware 3 has roughly one-eighth the memory bandwidth of Hardware 4, and Hardware 4 is three to five times faster for overall FSD workloads. The higher-resolution cameras on Hardware 4 add further capability gaps. He believes this effort stems partly from honoring Elon Musk's prior commitments to Hardware 3 owners (estimated 3–4 million vehicles), partly from a genuine engineering drive to understand system constraints, and that the optimization work likely benefited from pipeline work already done in a prior FSD version (referenced as an intermediate release in the v14.x series that involved a full-stack rewrite of data processing and movement). He does not expect Hardware 3 vehicles to ever achieve unsupervised FSD.

2. **Constraint-driven innovation:** Phil Beisel frames the Hardware 3 FSD work as exemplifying a broader engineering philosophy: working within severe constraints forces teams to deeply understand where compute cycles and data-movement bandwidth are actually spent, producing insights that benefit the broader FSD stack. He draws an analogy to biological analysis — observing a creature in granular detail reveals optimization opportunities invisible at a higher level.

3. **FSD breadth is a stretch on engineering resources:** Phil Beisel expresses concern — flagged as his personal opinion without internal data — that the FSD team may be spread thin across an unusually large number of simultaneous workstreams: supervised FSD on Hardware 3 and Hardware 4, FSD in Europe, left- and right-hand drive variants, Tesla Semi FSD, Cybertruck-specific features (e.g., summon), unsupervised FSD for robotaxi, and all associated operational systems. He notes it has been approximately one year since the robotaxi launch, which he interprets as evidence of more problems than were anticipated.

4. **Katy, Texas crash — media misreporting:** A Tesla crash in Katy, Texas prompted investigations from NHTSA and NTSB and was widely reported with implications of FSD involvement. Elon Musk responded publicly that FSD drives slowly through neighborhood streets and this was a high-speed crash. Phil Beisel elaborates that data showed FSD was manually overridden — the accelerator was pressed to 100% and the vehicle reached 73 mph — making driver fault clear. The hosts criticize media reporting as sensationalized and biased, while also noting an inherent irony: as FSD improves and human interventions become rarer, drivers become less prepared to intervene correctly when they do attempt to take control.

5. **"Full self-hearing" — in-factory audio diagnostics:** Lars Moravy described in the Herbert/Jeff Lutz interview a system (jokingly named "full self-hearing" by Lars) that uses the car's built-in microphones during end-of-line production testing to detect and localize rattles and other anomalies via AI analysis. The hosts note this technology has potential consumer-facing applications (e.g., helping service centers diagnose rattles without relying on driver descriptions) and fleet applications (e.g., autonomous vehicles self-diagnosing in the absence of a consistent human occupant).

## Energy

1. **Major European Megapack order — 25 GWh, phase one of 100+ GWh program:** Tesla secured a deal in Europe for 25 gigawatt-hours of Megapack energy storage systems, described as the first phase of a broader program targeting over 100 gigawatt-hours in total. For context, the hosts note Tesla sold nearly 47 gigawatt-hours of Megapack globally in 2025, making the 100 GWh target more than twice that figure. The deal also includes Autobidder trading software with long-term revenue warranties — the hosts flag this as a notable reemergence of a product Tesla has not publicly discussed in some time, describing it as AI-powered software to optimize Megapack dispatch and maximize revenue from grid arbitrage.

2. **Powerwall lease program in Massachusetts and Connecticut:** Tesla launched a discounted Powerwall lease program in Massachusetts and Connecticut tied to virtual power plant participation.

3. **Sunrun/Renew Home virtual power plant:** Tesla announced a partnership with Sunrun and Renew Home to aggregate home batteries, smart thermostats, and other distributed devices into what they describe as the largest distributed virtual power plant in the US, targeting more than 16 gigawatts of flexible capacity for hyperscalers, data centers, and utilities. The hosts flag this as flying under the radar despite being a significant strategic move.

4. **Megapod trademark — supercharger sites as distributed AI compute nodes:** Tesla filed a trademark application for "Megapod." The hosts theorize this refers to deploying Megapack-backed AI compute clusters at Tesla Supercharger sites across the US (noting approximately 7 gigawatt-hours of provisioned capacity at Supercharger locations). The concept is to use overprovisioned grid power at underutilized Supercharger sites to run inference workloads — potentially leased to third-party AI consumers similar to how Anthropic leases cloud compute — with Megapacks buffering cheap off-peak power for use during peak compute demand. The hosts emphasize this is inference compute, not training.

## Electric Vehicles

1. **Cybertruck earns top safety pick — safest pickup truck overall:** The Cybertruck received a top safety pick rating and was named the safest pickup truck, EV or otherwise.

2. **Q2 2026 delivery forecast:** Goldman Sachs raised its Q2 2026 delivery forecast to 420,000 vehicles. The hosts note that by the time of publication (estimated Friday, July 3, 2026), the actual Q2 numbers will already be known. Some trackers believe Q2 2026 could be a record quarter for Tesla.

3. **Tesla stock surge:** On June 29, 2026, Tesla stock surged approximately 8%, described as one of its largest single-day gains in over a year.

## Market & Competition

1. **Elon exercises options early:** Elon Musk exercised stock options ahead of an August deadline. The hosts note this has fueled speculation about a potential Tesla–SpaceX merger timeline but decline to add further detail.

2. **Tesla–SpaceX merger logic is growing:** The hosts make an extended case that a Tesla–SpaceX merger is increasingly inevitable, driven by: (a) deepening cross-company engineering collaboration (Lars Moravy on a first-name basis with SpaceX counterparts, shared materials and hardware between Starship and Cybertruck programs); (b) the impracticality of managing related-party transactions at scale (e.g., SpaceX purchasing millions of Optimus units, or Tesla using Grok in its vehicles, would generate taxable inter-company revenue); (c) Elon's desire for frictionless decision-making without independent board approval of cross-entity deals; and (d) the fact that Tesla — not SpaceX — hired the new director of the Terafab project (an 18-year Intel semiconductor manufacturing veteran), signaling Tesla's material stake in what might superficially appear to be a SpaceX project.

3. **The "Beisel Curve" — AI compute supply-demand gap:** Phil Beisel presents a proprietary chart (logarithmic scale, described as the "Beisel Curve") showing AI compute demand growing at approximately 3.4x per year since 2017, compared to the prior CPU-era growth rate of roughly 60% per year. Even after applying an efficiency discount (reflecting algorithmic and hardware improvements), the adjusted demand curve vastly outstrips the projected supply from existing fabs (primarily TSMC, with Samsung and smaller players). Terafab, if it achieves one terawatt of compute output and comes online around 2030 (which the hosts consider aggressive), makes a meaningful but still insufficient dent. The hosts argue this gap will drive compute prices significantly higher, benefiting Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic, and especially SpaceX as Cursor's new owner. Tim Cook and Apple are cited as a cautionary tale: Apple's late and weak AI investments caused a blind spot to GPU demand, resulting in Apple raising MacBook prices by $100–$300 due to memory cost pressure.

4. **Waymo competition framing:** The hosts use Waymo as a benchmark for robotaxi incident rates and operational scale, arguing Tesla must architect its entire operational loop — not just the vehicle AI — to be autonomous in order to run a fleet an order of magnitude larger than Waymo's without proportionally scaling human support staff.

5. **SpaceX Starfall — potential military application:** On June 23, 2026, SpaceX launched "Starfall," described as a temporary satellite capable of staying in orbit from one hour to a couple of weeks before returning to Earth via parachute (similar to Dragon). The hosts identify three potential use cases: rapid cargo delivery anywhere on Earth, in-orbit manufacturing or experiments with return capability, and future retrieval of cargo from other space objects. Both hosts believe the primary driver is military, though they acknowledge this is speculation.

6. **SpaceX / Echostar spectrum deal — direct-to-cell testing underway:** Last summer, SpaceX completed a deal with Echostar worth approximately $19 billion (paid in a mix of cash and SpaceX stock) to acquire wireless spectrum. Echostar received 261.8 million SpaceX shares, worth approximately $45 billion at current prices. The deal has cleared regulatory hurdles but is not scheduled to close financially until November 2027 unless SpaceX accelerates payments. A letter dated June 15, 2026 confirmed SpaceX is conducting interim period testing of next-generation direct-to-cell satellites using the acquired Echostar spectrum. Phil Beisel believes this testing likely involves prototype handset hardware built by SpaceX to validate antenna design and signal performance — and that this (rather than a consumer phone launch) is the most likely explanation for the Wall Street Journal's report that Elon Musk is developing a new AI device using Qualcomm Snapdragon chips, a report Elon publicly called "utterly false."

7. **AI device / "Starphone" speculation:** The hosts decline to fully dismiss the Wall Street Journal report about an Elon Musk AI phone, with Phil Beisel arguing that large organizations routinely build prototypes of adjacent hardware, and that a Snapdragon-based prototype device would be a logical tool for testing Starlink direct-to-cell capabilities. He sketches a longer-term vision of an AI-native device (no app ecosystem, pure information delivery via on-device and Starlink-offloaded inference through Star Mine) that could disrupt both carriers (Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile) and handset makers (Apple). He notes SpaceX's acquisition of Cursor AI as further evidence of an integrated AI stack ambition.

8. **Starlink in New Zealand — 27% rural broadband market share:** Elon Musk highlighted that Starlink has become New Zealand's largest rural internet provider, with 27% of the rural broadband market (up from 19% the prior year), 85,000 total connections (72,000 rural residential fixed), and download speeds averaging 226 Mbps — approximately four times faster than competing services. New Zealand now has the highest satellite broadband uptake per capita in the developed world.

9. **SpaceX IPO float and lockup schedule:** Per an analysis by Dillon Loomis, SpaceX's current public float is approximately 4.9% of total shares. Key lockup release milestones: ~20% of an early employee/investor block releases approximately two days after Q2 earnings (with an additional conditional 10% if the stock closes above $175.50 on more than five of ten days, bringing the potential float to ~15%); further tranches release between August 20 and October 24, 2026, bringing cumulative float to ~27–28%; Q3 earnings in November trigger another ~28% release (the largest single date); the 180-day lockup ends December 8, 2026, at which point ~40% of shares will be tradable. Elon Musk's shares carry a 366-day lockup — the longest of any individual — with his block not beginning to release until mid-2027. Full float (~100%) is expected by August 2027. NASDAQ-100 inclusion is scheduled for July 6, 2026; S&P 500 inclusion is expected mid-2027 or later, potentially coinciding with a Tesla–SpaceX merger.

10. **Terafab land acquisition near Austin:** Tesla (or an affiliated entity) has reportedly acquired approximately 2,700 acres of land east/northeast of Austin — comparable in size to the current Giga Texas footprint — as a likely site for Terafab. The hosts expect further land purchases. Separately, they reference a prior Elon Musk slide showing plans for 11 million square feet of manufacturing space near Bastrop, Texas (roughly 15–20 minutes from Giga Texas) for AI1 satellites (Star Mine).

Notable quotes and data:
- Hardware 3 has roughly **1/8 the memory bandwidth** of Hardware 4; Hardware 4 is **3–5x faster** for overall FSD workloads.
- Estimated **3–4 million Hardware 3 vehicles** exist globally.
- Goldman Sachs Q2 2026 delivery forecast: **420,000 vehicles**.
- Tesla stock surged **~8%** on June 29, 2026.
- European Megapack deal: **25 GWh** (Phase 1), targeting **100+ GWh** total; Tesla sold nearly **47 GWh** in 2025.
- Sunrun/Renew Home VPP target: **16+ GW** of flexible capacity.
- Starlink New Zealand: **27% rural broadband market share**, **85,000 connections**, **226 Mbps** average download, ~**4x faster** than competitors.
- SpaceX current public float: **~4.9%**; reaches ~40% by December 8, 2026; full float by August 2027.
- Echostar deal: **~$19 billion**, **261.8 million SpaceX shares** to Echostar, worth **~$45 billion** at current prices; closes November 2027.
- Terafab land acquisition: **~2,700 acres** east of Austin.
- Optimus production: **~40 sublines** to be built (per Tesla Zoa post); **12,000 human jobs** projected.
- Phil Beisel (on Cursor AI pricing): *"I've replaced a team of five for 60 bucks a month."*
- Phil Beisel (on compute supply gap): *"The United States produces today about half a terawatt. So you double that and you need that plus what it already uses… to run the air conditioners and the lights."*
- On the Katy, Texas crash: FSD was manually overridden with the accelerator pressed to **100%**, reaching **73 mph**.
- Phil Beisel (on robotaxi operational scale): *"He's thinking, 'I'm not having a 5,000-person call center.'"*
- Phil Beisel (predicting Austin unsupervised launch): *"Somewhere between two weeks to two months… we're going to wake up and Tesla's going to say we are running a service in Austin that includes a fleet of 150 cars."*
- Cern Basher (on Lars Moravy interview): *"The amount of AI that we put into the world… it's very specific — he's talking about embodied AI, real-world AI."*

2026-07-02.title: Tesla (TSLA) Q2 2026 deliveries jump 25% to 480,126, beating estimates
2026-07-02.body:
Tesla delivered 480,126 vehicles in Q2 2026, a 25% year-over-year increase that beat Wall Street's consensus estimate by roughly 74,000 units — the company's first quarterly delivery growth after two consecutive years of decline.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Record Q2 deliveries, massive beat vs. expectations:** Tesla produced 451,758 vehicles and delivered 480,126 in Q2 2026. Model 3/Y accounted for 442,936 produced and 467,762 delivered; Other Models (S, X, Cybertruck, Semi) contributed 8,822 produced and 12,364 delivered. The result surpassed analyst consensus of 406,024 and beat even the most bullish estimates from Goldman Sachs and Barclays (~418,000–420,000) by more than 60,000 units.

2. **Inventory drawdown marks reversal from Q1:** Tesla delivered ~28,000 more vehicles than it produced in the quarter, working down existing inventory — a reversal from Q1 2026, when the company built roughly 50,000 excess vehicles it couldn't sell.

3. **Historical context:** Q2 2026 is Tesla's best-ever second quarter, surpassing the 466,140 units delivered in Q2 2023. It also represents a 34% sequential jump from Q1 2026's 358,023 deliveries. Tesla's all-time quarterly record remains 497,099, set in Q3 2025.

## Energy
1. **Energy storage up 40%+ year-over-year:** Tesla deployed 13.5 GWh of energy storage in Q2 2026, up more than 40% from 9.6 GWh in Q2 2025, though slightly below analyst expectations of ~13.8 GWh.

## Market & Competition
1. **Tesla closing gap with BYD:** BYD delivered 557,090 fully electric vehicles in Q2 2026, maintaining its lead in global BEV sales. However, BYD's BEV deliveries fell ~8% year-over-year while Tesla's rose 25%, narrowing the gap from over 220,000 units a year ago to roughly 77,000 units.

## Editorial Stance
The author characterizes Q2 as a "genuinely strong" and real inflection point, attributing the demand surge primarily to a spike in gas prices triggered by the war in Iran, which drove EV demand while Tesla held ~50,000 units of excess inventory from Q1.

Notable quotes and data:
- Q2 2026 deliveries: 480,126 (+25% YoY, +34% QoQ)
- Q2 2026 production: 451,758
- Consensus estimate: 406,024; highest analyst estimates (Goldman Sachs, Barclays): ~418,000–420,000
- Beat over consensus: ~74,000 units (~18%)
- Model 3/Y deliveries: 467,762; Other Models: 12,364
- Energy storage deployed: 13.5 GWh (+40%+ YoY vs. 9.6 GWh in Q2 2025)
- BYD Q2 2026 BEV deliveries: 557,090 (down ~8% YoY)
