2026-07-06.title: Weekly Tesla Brief (Jun 29 – Jul 5, 2026)
2026-07-06.body:
## Brief

- Q2 deliveries hit 480,126, best Q2 ever, beat consensus by ~74K
- Stock fell ~7-8% on delivery day despite record beat
- Production Cybercab begins public road testing in Austin, no wheel
- Miami launches unsupervised Robotaxi, third unsupervised city
- Optimus line 1 installed at Fremont; ~40 more to go
- Katy, TX driver charged with manslaughter in fatal FSD-adjacent crash
- July 7 Giga Texas "scaling" announcement teased by Lars Moravy

---

## Robotaxi
- Miami launched unsupervised Model Y rides July 3, operating in rain on day one, though Electrek notes the published geofence covers only West Miami, Doral, and Sweetwater — excluding downtown, Miami Beach, and the airport. Unsupervised service now spans Miami, Dallas, and Houston; Austin runs mixed unsupervised/safety-monitor; Bay Area remains safety-monitor only.
- Production Cybercab — no steering wheel, no pedals — began engineering-test driving on Austin public roads, confirmed by both Musk and Ashok Elluswamy. Lars Moravy put Cybercab manufacturing automation at ~90%, called published analyst cost models wrong, and said the platform could hit 2M–10M+ units/year and outsell the Model Y.
- Nevada permit filed June 5 covers Clark County for up to 5,000 vehicles in year one including Reid Airport; a depot is built on Mohawk Street and gold-liveried robotaxis have been spotted in Las Vegas, but the permit remains under review with no rides yet.
- Lars Moravy teased a July 7 Giga Texas "scaling" announcement twice in his interview without elaborating; widely read as a multi-city robotaxi expansion signal. The mid-2026 seven-city commitment was missed — one channel counts service live in three cities as of July 5 (five counting Austin's mixed fleet and the Bay Area's safety-monitor service).
- Electrek disputes the bullish deployment narrative, citing city-official estimates of only ~50 vehicles in Austin's fleet, the unsupervised subset down to roughly 14 active cars from a ~25 peak, and wait times routinely exceeding 15 minutes.

---

## Electric Vehicles
- Q2 2026 deliveries: 480,126 (+25% YoY, +34% QoQ), beating consensus of ~406,000 by ~74,000 units — Tesla's best-ever Q2. Production was 451,758, with inventory drawdown of ~28,000 units confirming genuine demand versus Q1's overhang.
- Model Y L launched in the US at $61,990 (Launch Series AWD), roughly $8,000 above analyst expectations, with 325-mile range and September deliveries; also launched in the UAE (deliveries beginning November). Production-line commissioning for the 7-seat variant is underway at Giga Texas.
- Giga Berlin ramping from 6,200/week to a targeted 7,500/week by October, adding ~1,000 jobs, as VW simultaneously plans to close four German factories.
- Competitors lagged sharply: Ford EV sales -40.7% YoY, GM EV sales -41% YoY, Lucid delivered ~4,000 units and replaced its CFO; Rivian beat estimates and raised guidance. BYD's BEV lead over Tesla narrowed from 220,000+ units a year ago to roughly 77,000.

---

## Autonomous Driving
- Harris County prosecutors charged Tesla driver Michael Butler with manslaughter over the June 19 Katy crash that killed Martha Avila, alleging he overrode FSD twice and held the accelerator at 100% for six seconds, reaching ~73 mph; he had reportedly Googled making "FSD more aggressive" beforehand. He faces 2–20 years and $150,000 bond.
- FSD "V14 Lite" rolled out to Hardware 3 vehicles by June 30, distilling HW4's V14 behavior into HW3's constrained compute (~15% of HW4's memory bandwidth); early testers call it a major leap over v12.6, though Mad Max mode and other newer features are absent and HW3 is not expected to ever reach unsupervised capability.
- Mixed signals from Germany on FSD: the automotive regulator formally declined to approve FSD independently, deferring to an EU-wide vote expected October 2026 at earliest — while a parliamentary state secretary's response on autonomous-driving pilot rules was read by one commentator as opening the door to a surprise national approval "this month." The two statements, from different arms of the German government, are unreconciled.
- NHTSA eliminated the manual brake pedal requirement for fully autonomous vehicles; UNECE adopted the first global AV technical regulation, hardware-agnostic with no LiDAR mandate.

---

## Humanoid Bots
- First Optimus production line arrived and began installation at Fremont on the former Model S/X line; Musk toured the floor and posted photos. ~40 more sublines remain, each taking roughly one to two weeks to install and prove out, per Lars Moravy.
- Musk directly rejected "4D chess" delay theories: "Optimus production will be extremely slow at first, as everything is new. This is not like making a car." Fremont production timing points to late July/August at earliest; Texas factory is roughly a year from fully operational per Moravy.
- Stated 2026 targets of 50,000–100,000 units remain unconfirmed and widely doubted; unverified supply-chain rumors (Nomura-sourced) suggest ~25,000 units shipped in 2026 and 1,000/week by September — flagged as speculative.
- Neuralink announced it threaded electrodes through the dura without cutting it in a live trial; Musk called it a "very big deal" for brain-interface safety, with Optimus limb integration described as a 5–10+ year thread, not a near-term catalyst.

---

## Energy
- 25 GWh European Megapack deal signed as phase one of a 100+ GWh program — more than twice Tesla's full 2025 global Megapack sales — including Autobidder trading software with long-term revenue warranties.
- Q2 2026 energy storage: 13.5 GWh deployed (+41% YoY, +53% QoQ), slightly missing the ~13.8 GWh consensus but the second-best quarter on record; trailing-12-month deployment hit a new high of ~49 GWh.
- Orana BESS (415 MW / 1.66 GWh, $415M) reached commercial operation in New South Wales, Australia. A new ~50 GWh/year Megapack factory is planned in Texas.
- Tesla–Sunrun/Renew Home VPP targets 16+ GW of aggregated flexible capacity across residential batteries and smart thermostats for hyperscaler and data-center demand.

---

## Financials
- Tesla stock fell ~7-8% on delivery-report day despite the record beat, after running up ~12% into the report — read by multiple hosts as "sell the news," though Rivian's similar pattern on its own beat complicates that framing.
- Q2 2026 earnings call set for Wednesday, July 22, after market close.
- Michael Burry disclosed a new Tesla short at $416.22, part of a broader basket shorting Nvidia, Caterpillar, SOXX, and Applied Materials on a semiconductor-bubble thesis; position size undisclosed.
- Tesla capped employee AI spending at $200/week effective July 6, carving out an exemption for xAI beta products — flagged by Electrek as a potential internal conflict of interest favoring Grok over Claude.

---

## Market & Competition
- Grok 4.5 (1.5T-parameter "V9" model) entered private beta at SpaceX and Tesla, with Musk claiming performance "close to, perhaps exceeding" Anthropic's Opus.
- Terafab hired Gary Jiang (18 years at Intel, ran Arizona 18A fab) as director; ~2,700 acres acquired east of Austin as the likely site. Pilot line targeted ~2030, full facility ~2032-33 — still a multi-year-out bet.
- Tesla–SpaceX merger speculation continued to build on cross-company hiring, engineering ties, and Elon's early option exercise, though no formal announcement occurred this week.

---

## Bear Case of the Week
- Katy, TX driver Michael Butler charged with manslaughter (2nd-degree felony, 2-20 years) after allegedly overriding FSD and flooring the accelerator to 73 mph in a residential zone, killing Martha Avila; prosecutors cite prior searches about making FSD "more aggressive."
- Tesla Semi's first known fatal crash: on June 28 a Semi struck two stopped vehicles in Dayton, NV, killing two people; preliminary evidence suggests driver fatigue, no FSD involved, and it remains unconfirmed whether AEB engaged or a drowsiness camera exists on Semi.
- Tesla stock fell ~7-8% on Q2 delivery-report day despite a record 480,126-unit beat, an unexplained reaction multiple hosts flagged as concerning for near-term sentiment.
- Cybertruck Power Conversion System failures confirmed in ~41% of a 223-person owner forum poll, with failures as low as under 10,000 miles; Tesla is replacing units case-by-case without a recall, and pre-2026 Foundation Series trucks are not covered by the new 7-year warranty.
- Electrek disputes the robotaxi scale narrative: Austin's total fleet estimated at only ~50 vehicles by city officials, with the unsupervised subset down to ~14 active cars from a ~25 peak and wait times routinely exceeding 15 minutes.

2026-07-06.title: SpaceX Just Entered Another Massive Market
2026-07-06.relevance: tangential — The video is almost entirely about SpaceX (mobile service ambitions, Mesh acquisition, Starlink perks) with Tesla only entering via speculation about a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger and secondhand commentary on the robotaxi thesis.
2026-07-06.body:
This video (part of a discussion between the host and guest Larry Goldberg) focuses on three SpaceX developments — a possible consumer mobile service, Starlink direct-to-cell expansion, and the acquisition of optical transceiver startup Mesh — and uses them as a springboard to debate whether and when SpaceX might merge with Tesla, citing Cathie Wood's and Gwynne Shotwell's public comments. Tesla substance is thin and mostly speculative, centered on merger timing and relative valuation rather than Tesla's own operations.

## Market & Competition
1. **SpaceX reportedly eyeing US mobile market:** A report says SpaceX told investors it wants to launch a consumer mobile service in the US, competing with Verizon and AT&T; an Oppenheimer analyst described this as a "$2 trillion communications market" opportunity, with AI infrastructure and AI applications as the next-biggest areas for SpaceX. The guest cautioned that a full US mobile rollout is unlikely within a year and a meaningful nationwide network may not arrive until late next year, contingent on Starship deploying larger V3 satellite batches to expand bandwidth.
2. **Starlink direct-to-cell expands to Philippines:** The Philippines became the first Southeast Asian country to approve Starlink direct-to-cell service via partner Globe, allowing standard LTE phones to connect without extra hardware. The guest believes this initial service is text-based, not voice, with voice capability requiring further build-out and new phone compatibility.
3. **SpaceX offers Starlink perks near Memphis data center:** SpaceX is giving Memphis-area neighbors near its Colossus data center free Starlink hardware and roughly 50% off internet plans; the guest characterized this as a community goodwill gesture rather than a broader business shift, comparing it to friction Elon-affiliated projects have faced in other cities (e.g., the Boring Company in Tennessee).
4. **SpaceX acquires Mesh Optical Technologies:** SpaceX received regulatory approval to acquire Mesh, a startup founded by former SpaceX engineers building optical transceivers for AI data centers, aiming to manufacture 1,000+ units per day this year; the company raised a $50 million Series A in February. The guest described it as a classic SpaceX "aqua-hire" aimed at easing data bottlenecks in Colossus-style clusters and potentially SpaceX's orbital data center ambitions, calling it evolutionary rather than revolutionary.

## Financials
1. **Cathie Wood says Tesla-SpaceX merger not imminent:** Wood stated Elon Musk likely wants Tesla's robotaxi story to become clear to investors before combining Tesla with SpaceX/xAI, referencing Musk's recent framing of his companies as "convergent stories"; she believes Musk will "let Tesla run" for now.
2. **Guest's counter-view: merger could come sooner:** The guest (Larry Goldberg) argued a merger could happen anytime between now and mid-next year, leaning toward sooner rather than later, on the view that SpaceX holds as much unrealized value as Tesla and that combining the two would unlock value beyond what either achieves independently. He estimated (as personal judgment, not sourced data) that SpaceX stock "should be" in the low-200s and Tesla stock "should be" in the high-6000s.
3. **Gwynne Shotwell comments cited as merger breadcrumb:** The host noted that SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell, when asked about a Tesla merger, reportedly said it "would make Elon's life a lot easier," that she "can certainly see the synergies," and that she is currently focused on her present role rather than that future — read by the host as not a denial.
4. **Third-party analysis on data center revenue potential:** Referencing a separate video with an analyst named Brian Wang, the host relayed a claim (attributed to that analysis) that Tesla's terrestrial AI data center rental and related AI/Optimus opportunities could reach roughly $100 billion per year within a couple of years — a figure the host says would dwarf the robotaxi opportunity in scale.

Notable quotes and data:
- Oppenheimer analyst (Timothy Huran, per transcript name as best resolved): "It's a $2 trillion communications market... they're going to look to be disruptive there."
- Guest on mobile rollout timing: "I would say that it's highly unlikely we will see much of a network if any at all for a year in this country, and it could be late next year before we start seeing... a production roll out."
- Mesh Optical Technologies: former SpaceX engineers, targeting 1,000+ optical transceivers/day this year, raised a $50 million Series A in February.
- Memphis Starlink community offer: no upfront hardware cost and roughly 50% off internet plans for residential customers near the Colossus data center.
- Cathie Wood: "I think he's going to let Tesla run here for a while... he wants that story to become very clear to investors."
- Guest's personal valuation view (unsourced, his own judgment): SpaceX stock "should be in the 200s"; Tesla stock "should be in the 6700s."
- Guest: "The announcement could happen anytime between now and June of next year."
- Third-party estimate relayed by host: Tesla's terrestrial AI data center/Optimus-related revenue opportunity could reach ~$100 billion per year within a couple of years, per Brian Wang's analysis.

2026-07-06.title: The Moment Robotaxi Race Shifted to Tesla's Favor
2026-07-06.relevance: core — The video is centered on Tesla's Robotaxi/Cybercab expansion, FSD testing signals, and a direct competitive comparison with Waymo, all directly bearing on the Tesla investment thesis.
2026-07-06.body:
The video, hosted by brighterwithherbert with guest Jeff Le (a supply chain/manufacturing executive), argues that Tesla's robotaxi rollout is accelerating toward nationwide scale just as Waymo suffered a high-profile operational failure over the July 4th weekend — a contrast the hosts frame as a turning point favoring Tesla. Much of the discussion centers on fresh sightings of Cybercabs and robotaxi test vehicles across new US cities, alongside unresolved "convenience issues" (wait times, pickup locations) that still separate current operations from a true mass-market launch.

## Robotaxi
1. **Tesla launches unsupervised robotaxi service in Miami:** Tesla announced unsupervised robotaxi service is now live in Miami, with Ashok Elluswamy confirming it is fully unsupervised and encouraging owners to try it; video showed driverless Model Ys operating in heavy rain, including a rider sitting in the front seat. Tesla's robotaxi/Robotaxi network is now active across five regions: Miami, Dallas, Houston, Austin, and Bay Area (as Ride Hail). Miami's operating geofence was described as still much smaller than Waymo's Miami geofence, and only about four vehicles were spotted operating at one Miami intersection (count via a third-party spotter, not an official fleet figure).
2. **Cybercab sightings accelerate across new cities:** New production Cybercabs and Tesla testing/engineering vehicles were spotted in Dallas (reportedly ten in twenty minutes per one observer), Tampa, Jacksonville, and New Orleans, plus a fleet of Model Ys with camera washers spotted in New Orleans — a city not among Tesla's announced launch markets. The hosts interpret this as evidence Tesla is quietly staging infrastructure and operations ahead of a broader, faster nationwide rollout ("super slow, then all at once").
3. **Cybercab tests unprotected left turns and passenger drop-offs:** A widely-known difficult unprotected left-turn intersection in Florida (made famous by YouTube spotter Chuck Cook) was seen being tested by a Cybercab with a human driver, which Jeff Le characterizes as late-stage performance validation signaling proximity to a wider release. Separate footage appeared to show Cybercab passenger drop-off testing, though the host notes uncertainty about exactly what was being demonstrated.
4. **Cybercab is being fine-tuned as a new hardware form factor for FSD:** Le explains that Tesla can't simply port trained FSD models onto the Cybercab because of its different form factor (camera placement, geometry), requiring dedicated data collection and engineering — consistent with Lars Moravy's earlier statement that most Cybercabs currently being produced are going toward FSD field testing rather than public rides.
5. **Unresolved "convenience issues" still block a true mass launch:** Host Herbert and Le both describe current service in Austin, Dallas, Houston, and the Bay Area as not yet "real" services due to long wait times (up to ~20 minutes) and inconvenient pickup/drop-off locations, contrasting unfavorably with human-driven Uber/Lyft. Le argues Tesla should not scale to many cities until these issues are resolved, and notes Elon Musk has said upcoming releases will add memory of preferred pickup/drop-off locations (home, school, work) to address this.
6. **Tesla showcases Cybercab accessibility features for blind riders:** At the National Federation of the Blind's annual convention in Austin, Tesla demonstrated Cybercab accessibility features including braille on physical controls, space for service animals and assistive devices, and wheelchair-height seating for easier transfers; Musk said designing for blind riders was a specific goal. Le frames this as both socially meaningful and a signal of Tesla's scale-readiness and brand-building.

## Market & Competition
1. **Waymo suffers major operational failure in San Francisco over July 4th weekend:** Numerous Waymo vehicles reportedly became disabled or "froze" during holiday congestion, causing hours-long gridlock; described failure modes included vehicles stuck at intersections/stop signs awaiting remote assistance, dead batteries requiring 3-4 hour tows, and difficulty navigating heavy pedestrian traffic. Some vehicles were also vandalized/set on fire by bystanders. Le calls this a normal "edge case" of scaling but notes Waymo still operates under 4,000 cars after roughly six years of development, and contrasts the muted media coverage of this incident with the intense scrutiny Tesla receives for isolated incidents.
2. **New York Times criticized over Autopilot manslaughter story:** A Texas Autopilot-related crash previously reported globally as a Tesla/Autopilot failure was later revealed, per the hosts, to involve a driver who intentionally caused the crash (having searched how to override FSD while depressed) and who is now charged with manslaughter; Florida Governor Ron DeSantis publicly accused the New York Times of pushing an anti-Elon narrative despite this, and stated Florida is "reviewing possibilities" for adding Teslas to state agency fleets.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Order book momentum and possible capacity expansion:** Le speculates (without confirmed information) that an unspecified "cool news" announcement Musk teased for July 7th could relate to Tesla's order book/run-rate reportedly reaching its highest level in a couple of years exiting the prior quarter, and to potential US manufacturing capacity increases tied to earlier commitments Musk made; he notes Tesla appears to be adding headcount/capacity while other automakers report layoffs, though this is speculative and unconfirmed.

Notable quotes and data:
- "Tesla's robo taxi service is now active across five regions: Miami, Dallas, Houston, Austin, and as Ride Hail in the Bay Area."
- Roughly 24% increase in unsupervised robotaxis in Texas reported in a single day (day cited as Thursday, per host).
- Cybercabs/testing vehicles spotted in Dallas, Tampa, Jacksonville, and New Orleans; one observer reported seeing ten Cybercabs in Dallas within twenty minutes.
- Waymo vehicle count described as "under 4,000 cars after six years" of development, per Jeff Le.
- Recent California robotaxi wait time experienced by the host: approximately 20 minutes, with an inconvenient pickup location.
- Host's own Uber fare comparison in the Bay Area: approximately $250 for an airport-to-destination ride.
- Lars Moravy (recounted, not a new interview): "the vast majority of Cybercabs that we've been producing... is going out to the field to test Full Self-Driving."
- Ron DeSantis: New York Times "is pushing a narrative because they don't like Elon"; confirmed Florida is "reviewing possibilities" for adding Teslas to state fleets.
- First Model 3 rolled off the production line on July 7, 2017, per a social media post cited in the video (used as a coincidental comparison to an anticipated July 7 announcement).

2026-07-06.title: Tesla driver caught asleep at 100 km/h — how monitoring failed
2026-07-06.relevance: core — the article directly examines gaps in Tesla's FSD/driver-monitoring safety systems, which bears on the autonomous driving thesis investors track.
2026-07-06.body:
An Electrek report describes a viral video showing a Tesla driver apparently asleep at ~100 km/h on B.C.'s Trans-Canada Highway with two children in the car, and uses the incident to explain how the driver's sunglasses defeated Tesla's camera-based driver monitoring.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Incident details:** A witness ("Carleigh") filmed a Tesla driver slumped over and apparently asleep on Highway 1 between Golden and Revelstoke, B.C., on a Sunday; she reported it to Revelstoke RCMP, who said they had the license plate and would locate the driver. British Columbia's Motor Vehicle Act bars operating Level 3-5 automated vehicles on public roads, but since FSD is Level 2, the driver remains legally responsible regardless.

2. **How monitoring failed:** Since FSD v12.4 (2024), Tesla's primary driver-attention check is a cabin camera tracking eyes/face; per Tesla's own owner's manual, this vision-based monitoring will not activate if the camera is covered, lighting is poor, the driver isn't facing forward, or the driver wears sunglasses or a hat covering the eyes. The driver in the video wore large sunglasses, so the system reverted to the weaker steering-wheel torque "nag," which only detects force on the wheel, not actual driver alertness. Tesla's separate Driver Drowsiness Warning has the same camera-dependency flaw and, per the article, a recent update (2025.32.3) responds to detected drowsiness by suggesting the driver enable FSD.

3. **Broader pattern of monitoring gaps:** The article references Electrek's prior reporting that Chinese Tesla drivers have defeated the cabin camera using ~$30 plastic doll heads mounted near the mirror, tricking the system into classifying the "driver" as alert. It notes Tesla is still fighting court rulings over allegedly misleading claims about its self-driving capabilities.

## Editorial Stance
Electrek's Fred Lambert argues Tesla bears responsibility for building complacency through marketing (e.g., "time saved" messaging) while disclaiming liability for FSD-related accidents; he contends Tesla should do more to "dumb proof" the system and prevent misuse rather than relying solely on driver honesty.

Notable quotes and data:
- Witness described the driver as "fast asleep" while the vehicle traveled roughly 100 km/h.
- Tesla owner's manual: camera-based monitoring "will not be activated" when driver wears sunglasses/hat covering eyes, camera is obstructed, lighting is poor, or driver isn't facing forward.
- Reported use of ~$30 plastic doll heads by some Chinese Tesla drivers to spoof the cabin camera.
- Referenced software update 2025.32.3 reportedly prompts drowsy drivers to activate FSD.

2026-07-06.title: Tesla Cybercab: mass-producing a car it can’t sell or drive itself
2026-07-06.relevance: core — The article is a substantive analysis of Tesla's Cybercab production ramp, FSD limitations, and Robotaxi program timeline, directly bearing on the Tesla investment thesis.
2026-07-06.body:
Electrek's Fred Lambert argues Tesla is ramping Cybercab production at Giga Texas despite having neither regulatory/consumer sales approval nor unsupervised autonomy to actually operate the steering-wheel-less vehicle, questioning the rationale for building it now.

## Robotaxi
1. **Cybercab production ramping, but fleet has no path to use:** More than 100 steering-wheel-less Cybercabs have reportedly been spotted in Giga Texas outbound lots; the first unit rolled off the line in February 2026, with continuous production confirmed on Tesla's Q1 2026 earnings call in April. Musk described the ramp as a "stretched out S-curve" that will go "kind of exponential towards the end of the year." Tesla designed the Cybercab to self-certify against Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards, avoiding NHTSA's 2,500-unit annual cap on exemption vehicles.
2. **Austin robotaxi fleet remains small and reportedly shrinking:** City officials peg Tesla's Austin fleet at roughly 50 vehicles; per Electrek's own tracking, the unsupervised (driverless) portion has fallen from a peak of about 25 cumulative cars to roughly 14 active ones. Tesla expanded its Austin geofence to cover the metro area but runs only about 20 cars there; similar small geofences exist in Dallas and Houston, with a new sliver mapped in Miami — Tesla's first market outside Texas.
3. **Musk says safety validation, not mapping, is the bottleneck:** On the Q1 2026 earnings call, Musk said safety validation is limiting Robotaxi expansion and that Tesla is waiting for a rewritten FSD v15, now targeted for late 2026 or early 2027. He also said Robotaxi "likely will not see material revenue until at least 2027."

## Autonomous Driving
4. **Supervised FSD crash rate cited:** The article states Tesla's supervised fleet has been crashing at roughly four times the rate of an average human driver, and Tesla has reported a string of crashes to NHTSA in Austin.
5. **Camera-only sensor bet questioned:** Tesla's Robotaxi program relies solely on cameras (no radar or lidar); the author says he isn't convinced this technically precludes Level 4 autonomy, but notes companies running driverless cars at scale currently use radar/lidar, and Tesla's slow deployment a year in isn't a strong endorsement of the vision-only approach.

## Editorial Stance
The author's opinion: the Cybercab is a manufacturing achievement built ahead of a software promise (FSD v15) that keeps slipping, comparable to Tesla's earlier removal-then-reinstatement of the turn signal stalk on the Model 3 (which VP Lars Moravy admitted was "deleted too much"). The author argues Cybercabs won't be sold to consumers or aid Robotaxi improvement in the foreseeable future, and expresses doubt that FSD v15 will be sufficient for Tesla to let owners use FSD unsupervised, despite acknowledged improvements in v14.

Notable quotes and data:
- Musk: Robotaxi ramp is a "stretched out S-curve," going "kind of exponential towards the end of the year."
- Musk: Robotaxi "likely will not see material revenue until at least 2027."
- Lars Moravy (past admission): Tesla "deleted too much" with the turn signal stalk removal; Tesla now sells a $595 retrofit.
- Austin fleet: ~50 vehicles per city officials; unsupervised fleet down from peak ~25 to ~14 active cars per Electrek tracking.

2026-07-06.title: Tesla app code reveals cabin camera will verify driver before FSD
2026-07-06.relevance: core — The article discusses a potential new Tesla FSD/cabin-camera feature with direct implications for FSD subscription monetization and Robotaxi identity verification.
2026-07-06.body:
Electrek reports that decompiled code in Tesla's iOS app (version 4.58.5, built June 27) contains strings suggesting a future feature where the cabin camera would verify a driver's identity before allowing FSD to activate, blocking the system and showing an error dialog on mismatch. The author cautions this is unreleased code, not a confirmed shipping feature, and would require a corresponding vehicle firmware update.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Code strings found:** The decompile, surfaced by the account @Tesla_App_iOS, revealed strings named fsdIdentityCheckFailedTitle and showFsdIdentityCheckFailedDialog, describing a flow where the cabin camera checks driver identity and blocks FSD activation with an app error on failure.
2. **History of cabin camera use:** Tesla activated cabin-camera driver monitoring in 2021 and expanded it over time; since FSD v12.4 in 2024, the camera above the rearview mirror has been the primary attention monitor (tracking face/eye position) rather than relying on steering-wheel torque. The author notes identity verification would be a new, distinct function — a permission gate rather than an attention/safety check.
3. **Possible motivations:** The author speculates the feature could serve access control for Tesla's FSD subscription model (restricting activation to authorized account holders, useful for rentals, shared/fleet vehicles, and preventing unauthorized/teen use) and could support Robotaxi identity matching between riders and bookings.
4. **Hardware limitation:** The author notes Tesla's cabin camera is a standard RGB sensor, not an infrared depth-mapping system like Apple's Face ID, making it a weak biometric lock that would inherit existing blind spots in poor lighting, when covered, or when the driver wears sunglasses or a hat — issues Tesla's owner's manual already acknowledges for attention monitoring.

## Robotaxi
1. **Identity-matching relevance:** The author suggests the identity-check feature could support Tesla's driverless Robotaxi operations by matching the person in the vehicle seat to the person who booked the ride, though this is framed as a possible use case rather than a confirmed plan.

Notable quotes and data:
- Code strings: `fsdIdentityCheckFailedTitle`, `showFsdIdentityCheckFailedDialog`
- App version referenced: Tesla app 4.58.5, built June 27
- Source account: @Tesla_App_iOS

2026-07-06.title: Tesla's Insane New Product Will Pay You
2026-07-06.relevance: core — The video's central thesis is about a newly filed Tesla trademark and how Tesla's chip/power/cooling/fab/model stack could reshape its energy and AI compute business, directly bearing on the Tesla investment thesis.
2026-07-06.body:
The video analyzes a Tesla trademark filing for a product called "Megapod" — described as modular AI data-center hardware — and argues it signals Tesla's move from being an AI compute buyer (via Nvidia GPUs) to an AI compute seller. The host builds a thesis around Tesla owning five layers of the AI stack (chip, power, cooling, fab, model) and speculates that this could eventually extend to a consumer version bolted onto homes, combining Powerwall-like storage with AI inference and waste-heat home heating, that could eventually pay homeowners rather than cost them money.

## Financials
1. **Megapod trademark filing:** Tesla filed a US trademark on June 18, 2026 (serial number 99893717) for "Megapod," described in the filing as "modular data center hardware systems for artificial intelligence computing." It is an intent-to-use filing with no product, price, or ship date yet announced.
2. **AI compute leasing revenue at Musk companies:** The host states Anthropic is paying xAI for Colossus (SpaceX's Memphis supercomputer) compute at a rate cited as $14 billion a month, with that contract worth north of $40 billion over its life; Google reportedly signed a similar deal at roughly $900 million a month (unconfirmed figures relayed by the host, not independently verified in the transcript).

## Energy
1. **Nat Power Megapack deal:** On June 23, 2026, Tesla signed a deal with Nat Power to deploy 25 gigawatt-hours of Megapack storage across Italy and the UK in a first phase; the host says this phase alone exceeds half of all Tesla's global battery deployments in 2026 to date. The full program is described as exceeding 100 gigawatt-hours and worth over $15 billion over its life.
2. **Speculative home AI-energy box:** The host speculates (not an announced Tesla product) that a future Powerwall variant could embed an AI chip, using its battery and thermal system to run inference at the edge while heating homes with waste heat — citing existing "data furnace" companies (Hiatt in the UK, unnamed companies in France/Germany, and Microsoft piping data-center heat into a Danish town) as real-world precedent for the heat-reuse concept.
3. **Virtual power plant precedent:** Tesla's existing Powerwall program already pays homeowners for energy sent back to the grid via virtual power plants, which the host cites as the existing "baby version" of a pay-you-back business model he projects onto a future compute-selling home device.

## Market & Competition
1. **Tesla's AI5 chip vs. Nvidia GPUs:** Tesla's own AI5 chip taped out around April 2026, described by Musk as built for edge inference and consuming about 250 watts. Tesla's Cortex training cluster in Texas currently runs on roughly 67,000 Nvidia GPUs, making Tesla an Nvidia customer for training compute today.
2. **Terafab chip factory:** In March 2026, Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI announced a joint chip fab called Terafab in Texas, targeting over a terawatt of AI compute per year, with Intel joining the project shortly after; the host frames this as a 2027-and-beyond initiative that could slip in timing.
3. **Stack comparison vs. Nvidia:** The host contrasts Tesla's five-layer approach (chip, power, cooling, fab, model) against Nvidia, which sells a turnkey rack product (cited as the GB200 NVL72) but relies on utilities for power and TSMC for fabrication, arguing Tesla is unique in attempting to own the full vertical stack.
4. **Distributed edge compute vision:** The host references Musk's stated vision (via what's referred to as "Digital Optimus") of deploying AI inference units at Tesla Supercharger sites (citing ~7 gigawatts of power already available there) and using idle parked Teslas as distributed compute, up to a figure the host cites as 100 gigawatts of potential distributed compute.
5. **Realistic timeline caveat:** The host notes AI5 isn't expected to reach real production volume until mid-to-late 2027, meaning any home AI-energy box is far from shelf-ready and could initially rely on Nvidia chips or Tesla's existing AI4 chip rather than AI5.

Notable quotes and data:
- Megapod trademark filed June 18, 2026, serial number 99893717 — intent-to-use, no product/price/date yet.
- Tesla's Cortex cluster: ~67,000 Nvidia GPUs.
- AI5 chip taped out ~April 2026; runs on ~250 watts.
- Nat Power deal: 25 GWh Megapack (phase one) across Italy/UK, signed June 23, 2026; full program >100 GWh, >$15B lifetime value.
- Terafab (Tesla/SpaceX/xAI, joined by Intel) announced March 2026, targeting >1 terawatt of AI compute/year.
- Anthropic reportedly paying xAI $14B/month for Colossus compute (contract >$40B lifetime); Google reportedly ~$900M/month (host-relayed, unverified).
- Supercharger network cited as having ~7 GW of power available; distributed compute vision cited up to 100 GW.
- AI5 not expected at real production volume until mid-to-late 2027.

2026-07-06.title: YL is REAL, Polestar Half Off, Unsupervised Goes Wider, and MORE in the Monday News Roundup
2026-07-06.relevance: core — the video centers substantially on Tesla's robotaxi/FSD rollout, Q2 delivery numbers, stock reaction, and competitive EV market context relevant to the Tesla thesis.
2026-07-06.body:
This Monday news roundup from futureaza covers Waymo's citywide malfunction in San Francisco, Tesla's Q2 delivery beat and stock reaction, a fatal FSD-related crash investigation, expanding unsupervised Robotaxi rides, BYD's continued global sales momentum, EV battery longevity research, various China/EV policy stories, and a Q&A touching on speculation about a Giga Texas announcement.

## Robotaxi
1. **Unsupervised rides expand to Miami:** The host reports unsupervised Robotaxi rides launching in Miami, with a community member reportedly taking a ride there over the July 4th weekend; unsupervised operation is also noted continuing in Dallas, Houston, and Austin, alongside more Cybercab sightings nationally, including a reported sighting in Colorado Springs.
2. **Speculation on a Giga Texas announcement:** The host says he expects a Cybercab-related announcement at Giga Texas, based on a secondhand account of comments from Tesla VP Lars Moravy relayed to another commentator ("Herbert"); the host speculates it could relate to a "cyber SUV" concept but stresses this is unconfirmed ("That's not guaranteed. I don't know that").

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Fatal crash tied to driver override, not FSD:** Vehicle data in the Michael Butler crash (in which a Tesla hit a house, causing a fatality) reportedly shows the car was in FSD approaching a stop sign and slowing down when the driver pressed the accelerator, escalating to 100%, with the brake never applied; officers reportedly found search history showing the driver had searched for FSD being "not aggressive enough" and "too timid," which the host argues undermines any claim that FSD caused the crash.
2. **Y L (compact/next-gen vehicle) delayed:** In Q&A, the host and a viewer discuss "YL" (a next Tesla vehicle project), with the host saying he doesn't expect it before September and has not seen first delivery dates.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Tesla Q2 deliveries beat estimates:** Tesla reported deliveries of 480,000 for the quarter, beating Wall Street's expectation of 406,000 and the host's own projection of ~431,000; among trackers cited, James Stephenson was closest, followed by Randy Kirk (~490,000) and Troy Teslike (~460,000).
2. **UK EV market and Tesla growth:** The UK EV market reportedly surged 30%, with Tesla UK sales up 42% year over year, attributed to product strength rather than incentives.
3. **California's new EV rebate — Tesla mostly qualifies:** California is introducing a $3,500 rebate (funded partly by a $135 million state pool) for new EV buyers, requiring manufacturer price-matching and first-time EV buyer status; a cap on vehicle price applies but is higher for California-headquartered automakers (benefiting Rivian and Lucid), while Tesla, no longer HQ'd in California, faces the standard cap — though the host notes roughly half of Tesla's lineup still qualifies under it.
4. **BYD sustains overseas momentum despite domestic softness:** BYD sold 160,000 vehicles (including hybrids/PHEVs) overseas in May, its highest overseas monthly total ever, even as China domestic NEV sales have been soft industry-wide; BYD plans to showcase eight new vehicles across three brands at the Goodwill Festival of Speed in July, including the Denza Z Roadster (1,582 hp), launching in the UK on July 9.
5. **EV battery longevity better than expected:** Citing Stanford researchers, EV batteries held up roughly 40% longer than earlier lab-test predictions under real-world conditions; average EVs are expected to last 12–15 years of active service, comparable to combustion vehicles.
6. **Polestar 4 discounted amid US sales ban:** Due to a ban on Polestar 4 sales in the US, dealers are discounting inventory to around $31,400 (roughly half price), which the host calls a "heck of a bargain" despite the car lacking self-driving features; the host speculates the ban stems from software/national-security sourcing issues rather than the vehicle itself.

## Market & Competition
1. **Michigan startup building Tiny/TE electric truck:** Schwab Industries has signed on to build bodies-in-white for an electric truck targeting ~42,000 units in production this year, with a split battery pack supporting 400V or 800V charging; positioned as more capable but pricier than the "Slate," while Ford targets 30,000 units for its own entry-level electric truck next year.
2. **EU combustion ban pressure easing:** Per the EU climate chief, rising EV sales are reducing political pressure to roll back combustion engine phase-out plans, with some suggestion of a shift toward a ~90% emissions reduction target rather than a full ban, as more EV models now cover more market segments.
3. **Chinese automakers expanding manufacturing overseas:** Chery has taken over a former Nissan plant, creating roughly 3,000 jobs in Southeast Africa, part of a broader Chinese push to build (not just sell) cars abroad; separately, China's EV charging network has grown to 22.5 million charging points, described as the world's largest, with China's NEV fleet at 44 million and 12.9 million new registrations in the prior year.
4. **Sodium-ion battery materials use coconut-derived carbon, not burned coal:** A story framed around China's sodium-ion battery supply chain clarifies that "coal" references relate to biomass/hard-carbon lattice structures (including coconut-shell-derived precursors) used in electrode manufacturing, not coal combustion.

## Financials
1. **Stock reaction to Q2 deliveries:** Tesla shares reportedly moved only mildly higher despite the delivery beat, with the host noting a "sell the news" pattern after the report; SpaceX's internal share price is noted around $160, still up from its IPO reference point (no specific date given).

Notable quotes and data:
- "The accelerator was pressed increased to 67% and then increased to 100%... No data indicated the driver tried to turn away from the crash." — details from the Michael Butler crash investigation as relayed by the host.
- Tesla Q2 deliveries: 480,000 vs. Wall Street estimate of 406,000; host's own projection was ~431,000.
- UK EV market up 30%; Tesla UK sales up 42% year-over-year.
- California EV rebate: $3,500 per buyer, funded partly by a $135 million state pool; Rivian and Lucid get a higher price cap as CA-headquartered companies.
- BYD overseas sales: 160,000 units in May (including hybrids/PHEVs), its best overseas month ever.
- EV batteries held up ~40% longer than earlier lab predictions (Stanford research cited); typical EV lifespan estimated at 12–15 years.
- China EV charging network: 22.5 million charging points; NEV fleet at 44 million, 12.9 million new registrations.
- Michigan electric truck project (Schwab Industries/"Tiny TE"): targeting ~42,000 units this year; supports 400V/800V charging.
- Polestar 4 discounted to ~$31,400 amid US sales ban.
- Denza Z Roadster: 1,582 horsepower, launching in the UK July 9.

2026-07-06.title: After Thursdays Market Sell Off What's Next? And What about $TSLA ?
2026-07-06.relevance: core — the video centers on interpreting a market sell-off's implications for Tesla and covers Tesla-specific catalysts (delivery numbers, Model Y L launch, Miami robotaxi expansion, FSD performance).
2026-07-06.body:
The host, from the channel investingagainstthegrain, argues that Thursday's market sell-off — including Tesla's drop despite record deliveries — was driven by spillover fear from a South Korean market crash and overblown "AI bubble" narratives, not fundamentals, and that both the broader market and Tesla remain mispriced to the downside. He frames this as a buying opportunity for Tesla ahead of an anticipated announcement at the Giga Texas/Austin campus.

## Market & Competition
1. **South Korean market crash seen as sell-off trigger:** The host attributes Thursday's US sell-off largely to a crash in South Korea's Kospi index (down 8%, triggering trading halts) tied to concentration in memory/chip names like Samsung and SK Hynix, which he says has recently tended to spill over into US tech/AI-infrastructure stocks (Micron, SanDisk, Nvidia, Marvell, Bloom Energy).
2. **Meta's cloud-rental plan reframed as bullish, not bearish:** Reports that Meta will lease out excess data center capacity spooked markets over fears AI demand is overstated, but the host argues Meta (like SpaceX and Tesla) is monetizing excess compute while awaiting newer Nvidia chips — evidence of supply constraints (citing Anthropic and Google renting compute from Elon Musk/SpaceX), not weak demand.
3. **Dot-com bubble comparison rejected:** The host contrasts today's market — low P/E multiples, strong earnings, GPUs running at 70-90% utilization, no rush of unprofitable IPOs — with the 1999-2000 dot-com bubble's PE expansion without revenue and "dark fiber" overbuild, concluding current AI infrastructure spending is fundamentally different and not a bubble.
4. **Broadening market as bullish signal:** He notes the Magnificent 7 are down for the year while the S&P 500 overall and its equal-weight version are up and outperforming the cap-weighted index — a sign of market breadth that he says typically precedes continued bull markets rather than a top.

## Electric Vehicles
1. **Record Q2 deliveries beat expectations:** Tesla delivered numbers that blew past most estimates (host cites an expectation baseline around 406, with the highest bull estimates near 460-480); a Tesla community member, James Stephenson, was noted as among the closest with an estimate around 480. The host argues the more important story than headline deliveries will be how many buyers signed up for FSD.
2. **Model Y L launched in the US:** Tesla launched the Model Y L variant domestically, a version the host says has already been highly successful in China and Europe; he considers this a significant product event for the US market given consumer preference for larger vehicles.

## Robotaxi
1. **Robotaxi service launched in Miami:** Tesla launched robotaxi service in Miami, expanding beyond existing markets; the host and his wife traveled there specifically to try it, with a separate vlog-style video planned. He notes no additional new city or state (e.g., Vegas, Arizona) was announced alongside this.
2. **Anticipation builds for a Tuesday Giga Texas/Austin event:** Tesla VP Lars Moravy reportedly indicated something notable would happen at the Texas/Austin campus on the coming Tuesday; the host speculates (unconfirmed) this will involve Cybercab entering the Austin robotaxi fleet, which he believes could push the stock toward $500-600 if it signals a scaling blueprint for other cities.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **FSD performance praised on long road trip:** The host reports FSD drove nearly the entire Tampa Bay-to-Miami trip, including city driving, construction, police activity, and Fourth of July holiday traffic, with no interventions except manual takeovers for a hotel parking ramp (due to valet/no garage-parking setting) and one precautionary brake tap near a suspected speed trap.

## Financials
1. **Valuation comparison to prior year:** The host claims the overall stock market, and specifically companies like Nvidia and Micron, are cheaper today (on a P/E basis) than at this time last year despite significant price appreciation (citing Micron up roughly 10x and SanDisk up roughly 800%), attributing this to strong earnings growth outpacing price gains.

Notable quotes and data:
- "We do not have line of sight to when we will be able to fill all orders" — Micron CEO, cited by the host as evidence of AI infrastructure demand exceeding supply.
- South Korean Kospi index fell about 8% Thursday (breakers triggered) before rebounding roughly 6% Friday.
- Tesla Q2 delivery expectations baseline cited around 406, with bull estimates as high as 460-480; James Stephenson's estimate near 480 called closest by the host.
- MAG 7 stocks reportedly down for the year while the S&P 500 and its equal-weight index are up, with equal-weight outperforming cap-weight.
- Host's price target framing: a successful Austin Cybercab robotaxi scale-up could send Tesla stock to "$500-600."
- Nvidia and Micron described as cheaper on valuation now than a year ago despite large price gains, per the host's earnings-based analysis.

2026-07-06.title: Tesla Miami Robotaxi | The Good, Bad, and Ugly
2026-07-06.relevance: core — the video is a firsthand ride-along test of Tesla's driverless Robotaxi service in a new market (Miami), directly bearing on the pace and quality of robotaxi fleet expansion central to the Tesla thesis.
2026-07-06.body:
This vlog-style video follows the host and his wife on a spontaneous trip to Miami where they hunt down and ride Tesla's newly launched driverless Robotaxi service, comparing it against their personal car's FSD on the same route. Most of the runtime is personal vlogging (dinner, drinks, sponsor plugs) but the core substance is a real-world assessment of Robotaxi availability, ride quality, and rollout pace in Miami.

## Robotaxi
1. **Miami Robotaxi rides without a safety driver:** The host confirms Tesla is operating Robotaxi in Miami with no safety supervisor in the vehicle, which he contrasts with Elon Musk's guidance on a prior earnings call (described as "two earnings ago") that supervised rides would run for three to four months before removing the driver — a timeline that has clearly moved faster than stated, especially since Dallas and Houston reportedly launched unsupervised as well.
2. **Extremely limited fleet availability:** The host's app booking was cancelled once with no explanation, then re-booked after a "high demand" wait loop; from his experience and an evasive answer from a Tesla remote support agent, he estimates there may be only one to a few Robotaxi vehicles currently active in this part of Miami — not enough, in his view, to constitute a real service yet, though he notes similarly slow scaling in Austin.
3. **Ride quality praised, routing questioned:** Both the host and his wife found the driverless ride smooth and comfortable, with the wife specifically praising the ride comfort and suspension of the newer Model Y hardware used as the Robotaxi versus their personal Model Y performance. However, the host noted the Robotaxi took a notably inefficient, slower route compared to his own car's FSD navigating the same destination, arriving roughly 10–11 minutes later; he speculates the routing may reflect preset "comfortable" roads or deliberate route avoidance.
4. **Age restriction and pickup/drop-off friction:** The host notes Robotaxi rules currently prevent riders under age eight (even in a car seat) from being in the vehicle, which excluded his wife and son from riding along. He also flags awkward pickup logistics — being picked up in front of a random person's house rather than at a shopping plaza — as a customer-experience issue Tesla will need to address.
5. **NHTSA steering wheel/pedal rule change cited as evidence of readiness:** The host references a recent NHTSA decision no longer requiring steering wheels or pedals in these vehicles, arguing this shows regulators and Tesla's own software now consider the vehicle capable enough that such hardware is unnecessary — he speculates this regulatory shift may be timed to support the Cybercab rollout, alongside continued use of driver-hardware Model Ys for families needing multi-passenger rides.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Referenced "death loop" bug from prior earnings call:** The host recalls Ashok Elluswamy and Elon Musk discussing on a prior earnings call a known issue where the vehicle repeatedly attempts a route it doesn't "remember" is closed (e.g., due to a parade or road closure), looping ineffectively — characterized as a memory/mapping limitation rather than a fundamental driving capability problem.
2. **Anticipated near-term updates:** The host expects more clarity on Robotaxi scaling and city rollout plans from an unspecified Tuesday event referenced as being led by Lars Moravy, as well as from Tesla's upcoming earnings call, and speculates an additional city launch could occur before then.

Notable quotes and data:
- "It's just crazy... this drive is perfect... not a single thing have I had to do" — host describing zero interventions across a full day of Miami driving on personal FSD.
- Host estimate: Robotaxi fleet in this Miami area may be only "one, maybe two or three" vehicles — insufficient to be "a service" yet.
- Robotaxi arrival wait cited by host: booking initially failed/cancelled, then quoted an 11-minute wait, later resolved to about 9–10 minutes.
- Wife's route via personal FSD reportedly arrived roughly 10–11 minutes before the Robotaxi taking a different, less efficient path.
- Robotaxi minimum age restriction: riders under 8 not permitted, even with a car seat.
- Tech support declined to confirm whether more than one Robotaxi was operating in the area ("I don't think I'm at liberty to discuss that").
- Recent NHTSA rule change removing the steering wheel/pedal requirement cited as a signal of regulatory confidence in the technology.

2026-07-06.title: Why Tesla's Robot SHOCK REVEAL Is CLOSE
2026-07-06.relevance: core — The video centers on Tesla's Optimus production timeline and Robotaxi/Cybercab scaling, both central to the Tesla investment thesis.
2026-07-06.body:
The host (Jo Bhakdi) argues that Tesla's Optimus humanoid robot reveal and mass production ramp is much closer than the market believes, piecing together recent statements, leaked production-line footage, and executive comments to argue for a possible August 2026 launch shock. He contrasts this with his more cautious but still bullish view on Robotaxi/Cybercab scaling, and spends significant time mocking Waymo's operational problems in San Francisco.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Tesla China VP signals large-scale Optimus production by end of 2026:** The host cites reporting (via a Tesla-focused China commentator) that Tesla vice president Grace Tao stated at a Beijing digital economy conference that Optimus will officially enter large-scale mass production by the end of 2026, with a long-term target annual capacity of 1 million units at what she referred to as a "Freeman" factory (long-term target, not near-term).
2. **Elon Musk's recent comments frame Optimus 3 as near-complete:** In comments the host dates to around June 20, 2026, Musk said Tesla is in the "final stages of completion" of Optimus 3, calling it by far the most advanced robot in the world, said production would start this summer, ramp would follow a slow S-curve initially, and high-volume production would likely arrive around next summer, with Optimus 4 design finalized next year.
3. **Musk reportedly pushed back on pace, not on timeline, in an X exchange:** Per the host's account of an X exchange involving a commentator referred to as Dr. Jack, Musk responded that Optimus production "will be extremely slow at first as everything is new," which the host interprets as expectation-setting/sandbagging rather than a delay of the launch itself, since Musk did not dispute the timeline.
4. **Leaked footage allegedly shows an active Optimus production line:** The host highlights an official Tesla video (spotted by Sawyer Merritt) ostensibly about Model X/Y special-edition deliveries that contains background footage of what he identifies as a real, already-installed Optimus production line, including workers assembling robot hands — which he argues confirms production readiness rather than a distant, theoretical launch.
5. **Host's own projection: August reveal, thousands-scale ramp:** The host's personal (speculative, self-described "conspiracy-connecting") view is that Optimus 3 will likely be revealed in August 2026, not as a small-batch demo but backed by an already-installed line designed for high-volume output; he speculates about a run-rate reaching hundreds or low thousands per month by year-end, though he stresses this is his own inference, not confirmed guidance.
6. **Strategic case that Optimus is an easier commercial launch than Robotaxi:** The host argues Optimus can be sold to industrial/commercial customers (retail, agriculture, hospitals, warehousing) well before it reaches full labor-replacement capability, since failures don't carry the same safety/liability stakes as autonomous driving, making mass sales feasible years earlier than Robotaxi's economic viability threshold.

## Robotaxi
1. **Cybercab hardware ramp cited as the strongest signal for near-term Robotaxi progress:** The host says (as his own claim/estimate, not sourced to official guidance) that Tesla has already produced over a thousand Cybercabs, is running at roughly a 1,000/month rate in July, and is on track for a 5,000/month run rate within three months — he frames this as his personal, confident estimate ("I can guarantee you").
2. **Miami driverless Robotaxi launch:** The host notes Tesla Model Y robotaxis have launched driverless/unsupervised in Miami, part of what he expects to be expansion to many more cities soon.
3. **Third-party fleet size predictions diverge widely:** Commentator Keith Fitzgerald reportedly projected 1,500 robotaxis by year-end across Miami, Phoenix, Orlando, Tampa, and Las Vegas; another commentator ("Doge army") projected 5,000 by year-end and 30,000 by end of 2027; the host's own guess is 15,000 by year-end and roughly 100,000 by end of 2027.

## Market & Competition
1. **Waymo faces multiple operational incidents in San Francisco:** The host cites reports/footage of roughly 20 Waymo vehicles gridlocking streets near a fireworks display, some vehicles reportedly damaged and one destroyed by fire amid what's described as "external attacks," plus a separate incident of Waymo robotaxis entering freeway construction zones leading to a recall. He uses this to argue Waymo's LIDAR-based approach is fundamentally inferior to Tesla's vision-based approach.
2. **Google DeepMind–Apptronik partnership noted as competition, dismissed by host:** The host mentions a same-day announcement that Apptronik (a humanoid robotics startup) and Google DeepMind are partnering, with real-world data from Apptronik's Apollo 2 platform feeding Google's Gemini robotics efforts; he dismisses this as no threat to Tesla Optimus.

Notable quotes and data:
- "We're in the final stages of completion of Optimus 3, which is really going to be by far the most advanced robot in the world... I think we'll start production on Optimus 3 this summer... but very slow at first... probably reach high volume production around summer next year." — Elon Musk, cited by the host (~June 20, 2026 remarks)
- Grace Tao (Tesla VP, China), per reporting cited by the host: Optimus to enter large-scale mass production by end of 2026, with long-term annual capacity target of 1 million units at a planned factory.
- Host's own estimate (unconfirmed): Cybercab production already over 1,000 units, ~1,000/month run rate in July, targeting ~5,000/month within three months.
- Host's speculative Optimus ramp scenario: from a ~1,000/month run rate by September to 2,000–3,000/month by December (~30,000–40,000 annualized) — explicitly framed as his own guess, not company guidance.
- Third-party robotaxi fleet-size forecasts for year-end 2026: 1,500 (Keith Fitzgerald), 5,000 (Doge army), 15,000 (host's own estimate).
- Reported incident: ~20 Waymo vehicles gridlocked near a San Francisco fireworks display, with some vehicles damaged and one destroyed by fire.
- Host's overall call: expects a possible Optimus-related "shock" reveal in the second half of August 2026, describing it as an "upside risk" rather than downside risk.

2026-07-06.body:
