2026-07-24.title: Daily X Summary (2026-07-24)
2026-07-24.body:
## Executive Summary
The day's highest-signal items are fresh FSD safety/usage data showing continued strong growth and a wide-ranging 90-minute Elon Musk interview with The Economist covering taxes, politics, retail investors, and SpaceX's public listing rationale. On the SpaceX side, Starship's 13th test flight got a new launch date, Starlink Mini pricing dropped, and competitive commentary (AT&T CEO, Aurora, Ford/Apple) offers useful market-context signal for both theses.

---

## Key Posts / Themes

1. **New FSD safety and usage data:** Tesla released updated FSD (Supervised) safety statistics: miles per major collision are now 5,690,675 for FSD-supervised driving vs. 2,076,014 for manual driving with active safety features, 859,465 for manual driving without active safety features, and a U.S. average of 698,781 — implying FSD-supervised driving has a meaningfully lower collision rate than manual driving. Separately, Tesla's fleet-wide FSD usage is now running at an annualized rate of 13.7 billion miles/year, up 241% year-over-year, and the fleet is averaging 37.5 million miles per day on FSD, up from 28.8M/day "a few months ago" and 14.4M/day "earlier this year" — Tesla frames this as roughly 1,000 miles driven every 2.3 seconds. Tesla also published a new video showcasing FSD collision-avoidance instances.

2. **Elon Musk's Economist interview (90 minutes, filmed at Giga Texas):** Musk discussed several topics with notable investor relevance: on politics, he said "I think I got a little too involved in politics... I got carried away," framing the DOGE effort as an attempt to address the U.S. deficit; on retail investors, he called himself "a big fan," saying they are "on balance... very insightful and have very long-term views"; on his taxes, he stated he pays about 40% national income tax on stock options plus roughly 5% more due to California residency (~45% total), plus an estate tax of roughly another 45% upon death; on SpaceX, he said one reason he took SpaceX public was to let the public own a piece of the company, since private companies face shareholder-count limits.

3. **SpaceX Starship Flight 13 rescheduled:** SpaceX moved its 13th Starship test flight launch target to Friday, July 24 at 6:45 PM ET.

4. **Starlink Mini pricing update:** The Starlink Mini Kit is now available in the U.S. for $16/month for 12 months, with standard service plans starting at $55/month — a pricing move relevant to Starlink subscriber growth and unit economics.

5. **Competitive and industry context (autonomy market):** Aurora launched its second-generation driverless trucks, planning deployment across 10 driverless routes in the U.S. Sun Belt. Ford announced a partnership with Apple to integrate Apple Maps into Ford's upcoming Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) Platform and its next-generation self-driving development. The IIHS released a 25-page study recommending standardized autonomous-vehicle safety data reporting (uniform VMT reporting, standardized crash classifications, eliminating duplicate crash reports) — relevant to future AV regulatory frameworks Tesla's Robotaxi program would operate under. AT&T's CEO pushed back on the idea that Starlink will become a major wireless/broadband competitor, saying new entrants like Starlink are "coming to the game very late" in a mature industry.

6. **Adam Jonas SpaceX note:** Jonas (analyst) published commentary arguing that in space, "failure is not just an option... it's a vital part of the testing and improvement process," pushing back on the "failure is not an option" framing often applied to space programs — relevant context ahead of the Starship test flight.

---

## Signal Strength: **Bullish** — Continued strong FSD mileage/safety data growth (241% YoY usage increase, favorable collision-rate comparisons) reinforces the autonomy thesis, while SpaceX progress (Starship flight, Starlink pricing) and Musk's investor-friendly commentary add incremental positive signal, tempered by rising AV competition (Aurora, Ford/Apple).

2026-07-25.title: What Elon Musk and Ashok Elluswamy Actually Said
2026-07-25.relevance: core — the video is a detailed line-by-line analysis of Tesla's Q2 earnings call comments on robotaxi scaling, FSD, Optimus, and other growth initiatives, directly bearing on the Tesla investment thesis.
2026-07-25.body:
This video features analyst Cern Basher walking through three deep-dive breakdowns of Tesla's Q2 earnings call: Ashok Elluswamy's comments on robotaxi safety and scaling, an analysis of whether Tesla is being too cautious with robotaxi rollout versus Waymo, and 13 takeaways from Elon Musk's remarks. The core thesis is that demand and safety are no longer the bottleneck for Tesla's autonomy push — the constraint is now execution speed and scaling — and that investors focused on short-term linear progress are missing a nonlinear, exponential growth pattern that both Musk and Elluswamy described.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Ashok Elluswamy details unsupervised safety record:** Elluswamy stated Tesla has driven more than 380,000 unsupervised robotaxi miles across six cities in two states with zero notable incidents, framing this as validation of Tesla's camera-only approach without lidar, radar, or HD maps. He noted any reported incidents involved other actors impacting stationary vehicles.
2. **Double-digit weekly growth in unsupervised miles:** Elluswamy said unsupervised miles have grown at a double-digit rate week-over-week for several months and are expected to continue at that rate through the rest of the year; Musk separately said he believes it's "at least over 10%." Basher cautions this isn't necessarily a smooth 10% weekly rate — it could be higher, lower, or occur in stair-steps, and even the lowest interpretation implies large compounding growth (roughly 12x over six months, ~140x over a year at a steady 10%/week).
3. **New-city expansion effort declining, trending toward statewide operation:** Elluswamy said the engineering effort required to launch a new city is falling and should trend toward zero, with Tesla's eventual goal being to operate across entire states rather than city-by-city — a comment Basher calls the first explicit mention of state-by-state expansion.
4. **FSD V15 (10x parameter model) already partially deployed in robotaxi fleet:** Elluswamy said Tesla planned roughly seven major improvement tracks for V15, with about 40% already merged into early builds running in the robotaxi fleet — a detail Basher calls a surprise, noting it's still an early, incomplete version with no timeline given for full completion (Musk separately mentioned upcoming memory/destination-reasoning features, per Basher, to be taken with appropriate caution given the source).
5. **FSD attach rate cited as a demand driver:** Musk-era data cited: 55% of new vehicles delivered in North America had FSD attached at time of delivery, versus 42% globally, which Basher/Herbert frame as a major and underappreciated demand engine for vehicle sales.
6. **Tesla vs. Waymo architecture comparison:** Waymo has reportedly logged about 220 million fully autonomous miles — roughly 580 times Tesla's unsupervised mile count — with published safety stats (94% fewer serious/fatal crashes, 82% fewer injury-causing crashes than human driving) across cities including LA, San Francisco, Phoenix, Austin, and Atlanta. Basher notes Waymo's architecture defaults to inaction with remote-operator intervention when uncertain, which can cause stranded-vehicle incidents (e.g., during power outages), whereas Tesla is aiming for AI-driven reasoning without remote operators to enable scaling beyond a few thousand vehicles.

## Robotaxi
1. **Cybercab production aligned to unsupervised-mile growth rate:** Elluswamy said Tesla has aligned Cybercab manufacturing targets to roughly match projected unsupervised-mile growth. Basher and Herbert both infer (their own interpretation, not a direct quote) that this implies Cybercab will likely be added to the paid robotaxi network within a couple of months, since scaling production only makes sense if the vehicles enter revenue service rather than remaining employee-only test units.
2. **Multi-city rollout intended to prove generalization, not permanent city-by-city strategy:** Elluswamy said expansion across cities (rather than doubling down on one) is meant to prove the driving stack generalizes without heavy per-city engineering; once proven, Tesla's stated goal is to move to state-by-state and eventually near-instant activation, unlike Waymo's continued city-by-city approach.
3. **Assessment: Tesla not being "too cautious," per Basher:** Basher concludes Tesla's slower-than-hoped rollout reflects a deliberate long-term strategy — managing political/regulatory risk (citing a pending EU vote on supervised FSD where France has said it will vote no, and provisional approvals in five countries that could be revoked), waiting for Cybercab validation and Starlink connectivity integration, and avoiding Waymo/China-style backlash from stalled vehicles — rather than excess caution. He expects actual mass scaling more around mid-2027 rather than this year.
4. **Fleet mile accumulation and safety statistics context:** Beyond the 380,000 fully unsupervised miles, Basher/Herbert cite that Tesla has accumulated roughly 2.5 million robotaxi miles overall (including supervised safety-monitor miles) with no fatalities, and that a Cybercab is expected to log about three times more daily miles than a Waymo vehicle due to battery/charging efficiency, potentially accelerating mile accumulation once Cybercabs enter service.
5. **RobotaxiTracker.com fleet context:** (Not directly cited by number in transcript beyond general fleet discussion) Tesla's active robotaxi fleet stood at 791 vehicles as of 2026-07-24 per RobotaxiTracker.com, with the unsupervised (driverless) subset last reported at 39 as of 2026-05-09 (stale, unchanged for ~77 days).

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus timing remains least certain, deliberately slow-walked:** Musk reiterated Optimus has enormous opportunity but the least certain timing, citing all-new components and no existing supply chain. Basher notes Musk is not making the aggressive short-term promises here that he has for robotaxi, and interprets Tesla's approach as building for generalized robot intelligence (training via video/demo) rather than rushing narrow-task deployment — suggesting broad Optimus deployment won't occur until a version several generations from now.
2. **Major capex commitment to Optimus manufacturing capacity:** Tesla shared photos of the Model S/X line being repurposed for million-unit-capacity Optimus production, and a new large-scale factory in Texas is under construction. Basher argues this level of capital commitment is a strong long-term signal of confidence, arguing Musk would not build such capacity if he expected years of delay.
3. **Digital Optimus (software-only agent) framed as a potential independent revenue stream:** Musk said training a digital version of Optimus also aids physical robot training, since a humanoid robot needs to operate human-designed interfaces (touchscreens, terminals, machinery). Basher and Herbert discuss this as a possible major, non-manufactured revenue opportunity (compared informally to Anthropic's Claude Code), though its competitive advantage over existing AI agents from other companies remains unproven and undemonstrated.

## Energy
1. **Megapack framed as critical AI data-center infrastructure:** Musk discussed Megapack's role in smoothing power delivery to AI data centers, which Basher notes SpaceX has already proven out; falling Megapack cost per kilowatt-hour is expected alongside less price-sensitive data-center customers, a favorable margin dynamic going forward.
2. **Solar manufacturing and autonomous Semi mentioned without new specifics:** Musk referenced upcoming solar manufacturing plans (location unconfirmed) and an autonomous Semi, which Musk suggested could arrive around late 2026 or early 2027 (Basher suggests adding a buffer to that timeline).

## Financials
1. **Terafab framed as a major strategic value driver:** Musk emphasized chip production (Terafab) as a strategic constraint Tesla is trying to solve. Basher reiterates his own prior view that Terafab could represent roughly a trillion dollars in present value for Tesla if it works, even though the market isn't currently pricing that in.
2. **Micron memory allocation secured despite tight supply:** Musk indicated Tesla has secured a memory allocation from Micron that he seems satisfied with, despite Micron being largely sold out for the next year or more and other major customers (e.g., Apple) reportedly struggling to get supply.
3. **Capital efficiency being relaxed in favor of speed:** Musk indicated Tesla is prioritizing speed of execution somewhat over maximum capital efficiency at this stage of growth, a shift from Tesla's historically strict capital discipline.

Notable quotes and data:
- "We've driven more than 380,000 miles of unsupervised robotaxi now across six cities in two different states... zero notable incidents." — Ashok Elluswamy
- "I repeat, we have grown at such a high compounding rate on a week-over-week basis over the last several months... we expect to continue growing at such a large rate through the rest of this year." — Ashok Elluswamy
- Early V15 builds already running in the robotaxi fleet have about 40% of seven planned improvement tracks merged, per Elluswamy.
- 55% of new North American vehicle deliveries had FSD attached at delivery; 42% globally.
- Waymo: ~220 million fully autonomous miles reported; 94% fewer serious/fatal injury crashes and 82% fewer injury-causing crashes than human driving, per Waymo's published data.
- Tesla robotaxi program has accumulated roughly 2.5 million total robotaxi miles (including supervised) with no fatalities, per Basher.
- At a steady 10% weekly growth rate, unsupervised miles would roughly double every seven weeks, ~12x over six months, ~140x over a year (Basher's modeling, not a Tesla projection).
- Terafab could represent on the order of a trillion dollars in present value for Tesla, per Basher's own estimate.
- Basher's overall conclusion: "Tesla is being appropriately cautious" on robotaxi rollout, not reckless or unreasonably slow given the end goal.

2026-07-25.title: New Elon Interview: What He Actually Wants
2026-07-25.relevance: core — The video substantively analyzes a new Elon Musk interview covering Tesla's Optimus/AI strategy, robotaxi progress, China competition, taxes on his Tesla equity, and space-based data centers tied to Starship and Tesla Energy.
2026-07-25.body:
This video breaks down a new hour-long Elon Musk interview with The Economist's editor-in-chief, conducted the day after a rough Tesla Q2 earnings print, into five key clips the host says reveal Musk's real long-term goals: building for long-horizon retail investors, pursuing a "quasi infinite economy" via AI plus humanoid robots, racing China on electricity/compute by moving data centers to space, accepting he'll retain only about a quarter of his wealth after taxes, and no longer caring about media approval. The host frames this as directionally aligned with Tesla's and SpaceX's product roadmaps, while flagging genuine bear-case caveats (timeline slippage, unproven space-data-center economics, weak current margins).

## Financials
1. **Interview timing follows a rough Tesla print:** The interview was recorded the day after Tesla's Q2 earnings, which the host describes as "a very rough print" that gave the stock its worst week of the year; Musk used the interview to defend a 5-to-10-year investment horizon against what he called portfolio managers' 90-day mindset.
2. **Musk details his personal tax burden on Tesla equity:** Musk states he pays about 40% federal income tax on stock option exercises plus roughly another 5% in California taxes (since he spends about 30% of his time there), landing near 45% total, and then roughly another 45% (estate tax) is taken at death — leaving him with an estimated quarter of his total wealth; the host notes Musk previously set a record for the largest single-year tax bill by an individual (cited by the host as roughly $11 billion in 2021).
3. **Current financial picture called "bumpy":** The host notes Tesla's margins are "barely above break even" and free cash flow has been negative, cautioning that nothing in the interview changes near-term quarterly results.

## Autonomous Driving / Robotaxi
1. **Musk's robotaxi timeline record cited as a caution:** The host notes Musk originally promised robotaxi in 2020, with the first paying robotaxi ride not occurring until 2025 in Austin, used as evidence that his timelines run "fast" relative to reality.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Musk frames Optimus/AI as building a "quasi infinite economy":** Musk describes AI as currently confined to the "digital realm" lacking "endectors" (end-effectors/hands), arguing humanoid robots combined with digital intelligence let intelligence "shape atoms," removing the labor-hour cap on goods and services production — which he calls a "quasi infinite economy." Elsewhere in the interview he says work becomes optional, comparing it to choosing to garden versus buying from a store.
2. **Musk projects a 5-year timeline to AI surpassing human intelligence and a 2036 "age of abundance":** Musk states AI could surpass human intelligence in about five years and describes 2036 as a point where an "age of abundance" arrives where anyone can have anything they can think of; he also puts a 10–20% probability on AI going "very badly."

## Market & Competition
1. **Musk's central China argument centers on electricity, not just chips:** Musk says Chinese AI firms perform well despite relatively limited compute and would likely become AI leaders if given more compute; he identifies the constraints as electricity and chips, stating China has more electricity generation than the US, Europe, and India combined — a claim the host says checks out roughly on stacked totals. Musk also says China is "closer than most people realize" to solving its chip lithography problem, and that Washington can block Chinese AI models domestically but can't stop the rest of the world from using them.
2. **Musk's proposed fix: solar-powered orbital data centers to bypass the grid entirely:** To escape the electricity bottleneck, Musk describes putting data centers in space, powered by solar and free of permitting/transmission constraints, which would shift the bottleneck back to chips — an area the host says Musk believes the US still leads; the host notes this concept is unproven and depends on Starship's launch cadence and cost.
3. **The Economist's editor pushes back on Musk's media-favorability claims:** In a viral exchange, Musk tells the editor that journalism's favorability rating is around 15% and that the media/journalists are "loathed" more than he is; the editor responds that trust in journalism has real problems but also that Musk's platform (X) fosters polarization, and notes she personally has far less public recognition than Musk.

## SpaceX — Starship / AI & Compute
1. **Space-based compute idea is conceptual, not yet real:** The host clarifies there are currently no orbital data centers or training models in operation; the space-data-center concept depends entirely on Starship flying frequently and cheaply, which remains unproven "flight by flight."

Notable quotes and data:
- "I'm a big fan of the retail investors... I find our retail investors on balance are very insightful and have very long-term views." — Elon Musk
- "You need lots of bots... you have a sort of a quasi quasi infinite economy." — Elon Musk
- "China has more electricity than the United States, Europe, and India combined." — Elon Musk
- China is "closer than most people realize to solving the lithography problem" — Elon Musk
- Musk estimates paying ~40% federal tax plus ~5% California tax (~45% total) on stock option exercises, then ~45% more at death via estate tax, leaving him roughly a quarter of his wealth.
- Host's own math: after both tax layers, roughly 30% (a quarter to a third) of pre-tax value survives.
- Favorable view of journalists cited by Musk as around 15%.
- Musk puts a 10–20% probability on AI development going "very badly."
- Musk projects AI surpassing human intelligence in about 5 years and a 2036 "age of abundance."
- Host-cited historical figure: Musk paid roughly $11 billion in taxes in a single year (2021), described as a record.

2026-07-25.title: Tesla Actually Gave Us the Answers We Needed (TSLA) ⚡️
2026-07-25.relevance: core — The video is a detailed analysis of Tesla's earnings call disclosures on robotaxi/unsupervised mile growth, FSD attach rates, energy margins, and stock valuation, all central to the Tesla investment thesis.
2026-07-25.body:
The host (Dillon Loomis) walks through Tesla's Q2 earnings call, arguing that Elon Musk and Ashok Elluswamy finally gave the market a real metric to track — unsupervised robotaxi mile growth — and uses that data to build his own model for expected fleet size and mileage through Q3, while also flagging why he thinks Tesla stock had further downside even after its recent drop.

## Robotaxi
1. **New official metric: unsupervised miles, not just "paid miles":** Tesla disclosed it has driven more than 380,000 unsupervised robotaxi miles across six cities in two states. The host argues the previously-tracked "cumulative paid robotaxi miles" chart likely includes Bay Area supervised ride-hailing (not just Austin unsupervised rides), based on Elon Musk's comments grouping the Bay Area under the robotaxi umbrella, and estimates from a pixel analysis of that chart that monthly paid miles peaked around 445,000 in March before declining to roughly 155,000 in June — numbers he stresses are unofficial, derived estimates with wide error bars.
2. **Double-digit weekly growth in unsupervised miles:** Musk said the fleet is scaling at more than 10% weekly growth in miles driven; Ashok Elluswamy separately clarified this refers specifically to unsupervised miles, growing at a high compounding weekly rate since the start of the year, and said Tesla expects this pace to continue through the rest of the year.
3. **Cybercab production tied to unsupervised mile growth:** Elluswamy said Tesla will match Cybercab production/deployment rates to the growth rate of unsupervised miles, making that mileage metric the key number to track going forward.
4. **Host's model for Q3 fleet size:** Applying a sustained 10%-weekly growth assumption from a roughly 3,500-mile/week starting point in January, the host estimates Tesla reached about 38,000 unsupervised miles/week by mid-July (matching the ~380,000 cumulative figure), implying roughly 50 unsupervised vehicles doing just over 100 miles/day each. Extrapolating the same growth rate to late October would imply about 130,000 miles/week and a fleet needing to grow to around 173 unsupervised vehicles (adding ~123 over the quarter); under a decaying growth-rate scenario, the fleet might instead reach around 115 vehicles (adding ~65). The host's own Q3 expectation is up to roughly 200 deployed robotaxis, explicitly rejecting claims that Tesla will reach thousands of unsupervised vehicles this year.
5. **Comparison to Waymo:** A commentator's viral estimate pegs Waymo at roughly 570,000 driverless miles per day, versus Tesla's projected ~130,000 miles per week even under sustained growth — a comparison the host calls largely apples-to-oranges but useful for scale context.
6. **State-by-state expansion "trending toward zero," but not soon:** Elluswamy said time-to-launch in new cities will trend toward zero as Tesla moves toward operating across entire states rather than city-by-city. The host believes full-state approval won't happen this year at the earliest, more likely next year, and could be a multi-year process.
7. **Newer FSD version testing on robotaxi fleet:** The host notes that a newer FSD version is reportedly running on the robotaxi fleet in a deliberately controlled, small-scale environment, which he argues is actually the safest place to validate bleeding-edge autonomy software rather than deploying it broadly across the whole consumer fleet.
8. **Small sample size caveat:** The host emphasizes 380,000 unsupervised miles with zero "notable incidents" (a term Tesla did not define) is too small a sample to extrapolate safety conclusions to a nationally scaled fleet, given the concentrated, favorable-condition areas where robotaxis currently operate.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus remains highly uncertain:** The host argues Optimus deployment timelines, cost of goods sold, and pricing to third-party customers remain essentially unknown, with early production units expected to go first to an internal "Optimus Academy" rather than external customers; he criticizes analysts for not asking Tesla about Optimus Academy deployment timelines or scale during the earnings call.

## Financials
1. **AI hardware acquisition disclosed in 10-Q:** Tesla's Q2 10-Q confirmed an acquisition of an AI hardware company for up to $1.95 billion in common stock/equity, of which about $1.73 billion is contingent on service conditions or performance milestones (~$222 million allocated to patents/technology upfront). The host reiterates his unconfirmed Q1 speculation that this could be Density AI, founded by a former Tesla Autopilot Hardware senior director who worked on Dojo, joined by (per rumor) as many as 20 former Tesla Dojo engineers.
2. **FSD attach rate and recurring revenue:** Tesla's FSD attach rate in North America reached roughly 55% in Q2, spanning 1.48 million active subscriptions — 45% paying monthly (~666,000 users) and 55% purchased outright (~814,000 users). The host calculates this implies roughly $791 million/year in recurring FSD revenue, calling it one of the more encouraging Q2 stats, though he cautions it isn't yet enough to move Tesla's overall financials.
3. **Regulatory credit revenue declined sharply:** Regulatory credits came in at $146 million for the quarter, down from a prior-year low water mark of $380 million, which the host attributes to the expiration of CAFE penalties.

## Energy
1. **Energy gross margins guided lower:** Tesla's energy gross margin fell from about 39% to roughly 20% in Q2, and Tesla's CFO guided that energy gross margins are now expected to settle between 20-25% going forward — down from earlier expectations (per the host) that margins could exceed 30-40%.

## Market & Competition
1. **Valuation and stock outlook:** With TSLA around $313, the host highlights Tesla's forward P/E for fiscal 2027 at roughly 140x, versus Apple (35x), Amazon (23x), Google (22x), Microsoft (20x), Nvidia (17x), and Meta (17x), arguing this shows the market still prices in substantial robotaxi growth and thus retains significant downside risk when expectations are recalibrated lower. He states he sees more downside than upside in the near term, would not be surprised by TSLA testing $260-280, but says he is personally still buying shares and has not sold any, remaining bullish over a 3-5 year horizon.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Starlink and Semi FSD roadmap notes:** Musk said Starlink connectivity will eventually be added across the rest of Tesla's fleet where available, and that FSD for the Tesla Semi is expected to go active either later this year or early next year, with near-term focus remaining on FSD for high-volume passenger vehicles.

Notable quotes and data:
- Tesla has driven more than 380,000 unsupervised robotaxi miles across six cities in two states (per Ashok Elluswamy on the earnings call).
- Musk: "We've opened up in a number of cities in Florida and in Texas and obviously the Bay Area," and unsupervised miles are scaling "more than 10% a week."
- Elluswamy: "Since the beginning of this year, we have grown at double-digit growth rates to the number of unsupervised miles that the fleet drives every week... we expect to continue growing at such a large rate through the rest of this year."
- Host's derived monthly "paid mile" estimates (unofficial, from chart pixel analysis): Jan ~270,000; Feb ~340,000; Mar ~445,000 (peak); Apr ~365,000; May ~190,000; Jun ~155,000.
- Host's Q3 model: unsupervised fleet growing from ~50 vehicles/~38,000 miles per week to ~173 vehicles/~130,000 miles per week under sustained 10% weekly growth (or ~115 vehicles under a decaying growth scenario).

2026-07-25.title: STUNNING New SpaceX Starship Rocket Launch (Starship 13 w/ Starlink v3)
2026-07-25.relevance: core — This is a direct account of a SpaceX Starship test flight, including major Starship V3 and Starlink V3 milestones central to the SpaceX investment thesis.
2026-07-25.body:
This is a live webcast transcript of SpaceX's Starship Flight 13, the second test flight of Starship Version 3, covering booster launch, hot-staging separation, booster splashdown, deployment of 20 new Starlink V3 satellites, an in-space Raptor relight demonstration, atmospheric re-entry, and a soft ship splashdown in the Indian Ocean. The broadcast frames the flight as a major milestone-heavy success, with several "firsts" achieved across booster recovery, payload deployment, and ship survivability through splashdown.

## SpaceX — Starship
1. **Booster performs full ascent and controlled ocean splashdown:** All 33 Raptor engines on the Super Heavy booster ignited at liftoff; the vehicle passed through max aerodynamic pressure and executed hot-staging (shutting down all but five engines) before the ship's six engines ignited for separation. The booster then completed its boost-back burn — a objective it had missed on the prior flight — and executed a landing burn using its center engines, though hosts noted not all 13 planned engines appeared to light, resulting in a higher-than-targeted landing velocity before splashing down in the Gulf within a pre-cleared zone.
2. **Ship reaches orbit-like trajectory and later achieves softest-ever splashdown:** The ship's six Raptor engines burned for roughly eight minutes to reach a "nominal orbit insertion" call-out on a suborbital trajectory toward the Indian Ocean. After re-entry — during which hosts called out passing max heating and max dynamic pressure — the ship executed a landing burn (three engines down to two, then one) and achieved what hosts described as the softest splashdown yet recorded for Starship, remaining intact and afloat, which they called a "dream scenario" for data collection.
3. **In-space Raptor relight demonstrated with longer burn duration:** SpaceX successfully relit a single sea-level Raptor engine on the ship in space for about 14 seconds, longer than a roughly 3-second relight achieved on a previous flight. Hosts described this as a critical capability for future orbital missions requiring de-orbit burns.
4. **Heat shield imaging test conducted via satellite cameras:** Six of the deployed Starlink V3 satellites were fitted with engineering cameras and flashlights intended to image Starship's heat shield after ascent, a capability SpaceX says it needs to build confidence for eventually attempting to catch (recover) the ship itself, something not yet achieved (only the booster has been caught to date).

## SpaceX — Starlink
1. **First real Starlink V3 satellites deployed from Starship:** Starship deployed 20 Starlink V3 satellites — described as fully functional units rather than demonstration mass simulators used on a prior flight — via a "PEZ dispenser" mechanism, with SpaceX confirming contact and laser communication links established with all 20 satellites within minutes of deployment. Each V3 satellite is said to offer 1 terabit per second of downlink capacity, and hosts stated a Starship V3 launch of these satellites delivers roughly 20 times the constellation capacity of a single Falcon 9 launch carrying V2 satellites; a fully loaded Starship V3 flight is designed to carry up to 60 such satellites.
2. **Starlink powers real-time flight telemetry and video:** Hosts noted the existing Starlink constellation provides approximately 240 megabits per second of data rate from Starship in flight, enabling the extensive onboard camera views and real-time telemetry used throughout the broadcast and for rapid engineering iteration.

Notable quotes and data:
- "That is the softest splash down we have ever had with the Starship there in the Indian Ocean" — webcast host.
- All 33 Raptor engines lit on the Super Heavy booster at liftoff; hot-staging reduced this to 13, then 5 before shutdown.
- Booster completed its boost-back burn, an objective missed on the previous flight, per the host.
- Ship's six-engine burn lasted about eight minutes before orbital insertion call-out.
- 20 Starlink V3 satellites deployed; SpaceX confirmed contact and laser comms with all 20.
- Each Starlink V3 satellite: ~1 terabit per second downlink capacity, per the broadcast.
- A Starship V3/V3-satellite launch delivers ~20x the constellation capacity of a single Falcon 9/V2 launch, per the broadcast.
- Starship carries up to 60 Starlink V3 satellites per full deployment, per the broadcast.
- Starlink-enabled data rate from Starship in flight: ~240 megabits per second, per the host.
- Raptor in-space relight burn duration: ~14 seconds, up from ~3 seconds on a previous flight.
- Deployed satellites had a roughly 20-minute operational lifespan before atmospheric demise, being on the same suborbital trajectory as Starship.

2026-07-25.title: Why SpaceX Will Soon SHOCK Us (Upside!)
2026-07-25.relevance: core — The video is substantively about SpaceX's orbital AI satellite program and its implications for the SpaceX/AI-buildout investment thesis.
2026-07-25.body:
The host argues that SpaceX's orbital AI satellite program (Colossus-style compute in space) is advancing at a rapid pace and could eventually rescue the broader AI buildout from a looming terrestrial data-center bottleneck driven by energy, permitting, and political resistance. The core thesis: if SpaceX can scale orbital AI compute to gigawatt scale by roughly 2028, it arrives just in time to offset a predicted grinding halt in terrestrial data-center growth; if it takes until 2030–2035, markets tied to the AI buildout could face a serious setback.

## SpaceX — AI & Compute
1. **First-generation AI satellite specs unveiled:** On June 9th, Sawyer Merritt shared SpaceX's official unveiling of its first-generation AI satellite, with specs including 150 kilowatts of peak compute, a 70-meter wingspan, 20-meter deployed height, and 110 square meters of deployable liquid radiator for thermal management.
2. **Rapid redesign to a higher-power version:** Roughly 38 days after the June 9th unveiling, Elon Musk indicated on July 16th that SpaceX was already preparing an upgraded satellite design, boosting peak compute from 150 kW to 250 kW (a 67% increase) and adding batteries — illustrating, per the host, an extremely fast internal iteration cycle.
3. **Design upgrade tied to next-gen Nvidia GPUs:** The host attributes the power upgrade to SpaceX anticipating Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin GPU rack (Vera Rubin NVL 72), expected next year, which the satellite is reportedly being redesigned to accommodate; the host estimates that combining the power increase with Vera Rubin's expected generational compute gains over Blackwell could yield roughly five times more compute per satellite versus the original design.
4. **Terrestrial data center bottleneck as the setup for orbital AI:** The host cites growing political and regulatory resistance to data centers in the U.S. — noting New York State's move to bar data centers over 100 MW and resistance in over 20 states — as a structural bottleneck (alongside energy, permitting, and land constraints) that terrestrial AI buildout faces, and argues this friction will intensify sharply through 2029.
5. **Investment framing — timing risk for the AI buildout thesis:** The host frames the critical question as whether SpaceX can deliver gigawatt-scale orbital AI compute by 2028 (in time to offset a terrestrial buildout slowdown) versus 2030–2035 (which he argues would cause a "massive problem in the market" and short-term crashes across AI-linked stocks from Nvidia to Micron to AMD to hyperscalers); he explicitly states this satellite news itself is not expected to move SpaceX's stock price for at least 12 months.

Notable quotes and data:
- First-gen AI satellite (announced June 9): 150 kW peak compute, 70m wingspan, 20m deployed height, 110 sq m deployable liquid radiator.
- Upgraded satellite (announced ~July 16, ~38 days later): 250 kW peak compute (up 67%), added batteries, designed around Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL 72 rack.
- Host estimate: combined power and generational GPU gains could mean roughly 5x more compute per satellite versus the original design.
- Host claim: New York State has moved to ban data centers over 100 MW; resistance to data centers is active in over 20 U.S. states.
- Host prediction: data center resistance will rise "exponentially" through 2029, alongside "massive" job losses beginning next year.
- Host's investment framing: gigawatt-scale orbital AI by 2028 would be "just in time"; by 2030–2035 would cause a "massive problem in the market" for AI-linked stocks.
- Host explicitly states: this satellite development is not expected to affect SpaceX's stock price for at least 12 months.

2026-07-26.title: Tesla's $25 Billion Might Not Be Enough! Here’s Why
2026-07-26.relevance: core — The video is a detailed discussion of Tesla's capex strategy, financing, data center buildout, and competitive positioning, all central to the Tesla investment thesis.
2026-07-26.body:
This video features a discussion between host Herbert and guest Larry Goldberg debating whether Tesla's ramped-up capital expenditure — including a new debt facility — is sufficient given the scale of its simultaneous buildouts (robotaxi fleet, Cybercab production, Optimus lines, the Terafab chip plant, lithium and cathode refineries, battery cells, solar manufacturing, and Cortex data centers). Goldberg argues Tesla is unusually capital-efficient and that its "just-in-time," speed-over-scale approach to spending is a deliberate strategy rather than underinvestment.

## Financials
1. **Capex guidance likely to be exceeded:** Tesla guided capex toward roughly $25 billion for the year, but Goldberg predicts the company will exceed this figure by year-end (reversing its historical pattern of coming in under guidance), potentially even seeing capex roughly double from prior levels, driven by Cybercab buildout, Cortex 2 completion, and the new Terafab chip plant.
2. **Q2 capex and cash position:** Tesla spent $6 billion in capex in Q2, with cash declining by only $1.2 billion as the operating business funded much of the investment; Tesla holds close to $40 billion in cash and is generating $3–4 billion per quarter, which Goldberg expects to rise to $5–6 billion per quarter next year.
3. **New $30 billion debt facility:** Tesla secured a new $30 billion borrowing facility, which Goldberg says was within his expectations; he predicts long-term borrowing could rise to roughly $50 billion within a year, particularly to fund the Terafab, absent a Tesla–SpaceX merger (which he expects would instead resolve into a larger, longer-term combined loan facility).
4. **Robotaxi revenue already appearing, not delayed:** Goldberg pushes back on the idea that robotaxi revenue is delayed, saying it is already showing up in Tesla's services line and will scale from hundreds of thousands of dollars currently to millions next quarter, then hundreds of millions and eventually billions within roughly a year; he argues each robotaxi vehicle (a $30–40k investment) is easily financeable given fast payback.
5. **Micron memory supply deal framed as competitive advantage:** Citing an excerpt from an article by Cern Basher, the host notes Elon Musk thanked Micron and Nvidia on the earnings call for securing Tesla a significant, reasonably priced memory allocation for the foreseeable future despite what Musk called insane current memory pricing — framed as a supply-chain risk other "Mag 7" companies may not have managed as well.
6. **Capital efficiency vs. speed philosophy:** Musk told his team he prioritizes speed over maximum capital efficiency; Goldberg interprets this as Tesla optimizing for the combination of speed and cost together, arguing that faster execution lowers effective cost even if per-unit spending is sometimes higher, and cites Tesla's manufacturing time-to-market advantage over Ford and GM's EV programs as evidence.

## SpaceX — AI & Compute
1. **xAI's data center cost efficiency vs. hyperscalers:** Goldberg argues xAI (referred to as SpaceX AI in the discussion) has been able to sell compute capacity at premium prices despite lower investment than rivals like Google, because building data centers faster lets it deploy cutting-edge chips roughly a year ahead of competitors using conventional subcontracted buildouts, and those chips are lasting far longer than expected (around six years versus a predicted two to three).
2. **Tesla's own chip use for inference lowers costs:** Goldberg says Tesla/Cortex uses its own AI4 chips (with AI5 and AI6 upcoming) for inference rather than third-party GPUs, which he estimates cost three to four times more than building proprietary silicon, contributing to Tesla's low-capex efficiency.
3. **Prediction of another data center compute announcement before SpaceX's earnings:** Goldberg speculates that another company (he guesses Microsoft) may announce a deal similar to prior xAI compute arrangements before SpaceX's upcoming earnings date, but explicitly frames this as his opinion, not confirmed information.

## Autonomous Driving
1. **Cortex 2 buildout and FSD version 15:** Cortex 2 is reported at over 115 megawatts of production capacity, with compute roughly doubling over the recent quarter; Goldberg says Cortex 2's first half is currently being used for FSD (not Optimus), enabling rollout of a newer FSD version with a roughly 10x parameter increase, with a comparable magnitude of improvement expected from this version as was seen in the prior major FSD upgrade. The second half of the Cortex 2 building is still under construction and expected to roughly double total capacity to about a quarter-gigawatt by year-end.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Tesla's factory-first approach to Optimus:** The host argues Tesla appears behind in the humanoid robot race only because it hasn't shown flashy demos, while it is actually ahead in building manufacturing capacity — a roughly 1-million-unit-per-year line at Fremont and a next-generation, higher-capacity line planned at Giga Texas. Goldberg adds that Tesla is deliberately cautious given that robot usability involves far greater degrees of freedom than FSD, contrasting this with an unnamed competitor's robot project reportedly torn out by a client for not working.

Notable quotes and data:
- "Speed is efficiency." — Larry Goldberg's summary of Musk's capex philosophy
- Tesla capex guidance: ~$25 billion for the year; Goldberg predicts this will be exceeded
- Q2 capex: $6 billion; cash declined only $1.2 billion; cash on hand: ~$40 billion
- New Tesla borrowing facility: $30 billion; Goldberg predicts long-term debt could reach ~$50 billion within a year
- Cortex 2 capacity: over 115 megawatts currently, expected to roughly double to ~230 megawatts (quarter-gigawatt) by year-end
- Cash generation: currently $3–4 billion/quarter, projected to rise to $5–6 billion/quarter next year
- Robotaxi vehicle economics: each unit cited as roughly a $30–40k investment with fast revenue payback
- Elon Musk reportedly called Tesla's buildout "probably the fastest industrial scale-up in America since World War II" (per host)
- SpaceX earnings date cited as August 4th

2026-07-26.title: Go Big Or Go Home: Tesla’s Strategy
2026-07-26.relevance: core — The video is a detailed analysis of Tesla's Q2 earnings call commentary on robotaxi scaling strategy, Waymo comparisons, and Optimus development, all directly bearing on the Tesla investment thesis.
2026-07-26.body:
This video analyzes Tesla's Q2 earnings call, focusing on an analyst question about why Tesla's robotaxi fleet remains small, which drew answers from four executives (Lars Moravy, Vaibhav Taneja, Ashok Elluswamy, and Elon Musk). The host argues Tesla's consistent pattern — across Gigafactories, Superchargers, Model 3 production, robotaxi, and Optimus — is to solve the hardest, most general version of a problem first and delay scaling until it can go everywhere at once, contrasting this with Waymo's city-by-city approach.

## Robotaxi
1. **Four executives, four angles on the same strategy:** On the Q2 call, Lars Moravy said regulatory requirements differ city by city and must be cleared one at a time; Vaibhav Taneja said operational kinks (charging, cleaning, support, curbside pickup) need to be solved in a smaller fleet before scaling; Ashok Elluswamy said Tesla is deliberately expanding across many cities to prove its driving stack is general rather than doubling down on one city, describing growth as "just the early part of the exponential"; Elon Musk said Tesla is scaling as fast as possible while trying to ensure zero harm to humans or even pets.
2. **Waymo comparison — miles and safety record:** Through March, Waymo had logged over 220 million rider miles versus Tesla's roughly 2.5 million total paid robotaxi miles (Tesla's paid miles are compounding at roughly 10% a week). Waymo studies show roughly 90% fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers, but Waymo has filed roughly 1,400 incident reports with NHTSA since 2021, with 117 injuries and two fatal crashes (in both cases the Waymo was the vehicle struck, not at fault), plus a software recall covering more than 1,200 vehicles. Ashok said Tesla has driven approximately 380,000 fully unsupervised miles with zero notable incidents, with only other vehicles bumping into stationary Teslas recorded.
3. **State-by-state rollout as the strategic prize:** Ashok stated Tesla expects to eventually roll out to entire states at once rather than city by city — a claim the host says no other autonomy company makes, and one that only makes sense if the driving stack is fully generalized. The host frames this as the reason Tesla is protecting its clean safety record rather than flooding Austin now, since a single state approval (e.g., Texas at ~30 million people or Florida at ~23 million) would open a huge addressable market at once.
4. **FSD v15 deployed on the robotaxi fleet:** Robotaxis are running FSD version 15, which the host says includes seven major improvements over version 14; Elon reiterated that Tesla's camera-only (no lidar) approach is validated as safe for functional autonomy. The host notes no executive specified the exact validation milestone that would trigger a scale-up.
5. **Guidance repeatedly missed:** The host notes Tesla has missed its own short-term robotaxi guidance for three consecutive earnings calls, including an earlier target of covering the US population that did not happen, and cautions that "entire states" timing remains unspecified.

## Humanoid Bots
1. **Optimus following the same "go big" playbook:** The host predicts Optimus will take longer than expected to reach customers because Tesla is training it toward generalized intelligence rather than shipping a narrower pick-and-place robot now, even though Tesla could technically ship a limited-task version today (as some humanoid startups are reportedly doing with warehouse pilot deals).
2. **Optimus Academy and training approach:** Initial Optimus V3 production from Fremont was said to be starting around this quarter, feeding into a "Optimus Academy" training program where bots collect data to train other bots via reinforcement learning. Ashok described the method as "pixels in, controls out" — the same recipe as FSD — with bots learning from human demonstrations and internet how-to videos, aiming for a robot that can perform tasks it was never specifically programmed for. Ashok also claimed Optimus's hand has dexterity equal to or better than a human hand — a claim the host flags as unverified until shown in real work on video.
3. **Digital-first training and Fremont production ramp:** Tesla trains a software version of Optimus on computers first, with physical bots inheriting learned skills. Fremont's Model S/X lines were shut down and are being converted for Optimus, with production start expected later this year; Elon cautioned the ramp will be slow given roughly 10,000 unique parts that could each gate the line.
4. **Host's V3/V4 theory:** The host theorizes V3 is a "training generation" for the Academy while V4, to be built in Austin with manufacturing-friendly redesigns, will be the "scale generation," timed to pair with AI5 chip volume production which Elon said is hoped for next year. The host says he'll revise this view if V3 units start shipping directly to customers.
5. **Supplier investment as a scale signal:** The host cites Samsung and TSMC investments and Panasonic battery production ramp in support of Optimus as evidence suppliers are treating it as a scale product rather than a science project; Elon reiterated Optimus could be Tesla's biggest product ever while calling it some of the hardest engineering Tesla has undertaken.

## Financials / Market & Competition
1. **Bear case highlighted by the host:** Risks include Tesla's record spending against uncertain and possibly multi-year-out payoff timing, Waymo's substantial mileage and revenue lead continuing to compound while Tesla catches up, and regulatory approval processes that move on their own timeline — where even a single serious incident anywhere in the industry could stall state-level approval conversations.

Notable quotes and data:
- Waymo: 220+ million rider miles through March; ~1,400 NHTSA incident reports since 2021; 117 injuries; 2 fatal crashes (Waymo was the struck vehicle in both); recall of 1,200+ vehicles.
- Tesla: ~2.5 million total paid robotaxi miles (compounding ~10%/week); ~380,000 fully unsupervised miles with "zero notable incidents" (Ashok Elluswamy).
- Ashok Elluswamy: "The reason we have been expanding across different cities instead of just doubling down on a single city is that we want to make sure that our stack is a very general one."
- Ashok Elluswamy: Tesla expects to eventually roll out to "entire states" rather than city by city.
- Elon Musk: robotaxi scaling proceeds "trying to ensure that they do not harm anyone at all... no harm to humans or even pets."
- FSD version 15 is deployed on the robotaxi fleet with seven major improvements cited over version 14.
- Optimus V3 production start targeted for around this quarter at Fremont; Optimus has roughly 10,000 unique parts per Elon.
- AI5 chip volume production hoped for next year, per Elon.
- Host: Tesla has missed its own robotaxi guidance for three consecutive earnings calls.
